games.description:
Sega's 005 (1981), pronounced 'double-oh-five,' is a spy-themed maze game and an unusually early experiment in stealth. Agent 005 must deliver secret briefcases to an awaiting helicopter while guards pursue him through city streets, dark warehouses and slippery skating rinks. The guards' flashlight beams reveal where they can see, encouraging players to hide behind crates rather than simply attack every pursuer. A four-way joystick moves the agent, while a single button fires a temporary stun-gas weapon; collecting gas canisters extends its range.

Each delivery can involve a different route. The ice rink demands momentum control because the agent cannot stop on the ice, while warehouses reward careful avoidance of searchlights. After two deliveries the action changes to a helicopter escape, dodging bombs and engaging an enemy aircraft. This mixture of linked play areas and visible enemy sightlines makes 005 a notable precursor to later stealth games. Sega also marketed it as part of the G80 RasterScan Convert-a-Game program, which allowed operators to repurpose cabinets for new titles.

games.title: Eleven Beat
games.description:
Eleven Beat: World Tournament is a 1998 arcade football game by Hudson Soft, published for Seta's Aleck64 system. Built around Nintendo 64-derived hardware, it updates Hudson's J-League Eleven Beat 1997 with international teams and more refined controls. Players can enter a tournament against computer-controlled sides or challenge a friend to a standalone match.

Its conventional on-field soccer play is less historically unusual than its platform. The Aleck64 was an uncommon cartridge-based arcade system whose close relationship to home-console hardware makes Eleven Beat an interesting snapshot of the late-1990s crossover between Japanese coin-op and console development.

games.title: 1941 - Counter Attack
games.description:
Capcom's 1941: Counter Attack (1990) is the third entry in the 194X series and a World War II prequel to 1942. Running on the CPS-1 arcade system, it shifts the combat toward the North Atlantic and European theater. The first player pilots a Lockheed P-38 Lightning, while the second controls a de Havilland Mosquito, fighting through vertically scrolling formations of aircraft, ships and heavily armed bosses.

Unlike 1942's one-hit lives, 1941 uses a vitality meter that can absorb damage. Players collect weapon upgrades, hold the fire button to charge a powerful blast, and use a separate button for evasive rolls and destructive Mega-Crash attacks. These emergency moves must be weighed against the energy they consume, while unused loops can contribute to end-of-stage bonuses. The game's colorful CPS-1 presentation and more elaborate combat systems bridge the early 194X shooters and Capcom's later high-powered entries.

Capcom's 1942 (1984) helped define the vertically scrolling arcade shooter and launched the enduring 194X series. Set during a fictionalized World War II Pacific campaign, it puts the player in the cockpit of a Lockheed P-38 Lightning, known as the Super Ace, against waves of Japanese aircraft. The lengthy campaign spans 32 stages, unusually numbered in reverse order, with the fighter returning to an aircraft carrier after each completed sortie.

The signature maneuver is a limited-use loop, triggered with a dedicated button, that briefly renders the aircraft invulnerable. Shooting down an entire formation of red planes releases a POW item that can improve the guns, summon two escort fighters, grant a screen-clearing effect or award points. Larger bombers and enormous boss aircraft punctuate the waves, and even apparently minor decisions about when to collect a power-up or spend a loop can determine survival.

1942 became one of Capcom's most commercially successful early arcade releases and received numerous home conversions. Its deliberate appeal to Western audiences is reflected in the unusual choice, for a Japanese-developed game, of an American pilot fighting toward Tokyo. Its whistling soundtrack, carrier landings and precise dodge-and-shoot rhythm remain instantly recognizable features of the series.

games.title: 1943: The Battle of Midway
games.description:
1943: The Battle of Midway (1987) is Capcom's ambitious sequel to 1942, again placing players in P-38 Lightning fighters during a fictionalized Pacific naval campaign. The 16-stage route mixes aerial engagements with attacks on enormous battleships and aircraft carriers, culminating in a confrontation with the Yamato. Two players can cooperate, and the screen frequently fills with enemy aircraft, ship gunfire and destructible targets.

The most important change is the energy meter, which gradually drains and falls sharply when the fighter is hit. POW pickups restore it, while weapon items offer choices such as three-way fire, shotgun, shells and automatic bursts. Players can also spend energy on dramatic screen-wide attacks, including lightning, cyclones and tsunamis, or perform a defensive loop. In cooperative play, overlapping aircraft can even transfer energy from the healthier pilot to the other.

This shift from limited lives to fuel management makes 1943 more strategic than its predecessor. Shooting a power-up to cycle its contents, searching for hidden bonuses and dismantling the components of giant warships add layers of score-chasing depth to an already celebrated arcade shooter.

games.title: 1943 Kai: Midway Kaisen
games.description:
1943 Kai: Midway Kaisen is Capcom's substantially revised Japanese edition of 1943, released after the original arcade game. 'Kai' means 'modified,' and the changes extend beyond a simple difficulty adjustment: the weapon balance, music and stage sequence have been reworked, with a shorter campaign.

Players still pilot P-38 fighters through vertically scrolling attacks on enemy aircraft and warships, collecting upgrades and replenishing a steadily diminishing energy supply. Special attacks trade precious energy for immediate relief from enemy fire. Its different soundtrack and altered progression make Kai a worthwhile alternative to the original 1943 rather than merely another regional ROM set.

games.title: 1943: The Battle of Midway Mark II

variants.title: 1943: The Battle of Midway Mark II (US)

games.description:
1943: The Battle of Midway Mark II is the export version of Capcom's revised 1943 Kai. It retains the familiar vertically scrolling P-38 air campaign but uses the modified edition's shortened progression, revised weapons and different music rather than the complete stage structure of the original 1943.

Players fight both aircraft formations and heavily defended ships, collecting armaments and energy-restoring items while deciding when to spend energy on screen-clearing special attacks. The Mark II name distinguishes this overseas release from the standard Battle of Midway and preserves a lesser-known branch of Capcom's early 194X history.

games.title: 1944: The Loop Master
games.description:
1944: The Loop Master is a 2000 vertically scrolling shooter developed by Raizing (Eighting) and published by Capcom for CPS-2 hardware. Although it follows 19XX in the 194X series, its straightforward Pacific war imagery, aircraft formations and large naval targets evoke the earlier games. Players pilot a P-38 Lightning or a de Havilland Mosquito through increasingly dense defenses and oversized bosses.

Holding the fire button charges a maneuver that sends the plane into a brief invulnerable loop, making defense and offensive timing parts of the same control system. A separate bomb attack unleashes powerful missiles, while weapon upgrades improve the player's chances against aircraft, tanks, trains and battleships. The game is notable as the series' final mainline coin-operated release of the period, blending Capcom's historical shooter style with the denser enemy patterns associated with Raizing.

games.title: 1945k III
games.description:
1945k III is a Korean vertically scrolling shooter released in 2000 by Oriental Software. Despite its conspicuously similar name, it is not an official installment of Psikyo's Strikers 1945 series, and there are no earlier 1945k I or II games. It originated in the Korean game Solite Spirits and was reworked with new stage designs and imagery resembling contemporary arcade military shooters.

Players choose among modern combat aircraft such as the F-15 Eagle, F-14 Tomcat, F-22 Raptor and F-117A Nighthawk, each with different weapons, and collect power-ups while fighting waves of aerial and ground targets. Its distinctive history as a heavily reworked, unauthorized genre imitation makes it an interesting curiosity from the final years of mainstream 2D arcade shooting.

games.title: 19XX: The War Against Destiny

variants.title: 19XX: The War Against Destiny (Japan 960104, yellow case)

games.description:
19XX: The War Against Destiny (1996) brought Capcom's long-running World War II shooter series to CPS-2 hardware. Players choose among three aircraft with different speed and weapon characteristics, then fight through beautifully animated vertical-scrolling battles against fighters, armored installations and enormous mechanized bosses. The fictional war setting grows more extravagant as the campaign progresses, drawing as much from science-fiction superweapons as real military aviation.

Three primary weapon types, spread shots, lasers and missiles, offer distinct approaches to crowds and armored targets. Holding the fire button charges a shot that can mark a large enemy for rapid homing follow-up attacks, while bombs can also be charged to produce different effects. This lock-on system, lavish sprite work and fast-paced cooperative play make 19XX one of the most distinctive and technically accomplished entries in the 194X series.

games.title: 19YY
games.description: 19YY is a vertical-scrolling shoot-'em-up developed by Ichikyu Wai Wai, EKORZ, and Elrayzeur for the Neo Geo MVS platform in 2022. Inspired by classic 1940s-style military arcade shooters, players pilot a twin-propeller fighter aircraft across ocean and air stages, shooting down waves of enemy planes and bosses while collecting power-ups and deploying screen-clearing bombs.

games.title: 2020 Super Baseball
games.description:
2020 Super Baseball is a 1991 futuristic sports game from SNK and Pallas for the Neo Geo. It reimagines baseball as a commercial spectacle played in high-tech stadiums by armored humans and robots, yet keeps the recognizable structure of pitching, batting, fielding and base running. Matches feature exaggerated athletic abilities rather than strict simulation, making the game approachable as an arcade contest while retaining tactical decisions from traditional baseball.

Money earned during play can be spent on upgraded equipment and abilities, adding a game-long layer of team development. The stadium also includes unusual restrictions and hazards that make positioning and strong hits especially important. Its bright science-fiction presentation and blend of sports rules with character upgrades distinguish it from the many conventional baseball games released for arcades.

games.title: 280-ZZZAP
games.description:
280-ZZZAP is a 1976 black-and-white driving game produced by Midway using technology from Dave Nutting Associates. Named after the Datsun 280Z, it presents a nighttime road in first person, with roadside posts and bends conveying motion long before texture-mapped racing games existed. Players turn a steering wheel, control speed and brake to keep the car on the road while a timer counts down.

The dashboard displays speed and information about approaching curves, rewarding drivers who slow down appropriately rather than simply holding the accelerator. Its dedicated driving controls and convincing sense of speed for the period make it an important early example of arcade racing hardware.

games.title: 3 Count Bout / Fire Suplex
games.description:
SNK's 3 Count Bout, released in Japan as Fire Suplex (1993), is a Neo Geo professional wrestling game featuring ten exaggerated competitors. Players battle through a succession of championship matches in wrestling rings and less regulated venues such as parking lots and factories, where weapons and environmental hazards can enter the fight. Two players can also join forces in tag-team contests.

The action combines strikes, running attacks, rope maneuvers and grapples. When wrestlers lock up, rapid button pressing affects the outcome of the contest, turning a hold or throw into a physical arcade struggle. Its lively character animation and blend of conventional wrestling with hardcore brawling give it a very different tempo from standard one-on-one Neo Geo fighters.

games.title: XESS - The New Revolution
games.description:
XESS: The New Revolution is a 1997 Korean multi-game arcade compilation released by SemiCom. Its three selections are Cookie & Bibi, a competitive fruit-matching puzzle game in the style of Puzzle Bobble; Hyper Man, a version of SemiCom's unauthorized Hyper Pac-Man; and New Hyper Man, a separate maze-action game in which players maneuver and attack enemies with laser fire.

Rather than being an original game with one set of rules, XESS is notable for combining several previously developed Korean arcade designs on modified Snow Bros.-derived hardware. Its unofficial Pac-Man-like characters and reused game concepts make it a telling example of the region's inventive and legally loose compilation market.

games.title: Sankokushi
games.description: Sankokushi is a 1996 adult-themed mahjong-solitaire puzzle game by Mitchell. Unlike ordinary Shanghai-style solitaire, which removes matching pairs, it asks players to clear tiles in sets of three, either identical tiles or specified numerical sequences. Each stage identifies target sets that must be removed before the timer expires. Selecting a tile highlights possible partners, and on-screen hint and undo functions help with difficult layouts. Successful clears reveal more of the illustrated background, so the challenge comes from finding accessible tile combinations efficiently rather than playing competitive four-player mahjong.

games.title: The Three Stooges In Brides Is Brides
games.description:
The Three Stooges in Brides Is Brides is a 1984 comic action game by Mylstar based on the famous slapstick trio. Moe, Larry and Curly search for their kidnapped fiancées inside a mad scientist's mansion, smashing furniture with hammers to uncover the keys required to open each room's exit. Police officers, society guests and other nuisances interfere, while cream pies and comic attacks evoke the Stooges' screen routines.

The arcade cabinet supports three simultaneous players, giving each Stooge a role in the chaotic search. An opera-themed bonus sequence and the staged rescue of the missing brides add variety, making this an unusual licensed arcade game whose appeal comes from cooperative slapstick rather than traditional shooting or platforming.

games.title: Three Wonders
games.description:
Capcom's Three Wonders (1991) is an unusual CPS-1 arcade collection that puts three complete, visually coordinated games on one board. Midnight Wanderers is a side-scrolling fantasy action adventure starring Lou and Siva, who fight with ranged weapons, find upgrades and face elaborate monsters. Chariot continues the same fantasy world as a horizontally scrolling shoot-'em-up, replacing running and jumping with aerial combat and collectible weapons.

The third game, Don't Pull, is a colorful single-screen action puzzler in which players push blocks to crush enemies and clear each stage. The contrast between cinematic action, cooperative shooting and compact puzzle stages makes Three Wonders especially memorable, while its expressive art shows Capcom's CPS-1 hardware at its most imaginative.

games.title: Forty-Love
games.description: Forty-Love, also styled 40-0, is a Taito tennis game carrying a 1984 copyright date and first released in Japan in January 1985. Viewed from above, it presents a full-court tennis match in which players move their athletes with a four-way joystick and use four buttons to execute shots. Positioning, anticipation and shot placement are central to winning rallies. Its title is drawn from tennis scoring terminology, and its emphasis on a familiar competitive sport makes it a distinctive alternative to the shooters and action games that dominated Taito's mid-1980s catalog.

games.title: Idol Janshi Su-Chi-Pie 2
games.description:
Idol Janshi Su-Chi-Pie II is a 1994 Japanese mahjong game from Jaleco, presented with elaborately animated characters and a story about rescuing the kidnapped Shiho Katagiri. The player faces a succession of opponents in competitive mahjong; between matches, a tile-matching bonus game can also affect progress. Winning encounters unlocks further dialogue, characters and adult-oriented animated reward sequences.

The arcade game uses Jaleco's Mega System 32 hardware and character artwork overseen by Kenichi Sonoda. Its combination of conventional mahjong, playful supernatural heroines and extensive animation makes it one of the more distinctive releases in the Su-Chi-Pai series.

games.title: 4-D Warriors
games.description:
4-D Warriors is a 1985 horizontally scrolling shooter by Coreland and Sega in which a jetpack-equipped space soldier fights across linked parallel dimensions. Instead of simply flying from left to right, the player can move beyond the top of the playfield to shift between visually distinct red and blue worlds. Wormholes occasionally transport the character into stranger areas.

The two-button controls provide movement and fire as enemy formations build toward boss encounters. This ability to switch between dimensions while battling gives the game its name and makes it a creative variation on the conventional side-scrolling shooter.

games.title: 4 En Raya
games.description: 4 En Raya is a Spanish arcade adaptation of Connect Four, released by IDSA around 1990. Two sides, represented by a cowboy and an Indigenous warrior, compete to line up four colored pieces horizontally, vertically or diagonally. A moving crane positions the next piece while a timer governs its placement. The game complicates the familiar board-game rules with shooting attacks: the opposing characters can fire at pieces to interfere with the developing pattern. Its mixture of turn-based planning, timing and combative interruptions distinguishes it from a straightforward electronic board game.

games.title: 4 Fun in 1
games.description:
4 Fun in 1 is a 1981 multi-game arcade system associated with Armenia and Food and Fun. Its menu offers Galactic Convoy, Scramble Part 2, Galaxian Part 5 and The Ghost Muncher Part 3. Despite their sequel-like names, these are unauthorized derivatives of existing arcade games, respectively drawing on War of the Bugs, Scramble, Galaxian and Pac-Man.

The collection moves between insect-themed shooting, side-scrolling space combat, formation-based alien shooting and dot-collecting maze play. It captures an early period when operators could offer several familiar styles on a single cabinet, and when bootleg naming made unofficial games appear to belong to established series.

games.title: Puzzle King
games.description:
Puzzle King is a Korean multi-game arcade compilation from K1 Soft and HAN System, with an unauthorized version of Snow Bros. among its four offerings. The selections are Pac-Man 2 (derived from Hyper Pac-Man), a distinct Tetris-style block puzzle, Hyper Man 2 (originally New Hyper Man), and Snow, a repackaged Snow Bros. with altered audio.

Rather than merely presenting several games through one menu, Puzzle King rearranges earlier Korean releases and Toaplan's platform game into a new commercial package. Its Snow Bros.-derived hardware and the replaced endings of some included titles are distinctive signs of a compiled bootleg release.

games.title: Mahjong 4P Simasyo
games.description: Mahjong 4P Simasyo is a 1994 Japanese adult mahjong game from Sphinx and AV Japan. It begins with a four-player contest against three computer-controlled opponents, then moves into individual matches against selected rivals. Winning hands and reducing opponents' money advance the sequence, leading to photographic and video-style reward scenes featuring live-action performers. The alternating multiplayer-table and one-on-one structure makes it more varied than a simple series of two-player mahjong matches. Its live-action imagery also marks it as a distinctive product of Japan's adult arcade mahjong market.

games.title: 64th. Street - A Detective Story
games.description:
64th. Street: A Detective Story is Jaleco's 1991 side-scrolling beat-'em-up about detectives Rick Anderson and Allen Tombs, who pursue the kidnappers of a wealthy man's daughter. One or two players fight through six stages of criminals, armed thugs and bizarre bosses using punches, jumps, grabs and improvised weapons.

Its defining flourish is the ability to throw enemies into the background. A well-placed throw can send an opponent crashing into a wall or scenery, often breaking objects to expose useful pickups. This environmental interaction gives its familiar Final Fight-style brawling a distinctive tactical and visual touch.

games.title: 720 Degrees
games.description:
Atari's 720 Degrees (1986) is one of the earliest major arcade games devoted to skateboarding. Instead of following a fixed sequence of races, players roam Skate City, practicing spins, jumps and other tricks to earn points and tickets. Those tickets unlock timed competitions in specialized skate parks, where medals and rewards allow further progress.

Its dedicated rotating controller lets the skater steer and spin with unusual precision, while buttons govern jumping and acceleration. The game's notorious 'SKATE OR DIE' warning is literal: staying in the city too long attracts a swarm of bees that can end the run. Named for the difficult double-revolution aerial trick, 720 Degrees was a pioneering attempt to capture both the freedom and the risk-taking culture of skateboarding in a coin-operated game.

games.title: 7jigen no Youseitachi - Mahjong 7 Dimensions
games.description: 7jigen no Youseitachi: Mahjong 7 Dimensions is a 1990 Japanese mahjong arcade game from Dynax, released under a title that translates approximately as 'Fairies of the Seven Dimensions.' It uses the company's dedicated mahjong hardware and an extensive tile-selection control panel rather than ordinary joystick movement. The game also has a related version titled Mahjong X-Tal 7: Crystal Mahjong. Its specific match progression and any unusual rule variations are not reliably detailed in available historical references.

games.title: '88 Games
games.description:
Konami's '88 Games (1988), known in Japan as Hyper Sports Special, continues the company's Track & Field tradition with an international athletics competition modeled on the Seoul Olympics era. Events include the 100-meter dash, long jump, 400-meter relay, skeet shooting, hurdles, archery, javelin and high jump.

Each event demands a different combination of quick button presses, precisely timed jumps or careful aiming. Players must qualify for finals and chase gold medals, turning the classic Track & Field mix of reflexes and fiercely competitive button mashing into a broader sporting tournament.

games.title: Video Eight Ball
games.description: Video Eight Ball is an early-1980s electronic pool game from Century Electronics. The overhead view shows a billiards table with a movable aiming cursor; players choose a position and line up shots to pocket the colored balls before attempting the black eight ball. The joystick-and-button interface translates cue aiming and shot execution into simple arcade controls. Its appeal lies in strategic ball placement and increasingly awkward angles rather than reflex shooting, making it an example of the period's efforts to adapt familiar tabletop games to video arcades.

games.title: Eight Ball Action
games.description: Eight Ball Action is a 1984 arcade pool simulation in which the player uses a joystick to position an aiming point on an overhead billiards table. Shot strength cycles among soft, medium and hard settings, forcing players to time the shot as well as aim it. Unlike ordinary eight-ball, the game emphasizes scoring: each pocket has a multiplier, and the points for a sunk ball depend on its number, the pocket and the round. Players receive three attempts to pocket a ball, with successful shots extending the turn and scratches ending it. This score-oriented structure gives a traditional pub game an unmistakably arcade-style objective.

games.title: 9-Ball Shootout
games.description: 9-Ball Shootout is a 1993 billiards game offering nine-ball, eight-ball and straight-pool variations. The table is presented from above, and players select and execute shots with joystick-and-button controls. Computer opponents become more demanding as matches are won, so advancement depends on both accurate cue-ball positioning and understanding the different games' rules. Its inclusion of several recognizable pool disciplines distinguishes it from simpler single-mode arcade billiards games.

games.title: Area 51: Site 4
games.description:
Area 51: Site 4 (1998) is Atari Games' sequel to the live-action light-gun shooter Area 51. One or two players use gun controllers to fire at aliens, infected humans and other hostile targets as the action moves automatically through a secret military installation. The game retains the original's digitized, full-motion-video visual style while expanding its locations and enemy encounters.

Accuracy and rapid target recognition are essential as monsters appear suddenly, attack from different parts of the screen and overwhelm careless players. Its deliberately pulpy alien-invasion theme and mixture of film footage with shooting-gallery action make it a distinctive late-1990s American arcade light-gun game.

games.title: All American Football
games.description: All American Football is a 1989 American football arcade game from Leland, developed as an expanded follow-up to John Elway's Team Quarterback. It presents full-field football competition with passing, running, tackling and play selection, but favors brisk, accessible matches over a detailed simulation. Up to four people can compete, encouraging head-to-head teamwork on offense and defense. Improved presentation and sideline features distinguish it from its predecessor, making it a representative example of Leland's emphasis on multiplayer arcade sports.

games.title: Atari Baseball
games.description:
Atari Baseball (1979) is an early dedicated video baseball game built around an overhead diamond and a cocktail-table cabinet. Two players sit opposite each other and take turns batting and fielding, with the screen orientation adapting to the active side. A trackball controls fielders and contributes to the game's unusually direct physical feel.

Pitchers can select different deliveries, while the defending player must position the fielders to intercept balls in play. This attempt to condense the many roles of real baseball into a simple trackball interface makes Atari Baseball an important example of early arcade sports design.

games.title: A.B. Cop
games.description:
Sega's A.B. Cop (1990) is a futuristic motorcycle pursuit game built around high-speed law enforcement. The player rides an 'Air Bike' down a pseudo-3D roadway, weaving through traffic and obstacles in pursuit of criminals before the clock expires. Each mission ends with a moving target that must be caught and disabled rather than merely overtaken.

The game uses dedicated motorcycle-style controls and a dramatic scaling road presentation reminiscent of Sega's Super Scaler era. Combining racing, collisions and boss-like criminal encounters, A.B. Cop occupies an unusual position between traditional driving games and action shooters.

games.title: Abunai Houkago - Mou Matenai
games.description: Abunai Houkago: Mou Matenai is a 1989 Japanese adult-themed hanafuda arcade game from Green Soft. Rather than using the internationally familiar mahjong tiles or poker cards, it is based on hanafuda, the Japanese flower-card tradition. Players advance through matches against computer-controlled opponents in a character-oriented presentation. Its Japanese title can be translated loosely as 'Dangerous After School: I Can't Wait Any Longer.' It is one of the more obscure examples of late-1980s Japanese arcade gambling-style table games, and the available documentation does not establish further distinctive gameplay systems.

games.title: After Burner II
games.description:
After Burner II (1987) is Sega's spectacular jet-combat arcade game and a revised, expanded version of the original After Burner. Piloting an F-14 Tomcat from a rearward perspective, players steer into incoming enemy squadrons, unleash a rapid-fire cannon and launch limited homing missiles. The moving camera, huge sprite scaling and constantly changing aerial scenery produce an intense sensation of speed.

The revision adds a manual throttle, letting skilled pilots accelerate through dangerous encounters or slow down to line up targets, as well as revised stages and other refinements. Many cabinets used a moving cockpit assembly that pitched and rolled with the action, turning the game into a physical attraction as much as a shooter. Its thunderous soundtrack and dramatic launch sequence helped make After Burner II one of the defining showcases of Sega's late-1980s arcade technology.

games.title: Ace
games.description: Ace is a 1976 two-player aerial-combat arcade game from Allied Leisure. Each participant pilots a small biplane around a single-screen playfield and tries to shoot down the opponent while avoiding collisions with the scenery. The straightforward controls support immediate head-to-head dogfights rather than missions or stage progression. Direct hits score points, while crashing can benefit the opposing player, encouraging careful positioning as well as aggressive firing. Its competitive focus places it among the earliest attempts to turn aerial dogfighting into a self-contained video arcade sport.

games.title: Ace Attacker
games.description: Ace Attacker is a 1988 volleyball game from Sega. Viewed from above, it lets players select national teams and compete through a tournament progressing from preliminary matches to the final. A single athlete is controlled at a time, while other teammates are handled by the computer. Successful play requires positioning for receptions, setting up passes, blocking at the net and timing attacking smashes. The combination of team selection, rapid control changes and increasingly capable opponents gives the game more depth than a simple one-button ball-return simulation.

games.title: Ace Driver
games.description:
Ace Driver (1994) is Namco's polygonal Formula-style racing game, developed for its System 22 hardware. Players compete on fast circuits with a cockpit view, steering wheel, pedals and high-speed 3D graphics that emphasize the movement of the track and surrounding scenery. It was designed for arcade competition rather than exhaustive car setup or driving simulation.

An aggressive catch-up system boosts a trailing car, keeping races close and creating a distinctive competitive tactic: deliberately falling behind could allow a driver to exploit the temporary speed advantage for a late overtake. This interplay of driving skill and arcade balancing is one of Ace Driver's most memorable features.

games.title: Alien Command
games.description: Alien Command is an unusual early-1990s Jaleco redemption attraction combining electronic video hardware with a physical shooting gallery. Players aim an optical gun at five UFO targets that move up and down inside the cabinet, scoring by hitting them rather than by steering an onscreen spaceship. The moving targets and real light-based aiming make it closer to an electromechanical fairground shooting game than to a conventional scrolling shooter. It is also connected with Jaleco's E.D.F.: Earth Defense Force, making this obscure hybrid a curious physical offshoot of the company's science-fiction arcade line.

games.title: Acclaim PSX
games.description:
Acclaim PSX is the BIOS for Acclaim's version of Sony's ZN-1 arcade platform, introduced in 1995. The board adapts first-generation PlayStation architecture for coin-operated cabinets, combining a MIPS-based processor, Sony graphics hardware, and a standard arcade interface. Instead of being a standalone title, this entry contains the manufacturer-specific startup firmware required by the Acclaim configuration.

Acclaim's ZN-1 installation used a proprietary ROM daughterboard, with additional audio processing available through an Analog Devices ADSP-2181 board. Like other ZN systems, it relied on board-specific firmware and protection hardware, making the BIOS an important part of the original machine's identity.

games.title: Acrobat Mission
games.description: Acrobat Mission is a 1991 vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter by UPL and Taito. In a future where humanity has moved to Mars after devastating Earth's environment, pilots confront mysterious invaders in advanced Icarus fighters. The player navigates dense airborne and ground defenses, collecting power-ups and facing large mechanical bosses. Its action is built around rapid movement, adjustable weaponry and the spectacular changes in enemy formations typical of Japanese vertical shooters of the period. The game's unusually elaborate science-fiction background gives its aerial campaign more context than many comparable arcade releases.

games.title: Act-Fancer Cybernetick Hyper Weapon
games.description:
Act-Fancer: Cybernetick Hyper Weapon is Data East's 1989 side-scrolling action game starring a biomechanical soldier fighting alien creatures. Players dash through vividly drawn stages, firing at enemies and navigating platforms while collecting blue energy orbs. Gathering enough of these orbs transforms the protagonist into progressively stronger forms with different weapons.

The upgrades are not permanently secure: red orbs help maintain a transformation, while time and damage can strip it away. This unusual progression gives the action a constant risk-and-reward rhythm, as players press forward to keep their evolved weapons active. Fluid animation and grotesque enemy designs make Act-Fancer a recognizable Data East cult title.

games.title: Action Hollywood
games.description: Action Hollywood is a 1995 top-down arcade action game set on exaggerated movie sets. Players choose among themed productions such as Temples of Chaos, Excaliwood, Transilvania and Galaxy War, then battle monsters while traversing tiled rooms. The perspective and cooperative action recall Gauntlet, but the stages also require turning over floor squares to complete objectives. An eight-way joystick and three action buttons support movement and attacks against enemies that roam the set. Its mixture of arena combat, floor-clearing objectives and parody film themes gives it a more unusual structure than a conventional maze shooter.

games.title: A. D. 2083
games.description: A.D. 2083 is a 1983 space shooter that resembles Time Pilot but adds its own scrolling and perspective tricks. An eight-way joystick controls a spacecraft surrounded by enemy formations, with a single button for firing. Opponents can appear to fly out from the distant background before entering the combat area, creating an early pseudo-3D impression. The battlefield scrolls horizontally as the player's craft moves, while the scenery shifts at a different rate to suggest depth. Its looping, score-driven combat and unusual approach to perspective make this an interesting lesser-known entry in the early-1980s wave of omnidirectional arcade shooters.

games.title: Adventure Canoe
games.description: Adventure Canoe is a rare 1982 Taito action game about steering a canoe through a dangerous river. Players paddle downstream while avoiding rocks, whirlpools, islands and other obstacles, using the game's simple controls to keep the boat in safe water. Hostile wildlife can be shot for points, and each stage culminates in a confrontation with a larger enemy. Long considered extremely obscure because of its limited distribution, the game eventually became accessible through later Taito collections and Arcade Archives releases. Its river-navigation premise sets it apart from the space and military shooters that dominated its era.

games.title: Aero Fighters

variants.title: Aero Fighters
variants.version: (World / USA + Canada / Korea / Hong Kong / Taiwan) (newer hardware)

games.description:
Aero Fighters, known in Japan as Sonic Wings, is a 1992 vertically scrolling shooter developed by Video System. It puts an international roster of eccentric pilots into modern fighter aircraft, with each character and plane bringing different weapons and bomb effects. Solo players select from multiple national teams, while simultaneous two-player play adds cooperative firepower to the worldwide campaign.

Collecting power icons strengthens the weapons, bomb stocks permit emergency screen-clearing attacks, and destroying ground targets yields national-currency score items. Beneath the approachable controls is a fast, sometimes unforgiving game of memorizing enemy patterns and using limited resources efficiently.

Aero Fighters became the foundation of the Sonic Wings series, later continued on Neo Geo hardware. Its expressive pilot portraits, improbable aircraft arsenal and lighthearted character endings are an important part of the charm of this influential early-1990s shooter.

games.title: Aero Fighters Special
games.description:
Aero Fighters Special is the 1996 arcade adaptation of Sonic Wings Special, released in Japan as Sonic Wings Limited. It assembles a large selection of pilots and aircraft from the Aero Fighters series, giving players twelve playable fighters across six teams. Each aircraft has its own firing patterns and powerful special attacks.

The vertically scrolling campaign uses branching progression: performance during earlier stages determines some later destinations, including spectacular final confrontations in unexpected locations. Its broad roster and rearranged stages make it a celebratory remix of the series rather than a simple sequel to Aero Fighters 3.

games.title: Action Fighter, FD1089A 317-0018
games.description:
Action Fighter is a 1986 Sega action shooter built around a surprising sequence of vehicle transformations. The player begins on a motorcycle riding along a vertically scrolling road and shoots enemy bikes and cars while collecting lettered power-ups. Enough upgrades transform the motorcycle into a sports car, and later into a flying vehicle.

Once airborne, the gameplay shifts toward a more conventional scrolling shooter, with attacks against aircraft and ground targets. The alternating road and aerial sections, together with memorable boss encounters, make Action Fighter a distinctive mixture of Spy Hunter-style driving and fantasy combat.

games.title: Air Gallet
games.description:
Air Gallet is a 1996 vertically scrolling military shooter developed by Gazelle and published by Banpresto. Players fly a modern fighter against waves of tanks, helicopters and aircraft, confronting large bosses with densely layered attack patterns. The setting is recognizable military action, but the weapons quickly become extravagant.

Four main weapon types can be upgraded through repeated pickups, including a concentrated laser, homing support weapons and spreading shots. This choice of firepower allows different approaches to armored targets and wide formations. Its brisk pacing and elaborate sprite work earned it a following among enthusiasts of late-1990s arcade shooting games.

games.title: Agress
games.description: Agress is a 1991 competitive puzzle game by Palco that combines sliding-block challenges with a military attack theme. Each player rearranges colored tiles to recreate a target shape displayed above the board. Successful patterns expose hidden missile positions, launching attacks against the other side. The strategic twist is that completing a shape is not enough: its position determines which missile blocks are activated, so players must balance speed with placement. As shapes grow more complicated, the contest becomes a demanding mixture of pattern recognition, planning and direct competition.

games.title: Air Inferno
games.description:
Air Inferno is a 1990 helicopter rescue game from Taito, presented with early polygonal 3D graphics. Rather than destroying enemy aircraft, the player pilots a rescue helicopter into hazardous situations, extinguishes fires and lands near stranded people. Missions include burning skyscrapers, ships and dangerous weather conditions such as sandstorms.

The cabinet's flight controls demand careful positioning and altitude management, and approaching a landing site can be as challenging as reaching it. Its unusual emergency-service premise makes it a striking counterpoint to the many helicopter combat simulators of the period.

games.title: Air Attack
games.description: Air Attack is a 1996 vertically scrolling jet shooter from Korean developer Comad. Players fight through seven stages of airborne enemies and bosses, collecting pickups that alter the fighter's weapon. Available armaments include a concentrated Vulcan shot, rapid fire, a broad multi-directional spread and rockets. Repeatedly collecting the same weapon strengthens its effect, while a limited stock of powerful Phoenix-shaped bomb attacks offers a way out of dangerous formations. With one-hit vulnerability and no conventional score-based extra lives, its challenge depends heavily on learning stages and choosing the right weapon for each encounter.

games.title: Air Buster: Trouble Specialty Raid Unit

variants.title: Air Buster: Trouble Specialty Raid Unit (World)
Air Buster: Trouble Specialty Raid Unit (Japan)

games.description:
Air Buster: Trouble Specialty Raid Unit is a 1990 horizontally scrolling shooter developed by Kaneko. One or two players pilot compact Blaster fighters across six fast-moving stages filled with enemy aircraft, ground installations and enormous bosses. Its constantly shifting scenery and aggressive enemy formations are complemented by a broad selection of weapon pickups.

Players can equip homing missiles, multi-directional fire, rear shots and other specialized attacks, while protective items help prevent collisions with terrain. The game's speed and colorful visual design made it a cult favorite, and a later home conversion introduced it to a broader audience under the name Aero Blasters.

games.title: Air Combat 22
games.description:
Air Combat 22 is Namco's 1995 polygonal jet-combat arcade game and the successor to the original Air Combat. The title refers to the System Super 22 hardware, which allows more detailed scenery and aircraft. Players choose fighters such as the F-14 Tomcat, Su-27 and F-22 and pursue enemy squadrons using cannon fire and guided missiles.

A radar display and targeting indicators help locate enemies, while each mission demands that a specified number be shot down before time expires. Additional sequences include carrier landings and other flying challenges. Like its predecessor, it emphasizes the spectacle of aerial combat rather than the complexity of a full flight simulator.

games.title: Air Combat
games.description:
Namco's Air Combat (1992) is an early polygonal jet-fighting arcade game and the ancestor of the later Ace Combat series. Players pilot a modern fighter, commonly represented as an F-16, against enemy aircraft in missions viewed from behind the cockpit. Cannons and missiles handle close- and long-range attacks, while radar and targeting cues help track opponents.

A countdown timer makes every successful interception matter, with downed enemies extending the available time. Aircraft-carrier landing sequences break up the dogfights. Its dedicated cockpit-style controls and early 3D visuals made it an ambitious arcade aviation attraction and laid much of the groundwork for Namco's long-running console series.

games.title: Air Duel
games.description:
Air Duel is a 1990 vertically scrolling shooter from Irem distinguished by its choice of aircraft. Before each stage, players can select either a jet fighter with strong forward fire or a helicopter that turns its guns in the direction of movement. The helicopter's rotating attacks make side targets easier to hit, while the jet rewards direct, precise positioning.

Weapon upgrades expand each craft's strengths, and bomb attacks can be steered to lay down a chain of explosions. This ability to change aircraft between stages adds tactical variety to Irem's characteristic military environments and large boss battles.

games.title: Air Race
games.description: Air Race is an unreleased 1985 Atari Games prototype featuring futuristic vehicle racing around a flat-shaded polygonal course. Players would steer a flying craft through a race environment rather than drive a conventional car, an ambitious idea for arcade graphics hardware of its time. The project was never commercially released, reportedly because the proposed hardware was too costly. Work on its 3D technology later contributed to Atari's Hard Drivin' and S.T.U.N. Runner, making Air Race an important missing link in the company's transition to polygonal arcade racing.

games.title: Airwolf
games.description:
Airwolf is a 1987 side-scrolling helicopter shooter developed by Kyugo and based on the television series. Players pilot the high-tech Airwolf through four missions packed with jets, helicopters, armored vehicles, submarines and ground troops. The helicopter has a forward-firing cannon and diagonally dropping bombs, which can bounce along the terrain before striking their targets.

Firing both weapon buttons together performs an evasive loop, adding a defensive option to the constant barrage of enemies. Parachuting pickups provide bonuses, and the game cycles back to its opening after the fourth mission. It is a straightforward but distinctive licensed action game from the peak of the show's popularity.

games.title: Ajax
games.description:
Ajax, known as Typhoon in some markets, is Konami's 1987 military shooter combining multiple perspectives. Most stages show a helicopter in overhead vertical-scrolling combat, shooting at airborne enemies and bombing ground installations. Other sequences switch to a dramatic behind-the-aircraft perspective with fast-scaling sprites and oncoming targets.

Pickups provide lasers, spread fire and other upgrades as the campaign moves between hostile bases and formidable bosses. The shifting viewpoints and dynamic presentation make Ajax one of Konami's more technically distinctive late-1980s shooters, combining conventional arcade combat with cinematic pseudo-3D spectacle.

games.title: Akai Katana
games.description: Akai Katana is a horizontal-scrolling bullet-hell shoot-'em-up developed and published by Cave for the Cave CV1000-D arcade hardware in 2010. Set in a parallel Taisho-era Japan powered by a mystical mineral called Bloodstone, players choose between three fighter-pilot teams who can switch dynamically between a traditional Fighter craft and a giant phantom-warrior Soul form, altering their attack patterns, bullet-canceling mechanics, and katana-based scoring system.

games.title: Akai Katana Unlimited

modifications.description: Removes the phantom Soul timer drain so players can remain in Soul form indefinitely and alters katana generation mechanics.

games.description: Akai Katana Unlimited is a gameplay modification of Cave's 2010 horizontal shoot-'em-up Akai Katana created by IAmTheChuckster. It removes the time limit on the phantom Soul transformation, allowing players to stay in Soul form continuously and experiment freely with the katana-summoning and bullet-reflection mechanics.

games.title: Mahjong Angel Kiss
games.description: Mahjong Angel Kiss is a 1995 Japanese adult mahjong game from Jaleco, built on the company's Mega System 32 hardware. The player faces a sequence of illustrated opponents in mahjong matches, with victories advancing extensive animated character scenes. Unusually, opponents do not have a fixed pool of betting funds that can be exhausted to shorten the progression: a match must be completed for each reward sequence. The game's ornate character art was overseen by illustrator Satoshi Urushihara, and its comparatively large number of animations per opponent distinguishes it from less elaborate arcade mahjong releases of the period.

games.title: Akka Arrh
games.description:
Akka Arrh is an exceptionally rare Atari prototype tested in 1982, developed by Mike Hally and Dave Ralston. Players defend the central Sentinel cannon using a trackball-controlled cursor. On the wide battlefield, attacks target entire zones containing incoming alien formations; when attackers break through the perimeter, play switches to a closer view requiring direct fire against individual threats. A limited supply of screen-clearing bombs provides emergency protection.

Atari tested the game in a handful of specially built cabinets, but its unusual dual-perspective mechanics proved too difficult for many testers and the project was canceled. The name was an in-house joke on 'Another Ralston Hally' project; alternative development titles included The Sentinel and Target Outpost. The rediscovery of its playable software made it one of Atari's best-known unreleased arcade curiosities.

games.title: Aladdin
games.description:
Aladdin is an unauthorized 1993 arcade adaptation of Sega's Mega Drive platform game based on Disney's animated film. It retains the familiar side-scrolling adventure through Agrabah and other film-inspired settings, with Aladdin jumping, attacking enemies and negotiating hazards. The board uses Genesis-like technology rather than an original arcade engine.

The bootleg changes the console game's balance for coin-operated play: its normal damage tolerance is sharply reduced, though Genie-heart pickups can improve survivability, and the home version's options screen is absent. Unlike many arcade conversions, it does not introduce a stage timer. These alterations make it a particularly revealing example of home-console software being repackaged for arcades without official authorization.

games.title: Aleck64 PIF BIOS
games.description:
The Aleck64 PIF BIOS belongs to Seta's Nintendo 64-derived arcade hardware, introduced in 1998. Built around Nintendo's VR4300 processor and Reality Co-Processor architecture, the system adapted the console's 3D graphics and audio capabilities to a dedicated coin-operated motherboard. The Aleck64 used its own cartridge arrangement and additional arcade-oriented circuitry rather than accepting ordinary Nintendo 64 cartridges.

PIF stands for Peripheral Interface, the Nintendo 64 subsystem involved in early startup and controller communication. Its boot ROM is preserved separately because emulation of the Aleck64 requires this low-level system code in addition to the motherboard and cartridge data. The platform is a distinctive example of late-1990s arcade hardware developed directly from a home-console design.

games.title: Alex Kidd: The Lost Stars

variants.title: Alex Kidd: The Lost Stars (set 2, unprotected)
Alex Kidd: The Lost Stars (set 1, FD1089A 317-unknown)

games.description:
Alex Kidd: The Lost Stars is Sega's 1986 arcade platform game featuring Alex Kidd and, in two-player play, Stella. The heroes travel through colorful, frequently surreal side-scrolling stages in search of the twelve Miracle Balls, dodging hazards and monsters as a time-based vitality meter runs down. The controls emphasize jumping, positioning and collecting bonuses over the punch-heavy action of Alex Kidd's earlier adventures.

Its whimsical scenery, strange enemies and repeated 'I'm sorry!' cry when the character is hurt give it a distinctive personality. A later Master System conversion brought the game to a larger audience, although the arcade original remains notable for its cooperative play and bright visual style.

games.title: Ali Baba and 40 Thieves
games.description: Ali Baba and 40 Thieves is a 1982 maze game published by Sega and loosely inspired by the Arabian folktale. The player guides Ali Baba through corridors while fending off thieves attempting to steal his money. Enemies approach along the passages, making route choices and timing more important than indiscriminate shooting. The game combines the pursuit and evasion structure of early arcade maze titles with a recognizable storybook theme, offering an alternative to the science-fiction settings prevalent in the period.

games.title: Alien3: The Gun
games.description:
Alien3: The Gun is a 1993 Sega light-gun shooter that freely adapts the setting and creatures of the film Alien 3. Rather than following the movie's largely unarmed protagonist, players take the roles of Colonial Marines fighting through a facility overrun by xenomorphs. The arcade cabinet features a large, mounted gun inspired by the series' iconic pulse rifle, with a trigger for ordinary fire and an additional control for powerful attacks.

The game moves automatically between encounters as players shoot rapidly approaching aliens, facehuggers and enormous bosses. Weapon pickups, alternate routes and limited-use explosives provide variety, while occasional destructible scenery rewards accurate shooting. Its relentless action, detailed monster animation and imposing gun controller make it one of Sega's memorable licensed shooting-gallery attractions.

games.title: Alien Arena
games.description:
Alien Arena is a 1985 competitive action game by Duncan Brown featuring two opposing alien characters, Thor and Zespar. Each player tries to capture the rival's flag while protecting their own, maneuvering around a single-screen arena and using weapons and defensive aids. A solo participant fights the computer, while two players can battle each other directly.

Unusually, initial play is time-based, with additional coins extending the match. When the paid time runs out, the contest can continue in a survival-oriented solo phase, with the leading human player taking control against the computer. Its combination of capture-the-flag objectives and unusual coin-operated match structure sets it apart from standard maze combat games.

games.title: Alien Challenge
games.description:
Alien Challenge is a 1994 one-on-one fighting game from International Games System. Players choose from eight eccentric combatants, including martial artists and monster-like fighters, and compete in a tournament presented with large, colorful character sprites. The controls follow the six-button layout popularized by Street Fighter II, with light, medium and heavy punches and kicks.

Distinct attacks, special moves and the roster's mix of human and fantastical designs give it the recognizable structure of a mid-1990s arcade fighter. It is a lesser-known Taiwanese contribution to the era's fighting-game boom.

games.title: Aliens
games.description:
Konami's Aliens (1990) is a side-scrolling run-and-gun action game inspired by James Cameron's 1986 film. One or two players control Ellen Ripley and Corporal Hicks as they battle through LV-426, rescuing survivors and confronting swarms of xenomorphs on the way to a showdown with the Alien Queen. The game uses recognizable film settings but introduces many original creatures and extravagant enemy variants.

Players move along side-view corridors, firing weapons such as smart guns, flamethrowers and grenade launchers. Some sections switch to an over-the-shoulder shooting perspective, sharply changing the feel of the combat. Multiple health points, weapon pickups and striking boss designs help distinguish it from a conventional one-hit action game.

The detailed sprites, cooperative action and memorable final confrontation, including Ripley's power-loader fight, make Aliens a cult favorite among movie-licensed arcade games. Its creative liberties with the film's monsters are now part of its appeal.

games.title: Alien Syndrome
games.description:
Alien Syndrome is Sega's 1987 overhead-view run-and-gun game in which soldiers Ricky and Mary rescue hostages from spaceships infested with grotesque alien organisms. One or two players explore scrolling decks, gather the required number of prisoners and reach an exit before a time bomb detonates. Every level ends with a confrontation against an enormous organic boss.

The soldiers can fire in eight directions and replace their basic weapon with more powerful attacks collected around the ship. Route planning matters because clearing a stage requires finding hostages quickly rather than simply surviving an enemy wave. The grotesque creature designs, countdown pressure and cooperative rescue structure gave Alien Syndrome a lasting identity among Sega's late-1980s action titles.

games.title: Alligator Hunt
games.description:
Alligator Hunt is a 1994 arcade shooter by Spanish developer Gaelco in which two skateboarding teenagers defend Earth from an invasion of reptilian aliens. Its perspective resembles Cabal or Blood Bros.: the characters move across the bottom of the screen while players aim a separate crosshair at enemies approaching from the background. Later stages take the fight into space and toward the aliens' homeworld.

Rapid fire handles ordinary targets, while limited missiles and upgraded ammunition help against tougher opponents. Scenery, enemy projectiles and destructible targets fill the screen, making movement and aiming equally important. Its unusual heroes, bright art and surprisingly elaborate journey distinguish it from other gallery-style shooters of the period.

games.title: Alley Master
games.description: Alley Master is a 1986 arcade bowling game from Cinematronics. Designed for two players with a joystick and two buttons, it translates ten-pin bowling and the pursuit of strikes and spares into a compact video-game competition. Developed under the provisional name Up Your Alley, it reflects Cinematronics' attempts to bring familiar indoor sports into video arcades. Its dedicated upright cabinet contrasts with the real lanes and mechanical equipment found in traditional bowling alleys.

games.title: Alpha Fighter / Head On
games.description: Alpha Fighter / Head On is a late-1970s dual-game arcade release combining two different styles of early coin-operated action. Alpha Fighter is a fixed-screen alien shooter in the Space Invaders tradition, with descending enemies and a bonus encounter involving a larger spacecraft. Head On instead takes place on a top-down driving circuit, where players collect dots while trying to avoid an opposing car. The juxtaposition is historically interesting: Head On's collect-the-dots racing mechanic predates Pac-Man, while Alpha Fighter reflects the enormous influence of the first wave of fixed-screen space shooters. The combined board offered operators two recognizable, contrasting games in one installation.

games.title: Alpha Mission II / ASO II - Last Guardian
games.description:
Alpha Mission II, also known as ASO II: Last Guardian, is a 1991 vertically scrolling shooter from SNK for the Neo Geo. Players pilot a space fighter against airborne and ground-based enemies, using separate attacks for targets at different elevations. Ordinary weapons improve through pickups, but the game's distinguishing feature is a collection of specialized armor suits that dramatically change the ship's firepower.

Pieces of an armor set can be gathered during stages, and additional equipment may be purchased with credits earned during play. Armor abilities consume energy, which can be replenished by collecting the appropriate items. This combination of dual-plane shooting, equipment collection and resource management gives Alpha Mission II more customization than a typical straightforward Neo Geo shooter.

games.title: Alpha One
games.description:
Alpha One is Atari's 1983 vector-graphics prototype that became The Adventures of Major Havoc. The unusual design joins a spaceship shoot-'em-up against robotic defenders with a station-infiltration sequence, in which the protagonist sabotages a reactor and attempts to escape. A rotary controller and action button serve the game's different styles of play.

This early build preserves an intermediate stage of development: it has no music, some different sound effects and graphics, and a substantially different account of its alien enemies. It also includes the early Breakout-like warp-code challenge. Alpha One is therefore valuable not simply as a renamed game, but as a playable record of how one of Atari's most experimental arcade projects changed before release.

games.title: Alpine Ski
games.description:
Alpine Ski is Taito's 1982 downhill skiing game. Players steer a skier around other people, obstacles and gates on a scrolling mountainside, managing speed to avoid costly collisions. The game includes downhill, slalom and ski-jump challenges, progressing from basic obstacle avoidance to more demanding timed and precision-based competitions.

A speed-control button complements the joystick, allowing the skier to slow before a dangerous turn and accelerate on open stretches. Its multiple events and clear winter-sports theme make it an early predecessor to the specialized skiing simulators that appeared in 1990s arcades.

games.title: Alpine Racer
games.description:
Namco's Alpine Racer (1995) transformed arcade skiing into a full-body experience. Players stand on two ski-like platforms and hold handlebars while sliding their feet sideways to steer a polygonal skier downhill. The game's courses combine sharp turns, gates, slopes and obstacles in an early 3D mountain environment.

Race and time-trial modes challenge players to beat opponents or the clock, with several difficulty levels and routes. Unlike ordinary joystick games, the cabinet demands real balance and coordinated leg movement. This physical interface was central to Alpine Racer's appeal and made it a notable fixture of large-format amusement arcades.

games.title: Alpine Surfer
games.description:
Alpine Surfer is Namco's 1996 snowboarding companion to Alpine Racer. Instead of standing on two ski platforms, the player balances on a snowboard-like board and shifts weight to steer through a polygonal mountain course, holding the cabinet's bars for support. The dedicated physical controller is as important to the experience as the action on the screen.

Free-riding stages emphasize reaching the finish while performing aerial tricks, while gate-racing events reward fast and accurate navigation. Its combination of stunt scoring, speed and full-body control captures the mid-1990s fashion for snowboarding and experiential arcade machines.

games.title: Alpine Racer 2
games.description:
Alpine Racer 2 is Namco's 1996 sequel to its popular full-body skiing arcade game. Players once again stand on paired ski platforms and move their legs to guide a 3D skier downhill, negotiating slopes, gates and changing snow conditions. The game offers different skier types, races and timed events, refining the original's physically demanding approach to virtual winter sports.

A key addition is linked-cabinet competition, allowing two players to race directly against one another. The ability to compete side by side on imposing ski controllers made the sequel an especially social arcade attraction.

games.title: Altered Beast
games.description:
Altered Beast (1988) is Sega's mythological side-scrolling beat-'em-up, created by a team led by Makoto Uchida. Zeus resurrects fallen warriors and commands them to rescue Athena from the demon Neff. One or two players punch, kick and jump through five short but memorable levels of undead monsters and supernatural guardians.

Defeating white two-headed wolves releases Spirit Balls, and collecting enough transforms the hero into a beast with far more powerful attacks. The forms change between stages, including the iconic werewolf, a flying dragon and other creatures with distinctive abilities. The famous sampled command 'Rise from your grave!' and the rapidly swelling character sprites give the transformations an unforgettable theatrical quality.

A major arcade hit of Sega's late-1980s period, Altered Beast became especially familiar as a bundled game for the Sega Genesis/Mega Drive. Its transformations, enormous monsters and vivid voice samples made it one of the company's best-known early 16-bit showcases.

games.title: Soldier Girl Amazon
games.description:
Soldier Girl Amazon, also known as Sei Senshi Amatelass, is a 1986 overhead-view shooter by Nichibutsu. The heroine Amaterasu is a warrior pursuing escaped interplanetary criminals, advancing through hostile territory while firing energy shots in eight directions. Enemy forces attack from all sides, giving the game a pace reminiscent of Commando.

A motorcycle pickup improves mobility and endurance, and further upgrades can transform the vehicle into a more heavily armed flying craft. Limited bombs provide emergency firepower, while each stage leads to a spacecraft boss and the capture of another fugitive. The combination of run-and-gun action and progressive vehicle transformations gives this obscure shooter a distinctive personality.

games.title: Ambush
games.description: Ambush is a 1983 space-combat arcade game built around an unusual launch-and-fight sequence. Players first accelerate a spacecraft along a narrow runway, keeping it centered and initiating takeoff before running out of space. Failing to reach sufficient speed or striking the boundaries can end the attempt before any combat begins. After a successful launch, the viewpoint shifts to a behind-the-craft perspective, where the player dodges obstacles and fires on incoming enemies. The transition from precise takeoff control to arcade dogfighting makes Ambush more structurally varied than a conventional single-screen space shooter.

games.title: Ameri Darts
games.description: Ameri Darts is a 1989 arcade darts game from Ameri that uses a trackball to simulate aiming and throwing. Players position the dart with the ball, lock in the intended location and roll the trackball to determine the throw, translating a familiar pub-game motion into an electronic control scheme. Several rule sets are included, such as 301, Cricket, High Score, a bull's-eye challenge and a sector-target contest. Humorous result animations provide feedback between turns, while the choice of games encourages both precision play and head-to-head competition.

games.title: Amidar
games.description:
Amidar is Konami's influential 1981 maze game in which the player travels along a grid, completing rectangles while avoiding patrolling enemies. Stages alternate between a gorilla collecting coconuts and a paint roller drawing across the maze. Surrounding a rectangular space fills it in, and the aim is to complete the entire playfield without being caught.

The enemies follow distinctive movement patterns, including a pursuer that can trace the player's path, so success depends on planning routes rather than simply reacting. A limited-use jump button briefly disrupts enemy movement, offering a way out of tight situations. Completing corner sections can also create useful opportunities for bonus scoring.

With its clear visual rules and unusual territory-completion objective, Amidar established ideas later revisited by other maze and painting games. Its blend of predictable enemy behavior and constant route pressure remains challenging long after the simple controls are mastered.

games.title: American Poker II
games.description:
American Poker II is a 1990 video-poker machine from the Austrian Novomatic/AGI family. Unlike a plain five-card draw game, it uses a 52-card deck with a wild Joker and offers an optional paid second draw. A qualifying Jacks-or-Better hand only pays when the player has purchased that extra draw, so deciding whether to spend another credit is central to its risk-and-reward structure.

Designed for dedicated gambling cabinets rather than conventional action arcades, it runs on modest Z80-based hardware with an AY-3-8910 sound chip. Its success spawned numerous regional, revised, and unofficial derivatives, including Spanish Jackpot versions and Argentine adaptations. The many surviving program sets illustrate how extensively a popular video-poker design could be adapted to different markets.

games.title: American Speedway
games.description: American Speedway is a 1987 top-down racing game from Enerdyne Technologies, with a dedicated steering-wheel cabinet available for solo or head-to-head competition. Players guide small cars around a compact circuit shared with computer-controlled rivals, negotiating sharp corners and patches of oil that can send vehicles sliding. Qualifying rounds require five laps within a set time, while competitive rounds demand a sufficiently high finishing position to advance. The fixed overhead perspective keeps the whole tactical contest visible, making blocking, overtaking and recovery from a skid as important as outright speed.

games.title: Andro Dunos
games.description:
Andro Dunos is a 1992 horizontally scrolling space shooter from Visco, released for the Neo Geo. Players pilot a combat spacecraft through seven stages of mechanized opposition, moving across varied environments and confronting large end-of-stage bosses. Its main distinguishing feature is a selectable arsenal: four different weapon types are available from the outset and can be switched during play.

Each weapon gains power through pickups and, once sufficiently upgraded, can unleash a charged special shot. Losing a ship weakens the arsenal, so players must balance the tactical advantages of different guns against the need to preserve their upgrades. The colorful graphics and flexible weapons make it a solid example of early Neo Geo shooting design.

games.title: Andromeda
games.description: Andromeda is a 1979 fixed-screen space shooter by Irem, one of the company's earliest arcade releases. The player moves a ship horizontally along the bottom of the screen, firing at a formation of 33 Andro-Ships. Enemies break away to attack, and shots scored during a dive are worth more than hits on the stationary formation. The central Commander-Ship plays a crucial tactical role: as long as it survives, more enemies can be recruited, but destroying it prompts the remaining attackers to launch a general assault. A shrinking end-of-wave bonus adds an incentive to dispatch enemies efficiently. These details distinguish Andromeda from simpler Space Invaders imitations and anticipate the attack-formation design associated with Galaxian.

games.title: Angel Kids
games.description: Angel Kids is a 1988 Sega and Nasco arcade game with an unusually physical two-joystick control scheme. Two children hold a rope beneath a third child, and the player must pull the sticks apart to tighten the rope and bounce the airborne child upward. Careful timing and positioning allow the child to strike balloons above the playfield without falling. The action extends vertically over several screens, with changes in balloon movement altering the angle of the next bounce. Rather than relying on shooting or jumping buttons, the game challenges players to coordinate both hands as though controlling a trampoline. Its imaginative controls and pastel art make it a particularly unusual late-1980s arcade release.

games.title: Animalandia Jr.
games.description: Animalandia Jr., also released as Exciting Animal Land Jr. and Waiwai Animal Land Jr., is a 1993 animal-themed whac-a-mole arcade game by Nakanihon and East Technology, distributed under Taito license. It presents a simplified version of the earlier Waiwai Animal Land concept, asking players to react quickly to animal targets in a colorful, child-oriented setting. Its six-button input arrangement and optional ticket-redemption settings reflect the design of a family amusement attraction rather than a traditional joystick action game. English, Japanese and Spanish versions are known, illustrating its spread across different arcade markets.

games.title: Anteater
games.description:
Anteater is a 1982 maze game from Stern in which an anteater extends its long tongue into an underground network of passages to eat insect larvae. The player maneuvers the tongue through the maze, but only its tip can safely eat ants: contact with the middle of the tongue is dangerous. Different enemies have their own rules, including worms that are safe to consume from behind but not head-on.

Retracting the tongue quickly is essential when trouble approaches, and reaching a queen ant can temporarily clear the screen. A day-and-night cycle adds a spider threat as darkness falls. The resulting mixture of maze navigation, careful risk assessment and unusual creature behavior makes Anteater one of the most inventive obscure arcade games of its era.

games.title: Aggressors of Dark Kombat / Tsuukai GANGAN Koushinkyoku
games.description:
Aggressors of Dark Kombat, known in Japan as Tsuukai GANGAN Koushinkyoku, is a 1994 Neo Geo fighting game by ADK. Unlike conventional 2D fighters, its combatants can move toward and away from the screen as well as sideways, using the depth of the arena much like characters in a beat-'em-up. The cast includes eight unusual challengers with distinctive fighting styles.

Grabbing and grappling are central to the combat, and attacks can be countered while opponents struggle for control. Spectators sometimes throw weapons into the arena, giving fighters additional improvised options. This mixture of wrestling-like holds, side-scrolling brawler mechanics and one-on-one competition gives Aggressors a distinctive identity within the crowded Neo Geo fighting library.

games.title: Art of Fighting / Ryuuko no Ken
games.description:
Art of Fighting, known in Japan as Ryuuko no Ken, is SNK's influential 1992 Neo Geo fighting game starring Ryo Sakazaki and Robert Garcia. The two martial artists travel through South Town in search of Ryo's kidnapped sister Yuri, battling an underworld cast in dramatic one-on-one encounters. Its enormous, detailed character sprites and camera zoom that changes with the fighters' distance were striking technical showpieces for the time.

A separate spirit gauge governs many special moves, encouraging players to conserve energy or recharge between attacks, while a dedicated taunt can weaken an opponent's resources. Characters also show visible facial damage as fights progress, adding to the cinematic presentation.

Art of Fighting became one of SNK's defining early fighting-game series and helped establish characters and storylines that later crossed into The King of Fighters. Its blend of expressive animation, dramatic camera work and resource management remains distinctive even alongside the more famous Street Fighter II.

games.title: Art of Fighting 2 / Ryuuko no Ken 2

variants.title: Art of Fighting 2 / Ryuuko no Ken 2 (set 1)
Art of Fighting 2 / Ryuuko no Ken 2 (set 2)

games.description:
Art of Fighting 2 (1994) expands SNK's Neo Geo martial-arts series with a much larger selectable cast and a prequel story centered on Geese Howard's tournament in South Town. Ryo Sakazaki, Robert Garcia, Yuri and other familiar fighters return with reworked moves, new backgrounds and the same dramatic screen zooming that made the original memorable.

The spirit or rage gauge remains central: special attacks depend on maintaining enough energy, while taunts can undermine an opponent's resources. Bonus stages offer permanent improvements to health and spirit, and the computer-controlled opposition is famously aggressive. The game also includes a hidden encounter with Geese, connecting the Art of Fighting story more directly with the Fatal Fury universe.

games.title: Art of Fighting 3 - The Path of the Warrior / Art of Fighting - Ryuuko no Ken Gaiden

variants.title: Art of Fighting 3 - The Path of the Warrior / Art of Fighting - Ryuuko no Ken Gaiden
Art of Fighting 3 - The Path of the Warrior (Korean release)

games.description:
Art of Fighting 3: The Path of the Warrior (1996), released in Japan as Ryuuko no Ken Gaiden, is SNK's most technically elaborate entry in the original trilogy. Its story follows Robert Garcia to Mexico, where he searches for Freia Lawrence and becomes entangled with a new set of rivals. The cast is largely redesigned around newcomers, while Ryo returns as a familiar counterpart.

The game's unusually fluid, motion-capture-influenced animation is its most obvious attraction, but the combat also changes substantially. Attacks link into sequences and aerial juggles more reminiscent of contemporary 3D fighters, while the familiar spirit gauge, evasive movement and powerful special techniques remain. It is a distinctive finale to the classic trilogy, prized as much for its animation artistry as for its departure from the earlier games' fighting rhythm.

games.title: Age Of Heroes - Silkroad 2
games.description: Age of Heroes: Silkroad 2 is Unico's 2001 follow-up to The Legend of Silkroad, a Korean arcade beat-'em-up drawing on a fantasy version of East Asian martial-arts adventure. Players choose one of four warriors, Kai, Shuh, Shenmue, or Chamuku, and fight their way through enemy-filled stages in side-scrolling, belt-action combat. Its four-button, eight-way-joystick arrangement provides more options than the simplest punch-and-jump brawlers, while two-player cooperation lets partners tackle the mobs together. The sequel is an uncommon late example of the traditional scrolling beat-'em-up surviving into the 2000s, long after one-on-one fighters and 3D games had come to dominate arcades.

games.title: Apache 3
games.description:
Tatsumi's Apache 3 (1988) is a helicopter combat shooter that stages its missions in a fast-moving, pseudo-3D view from behind a yellow AH-64 Apache. A terrorist group called Blackslash has kidnapped three allied leaders, and the pilot must penetrate enemy territory, attack air and ground targets, destroy hostile bases, and rescue captives. Most of the action races forward over scaling terrain, with some sections shifting into a side-scrolling presentation. A flight stick and three buttons control the helicopter's movement and armament.

The elaborate arcade cockpit and multi-processor Tatsumi hardware made Apache 3 an ambitious alternative to ordinary two-dimensional shooters. Its distinctive road and landscape effects have also posed challenges for arcade emulation, making the surviving game an interesting showcase of the custom graphics hardware used in high-end Japanese cabinets of the period.

games.title: APB - All Points Bulletin
games.description:
APB: All Points Bulletin is Atari Games' 1987 comic police-driving game, designed by Dave Theurer, the creator of Missile Command and Tempest. Players become Officer Bob, driver of patrol car 54, and must meet an escalating daily quota of traffic citations and arrests. From a scrolling overhead view, Bob chases litterbugs, speeders, reckless drivers, and other offenders, using his siren to pull them over while juggling fuel, time, and a growing list of demerits. Donuts add time, gas stations replenish fuel, and a garage offers upgrades to the patrol car.

On special APB days, the police chief assigns a major fugitive.
