Catching the suspect is only half the challenge: back at the station, players rapidly alternate the controls to fill a satirical Confess-O-Meter before the chief catches Bob using excessive force. Enough demerits end his career in a cartoon dismissal.

APB's dedicated cabinet resembled a police cruiser, with steering wheel, accelerator, and flashing red-and-blue roof lights triggered by the siren button. Its high-resolution graphics, spoken effects, escalating objectives, and irreverent humor made it one of Atari's more eccentric late-1980s releases. Theurer later acknowledged that the unusually lengthy development had made its design more complicated than planned.

games.title: Attack Pla Rail
games.description: Attack Pla-Rail is an unusual 1998 train-driving arcade game made by Namco and Tomy for Namco's PlayStation-derived System 12 hardware. Rather than operating a full-size locomotive, players guide a miniature train over the bright plastic tracks associated with Tomy's Pla-Rail toy line. The principal control is a speed lever: moving quickly improves progress and score, but carrying too much speed into bends can derail the train. With its toy-scale setting and straightforward risk-versus-speed challenge, it is a playful, child-friendly counterpart to the more demanding Japanese train simulators of the late 1990s.

games.title: Apparel Night
games.description: Apparel Night is a Japanese adult-themed mahjong game released by Central Denshi in 1986. It uses a dedicated mahjong-button layout rather than a joystick, with conventional tile-game decisions framed by images of women and the presentation associated with Japan's mature arcade mahjong market. Its 1986 release and Z80-based hardware place it among the earlier wave of dedicated video-mahjong machines, a substantial but often overlooked part of the Japanese coin-operated industry. The surviving documentation establishes its theme and controls but provides little detail about any distinctive rule variations.

games.title: Appoooh
games.description:
Appoooh is a 1984 professional-wrestling arcade game developed by Sanritsu and published by Sega. Players choose from eight exaggerated wrestlers whose names and appearances parody contemporary stars, including G. Babu, H. Hogen, A. Inoke, and Tigerman. An eight-way joystick and three attack buttons produce a surprisingly varied repertoire of punches, kicks, grapples, throws, rope rebounds, and pin attempts. Opponents can even be thrown outside the ring, where the referee starts a count before they return.

Matches unfold in a large ring with a visible referee and a three-minute round timer. Colored waves around a fallen wrestler communicate whether they are briefly stunned or vulnerable to a decisive pin. The game's irreverent character designs and range of wrestling actions distinguish it from simpler early sports simulations, while its unlicensed roster preserves a snapshot of Japanese and international wrestling celebrity in the mid-1980s.

games.title: Aqua Jack
games.description:
Taito's Aqua Jack is a high-speed hovercraft shooter released in Japanese arcades in 1990. Viewed from behind the player's craft, the action races over waterways and land as helicopters, boats, aircraft, and ground vehicles attack. The hovercraft fires a regular cannon and limited explosives, and can jump over mines, obstacles, and other hazards that would otherwise destroy it. A turbo function adds speed to an already hectic eight-stage campaign.

Built for Taito's Z System, Aqua Jack uses scaling sprites and elaborate pseudo-3D scenery in the tradition of After Burner, but its low-flying watercraft, jumping maneuver, and surface hazards give it an identity of its own. The game also contains a cameo by Banglar, the villain from Taito's The Ninja Warriors.

games.title: Aqua Jet
games.description:
Namco's Aqua Jet (1996) turns jet-ski racing into a full-body arcade attraction. The original cabinet incorporates a large ride-on watercraft replica whose handlebars are used to steer, accelerate, and pitch the player's view up or down. Players race against eleven computer-controlled rivals, dodging rough water and obstacles and reaching checkpoints before the clock runs out. Novice and Expert courses vary the challenge, while ramps reward well-timed jumps; skilled riders can manipulate the handlebars for shorter hops and even brief dives beneath the water.

The game runs on Namco's System 22 family, using polygonal waterside scenery and a fast first-person viewpoint to create the impression of speed. Secret inputs unlock mirrored courses and a comical penguin rider. Although it offers a modest selection of tracks, the unusual physical cabinet is central to the experience and illustrates Namco's enthusiasm for large-scale motion-oriented racing attractions in the mid-1990s.

games.title: Clockwork Aquario
games.description: Clockwork Aquario is a two-player side-scrolling action platformer developed by Westone Bit Entertainment for the Sega System 18 arcade board. Originally planned for release in 1993, the project was cancelled after location testing and remained unreleased for nearly three decades before its prototype ROM was recovered and restored.

games.title: Aquarium
games.description: Aquarium is a fish-themed competitive falling-block puzzle game released in Japan by Excellent System in the mid-1990s. Players arrange descending pieces bearing different sea-creature shapes and clear groups by matching three of the same kind. Its colorful underwater presentation and chain-oriented matching resemble the Puyo Puyo school of puzzle games more than conventional line-clearing Tetris. An eight-way joystick and two buttons provide the controls, with support for two players. It is an obscure entry in the crowded Japanese puzzle-game market, notable for its aquatic theme rather than a radically different rule set.

games.title: Aqua Rush
games.description:
Namco's Aqua Rush (1999) turns the falling-block puzzle upside down. Bubbles rise from the bottom of the playfield instead of dropping from above, and players must join them to the existing formations to make complete horizontal rows disappear. The long-term goal is to work upward through an underwater course and burst the red bubbles marking each stage's ceiling. Three difficulty routes differ in puzzle layouts, pacing, and distance to the surface.

Every incoming piece consists of three bubbles side by side, but it cannot be rotated in the Tetris manner. Instead, separate buttons extend its three columns vertically, letting players sculpt a shape that precisely fills gaps in the formation. This unusually tactile shaping mechanic, together with a two-player split-screen mode, makes Aqua Rush one of Namco's more inventive System 12 puzzle games.

games.title: SportTime Table Hockey
games.description: SportTime Table Hockey is Arcadia Systems' 1988 video simulation of air hockey, presented from an angled view of a tabletop rink. Two opponents use joystick-controlled mallets to strike a red puck toward the opposing goal while defending their own. The digital table models gliding puck movement, wall rebounds, and collisions, with the score and remaining match time displayed on screen. Part of Arcadia's Amiga-derived Super Select lineup, it transforms a familiar physical amusement into a straightforward competitive video game rather than a full-scale sports management simulation.

games.title: Aaargh
games.description:
Aaargh! is a giant-monster action game developed for Arcadia Systems' Amiga-derived arcade hardware in 1987. Players choose a dinosaur-like beast or an ogre and tear across a lost island, destroying buildings, fighting hostile creatures, eating food and inhabitants to restore health, and searching for hidden Roc eggs. Each discovery leads to a one-on-one confrontation with the rival monster. The ultimate prize, claimed after the repeated battles, is the Golden Dragon's Egg at the island's volcano.

Its static, pseudo-isometric town scenes and destructible structures recall Rampage, but Aaargh! adds a hunt for concealed objectives and direct monster-versus-monster combat. It was one of Arcadia's earliest releases and an example of the company's unusual practice of bringing Amiga-class computer technology into coin-operated cabinets. Unlike typical Super Select cartridges, its arcade board had its own special connection arrangement.

games.title: Arcadia System BIOS
games.description:
The Arcadia System BIOS is the operating firmware for Arcadia Systems' Amiga-based coin-operated platform, introduced in the late 1980s. Its main board was derived from the Commodore Amiga 500, using a Motorola 68000 and the Amiga's custom graphics and audio hardware. Arcade-specific interfaces added coin handling, cabinet controls, and interchangeable ROM modules to what was otherwise recognizably home-computer technology.

Arcadia offered OnePlay and TenPlay control configurations. The former operated with a single installed software module; the latter could manage up to ten modules in one cabinet. Their Global Control Program provided an operator menu for coinage, difficulty, bookkeeping, and diagnostics, alongside the underlying Amiga Kickstart firmware. The BIOS set preserves this unusual meeting of microcomputer architecture and commercial arcade management.

games.title: Blastaball
games.description: Blastaball is a futuristic one-on-one sport game released on Arcadia Systems' Amiga-based arcade platform in 1988. Each player pilots a small spaceship around a scrolling rectangular arena and tries to drive a ball into the opponent's goal. Hitting the central goal is worth more than crossing other parts of the end line, so positioning matters as much as speed. The ball can be knocked by direct contact or pushed with a ship's weapon fire. A radar display keeps the two craft and ball visible even when they are beyond the current screen. Selectable ships differ in handling and firing characteristics, giving this odd mixture of space combat and ball sport a competitive edge.

games.title: SportTime Bowling
games.description: SportTime Bowling is a 1988 bowling simulation from Arcadia Systems, built for the company's arcade platform derived from Commodore Amiga hardware. One or two players take turns on a video bowling lane, competing to knock down pins and build a high score through successive frames. It belongs to the SportTime-branded series of familiar indoor sports brought to Arcadia's Super Select cabinets. The game illustrates the system's home-computer roots, offering a conventional bowling contest rather than a mechanical pin-setting machine.

games.title: World Darts
games.description: World Darts brings the classic pub game to Arcadia Systems' Amiga-based arcade platform. Players begin at 501 points and attempt to reach exactly zero, with a double required to finish. Accurate aiming at treble segments can produce the coveted 180-point turn, while mistakes can leave an awkward checkout. Released for Arcadia cabinets in the late 1980s, the game draws on the British computer-game tradition of titles such as 180! rather than on elaborate arcade action. Its competitive appeal comes from precise dart placement and the arithmetic of setting up a finishing double.

games.title: Delta Command
games.description: Delta Command is a scrolling military action shooter released for Arcadia Systems' Amiga-derived arcade platform in 1988. Seen from above, its on-foot combat follows the tradition of Ikari Warriors: the player moves through hostile territory, firing at enemy troops and surviving an advancing battlefield. The title was also associated with the computer game N.Y. Warriors, reflecting Arcadia's close relationship with contemporary home-computer software. Its comparatively conventional run-and-gun design contrasts with the stranger sports and experimental games in the Super Select library.

games.title: Magic Johnson's Fast Break
games.description:
Magic Johnson's Fast Break is a two-on-two basketball game associated with the NBA star and released on Arcadia Systems' arcade hardware in 1988. The full court scrolls horizontally as players dribble, pass, defend, and attempt baskets, with a referee able to call fouls. Matches use four timed quarters and five selectable skill levels, from Rookie to Professional, with increasingly aggressive opposition.

Instead of following a league season, the game frames progress as a climb through higher-paying contests: winning increases the team's earnings and can earn a place on the Big Earners leaderboard. Its arcade release is part of an unusual history in which an Amiga-era licensed basketball game was adapted to Arcadia's coin-operated computer-based platform.

games.title: Leader Board
games.description: Leader Board is a golf simulation brought to Arcadia Systems' Amiga-derived arcade platform in 1988. Players aim shots around a succession of holes, selecting direction and power while accounting for the course layout rather than competing in reflex-heavy sports action. Derived from Access Software's influential Leader Board computer-golf games, it reflects an era when home-computer sports simulations could be packaged for coin-operated amusement centers. Its focus on the mechanics of striking and placing the ball makes it a quieter counterpart to the fighting and shooting games normally associated with late-1980s arcades.

games.title: Ninja Mission
games.description: Ninja Mission is a side-scrolling martial-arts action game released through Arcadia Systems in 1987, adapted from the Amiga version of Mastertronic's Ninja. The player guides a lone ninja through a series of confrontations, battling armed enemies with close-range attacks and throwable weapons such as daggers and shuriken. Idol objects scattered through the stages restore strength and add to the score; collecting them is central to completing the mission. Its simple sequence of fights and pickups is a representative example of Arcadia's strategy of converting home-computer action titles into arcade offerings.

games.title: Pharaohs Match
games.description: Pharaohs Match is a tile-matching puzzle game from Arcadia Systems' 1988 Super Select lineup. Its rules follow the mahjong-solitaire tradition: players find matching pairs of exposed tiles and remove them from a layered arrangement, uncovering more possibilities as they work toward clearing the board. Only tiles not blocked from above and with an accessible side can be selected, so careless choices can leave a layout unsolvable. The Egyptian-themed title belongs to Arcadia's group of computer-derived puzzle and tabletop games, offering methodical play alongside the system's faster action titles.

games.title: RoadWars
games.description:
RoadWars is a futuristic vehicular combat game published for Arcadia Systems' arcade platform in 1988. One or two players control armed battle spheres hurtling along a seemingly endless elevated roadway, shooting obstacles and navigating spikes, barriers, and missing sections of track. A separate aiming direction allows weapons to target hazards without simply following the craft's movement.

The rival sphere can be an ally or another danger, especially when a player shoots away sections of roadside barrier and attempts to push an opponent through the opening. Its scrolling road effect and competitive interference make RoadWars a peculiar hybrid of driving, shooting, and arena combat, adapted from the same computer-game world that supplied much of Arcadia's library.

games.title: Sidewinder
games.description: Sidewinder is a vertically scrolling space shooter developed by Synergistic Software and issued on Arcadia Systems' Amiga-derived arcade hardware in 1988. Players pilot a small spacecraft upward through enemy territory, blasting hostile fighters and stationary defenses while maneuvering around incoming fire and scenery. Its straightforward overhead shooting action is reminiscent of contemporary home-computer shoot-'em-ups, unsurprising given the close connection between Arcadia's Super Select system and Commodore Amiga technology. The game is a compact example of the company's approach to putting computer-style arcade action into a coin-operated format.

games.title: World Trophy Soccer
games.description: World Trophy Soccer is a soccer simulation released for Arcadia Systems' arcade platform in 1989, adapted from Rick Davis' World Trophy Soccer for the Amiga. Players can arrange international friendly matches or a tournament, choosing match duration and difficulty. Normal play uses a side-on scrolling view, but the perspective changes as attacks approach the goal. Controlling passing, dribbling, and set pieces is more important here than spectacular special moves. Its tournament options were especially ambitious for a computer-derived soccer game, though the arcade configuration's available multiplayer arrangements depend on the installed setup.

games.title: Spot
games.description:
Spot is an abstract board-game adaptation featuring the red dot mascot of 7UP, produced for Arcadia's Amiga-derived arcade system around 1990. On a square grid, players try to finish with more pieces than their opponent. Moving a piece to an adjacent empty square duplicates it; jumping two spaces moves it without creating a copy. After either move, neighboring enemy pieces change to the moving player's color, allowing the balance of the board to swing dramatically in a single turn.

The simple rules reward careful control of space, especially around blocked squares and crowded corners. Spot is related to the game family later widely known through Ataxx, but its licensed character and uncommon Arcadia arcade format give it a distinct identity. The arcade version is notably rare, with sources uncertain whether it received a full commercial release.

games.title: Space Ranger
games.description: Space Ranger, also known as TASAR: Terran Armed Search and Rescue, is a horizontally scrolling science-fiction shooter brought to Arcadia Systems' arcade platform in the late 1980s. Rather than piloting a spaceship, the player controls a space-suited rescuer who can hover above the surface, shoot enemies, and protect vulnerable creatures from attackers. The action and long-range radar recall Williams' Defender, with threats appearing both in the air and on the ground. It is an unusual example of Arcadia repackaging the fast side-view rescue shooter for its Amiga-based coin-operated hardware.

games.title: Xenon
games.description:
Xenon is the Bitmap Brothers' 1988 vertical shooter, also offered on the Amiga-based Arcadia arcade system. The player fights alien Xenites threatening human colonies, but instead of using a single vehicle throughout, can switch between a flying spacecraft and a ground-based tank. The aerial form is suited to enemies and dangers above the terrain, while the tank can engage surface defenses and negotiate sections designed for land movement.

The transformation mechanic forces players to think about which form fits the immediate danger, giving an otherwise conventional scrolling shooter a distinctive tactical rhythm. Xenon was the Bitmap Brothers' debut and helped establish the British studio's reputation for stylish, technically polished action games; the Arcadia version is a rare instance of that computer-game lineage appearing in arcades.

games.title: Arabian Fight
games.description:
Arabian Fight is Sega's lavish 1992 four-player fantasy beat-'em-up, built for the System 32 arcade hardware. Four warriors, Sinbat, Ramaya, Goldor, and Datta, battle across seven stages to rescue Princess Lurana from the villainous Sheikh Sazabiss. Players mix punches, kicks, throws, and magical special attacks against human soldiers and supernatural foes, collecting recovery items and other rewards along the way.

Its signature visual trick is unusually aggressive sprite scaling. Characters can shrink into the distant background or loom into the foreground, creating a dramatic impression of depth on what is fundamentally a two-dimensional brawler. This theatrical staging and the capacity for four-player cooperation distinguish Arabian Fight from Sega's more familiar Golden Axe series, even though both share a colorful fantasy setting and screen-clearing magic attacks.

games.title: Arabian
games.description:
Arabian is a 1983 storybook platform game developed by Sun Electronics and released by Atari in North America. The player becomes a young prince traveling through a fantastical Arabian Nights setting to rescue a captive princess. Scenes unfold as successive pages of an illustrated tale, taking the hero through sea voyages, caves, and magical landscapes. With an eight-way joystick and kick button, the prince can climb, crawl, jump, and knock away enemies while negotiating platforms and environmental hazards.

Collecting the letters of A-R-A-B-I-A-N earns points, and finding them in the correct order produces an additional reward. Its combination of acrobatic movement, short themed scenes, and a framing narrative is more elaborate than the single-screen platform games that preceded it. The animated-book presentation gives Arabian a recognizable style among the early 1980s wave of post-Donkey Kong platform adventures.

games.title: Arabian Magic
games.description:
Arabian Magic is Taito's 1992 four-player fantasy brawler inspired by tales of the Arabian Nights. An evil wizard has turned the king into a monkey, leaving Prince Lassid, Princess Lisa, Sinbad, and Afshael to recover the Jewel of Seven Colors. Each selectable hero fights with a distinctive weapon, ranging from swords and a mace to Lisa's magical veil, as the party advances through seven stages guarded by powerful bosses.

Players smash containers for treasure and health boosts, improve their combat capabilities, and summon a giant genie for a devastating attack. Defeated guardians can also become spirits that aid the heroes in later battles, making the growing collection of allies part of the game's appeal. With detailed animation, colorful stages, and cooperative play, Arabian Magic is one of Taito's more imaginative alternatives to the Golden Axe formula.

games.title: Arbalester
games.description:
Arbalester is a 1989 vertically scrolling shooter developed by SETA and distributed in different territories under licenses including Taito and Romstar. One or two pilots fly combat aircraft over enemy territory, shooting airborne threats and bombing ground emplacements before facing large stage bosses. Missions are linked by a map, and stages are framed by the aircraft taking off from and returning to base. The player must manage attacks on targets at different heights while weaving through incoming fire.

Its combination of air-to-air and air-to-ground combat reflects the influence of Xevious and later military shooters, while the mission structure and brisk scrolling give Arbalester its own character. The original Japanese title is often rendered Arbalester even where arcade lists use the shorter Arbalest-derived name.

games.title: Arcade Classics
games.description:
Arcade Classics is an unreleased Atari Games prototype intended to revisit the company's arcade heritage around its twentieth anniversary. This arcade project is not the later Sega Genesis compilation of the same name: it contains two modernized games, Super Centipede and Missile Command II, with enhanced graphics and audio and a design that allowed cooperative play. Super Centipede reimagines the familiar defense against advancing segmented creatures, while Missile Command II expands the original's missile-base defense with additional spaceborne threats.

Only a very small number of arcade prototype machines are known to have survived. Its preservation offers a glimpse of Atari experimenting with updating its earliest hits for contemporary coin-operated audiences, years before retro compilations and remakes became common commercial products.

games.title: Arch Rivals
games.description:
Arch Rivals, released by Bally Midway in 1989, is a two-on-two basketball game proudly advertised as 'A Basket Brawl'. Players choose cartoonish athletes and fictional teams, then take part in full-court contests built around shooting, passing, blocking, and stealing the ball. The central twist is that punching an opposing player is not merely allowed but an effective way of taking possession. A joystick and two action buttons turn conventional basketball into a brisk, unruly fight for space and possession.

A match consists of four timed quarters, with sudden-death overtime if the teams remain tied. Spectators occasionally interfere with the action, adding to the game's chaotic sense of humor. Arch Rivals is widely regarded as an important predecessor to Midway's NBA Jam, anticipating its emphasis on personality, simplified team play, and outrageous physical competition. Its deliberate disregard for basketball etiquette is exactly what makes it memorable.

games.title: Area 51
games.description:
Area 51 is Atari Games' hit mid-1990s light-gun shooter, developed by Mesa Logic and originally released in 1995. The player is part of a military response team sent into the secret Area 51 facility, where the alien Kronn and their infected, zombie-like troops have overrun the base. The mission leads through warehouses, tunnels, and laboratories, with enemies popping into live-action and computer-rendered scenery. Players shoot hostile targets, reload by firing offscreen, avoid hitting friendly soldiers, and discover concealed routes and bonuses.

The game was built on CoJag hardware adapted from Atari's Jaguar console and helped revive interest in fast, accessible light-gun attractions. Its mixture of digitized actors, grotesque alien enemies, government-conspiracy imagery, and hidden features made it a defining shooter of its period. Shooting three friendly soldiers in succession can reveal the secret Kronn Hunter mode, which temporarily changes the player's role in the invasion.

games.title: Area 51 / Maximum Force Duo v2.0
games.description:
Area 51 / Maximum Force Duo is Atari's 1998 arcade conversion kit combining two separate light-gun shooters on one cabinet. Players can choose Area 51, in which soldiers battle aliens and zombies inside a secret military complex, or Maximum Force, a counterterrorism shooter staged across hostage situations and enemy strongholds. Both use rapid target shooting, reloading between bursts, and hidden areas or bonus opportunities.

The Duo release adds new secret locations to both games and a single-credit Tournament mode for Maximum Force, so it is more than a simple menu joining two existing titles. The Area 51 portion was also adapted to the Maximum Force software framework, with the side effect that the original game's hidden Kronn Hunter sequence does not behave in quite the same way. It is a representative example of the cost-conscious upgrade kits that kept light-gun cabinets earning in the late 1990s.

games.title: Air Rescue
games.description:
Sega's Air Rescue (1992) reinvents the premise of Choplifter as a first-person helicopter action game for System 32 arcade hardware. Players fly into hostile territory, destroy tanks, troops, and other threats with cannon and missile fire, then locate landing zones where stranded soldiers can board. Each rescue flight must return survivors safely to base, balancing offensive firepower with the risks of hovering under attack and the helicopter's limited passenger capacity.

The arcade version uses large scaling sprites to represent movement through a three-dimensional landscape and allows the helicopter to climb, descend, turn, and fly in multiple directions. It should not be confused with the Sega Master System game of the same name, which uses a conventional side-scrolling viewpoint and differs substantially in design.

games.title: Argus
games.description:
Argus is a 1986 vertical shooter developed by NMK and released by Jaleco, in the tradition of Xevious but with several imaginative complications. The player pilots the Wol-Arg fighter, using separate attacks against enemies in the air and targets on the ground. The scenery scrolls continuously upward, but the ship remains near the center while the landscape shifts sideways as the player steers, even wrapping horizontally around the playfield. Aerial obstacles, enemy formations, pickups, and bosses demand careful switching between the two attack types.

The later stages add unusual maze-like obstacles, giving the action an exploratory quality absent from many early scrolling shooters. This Argus has no relationship to Gottlieb's earlier unreleased superhero game of the same name, which is separately represented in arcade preservation collections.

games.title: Argus
games.description:
Argus is an unreleased Gottlieb superhero arcade prototype developed in the early 1980s, entirely unrelated to Jaleco's later shooter called Argus. Using a trackball and two buttons, the player guides a caped defender across a city, firing energy bolts at criminals and hazards while catching falling civilians and vehicles. Rubble from damaged buildings also threatens people below. The game continues only while citizens remain alive, so saving bystanders is as important as defeating attackers.

Designed and programmed by Tom Malinowski with contributions from Warren Davis, the project passed through working names including VideoMan, Protector, and Guardian before becoming Argus. Its creators considered a Superman license, but the game failed location and focus tests. Surviving accounts describe how attempts to replace the trackball with a joystick did not resolve its control problems. The prototype is a fascinating record of arcade designers experimenting with a more elaborate, destructible superhero world.

games.title: Arkanoid
games.description:
Taito's Arkanoid (1986) is one of arcade gaming's most influential block breakers, reviving the basic premise of Atari's Breakout with a science-fiction setting and a wealth of new mechanics. Players rotate a dedicated dial to move the small spacecraft Vaus along the bottom of the screen, bouncing a ball upward to destroy formations of bricks. Missing the ball costs a life, while tougher bricks, moving enemies, and intricate arrangements turn each round into a test of angles and control. The journey culminates in a confrontation with the mysterious alien DOH.

Colored capsules released from destroyed blocks transform the paddle or ball: they can extend the Vaus, catch the ball, split it into multiple balls, or equip twin lasers, among other effects. These bonuses introduce a tactical choice between immediate safety and greater destructive power.

Arkanoid was a major commercial success and established a template imitated by countless later puzzle-action games. Its responsive spinner control, distinctive sound effects, escalating level designs, and iconic power-up letters made a decades-old concept feel new, and the game spawned a long series of sequels and variations.

games.title: Ark Area
games.description: Ark Area is a 1988 overhead multidirectional shooter from UPL. The player pilots a futuristic craft through 23 increasingly dangerous stages, shooting enemies that arrive from many directions, collecting power-ups, and confronting one or more large bosses. Unlike an ordinary upward-only shooter, the craft can attack around the playfield, turning each encounter into a question of positioning as well as rapid fire. The game's stylized graphics, unconventional effects, and demanding one-life challenge reflect UPL's distinctive arcade design sensibility.

games.title: Arkanoid - Revenge of DOH
games.description:
Arkanoid: Revenge of DOH is Taito's 1987 sequel to its enormously successful block-breaking game. The player again steers the Vaus with a rotary dial, reflects a ball into walls of bricks, and catches power-up capsules that alter the craft's defenses and weapons. New brick patterns, enemy obstacles, and bonus effects give the basic loop more variety while retaining the precision and momentum of the original.

The sequel's key addition is a branching stage structure. After clearing a round, the player can choose between warp gates leading to different layouts, so a complete playthrough visits only part of the full stage set. This introduces route planning and replay value to a genre normally built around a strictly linear sequence of boards. Revenge of DOH is therefore a substantial redesign rather than a cosmetic update, and remains a favorite among Arkanoid players who enjoy its denser challenges and alternative paths.

games.title: Arkanoid Returns
games.description:
Arkanoid Returns is Taito's 1997 return to its celebrated brick-breaking series, produced for the F3 arcade platform. The player controls the familiar Vaus paddle, bouncing a ball into intricate walls of blocks while avoiding screen hazards and collecting capsules that modify the action. It retains established abilities such as catching or multiplying balls and adds the Giga Ball, which can tear through large sections of a formation.

The arcade campaign contains 50 stages, with changing visual themes and occasional layouts recalling previous installments. Its polished 1990s presentation and support for two players make it a late arcade revival of the spinner-controlled design that Arkanoid popularized in 1986.

games.title: Arlington Horse Racing
games.description: Arlington Horse Racing is an early-1990s coin-operated horse-race wagering game from Strata and Incredible Technologies, themed around the Arlington Park racecourse. Rather than controlling a jockey, players deposit credits, choose horses, and place win, place, or show bets before watching a simulated race unfold. Successful wagers return credit payouts that can be used on later races. Its appeal lies in predicting the result and managing bets, not in reflex-based racing controls, making it an example of arcade-video betting amusement rather than a traditional driving or sports-action game.

games.title: Arm Champs II
games.description:
Arm Champs II is Jaleco's 1992 arcade arm-wrestling attraction, notable for incorporating a physical robotic arm into the cabinet. Players grip the arm and attempt to pin a succession of increasingly difficult opponents, while the machine supplies resistance to create the sensation of an actual contest. The video display adds personality and match information, with a roster of twelve challengers that includes wrestlers identified as Trixie, Turk, Duke, and Goliath.

Unlike conventional joystick sports games, Arm Champs II is inseparable from its dedicated force-resisting hardware. This unusual hybrid of physical exertion and video-game progression made it a distinctive amusement-floor attraction and a successor to Jaleco's earlier Arm Champs.

games.title: Armed Formation
games.description:
Armed Formation is a 1988 vertically scrolling space shooter developed by Nichibutsu. The player pilots the Vowger, battling hostile formations and stage bosses while collecting power-ups that improve its firepower. Its central mechanic is the ability to change the arrangement and direction of supporting weapon units, allowing the ship to emphasize forward attacks, wider coverage, or protection against threats arriving from the sides.

This flexible formation system turns the usual shoot-and-dodge rhythm into a continual choice about where firepower is most useful. It belongs to the late-1980s wave of Japanese shooters exploring detachable and repositionable weapon systems, and should not be confused with SNK's similarly named ASO: Armored Scrum Object.

games.title: Armor Attack
games.description:
Armor Attack is Cinematronics' 1980 monochrome vector shooter, set in a city depicted with crisp outlines and enhanced in original cabinets by a colored screen overlay. One or two players drive small jeeps through a maze of streets, using rotation, thrust, and a forward-firing rocket launcher to destroy enemy tanks and helicopters. Each vehicle type requires different tactics: tanks follow the city streets while helicopters can cross the map more freely, forcing players to keep moving rather than hiding behind buildings.

The playfield's urban layout gives the game an unusually strong sense of place for an early vector title. Armor Attack is a notable example of how the vector era could create a tactical, maze-like combat game with only a handful of moving objects and carefully designed vehicle controls.

games.title: Armored Car
games.description:
Armored Car is Stern's 1981 scrolling maze game about moving cash safely through a city. Viewed from overhead, the player steers an armored money van along streets that scroll across the screen, collects cash, and delivers it to banks. Certain intersections enforce one-way travel, complicating route planning, while pursuing criminals can be slowed by dropping sawhorse roadblocks. Fuel is limited and must be replenished at service stations.

Rather than racing toward a finish line, Armored Car combines route selection, evasion, and delivery tasks in a compact urban maze. Its unusual banking premise distinguishes it from the many space-invasion and vehicle-combat games of the period.

games.title: Armored Warriors

variants.title: Powered Gear: Strategic Variant Armor Equipment (Japan 941024)
Powered Gear: Strategic Variant Armor Equipment (Japan 940916)

games.description:
Capcom's Armored Warriors (1994), released in Japan as Powered Gear: Strategic Variant Armor Equipment, is a CPS-2 side-scrolling beat-'em-up built around giant combat robots. Up to three players choose from four pilots and mechs, then tear through enemy forces on a distant world during a military conflict. The action is familiar belt-scrolling brawling, but the machinery changes dramatically as battles progress.

Defeated enemies drop interchangeable arms, legs, and weapons, allowing players to refit their robots in the middle of combat. A heavy drill, long-range gun, or alternative mobility unit can transform how a character fights, making scavenging almost as important as attacking. Cooperative combination maneuvers add another dimension to the multiplayer spectacle.

The game is closely linked to Capcom's later fighting game Cyberbots, which reuses its mecha designs in one-on-one combat. Armored Warriors remains one of the most inventive examples of the studio's 1990s arcade beat-'em-up craftsmanship.

games.title: Arm Wrestling
games.description:
Nintendo's Arm Wrestling (1985) is a cartoon sports game built on the hardware and visual language of the Punch-Out!! arcade series. The player takes on an escalating succession of eccentric opponents, including Texas Mac, Kabuki, the masked Mask X, and the formidable Frank Jr. Matches depend on timing, using the joystick and action button to resist an opponent's push, exploit openings, and force their arm down before time runs out.

The colorful characters, exaggerated reactions, and dual-screen cabinet presentation make a simple strength contest feel like a staged comic sporting event. Mask X even turns out to be Bald Bull from Punch-Out!!, tying the game directly to Nintendo's boxing hit. Arm Wrestling was the last arcade game developed independently by Nintendo before its focus shifted decisively toward home consoles.

games.title: Ashura Blaster
games.description: Ashura Blaster is a 1990 vertically scrolling helicopter shooter developed by Visco and published by Taito. Players pilot a military attack helicopter through waves of hostile aircraft and ground emplacements, collecting upgrades and destroying large bosses at the ends of stages. Before launching, the player can select from four bomb configurations, making the choice of screen-clearing weapon part of the strategy. Its dense military formations and fast action resemble Toaplan's Twin Cobra, but the selectable bomb loadout lends Ashura Blaster a modest tactical difference from its better-known inspirations.

games.title: ASO - Armored Scrum Object
games.description:
ASO: Armored Scrum Object, known internationally as Alpha Mission, is SNK's 1985 science-fiction vertical shooter. The player defends space installations against invading forces, destroying airborne enemies with forward-firing weapons and attacking ground emplacements with a separate missile system. Each stage builds toward a boss encounter, while collected upgrades expand the craft's offensive options.

Its divided air-to-air and air-to-ground attacks follow the example of Xevious, but ASO builds on that formula with a distinctive selection of armor and equipment upgrades. The title became an early part of SNK's arcade-shooter identity and later received a sequel, Alpha Mission II, for the Neo Geo.

games.title: Assault
games.description:
Assault is Namco's 1988 science-fiction tank shooter, distributed in North America by Atari Games. The player drives a heavily armed tracked vehicle across hostile, scrolling landscapes, destroying enemy installations and surviving eleven stages. Its signature dual-joystick controls are modeled on tank treads: pushing both sticks forward moves ahead, pulling them back reverses, and moving the sticks in opposite directions rotates the vehicle. The control scheme makes maneuvering part of the challenge, particularly when enemy fire arrives from several directions.

Assault combines an overhead view with Namco's sophisticated sprite rotation and scaling, letting the playfield twist and zoom dramatically during jumps and transitions. The tank can perform unusual maneuvers, including rolling for evasive movement and launching elevated attacks. Its audiovisual effects and complex controls made it a technically striking late-1980s shooter that feels very different from a conventional vertically scrolling aircraft game.

games.title: Asteroids Deluxe
games.description:
Asteroids Deluxe is Atari's 1981 follow-up to its groundbreaking vector shooter, designed to challenge players who had already mastered the original. A triangular spacecraft drifts through a wraparound asteroid field, rotating, thrusting, and shooting rocks that fragment into smaller, faster targets. Flying saucers still harass the player, but the sequel adds dangerous clusters of small ships known as Killer Satellites, whose pieces become threats of their own.

The original game's unpredictable hyperspace jump is replaced by a limited protective shield, shifting survival toward more deliberate defensive play. The game also uses a reflected vector display and a detailed space backdrop to give the monochrome lines a distinctive layered appearance.

Asteroids Deluxe preserves the precise, momentum-driven controls of Asteroids while altering enemy behavior and difficulty. Its innovations made it a worthy sequel rather than a straightforward reissue, and its vector graphics remain a memorable example of Atari's early-1980s arcade hardware artistry.

games.title: Asterix
games.description:
Konami's Asterix (1992) is a colorful two-player beat-'em-up based on the famous French comic books by René Goscinny and Albert Uderzo. Players choose the quick, compact Asterix or his towering companion Obelix and battle Roman legionaries across villages, camps, and other comic-inspired settings. The two heroes can punch, kick, grab and throw enemies, leap into the air, and deliver powerful dashing or spinning attacks.

The game stands out for its exceptionally faithful cartoon presentation. Roman soldiers react with exaggerated expressions and comic-book slapstick, while familiar characters, scenes, and jokes give the action the tone of the original stories. Although it shares the side-scrolling format of Konami's other arcade brawlers, Asterix has a particularly playful identity built around humor and animation rather than grim combat.

games.title: Asteroids
games.description:
Asteroids, created by Atari and released in 1979, is one of the foundational arcade games of the golden age. The player pilots a small triangular spaceship in a black vector-drawn field filled with drifting asteroids. Turning, thrusting, and firing follow the ship's direction, while inertia means a careless burst of acceleration can leave the craft sliding into danger. Shooting a large asteroid splits it into smaller rocks, so clearing the screen temporarily increases the number of threats. Enemy flying saucers intermittently appear and fire at the player.

The ship can cross one screen edge and reappear on the opposite side; a hyperspace button offers a risky emergency escape to an unpredictable location. Learning to control momentum, create safe routes through the rocks, and survive the increasingly accurate saucers is the essence of high-level play.

Designed by Lyle Rains and programmed by Ed Logg, Asteroids was an enormous commercial success and one of Atari's signature games. Its stark glowing vectors, resonant sound effects, and instantly understandable play made it a cultural landmark and inspired decades of multidirectional space shooters.

games.title: Astro Invader
games.description:
Astro Invader is a 1980 fixed-screen space shooter from Konami, published in some markets by Stern. The player moves a gunship left and right along the bottom and fires upward at alien craft descending from overhead. Rather than advancing in a simple marching formation, enemies are deposited into vertical storage columns; as a column fills, aliens drop out toward the player's position. Flying saucers can also swoop down, forcing rapid reactions.

The player can only have a single shot traveling at a time, so accurate timing is crucial. The unusual column-based enemy release system gives Astro Invader a different rhythm from Space Invaders, even though it shares the same basic left-right-and-fire controls.

games.title: Alien Storm

variants.title: Alien Storm (set 4, World, 2 Players, FD1094 317-0154)
differences: Hardware configuration: set 4, World, 2 Players, FD1094 317-0154.

variants.title: Alien Storm (set 3, World, 3 Players, FD1094 317-0148)
differences: Hardware configuration: set 3, World, 3 Players, FD1094 317-0148.

variants.title: Alien Storm (set 1, Japan, 2 Players, FD1094 317-0146)
differences: Hardware configuration: set 1, Japan, 2 Players, FD1094 317-0146.

variants.title: Alien Storm (set 2, US, 3 Players, FD1094 317-0147)
differences: Hardware configuration: set 2, US, 3 Players, FD1094 317-0147.

games.description:
Alien Storm is Sega's 1990 science-fiction beat-'em-up, combining the side-scrolling brawling of Golden Axe with shooting-gallery sequences and other short action diversions. Players select one of three Alien Busters: Gordon, Karla, or the robot Scooter. Each has a different energy weapon and special attack, used to drive back grotesque aliens disguising themselves as ordinary objects and people during an invasion of Earth. The arcade edition allows up to three players to fight together.

The action repeatedly changes pace. Standard street-fighting sections give way to first-person shooting sequences in which the player blasts enemies inside buildings, as well as fast-running segments demanding precise movement and attacks. Energy management and collecting restorative items add further pressure. The humorous monster designs and genre-switching structure make Alien Storm one of Sega's more varied and distinctive early-1990s arcade action games.

games.title: Astra SuperStars
games.description:
Astra SuperStars is a 1998 anime-styled fighting game developed by Sunsoft and released on Sega's ST-V arcade hardware. Instead of standing on a ground plane, its combatants hover and fly through an open arena, using aerial movement, normal attacks, and flashy magical special moves. The colorful cast battles for supremacy in a fantasy kingdom and ultimately confronts the villain Satan Volte.

The unusual airborne combat system distinguishes Astra SuperStars from conventional one-on-one fighters, encouraging movement throughout the screen rather than simple jumps over grounded opponents. In story mode, pre-fight dialogue choices can alter an opponent's behavior or difficulty, adding a playful narrative twist. Its extravagant animation and connection to Sunsoft's Waku Waku 7 place it among the more eccentric Japanese fighting games of the late 1990s.

games.title: Astro Blaster
games.description:
Astro Blaster is a 1981 space shooter produced by Sega/Gremlin, distinguished by spoken mission-control announcements and an unusually demanding pair of resource gauges. Players move a spacecraft left and right, firing at successive waves of enemies while monitoring laser temperature and remaining fuel. Rapid firing overheats the weapon and temporarily disables it; running out of fuel ends the game even if reserve ships remain. Successful pilots reach a mother ship and dock to refuel before continuing.

A limited-use time-warp function slows enemy movement and incoming shots without reducing the player's speed, creating opportunities to escape seemingly impossible attacks. Secret bonuses reward particular patterns of skillful play. With its computerized voice, fuel-management pressure, and strategic emergency system, Astro Blaster expanded the straightforward wave shooter into a more layered arcade challenge.

games.title: Astro Fighter
games.description:
Astro Fighter is Data East's 1979 space shooter, released during the first wave of games inspired by Space Invaders. The player steers a small fighter horizontally across the bottom of the screen and shoots down four successive formations of descending enemy craft, dodging bombs and projectiles. Fuel is constantly consumed, so missed shots and slow clearing make survival more difficult. After defeating the waves, the player can shoot a special GS ship to refuel before the cycle begins again at a higher difficulty.

The changing formations and refueling interval give Astro Fighter a brisk rhythm distinct from the static enemy march of Space Invaders. It is historically notable as one of Data East's earliest arcade releases, preceding the company's much broader catalog of shooters and action games in the 1980s.

games.title: Astropal
games.description: Astropal is an uncommon early-1980s Italian variant of Atari's Asteroids, produced by Sidam. It retains the core vector-space-shooter formula: rotate and thrust a small ship, fire at drifting rocks that break into smaller hazards, and survive as long as possible in a wraparound playfield. Contemporary arcade references identify it as an Asteroids-derived bootleg or hack rather than an independent new design. Its interest lies chiefly in documenting the European market for unauthorized versions of successful American arcade machines.

games.title: The Astyanax
games.description:
The Astyanax, released by Jaleco in 1989 and known in Japan as The Lord of King, is a side-scrolling fantasy hack-and-slash platform game. Players guide the mighty warrior Roche through monster-filled lands, using a legendary axe to defeat mythological creatures and enormous bosses. Carefully timed leaps, close-range strikes, and the management of powerful attacks are central to surviving its demanding stages. The arcade game supports cooperative play and emphasizes large animated enemies and imposing scenery.

The Astyanax is often confused with the Nintendo Entertainment System game bearing the same name, but the home version tells a substantially different story and changes the design. The arcade original stands on its own as one of Jaleco's more visually elaborate late-1980s fantasy action games.

games.title: Asuka & Asuka
games.description:
Asuka & Asuka is a vertically scrolling shooter created by Visco and released by Taito, with a 1988 copyright and a Japanese arcade release in early 1989. Players pilot a time-traveling fighter developed to resist the Galaxy Highters, invaders who have attacked multiple periods of Earth's history. The aircraft moves through enemy formations and ground defenses, firing its weapons, gathering enhancements, and facing powerful foes as the scenery scrolls beneath it.

The time-displacement premise allows stages with contrasting environments, while the action follows the fast, precision-driven style of Japanese military shooters. Its title is sometimes listed simply as Asuka & Asuka despite the more elaborate story attached to the aircraft's name.

games.title: Asura Blade - Sword of Dynasty
games.description:
Asura Blade: Sword of Dynasty is a 1998 weapon-based fighting game developed by Fuuki. Set in a world mixing ruined technology and fantasy, it centers on a legendary sword coveted by powerful combatants and the warlord S. Geist. Players select from eight unusual fighters and face opponents in one-on-one matches, using a three-button control scheme to combine normal attacks, special techniques, and weapon-centered tactics.

Its detailed two-dimensional sprites and imaginative character designs evoke the late-1990s boom in anime-styled fighting games, while the mixture of swords, monsters, and futuristic elements gives it a less conventional setting than most martial-arts tournaments. The game later received a direct sequel, Asura Buster.

games.title: Asura Buster - Eternal Warriors
games.description:
Asura Buster: Eternal Warriors is Fuuki's 2000 sequel to Asura Blade: Sword of Dynasty. Set several years after the original's conflict, it returns to a post-apocalyptic fantasy world destabilized by a new catastrophe. Familiar warriors and new challengers compete in one-on-one battles using an accessible three-button control system, combining weapon strikes, special moves, and dramatic attacks.

Rather than changing genres, Asura Buster refines the predecessor's unusual blend of fantasy and science fiction, expanding the cast and the range of fighting techniques. Its Japanese-only arcade release makes it a relatively obscure late example of the dedicated two-dimensional fighting games that flourished before polygonal competitors became dominant.

games.title: Asylum
games.description:
Asylum is an unreleased 1991 overhead action-shooter prototype developed by Leland. The player selects one of three captives attempting to escape a sinister institution operated by the villain Mr. G: Rip fights with knives, Rak carries a gun, and Rol wields a chain mace. The characters navigate maze-like rooms, jump around hazards, and attack grotesque creatures encountered along the way.

The combination of selectable fighters with different weapons and creepy maze exploration suggests a hybrid of run-and-gun action and top-down adventure. Although never commercially released, its surviving prototype preserves an unusually eccentric example of Leland's arcade experimentation.

games.title: Atari Football
games.description:
Atari Football is a pioneering 1978 American-football arcade game in which the two teams appear as simple X and O symbols on a black-and-white, vertically scrolling field. Each player chooses offensive or defensive plays and then rapidly rolls a large trackball to move an active athlete. The speed and direction of the rolling ball affect the action directly, making quick hands as important as tactical choices.

The tabletop-style cabinet positioned two opponents facing one another, with a prominent trackball for each side. Atari Football became a major commercial success and helped popularize the trackball as an arcade control device. Its remarkably abstract graphics did little to diminish its appeal: the combination of recognizably strategic football and frantic physical input made it one of the outstanding coin-operated sports games of the late 1970s. A four-player successor followed in 1979.

games.title: Atari System 1 BIOS
games.description:
Atari System 1 BIOS is the firmware for Atari Games' modular arcade hardware launched in 1984. The platform paired a Motorola 68010 main processor with a 6502 sound processor and used interchangeable cartridge boards on a reusable motherboard. Its audio hardware could combine Yamaha YM2151 FM synthesis, Atari POKEY chips, and a Texas Instruments TMS5220 speech synthesizer, while the video system typically produced a 336-by-240-pixel image.

The hardware existed in both early TTL-heavy and later LSI implementations. The later design consolidated numerous logic chips into custom integrated circuits, reducing manufacturing complexity while retaining compatibility with the platform. AdvanceMAME's BIOS entry represents the common motherboard firmware rather than a playable cartridge, and its preserved variants document these different physical board revisions.

games.title: Ataxx
games.description:
Ataxx is a 1990 arcade adaptation of an abstract territory-control board game, released by Leland. Two players begin with pieces at opposite corners of a seven-by-seven grid and take turns expanding their presence. Moving a piece one square creates an additional piece; jumping it two squares relocates the original. After either move, all opposing pieces immediately adjacent to the destination are converted to the moving player's color. The winner is the player controlling the most squares when play ends.

Despite its compact rules, Ataxx rewards positional planning and carefully timed reversals, since a single move can convert an entire cluster of enemy pieces. The arcade presentation adds colorful animated opponents and a trackball interface to the abstract contest. Its underlying rules became widely known through home-computer adaptations and similar games such as Spot.

games.title: Athena no Hatena ?
games.description:
Athena no Hatena? is a Japanese quiz adventure released by Athena in October 1993. Rather than presenting trivia as a succession of isolated questions, it combines a colourful fantasy board game with quiz-based encounters. One or two players choose among five stages and travel along board-game paths made up of event spaces, selecting numbered, colour-coded cards to determine how far they move. Some spaces offer treasure or useful cards, while others introduce characters who must be challenged before the journey can continue.

Encounters are decided by answering questions from a range of subjects, each with four possible responses. A correct answer damages the opponent, and successive answers are needed to defeat tougher characters. The player must also answer promptly: a row of flame icons counts down the available time, and quick responses earn more points. Wrong or unanswered questions cost a life, giving this unusual combination of board-game planning and Japanese-language trivia a distinct rhythm compared with more conventional arcade quiz titles.

games.title: Tetris
games.description:
Atari Games' Tetris, introduced to arcades in the late 1980s, adapts Alexey Pajitnov's Soviet falling-block puzzle into a fast, colorful coin-operated competition. Tetrominoes made of four squares descend into a tall well; players move and rotate them to complete horizontal lines, which vanish and award points. As the stack grows and pieces fall faster, each decision becomes a race to maintain space and recover from mistakes. The arcade game includes simultaneous two-player play and adjustable starting difficulty.

Atari's version was part of the complicated early history of international Tetris licensing, a dispute that also affected the company's planned home-console release. Although many other editions became famous on computers and handhelds, the arcade version remains notable for bringing the simple, endlessly replayable puzzle to dedicated video-game cabinets during Tetris's explosive rise in popularity.

games.title: Athena
games.description:
Athena is SNK's 1986 fantasy platform game starring a headstrong princess who leaves her sheltered kingdom in search of adventure. After entering a forbidden doorway, she finds herself in a hostile fantasy world filled with monstrous enemies and dangerous terrain. Initially armed with only kicks, Athena can seize weapons, shields, helmets, and armor from defeated enemies, gradually turning from a vulnerable wanderer into a well-equipped fighter. Powerful enemies and elaborate platforms guard the passage between its eight themed worlds.

Collected equipment can break or be lost when Athena takes damage, so adapting to what the current area offers is part of survival. The game's striking heroine, varied enemy designs, and unusually broad array of gear distinguished it from simpler platform action games. Athena later became an important character in SNK's fictional universe, especially through the Psycho Soldier and King of Fighters connections, although those games use different versions of the character.

games.title: Battle of Atlantis
games.description: Battle of Atlantis is an early-1980s underwater scrolling shooter derived from the Scramble formula. The player pilots a submarine through six hazardous sections, firing a forward laser and dropping torpedo-like bombs against ships, floating mines, sharks, and stationary defenses. The submarine must maneuver through changing obstacles while destroying targets and fuel tanks for points and bonuses. The unusual ocean setting and enemy designs distinguish this arcade variation from the rocket-and-cavern scenarios of its space-themed inspiration.

games.title: Atlus PSX
games.description:
Atlus PSX is the BIOS for Atlus's version of the Sony ZN-1 arcade motherboard, dating from the mid-1990s. ZN-1 technology was closely related to the original PlayStation, with a MIPS-based CPU, dedicated 3D graphics hardware, and Sony's sound-processing architecture adapted for commercial cabinets.

Atlus paired the Sony main board with its own ROM and audio circuitry. The documented configuration includes a Motorola 68000 support processor and Yamaha YMZ280B sample-based sound hardware, illustrating how different manufacturers could use the same graphics platform while designing their own peripheral electronics. The Atlus BIOS identifies and initializes that particular hardware arrangement; it is not a self-contained arcade title.

games.title: Atomic Point
games.description: Atomic Point is a 1990 falling-block puzzle game by Philko. Individual colored blocks descend onto a playfield containing fixed shapes and two illuminated diamond markers. The player's job is to arrange the falling pieces so that a complete horizontal row passes through the level of a highlighted diamond, clearing the row and bringing the target closer to completion. Its challenge is not simply to eliminate arbitrary lines as in Tetris, but to complete rows in strategically specified positions around the preexisting arrangement. The small-scale design reflects the wave of experimental puzzle games that followed Tetris's success.

games.title: Atari PSX
games.description:
Atari PSX is the historical AdvanceMAME name for the BIOS of Time Warner Interactive's Atari-branded Sony ZN-1 arcade hardware. Introduced in the mid-1990s, this platform used PlayStation-derived processing and graphics circuitry on a dedicated coin-operated motherboard, together with Atari's own auxiliary board and system firmware.

The preserved firmware belongs to the Time Warner ZN-1 configuration, later catalogued in MAME under the COH-1000W board identifier. Its supporting hardware used ROM storage and, in the documented arrangement, an IDE hard disk. The unusual naming reflects Atari's corporate ownership during this period and the wider adoption of PlayStation technology by independent arcade manufacturers.

games.title: Attack Ufo
games.description: Attack Ufo is a 1980 fixed-screen shooter produced by Ryoto Electric in Japan. It is an early Space Invaders-style derivative in which the player moves a gunship horizontally along the bottom of the display and shoots upward at descending alien formations. The familiar one-button attack and left-right movement establish it as part of the first boom in invasion shooters, rather than a substantially new action concept. Its main historical interest is as a comparatively obscure regional imitation of the blockbuster Taito formula.

games.title: Au
games.description:
Au is an unreleased 1983 Tehkan arcade shooter prototype prepared as a conversion kit for Swimmer hardware. Its name comes from the chemical symbol for gold. Played on a fixed screen, it asks the player to fire at airborne enemies, capture them, and use the captured targets to attack enemy bases below. Clearing a stage depends on destroying the bases, with the last surviving installation influencing the following round.

The capture-and-redirect mechanic gives Au a different objective from ordinary wave shooters. Because the kit was never commercially released, the preserved prototype is particularly interesting as evidence of Tehkan experimenting with alternative gameplay on existing arcade boards.

games.title: Aurail
games.description:
Aurail is Sega's 1990 mech-combat shooter, alternating between overhead battlefield action and a first-person view. Players pilot an armored machine against an army threatening a futuristic world, moving through hostile bases and defensive installations. In overhead stages, the mech travels across the scrolling terrain and fires in eight directions; holding the fire control can provide sustained attacks, but restricts movement. Gathered energy can be spent to create protective shields, forcing a trade-off between defense and other uses of the resource.

The perspective changes are the game's most distinctive feature. Overhead combat emphasizes positioning and projectile avoidance, while the first-person sequences suggest piloting a heavy machine directly through the enemy's territory. This mixture of viewpoints makes Aurail a curious entry in Sega's arcade-shooter catalog between conventional 2D action and the company's more elaborate cockpit games.

games.title: AV2Mahjong No.1 Bay Bridge no Seijo

variants.title: AV2Mahjong No.1 Bay Bridge no Seijo (Japan)

games.description: AV2 Mahjong No. 1: Bay Bridge no Seijo is a Japanese adult-themed mahjong arcade game released in 1991 by Nichibutsu and associated companies. It combines Japanese mahjong play with audiovisual reward sequences supplied through prerecorded video, a distinctive feature at a time when ordinary arcade boards could not easily reproduce lengthy full-motion footage. The dedicated mahjong controls and adult presentation place it in Japan's specialist video-mahjong market rather than among mainstream action games. Its significance lies as much in its video-playback apparatus as in its underlying tile game.

games.title: AV2Mahjong No.2 Rouge no Kaori
games.description: AV2 Mahjong No. 2: Rouge no Kaori is a 1991 Japanese adult video-mahjong game, following Bay Bridge no Seijo. Players engage in Japanese mahjong using a dedicated tile-control interface, while successful play leads to prerecorded video sequences used as the game's adult-themed rewards. The hybrid of mahjong and external video playback reflects the specialized multimedia hardware found in some Japanese amusement centers before full-motion video became routine in games. The surviving descriptions identify its format and presentation but do not establish any distinctive changes to conventional mahjong rules.

games.title: Avalanche
games.description:
Avalanche is a 1978 Atari reflex game in which rows of rocks drop from the top of the screen toward the ground. Players move a stack of horizontal paddles using a rotary control, catching falling rocks before they escape. At first the stack has six levels, but as the player clears successive waves, the top platforms disappear and the rocks become smaller and faster. With fewer opportunities to intercept each falling object, the challenge becomes increasingly severe.

The game predates Taito's Space Invaders boom and follows an inventive path away from the then-standard driving and paddle games. Its cascading rocks, shrinking safety net, and precise spinner control create a straightforward but demanding test of coordination. It is also an important early ancestor of the catch-and-deflect mechanics seen in later arcade puzzle-action games.

games.title: Avengers
games.description:
Avengers, known in Japan as Hissatsu Buraiken, is Capcom's 1987 overhead scrolling beat-'em-up. Players control martial artists Ryu and Ko as they fight through Paradise City to rescue six kidnapped women from the criminal mastermind Geshita. Unlike the side-on presentation that later became standard for the genre, combat is viewed from above, with foes attacking along the streets and through branching spaces. Punches, kicks, and special techniques are supplemented by collectible weapons and bonuses.

Power-ups include increased speed, stronger strikes, and weapons such as shuriken, nunchaku, and grenades, while hidden areas reward exploration. Directed by Takashi Nishiyama, who would go on to work on the original Street Fighter and several early SNK fighting titles, Avengers is an interesting transitional example of Capcom's approach to martial-arts arcade action before Final Fight.

games.title: Avengers In Galactic Storm
games.description:
Avengers in Galactic Storm is Data East's 1995-1996 Marvel Comics fighting game, inspired by the Galactic Storm storyline from the Avengers comics. Players select superheroes and villains for one-on-one matches, rendered with digitized-looking pre-rendered 3D character sprites on a two-dimensional fighting plane. Its space-themed cast and comic-book narrative give it a very different personality from the contemporary Marvel titles produced by Capcom.

The game's most distinctive mechanical feature is its roster of assist characters, which can be summoned briefly to interfere in a fight. This early use of helper attacks anticipated a technique that later became standard in team-based fighting games. The combination of elaborate character graphics and tactical support summons makes Avengers in Galactic Storm a notable, if comparatively obscure, experiment from the mid-1990s fighting-game boom.

games.title: Alien vs. Predator
games.description:
Capcom's Alien vs. Predator (1994) is a celebrated CPS-2 side-scrolling beat-'em-up that combines two science-fiction movie franchises into an original arcade action story. Up to three players choose from four fighters: the Predators Warrior and Hunter, cybernetically enhanced Major Dutch Schaefer, and Lieutenant Linn Kurosawa. Together they battle a city overrun by xenomorphs and uncover the forces responsible for the infestation. Although all four characters share basic movement and attacks, their weapons, reach, and special maneuvers are markedly different.

Three action buttons support melee strikes, jumps, and firearms, allowing players to juggle enemies, unleash powerful combinations, and control crowds with ranged weapons. Detailed animation, destructible foes, dramatic boss encounters, and a relentless pace make the combat unusually satisfying.

The game was never a conventional arcade-to-home port, helping its reputation grow among arcade enthusiasts. Its original characters and plot do not directly retell either film series, and its tight cooperative mechanics make it one of Capcom's most admired licensed beat-'em-ups.

games.title: Avenging Spirit
games.description:
Avenging Spirit is a 1991 Jaleco action-platformer, released in Japan as Phantasm, built around an unusually clever possession mechanic. Its hero is murdered while trying to protect his girlfriend, who is then kidnapped. Resurrected as a ghost by her father, he must infiltrate the criminals' hideout and rescue her. A disembodied spirit cannot fight directly for long, so the player enters the bodies of enemies encountered throughout the side-scrolling levels.

Different hosts possess different weapons, movements, and defensive abilities, from agile fighters to heavily armed opponents. The ghost has limited energy while outside a body, making the choice of when to abandon one host and possess another crucial to survival. This constant switching of abilities turns Avenging Spirit into a highly inventive variation on the run-and-gun platformer, and remains the feature for which the game is best remembered.

games.title: Aztarac
games.description:
Aztarac is a 1983 color-vector arcade shooter from Centuri, designed around defending a cluster of space outposts from attackers approaching across a wide scrolling battlefield. The player controls an armed tank whose body and turret can be operated independently, allowing it to drive one way while firing another. A separate scanner reveals enemies beyond the visible screen, so successful defense involves watching the broader situation as well as shooting immediate threats.

The game's specialized flight-style joystick and rotary turret control give it a distinctive physical feel, while the sharp vector lines convey large enemy formations without conventional bitmap graphics. Aztarac is a particularly rare example of a color-vector defense game and was one of the last vector-based releases associated with Centuri.

games.title: Azurian Attack
games.description: Azurian Attack is a 1982 fixed-screen space shooter in which the player's craft can move throughout the playfield and fire in the direction it faces. Enemy ships enter from the edges, circling and closing in as the player tries to pick them off without becoming trapped. Its eight-direction movement and relatively short-range attacks make the game less like a simple bottom-of-screen invader shooter and more like a compact single-screen arena battle. The game is an obscure early example of multidirectional space combat, with simple visuals and sound reminiscent of other arcade shooters of its era.

games.title: Bang Bang Busters
games.description:
Bang Bang Busters is a colorful Neo Geo action-platform game developed by Visco in the early 1990s but left without an ordinary commercial arcade launch. The player controls Lazy or Refia, space police officers who have been lured into a trap on the planet Palua. Across multiple compact stages, they defeat monsters by inflating or capturing them and throwing them into other enemies, setting off chain reactions in a style reminiscent of Snow Bros. and Bubble Bobble. The game supports two-player cooperation and culminates in boss encounters.

Its unusual release history is part of its appeal. Although the original MVS project dates to 1994, it survived chiefly as a rare prototype and eventually became available through later licensed Neo Geo editions. The playful enemy-throwing mechanic and bright sprite art make it an intriguing example of a finished-looking game that nearly disappeared from arcade history.

games.title: Backfire!
games.description: Backfire! is a 1995 rally-racing game from Data East, presented from an elevated, scrolling viewpoint. Players choose between two fictional cars, the Farco R4 Cup and Andula 2.0, and race over a sequence of six stages filled with turns and track hazards. Steering and speed control are central to reaching the finish ahead of the competition. The game also supports head-to-head play with the screen divided between two drivers. Its compact rally format and brightly rendered vehicles distinguish it from Data East's better-known action titles of the period.

games.title: Back Fire
games.description:
Back Fire is a Tecmo horizontal-scrolling shooter developed in the late 1980s but apparently given only a limited release, if any. The player's craft battles enemy formations through an 18-stage campaign, collecting upgrades that increase the speed and strength of the main gun or add alternate attacks such as lightning and three-way fire. The unusual continue rule sends players who lose late in the game back to stage 13, adding a punishing edge to the final stretch.

Back Fire has a close historical connection to Tecmo's better-known Silkworm: some of its background artwork was reused, and surviving accounts indicate that an unfavorable showing at a trade exhibition contributed to Tecmo changing direction toward Silkworm. This makes it an interesting preserved branch of the studio's arcade-shooter development.

games.title: Bad Dudes vs. Dragonninja
games.description:
Bad Dudes vs. Dragonninja is Data East's 1988 side-scrolling martial-arts game, famous for its outrageous premise: the DragonNinja clan has kidnapped President Ronnie, and two street fighters have been recruited to rescue him. One or two players control Blade and Striker across seven stages, punching and kicking their way through city streets, trucks, sewers, forests, and enemy hideouts. Foes attack from multiple heights, and defeated enemies sometimes drop knives, nunchaku, or restorative items.

Players can charge a powerful special strike by holding the attack button, while acrobatic jumps and double-deck stage layouts provide several ways to approach enemies. Each stage culminates in a memorable boss battle, including recurring clashes with the enemy's ninja leader.

Known in Japan as Dragonninja, the game became one of Data East's signature late-1980s arcade hits, helped by an exceptionally memorable opening challenge and a tongue-in-cheek portrayal of American action-movie heroism. Its camp humor and cooperative play remain central to its cult appeal.

games.title: Bad Lands
games.description:
Bad Lands is Atari Games' post-apocalyptic combat racer, released around the turn of 1990 as the final major arcade entry in the Sprint racing lineage. From a fixed overhead viewpoint, up to two players drive armed cars around compact circuits against rival vehicles. The goal remains to finish ahead of the opposition, but machine guns allow racers to disrupt each other rather than relying on steering alone. Collected wrenches can be exchanged between races for better speed, acceleration, tires, and other upgrades.

The wasteland scenery and aggressive driving contrast with the clean tracks of Super Sprint, while the familiar steering-wheel-and-pedal controls keep the racing immediately approachable. Bad Lands turns Atari's well-established single-screen racing formula into a rougher, weaponized contest suited to its late-1980s action aesthetic.

games.title: Bagman
games.description:
Bagman is a 1982 platform action game created by French developer Valadon Automation and published in arcades under various regional licenses. Players guide a thief through a multi-screen mine complex, collecting sacks of stolen gold and carrying them to a wheelbarrow at the surface. The job is complicated by roaming guards, moving mine carts, ladders, and elevators; getting caught or trapped wastes valuable time.

The hero can temporarily stun pursuers with a pickaxe, or drop heavy money bags onto guards below. Carrying treasure slows movement, so players must plan safe routes between underground pockets of loot and the exit. Its interconnected screens and focus on transporting objects, rather than merely collecting them, give Bagman a strategic dimension uncommon in early platformers. Its difficulty, memorable sound effects, and expressive little protagonist helped it earn a lasting cult following.

games.title: Bakatonosama Mahjong Manyuki
games.description: Bakatonosama Mahjong Manyuki is a 1991 Japanese Neo Geo mahjong game built around a comic feudal-lord character associated with Japanese television comedy. Players compete at mahjong in a lighthearted historical setting, with the game's humor and character presentation taking precedence over arcade-action spectacle. The original release supports the Neo Geo mahjong control panel, and its cartridge-based presentation makes it an unusual early entry in the MVS library. For collectors it is notable as a Japan-only, comedy-themed tabletop game on hardware internationally identified with fighting games.

games.title: Baku Baku Animal
