games.description:
Baku Baku Animal is Sega's 1995-1996 competitive falling-block puzzle game for the ST-V arcade system. Instead of removing rows, players arrange animal faces beside the foods they like: monkeys eat bananas, rabbits eat carrots, and other pairings work in the same way. Matching an animal with a connected group of its food makes the animal devour the pieces, possibly triggering further chain reactions as the remaining blocks fall.

The key to success is building large linked food groups and timing chain reactions to bury an opponent under extra pieces. Its simple, amusing visual metaphor makes the rules easy to grasp while allowing surprisingly sophisticated competitive play. The game's cartoon animals, expressive animations, and quick two-player matches made it one of Sega's most approachable puzzle titles of the mid-1990s.

games.title: Bakutotsu Kijuutei
games.description:
Bakutotsu Kijuutei is Namco's 1988 sequel to Baraduke, sometimes described as Baraduke II. Players control Takky and Hommy, suited explorers returning to battle the strange Octy creatures and rescue friendly one-eyed Paccets. Unlike the original, this is a more strictly directional scrolling shooter: the characters generally advance toward the right, and their weaponry and movement rules have been altered. New enemies and multiple types of capsules complicate the search-and-rescue action.

The game retains Baraduke's quirky biomechanical world and focus on saving Paccets, but changes its pacing and defensive system. A machine gun replaces the original shield-centered approach, and the revamped stage design makes it a distinct sequel rather than a mere expansion of the first game.

games.title: Bal Cube
games.description:
Bal Cube is a 1996 arcade block-clearing game from Metro that turns the Arkanoid concept inside out. Rather than moving a paddle to deflect a ball, the player directly influences the momentum of a rotating cube with the joystick. Different geometric blocks descend from the top of the screen and rebound the cube in different ways when struck. The objective is to clear the blocks before they reach the bottom, while preventing the cube from falling through the openings below.

Special blocks and power-ups alter the challenge, but the most important skill is judging how the cube will bounce after each contact. By transferring control from the paddle to the projectile, Bal Cube creates an unusually demanding variation on a familiar arcade formula.

games.title: Balloon Bomber
games.description:
Balloon Bomber is a 1980 fixed-screen shooter from Taito in which a small cannon moves left and right along the bottom of the playfield and fires at balloons carrying explosives. Enemy aircraft release the drifting balloon bombs from overhead, leaving players to shoot them before they descend. If a bomb reaches the ground, it creates a crater that permanently restricts the cannon's horizontal movement, making later waves harder to survive.

This persistent damage to the playfield is the game's defining idea. Unlike Space Invaders, where enemy shots mainly threaten the player's remaining lives, Balloon Bomber turns missed targets into obstacles that gradually remove escape routes. Its simple visuals hide a clever escalating risk, and it remains a distinctive curiosity from the first generation of Japanese fixed shooters.

games.title: Balloon Brothers
games.description: Balloon Brothers is a 1992 two-player puzzle game by East Technology, running on Taito X System hardware. Its twist on the familiar falling-block formula is that clusters of colored balloons rise from the bottom of the playfield instead of descending from above. Players arrange the differently shaped groups to complete horizontal rows, which then disappear and free space for more balloons. This inverted gravity gives an otherwise recognizable Tetris-style challenge a distinctive rhythm.

games.title: Vs. Balloon Fight
games.description:
Nintendo's Vs. Balloon Fight (1984), developed with HAL Laboratory, is an aerial combat platform game in which players steer balloon-equipped fighters through arenas populated by rivals. Flapping the character's arms provides lift, while horizontal movement carries momentum. The object is to swoop down on enemies from above, pop their balloons, then finish them off before they can inflate replacements. Losing one of your two balloons makes flying harder; losing both, falling into the water, or being struck by lightning can end a life.

Its height-based collisions recall Williams' Joust, but the buoyant movement, spinning bumpers, water-dwelling fish and intermittent lightning give the game its own personality. The Vs. System arcade edition preceded the better-known NES release and uses taller, vertically scrolling stage layouts on its dual-screen configuration. Unlike the NES game, it does not include the separate Balloon Trip endurance mode. Its combination of deceptively simple controls and chaotic multiplayer encounters helped make Balloon Fight an enduring Nintendo favorite.

games.title: Baluba-louk no Densetsu
games.description:
Baluba-louk no Densetsu (1986) is a Japanese platform action game by Able in which an explorer searches monster-filled rooms for treasure chests. Clearing a stage requires gathering every chest, but opening them first can change the rewards and provide tools for surviving the enemies. Striking platforms from below reveals coins or jewels, while strategically triggered bombs stun monsters and special traps fire across the screen to defeat them. Defeated enemies can leave behind unusual bonus items and warp opportunities.

The combination of collecting, platform jumping and trap manipulation makes this more intricate than a straightforward treasure hunt. It also has a small place in Japanese game history as the arcade predecessor to the related Aighina no Yogen: From the Legend of Balubalouk, released for home computers and the Famicom.

games.title: Mahjong Banana Dream
games.description: Mahjong Banana Dream is a 1989 Japanese medal-mahjong game by Digital Soft, played with a dedicated mahjong control panel. Players wager medals while competing in mahjong hands, with a suggestive reward presentation in which larger stakes are associated with progressively revealing illustrations. It belongs to the adult-oriented, wagering-based branch of Japanese arcade mahjong rather than the competitive action-game tradition.

games.title: Bandit
games.description:
Bandit is an unfinished 1989 vehicular-combat arcade prototype associated with Data East USA and Incredible Technologies. Players drive a sports car on a timed escape across the United States, starting in Los Angeles and aiming to reach New York while avoiding police pursuit and roadblocks. The game uses an unusual trackball-based control arrangement rather than a conventional racing wheel.

Its most memorable detail is a grim failure sequence: when time runs out, the pursuing police stop the getaway and the game depicts the fugitive's execution, followed by a warning that crime does not pay. The surviving prototype runs on hardware derived from Data East's Heavy Barrel board, making it a particularly curious example of an abandoned arcade project preserved through emulation.

games.title: Bang!
games.description:
Bang! is Gaelco's 1998 Wild West-themed light-gun game, released in Japan as Gun Gabacho. Rather than following a continuous shooting-gallery story, it strings together brief, cartoon-style challenges that test accuracy and reaction speed. Players may have to hit bandits appearing in a passing train, shoot objects tossed into the air, or carefully distinguish permitted targets from things that must be left alone.

Its structure closely resembles Namco's Point Blank: each round first explains a simple objective, then gives the player limited time and ammunition to complete it. Two players can compete for accuracy with physical light guns. The cheerful Western artwork and rapid shifts between shooting tasks distinguish Bang! from the darker rail shooters that dominated many late-1990s arcades.

games.title: Bang Bang Ball
games.description:
Bang Bang Ball (1996), published by Banpresto, is a colorful arcade puzzle-action game featuring mice on wheels trying to rescue a kidnapped companion from cats. Players move around a screen full of bouncing colored balls and throw balls toward others of the same color to remove them. Movement and timing matter as much as matching, because colliding with the roaming balls damages the characters.

The game reworks the earlier Mouse Shooter GoGo formula, replacing its instant-death collisions with a health gauge and introducing a cooperative two-player mode. Its related Korean release, Battle Bubble, retains the basic action but features different background graphics. The result sits somewhere between a bubble-matching puzzle and a hectic action game rather than a conventional falling-block puzzler.

games.title: Bang Bead
games.description:
Visco's Bang Bead is a fast-paced, two-player sports-action game for the Neo Geo MVS, following the cult favorite Battle Flip Shot. Its matches resemble an aggressive version of Pong: players dash across opposite sides of an enclosed court, deflect a speeding ball and attempt to drive it past their opponent. Each character has a standard return, a directional sliding dash and a character-specific special move powered by a meter.

The key change from Battle Flip Shot is that a goal is protected by a laser barrier until the attacking player has knocked out all the stars in front of it. Only then can a shot through the goal end the contest, leaving room for late comebacks. Its vivid characters and rapid exchanges make it one of the Neo Geo's more unusual competitive games.

games.title: Bank Panic
games.description:
Bank Panic (1984), developed by Sanritsu and published by Sega, is an ingenious Wild West shooting game about protecting a bank from outlaws without harming its customers. The player stands inside a circular bank with twelve numbered doors, only three of which can be viewed at once. A two-way joystick rotates between door groups, while three separate buttons fire at the left, middle and right doors. As doors open, the player must instantly distinguish robbers from depositors, allowing customers to leave money while stopping armed thieves before they shoot.

Clearing a stage requires securing a deposit at all twelve doors within the time limit. Robbers can steal deposited money, bombs must be defused by shooting them, and tied-up hostages must be freed with a precise shot. Even the timing of a fair gunfight matters: waiting for an outlaw to draw earns more points than firing before he is ready, but waiting too long is fatal. The numbered door indicators reward anticipation rather than indiscriminate shooting.

Distributed in North America by Bally Midway, Bank Panic remains notable for transforming a simple three-button shooting mechanic into a tense game of crowd recognition, timing and spatial awareness. Its distinctive circular-bank design has no need for a gun-shaped controller to create a convincing quick-draw challenge.

games.title: Baraduke
games.description:
Namco's Baraduke (1985), released in North America as Alien Sector, is a science-fiction run-and-gun game set in the alien-infested depths of Planet Paccet. Its space-suited protagonist, Kissy (or Takky for the second player), moves through interconnected, low-gravity rooms using a maneuverable jetpack-like suit and a wave gun. Every floor contains Octy enemies that must be destroyed to open the exit pipe, while capsules may yield upgraded weaponry, points or friendly one-eyed Paccets.

Those rescued Paccets affect the end-of-floor shield bonus and can help stun the enormous bosses. The journey spans eight worlds of six floors each, culminating in a battle with the Octy King. A single action button and directional movement support a surprisingly flexible blend of floating exploration and shooting, with the gun's recoil adding to the game's physical feel.

Baraduke stood out in Namco's mid-1980s catalogue for its eerie organic alien designs, moody atmosphere and distinctive armored heroine, whose identity is revealed more clearly at the end. It later received a sequel, Bakutotsu Kijutei, and became a recognizable cult entry in Namco's arcade history.

games.title: Bare Knuckle II

variants.title: Bare Knuckle II (scrambled bootleg of Mega Drive version)

games.description:
This Bare Knuckle II set is a scrambled Chinese arcade bootleg of Sega's Mega Drive beat 'em up Streets of Rage 2, catalogued as a 1994 coin-operated conversion. The underlying game follows Axel Stone, Blaze Fielding, Max Thunder and Skate Hunter through side-scrolling battles against Mr. X's criminal organization, combining punches, throws, improvised weapons and character-specific special attacks.

The arcade set is historically interesting because it adapts a console-exclusive style of play to unauthorized coin-op hardware, rather than representing a new Sega arcade release. The scrambled program and custom chips distinguish this bootleg implementation from other surviving Mega Drive-derived versions.

games.title: Bare Knuckle II

variants.title: Bare Knuckle II (bootleg of Mega Drive version)

games.description:
Bare Knuckle II in this set is an unauthorized arcade conversion of the Mega Drive's Streets of Rage 2, rather than a distinct official Sega sequel. Its four selectable fighters, Axel, Blaze, Max and Skate, battle through side-scrolling streets and hideouts, using throws, weapons, running attacks and powerful moves that can consume health.

This particular coin-operated bootleg is distinguished from the scrambled Chinese set by its own board and protection arrangements, including a PIC microcontroller documented in later emulation work. It preserves the home game's celebrated beat-'em-up action while showing how popular console titles were repackaged for arcades outside the original publisher's control.

games.title: Bare Knuckle III

variants.title: Bare Knuckle III (scrambled bootleg of Mega Drive version)
Bare Knuckle III (bootleg of Mega Drive version)

games.description:
Bare Knuckle III is a pirate coin-operated conversion of Sega's 1994 Mega Drive game Streets of Rage 3. Axel and Blaze return alongside Skate and the new robotic fighter Dr. Zan, fighting through a faster, more elaborate side-scrolling brawler with running attacks, weapon use and rechargeable special techniques. The Japanese Bare Knuckle III version is especially known for material and character details altered in the Western console release.

The AdvanceMAME set represents a scrambled bootleg of the Mega Drive program, with another protected arcade bootleg documented among its variants. It is a conversion of existing console software, not a purpose-built arcade installment in the series.

games.title: Bare Knuckle

variants.title: Bare Knuckle (scrambled bootleg of Mega Drive version)

games.description:
This Bare Knuckle set is a scrambled Chinese arcade bootleg of Sega's original Streets of Rage (Bare Knuckle), repackaged for coin-operated play in the 1990s. Players control former police officers Axel Stone, Blaze Fielding or Adam Hunter as they clear gangs from side-scrolling urban stages using punches, kicks, throws, dropped weapons and a limited police-support special attack.

The original was a 1991 Mega Drive release; this set instead documents an unauthorized hardware conversion. Surviving boards used custom-marked chips and rearranged program data, making the game notable as part of the history of console-to-arcade bootlegging rather than for an independently developed campaign.

games.title: Barricade
games.description:
RamTek's Barricade, dated 1976 in this set, is an early competitive maze game in the same family as Gremlin's Blockade and the later Snake and light-cycle games. Two or four players guide moving markers across a fixed arena, continuously leaving solid trails behind them. The aim is to survive by steering away from walls and all existing trails while forcing opponents to run out of space or crash.

There are no weapons or power-ups: each turn permanently changes the maze and makes the next decision harder. Operators could adjust the movement speed and the number of rounds needed to win. Its primitive monochrome presentation is an example of the earliest arcade designs built around head-to-head spatial strategy rather than shooting.

games.title: Barrier
games.description:
Barrier is a 1979 vector-graphics arcade game designed by Rob Patton and released by Vectorbeam. The action takes place on an obliquely drawn three-by-nine grid that suggests a three-dimensional corridor. Players steer a small triangular marker toward the far end while avoiding independently moving diamond-shaped hazards; reaching the end sends the marker back to the front to repeat the challenge and earn more points.

The stark line display and restricted grid make Barrier an unusual ancestor of later abstract action-puzzle games. Rather than offering combat or a conventional maze, it relies on judging safe paths and timing movements around obstacles.

games.title: Baryon - Future Assault
games.description:
Baryon: Future Assault is a 1997 vertically scrolling shooter from South Korea's SemiCom, based on an earlier Korean PC shooter developed by Acro Studio. Players pilot futuristic fighters through aerial, ground and space-themed stages, destroying formations of enemy craft and defensive installations while collecting weapon upgrades. Its busy action, multiple weapon systems and layered scrolling effects reflect the influence of Japanese shooters such as Raiden.

It is a particularly unusual example of a Korean PC game being reworked for coin-operated hardware. The arcade version uses a relatively modest sound system despite ambitious graphical effects and elaborate enemy patterns, making it a worthwhile curiosity for enthusiasts of lesser-known 1990s shooters.

games.title: Baseball The Season II
games.description: Baseball The Season II (1987) is a Cinematronics arcade baseball game designed around full matches against the computer or a second player. Batting, pitching and fielding are handled with a joystick and a six-button control layout, emphasizing hands-on baseball action rather than purely statistical management. The game also records team statistics and progress toward a championship, an unusually persistent element for a coin-operated sports title of its period.

games.title: Sega Bass Fishing
games.description:
Sega Bass Fishing, known in Japan as Get Bass, is a 1997 Sega Model 3 fishing game that brought an unexpectedly tactile sporting pastime into the arcade. Players choose lures, cast into a lake and attempt to hook largemouth bass, then carefully reel them in while responding to the fish's resistance. The original dedicated cabinet features a fishing-rod controller with a working reel and a moving line that communicates tension, making the physical experience central to its appeal.

A session progresses through four fishing spots or time-of-day stages. Each has a weight target to reach before the clock expires, culminating in a final stage focused on one particularly large catch. Fish are graded from small to huge, and choosing where and how to fish is as important as reeling quickly. Its distinctive cabinet and later Dreamcast port helped Sega Bass Fishing become one of the best remembered arcade simulations of an unconventional sport.

games.title: Battle Circuit
games.description:
Battle Circuit (1997) is Capcom's flamboyant final original arcade beat 'em up, developed for CPS-2 hardware. Set in a comic-book future, it follows eccentric bounty hunters pursuing a stolen computer disc containing the powerful Shiva System. Up to four players can join the side-scrolling melee, choosing from five radically different characters, including the elastic-armed Cyber Blue, the feline Yellow Iris and the plant-like Alien Green.

Like Final Fight, the action centers on clearing groups of enemies and defeating larger-than-life bosses, but Battle Circuit adds a progression system: money earned during each stage can be spent on upgrade discs that grant special techniques or improve existing abilities. Its exaggerated animation, absurd humor and highly differentiated fighters make it feel like a deliberately playful culmination of Capcom's cooperative brawler tradition. Initially confined to Japanese and European arcades, it later reached a wider audience through Capcom's beat-'em-up compilations.

games.title: Batman
games.description:
Atari Games' Batman (1991) is a coin-operated action adaptation of Tim Burton's 1989 film, combining side-scrolling combat with vehicle sequences. Batman fights the Joker's henchmen across Gotham City using punches, Batarangs and other gadgets; stages also put players behind the controls of the Batmobile and Batwing in first-person shooting sequences inspired by the movie.

The presentation uses digitized actor portraits and sampled dialogue from Michael Keaton and Jack Nicholson, giving the game unusually direct links to its cinematic source. Released primarily as a conversion kit rather than a widely distributed dedicated cabinet, it survives as an interesting example of Atari's movie-license arcade design at the start of the 1990s.

games.title: Batman Forever
games.description:
Batman Forever: The Arcade Game (1996) is Acclaim's spectacularly exaggerated two-player brawler based on the 1995 film. Players take the roles of Batman and Robin, fighting across Gotham against crowds of henchmen before confronting Two-Face and the Riddler. Unlike the earlier side-view console game of the same name, this is an arcade-specific belt-scrolling beat 'em up, with rapid combinations, juggling attacks, screen-filling effects and a collection of familiar gadgets.

Batarangs, grappling equipment and other tools complement punches and kicks, while the game's oversized character sprites and flashy audiovisual presentation reflect its Sega ST-V-based hardware. This was Acclaim's first arcade game, later brought to home platforms as Batman Forever: The Arcade Game.

games.title: Armed Police Batrider

variants.title: Armed Police Batrider - B Version (Japan) (Fri Feb 13 1998)
Armed Police Batrider - A Version (Japan) (Mon Dec 22 1997)
Armed Police Batrider - A Version (Taiwan) (Mon Dec 22 1997)

games.description: Armed Police Batrider is a vertical-scrolling manic shoot-'em-up developed by Raizing and published by Eighting in 1998. Set in the futuristic crime-ridden island city of Gigantea, players assemble a three-character team from a large roster of Batrider pilots and guest characters from earlier Raizing titles such as Battle Garegga and Kingdom Grandprix, featuring dynamic rank control and dozens of hidden bosses.

games.title: Batsugun
games.description:
Toaplan's Batsugun (1993) is one of the pivotal arcade shooters in the transition from traditional vertical shoot 'em ups to the modern bullet-hell style. Players choose a pilot and craft from the Skull Hornets squadron and fly through a campaign against a militaristic regime, unleashing enormous streams of firepower while weaving between densely layered enemy bullets. Three ship types offer different weapon characteristics, and a second button drops powerful screen-clearing bombs.

Its signature progression mechanic separates experience from score. Destroying enemies builds an experience gauge that upgrades the ship's firepower, while collectible power-up symbols further strengthen the current weapon level. The ship visibly changes as its weapon reaches higher levels, giving combat a distinct rhythm of escalating destruction. Two-player cooperative play adds even more spectacle, including coordinated bomb attacks.

Created by a team that included future Cave talent, Batsugun is frequently cited as a crucial precursor to DonPachi and the bullet-hell genre, even though it retains many conventional Toaplan shooter ideas. It was among Toaplan's final releases before the company's collapse, and its previously obscure Special Version became highly prized by collectors and shooting-game enthusiasts.

games.title: Battle Lane! Vol. 5
games.description:
Battle Lane! Vol. 5 (1986) is a vertically scrolling motorcycle combat shooter released through Taito, Tecmo and Romstar distribution arrangements. Players ride an armed bike through enemy checkpoints, shooting other vehicles and soldiers while dodging incoming fire. Bazooka pickups provide limited missiles powerful enough to breach fortified walls, and the mission culminates in an attack on a secret weapon inside an enemy base.

The six-part route combines continuous vehicle shooting with moments when the player must conserve heavy ammunition for obstacles. Its distinctive mounted-motorcycle premise sets it apart from the airplane shooters that dominated the genre.

games.title: Battlecry
games.description:
Battlecry is an unusual 1991 fighting game from Home Data, combining a side-scrolling brawler with a head-to-head battle mode. In the solo campaign, a muscular fighter named Mac crosses American-themed stages, defeating lesser opponents until a rope ladder opens the route to a stronger boss. The character can punch, kick, jump and roll, with attacks playing out from a side view.

A second player can instead participate in direct one-on-one fighting. The game was reportedly completed in 1989 but did not reach arcades until 1991, explaining some of its older-fashioned design during the early boom in versus fighters.

games.title: Battle Rangers
games.description:
Battle Rangers is the European title of Data East's Bloody Wolf (1988), a top-down, multi-directional run-and-gun game about two commandos sent to rescue a captured president. The soldiers fight through jungles and military installations, firing in several directions, rescuing prisoners and collecting replacement weapons, grenades and other supplies. Enemy motorbikes, helicopters, gun emplacements and large bosses turn the mission into a relentless series of firefights.

Two-player cooperative play and the ability to supplement gunfire with knives or other close-range attacks give the action a tactical edge. Its huge numbers of enemies, cinematic rescue objective and distinctive Data East presentation make it a strong late-1980s example of the Commando-inspired arcade shooter.

games.title: Battle Cross
games.description: Battle Cross (1982) is an early space shooter by Omori Electric. Players steer a small spacecraft freely around a fixed screen, shooting enemy vessels that enter from both sides and curl into moving formations. Rocky obstacles add a second threat, forcing the pilot to reposition while tracking the enemy waves. Its all-direction movement distinguishes it from the simpler left-and-right fixed shooters of the period.

games.title: Battlantis
games.description:
Konami's Battlantis (1987) is a fantasy-themed fixed-screen shooter that reinterprets Space Invaders as a battle against advancing armies and monsters. A human defender moves along the bottom edge, firing upward into formations of enemies that shift, swoop or rush toward the ground. Incoming projectiles and enemies reaching the bottom can cost a life; clearing the attackers leads to a larger boss encounter.

The medieval creatures and human soldiers give Battlantis an unusual visual identity compared with the genre's ubiquitous spacecraft. It remains a compact but demanding example of Konami's late-era single-screen shooters.

games.title: The Battle-Road
games.description:
Irem's The Battle-Road (1984) is an early vertically scrolling car-combat game built around a branching road system. Players drive an armed vehicle through traffic and military opposition, confronting motorcycles, trucks, helicopters and other enemies while firing both forward and sideways. At junctions, different route choices lead through different sections of the campaign, with 32 possible routes documented.

That combination of road shooting and nonlinear progression makes it an intriguing precursor to later vehicle-action games, several years before branching courses became a familiar feature of arcade racers.

games.title: Batsugun (Special Ver.)
games.description: Batsugun (Special Ver.) is an enhanced version of Toaplan's 1993 vertical-scrolling shoot-'em-up Batsugun. It introduces a smaller player hitbox, a protective shield when leveling up weapons, a reworked scoring system, and multiple loops with bullet-canceling mechanics that helped define the modern manic shooter genre.

games.title: Bay Route
games.description:
Bay Route (1989) is a side-scrolling run-and-gun game developed by Sunsoft for Sega arcade hardware. A soldier battles futuristic terrorists across multi-level industrial and military stages, using directional gunfire to eliminate infantry, vehicles, hovering craft and fortified positions. Defeated enemies may drop weapon upgrades, and reaching the end of a stage often means destroying a heavily defended installation rather than simply walking to the exit.

The arcade versions include Japanese, World and US sets, with some versions using Sega's FD1094 protection system and others appearing as unprotected or bootleg boards. Its fast-paced action and changing stage elevations place it in the tradition of Contra-like arcade shooters.

games.title: Bazooka
games.description:
Bazooka is a late-1970s black-and-white shooting game associated with Taito's Brazilian operation and the earlier Project Support Engineering design. Players aim a simulated bazooka at military targets crossing a side-view battlefield, firing at jeeps, tanks, trucks and motorcycles as they move into range. Ambulances and stretcher-bearing personnel must be spared, adding a recognition challenge to the simple shooting mechanics.

With its sparse monochrome graphics and focus on timing shots at passing vehicles, it resembles a land-combat counterpart to Sea Wolf rather than a later free-moving action shooter.

games.title: Bouncing Balls
games.description:
Comad's Bouncing Balls (1991) is a Korean arcade puzzle game built around numbered balls rather than simple color matching. Players drop balls in a chosen order to form the required numerical total, losing if the resulting sum is incorrect. The two-player game uses a joystick and two buttons, with puzzle decisions taking priority over reflex shooting.

Its visual presentation also includes recognizable cartoon characters such as Daffy Duck and Marvin the Martian, and a separate adult-oriented version was produced. Those details make it a curious example of the eclectic, sometimes unlicensed artwork found in smaller Korean arcade releases of the era.

games.title: Best Bout Boxing
games.description:
Best Bout Boxing (1994) is Jaleco's colorful one-on-one boxing game for Mega System 32 hardware. Players select one of seven international contenders, each with distinct punching techniques, and work through a tournament to challenge the reigning world champion. Bouts use life gauges, multiple rounds and knockout or technical-knockout outcomes rather than trying to simulate every rule of professional boxing.

Three-button attacks and character-specific special punches make the fights play more like an accessible arcade fighter than a strict boxing simulation. Two players can also step into the ring directly against each other.

games.title: Bomber Man World / New Dyna Blaster - Global Quest

variants.title: Bomber Man World / New Dyna Blaster - Global Quest

games.description:
Bomber Man World (1992), also known as New Dyna Blaster: Global Quest and New Atomic Punk, is Irem's second arcade Bomberman game, developed under license from Hudson Soft. Players navigate tightly packed grids, planting timed bombs to destroy enemies and clear breakable blocks while carefully avoiding their own expanding cross-shaped blasts. Power-ups improve bomb capacity, explosion range and movement options, turning each stage into a changing puzzle of safe and dangerous corridors.

The campaign spans six worlds with boss encounters and allows cooperative play, while the separate competitive mode turns the same mechanics into a frantic contest between up to four bombers. Its combination of single-player progression and multiplayer battles helped establish the format that later Bomberman games would exploit so successfully. Different regional sets and the unauthorized Bomber Lord variant document the game's unusually broad arcade distribution.

games.title: Bigfoot Bonkers
games.description:
Bigfoot Bonkers is a 1976 two-player maze game by Meadows Games, closely related to the early Blockade-style surround games. Each player guides a mouse across a grid, leaving a permanent trail that becomes an obstacle for both participants. Besides walls and the opponent's trail, giant footprints scattered around the arena must be avoided. The first player to crash gives a point to the survivor, and six points win the match.

There is no computer opponent, so its entire design depends on direct human competition. The oversized feet provide an extra hazard that differentiates it from the many plain trail-drawing games released during the industry's first wave of competitive video arcades.

games.title: Untitled Fighter 'BB'
games.description: Untitled Fighter 'BB' is an unfinished, unidentified one-on-one fighting-game prototype attributed to NIX and preserved under the working name 'BB'. Its surviving build is from a very early stage of development, rather than a finished or commercially released arcade title. The hardware supports two players with eight-direction joysticks and six attack buttons, in the mold of the fighting-game cabinets of the 1990s. The prototype is primarily significant as a surviving glimpse of an abandoned production; a complete roster, move system, and final title are not documented.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.
Original developer and publisher are not established.

games.title: Beast Busters
games.description:
SNK's Beast Busters (1989) is a horror-themed rail shooter in which a mysterious city has been overrun by zombies and grotesque monsters. Players use mounted light guns to shoot through streets, buildings and other danger zones, blasting enemies before they can attack while watching for targets suddenly appearing from all sides. The game's exaggerated gore and large, animated creatures contrast sharply with the military shooting galleries common at the time.

Its most notable hardware feature is support for three simultaneous light-gun players, an early milestone for cooperative gun games. Released shortly before SNK's shift toward the Neo Geo platform, Beast Busters later inspired further entries in the company's horror-shooter line.

games.title: Battle Chopper
games.description:
Battle Chopper (1987), called Mr. Heli no Dai-Bouken in Japan, is Irem's whimsical horizontally scrolling shooter starring a small armed helicopter. Instead of simply flying through open space, the player maneuvers through caves, platforms and blocked corridors, blasting cartoonish enemies and breaking pieces of the environment. Crystals collected from destroyed blocks become money, which can be spent on weapon upgrades revealed elsewhere in the stages.

This shop-like upgrade system changes the shooter's priorities: players must decide whether a risky detour to collect money is worth the resulting firepower. The helicopter's ability to hover and work through vertical as well as horizontal spaces makes the stages feel more exploratory than a conventional side-scrolling shooter. The Japanese title's Mr. Heli became a recognizable character in Irem's arcade history.

games.title: Battle Cruiser M-12
games.description:
Battle Cruiser M-12 is a 1983 submarine-themed shooting game from Sigma. Rather than piloting a fighter in open space, players attack waves of underwater vessels by dropping fast-moving depth charges from above. Enemy submarines and other craft fight back by launching mines and missiles toward the surface, so success depends on anticipating their positions and timing each drop.

Its unusual naval setting and rapid depth-charge attacks give it a different cadence from contemporary space shooters. The audio is also notable for arrangements reminiscent of popular songs, an audacious touch for an early-1980s arcade release.

games.title: B.C. Story
games.description: B.C. Story (1997) is a prehistoric-themed sports game from the Korean developer SemiCom. Rather than offering conventional athletics, it presents a series of cartoon Stone Age competitions featuring selectable caveman characters such as Sonlo, Milo and Ballo. Events include running and climbing challenges, with quick joystick-and-button inputs determining the outcome. Its playful prehistoric setting places it in the lineage of arcade sports mini-game collections rather than realistic simulations.

games.title: MPU4 Video Firmware
games.description:
MPU4 Video Firmware is the system BIOS for Barcrest's video-equipped MPU4 amusement-machine architecture. MPU4 began as a modular controller for British coin-operated machines, centered on a Motorola 6809 family processor. The video configuration supplemented this controller with separate display hardware, including a Motorola 68000-based video subsystem, rather than relying only on conventional mechanical indicators.

The firmware supports the underlying cabinet and video environment, with coin and service inputs, audio control, and operator-oriented functions forming part of the wider MPU4 design. This is a supporting ROM set, not a standalone gambling or action title. In later MAME sets the shared video firmware is generally catalogued under the identifier v4bios.

games.title: Beam Invader
games.description: Beam Invader (1979) is a Japanese Space Invaders-style fixed shooter by Tekunon Kougyou. Players control a cannon along the bottom of the screen, firing upward at descending formations of alien attackers. Its most conspicuous difference from Taito's original is physical: instead of moving the gun with buttons or a conventional joystick, the cabinet uses a rotary paddle for horizontal positioning. That analog movement changes the feel of an otherwise familiar early-arcade challenge.

games.title: Beastorizer
games.description:
Beastorizer (1997) is the original arcade incarnation of Bloody Roar, developed by Raizing and published with Hudson Soft. This polygonal one-on-one fighter centers on zoanthropes, people who can transform into powerful animal-human hybrids. A roster including a wolf, tiger, rabbit, gorilla and other beast forms battles while the sinister Tylon Corporation seeks to exploit their abilities.

Transformation is the decisive mechanic: fighters build or manage the ability to enter beast form, where they gain different moves, greater offensive potential and new combo routes. The approachable controls and dramatic mid-fight changes distinguish it from conventional 3D fighting games of the period. Its success launched the Bloody Roar series, with the game later reaching the PlayStation under the name by which the franchise is now best known.

games.title: BeatHead
games.description:
BeatHead is an unreleased 1993 Atari Games prototype built around a competitive tile-coloring contest. Players move characters around a patterned arena and jump on squares matching their own color, or squares showing both players' colors, to claim progress. The objective is to fill a designated quota of spaces before the opponent does.

Its joystick-and-two-button controls turn what could have been a static board puzzle into a kinetic contest of positioning and jumps. The surviving prototype offers a rare look at Atari experimenting with new multiplayer arcade ideas during the early 1990s, though it never became a regular commercial release.

games.title: Beezer
games.description:
Beezer (1982), by Tong Electronic, is an unusual trackball-controlled action puzzle game set inside a honeycomb-like maze. The player pushes and rotates gate segments to complete six-sided cells around dangerous bees, trapping them without accidentally sealing in the player character. The trackball makes movement precise but urgent as the insects roam the corridors.

A queen bee can rearrange barriers and lay eggs; eating the eggs before they hatch grants temporary power that allows the player to destroy bees directly. Beezer mixes territory control, maze construction and survival in a way few early-1980s arcade games attempted, and its trackball controls are central to the experience.

games.title: Ben Bero Beh
games.description:
Ben Bero Beh (1984) is a quirky Taito platform game about rescuing a young woman from a burning apartment building. Players guide a small superhero down through its floors, using stairs and carefully placed jumps while spraying flames with a fire extinguisher. Explosions, collapsing sections of floor, falling fixtures and creatures emerging from doorways continually disrupt the descent.

The building itself becomes an active hazard as the fire spreads, so players must balance extinguishing danger with moving toward the person waiting below. Its eccentric cast of characters and animated calamities exemplify the playful, experimental style of many Japanese arcade platformers of the mid-1980s.

games.title: Beraboh Man
games.description:
Beraboh Man, also known as Chou Zetsurinjin Berabowman or Bravoman, is Namco's 1988 side-scrolling superhero action game. The protagonist can stretch his arms and legs to strike robots, monsters and comic-book villains across colorful stages, with an assortment of attacks and unusual boss encounters. The exaggerated elastic-limbed hero and tongue-in-cheek Japanese presentation make it a striking departure from Namco's more conventional military action games.

The original cabinet is especially remembered for its pressure-sensitive button controls: pressing the attack and jump pads with different force changes the strength or length of the corresponding move. Those distinctive controls are an important part of the original design even though they must be mapped to ordinary buttons in many emulated configurations. The game later reached the PC Engine and became the basis for further appearances of the Bravoman character.

games.title: The Berlin Wall
games.description:
The Berlin Wall (1991), developed by Kaneko and released in Japan as Berlin no Kabe, is a bright platform action game built around the ideas pioneered by Space Panic. A boy armed with a hammer moves between tiers of platforms, breaking holes in the floor and luring patrolling monsters into them. Once an enemy is trapped, another blow drops it to a lower level and transforms it into collectible fruit.

Because the hammer is more useful for altering the arena than for striking monsters directly, successful play depends on setting up traps and positioning enemies. Its charming illustrations and deceptively demanding multi-level layouts give it a distinctive identity among the many single-screen platform games of the period. Its title appeared as the actual Berlin Wall was being dismantled, although the action is an abstract fantasy rather than a historical depiction.

games.title: Bermuda Triangle
games.description:
Bermuda Triangle (1987), also known in Japan as World Wars, is a vertically scrolling shooter by SNK built around a time-traveling warship. The large ZIG craft battles hostile forces across different eras, surviving waves of aircraft and defenses until it can destroy each stage's boss. Unlike the fragile fighters of most shooters, the ship has a damage gauge and can take multiple hits.

Its defining control feature is a rotary joystick that lets players aim an additional gun turret independently of their movement, supplementing the main forward fire. Smaller escort ships can be collected and arranged around the ZIG to provide protection and extra shots, while energy items restore health or enhance weapons. The stages sometimes scroll in different directions, giving this rotary-controlled shooter a more varied sense of movement than the genre's usual continuous upward advance.

games.title: Berzerk
games.description:
Stern Electronics' Berzerk (1980), created by Alan McNeil, is one of the foundational maze shooters of the golden age. The player guides a lone humanoid through an immense sequence of rooms populated by robots that move and fire lasers. An eight-way joystick controls movement and a separate button fires in the chosen direction; electric walls, enemy shots and the robots themselves are all lethal. The player can leave a room without destroying every enemy, but clearing it awards a bonus.

The game's most famous threat is Evil Otto, a bouncing, invulnerable smiling face that appears if the player lingers too long. Otto relentlessly pursues the humanoid, turning cautious defensive play into a frantic escape. Robots can also collide with the maze walls or each other, producing memorable moments in which the enemies' own clumsiness works in the player's favor.

Berzerk is also renowned for pioneering synthesized speech in arcades, with taunts such as 'Intruder alert!' and 'The humanoid must not escape!' giving the robots a remarkable personality for 1980. Its voice hardware was costly for the period, and its simple maze concept proved influential enough to produce the sequel Frenzy and a long legacy of robotic arena shooters.

games.title: Best Of Best
games.description:
Best of Best (1994) is a Korean head-to-head fighting game by SunA, released amid the worldwide wave of Street Fighter-inspired arcade challengers. Eight selectable combatants, including a wrestler, martial artists and military-styled fighters, face one another in two-out-of-three-round contests. Each uses punches, kicks and special techniques, with the option for two players to fight directly.

Unlike many contemporaries, it does not build toward a separate secret final boss. Its eccentric character designs, unusual animation and straightforward tournament structure give it the distinctive offbeat character of smaller Korean fighting-game productions of the time.

games.title: Battle Garegga

variants.title: Battle Garegga (Europe / USA / Japan / Asia) (Sat Feb 3 1996)
Battle Garegga - New Version (Austria / Hong Kong) (Sat Mar 2 1996)
Battle Garegga - Type 2 (Europe / USA / Japan / Asia) (Sat Mar 2 1996)

games.description:
Battle Garegga (1996), developed by Raizing and published by Eighting, is a landmark vertical shooter celebrated for its intricate scoring and unforgiving hidden difficulty system. Set in a dieselpunk world of industrial war machines, it offers four selectable aircraft with different shot spreads and options. Players collect power-ups, place auxiliary guns in various formations and bomb their way through dense formations of tanks, planes and enormous mechanical bosses.

The game's defining feature is its dynamic rank system: stronger weaponry, extra lives, survival time and other actions can increase enemy aggression. Playing well is therefore not simply a matter of maximizing firepower. Expert players deliberately manage rank, sometimes sacrificing a life at a carefully chosen moment to keep later stages survivable. Medal collection, weapon positioning and precise bomb use add further layers of strategy.

Designed by Shinobu Yagawa, Battle Garegga has become a touchstone of expert-level shooting-game design. Its realistic-looking bullets can blend into the detailed backgrounds, an infamous part of its challenge, while its branching optimization and scoring depth have supported decades of high-level play. It was followed spiritually by Armed Police Batrider and Battle Bakraid and later received the expanded Battle Garegga Rev.2016 release.

games.title: Big Bucks
games.description:
Big Bucks, also promoted as Big Bucks Trivia Quest, is a 1986 game-show-style trivia arcade game from Dynasoft. Players compete to accumulate virtual winnings by answering questions in themed categories, including sports and general-interest subjects, using a four-way joystick rather than a row of answer buttons. Dynasoft advertised a library of more than 10,000 questions and competition for up to four alternating participants, emphasizing both knowledge and quick decisions.

Its unusually long question bank was housed in a game running on modified Pac-Man-derived hardware, retaining the upright, vertically oriented monitor familiar from Namco's earlier maze games. The result is a striking example of an arcade conversion that replaces fast reflex action with a television quiz-show format, where the attraction lies in building a high score and outdoing other players' knowledge.

games.title: Big Deal
games.description: Big Deal is a 1986 video-poker machine by Austrian manufacturer Fun World, with surviving sets associated with the Hungarian market. It presents a single-player card-gambling format on a horizontal monitor, using a seven-button control panel rather than a joystick-driven arcade interface. The machine belongs to Fun World's early family of dedicated electronic poker products; its 65SC02 processor and AY-3-8910 audio hardware distinguish it from the more familiar action boards of the period.

games.title: Big Event Golf
games.description: Big Event Golf is a 1986 Taito arcade golf game built around a complete 18-hole championship course. Using a trackball and two buttons, players direct and strike shots from the tee through fairway and rough to the green, trying to complete the round with the lowest possible stroke count. Its conventional golf scoring and full-course progression provide a more deliberate sporting challenge than many short-format arcade competitions.

games.title: Big Fight - Big Trouble In The Atlantic Ocean
games.description:
Big Fight: Big Trouble in the Atlantic Ocean (1992) is Tatsumi's unusual crossover between a side-scrolling beat 'em up and a one-on-one fighting game. Its main mode follows three fighters, Gear, Kevin and Zill, through a succession of enemy encounters, with individual special moves and large bosses. Rather than ending there, the game also offers a distinct Battle mode in which players can choose from the heroes and several boss characters for direct duels.

This attempt to combine the cooperative street-brawling formula with the then-booming versus-fighting genre makes Big Fight a curiosity of the early 1990s. It was among Tatsumi's final traditional arcade video games before the company shifted its focus toward other amusement products.

games.title: Big Karnak
games.description:
Big Karnak (1991) is a Gaelco side-scrolling platform adventure set in a fantastical version of ancient Egypt. Players control a pharaoh-like warrior whose wife has been abducted, fighting through cobras, skeletons, mythological creatures and larger guardians. The adventure changes structure between stages: an early section emphasizes straightforward melee combat, a temple introduces branching passages and puzzles, and later areas focus more heavily on imposing bosses.

The hero can acquire a magical staff for ranged attacks, collect health or time bonuses and rescue characters encountered during exploration. Its shifting stage designs give it more of an adventure-game character than a simple left-to-right action platformer, while the Egyptian monsters and elaborate backgrounds lend it a distinctive visual identity.

games.title: The Big Pro Wrestling!
games.description:
The Big Pro Wrestling!, released internationally as Tag Team Wrestling, is a 1983 arcade wrestling game developed by Technos Japan and published by Data East. Players control the tag team Terry and Sunny against the villainous Heel Team, attempting to wear down their opponents and win through wrestling holds or pins. Rather than using a modern fighting game's many direct move buttons, the game presents a changing selection of wrestling techniques when the fighters grapple; the player must time a button press to choose the desired move.

The available attacks range from jabs and chops to piledrivers, lariats and submission holds. Tag-team positioning and the pressure of the match timer provide an early attempt to translate professional wrestling into arcade mechanics. It is historically notable as one of Technos Japan's first releases, years before the studio became associated with Double Dragon and other influential beat 'em ups.

games.title: Big Run
games.description:
Jaleco's Big Run (1989) is a pseudo-3D rally racer inspired by the grueling Paris-Dakar event, placing the player in a Porsche 959-like machine across roads, countryside and desert terrain. The objective is not merely to finish first in a short sprint: racers must survive six long stages, beat the clock and maintain a sufficiently strong position in the overall order to continue.

A two-speed gearbox and arcade-style driving controls keep the action accessible, while changing landscapes and rivals create the sensation of a prolonged cross-country competition. Big Run was an early arcade game to build its identity around the Paris-Dakar rally rather than circuit racing.

games.title: Big Striker

variants.title: Best League
variants.version: (bootleg of Big Striker, Italian Serie A)

games.description:
Big Striker (1992) is an isometric arcade soccer game from Jaleco, with an angled view of the pitch and fast, direct control of the action. Eight national teams are available, and three buttons handle passing, shooting or clearing, and evasive feints. Holding a pass changes its length and trajectory, while the attack button can produce different kinds of shots depending on the ball's height and the player's position.

Its third-button feint helps the ball carrier evade tackles, giving matches a distinctive tactical wrinkle. Rain and other changing conditions add atmosphere. A later unauthorized modification, Best League, replaces the international sides with Italian Serie A teams, making the game's bootleg history especially interesting.

games.title: Big Twin
games.description:
Big Twin (1995), from Italy's Playmark, is a falling-sphere puzzle game with adult-themed visual rewards. Players must arrange groups of three or more balls of the same color, horizontally, vertically or diagonally, before the pile fills the playfield. Balls that have already landed can be selected and moved to another open position, providing an extra layer of planning beyond simply choosing where to drop the next piece.

As matched balls disappear, portions of an illustration are gradually uncovered. Beneath the provocative presentation is a fast puzzle game where manipulating existing pieces is central to extending a run.

games.title: Bijokko Gakuen
games.description: Seishun Mahjong Bijokko Gakuen is a Japanese adult-themed mahjong game released by Nichibutsu in January 1988. Its title can be rendered as 'Youth Mahjong Cutie Academy', reflecting the school-themed presentation around a game of Japanese mahjong. Players use the specialized mahjong control panel rather than a conventional arcade joystick, selecting tiles and making calls during hands. It belongs to Nichibutsu's extensive late-1980s range of mature mahjong machines, whose appeal combined traditional tabletop play with illustrated character scenes. The cabinet also used an auxiliary LCD display arrangement characteristic of some Nichibutsu mahjong hardware.

games.title: Bijokko Yume Monogatari
games.description: Bijokko Yume Monogatari, roughly 'Cutie Dream Story', is a Japanese adult mahjong title released by Nichibutsu in September 1987. Built around the familiar tile-drawing and hand-completion play of Japanese mahjong, it presents that tabletop game through a character-driven, mature arcade format. Rather than joystick controls, it uses a dedicated mahjong button panel, and its hardware includes support for an auxiliary LCD display. It predates Bijokko Gakuen and illustrates Nichibutsu's prolific development of specialized mahjong machines during this period.

games.title: Bikkuri Pro Wrestling
games.description:
Bikkuri Pro Wrestling is a 1988 Japanese wrestling-themed prize game from Nichibutsu, and it is far stranger than a conventional joystick-controlled wrestling simulation. Players stake coins and select attacks using buttons, attempting to overcome a villainous wrestler with one of three depicted wrestling moves. Winning can award character stickers, making it a combination of illustrated wrestling contest, betting-style selection game, and physical redemption attraction. Its controls are accordingly classified as gambling buttons in modern MAME rather than a standard arcade joystick.

The machine capitalized on Japan's late-1980s collectible-sticker craze. A contemporary promotional leaflet described eight stickers to collect and offered a poster in return for sending the complete set to Nichibutsu. The surviving program is dated December 21, 1988 (version 1.05). This unusual prize mechanism explains why the game uses hardware more closely associated with Nichibutsu's specialized tabletop and medal games than with popular wrestling action titles.

games.title: Bikkuri Card
games.description:
Bikkuri Card is a Japanese prize-oriented memory game released by Peni Soft in 1987. The player uncovers cards in a three-by-three grid and tries to match pictures of foods such as hamburgers, sausages, doughnuts and fries. Successful pairs count toward a set of three matches needed to win a prize, while a running dog and a decreasing timer create urgency. The game also allows a player to abandon an unfavorable arrangement, ending the round.

Its blend of a simple picture-matching puzzle and physical prize redemption reflects a branch of Japanese arcade entertainment quite different from conventional high-score games.

games.title: Bio Attack
games.description:
Taito's Bio Attack (1983) is a vertically scrolling shooter with an unusual setting: the inside of a human body. Players pilot a microscopic craft through the bloodstream, firing at animated viruses, bacteria and other hostile organisms while avoiding their attacks. Pushing forward increases the scrolling speed, a valuable option because the craft has a limited oxygen supply; collecting oxygen capsules keeps the mission going.

The stages move through different organs and culminate in encounters with larger microorganisms, mixing rapid shooting with the pressure of managing a dwindling life-support gauge. Its medical-fantasy theme gives it a memorable identity among the many space-based shooters of the early 1980s. It should not be confused with the separate Atari 2600 game Fantastic Voyage, which appears in some catalogues as an unrelated source match.

games.title: BioFreaks
games.description:
Bio F.R.E.A.K.S. is Midway's 1997 arcade fighting-game prototype, developed before the title reached home systems in 1998. Set in a brutal futuristic world, it pits heavily armed, cybernetically modified warriors against one another in polygonal 3D arenas. Combat combines close-range strikes with special weapons and destructive attacks, giving its confrontations a more violent science-fiction tone than most traditional martial-arts fighters.

The planned coin-operated edition was tested but not commercially released, and the project eventually appeared on the PlayStation, Nintendo 64 and PC. The preserved arcade prototype is an example of Midway's late-1990s experimentation with 3D combat beyond Mortal Kombat.

games.title: Bio-Hazard Battle

variants.title: Bio-Hazard Battle (scrambled bootleg of Mega Drive version)

games.description:
This Bio-Hazard Battle set is a scrambled bootleg conversion of Sega's Mega Drive side-scrolling shooter, known in Japan as Crying: Aseimei Sensou. Players select one of four living, insect-like spacecraft to battle hostile biomechanical creatures across the planet Avaron. Colored weapon pickups alter the craft's attacks, and survival depends on navigating intricate enemy formations and using the selected ship's firing characteristics.

The original game debuted on Mega Drive in 1992. This coin-operated bootleg, catalogued with a later arcade date, repackages the console software on unauthorized hardware rather than adding a separate arcade-developed campaign.

games.title: Biomechanical Toy
games.description:
Biomechanical Toy (1995) is Gaelco's imaginative run-and-gun platform game set in a world of magically animated toys. The criminal Scrubby has stolen the Magic Pendulum that keeps the toy kingdom alive, and the hero Inguz must recover it while rescuing friendly toys scattered throughout the stages. The game scrolls in multiple directions as players jump between colorful platforms, dodge enemy toys and fire at creatures and machines that have turned hostile.

Inguz's pistol can be upgraded with stronger ammunition, automatic fire and explosive rounds, but ammunition magazines must be reloaded, leaving him briefly vulnerable. The combination of a lavish toy-box art style, exploration and constant shooting gives Biomechanical Toy a distinctive personality among European arcade action games of the mid-1990s.

games.title: Bionic Commando
games.description:
Capcom's Bionic Commando (1987), originally titled Top Secret in Japan, is one of the most inventive arcade platform shooters of the 1980s. Its commando protagonist infiltrates an enemy military installation armed with a gun and a remarkable telescopic bionic arm. Instead of relying on conventional jumps, players fire the grappling arm to catch overhead platforms, swing across gaps and climb through heavily defended vertical structures. The arm can also retrieve items or interfere with enemies, making it essential for both movement and combat.

The stages mix horizontally scrolling gunfights with demanding climbs and carefully positioned hazards. Parachutes periodically drop additional equipment and supplies, while the character's shooting capabilities are constrained by direction and positioning. Learning when to swing, hang and release is as important as shooting accurately.

Designed by Tokuro Fujiwara, Bionic Commando expanded ideas from the grappling mechanics of Konami's Roc'n Rope into a full action-platforming system. Though marketed in North America as connected to Capcom's Commando, its mechanical identity was entirely different. The later NES Bionic Commando developed the concept further into a beloved home-console adventure, but the arcade original remains a distinctive and demanding achievement in its own right.

games.title: Bio-ship Paladin
games.description:
Bio-ship Paladin (1990), known in Japan as Uchuu Senkan Gomora, is a horizontally scrolling shooter by UPL that gives the player control of a living battleship defending the planet Atlantal. Its most unusual feature is a separately aimed weapon: alongside a conventional forward-firing gun, the ship can target enemies elsewhere on the screen using a movable crosshair. This allows players to attack targets above, below or behind the ship while maintaining their flight path.

Power-ups increase firepower, add escort pods or strengthen the vessel's armor, sometimes causing the bio-ship itself to grow larger. The nine-stage campaign and simultaneous two-player action reward active use of both weapons, producing a distinctive combination of traditional side-scrolling shooting and target selection reminiscent of Missile Command.

games.title: Birdiy
games.description:
Birdiy (1983) is a rare Japanese single-screen action game developed by Mama Top. Players control a mother bird flying between branches and the ground to gather caterpillars and worms for her chick waiting in a nest. Predators threaten the baby while the mother is away, so collecting food must be balanced against returning to defend the nest. A button allows a burst of speed during downward movement.

A round ends after the chick has been fed all the required food. The unusual parental-rescue theme and interplay between feeding and protection give Birdiy a gentler premise than most early arcade action games, even though its timing demands can be unforgiving.

games.title: Birdie Try
games.description: Birdie Try (1988) is a Data East arcade golf game presented from an overhead view of the course. Players select and play their shots while accounting for the effect of wind, which is illustrated by clouds moving across the screen. A rotary control and buttons handle shot selection and execution. Its top-down presentation emphasizes course layout and ball placement rather than the behind-the-golfer perspective that became common in later golf simulations.

games.title: Bishi Bashi Championship Mini Game Senshuken

variants.title: Bishi Bashi Championship Mini Game Senshuken (ver JAA)

games.description:
Bishi Bashi Championship Mini Game Senshuken is Konami's 1996 original entry in the long-running Bishi Bashi series of frantic arcade party games. Up to three players compete through an ever-changing sequence of absurd, short challenges using only three large, colored buttons per person. Depending on the task, players may need to press rapidly, react to visual cues or follow a specific combination, with each contest explained just before it begins.

Its genius is the contrast between extremely simple inputs and deliberately unpredictable objectives, making it accessible to spectators and newcomers while keeping competitors under constant pressure. The first Bishi Bashi laid the foundation for later Super Bishi Bashi and Hyper Bishi Bashi cabinets, which expanded the same exuberant multiplayer formula.

games.title: Blue's Journey / Raguy
games.description:
Blue's Journey, known in Japan as Raguy, is a 1990 Neo Geo platform game developed by Alpha Denshi and published by SNK. Its small hero Blue sets out to save the planet Raguy from the polluting Daruma tribe, fighting through colorful forests, caves and other threatened environments. A large leaf serves as his primary weapon: hitting an enemy stuns it, allowing Blue to pick it up and throw it at other foes.

Blue can also shrink to enter narrow passages and discover hidden areas, adding a light exploratory element to the side-scrolling stages. A second player can join as Princess Fa, and the characters can interact with one another while using their special abilities. Its environmental theme, cheerful animation and cooperative platform action make it a distinctive alternative to the fighting games and shooters more commonly associated with the Neo Geo.

games.title: Bombjack Twin
games.description:
Bomb Jack Twin (1993), developed by NMK, updates Tehkan's 1984 single-screen platform classic with simultaneous two-player play. The heroes leap and glide through fixed arenas to collect bombs scattered among platforms while avoiding enemies. Picking up a lit bomb causes another fuse to ignite, so following the glowing sequence can produce substantial bonuses, whereas collecting bombs out of order sacrifices scoring potential.

A power ball can temporarily immobilize enemies, changing the rhythm from evasion to attack. Compared with the original, this sequel groups several stage layouts into themed rounds, adds bonus sequences and runs at a brisker tempo. Its colorful sightseeing backdrops and cooperative collection challenge make it a lively late continuation of the Bomb Jack formula.

games.title: Bare Knuckle III / Sunset Riders

variants.title: Bare Knuckle III / Sunset Riders (scrambled bootleg of Mega Drive versions)

games.description:
Bare Knuckle III / Sunset Riders is an unauthorized multi-game arcade conversion combining Mega Drive versions of two different action titles. Bare Knuckle III is Sega's Japanese Streets of Rage 3, a side-scrolling street brawler in which characters such as Axel, Blaze and Skate fight criminal gangs with punches, throws and special moves. Sunset Riders, originally a Konami arcade game later ported to Mega Drive, is a Western run-and-gun adventure featuring bounty hunters chasing outlaw bosses across frontier towns and trains.

The set is catalogued as a scrambled bootleg of the Mega Drive versions, not as an official crossover or newly designed game. Its significance lies in how pirate arcade boards repackaged recognizable console games into a single coin-operated product.

games.title: Birdie King
games.description: Birdie King is a 1982 arcade golf game from Taito, one of the company's earliest entries in a series that eventually reached three installments. Players use a trackball to control golf shots on a top-down course, aiming to reach each green and sink the ball in as few strokes as possible. Its physical trackball control was a natural fit for judging the direction and strength of a swing, and helped distinguish golf from the predominantly joystick-driven games of the early arcade period.

games.title: Birdie King 2
games.description: Birdie King 2 (1983) is Taito's follow-up to the 1982 trackball golf game Birdie King. It retains the series' overhead course presentation and tactile trackball-based shots, asking players to manage direction, distance and putting while pursuing a low score. The sequel continued a small but recognizable strand of early arcade golf games that used trackball motion to make the swing itself part of the physical challenge.

games.title: Birdie King 3
games.description: Birdie King 3 is the 1984 third installment in Taito's early arcade golf series. Like its predecessors, it uses trackball-based control to simulate the direction and strength of golf shots from an overhead view. This edition is distinguished by its expanded selection of 36 holes, offering a more substantial course variety than a typical single 18-hole round. It closed a compact series that helped establish trackball golf as a viable coin-operated sports format.

games.title: Battle Bakraid - Unlimited Version
games.description: Battle Bakraid - Unlimited Version is an updated release of Eighting's 1999 vertical-scrolling shoot-'em-up Battle Bakraid. Built around high-scoring chain multipliers and boss-rush style aerial combat, Unlimited Version expands the game beyond the original training and normal courses with an extended nine-stage Advanced Course.

games.title: Bakuretsu Quiz Ma-Q Dai Bouken
games.description:
Bakuretsu Quiz Ma-Q Dai Bouken is a 1992 Japanese quiz-adventure arcade game from Namco. Players guide two unlikely heroes, soldier Scott and the burly Stanley, on a mission to recover three jewels stolen from a crown by a sinister organization. Instead of fighting enemies through direct action, they progress through illustrated comic situations by answering multiple-choice questions using four dedicated answer buttons.

Each question has a time limit. Wrong answers or delays cost life hearts, while correct responses improve the heroes' situation and award points based on the remaining time. Its elaborate adventure framing and changing character illustrations set it apart from a bare question-and-answer trivia cabinet, although understanding its Japanese-language questions is essential to playing as intended.

games.title: Black Tiger
games.description:
This Black Tiger set is an unauthorized bootleg of Capcom's 1987 arcade fantasy platformer, rather than a distinct sequel or expanded edition. Players guide a barbarian warrior through monster-filled towers and ruins, swinging a chain-and-mace weapon and throwing daggers while trying to lift a curse laid upon the kingdom by three dragons. Treasure chests, breakable pots and rescued sages provide coins, equipment and chances to buy stronger armor or weapons.

The coin-and-shop system makes exploration rewarding, and the game's interconnected platforms invite detours for hidden treasure. The bootleg preserves the recognizable Black Tiger adventure while representing an unofficial board version documented separately from Capcom's original release.

games.title: Blades of Steel
games.description:
Blades of Steel (1987) is Konami's fast-moving arcade interpretation of ice hockey. Players control their skaters on the rink, pass and shoot toward the opposing goal, and compete either against the computer or another player. It favors quick action and immediately readable play over detailed team management, with enthusiastic synthesized speech adding to the atmosphere.

Its most famous flourish is the fight sequence: when opponents clash, the view cuts to a close-up boxing-style confrontation, and the losing player is sent to the penalty box. This combination of hockey and miniature fighting game became central to Blades of Steel's identity. A popular NES version brought the title to a wider audience, but the arcade original already had the fast play and spectacle for which the game is remembered.

games.title: Blandia
games.description:
Blandia (1992) is an early weapon-based versus fighter developed by Allumer and published by Taito, following the studio's earlier sword-fighting action game Gladiator. Set in a sword-and-sorcery world threatened by the evil Gildus, it features warriors armed with different weapons and protective armor. Players use attacks aimed at different heights to wear down opponents, with visible pieces of armor breaking away during combat.

The emphasis on destroying protection before winning gives the fights a distinct visual and tactical hook. Its fantastical cast and weapon duels appeared during the formative years of the post-Street Fighter II fighting-game boom, before games such as Samurai Shodown made armed combat a major subgenre.

games.title: Blasted
games.description:
Blasted (1988) is Bally Midway's unusual shooting-gallery game set around apartment buildings invaded by hostile aliens and cyborgs. Players aim a high-powered rifle through windows and across the building facade, eliminating attackers while avoiding innocent residents and incoming shots. The setting requires careful target selection, not just rapid fire, as a mistake can harm a tenant.

In its two-player mode, each participant attacks threats on the opposing player's building, creating a direct competitive variation on the gallery-shooter concept. The large urban backdrop and combination of hostile and innocent targets give Blasted a distinctive setting among late-1980s arcade shooters.

games.title: Blaster
games.description:
Blaster (1983) is Williams Electronics' spectacular first-person space shooter, designed by Eugene Jarvis and Larry DeMar as a loose narrative follow-up to Robotron: 2084. Humanity has been nearly wiped out by the Robotrons, and the player, one of its few survivors, pilots a spacecraft toward a rumored sanctuary called Paradise. Enemies rush directly toward the camera through fields of asteroids, grids and fantastical alien environments, while the ship must fire, steer and accelerate to survive.

The game is arranged as a succession of visually distinct waves, with stranded human astronauts appearing amid the dangers. Rescuing them by flying into them earns rewards, while shooting them is a costly mistake. Digitally scaled graphics give the impression of moving rapidly through three-dimensional space, an impressive spectacle for its period.

Blaster's ambitious visual technology and varied stage designs make it one of Williams' most adventurous early-1980s releases. Although it never achieved the fame of Defender or Robotron, its commitment to immersive viewpoint shooting anticipated later arcade space-combat experiences.

games.title: Blasto
games.description:
Blasto (1978), developed by Gremlin Industries for hardware related to Blockade, is a top-down minefield action game. Players steer a small tank or spacecraft around the arena and shoot stationary mines, trying to destroy as many as possible before the timer runs out. Shooting from too close is dangerous because the resulting explosion can destroy the player's vehicle.

In two-player play, the participants also have to avoid collisions and each other's gunfire while competing for targets. This mixture of deliberate positioning, shared hazards and simple shooting makes Blasto an early example of an arena game built around destructible obstacles rather than advancing enemy waves.

games.title: Blast Off
games.description:
Namco's Blast Off (1989) is a vertical scrolling space shooter and an unexpected sequel to the much earlier Bosconian. Instead of the original's free-roaming starfield battles, it adopts a conventional upward-scrolling format in which a single ship faces dense formations of enemies. The game's distinctive mechanic is the ability to switch between several colored firing patterns during play.

The different patterns cover the forward path, rear, flanks or diagonals, making weapon selection a continuing positional decision rather than a one-time pickup choice. Holding fire can produce more powerful attacks. Although the relationship to Bosconian is more historical than mechanical, Blast Off is an entertaining example of Namco adapting an older shooter property to late-1980s genre conventions.

games.title: Blaze On
games.description:
Blaze On, usually styled BlaZeon, is a 1992 side-scrolling shooter developed by Atlus. Its central invention is the Tranquilander, a weapon that allows the player's relatively weak fighter to capture certain enemy robots. After disabling a compatible foe, the player can enter its abandoned outline and transform into that machine, inheriting a new set of guns, movement properties and special attacks.

The captured forms often withstand additional hits, and losing one usually returns the player to the basic fighter instead of immediately ending a life. This gives each enemy encounter a second purpose: an opponent may also be a valuable weapon to acquire. The unusual transformation mechanic distinguishes Blaze On from more conventional weapon-pickup shooters and was retained in its Super Famicom adaptation.

games.title: Blazer
games.description:
Blazer (1987) is Namco's isometric scrolling combat shooter for System 1 hardware. Across a sequence of military missions, players alternate between a tank called Vanguard and a helicopter called Hardy, with a hovercraft called Atlanta appearing for the final operation. The angled view creates a battlefield where ground and aerial threats overlap, requiring careful positioning and attacks against enemies at different heights.

The tank can acquire upgrades and fuel supplies from defeated enemies, while the vehicle changes give later missions a different feel without abandoning the central shooting mechanics. Its isometric presentation and multi-vehicle structure place Blazer among Namco's more experimental action games of the late 1980s.

games.title: Blazing Star
games.description:
Blazing Star (1998), developed by Yumekobo and published by SNK for the Neo Geo, is a richly animated horizontal shooter and a successor in spirit to Pulstar. Set amid a conflict between planets corrupted by a sentient organic weapon called Brawshella, it offers six selectable ships with markedly different weapons. The player must dodge intricate enemy patterns, destroy giant biomechanical bosses and exploit each fighter's unique firing characteristics.

Alongside rapid shooting, players can charge attacks and use special variations that alter the coverage or direction of their weaponry. The scoring system rewards collecting bonus items and destroying enemy groups efficiently, giving expert players substantial incentive to master individual ships. Unlike Pulstar's austere R-Type-style challenge, Blazing Star places greater emphasis on speed, colorful effects and the spectacle of overwhelming firepower.
