Its digitized and pre-rendered visual elements pushed the Neo Geo's sprite hardware toward lavishly detailed results. It also became famous for its eccentric English voice samples and exuberant presentation. Today it is one of the system's signature late-period shooters, combining accessible action with surprising scoring depth.

games.title: Bloody Roar 2
games.description:
Bloody Roar 2 (1998) is the arcade sequel to Beastorizer, continuing Raizing and Eighting's distinctive 3D fighting series built around human-to-animal transformations. Fighters such as Yugo, Alice and Long can shift into powerful beast forms during a match, gaining new attacks, enhanced combinations and opportunities to recover momentum. The expanding roster, faster action and more elaborate presentation develop the original's emphasis on switching between human and beast fighting styles.

Transformation is not merely cosmetic: deciding when to enter beast form can change a round's tactical balance, and different characters gain different advantages. Known in various territories as Bringer of the New Age or The New Breed, the game was later adapted for the PlayStation and helped make Bloody Roar a recognizable alternative to more conventional polygonal fighters.

games.title: NFL Blitz
games.description:
NFL Blitz (1997) is Midway's outrageous arcade reinvention of American football, replacing strict simulation with spectacular tackles, oversized plays and relentlessly fast action. Official NFL teams compete in seven-on-seven matches where passing is flashy, defensive hits are brutal and many real-world penalties are simply ignored. A joystick and three-button arrangement make running, passing and tackling immediate rather than requiring a complicated simulation control scheme.

The game's 3D graphics, exaggerated animations and thundering presentation turn football into something closer to an action game. Its disregard for conventional sports-game restraint attracted players who might never approach a realistic NFL simulator. NFL Blitz became a substantial arcade and console franchise, establishing a distinctive late-1990s Midway style of over-the-top licensed sports entertainment.

games.title: NFL Blitz 2000 Gold Edition
games.description:
NFL Blitz 2000 Gold Edition (1999) is Midway's enhanced arcade entry in its spectacularly exaggerated NFL football series. Players select licensed professional teams and compete in fast seven-on-seven contests featuring huge tackles, aggressive passing and relaxed enforcement of real-world football rules. Up to four people can share a cabinet, while joystick-and-three-button controls keep games accessible even to players unfamiliar with simulation-style sports titles.

Gold Edition adds updated 1999 rosters, new offensive and defensive plays, team-specific formations, expanded animations and choices of fields or weather. The result is not merely a renamed earlier Blitz set, but a fuller late-1990s version of Midway's fast and confrontational arcade football formula.

games.title: NFL Blitz '99
games.description:
NFL Blitz '99 (1998) is Midway's second arcade entry in its exaggerated American football series. It retains the original's seven-on-seven action, official NFL teams and dramatic disregard for many real-world restrictions, favoring fast plays, long passes and bone-crunching tackles over detailed simulation. Updated rosters, additional plays and refinements to the established formula gave arcade regulars a fresh season of the same confrontational style.

The sequel also made four-player competition an important arcade attraction, allowing two players to cooperate on each side. With its mix of licensed teams, simple controls and outrageous collisions, Blitz '99 helped secure the series as one of the era's signature arcade sports franchises.

games.title: Black Dragon
games.description:
Black Dragon is the Japanese title of Capcom's Black Tiger (1987); this set is an unofficial bootleg of that fantasy platform game. A barbarian warrior journeys through interconnected ruins and towers, battling monsters with a spiked flail and thrown daggers while searching for the dragons responsible for the kingdom's ruin. Treasure chests, rescued sages and scattered coins support an equipment system in which better armor, stronger weapons and useful items can be purchased.

Unlike a pure linear brawler, Black Dragon rewards exploration of its many platforms and hidden areas. The bootleg documents an unauthorized arcade board implementation of the Japanese-titled game, not a separate adventure or an official Capcom redesign.

games.title: Black Heart
games.description:
Black Heart (1991) is a horizontally scrolling fantasy shooter developed by NMK and published by UPL. Instead of a spacecraft, the player rides a fire-breathing dragon through enemy-filled landscapes, battling flying creatures and large bosses while collecting items that strengthen its attacks. The combination of medieval-fantasy imagery and familiar scrolling-shooter action gives it a markedly different atmosphere from the military and science-fiction games that dominate the genre.

Originally released in Japanese arcades, Black Heart later became a minor cult discovery through preservation and re-releases, including Arcade Archives. Its dragon-mounted combat makes it a distinctive entry in UPL's final generation of arcade games.

games.title: Black Hole
games.description: Black Hole is a 1981 space shooter from TDS, running on hardware derived from Namco's Galaxian. Using a two-way joystick and a single firing button, players battle flying saucers and splitting neutron mines on a vertically oriented screen. The objective includes clearing obstacles, passing through special targets for bonus points, and attacking a moving target near the top of the playfield. Its unusual scoring arrangements distinguish it from the more straightforward alien-formation shooters of the period.

games.title: Black Panther
games.description: Konami's Black Panther (1987) is a side-scrolling action platformer with an unusual hero: a cybernetic black panther fighting to save Earth. Rather than controlling a human martial artist, the player races through enemy-filled stages, slashing with the animal's claws and leaping over hazards. Power-ups and additional time can be collected along the way, with a boss awaiting at the end of each stage. The eight-way joystick and two buttons handle movement, attack, and jumping, giving the game a brisk, acrobatic feel.

games.title: Black Tiger
games.description:
Black Tiger, released by Capcom in 1987 and titled Black Dragon in Japan, is a fantasy action platformer with a stronger emphasis on exploration than many contemporary arcade adventures. A barbarian warrior must cross eight dangerous regions to defeat three dragons threatening his kingdom. The screen scrolls both horizontally and vertically as he climbs pillars, leaps between ledges, and fights monsters with a chained mace while simultaneously throwing daggers.

Rescuing imprisoned wise men yields information, bonuses, or Zenny currency. Shops sell stronger weapons, protective armor, keys, and antidotes, while breakable walls and concealed dungeons reward careful investigation. Armor absorbs damage before the warrior's vitality is threatened, and poison temporarily prevents him from throwing daggers. The result is an unusual mix of arcade combat, route-finding, and resource management.

The Japanese Black Dragon is generally more demanding than the export version, with dearer shop items, additional falling-rock hazards, and tougher boss encounters. Hidden treasures even include nods to earlier Capcom games such as SonSon and Side Arms. Although often compared with Ghosts 'n Goblins, Black Tiger has a distinct personality thanks to its expansive stages and shopping system.

games.title: Black Touch
games.description: Black Touch is an unusual Korean puzzle game released in 1993, drawing on the tile-matching format of Dragon Punch. Its tiles replace conventional mahjong imagery with local motifs, including Korean traffic signs, baseball-team emblems, musical notation, fruit, and maps. The presentation also draws on a Korean comic about Byungitong's romantic misadventures. These distinctly local graphics are the chief documented feature of an otherwise obscure arcade release.

games.title: Blomby Car
games.description:
Blomby Car is a 1994 isometric rally racer made by the Italian team ABM & Gecas. Driving against the clock, players steer through winding tracks, reacting to roadside warnings of upcoming corners and hazards while using separate accelerator and brake buttons. Its elevated viewpoint and quick changes of direction recall Gaelco's World Rally, although the developers disputed claims that it was merely a graphics-swapped copy.

Distributed only as a conversion kit, Blomby Car had a relatively small arcade run. One unusual detail of its production is that a Peugeot 406 model supplied by a developer's family member was used in creating the player's car graphics. It remains a fascinating example of a small Italian team's contribution to the 1990s arcade-racing boom.

games.title: Block Block
games.description:
Capcom's Block Block (1991) is a polished, vertically oriented descendant of Breakout. Players move a paddle along the bottom of the screen, reflecting a bouncing ball into colorful brick formations while preventing it from escaping below. Its defining twist is a paddle-size gauge: when the counter runs down, the paddle contracts, making accurate returns progressively harder.

The full game offers 50 stages, with an introductory mode containing a smaller selection for beginners. Arcade sets exist for both dial and joystick controls, an unusually useful distinction for emulation and original-cabinet enthusiasts. Beneath its simple appearance, managing the paddle's size makes this more than a straightforward Arkanoid imitation.

games.title: Blockade
games.description:
Released by Gremlin in 1976, Blockade is one of the foundational arcade games of the maze-and-trail genre. Two players steer continually moving arrows around a rectangular field; each arrow leaves a permanent wall behind it. Turning is limited to right angles, and colliding with either player's trail or the outer boundary loses the round. The challenge rapidly becomes one of territory control, anticipating an opponent's route while preserving an escape corridor for yourself.

The original dedicated machine used four directional buttons per player rather than conventional joysticks. Operator settings determined whether a match ended after three, four, five, or six crashes. Its stark monochrome graphics and simple rules made it immediately understandable in an era when arcade video games were still establishing their vocabulary.

Designed by Lane Hauck with Ago Kiss, Blockade was Gremlin's first video arcade game and won recognition at the 1976 Music Operators of America exhibition. Its success inspired numerous competing implementations and a lineage of 'snake' and light-trail games, including later designs reminiscent of the light cycles in Tron. Gremlin itself followed the idea with titles such as Comotion and Hustle.

games.title: Block Carnival / Thunder & Lightning 2
games.description:
Block Carnival, also known as Thunder & Lightning 2, is a 1992 ball-and-paddle arcade game by Visco. It follows the colorful, character-driven approach of the original Thunder & Lightning rather than presenting only an abstract bat and ball. Players ricochet a ball through brick formations, keep it from dropping out of play, and contend with stage hazards while pursuing higher scores.

An interesting feature of the original arcade hardware is that a DIP-switch setting can change the displayed title between Block Carnival and Thunder & Lightning 2, including regional variations. It is a less familiar representative of the Japanese brick-breaker revival that followed Arkanoid.

games.title: Blocken
games.description: Blocken, released in 1994 by KID and Visco, turns the brick-breaker formula into a direct contest. Two players have separate wells filled with bricks and bounce balls against their own formations. Collecting enough power-ups sends additional blocks to the opponent's side, so an apparently successful rally can create trouble for the rival player. A match can end when one contestant clears the well, loses the ball, or has the paddle crushed by descending bricks. The competitive pressure and shifting balance of attack and defense set it apart from conventional single-player Breakout games.

games.title: Block Gal
games.description: Block Gal is a 1987 Sega and Vic Tokai brick-breaker with adult-oriented picture-reveal rewards. As in Breakout, the player uses a dial-controlled paddle to keep a ball aloft and knock away rows of blocks. Removing the obstruction progressively exposes an illustration of a woman, making the artwork itself an incentive to finish each board. The game runs on Sega System 1 hardware and also survives in bootleg form, an example of how the familiar paddle-game formula was repackaged for different arcade audiences.

games.title: Block Hole
games.description:
Block Hole, known as Quarth in Japan, is Konami's inventive 1989 combination of a shooting game and a geometric puzzle. Instead of shooting incoming enemies, players pilot a small craft at the bottom of the screen and fire square blocks upward. Descending arrangements must be completed into solid squares or rectangles, at which point the entire shape disappears and awards points. Larger completed shapes offer more reward but also require more precise placement.

The blocks steadily approach a danger line, and the game accelerates as rounds progress. Its rhythm is closer to a fixed shooter than to conventional falling-block games: players must aim quickly, choose whether to salvage an awkward shape, and prevent the pile from reaching their craft. Versions for the Game Boy, Famicom, and MSX2 helped preserve this unusual Konami design beyond the arcade.

games.title: Block Out
games.description:
Block Out is a striking 1989 attempt to take Tetris into three dimensions. Developed by California Dreams and released in arcades through Technos, it presents a deep rectangular pit viewed from above. Three-dimensional polycube pieces fall toward the floor, and the player uses three separate rotation controls to turn them around the X, Y, and Z axes before dropping them into place. Fully filled horizontal layers vanish, but any empty pocket can become a serious obstacle as the stack rises.

The extra axis transforms familiar falling-block strategy into a problem of spatial visualization. Players must judge shapes at different depths, predict hidden voids, and learn to rotate awkward pieces without losing track of their orientation. Arcade play supports a competitive two-player mode, while adjustable starting stages and pit dimensions add considerable variation. Block Out remains one of the most distinctive early interpretations of the three-dimensional puzzle genre.

games.title: Blood Bros.
games.description:
Blood Bros. (1990) is TAD Corporation's Wild West successor to Cabal, retaining its unusual combination of character movement and crosshair shooting. A cowboy and a Native American fighter pursue the outlaw Big Bad John through a series of gunfights. Seen from behind, the heroes dodge along the foreground while the player aims a cursor at bandits, gun emplacements, and destructible scenery deeper into the picture.

Ordinary ammunition is unlimited, but dynamite is scarce and particularly valuable against crowded screens and sturdy targets. Holding the fire button prioritizes aiming at the cost of mobility, creating a constant risk-and-reward decision. The lively frontier setting, collapsing cover, two-player cooperation, and numerous enemy entrances give Blood Bros. a flavor all its own despite its close mechanical relationship to Cabal.

games.title: Blood Storm
games.description:
BloodStorm is a 1994 one-on-one fighting game from Incredible Technologies, published by Strata and conceived as a spiritual successor to Time Killers. Set in a ruined future, it has combatants battling for power with specialized gauntlet weapons. Its notoriety comes from graphic dismemberment: fighters can lose arms during a round, and the corresponding attack buttons become unusable. Dedicated limb buttons and a separate block control give the game an unusual control scheme even among the experimental fighters of the mid-1990s.

Beyond the gore, BloodStorm includes special finishing attacks, character powers, and a password system for recording progress. It was positioned as a rival to Mortal Kombat but never achieved comparable popularity; announced Saturn and PlayStation ports did not reach release. Its blend of macabre spectacle and mechanically consequential injury makes it an instructive artifact of the arcade fighting-game arms race.

games.title: Blood Warrior
games.description: Blood Warrior, released by Kaneko in 1994 and titled Ooedo Fight in Japan, is a digitized-sprite fighting game set in a caricature of feudal Japan. It follows Shogun Warriors (Fujiyama Buster) but abandons hand-drawn character art in favor of photographed performers, blood effects, and violent finishing moves. The nine selectable fighters embody exaggerated Japanese historical and folkloric archetypes, while combat retains much of the familiar movement and special-move structure of Street Fighter II-style fighters. Its odd mixture of period satire and Mortal Kombat-inspired shock value distinguishes it from more conventional tournament games.

games.title: Bloxeed
games.description:
Sega's Bloxeed (1990) is a variation on Tetris that makes the contest less predictable. Familiar falling tetrominoes must be fitted together to complete horizontal lines, but occasional garbage rows rise into the playing field and special blocks introduce additional ways to manipulate the stack. These disruptions force players to adapt rather than rely on a rehearsed clearing pattern.

AdvanceMAME's represented versions include releases associated with Sega System C/C-2 and System 18 hardware. The System 18 edition added a counterclockwise rotation button, revised title-screen effects, and fixes to an earlier version. It is an intriguing example of Sega adapting a worldwide puzzle craze into a distinct coin-operated product.

games.title: Blasteroids
games.description:
Blasteroids is Atari Games' late-1980s reinvention of Asteroids, released in 1987-88 as the third major installment in the series. The spare vector graphics of its predecessors give way to colorful raster artwork, alien enemies, power-ups, and large end-of-game encounters. As before, a ship rotates and thrusts through open space, breaking rocks into smaller fragments, but momentum now has to be managed alongside a finite energy supply.

The player's spacecraft can change among three forms with different speed, firepower, and defensive characteristics, and crystals recovered from destroyed objects replenish energy. A branching sector map lets players choose routes toward the confrontation with the enormous boss Mukor. Two people can play together, adding cooperative tactics to a series originally known for solitary survival. The substantial changes make Blasteroids feel less like an update and more like a new interpretation of the arcade original.

games.title: Bells & Whistles
games.description:
Bells & Whistles is the European name of Konami's 1991 arcade shooter Detana!! TwinBee. The two pilots guide the colorful TwinBee and WinBee craft through seven vertically scrolling stages, firing at airborne foes and dropping bombs on ground targets. Shooting floating bells changes their colors, and catching the right ones awards upgrades, turning a simple-looking collectible into a demanding power-up management system.

The game expanded TwinBee's visual personality with expressive character art and elaborate, whimsical scenery. Its soundtrack, cooperative play, and chargeable attacks helped define the later 'cute-'em-up' style. Detana!! TwinBee was also notable for the involvement of artist Shūjirō Hamakawa, known as Shuzilow.HA, whose work became closely associated with the series.

games.title: Blue Hawk
games.description: Blue Hawk is a 1993 vertically scrolling military shooter from the Korean developer Dooyong. Piloting a jet fighter, players fight over naval and land battlefields, attacking enemy aircraft, tanks, warships, gun emplacements, and stage bosses. Destroyed targets release distinct power-ups, including stronger weapons, homing missiles, speed boosts, extra bombs, and additional lives. Two players can fly cooperatively, and the game's weapon selection recalls Dooyong's earlier Pollux. It is a comparatively obscure but fully featured example of Korea's early-1990s arcade shooting scene.

games.title: Blue Print
games.description:
Blue Print, released in 1982 by Zilec and distributed by Bally Midway in North America, mixes maze action with a comic construction puzzle. A burglar-like character races around a neighborhood opening houses to find pieces of a machine. Each collected part must be carried back to a central blueprint, where the contraption gradually takes shape. Houses can also contain bombs, which must be disposed of quickly, while pursuing enemies interfere with the search.

When the machine is completed, the player can use it to attack the monster threatening the girl at the top of the screen. The game alternates frantic collecting, route planning, and a brief action payoff, all set to jaunty audiovisual effects. This strange, multi-step objective makes Blue Print stand out among the many straightforward maze chases of its era.

games.title: Blue Shark
games.description: Blue Shark is a 1978 Midway underwater shooting game that places players behind a gun sight looking into a seascape. A pistol-shaped controller is used to aim and fire at sharks and other marine targets as they move across the display, with limited time to accumulate points. The game uses monochrome imagery combined with physical cabinet artwork to create an underwater scene, illustrating the elaborate presentation techniques manufacturers used before colorful raster displays became commonplace.

games.title: Blazing Tornado
games.description: Blazing Tornado is a 1994 professional wrestling game developed and published for Japanese arcades by Human Entertainment. It presents exaggerated wrestlers in the ring with grapples, throws, strikes, and spectacular finishing moves, emphasizing the theatrical side of the sport. Its arcade controls translate the complex exchanges of wrestling into fast, accessible bouts, while character designs and animated special attacks give each competitor a distinct style. It was also adapted for the Sega Saturn as Fire Pro Gaiden: Blazing Tornado.

games.title: beatmania
games.description:
Konami's beatmania, first released in 1997, was a landmark in arcade rhythm games and the foundation of the BEMANI music-game family. Instead of controlling a traditional on-screen character, players stand at a miniature DJ console equipped with five keys and a scratchable turntable. As note bars descend toward the timing line, each correctly timed key press or scratch adds part of the song, builds a combo, and helps maintain the performance gauge needed to continue.

Its physical controls were integral to the appeal: players appeared to be performing music rather than merely pressing buttons in response to it. The selection of dance, hip-hop, and electronic tracks, together with the possibility of playing side by side, made the cabinet a social as well as musical attraction. beatmania helped establish an arcade genre that Konami would develop through countless later mixes and related series.

games.title: beatmania 2nd MIX
games.description: beatmania 2nd MIX (1998) is Konami's follow-up to the original five-key DJ rhythm game. Players manipulate five piano-style keys and a turntable as scrolling notes reach the timing line, maintaining a performance gauge while performing successive songs. This revision refreshed the music selection and extended the early beatmania formula at a time when Konami's BEMANI line was rapidly gaining an audience. Its dedicated scratch controller remains central to the challenge, requiring coordination quite different from ordinary button-only rhythm games.

games.title: beatmania 4th MIX
games.description: Konami's beatmania 4th MIX (1999) continues the original five-key rhythm series with another collection of dance and club-oriented tracks. Players perform songs on the cabinet's five keys and scratch turntable, following falling note patterns while protecting the groove gauge that determines whether they advance. The combination of increasingly intricate note charts and a renewed song list gave established beatmania players fresh material without changing the recognizable DJ-console format.

games.title: beatmania 5th MIX
games.description: beatmania 5th MIX, released in 1999, is another installment in Konami's pioneering DJ-simulation rhythm series. Each player has five keys and a scratchable turntable, and must hit timed note patterns in sync with the selected track. Accurate performances raise the score and sustain the groove gauge, while mistakes can prevent progression. Like other early mixes, its identity is defined by the music selection and chart design, making it a distinct snapshot of the series' rapidly evolving late-1990s club-music repertoire.

games.title: beatmania 6th MIX
games.description: beatmania 6th MIX (2001) continues Konami's five-key DJ series with a selection emphasizing contemporary club music, including tracks associated with British artists. Players follow falling notes by pressing keys and scratching the turntable, balancing accuracy and gauge management over successive songs. This release also introduced a Free mode that gave players additional freedom to perform mixes. The mix illustrates how the original beatmania series continued experimenting with musical styles and play options after its initial breakthrough.

games.title: Blade Master
games.description: Blade Master is a 1991 fantasy side-scrolling beat-'em-up by Irem, also known as Cross Blades! in Japan. Players choose between the sword-wielding Roy and the spear-carrying Arnold, then fight through a succession of grotesque creatures and elaborate bosses to rescue Princess Emina from the King of Darkness. Breakable objects and pickups provide health or bonuses, while the two heroes' different weapons create a distinctive feel in combat. Its sweeping sprite work, imposing monsters, and two-player cooperation make it one of Irem's more memorable lesser-known action games.

games.title: BMC Bowling
games.description: BMC Bowling, also known as Konkyuu no Hoshi, is an obscure 1994 Japanese arcade bowling game from BMC. The documented machine is a single-player, button-controlled bowling simulation rather than a joystick-driven action title. Its Motorola 68000 hardware and unusual sound components give it a distinctive technical profile, but very little contemporary commentary survives about the details of its scoring or shot selection.

games.title: beatmania complete MIX 2
games.description: beatmania complete MIX 2 (2000) is Konami's follow-up compilation in the original five-key DJ rhythm series. It brings together substantial portions of the fourth and fifth mixes alongside additional material, offering a broad song selection in one cabinet. The core performance remains based on five keys, a scratch turntable, scrolling note charts, and the groove gauge. It was also marketed in North America under the hiphopmania Complete MIX 2 name.

games.title: beatmania complete MIX
games.description: Released in 1999, beatmania complete MIX gathers songs and modes associated with the earliest beatmania releases into a single arcade edition. Players mix by striking five keys and scratching a turntable precisely as notes descend, trying to keep the groove gauge high enough to finish each song. Rather than introducing a wholly new control scheme, this compilation offers a convenient retrospective of the series' formative music catalog. In North America it was known as hiphopmania Complete MIX.

games.title: beatmania CORE REMIX
games.description: beatmania CORE REMIX, released in 2000, takes a different approach to Konami's five-key arcade DJ formula by revisiting music from the earliest installments. Its track list combines classic compositions with newly arranged remixes spanning electronic and dance styles. Players still perform with five keys and the scratch turntable, but the familiar music receives fresh charts and arrangements. The game is especially interesting as an early example of BEMANI treating its own musical history as material for reinterpretation.

games.title: beatmania f. Dreams Come True

variants.title: beatmania f. Dreams Come True (ver JA-A)

games.description: beatmania featuring DREAMS COME TRUE is a 2000 Japanese rhythm-game collaboration devoted to the J-pop group Dreams Come True. The usual five-key and turntable controls are used to perform charted versions and remixes of the band's songs, giving this edition a more focused musical identity than the standard numbered mixes. Its distinctive MONKeY LIVE mode links songs with short turntable-scratching sections that can restore part of the player's gauge. This unusual licensed spin-off shows how flexible the original beatmania cabinet format had become.

games.title: BMX Stunts
games.description: BMX Stunts is a relatively obscure 1985 arcade cycling game associated with the BMX Trials home-computer release by JetSoft. It centers on bicycle stunt and racing action rather than motor vehicles, and its arcade implementation uses hardware derived from the Galaxian family with a 6502 processor. Surviving documentation is limited, making the coin-operated version an interesting footnote in the crossover between mid-1980s British computer games and arcade conversions.

games.title: Vs. Raid on Bungeling Bay
games.description:
Vs. Raid on Bungeling Bay is Nintendo's 1985 arcade adaptation of the helicopter-combat game designed by Will Wright and first published by Brøderbund for home computers. Viewed from above, the player's helicopter flies across enemy territory bombing factories that feed the Bungeling war machine. Hostile ships, aircraft, tanks, and shore defenses threaten the mission, while the friendly aircraft carrier serves as a place to refuel, rearm, and repair if it has not been destroyed.

The arcade edition uses Nintendo's Vs. System and derives from the Famicom adaptation. The game is historically notable as Wright's first published design, years before SimCity; the evolving map and enemy production systems already hinted at his fascination with complex simulated environments.

games.title: Bonanza Bros
games.description:
Bonanza Bros. is a 1990 Sega action game about two brothers, Robo and Mobo, carrying out elaborately staged burglaries. The objective in each building is to collect a specified set of valuables and escape to the rooftop before time runs out. Guards patrol balconies, doors, and staircases; the brothers can shoot them with stun guns or evade them by ducking behind scenery and using the building's multiple routes.

The screen shows an entire cross-section of a building, encouraging players to plan how to clear its floors efficiently. Split-screen two-player cooperation allows the thieves to divide the work, although bumping into guards or attracting attention can disrupt the plan. The stylized characters, slapstick animations, and blend of stealth with platform action give Bonanza Bros. a flavor unlike Sega's more straightforward shooters. It was an early showcase for the high-resolution Sega System 24 board.

games.title: Body Slam
games.description: Body Slam is Sega's 1986 women's professional wrestling game, released in Japan as Dump Matsumoto. Inspired by the Japanese joshi wrestling scene, it features recognizable performers associated with the sport, including Dump Matsumoto and the Crush Gals. Players grapple, strike, and attempt pins in the ring rather than simply trading attacks as in a conventional fighting game. Its theatrical presentation and real-wrestler connections distinguish it from the largely fictional wrestling rosters of other mid-1980s arcades. Sega later adapted the game for the Master System as Pro Wrestling, replacing the licensed wrestlers with fictional characters.

games.title: Bogey Manor
games.description: Bogey Manor, released in 1985, follows a young ghost hunter named Fritz through a succession of haunted buildings. Each level is a multi-floor maze filled with crystal balls that must be destroyed using his sword. Ghosts, witches, Frankenstein-like monsters, and other creatures pursue him through corridors and doors, while a map helps players navigate the house under a time limit. A magic glove can briefly immobilize enemies. Once the last crystal ball is broken, the house begins to collapse and Fritz must escape, giving the end of each round an extra burst of urgency.

games.title: Boggy '84
games.description: Boggy '84 is a 1983 Japanese platform game also represented in unofficial arcade sets. The player explores compact, multi-level stages collecting keys while avoiding roaming enemies. Ladders connect the floors, but springboards let the hero jump rapidly between levels and take routes unavailable to many pursuers. Its single-screen, floor-by-floor design recalls early maze platformers such as Space Panic and Mappy. The relatively simple presentation makes it a curious example of the many variations on the collecting-and-escaping formula that appeared in the early 1980s.

games.title: Bomb Bee
games.description:
Bomb Bee, released by Namco in 1979, is the second title in the company's early series combining Breakout with pinball. Instead of using a single horizontal bat, the player rotates a controller to move paddles at the sides of a compact table, keeping a ball in play as it strikes rows of bricks, bumpers, spinners, and scoring targets. Clearing bricks changes the scoring opportunities around the board, rewarding control of the ball rather than mere survival.

The game followed Gee Bee and preceded Cutie Q, forming a trilogy associated with designer Toru Iwatani before his work on Pac-Man. Its combination of digital pinball fixtures and brick-breaking mechanics shows Namco experimenting with familiar amusement-machine ideas during the formative years of video arcades.

games.title: Bomb Jack
games.description:
Bomb Jack is Tehkan's celebrated 1984 single-screen platform game, starring a masked hero who must gather 24 bombs scattered around famous-looking monuments. Jack can leap extraordinary distances and control his descent by fluttering through the air, an ability that turns each screen into a precise exercise in aerial navigation. Hostile birds, mummies, and transforming creatures steadily multiply, making it dangerous to hesitate.

Collecting a lit bomb causes the next bomb in a sequence to ignite, and gathering enough illuminated bombs in one round awards a substantial bonus. Special collectibles can temporarily freeze enemies or make them vulnerable, creating a constant trade-off between scoring ambition and survival. The stages' recognizable backgrounds, including Egyptian architecture and the Acropolis, give the simple arenas a distinctive visual theme.

Bomb Jack became a prominent arcade and home-computer favorite and inspired follow-ups such as Mighty Bomb Jack and Bomb Jack Twin. Its unusually responsive jumping and subtle high-score rules remain the heart of its appeal: a quick clear is not necessarily the best clear, and skillful players can plan a route through the bombs rather than collecting them at random.

games.title: Bomb Kick
games.description: Bomb Kick is a 1998 single-screen platform game built around using explosives to remove enemies. Players travel through compact stages, positioning bombs to catch moving targets while avoiding the hazards created by their own attacks. Its style closely resembles Compile's Bomber Through GoGo! Jump Hero Gaiden 2, a game distributed in the 1996 Japanese PC collection Disc Station 12. The arcade release is a comparatively obscure example of the late-1990s revival of simple action-puzzle platformers.

games.title: Bombs Away
games.description: Bombs Away is an unreleased 1988 Jaleco vertical shooter preserved in prototype form. Developed in Japan as Block Buster, it uses a scrolling, overhead playfield and an eight-way joystick with two buttons for combat. The surviving arcade program represents an export version that was never commercially launched under the Bombs Away name. Its historical interest comes as much from the recovered prototype and its relationship to Jaleco's Japanese release as from its conventional scrolling-shooter format.

games.title: Bongo
games.description: Bongo is an early-1980s side-view platform adventure in which an explorer flees a persistent red dinosaur across a long series of cavern screens. The route runs from left to right through narrow ledges, lava pits, falling rocks, birds, and other obstacles. Lingering too long gives the dinosaur time to catch up, so even when the way ahead looks difficult, standing still is seldom safe. The game also rewards collecting bonus objects and features a means of trapping the pursuing creature. Its flick-screen layout and cartoon prehistoric theme place it among the inventive but often forgotten platformers that followed Donkey Kong.

games.title: B.C. Kid / Bonk's Adventure / Kyukyoku!! PC Genjin
games.description: B.C. Kid / Bonk's Adventure / Kyukyoku!! PC Genjin is a 1994 arcade adaptation of the cartoon platform series made famous on NEC's PC Engine. The hero is a bald prehistoric boy whose oversized head is his principal weapon: he attacks enemies with headbutts while navigating colorful prehistoric landscapes filled with dinosaurs and other creatures. The arcade game spans 21 stages and preserves the lighthearted character of its console inspiration. It is notable as a comparatively uncommon example of a well-known home-console mascot being reworked for coin-operated play.

games.title: Bonze Adventure
games.description:
Bonze Adventure is Taito's 1988 fantasy platformer, known in Japan as Jigoku Meguri. The player controls a Buddhist monk journeying through an underworld filled with spirits, snakes, giant eyes, and other supernatural enemies. He attacks by sending out magical prayer beads, which can be strengthened until the projectiles become enormous. Careful jumping and deliberate shots are important because enemies often approach from awkward elevations.

The game's religious and folkloric imagery is unusually specific for an arcade platformer, and its time limit is displayed as a row of gradually melting candles. Power-ups supplied by helpful divine figures occasionally ease the journey. Its distinctive Japanese setting, later adapted for several home systems, makes Bonze Adventure an evocative alternative to more familiar medieval fantasy games.

games.title: Boogie Wings
games.description:
Boogie Wings, called The Great Ragtime Show in Japan, is one of Data East's most inventive horizontal shooters. Released in 1992, it begins with the player flying a World War I-style biplane carrying a large hook behind it. This hook can snag objects, vehicles, and even enemies; swinging or releasing the captured cargo turns the surroundings into improvised weapons. The stages are filled with elaborate visual jokes and absurd surprises, including a mechanical Santa Claus boss.

Losing the aircraft does not necessarily end the run. The pilot can continue on foot, commandeer other vehicles, or ride unexpected mounts, changing the rhythm from aerial shooter to a looser action game. Two-player play and a constant supply of interactive objects encourage experimentation rather than simply memorizing waves of bullets. Its eccentric mixture of aviation, slapstick, and shifting vehicles gives it a personality all its own.

games.title: Boomer Rang'r / Genesis
games.description: Boomer Rang'r, also known as Genesis, is a 1983 Data East Cassette System action game set in a cartoon prehistoric landscape. The hero Whirley searches for lost treasure while battling club-wielding cavemen, dinosaurs, and vultures that drop rocks. His principal weapon is a returning boomerang, but he can also seize an enemy dinosaur mount and use its fire-breathing attack. This combination of ranged combat, riding, and prehistoric hazards makes it a distinctive early example of a fantasy-themed arcade action game.

games.title: Boot Hill
games.description:
Boot Hill is Midway's 1977 Western gunfight game and a successor to Gun Fight. One cowboy stands on either side of a black-and-white arena, trying to shoot the opponent while making use of cacti and passing wagons as cover. Each player has a limited supply of bullets, and the scenery gradually breaks apart under gunfire, so safe firing lines become more exposed as a duel progresses.

The cabinet's most unusual feature is its pair of controls for each player: a smaller joystick for movement and a larger gunlike lever with a trigger for aiming and firing. A physical mirror and illuminated backdrop add depth to the otherwise simple monochrome graphics. Boot Hill captures a period when inventive cabinet hardware was as important to an arcade game's identity as its on-screen action.

games.title: Borench
games.description: Sega's Borench (1990) is an isometric puzzle game about guiding a constantly rolling ball toward a goal. Rather than steering the ball directly around corners, the player places or manipulates blocks on a grid to redirect its course as the screen advances. Poorly planned routes can send it over an edge or let it drift out of the playable area. The challenge comes from anticipating its motion and constructing a safe path quickly, giving the game a different feel from more directly controlled marble games such as Marble Madness.

games.title: Born To Fight
games.description: Born To Fight is an obscure military-themed arcade light-gun shooter designed around optical machine-gun controllers. One or two players aim directly at the display and fire on enemy soldiers and other targets from a first-person viewpoint. Its focus is on immediate gunfire rather than character movement, making it an example of the dedicated shooting galleries that remained popular alongside joystick-driven action games. The surviving documentation gives few further details about its missions or release history.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Bosconian
games.description:
Bosconian, Namco's 1981 space shooter, replaces the fixed formations of Galaxian with a freely scrolling battlefield. The player's Star Fighter moves in eight directions across a map studded with enemy space stations, asteroids, mines, and missiles. The ship fires forward and backward at the same time, while an on-screen radar shows the location of the remaining targets. To clear a round, every hexagonal Bosco base must be destroyed, either by taking out its six outer cannons or by aiming a precise shot through the narrow opening to its central core.

Later bases acquire additional defenses, and hostile squadrons can trigger more intense alert states. The need to steer, monitor the radar, and choose between risky direct attacks and safer dismantling makes the game unusually tactical for its era. Its spoken warnings, especially the memorable 'Alert! Alert!' call, helped give it an instantly recognizable personality.

Bosconian was a notable Japanese arcade success and became an important ancestor of later free-roaming shooters. It was followed indirectly by Namco's Blast Off and Final Blaster, and it remains an illuminating demonstration of how the company expanded its space-shooter formula beyond fixed screens and rigid enemy formations.

games.title: Botanic
games.description: Botanic is a 1984 maze game with a botanical twist: the player guides a silkworm around a network of branches, gathering leaves while evading spiders and other insects. The unusual complication is that connections between branches are not always apparent until the relevant leaf is collected, so the maze must be learned as it is explored. Its collecting-and-avoidance structure recalls Pac-Man, but the branching plant layout and partially concealed routes provide a different sort of navigation puzzle.

games.title: Battle of the Solar System
games.description: Battle of the Solar System, often abbreviated B.O.T.S.S., is a 1992 futuristic combat game from MicroProse. Players command a heavily armed giant robot through three-dimensional war zones, fighting opposing machines with weapons such as lasers and missiles. The game emphasizes a sense of scale and mechanical combat rather than the flat perspective of traditional arcade shooters. Shown at the 1992 ATE exhibition in London, it was MicroProse's second coin-operated game and an interesting attempt to bring the company's simulation-oriented sensibility into the arcade.

games.title: Bottom of the Ninth
games.description: Bottom of the Ninth is Konami's 1989 arcade baseball game, released in Japan as Main Stadium. Players choose teams representing major American baseball cities and compete against the machine or another player. Batters can adjust their stance and swing, while pitchers select from different deliveries, so each at-bat involves more than simply timing a button press. Its comparatively grounded baseball mechanics and strong emphasis on the pitcher-batter contest distinguish it from more extravagant sports games of the period.

games.title: Boulder Dash / Boulder Dash Part 2
games.description:
Boulder Dash / Boulder Dash Part 2 brings the classic digging-and-collecting puzzle adventure to arcades in 1990. As Rockford, the player tunnels through caves gathering enough diamonds to unlock the exit while avoiding roaming creatures and constantly shifting rocks. Boulders obey simple but dangerous physical rules: undermining them can release a deadly fall, yet the same falling stones can be used to crush pursuing enemies.

The arcade package draws on the game created by Peter Liepa and Chris Gray for home computers and pairs it with additional cave challenges. Successful play depends on planning the order of tunnels and anticipating chain reactions rather than merely moving quickly. The tension between collecting gems and reshaping the landscape gives Boulder Dash its lasting puzzle-action appeal.

games.title: The Bounty
games.description: The Bounty is a 1982 river-combat game by Orca in which the player pilots a boat upstream through a hostile waterway. Flags are collected for points, floating oil supplies keep the vessel fueled, and mines and enemy fire must be avoided or destroyed. The river setting adds a resource-management element to the shooting: staying alive is not enough if the boat runs out of fuel. Its modest scope and nautical theme make it an unusual early scrolling-action title.

games.title: Bowling Alley
games.description: Bowling Alley is a late-1970s black-and-white bowling arcade game from Midway, supporting up to four players. A trackball sends the ball toward a full rack of ten pins, while a separate control allows straight or hook shots. Players can choose ordinary regulation scoring or a Flash variation in which the timing of a shot affects the potential score. The original cabinet supplemented the screen with dedicated scoring indicators, reflecting the close relationship between video bowling and traditional coin-operated bowling amusements.

games.title: Bowl-O-Rama
games.description: Bowl-O-Rama (1991) is a bowling arcade game designed as an upgrade for Capcom Bowling hardware. It contains three variants: Regulation Bowling follows the standard ten-pin rules, Flash-O-Matic rewards carefully timed shots with scoring multipliers, and BlackJack turns pin counts into a target of 21. The games use familiar bowling presentation but give players different strategic goals and scoring rhythms. Its conversion-kit origins make it a good example of how operators could refresh an established cabinet without purchasing an entirely new machine.

games.title: Bowmen
games.description: Bowmen is a 1994 Spanish arcade shooter by Ten-Level, distinguished by its irreverent adult humor. The player controls a winged cherub who fires arrows and other projectiles at colored targets and block formations. The introductory sequence explains his unlikely transformation from a mischievous voyeur into an angelic archer, and the stages continue the mixture of religious imagery, comedy, and risqué artwork. It is a peculiar local variation on the arcade shooting-and-target-clearing formula.

games.title: Boxer
games.description: Boxer is an unreleased 1978 Atari black-and-white boxing prototype shown from an overhead perspective. Two figures circle one another in a compact arena, attempting to land punches in a one-on-one contest. Its most memorable feature was an experimental pair of swiveling punch controls, designed to make the physical action of striking part of the game itself. The mechanisms reportedly proved vulnerable to rough arcade use and required repeated strengthening; despite those efforts, the prototype did not perform well enough in testing to receive a commercial release.

games.title: Boxing Bugs
games.description:
Boxing Bugs is a 1981 Cinematronics vector shooter with an unusual combination of a gun and a boxing glove. The player's rotating turret sits inside an octagonal defensive wall while hostile insects move around the outside, carrying bombs into positions that threaten the enclosure. The turret can fire projectiles outward or extend a glove to punch enemies and bombs, requiring the player to judge both direction and attack type.

The game is one of the last vector-graphics productions associated with Cinematronics and was manufactured in small numbers. Its curious design resembles a reversal of Star Castle: instead of attacking a protected central object, the player must defend the center against encroaching foes.

games.title: Boxy Boy
games.description:
Boxy Boy is Namco's 1990 arcade adaptation of Sokoban, released in Japan as Souko Ban Deluxe. Players guide a small warehouse worker around compact rooms, pushing crates onto marked destinations. Each box can be pushed but not pulled, so a single careless move can trap it against a wall or block the route to another objective. The puzzle is solved only when every crate reaches its proper position.

Namco's System 1 hardware gives the austere original formula colorful sprites and a friendlier presentation, while a reset control allows an unsalvageable room to be restarted. Rather than demanding speed or reflexes, Boxy Boy rewards thinking several moves ahead and learning to recognize dead ends.

games.title: Block Panic DX
games.description: Block Panic DX is a fast-paced action puzzle game developed by Blastar for the Neo Geo MVS platform and released on January 1, 2025. Players clear and rearrange falling blocks under time pressure across single-player and competitive modes.

games.title: Bradley Trainer
games.description:
Bradley Trainer is a remarkable military training adaptation of Atari's vector-graphics Battlezone. Developed around 1980-81 after discussions with the United States Army, it was intended to help familiarize personnel with aspects of the Bradley fighting vehicle rather than to entertain arcade customers. The familiar first-person wireframe landscape remains, but the targets, control hardware, and rules were reworked for gunnery practice.

Unlike in Battlezone, opposing tanks generally do not fire back. Instead, the exercise emphasizes aiming and target recognition, with penalties for shooting friendly vehicles and a limited ammunition supply. Only a small number of units were made, making Bradley Trainer one of the most unusual crossovers between commercial arcade technology and military simulation.

games.title: Brain
games.description: Brain is a 1986 action shooter that shifts between vehicle combat and exploration on foot. The opening portions feature side-scrolling spacecraft or gunship action, with the screen able to move vertically as the player proceeds to the right. Later, the pilot lands and explores hostile interiors and tunnels as an armed space ranger, shooting enemies and collecting computer disks. The change in viewpoint and pacing gives Brain a more varied structure than the typical uninterrupted horizontal shooter, even though its atmosphere remains firmly science fiction.

games.title: B.Rap Boys
games.description:
B.Rap Boys is Kaneko's 1992 follow-up to DJ Boy, expanding the earlier game's roller-skating beat-'em-up formula into three-player cooperative mayhem. Its three selectable heroes ride a skateboard, bicycle, or roller skates and fight through side-scrolling urban stages using punches, kicks, weapons, and vehicles. Unlike simple palette-swapped teams, the characters have distinct looks and styles.

The game's personality comes from its exaggerated hip-hop aesthetic and extensive sampled voices and rap music, including recordings associated with the group 3 Stories High. With an energetic soundtrack and a broader combat system than its predecessor, B.Rap Boys is an unusual artifact of the period when arcade designers were experimenting with youth-culture imagery and cooperative brawlers.

games.title: Borderline
games.description:
Borderline is a 1981 Sega arcade game that combines vehicle shooting with maze-like route clearing. The player drives an armed jeep through four enemy sectors, trying to destroy refineries and energy installations while surviving tanks, missiles, and aircraft. The opening section resembles a forward-scrolling shooter, but later areas require maneuvering through vegetation and using the jeep's firepower to open routes through the landscape.

The changing stage rules make Borderline more varied than a conventional straight-line military shooter. It is also historically notable as a late entry on Sega's Vic Dual hardware, just as the company was moving toward more elaborate arcade systems.

games.title: Breakers
games.description:
Breakers is Visco's 1996 one-on-one fighting game for the SNK Neo Geo, known for exceptionally responsive controls and fluid combo play. Eight selectable characters bring distinct martial arts styles, special moves, and personal motivations to a colorful international tournament. The four-button layout, aggressive movement options, and ability to link attacks into long strings encourage a fast, offensive style of fighting.

Although its character archetypes recall the better-known Street Fighter and Fatal Fury series, Breakers won a dedicated following for the quality of its combat system. The prototype was previously shown as Tenrin no Syo Chicago, and the game was expanded into Breakers Revenge in 1998. Its reputation as a cult competitive fighter has outlasted its relatively modest original profile.

games.title: Brick Zone
games.description: Brick Zone is a 1992 arcade brick-breaker in the Arkanoid tradition, in which a paddle keeps a ball moving through patterned blocks. The game mixes conventional target-clearing action with unusual boss encounters and picture backgrounds that include adult-oriented imagery. Its blend of familiar paddle mechanics and provocative rewards reflects a niche in the early-1990s arcade market, when many small manufacturers sought to distinguish otherwise conventional puzzle games through themed graphics.

games.title: Burning Rival
games.description:
Burning Rival is a 1993 one-on-one fighting game developed by Sega AM2 for Sega System 32 hardware. Eight fighters, including a ninja, a martial artist, an American football player, and a flamboyant wrestler, meet in the fictional Destiny City tournament. Battles use a six-button layout with three punches and three kicks, special attacks, and best-of-three-round matches.

Although AdvanceMAME's catalog metadata sometimes dates it to 1992, the documented Japanese arcade release was in July 1993. Burning Rival was Sega AM2's first fighting game and was produced with Yu Suzuki's involvement shortly before Virtua Fighter changed the direction of the genre. Its large, expressive hand-drawn sprites and comedic tone make it an interesting companion to the studio's better-known 3D work.

games.title: Brixian
games.description: BriXian is a Korean puzzle arcade game released in 1993 by Cheil Computer System. Its basic challenge resembles Puzznic: players shift marked blocks around single-screen arrangements to bring matching pieces into contact and clear them. Many stages feature moving platforms or elevators that must be incorporated into the solution, and a strict timer makes even simple-looking layouts urgent. Its movement-based puzzles distinguish it from the more common falling-block games of the period.

games.title: Break Thru
games.description:
Break Thru, known in Japan as Kyohkoh-Toppa, is a 1986 Data East side-scrolling combat game in which the player drives an armored vehicle into enemy territory to recover the stolen PK430 aircraft. Its distinctive feature is a powerful jump ability: the vehicle can leap over gaps, obstacles, and incoming threats while firing forward at enemy vehicles and emplacements.

The journey takes in mountains, damaged bridges, jungles, and fortified urban areas, each filled with hazards that demand precise timing. Rather than offering a conventional racing challenge, Break Thru mixes the pace of a horizontal shooter with platform-style obstacle avoidance. Its unusually agile military vehicle and dramatic terrain shifts give it a recognizable identity among mid-1980s action games.

games.title: Burnin' Rubber
games.description:
Burnin' Rubber, released by Data East in 1982 and called Bump 'n' Jump in North America, is an overhead road-combat game built around two simple actions: bumping and jumping. The player's car speeds along scrolling highways, forcing rivals off the road for points while avoiding wrecks. With sufficient speed, it can leap over other traffic, trucks, broken bridges, and stretches of water.

A warning signal announces dangerous gaps, encouraging players to prepare a jump rather than simply react at the last moment. The roads narrow and hazards grow more frequent as the stages advance, with changing seasonal scenery distinguishing the routes. A particularly striking scoring rule rewards a large bonus for finishing without wrecking any enemy cars, providing a pacifist alternative to aggressive play. The game was a commercial arcade success and received numerous home conversions.

games.title: Brute Force
games.description: Brute Force is a 1991 Leland arcade beat-'em-up in which up to three players take on gangs controlling the streets. Viewed from a slightly elevated side perspective, the heroes fight through urban districts, battling groups of thugs and the leaders of seven gangs. Hand-to-hand attacks can be supplemented with dropped weapons, while destructible scenery, firearms, explosives, and temporary power-ups make the fighting unpredictable. Its emphasis on three-person cooperation and interactive surroundings places it among the brawler experiments that followed Final Fight and Double Dragon.

games.title: Brave Blade
games.description: Brave Blade is a 2000 vertically scrolling shooter from Eighting and Raizing that uses polygonal graphics to present a fantasy-mechanical world. The selectable Runeswords are flying weapons capable of transforming into humanoid combat forms. In flight they function as conventional shooting-game craft, but switching forms enables close-range attacks and defensive techniques that consume a special gauge. The need to decide when to keep firing from a distance and when to take the risk of melee combat gives Brave Blade a distinctive rhythm among late-era arcade shooters.

games.title: Battle Shark
games.description:
Battle Shark is Taito's 1989 underwater shooting game, played through a periscope-style viewpoint. The player commands a submarine and sights enemy vessels, aircraft, and incoming weapons while firing torpedoes from a limited but gradually replenishing supply. Shooting selected targets reveals power-ups that can repair damage, improve weapons, or increase available ammunition. Major enemies await at the ends of stages.

The arcade cabinet's physical controls and viewpoint make the experience feel closer to operating submarine equipment than piloting a conventional scrolling shooter. Battle Shark was recognized for its presentation and received a nomination for an innovation award from the American amusement industry in 1990.

games.title: Basketball
games.description:
Atari Basketball (1979) is an early one-on-one arcade sports simulation, designed and programmed by Chris Downend. Two players, or one player against the computer, move their basketball figures around a black-and-white court using large trackballs. The shooting button controls the height and timing of the shot, while dribbling and stealing the ball create a simple but recognizable contest of positioning and timing.

The cabinet's angled view of the court and its enormous trackball controls were distinctive for the period. A snippet of 'Sweet Georgia Brown' accompanied the opening tip-off, and the game helped establish conventions for representing human players in arcade sports titles. It should not be confused with Taito's earlier 1974 Basketball or Atari's different Basketball home-console cartridge.

games.title: Back Street Soccer
games.description: Back Street Soccer is a 1996 Korean arcade football game from SunA that takes a deliberately exaggerated approach to the sport. Players compete in street-styled settings with larger-than-life characters and improbable special shots, making the action resemble a colorful fighting game as much as a conventional football simulation. A second participant can join for competitive play. Its emphasis on spectacle rather than realistic tactics gives it a distinctive place among the arcade soccer titles of the 1990s.

games.title: Baseball Stars Professional
games.description:
Baseball Stars Professional was one of the inaugural Neo Geo arcade titles in 1990, bringing SNK's Baseball Stars name to a more powerful platform. Players select from a roster of fanciful teams and compete in conventional baseball matches, choosing pitches, timing swings, fielding balls, and running bases. Its large, expressive sprites and exaggerated team identities give the sport a cheerful, comic-book presentation.

The game offers a tournament against computer teams and direct two-player competition, with matches taking place in two stylized ballparks. It is historically interesting as an early demonstration of the Neo Geo's ability to handle detailed sports graphics and animation, before the system became best known for fighting games.

games.title: Baseball Stars 2
games.description:
Baseball Stars 2 is SNK's 1992 follow-up to its Neo Geo baseball game, expanding the vibrant cartoon presentation and fast arcade pacing. The roster is divided into two leagues, with an easier Exciting League and a more demanding Fighting League. Players pitch, bat, field, and run bases, while tactical substitutions and temporarily powered-up hitters add additional decisions to the standard baseball action.

Its broad character animations, dramatic close-ups, and emphatic sound effects make even ordinary hits feel theatrical. The accessible controls sit alongside enough team and player variation to reward repeated play, helping Baseball Stars 2 become one of the Neo Geo's best-remembered sports games.

games.title: Beat the Champ
games.description: Beat the Champ is a 1996 Konami arcade sports compilation built around trackball controls. Instead of using a joystick for a single sport, competitors perform a series of athletic challenges by rolling the trackball to regulate direction, speed, or power, with buttons handling contextual actions. The events include ball sports such as basketball and American football, and the cabinet supports up to four players. The original cabinet advertised nine events across five sports, split-screen competition, and two illuminated trackballs. Its PlayStation-derived Konami GV hardware and unusual physical controls make it a distinctive late-1990s multi-event arcade game.

games.title: Burger Time
games.description:
BurgerTime, released by Data East in 1982, is one of the most recognizable arcade maze-platform games. The player controls chef Peter Pepper as he runs across giant hamburger ingredients arranged on stacks of platforms. Walking across every section of a bun, patty, lettuce leaf, or other component makes it fall toward a plate at the bottom. Completing all the burgers clears the stage, but the chef is constantly chased by hostile food characters, including Mr. Hot Dog, Mr. Pickle, and Mr. Egg.

Peter Pepper can climb ladders to change floors and use a limited supply of pepper to stun approaching enemies. Letting ingredients fall onto pursuers can carry them downward or crush them, making enemy positioning part of the puzzle. The basic task of assembling burgers becomes increasingly demanding as the player must decide between efficient routes, defensive escapes, and opportunistic enemy traps.

Originally released as Hamburger in Japan, BurgerTime became a major early-1980s arcade success and received numerous home adaptations. Its food-themed enemies, instantly understandable goal, and clever relationship between movement and falling ingredients established a memorable alternative to the maze chases dominating the era.

games.title: Vs. Battle City
games.description:
Vs. Battle City is Nintendo's 1985 arcade presentation of Namco's Famicom game Battle City, itself an elaboration of the earlier Tank Battalion. Viewed from above, the player drives a tank around a compact battlefield, destroying successive waves of enemy armor while protecting an eagle-marked headquarters. Bricks can be shot away to open routes, while steel obstacles, water, ice, and other terrain features affect how the battle unfolds.

Each stage normally requires eliminating twenty enemy tanks, but the round can end abruptly if the base is destroyed, even by an ill-judged shot from the player's own tank. Power-ups and changing maze layouts add variety to the defense. The Vs. System release gives this highly replayable console tank game a dedicated coin-operated incarnation.

games.title: Battle Field
games.description:
Battle Field (bootleg) is an unauthorized arcade version of Alpha Denshi's 1987 action shooter Battle Field, better known internationally as Time Soldiers. One or two commandos travel through successive historical periods to rescue captured comrades from the villain Gylend. From an overhead perspective they move through enemy-filled landscapes, shooting soldiers, creatures, and bosses while entering time portals that can shift the setting to another era.

The original game was notable for its rotary joystick, which let players choose their firing direction independently of movement. The bootleg preserved in AdvanceMAME belongs to that game's arcade hardware family rather than being a separate military shooter. Specific gameplay changes unique to this unauthorized set are not reliably documented.

games.title: Battle K-Road
games.description: Battle K-Road is a 1994 arcade fighting game from Psikyo with a strong martial-arts tournament theme. Instead of fantasy warriors and spectacular projectiles, it emphasizes recognizable fighting disciplines and matches between athletes representing different styles. The single-player K-Road tournament begins with an opponent using the same style as the selected fighter, then introduces practitioners of other disciplines. Its grounded approach and comparatively technical hand-to-hand exchanges distinguish it from the increasingly elaborate supernatural fighters of the mid-1990s.

games.title: Battle Tryst
games.description:
Battle Tryst is a 1998 three-dimensional fighting game from Konami. Players choose from a cast of fighters and engage in one-on-one bouts using a three-button attack system, with movement and positioning recalling other 3D arcade fighters of the period. The matches are framed as part of a violent televised tournament, giving the contest a deliberately theatrical setting.

Beyond its polygonal combat, the game is remembered for its anime-style presentation, animated story scenes, and soundtrack. The animated sequences were storyboarded by filmmaker Mamoru Oshii, while character design and direction were associated with Shūjirō Hamakawa (Shuzilow.HA). Hidden characters and the distinctive visual framing help set Battle Tryst apart from more familiar Virtua Fighter imitators.

games.title: Battle Toads
games.description:
Battletoads is Rare's 1994 arcade beat-'em-up, a separate production from the earlier console games despite sharing their memorable characters. Up to three players simultaneously control Rash, Zitz, and Pimple as they battle through six stages to confront the Dark Queen. Rash is fast, Pimple is powerful, and Zitz provides a balance of strength and speed, while all three have exaggerated attacks in which fists and feet transform into comically oversized weapons.

The game combines traditional side-scrolling brawling with varied stage layouts, enemies, and huge bosses. Its colorful animation is paired with unexpectedly graphic slapstick violence, a sharper edge than some players might expect from the cartoon-like appearance. Three-player cooperative combat, impactful attacks, and aggressive arcade pacing make this a distinctive entry in Rare's action series.

games.title: Bubble Memories: The Story Of Bubble Bobble III

variants.title: Bubble Memories: The Story Of Bubble Bobble III (Ver 2.4O 1996/02/15)
Bubble Memories: The Story Of Bubble Bobble III (Ver 2.3J 1996/02/07)

games.description:
Bubble Memories: The Story of Bubble Bobble III is Taito's 1995 return to the original single-screen bubble-trapping formula, following Bubble Symphony. Bub and Bob again climb a tower of monster-filled stages, now on a quest to reclaim their original forms and defeat an evil dragon. Each room must be cleared of enemies by enclosing them in bubbles and then popping the bubbles, with score bonuses and power-ups rewarding efficient play.

A major addition is the ability to produce giant bubbles by charging a shot, allowing several enemies to be captured at once. The game also introduces large enemies, new objects, and themed stages while preserving the instantly recognizable cooperative gameplay of the original. Its combination of nostalgic design and expanded mechanics makes Bubble Memories a notable late-era chapter in Taito's platform series.

games.title: Bubbles
games.description:
Bubbles is an inventive Williams maze-action game bearing a 1982 copyright and commercially released in 1983, set inside a kitchen sink. The player controls a tiny soap bubble and must clean up crumbs, grease, and ants scattered around the basin. Each bit of dirt absorbed makes the bubble grow; as it becomes larger, it gradually develops a face and gains the strength to survive contact with some of the cleaning implements moving through the sink.

Sponges, brushes, cockroaches, and sharp objects complicate the cleaning task, and anything washed into the drain is lost. A small bubble is easily destroyed, while a grown bubble can withstand or repel certain hazards, producing a satisfying progression from vulnerability to strength. The unusual domestic setting and playful character animation give Bubbles a personality unlike almost any other arcade maze game of its day.

games.title: Bubble Trouble
games.description:
Bubble Trouble: Golly! Ghost! 2 is Namco's 1992 underwater-themed sequel to the original Golly! Ghost! shooting gallery. One or two players use light guns to fire at fish, crabs, seahorses, and other animated sea creatures while pursuing score targets in timed scenes. The change from a haunted house to a sunken-treasure setting gives the familiar shooting mechanics a wholly different visual personality.

The cabinet is particularly unusual because it combines real three-dimensional diorama scenery with projected or overlaid video-game action. Players are effectively firing into a miniature underwater set rather than an ordinary flat display. This hybrid of mechanical scenery and electronic targets makes Bubble Trouble an especially fascinating Namco amusement-machine experiment.

games.title: Bubble 2000
games.description: Bubble 2000 is a late-1990s adult-themed puzzle game by Tuning Electronic, modeled on Puzzle Bobble. Players aim and launch colored bubbles toward a formation at the top of the screen, trying to create matching groups and clear the field before it becomes overcrowded. Completing stages reveals photographs or illustrations of women, including nudity. It is an example of how the popular bubble-matching formula was reused in smaller, adult-oriented arcade releases.

games.title: Bubble Bobble II
games.description:
Bubble Bobble II, released in 1994 and also known as Bubble Symphony, is Taito's elaborate sequel to the 1986 platform classic. The central idea is unchanged: cartoon dragons trap enemies in bubbles and then burst the bubbles to clear each single-screen stage. This time players can select from four dragons with different abilities, including Bubblun, Bobblun, Cururun, and Cororon.

Holding the bubble button charges a multiple-bubble attack, while major enemies appear at regular intervals and the course branches after boss battles. New power-ups and collectible music-note items add variety, and two players can still work together to clear complicated rooms. Its brighter artwork, larger cast, and branching progression make Bubble Symphony both a faithful continuation and a substantial expansion of the original game's formula.

games.title: Bubble Bobble
games.description:
Bubble Bobble is Taito's landmark 1986 cooperative platform game, starring the small dragons Bub and Bob. Across 100 single-screen stages, the heroes must eliminate every monster by trapping it inside a bubble and then bursting the bubble with a touch or jump. Each room is a compact platform puzzle: players can use floating bubbles as temporary footholds, chase enemies across ladders and ledges, and manipulate air currents to reach difficult positions.

The apparent simplicity conceals an intricate scoring system. Defeated enemies become food and other collectibles, secret objects appear according to hidden conditions, and specialized bubbles grant extra abilities or screen-clearing effects. Enemies grow angry and faster if left trapped too long, while a dangerous invincible pursuer can appear when players delay a stage. Two-player teamwork is especially important, both for surviving difficult levels and for discovering the game's more complete endings.

With its catchy music, vivid characters, and unusually deep secrets, Bubble Bobble became one of the defining cooperative arcade games of the 1980s. Its influence extended through Rainbow Islands, Bubble Symphony, Bubble Memories, and countless imitators. It remains an exceptionally strong example of a game whose approachable controls and cheerful presentation support surprising mechanical depth.

games.title: Bubble Bobble (Ultra Version)

modifications.description: Replaces stage layouts and enemy placements with redesigned levels.

games.description: Bubble Bobble (Ultra Version) is a level and gameplay modification of Taito's 1986 arcade platformer Bubble Bobble, featuring redesigned single-screen stages and altered enemy arrangements.

games.title: Buccaneers
games.description: Buccaneers is a 1989 pirate-themed side-scrolling brawler that closely resembles Irem's Vigilante in its underlying action and sound. The player controls a sailor fighting through a port, town, castle, and dungeon to rescue captured comrades from a pirate captain. Punching and kicking form the basic combat system, with enemies and bosses blocking the way through each stage. Its apparent borrowing from Vigilante, combined with the swashbuckling setting and an eventual Amiga adaptation, gives this otherwise obscure game a curious history.

games.title: Buck Rogers: Planet of Zoom

variants.title: Buck Rogers: Planet of Zoom (not encrypted)

games.description:
Buck Rogers: Planet of Zoom is Sega's 1982 forward-scrolling space shooter, released in Japan as Zoom 909. The player's ship appears from behind as enemy craft and obstacles approach across a rapidly scaling pseudo-3D landscape. Different sequences involve shooting hostile formations, avoiding barriers, and navigating narrow routes, with the constant illusion of forward movement producing a much stronger sense of speed than most flat shooters of the time.

Its graphics build on Sega's earlier sprite-scaling racing technology, transforming the driving perspective of Turbo into a science-fiction flight experience. The export edition uses the Buck Rogers license, although the action is largely about piloting a spacecraft rather than portraying the television hero. The game was an important early experiment in the behind-the-craft perspective that Sega would refine further in Space Harrier.

games.title: Bucky O'Hare
games.description:
Bucky O'Hare is Konami's 1992 arcade action game based on the animated television series Bucky O'Hare and the Toad Wars. Up to four players can control Bucky, Jenny, Dead-Eye Duck, or the robot Blinky, each armed with a gun and distinctive abilities. Their mission is to fight through the Toad Empire's forces, liberate threatened planets, and confront the computer overlord KOMPLEX.

The game combines the movement and crowd control of a side-scrolling beat-'em-up with continuous ranged shooting, switching between varied stage layouts and spectacular bosses. Bright cartoon graphics, voice work linked to the animated series, and four-player cooperative action give the arcade game an energetic identity very different from Konami's earlier NES adaptation. It remains a notable example of the studio's skill at translating licensed animation into elaborate coin-operated action.

games.title: Buggy Boy (Single Monitor)
games.description:
Buggy Boy (Single Monitor) is the 1986 upright edition of Tatsumi's inventive off-road racer, also known as Speed Buggy in North America. The player drives an open buggy across a selection of five courses, weaving between rocks, fences, water hazards, and roadside obstacles while racing the clock. Colored flags and gates award points, while carefully striking ramps and logs launches the buggy into the air. Skilled drivers can even balance the vehicle on two wheels for extra rewards.

The original 1985 cockpit machine used three monitors to create a broad panoramic view; the single-monitor version adapts the same distinctive driving and stunt mechanics to a more conventional cabinet. With its exaggerated jumps, collecting routes, and playful physics, Buggy Boy occupies an unusual middle ground between realistic racing and arcade obstacle courses.

games.title: Buggy Challenge
games.description: Buggy Challenge is Taito's 1984 chase-view off-road driving game. Players steer a buggy across rough terrain, negotiating dirt mounds and avoiding rocks, fences, and competing vehicles while keeping the car moving toward the finish.
