The objective is to complete four stages before the fuel supply runs out. Its combination of a behind-the-vehicle viewpoint, rugged obstacles, and a fuel limit gave the early arcade driving format a rougher, rally-inspired character.

games.title: Bullet
games.description:
Sega's Bullet (1987) is an unusually ambitious overhead run-and-gun game for up to three simultaneous players, released on System 16B hardware. Teenage resistance fighters Emmy, Fred, and Chris descend through a devastated futuristic city, subway passages, and sewers to confront the Robot Master. Enemies pour in continuously from the edges of the screen, forcing players to fight their way towards each stage's exit.

Its defining feature is a Robotron-style pair of eight-way joysticks for each participant: one controls movement while the other independently aims and fires. Special platforms recharge and strengthen weapons through four power levels, but using upgraded shots consumes that power. Operators could configure two- or three-player operation. The original game's FD1094-encrypted processor also made it a notable challenge for arcade preservation and emulation.

games.title: Bullfight
games.description:
Bullfight (1984), developed by Coreland for Sega's System 1 hardware, turns Spanish-style bullfighting into a compact arcade action game. As a matador, the player must lure a charging bull with a cape, find an opening, and strike with a sword. The appearance of additional bulls can make the arena especially dangerous, emphasizing timing and positioning rather than ordinary sports scoring. The game uses an eight-way joystick and two buttons.

It appeared in Japan as The Togyu (also transliterated The Tougyuu), with Bally Midway distributing the Sega-licensed game overseas as a conversion kit. It should not be confused with Alpha Denshi's similarly named Bull Fighter, an ice hockey game released in the same year.

games.title: Bull Fighter
games.description: Bull Fighter is a 1984 ice hockey arcade game developed by Alpha Denshi and distributed by Sega, unrelated to Sega's bullfighting title Bullfight. It presents the rink on a vertically oriented monitor and supports one or two players. In solo play, the player works through a succession of opposing teams in brisk three-minute matches, using an eight-way joystick and three buttons. Its compact tournament format and unusually tall screen distinguish it from later hockey simulations. The arcade hardware combines a Motorola 68000 main processor with a dedicated sound processor and multiple sound generators.

games.title: Bulls Eye Darts
games.description:
Bulls Eye Darts (1985), developed by Shinkai and distributed through Magic Electronics, brings traditional pub darts to an arcade cabinet with a trackball and a single release button. Players choose from High Score, 301, and Round the Clock, each requiring a different approach to aiming and target selection. Rolling the trackball positions the player's throwing arm, and the direction of the final roll helps determine the throw before the dart is released.

The conversion kit was designed for modified Atari Centipede boards, retaining the host cabinet's trackball wiring and vertically mounted monitor. That practical reuse of existing machines is a distinctive part of this otherwise rare sports title's history.

games.title: Burglar X
games.description:
Unico's Burglar X (1997) combines an overhead maze game with cartoon brawling, timed explosives, and short puzzle challenges. Players choose Gukjung, who attacks with his head, or Guksoon, who wields a mallet. The three-button layout handles direct attacks, a comical gas attack, and bombs; collecting stars or coins while clearing enemies provides the route through early rounds.

Its five-stage structure mixes collection challenges with escape sequences, memory puzzles, and bomb-based boss fights. This repeated switching of objectives, alongside a three-heart damage system, makes Burglar X more varied than its simple maze-game classification might suggest.

games.title: Burning Force
games.description:
Namco's Burning Force (1989) is a colorful chase-view science-fiction shooter built for the System 2 arcade board. Blue-haired space cadet Hiromi Tengenji undergoes her final flight training aboard a futuristic airbike called the Sign Duck. The behind-the-rider perspective recalls Sega's Space Harrier, but Burning Force divides each world into distinct phases and places considerable emphasis on weapon management.

During the opening stretches, Hiromi steers left or right along the ground, accelerates or brakes, and fires both ordinary shots and limited missiles. At the boss encounter, the airbike transforms into a spacecraft capable of full-screen movement. Numbered spheres provide score bonuses in a subsequent collection stage. Weapon pickups include spread, long-range, and spiraling fire, along with two types of replenishable missile.

First released in Japanese arcades, Burning Force reached a broader audience through its 1990 Mega Drive/Genesis conversion. Hiromi later returned in several Namco crossover and sports titles, giving this comparatively overlooked shooter a lasting place in the company's character history.

games.title: Burning Fight
games.description:
Burning Fight (1991) is SNK's contribution to the arcade belt-scrolling brawler boom, released for the Neo Geo MVS. The action takes place in a stylized Osaka overrun by organized crime. American detectives Duke and Billy team up with Japanese martial artist Ryu, and players select one of the three to punch and kick their way through streets, stations, and gang hideouts.

Its structure follows the tradition of Final Fight and Double Dragon: enemies approach from both sides of the scrolling playfield, boss fights punctuate the levels, and destructible scenery conceals helpful items. Phone booths, signs, and other street fixtures can be smashed, while dropped weapons temporarily expand the fighters' options. Two people can cooperate on the same screen.

Although it did not become a flagship SNK series, Burning Fight illustrates how the Neo Geo's large sprites and colorful urban backdrops were applied beyond one-on-one fighting games. Duke later made a cameo as a striker in The King of Fighters 2000.

games.title: Butasan
games.description:
Butasan (1987), developed by NMK and published by Jaleco, is an eccentric overhead arena game in which rival cartoon pigs try to blow one another up. Instead of firing a conventional weapon, players snatch bombs that appear around the field and throw them at opponents. Their visible countdowns vary, making positioning and the timing of each toss essential; a direct hit detonates immediately.

Power-ups alter the chaos, including gas that puts other pigs to sleep, while a whack-a-mole-style bonus stage challenges players to knock pigs back into their holes. The Japanese arcade original later reached European home computers under the name Psycho Pigs U.X.B. Its blend of comic violence, bomb juggling, and competitive arena tactics gives it a recognizable personality distinct from conventional maze shooters.

games.title: Boardwalk Casino
games.description:
Boardwalk Casino is a 1983 casino-themed arcade title from Epos Corporation, also preserved as Atlantic City Action. Its six-button, portrait-screen presentation uses betting/card-game imagery instead of the joystick-and-maze action associated with the hardware it runs on. The game is particularly notable as a conversion for Pac-Man-compatible boards, allowing operators to reuse existing cabinets and electronics for an entirely different sort of coin-operated attraction.

Despite its casino name, its exact gambling or payout mechanics are not well documented in the surviving historical descriptions. The two known program identities and unusual Pac-Man platform are its most firmly established distinguishing features.

games.title: Black Widow
games.description:
Atari's Black Widow, bearing a 1982 copyright and released to arcades in early 1983, is a color-vector twin-stick shooter set on a giant spiderweb. The player controls a spider with one eight-way joystick and fires independently with the other, eliminating invading insects while avoiding contact. Each enemy type has its own behavior, so success depends on more than simply shooting everything as it appears.

Some insects lay eggs that can be pushed off the web before they hatch, while defeated enemies leave temporary food bonuses whose value decreases over time. A roaming Bug Slayer can destroy pests for the player, but that assistance can also cost valuable scoring opportunities. The interplay between fighting, collecting, and manipulating the web's hazards makes it an unusually tactical descendant of Robotron: 2084.

Black Widow was also sold as a conversion for Atari's earlier vector game Gravitar, allowing operators to reuse much of the existing equipment. Its bright vector lines and independent movement-and-fire controls have made it a favorite among collectors of Atari's early-eighties arcade output.

games.title: B-Wings
games.description:
B-Wings, also known as Battle Wings, is a 1984 vertically scrolling shooter by Data East whose main attraction is an extensive selection of detachable weapon configurations. The player's aircraft can take on different wing formations that drastically change how it attacks, from focused forward fire to wider coverage or protective arrangements. Learning which setup suits an approaching obstacle or enemy formation is central to survival.

The game stretches this idea across a lengthy series of stages and demanding boss encounters. Wing choice introduces a strategic layer beyond the reflex shooting typical of its contemporaries. A later Family Computer adaptation became particularly familiar to players who encountered it through imported cartridges and unofficial multicart collections.

games.title: Battle Zone
games.description:
Atari's Battlezone (1980) is one of the foundational arcade demonstrations of real-time first-person 3D graphics. Viewed through a tank's gunsight, a stark vector landscape of mountains, geometric obstacles, and enemy armor stretches into the distance. The player hunts hostile tanks and incoming missiles, using the radar to locate threats that may be outside the narrow forward view. A single direct hit can end a life, so anticipating enemy movement matters as much as accurate firing.

Two levers control the tank's left and right tracks independently. Pushing both forward advances, pulling both back reverses, and moving them in opposite directions turns the vehicle in place. This physical tank-control scheme gives the game a much more deliberate character than a standard joystick shooter. Wireframe enemy silhouettes grow convincingly as they approach, making the virtual battlefield feel spacious despite the limited hardware.

Battlezone became a major commercial success and a landmark in the evolution of 3D games. Its reputation also grew from the military-training adaptation commissioned for the US Army, an unusual afterlife for a coin-operated game. The combination of simulated movement, radar awareness, and first-person combat influenced generations of later vehicle and action games.

games.title: Cabal

variants.title: Cabal (bootleg of Joystick version)
variants.version: (bootleg of Joystick version, set 1, alternate sound hardware)

games.description:
Cabal (1988), developed by TAD Corporation, helped establish the arcade 'shooting gallery' format that combines a visible player character with a movable targeting cursor. One or two commandos occupy the foreground while enemy soldiers, trucks, helicopters, and defensive positions fill the battlefield beyond them. Players move laterally, aim across the screen, and use guns and grenades to demolish enemies and scenery before progressing to the next area.

The unusual tension is that aiming and protecting the commando compete for attention. Remaining behind obstacles provides cover, but that protection is gradually destroyed by incoming fire, and evasive rolls are often essential. Each of the five stages consists of multiple combat screens and culminates in heavier opposition.

Cabal was TAD's debut arcade release and proved adaptable to a wide variety of home computers and consoles. Its perspective and mixture of cover, destruction, and crosshair shooting were influential on later games such as Blood Bros. and NAM-1975.

games.title: Cabaret
games.description: Cabaret is an adult-oriented video-poker machine released by IGS in the early 1990s. It combines card-based gambling play with mature presentation rather than traditional arcade combat or movement. The game runs on Z180 hardware with a Yamaha YM2413 sound chip; its numerous operator-adjustable settings cover such matters as betting limits, holding cards and double-up percentages, reflecting its origins as a configurable gambling cabinet. Although some older database records describe joystick controls, later emulator research identified a dedicated multi-button poker control scheme.

games.title: Cachat
games.description:
Cachat (1993), known internationally as Tube-It, is a fast-moving puzzle game from Taito. Sections of pipe fall into a vertical playfield, and the player rotates and positions them to build a continuous connection between electrical terminals along the sides. Straight, curved, and branching pieces can all contribute to a completed circuit, after which the connected arrangement disappears and makes room for further pieces.

Unlike puzzles built around matching colors, Cachat rewards planning the geometry of the entire stack. An awkwardly placed elbow can block a promising route, while a branching piece can create several possible connections. The game becomes increasingly demanding as the pile rises toward the top of the screen.

games.title: Angler Dangler
games.description: Angler Dangler, released by Data East for its DECO Cassette System in 1982 and known in Japan as Fishing, is an early arcade fishing simulation. The player positions the cast with a joystick, throws a hook toward promising groups of fish, and reels in the catch while avoiding rocks and other underwater hazards. Pulling too aggressively can snap the line, so a successful catch requires controlled timing rather than simply pressing the button as fast as possible. With a limited supply of hooks and a time limit, the goal is to land the most valuable fish before the outing ends.

games.title: Cadash
games.description:
Cadash, developed by Taito with a 1989 copyright and released in arcades in 1990, is an unusually ambitious fusion of side-scrolling action and fantasy role-playing. Players embark on a quest to rescue a princess, choosing between a fighter, priestess, mage, and ninja. Each class has its own strengths, and the journey involves jumping through dangerous landscapes, fighting monsters, exploring dungeons, and visiting settlements.

Unlike most contemporary arcade platform games, Cadash includes experience levels, statistics, equipment upgrades, money, and shops. Enemies award experience and gold, so players must balance forward progress against the benefits of additional preparation. Its linked-cabinet configuration could support up to four adventurers, an especially unusual social RPG arrangement for coin-operated hardware.

Cadash was later adapted for the TurboGrafx-16 and Mega Drive/Genesis, but the original remains distinctive for putting a substantial role-playing campaign inside the time-sensitive economy of an arcade machine.

games.title: Change Air Blade
games.description:
Change Air Blade (1999), developed by Sammy for Seta's SSV-based arcade hardware, turns the vertically scrolling shooter into a succession of duels against heavily armed rival aircraft. Players select from eight fighters with different capabilities and special forms, then confront opponents that function more like major bosses than ordinary waves of disposable enemies. Smaller support craft may join the fight, but the central objective is to deplete the opposing machine's substantial energy bar.

Standard gunfire and limited bombs must be balanced against enemy patterns and positioning. Its boss-rush structure, airborne transformations, and emphasis on one-on-one confrontations make this Japan-only release a curiosity among late-1990s shooters.

games.title: Caliber 50
games.description:
SETA's Caliber .50 (1989) is an overhead military run-and-gun game that follows American pilots escaping captivity in a Vietnam War setting. One or two players cross hostile terrain, shooting soldiers, vehicles, and aircraft while attempting to survive a constant stream of attacks. Machine guns are supplemented by grenades and more powerful weapons encountered along the route.

Its signature control system uses a rotary joystick, allowing the character to travel in one direction while aiming independently at threats elsewhere. That freedom connects Caliber .50 to Ikari Warriors and Heavy Barrel, but its escape narrative, dense ambushes, and wide-ranging battlefield give the game a personality of its own. A later Sega Genesis adaptation substantially changed the presentation.

games.title: Calipso
games.description: Calipso (1982) is an underwater action game in which a diver must recover treasure from the sea floor and carry it back to a boat at the surface. Fish and other sea creatures obstruct the route, while a depleting air supply creates an urgent time limit. Holding the action button and pressing a direction fires a shot, but the diver cannot swim while aiming, so every attempt to clear a path leaves the character briefly exposed. In competitive play, another diver adds to the hazards. The combination of oxygen management, treasure hauling, and stationary shooting distinguishes it from ordinary aquatic maze games.

games.title: Calorie Kun vs Moguranian
games.description: Calorie Kun vs Moguranian (1986), developed by Vic Tokai and published by Sega, is a compact underground platform-and-maze game. The player guides a small creature through connected passages and ladders, gathering the scattered items needed to finish each stage while avoiding patrols. A limited supply of bombs can destroy or temporarily disable enemies, but the objective remains collection and reaching the exit rather than defeating everything onscreen. The confined tunnels, ladders, and cautious use of explosives give it a puzzle-like rhythm alongside its arcade action.

games.title: California Speed
games.description:
California Speed (1998) is Atari Games' exuberant arcade tour of California, trading strict driving realism for broad roads, shortcuts, and improbable scenery. Drivers race a varied selection of vehicles through city streets, desert highways, mountain routes, and locations inspired by famous California circuits. Branching paths and hidden shortcuts reward familiarity with each course, while timed checkpoints keep every run urgent.

The original cabinets offered steering-wheel controls and a choice of automatic or manual transmission. Its bright presentation, unusual car selection, and deliberately exaggerated tracks reflect the late-1990s arcade-racer tradition of encouraging risky driving and repeated attempts. A Nintendo 64 conversion followed in 1999, bringing the game to a much larger home audience.

games.title: Cameltry
games.description:
Taito's Cameltry, copyrighted 1989 and released in Japanese arcades in 1990, is a maze-action puzzle game built around a striking reversal of familiar marble games: instead of directly steering a ball, the player rotates the entire maze around it. A rotary control swings the level while gravity pulls the ball through corridors, around corners, and past traps. The jump button offers another way to escape awkward positions or maintain momentum.

The goal is to reach the exit within a strict time limit, collecting useful bonuses along the way. Mastery depends on understanding inertia, planning rotations in advance, and avoiding obstacles that waste precious seconds. The spinning screen produces a distinctive visual effect and a sense of physical manipulation rarely seen in conventional arcade puzzles.

Cameltry later reached the Super Nintendo, where it was called On the Ball outside Japan. Its clear central idea and unconventional rotary controls make it one of Taito's more inventive departures from the standard joystick formula.

games.title: Candy Candy
games.description: Candy Candy (1999) is a Korean arcade puzzle game by Eolith centered on matching colored pieces. Players manipulate the pieces with a joystick, arranging groups of four of the same color so that they disappear and free space in the playfield. Its quick succession of falling pieces and gravity-driven rearrangements place it in the competitive tradition of post-Tetris arcade puzzles. The simple two-button control scheme belies the importance of anticipating where new pieces will settle after a match.

games.title: Cane
games.description:
Cane is an unreleased, unfinished arcade shooter project created at the Italian company Model Racing around 1979. The name, Italian for 'dog', is not a documented marketing title: it was found on the original development floppy disks. The surviving code suggests an early joystick-and-fire-button design, but the unfinished program does not provide enough evidence to reconstruct a fully intended gameplay loop.

Its preservation story is unusually well documented. Source files by former Model Racing developer Adolfo Melilli were recovered from his original disks by Alessandro Bolgia and Lorenzo Fongaro, digitally extracted by Piero Andreini, and later assembled into a working historical reconstruction. Jean Paul Piccato used the code and comments, supported by comparisons with contemporary Model Racing projects and input from Melilli, to infer an emulated hardware configuration. Cane is valuable above all as a rare surviving piece of original late-1970s arcade source code, not as a completed commercial game.

games.title: Cannon Ball
games.description:
Cannon Ball (1995) is a Korean color-matching puzzle game from Yun Sung, developed for its horizontal-screen release by Soft Vision. Players fire colored balls upward at an advancing cluster, clearing groups of three or more touching balls of the same color. Groups that lose their support also drop away, making carefully chosen shots more effective than indiscriminate firing. Shots can be directed vertically or at diagonal angles, and a limited bomb provides an emergency escape when the cluster gets too close.

Clearing stages reveals digitized glamour photographs, placing the game in the adult-oriented Korean puzzle-arcade tradition. A separate vertical-screen version, developed by J&K Production, changes the well's proportions and matching rules. An oddity of the horizontal release is that its score resets after each completed stage.

games.title: Cannon Ball
games.description:
Cannon Ball (1985) is a distinctive Breakout-style game originally produced by Novomatic, here represented by Soft's unauthorized conversion to Crazy Kong hardware. The goal is not simply to clear bricks: the player must break through a protective wall to destroy a bat-like enemy. This opponent retaliates by throwing monsters into the playfield, and contact with them gradually shrinks the player's paddle. Some of the creatures can be eliminated by colliding with them under the right conditions.

This bootleg adapts a game originally built for Pac-Man-derived hardware to a very different arcade board. The conversion is known for a protection-related fault after its bonus game, an important distinction from the original Novomatic version.

games.title: Canvas Croquis
games.description: Canvas Croquis (1985) is a Japanese adult-oriented arcade maze game in which the player controls a painter trying to complete images of women. The painter navigates a crowded playfield while hostile creatures interfere with the work, forcing the player to evade or eliminate them before finishing the picture and moving to the next stage. Its unusual painting objective gives an otherwise straightforward maze-action structure an identifiable theme, while the gradually revealed pictures provide the game's adult reward element.

games.title: Canyon Bomber
games.description:
Atari's Canyon Bomber (1977) is an early exercise in timing and precision rather than continuous movement. Aircraft fly automatically over a canyon filled with colored layers of rock; the player's task is to release bombs at exactly the right moment to blast away as much material as possible. Different targets carry different point values, and missed bombs are limited, so reckless firing quickly ends a run.

Players can compete to achieve the higher score, with the focus entirely on predicting where a dropped bomb will land as the aircraft travels overhead. The original arcade game was programmed by Wendi Allen, credited at the time as Howard Delman, and later received an Atari VCS adaptation. Its simplicity highlights a period when developers could build a full coin-operated game around a single carefully judged action.

games.title: Capcom Bowling
games.description:
Capcom Bowling (1988), developed by Incredible Technologies and published by Capcom, is a remarkably direct translation of ten-pin bowling to an arcade cabinet. Up to four people compete in alternating turns, using a trackball to position the bowler and roll the ball. Two additional buttons control left and right hook, allowing players to adjust their approach to the pins rather than depending solely on throwing power.

The overhead view keeps the lane and pin arrangement easy to read, while playful animations celebrate notable shots. Distributed substantially as a conversion kit, Capcom Bowling showed how a familiar recreational sport could work well in a compact coin-op format, with the trackball providing a convincing physical connection to the act of rolling a bowling ball.

games.title: Captain America and The Avengers

variants.title: Captain America and The Avengers (Asia Rev 1.9)
Captain America and The Avengers (Asia Rev 1.0)
Captain America and The Avengers (UK Rev 1.4)
Captain America and The Avengers (Japan Rev 0.2)
Captain America and The Avengers (US Rev 1.9)
Captain America and The Avengers (US Rev 1.6)

games.description:
Captain America and the Avengers (1991) is Data East's comic-book beat-'em-up starring four Marvel superheroes. Captain America, Iron Man, Hawkeye, and Vision battle the Red Skull and an assortment of recognizable villains in a campaign combining side-scrolling hand-to-hand combat with flying and shooting sequences. Each hero has characteristic attacks, ranging from Captain America's shield to Iron Man's repulsors and Vision's energy powers.

The cooperative arcade version can accommodate up to four simultaneous players, making the crowded fights a showcase for the team's combined abilities. Boss encounters, digitized speech, brightly outlined comic-book art, and intentionally melodramatic dialogue contribute to its distinctive atmosphere. The action moves between city streets, enemy installations, and other comic-inspired locations.

Although several home adaptations followed, the original remains notable for its full four-player superhero roster and for alternating brawling stages with shooting sections, giving it more variety than the typical licensed arcade fighter of its era.

games.title: Captain Commando
games.description:
Capcom's Captain Commando (1991) is a four-player science-fiction beat-'em-up for the CPS-1 arcade system. Set in a futuristic Metro City, it follows the armored Captain Commando and three unlikely allies, ninja Sho, alien mummy Jennety, and a genius baby named Hoover operating a robot suit. Their mission is to defeat the Scumocide criminal organization, whose mutant members have infiltrated society.

The heroes fight across scrolling streets, museums, underground passages, and high-tech bases, using an assortment of throws, special attacks, and weapons. Some encounters allow them to take over powerful robotic mounts, adding a memorable mechanical twist to the brawling. The Western release renamed three characters Ginzu the Ninja, Mack the Knife, and Baby Head.

Captain Commando himself predates the game: Capcom originally used the character as a mascot in the packaging and manuals for its American console releases. His arcade starring role eventually became a cult favorite, and the character later appeared in the Marvel vs. Capcom series.

games.title: Project Neon Caravan Edition
games.description: Project Neon Caravan Edition is a pre-alpha score-attack demo of the homebrew vertical-scrolling shoot-'em-up Project Neon developed by Team Fullset for the Neo Geo MVS in 2019. Designed in the tradition of classic caravan shooting competitions, it challenges players to achieve the highest possible score within a timed stage.

games.title: Card Line
games.description: Card Line is a Dutch electronic card-gambling machine produced by Veltmeijer Automaten, probably during the 1990s. It is a single-player, button-operated game presented on a horizontal CRT, with hardware built around an Intel 8051-family microcontroller and an MC6845 display controller. Its obscure circuit board, including an initially unidentified custom I/O component, made the game unusually challenging to document and emulate. The exact card rules are not established by the surviving descriptions, so it should not be confused with a specifically identified poker variant.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Car Jamboree
games.description: Car Jamboree (1983) is an overhead demolition-driving game in which the goal is to knock three rival cars out of a compact arena. The player must ram opponents from the side rather than simply meeting them head-on, which makes steering angle and approach more important than speed alone. Later arenas introduce ponds, ramps, and other obstacles that can turn a straightforward collision into a dangerous maneuver. With a four-way joystick and one button, it emphasizes positioning and quick changes of direction over conventional racing laps.

games.title: Carket Ball
games.description: Carket Ball (1996), developed by South Korean studio SemiCom, is an unusual arcade billiards game incorporating playing-card elements. Players work with sets of balls and cards, using joystick controls and three action buttons in a compact, competitive table-game presentation. Operator settings allow the starting number of balls and cards to be adjusted, showing how central those two elements are to its rules. It is a rare example of a mid-1990s Korean sports title that mixes cue-sport imagery with an unconventional arcade scoring concept.

games.title: CarnEvil
games.description:
Midway's CarnEvil (1998) is a horror-themed light-gun shooter with a gleefully grotesque carnival setting. A sinister amusement park is summoned by placing a golden token into the mouth of a jester-headed tombstone, trapping its visitors amid murderous clowns, undead creatures, carnival attractions, and monstrous bosses. Players shoot their way through several themed areas in a rail-shooter format, with branching stage choices shaping the journey.

The cabinet's shotgun-style light gun is operated with a pump action for reloading, giving every encounter a physical rhythm unlike the standard pistol-shaped arcade gun. Temporary weapon upgrades provide extra firepower against the game's often crowded scenes. Its digitized imagery and elaborate enemy animations push the exaggerated horror-comedy aesthetic characteristic of late-1990s Midway games.

Released around Halloween, CarnEvil became a cult favorite precisely because of its excess: unsettling scenery, dark humor, and relentless gallery shooting distinguish it from the more conventional military and police light-gun titles of the period.

games.title: Carnival
games.description:
Carnival (1980), developed by Gremlin and released by Sega, is a carnival shooting-gallery game in which conserving ammunition matters as much as hitting targets. The player moves a gun horizontally along the bottom of the screen, firing at rows of moving ducks, rabbits, owls, and bonus items. Every shot reduces a finite bullet supply, and some ducks that escape the target rows become dangerous airborne attackers.

The game periodically switches to a bonus sequence featuring a moving bear, one of the early examples of a distinct bonus round in arcade video games. Its colorful fairground imagery and mechanical shooting-gallery premise made it immediately accessible, while the need to prioritize high-value targets added more strategy than the simple controls suggest. Carnival was subsequently adapted to several popular home systems.

games.title: Car Polo
games.description:
Car Polo (1977) is an unusually early four-player competitive arcade game that combines overhead driving with a team ball sport. Two pairs of cars try to shove a ball into the opposing goal, using steering, blocking, and collisions to gain possession. When fewer than four people join, computer-controlled cars fill the remaining positions. Short timed matches make the result depend on rapid cooperation and positioning rather than long-term vehicle upgrades or race strategy.

Developed by Exidy, it is particularly interesting as an early example of simultaneous team play in a color arcade video game. Its design anticipates later vehicular sports games, replacing direct ball control with the unpredictable physics of bumping it around the arena.

games.title: CART Fury Championship Racing
games.description:
CART Fury: Championship Racing (2000) is Midway's arcade interpretation of American open-wheel motor racing, licensed from Championship Auto Racing Teams. Players climb into high-speed formula-style cars associated with recognizable CART drivers and circuits, including appearances by Michael Andretti and Juan Pablo Montoya. Courses combine real racing venues with the dramatic checkpoint pressure and close competition expected of coin-operated driving games.

Rather than attempting a strict motorsport simulation, CART Fury adds a boost meter that encourages aggressive overtaking and spectacular recoveries. The arcade version featured commentary by former champion Danny Sullivan and music by Midway composer Dan Forden. A PlayStation 2 adaptation followed, but the original cabinet is most closely associated with the late era of large, dedicated arcade racers.

games.title: Astro Fantasia
games.description:
Astro Fantasia (1981), produced by Data East for the DECO Cassette System, is an early space shooter that alternates between two visually different battlefields. One section presents a pseudo-three-dimensional view of an alien installation, with the player's fighter maneuvering across a limited surface while hostile craft approach from ahead. The other adopts a more conventional shooting arrangement, changing the attack patterns and positioning requirements.

The shifting perspectives make Astro Fantasia more experimental than a standard fixed-screen alien shooter. It was an early entry in Data East's cassette-based arcade program, a system that allowed operators to change games by exchanging media rather than buying a new dedicated board.

games.title: Catapult
games.description: Catapult (1982), produced by Photar, is an unusual single-screen action game starring Bruno, a dog trying to protect his owner's house. Cats and mice invade the rooms and threaten the furniture, and Bruno must use a catapult to eject the pests before they cause too much destruction. Its domestic cartoon premise and emphasis on clearing threats away from vulnerable objects separate it from the era's more common space shooters and maze chases.

games.title: Cat and Mouse
games.description:
Cat'n Mouse (1982), developed by Italian arcade manufacturer Zaccaria and also displayed as Cat and Mouse, is a fixed-screen action game about protecting a collection of food from hungry rodents. The player controls a cat moving along the bottom of the screen, throwing projectiles upward to knock advancing mice back toward holes in the wall. Mice pushed back into their holes become temporarily trapped, but they can gnaw their way out again.

The challenge is to get every mouse confined at the same time before they consume the food. Unlike a conventional shooter, simply hitting the enemies does not permanently remove them, so timing and juggling several escaping mice are essential.

games.title: Cavelon
games.description:
Cavelon (1983) is a horizontally scrolling castle maze game in which an armored knight climbs toward the lair of a Black Wizard to rescue a captive maiden. Each level is a network of guarded passages, and the player must collect the eight pieces of a door before the exit becomes available. Bows provide ordinary ranged attacks, while a limited-use magic sword can clear dangerous enemies from the screen.

As the knight moves through the castle, the playfield scrolls horizontally and guards obstruct narrow routes between platforms. The game combines a simple collection objective with the tension of deciding when to spend a valuable screen-clearing attack.

games.title: Cosmic Avenger
games.description:
Universal's Cosmic Avenger (1981) belongs to the first wave of continuously scrolling horizontal shooters. The player pilots a spacecraft over a hostile planet, firing forward at aerial threats while dropping bombs on ground installations, tanks, and other defenses. Enemy missiles, flying saucers, and moving obstacles create an unbroken sequence of dangerous encounters rather than a series of separate, stationary screens.

The ship can maneuver in multiple directions, and awareness of enemies approaching from behind is important. Released close to Konami's Scramble and SNK's Vanguard, Cosmic Avenger illustrates how quickly the side-scrolling shooter was evolving in 1981. Its later ColecoVision conversion brought this early arcade design to home players.

games.title: Carrier Air Wing
games.description:
Carrier Air Wing (1990), released in Japan as U.S. Navy, is Capcom's military-themed horizontal shooter for CPS-1 hardware. A spiritual successor to U.N. Squadron, it lets one or two players choose among three different jet fighters and attack waves of aircraft, armored vehicles, ships, and enormous mechanical bosses. Each mission advances through densely populated side-scrolling combat zones, with careful weapon use essential for surviving the larger encounters.

Before stages, accumulated money can be spent on special weapons, fuel, and defensive equipment. The aircraft's energy supply gradually declines and is further reduced by damage, creating a reason to conserve resources as well as avoid bullets. The combination of equipment purchasing and distinct aircraft types gives the campaign a useful tactical dimension.

Its detailed hardware-era artwork, large enemy machines, and elaborate military settings make Carrier Air Wing one of Capcom's notable early-1990s scrolling shooters, even though it never acquired the extensive home-conversion history of U.N. Squadron.

games.title: Cool Boarders Arcade Jam
games.description: Cool Boarders Arcade Jam (1998), developed by Tecmo for PlayStation-derived arcade hardware, takes the popular late-1990s snowboarding theme into the coin-operated sports market. Players guide snowboarders down courses with a joystick and a six-button control arrangement, emphasizing quick arcade responsiveness rather than a complex simulation interface. Its connection to the Cool Boarders name and the use of Sony-derived arcade electronics place it among the numerous Japanese sports games that bridged console and arcade technology during the period.

games.title: Cannonball
games.description:
Atari's Cannonball is an unfinished 1976 prototype created by programmer Owen Rubin, one of the company's earliest coin-op software engineers. The premise is to launch a human cannonball through a hole in a wall: the player charges the cannon with powder to set the trajectory, then fires and tries to thread the opening. A successful shot scores, while a miss sends the unfortunate performer crashing into the wall or ground in a comic animation.

Rubin later recalled building the graphics and programming much of the game by hand, entering machine instructions through a Motorola 6800 development system and saving his work on paper tape. The prototype was reportedly well advanced, but whether it ever received a commercial release remains uncertain. It survives as a fascinating snapshot of early microprocessor-based arcade development.

games.title: Captain Barrel
games.description: Captain Barrel is a homebrew arcade action game developed and published by Neo Byte Force Ltd for the Neo Geo MVS platform in 2024.

games.title: Capcom Baseball
games.description: Capcom Baseball (1989) is a Japanese-only arcade baseball game that puts conventional pitching, batting, and fielding into a short-form coin-operated format. It uses an eight-way joystick and three action buttons to control the plays, with players managing the contest rather than simply watching an animated match. Its colorful presentation and rapid input scheme reflect Capcom's attempts to bring familiar sports to arcades alongside the company's better-known action games. Its humorous Japanese subtitle refers to the unruly exploits of foreign players.

games.title: Boulder Dash
games.description:
Boulder Dash, presented here in Data East's 1985 DECO Cassette System version, is the arcade adaptation of the influential cave-exploration puzzle game created by Peter Liepa and Chris Gray. Players guide Rockford through underground chambers, digging dirt and collecting enough diamonds to open each exit. The challenge is not simply finding gems: removing dirt can unleash falling boulders, block passages, or create deadly chain reactions.

Creatures wander through the caves, and clever players can turn loose rocks into weapons against them. Every cave combines a fixed layout with a time limit, demanding that the player understand how gravity and moving obstacles interact. The original computer game appeared in 1984, and Data East's cassette release brought its ingenious blend of action and environmental puzzle-solving into the arcade.

games.title: Chase Bombers
games.description:
Taito's Chase Bombers (1994) is a chaotic chase-view racing game that replaces police pursuits with weapon-equipped competition. Players select customized vehicles and race through hazardous courses littered with mines, poles, and other obstacles. Item gates dispense offensive and defensive equipment, allowing racers to attack opponents while trying to maintain speed and reach the finish line.

Its exaggerated crashes and tactical weapon use make it closer to combat kart racing than a conventional driving simulation. Chase Bombers is also connected thematically to Taito's Chase H.Q. family, with appearances that recall the police characters from that series, but it redirects the emphasis from catching criminals to battling rival racers.

games.title: Burger Time
games.description:
BurgerTime, represented here by its Data East cassette-system incarnation, is a classic single-screen platform game starring chef Peter Pepper. The kitchen is arranged as interconnected platforms and ladders covered with enormous hamburger ingredients. Walking across every segment of an ingredient sends the entire layer tumbling downward, sometimes carrying other ingredients with it. The objective is to assemble all the burgers on plates at the bottom before the chef's lives are exhausted.

Living hot dogs, fried eggs, and pickles patrol the ladders and platforms. Peter can temporarily stun them with a limited supply of pepper, and dropping ingredients onto enemies provides another way to clear a path. The timing of descending layers encourages players to plan efficient routes rather than simply run away.

Originally introduced in 1982 as Hamburger in Japan, BurgerTime became one of Data East's best-known arcade characters and a fixture of early home-console ports. The DECO Cassette System edition shows how the company's adaptable arcade hardware could host a major commercial hit.

games.title: Burnin' Rubber
games.description:
Burnin' Rubber (1982), internationally better known as Bump 'n' Jump, is Data East's overhead vehicular action game, here in its DECO Cassette System release. The player races along scrolling roads packed with hostile traffic, forcing opponents into roadside hazards while keeping the car out of danger. The signature mechanic is a spectacular jump that allows the vehicle to clear gaps, waterways, and other obstructions.

Road layouts, opponents, and hazards continually change, creating a brisk mixture of driving, collision tactics, and platform-like leaps. Burnin' Rubber's jump mechanic was an inventive addition to the early racing genre, helping make it recognizable well beyond the arcade through later home adaptations.

games.title: Crude Buster
games.description:
Crude Buster (1990), released internationally as Two Crude, is Data East's unruly side-scrolling beat-'em-up and a follow-up in spirit to Bad Dudes vs. DragonNinja. Biff and Spike, two exceptionally strong mercenaries, are hired to defeat the criminal organization Big Valley in a ruined futuristic city. Their enemies include gang members, mutants, and elaborate mechanical bosses.

The game's great pleasure is the sheer range of objects that can become weapons. Players can lift and throw pipes, rocks, signs, vehicles, and even defeated enemies, turning much of the scenery into ammunition. Two-player cooperative action makes the chaotic environmental combat even more pronounced. Crude Buster's exaggerated physical strength and destructible cityscape distinguish it from beat-'em-ups based chiefly on punches and kicks.

games.title: Chinese Casino
games.description: Chinese Casino is a 1987 Japanese mahjong medal game from V-System, released in September of that year. It translates the familiar strategy of drawing and discarding mahjong tiles into a coin-operated betting format, with a dedicated mahjong keyboard instead of an action-game joystick. A single player works through the tile game while the machine's medal-oriented design supplies the gambling context. Its compact Z80-based hardware and AY-3-8910 and MSM5205 sound devices are typical of the specialized Japanese tabletop machines of the era.

games.title: Crystal Castles
games.description:
Atari's Crystal Castles (1983) is an isometric maze game starring Bentley Bear, who must collect every gem scattered across intricate, multi-level castles. Unlike the flat corridors of Pac-Man, the castles have raised walkways, slopes, tunnels, and visual overlaps that make their geometry part of the challenge. A trackball controls Bentley with impressive fluidity, while a separate button allows him to jump over hazards.

Monsters pursue Bentley, some compete for the same gems, and special items such as a magical hat can briefly change his chances of survival. Because enemies may remove gems from the map, fast collection and route planning are rewarded. The memorable castles also include hidden passages and unusual bonus opportunities for players who learn their layouts.

Programmed by Franz Lanzinger, Crystal Castles became a showcase for Atari's colorful pseudo-3D graphics and intuitive trackball control. Its detailed stages and distinctive bear protagonist set it apart from the many straightforward maze-chase games of the early 1980s.

games.title: Cosmic Chasm
games.description:
Cosmic Chasm (1983) is Cinematronics' vector-graphics adaptation of a game first created for the Vectrex home console. A small spacecraft infiltrates a complex underground alien installation, moving from chamber to chamber toward a central power core. Each room contains enemy drones and hazards, and passageways into deeper parts of the fortress may need to be opened with the ship's weapons. The player must reach the center, sabotage it, and escape.

The controls emphasize classic spaceflight handling: rotation, thrust, firing, and shielding are all important when navigating enclosed vector-lined chambers. A map gives the maze an overall structure, and the pressure increases as the player penetrates farther toward the installation's heart.

Cosmic Chasm is historically remarkable for reversing the usual conversion path. The Vectrex game came first, and Cinematronics transformed it into a coin-operated color-vector release, one of the company's final efforts in that visually distinctive hardware tradition.

games.title: Crazy Climber
games.description:
Crazy Climber (1980), developed by Nichibutsu with Jorudan, is one of the arcade industry's earliest and most distinctive climbing games. The player guides a daring mountaineer up the face of a skyscraper using two joysticks, independently controlling the character's arms. Alternating hand movements raises the climber, while repositioning both arms allows sideways movement and careful passage around dangerous windows.

The buildings are alive with hostile residents and absurd hazards. Opening windows can crush the climber's hands, people throw objects from above, giant birds drop hazards, and an enormous ape threatens to knock the player from the wall. The goal is to reach the roof and catch a waiting helicopter before the accumulation of threats causes a fall.

Crazy Climber predates Donkey Kong and established a style of character-driven vertical action that did not rely on conventional jumping. Its awkward-looking yet remarkably expressive twin-joystick control scheme remains central to its identity and is one reason it feels unlike almost any later platform game.

games.title: Crazy Climber 2
games.description:
Crazy Climber 2 (1988) returns to Nichibutsu's skyscraper-climbing formula with brighter graphics, new obstacles, and six buildings to scale. Both eight-way joysticks control the climber's arms independently, requiring players to coordinate their movements while searching for safe holds. Shutting windows, birds, falling objects, cranes, wandering gorillas, and other hazards make each ascent a dangerous exercise in timing.

The basic objective remains to climb to the roof and board a helicopter, but the sequel expands the visual variety and surprises, including occasional bonus encounters at windows. It was released in Japanese arcades rather than receiving the broad international exposure of its 1980 predecessor, making it a lesser-known continuation of one of arcade gaming's most unusual control systems.

games.title: Crazzy Clownz
games.description: Crazzy Clownz (1999) is a video-redemption game built around a bouncing circus performer. A clown shoots from a cannon and repeatedly rebounds from a movable trampoline toward balloons hanging above the arena. The player turns a wheel to reposition the trampoline, aiming to keep the clown airborne and burst balloons carrying different point values. The game resembles a paddle-and-ball arcade design, but its scoring and presentation are framed as a carnival attraction rather than a traditional brick-breaking challenge.

games.title: Disco No.1
games.description:
Disco No. 1 (1982), also released as Sweet Heart, is Data East's eccentric roller-rink action game for the DECO Cassette System. The player controls a shy skater trying to impress girls by outmaneuvering tougher rivals on the rink. Rather than attacking them directly, the skater earns points by circling opponents and completing loops around them, while collecting bonus objects that glide across the floor.

The skating theme, lighthearted romantic premise, and emphasis on encircling enemies make Disco No. 1 stand apart from the more common maze chases of its era. The game was among the early releases for Data East's cassette-based arcade platform.

games.title: Castle Of Dracula
games.description:
Castle of Dracula (1994) is a Korean puzzle game by Yun Sung, loosely framed as a rescue quest in which the knight Sonnie seeks a kidnapped woman named Lydia. Despite its fantasy story, the central gameplay is not combat: the player shoots or places matching blocks within a confined playfield to create a route to a key that unlocks the next stage. Rounds impose a time limit and a finite number of attempts.

Its puzzle mechanics closely resemble Taito's Plotting/Flipull, but the key-collection objective and story interludes give Castle of Dracula a separate identity. Comic-style cutscenes show the hero confronting enemies between the puzzle rounds, even though those scenes are not direct representations of the underlying gameplay.

games.title: ChuckECheese's Match Game
games.description: Chuck E. Cheese's Match Game (1993), also known on its marquee as Chuck E. Cheese's Memory Match, is a children's arcade matching game produced by Coastal Amusements for ShowBiz Pizza Time locations. Players uncover and pair matching images in a simple memory challenge, using a dedicated array of selection buttons rather than a conventional movement joystick. Its cheerful licensed presentation and straightforward rules were tailored to the family amusement environment of Chuck E. Cheese restaurants rather than to the traditional high-difficulty video arcade.

games.title: Magnet System
games.description:
The Magnet System was a Spanish arcade platform developed by EFO SA, using technology derived from Cedar Computer equipment, around 1987. Unlike fixed-program arcade boards, it was designed around changeable magnetic-disk media. Its architecture employed several Z80 processors distributed across the main, sound, and graphics subsystems, with AY-3-8910 sound generators and OKI sampled-audio hardware.

The BIOS represents the system's master firmware, while the software was distributed on separately priced disks. Contemporary pricing information lists the hardware at 198,000 Spanish pesetas and individual disks at approximately 15,000 to 25,000 pesetas. The extent of its original commercial distribution is uncertain, making the preserved firmware and disk-format research especially valuable evidence of an ambitious, little-known European arcade design.

games.title: Centipede
games.description:
Atari's Centipede, carrying a 1980 copyright and released in arcades in 1981, is one of the defining fixed-screen shooters of the golden age. The player operates a Bug Blaster at the bottom of a mushroom-filled field while a segmented centipede snakes across the screen, descending whenever it encounters an obstacle or the playfield edge. A trackball allows unusually agile movement inside the player's restricted zone, and the single fire button launches a continuous stream of shots.

Shooting a centipede segment turns its location into a mushroom, while destroying a middle segment splits the creature into independently moving sections. Fleas seed the field with new mushrooms, spiders roam the lower area, and scorpions poison mushrooms so the centipede can descend more rapidly. These interacting enemies continuously rearrange the battlefield, turning basic shooting into a surprisingly sophisticated exercise in managing the environment.

Designed by Ed Logg and Dona Bailey, Centipede was a major commercial hit and is especially remembered for attracting a broad audience, including many women, at a time when arcade gaming was heavily male-dominated. Its pastel palette, responsive trackball, and constantly changing attack patterns made it one of Atari's most enduring creations.

games.title: Cerberus
games.description:
Cerberus (1985), developed by Cinematronics for its Cinemat system, is a space rescue shooter in which the player tries to recover drifting fuel pods before hostile ships can steal them. At the start of each stage, an attack scatters pods around the screen. The player's craft must collect each one individually and return it to the station while fending off enemy vessels that threaten both the pilot and the cargo.

The action is shown on a single screen with a moving background, and rotary-style controls let the craft maneuver and fight amid the drifting objects. Its rescue-and-return objective makes Cerberus more tactical than a simple score-based space shooter and is a defining example of the short-lived Cinematronics convertible arcade platform.

games.title: Explorer
games.description: Explorer (1982) is an early Data East space shooter released on the DECO Cassette System. The player pilots a craft through an environment presented with a rudimentary three-dimensional perspective, firing on approaching enemies instead of fighting across a conventional fixed alien formation. Its main historical distinction is its place in Data East's experimental cassette library, where short-form arcade concepts could be exchanged on compatible cabinets without replacing the entire hardware setup.

games.title: Chicken Farm
games.description: Chicken Farm is a colorful video-redemption arcade machine introduced by LAI Games in 1999. Instead of progressing through a conventional long-form adventure, players take part in a short, chicken-and-egg-themed arcade challenge whose outcome can be exchanged for tickets. The original cabinet uses a tall, vertically oriented screen and three gameplay buttons, accompanied by cheerful animal graphics, music, and sampled effects. Operator settings include a starting jackpot and an 'eggs per ticket' value, underscoring its role as a prize-earning amusement-center machine. The preserved Version 2.0 runs on Texas Instruments TMS34010 video hardware.

games.title: Fighting Ice Hockey
games.description: Fighting Ice Hockey (1984) is a top-down ice hockey game released by Data East as cassette number 40 for its DECO Cassette System. Players select from six fictional teams, each fielding five skaters and a goalkeeper, and compete on a vertically scrolling rink that follows the puck. The joystick controls the action while two buttons handle hockey maneuvers such as passing, shooting, and challenging an opponent. Its overhead presentation and familiar team-sport rules made it a straightforward alternative to the more experimental action games in Data East's cassette-based arcade library.

games.title: Flying Ball
games.description: Flying Ball (1985) is a ball-and-paddle arcade game released by Data East on its DECO Cassette System. Its basic objective follows the Breakout tradition: keep a ball in play and use its rebounds to remove a field of targets. The design is closely related to Data East's earlier Cluster Buster, also known as Graplop, rather than to conventional action platform games. A planned export version called Bumpoline was reportedly abandoned, leaving Flying Ball as a little-known entry in the manufacturer's cassette catalog.

games.title: Cosmo Gang the Puzzle
games.description:
Cosmo Gang the Puzzle (1992) is Namco's lively falling-block game starring the mischievous aliens from Cosmo Gang the Video. Groups of blocks and alien Jammers descend into a vertical well. Completing horizontal rows removes ordinary blocks, while special attack pieces clear the Jammers that otherwise clog the field. Players must juggle the two types of obstruction rather than relying on the simple line-making logic of Tetris.

The game supports competitive play, where efficient combinations help pressure the opposing player. Its playful graphics disguise a surprisingly demanding puzzle system built around keeping alien groups under control. Namco later adapted the concept for consoles under names including Pac-Attack and Pac-Panic, replacing the Cosmo Gang cast with Pac-Man characters in some versions.

games.title: Graplop
games.description: Graplop (1983), also known as Cluster Buster, is a Data East ball-and-paddle game for the DECO Cassette System. A bouncing ball must be kept in play and directed against shifting clusters of grape-like targets, creating an unusual take on the Breakout formula. The changing arrangement of objects requires players to adapt their rebound angles rather than simply work across uniform rows of bricks. Its arcade release predates the later surge in elaborate brick-breakers such as Arkanoid, making it an interesting early experiment in the genre.

games.title: Chain Reaction
games.description:
Chain Reaction (1995) is the overseas title of Data East's original Magical Drop, a fast competitive puzzle game in which colored drops descend from the top of the screen. A small character moves along the bottom, grabbing drops from a column and throwing them back upward to build vertical groups of matching colors. Clearing multiple groups in sequence creates the chain reactions that give the export release its name.

The original roster uses colorful characters inspired by tarot imagery, and single-player competition takes the form of a series of increasingly difficult puzzle battles. Rather than dropping shapes as in Tetris, the player actively rearranges existing columns, giving the game a distinctive speed and rewarding confident pattern recognition. Magical Drop went on to become one of Data East's best-known puzzle series.

games.title: Chack'n Pop
games.description:
Chack'n Pop, released by Taito in Japanese arcades in 1984 despite a 1983 copyright, is a curious precursor to Bubble Bobble. The player controls Chack'n, a small yellow creature who must recover stolen hearts from maze-like rooms populated by Monstas and Mightas. Chack'n moves along floors and ceilings, negotiates narrow passages, and tosses bombs that can be used to defeat enemies or clear obstacles.

Monstas hatch from hanging eggs, introducing an escalating threat as the player searches for the hearts and reaches the exit. The unusual movement and bomb physics make it more demanding than its cute appearance suggests. Several of its enemy designs later reappeared in Bubble Bobble, giving it an important place in Taito's arcade lineage. Although the supplied set is classified as a hack, the available documentation does not establish any specific gameplay modifications to describe.

games.title: Challenger
games.description:
Challenger (1981), released by Centuri, is a single-screen science-fiction shooter built around successive waves of geometric threats. The player's spaceship moves along the bottom of the playfield and fires angled bursts at drifting energy rings. Large rings fragment into smaller, more difficult targets when hit, while other approaching creatures must be shot before they can reach the ship.

The game is organized into sixteen sectors with changing attack combinations, so mastering the rhythm of each wave matters as much as dodging stray obstacles. Its mix of splitting targets, fixed-screen movement, and increasingly crowded patterns is characteristic of the inventive early-1980s arcade shooter boom. This title is unrelated to Hudson's later Famicom game Challenger.

games.title: Chameleon
games.description:
Chameleon (1983) is a colorful single-screen platform game developed by Donga-Seiko. The player controls a long-tongued chameleon raiding nests for eggs while trying to avoid protective chickens. The tongue is both a weapon and a means of reaching higher surfaces: it can catch enemies and help the character pull itself up through the tiered playfield. Bombs found around the stage provide another way to deal with particularly troublesome birds.

The game's climbing and egg-collecting objective gives the action a different rhythm from ordinary jump-and-run titles. It should not be confused with the unrelated 2006 arcade puzzle game of the same name.

games.title: Champion Baseball
games.description:
Champion Baseball (1983), developed by Alpha Denshi and published by Sega, was an early arcade attempt to represent baseball with more sophistication than a simple batting contest. It uses multiple camera angles, including a close view of pitcher and batter and a wider perspective for field action. Players can manage substitutions such as relief pitchers and pinch hitters, and an onscreen umpire calls the plays.

Its combination of tactical decisions, animated players, and baseball-specific presentation made it a notable sports attraction in Japanese arcades. The game was successful enough to receive a sequel the same year, during a period when arcade baseball titles were beginning to move beyond abstract representations of the sport.

games.title: Champion Baseball II
games.description:
Champion Baseball II (1983), also subtitled Champion Base Ball Part-2: Pair Play, is Alpha Denshi's follow-up to its successful baseball arcade game. It retains the original's accessible joystick-and-button approach to pitching, batting, and fielding while emphasizing competitive play. The presentation continues to mix the view of the playing field with close-up baseball action, preserving the first game's unusually detailed treatment of the sport for its era.

Released in Japan through SNK and distributed in North America through Sega-related channels, the sequel is much less widely remembered than Champion Baseball. It represents the short-lived arcade series before Alpha Denshi moved on to other sports and action projects.

games.title: Championship Bowling
games.description:
Championship Bowling (1989), developed by Athena and distributed in arcades by Romstar, offers a straightforward ten-pin bowling contest. The player uses a trackball to aim and deliver the ball, with action buttons helping control the shot. As in real bowling, the goal is to achieve strikes and spares across a complete game rather than merely knock over the pins in a single throw.

The arcade game appeared in relatively limited numbers and was followed by a home adaptation for the NES. Its trackball input belongs to the same practical tradition as Capcom Bowling, bringing a tactile element to an otherwise familiar sport.

games.title: Champion Wrestler
games.description:
Taito's Champion Wrestler (1989) is an arcade professional wrestling game featuring eight colorful competitors, each with a recognizable persona and fighting style. The action is shown from an elevated side view of the ring, where players exchange punches, kicks, grapples, and throws in singles or tag-team competition. Leaving the ring introduces the risk of a count-out, so controlling the opponent's position matters as well as landing attacks.

The roster includes Miracle Rastan, a wrestler modeled after the hero of Taito's Rastan saga, an amusing crossover for fans of the company's action games. With championship progression and varied moves, Champion Wrestler aims to reproduce the theatrical rhythm of professional wrestling while keeping each match suitable for quick arcade play.

games.title: Change Lanes
games.description:
Change Lanes (1983), published by Taito America, is an overhead driving game with an unusual amphibious car. The player steers along highways and navigable waterways, switching between road and river routes at designated points while racing toward the next checkpoint. Traffic, scenery, and other hazards can damage the vehicle's progress, and every crash consumes precious fuel.

The fuel gauge acts as an overall time limit, with successful checkpoint runs awarding additional supplies. Its steering-wheel and gear-shift controls give the cabinet a driving-game feel, while the ability to leave the road for a water route creates a distinctive challenge not found in most conventional early arcade racers.

games.title: Changes
games.description:
Changes (1982), also released under the name Looper, is a maze-action game in which the player controls a caterpillar crawling among the branches of a large tree. The objective is to eat every nut and strawberry while avoiding insects and a hungry bird. Collecting a strawberry temporarily grants the ability to defeat enemies, turning a moment of vulnerability into an opportunity to clear dangerous parts of the tree.

Once the required food has been eaten, the caterpillar transforms into a butterfly, providing a memorable reward for successfully navigating the twisting pathways. The botanical setting and transformation theme give this Pac-Man-era maze game a character of its own.

games.title: Charlie Ninja
games.description:
Charlie Ninja (1995), developed by Mitchell, is a lively side-scrolling action platform game starring the ninja characters Roy and Lon. One or two players fight through five themed stages, hurling projectiles, jumping over hazards, and confronting bosses at the end of each area. Collectible items improve the characters' weaponry, while barrels can be smashed for rewards or picked up and thrown at enemies.

The ninja can also perform higher jumps and use a disappearing technique to evade danger. Settings range from a Western town to industrial and military locations, giving the game a deliberately playful mixture of styles. Its colorful character animation and quick cooperative action made it a small but memorable entry among mid-1990s arcade platform shooters.

games.title: Chase H.Q.
games.description:
Taito's Chase H.Q. (1988) transformed the arcade driving game into a police pursuit thriller. As undercover officer Tony Gibson, accompanied by partner Raymond Broady, the player races a powerful black sports car along highways in search of wanted criminals. Each mission has two crucial parts: catch the suspect before time expires, then repeatedly ram the fleeing vehicle until it is too damaged to escape.

The driving uses a behind-the-car perspective, branching routes, traffic hazards, gear changes, and a limited supply of turbo boosts. Checkpoints add time, but crashes and poor route choices can allow a criminal to pull away. Unlike conventional racers, finishing in first place is irrelevant: the whole challenge is a dramatic moving takedown.

Chase H.Q. was an enormous arcade success, particularly in Japan, and spawned numerous home-computer and console conversions as well as sequels. Its combination of racing speed, voice announcements, and vehicle combat helped establish the police-chase arcade subgenre.

games.title: Champion Boxing
games.description:
Champion Boxing (1984) is an early Sega boxing game in which players compete in the ring using a straightforward selection of punches and defensive movement. Jabs, straight punches, and uppercuts must be mixed with positioning to overcome an opponent; a referee counts knockdowns, and the matches can be played at different difficulty levels.

The game is notable in Sega's history as an early project associated with Yu Suzuki and artist Rieko Kodama, both of whom later contributed to some of the company's best-known releases. Originally developed for the SG-1000 and subsequently adapted to arcade hardware, it captures a period when home and coin-operated game development often overlapped.

games.title: Check Man
games.description:
Check Man (1982), developed by the British company Zilec-Zenitone, is a devious overhead puzzle game played on a grid of disappearing squares. The player must reach and defuse timed bombs as they appear, but every ordinary square vanishes after being crossed. A careless route can therefore trap the player or make the next bomb impossible to reach. Deadly skull tiles and, in later stages, moving threats further complicate the task.

Success depends on planning a route that leaves enough floor for future emergencies, rather than racing toward the nearest target. Built on Galaxian-derived arcade hardware and associated with the early work of the Stamper brothers, Check Man was among the British-developed arcade titles to find an audience in Japan during the early 1980s.

games.title: Checkmate
games.description:
Midway's Checkmate (1977) is an early four-player competitive arcade game in the trail-making tradition of Blockade. Each participant steers a continuously moving line around a shared rectangular arena. The line leaves a permanent trail, and colliding with another trail or the boundary eliminates that player. The last survivor scores the round.

Up to four people can compete simultaneously, with the computer controlling unused positions. With no shooting, jumping, or elaborate power-ups, the entire game is about cutting off escape routes and predicting rivals' next turns. Its support for four simultaneous players was especially notable for Midway hardware in the 1970s.

games.title: Cheeky Mouse
games.description: Cheeky Mouse (1980) is a compact arcade action game based on the familiar cartoon rivalry between mice and a human defender. The player operates a hammer to strike mice as they emerge from openings in a wall and rush toward cheese on the opposite side. Accurate timing is more important than exploration, because the mice appear at different positions and must be intercepted before reaching their goal. The play resembles an electronic whack-a-mole challenge, with a moving target and the pressure of protecting the food.

games.title: Cheese Chase
games.description:
Cheese Chase (1994), developed by Belgian studio Art & Magic, is an overhead maze game starring a mouse named Fantasy who searches for cheese while avoiding rats, beetles, and dangerous environmental effects. The scrolling playfield contains rotating wooden doors and electrically operated barriers, so navigating each level is as much a matter of planning routes as dodging enemies.

The mouse can deploy mines that explode after a short delay, turning narrow passages into useful traps. Sparks, ice, and moving obstacles complicate the chase, and two-player support adds to the arcade appeal. Its unusually large, expressive sprites and detailed 2D environments give Cheese Chase a distinctive visual identity among early-1990s maze games.

games.title: Chelnov - Atomic Runner
games.description:
Atomic Runner Chelnov (1988) is Data East's unusual fusion of a platform game and a forced-scrolling shooter. Chelnov, a miner transformed by a catastrophic nuclear accident, gains superhuman abilities and becomes the target of a mysterious organization. The scenery scrolls relentlessly forward, and the character keeps running even when the player releases the controls, so survival demands constant anticipation of enemies, pits, and obstacles.

Players can jump, fire, and change the direction Chelnov faces, allowing them to attack threats approaching from behind without stopping the advance. Collectible weapons include lasers, boomerangs, and other exotic projectiles, while power-ups improve fire rate, range, or jumping ability. Boss encounters temporarily halt the scrolling and turn the action into a more conventional duel.

The game's striking mechanical design was complemented by notoriety around its nuclear-accident setting, which evoked contemporary memories of Chernobyl. A substantially reworked Mega Drive/Genesis version later appeared, but the arcade original remains best known for making automatic forward movement the central challenge rather than an occasional gimmick.

games.title: Chewing Gum
games.description: Chewing Gum is an unidentified manufacturer's conversion of Sigma's Lucky Today, an early electronic slot game. Like its parent, it uses Galaxian-derived hardware with a vertically oriented display and simple two-way-joystick-and-button inputs. Players insert credits, choose a wager and start the slot-machine play rather than steering a spaceship or navigating a maze. Its significance lies in showing how early shooter PCBs could be recycled for gambling software; the alternate name and graphics distinguish this unofficial set from Lucky Today.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.
Original developer and publisher are not established.

games.title: Cheyenne
games.description:
Exidy's Cheyenne (1984) is a Western-themed light-gun shooting gallery in which the player must protect lawman Buster Badshot through a series of dangerous frontier scenes. Outlaws, animals, and environmental hazards appear in saloons, graveyards, mines, and other locations, and the gun can be used to dispatch threats before they reach the sheriff. Players select episodes by shooting their pictures, giving the campaign a degree of freedom in stage order.

The cabinet uses a mounted gun rather than a conventional joystick, and the action mixes precise target shooting with escort-style defense. Its illustrated scenes and cinematic Western premise helped establish the format that Exidy would continue exploring in Crossbow and other gun games.

games.title: Chiller
games.description:
Exidy's Chiller (1986) is one of the most notorious early arcade light-gun games, remembered for its graphic horror imagery and willingness to make human victims part of the shooting-gallery scenery. Players shoot targets in torture chambers, graveyards, and other macabre locations, trying to uncover hidden scoring opportunities and complete each scene before the time expires.

Rather than presenting a conventional heroic mission, the game deliberately uses shock and transgression as attractions. Its static, densely populated screens reward precise shooting and knowledge of concealed interactions, with different scenes and bonus sequences varying the objectives. Chiller became a cult curiosity and an early reference point in discussions of extreme violence in video games, years before similar controversies surrounded more famous 1990s titles.

games.title: Chimera Beast
games.description:
Chimera Beast (1993) is an unreleased Jaleco arcade shooter developed by C.P. Brain, preserved through an advanced prototype rather than a normal commercial launch. It takes place on an alien world inhabited by creatures called Eaters, which gain characteristics from the life forms they consume. The player guides one of these organisms through horizontally scrolling environments, eating enemies and growing into increasingly strange forms.

The campaign follows a food-chain concept, beginning with smaller aquatic creatures and advancing toward more complex prey. Absorbing different organisms changes the Eater's capabilities, making predation and transformation central to progress rather than mere background story. Its grotesque creature art and branching outcomes give the game a highly unusual identity for an arcade shooter.

Although the software was substantially complete, Jaleco never brought Chimera Beast to ordinary arcades. Its survival as a playable prototype has made it a favorite example of the unusual projects that arcade preservation can recover from obscurity.

games.title: China Gate

variants.title: Sai Yu Gou Ma Roku (Japan bootleg 1)
Sai Yu Gou Ma Roku (Japan bootleg 2)

games.description:
China Gate (1988), originally released in Japan as Sai Yu Gou Ma Roku, is a colorful platform-and-brawling game inspired by characters from Journey to the West. Players choose among Gocoo, Hakai, and Gojou, based on the monkey, pig, and river-spirit companions, and fight their way through rooms of enemies to recover a stolen sacred book. Up to two players can cooperate.

Rather than simply walking through a continuous scrolling street, the heroes jump between platforms, attack enemies approaching from multiple directions, and confront bosses after clearing each area. Distinct character attacks and a dedicated power-up button add variety to the basic three-button controls. The mixture of mythological characters and compact arena combat made it a recognizable late-1980s arcade action title.

games.title: China Town
games.description:
China Town (1991) is a Korean mahjong-themed falling-tile puzzle game that combines elements of Tetris with the pattern-building rules of mahjong.
