Players arrange numbered and character-marked tiles into groups of three, making either matching sets or consecutive sequences. Valid combinations can be formed in several orientations, including straight lines and certain corner configurations, while a time limit discourages prolonged hesitation.

The objective is to assemble useful mahjong combinations quickly enough to keep the playing area under control. Some versions add lighthearted bonus challenges between rounds, including a balloon-inflating contest. The unusual tile vocabulary makes China Town distinct from ordinary color-matching puzzle games.

games.title: Chinese Hero
games.description:
Chinese Hero (1984), also known as Super Chinese, is a top-down kung-fu action game that launched the long-running Super Chinese/Ninja Boy line. Players control the young martial artists Lee and Loo as they fight through rooms full of enemies in an effort to rescue a kidnapped princess and recover stolen treasures. The action takes place on compact single-screen arenas, where punches, kicks, and quick movement are needed to avoid being surrounded.

The game combines cooperative combat with a playful Chinese-fantasy setting and a cast of varied opponents. Its importance extends beyond the arcade release: the concept was adapted for the Famicom as Kung-Fu Heroes, establishing characters and a style that would continue through numerous console sequels.

games.title: Mahjong Chinmoku no Hentai
games.description: Mahjong Chinmoku no Hentai (1990) is a Japanese mahjong game from Nichibutsu with a military theme and adult-oriented presentation. Traditional mahjong tile play is supplemented by occasional random bonus items, while the character suit, or manzu tiles, uses English markings instead of the usual Chinese numerals. Its title, meaning approximately Mahjong: Silent Formation, plays on the name of the Japanese submarine drama The Silent Service. The result is a niche example of Nichibutsu's extensive mahjong output, distinguished mainly by its wartime motif and unconventional tile artwork.

games.title: Chance Kun
games.description:
Chance Kun (1988), developed by Peni Soft, is a Japanese baseball-themed redemption and wagering game starring cartoon cats. Instead of controlling a full baseball team, the player makes bets on the outcome of a batter's swing, selecting targets corresponding to a single, double, triple, or home run. An out or a caught ball can wipe out the attempted gain, while successful choices increase the player's reward.

The playfield is viewed from above and controlled through a bank of selection buttons. Its mixture of baseball imagery, prediction, and betting mechanics makes it an unusual arcade attraction rather than a conventional sports simulation.

games.title: Long Hu Bang II
games.description: Long Hu Bang II (1996) is a Taiwanese mahjong-based gambling arcade game developed by International Games System. It uses a dedicated mahjong control panel and supports wagering and payout settings, with optional automatic declaration of a ready hand. Operators could also configure adult-oriented character illustrations. The game appeared in multiple regional forms, including the Hong Kong Lung Fu Bong II release, China's Cuo Pai Gaoshou revisions, and Japan's Mahjong Nenrikishu SP. These variations, together with a later joystick-operated edition, illustrate how IGS adapted the same mahjong hardware and game family for different amusement markets.

games.title: Choky! Choky!
games.description: SemiCom's Choky! Choky! (1995) is a Korean arcade variation on the bubble-bursting formula popularized by Pang, also known as Buster Bros. Its action centers on clearing bouncing balls, but its most distinctive feature is competitive two-player play on a divided screen rather than the original game's straightforward cooperative format. Each player fights through a separate area while racing against the other, giving the familiar ball-splitting challenge a head-to-head twist. The cartoon presentation and modest sound effects reflect its small-budget origins, while the unusual versus arrangement sets it apart from many other Pang-inspired games.

games.title: Janpai Puzzle Choukou
games.description:
Janpai Puzzle Choukou, also known as Jong Pai Puzzle Choko, is a late Capcom CPS-2 puzzle title developed by Mitchell and released in Japan in 2001. Instead of playing a conventional hand of mahjong, players remove matching mahjong tiles from a board. A pair is valid only when the tiles can be connected by a clear route containing no more than two turns, introducing a spatial planning challenge alongside the race against time.

The columns of tiles and surrounding barriers steadily advance toward the center; each successful match briefly pushes them back. A once-per-stage assistance feature reveals available pairs and restores space, but a deadlock or collision means defeat. Clearing stages quickly reveals increasingly risqué character illustrations, making this an adult-oriented curiosity from the very end of the CPS-2's commercial life.

games.title: Chopper I

variants.title: Koukuu Kihei Monogatari - The Legend of Air Cavalry (Japan)

games.description:
SNK's Chopper I (1988), released in Japan as Koukuu Kihei Monogatari: The Legend of Air Cavalry, is a vertically scrolling combat shooter starring one or two helicopters. Players fly over hostile territory, firing on ground troops, military installations, and airborne enemies while gathering upgrades to strengthen their weapons. Large enemies punctuate the campaign, including bosses capable of firing nets that briefly immobilize a helicopter and disable its weapons.

The simultaneous two-player option makes this a notable cooperative entry in SNK's late-1980s shooter catalog. Its straightforward overhead battlefield action predates the company's Neo Geo era and emphasizes continuous movement and threat management over elaborate weapon systems.

games.title: Choplifter
games.description:
Sega's 1985 arcade Choplifter is a lavish, faster-moving reworking of Dan Gorlin's 1982 Apple II hit, a rare case of a successful computer game making the journey into arcades rather than the other way around. Players pilot a rescue helicopter into enemy territory, break open prisoner barracks, land to collect hostages, and ferry them back to safety. Merely destroying tanks and aircraft is not enough: the heart of the game is bringing people home alive.

The chopper can aim to the left, right, or toward the foreground, allowing pilots to change firing direction independently of their travel. Landing under fire is particularly tense, because escaping prisoners can be killed by enemies or by a careless pilot. Sega expanded the original concept with more varied scenery, including deserts, caves, and urban environments, and more elaborate arcade action.

Choplifter stands out among 1980s shooters for combining combat with a rescue-and-transport mission. Its shifts between aggressive attack runs and careful landings create a distinctive rhythm, and the arcade adaptation became the basis for later home-console conversions.

games.title: Chequered Flag
games.description:
Konami's Chequered Flag (1988) is an overhead-view racing game using rotating and scaled sprites to convey fast turns and changes in direction. Drivers steer through a series of circuits against the clock, with courses inspired by famous motor-racing venues, including Suzuka and Le Mans. Unlike a simple sprint to the finish, the game demands attention to the car's mechanical condition.

Collisions can damage the engine, front and rear tires, and brakes, all of which are tracked separately on the dashboard. Players must enter the pits for repairs and choose appropriate tires when rain makes the track slippery. Dedicated driving controls, including a steering wheel, pedals, and gear selection on arcade cabinets, give it a more technical character than many contemporary top-down racers. It should not be confused with the unrelated 1983 ZX Spectrum game of the same name.

games.title: Chuka Taisen
games.description:
Chuka Taisen (1988), released internationally as Cloud Master, is one of Taito's more whimsical horizontally scrolling shooters. Instead of a spaceship, players guide the young magician Mike Chen as he rides a cloud through a fantasy world inspired by Chinese folklore. His energy blasts repel bizarre enemies, including flying noodle bowls, while collectible items improve attack speed and strength.

Doorways lead to shops where accumulated credits can be exchanged for special weapons and other improvements. Each stage includes a mid-boss and a larger end-of-stage confrontation, and losing a life sends the hero back to a checkpoint. The fanciful creatures, bright scenery, and shop-based power-ups make it a distinctive alternative to the military and science-fiction shooters of the period.

games.title: Champion Pro Wrestling
games.description: Champion Pro Wrestling is Sega's 1985 arcade follow-up to Champion Boxing, trading the boxing ring for a colorful, cartoonish professional-wrestling contest. Players choose wrestling moves such as chops, kicks, dropkicks, and piledrivers, trying to knock down opponents long enough for the referee's count. Progression is organized as a climb through ranks C, B, and A, with promotion awarded after winning two of three matches at a given rank. Built on hardware related to Sega's SG-1000, it is an early example of the company's sports games experimenting with character-based wrestling before the genre became a major arcade attraction.

games.title: Highway Chase?
games.description:
HWY Chase, also listed as Highway Chase, is an early Data East DECO Cassette System shooter released in Japan in December 1980. Despite its road-themed name and automobile imagery, contemporary descriptions liken the action to Galaxian: the player fires at targets presented as cars or aliens, with a flashing target that must be destroyed to clear the screen.

It is historically significant as one of the first games made for Data East's cassette-based arcade platform, identified as cassette number 01. Its unusual combination of driving imagery and fixed-screen shooting also reflects a reported connection to Data East's earlier Mad Rider, exported as Mad Alien. The 1985 date sometimes attached to the emulated set does not match the documented original release.

games.title: Circus
games.description:
Exidy's Circus (1977) turned the paddle-and-ball formula of Breakout into a memorable slapstick act. Rather than bouncing a ball from a bat, players use a rotary controller to position a seesaw beneath a falling clown. Catching him launches another clown upward into colored rows of balloons; missing him sends the unfortunate acrobat crashing to the ground. The goal is to keep the act going while bursting balloons for points and row-clearing bonuses.

The higher balloon rows award more points, and the speed and angle of each landing determine whether the next clown will reach them. The game's famous morbid joke arrives when a clown is lost: a brief excerpt of Chopin's funeral march accompanies the mishap. Its stark black-and-white monitor used a colored overlay to tint the balloon rows.

Created by Exidy designers Edward Valeau and Howell Ivey, Circus was an early success for CPU-driven arcade hardware, using a 6502 rather than entirely fixed logic. It sold in substantial numbers and inspired licensed releases and imitators, including Midway's Clowns, helping establish the seesaw-and-balloons subgenre of late-1970s arcade games.

games.title: Circus Charlie
games.description:
Konami's Circus Charlie (1984) is a collection of six circus acts turned into a run-and-jump arcade platform game. Players guide Charlie the clown through stunts involving flaming hoops, tightrope obstacles, trampolines, rolling barrels, and a flying trapeze, with each event testing a different pattern of timing and movement. The simple two-way joystick and single jump button make the game immediately approachable, but the precise timing required becomes increasingly unforgiving.

Scoring rewards both fast completion and optional feats such as collecting money bags or performing particular tricks. Completing the full program restarts it at a higher level of difficulty, providing a traditional arcade endurance challenge. A level-selection feature appears in some versions, while other sets require the acts to be tackled in sequence.

Circus Charlie became one of Konami's recognizable mid-1980s character games. Its cheerful fairground aesthetic, animated animal performances, and use of familiar melodies such as The Blue Danube give it a personality quite unlike the company's contemporary military action titles.

games.title: Cisco Heat
games.description:
Cisco Heat: All American Police Car Race (1990) is Jaleco's fast, flamboyant arcade drive through San Francisco. Players choose between police cars emphasizing speed or cornering and race against rival patrol cars, civilian traffic, and a ticking clock. The routes feature city landmarks including the Golden Gate Bridge, steep streets, and tight ninety-degree turns, with branching paths offering different ways to approach checkpoints.

The game borrows the staged progression of Out Run but adds a deliberately chaotic urban setting, complete with trams, emergency vehicles, and a police-car horn. Jaleco produced upright, sit-down, and deluxe motion cabinets, with versions that could be linked for multiplayer racing. Its ambitious scaling effects and unusual police-championship premise make it a distinctive, if technically rough, arcade racer.

games.title: City Bomber
games.description:
Konami's City Bomber (1987) mixes an overhead car chase with weapon-heavy arcade shooting. The protagonist, a thief known as Cat Burglar 306, escapes after stealing money from a corrupt casino and must outrun the criminals pursuing him. The car can fire missiles at enemy vehicles and leap over obstacles, and each section must be completed before the checkpoint timer expires.

Destroyed vehicles may leave upgrades, including stronger missiles, longer jumps, and speed boosters. The constantly scrolling road, aggressive traffic, and ability to jump turn the chase into something closer to an action shooter than a conventional racing game. An airborne escape at the end provides a suitably extravagant finish to this unusual Konami title.

games.title: City Connection
games.description:
City Connection (1985) is Jaleco's quirky hybrid of maze-chase and platform driving. Players guide Clarice, a teenage driver in a small hatchback, across multilayered roads in cities around the world. Every stretch of pavement changes color when driven over; covering every section completes the stage. The car can jump between roadway levels, creating a nimble platform-game feel despite the automotive theme.

Police and other vehicles patrol the roads, but collectible oil cans can be thrown to stun them. Cats are a particularly troublesome obstacle, while balloons offer occasional rewards and opportunities to advance. The need to cover the entire layout while dodging pursuit recalls Pac-Man, yet the combination of jumping, car handling, and scenic backdrops gives City Connection a character of its own. The game also circulated in North America under the title Cruisin'.

games.title: City Love
games.description: Nichibutsu's City Love (1986) is a Japanese adult-oriented mahjong game built around encounters with female opponents. Winning mahjong hands advances the player's encounters, while an unusual rock-paper-scissors bonus round determines additional rewards and opportunities to reveal character illustrations. The combination of conventional mahjong competition and the separate luck-based bonus makes it a distinctive example of Nichibutsu's mid-1980s mahjong catalog. A separate medal or betting version also existed.

games.title: Crazy Kong
games.description:
Falcon's Crazy Kong (1981) is an alternative arcade version of Nintendo's Donkey Kong, developed for different, less expensive hardware with redrawn graphics, altered colors, and distinctive sounds. Players still guide the carpenter hero up a succession of construction-site screens, jumping barrels and other hazards to rescue a captive woman from a giant ape. Its familiar obstacle patterns reveal the Nintendo original beneath the visual changes.

Crazy Kong has an unusual legal history. Falcon originally obtained a license to sell the game in Japan while demand for Donkey Kong outstripped supply, but machines were also exported without authorization, leading to a dispute with Nintendo and termination of the license. Numerous unauthorized copies and hardware conversions followed, making it one of the most tangled early arcade families. In AdvanceMAME it represents both the popularity of Donkey Kong and the proliferation of alternative boards during the early-1980s arcade boom.

games.title: Rootin' Tootin'
games.description: Rootin' Tootin', originally known as La Pa Pa, is a 1983 Data East maze game for the DECO Cassette System. The player controls a tuba moving around a maze, collecting musical notes and bonus objects while avoiding hostile musical instruments. The unusual cast of animated instruments gives this otherwise straightforward chase-and-collection game its identity. It was cassette number 29 in Data East's interchangeable arcade library, and Rootin' Tootin' was the name used for export releases.

games.title: Clay Pigeon
games.description: Exidy's Clay Pigeon (1986) recreates clay-target shooting with a cabinet-mounted light gun fashioned like a shotgun. Players select trap shooting, with targets flying away from the shooter, or skeet shooting, with targets crossing the field of view. The game emphasizes careful aim and quick reactions against outdoor backdrops, while a voice repeatedly calls for each target to be launched. Later rounds introduce different shooting challenges. Clay Pigeon was offered both as a dedicated game and as a conversion for Exidy's earlier light-gun cabinets, continuing the company's tradition of arcade shooting galleries.

games.title: Clay Shoot
games.description: Clay Shoot (1979) is an early American clay-target shooting arcade game manufactured by Allied Leisure. Its subject is the target-shooting sport rather than combat: players try to hit flying clay targets in a shooting-gallery setting. Released near the end of Allied Leisure's video-game production, it is a relatively obscure survivor from the period when specialist sports simulations were beginning to appear alongside fixed-screen space shooters.

games.title: Cleopatra Fortune
games.description:
Cleopatra Fortune, released for Taito's F3 arcade hardware in 1996, is a falling-block puzzle game with a colorful ancient-Egyptian theme. Instead of relying solely on matching colors, players stack falling stones and gems so that treasures become completely enclosed by stone blocks. Completed horizontal rows also disappear, and gravity can trigger cascades of additional clears.

The unusual enclosure rule rewards planning the shape of a pile rather than simply making immediate matches. Endless play, competitive two-player matches, and preset puzzle challenges provide different ways to explore the system. Created in collaboration with Natsume, Cleopatra Fortune became a cult favorite for its deceptively elaborate mechanics, cheerful character art, and soundtrack associated with Taito's Zuntata music team.

games.title: Cloak & Dagger
games.description:
Cloak & Dagger is Atari's 1983 arcade spy thriller, developed under the working title Agent X and later linked to the 1984 film of the same name. Players guide a trench-coated secret agent into the underground headquarters of Dr. Boom, searching for stolen plans and trying to stop a bomb factory. Each room is filled with hostile robots, dangerous machinery, conveyor belts, and explosives, while a large countdown bomb maintains the pressure.

Its twin-joystick controls allow movement and firing in different directions, encouraging the rapid defensive shooting associated with Robotron while adding room-by-room infiltration and environmental hazards. After penetrating the complex, the agent must make his escape.

The game's cinematic connection is particularly unusual. Atari's original design was already well advanced when filmmakers sought a plausible fictional arcade game to feature in their movie, prompting the new name and shared imagery. The eventual arcade release was limited, primarily through conversion kits, leaving Cloak & Dagger as both a distinctive action game and a curious artifact of early video-game and film cross-promotion.

games.title: Lock'n'Chase
games.description:
Data East's Lock'n'Chase (1981) reinterprets Pac-Man as a comic bank robbery. Players control a thief racing through a vault-like maze, collecting all the gold dots while four policemen pursue him. Instead of eating a power pellet to turn the tables, the robber can temporarily close doors behind him, changing routes and trapping the police. Only two doors can remain shut at once, and they reopen after a short interval.

Once the loot has been gathered, the thief must reach an exit to clear the stage. The door mechanism creates a satisfying strategic difference from more direct Pac-Man imitators: the maze itself becomes a tool for escape. Lock'n'Chase debuted on Data East's DECO Cassette System and later appeared on home platforms, becoming one of the more recognizable early maze-chase alternatives.

games.title: Cloud 9
games.description:
Cloud 9 is an unreleased Atari shooter prototype from 1983, originally conceived under the name Weather War. Players shoot apart clouds while avoiding falling raindrops and other hazards, trying to eliminate the weather threats before the lower area floods. Its playful premise turns the accumulation of water into an immediate environmental danger rather than using a conventional enemy invasion.

The project developed from a concept initially intended for Centipede co-creator Dona Bailey, before another programmer took it over. An earlier design reportedly let the player drain the water through a plug at the bottom of the screen. Atari canceled Cloud 9 after very limited location testing, making its surviving prototype a glimpse of an arcade design that never reached full production.

games.title: Clowns
games.description:
Midway's Clowns (1978) is a licensed adaptation of Exidy's Circus, exchanging Breakout's paddle and ball for a pair of acrobats and a seesaw. A rotary control moves the seesaw along the bottom of the screen; catching a falling clown sends his partner flying into rows of colored balloons. The higher balloons are harder to reach and worth more points, while missing a catch costs one of the player's clowns.

Although mechanically close to Circus, Clowns is an important example of how successful early arcade ideas circulated through licensing and regional releases. Its simple physical timing challenge, with the seesaw's position determining the launch angle, remains the entire appeal.

games.title: Clash-Road
games.description: Clash-Road is a 1986 side-scrolling bicycle-racing game developed by Wood Place and distributed by different publishers in various regions, including Data East in the United States. Its premise trades the cars and motorcycles of contemporary racers for bicycles, with riders competing across horizontally scrolling courses. The unusual choice of vehicles and compact mid-1980s presentation make it a modest curiosity among arcade racing games.

games.title: Clutch Hitter
games.description:
Sega's Clutch Hitter (1991) is a baseball arcade game with batter-versus-pitcher action and full on-field play. The Japanese release features Nippon Professional Baseball teams and players, while the North American version uses Major League Baseball Players Association licensing for recognizable athletes without official MLB team names, substituting cities instead.

The arcade version presents the field from a perspective behind the batter, putting emphasis on pitch timing and strategic batting as well as fielding. Its regional licensing differences make the two editions interesting snapshots of professional baseball's marketing in Japanese and American arcades during the early 1990s.

games.title: Mahjong CLUB 90's
games.description: Mahjong CLUB 90's (1990) is a Nichibutsu adult mahjong game framed around an upscale nightclub. Players compete in Japanese mahjong against a succession of female opponents, with winning hands unlocking character scenes and special 'Showtime' events. An in-game vending machine can also be visited to purchase items, adding a small element of preparation to the usual mahjong progression. Its club setting and character-focused presentation are typical of Nichibutsu's specialized mahjong cabinets around the turn of the decade.

games.title: Pacman Club / Club Lambada
games.description:
Pacman Club / Club Lambada is an Argentine arcade modification dating to 1989 that reworks Pac-Man and Ms. Pac-Man-style maze play into a faster, music-driven challenge. Players still clear dots, chase fruit, and use power pellets to escape pursuing ghosts, but this version adds accelerated movement after taking a pellet, quicker bonus fruit, and speed options. The ghosts also become faster as the player improves, altering the rhythm of the familiar maze game.

The Club Lambada identity draws on the late-1980s popularity of lambada music, while the on-screen 'MIKY' name refers to developer Miguel Ojeda and his Argentine arcade business. Unlike an ordinary regional ROM revision, it is a localized hack with deliberate gameplay changes and a distinctive soundtrack.

games.title: Lucky Poker
games.description:
Lucky Poker is a Data East casino-card game released in February 1981 as cassette number 15 for the DECO Cassette System. It brings a poker-themed betting game to the same reusable arcade hardware that hosted titles such as Lock 'n Chase, illustrating how Data East could offer operators very different genres without replacing the entire machine.

Unlike the dedicated poker cabinets of the period, Lucky Poker was distributed as a cassette-based program (model DT-115). Its unusual medium and early date are better documented than the precise details of its poker rules, but its place in the DECO library makes it an interesting example of commercial arcade experimentation beyond action games.

games.title: Vs. Clu Clu Land
games.description:
Vs. Clu Clu Land is Nintendo's 1984 arcade adaptation of its unusual underwater puzzle game, released for the Nintendo VS. System. Players guide Bubbles, a round fish, around a grid of posts to reveal hidden gold ingots. Unlike a conventional maze game, movement is controlled by grabbing a post and swinging around it before releasing in a new direction. Steering therefore becomes a puzzle of momentum and timing rather than simple four-way navigation.

Sea urchins patrol the maze, and a sound-wave attack can temporarily stun them; black holes and the stage timer add further danger. Each completed board reveals a patterned arrangement of treasure. Simultaneous two-player play and changes from the Famicom release make the VS. edition a particularly interesting arcade version of Nintendo's early puzzle design.

games.title: Cherry Master II v8.41
games.description:
Cherry Master II v8.41 is a 1991 video-slot release attributed to Dyna Electronics and part of the long-running Cherry Master family of eight-line gambling machines. The familiar format arranges symbols in a grid and checks multiple horizontal, vertical and diagonal winning lines instead of using only the center payline of a traditional three-reel slot. This creates several simultaneous ways to win on each spin.

Preserved in at least two North American sets, this release uses Z80 and AY-3-8910 hardware with a compact horizontal display. The v8.41 designation identifies a particular program revision rather than a conventional action-game sequel.

games.title: Mahjong Circuit no Mehyou
games.description: Mahjong Circuit no Mehyou (1992) is an unusual adult-oriented Japanese mahjong game developed by Kawakusu and released through Nichibutsu. Instead of presenting each win as a conventional match result, it combines mahjong with a motor-racing theme: successful hands advance the player's race car around a circuit, with the distance linked to the value of the hand. Encounters with rival cars turn the race into an additional layer of competition. Its mix of tile strategy, racing imagery, and character-focused presentation makes it one of the stranger thematic experiments in Nichibutsu's mahjong catalog.

games.title: Mission-X
games.description: Mission-X (1982) is a military aerial shooter released for Data East's DECO Cassette System, and also produced on a conventional arcade board. Players pilot an aircraft over enemy territory, using bombs against ships, bridges, tanks, and installations while firing on hostile planes. Low-altitude bombing can improve accuracy but increases the danger, and at the end of a mission players attempt to land on a runway for bonus points. The contrast between air-to-air combat, ground attacks, and the final landing sequence gives this early scrolling shooter more variety than a simple wave-clearing game.

games.title: Cherry Master
games.description:
Cherry Master, represented here by Corsica's v8.01 program, is an electronic eight-line fruit machine. Its video display replaces physical reels with a grid of fruit and slot symbols; winning combinations are evaluated across multiple lines, including diagonals. The five-button panel suits a gambling cabinet built around placing wagers and initiating rounds rather than joystick movement.

This particular version was documented as an amusement/redemption machine capable of awarding tickets or tokens. As with many Cherry Master-style products, software revisions and similar-looking boards can represent quite different manufacturers and payout arrangements, so the v8.01 identifier is an important part of its identity.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Codename: Blut Engel
games.description: Codename: Blut Engel is a homebrew horizontal shoot-'em-up developed by Blastar for the Neo Geo MVS platform, represented here by its September 5, 2018 revision.

games.title: Night Star
games.description: Night Star is a vertically scrolling space shooter released by Data East in April 1983 as cassette number 32 for the DECO Cassette System. Players pilot an armed spacecraft toward a rendezvous point while fighting the enemies blocking the route. Rescuing stranded astronauts upgrades the ship's standard forward-firing weapon to a more powerful penetrating laser, giving the rescue element a practical role in survival. Like other DECO Cassette titles, Night Star was distributed on interchangeable magnetic media for a reusable arcade cabinet, an ambitious approach that later became notorious for slow loading and cassette reliability problems.

games.title: Caveman Ninja
games.description:
Caveman Ninja, also known as Joe & Mac, is Data East's 1991 prehistoric run-and-jump action game. One or two players take control of Joe and Mac, brightly haired cavemen setting off to rescue women abducted by a rival tribe. Their journey passes through jungle, caves, and other cartoon Stone Age environments populated by enemy cavemen, dinosaurs, and oversized prehistoric creatures. Throwing axes and other weapons can be aimed across the screen, while holding the attack button produces a more powerful shot.

Different pickups provide weapons such as bones, boomerangs, and fiery projectiles. The game balances quick platforming with large, elaborately animated boss fights, and its exaggerated comic expressions help soften the constant danger. The arcade success led to several home conversions and subsequent Joe & Mac games. A pirate edition called Stoneage also circulated, reflecting the original's appeal beyond officially licensed releases.

games.title: Counter Steer
games.description: Counter Steer is a little-known 1985 motorcycle racing game from Data East, released in Japan. Viewed from above, the action places the player on a motocross-style course rather than on the pseudo-3D highways favored by many mid-1980s racers. It is a straightforward early motorcycle competition title, notable primarily for its top-down presentation and relative obscurity within Data East's arcade racing catalog.

games.title: Cobra-Command
games.description:
Data East's Cobra-Command (1988) is a horizontally scrolling helicopter shooter, not the laserdisc-based Cobra Command that the company released in 1984. Players pilot an armed helicopter through six missions across Southeast Asian locations including Sumatra, Java, Borneo, the South China Sea, and Siam. Tanks, coastal batteries, submarines, aircraft, and gunboats turn the journey into a constant battle across both land and sea.

The action emphasizes forward movement, dodging enemy fire, and using the helicopter's weapons to clear heavily defended routes. Though it shares a name and military-helicopter theme with the earlier animated laserdisc game, this is a conventional sprite-based action title with directly controlled movement. Its later NES adaptation helped preserve the less-famous of Data East's two Cobra Command games.

games.title: Video System PSX
games.description:
Video System PSX is the BIOS for Video System Co.'s Sony ZN-1-based arcade hardware, introduced in the mid-1990s. The underlying Sony motherboard offered PlayStation-derived MIPS processing, textured-polygon graphics, and digital sound capabilities in a coin-operated format.

Video System provided a manufacturer-specific ROM daughterboard, identified in hardware documentation as VS34, together with matching firmware and protection information. This BIOS is the shared startup component of that configuration. Its separate preservation illustrates the modular nature of the ZN family: a common Sony foundation could be paired with different publishers' circuitry and system ROMs.

games.title: Columns '97
games.description:
Columns '97 is Sega's 1996 update of its influential falling-jewel puzzle game, released on the Sega ST-V arcade system. Players maneuver falling vertical trios of colored gems, cycling their order to align three or more matching jewels horizontally, vertically, or diagonally. Successful matches disappear, and the resulting falling pieces can produce valuable chain reactions.

Its distinctive feature is not a new premise but a later arcade presentation of the original Columns rules on Saturn-derived hardware. The game illustrates Sega's continued use of its familiar match-three formula well into the late 1990s, long after the first Columns had helped establish the genre in arcades and on home consoles.

games.title: Colony 7
games.description:
Colony 7 (1981), developed by Taito's American division, is a fixed-screen defensive shooter that blends the threats of Space Invaders with the protective duties of Missile Command. Alien formations attack a vulnerable settlement and its power generators, while the player operates defensive guns and tries to preserve the colony's temporary shield. Enemy fire gradually erodes its defenses, so surviving a wave depends on intercepting attackers before the damage becomes irreversible.

The game's most remarkable feature is its 'extended weaponry' system. Beyond ordinary cannon fire, players could insert additional coins to obtain limited-use superweapons such as a localized Mega-Blaster or a screen-clearing Eradicator. This very early form of paid in-game upgrades is a striking piece of arcade history, decades before microtransactions became common elsewhere. Colony 7 also influenced Imagic's later Atari 2600 game Atlantis.

games.title: Columns
games.description:
Sega's Columns (1990) is one of the landmark falling-block puzzle games of the early 1990s. Three differently colored jewels descend together as a vertical group, and players can shift the column sideways or rotate the order of the jewels before it lands. Any line of at least three matching jewels disappears, whether arranged vertically, horizontally, or diagonally. The real depth comes from setting up cascades: clearing one group makes unsupported gems fall and potentially complete further matches.

Where Tetris focuses on filling rows, Columns rewards color planning and diagonals, creating a rhythm of advance preparation and sudden chain reactions. Different play options, including a Flash mode centered on clearing a particular target, offer variations on the basic survival challenge.

The design originated with Jay Geertsen on a computer workstation before Sega adapted it for arcades and its home systems. Columns became one of Sega's best-known puzzle properties, especially through the Genesis/Mega Drive, and inspired many later color-matching games. Its jewel imagery and distinctive music remain closely associated with Sega's early-1990s catalog.

games.title: Columns II: The Voyage Through Time

variants.title: Columns II: The Voyage Through Time (World)
Columns II: The Voyage Through Time (Japan)

games.description:
Columns II: The Voyage Through Time (1990) is Sega's Japanese-only arcade sequel to Columns, built on Sega System C hardware. Players again manipulate falling trios of colored objects and clear lines of three or more identical pieces horizontally, vertically, or diagonally. Chain reactions remain central to high scores, with the challenge becoming more demanding as the playing field fills.

Rather than abandoning the original's elegant rules, the sequel expands the presentation with different visual themes suggestive of past and future eras. For many years it was far less familiar than the original because of its limited arcade distribution, although it later appeared in Sega compilations. It is an interesting early attempt to develop Columns as an arcade series rather than merely a single successful puzzle game.

games.title: Columns
games.description: Columns is an unofficial homebrew adaptation of Sega's tile-matching puzzle game created by Jeff Kurtz for the Neo Geo platform, where players align falling vertical triplets of colored jewels horizontally, vertically, or diagonally.

games.title: Combat School
games.description:
Combat School, known as Boot Camp in North America, is Konami's 1987 military-training sports game. Like an army-themed descendant of Track & Field, it makes players prove their fitness through a sequence of boot-camp events, including obstacle courses, shooting exercises, and other tests of speed and coordination. A stern drill instructor judges each performance, and failing to meet the qualification standard can end the recruit's career.

The original arcade game uses trackball-driven physical action, although alternate control arrangements exist. Its multi-event format requires different skills in rapid succession and supports competition between recruits. After completing the basic training program, the game culminates in a combat-themed challenge. The mix of comic drill-sergeant personality and demanding sports-game mechanics helped it stand apart from Konami's better-known conventional athletics titles.

games.title: Combat
games.description:
Exidy's Combat (1985), later also known as Catch-22, is a military-themed light-gun shooting gallery. Rather than controlling a soldier directly, the player aims a cabinet-mounted gun at targets across a series of battlefront scenes, shooting enemy troops and threats while avoiding friendly units. Allies and enemies are distinguished by color, making quick target identification as important as marksmanship.

Successful protection of friendly forces allows progress through the military campaign and advancement in rank, ultimately toward General of the Army. Its emphasis on choosing the right targets distinguishes this Exidy coin-op game from the unrelated Atari 2600 title Combat, a two-player tank and aircraft duel.

games.title: Combat Hawk
games.description: Combat Hawk is a 1987 arcade shooter developed by Sanritsu and associated with Sega. It presents the player as an infantry soldier in a military action scenario, with progress relying on quick reactions to threats. Contemporary descriptions characterize it as a reaction-based shoot-'em-up rather than an elaborate campaign game. The surviving information about its precise enemy patterns and stage objectives is limited, making it a comparatively obscure entry in the late-1980s military-action genre.

games.title: Commando
games.description:
Capcom's Commando (1985), released in Japan as Senjou no Ookami, helped define the top-down run-and-gun shooter. Players guide the lone soldier Super Joe deep into enemy territory, advancing through vertically scrolling battlefields filled with troops, bunkers, and vehicles. An unlimited-ammunition machine gun can fire in eight directions, while a limited supply of grenades arcs forward to destroy enemies and fortified positions. Each area ends with a concentrated enemy assault near a gate or stronghold.

The appeal lies in its relentless pace and readable but demanding battlefield movement. Bullets approach from multiple directions, cover provides only brief relief, and grenades must be saved for difficult clusters of enemies. Prisoners of war can also be rescued for bonuses, adding a small secondary objective to the advance.

Designed by Tokuro Fujiwara, Commando was a major arcade hit and a foundational influence on games such as Ikari Warriors and Capcom's own Mercs. Its familiar two-button combat system and constant forward pressure became genre conventions. It was ported to numerous computers and consoles, while later appearances of Super Joe connected the game to a wider Capcom action lineage.

games.title: Command War - Super Special Battle & War Game

variants.title: Command War - Super Special Battle & War Game (Ver 0.0J) (Prototype)

games.description:
Command War: Super Special Battle & War Game is an unreleased Taito prototype dated 1992, preserved in a very early Version 0.0J build. It is a futuristic combat game designed for Taito's F3 arcade hardware, with support for four players and an unusually elaborate control configuration involving four action buttons and joystick or rotary-style inputs. The surviving material does not establish all of its intended combat rules or progression.

The project is particularly interesting for its connection to Taito's later Riding Fight. Material from the canceled game was reused in that production, and its round-selection presentation is notably similar. Consequently, Command War documents an abandoned branch of Taito's early-1990s arcade development rather than simply an unfinished regional release of a familiar game.

games.title: Commando
games.description:
Commando is a little-known 1983 Sega arcade shooter built on hardware closely related to Konami's early-1980s Rally-X-derived designs. It uses a vertically oriented display, a four-direction joystick, and two buttons, with two-player turn-taking supported by the cabinet. Its Z80-based board and AY-3-8910 sound hardware place it firmly among the compact sprite-and-tile arcade games of the period.

Despite sharing a name, this is not Capcom's much more famous 1985 Commando (Senjō no Ōkami), and its gameplay should not be confused with Super Joe's machine-gun-and-grenade campaign. The Sega title survives as a separate, substantially more obscure arcade production with comparatively little detailed gameplay documentation.

games.title: Comotion
games.description:
Comotion (1976) is Gremlin's multiplayer extension of Blockade, an important precursor to the light-cycle games that followed. Up to four players steer continuously moving lines around a rectangular playfield, turning at right angles while leaving permanent trails behind them. Running into the boundary or another trail eliminates a player, so the challenge is to survive while gradually restricting opponents' remaining space.

The game's main attraction was its unusual social setup: it was housed in a four-sided, standing cocktail-style cabinet with controls for several people around the display. All players shared the same small arena, producing fast contests based on anticipation rather than reflex shooting. Comotion is an early and historically interesting example of four-person arcade competition.

games.title: Competition Golf Final Round
games.description: Competition Golf Final Round is a Data East golf game associated with a 1985 Japanese release and a 1986 version. Players compete over a course of holes, aiming to finish each in the fewest strokes; the game supports solo play or alternating competition between two golfers. Its straightforward coin-operated approach emphasizes shot selection and scorekeeping rather than a complex sports simulation. It belongs to Data East's series of early golf games, which brought a quieter, turn-based alternative to the action-heavy arcade floor.

games.title: Complex X
games.description:
Complex X is an unusual 1984-85 platform shooter set inside a flooding nuclear reactor. Players control a scientist trying to reach each level's exit before rising water and the dwindling air supply overwhelm him. One eight-way joystick moves the character, while a second aims his shots independently; a button allows jumping between platforms and other obstacles. Ammunition is limited, but collectible items replenish it, creating a tension between spending shots on hostile creatures and preserving them for a completion bonus.

The level design also permits wrapping around the screen edges, while moving platforms demand precise timing. Originally associated with Taito America, the game eventually appeared through Progressive Game Distributors after Taito's American manufacturing operation closed. Its two-stick control scheme and rising-water threat make it a distinctive late survivor of the hardware family used by games such as Zoo Keeper and Space Dungeon.

games.title: Congo Bongo
games.description:
Sega's Congo Bongo (1983), also known as Tip Top, is an isometric platform game that combines the three-quarter view of Zaxxon with a mischievous variation on Donkey Kong. Players control a safari explorer whose campsite has been set alight by Bongo the gorilla. Determined to catch him, the explorer traverses four distinct single-screen environments, jumping over obstacles, climbing through precarious terrain, and evading aggressive jungle animals.

Unlike a conventional side-view platformer, the diagonal isometric perspective makes judging the height and alignment of jumps part of the challenge. Different stages introduce their own hazards, from coconut-throwing apes to dangerous crossings and roaming wildlife. The hero generally survives through movement and well-timed leaps rather than combat.

Developed with work credited to Ikegami Tsushinki, Congo Bongo was one of Sega's most visible attempts to capitalize on the platform-game boom that followed Donkey Kong. Its striking perspective gave the familiar ape-chase premise a distinctive visual identity, and it was converted to several home computers and consoles.

games.title: Conquer
games.description:
Conqueror, listed as Conquer in MAME, is an obscure early-1980s arcade space shooter built on Scramble-derived hardware and closely related to Hot Shocker. Its manufacturer and exact release year remain unknown. Analysis of its surviving graphics ROMs revealed sprites, tiles, and artwork borrowed from Hot Shocker, including an altered Domino logo in place of the earlier Dudley branding. MAME developer Tomasz Slanina suggested in January 2004 that it was probably a ROM-swap conversion, although its gameplay appeared to differ from the original. The board uses two Z80 processors, two AY-3-8910 sound chips, and a vertically oriented display.

The original circuit board was obtained from arcade hardware seller Kirk Weaver and examined by the MAME preservation community in January 2004. It featured an unusually crude, epoxy-encapsulated module containing two unmarked 20-pin integrated circuits. Developers suspected that this module implemented a simple form of program-ROM encryption, since the main CPU data appeared corrupt or encrypted while the sound ROMs were readable. The protection scheme was never conclusively identified, and the game remains non-working in MAME. Conqueror is a rare surviving example of how early arcade hardware could be repurposed through ROM and circuitry modifications, with its precise gameplay still largely undocumented.
research_notes: Original developer and publisher are not established.

games.title: Conquest
games.description:
Conquest is an unfinished 1982 space-combat project by Larry DeMar of Vid Kidz, the celebrated studio he formed with Eugene Jarvis after their work on Defender and Stargate. Conceived as a free-roaming two-dimensional universe rather than a conventional scrolling shooter, its prototype lets the player pilot a craft using rotational control, thrust, and firing, with a scanner to show activity beyond the immediate view. DeMar developed the basic movement, enemy tracking, collision detection, and animated projectile and explosion systems, including a circular explosion effect later adapted for Blaster.

The game never advanced beyond an early demonstration. DeMar shifted attention to the more promising Robotron: 2084, and the team later discovered that Williams was independently developing the somewhat similar Sinistar. DeMar's surviving source code, historical interviews, and a reconstruction produced by Jeff Vavasour eventually brought this long-lost experiment back to public view. It offers a rare glimpse into ideas circulating among the creators of some of the most influential American arcade shooters.

games.title: Continental Circus
games.description:
Continental Circus is Taito's ambitious Formula One-style arcade racer, carrying a 1987 copyright and released in Japanese arcades in 1988. Players race through a succession of Grand Prix courses, trying to pass checkpoints and finish laps before the time limit expires. Cars can suffer progressive damage after collisions, requiring a visit to the pits before smoke becomes a catastrophic fire. Weather also matters: rain can affect handling and make tire choice important.

Its most remarkable attraction was the optional stereoscopic presentation. Dedicated cabinets employed synchronized shutter glasses to create a three-dimensional racing effect, an uncommon technology in 1980s arcades. A shifting field of cars, roadside obstacles, and hills added to the sensation of speed.

The unusual title is commonly attributed to a mistranslation of Continental Circuits, although Formula One was also popularly called a traveling circus. Whatever the origin, the game remains a notable example of Taito experimenting with driving realism, pit-stop management, and display technology at the same time.

games.title: Contra
games.description:
Konami's Contra (1987) is one of the defining arcade run-and-gun games and the beginning of a major action series. Soldiers Bill Rizer and Lance Bean are sent to stop the Red Falcon threat on the Galuga archipelago, battling through enemy bases, jungle defenses, and grotesque alien installations. One or two players can run, jump, duck, and fire in multiple directions, with a single enemy hit normally costing a life. The relentless shooting is punctuated by large bosses and increasingly otherworldly enemies.

The arcade game alternates side-scrolling stages with pseudo-3D corridor sections, changing the movement and aiming challenge without breaking the campaign. Weapon capsules supply powerful upgrades, most famously the Spread Gun, while careful coordination is crucial in simultaneous two-player play. Despite the simple two-button controls, success depends on memorizing hazards and mastering tight movement.

Contra was a major international hit and became even more widely known through its 1988 NES adaptation. The European arcade edition carried the title Gryzor, and later regional console versions appeared under other names. Its cinematic action style, unforgiving difficulty, and cooperative combat set the template for numerous arcade and console shooters that followed.

games.title: Cookie & Bibi
games.description: Cookie & Bibi (1995) is SemiCom's Korean take on the Puzzle Bobble formula. Players aim and launch colored, fruit-themed bubbles toward clusters suspended above the play area. Joining three or more of the same color clears them, while poor placement causes the growing mass to become harder to manage. The game replaces Taito's familiar bubble-dragons with its own characters and playful food imagery. Though closely derivative in structure, it is representative of the small-studio puzzle games that followed Puzzle Bobble's arcade success.

games.title: Cookie & Bibi 2
games.description: Cookie & Bibi 2, released around 1995-96 by SemiCom, continues the Korean puzzle series built around Puzzle Bobble-style aiming and matching. Players launch colored pieces into an overhead arrangement and try to create groups of three or more identical pieces to make them disappear. New layouts and a revised presentation give this sequel a slightly different pace while preserving the basic appeal of clearing increasingly awkward formations. It is best understood as an incremental follow-up rather than a completely new puzzle system.

games.title: Cookie & Bibi 3
games.description: SemiCom's Cookie & Bibi 3 (1997) is another Korean bubble-shooter puzzle game in the style of Puzzle Bobble, this time featuring food-shaped pieces. Players fire from a cannon at clusters hanging above, aiming to connect at least three matching pieces and remove them before the mass becomes unmanageable. The game includes a stage-based puzzle mode, cooperative play, and a competitive option for players who prefer head-to-head matches. Its colorful food theme and variety of modes make it a modest but recognizable entry in SemiCom's long-running imitation of Taito's puzzle formula.

games.title: Cool Minigame Collection
games.description:
Cool Minigame Collection (1999) is a Korean arcade compilation by SemiCom containing 36 short challenges rather than one continuous game. The selection is arranged as a six-by-six collection of activities with deliberately varied themes, including quick-action exercises, sports-like trials, puzzles, and comic situations. Games bearing names such as TNT, Fencer, Hamburger, Snowball, Penguin, and Pong Pong emphasize the anthology's playful breadth.

Its appeal lies in switching rapidly between small rule sets, rewarding adaptable timing and observation instead of mastery of a single long campaign. Cool Minigame Collection represents the party-game side of late-1990s arcades, where many compact challenges could be packed into one machine.

games.title: Cool Pool
games.description:
Cool Pool (1992) is a digitized billiards game developed by Catalina with a trackball-based control scheme. Players can choose straight pool, eight-ball, or nine-ball, while the trackball provides a physical way to line up and control shots. The game also offers selectable background music in styles such as jazz, rock, and fusion.

An optional adult-oriented Strip Pool mode was included, with several selectable characters; operators could configure this content for their venue. The mixture of traditional cue sports, tactile controls, and adult novelty made Cool Pool an unusual coin-op billiards machine rather than a standard sports game.

games.title: Cool Riders
games.description:
Sega's Cool Riders (1995) is a colorful motorcycle racer in the tradition of Out Run and OutRunners. Players select from an eccentric assortment of riders and machines, including conventional sport bikes, cruisers, and scooters, then speed across a succession of American highways. Each section must be completed before time expires, while competition with a computer-controlled rival determines who chooses the next route.

The game is notable for its lively digitized visual style, branching stage progression, and distinctive soundtrack, including use of Steppenwolf's Born to Be Wild. It was also the only released arcade game built around Sega's H1 board, whose unusual graphics compression later presented a significant emulation challenge. Cool Riders is a late, exuberant variation on Sega's checkpoint-based road-racing tradition.

games.title: Cop 01
games.description: Cop 01 is a 1985 Nichibutsu side-scrolling action game starring a futuristic policeman on a rescue mission. The hero runs and jumps through hostile environments while shooting enemies, and a wall of fire advancing from behind discourages lingering in one area. The need to keep moving creates a pressure distinct from the more methodical platform shooters of the period. Released originally in Japan, Cop 01 mixes cinematic spy-action influences with straightforward arcade platforming and is a relatively obscure title from Nichibutsu's mid-1980s catalog.

games.title: Cops'n Robbers
games.description:
Atari's Cops'n Robbers (1976) is an early four-player arcade shootout staged as a chase between police cars and criminals. The screen shows a city street from overhead: police vehicles occupy lanes on one side, robbers occupy the other, and the players move their cars vertically while firing across the road. A large truck drives along the center and can block shots at the most inconvenient moment. Computer-controlled participants fill unused positions when necessary.

The game is historically notable for accommodating four people side by side at one upright cabinet, rather than relying on a cocktail table. Its simple lane-based movement and opposing teams anticipate later multiplayer arcade competitions, while the cartoon police-and-robber setting gives a clear social identity to a very early shooting game.

games.title: Cosmic Cop
games.description:
Cosmic Cop, released by Irem in 1991 as Armed Police Unit Gallop in Japan, is a side-scrolling shooter connected to the R-Type universe. Instead of a conventional starfighter, players control an armed police craft sent to destroy criminal spacecraft. Standard forward fire and missiles can be strengthened with power-ups, but its signature weapon is a homing laser that automatically seeks threats on screen.

The laser is governed by an overheat meter, so keeping it active continuously is impossible. This makes weapon timing a central part of survival, rewarding players who reserve the laser for dangerous moments rather than relying on it constantly. With Irem's trademark elaborate enemies and demanding stages, Cosmic Cop offers an interesting variation on the R-Type formula rather than a straightforward sequel.

games.title: Cosmic Alien
games.description:
Cosmic Alien, carrying a 1979 copyright and documented as released in early 1980, is Universal's early fixed-screen space shooter in the tradition of Galaxian. The player's ship slides along the bottom of the screen and shoots into formations of different alien ranks, including guards, commanders, and chiefs. Enemy craft break away from formation to dive toward the player, and shooting a diving attacker can be worth more than destroying it in place.

The different enemy types follow distinct attack and firing patterns, while special scoring opportunities reward eliminating leaders together with their escorts. Released at the dawn of the arcade space-shooter boom, Cosmic Alien is a lesser-known example of the transition from static Space Invaders formations to more animated, aggressive alien attacks.

games.title: Cosmic Guerilla
games.description:
Cosmic Guerilla (1979) is Universal's inventive twist on the fixed-screen alien shooter. The player's gun moves along the bottom of the display, defending two reserve laser cannons positioned inside a cluster of barriers above. Rather than merely descending toward the player, enemy attackers advance from the sides and physically carry away protective blocks, gradually opening a route to the vulnerable cannons.

This creates a defensive puzzle alongside the usual shooting. Players must decide which enemies pose the greatest danger to the shield network, because allowing too many barriers to disappear exposes the reserve weapons. Its unusual arrangement and the impression of aliens dismantling defenses piece by piece distinguish Cosmic Guerilla from many Space Invaders imitators.

games.title: Cosmo
games.description: Cosmo is a 1979 fixed-screen space shooter published by TDS and developed with Mints. The player's spacecraft moves horizontally along the bottom of a vertical monitor, firing upward at successive waves of colorful aliens. Different enemy types follow their own descending and dive-bombing trajectories, making the timing of each shot and evasive movement important. The simple two-way joystick and single fire button recall Space Invaders, but its variety of attacker formations and individual alien behaviors give this obscure early shooter a distinct identity.

games.title: Cosmo Gang the Video
games.description:
Cosmo Gang the Video is Namco's exuberant 1992 reinvention of the Galaxian formula, featuring characters from its earlier Cosmo Gangs redemption machine. One or two players control Hyper Beat spacecraft at the bottom of a fixed screen, shooting down colorful alien invaders as they enter formation, break ranks, and swoop toward the player. Defeated enemies can leave behind weapon upgrades, shields, bombs, and other useful items, giving the familiar formation shooter a richer set of tactical possibilities.

Its distinctive bonus rounds reverse the usual objective: the mischievous Cosmo Gang attempts to steal the player's energy containers, and the players must prevent enough thefts to survive the timed challenge. Cooperative play is particularly unusual because the two ships share lives and can interact through special power-ups.

The bright cartoon art, speech samples, and variety of enemy behavior give Cosmo Gang the Video a much lighter personality than Namco's original space shooters. It was followed by Cosmo Gang the Puzzle and became a well-regarded late descendant of the fixed-screen arcade shooter tradition, combining nostalgia with a surprisingly elaborate set of twists.

games.title: Cosmos
games.description:
Cosmos is an early space shooter developed for Century Electronics' CVS arcade hardware, with a 1981 copyright and a documented 1982 release. Players fire on waves of alien craft and asteroids while managing threats that can quickly overwhelm the screen. Its notable defensive feature is a time-warp effect that temporarily slows enemies, offering breathing room during dense attacks.

Contemporary descriptions also note similarities to other space games in its treatment of fuel, weapon heat, and docking with a mothership. These borrowed elements and the ability to slow the action give Cosmos a peculiar identity among the many small arcade shooters released in the wake of Space Invaders and Galaxian.

games.title: Cotton
games.description:
Cotton: Fantastic Night Dreams (1991) introduced Success's candy-obsessed young witch in a playful horizontally scrolling shooter. Riding a broomstick and accompanied by the fairy Silk, Cotton battles through a magical world of monsters, ghosts, and enormous fantasy bosses in pursuit of her favorite Willow candy. The colorful environments and exaggerated characters replace the usual spaceships and military hardware with storybook imagery.

Fallen enemies and other targets produce crystals that can increase Cotton's firepower, while magic attacks and bombs provide more spectacular ways to clear the screen. Repeated play rewards learning enemy formations and making careful use of limited special weapons. Its mixture of accessible shooting, character humor, and fantasy art established the identity later retained by the series.

Originally released through Sega's arcade distribution, Cotton became a long-running cult favorite across arcades and home systems. Its importance lies not in inventing horizontal shooting but in giving the genre a distinctively cheerful heroine and a magical-comedy personality that remained recognizable through numerous sequels.

games.title: Cotton 2
games.description:
Cotton 2: Magical Night Dreams (1997) is Success's Sega ST-V sequel to its fantasy-themed arcade shooter. The candy-loving witch Cotton and her rival Appli, assisted by Silk the fairy and Needle the talking hat, travel through a magical kingdom in pursuit of the missing Bluewater Willow. One or two players fly through colorful side-scrolling stages, shooting fantastical enemies and confronting large bosses.

Compared with the original, Cotton 2 adds a more elaborate command system resembling fighting-game inputs. Special moves can capture enemies and projectiles inside bubbles, which can then be thrown or used defensively. Elemental crystals change weapons and magic properties, and the health meter allows more than one hit before a character is defeated. These systems make the action unusually tactical for a scrolling shooter.

The sequel was admired for its detailed animation and inventive combat, and was later ported to the Sega Saturn. Its mechanics also provided the foundation for Cotton Boomerang, which remixed many of the same assets into a faster, more aggressive game.

games.title: Cotton 2 (English translation)

modifications.description: Translates the attract-mode prologue, character profiles, stage-continue hints, all story dialogue scenes (VS0-VS6), ending sequence (VS7), and staff roll into English.

games.description: Cotton 2 (English translation) is an English localization patch by Zanac (with help from Katrin and Danthrax) for Success's 1997 Sega ST-V cute-'em-up Cotton 2: Magical Night Dreams. Adapting the script and graphics from the Sega Saturn fan translation to native ST-V arcade hardware, it translates the attract-mode prologue scroll, character profiles, continue-screen hints across all seven stages, in-game story cutscenes, and the ending credits into English while preserving original arcade gameplay timing.

games.title: Cotton Boomerang
games.description:
Cotton Boomerang (1998) is Success's exuberant remix of Cotton 2 for Sega's ST-V arcade hardware. Although it shares much of the earlier game's artwork, enemies, and magical setting, it substantially changes the rules. Instead of a character with a refillable health bar, players choose a team of three characters from a larger roster, each with distinct weapons and special attacks. A character can be lost to a single hit, but the player can switch to a surviving teammate during play.

Switching also triggers a screen-clearing attack, transforming character selection into a tactical weapon. Power-ups and magic have been rebalanced, stage layouts are remixed, and the action moves at a more aggressive pace than Cotton 2's relatively deliberate bubble-combo combat.

Far more than a simple reissue, Cotton Boomerang became a cult favorite for its replay value and layered character strategies. It offers a clear example of how an arcade revision can build an almost new shooter from an existing visual foundation.

games.title: Counter Run
games.description:
Counter Run (1988), developed by Nihon System and released by Sega, is a maze-chase game in which the player drives a small car around a network of corridors. The goal is to collect the fruit or dots scattered through each course while avoiding an opposing car that patrols the same maze. The entire level is visible from an elevated angle, and players must navigate the narrow gaps and walls without colliding with the pursuer.

Car handling provides the unusual twist: players can accelerate and reverse, but steering and accelerating are restricted while reversing. Some barriers can be crossed and bonus objects appear, while multiple course layouts increase the challenge. Its dial-based controls and automotive theme make it a peculiar descendant of Pac-Man-style maze games.

games.title: The Couples
games.description:
The Couples is an unofficial 1988 variation of Merit's 1986 memory game Match'em Up, rather than an original release developed by Merit. The underlying challenge is to uncover concealed symbols and remember their positions so that matching pairs can be found before the timer expires. An eight-way joystick and selection buttons are used to work across the fixed screen, making speed and short-term memory more important than reflex-based combat.

Its adult-oriented presentation and altered title distinguish this bootleg from Merit's original. Several closely related PCB sets survive in arcade preservation projects, with some boards marked January 1988; the title screen also gives 1988, although the precise release history is uncertain.

games.title: Peter Pepper's Ice Cream Factory

variants.title: Peter Pepper's Ice Cream Factory (Cassette, set 1)
Peter Pepper's Ice Cream Factory (Cassette, set 2)

games.description:
Peter Pepper's Ice Cream Factory (1984) is Data East's whimsical follow-up to BurgerTime, released for the DECO Cassette System. Instead of assembling hamburgers by walking over ingredients, chef Peter Pepper must move scoops of ice cream into waiting cones scattered across multilevel platforms. All scoops must be placed correctly to clear a stage, but hostile sweets and animated kitchen utensils continually get in his way.

The main mechanical innovation is direct interaction with the food. Peter can push or throw scoops, sometimes launching them to higher levels or using them to defeat enemies, and he can jump as well as climb ladders. The result is a more physical and puzzle-like version of BurgerTime's arcade formula. This relatively obscure sequel replaces the original's memorized ingredient routes with a fresh emphasis on manipulating objects.

games.title: Pro Bowling
games.description: Pro Bowling is a 1983 ten-pin bowling game released on Data East's DECO Cassette System, an interchangeable arcade platform that also hosted the company's early golf and tennis games. It brings the familiar objective of knocking down pins and completing frames to a compact coin-operated sports format. While its exact throwing controls are poorly documented, its historical interest comes from Data East's attempt to diversify arcade cabinets with recognizable recreational sports alongside fast-action games.

games.title: Pro Golf
games.description:
Pro Golf, also known in some versions as Tournament Pro Golf, is Data East's 1981 arcade golf game, offered both as a regular board and on the DECO Cassette System. Players choose shot direction and power, with the game handling club selection, and try to complete a series of holes within the permitted number of strokes. Bunkers, rough, trees, and water hazards force careful choice of angles and distances.

Its straightforward controls translate the basic decisions of golf into short turns suitable for coin-operated play. The arcade game is organized around a repeating set of nine holes, and two players can compete in alternating turns. It is a relatively early example of a recognizable sporting simulation on an interchangeable arcade system.

games.title: Pro Soccer
games.description: Data East's Pro Soccer (1983) is an early top-down arcade football game offered both as a standalone machine and as cassette number 33 for the DECO Cassette System. The field is shown vertically, with goals at opposite ends, and players try to outscore the opposing side within the match. Simple joystick controls direct the action, with separate buttons for passing between teammates and shooting. Its uncomplicated presentation places it among the early attempts to turn the movement and teamwork of association football into a real-time coin-operated sports game, well before the more elaborate soccer titles of the 1990s.

games.title: Pro Tennis
games.description: Pro Tennis is an early 1982 arcade tennis game by Data East, issued as cassette number 22 for the DECO Cassette System. It brings the familiar contest of returning shots across the net and winning points to the company's interchangeable coin-operated hardware. Although detailed descriptions of its stroke controls and match options are scarce, its release demonstrates how the DECO platform accommodated conventional sports such as tennis alongside shooters and maze games.

games.title: ZN1
games.description:
ZN1 is the BIOS for Capcom's implementation of the Sony ZN-1 arcade platform, introduced in 1995. ZN-1 brought the original PlayStation's MIPS-based architecture into the arcade, combining dedicated geometry and textured-graphics hardware with a modular main board and manufacturer-specific ROM circuitry. Its shared design helped bridge the transition from sprite-dominated systems to affordable real-time 3D hardware.

Capcom supplemented the Sony board with its own daughterboard containing a Z80 audio controller and QSound digital sound hardware. The BIOS provides the startup environment for this Capcom configuration and works alongside board-specific security devices. The preserved set also includes historical firmware revisions, including development material, rather than representing a playable program by itself.

games.title: ZN2
games.description:
ZN2 is the BIOS for Capcom's Sony ZN-2 arcade hardware, introduced in 1997 as an evolution of the ZN-1 platform. It retained the PlayStation-derived MIPS instruction set and Sony graphics architecture but used revised chips and a faster processor configuration, giving developers more room for complex 3D scenes and animation.

The Capcom implementation continued to use dedicated ROM boards and QSound-based audio circuitry, while the ZN-2 main board provided expanded video-memory arrangements and interfaces for specialized controls. Its manufacturer-specific BIOS and protection data distinguish the system from otherwise similar Sony-derived arcade boards. This entry preserves those shared startup components, not a standalone title.

games.title: Crackshot
games.description:
Exidy's Crackshot (1985) is a light-gun shooting gallery built around choosing the correct targets before time runs out. Players aim a cabinet-mounted gun through a changing sequence of scenes, hitting designated threats while avoiding objects or characters that should be left unharmed. The stages range from western-style barrooms and bank robberies to birds, robots, and outer-space targets, with a novelty slot-machine bonus round.

The rapidly changing themes make it closer to a carnival shooting gallery than to a single continuous combat story. Accuracy and quick discrimination matter more than simply firing as fast as possible. Crackshot was another distinctive entry in Exidy's line of arcade gun games, which often reused specialized light-gun cabinets for new target-shooting experiences.

games.title: Crash
games.description:
Crash (1979) is Exidy's early maze-driving game, designed and programmed by Edward Valeau. Players guide a continuously moving car along a compact grid of roadways, collecting dots while avoiding enemy cars approaching from the opposite direction. The player can change lanes at junctions and vary the car's speed, but cannot simply stop to wait for danger to pass.

The challenge comes from timing lane changes and anticipating oncoming traffic as the maze gradually empties of collectibles. Clearing one layout leads to another round with renewed hazards. Crash is an important early example of a car-based maze game, combining dot collection with a more constrained form of steering than the free movement found in Pac-Man.

games.title: Crater Raider
games.description:
Crater Raider (1984) is Bally Midway's unusual multidirectional tank shooter set on an alien world covered in craters. Players steer a futuristic tank around the landscape, rescuing stranded humans while fighting enemy tanks and UFOs. Completing a level requires collecting the hostages rather than simply destroying everything in sight, giving the action an objective beyond survival.

The crater-filled terrain is more than decoration. Entering certain craters transports the tank to another location, while special marked craters can replenish shields. A rotary control handles steering, and a protective shield can be activated when danger becomes overwhelming. This combination of rescue objectives, teleporting terrain, and tank combat distinguishes Crater Raider from Bally Midway's more conventional shooting games.

games.title: Crazy Fight
games.description: Crazy Fight is a 1990s arcade action shooting game associated with Subsino, with surviving sources giving inconsistent dates around 1996-98. Across six stages, players fire at hostile targets while trying to avoid hitting hostages who appear among them. Correctly distinguishing threats from innocent bystanders is therefore essential to progress. The game's documented appeal is its rapid target selection and rescue theme, rather than a fully described platform or fighting system; more detailed information about its stages and controls remains scarce.

games.title: Crazy Balloon
games.description:
Taito's Crazy Balloon (1980) is an unusually delicate arcade maze game. Players guide a small box suspended below a balloon through narrow passages lined with spikes and pinwheel-like obstacles. The balloon sways as the box changes direction, so steering the lower part safely through an opening does not guarantee that the balloon above will clear it. A single touch against a thorn bursts it and costs a life.

There is no ordinary countdown timer, but lingering too long summons a face that blows the balloon toward danger. Later mazes introduce moving obstacles and more difficult passages, making careful control increasingly important. Crazy Balloon stands out among early maze games for turning the physical behavior of a fragile, swinging object into the central challenge rather than relying on pursuing enemies.

games.title: Crowns Golf
games.description: Crowns Golf (1984), also distributed under the title Champion Golf, is an early golf arcade game developed by Nasco and licensed through Sega and other regional publishers. Players attempt to complete a golf course in as few strokes as possible, using joystick and button controls to manage their shots. Its appeal is the straightforward transfer of golf's aim, distance, and scoring decisions into a coin-operated cabinet. Regional releases and licensing arrangements made Crowns Golf familiar under more than one name, and it was followed by a Hawaii-themed sequel.

games.title: Crowns Golf in Hawaii
games.description: Crowns Golf in Hawaii is Nasco's 1985 sequel to Crowns Golf, issued through Sega's arcade distribution network. It carries the earlier game's golf competition into a Hawaiian setting, asking players to navigate the course and minimize the strokes taken on each hole. The continuation is more of a themed extension of Nasco's arcade golf format than a radically new sports game. Its release shows the popularity of compact golf simulations in mid-1980s amusement centers, with a further sequel, Super Crowns Golf, following in 1989.

games.title: Crime City
games.description:
Crime City (1989) is Taito's side-scrolling police action game and an official offshoot of the Chase H.Q. world. Instead of chasing suspects by car, officers Tony Gibson and Raymond Broady take to the streets on foot to confront criminal gangs. The six stages involve different crimes, including robberies and smuggling, and end with the defeat and arrest of a gang leader.
