Up to two players can cooperate, firing at enemies, taking cover behind scenery, and advancing through crowded urban settings.

The officers start with pistols but can obtain more powerful guns, including machine guns and spread-fire weapons. Ammunition is limited, and once their guns run dry they must rely on punches and acrobatic attacks. Its mixture of gunplay, close combat, and police-drama staging makes Crime City a distinctive alternative to the fantasy and military run-and-gun games common at the time.

games.title: Crime Fighters
games.description:
Konami's Crime Fighters (1989) helped establish the company's urban beat-'em-up line before Vendetta and the better-known Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles adaptations. Players take the role of undercover fighters battling through eight city locations to rescue kidnapped women from a criminal organization. Street punks swarm from both sides, while weapons such as pipes, knives, and firearms can be seized from opponents. Punching, kicking, and grappling are supplemented by boss battles against eccentric villains.

Different arcade editions offer different multiplayer configurations and rules. Some versions support up to four simultaneous players, while two-player sets have a more traditional setup; the four-player edition is especially notable for a health reserve that can be extended by inserting additional credits.

Crime Fighters retains the rough, sometimes deliberately comic atmosphere of late-1980s street brawlers, with crowded fights and exaggerated hazards. It represents an early step in Konami's refinement of the cooperative beat-'em-up formula that would become one of its arcade specialties.

games.title: Critter Crusher
games.description: Critter Crusher (1995), known as Tatakot in Japan, is Sega's arcade variation on whack-a-mole, released for its ST-V hardware. Rather than striking mechanical targets, players hit on-screen bugs and creatures using the cabinet's special hammer-style input device, turning a familiar amusement-park reflex challenge into a video game. The goal is to respond quickly to the creatures that appear, emphasizing physical timing rather than character movement or shooting. Its unusual controller is central to the experience and historically caused difficulties when the game was first emulated.

games.title: Crack Down
games.description:
Sega's Crack Down (1989) is an overhead-view infiltration shooter for one or two players, released on the System 24 arcade hardware. Special agents Ben and Andy must penetrate a city seized by an army of artificial soldiers and place timed explosive charges at designated points. Each stage is a maze of corridors, armed guards, and equipment; the agents must reach all marked locations and escape before the countdown expires.

Unlike a conventional endless firefight, success depends on plotting an efficient route through the map. Players can fight with limited-ammunition guns and explosives, collect supplies, and cooperate or divide tasks. The arcade game's split-screen presentation lets each agent explore independently, a particularly effective use of Sega's high-resolution System 24 display. Crack Down was later adapted for the Mega Drive/Genesis and home computers, but the arcade original remains distinctive for combining tactical movement, action shooting, and timed demolition objectives.

games.title: The Crystal Maze: Team Challenge
games.description:
The Crystal Maze: Team Challenge is a 1994 Barcrest video amusement and skill-with-prizes game based on the British television show The Crystal Maze. Players participate in a series of short challenges intended to win crystals, which in turn determine how much time is available for the concluding Crystal Dome round. The format adapts the television program's varied tests of quick thinking and dexterity into a coin-operated machine.

Rather than being a conventional platformer or quiz, it is a collection of themed minigames tied together by the crystal-collection objective. Its connection to the Channel 4 program and Barcrest's MPU4 Video hardware make it an unusual crossover between television game shows and British amusement-machine design.

games.title: The Crystal Maze
games.description: The Crystal Maze is an earlier Barcrest arcade amusement-machine edition based on the British Channel 4 television game show, associated with a 1993 UK release. Like The Crystal Maze: Team Challenge, it translates the program's premise into short skill-based challenges in which winning crystals contributes to a final Crystal Dome round. The game's identity rests on its television license and variety of self-contained tests rather than one continuous action scenario. This set represents a related edition within the Barcrest Crystal Maze family, not an unrelated game with the same title.

games.title: The Crystal Maze - Now Featuring Ocean Zone

variants.title: The Crystal Maze - Now Featuring Ocean Zone (AMLD Version SWP)

games.description: The Crystal Maze: Now Featuring Ocean Zone is a themed Barcrest edition of its television-inspired arcade amusement game. It retains the series' structure of completing short challenges to earn crystals and time for the final Crystal Dome, while the Ocean Zone branding reflects the addition of the show's nautical-themed area. This version belongs to the early-1990s British MPU4 Video family and is related to The Crystal Maze and Team Challenge releases. Its distinguishing feature is the Ocean Zone update rather than a completely different gameplay concept.

games.title: Cross Pang
games.description: Cross Pang is a Korean arcade puzzle game released by F2 System in April 1998. Its bright presentation centers on colored balls arranged in a compact playfield, with two-player competition supported by four-way joysticks and two buttons per player. Configurable settings include the number of extra balls per move and rewards for chain reactions, indicating an emphasis on managing the board and building combinations. It was followed in 1999 by New Cross Pang, which developed the colorful ball-matching concept further.

games.title: Crossbow
games.description:
Exidy's Crossbow (1983) is an unusually atmospheric light-gun game that turns the player into the unseen guardian of a party of fantasy adventurers. Rather than simply shooting everything on screen, the task is to keep vulnerable companions alive as they march across towns, deserts, jungles, caves, and castles. Scorpions, monsters, and environmental hazards must be eliminated before they reach the adventurers, but careless shots can injure the very people being protected. The number of survivors carries over between scenes, giving every rescue and mistake lasting consequences.

A branching route is selected by shooting destinations on a map. Eventually the expedition confronts the Master of Darkness, whose vulnerable eyes must be hit at the right moment. The arcade cabinet's large crossbow-shaped gun makes aiming a physical part of the experience, while the game's extensive sampled speech, music, and screams were exceptionally ambitious for 1983.

Designed by a team led by Nick Ilyin, Crossbow inaugurated Exidy's 440-series shooting games. The company subsequently reused the technology in conversion titles such as Cheyenne, Chiller, and Combat. Its mixture of target shooting, route choice, and protecting non-player characters makes it quite different from later reflex-driven rail shooters.

games.title: Lethal Crash Race
games.description:
Lethal Crash Race, known in Japan as Bakuretsu Crash Race, is a 1993 top-down racing game from Video System. Players choose from eight eccentric international drivers and compete in one-on-one races through courses set in different parts of the world. Each rival has a distinct personality, and the character-specific endings give the tournament a structure reminiscent of the same developer's Sonic Wings shooters.

Despite its racing format, the attraction is as much the cast as the competition. The game introduced Ellen and Cincia, characters who later appeared in the Sonic Wings series, making it an unexpected part of Video System's shared arcade universe. It uses a vertically oriented screen and joystick-and-button controls rather than a conventional steering-wheel cabinet.

games.title: Crossed Swords 2
games.description:
This AdvanceMAME entry is an unofficial Neo Geo MVS cartridge conversion of Crossed Swords II, a sequel originally released for the Neo Geo CD in 1995. The arcade-compatible version is associated with the Neo Geo hacker Razoola; it is not a separate official arcade sequel or a mere recoloring of the first Crossed Swords.

Like its predecessor, the game presents fantasy sword fights from an over-the-shoulder perspective, with the player's warrior shown as a translucent outline so incoming enemies remain visible. The sequel adds a choice of Knight, Dancer, or Ninja, along with jumping and dashing maneuvers that widen the defensive and offensive options. In addition to the story campaign, it offers an arena-style succession of battles. The conversion is historically notable for bringing a CD-exclusive Neo Geo title to cartridge-based MVS hardware.

games.title: Crossed Swords
games.description:
Crossed Swords (1991) is Alpha Denshi's distinctive fantasy action game for the Neo Geo. Instead of the sideways view common to beat 'em ups, combat unfolds from directly behind the player, whose hero appears as a transparent, wireframe-like silhouette. This makes it possible to watch monstrous enemies telegraph attacks while still seeing the action from the knight's viewpoint. Two players can undertake the journey together.

Success depends more on reading opponents than on constant attacking. The knight can shift position, raise a shield to guard different heights, and retaliate with slashes or thrusts. Magical sword attacks and equipment obtained along the way add variety, while branching routes allow different journeys through the kingdom of Belkana and its demon-infested strongholds.

Often compared with SNK's The Super Spy because of its perspective, Crossed Swords stands apart through deliberate melee combat and its unusually strong emphasis on blocking. It was followed by Crossed Swords II on the Neo Geo CD in 1995.

games.title: Crush Roller
games.description:
Crush Roller, developed by Alpha Denshi and released in 1981, is a wonderfully eccentric maze game in which the player controls a paintbrush instead of a hungry yellow character. The objective is to cover every corridor of the maze in paint while two persistent fish escape their aquariums and give chase. Merely passing through a corridor is not enough if an intruder later spoils the paint: damaged sections have to be painted again before the stage can end.

Two heavy rollers positioned on overpasses provide the paintbrush's only reliable means of fighting back. Timing a roller's movement can flatten pursuing fish for bonus points, although they return after a short absence and eventually learn to avoid the traps. A mischievous third visitor periodically crosses the playfield leaving marks, introducing a second kind of interference.

The game circulated under several identities: Exidy distributed Crush Roller in Europe, while Williams marketed it in North America as Make Trax. Other versions and hacks include Korosuke Roller, Paint Roller, and Magic Brush. Its unusual painting objective and adaptive pursuers make it one of the more imaginative maze games to emerge in the wake of Pac-Man.

games.title: Crusher Makochan
games.description:
Crusher Makochan is a 1999 Japanese medal game by Takumi that disguises its risk-and-reward structure as a cartoon combat contest. The player moves through a succession of short stages where button-pressing challenges are affected by randomly awarded beneficial or harmful items. Different routes change the apparent difficulty and potential medal returns.

Unlike a conventional fighting game, the outcome is strongly influenced by chance. Players can collect a reward and stop at designated points or continue toward a third stage in pursuit of a larger payout, risking what they have accumulated. Its preservation is notable because Japanese medal games of this sort were seldom documented or dumped as extensively as ordinary arcade action titles.

games.title: Cruis'n Exotica
games.description:
Midway's Cruis'n Exotica (1999) takes the extravagant, arcade-first racing of Cruis'n USA and Cruis'n World to its most surreal extreme. Players still race point to point against nine rivals, dodging traffic and obstacles while charging through checkpoints, but the itinerary now extends beyond familiar cities to fantasy settings such as Atlantis, a dinosaur-filled Amazon, and even Mars.

The selection includes conventional sports cars alongside deliberately absurd vehicles and selectable drivers, turning what began as a cross-country road trip into a playful spectacle. A PIN-based progress system lets returning arcade players retain their advancement, a notable addition to the series' straightforward pick-up-and-play formula.

Built on Midway's Zeus 2 hardware, Exotica continued the series' tradition of bold, colorful 3D scenery and exaggerated collision physics. Nintendo 64 and Game Boy Color adaptations followed in 2000, although the home versions changed aspects of the arcade courses and vehicle selection.

games.title: Cruis'n USA
games.description:
Cruis'n USA (1994) is Midway's exuberant coast-to-coast racer and the first installment of the Cruis'n series. Under the direction of arcade veteran Eugene Jarvis, it traded driving simulation for accessible controls, broad powerslides, outrageous crashes, and a colorful road trip across the United States. Drivers race against nine opponents while avoiding civilian traffic and roadside hazards, beginning around San Francisco and eventually reaching Washington, D.C.

The original cabinet featured a steering wheel, accelerator and brake pedals, a gear selector, and buttons for changing the camera view or music. Races are point-to-point sprints with time limits and checkpoints, while linked machines allow head-to-head competition. Hidden vehicles, alternate tracks, and intentionally exaggerated handling reward experimentation rather than realistic driving technique.

Cruis'n USA was promoted as part of Nintendo and Midway's 'Ultra 64' initiative, but the arcade machine actually ran on Midway's own V-Unit hardware, not the technology later used in the Nintendo 64 console. Its arcade popularity helped establish a distinctly American alternative to Sega's Daytona USA and launched a long-running line of over-the-top racing games.

games.title: Cruis'n World
games.description:
Cruis'n World (1996) expands Midway's arcade racing formula from the highways of the United States to a globe-spanning itinerary. Players race against nine other cars through locations inspired by Hawaii, Japan, Australia, Egypt, Europe, and other destinations, negotiating traffic, shortcuts, and checkpoints before time runs out. The colorful landscapes and deliberately implausible collisions preserve the original game's accessible style.

The biggest change is the introduction of stunts. Wheelies can produce speed bursts, and well-executed jumps or flips can improve a race result. More cars, additional secrets, and an expanded route selection make the sequel livelier than its predecessor. The cabinet again uses a wheel and pedals, with linked competition available.

Cruis'n World retained Midway's V-Unit arcade technology and was later adapted to the Nintendo 64, where it gained additional modes. Its stunt-focused racing became an important part of the series' identity.

games.title: Crypt Killer
games.description:
Konami's Crypt Killer (1995), released in Japan as Henry Explorers, is a horror-themed light-gun shooter built around a succession of monster-filled archaeological expeditions. Up to three players can shoot simultaneously as the camera moves automatically through crypts and other sinister environments. Skeletons, gargoyles, and other creatures are rendered as sprites against polygonal scenery, producing the distinctive mixture of 2D and 3D graphics typical of its era.

Players can select among six opening stages, shoot breakable objects for concealed weapon upgrades, and choose alternate routes at branching points. Each expedition ends in a boss encounter guarding an Eye of Guidance. Collecting different combinations of these artifacts leads to several endings, some of them deliberately comic rather than straightforward horror.

The arcade game stands out for its three-player cabinet and its non-linear progression at a time when many gun shooters followed a single fixed route. Conversions for the PlayStation, Saturn, and Japanese personal computers followed in 1997.

games.title: Crystal System BIOS
games.description:
Crystal System BIOS belongs to Brezzasoft's compact arcade platform introduced in 2001. The hardware was built around the Magic Eyes VRender0, an integrated device combining an ADC SE3208 32-bit RISC processor with 2D graphics, texture mapping, scaling, rotation, alpha blending, and sample-based audio. Its tightly integrated design allowed the main printed circuit board to be unusually small.

The board used separate pools of main, texture, and frame memory and connected to arcade cabinets through JAMMA. It was presented as a modern, cartridge-oriented platform for high-quality 2D presentation at a time when much of the industry was turning to more elaborate 3D systems. The BIOS contains the platform's essential startup code and is preserved independently of the removable software media.

games.title: The Crystal of Kings
games.description:
The Crystal of Kings (2001) is a fantasy side-scrolling beat 'em up released by BrezzaSoft on the Crystal System arcade board. Players select from four heroes and push through groups of monsters and armed enemies, using close-range attacks and special powers to survive the journey. The character choices provide different approaches to combat, while large fantasy bosses punctuate the stages.

Its hand-drawn, late-arcade-era presentation recalls the cooperative fantasy brawlers of the early 1990s, but it appeared when such games were becoming uncommon in coin-operated arcades. The title is also a principal showcase for BrezzaSoft's relatively obscure Crystal System hardware.

games.title: Crystal Gal 2
games.description: Crystal Gal 2 is a Japanese mahjong arcade game released in 1986, following Crystal Gal. Like its predecessor, it belongs to the adult-themed mahjong genre that occupied a substantial niche of Japanese amusement centers during the 1980s. Play is built around mahjong matches rather than action sequences; its significance is primarily as a surviving example of that specialized market.

games.title: Crystal Gal
games.description: Crystal Gal is a Japanese adult-oriented mahjong game released in May 1986. It uses the familiar turn-based tile-drawing and hand-building conventions of arcade mahjong, pairing the tabletop contest with character imagery aimed at an adult audience. A follow-up, Crystal Gal 2, appeared shortly afterward. Both titles illustrate the range of specialized mahjong machines available in Japanese arcades alongside mainstream action games.

games.title: Crazy Rally
games.description:
Crazy Rally is a vertically scrolling driving game released by Spanish developer Tecfri in 1985. The player steers a car along a busy road, slipping around ordinary traffic, emergency vehicles, and other obstacles while the scenery scrolls downward. With steering handled by a two-direction joystick and separate action buttons, it takes a compact, overhead approach to racing rather than attempting a cockpit simulation.

The emphasis is on avoiding collisions and maintaining progress through increasingly congested roads. Its modest hardware and straightforward presentation make it representative of the independently developed European coin-op games of the mid-1980s.

games.title: Capcom Sports Club
games.description:
Capcom Sports Club (1997) combines three accessible sporting games on a single CPS-2 cartridge: soccer, basketball, and tennis. Players select a sport from the menu and take part in quick, exaggerated contests whose colorful characters and immediate controls are closer to arcade action than to detailed athletic simulations.

Each sport has its own rules and scoring, and the cabinet can support competition between human players. The compilation's variety is its main attraction, offering short matches and rapid changes of pace without changing machines. Released relatively late in the CPS-2's commercial life, it is an unusual example of Capcom using hardware more closely associated with fighting games for an all-in-one sports cabinet.

games.title: Scrum Try
games.description: Scrum Try is Data East's 1984 arcade rugby game for the DECO Cassette System. It presents rugby as a compact, joystick-controlled sporting contest rather than a detailed simulation, with players trying to advance the ball and score against the opposing side. Its appearance on Data East's cassette-based arcade platform is a reminder that the system hosted a diverse catalog extending well beyond conventional shooting and maze games.

games.title: Chicken Shift
games.description:
Chicken Shift (1984) is one of Bally/Sente's most unusual early arcade puzzle games. The player does not directly guide a character through a maze. Instead, chickens at the top of the screen lay eggs that roll through a complicated network of pipes toward a basket below. Two buttons rotate groups of red and blue pipe sections, and the challenge is to align the correct route just before each egg reaches a junction.

Since different parts of the network need attention at the same time, a switch thrown too early or too late may send an egg into danger. The combination of indirect control, precise timing, and elaborate farmyard machinery gives Chicken Shift the feeling of an interactive mechanical puzzle rather than a conventional platform game.

games.title: Cross Shooter
games.description:
Cross Shooter, also released as Air Raid, is a 1987 vertically scrolling shoot-'em-up from Seibu Kaihatsu. The player pilots a small fighter through colorful enemy formations, using forward fire and a limited supply of bombs to clear the screen. Defeated enemies release power-ups whose colors change over time, rewarding players who time their collection to obtain the desired weapon upgrade.

Its bright, almost cartoon-like visual style is notably different from the harder military aesthetic of Seibu's later Raiden series. Cross Shooter is an obscure but historically interesting predecessor to that company's better-known arcade shooters.

games.title: Captain Silver
games.description:
Captain Silver (1987) is Data East's pirate-themed side-scrolling action game, starring a young adventurer hunting the treasure of the legendary Captain Silver. The hero travels through towns, harbors, caves, and hostile territory, fighting pirates and fantastic creatures with a sword while jumping between platforms and climbing ladders.

Collectible items improve the hero's capabilities, and equipment bought or found along the way provides welcome help against the game's demanding enemies. The combination of swordplay, platforming, shops, and treasure-hunting scenery gives it a flavor of an arcade adventure rather than a simple left-to-right brawler. It later appeared on home systems, although the arcade original is the reference point for this entry.

games.title: Champion Skill
games.description:
Champion Skill is an IGS video gambling and redemption game preserved in versions labelled With Ability and Ability, Poker & Symbols. Its single-player, five-button layout and Z80-based hardware belong to the borderland between video poker, symbol matching and amusement-with-prizes machines. The 'ability' designation distinguishes it from conventional chance-only gambling products, although the precise skill sequence and scoring rules are not adequately described in surviving sources.

The game also has an unusual emulation history: it appeared in early MAME releases, was removed when gambling and payout machines fell outside the project's then-current scope, and was later restored. That history makes it a revealing example of how arcade preservation expanded beyond coin-operated action games.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Championship Sprint
games.description:
Atari Games' Championship Sprint (1986) is an overhead racing game that follows the hugely successful Super Sprint formula with more demanding tracks and sharper competition. Up to three players use large steering wheels and accelerator pedals to guide miniature Formula-style cars around compact circuits viewed entirely from above.

The tracks are full of tight corners, hazards, shortcuts, and opportunities to outmaneuver rivals. Wrenches collected during races can be spent on upgrades, introducing a light element of long-term strategy to the frantic short events. Much of the appeal comes from the physical steering controls and the chaos of three human drivers fighting for the same section of road.

Championship Sprint is more an expanded successor than a new genre: its additional circuits and competitive tuning preserve the clarity and immediacy that made Atari's overhead racers popular in arcades.

games.title: Vs. Castlevania
games.description:
Vs. Castlevania (1987) is the Nintendo Vs. System arcade adaptation of the original Castlevania. Players control vampire hunter Simon Belmont as he enters Dracula's castle, climbing stairways, leaping over traps, and battling skeletons, bats, and other monsters on a quest to confront the Count.

Simon attacks with a whip that can be upgraded, while secondary weapons such as daggers, axes, and holy water consume hearts collected from candles and enemies. The fixed jump trajectory and exacting enemy placement demand careful timing. As a coin-operated adaptation of the NES game, Vs. Castlevania brings a landmark home-console action platformer into Nintendo's arcade hardware ecosystem, with game settings tailored to arcade operation.

games.title: Super Astro Fighter
games.description:
Super Astro Fighter (1981) is Data East's enhanced follow-up to Astro Fighter, produced for the DECO Cassette System. The player defends successive sectors of space from waves of invading UFOs, shooting down alien craft before confronting the larger enemy vessel known as the Space Master. Destroying and docking with that vessel provides an opportunity to refuel before the mission continues.

Its revised graphics and sounds build on a simple early-space-shooter foundation. The game is also part of Data East's notable cassette-based system, which let operators exchange software without replacing the entire arcade cabinet.

games.title: Terranean
games.description: Terranean is an early Data East space shooter released on the DECO Cassette System in 1981. The setting casts the player as a defender of Earth against approaching alien raiders, in a compact arcade format built around shooting down attackers before they can break through. It belongs to the first wave of interchangeable cassette games produced for Data East's unusual arcade platform.

games.title: Treasure Island
games.description:
Data East's Treasure Island (1981) is an early isometric maze-action game whose central danger is a sinking island. The player guides an explorer upward through winding routes, collects scattered treasure, and tries to reach the building at the summit before the terrain disappears beneath them. Hostile creatures patrol the passages, but stones can be thrown to clear a path.

Tunnels provide shortcuts through the maze, although they can also hide enemies. The game combines the urgency of a rising environmental threat with the navigation and item collecting of an arcade maze game. It appeared both as a DECO Cassette System title and in a dedicated cabinet, making it a historically interesting example of isometric perspective before that visual style became widespread.

games.title: Captain Tomaday
games.description:
Captain Tomaday (1999) is a charmingly eccentric vertically scrolling shooter from Visco for the Neo Geo. Its unlikely hero is a tomato transformed into a superhero, facing swarms of bizarre creatures and mechanical enemies in a brightly colored cartoon world. Instead of a conventional fighter plane, the player steers the flying tomato and attacks with its fists.

Power-ups change the character's form and fighting abilities, while the continual stream of humorous enemy designs gives the game a distinctive look. It offers a lighter, more comic alternative to the militaristic and bullet-heavy shooters that dominated the late-1990s arcade scene.

games.title: Tornado
games.description:
Tornado is a 1982 Data East shooter for the DECO Cassette System, built around a circular, tube-like playfield reminiscent of Tempest. The player controls a robot moving around the perimeter and fires toward the center at enemies emerging from within. At the same time, capsules positioned around the outer edge must be protected from destruction.

Its unusual geometry shifts the emphasis from conventional left-to-right movement to choosing firing positions around a ring. The game is one of the less familiar experiments in Data East's cassette-based arcade catalog.

games.title: The Combatribes
games.description:
The Combatribes (1990) is Technos Japan's tough, street-level beat 'em up starring three cyborg vigilantes: Berserker, Bullova, and Blitz. In a crime-ridden New York, they battle gangs through stages set in locations such as an amusement park, a nightclub, and a baseball stadium. The large character sprites, urban atmosphere, and deliberate pacing distinguish it from the faster River City and Double Dragon branches of Technos' catalog.

Players can punch, kick, grab, and throw enemies, but the game's most memorable moves are spectacularly brutal, including slamming opponents against the ground or using one thug as a weapon against another. Two or three players can join the brawl depending on the cabinet arrangement. Each hero has different strengths, encouraging coordination when the screen fills with opponents.

The Combatribes later received a Super Nintendo adaptation, but the arcade original retains its distinctive large sprites and punishing combat. It is a cult favorite for enthusiasts of Technos' particular style of close-quarters brawling.

games.title: Test Tape
games.description:
Test Tape is a 1981 service and diagnostic cassette for Data East's DECO Cassette System, not a conventional arcade title. Data East's system used interchangeable magnetic cassettes to load programs into a reusable cabinet, reducing the need to replace a complete circuit board when changing software.

This test cassette belongs to the maintenance side of that model. It provided technicians and operators with a dedicated system-test program running on the same 6502-based hardware and cassette-loading arrangement as ordinary releases. Its preservation is especially useful because it documents how early interchangeable-media arcade equipment could be checked and maintained.

games.title: Cuby Bop
games.description:
Cuby Bop is an unreleased arcade puzzle prototype that reached location testing but not general commercial release. Two players, or one player against the computer, compete to break colored blocks by throwing a ball upward. Each side has its own block color, blue for one player and red for the other, and a ball only destroys blocks belonging to the player whose color it currently carries. Against the other color, the ball simply rebounds.

This simple restriction turns ball timing and control into a tactical contest rather than a conventional block-breaking game. The surviving prototype is a glimpse of an arcade design that never reached the broader market.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Cue Brick
games.description:
Konami's Cue Brick (1989) is an isometric sliding-block puzzle game that revisits ideas from the company's earlier Guttang Gottong. Players rearrange track-like pieces and move blocks through compact puzzle layouts, trying to make the necessary connections or reach the required arrangement. Its clean angled perspective makes the relationship between pieces easy to read while concealing surprisingly tricky solutions.

The game stands apart from the reflex-heavy arcade puzzle boom through its slower emphasis on spatial reasoning and planning. It offers a rare example of a major Japanese arcade manufacturer producing a cerebral block puzzle instead of another action game.

games.title: Seimei-Kantei-Meimei-Ki Cult Name
games.description:
Seimei-Kantei-Meimei-Ki Cult Name is a 1996 Japanese arcade fortune-telling and name-analysis machine published by I'Max, with development associated with KID. Rather than an action game, it offers a form of onomancy, the Japanese practice of interpreting the presumed fortune or character associated with a person's name. Players interact with the machine to receive a personalized assessment and an auspicious alternative name. It runs on the Multi Amenity Cassette System, a platform used for unusual coin-operated attractions.

A contemporary 1996 coin-op trade report described Cult Name as a machine that would provide customers with a 'lucky second name', placing it alongside photo-sticker booths and other inexpensive personalized attractions aimed at Japanese amusement-center visitors. It is a distinctive example of the arcade as a home for novelty services as well as games.

games.title: Cuore Uno
games.description:
Cuore Uno, also known as Cuore 1, is an Italian card-gambling machine associated with C.M.C. and dated to the mid-1990s. Instead of standard playing-card suits, it asks players to assemble valuable hands from hearts differentiated by numbers and colors. A higher-or-lower gamble offers a further chance to increase winnings after the main hand, giving this video-poker variation a recognizable second decision point.

The surviving Italian-language sets include revisions and possible bootlegs. It runs on 65C02-family hardware with AY-3-8910 sound and a seven-button control panel. Its unconventional heart cards are a stronger identifying feature than its many closely related PCB versions.

games.title: Taito Cup Finals
games.description:
Taito Cup Finals is the international version of Hat Trick Hero '93, a 1993 soccer game running on Taito's F3 arcade hardware. Players guide national teams through fast, direct matches using a joystick and action buttons for passing, shooting, and defending. The game favors aggressive challenges and spectacular goal attempts over the tactical depth of a simulation.

Its exaggerated tackles and brisk pace reflect the arcade soccer tradition of turning the sport into an immediate, competitive spectacle. The regional naming also makes it an interesting example of the same Japanese release being presented differently to overseas arcade audiences.

games.title: Seibu Cup Soccer
games.description:
Seibu Cup Soccer (1992) is a quick-playing international soccer game from Seibu Kaihatsu. Players select one of eight national teams, including Brazil, Argentina, Italy, England, Japan, and Korea, and compete through a succession of short matches. A draw can lead to extra time or a penalty shootout rather than simply ending the competition.

A distinctive feature is the 'dynamite kick' gauge, which periodically enables a powerful shot and adds an unpredictable arcade flourish to otherwise recognizable soccer play. The game also circulated under names including Goal! '92 and Olympic Soccer '92, illustrating the complicated regional distribution of some early-1990s football games.

games.title: Curve Ball
games.description: Curve Ball is a 1984 arcade baseball game built for short, self-contained matches. One or two players take part in games lasting just three innings, concentrating the familiar sequence of pitching, batting, and fielding into a coin-op-friendly format. Its appeal is the simplicity of the sport translated into a compact arcade contest rather than a full-season simulation.

games.title: Cute Fighter
games.description: Cute Fighter is a 1998 arcade fighting game whose defining characteristic is a cast of twelve deliberately small, cartoonish fighters. It follows SD Fighters, continuing the super-deformed visual style that replaces muscular realism with exaggerated proportions and playful character designs. Beneath its lighthearted presentation is a conventional head-to-head fighting format based on choosing a character and defeating an opponent in successive bouts.

games.title: Cutie Q
games.description:
Namco's Cutie Q (1979) is an early hybrid of video pinball and block-breaking action, and the final installment in the Gee Bee trilogy. A rotary controller moves sets of paddles to keep the ball in play and redirect it into rainbow-colored bricks, spinners, small ghosts called Minimon, and bonus targets. Lighting a row of sad faces changes them to smiling faces and increases the scoring multiplier, adding a little strategy to the fast rebounds.

Designed by Shigeru Yokoyama with character artwork by Toru Iwatani, Cutie Q was one of Namco's earliest experiments with a cute, character-driven visual style. Iwatani went on to create Pac-Man, making this modest paddle game an intriguing precursor to Namco's defining arcade hit. It was originally marketed as a conversion for earlier Gee Bee-family machines.

games.title: CVS Bios
games.description:
The CVS BIOS belongs to Century Electronics' Convertible Video System, introduced in Britain in 1981. CVS was an early modular arcade platform designed so that operators could change the installed software by replacing a compact program module while retaining the principal cabinet electronics. Developed with Philips technology, the system used a Signetics 2650 processor and a separate sound board with speech-synthesis capability.

The acronym CVS stood for Convertible Video System. Its interchangeable program modules and common motherboard anticipated a business model that would become more widespread in later arcade generations. This entry represents the platform's shared system code rather than a standalone program, and it preserves the architecture of a relatively overlooked British coin-operated system.

games.title: Capcom World
games.description:
Capcom World: Adventure Quiz is a 1989 Japanese arcade quiz game that turns a trivia contest into a lighthearted tour of Capcom's own fictional universe. The Princess of Capcom Kingdom has been kidnapped, and players travel across a series of board-game-like worlds by rolling dice and moving between spaces. Encounters trigger timed multiple-choice questions, with four dedicated answer buttons used to progress. The result is part quiz machine, part tabletop adventure, and a playful departure from Capcom's better-known action games.

Its chief attraction for arcade historians is the cast of familiar Capcom characters used as obstacles and opponents. Dr. Wily from Mega Man, Red Arremer from Ghosts 'n Goblins, the Unknown Soldier from Forgotten Worlds, and the tiny Mobi-chan from Side Arms all make appearances. Released in Japan in November 1989, Capcom World later inspired a sequel and received a PC Engine CD adaptation, making it an early example of Capcom celebrating its own expanding arcade heritage.

games.title: Capcom World 2
games.description:
Adventure Quiz: Capcom World 2 is a 1992 Japanese arcade quiz game produced for Capcom's CPS-1 hardware. Rather than presenting questions as an isolated television-style test, it frames them as a lighthearted adventure through a world built around Capcom characters and references. Players advance by answering multiple-choice questions, with progress depending on both knowledge and quick decisions.

The game follows the original Capcom World and belongs to a line of Japanese arcade trivia adventures that rarely received international releases because their questions and wordplay were closely tied to Japanese language and popular culture. It is a curiosity in Capcom's CPS-1 catalog, which is otherwise better known for shooters, platform action, and fighting games.

games.title: Cybattler
games.description:
Cybattler (1993) is a vertically scrolling mecha shooter from Jaleco that gives its robot pilot a more varied arsenal than the usual single forward-firing weapon. The player commands the armored machine Blanche through a series of futuristic battlefields, attacking with guns and a close-range beam sword while collecting equipment that changes its offensive options.

The ability to engage enemies at melee range makes positioning unusually important for a scrolling shooter. Its large mechanical designs and alternating combat ranges set it apart from more conventional fighter-plane games, while the demanding enemy waves preserve the precision expected of early-1990s Japanese arcades.

games.title: Cyberball 2072
games.description:
Cyberball 2072 is Atari Games' 1989 update to its futuristic robot-football game Cyberball. This entry represents the compact, single-monitor two-player arcade version rather than the large twin-monitor Tournament cabinet. Both share major gameplay revisions, including Rookie and Game Breakers modes, many additional offensive and defensive plays, and new roles such as the powerback.

The signature explosive football remains central. As the ball heats from cool to critical, a robot tackled while holding it risks being destroyed, so the attacking team must balance yardage against the danger of one play too many. Improvements to the teams and expanded tactical choices make 2072 more than a cosmetic revision of the 1988 original.

games.title: Cyberball
games.description:
Atari Games' Cyberball (1988) transforms American football into a violent futuristic sport contested entirely by robots. Each team fields seven machines with different capabilities, and offensive and defensive plays are selected from extensive tactical menus. The familiar aim of reaching the end zone remains, but the football itself is a bomb whose temperature rises as plays continue.

The ball moves from 'cool' to 'warm', 'hot', and finally 'critical'. A tackle at the critical stage destroys the ball carrier, so teams must decide whether to push for another gain or make a safer play that resets the danger. Crossing midfield or a change of possession can cool the ball, turning possession management into a tactical game within the sport.

Cyberball's distinctive cabinets could accommodate multiple simultaneous players, making it a popular social competition. Its explosive rule change and mechanical athletes are more than cosmetic gimmicks: they meaningfully alter the strategy of arcade football. The series expanded with Cyberball 2072 and tournament-oriented revisions.

games.title: Cyberball
games.description:
This entry preserves a prototype build of Atari Games' Cyberball, the 1988 seven-on-seven robot-football game. It already centers on the defining mechanic of the finished release: a football that grows progressively hotter, with a critical ball capable of exploding and destroying the robot carrying it when tackled. Players select plays, move robotic athletes, and try to advance downfield before the explosive rule turns against them.

Its importance is archival rather than that of a separate sequel. The prototype documents a stage in the development of the original Cyberball, allowing comparison with the later commercial revisions.

games.title: Tournament Cyberball 2072
games.description:
Tournament Cyberball 2072 is the four-player, twin-monitor version of Atari Games' major 1989 update to Cyberball. Two sides select plays and maneuver seven robotic football players, while the ball heats up toward a critical state that can destroy a tackled carrier. The oversized cabinet allows pairs of players to cooperate on opposing teams, recreating the original game's social, competitive appeal.

Compared with the 1988 Cyberball, the 2072 update adds Rookie and Game Breakers modes, approximately 100 additional plays, new player roles including the powerback, and corrections to the onside-kick system. These changes expand the tactical possibilities while preserving the explosive-ball rule that defines the series.

games.title: Cyber-Lip
games.description:
Cyber-Lip (1990) is an early Neo Geo run-and-gun platform shooter from SNK. Two soldiers battle through a near-future military disaster after a powerful defense computer turns its robotic forces against humanity. The characters move through side-scrolling installations, shooting enemy troops and machines, collecting weapons, and surviving imposing stage bosses.

Its appeal lies in the heavy military hardware, cooperative two-player action, and the varied arsenal available from weapon pickups. Interludes and branching route choices give the campaign more personality than a straightforward sequence of shooting galleries. The game also features a famously abrupt and unsettling conclusion that has helped sustain its cult reputation.

As one of the early Neo Geo action titles, Cyber-Lip shows SNK experimenting with genres beyond the fighting games that would later define the hardware.

games.title: Cyber Tank
games.description:
Cyber Tank is a rare, unreleased 1988 arcade shooter developed by Coreland, the company that would become Banpresto. It was tested publicly but never entered normal commercial production. The unusual two-player arrangement divides the action between a player handling the vehicle's horizontal movement and a second player operating a separate gun to shoot approaching enemies.

The second player can join while the first is already playing, turning the cockpit into a cooperative action station. Its surviving hardware and location-test history make it a particularly intriguing example of an arcade project abandoned before wide release.

games.title: Cyborg Force
games.description: Cyborg Force is a homebrew run-and-gun action game developed and published by Neo Byte Force for the Neo Geo MVS platform in 2023.

games.title: Cyberbots: Fullmetal Madness
games.description:
Capcom's Cyberbots: Fullmetal Madness (1995) is a one-on-one fighting game in which enormous combat robots, rather than human martial artists, occupy the screen. Emerging from the mechanical designs of Armored Warriors, it allows players to choose pilots and select different machines whose weapons, speed, reach, and special attacks change the rhythm of a match.

Battles use the familiar facing-off structure of a 2D fighting game, but giant limbs, energy weapons, and spectacular mechanical effects give every attack a sense of mass. The pilot-specific story routes add an anime-style narrative framework, and the intricate robot sprite work showcases Capcom's CPS-2 technology.

Although less famous than Street Fighter, Cyberbots developed a dedicated following for its unusual cast and tactical distinctions between machines. The character Jin Saotome subsequently appeared in Capcom crossover fighting games, bringing one of its pilots to a much wider audience.

games.title: Cyber Commando
games.description:
Namco's Cyber Commando (1994) is a polygonal arena-combat game and the successor to Cyber Sled. The player pilots one of six futuristic armored vehicles inside a space colony whose security systems have run out of control. Using two analog joysticks, the pilot maneuvers across enclosed battlegrounds while firing guns and missiles at opposing machines.

The action can be viewed either from behind the vehicle or through a first-person perspective, and on-screen instruments track radar contacts, shields, and the remaining time. Unlike Cyber Sled's strong emphasis on two-player duels, Cyber Commando concentrates on a single-player campaign against computer-controlled opponents. It is an ambitious example of Namco's mid-1990s System 22 3D arcade technology.

games.title: Cyber Cycles
games.description:
Cyber Cycles is Namco's 1995 3D motorcycle racer, played with motorcycle-style handlebars and an accelerator pedal rather than a car's steering wheel. Players select from three main bikes with different handling characteristics, plus hidden alternatives, and race against opponents on two contrasting circuits: coastal Greenhill and futuristic Neo Yokohama.

Passing checkpoints extends the time available to reach the finish, giving the races the same urgency as Namco's Ridge Racer. With linked cabinets supporting up to four players, Cyber Cycles combines the physical appeal of a dedicated motorcycle machine with the vivid polygonal scenery of Namco's System 22 era.

games.title: Cyber Sled
games.description:
Cyber Sled (1993) is Namco's pioneering polygonal vehicle-combat game, placing players in heavily armed hover tanks inside enclosed futuristic arenas. Rather than racing to a finish line, the objective is to hunt down and destroy a rival machine while protecting the player's own shields. Each combat vehicle has different movement and weapon characteristics, adding variety to the duels.

The distinctive twin-stick controls allow the player to steer and rotate the tank, while a choice of camera views changes how the battlefield is read. Obstacles provide cover from enemy fire, and the radar becomes an important tool for tracking a fast-moving opponent.

Cyber Sled was one of Namco's early showcases for real-time texture-mapped 3D action, with linked cabinets permitting direct competition. Its blend of tank tactics and arcade immediacy led to the single-player-oriented sequel Cyber Commando in 1994.

games.title: Cyberstorm
games.description:
Cyberstorm is an unreleased 1993 Atari Games fighting-game prototype built around futuristic robot combat. Its surviving version presents one-on-one battles between mechanical characters rather than human martial artists. The project ran on an expensive experimental arcade platform that never became a commercial product, leaving Cyberstorm as a rare look at Atari's attempts to enter the early-1990s fighting-game market.

Because it never received a normal arcade release, the prototype is most significant as preserved development history rather than a familiar tournament-era cabinet.

games.title: Cycle Shooting
games.description:
Cycle Shooting, released by Taito in 1986 and known in Japan as Violent Shooting, is a light-gun shooting game in which the player fires at motorcycles moving across the screen. Instead of steering a vehicle, the player aims the gun at moving targets, making observation, accuracy, and quick reactions the focus of play.

The game also circulated in unauthorized form under the name Bronx. It is an obscure example of Taito's mid-1980s gun-game experiments before the more elaborate shooting attractions of the following decade.

games.title: Cycle Warriors
games.description:
Cycle Warriors (1991) is an unusual arcade beat 'em up that keeps its characters on motorcycles. Players control a biker fighting rival riders while moving along scrolling roads, using punches and other attacks to knock enemies off their machines. Threats are not limited to other bikes: airborne attackers and other obstacles interrupt the ride.

The mixture of forward movement, road combat, and brawling creates a different rhythm from a conventional walking beat 'em up. Its appeal lies in that rough-edged combination of a motorcycle chase with close-range arcade fighting.

games.title: Cyvern
games.description:
Cyvern: The Dragon Weapons (1998) is Kaneko's spectacular vertical shooter for the Super Nova arcade system. Players choose from three biomechanical dragons, each possessing its own primary shot and a devastating close-range flame attack. The machines sweep across intensely detailed stages filled with enemy aircraft, armored creatures, and giant bosses.

The flamethrower is central to the game's identity: it is immensely powerful but requires approaching enemies at dangerous distances. This creates a constant tension between safe long-range shooting and aggressive attacks that clear threats quickly. The elaborate mechanical designs and dense projectile patterns make Cyvern a striking example of the late-1990s Japanese shooter.

Released at a time when dedicated arcade shooting games were becoming more specialized, it acquired a cult following for its demanding difficulty and unusual fusion of fantasy dragons with science-fiction weaponry.

games.title: Zeroize
games.description: Zeroize is an unusual maze and vehicle-combat game released by Data East in October 1983 for the DECO Cassette System. Played on a vertically oriented screen with an eight-way joystick and two action buttons, it combines navigating enclosed routes with the science-fiction imagery of armed vehicles. It was issued as cassette number 37, model DT-137, late in the lifetime of Data East's interchangeable tape-based arcade platform. Its more tactical, maze-oriented format stands apart from the system's straightforward shooters and sports titles.

games.title: Dacholer
games.description:
Dacholer (1983) is an eccentric single-screen action game from Nichibutsu in which the player controls an ostrich rather than an armed soldier. The bird kicks turtles or ball-like objects toward enemy animals moving around the playfield. A successful kick sends the projectile ricocheting through the area, knocking out targets, while a collision with an enemy can cost a life.

Because the ostrich cannot simply shoot at will, success depends on lining up a moving object and predicting its rebounds. The game also features bonus items and a variety of animal opponents. It later appeared in altered form under the name Kick Boy.

games.title: Daikaiju no Gyakushu
games.description:
Daikaiju no Gyakushu, meaning 'Great Monster Counterattack', is Taito's 1986 homage to Japanese giant-monster films. Instead of defending a city, the player controls a towering, Godzilla-like creature rampaging through it. Tanks, aircraft, and buildings become targets as the monster stomps across the landscape.

An eight-way joystick controls movement, while buttons activate fire-breathing attacks and jumps. A fire-power meter limits indiscriminate attacks, and an energy meter records damage from human resistance. Five distinct stages cycle into harder repetitions, creating a straightforward but wonderfully inverted arcade shooter in which the player is the kaiju.

Released only in Japan, it evokes Toho's monster-movie tradition without being an official Godzilla license.

games.title: Daioh
games.description:
Daioh (1993) is a vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter by Athena, notable for its emphasis on managing several weapon types instead of relying on a single evolving cannon. The player's fighter faces waves of enemy spacecraft, ground defenses, and enormous bosses while collecting upgrades and dodging increasingly intricate streams of fire.

The Japanese and overseas releases are especially interesting because their control schemes differ: some versions provide dedicated buttons for distinct weapon types, while others condense the action into fewer controls. That distinction gives the game a different feel depending on which arcade board is played.

With sharply drawn mechanical enemies and fast, technical combat, Daioh occupies a rewarding middle ground between traditional early-1990s shooting and the more elaborate bullet patterns that later became common.

games.title: Mahjong Daireikai
games.description: Mahjong Daireikai is a 1989 Japanese arcade mahjong title associated with Jaleco and NM. It uses the familiar head-to-head tile game as the basis of play, requiring players to build winning hands through draws and discards. The release is part of the specialist mahjong cabinet market that flourished in Japanese amusement centers alongside mainstream video games.

games.title: Daisu-Kiss
games.description:
Konami's Daisu-Kiss (1996) blends short arcade mini-games, trivia, and a playful high-school romance. Players choose from eight students and spend an in-game school year trying to win the affection of another character. Success in brief challenges builds a relationship meter, with the possibility of reaching a romantic ending at graduation.

The activities range across different genres, including dancing, cooking, racing, and quick-response puzzles, keeping the controls simple enough for immediate play. Its mixture of lighthearted dating comedy and competitive mini-games makes it a close relative of the Bishi Bashi style, but with a more persistent narrative goal.

Released in Japan on Konami's arcade hardware, Daisu-Kiss is memorable for turning a series of short skill tests into an eccentric, character-driven social comedy.

games.title: Daitoride
games.description:
Daitoride (1995) is an arcade solitaire-mahjong puzzle game developed by Metro. Instead of playing a traditional four-player mahjong match, the objective is to remove matching pairs of exposed tiles from a layout, working around pieces that remain blocked by their neighbors. Planning the removal order is essential, since an apparently convenient match can leave no legal moves later.

The simple rules and tile-based visual design make it approachable without knowledge of mahjong scoring. Its arcade format adds the pressure of solving puzzles efficiently rather than leisurely studying a tabletop arrangement.

games.title: Mahjong Daiyogen
games.description: Mahjong Daiyogen (1990) is a Japanese adult-oriented mahjong game from Video System. Traditional tile-based competition is combined with a fortune-telling theme, including tarot imagery and randomly awarded bonus items. The result is a distinctive blend of mahjong play and supernatural presentation, reflecting the inventive ways Japanese arcade developers differentiated games within a crowded specialty market.

games.title: DakkoChan Jansoh
games.description: DakkoChan Jansoh is a Japanese mahjong game released for Sega System 2 hardware in 1987. The title is built around the country's specialized arcade mahjong format rather than action gameplay, with players competing to complete tile hands. Its importance to arcade preservation lies partly in its unusual use of Sega hardware for a genre more commonly associated with dedicated mahjong boards.

games.title: Dambusters
games.description:
Dambusters is an early Data East horizontal-scrolling shooter for the DECO Cassette System. The player pilots a bomber across a hostile landscape, firing at approaching aircraft and dropping attacks toward targets below. Survival depends on handling threats at different heights while maintaining forward progress through enemy territory.

Its mixture of air-to-air combat and ground attacks anticipated a common feature of later scrolling shooters, although here it appears in a simpler, early-1980s form.

games.title: Dancing Eyes
games.description:
Dancing Eyes (1996) is one of Namco's strangest arcade puzzle games, using textured 3D characters and a territory-clearing mechanic inspired by Qix. Players guide a small monkey, Urusu-San, around the surface of a three-dimensional object and trace closed paths to remove its tiled sections. Hazards patrol the surface, so the challenge is to expose territory without being caught while a line is being completed.

The objects include boxes and other props, but the game is especially remembered for stages in which clearing tiles removes pieces of a female character's clothing. This overtly cheeky premise is paired with colorful graphics, comic animation, and the characteristic experimental spirit of Namco's mid-1990s arcade output.

Running on Namco System 11 hardware, Dancing Eyes remains a cult curiosity because its unusual 3D puzzle mechanics are more substantial than its provocative presentation initially suggests.

games.title: Danchi de Hanafuoda
games.description: Danchi de Hanafuda is a 1999 Japanese arcade card game developed by Altron for Sega's ST-V hardware. It uses hanafuda, the traditional Japanese playing-card system based on matching illustrated seasonal cards, as the core of its matches. Presented with adult-oriented character artwork, it belongs to a specialized branch of Japanese arcade tabletop games rather than to the action-heavy ST-V catalog.

games.title: Dangar - Ufo Robo
games.description:
UFO Robo Dangar (1986) is Nichibutsu's vertically scrolling shooter built around the spectacular idea of assembling a giant robot during flight. The player begins with a combat craft and collects additional sections, gradually transforming it into a larger and more heavily armed machine. Its weapons can include forceful projectile attacks from the robot itself, while separating the machine offers an alternative tactical response to danger.

The game follows the modular-ship tradition of Nichibutsu's Moon Cresta and Terra Cresta, but exaggerates the transformation into something closer to a Japanese robot anime. Enemy formations and large targets make maintaining the assembled form difficult, so collecting upgrades is only half the challenge.

Its mixture of spaceship shooting and transforming-super-robot imagery gives Dangar an unmistakable mid-1980s personality.

games.title: Danger Express
games.description:
Danger Express is a 1992 Atari Games prototype that was tested but never commercially released. It follows government agents pursuing criminals who have seized a train carrying sensitive cargo. The action uses a forward-looking, corridor-style perspective rather than a conventional sideways beat 'em up, with digitized human figures giving the brawls a semi-live-action appearance.

Players move through train cars and other urban locations, using punches, kicks, and weapons to fight attackers. The mixture of shooting and hand-to-hand combat, together with unusual camera staging, makes it one of Atari's more experimental unreleased action projects.

games.title: Danger Zone
games.description:
Danger Zone is a 1986 arcade combat game from Cinematronics set around the defense of a military installation in a desert landscape. Fighters, bombers, and helicopters attack from beyond the mountains, and the player must spot and destroy threats before the base is overwhelmed.

A radar display helps track the incoming aircraft, adding an element of surveillance and target selection to the shooting. The result is closer to a stationary defensive gun emplacement than to the free-flying aircraft games that dominated much of the era.

games.title: Dangerous Seed
games.description:
Dangerous Seed (1989) is Namco's vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter featuring three distinct spacecraft, Alpha, Beta, and Gamma. Each stage begins with a different craft and its own weapon characteristics, while the game's evolving structure eventually allows the machines to combine into a single more formidable vessel.

The action takes place against a succession of alien organisms and mechanical enemies, with enormous bosses and shifting visual themes reinforcing its strange biological aesthetic. The combined spacecraft has different capabilities from its individual components, so the transformation changes strategy rather than simply increasing firepower.

Its multi-ship design and elaborate enemy art are among the reasons Dangerous Seed remains a favorite with enthusiasts of Namco's less widely distributed late-1980s shooters.

games.title: Daraku Tenshi - The Fallen Angels
games.description:
Daraku Tenshi: The Fallen Angels (1998) is a cult one-on-one fighting game from Psikyo, created by a development team that included former SNK staff. Set in a gloomy contemporary city, it abandons the bright fantasy of many late-1990s fighters for street clothes, brooding characters, realistic urban backgrounds, and unusually detailed animation.

Combat emphasizes timing, special attacks, and positioning, with character designs that feel closer to a gritty action comic than to an anime tournament. The game's comparatively restrained visual style makes its powerful attacks and dramatic win poses especially striking.

The project is often described as unfinished, and its limited distribution kept it from achieving the recognition of larger fighting series. Nevertheless, its atmosphere, expressive pixel art, and unconventional cast have given it a lasting reputation among dedicated arcade fighting-game fans.

games.title: Darius
games.description:
Taito's Darius (1986) is a landmark horizontally scrolling shooter famous for its extraordinary three-monitor arcade cabinet. A system of mirrors joins the screens into an immense, continuous panoramic playfield, giving the Silver Hawk spacecraft an unusually wide battlefield. The player travels through hostile zones fighting mechanical creatures, aircraft, and giant bosses, many famously modeled after fish and other aquatic life.

The Silver Hawk's arsenal combines forward-firing missiles, bombs for targets below, and a defensive shield known as the Arm. Destroying specially colored enemies produces upgrades for these systems. At the end of each stage, a branching route lets players choose between two destinations, producing different paths through the campaign and multiple endings. This structure offers substantial replay value without requiring every stage to be played in a single run.

Darius became one of Taito's most recognizable shooting series, celebrated for its huge boss designs, branching progression, and music by the company's Zuntata sound team. The original cabinet remains a memorable example of arcade hardware being built around a visual experience that contemporary home systems could not easily reproduce.

games.title: Darius II
games.description:
Darius II (1989) expands Taito's panoramic shoot-'em-up series into the inner Solar System, with the Silver Hawk battling enormous fleets and aquatic-inspired mechanical bosses. The game preserves the series' distinctive choice of routes at the end of stages, so each playthrough follows only one path through a much larger network of levels.

The arcade release is particularly associated with a two-screen widescreen cabinet, although a three-screen configuration also exists. Forward weapons, bombs, and shields can be upgraded with colored power-ups, while additional weapons broaden the firepower available to experienced pilots. Boss battles are grand, often requiring careful destruction of vulnerable sections amid dense enemy fire.

Darius II's expansive presentation, branching campaign, and distinctive electronic soundtrack made it a notable sequel to the 1986 original. Its technology-driven spectacle remained central to the series even as many competing shooters moved toward more compact cabinets.

games.title: Darius Gaiden - Silver Hawk

variants.title: Darius Gaiden - Silver Hawk Extra Version (Ver 2.7J 1995/03/06) (Official Hack)

games.description:
Darius Gaiden: Silver Hawk (1994) revitalized Taito's famous shooter series on a single standard-size monitor after the panoramic cabinets of the first two arcade games. Players pilot the Silver Hawk through beautifully animated underwater, industrial, and outer-space environments, fighting mechanical sea creatures and enormous bosses while selecting alternate routes between stages.

Its defining addition is the Black Hole Bomb, a spectacular emergency attack that forms a swirling vortex, draws in projectiles and enemies, and unleashes destructive energy across the screen. Another distinctive mechanic allows the player to capture certain minibosses: destroying an orb on the enemy's head releases it for collection, temporarily turning that formidable opponent into an ally. Colored power-ups improve the ship's main shot, bombs, and protective Arm shield.

The game's intricate boss designs, vivid 2D artwork, and memorable Zuntata soundtrack helped make Darius Gaiden one of the most admired horizontal shooters of the 1990s. It combines a familiar arcade formula with unusually lavish presentation and deep replayability.

games.title: Dark Edge
games.description:
Dark Edge is Sega's unusual early-1990s one-on-one fighting game, copyright dated 1992 and commercially released around 1993. Instead of using true polygons, it manipulates and scales large sprites to simulate fighters moving around a three-dimensional arena. The result is a striking transitional design between 2D fighting games and the fully polygonal Virtua Fighter.

Characters can circle around one another rather than being confined to a single line, and a dedicated jump button accommodates movement controls that serve the simulated 3D space. Its futuristic cast includes both human warriors and bizarre creatures.

Running on Sega System 32 hardware, Dark Edge is historically interesting as an experimental solution to 3D fighting before polygonal characters became standard. Its unusual perspective can initially feel unfamiliar even to experienced fighting-game players.

games.title: Dark Horse
games.description:
Dark Horse is a 2001 unauthorized version of Seta's Jockey Club II, a Japanese video horse-racing betting game. Players wager on simulated races rather than controlling the horses directly. Its name, American-targeted v4.00 program, and modified circuit board distinguish it from the original Seta releases.

The conversion is technically remarkable: the bootleggers rewrote the original graphics routines to replace expensive zooming and floating-tilemap effects with simpler sprites and tilemaps, and substituted low-rate sampled sound through an OKI chip. Emulator developer Luca Elia documented this as a deliberate adaptation of a sophisticated racing-betting game to cheaper hardware. This makes Dark Horse an especially informative example of arcade bootlegging driven by PCB cost rather than just renamed artwork.

games.title: The Lost Castle In Darkmist
games.description:
The Lost Castle in Darkmist (1986) is a fantasy action game from Taito in which a knight fights through vertically scrolling landscapes crowded with monsters and magical hazards. The player advances up the screen, swinging a sword at enemies and incoming projectiles while watching for treasures left behind after battles.

Potions and other pickups improve the knight's prospects, but care is required when collecting objects from treasure chests. Boss encounters punctuate the journey, giving the game the structure of an adventure even though its combat is immediate and arcade-focused. Its overhead viewpoint and supernatural setting make it an appealing curiosity among Taito's less famous mid-1980s action games.

games.title: Dark Planet
games.description:
Dark Planet (1982) is an unusual Stern Electronics space shooter that creates the illusion of a three-dimensional battlefield using a specially illustrated planetary backdrop. A spacecraft moves over the surface of a mysterious alien world, attacking hostile vehicles and installations before they can establish control.

The player can use ordinary shots as well as a more limited laser attack, making weapon choice part of the scoring and survival strategy. Because much of the scenery is supplied by physical artwork rather than conventional moving graphics, Dark Planet has a distinctive appearance unlike most contemporary raster shooters.

Its hybrid of cabinet artwork and video action is a reminder of the experimental presentation techniques arcade manufacturers explored before real-time 3D graphics became practical.

games.title: Dark Seal
games.description:
Dark Seal (1990), released in North America as Gate of Doom, is Data East's fantasy action adventure viewed from a richly detailed isometric perspective. Players select from four different heroes, including a knight, wizard, bard, and ninja, then fight through monster-infested rooms while collecting treasure, casting spells, and avoiding traps.

The diagonal viewpoint gives combat a different rhythm from a conventional side-scrolling beat 'em up. Enemies approach from several directions, so positioning and character-specific abilities become important, particularly in cooperative play. The stages mix combat with small environmental hazards and impressive fantasy bosses.

With its colorful monsters and tabletop-role-playing imagery, Dark Seal is a memorable counterpart to games such as Gauntlet. A sequel, Dark Seal II, later continued the series' isometric fantasy format.

games.title: Dark Tower
games.description:
Dark Tower (1992) is an obscure single-screen arcade platform-action game by The Game Room. The player controls a baseball-bat-wielding hero who must eliminate all enemies on each stage before moving to the next, in a structure reminiscent of Snow Bros. and Bubble Bobble. Defeated opponents leave bonuses that can be collected for points.

The game's most notorious characteristic is its eclectic presentation: graphics and music borrow heavily from other contemporary arcade titles, including recognizable material associated with Ghosts 'n Goblins, Black Tiger, and Double Dragon. Although the rules are not a direct copy of any one of those games, the audiovisual collage gives Dark Tower an unmistakably bootleg-like personality.

games.title: Dark Warrior
games.description:
Dark Warrior (1981) is an early fixed-screen shooter for Century Electronics' CVS arcade system. The player defends a ship against formations of aliens moving across the screen, while ground-based walking machines threaten vital fuel tanks with missiles. The two types of danger require attention to both the player's own survival and the equipment being protected.

Its synthesized voice effects were a notable attraction when speech in arcade games was still unusual. Dark Warrior belongs to the experimental period before shooting-game conventions had fully settled into the familiar patterns of later classics.

games.title: Darwin 4078
games.description:
Darwin 4078 (1986) is Data East's surreal vertically scrolling shooter built around evolution rather than conventional weapon upgrading. The player flies a small craft through microscopic-looking alien environments, destroying bizarre organisms and collecting capsules that cause the ship to transform into increasingly elaborate life forms.

Different evolutionary stages change the shape and firepower of the craft, and the transformations are temporary unless the player continues collecting the appropriate items. This creates a distinctive rhythm of building power, trying to maintain it, and recovering after a setback. Standard forward shots and attacks against ground targets give the action a recognizable scrolling-shooter foundation beneath its strange biological imagery.

Darwin 4078 initiated a small lineage that included Super Real Darwin. Its transformations, abstract creature designs, and almost evolutionary-science-fiction atmosphere make it one of Data East's more original shooters.

games.title: Daytona USA 2 Power Edition
games.description:
Daytona USA 2: Power Edition is Sega's updated 1998 version of Daytona USA 2: Battle on the Edge. The core Model 3 stock-car racing remains intact, but this revision changes the beginner track's scenery to a more conventional oval-racing environment and adjusts certain vehicle details and handling.

Most importantly, Power Edition adds a Challenge or Mix Course that links sections of the three main tracks into a much longer event. The original Daytona USA's familiar Hornet car becomes selectable, giving longtime players a nostalgic alternative to the sequel's vehicles. Reverse-direction driving also expands the possibilities.

Rather than being a separate numbered sequel, Power Edition is an enhanced arcade revision, particularly rewarding for players who already know the original Daytona USA 2 courses.

games.title: Daytona USA 2
games.description:
Daytona USA 2: Battle on the Edge (1998) is Sega's spectacular Model 3 successor to one of the most influential 3D arcade racing games. It updates the stock-car formula with far more detailed circuits, realistic-looking smoke and crashes, and a choice of driver and car combinations with different handling characteristics.

Three principal tracks offer distinct challenges: the fast beginner circuit Forest Dome, the winding amusement-park-themed Joypolis course, and the demanding Virtua City layout. Players use a steering wheel, pedals, and gear shifter, trying to master drifting, drafting, and close racing against computer opponents or linked cabinets. Slipstreaming behind another car can provide a useful speed advantage before an overtake.

The original release was followed later in 1998 by Power Edition, which revised the beginner-course setting, added a combined Challenge course, and restored the classic Hornet from the first Daytona USA. Together the two versions remain benchmarks for Sega's exuberant approach to arcade racing.

games.title: Dazzler
games.description:
Dazzler (1982) is a quirky maze-platform game for Century Electronics' CVS hardware. Its action combines climbing and navigation with the task of collecting bananas to feed a gorilla companion, while aggressive vultures threaten the player. Snakes can be dropped to delay the birds, turning the maze into a small sequence of timed defensive problems.

The game also uses synthesized voice effects, a feature that helped distinguish some Century titles from other early-1980s arcade releases. Its odd combination of animal characters, maze traversal, and environmental interactions makes it more distinctive than its simple graphics suggest.

games.title: Double Axle
games.description:
Double Axle (1991), known in Japan as Power Wheels, is Taito's monster-truck racing game. Players drive huge-wheeled vehicles over rough tracks, attempting to finish each event in third place or better to remain in the competition. Oversized trucks, jumps, and uneven terrain give the races a very different feel from conventional road-car games.

Successful results earn prize money that can be spent improving the truck, while bonus events provide additional opportunities to build a stronger machine. The upgrade system gives each race lasting importance: a poorly prepared truck may struggle against the increasingly difficult opposition.

The game's emphasis on heavy vehicles and incremental mechanical improvement distinguishes it among the early-1990s arcade racing titles.

games.title: Double Wings
games.description:
Double Wings (1993) is a vertically scrolling shoot-'em-up in which the player pilots a vintage military aircraft through waves of enemy planes and ground targets. The fighter uses direct gunfire and bombs, so targets at different elevations call for different attacks. Its style recalls the World War II aerial shooters popularized by Capcom's 1942, but with its own enemy formations and visual presentation.

The game is a straightforward example of the genre's early-1990s continuation, relying on careful movement, weapon timing, and a steady stream of airborne threats.

games.title: Super Baseball Double Play Home Run Derby
games.description:
Super Baseball Double Play Home Run Derby (1987) is a baseball arcade game developed by Leland. It combines a conventional baseball contest with a separate home-run-hitting challenge, allowing players to concentrate either on the complete sport or on batting for distance.

The baseball mode includes pitching, hitting, and fielding over a selectable number of innings, while Home Run Derby strips the experience down to a more immediate competition in powerful swings.
