The dual format gives the cabinet flexibility for both longer games and quick head-to-head arcade sessions.

games.title: Double Point
games.description: Double Point is a 1995 adult-themed arcade pattern-matching puzzle game associated with Dong Bang Electron. Its gameplay is based on recognizing and completing matching arrangements on a compact, fixed-screen playfield, using an eight-way joystick and three buttons; the mature material appears in the game's presentation rather than being its puzzle mechanic. A curious production detail is the reuse of cartoon chipmunk and rabbit graphics from Don't Pull, the puzzle game in Capcom's Three Wonders. The game belongs to a group of inexpensive 1990s puzzle boards built around simple repeated challenges and borrowed artwork.

games.title: Dragon Breed
games.description:
Irem's Dragon Breed (1989) is one of the most imaginative side-scrolling shooters of its generation. The player controls King Kayus, who rides a giant articulated dragon named Bahamoot through a haunted fantasy world. While Kayus fires a crossbow, the dragon's long body is effectively invulnerable and can block incoming shots, damage enemies, or curl around its rider as protection.

Unlike the rigid option pods of most shooters, Bahamoot's body follows the player's movements like a flexible chain. Skilled pilots can wrap it around enemies, sweep it across the screen, or position it as a moving shield. Power-ups alter the dragon's color and attacks, and charging the fire button can unleash stronger abilities. The central challenge is protecting the vulnerable rider while using the dragon as both weapon and armor.

Its organic animation and medieval setting set Dragon Breed apart from the spaceships and military aircraft typical of the genre. Even among Irem's visually inventive shooters, its dragon-control mechanic remains memorable.

games.title: Dragonball Z
games.description:
Dragon Ball Z (1993) is Banpresto's arcade fighting-game adaptation of Akira Toriyama's hugely popular manga and anime. It uses large, colorful sprites and head-to-head battles featuring eight characters drawn mainly from the series' early Dragon Ball Z story arcs, including Goku, Gohan, Piccolo, Vegeta, Captain Ginyu, and Frieza.

Fighters can take to the air and unleash signature energy attacks, bringing familiar techniques such as the Kamehameha into the arena. The game emphasizes recognition of the characters and their special powers over the elaborate systems found in dedicated competitive fighting series of the period.

Its historical appeal is as an early coin-operated Dragon Ball Z fighter, preceding the more polished Dragon Ball Z 2: Super Battle and the unusual perspective-based Dragon Ball Z V.R.V.S.

games.title: Dragonball Z 2 - Super Battle
games.description:
Dragon Ball Z 2: Super Battle (1994) is Banpresto's follow-up to its earlier Dragon Ball Z arcade fighting game. The sequel expands the roster to ten fighters, including Goku, Gohan, Vegeta, Future Trunks, Piccolo, Androids 16, 18, and 20, Cell, and Mr. Satan. Its large, detailed sprites reproduce the exaggerated poses and colorful energy attacks of the anime.

Battles are fought one-on-one, but players can shift between ground and aerial fighting areas, giving the stages a sense of vertical scale. A super-power gauge supports stronger attacks and adds another layer to the timing of special moves. The game is an interesting link between conventional 2D arcade fighting mechanics and the aerial combat for which Dragon Ball is known.

games.title: Dragon Ball Z V.R.V.S.
games.description:
Dragon Ball Z V.R.V.S. (1994) is Sega and Banpresto's unusual arcade fighting game based on the Dragon Ball Z franchise. Instead of using a traditional side-on fighting-game view, it places the camera behind the combatants to suggest a three-dimensional duel, with characters moving through the arena and attacking with familiar martial-arts and energy techniques.

Players can choose heroes including Goku, Gohan, Piccolo, Vegeta, and Future Trunks, then fight through a sequence of opponents culminating in a special original boss. The regular version uses a joystick and buttons, while a larger deluxe installation experiments with motion-sensitive controls, turning the player's physical movements into commands.

Its unconventional camera and optional body-motion interface make V.R.V.S. a fascinating side branch of early Dragon Ball arcade games rather than a straightforward sequel to Banpresto's 2D fighters.

games.title: Dynamic Country Club
games.description:
Dynamic Country Club is a 1991 Sega arcade golf game for the System 24 platform. It presents courses using polygon-based scenery and asks players to judge the direction, strength, and placement of shots as they work through the holes. Unlike Sega's more action-oriented arcade offerings, it concentrates on the measured rhythm of golf, with the unusual 3D course presentation providing the main technical attraction.

The disk-based System 24 release is also a reminder of the period when arcade manufacturers experimented with storage media and graphical techniques beyond standard ROM-cartridge action games.

games.title: Dynamic Country Club
games.description:
This Dynamic Country Club entry represents a floppy-disk-based revision of Sega's 1991 System 24 golf simulation. The same golf fundamentals apply: players select shots and try to navigate polygon-rendered fairways, hazards, and greens in as few strokes as possible.

Its distinction in AdvanceMAME is the specific floppy-disk and security-chip configuration, not a separately documented set of golf rules. Preserving such revisions is valuable because Sega's disk-based arcade hardware often exists in multiple technical versions of the same game.

games.title: Double Cheese
games.description: Double Cheese is a 1993 video-redemption amusement machine from HAR Management. Unlike a traditional platform or maze game, it is built around brief chances to line up or match numbered results for ticket awards. The original machine uses a rotary control arrangement, with additional buttons, on a vertical display, making physical timing and selection central to its presentation. Its elaborate 68000-based audio/video hardware and BSMT2000 sound chip are striking for a prize-focused game of this sort. The separate, sometimes contradictory catalog descriptions of its control panel should not be confused with a conventional Midway action-game release.

games.title: D-Con
games.description: D-Con is a 1992 science-fiction shooter from Japanese developer Success. One or two players simultaneously pilot spacecraft tasked with defending a city against attacking alien ships, using eight-way joysticks and two action buttons. Its emphasis is on clearing successive enemy waves while keeping the threatened city safe, rather than on the unrelated anime convention that shares its name.

games.title: D-Day
games.description: Olympia's D-Day (1982) is an early military-themed arcade shooting game, entirely separate from Jaleco's 1984 title of the same name. The player operates a gun emplacement, aiming with a paddle-style controller and firing at approaching tanks and other enemy targets on a horizontal battlefield. Its compact, single-screen action reflects the shooting-gallery design of the early 1980s. North American releases include a Centuri-branded version, whose control configuration differs from the Olympia set.

games.title: D-Day
games.description:
D-Day, released in Japan in January 1984 by Jaleco and developed by E.L.S., is a vertically scrolling naval shooter inspired by the Allied landings in Normandy. The player steers a warship toward the enemy-held coast, shooting at attacking aircraft and surface or ground defenses. A distinguishing feature is its separation of attacks against airborne targets, which can be engaged in different directions, from attacks directed ahead at ground targets. The cumbersome ship must be positioned carefully because it cannot dodge sudden threats quickly.

This is not a revision of Olympia's 1982 D-Day, but a completely different arcade game. Jaleco's release received an MSX conversion, while a planned Famicom edition never appeared. The original subsequently gained a modern Arcade Archives reissue, bringing this relatively obscure Japanese shooter to a wider audience.

games.description:
Sega's D. D. Crew (1991) is a cooperative, side-scrolling beat 'em up built for its System 18 hardware. Players take the roles of street fighters battling a gang threatening to destroy parts of the city. Progress through each crowded scene depends on defeating the enemies appearing from doorways and both edges of the screen; fights culminate in tougher stage bosses. Characters can punch, kick, grapple and throw opponents, and pick up weapons such as knives and grenades. A quick double-tap of the joystick allows running attacks, giving the combat more momentum than simple standing combos.

Arcade configurations accommodate two, three or four participants, with regional ROM sets adapted to different cabinets. The game is an interesting example of Sega entering the multiplayer brawler boom associated with Final Fight and Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, although it never acquired the reputation of Sega's Streets of Rage series.

games.title: Don Den Lover Vol. 1
games.description:
Don Den Lover Vol. 1 is Dynax's adult-oriented arcade adaptation of Othello, also known as Reversi. One or two players place black or white discs on an eight-by-eight board, turning the opponent's discs by enclosing them in straight lines. In the solo game, winning against a succession of female opponents unlocks animated adult-themed scenes. A countdown clock adds pressure, and a limited assistance feature can suggest moves or undo the last turn.

The AdvanceMAME entry represents the Hong Kong edition, which uses Korean character names and voices. Its gameplay is a board-game contest rather than mahjong or a chance-based gambling machine.

games.title: DoDonPachi
games.description:
Cave's DoDonPachi (1997), published by Atlus, is one of the formative works of the bullet-hell shooter genre. Following DonPachi, it puts players in one of three craft: a narrow-firing fighter, a helicopter with swiveling side guns, or a wide-spread fighter. Each can be configured for stronger standard shots or a more powerful laser. Holding the fire button concentrates the ship's fire into a continuous beam but reduces movement speed, creating a tactical choice between mobility and damage during ever-denser enemy patterns. Bombs behave differently depending on whether the ship is firing ordinary shots or its laser.

The game's lasting contribution is its demanding Get Point System, which rewards continuous enemy destruction and sustained laser contact with increasingly valuable hit chains. Hidden golden bee medals, careful bomb management and a MAXIMUM bonus for surplus bombs give expert players additional layers of scoring strategy. Clearing six stages on one credit while meeting special conditions unlocks a harder second loop and the notorious mechanical-bee bosses Hachi and Hibachi.

With its spectacular projectile patterns, distinctive orange explosions and deep scoring, DoDonPachi helped define Cave's approach to arcade shooting. Its reputation rests as much on the enormous skill ceiling of maintaining chains and surviving Hibachi as on the visual spectacle that inspired later manic shooters.

games.title: DoDonPachi II - Bee Storm
games.description:
DoDonPachi II: Bee Storm (2001) is the unusual entry in the series developed by Taiwan's International Games System rather than Cave. Released on IGS's PolyGame Master arcade hardware, it retains the familiar vertical shooter formula: choose among three aircraft, destroy waves of mechanized enemies, dodge intricate bullet patterns and collect weapon enhancements and score items. Multi-part bosses punctuate its stages, while a high-score requirement can unlock a secret seventh stage.

Its different developer, visual presentation and scoring balance make Bee Storm a distinct offshoot rather than a direct expression of Cave's evolving design. The game also has an unusual preservation history: its additional ARM processor performs essential gameplay tasks, including creating bullet patterns, and needed to be properly emulated before the arcade program would function accurately.

games.title: DoDonPachi III
games.description:
DoDonPachi III is a rare overseas version of Cave's 2002 vertical shooter DoDonPachi DaiOuJou, developed for the IGS PolyGame Master platform. The player chooses a narrow-shot or wide-shot fighter and an Element Doll partner emphasizing shots, lasers or both. Eliminating enemies in rapid succession, or holding the laser on large targets, builds long score chains. The Hyper system rewards aggressive play with temporary heightened firepower and faster combo building, even as increasingly severe bullet patterns test precision.

Unlike the ordinary Japanese DaiOuJou release, the version titled DoDonPachi III was an international export build that did not see a normal commercial launch. A surviving 2002 program was recovered and documented in 2016. Its rules and balance sit between the original 'White Label' game and the later Black Label revision, making it particularly valuable to enthusiasts studying the development of one of Cave's most demanding shooters.

games.title: DoDonPachi Dai-Ou-Jou (Black Label)
games.description: DoDonPachi Dai-Ou-Jou (Black Label) is Cave's updated 2002 edition of the vertical bullet-hell shoot-'em-up DoDonPachi Dai-Ou-Jou on PolyGame Master (PGM) hardware. It allows players to choose between a single-loop (1-ALL) or two-loop (2-ALL) game at the start, lets Hyper items carry over across lives, and adjusts rank progression and scoring balance.

games.title: DoDonPachi Dai-Fukkatsu Ver 1.5
games.description:
DoDonPachi Dai-Fukkatsu Ver. 1.5 is Cave's 2008 revision of the bullet-hell sequel also known as DoDonPachi Resurrection. Against an army of mechanized invaders, players fly vertically through extravagant patterns of bullets, selecting different ship types and fighting styles. Ordinary shots are suited to sweeping away enemies, while a focused laser attacks durable targets. A Hyper Counter can intensify firepower and help cancel incoming bullets, making the choice of when to activate it central to both survival and scoring.

The game modernizes the DonPachi chaining tradition with elaborate counters, large mechanical bosses and weapon systems that encourage aggressive play under pressure. Version 1.5 became the widely recognized arcade revision, distinct from the later, more demanding Black Label release.

games.title: DoDonPachi Dai-Ou-Jou Tamashii
games.description:
DoDonPachi DaiOuJou Tamashii is a 2010 Chinese and Taiwanese adaptation of Cave's 2002 shoot 'em up, released on IGS PolyGame Master 2 hardware rather than the original PGM system. It preserves the central idea of negotiating dense vertical bullet patterns while building scoring chains with sustained fire, collecting bee items and using powerful Hyper attacks. Players can select an Original mode closer to the source arcade game or an Easy mode with slower projectiles and less crowded patterns.

Because Tamashii is a separate hardware adaptation, not merely an alternate language ROM, it has its own identity within the numerous DaiOuJou variants preserved by emulators.

games.title: DoDonPachi SaiDaiOuJou

variants.title: DoDonPachi SaiDaiOuJou (dirty dump)
differences: Alternate ROM dump with pre-populated NVRAM/EEPROM data.

games.description: DoDonPachi SaiDaiOuJou is a vertical-scrolling bullet-hell shoot-'em-up developed and published by Cave for the Cave CV1000-D arcade platform in 2012. As the final arcade installment in the DoDonPachi series, it features three playable Element Dolls with customizable Shot, Laser, and Expert outfits, a Hyper Overflow system that increases both firepower and enemy bullet density, and five stages culminating in the true final boss Hibachi.

games.title: Double Dragon
games.description:
Double Dragon (1987), developed by Technos Japan and distributed internationally by Taito, was a landmark of cooperative arcade fighting. Brothers Billy and Jimmy Lee fight through city streets, factories and gang hideouts to rescue Marian from the Black Warriors. An eight-way joystick and dedicated punch, kick and jump buttons allow a remarkable range of moves, including elbow strikes, throws, flying kicks and attacks against enemies holding the player. Baseball bats, whips, knives and even oil drums can be taken from enemies or the scenery.

Building on Technos's earlier Renegade, Double Dragon made two-player teamwork a defining attraction of the scrolling beat 'em up. Players could approach and attack enemies from different positions while moving freely up and down the street. Its memorable final confrontation contains an additional twist when both brothers survive: they must fight each other to decide who wins Marian's affection.

The game became a worldwide arcade hit, inspired numerous home conversions and helped establish the template followed by later favorites such as Final Fight and Streets of Rage. Its combat depth and cinematic street-gang setting made it one of the most influential action games of the late 1980s.

games.title: Double Dragon II - The Revenge
games.description:
Double Dragon II: The Revenge (1988) returns to Billy and Jimmy Lee after the Black Warriors murder Marian, changing the brothers' motivation from rescue to retaliation. The cooperative side-scrolling action remains familiar, with waves of thugs, collectible weapons and progressively dangerous bosses. The greatest mechanical change is its directional attack scheme: buttons deliver strikes to the left or right relative to the character, encouraging precise positioning and enabling powerful techniques such as the spinning cyclone kick.

Technos reused elements of the original arcade game's technology and structure but revised character graphics, locations, attacks and enemy behavior. The darker opening, harder combat and recognizable new moves give the sequel a distinct identity, separate from the more extensively redesigned home-console versions.

games.title: Double Dragon 3 - The Rosetta Stone
games.description:
Double Dragon 3: The Rosetta Stone (1990) sends Billy and Jimmy Lee on an international quest to recover three sacred Rosetta Stones and uncover the mystery surrounding an ancient Egyptian power. The arcade game expands the series' martial-arts roster beyond its original heroes, allowing additional fighters to join the adventure, while combat emphasizes running moves, cooperative techniques and battles against opponents with very different styles.

Its most infamous feature is an in-game shop that originally allowed players to spend additional real arcade credits on upgrades and extra characters. This unusual attempt to monetize progress contributed to the game's controversial reputation. Developed for arcades by East Technology under Technos's supervision, it differs substantially from the better-known Nintendo Entertainment System game with the same title.

games.title: Double Dribble
games.description:
Konami's Double Dribble (1986) was a milestone in arcade basketball for its dynamic presentation of the sport. Two teams of five players compete on a scrolling court, passing, dribbling, shooting and contesting possession under a countdown clock. The action switches to large, animated close-ups for dramatic slam dunks, a striking audiovisual effect for its time. Three-button controls separate passing, shooting and other court actions, with two players able to compete head to head.

A digitized voice calls the game's name at startup, and the combination of fast play, exaggerated dunks and simulated basketball rules gave it a distinctive arcade personality. The popular NES adaptation later became particularly famous, but the coin-operated original established the series' visual style and immediate competitive appeal.

games.title: Dungeons & Dragons: Shadow over Mystara
games.description:
Dungeons & Dragons: Shadow over Mystara (1996) is Capcom's expansive CPS-2 fantasy beat 'em up and the sequel to Tower of Doom. Up to four adventurers travel through branching routes, battling goblins, trolls, dragons and other creatures from the Dungeons & Dragons universe. Six character classes offer dramatically different tactics: warriors rely on physical combinations, while spellcasters manage limited magic and specialized abilities. Equipment, consumables, shops and treasure create a progression system with much more depth than most scrolling brawlers.

The combat combines standard attacks, grabs and evasive maneuvers with spell selection and item management. Cooperative parties can divide roles, recover resources and tackle formidable bosses through different stage paths. Its multiple endings, hidden items, elaborate animation and wealth of tabletop-inspired details have made Shadow over Mystara a cult favorite and one of the most ambitious arcade beat 'em ups of the 1990s.

games.title: Dungeons & Dragons: Tower of Doom
games.description:
Capcom's Dungeons & Dragons: Tower of Doom (1993) turns the fantasy role-playing license into a cooperative side-scrolling action game. Players choose among a fighter, cleric, dwarf and elf, each with distinctive attacks and abilities, and journey through branching stages filled with monsters, traps, treasure and imposing bosses. Unlike a conventional brawler, the game includes an inventory for weapons, potions and magic, along with occasional choices that determine which areas the party visits next.

Adapted from the atmosphere and creatures of tabletop Dungeons & Dragons, Tower of Doom rewards cooperation and the intelligent use of limited equipment. Its class-based combat and branching adventure were ambitious additions to Capcom's arcade formula, laying the foundation for the deeper sequel Shadow over Mystara.

games.title: Dangerous Dungeons
games.description: Dangerous Dungeons (1992), released by The Game Room, is a top-down digging and maze game in the tradition of Boulder Dash. Players tunnel through underground stages collecting blue crystals and fruit, then search for the exit once the required gems have been gathered. Moving rocks can crush pursuing creatures, while dynamite opens blocked passages or removes troublesome enemies. Each screen is a compact puzzle of gravity, timing and safe routes rather than a simple race to collect everything.

games.title: Dynamite Dux
games.description:
Dynamite Dux is Sega's quirky late-1980s side-scrolling action game starring the feathered heroes Bin and Pin. The ducks fight their way through colorful stages to rescue a kidnapped girl, using punches and a variety of pick-up weapons against comical enemies and oversized bosses. Its exaggerated cartoon animation and offbeat enemy designs distinguish it from the gritty street-fighting games of the period. Two-player action allows both ducks to tackle the mayhem together, and special boxing bonus rounds even let them fight each other for extra points.

Produced in the era of Sega System 16, the game stood out for its Tex Avery-like absurdity and was also copied onto unofficial arcade hardware.

games.title: Dead Angle
games.description:
Dead Angle (1988), developed by Seibu Kaihatsu, is a gangster-themed shooting gallery with a distinctive cinematic presentation. Playing a man trying to rescue his kidnapped girlfriend, the player confronts mobsters across a sequence of urban locations, aiming a gun at enemies displayed beyond the silhouetted outline of the hero. When the outline turns red, the protagonist is exposed to enemy fire; crouching provides temporary cover but cannot be maintained indefinitely.

The combination of timed shootouts, limited protection and stylized gangster imagery makes Dead Angle feel like an interactive crime film, rather than a conventional run-and-gun shooter.

games.title: Dead Connection
games.description:
Taito's Dead Connection (1992) is an unusual crime-themed, single-screen action shooter set in a stylized 1950s America. Players choose among four investigators seeking to dismantle a powerful criminal organization. Each scene unfolds in a confined location full of furniture, platforms and destructible objects, as armed gangsters rush in from different directions. Players must defeat a set number of enemies before time runs out, using precise movement and attacks while collecting dropped items and bonus evidence.

Its theatrical characters, detailed environments and episodic story give the game the flavor of a gangster movie. Rather than scrolling continuously through a city, it uses intricate arena-like stages where cover, jump positions and environmental interactions matter.

games.title: Dead Eye
games.description: Dead Eye is an early Western-themed arcade shooting game in which a cowboy demonstrates his marksmanship by firing at coins tossed into the air and at birds. Its challenge revolves around timing repeated shots to keep the airborne coin in play and score points without letting it escape the permitted area. The simple shooting-gallery premise and cowboy theme place it among the experimental target games of the 1970s.

games.title: The Dealer
games.description:
The Dealer is a 1984 video-poker game from Epos Corporation. Designed for button-operated card play rather than action controls, it displays its gambling interface on a portrait CRT driven by a Z80 and AY-3-8910 sound hardware. The coin-operated poker format and dedicated panel place it among the early electronic replacements for mechanical and tabletop card machines.

The original program initially posed problems for emulator developers because of its ROM banking and color handling. Later discoveries restored the correct banking scheme and input behavior, making this comparatively obscure Epos title playable and documenting another use of the company's arcade technology outside standard video games.

games.title: Deathsmiles
games.description:
Deathsmiles (2007) is Cave's gothic-fantasy take on the bullet-hell shooter, replacing its familiar vertically scrolling spacecraft with young witches flying across a haunted kingdom. Windia, Follett, Casper and Rosa battle monsters in a world of graveyards, forests, villages and demonic castles. Players can fire to either the left or right, a vital ability in stages where enemies attack from both sides. Each heroine has a familiar, and the scoring system rewards the careful use of different firing modes and collection of cascading point items.

Instead of a wholly fixed route, Deathsmiles offers stage choices and selectable difficulty levels that let players shape the progression of a run. Its distinctive Halloween imagery, elaborate sprite art and accessible opening stages conceal a demanding scoring game and formidable late bosses. It helped Cave reach a wider audience beyond its traditional military and science-fiction shooters.

games.title: Deathsmiles (Hidden Elements Full Open + Character Enhancement)

variants.title: Death Smiles (Hidden elements full open + character enhancement)

modifications.description: Unlocks hidden stage routes and boss content by default and enhances player character attack capabilities.

games.description: Deathsmiles (Hidden Elements Full Open + Character Enhancement) is a modified version of Cave's 2007 horizontal gothic shoot-'em-up Deathsmiles on Cave CV1000 hardware, unlocking secret elements and boosting character firepower.

games.title: Decathlete
games.description:
Sega's Decathlete, also known as Athlete Kings, is a 3D athletics game for the ST-V arcade system, commercially released in 1996 despite its 1995 copyright. Players choose international competitors and tackle all ten events of a decathlon, from the 100-metre sprint and hurdles to the pole vault, discus and 1500 metres. Rapid button tapping builds running speed, while carefully timed presses determine jumps and throws. Each event requires meeting a qualifying target to advance.

A descendant of the button-bashing tradition established by Konami's Track & Field, Decathlete stands out for its polygonal athletes, lively animations and event-specific challenges. Competition between friends is as much a test of rhythm and timing as of sheer button speed.

games.title: Cassette System
games.description:
Data East's DECO Cassette System, introduced in Japan in 1980 and subsequently sold overseas, was a pioneering attempt to make arcade games interchangeable without replacing an entire circuit board or cabinet. Operators purchased a common machine and installed a game by inserting a magnetic cassette together with a matching security key. On startup, the program loaded into RAM, typically taking several minutes before play could begin. In AdvanceMAME, this entry represents the system BIOS rather than an individual playable game.

Its library included varied early-1980s releases such as Astro Fantasia, Lock 'n' Chase, and Mission X. The unusual tape-based arrangement made updates comparatively inexpensive, but long loading times, vulnerable media, and unreliable security modules undermined its appeal. It remains an important precursor to later arcade platforms built around replaceable games, and accurately preserving the loading process has been a particular challenge for emulation.

games.title: Deer Hunting USA V4.3
games.description:
Deer Hunting USA V4.3 (2000) is a light-gun hunting simulation from Sammy, built around a distinctive shotgun-shaped cabinet controller. Players select a wilderness area, choose a hunting weapon and visit different locations to find and shoot male deer while avoiding females. Each hunting ground presents its own targets and timing challenges, and a successful expedition may involve several areas in succession.

The physical gun, which must be pumped after shots, is central to the experience. Unlike a typical military shooting gallery, the game's rules distinguish legal targets from animals that must be spared, and success depends on recognition and careful aim rather than simply firing at everything on screen.

games.title: Defender
games.description:
Williams' Defender (1980) is a towering landmark of arcade shooting, created under the leadership of Eugene Jarvis. The player pilots a powerful spaceship across a horizontally scrolling, wraparound planetary landscape, protecting humanoids from alien abductors. A radar strip at the top of the screen tracks threats far beyond the current view. Landers swoop down to seize civilians and, if allowed to escape with them, transform into faster and deadlier mutants. Shooting an abductor is only half the rescue: the falling captive must be caught and safely delivered back to the surface.

Defender's demanding control panel was revolutionary. A two-way joystick controls altitude, while separate buttons handle thrust, reversing direction, laser fire, smart bombs and unpredictable hyperspace jumps. The ship's movement and screen direction require constant attention, and an experienced player must balance eliminating enemies with preserving the vulnerable population. If the planet loses all its humans, the battlefield becomes dramatically more hostile.

Initially regarded by some industry observers as excessively difficult, Defender became a massive arcade success and one of the defining shooters of the golden age. Its speed, synthesised explosions, complex enemy behavior and unusual rescue mechanics influenced generations of horizontally scrolling action games and established Jarvis as a major arcade designer.

games.title: Deluxe 5
games.description: Deluxe 5 (2000) is a Korean arcade multi-game collection rather than a single continuous adventure. Its selection comprises Blackjack, Bingo, Search Point, Pang and Land Cutter, combining card and number-based play with different short arcade challenges. Players choose the included game from the machine's menu. A related Deluxe 4 U release removes Blackjack, illustrating how the collection was tailored for different markets.

games.title: Demons and Dragons
games.description:
Demons & Dragons is an unreleased 1982 Bally Midway arcade prototype created by Dave Nutting Associates. The player explores a fantasy castle under threat from flying dragons, trolls and other monsters, using a trackball-based control scheme to evade hazards and throw magic missiles. A central objective is to gather three keys in a wave to free the imprisoned princess, while protecting the castle from attacking creatures.

Designed by Pat Lawlor, who would later become well known for pinball, the game survives as an unusual example of an early-1980s arcade fantasy experiment that never reached regular commercial distribution.

games.title: Demolition Derby
games.description:
Bally Midway's Demolition Derby is an arena-based driving combat game from the mid-1980s. Rather than racing to a finish line, players steer cars around a crowded enclosure and try to disable their opponents by ramming vulnerable radiators, all while protecting their own vehicles from the same fate. Wrenches, screwdrivers and keys can be collected for bonuses, and the tightly packed field turns every collision into an opportunity or a risk.

The game appeared in two-player and four-player configurations, using a rotary driving control. A noteworthy multiplayer feature lets additional drivers join while a derby is already underway, preserving the chaotic feel of a real demolition event.

games.title: Demon
games.description:
Demon (1982) is a vector-graphics space shooter produced by Rock-Ola for Cinematronics-style hardware. Viewed from above, it combines shooting enemy craft with the unusual task of collecting energy crystals and delivering them to a moving shuttle to replenish the player's laser. Without a steady supply, weapon power runs down even if the player survives the attackers.

Its spare luminous vector visuals, resource-management mechanic and simultaneous two-player option distinguish it from the more conventional wave shooters of the era.

games.title: Demoneye-X
games.description:
Irem's Demoneye-X (1981) is a fixed-screen space shooter in which the player moves a ship horizontally across the bottom of the screen and fires upward at formations of strange alien organisms. Hit enemies may split or transform into different creatures, creating new targets instead of disappearing immediately. The ultimate challenge of each wave is to expose and strike the heart of the giant Demoneye after destroying its smaller defenders.

The changing enemy shapes and multi-stage destruction give the game more variety than a straightforward Space Invaders imitation. It was also one of the earliest titles made for Irem's M27 arcade hardware.

games.title: Demon's World / Horror Story

variants.title: Demon's World / Horror Story (Taito license. set 2)

games.description:
Toaplan's Demon's World, released in Japan as Horror Story, is a horror-comedy run-and-gun platform game from 1989. One or two ghost hunters advance through side-scrolling, often automatically moving stages populated by zombies, spirits and monstrous creatures. The heroes jump between platforms, shoot supernatural enemies and confront bosses drawn from a variety of horror traditions. Its playful visual style contrasts with the elaborate military shooters for which Toaplan is better known.

Regional settings can change the displayed title and licensing information, so Horror Story and Demon's World refer to the same underlying arcade game rather than separate sequels.

games.title: Densya De Go
games.description:
Taito's Densha de Go! (1997) is an arcade train-driving simulator that asks the player to operate Japanese commuter trains according to strict schedules. Instead of racing, the challenge is to accelerate smoothly, obey speed restrictions, respond to track signals and brake accurately enough to stop at the correct station position. Late arrivals, rough braking and other mistakes cost performance points.

Its dedicated train-style throttle and brake controls helped make ordinary railway operations into an unusually absorbing arcade challenge. The authentic routes and emphasis on precision created a major Japanese series with a very different rhythm from conventional driving games.

games.title: Densya De Go 2
games.description:
Densha de Go! 2 (1998) expands Taito's distinctive arcade railway simulation with additional routes, trains and operational challenges. Players drive from station to station using train-specific acceleration and braking controls, following speed limits and arriving on time while trying to stop precisely at each platform. Poor timing or harsh handling is penalized, turning a seemingly calm journey into a demanding exercise in anticipation.

The sequel builds on the first game's success as a Japanese arcade phenomenon, preserving the unusually realistic train-controller cabinet and a focus on everyday railway discipline rather than racing.

games.title: Denjin Makai
games.description:
Denjin Makai (1994), developed by Winkysoft and published by Banpresto, is a science-fiction side-scrolling beat 'em up built around colorful characters and expressive combat. One or two players fight through futuristic streets and hostile installations, combining punches, jumps, throws and special attacks. Each character has a distinctive fighting style, and an energy gauge governs some stronger moves.

Beyond standard brawler combinations, Denjin Makai includes more elaborate techniques and enemy interactions than many contemporaries. Its arcade action was later reworked for the Super Famicom as Ghost Chaser Densei, a title that should not be confused with the separate pirate arcade conversion of that console game.

games.title: Ghost Chaser Densei
games.description:
Ghost Chaser Densei is an unauthorized coin-operated adaptation of the Super Famicom beat 'em up derived from Denjin Makai. Rather than being a wholly new arcade sequel, it brings the console game's side-scrolling fights to arcade hardware, with protagonists battling gangs of futuristic enemies through stages using character-specific attacks and special moves.

Its unusual origin makes it a useful example of a console-to-arcade pirate conversion. It is related to Banpresto's original Denjin Makai but does not represent an official new entry in the series.

games.title: Depthcharge
games.description:
Depthcharge (1977), developed by Gremlin and distributed in Japan by Sega as Depthbomb, is an early naval action game viewed in cross-section. The player steers a destroyer left and right across the ocean surface, dropping depth charges toward submarines traveling at different depths. Deeper targets are worth more points, but their positions must be anticipated while rising mines threaten the ship.

Its simple two-button attack arrangement, moving targets and pursuit of a high score make Depthcharge a clear ancestor of later undersea shooting games. The same concept also appeared under other regional titles, including Sub Hunter.

games.title: Deroon DeroDero
games.description:
Tecmo's Deroon DeroDero is a quirky Japanese competitive puzzle game, first released in arcades around 1995-1996 and later adapted for PlayStation as Tecmo Stackers. Players arrange falling pairs of soft, stretchy creatures so that matching colors connect and disappear. The elastic shapes deform and shift as other pieces move, producing chain reactions that are less predictable than those in a conventional rigid-block puzzler.

With expressive character animation and head-to-head battles, the game offers a distinctive variation on the Puyo Puyo style of match-and-clear competition.

games.title: Desert Breaker
games.description:
Desert Breaker (1992) is Sega's military-themed, vertically scrolling run-and-gun shooter for System 18 hardware. Players choose among three soldiers and advance through enemy territory, battling infantry, tanks and fortified positions from an overhead perspective. Weapons and other power-ups scattered through the stages encourage aggressive movement and constant changes of firepower.

The gameplay closely follows the arcade style popularized by Capcom's Mercs, combining crowded battlefields with cooperative action. Its distinctive Sega hardware presentation and relatively limited release have made it a less familiar entry in the early-1990s commando-shooter genre.

games.title: Desert Gun
games.description:
Midway's Desert Gun (1977) is a first-person electro-mechanical-style video shooting gallery set in the American desert. The player operates a light gun to pick off moving roadrunners, buzzards and other targets against a stylized Western landscape. Its appeal lies in quick recognition and accuracy, not movement through a scrolling world.

The game originally carried the name Road Runner before being renamed Desert Gun, distinguishing it from later games using the famous cartoon character. It is unrelated to Atari's 1985 Road Runner chase game, despite misleading descriptions sometimes attached to it.

games.title: Desert War / Wangan Sensou
games.description:
Desert War, known in Japan as Wangan Sensou, is a 1995 vertically scrolling military shooter developed by NMK and released by Jaleco on Mega System 32 hardware. The player advances through hostile battlefields while attacking enemy forces and rescuing prisoners of war. Its mission-based premise combines the constant forward pressure of an overhead shooter with the additional objective of reaching captives amid enemy fire.

The game is notable as one of NMK's final arcade productions, combining the studio's experience with scrolling shooters and the more powerful graphics hardware of the mid-1990s.

games.title: Destroyer
games.description:
Atari's Destroyer (1977) is an early submarine-hunting arcade game with an unusual physical control panel. A surface destroyer moves over underwater targets, while the player sets a depth-charge detonation depth with a dial and regulates the ship's speed with a separate lever. Accurate shots require anticipating both the submarine's travel and the delay before the charge reaches the chosen depth.

The dedicated controls, naval sound effects and physical artwork around the monitor helped create the illusion of commanding a warship. It is a distinctive example of the experimental cabinet design of the late 1970s.

games.title: Devil Fish
games.description:
Devil Fish (1982) is a curious single-screen maze game starring Sea Dog and a collection of hungry sea creatures. The player moves through narrow passages, feeding the pursuing Devil Fish until they become too large to slip through the corridors. Once a creature is trapped, Sea Dog can approach and touch it to complete the capture. Successful captures reveal sections of a hidden picture, and finishing the illustration advances to the next challenge.

Its combination of enemy manipulation, maze navigation and picture-reveal rewards is more involved than its simple cartoon appearance suggests. A later bootleg was converted to Galaxian-type hardware.

games.title: Devil World
games.description:
Devil World is the Japanese version of Konami's 1987 overhead action adventure also known as Majuu no Oukoku and related to Dark Adventure. Players guide explorers through monster-filled labyrinths after a mysterious artifact unleashes supernatural forces. Rather than advancing through a linear shooting stage, the heroes search connected rooms, collect helpful objects and fight enemies while discovering routes through the hostile world.

Different regional releases alter the cast and presentation: the Japanese version focuses on Labryna and Condor, while the three-player Dark Adventure arrangement adds Zorlock. Its exploration, fantasy setting and simultaneous cooperative action draw comparisons with Atari's Gauntlet. It is unrelated to Nintendo's similarly titled 1984 maze game featuring Tamagon.

games.title: Devastators
games.description:
Konami's Devastators (1988), released in Japan as Garuka, is a military shooting game with an unusual behind-the-soldier viewpoint. The player advances into the screen through deserts, bases and ruined settlements while shooting enemy troops and vehicles. Unlike many stationary-gallery shooters, the commandos can deliberately move forward and maneuver laterally, creating a distinctive sense of physically pushing through enemy territory.

Its pseudo-3D scaling backgrounds and over-the-shoulder combat place it between the perspective stages of Contra and the shooting-gallery action of Cabal. Weapons and grenades help the soldiers survive seven missions against escalating resistance.

games.title: Devil Zone
games.description:
Devil Zone is an early fixed-screen alien shooter from Universal, developed around 1980 and introduced to arcades in the early 1980s. The player's craft moves horizontally across the bottom of the screen and fires at demonic-looking aliens that gather overhead before diving to attack. A perspective-grid background gives the action an unusual illusion of depth, combining ideas familiar from Galaxian and Radar Scope.

Its restrained controls and wave-based scoring make it an example of the period when companies were rapidly experimenting with variations on Space Invaders.

games.title: Dangun Feveron
games.description:
Dangun Feveron (1998), known internationally as Fever SOS, is one of Cave's strangest and most energetic shooters. Instead of a grim military campaign, it embraces disco music, bright colors and a deliberately theatrical sense of speed. Before playing, pilots choose their craft's movement speed and weapon characteristics, then race through vertical stages filled with aggressive enemies. Destroyed foes release tiny disco-dancing figures that must be collected quickly to build the score, encouraging constant movement and dangerous close-range play.

Its unusually fast pacing and scoring system set it apart from Cave's more methodical chaining shooters. The mix of pulsating soundtrack, retro science-fiction imagery and high-risk item collection has made it a cult favorite among players seeking an alternative to the studio's more familiar DonPachi games.

games.title: The Destroyer From Jail
games.description:
The Destroyer From Jail is a 1991 Korean arcade action game developed by Philko and distributed in the United States by Four J International. Despite being classified as a fighter in some arcade databases, it plays as a belt-scrolling action shooter: players move through the depth of the battlefield like a beat-'em-up while using firearms to fight enemies, rather than trading punches in a fixed one-on-one arena. The protagonist is a convict trying to win his freedom by defeating a criminal boss and his followers over five stages.

It supports two simultaneous players using eight-way joysticks and three action buttons. That blend of multidirectional gunplay and side-view beat-'em-up movement gives it a distinctive identity among the many early-1990s Korean arcade action games. The surviving release dates to March 1991.

games.title: DoDonPachi Dai-Fukkatsu Black Label

variants.title: DoDonPachi Dai-Fukkatsu Black Label (2010/1/18 BLACK LABEL)

games.description:
DoDonPachi Dai-Fukkatsu Black Label (2010) is Cave's substantial revision of the shooter also known as DoDonPachi Resurrection. Players still weave through dense vertical projectile patterns using standard shots, focused lasers and spectacular Hyper abilities, but the Black Label rules change how those systems interact. Fighter selection is followed by a choice of Bomb, Power or Strong style, each with a different difficulty profile, and players may decide whether to enable automatic bombing.

Most notably, shot and laser can be fired together, producing a different tactical rhythm from the original game. Revised scoring and more aggressive enemy patterns make this a distinct expert-oriented version rather than a simple cosmetic update.

games.title: Dharma Doujou
games.description:
Dharma Doujou, released by Metro in 1994, is a whimsical Japanese puzzle game in which a monk or shrine maiden attacks stacks of colorful blocks with an oversized mallet. Players move the character to the appropriate height and strike blocks into a collection area, trying to arrange matching pieces so they disappear. Meanwhile a demon climbs a rope beside the playfield; letting it reach the top brings a dangerous temple bell down on the board. Matching groups creates a protective spirit that knocks the demon back, buying precious time.

The combination of character movement, block positioning and a visible pursuing threat gives Dharma Doujou a personality different from ordinary falling-block games. It was later adapted for the Super Famicom, where some of the character-control mechanics were simplified.

games.title: Diamond Run
games.description:
Diamond Run (1989), by KH Video, is an underground puzzle game in the Boulder Dash tradition. Players excavate passages and collect the required diamonds on each screen while avoiding spiders, dangerous faces and rocks that tumble when unsupported. Environmental objects complicate the route: green stones can explode near enemies, red balls detonate on impact, and some walls can be destroyed while others remain solid.

Progress requires planning around gravity and enemy movement rather than simply moving toward the nearest gem, since the same falling objects that threaten the player can also eliminate enemies and reveal more diamonds.

games.title: Dice - The Dice Game
games.description:
Dice: The Dice Game! is a 1991 unauthorized arcade version of Irem's unreleased Dice Dice Dice, distributed by Tuning. Its maze-based puzzle action involves pushing and rolling large dice around the playfield while dealing with hostile creatures. Manipulating the dice is the central activity, rather than simply firing at enemies or gathering objects.

The game survives in emulation as an unusual bootleg of a title that never received a standard commercial Irem release, making its existence an interesting piece of arcade preservation history.

games.title: Die Hard Arcade
games.description:
Sega's Die Hard Arcade (1996), known in Japan as Dynamite Deka, brought cinematic 3D spectacle to the scrolling beat 'em up. One or two police officers fight through a skyscraper held by terrorists, rescuing the president's daughter. Characters can punch, kick, grab and throw opponents, but the real pleasure is the astonishing assortment of improvised weapons: chairs, brooms, firearms and household objects can all become part of a fight.

Its short, heavily staged encounters are linked by quick-time events that require a timely button press or direction to avoid danger or enter the next area advantageously. The polygonal characters and rapidly shifting camera angles made it feel very different from traditional sprite-based brawlers. The Japanese original was not originally based on the Die Hard film; the movie branding was applied to its Western release.

Running on Sega's ST-V hardware, Die Hard Arcade is remembered as an exuberant bridge between the arcade beat 'em ups of the early 1990s and later 3D action games, with a deliberately over-the-top approach to combat.

games.title: Diet Go Go
games.description:
Diet Go Go (1992) is Data East's cheerful single-screen platform game built around the hazards of overeating. One or two players throw food at monsters to inflate them, then touch the swollen creatures to make them burst and knock into other enemies. The monsters can retaliate with food of their own, and a character who becomes too fat loses a life. Diet drinks and other collectible bonuses help keep the heroes in shape.

With its colorful enemies, chain reactions and absurd health-bar alternative, the game offers a comic variation on the screen-clearing design of Bubble Bobble and Snow Bros.

games.title: Dig Dug
games.description:
Namco's Dig Dug (1982) is one of the defining maze-action games of the golden arcade era. Players guide Taizo Hori through layers of underground earth, digging tunnels on the fly while hunting two unforgettable enemies: goggle-wearing red Pookas and green, fire-breathing Fygars. The hero can inflate creatures with an air pump until they burst or maneuver beneath precarious rocks and let gravity crush them. Enemies eventually turn into ghosts and pass through intact soil, preventing the player from remaining safe behind carefully excavated walls.

The scoring system gives extra rewards for eliminating multiple enemies with a single rock, and the depth of each encounter depends on the layout of tunnels and the timing of monster movements. Even the act of moving changes the stage by carving open new routes for both the player and pursuers.

With endearing character designs, bouncy sound effects and a remarkably readable visual style, Dig Dug became a major arcade success and an enduring Namco property. Its combination of freeform digging, indirect attacks and spatial puzzles continues to distinguish it from the maze-chase games that surrounded its release.

games.title: Dig Dug II
games.description:
Dig Dug II (1985) takes Namco's underground original in a surprising direction: the action is now viewed from above on small islands surrounded by water. Taizo Hori still fights Pookas and fire-breathing Fygars with his trusty air pump, but he also carries a drill that creates cracks along designated fault lines. Connecting these cuts can break off whole sections of island, sending enemies plunging into the sea.

The new mechanic turns each stage into a spatial puzzle. Sinking a large piece of land can defeat several monsters at once, but careless drilling can leave the hero stranded or cause him to fall with the island. Although less commercially celebrated than the original, Dig Dug II is remembered for replacing digging tunnels with a genuinely different environmental weapon.

games.title: Digger
games.description:
Sega/Gremlin's Digger (1980) is an early top-down trapping game based on the design of Heiankyo Alien. An explorer moves through a maze-like canyon while pursued by spider-like aliens. Two buttons allow the player to dig a hole and fill it in, and enemies must be lured into these temporary traps before they escape. The aim is to eliminate every creature while avoiding contact with the wandering monsters.

The appearance of a red enemy creates an additional scoring challenge: trapping it before any green enemy yields a special bonus. Digger predates the better-known 1983 computer game of the same name and belongs to the earlier family of maze games in which players defeat enemies by shaping the ground itself.

games.title: Digger
games.description: Digger (1982) is a maze and excavation game released for the Century Electronics CVS arcade system, distinct from Sega/Gremlin's 1980 game with the same title. Players navigate underground maze layouts using digging mechanics, although reliable descriptions of the exact stage objectives are scarce. The surviving documentation establishes its early arcade maze-game format but offers little reliable detail about its exact stage rules, so it should not be confused with the emerald-collecting PC game Digger released the following year.

games.title: Digger Man
games.description:
Digger Man is an independently produced Neo Geo arcade puzzle game dating from around 2000. Across 32 underground levels, players explore and collect 20 jewels to unlock the exit, while avoiding insects, falling rocks and other dangers. The life meter steadily runs down, but fruit can replenish it, creating pressure to plan efficient routes and gather supplies.

Its compact maze designs and treasure-hunting structure recall Boulder Dash, and its graphics reuse elements associated with the Neo Geo puzzle game Gururin.

games.title: Dimahoo
games.description:
Dimahoo (2000), released in Japan as Great Mahou Daisakusen, is a remarkable fusion of fantasy role-playing imagery and vertically scrolling shooter action. Developed by Eighting/Raizing and published by Capcom on CPS-2 hardware, it sends an eccentric group of aerial adventurers against the Gobligan Empire. Each selectable hero has distinctive attacks, and the elaborate bosses range from mechanical contraptions to fantastic monsters.

Its most unusual feature is an enormous collection of hidden treasure: food, armor, swords and other equipment items can be revealed by defeating enemies under specific conditions. Collecting the sets adds a strong treasure-hunting dimension to normal shoot 'em up scoring. Charge attacks, elemental interactions and constantly changing power levels reward experimentation as well as reflexes, making Dimahoo a memorable late entry in Raizing's Mahou Daisakusen series.

games.title: Dingo
games.description:
Dingo (1983) is a colorful maze game produced by Ashby Computers & Graphics, the British company also known as Ultimate Play the Game and later associated with Rare. Players guide Big Ted, a fruit-loving bear, around a single-screen orchard, gathering fruit while purple dingoes invade from the corners. Fruit can also be thrown at the marauders, giving the player a limited means of defense as the field becomes more crowded.

The game is a fascinating early arcade credit for the Stamper brothers and their collaborators. Its Z80 hardware and character fonts share visible ties with the team's contemporary British home-computer development work.

games.title: Dingo
games.description:
Dingo (encrypted) is an alternate protected program set of Ashby Computers & Graphics' 1983 arcade maze game. As Big Ted, the player harvests fruit in a compact orchard while evading invading dingoes and occasionally throwing fruit to keep them away. The scoring and playfield are those of the familiar Dingo game rather than a separate sequel.

This set is principally important as a hardware and preservation variant: its encrypted program and slightly different sound-chip clock configuration distinguish it from the unencrypted release.

games.title: Cadillacs and Dinosaurs
games.description:
Capcom's Cadillacs and Dinosaurs (1993) is a lavish CPS-1 side-scrolling beat 'em up based on Mark Schultz's Xenozoic Tales comic world. In a future where humans and dinosaurs share a fragile environment, heroes Jack Tenrec, Hannah Dundee, Mustapha Cairo and Mess O'Bradovich battle poachers and criminal gangs. Up to three players fight simultaneously through eight stages using punches, throws, running attacks and an extensive range of weapons, including guns and explosives.

Each hero has a different combination of reach, speed and strength, while dinosaurs roaming the stages can threaten both the villains and the players. The game's huge sprites, energetic animation and creative set pieces have made it one of Capcom's most admired arcade brawlers, often celebrated alongside Final Fight and The Punisher.

games.title: Dino Rex
games.description:
Taito's Dino Rex (1992) is a delightfully bizarre one-on-one fighting game in which prehistoric warriors command enormous dinosaurs. Players select from several species and battle opponents with bites, claws and special moves until one creature wins the best of three rounds. The beasts are rendered using digitized graphics, giving their lumbering attacks a distinctive stop-motion-like appearance. Between fights, the game features eccentric interludes, including a sequence in which a dinosaur rampages through a modern city.

Developed during the fighting-game boom following Street Fighter II, Dino Rex is remembered less for competitive precision than for its strange concept, extravagant presentation and giant-monster spectacle.

games.title: Dirt Devils
games.description:
Sega's Dirt Devils (1998) is an off-road racing game built around exaggerated slides, jumps and rugged terrain. Players choose from vehicles such as dune buggies and military-style trucks, then race against rivals across courses with sharp turns, water, potholes and changing visibility. Checkpoints extend the available driving time, while a rear-view mirror and radar help the driver keep track of competitors.

Its emphasis on handling heavy vehicles over uneven ground sets it apart from Sega's road-racing titles. Several standard courses and a hidden arena provide variety for players mastering the game's loose, aggressive driving model.

games.title: Dirt Fox
games.description:
Namco's Dirt Fox (1989) is an overhead-view off-road racing game released in Japan on System 2 arcade hardware. Competitors race brightly colored cars over a course divided into timed sections, gaining additional time whenever they pass a checkpoint. Dirt racing is complicated by numerous computer-controlled cars and the need to maintain speed through the bends. Failure to finish a section before the countdown expires eliminates that driver.

Linked cabinets can bring up to four human competitors into the same event. This combination of time-attack pressure and arcade multiplayer racing makes Dirt Fox an interesting companion to Namco's better-known Final Lap series.

games.title: Disco No.1
games.description:
Disco No. 1, also known as Sweet Heart, is a 1982 Data East maze game set inside a lively roller-skating rink. The player controls an awkward young skater trying to impress the girls while navigating around tougher rivals. By skating loops around characters and picking up moving bonus objects, the player earns points and clears challenges on the crowded rink.

Its playful courtship theme and territory-enclosing mechanics distinguish it from more conventional chase games. Disco No. 1 appeared both on Data East's interchangeable DECO Cassette System and in dedicated arcade form.

games.title: Diver Boy
games.description:
Diver Boy (1992), produced by Electronic Devices in Italy, is a colorful aquatic platform game inspired by the single-screen movement of Bomb Jack. The player dives through an underwater area collecting shells and pearls while avoiding roaming sea creatures that guard the treasure. Movement around the playfield and the order in which items are collected are central to surviving each stage.

Its unusual underwater setting and reversed gravity-like motion give a different flavor to the collect-and-avoid formula popular in earlier platform games.

games.title: DJ Boy
games.description:
Kaneko's DJ Boy (1989) is a street-fighting beat 'em up that brings roller skates and hip-hop imagery to the arcade. The hero rolls through city districts, battling flamboyant gangs and confronting bosses with punches, kicks and acrobatic moves. The skates give the action an unusual visual rhythm, with characters gliding rather than walking as they attack.

Regional editions are especially interesting for their different disc-jockey voices: the Japanese game featured musician Demon Kogure, while the overseas release used American radio personality Wolfman Jack. The arcade version differs in important ways from its home-console adaptations, which expanded some of the power-up and shopping systems.

games.title: Donkey Kong
games.description:
Nintendo's Donkey Kong (1981) is one of the most consequential games in arcade history. The player controls a carpenter known initially as Jumpman, later Mario, who must climb a construction site to rescue a captive woman, later named Pauline, from a giant ape. Across four distinct screens, he dodges rolling barrels, climbs ladders, crosses moving platforms and jumps over fireballs and other hazards. A temporary hammer can destroy enemies, but prevents climbing and jumping while active. Each stage has a falling bonus counter, keeping the pressure on even when the route is safe.

Designed by Shigeru Miyamoto, the game introduced Mario and Donkey Kong and made jumping a central mechanic of the emerging platform genre. Its changing level layouts, expressive characters and brief story scenes were striking at a time when many arcade games consisted of repeated variations on a single field.

Donkey Kong was a breakthrough commercial success for Nintendo, particularly in North America, and established two characters who would become cornerstones of video-game culture. Its barrel stage, memorable sound effects and famous difficulty remain instantly recognizable, while its influence runs through decades of platform and action games.

games.title: Donkey Kong 3

variants.title: Donkey Kong 3 (bootleg on Donkey Kong Jr. hardware)

games.description:
Donkey Kong 3 (1983) takes Nintendo's famous ape into a completely different genre. Instead of controlling Mario in a climbing game, players guide Stanley the exterminator through a greenhouse, spraying insects and pushing Donkey Kong upward with bursts of bug repellent. Flying bees, creeping caterpillars and other pests threaten both Stanley and the flowers growing at the bottom of the screen. Saving flowers improves the round bonus, and a temporary Super Sprayer greatly strengthens the attack.

The arcade game is an unusual hybrid of fixed-screen shooter and platform action. Its change of protagonist and focus on protecting the greenhouse make it an eccentric installment in the Donkey Kong series, very different from the jumping adventures that preceded it.

games.title: Donkey Kong Junior
games.description:
Donkey Kong Junior (1982) reverses the roles of Nintendo's original arcade hit. Mario has captured Donkey Kong and locked him in a cage, so the player controls the ape's young son on a mission to free his father. Junior runs, jumps and climbs through four different screens, avoiding Snapjaw creatures, birds and electrical hazards while reaching the keys needed to open the cage. Fruit can be knocked loose to defeat enemies or collect bonus points.

Its signature mechanic is climbing vines and chains. Holding two adjacent vines allows Junior to ascend more quickly, while sliding down a single vine is faster, a small detail that becomes critical when enemies close in. The changing layouts, including a final screen requiring several keys to be inserted into locks, make it a distinctly different platform challenge from the original Donkey Kong.

It remains one of Nintendo's classic early sequels and a rare appearance of Mario as the villain, years before he became the company's universally recognized hero.

games.title: Dragon's Lair
games.description:
Dragon's Lair (1983), developed by Advanced Microcomputer Systems and released by Cinematronics, transformed the appearance of arcade games with animated footage stored on a laserdisc. The player guides Dirk the Daring, an inept but courageous knight, through a perilous castle in search of Princess Daphne, who is held by the dragon Singe. Instead of moving Dirk continuously through computer-drawn environments, players make precisely timed directional inputs or sword attacks as full-motion animated scenes unfold. Success leads to another sequence; hesitation or a wrong action triggers one of the game's many elaborate death animations.

The spectacular artwork was created by animator Don Bluth and his team, giving the cabinet the look of an interactive animated film. The technology delivered visual detail far beyond contemporary sprite-based games, although it also meant that mastering the adventure depended heavily on memorizing correct responses to each scene.

Dragon's Lair became a major arcade sensation and a cultural symbol of the laserdisc-game boom. Its impressive presentation and steep learning curve remain inseparable from its reputation, and its influence can be seen in later cinematic games built around timed reactions and interactive cutscenes.

games.title: Dynamite League
games.description: Dynamite League (1990) is Taito's arcade baseball game, presenting the confrontation between pitcher and batter with a distinctive horizontally divided view. Players control their team through innings, making decisions about pitches, batting and fielding while trying to outscore the opposing side. The split-screen presentation puts both sides of the duel in view and gives this Japanese baseball title a different look from games that show the entire diamond from a single angle.

games.title: Diamond Derby
games.description:
Diamond Derby is an Electrocoin horse-race betting game represented in arcade preservation by several software and circuit-board revisions. Rather than steering a vehicle or controlling a jockey, the player places a wager and watches a simulated race unfold on a horizontal display. The documented versions distinguish ordinary win bets from a bootleg offering quinella bets, which concern the first two finishers.

The surviving sets include an original 1986 version and a later revision associated with 1994. Its animated racetrack, horse sprites, and wager-management controls make it a distinctive example of the video-assisted betting machines that occupied a different corner of the coin-op business from action-oriented racing games.

games.title: Demon Front / Moyu Zhanxian

variants.title: Demon Front / Moyu Zhanxian (68k label V105, ROM M105XX 08/05/02) (ARM label V105, ROM 08/05/02 S105XX)
Demon Front / Moyu Zhanxian (68k label V102, ROM M102XX 06/19/02) (ARM label V102, ROM 05/24/02 S101XX)

games.description:
Demon Front (2002), developed by IGS for its PolyGame Master arcade system, is a colorful science-fiction run-and-gun platformer that openly recalls SNK's Metal Slug. Up to two players simultaneously select from four fighters and battle mutated creatures across a distant planet suffering from a mysterious catastrophe. The heroes run, jump and fire through layered side-scrolling stages, collecting new weapons and facing large, heavily animated bosses.

Its defining addition is a small companion creature that assists with attacks and can generate a protective effect, lending the familiar shooting formula a tactical twist. The game's branching opening stage choices, expressive characters and substantial boss encounters have earned it a following among fans of late-period arcade action.

games.title: Dead Or Alive ++
games.description:
Dead or Alive ++ (1998) is an enhanced arcade edition of Tecmo's 3D fighting game, running on PlayStation-derived ZN-1 hardware. Players choose from a roster of martial artists and battle in fast, close-range one-on-one matches that emphasize striking, throws and rapid counterattacks. The series' hallmark hold system lets a well-timed defensive command catch an opponent's attack and turn it into a counter, making anticipation and reading the opponent essential.

This revision updates the original Dead or Alive's balance and presentation for the arcade, offering an important intermediate version in the series' early history before the more elaborate sequels moved to newer hardware.

games.title: Mr. Do's Castle
games.description:
Mr. Do's Castle (1983) transforms Universal's popular digging-game hero into the star of a platform-and-ladders puzzle action game. Mr. Do moves through a multi-storey castle collecting cherries and dodging persistent unicorn-like enemies. His hammer removes blocks from platforms, opening holes that can trap monsters, while knocking loose blocks down onto pursuers provides another way to eliminate them. Some diagonal ladders can be moved, allowing the player to change access routes through the building.

A stage can be cleared by collecting the required cherries or defeating all the enemies, creating opportunities for different strategies. Its mix of climbing, excavation, environmental traps and movement puzzles makes it a thoughtful sequel rather than a simple reskin of Mr. Do!.

games.title: Dock Man
games.description:
Dock Man (1982), also known as Port Man, is a dockside action game in which the player plays a frantic cargo handler. In the first phase, luggage drops from an overhead conveyor belt and must be caught and thrown into the appropriate berths on a waiting ship. Hazards include moving carts, objects thrown by troublemakers and the risk of letting too much cargo fall. Later phases involve dislodging and catching explosive crates before they reach the ground.

Its changing cargo-handling tasks, timing demands and comic port setting make it an unusual early arcade game built around catching and throwing rather than shooting or jumping over enemies.

games.title: Dodgem
games.description:
Dodgem (1979), produced by Zaccaria, is an early maze-driving game closely modeled on Sega/Gremlin's Head On. Players steer a small vehicle around looping lanes, collecting dots while avoiding oncoming traffic. Lane changes must be carefully timed because a collision ends the attempt, and the remaining dots determine which paths must still be traversed.

The simple combination of a fixed maze, constantly moving vehicles and constrained lane changes makes it an early ancestor of driving-based maze-chase games. Some descriptions refer to the vehicle as a boat, but the central play remains the same Head On-style collision-avoidance challenge.

games.title: Dodge Man
games.description: Dodge Man is a 1983 arcade shooter by Omori Electric built around a small astronaut exploring the Moon. The game begins after the character disembarks from a spacecraft and starts traversing the lunar surface, with joystick movement and two action buttons used during the encounter with hazards and opponents. Presented on a horizontal raster display, it offers a science-fiction alternative to the military and alien-invasion themes more commonly found in shooters of the period. Its uncommon hardware and relative obscurity have made the surviving board of interest to arcade preservationists.

games.title: Acrobatic Dog-Fight
games.description:
Acrobatic Dog-Fight (1984) is Technos Japan's lively cartoon-style aerial combat game. Players pilot a small aircraft through horizontally scrolling stages, shooting opposing planes while avoiding obstacles between the ground and the upper limits of the screen. Unlike many shooters, the hero can eject from a damaged plane and attempt to hijack an enemy aircraft in midair. If the attempt fails, the parachuting pilot can recover another plane on the ground and continue.

This unusual ejection-and-recovery feature gives the game a playful sense of improvisation and sets it apart from the conventional one-life-per-aircraft design of most early shooting games.

games.title: Dog Fight
games.description: Dog Fight is a little-known 1983 arcade air-combat shooter developed by Orca and licensed to Thunderbolt. Using a two-way joystick and a fire button, the player controls an aircraft in a shooting contest against opposing planes. It predates and is unrelated to Technos's better-documented Acrobatic Dog-Fight, which appeared in 1984. Surviving references provide few reliable details about its stage structure or scoring beyond the basic aerial-combat premise.

games.title: Dogou Souken

modifications.description: Adapts the rotary/positional control scheme for standard 8-way joystick input.

games.description:
Dogou Souken is the Japanese title of SNK's 1986 arcade run-and-gun shooter known internationally as Victory Road, the sequel to Ikari Warriors. The heroes enter a bizarre alien and fantasy environment, fighting strange creatures and enormous bosses with guns, grenades and special weapons. Its distinctive rotary joysticks let players move in one direction while turning to fire in another, an important part of managing enemies that approach from all sides.

Compared with the military setting of Ikari Warriors, the sequel leans into science-fiction and supernatural imagery while retaining the same demanding twin-commando style. This AdvanceMAME version is a gameplay hack of the Japanese release, adapting the original rotary aiming scheme for a standard eight-way joystick. It therefore changes how movement and firing are controlled, rather than adding new stages or enemies.

games.title: Dog Patch
games.description:
Dog Patch (1977-1978) is a lighthearted two-player shooting game from Midway in which hillbilly characters take aim at tin cans tossed into the air. Rather than navigating a world, players line up shots and compete for points by hitting moving targets at the right moment. A special bonus round introduces a goose that can be shot for extra points.

Its cartoon rural theme and simple competitive shooting-gallery action are characteristic of the period before scrolling arcade shooters became dominant.

games.title: Dogyuun
games.description:
Toaplan's Dogyuun (1992) is a technically impressive vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter known for its huge mechanical enemies and punishing precision. The player pilots a Sylfers craft on a mission to reclaim a distant colony from hostile alien machines. Weapons can be upgraded or exchanged as the ship advances through increasingly dense formations of fighters, turrets and massive bosses. The game combines the fluid movement and screen-filling explosions associated with Toaplan with a notably unforgiving challenge.

Its unusual two-player system allows the fighters to connect into a stronger combined craft, creating a trade-off between separate fire coverage and concentrated power. With bold pixel art and dramatic boss machinery, Dogyuun became one of the company's standout late-period shooters and remains a favorite among dedicated genre enthusiasts.

games.title: Dokaben
games.description:
Dokaben (1989) is Capcom's Japanese arcade baseball game based on Shinji Mizushima's popular manga about high-school players. Instead of representing every decision purely through reflex-based batting and pitching, it uses a deck of randomly dealt cards to influence baseball actions and strategy. Players must manage the flow of a match through this unusual combination of sporting simulation and card play.

The well-known comic license and hybrid mechanics give Dokaben a distinctive place among the many arcade baseball titles of its era.

games.title: Dokaben 2
games.description: Dokaben 2, released by Capcom in 1989, continues the Japanese manga-inspired baseball and card-game hybrid introduced in Dokaben. Players contest baseball matches using randomly dealt cards to help determine strategic actions, rather than relying entirely on conventional joystick-and-button fielding. Released only months after the first game, this follow-up is primarily of interest for its unusual sports-meets-cards formula and its connection to Shinji Mizushima's long-running baseball story.

games.title: Doki Doki Penguin Land
games.description:
Sega's Doki Doki Penguin Land, developed in 1985 and released in Japanese arcades around 1986, is an inventive vertical puzzle-platform game starring a penguin named Adelie. The objective is to guide an egg from the top of an icy cavern to the bottom without breaking it. Players can push the egg along ledges, dig or melt away blocks and work out safe drops, but a fall that is too long will shatter the precious cargo. Polar bears, falling rocks and the geometry of each stage complicate the descent.

Its central challenge is not merely reaching the exit yourself, but engineering a safe route for an object that obeys gravity and cannot survive careless handling. The combination of cheerful visuals and demanding egg physics made Penguin Land a memorable Sega puzzle series.

games.title: Mahjong Doukyuusei
games.description:
Mahjong Doukyuusei (1995) is a Japanese adult-themed riichi mahjong game based on the popular Doukyuusei romance-adventure franchise. Players compete against a succession of animated female opponents, progressing by winning mahjong hands.
