Each defeated character reveals additional illustrated sequences, making the character presentation as prominent as traditional Japanese mahjong rules.

The arcade edition combines authentic mahjong decision-making with 1990s anime-style art and adult fan-service, reflecting a distinctive niche in Japanese amusement centers rather than a conventional action or gambling-slot machine.

games.title: Mahjong Doukyuusei Special
games.description:
Mahjong Doukyuusei Special (1995) is an expanded follow-up to the adult-themed mahjong game inspired by the Doukyuusei visual novels. It retains riichi mahjong competition against illustrated female characters while introducing a revised roster, more elaborate animated scenes and additional character interactions. Some opponents return from the earlier game, but the overall selection and presentation are different.

Its appeal lies in a combination of conventional Japanese mahjong play and the animated character rewards familiar from mid-1990s Japanese arcade mahjong titles.

games.title: Dolmen
games.description:
Dolmen (1995), also released as Goindol, is a Korean prehistoric-themed puzzle game inspired by Puzzle Bobble. Players launch colored objects toward groups suspended overhead, trying to make matching clusters disappear and clear the board before the advancing mass becomes dangerous. Cartoon cavemen, ropes and obstacles create unusual arrangements, including stages requiring the player to knock figures from their supports.

Its visual material borrows noticeably from other prehistoric-themed games of the period, making this an unusual and somewhat cheeky entry in the wave of competitive color-matching arcade puzzlers.

games.title: Domino Man
games.description:
Bally Midway's Domino Man (1982) is an inventive single-screen action game built around the unlikely occupation of arranging giant dominoes. Players guide a mustachioed domino setter around a crowded public space, placing a tile on every marked spot while avoiding pedestrians who can accidentally knock the work over. A troublesome bee and a much larger bully add extra pressure, while the player can shove bystanders away or stun certain threats.

Once the chain is complete, the dominoes can be knocked down in a satisfying cascade. The game's ragtime soundtrack, including Scott Joplin's Maple Leaf Rag, contributes to its comical atmosphere. Its unusual nonviolent objective and carefully timed positioning stand apart from the shooting and maze-chase games of the same era.

games.title: Dominos
games.description:
Atari's Dominos (1977) is an early multiplayer action game that translates the idea of leaving a trail into an escalating contest of movement and space. Each player steers a continuously moving line of dominoes around a rectangular arena, trying to force an opponent into a wall or an existing trail. Colliding with an obstacle ends the round, and the defeated trail tumbles over like real dominoes.

As play speeds up, every turn permanently reduces the room left to maneuver. Dominos appeared in dedicated and cocktail cabinets, including multiplayer configurations, and helped establish the basic competitive trail-game formula later associated with Snake and light-cycle games.

games.title: Dommy
games.description:
Dommy (1983) is a single-screen maze action game from Technos Japan with an unusual block-collecting objective. The player pushes blocks toward the edge of the playfield while avoiding or temporarily stunning roaming enemies. Once enough blocks have gathered together, standing on a special marked arrow and pressing the action button allows the player to claim the collection.

Instead of clearing a maze through straightforward pursuit or shooting, Dommy asks players to manipulate the arrangement of objects while staying ahead of threats, making it a distinctive early Technos arcade curiosity.

games.title: Hanabi de Doon! - Don-chan Puzzle
games.description:
Hanabi de Doon! - Don-chan Puzzle is a Japanese falling-block puzzle game published by Aruze in December 2003 and developed by Takumi Corporation. Its fireworks theme draws on Don-chan, the mascot of Aruze's popular Hanabi pachislot series, rather than on an established action-game franchise. Two players are supported, with the game presented through the colorful, compact Seta Aleck64 arcade system.

The cartridge is a curious meeting of pachislot branding and conventional arcade puzzle gaming. Aleck64's Nintendo 64-derived architecture and the title's limited Japanese release make it a particularly uncommon puzzle entry in the early-2000s arcade landscape.

games.title: Don Den Mahjong
games.description: Don Den Mahjong is a 1986 Japanese adult mahjong game from Dyna Electronics, also associated with the Dynax name. Played with a dedicated mahjong-button panel, it combines traditional tile-based competition with strip-mahjong presentation: successful play reveals progressively more of the female opponents. A separate betting-oriented edition is also documented, illustrating the overlap between adult mahjong and wagering-style arcade machines during the period.

games.title: Don Doko Don
games.description:
Taito's Don Doko Don (1989) is a colorful single-screen platform game starring Bob and Jim, two hammer-wielding lumberjacks on a mission to rescue the princess of Marry Land. One or two players clear each round by stunning monsters with their mallets, picking them up, and hurling them against walls or into other enemies. Well-aimed throws can eliminate several creatures in one move, multiplying the score, while defeated foes leave fruit and helpful items. The two-button controls make this deceptively elaborate system easy to learn.

Across five worlds of ten rounds each, the layouts grow trickier and culminate in inventive boss encounters, often requiring players to throw smaller enemies at a giant adversary. Drinks, magic books, and special hammers change movement speed or attack power. Spending too long on a round summons an invulnerable flying pursuer, another reminder of the game's Bubble Bobble ancestry.

Don Doko Don hides an unusually substantial second half: collecting secret keys can unlock five additional worlds and the true ending, which rescues the king as well as the princess. Its expressive characters, cooperative tactics, and secret-room structure make it one of Taito's more rewarding late-1980s variations on the single-screen platform formula.

games.title: DonPachi
games.description:
DonPachi (1995) was the debut arcade release from Cave, the studio founded by former Toaplan developers that would become synonymous with bullet-heavy shooting games. Published by Atlus, this vertically scrolling military shooter lets one or two players choose among three craft: a narrow-shot fighter, a helicopter with direction-sensitive side guns, and a wide-spread fighter. Tapping fire releases normal shots, while holding it produces a powerful focused laser at the cost of movement speed. Bombs provide an emergency escape from enemy formations and ground defenses.

Its defining contribution is the Get Point System. Destroying enemies in rapid succession builds a hit chain, rewarding players who plan an uninterrupted route through each stage instead of merely surviving. Hidden bee medals add another layer of score optimization. Five stages lead to a second, more punishing loop, complete with revenge bullets from destroyed enemies and an eventual confrontation with Hachi, the series' giant mechanical bee. The game's adaptive rank system can also increase enemy aggression as a run progresses.

DonPachi bridged Toaplan's classic shoot-'em-up design and the scoring-intensive approach developed in its successor, DoDonPachi. Cave's respect for its predecessors even appears in the default initials on the high-score table, which spell out 'TOAPLAN FOREVER' when read vertically. Its intricate chaining system helped define the identity of one of arcade shooting's most influential studios.

games.title: Dorachan
games.description: Dorachan is an unusual early Japanese maze game made by Craul Denshi in 1980, using a character resembling Doraemon from the popular manga and anime series. Its vertically oriented screen and eight-way joystick place it among the experimental maze releases that appeared around the time of Pac-Man. The game is particularly remembered for the reported withdrawal of its boards because the Doraemon character had been used without authorization. The precise maze rules are not well documented, but its unlicensed character connection gives this otherwise obscure game a distinctive place in arcade history.

games.title: Dorodon
games.description: Falcon's Dorodon (1982) is an overhead maze game in which a small, blue-trousered character gathers question marks, fruit, and other pickups while avoiding roaming monsters and dangerous flames. Its unusual twist is a set of walls that can flip, changing the routes through the maze and allowing a quick-thinking player to evade or trap pursuers. Collecting a whirlwind symbol changes the walls more broadly, turning navigation into a continually shifting puzzle rather than a fixed Pac-Man-style circuit. A four-way joystick and two buttons control the action. The game later reached the MSX home computer.

games.title: Do! Run Run

variants.title: Do! Run Run (Do's Castle hardware, set 2)
Do! Run Run (Do's Castle hardware, set 1)

games.description:
Do! Run Run (1984), known in Japan as Super Pierrot, is Universal's fourth original Mr. Do! arcade game. It returns the clown's bouncing powerball, but replaces the digging of the original with a sloping, overhead-style playfield. Mr. Do runs over colored dots, dodges monsters, and releases heavy logs that roll downhill and crush anything in their path. A stage ends when the required dots and fruit have been collected or the ordinary monsters have been eliminated.

The key innovation is territory-making. As Mr. Do moves, he traces a line; enclosing sections of the playfield converts ordinary dots into cherries. Repeating the process can upgrade fruit through apples and lemons to valuable pineapples. The powerball recharges through collecting items, and shots that rebound off walls earn greater rewards. The series' familiar EXTRA letters can still be collected for additional lives.

Released primarily as a conversion kit in the difficult post-crash North American arcade market, Do! Run Run is an inventive hybrid of Pac-Man-like chasing, Qix-style enclosure, and Mr. Do!'s environmental traps. Some alternate boards were converted to Mr. Do's Castle hardware, while the Japanese Super Pierrot release features its own maze arrangements.

games.title: Dottori Kun
games.description:
Dottori Kun is a deliberately minimal Sega maze game from 1990, effectively a tiny reinterpretation of the company's 1979 Head On. The player guides an arrow around a rectangular course, gathering dots while avoiding an X-shaped opponent. Movement follows the paths of the maze, with automatic turns at corners and no immediate reversal; holding a button accelerates the arrow, while another pauses the action.

Its historical interest is greater than its modest presentation. Sega built the exceptionally small, monochrome circuit board primarily as an inexpensive cabinet-testing and compliance game rather than a major commercial attraction. Many boards were reportedly removed when their host cabinets received full games, leaving Dottori Kun as a fascinating example of software created to satisfy the practical needs of arcade manufacturing.

games.title: Discs of Tron
games.description:
Bally Midway's Discs of Tron (1983) transforms the disc-duel sequences from Disney's Tron into a dedicated arcade contest. Viewed from behind the hero, players battle the villain Sark across a futuristic arena of raised circular platforms. A joystick moves Tron, a rotary aiming control targets throws, and trigger and thumb controls handle disc attacks and defensive deflection. Unlike a conventional shooting gallery, both combatants can return or intercept thrown discs, forcing the player to balance offense with survival.

As the twelve-stage challenge advances, platforms disappear when struck, move vertically, or become separated by a wall of destructible blocks. Sark fires increasingly troublesome projectiles, including homing hazards that cannot simply be deflected. Players can knock Sark down directly or destroy the platforms supporting him; a careless throw or movement can also send Tron plunging from his own foothold.

The disc battle was originally planned as part of Midway's earlier Tron arcade game, but was removed and developed into its own release. The spectacular enclosed 'Environmental' cabinet surrounded the player with themed lighting and sound, turning the match into an attraction in its own right. Its highly specialized aiming and defensive controls remain one of the most distinctive arcade interpretations of a film scene.

games.title: Double Dragon One
games.developer: La Casa De Ruivo / Neo Byte Force
games.publisher: La Casa De Ruivo / Neo Byte Force
games.description: Double Dragon One is a homebrew side-scrolling beat-'em-up adaptation for the Neo Geo MVS developed by La Casa De Ruivo and Neo Byte Force in 2025.

games.title: Double Dragon
games.description:
Double Dragon (1995) is Technos Japan's Neo Geo one-on-one fighting game, an unexpected transformation of the side-scrolling beat-'em-up franchise popularized in 1987. Loosely associated with the live-action Double Dragon film, it brings Billy and Jimmy Lee into a tournament against a colorful roster of opponents, with characters and visual references drawn from several parts of the series. The pace and presentation belong to the mid-1990s fighting-game boom rather than to the original street-brawling formula.

Instead of the familiar separate punch and kick buttons, four attack buttons offer different strengths and speeds, producing an unusual approach to normal attacks and combinations. The game also uses a power meter for stronger moves, and matches emphasize fast exchanges and elaborate special attacks. Its existence is especially noteworthy because the Neo Geo later hosted other games inspired by Double Dragon, but this was the series' official departure into competitive fighting.

games.title: Mr. Do's Wild Ride
games.description:
Mr. Do's Wild Ride (1984) takes Universal's clown mascot to a perilous amusement-park roller coaster. Rather than digging tunnels or collecting fruit, Mr. Do must climb across the track and reach a goal near the top of each screen while avoiding speeding coaster cars and other moving hazards. Ladders provide temporary refuge, and a dedicated speed button lets him sprint through short openings in traffic, though timing remains essential.

The roller-coaster setting gives this third arcade Mr. Do! installment a very different rhythm from its maze-oriented predecessors. Routes must be judged around the movement of the cars, with increasingly hazardous layouts demanding precise, stop-and-go platforming. Bonus cherries remain as a nod to the series, but reaching the destination alive is the central challenge.

games.title: DownTown

modifications.description: Adapts the rotary/positional control scheme for standard 8-way joystick input.

games.description: This alternate DownTown set adapts Seta's 1989 overhead street-fighting game for standard eight-way joystick control rather than the original positional or rotary-style input arrangement. The underlying adventure still follows two law-enforcement protagonists fighting through city streets crowded with gangs and corrupt officers, using close-range attacks to reach the criminal leaders. Its significance in AdvanceMAME is practical: the revised input mapping makes the same unusual overhead brawler more accessible on conventional arcade sticks without reproducing the original specialized controls.

games.title: DownTown
games.description:
DownTown is Seta's 1989 overhead-view beat-'em-up, following two public officials as they fight through a crime-ridden city to confront the gang responsible for its collapse. Rather than using the horizontal side view of Double Dragon or Final Fight, it looks down onto the streets as enemies surround the player from several directions. Punching and kicking therefore depend heavily on positioning and the orientation of attacks.

The original arcade controls are particularly unusual, using positional or rotary-style input to manage the direction of combat. This separates DownTown from other late-1980s brawlers: merely approaching an opponent is not enough, because facing the correct way matters just as much as moving through the environment. Alternate joystick-adapted versions exist for more conventional control panels.

games.title: DownTown
games.description: This prototype version of Seta's DownTown preserves a pre-release form of the company's 1989 overhead-view street brawler. As in the finished game, players guide public-official heroes through gang-controlled urban streets, fighting criminals and crooked police officers from a top-down perspective. The prototype is noteworthy as development material rather than a separate sequel. Without firmly documented, set-specific gameplay changes, it should not be assumed to have different stages, enemies, or balance from the released game.

games.title: Double Play
games.description:
Double Play is a 1977 Midway baseball game from the first generation of microprocessor-driven arcade sports titles. Its action resembles an electronic pitch-and-bat machine: in a solo game the player bats against the computer, while in two-player competition one person pitches and fields as the other bats. Teams change sides after three outs, reproducing baseball's essential contest with very simple on-screen figures and controls.

Powered by an Intel 8080, Double Play is a snapshot of the period before detailed animated athletes and licensed teams became standard. Its appeal lies in timing a swing, choosing pitches, and competing directly at the cabinet rather than in elaborate presentation.

games.title: Dragon Blaze
games.description:
Psikyo's Dragon Blaze (2000) is a fantasy-themed vertical shooter in which four heroes ride dragons into battle against grotesque monsters and enormous transforming bosses. Each rider has different shot characteristics and magic attacks, giving the usual Psikyo character selection greater tactical meaning. Although the game retains the studio's rapid enemy formations and sharply aimed projectiles, its denser purple bullet patterns place it closer to the emerging bullet-hell style.

The signature technique is Dragon Shot: the rider launches the dragon forward as a powerful attack, then fights separately until calling the mount back. Dividing rider and dragon changes movement, firing coverage, and scoring opportunities, making this far more than a cosmetic variation on a spaceship shooter. Magic attacks, power-ups, and increasingly ferocious boss phases reward mastering this unusual two-part offense. Dragon Blaze is among Psikyo's most demanding and inventive late arcade shooters.

games.title: Dragon Gun
games.description: Data East's Dragon Gun (1993) is a fantasy light-gun shooting game that sends one or two players through monster-filled environments from a first-person perspective. Rather than maneuvering an on-screen character, players aim physical guns at skeletons, beasts, and other supernatural threats as the scenery advances along a preset route. The emphasis is on rapid target recognition, accurate firing, and surviving spectacular enemy encounters. Its medieval horror imagery and shared two-player gunplay distinguish it from Data East's military-oriented shooting games.

games.title: Dragoon Might
games.description:
Konami's Dragoon Might (1995) is a Japanese one-on-one fighting game with a varied cast and an emphasis on aggressive, technical combat. Players choose among human and supernatural combatants, exchanging special moves, aerial attacks, and close-range combinations in side-view arenas. The game offers both an individual-match mode and a tournament-style progression, with each character's techniques encouraging different strategies.

Although released during an extremely crowded period for 2D fighting games, Dragoon Might stands out for its elaborate character animation, stylish special attacks, and combination-oriented play. Its limited arcade profile outside Japan helped make it a lesser-known Konami fighter rather than a major international franchise.

games.title: Drag Race
games.description:
Atari's Drag Race (1977) reduces motorsport to a fiercely timed straight-line contest. Two drivers line up at a starting tree, wait for the green light, and accelerate through the gears toward the finish. Success comes from shifting at the right moment and controlling speed without losing time or damaging the engine. It is a direct two-player challenge rather than a circuit racing simulation.

The sparse monochrome presentation is typical of Atari's early video games, but the manual gear-changing and drag-strip starting lights gave the cabinet a mechanical, competitive feel. Its distinctive appeal is how much of a race depends on a few precisely timed decisions.

games.title: Drakton
games.description: Drakton is a 1984 space-themed maze shooter, also found as a conversion for Donkey Kong hardware. Players pilot the Drakton Fighter through hostile sectors, firing plasma torpedoes at enemies while negotiating the game's maze-like layouts. Its mixture of navigation and shooting sets it apart from the straight vertical and horizontal scrolling space shooters of the period. The availability of a conversion version also reflects the mid-1980s market for giving established arcade cabinets a different game without replacing the entire machine.

games.title: Dream World
games.description:
Dream World (2000) is a Korean cooperative platform game by SemiCom that combines the colorful single-screen tradition of Bubble Bobble with the digging and route-planning of Lode Runner. Its two small magician heroes move through stages that scroll in multiple directions, collecting gems and making their way to the exit or eliminating every enemy. Ladders and overhead bars are essential to movement because the characters cannot jump very high.

Their wands can create holes in suitable floors, allowing armored enemies to be trapped rather than attacked directly. Other monsters can be jumped on, carried, and thrown at their companions, while rare invincibility potions or spellbooks offer ways out of difficult situations. Every tenth stage brings a boss. An earlier prototype is known as Lode Quest, a title that aptly reflects the game's unusual mixture of platform action and environmental puzzles.

games.title: Dream Shopper
games.description:
Sanritsu's Dream Shopper (1982) is a memory-and-chase game running on hardware derived from Namco's Pac-Man. The playfield is a grid of shop goods whose contents and values are revealed briefly before the round begins. Players then move a shopper across the tiles, trying to uncover at least 10,000 points' worth of merchandise before closing time while avoiding hidden bombs and pursuing threats.

The challenge is to remember where high-value goods were displayed and plan a safe route across the board. Unlike a conventional maze game, the important information is momentarily visible at the start of each round, turning visual memory into a practical scoring skill. Its unusual shopping theme makes it one of the more inventive uses of early-1980s chase-game hardware.

games.title: Dragon Bowl
games.description:
Dragon Bowl is a 1992 Korean side-scrolling beat-'em-up from Nics, notable for combining the mechanics of Tecmo's arcade Ninja Gaiden with unauthorized Dragon Ball-inspired imagery. Players move through platform-filled action stages, battling enemies at close quarters with attacks drawn from the earlier game's design. Familiar-looking anime characters and conspicuously reworked graphics replace Ninja Gaiden's original visual identity.

Its historical interest comes less from innovative mechanics than from this unusually blatant adaptation of both a popular arcade game and a major anime franchise. It is an example of the unlicensed and heavily derivative games that circulated in parts of the Korean arcade market.

games.title: Dragon Buster
games.description:
Namco's Dragon Buster, developed in 1984 and released in Japanese arcades in early 1985, is an early blend of side-view platform action and fantasy dungeon exploration. The hero Clovis crosses a branching map in pursuit of Princess Celia, entering caves, castles, and other monster-filled areas on the way to the dreaded Dragon Mountain. Within each location he swings a sword at enemies, leaps over obstacles, and defeats imposing guardians, sometimes using magic items collected along the journey.

A particularly distinctive feature is Clovis's ability to jump again while in midair, an early example of the double jump in arcade platforming. Routes through the world map provide an element of choice, and the combination of swordplay, spells, health management, and boss encounters makes the game feel more adventurous than a typical one-screen action title.

Dragon Buster helped establish the action-RPG vocabulary that would become familiar later in the 1980s. Its fantasy atmosphere, sprawling stage structure, and fluid airborne combat gave Namco an important bridge between traditional arcade platformers and larger exploratory action games.

games.title: Dragon Master
games.description: Dragon Master is a 1994 arcade fighting game by the Korean company Unico, created during the worldwide surge of interest in one-on-one combat games after Street Fighter II. It offers eight selectable fighters and three boss opponents, each distinguished by martial-arts attacks and special moves. Players face a succession of side-view duels, managing spacing and timing against both human and computer-controlled rivals. Its regional origins and relatively small distribution make it an interesting example of the many independent fighting games that emerged outside Japan's dominant studios.

games.title: Dragon Unit / Castle of Dragon
games.description:
Dragon Unit, also released as Castle of Dragon, is a 1989 fantasy action game developed by Athena and distributed on Seta-related arcade hardware. One or two players control armored knights crossing dangerous landscapes to rescue a princess from a dragon. Side-scrolling combat combines sword strikes, jumping, and a shield that can block incoming attacks; players can also shift between foreground and background paths to avoid threats or find a safer angle of attack.

The knights acquire temporary enhanced swords and other helpful items while fighting monsters and stage bosses. The combination of defensive positioning, several attack options, and timed stages gives Castle of Dragon a character of its own among late-1980s sword-and-sorcery platform games. The arcade original should not be confused with the substantially redesigned NES version.

games.title: Dragon World
games.description: Dragon World is a 1997 tile-matching arcade puzzle game from IGS, issued in several regional versions under names including Zhong Guo Long. Its board resembles mahjong solitaire, but instead of removing pairs directly, the player selects exposed tiles and transfers them to a holding rack. Three matching tiles disappear; allowing too many unmatched tiles to accumulate fills the rack and ends the attempt. Success therefore depends on choosing the order of removals, anticipating which tiles will become accessible, and conserving limited rack space. Some versions include adult-themed reward pictures between stages.

games.title: Dragon Punch
games.description:
Dynax's Dragon Punch (1989), developed from a game by LOG, is a Japanese mahjong-solitaire puzzle title with adult-themed intermissions, not a boxing simulator despite its name. Players remove matching mahjong tiles from a crowded arrangement in a game related to the Shisen-sho style of tile-matching. A comic on-screen figure reacts to successful matches while the player works to clear the layout.

Its overseas counterpart Sports Match replaces the traditional mahjong symbols with sports-themed tile pictures and changes the background and attendant character, presenting a more general-audience version of essentially the same puzzle design. The contrast between these two appearances makes Dragon Punch an illuminating example of how Japanese adult puzzle games were repackaged for export.

games.title: Dragon World II
games.description: Dragon World II is a 1997 IGS arcade mahjong-solitaire puzzle released for the company's PGM cartridge system. Players select accessible tiles from a board and transfer them into a limited rack; collecting three identical tiles eliminates the set. Selecting poorly can clog the rack before the board is cleared, so success depends on reading the layout and planning several moves ahead. Known in China as Zhongguo Long II and in Japan as Chuugokuryuu II, it expands the line of accessible but increasingly intricate triple-matching tile puzzles.

games.title: Dragon World 3 / Zhongguo Long 3 / Dungfong Zi Zyu 3 / Chuugokuryuu 3 Special

variants.title: Dragon World 3 / Zhongguo Long 3 / Dungfong Zi Zyu 3 / Chuugokuryuu 3 Special (ver. 106)

games.description: Dragon World 3, also known as Zhongguo Long 3 and Chuugokuryuu 3 Special, continues IGS's series of mahjong-inspired puzzle games on PGM hardware in 1998. The familiar objective is to clear a layout by selecting available tiles and collecting three of the same design in a temporary holding area. Because rack space is limited, apparently simple matches can close off more valuable combinations later. The game preserves the series' emphasis on careful tile order rather than the direct hand-building rules of competitive mahjong, and circulated under several regional names.

games.title: Dribbling
games.description:
Dribbling is a 1983 Italian arcade soccer game by Model Racing, designed by Lanfranco Chinea. Two players compete on an overhead pitch with seven-man teams, but the unusual cabinet controls owe more to table football than to later joystick-driven soccer games. Separate handles direct the attacking and defending players, while shooting is triggered with buttons; the goalkeeper is handled automatically. The result is a fast contest of positioning, possession, and timing with a distinctly physical control scheme.

The game was also licensed to Olympia and Zaccaria, and its design was associated with European patent EP0071690. Its combination of an electronic soccer field and table-football-style operation makes it a revealing experiment in how arcade manufacturers tried to translate familiar physical sports into video games.

games.title: Drift Out '94 - The Hard Order
games.description:
Drift Out '94: The Hard Order is Visco's 1994 continuation of its overhead arcade rally series. Drivers tackle winding courses viewed from above, steering through tight corners and trying to maintain speed without sliding off the ideal racing line. The compact view makes approaching bends easy to see but puts a premium on judging their severity and controlling the car's drift.

The game builds on the accessible, arcade-oriented handling of the original Drift Out, concentrating the appeal of rally racing into short, demanding stages rather than a realistic driving simulation. It remains a lesser-known entry in the wave of specialized overhead racing games that appeared before fully textured 3D racers dominated arcades.

games.title: Drift Out
games.description:
Visco's Drift Out (1991) is an overhead rally-driving game that challenges players to race through twisting courses rather than around a conventional enclosed circuit. The car is viewed from above, and the action focuses on negotiating corners cleanly, keeping momentum on narrow roads, and racing against the clock. A joystick handles steering while a button supplies acceleration, providing simple controls but surprisingly demanding precision.

The game appeared during a period when arcade racing was experimenting with views other than the familiar chase camera. Its emphasis on controlled sliding and compact rally stages later continued in Drift Out '94 and Visco's Neo Geo racer Neo Drift Out.

games.title: Driver's Edge
games.description:
Driver's Edge is a 1994 Formula One-style arcade racing game developed by Incredible Technologies and published by Strata. It puts the player in a high-speed competition against computer-controlled racing cars, with track positioning and clean cornering determining whether a lap gains or loses valuable time. Its polygonal 3D presentation belongs to the transitional generation of American arcade racers that followed the industry's move away from sprite-scaling road effects.

Although far less familiar than Daytona USA or Ridge Racer, Driver's Edge shows an American developer exploring the same era's appetite for immersive, dedicated driving cabinets and real-time 3D racing.

games.title: Driver's Eyes
games.description:
Namco's Driver's Eyes is an ambitious Formula One arcade simulator from the early 1990s, commonly dated to 1991, built on the company's polygon-based System 21 technology. Its most dramatic feature is a three-monitor panoramic display surrounding a cockpit with a steering wheel and racing instrumentation. Players choose a difficulty level and either easy or technical driving before competing from a driver's-eye perspective on a demanding circuit.

The presentation emphasizes the sensation of sitting inside a Formula One car: the camera stays at cockpit height, the broad field of view makes nearby rivals and corners more visible, and the controls require committed braking and steering. Rather than chasing a simple top speed on a straight line, drivers must manage lap consistency and avoid mistakes. A descendant of Namco's pioneering Winning Run, Driver's Eyes is remembered for its imposing cabinet and unusually elaborate attempt to bring a full racing cockpit to the arcade.

games.title: Driving Force
games.description:
Driving Force is a 1984 arcade road racer built around a behind-the-car view and a strict time limit. The player drives through changing conditions that include ordinary daylight, snow, fog, and nighttime, avoiding traffic while trying to reach checkpoints before the clock expires. Overtaking cars earns bonus points, and the distance traveled contributes to the final score.

The game circulated in several conversion configurations, including versions adapted to Pac-Man and Galaxian-derived hardware. Those board conversions are historically interesting because they brought a chase-view racing game to equipment originally built for very different genres, reflecting the arcade industry's busy conversion-kit market.

games.title: Vs. Dr. Mario
games.description:
Vs. Dr. Mario is Nintendo's 1990 competitive arcade edition of the familiar capsule-matching puzzle game. Mario drops two-colored capsules into a medicine bottle inhabited by stationary red, yellow, and blue viruses. Players move and rotate the falling capsules, trying to align groups of four or more identical colors so that both capsules and viruses disappear. Clearing every virus wins the round, but poor placement quickly fills the bottle and leaves no room to recover.

The two-player format turns careful organization into direct rivalry, with strong clearing sequences disrupting an opponent's field. It carries over the elegant strategy of the home-console Dr. Mario while adapting the game to the short, competitive rhythm of Nintendo's Vs. arcade system. Its seemingly simple premise rewards advance planning, efficient color placement, and awareness of the next capsule.

games.title: Dr. Micro
games.description:
Sanritsu's Dr. Micro (1983) is an inventive early platform game that mixes several kinds of action within a short, screen-by-screen adventure. The player confronts a mad scientist's inventions, first crossing a room of moving pillars while shooting enemies, then controlling a floating ball through another chamber. Later challenges change the hazards and movement rules again, making the game more varied than its modest graphics suggest.

Running on hardware related to Pac-Man, Dr. Micro is a good example of developers stretching familiar circuit boards into new genres. Its constantly changing mini-adventures, shifting modes of movement, and whimsical laboratory setting give it a personality distinct from simpler early arcade platformers.

games.title: Dr. Tomy
games.description:
Dr. Tomy is a 1993 adult-themed puzzle game by Playmark that closely imitates Nintendo's Dr. Mario. Colored, two-part pills descend into a bottle containing viruses, and players rotate and arrange them to create lines of four matching colors. Successful matches remove the pills and viruses, with the goal of clearing each board before the playfield becomes obstructed.

Progression reveals increasingly undressed pictures of women, replacing Dr. Mario's family-friendly presentation with the adult-reward structure found in many European and Japanese arcade puzzle games of the period. One of the depicted characters is an unauthorized version of Chun-Li, another example of the game's reliance on familiar popular imagery.

games.title: Dr. Toppel's Adventure
games.description:
Dr. Toppel's Adventure is a whimsical vertically scrolling shooter developed by Kaneko and published by Taito, bearing a 1987 copyright and reaching some markets in 1988. Players control a small green flying creature through colorful fantasy landscapes filled with insects, aquatic monsters, and bizarre mechanical threats. The game follows the classic shoot-'em-up pattern of dodging hostile formations, attacking ground or airborne targets, and defeating an oversized boss at the end of each stage.

Its cheerful, cartoon-like creatures and strange scenery contrast with the military themes common in late-1980s shooters. The Japanese title, Dr. Toppel's Tankentai, means roughly Dr. Toppel's Expedition, matching the game's playful sense of exploring an eccentric world.

games.title: Dragon Saber
games.description:
Dragon Saber (1990) is Namco's fantasy-themed vertical shooter and a direct sequel to Dragon Spirit. The blue dragon Huey and red dragon Siria can be controlled together by two players, traveling through spectacular landscapes to confront demonic creatures and enormous bosses. Like its predecessor, the game separates attacks against airborne enemies from those directed toward the ground, requiring constant attention to two layers of danger.

A major addition is the ability to build up a stronger flame attack by withholding fire and then releasing it, adding a risk-and-reward decision to the familiar dragon-shooting formula. Power-ups enhance the dragons' heads and attacks, while the detailed System 2 graphics give the stages greater scale and dramatic variety. Dragon Saber is a particularly attractive evolution of Namco's unusual fantasy answer to Xevious.

games.title: Deathsmiles MegaBlack Label

variants.title: Deathsmiles MegaBlack Label (2008/10/06 MEGABLACK LABEL VER)

games.description:
Deathsmiles Mega Black Label is Cave's enhanced 2008 edition of its gothic horizontal bullet-hell shooter Deathsmiles. Players guide young witches through the monster-infested kingdom of Gilverado, firing toward enemies on either side while using a small familiar and a timed power-up mode to manage dense projectile patterns. The unusual side-view action and stage-selection structure distinguish the series from Cave's more familiar vertical shooters.

Mega Black Label is a substantial revision rather than a simple difficulty adjustment. It adds Sakura as a fifth playable character, an extra Ice Palace stage, and a punishing Level 999 setting. The item threshold for entering power-up mode is reduced, opening new scoring strategies, while players who survive the most extreme course without continuing can encounter the hidden boss Bloody Jitterbug. Produced in comparatively small quantities, this edition became a coveted challenge for experienced Cave players.

games.title: Dream Soccer '94
games.description:
Dream Soccer '94 is Irem's arcade soccer game released during the 1994 FIFA World Cup, with Data East distributing certain versions. Players choose national teams and compete in quick, overhead-view matches built for direct joystick-and-button play. The arcade progression emphasizes defeating successive opponents rather than running a complete league simulation, and the game supports multiplayer competition.

Regional releases used different Irem boards, including the M92 and M107 systems. Its exaggerated, immediately accessible approach fits the early-1990s preference for fast sports action with little time spent configuring a match, making it a compact arcade alternative to contemporary home-console football games.

games.title: Dragon Spirit
games.description:
Namco's Dragon Spirit (1987) is a vertically scrolling fantasy shooter that replaces the usual aircraft with Amul, a warrior transformed into a blue dragon. His mission is to rescue Princess Alicia from the demon Zawell across nine environments packed with prehistoric beasts, strange insects, and mythical monsters. Much like Namco's earlier Xevious, the controls distinguish air-to-air fire from attacks on ground targets, forcing the player to watch two different levels of the battlefield.

Power-ups can give Amul extra heads, greater firepower, and other temporary advantages, while a limited damage capacity makes careful maneuvering essential. The stages introduce striking changes of scenery, from volcanic regions to nightmarish organic landscapes, and culminate in huge boss encounters.

Dragon Spirit was one of the most recognizable fantasy-themed arcade shooters of its period, noted for its imaginative monster designs and memorable music. Its unusual pairing of dragon mythology with the established vertical shooter formula proved durable enough to inspire the cooperative sequel Dragon Saber in 1990.

games.title: Darkstalkers: The Night Warriors
games.description:
Darkstalkers: The Night Warriors, released by Capcom in 1994 and called Vampire: The Night Warriors in Japan, gave the CPS-2 fighting-game platform an unusually vivid supernatural cast. Rather than another martial-arts tournament of ordinary people, it pits monsters drawn from horror and folklore against one another: Morrigan the succubus, Demitri the vampire, Felicia the catwoman, Victor the Frankenstein-like giant, and other bizarre contenders. The alien menace Pyron provides the central threat.

Underneath its colorful monster designs is a fast, technically ambitious fighting system with chainable normal attacks, special moves, aerial defense, and enhanced attacks fueled by a special meter. Each character animates with elastic, cartoon-like transformations that would be impossible in a conventional realistic fighter, helping the action feel as distinctive as the roster.

Darkstalkers established one of Capcom's most beloved fighting-game series and introduced characters who became popular far beyond the original arcades. Its sophisticated pixel animation and willingness to use comic horror instead of another Street Fighter-style setting made it an important showcase for the CPS-2 hardware.

games.title: Diet Family
games.description: Diet Family is an eccentric 2001 vertical shooter in which players choose from five cartoon characters and battle waves of food-themed targets. The comic premise turns eating and weight gain into shooting-game hazards: the object is to destroy the incoming food and survive the scrolling stages rather than collect it. Its deliberately silly subject matter and unconventional playable cast set it apart from the spaceships, soldiers, and fantasy heroes typical of the genre.

games.title: Vs. Duck Hunt
games.description:
Vs. Duck Hunt is Nintendo's 1985 arcade adaptation of the light-gun hunting game, using the company's Vs. system and an optical gun. On a quiet marshland screen, a dog flushes ducks into flight and the player has only a few shots to hit them before they escape. Later rounds demand quicker aim and greater accuracy, while the dog's teasing reactions give the simple shooting contest its unmistakable personality.

The familiar duck-hunting action sits alongside clay-target shooting in the wider Duck Hunt design, with moving targets that reward anticipation rather than continuous firing. The arcade version brings one of the NES's signature light-gun experiences back into coin-operated competition, where its short rounds and increasing hit requirements are naturally suited to quick play.

games.title: Dungeon Magic
games.description:
Dungeon Magic, titled Light Bringer in Japan, is Taito's 1993 fantasy beat-'em-up on F3 hardware, notable for its isometric perspective and unusually adventurous structure. Up to four players choose between Ash the knight, Gren the martial artist, Cisty the elven archer, and Vold the wizard, each with different weapons and fighting styles. The party battles monsters across towns, dungeons, and castles while attempting to rescue a princess and defeat an evil magician.

Unlike most straight-line arcade brawlers, the game offers branching routes, hidden rooms, environmental puzzles, and treasure that rewards exploration. Characters can gain experience, strengthen charged attacks, collect equipment, and recover health with food, making their progression feel closer to a compact action RPG than a simple sequence of fights.

Dungeon Magic is one of Taito's most distinctive multiplayer arcade adventures. Its combination of cooperative combat, secret passages, detailed hand-drawn scenery, and limited role-playing mechanics makes it an intriguing companion to Capcom's contemporary Dungeons & Dragons arcade games.

games.title: Dunk Mania
games.description:
Dunk Mania is Namco's 1995 two-on-two arcade basketball game, created around spectacular slam dunks rather than detailed league simulation. Players compete from a sideline view, dribbling, passing, blocking, and driving toward the basket. Successful dunks trigger dramatic replay angles that showcase the game's motion-captured animation, turning each score into a miniature highlight reel.

The game uses fictional American-city teams rather than licensed NBA rosters, with simplified possessions that restart near midcourt after a basket. Its emphasis on quick attacks, physical defense, and theatrical finishing moves places it firmly in the arcade-sports tradition.

games.title: Dunk Shot
games.description:
Sega's Dunk Shot, copyrighted 1986 and released in Japanese arcades in January 1987, is an overhead basketball game for as many as four simultaneous players. Its most distinctive feature is the use of trackballs to move the athletes, accompanied by two buttons for basketball actions. The control scheme makes acceleration and direction changes immediately physical, while the top-down view reveals passing lanes and open space across the court.

In a single-player game, the team begins behind the computer in points and must overturn the deficit before time expires. Approaching the basket and shooting can produce a dramatic slam dunk, bringing an arcade flourish to the relatively simple match. Built for Sega System 16B hardware, Dunk Shot is an unusual, energetic experiment in multiplayer basketball controls.

games.title: Dwarfs Den
games.description:
Dwarfs Den is a 1981 Electro-Sport gambling game preserved under the more revealing title Draw Poker III / Dwarfs Den. Its principal activity is draw-poker play, with a distinctive dwarf-themed graphic set replacing more conventional card imagery in one version. Another surviving ROM set instead displays card graphics, confirming that the decoration could change while the underlying poker machine remained related.

The machine uses an Intel 8085-family processor and an unusual CRT-controller arrangement. The twin graphics versions are an excellent example of the way early casino videogames were reskinned or sold in visually distinct cabinets without becoming entirely new games.

games.title: Dyger
games.description:
Dyger is a 1989 Korean vertically scrolling shooter that casts the player as a lone female pilot fighting an alien invasion of Earth. Its unusually elaborate science-fiction backstory involves a catastrophic military accident, cryogenic suspension, and the heroine awakening decades later to face a new threat. On screen, the action follows a traditional vertical shooter format: a small craft moves through enemy formations and heavily defended territory, firing at approaching targets while dodging attacks.

The contrast between its melodramatic narrative and compact arcade shooting makes Dyger a curiosity among Korean late-1980s releases, when local developers were beginning to produce original games in genres dominated by Japanese manufacturers.

games.title: Dynablaster / Bomber Man
games.description:
Dynablaster, also known as Bomber Man or Atomic Punk in different markets, is a 1991 arcade installment of Hudson Soft's celebrated Bomberman series, developed for Irem hardware. Players guide small robot heroes around single-screen mazes, dropping bombs that explode in cross-shaped blasts. The objective is to eliminate enemies without being caught in one's own explosions; destructible blocks open new routes and reveal helpful power-ups, including greater bomb capacity and longer blast range.

The arcade story follows Bomberman as he challenges King Bomber and his minions, with cooperative play allowing two participants to clear stages together. Timing explosions, manipulating enemy paths, and choosing safe escape routes create a mixture of action and spatial puzzle-solving that made Bomberman so enduring.

Its international titles reflect the complicated history of the franchise's branding, but the underlying game remains instantly recognizable. The coin-op release brought Bomberman's maze-bombing formula into arcades at a time when the series was becoming a major multiplayer fixture on home systems.

games.title: Dynamic Dice
games.description: Dynamic Dice is an obscure early-1980s electronic dice-gambling game whose circuit board survived without a clearly identified manufacturer. It has a button-operated casino interface rather than an action-game joystick, and period emulation notes place it near other compact gambling programs, including craps-themed titles. The original board recovered for emulation was reportedly old, corroded and nonfunctional, which helps explain the limited documentation of its precise betting options and payout rules.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.
Original developer and publisher are not established.

games.title: Dyna Gear
games.description:
Dyna Gear: An Action Adventure on the Era of Dinosaur is a 1993 side-scrolling action-platform game from Sammy. A time-travel accident brings the hero Roger and his adversary Gustaf to a prehistoric world, where dinosaurs and strange creatures become part of a fast-moving rescue adventure. Players can choose Roger or the animal-like Wolf and fight through varied environments using swords, flails, bows, and other weapons.

The game mixes jumping and ranged combat with close-range attacks, oversized enemies, and colorful fantasy scenery rather than following a strictly military run-and-gun formula. Its two-player action, animated dinosaur opponents, and changeable weapons make it an appealing lesser-known alternative to the era's more famous action-platform games.

games.title: Dynamic Ski
games.description:
Dynamic Ski is a 1984 winter-sports arcade game developed by Taiyo System and published by Nichibutsu. It combines ski-jumping events with slalom and downhill challenges rather than restricting the player to one kind of run. The jumping events demand a controlled approach and accurate timing at takeoff, while the downhill courses require steering through gates, avoiding trees and rocks, and maintaining speed.

The succession of disciplines gives the compact arcade game a varied sporting structure. Instead of racing a rival on a common screen, players are primarily judged on the precision and quality of individual performances, with higher scores and faster runs rewarding practice.

games.title: Dynamic Shoot Kyousou
games.description:
Dynamic Shoot Kyousou, also called Dynamic Shooting, is Jaleco's 1988 soccer-themed arcade action game. Instead of controlling an entire team through a full match, players concentrate on an attacking striker, advancing past defenders and trying to beat the goalkeeper with a well-timed shot. The selection of four international football-star likenesses, including figures associated with Maradona, Platini, and Gullit, gives the game an unmistakable late-1980s sporting flavor.

Its focused run-and-shoot structure makes it closer to a soccer skills challenge than to a conventional eleven-a-side football simulation, emphasizing quick reactions and scoring opportunities.

games.title: Dynamite Duke
games.description:
Dynamite Duke (1989) is a Seibu Kaihatsu shooting game that combines the behind-the-character gallery combat of Cabal with occasional close-range brawling. Players control a heavily armed soldier with a powerful cybernetic arm, advancing against a mad scientist's military forces. The hero moves across the foreground of each combat screen, firing into enemy soldiers, vehicles, and installations while dodging incoming attacks.

The mechanical arm gives Duke an identity beyond an ordinary gunner, with powerful punches used when opponents reach close quarters. Across nine arcade stages, large enemy encounters and military set pieces alternate with aggressive gunfire. The game was also released under the name The Double Dynamites in certain territories, and later received home-console conversions.

Its blend of shooting-gallery action and hand-to-hand attacks makes it a distinctive branch of Seibu's late-1980s output, sitting between the studio's earlier crime-themed shooters and its more elaborate later action games.

games.title: Dyno Bop
games.description:
Dyno Bop is a 1990 video redemption game from Grand Products, with software created by Incredible Technologies. Players physically roll hard plastic balls into the machine, trying to strike animated dinosaurs and their eggs on the screen. An infrared tracking system measures the trajectory of each real ball and recreates its movement as a virtual projectile, with successful hits contributing to a ticket-awarding score.

The technology was also used in Slick Shot and Super Strike Bowling. This combination of actual rolling balls, optical motion sensing, and video targets makes Dyno Bop a particularly distinctive hybrid of arcade video gaming and traditional redemption amusement.

games.title: Dynasty Wars
games.description:
Capcom's Dynasty Wars (1989), known in Japan as Tenchi wo Kurau, is a side-scrolling horseback combat game inspired by the historical fiction of Romance of the Three Kingdoms. One or two players choose from four Chinese warriors and ride into battle against rebel armies during the collapse of the Han dynasty. Unlike a typical belt-scrolling beat-'em-up, the action constantly advances to the right, with mounted fighters striking enemies using long weapons and special attacks.

The cavalry theme gives the game its unusual rhythm. Players must judge the range of their weapons, attack foes approaching from either direction, and survive massed troops before confronting enemy commanders at the end of each stage. Magical attacks provide a way to break out of particularly dangerous encounters.

Dynasty Wars was an early example of Capcom's interest in adapting East Asian historical epics to the arcade action format. It was followed by Warriors of Fate, which transformed the same setting into a more conventional and elaborate multiplayer brawler.

games.title: Eagle Shot Golf
games.description:
Eagle Shot Golf is a 1994 arcade golf game from American Sammy. Players select among golfers with different strengths, choose a club, and play rounds on courses arranged around beginner, amateur, and professional difficulty levels. Up to four people can participate in turn, lining up shots and judging their power and direction before addressing the next lie.

The game emphasizes the familiar rhythm of selecting a club, measuring a swing, and managing the course rather than turning golf into a simple target shooter. Its arcade cabinet format makes each hole a short contest of placement and precision.

games.title: U.N. Defense Force: Earth Joker
games.description:
U.N. Defense Force: Earth Joker is a 1993 vertically scrolling shooter by Visco in which players choose among four pilots and their aircraft to defend Earth from hostile forces. Each ship has its own offensive characteristics, encouraging different approaches to dense enemy formations and large mechanical bosses. Holding the fire button charges a stronger shot, creating a tradeoff between sustained ordinary fire and timing a powerful attack.

With its military aircraft, dramatic boss encounters, and challenging projectile patterns, Earth Joker fits the tradition of Japanese vertical shooters while retaining a distinctive selection of pilots and charged weapons. It is a relatively obscure but accomplished example of Visco's work outside its better-known racing and Neo Geo releases.

games.title: Extra Bases
games.description:
Midway's Extra Bases (1980) is an early arcade baseball simulation operated with a trackball and a button. Each credit buys a brief baseball contest in which the player alternates between batting and fielding, either against the computer or a second participant. At bat, timing the swing determines whether the ball can be put into play; in the field, the controls allow the player to respond to the hit and try to retire runners.

The restrained graphics and innings-based coin structure reflect the period when arcade sports games still borrowed heavily from tabletop and electromechanical amusements. Extra Bases is notable for using a trackball to add physical precision to a familiar sport.

games.title: Emergency Call Ambulance
games.description:
Sega's Emergency Call Ambulance (1999) is an unusual emergency-driving arcade game that replaces competitive racing with the urgent task of saving injured people. Players drive an ambulance through the streets of Chicago, steering with a wheel, managing the accelerator and brakes, and choosing either automatic or manual transmission. Each mission begins at an emergency scene and becomes a tense journey to the hospital.

The central mechanic is the patient's condition: a health indicator falls as time passes and can worsen after collisions or rough driving. Reaching the emergency room quickly is important, but reckless shortcuts can be disastrous. Different calls introduce more difficult routes and pressure, giving the game a surprisingly dramatic structure.

Built around realistic-feeling dedicated driving controls, Emergency Call Ambulance stands out in Sega's arcade catalog because speed is a means to an altruistic objective, not a race against another driver. Its mixture of route memorization, careful driving, and urgent time management creates a distinctive high-pressure experience.

games.title: Eco Fighters
games.description:
Eco Fighters, released by Capcom in 1993 and known in Japan as Ultimate Ecology, is a colorful horizontal scrolling shooter with a pointed environmental theme. Players pilot small craft against the pollution-spewing machinery of the Goyolk corporation, encountering junk-filled factories, mechanical monsters, and enormous industrial bosses. Its cheerful graphics contrast with a surprisingly demanding stream of incoming fire.

The signature feature is an independently rotating weapon mounted to the ship. Players can aim it around the craft, firing backward or upward while moving in another direction. This adds a major tactical dimension to positioning and transforms encounters that would be routine in a forward-firing shooter. Different weapon upgrades invite experimentation as the stages introduce new firing angles and hazards.

Capcom developed the concept from a game-design contest idea, giving Eco Fighters a distinctive origin as well as a distinctive control scheme. Its imaginative industrial enemies and 360-degree attack mechanic make it one of the more memorable late CPS-2 shooting games.

games.title: E.D.F. : Earth Defense Force
games.description:
E.D.F.: Earth Defense Force is Jaleco's 1991 horizontal shooter, in which a lone advanced fighter battles an alien armada across a succession of heavily defended stages. Players choose between different weapon types and navigate dense formations of enemy craft, ground installations, and large bosses. A shield system lets the ship survive several hits, changing the usual one-mistake-and-you-die rhythm of the genre.

Weapon experience accumulates during play, allowing the chosen armaments to become more powerful over time. Surviving and keeping the right weapon for a given stage therefore becomes part of the challenge. Although often overshadowed by contemporary Konami and Irem shooters, E.D.F. has its own identity through its upgradeable weapons, sturdy defensive system, and detailed mechanical opponents.

games.title: The Cliffhanger - Edward Randy
games.description:
The Cliffhanger: Edward Randy is Data East's spectacular early-1990s cinematic action game, released with a 1990 copyright. Inspired by pulp serials and adventure films, it stars Edward Randy as he battles an army of soldiers in pursuit of a kidnapped woman and a mysterious prism stone. The story unfolds through seven stages filled with dramatic chases, collapsing scenery, and enormous mechanical set pieces.

The action combines platform fighting with grappling and whip-like attacks, while some sections shift into vehicle sequences and perspective tricks that create the illusion of a moving camera. Enemies frequently attack from unexpected angles, and bosses feel like the climax of elaborate movie scenes rather than isolated combat arenas.

Edward Randy is particularly celebrated for its aggressive use of Data East's sprite and scrolling hardware to imitate cinematic motion. Its inventive transitions and blockbuster pacing make it a cult favorite for players who appreciate ambitious arcade spectacle.

games.title: Eeekk!
games.description: Eeekk! is a 1983 single-screen arcade platform/action game produced by Epos Corporation and developed by Shinkai. Players maneuver through compact stages while dealing with moving threats, using an eight-way joystick and two buttons. Its character-based, vertically oriented playfield distinguishes it from Epos's more familiar shoot-'em-up conversions. An additional preserved version was adapted to run on Pac-Man-derived arcade hardware, illustrating the early-1980s business of repurposing existing cabinets rather than building new machines for every game.

games.title: Egg Hunt
games.description: Egg Hunt is a 1995 puzzle game from Invi Image, an obscure Korean arcade developer. It is a two-player-capable, vertically arranged drop-style puzzle game presented on a horizontal monitor, using an eight-way joystick and two buttons for each participant. The title is also cataloged among mature-themed puzzle machines, a small but widespread corner of the 1990s arcade market. Its dual-Z80 hardware and OKI sound chip are notably modest for a game released well into the 32-bit era.

games.title: Eggor
games.description:
Eggor is a 1983 maze shooter released by Telko, built on Pac-Man-derived arcade hardware and closely related in design to the earlier game Eyes. The player controls a young vulture moving through a sequence of mazes and shooting eggs scattered around the passages. Five adult vultures pursue the hero, while the player can temporarily remove threats by shooting at them. The challenge is to clear the eggs efficiently before being trapped in a narrow corridor.

The combination of four-way maze movement and directional firing changes the familiar Pac-Man formula: pursuers are not merely obstacles to evade, because they can also be pushed back with carefully placed shots. Its unusual bird-and-egg theme gives an otherwise demanding chase game a playful twist.

games.title: Egg Venture
games.description:
Egg Venture is a 1997 arcade light-gun game produced through a collaboration involving The Game Room and Innovative Concepts in Entertainment. Its animated targets are deliberately non-threatening: players shoot villainous eggs and other 'bad' figures while avoiding friendly eggs that must be left unharmed. Rounds unfold as a sequence of cartoon shooting galleries with different arrangements of moving targets.

Unlike many 1990s gun games built around soldiers or horror, Egg Venture aims at a broad family audience, rewarding fast aiming and restraint rather than simply firing at everything. Its variety of stages and the different editions released by the participating amusement companies make it a distinctive late-period shooting-gallery game.

games.title: Egg Venture Deluxe
games.description:
Egg Venture Deluxe is The Game Room's revised 1997 edition of Egg Venture, the cartoon light-gun shooting game built around good and bad anthropomorphic eggs. Players shoot hostile targets while protecting friendly characters in missions that include target practice, underwater rescues, and other playful scenarios. Fast aiming matters, but firing indiscriminately can harm the very eggs the player is supposed to defend.

Unlike the original game's day-by-day sequence of challenges, the Deluxe edition follows an egg traveling around the world and visiting recognizable landmarks. Most missions remain related to those in the original, but this version fixes reported glitches and adds a proper ending instead of simply escalating in difficulty indefinitely. It is therefore a meaningful revised edition, not merely a cabinet-name variation.

games.title: Ehrgeiz
games.description:
Ehrgeiz: God Bless the Ring is a 1998 three-dimensional fighting game developed by DreamFactory in collaboration with Square and published by Namco for System 12 arcade hardware. Its fighters move freely around the arena rather than remaining locked onto a strict left-right fighting line, using strikes, throws, and interactive environments to outmaneuver opponents. The international title is a German word meaning ambition, appropriately matching a tournament whose prize is a mysterious legendary sword.

The game also became famous for featuring Cloud Strife and Tifa Lockhart from Final Fantasy VII in its original arcade roster, bringing role-playing characters into a very different type of combat. Rather than imitating the reigning 2D tournament formula, Ehrgeiz explores more spatial, arena-oriented fighting, with elevation and positioning playing important roles.

The PlayStation adaptation expanded its reputation beyond arcades and introduced additional material, but the original coin-op game remains an unusual meeting of Namco arcade technology, DreamFactory's combat design, and Square's character universe.

games.title: Eight Forces
games.description: Eight Forces is a 1994 vertically scrolling shooter by Tecmo, built around a choice of four different fighter aircraft. Each craft gives the player a distinct way to attack the waves of aerial enemies and large bosses appearing from the top of the screen. The game follows the traditional arcade shooter emphasis on quick movement, route learning, and avoiding concentrated enemy fire. Its straightforward military presentation and small release profile make it a comparatively obscure entry in the crowded early-1990s vertical shooter genre.

games.title: Eight Man
games.description:
Eight Man is a 1991 Neo Geo side-scrolling action game developed by Pallas and published by SNK, based on the classic Japanese cyborg superhero 8 Man. One or two players control 8 Man and his ally 9 Man through futuristic stages filled with hostile robots and mechanical defenses. Unlike the belt-scrolling brawlers popular at the time, movement is primarily left and right, with jumping, punches, and character-specific special attacks used to break through each wave of enemies.

The game is especially remembered for its high-speed running sequences, when the heroes rush forward at spectacular speed while enemies and obstacles stream past. Large bosses, sharply defined Neo Geo sprites, and the science-fiction character designs give it the feel of an animated superhero adventure. Its adaptation of a vintage manga and anime property also makes it one of the more unusual licensed titles in the early Neo Geo catalog.

games.title: Extra Inning / Ball Park II
games.description: Extra Inning, also released as Ball Park II, is Midway's 1978 baseball game and a follow-up or revised presentation of the company's earlier Double Play. Two competitors take turns batting and pitching through a simplified game represented by small stick-figure players. The pitcher chooses deliveries and directs fielders, while the batter tries to time a swing and put the ball into play. Its compact innings structure and direct head-to-head controls reflect the early arcade era's attempt to recreate popular tabletop and sporting contests with minimal graphics.

games.title: E-Jan High School
games.description: E-Jan High School is a 1996 Japanese mahjong arcade game produced by Seibu Kaihatsu. Its school-themed presentation places conventional competitive mahjong in the context of the adult-oriented Japanese arcade market. Play uses the specialized mahjong controls typical of the genre rather than a standard action-game joystick, with the player choosing tile actions and working toward a winning hand. Detailed stage-specific rules and character events are not reliably documented, so its identifiable features are its mahjong format, theme, and mid-1990s arcade origin.

games.title: Ejihon Tantei Jimusyo
games.description:
Ejihon Tantei Jimusyo, or Ejihon Detective Agency, is a 1995 Japanese visual puzzle game released by Sega for the Saturn-derived ST-V arcade system. Rather than relying on reflex-based combat, it asks players to search busy illustrated screens and identify small visual differences or irregularities. The detective-agency framing turns each puzzle into an exercise in observation and careful inspection.

The game is distinguished by its heavy use of Japanese written characters and visual wordplay, making it much more language-dependent than most arcade puzzle titles. Its quirky detective theme and detailed illustrated scenes place it alongside Sega's unusual 1990s experiments with short, accessible puzzle challenges.

games.title: Touryuu Densetsu Elan-Doree / Elan Doree - Legend of Dragoon

variants.title: Touryuu Densetsu Elan-Doree / Elan Doree - Legend of Dragoon (JUET 980922 V1.006)

games.description:
Touryuu Densetsu Elan Doree, also known as Elan Doree: Legend of Dragoon, is a 1998 Japanese fighting game by Sai-Mate for Sega's ST-V arcade system. The fighters do not simply stand on a floor exchanging punches: they ride flying dragons, dueling in fantasy arenas with physical strikes and magical attacks. Combat primarily follows a two-dimensional fighting plane, but the mounts also allow movement through three-dimensional space, creating a very different feeling from conventional tournament fighters.

A combatant can be knocked off the dragon and left vulnerable, making aerial positioning and control of the mount important to the fight. The unusual dragon-riding premise and elaborate fantasy presentation earned it a cult following, while a later Sega Saturn version preserved the concept for home players.

games.title: The Electric Yo-Yo
games.description:
The Electric Yo-Yo is a 1982 arcade maze game from Taito America, running on hardware related to the company's Qix and Space Dungeon boards. Players guide a small yo-yo-like character around a collection of blocky obstacles, extending its string to collect the dots or blocks needed to clear a round. Enemies move through the playfield and must be avoided, although some pickups provide temporary protection from lesser threats.

The title's unusual visual conceit is also its control idea: the yo-yo reaches out with its string rather than simply walking over every collectible like a conventional maze hero. The need to judge distances and openings makes it a distinctive experiment in post-Pac-Man maze design.

games.title: Elephant Family
games.description:
Elephant Family is an Italian video-slot game produced by C.M.C. in the mid-1990s, with preserved early and later national program sets. It uses a button-controlled gambling interface on horizontally oriented 65C02/AY-3-8910 hardware. The two documented Italian revisions are not completely interchangeable: one lacks a test mode and handles the minimum/maximum bet selection differently.

The game's circuit boards have also been important to emulator preservation because the original color PROMs and protection devices required further study before its graphics could be reproduced faithfully. It represents the highly localized Italian electronic-gambling market of the period.

games.title: Elevator Action
games.description:
Elevator Action (1983) is one of Taito's defining early action games, casting the player as Agent 17, codename Otto, on an espionage mission inside a succession of enemy buildings. Each stage begins on the roof and requires the agent to work downward, entering every red door to collect secret documents before reaching an escape car at street level. Guards patrol the hallways and emerge from doors, forcing Otto to run, duck, leap, and fire his pistol while using elevators and escalators to change floors.

The building itself is the central puzzle. Elevators can provide cover, unexpectedly separate the agent from a pursuer, or leave him exposed to gunfire; elevators and light fixtures can also be manipulated tactically. The objective is not merely to shoot every guard, because missed red doors prevent a successful escape. The combination of route planning, combat, and moving machinery gives the game a pace unlike straightforward platform shooters.

Widely ported to home computers and consoles, Elevator Action became one of Taito's most enduring arcade properties. Its spy-film atmosphere, distinctive red-door objectives, and innovative use of the entire building as a navigable machine led to the elaborate 1994 sequel Elevator Action Returns.

games.title: Eliminator
games.description:
Eliminator is Sega/Gremlin's 1981 vector-graphics space shooter, presented here in its two-player configuration. The players pilot small ships in an enclosed arena, firing at hostile drones while confronting the enormous Eliminator, a mechanical fortress whose vulnerable parts must be destroyed. Movement is free within the field, and enemy collisions and rebounding projectiles demand constant awareness of the arena's boundaries.

A major difference from conventional space shooters is the way struck objects can be pushed around the screen, adding an element of ricochet-based positioning to combat. The game was also produced in more elaborate multiplayer configurations, but the two-player version preserves the central challenge of coordinating attacks against a massive opponent. Its crisp vector lines and unusual arena combat make Eliminator one of Sega's more inventive early science-fiction coin-ops.

games.title: Elevator Action Returns
games.description:
Elevator Action Returns, known in some regions as Elevator Action II, is Taito's 1994 action-packed sequel to the 1983 spy classic. Instead of a lone secret agent descending simple office buildings, players choose among three operatives, Kart Bradfield, Edie Burrett, and Jad the Taff, and infiltrate sprawling terrorist-controlled installations. The mission remains recognizable: enter the marked red doors, complete the required objectives, and reach the exit alive.

The sequel dramatically expands the combat with different character abilities, firearms, grenades, close-range attacks, destructible scenery, and detailed animation. Elevators, lifts, and multi-level buildings still determine movement, but the environments now include industrial machinery, explosions, and far more elaborate enemy encounters. Cooperative play rewards complementary movement and weapon choices.

Running on Taito's F3 hardware, Elevator Action Returns is celebrated for its cinematic pixel art, weighty weapons, and precisely choreographed action. It is both a faithful reinterpretation of the original game's door-and-elevator objectives and a standout mid-1990s run-and-gun title in its own right.

games.title: Embargo
games.description:
Embargo is a 1977 four-player arcade strategy game by Cinematronics, set around a simplified map of Cuba. Each player controls a boat that sails from one corner of the field, laying a continuous line of mines in its wake. Colliding with land, the screen edge, another boat, or a mine destroys the craft, while the surviving players earn points. Computer-controlled boats fill the unused positions when fewer than four people join.

The directional controller and a button allow a player to steer and occasionally leave brief gaps in the mine trail, creating an opportunity to double back through an otherwise blocked route. The challenge is to enclose rivals without trapping oneself. This use of hazardous trails anticipated the territory-blocking competition that later became familiar through light-cycle games.

games.title: Emeraldia
games.description:
Emeraldia is Namco's 1993 arcade puzzle game built around falling blocks and a distinctive two-step matching system. Players arrange groups of colored blocks vertically; lining up three matching pieces cracks them, but a further matching piece is needed to shatter and remove the damaged blocks. This encourages building useful formations in advance rather than merely clearing every three-piece match as soon as it appears.

The game includes Adventure, Normal, and Versus modes, giving it both solo puzzle progression and direct competition. Its friendly presentation disguises a demanding system in which the placement of cracked blocks can help set up a cascade or create a dangerous obstruction. Emeraldia is one of Namco's more inventive contributions to the crowded early-1990s falling-block puzzle field.

games.title: Empire City: 1931
games.description:
Empire City: 1931 is a 1986 shooting-gallery game developed by Seibu Kaihatsu, with this arcade set identified as a bootleg version. Set in Prohibition-era New York, it follows a young man pursuing revenge against the mobsters responsible for his family's murder. Enemies appear in street scenes, windows, and other hiding places, and the player aims a screen cursor with a joystick before firing at exposed gangsters.

Rather than shooting continuously, the game emphasizes noticing enemies, tracking their movements, and reacting before they attack or disappear. The period crime setting and revenge narrative distinguish it from contemporary military target shooters. As a bootleg set, its historical interest includes unauthorized distribution, but no particular change to the original shooting rules should be assumed without further evidence.

games.title: Gundam Wing: Endless Duel

variants.title: Gundam Wing: Endless Duel (SNES bootleg, set 1)
Gundam Wing: Endless Duel (SNES bootleg, set 2)

games.description:
