Gundam Wing: Endless Duel is an unauthorized arcade adaptation of the 1996 Super Famicom fighting game developed by Natsume and published by Bandai. Based on the Mobile Suit Gundam Wing anime, it features one-on-one battles between giant mobile suits, with attacks, special techniques, and character-specific weapons inspired by the television series. Players fight in side-view arenas, using combinations and ranged attacks to overcome opposing machines.

The arcade version is a bootleg conversion of the console title rather than an officially developed new coin-op installment. Its preservation is interesting because it demonstrates how a popular Japan-only licensed console fighter was repackaged for arcade use, retaining the distinctive mecha combat and anime roster of the original game.

games.title: Enduro Racer
games.description:
Sega's Enduro Racer (1986) is a motorcycle racing arcade game built around off-road riding, dangerous obstacles, and dramatic jumps. Viewed from behind the bike, the player speeds through five courses filled with other riders, rocks, logs, and irregular terrain. Unlike an ordinary road-racing game, clearing hazards often requires deliberately lifting the front wheel or hitting a ramp at just the right moment.

The dedicated motorcycle-style controls make the physical act of leaning and pulling up on the handlebars a central part of play. Correctly timed wheelies help the rider cross obstacles, while poorly judged jumps waste speed or result in collisions. The constantly changing terrain turns each course into a succession of quick tactical decisions.

Enduro Racer belongs to Sega's celebrated mid-1980s generation of immersive arcade driving machines, alongside games such as Hang-On and Out Run. Its dirt-bike theme and stunt-oriented handling give it an identity quite different from Sega's smoother tarmac racers.

games.title: Enforce
games.description:
Enforce is a late-1980s Taito 3D tank shooter, built around the spectacle of driving an armored vehicle into hostile territory. Using a forward-looking pseudo-3D view, players steer through battlefields, line up targets, and fire on enemy forces while trying to survive their attacks. The game's visual approach is related to the scaling and perspective techniques used in Taito's contemporary racing games, especially Continental Circus.

Its mixture of combat and vehicle movement gives it a more immersive presentation than a traditional fixed-screen shooting game. Enforce remains a relatively obscure experiment in applying arcade driving technology to a military action scenario.

games.title: Enigma 2
games.description:
Enigma II is a 1981 fixed-screen space shooter associated with Zilec Electronics and Game Plan, also connected with the earlier title Phantoms II. The player commands a spacecraft at the bottom of a vertically oriented screen, firing upward into formations of alien craft and creatures while dodging enemy attacks. Larger hostile vessels, including a mother ship, add variety to the otherwise straightforward wave-based combat.

Its simple controls and familiar space-invasion structure reflect the genre's early years, when designers experimented with new enemy patterns and formations on hardware descended from the original wave of fixed-screen shooters.

games.title: Escape from the Planet of the Robot Monsters

variants.title: Escape from the Planet of the Robot Monsters (set 1)
Escape from the Planet of the Robot Monsters (set 2)

games.description:
Escape from the Planet of the Robot Monsters is Atari Games' 1989 science-fiction action game, presented in the style of a campy 1950s serial. Players control the heroes Jake and Duke as they storm Planet X to rescue Dr. Sarah Bellum and free humans enslaved by the Reptilons. The action is shown from an isometric perspective, with corridors, platforms, conveyor belts, and rooms crowded with dangerous robots.

Using specialized aiming controls, the heroes shoot mechanical enemies while navigating the labyrinthine facilities, rescuing captives, and collecting helpful equipment. Environmental switches, elevators, and sudden ambushes make exploration more involved than simply moving between shooting arenas. Large bosses and deliberately exaggerated pulp imagery give the campaign an amusing B-movie character.

Its combination of isometric movement, dual-player action, distinctive controls, and a tongue-in-cheek title makes it one of Atari's most memorable late-1980s arcade adventures. It also stands out for blending shooting-gallery intensity with a genuine sense of exploring a dangerous mechanical world.

games.title: Equites
games.description:
Equites is a 1984 vertically scrolling shooter from Alpha Denshi, centered on a transformable, jump-capable robot fighting across hostile terrain. The player fires lasers at surface-based enemies while confronting threats on other levels of the battlefield, requiring more than indiscriminate shooting. Certain passages lead into separate side-view encounters or sub-stages, giving the game a structure more varied than a continuous flight down a single route.

Its hybrid of robotic combat, layered targets, and bonus excursions anticipates some of the experimentation that made mid-1980s arcade shooters increasingly elaborate. Equites is an intriguing lesser-known transitional title between the fixed-pattern shooters of the previous decade and later scrolling action games.

games.title: Erotictac/Tactic
games.description: Erotictac, also called Tactic, is a 1990 adult-themed falling-block puzzle game. Players manipulate descending colored stones and try to bring three of the same color into contact, causing them to disappear and opening room for further pieces. Clearing stages reveals erotic pictures, pairing the straightforward matching puzzle with the adult-reward presentation familiar from numerous arcade titles of the period. Its main challenge is managing the arrangement of the growing pile while creating successive color matches.

games.title: The Empire Strikes Back
games.description:
Atari Games' Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back (1985) is a vector-graphics shooting game based on the 1980 film, created as a conversion for the original Star Wars arcade machine. Players pilot a Rebel snowspeeder during the defense of Hoth, then survive the pursuit through space aboard the Millennium Falcon. The first-person viewpoint, luminous wireframe graphics, cockpit-style controller, and film dialogue preserve the atmosphere of Atari's earlier 1983 hit.

On Hoth, players shoot Imperial probe droids and defend the Rebel base against AT-AT walkers. A limited supply of tow cables can trip the enormous machines by targeting their legs, adding a distinctive tactical weapon beyond the usual lasers. Later sequences involve shooting TIE fighters and surviving a dangerous asteroid field. Collecting the letters J-E-D-I by meeting stage targets can grant a temporary protective Jedi Force bonus.

The game is notable for turning a successful film-licensed arcade system into a new sequence of missions rather than creating a completely unrelated follow-up. Its mixture of familiar vector-flight action, memorable Hoth combat, and a few new defensive mechanics makes it a worthy companion to Atari's original Star Wars.

games.title: Escape Kids
games.description:
Escape Kids is Konami's 1991 competitive foot-racing arcade game, featuring brightly dressed children sprinting around single-screen obstacle courses. Up to four players race for three laps, repeatedly pressing the running control to build speed and using a limited supply of super jumps to clear hazards. Obstacles, collisions, and pickups can quickly change the lead, and the black-clothed champion provides a particularly tough opponent.

Coins gathered during a race can improve the character's abilities between contests, including recovery, handling, and jumping. A player who strings together victories can reach a bicycle-riding bonus game. The combination of frantic button pressing, changing tracks, and light character progression makes Escape Kids a lively alternative to vehicle-based arcade racers.

games.title: EspGaluda
games.description:
Espgaluda is Cave's 2003 vertically scrolling bullet-hell shooter and the spiritual successor to ESP Ra.De. Players choose between the psychic siblings Ageha and Tateha, whose different firing patterns and movement characteristics encourage different strategies. Fighting through mechanical armies and dense projectile patterns, they combine ordinary shots with a focused attack and a defensive barrier powered by a limited energy supply.

The game's defining feature is Kakusei, an altered state that slows enemy bullets and transforms the scoring system. Defeating enemies during this mode can turn dangerous projectiles into valuable gold, but the ability consumes collected resources and becomes dangerous when mismanaged. Skilled play therefore depends not just on dodging but on choosing when to slow the screen and convert a dangerous enemy formation into a scoring opportunity.

Espgaluda is admired for making Cave's intricate scoring design accessible without sacrificing depth. Its combination of character-driven fantasy, elegant bullet patterns, and the unusual time-manipulation mechanic made it one of the studio's defining early-2000s shooters.

games.title: Espgaluda II

variants.title: Espgaluda II (2005/11/14 MASTER VER, newer CV1000-B PCB)
Espgaluda II (2005/11/14 MASTER VER, original CV1000-B PCB)

games.description:
Espgaluda II is Cave's 2005 sequel to its acclaimed psychic-themed vertical shooter, expanding the first game's bullet-hell combat and scoring mechanics. Ageha and Tateha return alongside the new playable character Asagi, each using different shot arrangements and focused attacks. The stages feature elaborate mechanical enemies, screen-filling bullet patterns, and large bosses that demand precise movement.

The Kakusei system again lets players temporarily slow enemy projectiles and convert them into scoring rewards, but the sequel introduces additional possibilities through its modified resource and counter mechanics. Rapid fire is available by default, and the scoring system offers experienced players more opportunities to turn dangerous patterns into spectacular chains of gold. The result is a demanding sequel that rewards planning as much as reflexes.

Released for Cave's SH-3-based arcade hardware, Espgaluda II represents the studio's mature mid-2000s style: ornate bullet choreography, powerful character-specific weapons, and a complex but rewarding relationship between survival and score.

games.title: Espial
games.description:
Espial is a 1983 vertically scrolling shooter developed by Orca, strongly influenced by Namco's Xevious. The player pilots a spacecraft over a succession of hostile landscapes, battling airborne enemies while attacking installations on the terrain below. Movement and shooting demand attention to more than a single line of threats, with fast formations and ground defenses creating overlapping hazards.

Its colorful environments and lively introductory music distinguish it from the many anonymous space shooters of the period. The game received licensed releases in other markets and was later adapted to home computers, including the Atari 8-bit family. Espial is a notable example of how quickly Xevious's combination of scrolling scenery and layered targets influenced other arcade developers.

games.title: ESP Ra.De.
games.description:
Cave's ESP Ra.De. (1998, pronounced 'ESP-ra-de') is a landmark of the bullet-hell shooter genre, replacing the familiar fighter aircraft with three teenagers possessing psychic powers. Set in a futuristic Tokyo threatened by the criminal Yaksa syndicate and its leader Lady Garra, it follows Yusuke Sagami, J-B 5th and Irori Mimasaka through five elaborate vertically scrolling stages. Dense bullet patterns, meticulously illustrated urban scenery and a distinctive blend of science fiction and contemporary Japanese imagery give it an identity quite different from Cave's earlier DoDonPachi.

A three-button system combines standard fire, a limited piercing attack and a psychic barrier. Holding the barrier makes the character temporarily invulnerable and converts incoming bullets into collectible cubes; releasing it unleashes an offensive blast. The piercing attack is central to the elaborate scoring system: marking enemies before destroying them activates multipliers, while careful cube collection maintains scoring chains and helps replenish barrier energy. Holding the ordinary shot also slows movement for precise dodging.

ESP Ra.De. was the first Cave title with Junya Inoue as art director, and its human protagonists helped establish the visual direction of the later Espgaluda games. Long unavailable at home because of publishing rights, it finally received a dedicated console revival as ESP Ra.De. Psi in 2019, more than two decades after its arcade debut.

games.title: E-Swat - Cyber Police
games.description:
Sega's Cyber Police ESWAT (1989) is a side-scrolling run-and-gun action game set in crime-ridden Liberty City. Players control police officer Duke Oda, pursuing wanted criminals across 15 stages. The opening missions resemble Sega's Shinobi, with gunfights, platform jumping and movement between different levels of the scenery; each assignment culminates in the arrest of a major criminal.

After the first three arrests, Duke is promoted to the elite ESWAT unit and receives a heavily armored powered suit. Its mounted machine gun, enhanced firepower and limited special weapons transform the feel of later stages, although ammunition still has to be collected and running out leaves Duke relying on kicks. The arcade release runs on Sega System 16 hardware. The later Mega Drive/Genesis game ESWAT: City Under Siege is a substantially different adaptation, not a straight arcade conversion.

games.title: Kokontouzai Eto Monogatari
games.description: Visco's Kokontouzai Eto Monogatari (1994) is a Japanese puzzle game built around arranging matching colored blocks. Rather than relying exclusively on straight lines, it accepts groups of three matching pieces aligned horizontally, vertically or around an L-shaped corner, with the corner allowed to face in any direction. Its lighthearted presentation draws on the animals of the Chinese zodiac, as suggested by its extended Japanese title. The two-player arcade game uses an eight-way joystick and two buttons, giving an unusual twist to the familiar early-1990s matching-puzzle formula.

games.title: Evil Night
games.description:
Konami's Evil Night (1998), also released as Hell Night, is a horror-themed light-gun shooter in which three police officers enter a haunted house to rescue an abducted girl. Players blast zombies and other supernatural threats as the action advances through the mansion, with hidden details helping unfold the story. It belongs to the same late-1990s arcade horror tradition as The House of the Dead, but stands out through its three-gun arrangement.

The first and third players wield pistols that can be charged by tilting the guns upward, producing powerful penetrating shots, while the middle player uses a shotgun with a wider spread. The game runs on Konami's unusual PowerPC-based M2 arcade platform and was originally distributed on CD-ROM, making it a distinctive piece of late-era light-gun hardware history.

games.title: Evil Stone
games.description: Evil Stone (1990), developed by Spacy Industrial for Taito's L-System hardware, is an unconventional action-platform game set across grids of floating stone platforms. Instead of advancing along a conventional side-scrolling street, the player moves through vertically arranged rocky arenas and fights enemies while navigating gaps and platforms. Its most peculiar rule is the absence of a conventional health meter: ordinary hits do not simply subtract from a visible reserve of life, so survival depends on the game's unusual movement and combat rules. Two players can take part using four-way joysticks and two buttons.

games.title: Evolution Soccer
games.description: Evolution Soccer, also called ES Evolution Soccer, is a 2001 football arcade game associated with Evoga and BrezzaSoft's Crystal System hardware. Up to four players can take part in matches using an eight-way joystick and four action buttons. The controls distinguish low passes and shots, high passes and tackles, a turbo action and special techniques, creating a deliberately fast arcade approach rather than a simulation-heavy one. Winning through the available matches can lead to an additional all-star team challenge. It is one of the relatively few known games for the Crystal System, alongside The Crystal of Kings.

games.title: Excelsior
games.description:
Playmark's Excelsior (1996) mixes overhead shooting with a block-clearing puzzle game and adult photographic imagery. Players select a character and use a drilling tool to remove portions of a wall, gradually uncovering a concealed photograph while hostile creatures move around the playfield. Guns, bombs and collectible upgrades help clear obstacles and defend against enemies. Revealing roughly two-thirds of the background restores the picture's full colors, while clearing a larger proportion completes the stage.

Between regular rounds are enemy-free bonus stages in which players excavate bricks to uncover items and score rewards. The game includes several selectable photographic subjects and was connected with an Italian adult magazine of the same name. Its blend of shooting, excavation and image-reveal mechanics places it among the more unusual European responses to the Gals Panic phenomenon.

games.title: Vs. Excitebike
games.description:
Nintendo's Vs. Excitebike (1984) adapts Shigeru Miyamoto's pioneering motocross racer to the coin-operated Nintendo Vs. System. Viewed from the side, the action challenges players to negotiate jumps, bumps, narrow lanes and rival motorcycles while making a qualifying time. Steering vertically changes lanes, while leaning the bike forward or backward controls wheelies and landing angles. A normal throttle provides reliable speed, whereas turbo acceleration risks overheating the engine unless cooling strips are used effectively.

Unlike the original Famicom game, this arcade edition replaces its track editor with two additional courses and alternates solo qualifying runs with races against other riders. A special truck-jumping bonus stage adds a playful interlude. Learning to land without losing momentum, judge the engine temperature and weave through traffic is more important than simply holding the faster throttle. The game became one of Nintendo's most familiar Vs. System attractions and helped cement Excitebike's enduring place in the company's racing history.

games.title: Excite League
games.description: Excite League (1988) is a baseball arcade game from Sega, running on the System 16B platform and related to the company's earlier Major League sports titles. Players take part in batting, pitching and fielding contests through arcade-oriented controls, with the game's cabinet configurations using specialized baseball inputs. The surviving game is notable among Sega collectors for its uncommon protected System 16 hardware, identified by the FD1094 security CPU, and for the scarcity of original circuit boards. It represents Sega's late-1980s attempts to bring accessible competitive ball sports into the arcade.

games.title: Exciting Soccer II
games.description:
Alpha Denshi's Exciting Soccer II carries forward the overhead football action of the original Exciting Soccer with only modest changes. Players choose from six national teams, with Japan replacing Austria, and contest matches that include passing, shooting, tackles, throw-ins, corner kicks and penalty shoot-outs. New music accompanies an otherwise largely unchanged game, including the escalating difficulty of its single-player competition.

Although the title screen retains a 1984 copyright, arcade historical records place the Japanese release in February 1985. Its angled overhead pitch, lively presentation and speech effects belong to an early generation of arcade football games, preceding the better-known Tehkan World Cup.

games.title: Exciting Soccer
games.description:
Exciting Soccer (1983) is Alpha Denshi's early overhead-view football game, notable for representing a surprisingly broad set of the sport's rules at a time when most coin-operated sports games were highly abstract. Players can choose Italy, England, Brazil, West Germany, Austria or France, passing and shooting down a vertically oriented pitch while tackling opponents and taking throw-ins, corners and penalty shoot-outs. Winning against the computer advances to increasingly difficult matches, and two-player competition is supported.

Cheerleaders, sampled voices and its prominent top-down presentation gave the game a lively stadium atmosphere. It preceded the overhead football style later made famous by Tehkan World Cup, and was followed by Exciting Soccer II, which kept the same core play while changing some music and replacing Austria with Japan.

games.title: Exed Exes
games.description:
Capcom's Exed Exes (1985), marketed as Savage Bees in some territories, is a vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter built around a revolt by giant insect-like creatures on a distant planet. Players pilot combat craft through waves of mechanized bugs and alien defenses, with the enormous Exed Exes weapon looming as the ultimate threat. Its colorful, unusually intricate backgrounds and large formations give the game a distinct visual style compared with Capcom's earlier Vulgus.

A fast-moving sequence of enemy patterns, power-ups and increasingly dangerous opponents rewards careful positioning and accurate shooting. Built on hardware closely related to 1942, Exed Exes is a lesser-known but characteristic example of Capcom's mid-1980s experimentation with vertical shooters, especially in its detailed parallax scenery and insect-inspired enemy designs.

games.title: Exerion
games.description:
Jaleco's Exerion (1983) is a vertically oriented space shooter remembered for its layered parallax scenery and unusually weighty flight controls. Instead of stopping instantly, the player's craft drifts with simulated inertia while enemy formations swoop over a detailed planetary landscape. The combination makes even small movements matter, demanding anticipation rather than reflexive left-right dodging.

Two weapons create an elegant resource trade-off: an unlimited but relatively slow double shot and a faster single-shot gun with finite ammunition. Hitting enemies with the standard weapon replenishes the rapid-fire supply, and periodic challenge rounds offer opportunities to build reserves. Exerion's background effects and movement physics made it stand out from the many more conventional formation shooters of its era.

games.title: Explosive Breaker
games.description:
Kaneko's Explosive Breaker (1992), known in Japan as Bakuretsu Breaker, is a vertically scrolling shooter with an unusually colorful cast of pilots and spacecraft. Players select from several characters whose ships differ in shot patterns and specialized bomb attacks, then fight through asteroid fields, enormous machines and waves of aircraft. Some special attacks are particularly eccentric, ranging from electrical storms to an oversized sword-wielding figure.

The combination of character-specific firepower, dramatic screen-clearing weapons and elaborate enemy bosses makes Explosive Breaker a distinctive late-period Kaneko shooter. It remained an arcade exclusive, without a contemporary official console conversion.

games.title: Express Raider
games.description:
Express Raider (1986), known as Western Express in Japan, is Data East's comic-book-styled Wild West action game about a bandit robbing moving trains. Its stages alternate between two very different activities. In the side-scrolling sections, the robber runs and fights along railway cars, dodges thrown objects and knocks down guards to seize money bags. In the shooting sections, the action shifts to a horse-riding chase in which enemies must be shot while the train races past.

This blend of close-range brawling and mounted gunplay gives the game more variety than a typical mid-1980s platform action title. Timing punches, jumps and shots against the constant movement of the train is central to its appeal.

games.title: Extreme Downhill
games.description: Extreme Downhill (1995) is a downhill skiing arcade game developed by Scarab and published by Sammy. Rather than conventional racing cars, it puts players on skis for fast descents governed by steering and timed reactions. Its simple two-direction input and action button make it a compact, arcade-oriented interpretation of winter racing. A small historical curiosity is its high-score entry filter, which substitutes a fixed set of initials for certain forbidden names.

games.title: Exterminator
games.description:
Exterminator (1989) is one of the strangest commercial arcade games of its decade. Developed by Premier Technology and released under the Gottlieb name, it casts players as a digitized, disembodied human hand moving through houses infested with bizarre insects and other pests. Rather than controlling a conventional hero, players grab flying creatures, pound crawling enemies with a fist and use an aimed beam from the edge of the playfield. Eliminating pests gradually fills a pattern of floor tiles, allowing progress from room to room.

The entire presentation relies heavily on digitized imagery, including its giant human hand, an extraordinary visual choice for 1989. Its peculiar controls, surreal perspective and complex rules proved divisive in arcades, and relatively few machines were produced. Exterminator remains a memorable example of how experimental Gottlieb's final generation of video games could be.

games.title: Extermination
games.description:
Extermination (1987) is a vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter developed by Taito and distributed in North America by World Games. Set in a future threatened by mutant creatures, it sends armed survivors into hostile territory to destroy the invaders. Players advance up the screen, firing at ground-based enemies and other threats before confronting larger mutants at the ends of stages. The game supports simultaneous two-player action, using a joystick and two firing controls.

Its alien-infested landscapes and on-foot protagonists distinguish it from Taito's aircraft shooters of the same period. This is the 1987 arcade game, not the unrelated survival-horror title released for PlayStation 2 years later.

games.title: Exvania
games.description:
Namco's Exvania (1992) is a medieval-themed arena game that anticipates the competitive chaos of Bomberman while adding a few twists of its own. Four rival nobles, Ward, Emilio, Charles and Karl, fight through a succession of castles in a contest to dominate the kingdom. Each occupies a corner of an enclosed maze and can place explosive bombs to trap rivals, while a whip stuns opponents and can break through obstacles.

Winning a round earns a medal, and three medals secure control of a castle before the competition moves onward. Items and changing layouts keep the fights unpredictable, while up to four human contestants can compete instead of facing computer-controlled lords. Originally a Japan-only release, Exvania is a distinctive multiplayer curiosity from Namco's early-1990s arcade catalogue.

games.title: Exzisus
games.description:
Taito's Exzisus (1987) is a horizontally scrolling shooter in which players battle across four hostile planets using a flying humanoid robot that can transform into a faster spaceship. The robot can move along the ground, crouch and attack with both forward shots and bombs, while mechanical bird- and dog-like companions can help fight enemies. Collecting lettered items upgrades weapons and can activate the ship form, providing greater speed and extra protection at the cost of vulnerability to contact with the ground.

Its mixture of transformations, companion robots and air-to-ground combat lends variety to an otherwise traditional scrolling shooter. The game's unusual mechanical designs, including a player craft reminiscent of Taito's Darius, have helped it retain a cult following among fans of obscure shooters.

games.title: Eyes
games.description:
Eyes (1982), developed by Digitrex Techstar and released by Rock-Ola, turns the Pac-Man maze formula into a shooting game. The player controls a bowler-hatted eyeball, navigating corridors and firing at the small objects scattered around each maze rather than eating them. Hostile eyeballs pursue the player and shoot back; hitting one temporarily removes it from play, but it returns shortly afterward. A single enemy projectile is fatal.

Eight different mazes and increasingly aggressive opponents make accuracy and route planning essential. The peculiar character designs and combination of pellet collection with direct combat make Eyes one of the most inventive early Pac-Man-inspired arcade games. Italian manufacturer Zaccaria also distributed a version in Europe.

games.title: F-15 Strike Eagle
games.description:
MicroProse's F-15 Strike Eagle (1991) brought its well-known home-computer combat flight series to dedicated arcade hardware. Viewed from the cockpit of an F-15E fighter, the game combines aerial combat with attacks on ground targets, letting players engage hostile aircraft and destroy strategic installations. Missions offer different objectives and difficulty settings, while fuel and limited ordnance force players to manage their sortie rather than simply keep firing.

The coin-operated version draws heavily on F-15 Strike Eagle II but uses a dedicated graphics system to provide a more imposing 3D cockpit experience. Sold in upright and sit-down configurations, it is notable as MicroProse's first arcade release and a rare example of a simulation-oriented computer game being adapted for short, paid sessions.

games.title: F-1 Dream
games.description:
Capcom's F-1 Dream (1988) is an overhead Formula racing game whose cheerful, slightly exaggerated graphics conceal a surprisingly involved motorsport structure. Players begin in Formula 3000 and must earn enough results to advance to Formula One, selecting turbocharged or normally aspirated cars and racing across multiple circuits. Qualifying laps establish grid positions, while races against seven opponents demand careful handling and tactical overtaking.

Changing weather, tire wear, vehicle damage and optional pit stops add depth rarely seen in compact coin-operated racers. Progression rewards successful finishes with faster machinery, and the game evokes late-1980s Formula One through recognizable racing personalities and sponsors. Published in North America by Romstar, F-1 Dream is an appealing alternative to the pseudo-3D driving cabinets that dominated the genre.

games.title: F1 Exhaust Note
games.description: Sega's F1 Exhaust Note (1991) is a Formula One racing game for the company's System 32 hardware, designed around a substantial two-player driving cabinet. Each station supplies its own monitor, steering wheel, pedals, gear controls and molded seat, while speakers placed behind the driver emphasize the engine noise. The racing action follows a high-speed Formula One format, with its cabinet's physical immersion as much a part of the experience as the onscreen competition. It was an important step in Sega's early-1990s movement toward increasingly elaborate connected racing attractions.

games.title: F-1 Grand Prix
games.description:
Video System's F-1 Grand Prix (1991) is an officially licensed overhead racing game based on that year's Formula One season. Unlike many arcade racers, it pays close attention to car preparation: players can adjust their machines, monitor mechanical wear and visit the pits to repair damage accumulated in collisions. The selected car remains near the center of the screen as the track rotates around it, giving corners an unusual sense of movement.

Modes include individual races, a full championship and best-lap attempts. The licensed teams and drivers, combined with mechanical strategy, set this title apart from simpler overhead racing games and established the foundation for Video System's subsequent F-1 Grand Prix sequels.

games.title: F-1 Grand Prix Part II
games.description: F-1 Grand Prix Part II (1992) is Video System's follow-up to its licensed Formula One racing game. It retains the overhead perspective and emphasis on circuit racing rather than an immersive driving cabinet, challenging players to handle tight corners, overtake opponents and maintain consistent lap times. Released in Japan during the height of Formula One's early-1990s popularity, it continues the series' unusual approach to displaying the car against a rotating track. The sequel is a comparatively obscure arcade-only chapter in Video System's F-1 Grand Prix line.

games.title: Grand Prix Star
games.description:
Grand Prix Star (1991) is Jaleco's Formula One arcade racer, built around steering-wheel controls and the spectacle of a dedicated driving cabinet. Players negotiate circuits modeled on famous Grand Prix venues, including Monaco and Germany, while chasing fast lap times. Regional cabinet settings change speed readouts between kilometers and miles per hour, and the game emphasizes recorded times rather than an ordinary numeric score.

Two cabinets can be linked for head-to-head racing. Its combination of recognizable racing locations, wheel-and-pedal controls and competitive lap timing places it among the ambitious Formula One arcade attractions of the early 1990s.

games.title: F-1 Grand Prix Star II
games.description: F-1 Grand Prix Star II (1993) is Jaleco's sequel to Grand Prix Star, continuing its Formula One racing series with dedicated driving controls and an emphasis on rapid circuit competition. It preserves the physical arcade experience of steering through bends and competing for racing positions rather than abstract points. Released in Japan in March 1993, it is one of Jaleco's less familiar driving games, sitting between the original Grand Prix Star and the later F1 Super Battle.

games.title: F1 Super Lap
games.description: Sega's F1 Super Lap (1993) is a Formula One racing game with detailed pseudo-3D racing graphics and a dedicated cockpit-style control setup. Closely related in spirit to F1 Exhaust Note, it emphasizes driving speed, steering precision and the atmosphere of real Grand Prix competition. Contemporary Formula One team, driver, car and sponsor names add to its sporting authenticity. Although its title screen retains a 1992 copyright, the arcade release followed in 1993, during Sega's transition toward a new generation of sophisticated racing cabinets.

games.title: F1 Super Battle
games.description:
Jaleco's F1 Super Battle (1994) brings Grand Prix-style racing to Mega System 32 arcade hardware. Players race against seven computer-controlled cars on three courses inspired by Belgium, France and the United States, each presenting different corners and difficulty. Checkpoints must be reached before time expires, and a full race lasts three laps. Wet conditions and tight hairpins make choosing a good line essential.

Although released under a new name, it belongs to the same broad style as Jaleco's earlier Grand Prix Star games. Its colorful graphics and straightforward checkpoint-based racing favor short, competitive arcade sessions.

games.title: Face Off
games.description:
Namco's Face Off (1988) is an overhead ice-hockey game with an unusual emphasis on multiplayer arcade competition. Players select national squads representing Canada, the Soviet Union, Sweden, Czechoslovakia, the United States, Finland, France or Japan. In tournament mode, one or two players take on a series of computer-controlled teams; versus mode allows as many as four people to play, with two on each side.

Teams can be configured with different numbers of skaters, and the top-down viewpoint keeps the puck, players and goalmouth visible during rapid changes of possession. Face Off is an early example of Namco using the arcade format to stage a lively, social interpretation of a full-contact team sport.

games.title: Falcon
games.description:
Falcon is an unauthorized arcade variant of Phoenix, the influential 1980 fixed-screen space shooter. The player moves a small ship horizontally across the bottom of the screen, shooting descending birds and surviving with the help of a temporary protective shield. The cycle begins with small formations, continues through larger birds that hatch from eggs, and culminates in an assault on a heavily defended alien mothership.

The Falcon set preserves the recognizable five-wave structure and basic firing-and-shielding mechanics of Phoenix. Its significance is chiefly as one of the game's many contemporary unofficial releases, documenting how widely successful arcade designs circulated through alternative manufacturers.

games.title: Fantasia
games.description:
Fantasia (1994), developed by Comad and New Japan System, is an adult-oriented territory-capture puzzle game heavily influenced by Qix and Gals Panic. Players travel away from a safe boundary to trace lines and claim enclosed portions of a picture, gradually revealing a photograph while avoiding enemies that patrol the exposed playfield. Clearing enough of the image within the time limit completes a round.

Its distinctive twist is an indicator that shifts between a normal portrait and a monster image depending on the areas revealed. Claiming the wrong sections can push the indicator toward the monster side, forcing a replay even when the required area has been uncovered. This extra risk-management layer distinguishes Fantasia from many more straightforward image-reveal games.

games.title: Fantastic
games.description:
Fantastic is a Brazilian adaptation of Namco's Galaga produced by Taito do Brasil, apparently during the 1980s. Rather than running on Galaga's original hardware, it recreates the formation-shooting action on an earlier Galaxian-derived board. The player moves a ship from side to side, firing at alien formations and their diving attackers with a single button.

This technically unusual conversion is slower and behaves differently from the original Galaga, especially in enemy movement. Its interest lies less in adding new game ideas than in demonstrating how arcade operators and manufacturers repurposed widely available hardware to reproduce a popular hit.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Fantasy
games.description:
SNK's Fantasy (1981) is a whimsical multi-scene action adventure, unusually ambitious for the early years of arcade gaming. A young man sets out to rescue his girlfriend from pirates, only for the couple to face a succession of further kidnappings and hazards. Rather than repeat one fixed playfield, the game moves through contrasting situations involving pirate ships, balloon travel, jungle dangers and village encounters. The hero is guided by joystick alone, with each scene demanding different timing and movement.

Its episodic structure, animated sequences and memorable synthesized soundtrack give Fantasy an almost storybook quality. Often cited as one of the first arcade games to offer a continue feature, it was released by SNK in Japan and licensed to Rock-Ola for North American distribution in 1982.

games.title: Fantasy Land
games.description: Fantasy Land is a side-scrolling fantasy platform game released by Electronic Devices around the beginning of the 1990s. Its hero sets off to rescue a kidnapped girlfriend, passing through themed stages including medieval landscapes, winter settings, underwater passages and dungeons. Players jump across hazards and fight melee and ranged enemies before confronting stage bosses. The changing scenery and mixture of platform navigation with weapon-based combat make it a comparatively elaborate but little-known fantasy arcade adventure.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Fantasia II
games.description: Fantasia II (1997) is Comad's follow-up to its adult-themed Qix-style puzzle game. Players leave the safety of the playfield's border to trace lines, enclose territory and uncover concealed photographic images. Roaming enemies and a restrictive timer punish ambitious moves, while claiming sufficient territory advances to the next picture. Two-player play is supported, retaining the competitive attraction of the earlier game. Its main appeal is the familiar risk-versus-reward tension of cutting into dangerous space to reveal a larger portion of the image.

games.title: Fantasy '95
games.description: Fantasy '95 (1995), by Hi-max Technology, is a Korean adult-oriented territory-capture puzzle game in the style of Gals Panic and Comad's Fantasia series. Players guide a marker around a playfield, draw dividing lines and claim areas to reveal photographic portraits while avoiding enemies. Unusually for this type of game, its picture selection includes male subjects as well as female models, including Korean entertainer Hyung-rae Shim. This change of visual subject matter makes it stand out from the many near-identical photographic Qix derivatives of the period.

games.title: Fantasy Zone 2
games.description:
Fantasy Zone II: The Tears of Opa-Opa reached arcades in 1988 as an adaptation of Sega's 1987 Master System sequel. The colorful, winged spaceship Opa-Opa once again fights to save his world by destroying enemy bases, collecting money and purchasing engines, bombs and new weapons from shops. Players can fly left or right around looping horizontal stages, but the sequel divides each level into several connected zones. Warp gates discovered during play link these areas, and clearing their bases opens the way to a large boss.

The arcade version runs on Sega System E hardware, rather than the System 16 board of the original Fantasy Zone. It largely preserves the console game's graphics and structure while introducing arcade-oriented changes, including a time pressure absent from the original home version. It should not be confused with M2's extensively redesigned System 16 remake from 2008.

games.title: Fantasy Zone II - The Tears of Opa-Opa

variants.title: Fantasy Zone II - The Tears of Opa-Opa (System 16C version)
Fantasy Zone II - The Tears of Opa-Opa (System 16C version, prototype)

games.description:
Fantasy Zone II: The Tears of Opa-Opa (System 16 version, 2008) is M2's remarkable reimagining of Sega's 1987 sequel. Instead of simply emulating the Master System game, M2 rebuilt it for genuine System 16-class arcade hardware, imagining what Fantasy Zone II might have looked and played like had it been developed for the more powerful board used by the first game. The result has richer pixel art, denser enemy formations and a redesigned progression system while retaining Opa-Opa, shops, money collection and the familiar base-destruction objective.

Each area now has connected Bright and Dark versions. The darker side offers more aggressive enemies and greater rewards, giving skilled players reasons to take a risk rather than remain in the safer zone. This unusual remake first appeared as part of Sega Ages' Fantasy Zone Complete Collection for PlayStation 2 and was later preserved in arcade-compatible form. It is a deliberate alternate-history arcade game, not the same program as the 1988 System E conversion.

games.title: Fantasy Zone
games.description:
Sega's Fantasy Zone (1986) is one of the defining 'cute-'em-up' shooters, blending pastel-colored, playful visuals with surprisingly demanding arcade action. Players control Opa-Opa, a small sentient craft with wings and feet, traveling through a series of looping horizontal worlds. Instead of advancing automatically, they may fly in either direction to hunt down enemy-producing bases. Destroying every base summons a large, characterful boss, and the final stage revisits earlier bosses before the climactic confrontation.

Defeated enemies drop money rather than merely points, and shops scattered through each world sell more powerful shots, bombs and engines. Deciding when to spend and which weapon to buy is fundamental to survival, especially because some upgrades are temporary. The combination of free movement, an in-game economy and charming but challenging boss design created a distinctive identity at a time when science-fiction shooters tended to be grim and militaristic.

Fantasy Zone was a major Sega arcade hit and the beginning of a long-running series. Opa-Opa became an enduring Sega mascot, and the game's shop-based upgrades and whimsical visual language influenced generations of later shooters.

games.title: Fast Lane
games.description:
Konami's Fast Lane (1987) turns the classic Head On driving-maze formula into a colorful chase game. Viewed from above, the player drives continuously along interlocking roads, changing the color of untraveled sections while avoiding a hostile vehicle. The car cannot simply reverse direction, so careful use of junctions and passages is crucial. Power-ups collected around the course can enable jumping, shooting or attacks to escape danger.

The combination of maze clearing, one-way momentum and active pursuit gives Fast Lane a distinctive rhythm somewhere between a racing game and Pac-Man. Each new layout demands a planned route rather than raw driving speed.

games.title: Fatal Fury Special / Garou Densetsu Special

variants.title: Fatal Fury Special / Garou Densetsu Special (set 1)
Fatal Fury Special / Garou Densetsu Special (set 2)

games.description:
Fatal Fury Special (1993) is SNK's expanded and refined version of Fatal Fury 2, and one of the defining early fighting games on the Neo Geo. The roster brings back popular fighters from the first game, including Duck King, Tung Fu Rue and Geese Howard, while preserving the sequel's exotic international cast. Faster action, revised damage, smoother combinations and improved controls make the fights markedly more fluid than in its immediate predecessor.

Its signature two-plane stages allow fighters to shift between the foreground and background, changing how attacks and spacing work. A celebrated secret encounter with Ryo Sakazaki from Art of Fighting also helped establish SNK's tradition of crossover fighting-game appearances. More than a minor update, Fatal Fury Special became a competitive favorite and an important foundation for later entries in the series.

games.title: Fatal Fury - King of Fighters / Garou Densetsu - shukumei no tatakai
games.description:
SNK's Fatal Fury: King of Fighters (1991) was one of the first major challengers to Street Fighter II and introduced a cast that would become central to the Neo Geo's identity. Brothers Terry and Andy Bogard enter Southtown's King of Fighters tournament to confront crime lord Geese Howard, the man responsible for their father's death. Their friend Joe Higashi joins them in a martial-arts contest against colorful opponents including Tung Fu Rue and Raiden.

Combat uses punch, kick and throw buttons and distinctive joystick-driven special moves, but the game's most unusual idea is its two-plane arena. Fighters can shift between foreground and background paths, adding an extra positional dimension to its one-on-one bouts. The original release has only three selectable heroes, yet emphasizes story presentation and dramatic rival encounters more than many of its contemporaries.

Fatal Fury launched one of SNK's defining franchises and introduced Terry Bogard and Geese Howard, characters who would remain fixtures of the genre. Its tournament title also foreshadowed SNK's later King of Fighters crossover series, although the two franchises are distinct.

games.title: Fatal Fury 2 / Garou Densetsu 2 - arata-naru tatakai
games.description:
Fatal Fury 2 (1992) greatly expands SNK's original one-on-one fighting game. Terry and Andy Bogard and Joe Higashi return alongside newcomers including Mai Shiranui, Kim Kaphwan, Big Bear, Jubei Yamada and Cheng Sinzan, while the mysterious Wolfgang Krauser waits beyond the main competition. The roster grows to eight selectable fighters and the control scheme now uses four attack buttons for different strengths of punches and kicks.

The sequel also makes switching between its foreground and background combat planes an active tactical choice, rather than a mostly opponent-driven event. Faster play, larger character sprites and a more international cast helped establish the Fatal Fury formula that Fatal Fury Special would refine the following year.

games.title: Fatal Fury 3 - Road to the Final Victory / Garou Densetsu 3 - haruka-naru tatakai
games.description:
Fatal Fury 3: Road to the Final Victory (1995) returns to Southtown with a new storyline centered on the mysterious Jin scrolls and a fresh group of rival fighters. Terry and Andy Bogard, Joe Higashi and Mai Shiranui are joined by characters such as Blue Mary, Bob Wilson, Franco Bash and Hon-Fu. Its distinctive presentation uses dramatically animated backgrounds and large, expressive character artwork.

The major mechanical change is the Oversway System, which replaces the older two-plane arrangement with a central fighting lane and two temporary sidestep lines, one in front and one behind. Fighters can evade strikes, counterattack from these side lanes and chain combinations through a more technical move system. The result is an ambitious and sometimes demanding installment that pointed toward the later Real Bout Fatal Fury games.

games.title: Fax
games.description:
Exidy's Fax (1983) is an unusually elaborate early arcade trivia machine rather than a conventional action game. Players answer multiple-choice questions covering general knowledge, history, sports and entertainment, with several difficulty levels and a large bank of stored questions. A countdown indicator limits deliberation, while a separate timer influences the points awarded for correct answers. Competitive two-player play allows opponents to test their knowledge head to head.

Fax came in a distinctive woodgrain cabinet resembling a small jukebox, complete with a compact central monitor and answer buttons mounted on either side. Exidy also offered replacement question sets, making it an early attempt to create a refreshable quiz attraction for bars and other venues beyond the traditional arcade.

games.title: Fire Ball
games.description: Fire Ball (1992) is a Korean maze-action game built around the bomb-placement formula familiar from Bomberman. Players move through enclosed arenas, dropping timed explosives to blast opponents or clear routes while avoiding the expanding explosions. Its appeal comes from positioning bombs to restrict escape paths and then moving clear before detonation. Released during the early-1990s boom in competitive arcade maze games, it is a relatively obscure regional variation on a proven multiplayer formula.

games.title: Football Frenzy
games.description:
Football Frenzy (1992) is SNK's energetic American football game for the Neo Geo MVS. Players choose from ten fictional teams, then enter either a knockout tournament against the computer or a two-player head-to-head game. The field is shown from a high diagonal angle, giving a clear view of the offensive and defensive formations.

Before each offensive snap, the player can choose from a variety of running and passing plays, or opt for a punt or field-goal attempt. Tackles, forward passes and the tactical choices of gridiron football are streamlined into a quick, button-driven arcade contest. The combination of accessible play selection and colorful, oversized player sprites makes it a distinctive sports entry in the Neo Geo library.

games.title: Field Combat
games.description:
Jaleco's Field Combat (1985) is an unusual vertically scrolling battlefield shooter in which players command the hovering combat craft Genesis against an invading red army. The craft can fire missiles at enemy infantry, tanks and helicopters, but simply destroying everything is not always the best strategy. Its special capture beam can seize enemy units, adding them to the player's reserves, and captured troops can later be deployed as friendly reinforcements on the battlefield.

This blend of shooting and rudimentary force management gives Field Combat a tactical element uncommon in early arcade shooters. The game's use of Wagner's Ride of the Valkyries further emphasizes its theatrical military setting. Although an obscure Jaleco title, it stands out for treating enemy soldiers as potential resources rather than mere targets.

games.title: Frog Feast
games.description: Frog Feast is a homebrew two-player action game developed by Rastersoft (Charles Doty) for the Neo Geo platform in 2006, inspired by classic frog-catching pond games where players leap across lily pads and use their tongues to catch flies.

games.title: Final Fight
games.description:
Capcom's Final Fight (1989) is one of the most influential side-scrolling beat-'em-ups ever made. When the Mad Gear gang kidnaps Jessica, daughter of Metro City's new mayor Mike Haggar, Haggar joins forces with Jessica's boyfriend Cody and martial artist Guy to fight through the city's criminal underworld. Players choose one of three distinctly balanced characters and march through six increasingly hostile urban areas, brawling with street gangs, wrestlers and towering bosses. The simple combination of an eight-way joystick, attack and jump buttons hides a flexible range of throws, jumping kicks, grabs and crowd-control techniques.

The game set a new benchmark for scale and spectacle in the genre: huge, expressive character sprites, busy urban backgrounds and large numbers of enemies on screen made its street fights feel more physical than earlier brawlers. Weapons picked up from the scenery, destructible objects containing food and money, and cooperative play for two players add tactical variety. Haggar's wrestling moves and the contrast between Cody's strength and Guy's speed encourage different styles of play.

Originally developed under the working title Street Fighter '89, Final Fight became a defining early showcase for Capcom's CPS-1 hardware. Its impact can be traced through later beat-'em-ups from Capcom, Konami and many others, while several of its characters went on to appear in the Street Fighter series. The game remains a genre cornerstone, equally memorable for its atmosphere, animation and demanding cooperative action.

games.title: Final Fight 2
games.description:
Final Fight 2 (1996 arcade bootleg) is an unauthorized coin-operated conversion of Capcom's Super Famicom/Super Nintendo beat-'em-up, not an official Capcom arcade sequel. It runs on hardware derived from Nintendo's 16-bit console technology, adapted with coin inputs and arcade controls. The underlying game follows Haggar, ninja fighter Maki and swordsman Carlos as they battle a revived Mad Gear organization through a series of international locations.

Like the console original, the action features two-player cooperative brawling, character-specific attacks, grabs and special moves. This bootleg is primarily interesting as a surviving example of 1990s arcade operators repackaging popular home games for coin-operated cabinets, rather than as a redesigned version of Final Fight 2.

games.title: Final Fight 3
games.description:
Final Fight 3 is an unauthorized arcade adaptation of Capcom's Super Nintendo game, assembled for coin-operated hardware using components closely related to the original console. It is not a lost official CPS-series sequel. The game returns to Metro City with four selectable fighters: Haggar, Guy, Lucia and Dean. Players punch, kick and throw their way through gang-controlled streets, with a broader move set than in the earlier games.

Dashes, special command attacks and branching routes make this installment more elaborate than the original Final Fight. A human partner can join the brawling, and the underlying console game also supports computer-assisted cooperative play. The bootleg is chiefly notable for preserving an unofficial arcade incarnation of a home-only Capcom sequel.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Final Fight Revenge
games.description:
Final Fight Revenge (1999) is an unlikely transformation of Capcom's celebrated street-brawling series into a one-on-one 3D fighting game. Developed by Capcom's American team for Sega's Saturn-based ST-V arcade platform, it brings together characters from the original Final Fight, including Cody, Guy, Haggar and several former Mad Gear enemies, in arena-style duels rather than cooperative side-scrolling battles.

The fighting system uses four attack buttons plus a special-action control for sidestepping and picking up objects. Weapons and restorative items appear during matches, giving the action a chaotic flavor unlike Capcom's more traditional competitive fighters. Its cartoonish character reinterpretations and unusual finishing moves made it a curiosity among fans. A Japanese Sega Saturn conversion followed in 2000, but the game never established itself as a major competitive series.

games.title: Fighter & Attacker
games.description:
Namco's Fighter & Attacker (1992), commonly abbreviated F/A, is a vertically scrolling military shooter with an exceptionally large selection of modern aircraft. Players choose among sixteen jets, including recognizable American and Japanese fighter designs, and fight through eight stages of enemy aircraft, ground defenses and large bosses. Each plane has a characteristic speed and firing pattern, making the opening choice central to the game.

Unlike many contemporary shooters, F/A does not rely on collecting conventional weapon upgrades or deploying screen-clearing smart bombs. Players instead master the fixed capabilities of their selected aircraft, using separate attacks to destroy aerial and ground targets. The austere weapon system and choice of real-world aircraft distinguish this Namco title from more fantastical shooters of the early 1990s.

games.title: Fighting Basketball
games.description: Fighting Basketball is a 1984 arcade basketball game developed by Paradise. Viewed from above, its compact court and simplified player graphics emphasize fast movement and direct shooting rather than a detailed simulation of the sport. Players move their team around the court, seek scoring opportunities and compete against opposing sides using an eight-way joystick and a single action button. An obscure early basketball release, it reflects the period when arcade manufacturers were still experimenting with how to translate team sports into simple digital controls.

games.title: Fighter's History
games.description:
Data East's Fighter's History (1993) is a traditional one-on-one fighting game created during the worldwide boom inspired by Street Fighter II. Its roster includes martial artists such as Mizoguchi, Ryoko, Jean and Ray, along with the flamboyant bosses Clown and Karnov, a returning Data East character. Fighters use the familiar six-button punch-and-kick arrangement and individual command-based special moves, but the central twist is a visible weak point on each opponent.

Repeatedly striking that vulnerable area can stun a fighter and create an opening for further attacks, rewarding deliberate target selection instead of constant aggression. Fighter's History is also historically notable for the copyright lawsuit Capcom brought against Data East over similarities to Street Fighter II. Data East prevailed, making the case a frequently cited example in discussions of the limits of copyright protection for game mechanics. The series continued with Fighter's History Dynamite, also known as Karnov's Revenge.

games.title: Field Goal
games.description:
Taito's Field Goal (1979) is an American-football-themed adaptation of Breakout rather than a conventional football simulation. A paddle moves horizontally along the bottom of a fixed screen, keeping a football-shaped ball in play and bouncing it toward rows of colored helmets. The angle of each rebound determines which targets can be struck, while a moving football-player figure offers bonus scoring opportunities.

Its mixture of a familiar paddle game with sporting imagery is typical of late-1970s arcade experimentation. Field Goal appeared in both upright and cocktail cabinets, with the tabletop version marketed in Japan as T.T. Field Goal.

games.title: Fighting Layer
games.description:
Fighting Layer (1998) is a 3D fighting game developed by Arika and published by Namco, closely related in design to Arika's Street Fighter EX series. Two returning EX characters, Allen Snider and Blair Dame, join a new cast of fighters in one-on-one matches built around six-button attacks, command moves and elaborate super combinations. Although the characters are rendered in 3D, combat retains the precise side-on structure of a traditional two-dimensional fighter.

Players can chain super moves into one another, perform universal guard-breaking attacks and use rapid dashes or sidesteps for positioning. Defensive options include special recovery and evasive techniques that reward mastery of timing. Released in Japanese arcades without a contemporary home conversion, Fighting Layer became an elusive cult title among fans of Arika's distinctive style of fighting games.

games.title: Fighting Hawk
games.description:
Taito's Fighting Hawk (1988 copyright, released in Japan in 1989) is a vertically scrolling aerial shooter in which players pilot a combat aircraft called Falcon across grasslands, snowfields, glaciers and urban battle zones. Aircraft and ground defenses attack from all directions as the player collects shot upgrades and fires homing missile-like bombs at tougher targets. The campaign eventually leads toward a confrontation with the advanced enemy bomber Dragon Hat.

Its military setting and straightforward power-up system invite comparison with Toaplan's airborne shooters, although its pacing and enemy patterns have their own character. It is a relatively obscure late-1980s Taito shooter, with artwork and music ideas that were later reused in Master of Weapon.

games.title: Funky Head Boxers
games.description:
Sega's Funky Head Boxers (1995) is a whimsical 3D boxing game for the Saturn-derived ST-V arcade system. Its fighters have oversized, almost cube-shaped heads that squash, change expression and display increasingly comical injuries as punches land. Six boxers from different countries compete in matches where timing, defense and well-placed blows matter more than visual realism.

The exaggerated animation extends to the spectators and gives the game an unmistakable personality among the more serious arcade boxing titles of the period. The combination of polygonal characters, texture-mapped facial reactions and traditional ring action is its main appeal.

games.title: Field Day
games.description:
Taito's Field Day (1984), known in Japan as The Undoukai, is a comic sports compilation built around a school athletics festival rather than Olympic competition. Players tackle a succession of short events such as tug-of-war and three-legged racing, using quick button presses and careful timing to meet each event's qualifying condition. Failing to achieve a required result ends the attempt, while successful players advance through seven contests.

Its lighthearted theme and exaggerated animated competitors give it a different atmosphere from Konami's Track & Field, despite sharing the button-driven sports format. The game is an appealing record of Japan's school sports-day traditions translated into arcade competition.

games.title: Fight Fever
games.description:
Fight Fever (1994), developed by Korean studio Viccom for the Neo Geo MVS, is an early Korean entry into the one-on-one fighting-game boom. Eight selectable competitors face off in a tournament inspired by martial arts, particularly taekwondo, before confronting eccentric boss fighters. The four-button system emphasizes punches, kicks and command-based special attacks, including powerful character-specific Danger Moves.

Known in Korea as Wang Joong Wang, or King of the Kings, the game borrows elements of SNK's Fatal Fury and Art of Fighting but has its own deliberately flamboyant cast and presentation. It was Viccom's only commercially released Neo Geo MVS game and remains a curiosity in the system's crowded fighting catalogue.

games.title: Fighting Roller
games.description: Fighting Roller (1983), developed by Kaneko and distributed by Taito, is an arcade obstacle race on roller skates, released internationally as Roller Aces. The player races along a scrolling course while avoiding barriers and other dangers, using joystick movement and action buttons to preserve momentum and reach the finish. Despite sometimes being classified as a fighting game in emulator databases, its actual premise is speed-skating through hazards rather than hand-to-hand combat. Its quirky sports theme makes it an unusual early-1980s arcade release.

games.title: Final Lap 2
games.description:
Namco's Final Lap 2 (1990) continues the Formula One racing style of the original with more circuits and the same emphasis on linked-cabinet competition. Players choose among racing teams inspired by contemporary Formula One machinery and drive from a behind-the-car perspective, braking and changing gears through demanding corners. The familiar Suzuka circuit returns alongside courses in Italy, Monaco and the United States.

As with its predecessor, connected two-seat cabinets can accommodate as many as eight simultaneous racers, making it a particularly impressive group attraction. Final Lap 2 expands the original's circuit selection without abandoning the responsive, unforgiving arcade handling that defined the series.

games.title: Final Lap 3
games.description:
Final Lap 3 (1992) is the third major Formula One racing installment in Namco's Final Lap line. Running on Namco System 2 hardware, it brings a fresh set of courses inspired by Silverstone, Paul Ricard, Imola and Spain's Barcelona-Catalunya circuit. Players race recognizable Formula One-style cars from a behind-the-vehicle perspective, trying to maintain speed through corners while contending with rival drivers.

The game's chief strength remains multiplayer scale: up to four linked two-person racing cabinets can host eight competitors in a single event. The updated circuits and vehicle graphics offer enthusiasts another set of challenges within Namco's established arcade racing formula.

games.title: Final Lap R
games.description:
Final Lap R is Namco's later and final arcade entry in the Final Lap Formula One series, bringing upgraded graphics and hardware to the longstanding behind-the-car racing formula. Four circuits inspired by Germany's Hockenheimring, Hungary's Hungaroring, Belgium's Spa-Francorchamps and Brazil's Interlagos replace the locations of earlier installments. Players must judge braking distances, steer through demanding turns and battle other cars while the race clock keeps pressure on.

As in earlier Final Lap titles, linked cabinets support up to eight people competing at once. The combination of real-world circuit inspiration and large-scale multiplayer racing remained the series' defining feature, even as the arcade market shifted toward fully polygonal driving games.

games.title: Final Blow
games.description:
Final Blow (1988 copyright, released in Japanese arcades in 1989) is Taito's side-view boxing game with dramatically oversized fighters. Players choose from a small roster of fictional champions, move around the ring and deliver jabs, hooks and heavier punches while judging distance and the opponent's guard. A precisely timed finishing blow can score a sudden knockout, giving even an apparently even contest a dramatic ending.

Its large sprites, emphatic punch animations and straightforward championship structure make it more theatrical than a serious boxing simulation. A later Mega Drive/Genesis adaptation was marketed in North America as James 'Buster' Douglas Knockout Boxing, taking advantage of the boxer's 1990 world title victory.

games.title: Finalizer - Super Transformation
games.description:
Konami's Finalizer: Super Transformation (1985) is a vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter built around an aircraft that can develop into a powerful humanoid combat robot. Flying above landscapes inspired by the United States, the player battles enemy formations while collecting equipment that upgrades the craft's weapons and changes its appearance. Its transformation motif gives the action a mechanical-anime flavor uncommon in the company's earlier shooters.

Progress depends on surviving waves of enemies and selecting useful power-ups as the screen scrolls upward. Finalizer occupies an interesting position between Konami's straightforward early vertical shooters and the more elaborate weapon systems of its later arcade action games.

games.title: Final Lap
games.description:
Namco's Final Lap (1987) is an important milestone in the history of competitive arcade racing. Built as a successor to Pole Position, it places players in Formula One-style cars on a condensed but carefully recognizable version of Japan's Suzuka Circuit. Viewed from behind the car, racers use a steering wheel, accelerator, brakes and gear changes to negotiate corners, avoid collisions and beat the clock. Contact with other vehicles causes spins rather than the spectacular explosions familiar from Pole Position.

Its greatest innovation was the scale of its linked multiplayer system. Multiple two-seat cabinets could be joined for races with as many as eight drivers, transforming a solitary driving game into a loud, shared social event. This concept became enormously influential on the design of later arcade racing installations.

Featuring teams inspired by the 1987 Formula One season and a circuit newly prominent on the world championship calendar, Final Lap combined sporting authenticity with accessible arcade competition. The series went on to produce several sequels, each expanding the circuit selection while preserving the multiplayer concept.

games.title: Final Tetris
games.description:
Final Tetris (1993) is an unauthorized Korean competitive puzzle game based on the falling-block rules of Tetris. Its matches are built around two opposing playfields, where clearing lines containing special blocks grants abilities that can upset the opponent's game. Victory comes by forcing the rival to fill the board or by having the safer field when the time limit expires.

Its three-button control arrangement is unusual: one button drops a piece instantly, while another rotates it counterclockwise. The mixture of familiar line clearing, temporary special abilities and head-to-head pressure makes it a regional counterpart to the competitive Tetris variations appearing in Japanese arcades in the same period.

games.title: Zenkoku Seifuku Bishoujo Grand Prix Find Love

variants.title: Zenkoku Seifuku Bishoujo Grand Prix Find Love (J 971212 V1.000)

games.description: Zenkoku Seifuku Bishoujo Grand Prix: Find Love (1997) is a Japanese image-based jigsaw puzzle game developed for Sega's Saturn-derived ST-V arcade hardware. Players choose from ten illustrated female characters and assemble scrambled pictures against a strict time limit. Successfully completing each arrangement reveals another image and allows progress through the selection. Its anime-styled portraits and timed puzzle format distinguish it from the territory-capture adult puzzle games that were more common in arcades of the era. A Sega Saturn edition also exists.

games.title: Find Out
games.description: Find Out is an Italian quiz and word-puzzle arcade game released by Elettronolo in 1987. Its central idea follows the television game-show format of Wheel of Fortune: players work toward identifying a concealed word or phrase instead of answering a simple string of unrelated trivia questions. The machine uses five buttons and a horizontal screen, with a Z80 processor and very simple digital sound. It is an unusual example of a locally produced European arcade game drawing on a television format rather than the Japanese action-game conventions that dominated the industry.

games.title: Finest Hour
games.description:
Namco's Finest Hour (1989) is a side-scrolling mecha action game for the System 2 arcade platform. Players pilot Sygnus, an armored machine equipped with a laser cannon, automatic target acquisition and jump jets, through industrial battlefields crowded with hostile robots and defenses. Double-tapping a direction initiates a dash, and managing momentum is vital because the machine cannot freely reverse its facing direction in midair.

Instead of an ordinary health meter, Sygnus has a temperature gauge. Enemy attacks raise the temperature, while the onboard cooling system lowers it during safer moments. Overheating destroys the mech, and running out of time disrupts the cooling system, making speed and caution equally important. This unusual combination of movement physics and thermal management gives Finest Hour a markedly different feel from conventional run-and-gun games.

games.title: Final Furlong 2
games.description:
Namco's Final Furlong 2 (1999) expands the unusual physical horse-racing attraction introduced by Final Furlong. Instead of simply pressing a button to accelerate, players mount life-sized fiberglass horses and rock their bodies back and forth to urge their steeds forward, using the handles to guide their racing line. A whip control provides extra bursts of speed, while jockeying for position and avoiding rivals are essential to a successful race.

Running on Namco's Super System 23 hardware, the sequel combines impressive 3D horse racing with a demanding full-body arcade experience. Its novelty is inseparable from the dedicated cabinet: the act of riding is a physical performance as much as a video-game control scheme.

games.title: Fire Barrel
games.description:
Irem's Fire Barrel (1993 copyright, released in Japan in 1994), also known as Air Assault, is a vertically scrolling military shooter with an unusual aircraft-selection system. Players can choose a jet or helicopter at the beginning of each stage rather than being locked into one craft for the entire campaign. The jet fires straight ahead with increasingly broad weapons, while the helicopter can direct its gunfire in the direction of movement, trading raw firepower for versatility.

Ground batteries, aircraft and major bosses fill the scrolling battlefields, while pickups strengthen weapons and powerful bombs offer emergency firepower. The contrast between the two aircraft makes stage-by-stage vehicle choice a meaningful part of the challenge.

games.title: Fire Battle
games.description:
Fire Battle (1984) is a vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter developed by Woodplace and released by Taito. The player pilots a spacecraft over enemy territory, firing a forward-facing gun at airborne targets and dropping slower bombs onto ground installations. Opponents include moving fighters, gun emplacements and mechanical enemies, and the score rises as their defenses are destroyed.

The separation of air and ground attacks closely resembles Namco's Xevious and requires players to monitor two kinds of danger at once. Its straightforward dual-weapon system and layered targets make Fire Battle a characteristic, though comparatively obscure, entry in the early Xevious-inspired shooter wave.

games.title: Firebeast
games.description:
Firebeast (1983) is an unreleased Atari arcade prototype designed and programmed by Ed Rotberg. Players fly a dragon across a dangerous valley, protecting dwarves on the ground from falling projectiles and other hazards while helping them reach safety. The dragon is moved with a trackball and can fire toward either side; dwarves sometimes stop in shelters and must be nudged to continue their journey. Later areas introduce treasure caves and different challenges.

Originally conceived as Dragon Rider and reportedly inspired by the Dragonriders of Pern books, the project was renamed after licensing problems. It performed poorly in testing and was canceled before commercial manufacture. The preserved prototype offers a rare view of Atari experimenting with an escort-based action game rather than a conventional shooter.

games.title: Fire Hawk
games.description:
Fire Hawk (2001) is a vertically scrolling shooter developed by Korean arcade manufacturer ESD. Players select one of five fighter aircraft and fly through waves of enemies, collecting weapon power-ups and deploying a limited supply of bombs against dense formations and bosses. Its straightforward two-button controls and military-looking craft follow the conventions of late-period arcade shooters.

One of its more peculiar traits is an audio presentation that draws on music associated with earlier arcade games, including Andro Dunos. Fire Hawk is a relatively obscure example of traditional scrolling shooting surviving into the 2000s in regional arcade markets.

games.title: Fire One
games.description:
Exidy's Fire One (1979) is an inventive two-player submarine duel that splits the monitor into separate periscope views. Each contestant scans the sea by rotating a paddle control, launches torpedoes at enemy vessels and attempts to locate and destroy the opposing submarine. Shots are limited by torpedo capacity and reloading delays, rewarding anticipation over constant firing.

A submerge control lets a player hide temporarily, but also prevents attacking while submerged. The game can be played against a computer opponent or another person, turning its two periscope stations into a tense contest of concealment, observation and carefully timed torpedo strikes. Licensed to Sega in Japan, it is a particularly unusual example of Exidy's experimental late-1970s arcade designs.

games.title: Fire Shark
games.description:
Toaplan's Fire Shark (1990), known in Japan as Same! Same! Same!, is a ferociously demanding vertically scrolling shooter in which players pilot a lone biplane against an enormous enemy armada. Tanks, warships, fighter formations and gun emplacements pour into view as the aircraft advances through a series of battlefields. The game builds on the military action of Flying Shark, but emphasizes still larger enemy formations and relentlessly escalating danger.

Power-ups allow the plane to switch between a wide spread shot, a focused laser and a spectacular flamethrower that grows into an enormous stream of fire. Speed upgrades and limited bombs help manage the most dangerous patterns. The Japanese and export editions differ in important respects, including their handling of player deaths and multiplayer play.

Fire Shark is remembered as a demanding Toaplan classic and for its striking flame weapon, one of the most visually memorable attacks in the company's catalogue. Its fast, unforgiving action represents the studio's influential approach to arcade shooters on the eve of the bullet-hell era.

games.title: Fire Trap
games.description:
Fire Trap (1986) takes the climbing action of Crazy Climber into a burning high-rise. The player guides a firefighter up the exterior of the building, extinguishing flames and rescuing trapped people and animals while dodging falling debris and other hazards.
