Gaplus reverses one of Galaga's best-known ideas by allowing the player to acquire a tractor beam and capture enemy fighters. The converted enemies become temporary allies and can add to the player's firepower. Other bonuses, changing enemy races and special stages make the action unusually varied for a single-screen shooter.

Its intricate enemy patterns, player-controlled tractor beam and higher movement freedom make Gaplus more than a straightforward sequel. The alternate Galaga 3 name was a marketing attempt to associate it more directly with the better-known Galaga, even though the actual series chronology already included Galaxian.

games.title: Gardia
games.description: Gardia (1986), developed by Coreland for Sega, is a vertically scrolling aerial shooter that distinguishes between airborne and ground targets. The aircraft fires rapid forward shots at enemies in the sky while separately launching missiles at installations and vehicles below. Collectible enhancements increase firepower and protection, helping the player survive waves of opponents and encounters with large mid-stage and end-stage bosses. The game runs through four main stages before looping, a structure that rewards pattern memorization and sustained high-score play.

games.title: Garogun Seroyang
games.description: Garogun Seroyang is a Korean-language arcade quiz game released by Yun Sung in January 2000. A single player answers trivia questions using joystick-and-button controls, in a presentation that reflects the small, low-cost Korean coin-op market of the period. Its most distinctive documented feature is its artwork: background images were taken from Japanese bishōjo computer games, including White Album and Pia Carrot e Yōkoso!! 2. The unexpected juxtaposition of borrowed visual-novel illustrations and straightforward quiz play makes it a particularly revealing example of late-1990s arcade asset reuse.

games.title: Garou - Mark of the Wolves
games.description:
Garou: Mark of the Wolves (1999) is SNK's acclaimed late Neo Geo fighting game and the ninth main installment in the Fatal Fury lineage. Set years after Geese Howard's death, it introduces a new generation of combatants in Southtown, led by Rock Howard, Geese's son and Terry Bogard's protégé. The cast includes a small group of returning veterans alongside newcomers, and the game's exceptionally fluid sprite animation became one of the defining showcases of SNK's mature 2D fighting technology.

Garou abandons Fatal Fury's traditional foreground-background lane switching in favor of a single combat plane, replacing it with two systems that reward tactical precision. Just Defend grants benefits for blocking an attack at the last instant, including slight health recovery and counterattack opportunities. The Tactical Offense Position, or T.O.P., is a player-chosen segment of the health gauge that temporarily boosts offense and enables a special attack when the fighter's remaining life enters that range. These features create dramatic shifts in momentum without sacrificing the demands of spacing and execution.

Highly regarded for its character designs, responsive controls and competitive depth, Garou is often considered one of the Neo Geo's finest fighting games. Its distinct mechanics and unusually polished presentation helped it build a long-lasting tournament following well beyond the end of the original arcade hardware's commercial life.

games.title: Garyo Retsuden
games.description: Garyo Retsuden (1987) is a top-down action shooter inspired by the Chinese Romance of the Three Kingdoms. Players choose among the heroes Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei, each associated with different thrown or ranged weapons, and advance through hostile territory to rescue a captive princess from Lu Bu. Enemies press in from multiple directions while pickups improve attack strength, movement speed or protection. The heroes can also ride horses, which offer a little extra resilience and can be restored with scattered carrots. Its unusual combination of historical-warrior characters and arcade run-and-gun mechanics gives this Japanese release a very different tone from conventional military shooters.

games.title: Gauntlet II
games.description:
Atari Games' Gauntlet II (1986) expands the enormously successful four-player fantasy dungeon crawler without abandoning its immediate cooperative action. Players choose a Warrior, Valkyrie, Wizard or Elf, explore maze-like rooms, destroy monster generators and search for exits while their health drains from both attacks and the passage of time. Food, treasure and magic remain essential, and the constant scramble for resources creates a lively mix of cooperation and competition.

The sequel's major multiplayer change is the freedom to choose duplicate character classes. Fighters are identified by color rather than being locked to four distinct roles, prompting new digitized voice announcements such as 'Red Wizard'. Gauntlet II also introduces additional hazards, rotating maze layouts, reflected shots and the mischievous 'It' condition, which causes enemies to pursue one marked player until the curse is transferred or cleared. These additions make the labyrinths less predictable and add new reasons for players to jostle for position.

games.title: Gauntlet Dark Legacy
games.description:
Gauntlet Dark Legacy is Midway's expanded follow-up to Gauntlet Legends, reaching arcades in 2000 despite a 1999 copyright. It carries the classic series into a three-dimensional fantasy world where as many as four players battle through enemy-packed dungeons, collect treasure and level up persistent characters. The familiar Warrior, Valkyrie, Archer and Wizard are joined by the Knight, Sorceress, Dwarf and Jester, greatly broadening the party combinations.

Dark Legacy expands the original four realms with new areas including Ice, Town, Sky and Dream, plus additional characters and secret content. Combat is also richer, with faster and slower melee attacks that can be chained into combinations, individual turbo abilities and special team attacks performed by nearby players. Character passwords and progression encourage return visits, making the arcade cabinet function almost like a shared campaign game. Its sprawling content represents the most ambitious form of the late-1990s 3D Gauntlet formula.

games.title: Gauntlet Legends
games.description:
Gauntlet Legends (1998) revives Atari's classic dungeon-crawling series as a fully three-dimensional arcade adventure for up to four players. The heroes battle through fantasy realms to recover scattered Runestones and ultimately confront the demon Skorne. Each character has strengths and weaknesses, and familiar activities such as destroying monster generators, collecting treasure, finding food and escaping mazes remain central to the experience.

Its biggest departure from the original formula is persistent character growth. Defeating enemies and collecting valuables improves a hero's abilities, while passwords allow players to return to developed characters in later arcade visits. Large bosses, secrets and an interconnected quest give the game a clearer long-term objective than the endless dungeon survival of 1985's Gauntlet. Legends helped reintroduce cooperative fantasy action to arcades at a time when 3D graphics and progression systems were reshaping the medium.

games.title: Gauntlet
games.description:
Atari Games' Gauntlet (1985) is a landmark cooperative dungeon-crawler that brought four simultaneous players together around a single arcade cabinet. Each player takes a distinct fantasy hero: Thor the Warrior, Thyra the Valkyrie, Merlin the Wizard or Questor the Elf. From a top-down view, the party traverses labyrinths crowded with ghosts, grunts, demons, generators and other hazards, firing weapons, gathering treasure and trying to reach the next exit. Character classes differ in movement, combat power, armor and magic, making teamwork valuable but never compulsory.

The crucial resource is health. It drains continuously over time as well as from enemy attacks, while scarce food restores it. This creates a constant tension between exploration, fighting and racing fellow players for supplies. Potions destroy or weaken enemies, keys open doors, and monster generators must often be eliminated to keep the maze manageable. Digitized speech, including the iconic warning that a particular hero 'needs food badly', gives the cabinet a personality that became inseparable from the game.

Designed by Ed Logg, Gauntlet drew on tabletop fantasy adventures and Jack Palevich's earlier computer game Dandy. Its open-ended levels, class-based play and shared-screen action established a template for many later cooperative action RPGs and dungeon games. It also showed how four-player competition for limited resources could coexist with a common objective, a design tension that helped make Gauntlet an arcade institution.

games.title: Golden Axe - The Duel
games.description: Golden Axe: The Duel (1995, with a 1994 copyright) is Sega's one-on-one fighting-game spin-off of its fantasy beat-'em-up series. Released for the ST-V arcade system, it turns the world of Golden Axe into a tournament of warriors seeking a legendary magical axe said to grant its owner extraordinary power. Players select from a colorful roster of fighters and use punches, kicks and special attacks in two-dimensional duels rather than progressing through scrolling fantasy stages. Its anime-influenced sprites and sword-and-sorcery setting connect it visually with the original Golden Axe while its six-button competitive mechanics place it firmly in the mid-1990s fighting-game boom.

games.title: Green Beret
games.description:
Konami's Green Beret (1985), known in North America as Rush'n Attack, is a demanding Cold War-era side-scrolling action game. A lone commando infiltrates enemy bases to rescue prisoners, relying primarily on a combat knife at close range. Certain soldiers drop limited-use weapons, including flamethrowers, rocket launchers and grenades, but ammunition is scarce and the knife remains the player's main defense. The soldier can run, jump, crouch and climb ladders while avoiding armed guards, dogs, mines and other threats.

Each of the four principal areas culminates in a distinct enemy confrontation, and hesitation invites tougher opposition. The game's emphasis on pressing forward with a short-range weapon creates a particularly aggressive rhythm. Its memorable music, harsh difficulty and instantly recognizable knife attack made it a favorite among Konami's mid-1980s arcade action titles.

games.title: Gang Busters
games.description: Konami's Gang Busters (1988), released in Japan as Crazy Cop, is an overhead run-and-gun game featuring police officers pursuing a criminal gang. Moving through vertically oriented city streets with an eight-way joystick, players shoot at armed enemies and dodge incoming attacks, with support for two-player action. The Japanese presentation features an unusually colorful, green-haired hero, while the story centers on a bank robbery by the Dagrus gang and the officers' attempt to recover the stolen money. Its top-down viewpoint and simultaneous shooting place it among Konami's lesser-known late-1980s action games.

games.title: Grand Cross
games.description: Grand Cross (1994) is a futuristic video pinball game from Excellent System. Instead of a physical table, it depicts a science-fiction playfield populated by space-themed targets and enemies, with the player using a pair of flippers to redirect the ball, trigger scoring events and keep it from draining. The cabinet's multiple buttons support the game's virtual table controls. It is an unusual entry in the arcade pinball tradition, trading conventional bumpers-and-ramps presentation for an animated space-combat theme.

games.title: G-Darius
games.description:
Taito's G-Darius (1997) is a visually ambitious installment in the long-running Darius shooter series, replacing hand-drawn scenery with polygonal environments and gigantic mechanical sea-creature bosses. The player pilots the Silver Hawk through horizontally scrolling combat, upgrading forward missiles, bombs and protective equipment while choosing branching routes after major encounters. Although the graphics are three-dimensional, movement and firing remain on a two-dimensional plane, preserving the precise feel of earlier Darius games.

Its major gameplay innovation is the Capture Ball system. Instead of merely destroying enemies, players can seize many hostile craft and turn them into temporary allies, each with its own attack behavior. Captured enemies can also be sacrificed for powerful offensive effects, including the spectacular Alpha Beam. Bosses can fire opposing beams, leading to dramatic beam struggles that reward skilled timing. The decisions of which enemies to capture and when to expend them add a tactical layer to each stage.

With its enormous bosses, branching campaign, distinctive Zuntata soundtrack and elaborate visual effects, G-Darius stands as one of the most celebrated late-1990s arcade shoot-'em-ups. It marked the series' transition into 3D-rendered presentation without surrendering the mechanical identity that made Darius recognizable.

games.title: Mobil Suit Gundam Final Shooting
games.description: Mobile Suit Gundam: Final Shooting (1995) is Banpresto's rail-style light-gun shooter based on the Gundam science-fiction franchise. One or two players use gun controllers to blast successive waves of enemy mobile suits as the viewpoint advances through scripted battle scenes. Accurate shooting is vital both for destroying opponents and for intercepting their incoming missiles. Between major encounters, the player's mobile suit may receive repairs and a limited supply of more powerful secondary ammunition, while each stage ends in a large boss battle. Its combination of dedicated gun hardware, animated mecha and relentless target pressure turns Gundam's robot warfare into a physical arcade shooting challenge.

games.title: Gee Bee
games.description:
Gee Bee (1978) is a historically important Namco arcade release, designed by Toru Iwatani before he created Pac-Man. It combines the brick-breaking premise of Breakout with the scoring features of pinball. The player turns a rotary dial to position linked paddles, bouncing a single ball into block formations, bumpers and spinning targets arranged around the field. Clearing areas and lighting rollover symbols can raise the value of subsequent hits, so careful ball placement is more valuable than simply keeping it in play.

Gee Bee was Namco's first independently developed video game and grew from Iwatani's interest in building pinball machines. The hybrid approach continued in its successors Bomb Bee and Cutie Q. Though far less famous than Pac-Man, it is a revealing early work from a major arcade designer and an important milestone in Namco's transition from amusement rides and electromechanical attractions to video games.

games.title: Quiz Gekiretsu Scramble
games.description: Quiz Gekiretsu Scramble (1992) is a Japanese trivia game and a follow-up to Quiz Gakuen Paradise. Using four answer buttons, players respond to multiple-choice questions under time pressure against a school-themed presentation. The two title characters, Geki and Retsu, provide its distinctive identity, and the challenge revolves around recognizing correct answers quickly rather than mastering action-game controls. Like many Japanese arcade quizzes of the period, much of its appeal depends on familiarity with the language and cultural references used in the questions.

games.title: Gekirindan
games.description:
Taito's Gekirindan (1995) is a vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter whose storyline jumps through different eras of human history. A mechanized villain called Huge Boss steals a time machine in the year 3195, prompting pilots from different periods to pursue him across five stages. Players select from three unusual craft, including a futuristic jet, a space-capable helicopter and a modified old-fashioned aircraft, each with distinctive weapon behavior.

Combat mixes weapon upgrades, dense enemy formations and large bosses, with a structure closer to classic arcade shooters than the extreme bullet patterns of later Cave games. The changing historical environments and contrasting aircraft add variety to what is otherwise a demanding traditional shooter. Released on Taito's F3 hardware, Gekirindan is remembered for its polished pixel art, energetic soundtrack and time-travel theme.

games.title: Gekisou
games.description: Gekisou (1985), also exported as Violent Run, is a fast scrolling vehicle-action game from Eastern Corporation. The player drives an armored futuristic car through city roads filled with hostile vehicles and obstacles, attacking pursuers with onboard weapons and by ramming them. A jump maneuver helps evade road hazards or strike enemies from an unexpected angle. The aim is to survive the hazardous journey and reach a garage that leads to the next stage. Its combination of racing speed, armed combat and jumps places it midway between a driving game and a scrolling action shooter.

games.title: Gemini Wing
games.description:
Tecmo's Gemini Wing (1987) is a vertically scrolling shooter whose unusual weapon system distinguishes it from most contemporary aircraft games. One or two players fly futuristic fighters over landscapes overrun by bizarre, insect-like and organic enemies, dodging fire and shooting at enemies that emerge from the scenery itself.

Instead of simply upgrading a permanent main gun, players collect colorful 'gunballs' that trail behind their craft like a chain. Each stores a special attack or useful effect, and pressing the second button releases the frontmost one, making collection order as important as timing. Its vivid biological scenery and distinctive reserve-weapon mechanic give Gemini Wing a recognizable identity among late-1980s shooters.

games.title: Genix Family
games.description: Genix Family is an obscure 1994 arcade action game by NIX that adapts the basic formula of Mitchell's Pang to a comical Wild West setting. Players move across single-screen arenas, attacking bouncing hazards and trying to clear the playfield without being hit, in a style built around positioning and fast reactions. Its visuals borrow notably from other arcade fighting games, including graphics associated with Fatal Fury and Art of Fighting. With two-player support and three buttons, it is an unusual Korean-era variation on the bubble-bursting arcade formula rather than a conventional scrolling shooter.

games.title: Genpei ToumaDen
games.description:
Namco's Genpei ToumaDen (1986), later introduced to Western audiences as The Genji and the Heike Clans, blends Japanese history, folklore, and elaborate arcade spectacle. Its hero is the resurrected Taira no Kagekiyo, a warrior associated with the Genpei War, who journeys through a demon-haunted vision of medieval Japan to confront Minamoto no Yoritomo. Historical opponents such as Yoshitsune and Benkei share the stage with supernatural figures drawn from Japanese mythology.

What makes the game remarkable is its continual shift among three presentation styles: conventional side-scrolling platform action with small sprites, dramatic close-up sword fights featuring enormous characters, and overhead exploration. Torii gates lead to branching destinations, making route choice an important part of the quest. Kagekiyo must manage health, money, sword strength, and three sacred treasures, while a fall into certain pits can send him into a perilous underworld area.

Built for Namco System 86 and originally limited to Japanese arcades, Genpei ToumaDen remains especially distinctive for its striking giant-character scenes, expressive soundtrack, and willingness to mix different types of action in one adventure. The PlayStation compilation Namco Museum Vol. 4 finally gave the original arcade version an official release outside Japan.

games.title: Poker
games.description:
Greyhound Electronics' Poker, released in 1984, is more than a single video-poker program. Its cabinet houses a collection of electronic casino games, documented as Joker Poker, Blackjack, Horse Race, Rolling Bones and Casino Slots. Players use a dedicated eight-button panel to choose among card, dice, racing-bet and slot-style activities, turning one coin-operated machine into a compact electronic casino.

Multiple version 50.02 ICB program sets survive, some differing in the number of installed games. This unusual multi-game structure, at a time when most arcade cabinets ran only one title, is what makes Greyhound's Poker historically interesting.

games.title: Poker
games.description:
Greyhound Electronics' Poker (1984) belongs to a family of American coin-operated casino compilations, rather than being limited to a single draw-poker game. The documented selection encompasses Joker Poker, blackjack, horse racing, dice-based betting, and slot-style games, with the exact mix varying between related Greyhound boards. Players choose games and make wagers using a bank of physical buttons, with on-screen credits standing in for casino chips.

Greyhound marketed this equipment as amusement-only entertainment, without cash or prize redemption, in an era when countertop and barroom video games were increasingly borrowing casino themes. Some Greyhound systems accepted separate game boards to change their offerings. The surviving Poker ROM revisions also illustrate how the same basic Z80-based hardware could support different gambling-themed programs without requiring a dedicated cabinet for each.

games.title: Guardian
games.description:
Guardian, called Get Star in Japan, is a 1986 side-scrolling action game developed by Toaplan and published by Taito. Its hero is a powerful humanoid robot traveling across six science-fiction worlds, each culminating in a boss encounter. Movement, jumping, and crouching combine with separate punch and kick attacks, while pickups can provide stronger blows, temporary invulnerability, restored energy, or a ranged laser weapon.

Its continuous left-to-right fights recall Kung-Fu Master more than Toaplan's later shooting games. Punch power can be raised through collectible red orbs, but losing a life resets that advantage. The game is also a notable early graphic-design credit for Toaplan artist Kōetsu Iwabuchi. Despite its colorful planetary settings, it was reportedly a commercial disappointment, and surviving bootleg sets differ in their protection circuitry and reliability.

games.title: Golden Fire II
games.description: Golden Fire II is a 1992 two-player abstract strategy game from Topis Corporation, closely modeled on Ataxx. Opponents begin with pieces at opposite corners of a seven-by-seven board and compete to control the largest number of squares. Moving one space creates a new piece while jumping two spaces relocates an existing one; either way, adjacent opposing pieces are converted to the active player's color. The simple rules create a tactical contest in which a promising expansion can suddenly give an opponent a large counterattack. Its mature-themed presentation surrounds what is fundamentally a turn-based territory game.

games.title: Galaxy Force 2
games.description:
Sega's Galaxy Force II (1988) is a spectacular rail shooter built around the company's ambitious sprite-scaling technology. From behind a futuristic space fighter, the player flies through enormous fleets, planetary landscapes, and fortified tunnels, shooting enemies while controlling flight direction and speed. The open-space battles give way to twisting passages inside enemy bases, where avoiding the walls becomes as important as destroying targets.

Running on Sega's powerful Y Board, the game uses layers of rapidly scaling sprites to create an extraordinary illusion of three-dimensional flight. Its volcanic landscapes and massive spacecraft were showpieces for late-1980s arcade hardware. Galaxy Force II was also offered in deluxe motion cabinets, including a Super Deluxe unit with its own motor-control hardware. Although related to the original Galaxy Force, the revised second version became the better-known arcade edition and a memorable successor to Sega's Space Harrier and After Burner tradition.

games.title: Goalie Ghost
games.description: Bally/Sente's Goalie Ghost (1984) turns soccer into an unusual head-to-head goalkeeper duel. Each player sees the field from behind their own keeper, with the screen divided into upper and lower viewpoints. One to three balls move between the two goals, and players use trackballs to position their keepers and a jump button to intercept high shots. Blocking a ball also sends it back toward the opponent, so defense immediately becomes attack. Against a computer keeper or another person, the game is a compact test of positioning and reaction rather than a full-team soccer simulation.

games.title: Gain Ground

variants.title: Gain Ground (FD1094 317-0058-03?)
variants.version: (World, 3 Players, Floppy Based, FD1094 317-0058-03d Rev A)

games.description:
Gain Ground is one of Sega's most inventive late-1980s arcade action games. Released for System 24 in 1988, it places up to three players inside a malfunctioning computer's war simulation, where they must traverse 40 compact, overhead-view battlefields inspired by different historical eras. Each screen can be completed either by defeating every enemy or by carrying a warrior safely to the exit before time expires.

Its real strategic depth comes from the roster of 20 different character types. Warriors vary in speed, attack range, normal weapon, and special ability, so archers, gunfighters, and futuristic soldiers solve different tactical problems. Captives found on the battlefield can be rescued and added to the roster; fallen characters can sometimes be recovered in the same way, but anyone left behind at the exit is lost. The resulting need to choose who enters the field, who gets rescued, and when to retreat makes every apparent action puzzle a resource-management decision.

The original arcade version is especially recognizable for its tall, high-resolution System 24 display and simultaneous three-player support. Home versions on the Master System and Mega Drive adapted its unusual mix of shooting, planning, and rescue missions, but the arcade game's balance between cooperation and deliberate character selection remains its defining quality.

games.title: Ghoul Panic
games.description:
Ghoul Panic is a 1999 light-gun arcade game developed by Raizing and published by Namco, originally known in Japan as Oh! Bakyuuun. Using Namco System 12 hardware, it applies the rapid-fire shooting challenges of Point Blank to a whimsical haunted-house setting. Up to two players complete short timed tasks such as shooting a specified number of monsters, stopping incoming projectiles, or protecting small yellow cats from danger.

Accuracy matters as much as speed: hitting a protected cat or a dangerous 'bomb ghost' costs a life. Groups of minigames lead to monster-themed boss confrontations involving a vampire, a witch, and other comic horrors. Raizing's involvement gives this light-gun party game an unusual pedigree, connecting it to the studio better known for demanding scrolling shooters such as Battle Garegga.

games.title: Ghost Hunter
games.description: HanaHo Games' Ghost Hunter (1996) is a light-gun shooting-gallery game for up to two players. Contemporary catalogues compare it with Tickee Tickats, another arcade attraction built around hitting on-screen targets. Its ghost-shooting theme and gun-based competition make it distinct from story-driven light-gun adventures. It should not be confused with Kurokishi no Kamen, an unrelated Japanese computer role-playing adventure sometimes incorrectly associated with this title.

games.title: The Real Ghostbusters
games.description:
Data East's The Real Ghostbusters (1987) is an overhead, diagonally scrolling shooter based on the animated television series. Up to three players take the roles of the Ghostbusters and fight through ten timed stages filled with supernatural enemies. After shooting a monster, the player can use a second button to capture the ghost it leaves behind with a proton beam, creating a distinctive two-step attack-and-collect rhythm.

Stages include hidden weapon upgrades, bonus items, and boss encounters, while capturing enough ghosts can earn extra lives. Its multiplayer chaos and recognizable theme music helped make it a memorable licensed arcade adaptation. In Japan, the underlying game appeared as Meikyuu Hunter G, an earlier non-Ghostbusters-themed version with different characters and a different function for its second button.

games.title: Ghostlop
games.description:
Ghostlop is a colorful puzzle-action game developed by Data East for Neo Geo hardware and location-tested in 1996, but never commercially released. Players control ghost hunters Bruce and McCoy, who try to clear descending formations of colored ghosts by bouncing a ball upward from their position at the bottom of the screen. Combining ricochet aiming with the pressure of a falling-block puzzler, it punishes missed returns by adding more ghosts to the playfield.

Single-player and competitive modes build on the same simple concept, with the arrangement of ghosts and the direction of each rebound shaping the tactics. As a completed but unreleased Neo Geo project, Ghostlop is now best known through its surviving prototype and the game-preservation scene rather than original arcade distribution.

games.title: Ghouls'n Ghosts
games.description:
Capcom's Ghouls'n Ghosts (1988), known in Japan as Dai Makaimura, brought Sir Arthur back for a more elaborate and equally punishing quest. His goal is to battle through demonic landscapes and restore Princess Prin-Prin and the kingdom's victims to life. Arthur still loses his armor after one hit, fighting on in his underwear until another strike ends his life, and his leap retains the series' famously unforgiving commitment once launched.

This sequel expands combat by allowing upward firing and downward attacks while airborne. Hidden treasure chests can reveal new weapons or armor, including golden armor that enables powerful charged magic associated with the currently equipped weapon. Stages are packed with hostile terrain, enormous bosses, and enemies that require both memorization and precise timing. Completing the adventure once is not enough: a second journey is needed to reach the true ending.

Its lush graphics and detailed animation made it a showcase of Capcom's late-1980s arcade technology. A major success that received influential home conversions, notably on the Mega Drive/Genesis, Ghouls'n Ghosts helped cement the series' reputation for spectacle, memorable monsters, and fearsome difficulty.

games.title: Ghox
games.description: Ghox is Toaplan's unusual 1991 fantasy take on Breakout, built around an elaborate ball-and-paddle battle against the evil magician Jagula. One or two players use rotary paddle controls to deflect magical balls through bricks, monsters, and obstacles, clearing stages in a top-down view. Boss fights periodically interrupt the brick-breaking, and treasure chests can provide useful items and special effects. The combination of eerie fantasy art, two-player play, and a much more active battlefield makes Ghox stand apart from simpler Arkanoid-style games. It was also one of the comparatively few Toaplan titles that did not receive a contemporary home-console conversion.

games.title: Gigandes
games.description:
Gigandes is a horizontally scrolling science-fiction shooter created by East Technology, carrying a 1989 copyright and released in arcades around early 1990. Players pilot the Round-37 fighter through eight stages of alien forces and large bosses, but its weapon arrangement is much less conventional than that of most scrolling shooters.

Collected weapons are mounted around the ship in different directions, allowing firepower to be concentrated forward, backward, above, or below according to how an item is taken. The player can also change the craft's facing direction. Most unusually, a lost life does not immediately erase the current power-ups, although the accumulated loadout is reset at the start of the next stage. This system rewards planning where weapons are mounted rather than merely collecting every item that appears.

games.title: Gigas
games.description: Gigas is a 1986 arcade brick-breaker from Sega, represented here by a bootleg board set. Players use a rotary controller to move a paddle, rebound a ball, and clear formations of blocks in compact single-screen stages. The underlying game belongs to the wave of Breakout-style releases that followed Arkanoid, with straightforward ball control and collectible bonuses. This entry documents an unauthorized hardware version of Gigas rather than a distinct sequel; another known bootleg circulated under the name Oigas.

games.title: Gigas Mark II
games.description: Gigas Mark II is the 1986 follow-up to Sega's Gigas, preserved here in a bootleg arcade set. It retains the rotary-paddle, ball-and-brick formula of the original and offers a campaign of 32 block-breaking stages. Keeping the ball in play while finding angles through increasingly awkward block formations is the central challenge. Its historical interest lies partly in this unauthorized version of an otherwise modest Sega paddle-game sequel.

games.title: Giga Wing
games.description:
Giga Wing is a 1999 vertical shooter developed by Takumi and published by Capcom on CPS-2 hardware. Set in a fantastical world of advanced aircraft and ancient technology, it offers four pilots with different ships and weapon styles. The game is famous for filling its horizontally oriented arcade screen with enormous clouds of bullets and for awarding scores that can climb to astonishing numbers.

The key to surviving this apparent impossibility is the Reflect Force, a rechargeable defensive field that turns incoming enemy fire back against its source. A well-timed reflection not only clears a path but creates medals and scoring opportunities, making deliberate exposure to danger central to high-level play. Bombs offer a separate emergency escape. With its intense two-player action and unusually aggressive risk-reward scoring, Giga Wing helped establish the bullet-reflection style later revisited by Takumi in further shooters.

games.title: GI Joe
games.description:
Konami's G.I. Joe (1992) is a fast-moving rail shooter based on the animated toy franchise rather than a conventional side-scrolling beat 'em up. Up to four players select Duke, Snake Eyes, Scarlett, or Roadblock and advance automatically through battlefields controlled by the terrorist organization Cobra. The view follows the characters from behind, allowing players to maneuver, sweep aiming sights across the screen, and destroy soldiers, vehicles, and even parts of the scenery.

Rapid shooting, explosive attacks, and large boss machines give the game a spectacular arcade rhythm. Its pseudo-3D camera evokes Space Harrier and Konami's other dramatic action shooters, but the familiar characters and cooperative four-player format make it a particularly distinctive early-1990s license.

games.title: Gimme A Break
games.description: Gimme A Break is a 1985 overhead billiards game for Bally/Sente's SAC-I platform. Rather than simulating a cue with a joystick, it uses a trackball to aim and control shots, giving the cabinet an unusually physical relationship to the game of pool. Players can compete against one another or the computer, with the familiar distinction between solid and striped balls shaping the contests. Its top-down table and tactile input make it a small but notable example of Sente's experiments with trackball-based sports and competitive arcade games.

games.title: Ginga NinkyouDen
games.description: Jaleco's Ginga NinkyouDen (1987), roughly 'Galactic Chivalry Story,' is a side-scrolling action-platform game built around parodies of Japanese anime, manga, and popular culture. The hero fights his way through enemy-filled scenes in an effort to rescue his kidnapped girlfriend, moving, jumping, and attacking through a succession of comic encounters. Its appeal lies less in a straightforward historical or science-fiction setting than in the exaggerated characters and pop-culture references scattered through the action. Released in Japan, it remains an unusual example of how closely some arcade games drew on contemporary Japanese media jokes.

games.title: Ganbare Ginkun
games.description:
Ganbare Ginkun is Tecmo's outrageous 1995 collection of short competitive minigames, released only in Japanese arcades. Up to two players control crudely drawn stick figures through an escalating sequence of bizarre challenges, from dodging hazards to timing cannon shots and attempting increasingly absurd feats. Each task has a simple objective and a tight time limit, with failure costing a life and a successful player influencing the next event.

Its deliberately crude cartoon look conceals a surprising variety of timing and reaction tests. The game's grotesque and occasionally adult humor made it particularly difficult to reissue on later platforms. Its central character also gained an afterlife as the Doodle monster in Tecmo's Monster Rancher series, making this odd arcade release part of a much better-known lineage.

games.title: Gionbana
games.description: Gionbana is a 1989 Japanese adult-themed hanafuda arcade game from Nichibutsu. Instead of a standard mahjong match, players use a mahjong-style control panel to play a traditional Japanese flower-card game against female opponents. Winning progresses through character encounters and reveals suggestive illustrations. Its combination of hanafuda rules, dedicated tabletop-style controls, and mature presentation places it within Nichibutsu's late-1980s line of adult amusement games.

games.title: Gekitoride-Jong Space
games.description: Gekitoride-Jong Space is a 2001 Japanese Namco System 10 compilation developed by Metro, combining two puzzle games that use mahjong tiles rather than traditional mahjong hands. In GekiToride, players select matching tiles or number sequences in groups of three to remove them before time expires. Jong Space moves the same idea onto a rotating three-dimensional cube, changing the way hidden and visible tiles must be considered. The joystick and several buttons select and manipulate tiles, making this a timed pattern-recognition puzzle collection rather than a conventional wagering mahjong game.

games.title: Gladiator
games.description:
Gladiator, developed by Allumer and published by Taito in 1986, is a distinctive sword-fighting action game also known in Japan as Ougon no Shiro. Players guide the armored Great Gurianos through a dangerous castle, blocking flying weapons and other hazards before entering one-on-one duels against hostile warriors. The joystick controls movement and shield height, while three attack buttons deliver sword blows at high, middle, or low levels.

Combat depends on finding openings in an opponent's guard and stripping away pieces of armor rather than simply depleting a conventional health bar. The variety of defensive postures gives the duels an unusually deliberate pace for an arcade action game. Its armor-damage effects also vary by region: the American Gladiator edition removes some nudity present in Japanese releases. Allumer later revisited this combat style in Blandia.

games.title: Gladmort
games.description: Gladmort is a dark-fantasy run-and-gun action platformer developed by ChipsOnSteroids and published by PixelHeart for the Neo Geo MVS platform in 2024. Inspired by classic arcade action-platformers such as Ghosts'n Goblins, players battle through undead legions using medieval weaponry and armor upgrades.

games.title: Glass

variants.title: Glass (ver 1.1, Break Edition, checksum 49D5E66B, Version 1994, set 1)
Glass (ver 1.1, Break Edition, checksum D419AB69, Version 1994, unprotected, Korea)

games.description: Glass is a 1994 adult-themed single-screen action game designed by OMK and distributed by Gaelco, related to the earlier Splash! and also represented by the title Super Splash. Its gameplay follows Splash!'s single-screen picture-revealing concept, asking players to uncover concealed imagery while avoiding hazards and working against a time limit. Safe routes and playfield coverage matter more than conventional enemy elimination. The 1994 'Break Edition' sets include different revisions, and some regional versions replace the original adult illustrations with censored artwork.

games.title: Golden Crown
games.description: Golden Crown is a 1997 Dutch-market video-slot game made for the BFM/ELAM gambling platform. Its single-player, six-button cabinet uses a game-card program on a 6809-based system rather than a conventional cartridge or arcade action board. The surviving Dutch set is identified by its game-card number 95-752-011, while related Golden Crown Hopper versions show how payout hardware and regional requirements affected the same underlying amusement-machine family.

games.title: Golfing Greats
games.description: Golfing Greats is Konami's 1991 arcade golf game, featuring perspective views of the course with camera pans and zooms that convey the path of each shot. Up to four players choose among golfers with different strengths and compete in either stroke play or head-to-head match play across 18 holes. Shot planning requires weighing each character's distance and accuracy rather than simply selecting the strongest swing. Match play also introduces special longest-drive and nearest-the-pin contests, creating extra opportunities to win bonus balls. The game's distinctive presentation offers a more theatrical alternative to straightforward overhead golf simulations.

games.title: G-LOC Air Battle
games.description:
G-LOC: Air Battle is Sega's 1990 combat-flight arcade game, continuing the company's tradition of spectacular pseudo-3D action established by After Burner. The player pilots a high-performance jet through timed missions, identifying targets and firing machine guns and guided missiles against hostile aircraft, ships, and ground forces. The action is primarily viewed from inside the cockpit, occasionally switching viewpoint to emphasize the motion of the fighter.

Its title refers to 'G-force induced loss of consciousness,' an apt theme for a game celebrated as much for its cabinets as for its aerial combat. Sega produced the extraordinary R360 version, which could rotate the seated player through full loops to simulate aerobatic maneuvers. The sense of motion, rapid perspective changes, and specialized flight controls made G-LOC a major attraction in high-end arcades even as conventional upright versions offered a less physically demanding experience.

games.title: Gallop Racer 2 Link HW
games.description: Gallop Racer 2 Link HW is a linked-hardware variant of Tecmo's 1997 horse-racing sequel. It retains the series' three-dimensional jockey view and race-timing gameplay, in which players steer their mounts, manage pace, and use the whip strategically to compete for position. The linked configuration emphasizes racing against another connected cabinet rather than changing the underlying sport or presenting an entirely new game. It belongs with Gallop Racer 2 rather than the original Gallop Racer, which did not offer the sequel's expanded head-to-head arcade competition.

games.title: Gallop Racer
games.description: Gallop Racer is Tecmo's 1996 three-dimensional horse-racing arcade game. Players ride a racehorse from a jockey's perspective, controlling direction and maintaining speed by rhythmically working the cabinet's racing control, with a whip button for extra encouragement. Its arcade appeal lies in judging the pace and timing of a race, staying clear of rivals, and knowing when to make a final push for the finish. The title launched an extensive series of horse-racing games that later explored more elaborate horse management and breeding on home platforms.

games.title: Gallop Racer 2
games.description: Gallop Racer 2, released by Tecmo in 1997, develops the company's jockey-perspective horse-racing game with updated three-dimensional presentation and a more competitive arcade format. Players guide their mounts through races, preserving momentum and timing bursts of speed while maneuvering around other horses. Its most important change from the first Gallop Racer is support for two-player versus racing, giving the physical racing controls a direct head-to-head purpose. It later appeared in a linked-hardware configuration designed for connected arcade units.

games.title: Gallop Racer 3
games.description: Gallop Racer 3 is Tecmo's third three-dimensional horse-racing arcade game, released in 1999. Players compete as jockeys rather than driving vehicles, trying to keep their horses at an effective pace and choose the right moment to accelerate past rivals. It follows the original Gallop Racer and its two-player-oriented sequel, continuing the series' distinctive attempt to turn professional horse racing into a cabinet-based arcade sport. The emphasis remains on race positioning and timing rather than an overhead management simulation.

games.title: Ghostmuncher Galaxian
games.description: Ghostmuncher Galaxian is an unusual 1981 multi-game bootleg combining unauthorized versions of Pac-Man and Galaxian on one arcade board. Operators select between the maze game and the fixed-screen space shooter through a DIP-switch setting rather than a normal in-game menu. Its Pac-Man derivative changes ghost names, colors, and sounds, while its Galaxian game runs noticeably faster than the original. Associated with distribution in Australia and New Zealand, this board is a revealing example of early arcade operators and manufacturers combining familiar hits when official machines were difficult to obtain.

games.title: Guided Missile
games.description: Guided Missile, also known as Missile-X, is a 1977 target-shooting arcade game associated with Taito and Midway. The player launches missiles toward targets traveling horizontally across the upper screen, using simple directional controls to position shots and scoring as many hits as possible within a 90-second session. Its combination of launch timing and moving-target prediction predates the later wave of missile-defense games. The spare graphics and short fixed-duration challenge place it firmly in the transitional years between electromechanical shooting attractions and the more complex video shooters of the 1980s.

games.title: Gunbarich
games.description: Gunbarich is a 2001 Psikyo arcade game that combines brick-breaking action with shooting-game hazards. Players maneuver a flipper to keep a pink ball or puck in motion and break all the blocks in a stage before the timer expires. Unlike a straightforward Breakout imitation, the flipper can also reflect enemy bullets back at the attackers, turning incoming danger into an offensive weapon. Losing the ball or running out of time means failure, and aiming rebounds becomes increasingly important as hazards accumulate. The game is a playful Gunbird spin-off starring Marion, making its blend of paddle control and shooter combat particularly appropriate to the series.

games.title: Ghosts'n Goblins
games.description:
Capcom's Ghosts'n Goblins (1985) is one of the defining arcade platform games of its era and the origin of the long-running Makaimura series. The knight Sir Arthur ventures into a demon-infested world to rescue Princess Prin-Prin from Astaroth, battling zombies, flying demons, armored monsters, and enormous bosses. The game mixes side-scrolling and vertical platforming sections with a notoriously punishing system in which one hit removes Arthur's armor, leaving him in his underwear, and a second hit kills him.

Arthur can throw a succession of weapons, including lances, knives, and axes, but jumping requires careful commitment: unlike many later platform heroes, he cannot freely redirect himself in midair. Enemies often appear in unpredictable positions, and reaching the apparent ending only begins the second half of the challenge. Players must complete the whole game twice, using the required special weapon on the final confrontation to achieve the genuine ending.

Created before the arcade action-platform formula was fully standardized, Ghosts'n Goblins became a major international success and inspired a succession of sequels and home conversions. Its graveyard opening, relentless Red Arremer demons, and almost comically fragile hero remain some of Capcom's most enduring arcade images.

games.title: Ghosts'n Goblins - Knight Artoria Edition

Enhanced variants add fluid crouching and smooth ladder-climbing mechanics.

games.description: Ghosts'n Goblins - Princess Prin Prin Edition is a 2026 sprite and gameplay modification of Capcom's 1985 arcade action-platformer Ghosts'n Goblins (and its Japanese counterpart Makaimura) created by GoodLuckTrying (Wolfric) and Poody. Players control Princess Prin Prin on a quest to rescue Sir Arthur while battling enemy sprites redrawn as monster girls. The family covers World, US, and Japanese revisions alongside Enhanced Gameplay variants with fluid crouching and smooth ladder climbing.

games.title: Go 2000
games.description: Go 2000 is a Korean tabletop arcade game released around 2000, associated with the flower-card tradition of Go-Stop. This Korean card game developed from Japanese hanafuda but uses its own combinations and quicker scoring conventions. The cabinet presents the card contest on screen with dedicated controls rather than depicting a platform or action game. Documentation for this particular release is limited, but its connection to Korean Go-Stop places it among the region's electronic adaptations of traditional card games.

games.title: Goal! Goal! Goal!
games.description: Goal! Goal! Goal! is a colorful 1995 soccer game from Visco for SNK's Neo Geo MVS. Players choose from 28 national teams and compete in an abbreviated World Cup-style tournament, progressing from early fixtures to knockout matches. Short games keep the pace high, and holding the shoot button charges a powerful shot that can dramatically change a scoring chance. Its bright oversized players and arcade-oriented rules favor quick attacks over an elaborate football simulation. Notably, the title was released on Neo Geo arcade hardware without a corresponding original AES home-cartridge version.

games.title: Godzilla
games.description: Banpresto's Godzilla (1993) is a Japanese arcade action game built around Toho's famous giant monster. Players control Godzilla alone through seven stages, first trampling city structures and military forces as civilians flee, then facing an opposing monster in a side-view duel. These confrontations resemble fighting games, with attacks and positioning deciding the victor before the clock expires. The alternation between mass destruction and one-on-one kaiju combat recreates two familiar sides of the films: Godzilla as an unstoppable urban threat and Godzilla as a battling monster hero.

games.title: Go Go! Mile Smile
games.description: Go Go! Mile Smile, originally Susume! Mile Smile, is a 1995 maze-action game from Fuuki that recalls Stern's Anteater. Players guide a long-reaching character around intricate fields of pellets, collecting them in uninterrupted chains to build increasingly valuable scores while avoiding hazards. Its colorful presentation adds unusual entry points, boss encounters, and lively music to a classic maze-clearing idea. The scoring incentive for continuous collection gives even seemingly simple passages a route-planning challenge.

games.title: Goindol
games.description: Goindol is a 1987 Korean-developed brick-breaking game from SunA Electronics, related to Arkanoid but featuring several unusual playfield devices. Players turn a dial to position a paddle, rebound a ball through blocks, and avoid letting it escape the bottom of the screen. Angled rebound surfaces near the paddle change the ball's trajectory, while three special numbered blocks can be aligned to trigger bonus rounds. Across a lengthy succession of stages, these devices add elements of puzzle timing and pinball-style deflection to the familiar brick-breaking formula.

games.title: Gokujyou Parodius
games.description:
Konami's Gokujyou Parodius (1994), also known as Fantastic Journey, is the riotously inventive arcade sequel to Parodius Da! and a comic offshoot of Gradius. Players choose from eight wildly different pilots, ranging from the Vic Viper and TwinBee to penguins, octopuses, and absurd human or animal characters riding unlikely vehicles. Each has a distinctive loadout that parodies the serious military science fiction of conventional scrolling shooters.

Weapons use a Gradius-style power meter activated by collecting capsules, while color-changing bells borrowed from TwinBee provide an additional risk-reward system. Its seven horizontally scrolling stages transform familiar shooter patterns into visual jokes, from oversized amusements to casino-themed scenery and deliberate references to rival games such as R-Type. Two-player participation adds alternate character appearances. With its lavish sprite work, irreverent humor, and demanding bullet patterns, Gokujyou Parodius is one of the more celebrated examples of Konami turning its own arcade heritage into a parody.

games.title: Gold Bug
games.description: Gold Bug is a 1982 maze-action game from Century Electronics for its modular CVS arcade system. The player digs through soil, collects gold and treasure, and fills trucks at the bottom of the playfield while avoiding wandering monsters. Some enemies become vulnerable under particular conditions, and releasing a dangerous roaming bug can wipe out monsters but also harm the player. This mixture of tunneling, collecting, and indirect attacks places Gold Bug alongside early Dig Dug-style games, with its own emphasis on manipulating threats rather than simply shooting everything on sight.

games.title: Gold Medalist
games.description: Gold Medalist is SNK's 1988 multi-event athletics game, released in connection with the Seoul Olympics. Up to four players compete across nine events including sprinting, hurdles, swimming, long jump, high jump, discus, gymnastics, boxing, and relay running. Each discipline has its own timing or button-pressing challenge, favoring quick adaptation and determined arcade competition rather than a detailed sports simulation. Heavily influenced by Konami's Track & Field tradition, it packages a complete miniature athletics meeting into a single cabinet.

games.title: Golden Axe
games.description:
Golden Axe (1989) is one of Sega's defining fantasy beat 'em ups, designed under the direction of Makoto Uchida, who had previously worked on Altered Beast. The kingdom of Yuria has fallen under the rule of Death Adder, and three adventurers set out to defeat him: Ax Battler, an axe-wielding barbarian; Tyris Flare, an Amazon warrior skilled in fire magic; and Gilius Thunderhead, a dwarf whose modest magical ability is offset by his combat strength. The arcade game blends classic sword-and-sorcery imagery with the accessible side-scrolling brawling that had become popular in the late 1980s.

Players slash, kick, grapple, charge, and jump-attack through waves of enemies, sometimes seizing rideable creatures that breathe fire or knock enemies aside. Each hero also has a distinct form of screen-clearing magic, fueled by potions taken from blue thieves encountered during and between stages. Deciding when to spend those limited resources adds an important tactical layer to the melee combat, especially in cooperative play.

Golden Axe became a major arcade favorite and an influential model for later fantasy brawlers. Its chunky character sprites, dramatic spells, enemy mounts, and memorable soundtrack helped establish a distinctive Sega identity. A successful Mega Drive/Genesis conversion introduced the game to a still wider audience and helped turn its world into a continuing series.

games.title: Golden Star
games.description:
Golden Star is a mid-1990s IGS video medal/slot machine with a dedicated six-button panel. Instead of a joystick-driven contest, the player interacts with a gambling-style reel interface, with physical payout hardware available on certain original boards. Its numerous surviving revisions and close relatives, including Golden Star Blue and Moon Light, demonstrate how widely the same basic slot architecture was reused and rethemed.

Much of the game's preservation history concerns reel graphics, color decoding and hopper operation, all essential to recreating a gambling cabinet accurately even when its gameplay is simpler than that of a conventional videogame.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Golgo 13
games.description:
Namco's Golgo 13 is a 1999 arcade sniper-shooting game based on Takao Saito's long-running manga about the assassin Duke Togo. Instead of the frantic spray of bullets common to light-gun shooters, the player uses a rifle-shaped controller to take carefully aimed shots during individual assassination assignments. Short comic-book story sequences introduce the missions, which combine two-dimensional artwork and three-dimensional target scenes.

Accuracy is the central measure of success: missing or striking the wrong target jeopardizes a mission, and the game tracks the player's performance as a professional marksman. The cabinet's specialized sniper-rifle presentation makes it a markedly different arcade experience from Namco's Point Blank or Time Crisis. Although its title carries a 1999 copyright, Japanese arcade release records place it in early 2000.

games.title: Golly! Ghost!
games.description:
Golly! Ghost! is Namco's remarkable haunted-house shooting attraction, copyrighted 1990 and released in Japan in 1991. Two players use light guns, nicknamed Zip and Zap, to shoot comic ghosts appearing in a Victorian-style house, with each short scene demanding enough points before time expires. Some targets are more valuable than others, encouraging fast, selective shooting rather than indiscriminate fire.

Its special attraction is a real miniature house inside the cabinet, complete with electrically operated doors and moving fixtures. A monitor and partially reflective glass make animated ghosts appear to inhabit the physical model. This hybrid of video projection, electromechanical effects, and light-gun shooting gives Golly! Ghost! an unusually tangible stage setting, and makes it one of Namco's most inventive arcade curiosities.

games.title: Gomoku Narabe Renju
games.description: Gomoku Narabe Renju is a 1981 Nichibutsu arcade adaptation of a traditional Japanese five-in-a-row board game. Two sides alternately place stones on the intersections of a grid, each aiming to create an unbroken straight line of five stones horizontally, vertically, or diagonally. The Renju variation adds restrictions on certain powerful opening moves, giving the apparently simple game a considerable strategic depth. A joystick and selection button replace physical stones and board, making this an early example of a familiar tabletop contest transferred to an arcade screen. It is unrelated to the territorial-capture game of Go despite sharing the style of board and pieces.

games.title: Gondomania
games.description:
GondoMania, known in Japan as Makyō Senshi, is Data East's 1987 vertical scrolling shooter with an unusual mixture of futuristic weaponry and mythic enemies. Players maneuver a flying craft through landscapes filled with dragons, soldiers, and hostile fortifications. Unlike many shooters, its rotary control allows the firing direction to be adjusted independently of movement, making threats from the side or rear part of the normal tactical challenge.

Defeated enemies drop money that can be spent on useful weapons and upgrades, while some stronger attacks have limited ammunition. This creates choices between improving firepower and conserving resources for later sections. Its combination of multidirectional aiming, shopping, and fantasy imagery makes GondoMania a distinctive alternative to the more straightforward vertically scrolling aircraft games of the period.

games.title: Vs. The Goonies
games.description:
Vs. The Goonies is Konami's arcade adaptation of its 1986 Famicom action-platform game, itself inspired by the 1985 adventure film. Players control Mikey through underground caverns, corridors, and dangerous hideouts, searching for his friends and the treasure associated with One-Eyed Willie. Each stage requires collecting keys hidden behind doors, with bombs used to open passages and reveal useful objects.

Mikey fights enemies mainly with kicks, although he can also obtain a slingshot. The maze-like stage layouts reward searching and remembering where doors and keys appear. While the Famicom original was not formally sold for the NES in North America, players there could encounter the game on Nintendo's Vs. arcade hardware, making this coin-operated edition an important route by which the first Goonies game reached Western audiences.

games.title: Gorf
games.description:
Gorf (1981), developed by Dave Nutting Associates and released by Midway, is one of the earliest major arcade shooters to present a sequence of substantially different game types rather than repeating a single formation. Players command a spacecraft in the defense against the Gorfian Empire, advancing through five missions that include Space Invaders-like ranks, Galaxian-inspired attacks, and a final confrontation with a vulnerable mothership.

The player's craft can maneuver in two dimensions across the lower part of the screen rather than simply sliding from side to side. A distinctive firing system allows a newly launched shot to replace the previous projectile, rewarding deliberate timing. More memorably, the cabinet uses synthesized speech to taunt the player and announce progress, giving its robotic enemy a personality unusual for 1981.

Gorf became a recognizable early-1980s arcade hit through its variety and theatrical presentation. Later home versions generally omitted the Galaxian-based mission because of licensing issues, making the complete five-stage original an important part of the game's historical identity.

games.title: Got-cha Mini Game Festival

variants.title: Pasha Pasha Champ Mini Game Festival

games.description: Got-cha Mini Game Festival, also distributed as Pasha Pasha Champ, is a 1997 Korean arcade party-game collection clearly inspired by Konami's Bishi Bashi series. Up to three players face a rapid succession of approximately twenty brief challenges that test reactions, timing, and speed. Instead of a joystick, each player relies on three large colored buttons, red, green, and blue, whose meaning changes with each minigame. Its fast turnover and easily understood contests made it well suited to quick multiplayer arcade sessions. The English edition is also known for unusually fast spoken instructions, reportedly recorded under tight timing constraints.

games.title: Voltage Fighter - Gowcaizer / Choujin Gakuen Gowcaizer
games.description:
Voltage Fighter Gowcaizer, called Choujin Gakuen Gowcaizer in Japan, is a 1995 Neo Geo fighting game developed by Technōs Japan. Its exaggerated superhero cast fights in a futuristic city surrounding the mysterious Belnar Institute, with character designs by anime artist Masami Ōbari. The flamboyant art, large special attacks, and transformations draw heavily on Japanese action animation.

Its defining mechanic is the Trade System: after defeating an opponent, the winner may take one of that fighter's special moves and incorporate it into their own arsenal. This adds a small element of long-term customization to the otherwise traditional one-on-one fighting ladder. Desperation attacks become available at low health, giving endangered players a chance to reverse a fight. The game later inspired an animated adaptation and remains a distinctive, short-lived branch of the Neo Geo fighting-game boom.

games.title: GP500
games.description: GP500 is a late-1990s arcade motorcycle-racing game in the tradition of Namco-style and Sega-style 3D circuit racers. It features licensed 500cc Grand Prix motorcycles from Honda, Suzuki, and Yamaha, with appearances by professional riders and courses including Jerez, Paul Ricard, and Suzuka. Players compete around the circuit rather than simply navigating a traffic-filled highway, making corner entry and throttle timing central challenges. It is a separate arcade title from the 1999 PC racing simulation that shares the GP 500 name.

games.title: Gals Panic II - Quiz Version
games.description: Gals Panic II: Quiz Version is an adult-themed variation of Kaneko's territory-revealing Gals Panic II. The central game remains a Qix-style challenge: players move around the field and claim sections of the concealed picture while evading hazards. This edition adds a special event triggered by collecting question-mark items. A female character then poses three rapid two-choice questions, with only a couple of seconds to answer each one. Correct replies award helpful power-ups, while incorrect answers accelerate the drain of the remaining time. The added quiz sequences distinguish this release from an ordinary graphical revision of Gals Panic II.

games.title: Golden Par Golf
games.description: Golden Par Golf is a 1992 arcade golf game developed by Incredible Technologies and distributed by Strata, closely related to the early Golden Tee Golf releases. It preserves the earlier games' accessible approach to controlling a golf swing, although the AdvanceMAME parent set is specifically the joystick-controlled version rather than the better-known trackball configuration. The principal new content is a set of three courses, Hilldale, Sherwood Links, and Lake Oaks Country Club. As a result, this edition is best understood as an expanded course selection for an established arcade golf formula rather than a fundamentally new simulation.

games.title: Ghost Pilots
games.description:
Ghost Pilots is a 1991 Neo Geo vertically scrolling shooter from SNK, set in a fictionalized World War II campaign. One or two players pilot armed seaplanes against enemy fighters, tanks, boats, and heavily defended military installations, fighting through large formations and boss encounters. The adventure branches between land-attack and air-combat routes, adding variety to the otherwise traditional overhead shooting action.

Before missions, players choose bomb types with different effects, including specialized weapons available on particular routes. Limited bomb supplies must be balanced against regular gunfire, while red-plane formations yield upgrades and bonuses. With its lengthy stages, military hardware, and prominent use of the Neo Geo's colorful sprite graphics, Ghost Pilots occupies a distinctive place among SNK's early MVS shooters.

games.title: GP Rider
games.description:
Sega's GP Rider (1990) brings Grand Prix motorcycle racing to arcade cabinets with specialized riding controls, including a two-player motion-style installation. Players negotiate high-speed bends against computer riders or a human opponent, trying to maintain momentum without losing control. The game uses a split-screen presentation even during single-player sessions and offers different ways to tackle its collection of racing circuits.

Its head-to-head format distinguishes it from the more solitary time-trial structure of many earlier bike racers. Coming from Sega during the company's period of elaborate driving and flight cabinets, GP Rider combines accessible competition with the physical sensation of steering a racing motorcycle.

games.title: Gradius III
games.description:
Gradius III (1989) is Konami's enormous, exceptionally demanding continuation of its landmark side-scrolling shooter series. Players pilot the Vic Viper against Bacterion forces through ten visually varied stages, from organic hazards and claustrophobic tunnels to a special high-speed, behind-the-ship navigation section. The familiar power-meter system returns, allowing collected capsules to be spent on speed, missiles, lasers, Options, and shields, with a much broader weapon selection than before.

Success depends on creating a powerful configuration while preserving a route through complex enemy patterns. Losing a life can leave the ship poorly equipped in situations that seem nearly impossible to recover from, and the arcade release offers no conventional continue option. The game's elaborate bosses and punishing difficulty have made it a favorite among dedicated shooter specialists rather than an easy introduction to the genre.

Released in Japan, Gradius III eventually reached a much wider audience through a considerably modified Super Nintendo version. The original arcade edition remains famous for the scale of its ambition and for pushing the traditional Gradius power-up formula to a particularly unforgiving extreme.

games.title: Gradius 4: Fukkatsu
games.description:
Gradius IV: Fukkatsu, or 'Gradius IV: Revival,' bears a 1998 copyright but reached Japanese arcades in February 1999. It returned Konami's long-running shooter series to the arcades with upgraded graphics, dramatic colored lighting, and a new succession of horizontally scrolling hazards for the Vic Viper. As ever, players collect capsules to advance a power meter and choose when to purchase upgrades before tackling increasingly dangerous stages and bosses.

Unlike Gradius III, this sequel removes the freely assembled edit-mode equipment list and instead offers six predefined weapon configurations. It also introduced a score-registration system using passcodes for an online ranking service, a noteworthy experiment for a traditional arcade shooter near the end of the 1990s. Its revised weapons and modern presentation give it an identity distinct from both the earlier arcade games and the console spin-offs.

games.title: SD Gundam Sangokushi Rainbow Tairiku Senki

variants.title: SD Gundam Sangokushi Rainbow Tairiku Senki (Japan)

games.description: SD Gundam Sangokushi Rainbow Tairiku Senki is a 1993 Banpresto side-scrolling run-and-gun game built around super-deformed Gundam mobile suits. Players advance through hostile stages, firing at enemy machines, jumping over obstacles, and collecting stronger weapons such as spread and homing shots. The colorful, large-headed robot designs contrast with the relentless combat and stage-by-stage action, which resembles a Gundam-flavored variation on Contra. It supports multiple players and was released for Japanese arcades rather than as a conventional console Gundam strategy game.

games.title: Grasspin
games.description: Grasspin is a 1983 maze-action game created by Zilec Electronics and distributed in Japan by Jaleco. Like Lady Bug, it lets players push movable walls to change the routes through a maze while avoiding pursuing enemies. The objective is to collect lettered flags in alphabetical order, with portable lifebuoys serving as escape aids. At the edges of the maze, a river provides an alternative route: a character equipped with a life jacket can jump in and ride the current to evade pursuers. Its shifting corridors, ordered pickups, and unusual river escape make it more than a straightforward Pac-Man imitation. The game is also linked to early British arcade developers who later became prominent in the home-computer industry.

games.title: Gratia - Second Earth
games.description: Gratia: Second Earth is a 1996 horizontally scrolling science-fiction shooter from Jaleco, developed for the company's Mega System 32 hardware. One or two players pilot aircraft through successive waves of enemy ships, ground defenses, and large mechanical encounters. The game is an example of the richly detailed, sprite-heavy shooting games that continued to appear in Japanese arcades late in the decade despite the growing dominance of three-dimensional graphics. Its 1996 release makes it one of Jaleco's later original arcade scrolling shooters.

games.title: Gravitar
games.description:
Atari's Gravitar (1982) is a demanding color-vector space shooter designed by Mike Hally that combines the momentum of Asteroids with the lunar-landing physics of Lunar Lander. Players steer a small ship between star systems, descend onto planets, and attack enemy defenses or reactors while contending with a persistent gravitational pull. Ship rotation, thrust, firing, and a combined shield/tractor beam are separate controls, and nearly every maneuver consumes precious fuel or risks a collision.

Planetary missions take place in enclosed caverns and surface landscapes where accurate piloting matters more than rapid shooting. Destroying a reactor triggers a tense escape, while collecting fuel and clearing hostile installations demand careful planning. There is little margin for error: even reaching the correct location can become a challenge when the ship is moving too quickly to turn or brake in time.

Known for its uncompromising difficulty, Gravitar showcased Atari's bright color-vector display and the appeal of sophisticated physics-based arcade challenges. Its design is an important bridge between the minimalist vector shooters of the late 1970s and the more involved action adventures that followed.

games.title: Gravitar
games.description: This Gravitar prototype preserves a developmental version of Atari's 1982 color-vector space shooter. The essential design is recognizable: a rotating and thrusting spacecraft travels between planets, descends into gravity-filled landscapes, and destroys enemy defenses while managing its fuel. The build belongs to the title's early development history rather than representing an unrelated sequel or new game mode. It is especially interesting for players comparing the surviving prototype with the finished arcade release and the evolution of Mike Hally's unusually demanding physics-based shooter.

games.title: Grand Champion
games.description: Grand Champion is a 1981 overhead racing game from Taito in the tradition of its earlier Speed Race titles. Players drive a red car through scrolling circuits, using a steering control, accelerator, and high/low gear shift to overtake computer opponents. Each stage starts from behind the field and challenges the player to finish among the leading cars. Weather and scenery affect the drive: storms make handling hazardous, darkness limits visibility, and other obstacles demand quick changes of direction. Its stage-based progression and environmental complications add variety to the straightforward early arcade driving formula.

games.title: Guardian Force
games.description: Guardian Force is a 1998 scrolling tank shooter from Success, released for Sega's ST-V arcade platform and later the Saturn. Unlike most vertically scrolling shooters, the player controls an armored vehicle with a turret that rotates independently through 360 degrees. The screen advances automatically through battlefields packed with enemies and large bosses, while power-ups modify the tank's available weapons. Keeping the turret aimed at threats coming from different angles gives the game its own rhythm, closer to a constantly moving multidirectional shooter than to a conventional aircraft game. Its limited arcade distribution helped make it a cult favorite among Saturn-era shooter enthusiasts.

games.title: Guardians / Denjin Makai II
games.description:
Guardians, also called Denjin Makai II, is a 1995 side-scrolling beat 'em up developed by Winkysoft and published by Banpresto. A sequel to Denjin Makai, it pits a choice of eight unusual fighters against gangs of enemies across large scrolling stages. Each character has an individual fighting style, with combinations of normal strikes, throws, aerial attacks, and energy-consuming special techniques.

Players can grab opponents simply by moving close, then choose between follow-up strikes and throws. Timing the final hit of a combo can also produce a different finishing move, while two-player combinations reward cooperation. Its broad roster, varied combat options, and elaborate animated attacks have helped make Guardians one of the more admired lesser-known beat 'em ups of the mid-1990s.

games.title: Sen Jin - Guardian Storm
games.description: Sen Jin: Guardian Storm is a 1998 vertically scrolling shooter from Korean developer Afega, related to its earlier Red Hawk. Players guide eccentric flying heroes and machines through waves of enemies, mixing traditional shooting with deliberately cartoonish imagery and folklore-inspired opponents. One available character is based on Sun Wukong riding a cloud. Many defeated enemies drop money rather than weapons, and players buy upgrades from a shop between stages. The scarcity of direct power-up drops makes resource management unusually important and contributes to the game's demanding difficulty. Several regional releases and retitlings circulated outside Korea.

games.title: Great Guns
games.description: Great Guns is a 1983 light-gun target shooter from Stern Electronics. One or two players aim physical guns at animated targets across a series of colorful shooting-gallery scenes, including circus, prehistoric, and fantasy settings. The objective is to hit as many targets as possible, with progress through the available scenes determined by shooting performance. Its constantly changing visual themes distinguish it from simpler fixed-range gun games. Some arcade installations also offered an operator-adjustable skill reward that returned a player's coin or token after reaching a specified score.

games.title: Green Beret
games.description: Green Beret is an early Irem arcade run-and-gun game released in 1980 on the company's M10 hardware. It uses a simple two-direction joystick and one action button, and belongs to a much earlier generation of action games than the famous Konami title with the same name. Surviving information about the gameplay is limited and early emulation records reported an incomplete ROM set, so its exact sequence of encounters and stage objectives are not well documented. Its historical significance is principally as a rare, early Irem military action game, entirely separate from Konami's 1985 Green Beret, known in North America as Rush'n Attack.

games.title: Gridiron Fight
games.description:
Gridiron Fight is Tehkan's 1985 top-down American football game, known in Japan as All American Football. Instead of direct control of an entire team, players use a trackball to guide the athlete nearest the ball, with the speed and direction of the roll influencing how quickly the character moves. A button releases or kicks the ball according to the ball carrier's movement, giving the game a physical, almost tabletop style of control.

The title was designed by members of the team that soon created Tehkan World Cup, another influential trackball sports game. Its cocktail-style cabinet and one-on-one competition made it part of Tehkan's distinctive mid-1980s approach to translating team sports into quick arcade matches.

games.title: Gridlee
games.description: Gridlee is an unreleased early-1980s arcade action game developed by Videa, the studio whose technology helped lead to the Bally/Sente arcade system.
