Players control a small, bottle-shaped character on a grid, collecting colored balls for points while firing at enemies passing overhead. Their shadows reveal where they are flying, and every enemy must be destroyed to clear a stage. The game was originally called Pogoz and received only limited field testing before being abandoned. Its survival is historically important because it preserves an obscure experiment from the company that would become part of Sente Technologies.

games.title: Grudge Match
games.description: Grudge Match is a 1989 professional-wrestling arcade game from Yankee Game Technology, unrelated to Bally/Sente's racing prototype of the same title. One or two players select from six exaggerated wrestlers and compete in no-holds-barred ring matches. A player must defeat an opponent three times before advancing to the next challenger, eventually seeking the world championship. Its arcade format also allows a defeated rival to request another match through a continue, preserving the spirit of a competitive grudge rematch.

games.title: Grand Tour
games.description: Grand Tour is a 1993 adult-themed falling-block puzzle game from IGS, modeled on the column-matching style of Sega's Columns. Players arrange descending groups of colored pieces to form matching combinations and clear the playfield before it fills. Completing levels rewards the player with photographs or illustrations of women, giving the otherwise conventional tile-matching contest a mature arcade presentation. Its main challenge remains the familiar mixture of quick placement and setting up chain reactions.

games.title: Grobda
games.description:
Grobda is Namco's 1984 arena-based tank shooter, built around an enemy vehicle that previously appeared in Xevious. Players command the nimble, screw-propelled Grobda through a succession of compact overhead battlefields, destroying hostile tanks while navigating obstacles and deadly crossfire. The title's 99 increasingly difficult 'battlings' favor quick positioning over long scrolling stages.

A temporary energy shield can prevent damage but must be used carefully. More importantly, destroying an enemy can trigger an explosion that catches neighboring tanks, sometimes eliminating several at once and sometimes threatening the player. These chain reactions give Grobda a tactical puzzle-like quality beneath its fast action. The reuse of a minor Xevious enemy as a playable hero makes it an early and rather unusual arcade spin-off.

games.title: Power Instinct 3 - Groove On Fight

variants.title: Power Instinct 3 - Groove On Fight (J 970416 V1.001)

games.description:
Groove on Fight: Gōketsuji Ichizoku 3 is an eccentric 1997 Japanese fighting game from Atlus for Sega ST-V hardware, belonging to the Power Instinct family. Set in a bizarre future and featuring distinctive character art by Range Murata, it replaces the earlier games' conventional confrontations with team-based battles. Players select two fighters and can tag between them, letting a recovering partner wait off-screen until needed.

The combat is memorably unconventional: fighters can pick up and throw defeated characters as projectiles, and various special systems support partner attacks and tactical switching. Veterans Oume and Otane return alongside an otherwise largely new cast. Its darker visual style and offbeat team mechanics make Groove on Fight one of the strangest entries in an already eccentric fighting series.

games.title: Ground Effects / Super Ground Effects
games.description: Ground Effects, also called Super Ground Effects, is Taito's 1992 three-dimensional Formula One-style racing arcade game. Drivers navigate high-speed circuits against a field of rivals, balancing acceleration and cornering while trying to reach the front. The game uses specialized racing controls and Taito's contemporary 3D-capable arcade hardware rather than a conventional overhead viewpoint. Official association with McLaren International gave the racing presentation an additional touch of motorsport authenticity. It belongs to the transitional generation of early-1990s arcade racers that emphasized simulated depth and fast camera movement.

games.title: Growl
games.description:
Growl, released in Japan as Runark, is Taito's beat 'em up about four wildlife rangers fighting an army of ruthless poachers. Although it bears a 1990 copyright, the game reached Japanese arcades in early 1991. The rangers battle through crowded side-scrolling stages, rescuing threatened animals and facing gangs equipped with knives, firearms, and other weapons. Players can seize dropped weapons, throw explosives, and use jump attacks to survive the large enemy crowds.

The game's conservation theme is unusually direct for a genre more often concerned with street gangs or kidnapped relatives. Some of its most memorable moments involve rescued animals retaliating against their captors. Growl could be configured for two or four players, making its big brawls especially frantic on multiplayer cabinets.

games.title: Grudge Match
games.description:
Grudge Match is an unfinished 1987 overhead racing game developed for Bally/Sente, associated with designer Owen Rubin and originally titled Race for Pink. Players race against one another for more than a finishing position: the winner can claim a vehicle part from the loser, making each contest a step toward improving the car. The surviving arcade prototype simplifies the car-upgrade mechanics that had been planned for a fuller release.

The abandoned design envisaged garage-based purchasing, improved tires, suspension, brakes, engines, and transmission, longer races, and even city police traffic enforcement. Although these ambitious additions were not completed, the surviving prototype is a fascinating record of an arcade racer that tried to tie competitive driving to persistent vehicle upgrades. It is unrelated to Yankee Game Technology's 1989 wrestling game also titled Grudge Match.

games.title: Selection (Version 40.02TMB) set 1
games.description:
Selection is a 1982 multi-game casino title from Greyhound Electronics, also identified as G.E.I. Rather than presenting a single arcade action game, it brings together a set of betting-oriented diversions on one screen. The preserved program contains separately labeled material for blackjack, poker, a dice game, slot-style play, and a game called Beat the Spread. A button-only control panel supplies the selections and betting commands.

Version 40.02TMB survives in two sets in arcade emulation. Its Z80 processor, horizontal monitor, and small library of interchangeable-looking casino programs make Selection an early example of the multi-game countertop approach that Greyhound continued to develop during the 1980s.

games.title: Grid Seeker: Project Storm Hammer
games.description:
Grid Seeker: Project Storm Hammer is a 1992 vertically scrolling shooter from Taito, presenting an alternate-history military conflict in the Middle East. Players select among modern-style aircraft including an F-14 fighter, attack helicopter, and stealth bomber, flying over battlefields packed with aircraft, armor, and heavy defenses. Its memorable feature is the pair of 'Grid' units accompanying the craft, which can catch incoming enemy bullets instead of merely dodging them.

Absorbed shots can be converted into offensive power, encouraging players to turn a defensive maneuver into an attack. The weapon and aircraft choices lend the game more variety than its apparently conventional military setting suggests. Released on Taito's F3 arcade hardware, Grid Seeker is also remembered for a strong soundtrack and as a comparatively overlooked early-1990s shooter.

games.title: Great Sluggers '94
games.description: Great Sluggers '94 is Namco's 1994 baseball arcade game for its NB-1 hardware, following the Japanese Great Sluggers from the previous year. This edition replaces the earlier Japanese league lineup with 28 American League and National League teams, bringing it closer to the expectations of North American players. Batting, pitching, stealing bases, and fielding use accessible joystick-and-button controls while retaining the familiar structure of a baseball contest. The game's player representation was licensed through the Major League Baseball Players Association, an important distinction from generic unlicensed arcade sports games.

games.title: Great Sluggers
games.description: Great Sluggers: New World Stadium is a 1993 baseball game from Namco and the first release on the company's NB-1 arcade hardware. Players choose among 12 Japanese professional baseball teams from the Central and Pacific Leagues, then compete through complete baseball innings using joystick-based pitching, batting, and base-running controls. Its style builds on Namco's long-running World Stadium and Family Stadium tradition, with colorful players and a brisk arcade interpretation of the sport. The following year's Great Sluggers '94 adapted the formula for a lineup of American baseball teams.

games.title: Grand Striker 2
games.description: Grand Striker 2 is a 1996 soccer arcade game from Human, following the earlier Grand Striker: Human Cup. It retains quick joystick-based football matches while expanding the selection of teams and improving the visual presentation. The sequel focuses on immediate arcade competition rather than elaborate management, offering players another opportunity to master passing, positioning, and goal scoring. Its stadium advertising even references Human's wrestling game Blazing Tornado, an unusual in-house promotional detail.

games.title: Grand Striker
games.description: Grand Striker is Human's 1993 arcade soccer game, also known as Grand Striker: Human Cup. Players progress through a short tournament of preliminary and knockout fixtures to claim the Human Cup, then face a special opponent, Sepia Dreams, for the ultimate Greatest Cup. Matches emphasize quick arcade football action with a joystick and multiple control buttons rather than long-term team management. A distinctive feature is its treatment of drawn matches: instead of automatically deciding the result through a penalty shootout, the arcade version can demand another credit to continue the contest.

games.title: Great Swordsman
games.description:
Great Swordsman is a 1984 one-on-one weapons fighting game developed by Allumer and published by Taito. Rather than choosing from fantasy warriors, players advance through three disciplines: Western fencing, Japanese kendo, and gladiator-style sword combat. The side-view duels use a two-direction joystick and three buttons for attacks at different heights, while careful weapon positioning can intercept an opponent's blow.

Victory comes from landing precise hits or forcing an opponent out of bounds, making spacing and timing more important than a flurry of attacks. Fifteen opponents are spread across the disciplines, with an arrow-blocking bonus challenge between sections. Its structured progression through distinct fighting styles makes Great Swordsman an interesting precursor to later weapon-based arcade fighters.

games.title: Trivia
games.description:
Greyhound Electronics' Trivia (version 1.02B) is a 1984 English-language coin-operated quiz game from the company's long-running tavern and countertop trivia line. Players respond to on-screen questions through dedicated answer buttons rather than a joystick, making factual recall, not reflexes, the focus. This version was later organized in MAME's collection as Questions Series 2, with surviving question material covering comics, television, sports, general knowledge, and entertainment.

The replaceable question sets were a practical feature for arcade and bar operators: fresh subjects could renew interest without requiring a completely different game. This is Greyhound's electronic quiz system, not the unrelated 1975 trivia machine sometimes mistakenly described in game databases.

games.title: Trivia
games.description:
Trivia (version 1.02C) is a 1984 revision of Greyhound Electronics' coin-operated, button-controlled quiz game. In MAME's later organization it corresponds to Questions Series 1, a collection of English-language questions covering science, general knowledge, sports, music, and movies and television. Players answer questions on screen, with the attraction coming from knowledge of popular culture and current affairs rather than animated action.

Several preserved variants carry different question ROMs, and some versions of the hardware support ticket dispensing. These alternatives document how Greyhound kept its bar and amusement-location machines supplied with fresh material. The version labels identify software and question-set differences, not an entirely new style of gameplay.

games.title: Trivia
games.description:
Trivia (version 1.03) is a 1986 entry in Greyhound Electronics' series of English-language arcade quiz machines. It is a dedicated question-and-answer game operated with a bank of buttons, rather than an action title with joystick controls. Surviving arcade listings also identify this release as Trivia 4, distinguishing it from the earlier 1.02 and 1.03a software families.

The horizontal Z80-based hardware and straightforward button interface suit the bar and countertop format for which Greyhound's trivia games were known. Individual questions and rule variations for this particular program revision are not well documented, so it is best understood as a preserved edition of the company's established electronic quiz format.

games.title: Trivia
games.description:
Greyhound Electronics' Trivia (version 1.03a) is part of its mid-1980s arcade quiz family, built around English-language questions answered with dedicated buttons. The standard game presents themed factual and popular-culture challenges, while the preserved versions differ substantially in which question ROMs are installed. The broader 1.03a family includes revised collections and alternate question packs, some of them intended for adult bar audiences.

This software family became a useful case study in arcade preservation because numerous apparently separate ROM sets were eventually reorganized by question series rather than by their original revision labels. It illustrates how the same coin-operated quiz platform could remain in service through changes of content, with little need to alter the physical controls or main hardware.

games.title: Golden Tee 2K
games.description: Peter Jacobsen's Golden Tee 2K is Incredible Technologies' 2000 entry in its enormously successful arcade golf series. As in earlier Golden Tee games, players select clubs and use a large trackball to control swing strength and direction, making each drive, approach, and putt a physical gesture. This edition adds three courses, Stone Valley, Sea Haven, and Coyote Run, giving returning players new hazards and greens to learn. Its easy-to-understand controls and turn-based competition reflect the formula that made Golden Tee a familiar fixture in bars and arcades well beyond the peak years of traditional coin-operated video games.

games.title: Golden Tee 3D Golf
games.description:
Golden Tee 3D Golf (1995) marked the breakthrough of Incredible Technologies' golf series in American bars and amusement venues. Moving to more powerful 32-bit hardware, it presented digitized golfers and a more polished version of the series' defining control scheme: the player rolls a trackball to swing, with the direction and force of the movement shaping each shot. The approachable controls concealed a game of careful club selection, positioning and putting, equally suited to casual rounds and competitive score chasing.

Professional golfer Peter Jacobsen advised the project and served as a model for its players. The game established the foundation that Incredible Technologies would refine through successive annual Golden Tee editions into 2001. AdvanceMAME includes several software revisions and Tournament sets, preserving the variations found in commercial cabinets.

games.title: Trivia
games.description: Grayhound Electronics' Trivia is a mid-1980s electronic quiz game designed for a button-operated arcade cabinet. Players answer questions drawn from installed question sets rather than navigating an action game, with the five-button panel providing the interface. This entry represents the Version 5 branch of Grayhound's trivia software, not the unrelated 1975 electromechanical Trivia machine sometimes mistakenly described in general game databases.

games.title: Trivia
games.description: Trivia (UK Version 5.07) is a 1986 British-market revision of Grayhound Electronics' arcade quiz game. Players select a question category and answer on-screen trivia using a five-button control panel. Preserved question ROMs include categories such as general facts, popular music, sport and horror, reflecting the localized subject matter of this edition. It is a revision of an electronic trivia platform rather than the much earlier tape-based quiz machine with which some database descriptions confuse it.

games.title: Golden Tee '97
games.description:
Golden Tee '97 continued Incredible Technologies' successful trackball golf formula with a new annual arcade edition, released in 1997. Players control the swing by rolling the trackball, making the speed and direction of the physical motion central to drives, approach shots and putting. Its digitized golfers and accessible, competitive rounds built on the 32-bit Golden Tee 3D Golf engine rather than reinventing the controls.

In addition to several standard revisions, the preserved arcade sets include a Tournament edition. The series' increasingly familiar combination of easy entry and demanding shot control helped make golf a fixture in bars and other venues that rarely specialized in video games.

games.title: Golden Tee '98
games.description:
Golden Tee '98 is Incredible Technologies' 1998 installment of its popular arcade golf series. It retains the tactile trackball swing introduced in earlier entries, challenging players to judge shot strength and direction over a full round instead of relying on a conventional joystick-and-button timing meter. Its 32-bit hardware continues to display digitized golfers and a course view suited to spectators as well as players.

The edition was offered in standard and Tournament software versions, and its multiplayer tournament format made it well suited to friendly competition in bars. Golden Tee '98 represents a yearly refinement of the established Golden Tee 3D design, not a completely new golf engine.

games.title: Golden Tee '99
games.description:
Golden Tee '99 (1999) brought three new courses to Incredible Technologies' established trackball golf series: Aspen Lake, Coconut Cove and Rancho Saguaro. As in the preceding editions, players roll the trackball to strike the ball, using the speed and direction of their physical swing to determine the shot. The contrasting settings add variety while retaining the familiar digitized golfers and competitive round-based play.

Built on the Golden Tee 3D Golf engine, this edition appeared in both ordinary and Tournament versions, including a Royal Edition Tournament variant. A small but memorable feature is the ability to call up an instant replay by tapping Start while the ball is still moving.

games.title: Golden Tee Classic
games.description:
Golden Tee Classic (2001) is one of the final installments in the long-running 32-bit generation of Incredible Technologies' golf games. Following Golden Tee 2K, it offers three additional courses, Mountain Springs, Anchor Cove and Scorpion Bend. Players still control every stroke with the series' distinctive trackball, turning a simple physical gesture into a test of distance, angle and precision.

Although the presentation and play have the recognizable feel of Golden Tee 3D Golf, the new courses provide different challenges for regular competitors. Its preserved ROM revisions also include alternative protection and board configurations, reflecting the commercial hardware's evolution near the end of this generation.

games.title: Golden Tee Golf
games.description:
Golden Tee Golf, developed by Strata and Incredible Technologies and appearing in arcades around 1989-1990, introduced one of the most enduring interfaces in coin-operated sports games. Instead of using only a button to set shot strength, its best-known cabinets let players roll a trackball to simulate a golf swing. The motion governs power and direction and makes every drive, chip and putt feel physically connected to the player's hands.

Courses and modes encourage both individual play and friendly competition, including conventional golf rounds and closest-to-the-pin challenges. Early arcade revisions also existed with joystick controls, a reminder that the series' now-iconic trackball was not its only original configuration. What began as a relatively modest golf title eventually grew into a lasting competitive arcade institution.

games.title: Golden Tee Golf II
games.description:
Golden Tee Golf II (1992) is the sequel to Strata and Incredible Technologies' original arcade golf game. It preserves the emphasis on choosing shots and guiding the swing through physical controls, but replaces the original selection of courses with four new ones. Different cabinet and ROM configurations support either trackball or joystick play, creating noticeably different ways to approach the same golf challenges.

Like its predecessor, the appeal lies in the tension between approachable controls and the fine judgment needed to shoot consistently low scores. It belongs to the early 8-bit era of Golden Tee, before the later 3D-branded games transformed the series' commercial reach.

games.title: GTI Club
games.description:
GTI Club: Rally Côte d'Azur (1996) is Konami's distinctive polygonal racer set in a compact French Riviera town, complete with steep streets, tight corners and opportunities for creative route finding. Players choose among small classic rally cars, including a Mini Cooper and a Renault 5 Alpine Turbo, with a faster supercar available under a special credit arrangement. Rather than confining the action to a rigid track, the environment offers alternate roads and shortcuts that reward experimentation.

The handbrake is especially important: sharp handbrake turns can save valuable seconds while navigating the narrow streets and reaching checkpoints. Three course variations change the route and challenge, with the medium course opening additional shortcuts and the difficult course mirroring the layout. Built for Konami's ambitious PowerPC-based Cobra arcade hardware, GTI Club helped bring an unusually open, playground-like approach to arcade racing.

games.title: 1000 Miglia: Great 1000 Miles Rally
games.description:
1000 Miglia: Great 1000 Miles Rally (1994) is Kaneko's isometric-style arcade racer inspired by the historic Mille Miglia endurance event, which ran between Brescia and Rome and back. Instead of contemporary formula cars, it showcases vintage racing machinery associated with marques such as Ferrari, Alfa Romeo and Mercedes-Benz. The viewpoint looks down diagonally on winding roads, emphasizing quick steering corrections and anticipation of corners.

Its fast, sprite-based presentation places it alongside the overhead rally games of the early 1990s, but its classic-car theme gives it a different personality. The arcade family includes alternate releases titled Evolution Model!!! and U.S.A Version!, preserving different regional and revised versions of the original racing game.

games.title: Mille Miglia 2: Great 1000 Miles Rally
games.description:
Mille Miglia 2: Great 1000 Miles Rally (1995) expands Kaneko's vintage-car racing formula with ten selectable cars and routes linked to the vehicle choice. Each short rally stage is a race against a 60-second limit: reach the finish quickly enough to continue, or use a credit to try again. The rapidly scrolling, overhead pseudo-3D scenery demands that players watch for on-screen warnings of hairpins, zigzags and other sudden changes of direction.

Arcade operators could configure the game for joystick-and-button controls or a steering wheel and pedals. The sequel also circulated as Great 1000 Miles Rally 2 USA, retaining its inspiration from Italy's historic Brescia-to-Rome endurance race. Its combination of classic vehicles, tight checkpoints and unforgiving cornering makes it a particularly demanding example of the genre.

games.title: Guardians of the 'Hood
games.description:
Guardians of the 'Hood (1992) is Atari Games' unusual three-player street brawler, combining the side-scrolling structure of a beat 'em up with the digitized human fighters and exaggerated motion familiar from Pit-Fighter. Players choose among Conner, Chief, Javier and Tanya, then fight through gang-controlled neighborhoods, subway areas and other city locations. Each guardian has distinct moves, can use or throw objects found along the way, and has access to a special projectile attack.

Between some street battles, the heroes return to a gym for sparring matches. Defeated gang leaders can be recruited and become playable characters, gradually enlarging the roster as the campaign progresses. The result is a curious blend of cooperative brawling and one-on-one fighting, culminating in the confrontation with the mysterious Mr. Big. Its digitized look and rough-edged presentation make it one of Atari's most recognizable attempts to move the Pit-Fighter aesthetic into a scrolling action game.

games.title: Gulf Storm
games.description:
Gulf Storm (1991) is a vertically scrolling military shooter by the South Korean developer Dooyong. Cast as an Allied commando during the Gulf War, the player changes vehicle according to the stage, fighting from a speedboat, helicopter or motorcycle against tanks, ships, aircraft and gun emplacements. Two players can tackle the action together, collecting weapon upgrades, faster-fire bonuses and limited-use bombs from defeated enemies.

According to the game's historical notes, Dooyong rethemed the project around the contemporary Gulf conflict during development. The resulting topical setting and varied vehicles distinguish it from many more conventional aircraft-only shooters. A Japanese version was distributed under license by Media Shoji.

games.title: Gulf War II
games.description:
Gulf War II (1991) is a Korean vertically scrolling shooter from Comad, set amid a fictionalized conflict in the Persian Gulf. The player pilots an armed aircraft through waves of military targets, enhancing its main gun with power-ups and using a limited supply of powerful bombs against especially dangerous formations. An eight-way joystick and two buttons supply the familiar control scheme.

Its development history is more unusual than its mechanics: substantial portions of the program were taken from Taito and Toaplan's Twin Cobra, while the graphics and theme were changed. Consequently, Gulf War II is best understood as an extensively reworked, unauthorized derivative of that earlier shooter rather than a wholly independent design.

games.title: Gulun.Pa!
games.description:
Gulun.Pa! is an unreleased 1993 Capcom puzzle-game prototype for the CPS-1 arcade system. The surviving build is a two-player-capable dropping-piece puzzle game controlled with an eight-way joystick and two buttons, but it is notably incomplete, with only a limited amount of playable content. The extant board is dated December 20, 1993, and contains unused material suggesting that additional stages or features were planned.

The program ROM also contains the English working title Piyo Piyo, although no complete English-localized graphics have been identified. Unlike Capcom's major CPS-1 arcade releases, Gulun.Pa! never received a commercial release, making it a rare record of an abandoned arcade puzzle project during the company's transition to more advanced hardware.

games.title: Gumbo
games.description:
Gumbo (1994), from South Korea's Min Corp., is an adult-themed falling-block puzzler closely related to Columns. Three symbols descend together, and the player shifts their position and order to create lines of at least three identical blocks horizontally, vertically or diagonally. New rows periodically rise from the bottom, adding pressure even when the falling pieces are being managed successfully.

Clearing blocks can remove bottom rows and advance a progress meter, while a limited helper converts the active piece into special blocks that clear matching symbols. Completing a stage triggers a timed sliding-picture bonus round. Its mixture of chain-reaction strategy, rising-board pressure and photographic or illustrated adult backgrounds distinguishes Gumbo from a straightforward Columns clone.

games.title: Gunbird
games.description:
Gunbird (1994) is Psikyo's whimsical fantasy shooter, exchanging military aircraft for a cast of eccentric adventurers flying broomsticks, gadgets and other unlikely machines. Five playable characters, including Marion, Ash and the robot Valnus, pursue the pieces of a magical mirror while battling pirates, mechanical monsters and elaborate bosses. Each character has a different main shot, charged attack and bomb, giving the same vertically scrolling stages a different rhythm depending on the selection.

The campaign mixes fixed later stages with early stages chosen in changing order, and clearing it opens a harder second loop. Its sharp enemy patterns and brisk boss encounters display the precision associated with Psikyo's shooters, while the character interactions and alternate endings add a comic-adventure personality. The arcade game became a cult favorite and established a series that continued with Gunbird 2.

games.title: Gunbird 2
games.description:
Gunbird 2 (1998) advances Psikyo's fantasy-themed shooting series with faster bullet patterns, eccentric characters and another quest involving magical treasures and elemental potions. Its arcade cast includes five principal playable characters, each bringing a different shot, charge attack and bomb to the vertically scrolling campaign. The first stages vary in order before the game advances into setpiece boss battles and a more difficult second loop.

A notable addition is medal chaining: collecting flashing 2,000-point medals in succession builds a separate chain, rewarding precise movement even when the screen is dangerous. Character combinations and post-campaign wishes affect the endings, adding replay value beyond high scores. The later Dreamcast conversion added Morrigan from Darkstalkers as a guest; that character is not part of the original arcade roster.

games.title: Gunbuster
games.description:
Gunbuster (1992), also known as Operation Gunbuster, is Taito's early first-person action shooter set in a futuristic city plagued by dangerous cyborg criminals. Unusually for its era, it combines a joystick for moving and strafing with a gun controller for aiming and turning, allowing players to navigate 3D arenas rather than simply shoot targets passing across a fixed screen. Its machines could support cooperative missions and competitive team battles across linked play positions.

Players hunt cyborg opponents through maze-like environments, using automatic gunfire and secondary weapons such as mines, lasers, fire and electricity. Different weapon properties, cover and movement are central to the battles. Released before first-person shooters became a dominant commercial genre, Gunbuster is an ambitious arcade experiment in combining gun-game spectacle with free-roaming movement.

games.title: Mobile Suit Gundam EX Revue
games.description:
Mobile Suit Gundam EX Revue (1994) is a Japanese one-on-one fighting game developed by Allumer and published by Banpresto. It brings the giant robots of Mobile Suit Gundam into a conventional side-view fighting format, with selectable mobile suits trading close-range strikes and special attacks under health-bar rules. The four-button controls and faster fighting engine reflect the influence of the early-1990s arcade fighting boom.

A notable addition is the MS-19 Dolmel, an original mobile suit associated with this game. EX Revue follows an earlier Gundam arcade fighter, making it an interesting step in the franchise's experiments with competitive fighting long before later 3D Gundam arena games.

games.title: Gun Dealer
games.description:
Gun Dealer (1990) is a Korean puzzle game by Dooyong that mixes falling-block action with the logic of poker hands. Playing cards enter a narrow vertical field, and the player shifts their position and cycles the cards in the active group to arrange combinations such as straights and flushes. Successful combinations are removed from the stack, making foresight and rapid recognition of card patterns more important than simply matching colors.

The game also features adult-themed intermissions between rounds, reflecting a common niche in Korean and Japanese arcade puzzle design of the period. Its use of cards rather than abstract shapes gives Gun Dealer an unusual identity among Tetris-inspired games.

games.title: Gundhara
games.description:
Gundhara (1995) is a top-down, vertically progressing action shooter published by Banpresto. Players choose either Jerry Scott or Jinn Ayakawa and fight through armed soldiers, robots and fortified enemy positions while rescuing kidnapped children. The story frames the mission as an attempt to stop a conspiracy involving brainwashing and a threatened world conflict.

Its brisk run-and-gun action uses an eight-way joystick, with gunfire, close-range kicks and special weapons. Weapons can be upgraded or exchanged for heavier firepower, and major bosses punctuate the stages. The two-player cooperative mode makes Gundhara particularly reminiscent of arcade commandos such as Ikari Warriors, although its presentation belongs to a later generation.

games.title: Gun Dealer '94
games.description: Gun Dealer '94 (1994) is Dooyong's follow-up in name to its earlier card-based puzzle game, but its matching mechanic uses colored, numbered blocks instead of poker hands. The player arranges pieces so that suitable groups disappear from the playfield, balancing the urge to clear blocks quickly against the risk of filling the board. It supports one or two players and was also released internationally under the title Primella, through an NTC license.

games.title: Gun Fight
games.description:
Gun Fight (1975) is Midway's influential two-player western showdown, adapted from Taito's Western Gun. Each player moves a cowboy around one side of a single screen, aims a revolver independently and tries to shoot the opposing gunfighter before time expires. Cacti, moving obstacles and ricochets off the screen edges complicate what would otherwise be a simple duel. The game's gun-grip controller gives aiming a physical quality very different from later one-joystick shooters.

One of the historically important distinctions of Midway's adaptation is its use of a microprocessor-based design where the Japanese original relied on discrete logic. The game became an early landmark in arcade character combat, with its unmistakable 'GOT ME!' message appearing when a cowboy is hit. It remains an unusually direct example of competitive video gaming from before the rise of maze games and scrolling shooters.

games.title: Gunforce 2
games.description:
Gunforce 2 (1994), also known as Geo Storm, is Irem's explosive sequel to Gunforce and an important precursor to the style later made famous by Metal Slug. Across five sprawling side-scrolling stages, soldiers Max and Lei battle troops, mutants and aliens amid collapsing structures and huge mechanical enemies. The characters carry two firearms at once, with overlapping fire directions, and can upgrade one of their weapons while keeping the other available.

Rescuing prisoners, collecting medals and commandeering motorcycles, walkers and other vehicles add layers to the action. Much of the spectacle comes from the enormous number of animated objects and destructible-looking battlefield setpieces on screen. Several members of Irem's development staff later helped create Nazca's Metal Slug, making Gunforce 2 a particularly revealing link between two generations of arcade run-and-gun design.

games.title: Gunforce - Battle Fire Engulfed Terror Island

variants.title: Gunforce - Battle Fire Engulfed Terror Island (World)
Gunforce - Battle Fire Engulfed Terror Island (Japan)
Gunforce - Battle Fire Engulfed Terror Island (US)

games.description:
Gunforce: Battle Fire Engulfed Terror Island (1991) is Irem's side-scrolling military run-and-gun game for one or two cooperating players. Soldiers advance through enemy-filled terrain, firing horizontally, upward or diagonally and swapping their unlimited-ammunition standard weapon for powerful but finite-use pickups such as a flamethrower or laser. The stages also feature vehicles that players can enter and use against enemy forces.

Time limits and destructible end-of-stage objectives keep the action moving, while the opportunity to climb aboard jeeps and helicopters introduces variety into the otherwise straightforward combat. Gunforce's mixture of foot soldiers, weapon pickups and military vehicles became much more elaborate in its 1994 sequel, Gunforce 2.

games.title: Gun & Frontier
games.description:
Gun & Frontier, also known as Gun Frontier (1990), is Taito's striking space-Western vertical shooter. On the distant colony planet Gloria, settlers fight back against the Wild Lizards, space pirates who have enslaved their population. The player's aircraft is shaped like a revolver, enemy machines evoke Wild West imagery, and power-ups appear as coins and gold bars, making the setting integral to nearly every detail of its visual design.

Destroyed enemies release dimes that improve the aircraft's main guns, while gold bars build the stock of increasingly powerful bombs. The six-stage campaign mixes airborne foes, ground installations and large mechanical bosses. Its elaborate presentation and deliberate pacing are particularly associated with designer Takatsuna Senba, and its Western motifs give it a lasting identity among Taito's early-1990s shooters.

games.title: Gunlock
games.description:
Gunlock (1993), known in Japan as RayForce and in some overseas releases as Galactic Attack, is Taito's dramatic vertically scrolling shooter built around attacking enemies at two different altitudes. The player's craft fires straight ahead at airborne targets while a separate lock-on system marks enemies far below; releasing the lock sends homing lasers at the selected targets. Managing both planes of combat is essential, because threats and scoring opportunities often occupy different depths of the battlefield.

Its seven stages move from orbital fighting to planetary installations and enormous mechanical bosses, with smoothly layered scrolling and cinematic transitions that give the impression of a continuous descent. The lock-on mechanic, powerful music and detailed pixel art made RayForce a celebrated late-era 2D shooter and the starting point for Taito's Ray series.

games.title: Gun Master
games.description:
Gun Master (1994) is Metro's unusual hybrid of a beat 'em up and boss-rush fighting game. Rather than progressing through conventional streets full of disposable enemies, one or two players confront specific major adversaries across fourteen stages. Most of the central stages can be tackled in a chosen order, giving the campaign an uncommon degree of freedom for an arcade action title.

The hero can punch, kick, throw opponents and fire a gun, combining close-quarters fighting moves with ranged attacks. Its side-view action and oversized bosses make Gun Master feel closer to a sequence of arcade fighting encounters than to a standard scrolling brawler.

games.title: GunNail
games.description:
GunNail (1993) is NMK's fast, vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter, distributed with Tecmo involvement. Players pilot a spacecraft accompanied by smaller support craft and collect weapons, bombs and upgrades while surviving dense attack patterns and bosses. The game introduces an unusual reward for risk: taking damage strips away shield sections but can improve scoring multipliers and available firepower.

The ship can therefore become more dangerous as it becomes more vulnerable, creating a constant tension between maximizing score and preserving a margin for error. Its support craft remain active even after the main ship takes a hit, adding to the tactical use of upgrades. GunNail has earned a following among shooter enthusiasts for this distinctive relationship between damage and power.

games.title: Gunpey
games.description:
Gunpey (2000) is Banpresto's arcade adaptation of the line-connecting puzzle concept named in tribute to influential designer Gunpei Yokoi. A five-column grid fills with fragments of diagonal and angled lines; players swap vertically adjacent cells to make an unbroken path connecting the left and right edges. Completed paths vanish, and extensions or branches built before they disappear can increase the score.

Unlike block-dropping puzzle games, Gunpey is about rearranging pieces already in the field while new material rises from below. That simple difference makes it a game of spatial planning and rapidly recognizing possible connections. The concept originated on Bandai's WonderSwan, a handheld associated with Yokoi's final hardware work, giving the arcade edition an unusually personal name and history.

games.title: Gun.Smoke
games.description:
Gun.Smoke (1985) is Capcom's celebrated Wild West vertical shooter, following a lone gunslinger through bandit-filled towns, canyons and other frontier settings. The screen scrolls steadily upward as the hero moves around obstacles and defeats gunmen, animals and stage bosses. Its famous three-button firing system lets the player shoot left-diagonally, straight ahead or right-diagonally, with combinations producing additional firing patterns. Learning to aim while maneuvering is the game's defining skill.

Barrels conceal useful pickups, including boots for speed, ammunition upgrades, rifles for longer range and even a horse that can absorb damage. At the end of each stage awaits a wanted outlaw wielding a distinctive weapon, from boomerangs to knives. The mixture of Commando-like forward momentum and independent directional fire made Gun.Smoke a memorable arcade favorite, and its controls remain distinctive among Capcom's mid-1980s action games.

games.title: Gururin
games.description:
Gururin (1994) is Face's inventive Neo Geo puzzle game, featuring pairs of brightly dressed people descending into a circularly organized playfield. Instead of rotating the falling pair, the player rotates the entire arena clockwise or counterclockwise, repositioning its inhabitants so that three people of the same color line up and disappear. This reversal of the usual falling-block control scheme makes each move feel like a small spatial puzzle.

Matches can cascade as people settle into new positions, and a two-player mode pits competitors against one another. Published by SNK for the Neo Geo MVS, Gururin is a distinctive example of developers experimenting with the Columns formula rather than merely changing the pieces' appearance.

games.title: Guts n' Glory
games.description:
Guts n' Glory is an unreleased 1989 Atari Games prototype organized as a collection of military-themed shooting challenges. Players choose among mini-games such as Antiaircraft, Bombing, Depth Charge, Machine Gun and Submarine, each demanding that a quota of targets be destroyed within a time limit. Steering, weapon selection and firing vary with the scenario rather than forming a single continuous scrolling campaign.

The preserved prototype includes two-player support and work by Atari veterans Ed Logg and Dave Theurer. Its collection of short war-game situations makes it an unusual piece of arcade history from a period when coin-operated action games increasingly emphasized larger, continuous adventures.

games.title: Guts'n
games.description:
Guts'n (2000) is a highly unusual action-puzzle game developed by Kouyousha's Nova Project Team for Kaneko's Super Nova arcade hardware. Instead of manipulating falling blocks from outside the board, players control a small nurse moving directly around the playfield. She injects medicine into virus blocks to push them into position, creating horizontal groups that disappear when matched. The game therefore combines the spatial planning of a tile-matching puzzle with active movement inside the puzzle itself.

Released late in the commercial life of the Super Nova system, Guts'n supports two-player play and is among Kaneko's less widely seen arcade releases. Its medical theme and hands-on virus-pushing mechanic make it notably different from conventional Dr. Mario-style falling-piece games.

games.title: Guwange
games.description:
Guwange (1999) is Cave's sumptuous bullet-heavy shooter set in a supernatural version of Japan's Muromachi period. Rather than piloting aircraft, players select from three people possessed by powerful shikigami spirits and move on foot through villages, shrines and demon-infested landscapes. The story follows their attempt to escape the fatal curse of possession by confronting the god Guwange and his servants.

Its defining mechanic is the controllable shikigami, which can attack away from the character's usual firing direction and turn enemy bullets into a source of scoring opportunities. The screen scrolls not only vertically but also sideways and diagonally as the route winds through elaborate scenery. Deliberate movement, dense projectile patterns, occult imagery and complex scoring have made Guwange one of Cave's most admired and visually distinctive arcade shooters.

games.title: Guzzler
games.description:
Guzzler (1983) is a strange maze-action game in which a small, thirsty firefighter creature attempts to extinguish flames that spawn pursuing monsters. The player moves through fixed-screen mazes, drinking from puddles to refill a limited supply of water and spraying liquid to defeat enemies and put out the fires required to clear each stage.

Each shot drains the character's supply, but an emptier character also moves faster, creating an unusual trade-off between offensive ability and mobility. Occasional special drinks refill the supply and temporarily freeze the fires. Its comical premise and carefully balanced water-management mechanic make Guzzler more than a conventional Pac-Man-style maze chase.

games.title: Guerrilla War
games.description:
Guerrilla War (1987) is SNK's overhead run-and-gun successor in spirit to Ikari Warriors. One or two commandos advance through enemy territory, attacking soldiers, tanks and fortifications while freeing captives tied to stakes. Guns, grenades, ammunition pickups and vehicles keep the combat varied, while inadvertently shooting prisoners costs points. Rotary-style aiming lets players fire independently of their movement direction on the original arcade controls.

The Japanese release, Guevara, explicitly cast the two players as Che Guevara and Fidel Castro during the Cuban Revolution; the overseas story was rewritten to avoid those politically contentious identities. This unusual localization history sits alongside a demanding, action-packed design that became one of SNK's recognizable late-1980s arcade shooters.

games.title: Galactic Warriors
games.description:
Galactic Warriors (1985) is Konami's remarkably early one-on-one robot fighting game. Players select one of three machines, Samson, Gaea or Poseidon, each with different weapons and reach, then fight a succession of robotic opponents on planets and space installations. The side-view battles involve positioning, guarding and using both armed and unarmed attacks, while the environments can incorporate different gravity conditions.

A joystick and separate attack, guard and weapon-selection buttons produce a surprisingly elaborate combat system for 1985. Distinct playable fighters, health bars, projectiles and aerial defense anticipate features that would become common during the fighting-game boom years later. Its mechanical cast and science-fiction stages give this historical curiosity a personality all its own.

games.title: Gypsy Juggler
games.description: Gypsy Juggler (1978) is an early Atari arcade game built around the simple physical challenge of juggling. A character at the foot of the screen catches and tosses falling eggs or balls, attempting to keep multiple objects aloft as additional ones enter from a chute above. The number of simultaneous objects rises, and allowing too many to fall ends the round. The game turns a single recognizable skill into a deceptively demanding test of timing and positioning.

games.title: Gyrodine
games.description:
Gyrodine (1984), developed by Crux and also known as Buzzard, is a vertically scrolling helicopter shooter. Players pilot an armed helicopter across coastlines, military positions and other terrain while attacking airborne aircraft and ground targets. The challenge is continuous rather than story-led, demanding accurate positioning and steady fire against helicopters, tanks, bunkers and fighter planes.

The game is notable in Japanese arcade history for its links to former Orca staff and the development lineage that later fed into Toaplan. Its straightforward air-to-ground action captures an early stage in the evolution of the vertically scrolling military shooter.

games.title: Gyruss
games.description:
Gyruss (1983) is Konami's spectacular variation on the fixed-screen space shooter, designed by Yoshiki Okamoto after his work on Time Pilot. Instead of flying along the bottom of the screen, the player's craft travels around a circular track at the edge, firing inward toward the vanishing point. Waves of enemy ships spin into view, gather near the center and then break formation to attack. This unusual perspective gives the action a sensation of plunging through a space tunnel.

The voyage progresses through the Solar System toward Earth, with a number of 'warps' to complete between planets. Chance Stages offer opportunities for bonus points, and a double-shot upgrade rewards accurate attacks on special targets. The circular movement takes practice, but once mastered it allows dramatic sweeps around enemy formations.

Gyruss is also remembered for its energetic electronic arrangement of Bach's Toccata and Fugue in D minor and a sound presentation more elaborate than many contemporary shooters. Its combination of music, pseudo-3D visual motion and distinctive controls earned it lasting status as one of the most original early-1980s arcade space games.

games.title: Hacha Mecha Fighter

variants.title: Hacha Mecha Fighter (unprotected)
variants.version: (19th Sep. 1991, unprotected, bootleg Thunder Dragon conversion)

games.description:
Hacha Mecha Fighter (1991) is NMK's brightly colored, horizontally scrolling cute-'em-up. Instead of military pilots, the two players control flying animal heroes, an otter and an aardvark, confronting improbable waves of other cartoon creatures. Weapons fire an assortment of playful projectiles, and upgrades help the tiny aircraft survive increasingly crowded stages.

A limited special attack enlarges the player's character and boosts offensive power, producing an especially comic contrast with the normally small protagonists. Beneath the cuddly appearance lies a demanding shooter that depends on careful positioning and knowledge of enemy patterns.

games.title: Hachoo!
games.description:
Hachoo! (1989) is Jaleco's side-scrolling martial-arts beat 'em up set in a fantasy version of China. The hero sets out to prevent a creature sealed inside an ancient statue from breaking free, fighting the guards and monsters that stand in the way. An eight-way joystick and attack and jump controls allow kicks, punches and evasive moves, while some enemies can be hurled directly toward the screen.

Two players can cooperate through the stages, facing opponents that use rocks, fire and hand-to-hand techniques. Its stylized Chinese scenery, unusual enemy-throwing animation and supernatural premise distinguish it from more conventional urban brawlers.

games.title: HAL21
games.description:
HAL21 (1985) is an SNK vertically scrolling aerial shooter in the mold of Xevious. The player pilots a fighter over enemy-held territory, using separate attacks against airborne craft and ground defenses marked by a targeting sight. Success depends on watching both kinds of targets while dodging heavy fire as the landscape scrolls downward.

A memorable feature is its large multipart enemies: damaged sections can break away and then reattach, making major encounters more elaborate than a simple single-sprite target. HAL21 is an early example of SNK's attempts to combine air-to-air and air-to-ground combat, preceding the company's better-known Alpha Mission shooters.

games.title: Halley's Comet
games.description:
Halley's Comet (1986) is Taito's vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter built around an unusual defensive objective. The player protects planets of the Solar System from the comet and the hostile alien forces accompanying it. Enemies that slip past the player's spacecraft threaten the planet below, so survival alone is not enough: allowing too many attackers through can end the mission even with ships remaining.

Each planetary campaign combines waves of enemy craft, a confrontation with larger defenders and an attack into the comet itself. The visible planetary-damage pressure encourages aggressive interception, while the scrolling action and weapon pickups retain the familiar immediacy of a classic mid-1980s shooter. Its appearance in the year of Halley's Comet's celebrated return gave the theme a particularly timely resonance.

games.title: Hammer Away
games.description: Hammer Away is an unreleased vertical shooter developed by Santos for Sega's System 18 hardware. Exhibited at Japan's 1991 Amusement Machine Show, it was cancelled before a general arcade release, although a working prototype later survived. The game belongs to the wave of military-themed scrolling shooters that followed the success of titles such as Raiden, and its preserved build provides a rare opportunity to see a Sega-published project that never reached commercial cabinets.

games.title: Hana Awase
games.description: Hana Awase is an early-1980s Japanese arcade adaptation of hanafuda, the traditional flower-card game. Produced by Seta as a video-based medal game, it uses a dedicated panel of selection buttons instead of an action joystick. Its appeal lies in recognizing flower-card combinations and choosing which cards to play or collect, offering traditional tabletop play in coin-operated electronic form rather than an action or puzzle game.

games.title: Hanagumi Taisen Columns - Sakura Wars

variants.title: Hanagumi Taisen Columns - Sakura Wars (J 971007 V1.010)

games.description:
Hanagumi Taisen Columns: Sakura Wars brings Sega's Columns puzzle mechanics into the cast and setting of Sakura Taisen, or Sakura Wars. Players arrange falling groups of three colored gems, making vertical, horizontal or diagonal matches to remove them and create chain reactions. The competitive focus pits familiar Sakura Wars characters against one another, using the match-making system as the basis for head-to-head play.

Released for Sega's ST-V arcade hardware in the late 1990s, the game combines a well-established falling-piece puzzle formula with the strong character appeal of Sega's theatrical adventure series. It is especially notable as a Sakura Wars spin-off designed around quick arcade matches rather than story-driven role-playing.

games.title: Hana Kanzashi
games.description: Hana Kanzashi is a Japanese hanafuda medal game released by Dynax in December 1996. Its name means 'ornamental flower hairpin'. Players use traditional flower-card combinations as the basis for a coin-operated tabletop game, choosing cards through a specialized button interface rather than controlling a moving character. This title belongs to Dynax's later generation of games built around sophisticated blitter-driven graphics and Japanese traditional card games. Its elaborate operator menus and dedicated hardware are part of its appeal to collectors of unusual Japanese medal machines.

games.title: Hana no Mai
games.description: Hana no Mai (1988) is a Dynax hanafuda arcade game with an unusual time-travel framing. Players compete in Japanese flower-card matches against computer opponents, with the card game integrated into scenes from different periods rather than presented as an entirely abstract tabletop simulation. The title translates as 'Flower Dance', and one revised release is known as Hana Kochou. It exemplifies the narrative embellishments Japanese arcade developers brought to traditional card games in the late 1980s.

games.title: Mahjong Hana no Momoko gumi
games.description: Mahjong Hana no Momoko gumi (1988) is a Japanese adult-themed mahjong game played against computer-controlled female opponents. It follows the recognizable structure of Japanese mahjong, with players drawing and discarding tiles to construct winning hands, while victories advance the character encounters and reveal additional artwork. Unlike action-oriented arcade releases, its challenge depends on tile recognition, hand construction and the risk of committing to particular combinations.

games.title: Hana to Ojisan
games.description: Hana to Ojisan (1991) is a Japanese adult-themed video medal game based on hanafuda, the traditional flower-card deck. Its card play draws on the familiar matching and set-building traditions of koi-koi, while its arcade reward presentation includes revealing character artwork. Developed for a specialized Japanese coin-operated audience, it belongs to a different branch of tabletop arcade games from the more common electronic mahjong machines.

games.title: Hanaroku
games.description: Hanaroku, literally 'Six Flowers', is a 1988 Japanese hanafuda medal game developed by Alba. The play is based on matching the seasonal flower illustrations on Japanese hanafuda cards and assembling scoring combinations, presented through a dedicated ten-button arcade control panel. It is a specialized tabletop attraction rather than a joystick-driven action game, and its medal-machine format reflects the Japanese tradition of adapting established card games for coin-operated entertainment.

games.title: Hangman
games.description:
Hangman (1984), produced by Status, translates the familiar pencil-and-paper word-guessing game into an arcade machine. Players identify a hidden word by choosing letters; every incorrect choice adds another element to the drawing of a condemned figure. Guess the word before the drawing is completed to win, or allow too many incorrect choices and the round ends.

With difficulty choices ranging from elementary-school to high-school vocabulary, Hangman emphasizes knowledge and deduction rather than reflexes. The simple button-operated interface shows how arcade manufacturers adapted recognizable educational and parlour games to coin-operated play during the early 1980s.

games.title: Hang-On
games.description:
Hang-On (1985) is Sega's pioneering motorcycle racing game and one of the major achievements of designer Yu Suzuki. Viewed from directly behind the bike, players race through five consecutive stages, leaning into bends, overtaking traffic and reaching checkpoints before the timer expires. Crashing into rivals or roadside objects sends the rider flying and wastes precious seconds. Its smooth, rapidly scaling scenery creates a convincing sense of speed without conventional polygonal graphics.

The famous deluxe cabinet is as important as the software: players physically straddle a motorcycle-shaped machine and lean their bodies to steer, twisting a handlebar throttle to accelerate. More conventional upright controls were also available. Combined with Sega's 16-bit Super Scaler technology, the ride-on setup made Hang-On an amusement attraction as much as a video game.

The game's commercial and technical success helped establish Sega's line of spectacular motion-oriented racers, leading toward Space Harrier, Out Run and Super Hang-On. It remains a defining example of how specialized arcade hardware could deliver an experience impossible to reproduce fully with an ordinary home controller.

games.title: Hang-On Jr.
games.description:
Hang-On Jr. (1985-1986) adapts Sega's famous motorcycle racing formula to the more modest System E arcade hardware. Players steer a superbike down a winding pseudo-3D course, overtaking riders and reaching checkpoints before time runs out. The action retains the original's behind-the-bike viewpoint but uses simpler visuals and conventional cabinet controls instead of the renowned full-size leaning motorcycle.

A new hazard is the presence of puddles, which slow the bike, and the course is divided into novice and advanced sequences of stages. Rather than a wholly new sequel, Hang-On Jr. is best regarded as an accessible, reduced-hardware interpretation of the original arcade hit.

games.title: Hang Pilot
games.description:
Hang Pilot (1997) is Konami's unusual 3D hang-gliding arcade simulation, designed around a physical control setup that imitates the posture and handling of a real glider. Players choose from three pilots and courses, then launch into the air and guide their craft through checkpoints while avoiding terrain and obstacles. The controls involve leaning or positioning the body on supports and manipulating a handlebar assembly to affect direction and speed.

The dedicated machine could use two displays, one showing the view ahead and another emphasizing the terrain below, reinforcing the sensation of suspended flight. Its uncommon subject and specialized cabinet make Hang Pilot stand apart from Konami's better-known racing games; the challenge is controlling a glider's path, not simply accelerating along a road.

games.title: Hangzo
games.description:
Hangzo is a surviving prototype of an unreleased 1992 side-scrolling ninja action game, associated with Hot-B and Data East arcade hardware. Players can select Hangzo, Kotaro or Kasumi and fight through platforming stages with different melee weapons and ranged attacks. A rope-like movement ability gives the heroes an additional way to navigate the environment.

The known build is dated January 1992 and was never released commercially. Its combination of sword-fighting and platform traversal gives it a distinct identity among the action-game experiments preserved only through prototype ROMs.

games.title: Hard Drivin'
games.description:
Hard Drivin' (1988-1989) is Atari Games' landmark polygonal driving simulator, created to make handling a sports car feel more physical and demanding than in conventional sprite-based arcade racers. Players take on a closed road network with two interconnected routes: the faster Speed Track and the notorious Stunt Track, featuring a full vertical loop, steep slopes and a drawbridge jump. Failure often produces a dramatic instant replay from an external camera instead of merely resetting the car without ceremony.

Its elaborate cockpit controls include a steering wheel, pedals and, on suitable cabinets, manual shifting with a clutch. Steering feedback, simulated vehicle dynamics and obstacles such as oncoming traffic make learning the car part of the experience. The game also introduced the intimidating Phantom Photon computer opponent as a high-score challenge.

At a time when most arcade driving games used scaled 2D graphics, Hard Drivin's filled 3D environment and vehicle simulation were technological showpieces. The result could be less forgiving than a typical arcade racer, but its ambition influenced the development of later polygonal driving games and established a memorable identity for Atari's simulation-focused design.

games.title: Hard Dunk
games.description:
Hard Dunk (1994) is Sega's energetic three-on-three street basketball game for System Multi 32 hardware. Its dedicated double-screen cabinet supports up to six human players, three per side, with the remaining team members controlled by the computer when fewer people join. The view follows the action around a shared basket, emphasizing fast moves, quick shots and direct competition.

Each match is played to eleven points, and the game features seven stages with different locations. The twin-screen cabinet and unusually large player count made Hard Dunk a social arcade sports attraction rather than a standard one-person basketball simulation.

games.title: Hard Hat
games.description:
Hard Hat (1982) is Exidy's distinctive combination of maze chase and word puzzle, designed by Larry W. Hutcherson Sr. Players guide a carpenter through a grid of scaffolding while dodging pursuing hammers and whirlwinds. The objective is not merely to survive: the carpenter must rearrange letters and scaffolding to spell words such as EXIDY and HARD HAT.

The game uses four-direction movement and can be played alternately by two people. Marketed as an early educational coin-operated title, it offers an unusual example of arcade designers combining action-game hazards with a concrete spelling objective. It shares hardware roots with Exidy's Pepper II but has a markedly different gameplay emphasis.

games.title: Hard Head 2
games.description:
Hard Head 2 (1991) continues SunA's eccentric platform-game series with another rescue mission for its round-headed heroes. Players cross eight side-scrolling stages filled with bizarre animal and fantasy enemies, traps and end-stage bosses. The heroes can attack with a changing assortment of weapons, including a club, mace and bubble gun, and collect upgrades while working toward the kidnapped heroine.

Where the original Hard Head emphasized bubbles and football-goal exits, the sequel leans further into varied weapon use and obstacle-course action. Its bright graphics and strange character designs retain the Korean series' offbeat, cartoonish personality.

games.title: Hard Head
games.description:
Hard Head (1988) is SunA's oddball Korean platform game, superficially reminiscent of Super Mario Bros. but full of its own eccentric ideas. One or two players guide round-headed characters through sixteen side-scrolling stages, breaking overhead blocks with their heads and using a bubble gun to trap bizarre enemies. Captured enemies can be finished by jumping on them, while hidden blocks and power-ups encourage exploration.

A particularly unusual objective is ending stages by finding a soccer ball and kicking it into a goal. The combination of bubble-based attacks, strange monsters and football imagery makes the game difficult to mistake for any of its inspirations. Classical music excerpts, including works by Tchaikovsky and Mozart, add another unexpected note to its presentation.

games.title: Hard Yardage
games.description:
NFL Hard Yardage (1993) is Incredible Technologies' licensed American football game, designed for up to four participants and featuring digitized players and a broadcast-inspired presentation. Players run offensive and defensive plays in fast arcade matches, with the NFL license providing an authentic professional-football frame for the action.

The game features announcing by Wayne Larrivee, known for his work broadcasting Chicago Bears games. Its combination of recognizable league branding, multiplayer competition and television-like sound and visuals made it part of the early-1990s wave of arcade sports games aimed at groups rather than solitary players.

games.title: Harem
games.description:
Harem (1983) is an unusual desert-themed maze-action game in which a sheikh tries to bring women from tents and passing transport back to the chambers of his harem. Enemies patrol the playfield, and the player can defend himself by throwing stones while moving between the tents and the lower part of the screen. Hazards include hostile guards and a particularly dangerous giant pink snake.

Produced by I.G.R. and shown at an Italian amusement exhibition, Harem is a strange example of early-1980s arcade design, combining rescue-and-return objectives with maze movement and a conspicuously period-specific fantasy setting.

games.title: Harley-Davidson and L.A. Riders
games.description:
Harley-Davidson and L.A. Riders (1997) is Sega's free-roaming motorcycle game set around a stylized Los Angeles. Players select from five Harley-Davidson models, including the Fat Boy, Panhead and Sportster, and navigate streets and freeways to reach successive destinations before the timer runs out. Rather than completing laps on a traditional circuit, the game emphasizes route choice, traffic avoidance and maintaining momentum between checkpoints.

The dedicated motorcycle-style controls include handlebars and, for manual riding, gear selection. Landmarks and road layouts give the city a sightseeing quality, while collisions consume valuable time. Running on Sega's Model 3 hardware, the game combines the spectacle of late-1990s 3D racing with a touring-oriented structure that anticipates later open-route arcade driving games.

games.title: Hasamu
games.description:
Hasamu (1991) is an Irem solitaire-style mahjong-tile puzzle with a twist on traditional tile matching. Players remove matching tiles when they satisfy positional rules, such as being adjacent or aligned appropriately in a row. Certain pieces can be moved, adding a spatial-planning element absent from the familiar fixed-layout mahjong-solitaire format.

The challenge is to plan removals without isolating tiles needed later, making Hasamu a compact strategy puzzle rather than a conventional Japanese four-player mahjong simulation.

games.title: Adventure Quiz 2 Hatena Hatena no Dai-Bouken

variants.title: Adventure Quiz 2 Hatena Hatena no Dai-Bouken (Japan 900228)

games.description:
Adventure Quiz 2: Hatena? no Daibouken (1990) is Capcom's Japanese quiz-adventure sequel. Instead of presenting only an isolated series of questions, it places the player on an adventure through seven maps, with trivia challenges determining progress. The character Hatena leads the journey, and guest enemies from Kamen no Ninja Hanamaru appear along the route.

The game later appeared on PC Engine Super CD-ROM² alongside Adventure Quiz: Capcom World. Its map-based framing and Capcom character connections distinguish it from conventional stand-alone quiz machines, even though understanding the Japanese questions remains central to play.

games.title: Hatris
games.description:
Hatris (1990) is an inventive falling-object puzzle game designed by Tetris creator Alexey Pajitnov. At a busy hat factory, pairs of hats descend toward six mannequin heads. Players arrange the different styles so that five identical hats stack together and can be shipped away for money. Unlike the rigid blocks in Tetris, hats have different silhouettes and stack in different ways, making spatial judgment important.

As production advances through the factory's shops, more hat varieties enter circulation and the towers become increasingly difficult to manage. Occasional flame items can eliminate hats or entire stacks, providing emergency relief. The combination of familiar falling-piece tension with unusual shapes and a playful industrial theme makes Hatris one of Pajitnov's most recognizable post-Tetris arcade experiments.

games.title: Hat Trick
games.description:
Hat Trick (1984) is a brisk overhead ice-hockey game in which each side fields a skater and a goalie. Players control their team's two roles while trying to carry or shoot the puck into the opposing net, with a match lasting just two minutes. The small number of characters keeps the action fast and makes defensive positioning as important as aggressive shooting.

Developed by Bally Sente, Hat Trick was remembered for fluid-looking skaters, trails left by their blades and the Zamboni ice-resurfacing machine between games. Its accessible two-player competition made it a particularly approachable sports title for mid-1980s arcades.

games.title: Hayaoshi Quiz Ouza Ketteisen
games.description: Hayaoshi Quiz Ouza Ketteisen (1993-1994), subtitled The King of Quiz, is Jaleco's Japanese competitive trivia arcade game. Its name refers to rapid-response or buzzer-style quizzing: the challenge is to recognize a question and respond correctly before a rival. Unlike a maze or action game, play is built around reading Japanese questions and using the cabinet's answer buttons. Its format is that of a televised quiz contest, with speed as well as knowledge influencing the competition.

games.title: Heavy Barrel
games.description:
Heavy Barrel (1987) is Data East's muscular overhead run-and-gun adventure, sending one or two commandos into a nuclear-missile complex seized by terrorists. As in Ikari Warriors, the original arcade controls allow movement and the direction of fire to be handled separately using rotary joysticks. Players advance through enemy-filled corridors and outdoor defenses, collecting gun upgrades, grenades and keys for locked supply crates.

The game's signature objective is assembling the devastating Heavy Barrel weapon from six separate pieces hidden in those crates. Once completed, this enormous energy cannon can annihilate ordinary enemies and bosses, rewarding players who explore the dangerous battlefield and gather the necessary parts. This treasure-hunt element gives Heavy Barrel more structure than a simple sequence of military firefights.

games.title: Haunted Castle
games.description:
Haunted Castle (1988) is Konami's arcade interpretation of Castlevania, released in Japan under the familiar title Akumajou Dracula. Simon Belmont's wedding is interrupted when Dracula abducts his bride, Selena, forcing Simon to cross six stages of haunted forests, crumbling structures and monster-filled halls. He starts with a whip and can acquire stronger primary weapons, including a morning star and sword, along with sub-weapons such as crosses, bombs and boomerangs that consume collected hearts.

Compared with the home-console Castlevania games, Haunted Castle features larger, detailed arcade sprites, striking horror scenery and a notoriously punishing difficulty curve. The game is not a direct conversion of the Nintendo Entertainment System original: its level designs, presentation and storyline are distinct. Its energetic soundtrack and unusual place within the Castlevania chronology have made it a frequent subject of discussion among series enthusiasts.

games.title: Hyper Crash
games.description:
Hyper Crash (1987) is Konami's eccentric behind-the-car driving game, built around deliberately smashing rival vehicles rather than merely overtaking them. The player races along a twisting road toward successive checkpoints while a fuel supply steadily drains. Ramming other cars or performing airborne attacks destroys them and replenishes fuel, turning aggressive driving into the only reliable way to stay on the road.

Players must decide whether to batter opponents repeatedly or spend extra fuel on a powerful jump-and-flip attack. Barrels, rival cars capable of similar tricks and the approaching empty fuel gauge make every encounter risky. Its mixture of racing, vehicular combat and resource management sets Hyper Crash apart from more conventional Out Run-style driving games.

games.title: Hard Drivin's Airborne
games.description: Hard Drivin's Airborne is an unreleased 1993 Atari Games prototype extending the ideas of Hard Drivin' into an unusual car-and-glider hybrid. The player drives a vehicle that can transform for airborne travel, shifting the experience away from the grounded road simulation of the original. Only prototype software survives, making it a glimpse of an experimental branch in Atari's polygonal driving-game development rather than a completed commercial sequel.

games.title: Head On
games.description:
Head On (1979) is Sega and Gremlin's influential maze-driving game, predating Pac-Man's famous dot-collecting formula. From a top-down view, the player's car circulates around a rectangular set of lanes, collecting all the dots while avoiding a computer-controlled car moving in the opposite direction. Gaps at the sides of the course allow lane changes; accelerating increases speed but makes those changes harder to judge.

Each cleared board introduces a harder combination of traffic and speed, eventually requiring precise timing to slip around several hostile cars. The simple interplay of collecting, pursuit and fixed routes made Head On an important early arcade maze game and a precursor to the dot-eater genre that soon became hugely popular.

games.title: Head On 2
games.description:
Head On 2 (1979) expands Sega and Gremlin's early maze-driving concept by redesigning the lanes and giving cars more ways to move around the circuit. As before, players guide a constantly moving car over dots while avoiding opponents, but additional outer routes allow changes in direction that were impossible in the original layout. Rival cars can therefore threaten from behind as well as from ahead.

Later stages introduce more computer-controlled cars, up to four in the game's more difficult arrangements. The added route choices and more complicated traffic turn a deceptively simple dot-collection exercise into a tighter game of prediction and evasive driving.

games.title: Head On Channel
games.description:
Monita to Rimoko no Head On Channel is an unreleased 1994 Sega System C2 prototype that revisits the company's 1979 maze-driving game Head On. It transforms the familiar dot-collecting and obstacle-avoidance concept into a colorful, comedic presentation inspired by Japanese television. Designed for one or two players, it was tested at a Tokyo location but never received a normal commercial arcade release.

Its surviving prototype is interesting both as a late reinterpretation of a foundational Sega game and as a look at the company's experiments with retro ideas during the 1990s.

games.title: Head On
games.description:
Head On, in Irem's 1979 Play Table adaptation, retains the basic challenge of guiding a car around a maze to collect dots without colliding with hostile traffic. This version has its own visual and scoring details rather than being a completely identical copy of the Sega and Gremlin game. In particular, Irem letters appear in the course, and the colors collected in the maze's quadrants can affect the end-of-round bonus.

That bonus wrinkle gives careful route planning an additional purpose beyond simply clearing every dot. The version is a useful example of how different arcade manufacturers adapted and modified successful early maze-game ideas for their own hardware.

games.title: Heart Attack
games.description:
Heart Attack (1983) is a maze game from Century Electronics in which the player's task is to fill the pathways with dots before a timer expires. Instead of removing dots from a board, the action reverses the usual maze-collection premise and demands that the entire route be marked while an enemy pursues the player.

A defensive plug can be dropped to obstruct the pursuer or freeze it temporarily, creating opportunities to complete dangerous sections of the maze. The combination of timed route coverage and limited defensive interference gives Heart Attack a recognizable identity among early maze-action games.

games.title: Heated Barrel
games.description:
