Heated Barrel (1992) is TAD Corporation's exuberant Wild West action shooter, featuring four exaggerated frontier heroes with different weapons. Players can choose Howdy Pardner, Chi Chi Gringo, Little Plum or Billy Six Guns, then fight through towns, deserts and river settings overrun by bandits, supernatural enemies and enormous bosses. Its sideways-progressing action allows shots in multiple directions and encourages cooperative play, with up to four participants battling together.

Weapon upgrades increase damage, special pickups can add a second weapon and a barrel item delivers a powerful screen-clearing attack with temporary protection. The wild cartoon designs and frantic action give the game a very different tone from realistic western shooters. Released shortly before TAD closed in 1993, Heated Barrel was the company's final arcade video game.

games.title: Heat of Eleven '98
games.description:
Heat of Eleven '98 (1998), known in Japan as World Soccer Championship, is Konami's soccer game for the uncommon Konami M2 arcade hardware. Players select from 32 national teams and compete in an international tournament using short and long passing, shooting, tackles and sliding challenges. Wide, normal and close camera views allow different perspectives on the match, while commentary adds a television-broadcast flavor.

Its significance lies partly in the platform: Konami released only a handful of games for its M2-based arcade system. Heat of Eleven '98 is therefore both a late-1990s international football title and a relatively unusual piece of Konami arcade hardware history.

games.title: Hebereke no Popoon
games.description:
Hebereke no Popoon (1994) is Sunsoft's lively competitive puzzle game starring characters from its Hebereke series. Pairs of colored pieces drop into a field, and players rotate and place them to form groups of at least three matching colors. Cleared groups cause pieces above to fall, allowing chain reactions, while certain attacks send awkward character-shaped blocks into the opponent's playfield.

Different characters have their own disruptive abilities, turning careful matching into an energetic head-to-head contest. The arcade version follows an earlier Super Famicom release and blends familiar Dr. Mario-style pairing with the unmistakable personality of Sunsoft's oddball mascot cast.

games.title: Head Panic
games.description:
Head Panic (1999-2000) is a Korean single-screen platform action game in the tradition of Snow Bros. Players guide Polly and Sally through a series of themed locations, throwing projectile attacks at roaming monsters and clearing enemies from each screen. The travelogue backdrop draws on recognizable landmarks and scenery from around the world, making each area visually distinct.

With straightforward movement, two attack buttons and colorful cartoon characters, it favors quick arcade action and cooperative play over elaborate exploration. Its enemy-clearing structure places it in the long-running family of Bubble Bobble-inspired platform games.

games.title: Heiankyo Alien
games.description:
Heiankyo Alien (1979-1980) is a pioneering Japanese maze game set in an imagined ancient Kyoto invaded by extraterrestrials. The player controls a kebiishi, a Heian-era law-enforcement officer, whose only way to defeat the aliens is to dig holes in the ground. An alien that walks into a completed hole becomes trapped, but must be buried by filling the hole before it escapes.

The resulting action is a blend of pursuit, baiting and timing: rather than directly attacking monsters, players must predict their movement through the maze and prepare traps in advance. The game was adapted for Western arcades as Digger and became a notable early example of a digging-and-trapping mechanic that later games would explore in different ways.

games.title: HeliFire
games.description:
HeliFire (1980) is an early Nintendo arcade shooter with a striking sea-and-sky battlefield. Players control a submarine that can move across the underwater portion of the screen and fire missiles upward at incoming helicopters. Above-water attackers drop bombs and depth charges, while underwater ships, mines and sea creatures restrict the submarine's movement.

Different-colored helicopters behave at different speeds, and later waves become increasingly crowded. With its combination of targets above and hazards below, HeliFire offers more spatial complexity than a simple fixed-row shooting gallery and reflects Nintendo's early experiments before its best-known character-driven arcade successes.

games.title: Hellfire
games.description:
Hellfire (1989) is Toaplan's inventive horizontally scrolling space shooter, built around changing the direction of the player's fire. Captain Lancer pilots the CNCS1 craft through a campaign against the robotic tyrant Super Mech and his forces, facing waves of enemy machines, hazardous terrain and large stage bosses. The spacecraft can switch between several firing patterns, including forward, backward, vertical and diagonal shots, allowing enemies to be attacked from angles normally inaccessible in side-scrolling shooters.

That direction-switching system is the heart of the game: particular obstacles and gun placements are easier to tackle by passing them and firing backward or by choosing the correct multi-direction pattern. Six demanding stages and Toaplan's dense mechanical designs make Hellfire an unusually tactical take on its genre. It remains a favorite with shooter enthusiasts for rewarding planning as well as quick reflexes.

games.title: Hero

variants.title: Hero in the Castle of Doom (DK conversion)
Hero in the Castle of Doom (DK conversion not encrypted)

games.description:
Hero, also distributed as Hero in the Castle of Doom, is an early-1980s maze adventure for Century Electronics' CVS arcade hardware. Players traverse fixed-screen passages while collecting symbols associated with a deck of cards, including hearts, diamonds, spades and clubs, and later a letter J. Gathering the required symbols allows progression toward rescuing Esmeralda.

Fireballs and arrows patrol the maze, so success requires choosing routes and timing movement around hazards rather than defeating everything in sight. Its compact objective-based rooms give the game the feel of an early arcade rescue adventure.

games.title: Hexa
games.description:
Hexa (1990) is a Korean falling-block puzzle game closely modeled on Sega's Columns. Players move and reorder descending symbols, clearing groups of three or more that line up horizontally, vertically or diagonally. As the game becomes more demanding, the speed of falling pieces varies, forcing players to plan matches quickly.

It adds a limited-use special piece called a Poby, which can be triggered deliberately rather than simply appearing as a rare random bonus. The game is also notable for borrowed assets, including music associated with Konami's MSX game The Treasure of Usas, making it an example of the unlicensed reuse sometimes found in early Korean arcade software.

games.title: Hexion
games.description:
Hexion (1992) is Konami's arcade reworking of Hextris, a puzzle design using hexagonal cells instead of the square blocks familiar from Tetris. Groups of hexagons fall into a honeycomb-like board, and players must arrange them into complete lines that disappear to make room for more pieces. The angled geometry creates unfamiliar gaps and interlocking shapes, forcing even experienced Tetris players to rethink their spatial instincts.

Besides its standard field, Hexion provides alternate playfield shapes, including wide, tall and diagonal arrangements. It also offers competitive and cooperative two-player modes. The underlying Hextris concept originated in software by David Markley, while Konami turned it into a polished arcade release with its own variations and character cameos.

games.title: Huang Fei Hong
games.description:
Huang Fei Hong (1994) is the Chinese-region version of IGS's one-on-one fighting game Alien Challenge. It features eight selectable fighters drawn from a deliberately eccentric mix of martial-arts, fantasy and comic-book archetypes, including the Chinese folk hero Huang Fei Hong, a ninja, a werewolf and a flaming creature. Matches are fought in a conventional side-view arena with punches, kicks and special moves, generally under best-of-three rules.

The game also features a final opponent named Claus and occasional bonus challenges. Its Chinese-region program differs from the international Alien Challenge software, making this entry a regional revision of the same fighting game rather than a separate franchise.

games.title: Taisen Hot Gimmick Kairakuten
games.description:
Taisen Hot Gimmick Kairakuten (1998) is Psikyo's adult-oriented Japanese mahjong game, built around one-on-one matches against a cast of twelve illustrated opponents. Players draw and discard tiles to build winning hands while managing a limited pool of betting funds. Victories advance the character encounters, and the game includes adult reward scenes selected after defeating an opponent.

Between matches, players can purchase special assistance items to improve their chances in later rounds. Its combination of conventional mahjong strategy, character-based progression and elaborate animated reward sequences is characteristic of the Hot Gimmick arcade series.

games.title: Hammerin' Harry
games.description:
Hammerin' Harry (1990), known in Japan as Daiku no Gen-san, is Irem's colorful side-scrolling action game about a carpenter fighting back against a corrupt construction organization. After his house is demolished, Harry takes up an oversized wooden mallet and fights through building sites, sewers, docks and the enemy's headquarters. He can hit foes directly or pound the ground to send shockwaves along the floor, adding range to his otherwise close-quarters weapon.

The stages feature machinery, hazardous platforms and oversized bosses, with a comic style that makes the action feel like a slapstick workplace rebellion. Its immediately recognizable hero and hammer attacks proved distinctive enough to launch a small series beyond the arcade original.

games.title: Hidden Catch 2
games.description:
Hidden Catch 2 (1999) is Eolith's follow-up to its successful spot-the-difference arcade puzzle. Two nearly identical pictures appear side by side, and players must identify several discrepancies before the timer expires. Dedicated cabinets used a pen-like pointing controller to select suspected differences and deliver strong vibration feedback for mistakes.

This edition wraps the picture comparisons in a light fantasy story about restoring peace to Picture World, with colored-pencil knights confronting a wicked wizard. The combination of quick visual recognition, physical pen controls and short timed rounds made Hidden Catch especially suited to casual arcade audiences.

games.title: Hidden Catch 3
games.description:
Hidden Catch 3 (2000) continues Eolith's arcade spot-the-difference series. Players compare paired pictures, locate the five altered details and indicate their findings before time runs out. On the original dedicated hardware, an interactive pointing pen lets players select locations directly and vibrates to signal unsuccessful choices.

The game retains the series' accessible, observation-based challenge rather than introducing a conventional joystick action format. Later entries in the series became a recognizable fixture of the Korean casual arcade scene.

games.title: Hidden Catch 2000
games.description:
Hidden Catch 2000 (1999) is another Eolith arcade entry in the spot-the-difference puzzle format. Players inspect two images displayed together and try to find five mismatched details under a time limit. The series' original pen-based input gives the activity the feel of marking discrepancies on a printed puzzle, with vibration feedback when players make an incorrect selection.

Its short, visually intuitive rounds are aimed at observation and accuracy rather than reflex-driven combat, making it a representative late-1990s casual arcade puzzle game.

games.title: Hidden Catch (World) / Tul Lin Gu Lim Chat Ki '98

variants.title: Hidden Catch (World) / Tul Lin Gu Lim Chat Ki '98 (Korea) (pcb ver 3.03)
variants.version: (World) / Tul Lin Gu Lim Chat Ki '98 (Korea) (pcb ver 3.03)

games.description:
Hidden Catch, also known in Korea as Tul Lin Gu Lim Chat Ki '98 (1998), introduced Eolith's enduring spot-the-difference arcade formula. Each round displays two near-identical scenes, and the player must find and select five details that do not match before the countdown runs out. The concept is immediately recognizable, but the dedicated cabinet gives it a memorable physical twist: players use an interactive pen rather than simply pressing direction buttons, and the pen vibrates when a selection is wrong.

This combination of familiar picture-puzzle rules and force-feedback pointing controls helped distinguish Hidden Catch from the more conventional falling-block games of the era. Its success led to several sequels and revised editions, including Hidden Catch 2, Hidden Catch 3 and Hidden Catch 2000.

games.title: Pirate Ship Higemaru
games.description:
Pirate Ship Higemaru (1984) is an early Capcom maze-action game with a wonderfully direct idea: a small sailor named Momotaro must clear pirate-infested ship decks by picking up barrels and throwing them at enemies. Each stage is a fixed overhead playfield filled with barrels, bags and other obstacles. The hero has no conventional weapon, so players must use the scenery itself, choosing firing lanes and positioning throws to knock pirates off the deck.

Some objects break on impact while others can be reused, and hitting several enemies with a single rolling barrel yields increased rewards. The stages become progressively more crowded, culminating in encounters with pirate leaders. Its cheerful character designs and object-throwing mechanics foreshadow some of the playful action ideas Capcom would revisit in later years.

The game's music is also associated with Tamayo Kawamoto, an important composer in Capcom's early arcade history. Higemaru remains a distinctive pre-Mega Man and pre-Street Fighter example of the studio's talent for giving simple controls inventive consequences.

games.title: Space Fever High Splitter
games.description:
Nintendo's Space Fever High Splitter (1979), also advertised as SF-HiSplitter, is a variation of the Space Invaders formula with a particularly mischievous scoring rule: shooting an alien off-center can split it into two smaller enemies instead of destroying it. A direct hit through its center is more efficient, while careless shooting actually increases the number of targets to clear. Aliens descend behind destructible defensive barriers, UFOs offer bonus opportunities, and the formation accelerates as it thins out.

The game offers three alternative movement patterns, including aliens that change vertical direction and a mode that adds rows as the formation advances. This makes High Splitter more than a simple Nintendo imitation of Taito's hit: aiming accuracy matters as much as survival, and the changing formations alter the rhythm of play.

games.title: High Impact Football
games.description:
This December 9, 1990 prototype revision 8.6 of Williams' High Impact Football preserves an early development build of the company's four-player arcade football game. Players can pair up on opposing sides, select offensive plays or defensive formations, and direct the action with eight-way joysticks and a single multipurpose button for passing, jumping, kicking and player switching.

High Impact combines surprisingly elaborate play selection with aggressive, exaggerated on-field action and boisterous commentary. The prototype is valuable as a snapshot of the game's development before the later LA-series production revisions; the available documentation does not establish specific gameplay changes unique to this build.

games.title: High Impact Football
games.description:
High Impact Football is Williams' 1990 attempt to give American football the immediate appeal and noisy personality of a four-player arcade game. Up to two players can cooperate on each side, selecting from a wide selection of offensive plays and defensive formations before throwing passes, running with the ball, tackling and kicking. A single action button changes function with the situation, while the eight-way joystick handles play selection and the currently controlled athlete.

Rather than relying on licensed real-world players, High Impact uses a colorful selection of fictionalized city and regional teams, exaggerated action and enthusiastic stadium presentation. Its over-the-top play-by-play announcer, Manic Max, and boisterous crowd help make each possession a spectacle. Built on Williams' Y-Unit hardware, the game occupies a distinctive place just before Midway's more streamlined, spectacularly violent NFL Blitz style of arcade football.

games.title: Hippodrome
games.description:
Hippodrome, released by Data East in 1989 and known in Japan as Fighting Fantasy, is a fantasy gladiatorial fighting game set in a succession of monster-filled arenas. The player chooses a human warrior and faces such opponents as a gargoyle, lizard man, scorpion man, armored dragon and wizard. Each bout is fought on a side-on screen using a joystick and separate attack and jump buttons, making positioning, timing and enemy attack patterns crucial.

Victories earn money that can be spent between matches on equipment improving attributes such as attack power, reach and endurance. A second player can interrupt the tournament to challenge the current fighter, but only the winner continues the campaign. The mixture of one-on-one monster battles and persistent equipment upgrades gives Hippodrome an unusual role-playing flavor for a late-1980s arcade fighter.

games.title: The History of Martial Arts
games.description:
The History of Martial Arts is an obscure, unlicensed fighting game produced by NIX during the 1990s, heavily borrowing characters and artwork from Data East's Fighter's History. Its nine selectable combatants fight one-on-one matches using an eight-way joystick and six attack buttons, echoing the control layout popularized by Street Fighter II.

Rather than being an official revision of Fighter's History, it is a reconstructed, sprite-ripped imitation running on different arcade hardware. Its appropriated character graphics and altered presentation make it a revealing example of the unauthorized fighting-game derivatives that circulated during the genre's early-1990s boom.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Hit the Ice
games.description:
Hit the Ice is Taito's 1990 cartoon hockey game, distributed in North America by Williams, and it treats the sport more like a brawl than a rulebook. Each side fields only a forward, a defender and a goalie, with up to four human players participating. Skating, passing and shooting remain essential, but opponents can also be checked, tripped, elbowed and dragged into fistfights without the usual sporting consequences.

The game's signature super shot is powerful enough to knock the goalie into the net with the puck. A trailing team can receive a temporary super-drink advantage, and the arcade operator could offer an additional-credit power drink before a period. With its expressive characters, frantic puck exchanges and intentionally rough contact, Hit the Ice is a particularly memorable example of late-arcade-era sports games built for spectacle and multiplayer rivalry.

games.title: Hit Me
games.description:
RamTek's Hit Me (1976) is an early video adaptation of blackjack, using a monochrome display and dedicated buttons rather than the mechanical reels of later gambling machines. Up to four players can take part, deciding whether to take another card or stand while trying to finish closer to 21 than the dealer without going bust. A two-card total of 21 counts as blackjack.

Its restrained presentation reflects the first generation of microprocessor arcade games: the familiar card-game decisions, rather than elaborate graphics or animations, provide the entire challenge. Versions included an upright and a cocktail-table cabinet.

games.title: Hit 'n Miss
games.description:
Hit 'n Miss is a 1987 Exidy light-gun shooting-gallery game designed with younger players in mind. Instead of simply blasting everything on the screen, the player must recognize appropriate targets and avoid shooting the wrong ones. Across seven kinds of stages, objectives vary from quickly hitting moving targets to dropping apples onto passing objects with carefully timed shots.

Stages award bonus points for unused time, but poor target choices or letting the timer run out can end a game. The shifting rules give this child-friendly entry in Exidy's 440 light-gun range more variety than a conventional target gallery.

games.title: Hana Kagerou
games.description: Hana Kagerou is a 1997 Japanese medal-style hanafuda game from Nakanihon and Dynax. It uses traditional Japanese flower-card play rather than Western cards and belongs to the betting-oriented side of the country's arcade market. The game's horizontal display and Dynax blitter-based hardware support an illustrated presentation typical of the company's later tabletop titles. Its name is often translated as Hanafuda Heat Haze.

games.title: Hana Yayoi
games.description: Hana Yayoi is a 1987 Japanese hanafuda title from Dyna Electronics, played with a dedicated flower-card control panel. The player competes in traditional Japanese card play against a female opponent, with adult-themed visual rewards forming part of the presentation. A related version is known as Hana Fubuki, including betting-oriented configurations. The game belongs to the substantial niche of Japanese arcade machines that combined familiar card games with character artwork.

games.title: Hana Oriduru
games.description: Dynax's Hana Oriduru (1989), also romanized Hana Orizuru, is a single-player Japanese hanafuda game. Rather than involving movement or action controls, play centers on flower-card matches, with the machine associated with the betting or medal-game market. A related medal version was released under the title Hanajingi. The original title refers to a folded-paper crane decorated with flowers.

games.title: Hoccer
games.description:
Hoccer (1983) is Eastern Micro Electronics' strange futuristic mixture of ice hockey, soccer and arena combat. The player controls Andrew, a one-man team attempting to score goals and strike side targets while being hunted by two hostile robots, Ord and Clee. These opponents can ram Andrew into the boards or a spinner and attack him with a charged ball.

Andrew can fight back by throwing the ball at the robots or knocking them into the rink's edges. Seen from above on a vertically oriented screen, the game turns an apparently ordinary sporting contest into a frantic survival challenge where scoring and disabling opponents are equally important.

games.title: Vs. Hogan's Alley
games.description:
Vs. Hogan's Alley is Nintendo's 1985 arcade light-gun game, built for the NES-derived Vs. System. The player takes part in police-style target practice, using a gun to distinguish gangsters from innocent bystanders as cardboard silhouettes suddenly turn or appear in windows. Successful shots score according to the criminal's value, but shooting a civilian or missing a threat counts against the player.

The different target scenarios include a conventional firing range and a simulated city street. A contrasting trick-shot game asks the player to keep thrown tin cans airborne and guide them onto scoring ledges. The challenge comes from instant visual recognition as much as marksmanship, making Hogan's Alley one of Nintendo's early demonstrations of light-gun gameplay in arcades and on home hardware.

games.title: Hole Land
games.description:
Hole Land is a 1984 fixed-screen action shooter developed by Spain's Tecfri. The player controls a brightly colored robot along the bottom of the screen, moving horizontally, jumping and firing upward at enemies emerging from holes overhead. Rats, ghosts, snakes and other creatures advance downward, while bombs and falling rocks can temporarily disable the robot's movement and weapons.

The short campaign includes a memorable final confrontation with a giant, tooth-filled monster: the player must shoot out its teeth before it reaches the robot. Completing the encounter loops the game back to the beginning. Its unusual enemies, jump mechanic and friendly repairman distinguish Hole Land from more conventional alien-formation shooters.

games.title: Holosseum
games.description:
Holosseum is Sega's 1992 one-on-one fighting game created specifically for its remarkable Hologram Time Traveler theater cabinet. Four selectable martial artists face one another in best-of-three bouts, using largely realistic punches, kicks and grappling techniques. A solo tournament pits the chosen fighter against the remaining roster and ultimately a mirror opponent.

Its headline attraction is not a conventional display: a monitor image reflected through a concave mirror appears to float inside a darkened viewing chamber, an illusion promoted as holographic imagery. Following Time Traveler, Holosseum was only the second game made for this expensive cabinet format, and the last. Its small cast and comparatively basic combat have aged more than the visual trick, but it remains an intriguing arcade experiment from the period when Sega was exploring alternatives to ordinary flat-screen presentation.

games.title: Moero Pro Yakyuu Homerun
games.description: Moero!! Pro Yakyuu Homerun Kyousou is an unusual 1988 Jaleco baseball-themed medal arcade game. Its home-run competition places the emphasis on batting skill rather than managing a full professional baseball match, while the medal-machine format also incorporates an element of chance and rewards successful play through a payout hopper. The single-player cabinet uses a joystick and one action button. Its hardware draws on the Nintendo Famicom architecture, an interesting technical connection to Jaleco's better-known Moero!! Pro Yakyuu home baseball games.

games.title: Honey Dolls
games.description:
Honey Dolls is an adult-themed 1995 puzzle game built around the block-clearing mechanics of Dharma Dojo. Players strike blocks so that identical types line up and disappear, with the required length of each matching group increasing as the game progresses. Unlike its inspiration, blocks can be punched from either side of a row, opening up additional ways to set up combinations.

Matching blocks releases letters that can be collected to spell GO HONEY, unlocking one of several bonus stages. Clearing stages reveals photographs of nude models, though the adult imagery can be disabled through a cabinet setting. Beneath that presentation is a timing-and-planning puzzle about arranging matches efficiently.

games.title: Hook
games.description:
Irem's Hook (1992) is a side-scrolling beat 'em up based on Steven Spielberg's 1991 Peter Pan film. Peter Banning has returned to Neverland to rescue his children from Captain Hook, and the arcade game lets players take the roles of Peter Pan and several Lost Boys, including Rufio. Its colorful stages are populated by pirates, hostile creatures and characters drawn from the film's story.

The action is built around movement across multi-plane environments, sword attacks, jumps and special moves, with enemies often surrendering rather than being killed. The cooperative cabinet supports several players working together, a natural fit for the Lost Boys' ensemble. Unlike the numerous home-console platform games also called Hook, Irem's version is a dedicated arcade brawler distinguished by large animated sprites, movie-inspired settings and a lighter, storybook tone than most contemporary beat 'em ups.

games.title: Hoops '96
games.description:
Hoops '96 is Data East's arcade basketball sequel to Street Hoop, also known as Dunk Dream '95 in Japan. It keeps the predecessor's fast side-view street-basketball action but adds exaggerated super shots and a Super Defense maneuver that can repel an opponent's spectacular Super Dunk. Athletes from twelve national teams battle on a scrolling court, with a finite power reserve governing special techniques.

A third action button lets the player choose a pass recipient on offense or switch the controlled defender. This extra control gives the game a more deliberate team-play element beneath its flamboyant presentation. Its combination of showy scoring, defensive counters and accessible multiplayer play makes it a distinct continuation of Data East's arcade basketball formula.

games.title: Hopping Mappy
games.description:
Hopping Mappy is Namco's 1986 sequel to Mappy, developed by Game Studio and originally released in Japan. The mouse policeman returns to recover eight stolen treasures from garden-like checkerboard stages, but now he moves by bouncing on a pogo stick. His old adversaries, the pink Meowky cats and the larger Nyamco, patrol the paths and force the player to plan each jump carefully.

Because Mappy lands on fixed squares rather than moving freely, escaping a line of cats depends on anticipating their routes. Holding the acceleration button makes him hop faster, at the cost of more demanding control. Balloon-collecting bonus stages break up the chase. Moving the action outdoors and replacing the original game's doors and trampolines with grid-based pogo hopping made this an unusually substantial sequel rather than a cosmetic update.

games.title: Hopper Robo
games.description:
Hopper Robo is a 1983 Sega-released platform game set inside a robot-filled factory. The player guides a small robot across platforms to collect numbered boxes in the correct order, then deposits them onto conveyor belts at the bottom of the screen. The next required box flashes, turning each stage into a route-planning problem as well as a jumping challenge.

Hostile robots follow predictable patrol patterns, while flying hammers and spring hazards complicate the journey. Learning the timing of those dangers is essential because touching an enemy costs a life. The game's combination of ordered collection and hazardous industrial scenery gives it a different rhythm from the more familiar rescue-oriented platform games of the period.

games.title: Kid no Hore Hore Daisakusen
games.description:
Kid no Hore Hore Daisakusen is Nichibutsu's 1987 maze-action game, whose title roughly means Kid's Great Digging Operation. Players steer children through overhead maze stages and dig holes to trap pursuing enemies, then fill those holes to dispatch their captives. The core idea recalls Heiankyo Alien, but this game adds doors that can be opened or shut, temporary weapons, varied stage layouts and a more comical style.

One button handles digging or the currently held weapon, while the other controls doors, making traps and escape routes closely linked. The game was initially associated with the name Booby Kids, later used for an unauthorized variant. Its deceptively simple digging mechanic supports a surprisingly tactical style of pursuit and crowd management.

games.title: Horizon
games.description:
Horizon is Irem's 1985 horizontally scrolling action shooter, a little-known successor in spirit to Moon Patrol. The player pilots an armed hover vehicle over a hostile landscape, switching between three depth lanes while firing at enemies and negotiating obstacles. The alternating lanes change not only the position of threats but also the musical arrangement, which becomes more percussion-heavy nearer the foreground.

Fuel and useful pickups must be collected while avoiding enemy fire and terrain hazards. Where Moon Patrol emphasized jumping over craters in a single side-view lane, Horizon experiments with changing the apparent depth of the battlefield, giving its familiar vehicle-shooter premise a distinctive three-lane structure.

games.title: American Horseshoes
games.description:
American Horseshoes (1990) turns the traditional lawn game into a coin-operated contest for as many as four alternating players. Competitors choose from four cartoon characters, set the grip and angle of each throw, and roll a trackball to control the distance of a horseshoe's flight toward the stake. Aiming is evaluated from an overhead view of the landing area after each inning.

Players receive two throws per inning, with three innings provided initially and the option to continue for a longer match. Its physical trackball control is central to the appeal: throwing a successful ringer depends on a measured gesture rather than simply pressing a button.

games.title: Hot Blocks - Tetrix II
games.description: Hot Blocks: Tetrix II is a 1993 falling-block puzzle game built around the familiar Tetris formula. Players arrange descending shapes to clear completed horizontal lines and survive as the board fills. Its distinguishing addition is adult-oriented imagery that is revealed as the player makes progress through the stages. The combination of an established block-stacking ruleset with risqué visual rewards typifies a small but persistent niche in 1990s arcade puzzle games.

games.title: Hot Chase
games.description:
Hot Chase is Konami's 1988 driving-action game about a stolen supercar rigged with a bomb. The player must steer the white sports car through hostile territory and reach a friendly border before its countdown reaches zero. Narrow roads, traffic, military roadblocks, aircraft and helicopters threaten to delay or destroy the escape.

Rather than awarding victory simply for overtaking opponents, Hot Chase makes each run a timed mission with the feeling of an action-film pursuit. The original arcade controls use a steering mechanism and buttons to manage the car, while the changing scenery and military threats produce a very different experience from circuit racing. Reaching the border triggers a cinematic conclusion to the mission.

games.title: Quiz de Idol! Hot Debut
games.description: Quiz de Idol! Hot Debut is a 2000 Japanese quiz game developed by Moss and published by Psikyo. Its trivia challenges are presented within an idol-entertainment setting rather than as a conventional, anonymous question bank. Players answer multiple-choice questions using four selection buttons, with the idol-production theme supplying the characters and surrounding presentation. It is a relatively unusual late arcade release for Psikyo, better known for its shooting games.

games.title: Hotdog Storm
games.description: Hotdog Storm (1996) is a Korean vertically scrolling shoot 'em up. Piloting a spacecraft, the player flies over stages filled with enemy helicopters, mechanical units and other aircraft, destroying formations while maneuvering through incoming fire. The ship carries a standard forward weapon, a limited supply of bombs and collectible upgrades that improve its fighting power. The conventional shooting structure and energetic mix of airborne and ground-based enemies place it firmly in the mid-1990s arcade shooter tradition.

games.title: Taisen Hot Gimmick 4 Ever
games.description:
Taisen Hot Gimmick 4 Ever is Psikyo's fourth adult-themed mahjong game, released in Japan in 2000. In its principal mode, players challenge a roster of illustrated female opponents at Japanese mahjong, advancing by winning hands and depleting the opponents' funds. Between matches they can purchase items that influence subsequent games; optional post-victory scenes provide the series' characteristic mature-content rewards.

This installment expands the formula with a Mahjong Detective single-player mode and a Jan-God versus Jan-Devil competition for two players. It also allows a non-punishing response when an opponent is defeated, an unusual option for a series normally organized around its punishment animations. The additional modes are what most clearly distinguish 4 Ever from the earlier releases.

games.title: Taisen Hot Gimmick
games.description:
Taisen Hot Gimmick (1997) established Psikyo's adult-themed, one-on-one mahjong series. Players work through eight principal female opponents and additional hidden challengers, attempting to win hands or exhaust an opponent's betting funds. Victories lead to interactive punishment scenes with erotic imagery, while the player can purchase special-use items between matches to gain an advantage.

Its underlying competition is Japanese mahjong rather than a tile-matching action puzzle: the drama comes from risk, hand completion and the changing funds of the players. The game's character artwork, animation and interstitial bonus sequences established a recognizable formula that Psikyo would revisit through several sequels.

games.title: Taisen Hot Gimmick 3 Digital Surfing
games.description:
Taisen Hot Gimmick 3: Digital Surfing is Psikyo's 1999 continuation of its adult mahjong series. Its headline mode dresses the usual sequence of one-on-one matches and erotic post-victory animations in a fictional computer-and-Internet interface. Players challenge ten featured opponents and a secret opponent, using winnings and purchased items to advance through the roster.

More importantly, this is the first Hot Gimmick to offer three distinct modes. Alongside the mature-content Digital Surfing game is a solo Mahjong Fighters story and a two-player Jan-Prince versus Jan-Shogun contest. That broader structure gives the third installment more to offer than its changing cast and visual theme alone.

games.title: Taisen Hot Gimmick Integral
games.description:
Taisen Hot Gimmick Integral (2001) is Psikyo's fifth entry in the adult mahjong series and an anthology drawing characters and animations from its first four installments. It concentrates exclusively on single-player mahjong rather than retaining the alternate modes introduced in the previous games. Players face a large returning roster, buy advantageous items between matches and try to preserve their betting funds.

Integral also changes the progression rules: winning three hands without exhausting an opponent's funds advances the player but skips the optional punishment sequence, and each opponent now has only one such scene. This makes the game a remix of the series' existing material with a somewhat different reward and difficulty structure, not simply a collection of the earlier ROMs.

games.title: Hot Mind
games.description: Hot Mind is a 1995 Italian arcade puzzle game by Playmark, presented on a horizontal display and operated with an eight-way joystick and two buttons. Unlike a major Japanese arcade release with dedicated proprietary hardware, it survives in several distinctive board configurations, including versions adapted to the hardware of Playmark's Hard Times and Fit of Fighting. Some builds also include configurable ticket or token dispensing, linking its puzzle play to redemption-machine operation. Its preservation required emulation work on both the video circuitry and the PIC-controlled sound system.

games.title: Hot Pinball
games.description: Hot Pinball is a 1995 arcade video-pinball game from Comad, combining simulated flipper action with adult-themed illustrations of women. Rather than a physical pinball table, it presents the playfield on a vertical video display and uses dedicated buttons for the pinball controls. It is part of the same small Korean arcade niche as the later Gals Pinball, offering pinball scoring and ball control alongside provocative visual rewards.

games.title: Hot Rod
games.description:
Sega's Hot Rod (1988) is a lively overhead racing game designed for three-player upright and four-player cocktail cabinets. Its small cars race on winding tracks across different surfaces, while the scrolling screen keeps the contest moving. Falling too far behind the visible playfield costs fuel, so it is not enough to drive cleanly: competitors must remain close to the leaders while collecting gas refills on the track.

Between races, prize money can be used to improve a car, introducing a simple upgrade strategy to the multiplayer chaos. Fuel pickups, shortcuts and the continual risk of being pushed offscreen make each race a struggle for position. Running on Sega's disk-based System 24 hardware, Hot Rod is notable for turning the familiar top-down racer into a deliberately social, cabinet-centered competition.

games.title: Hot Shocker
games.description: Hot Shocker is a 1982 maze game by E. G. Felaco, published by Domino, in which the character Dudley must recolor a web-like network by walking along its lines. Enemies chase him through the same interconnected paths, forcing the player to balance territory coverage with escape. Unlike a pellet-collection maze game, progress is visibly marked by the route Dudley has traced, making the network itself the main puzzle.

games.title: Vs. Hot Smash
games.description: Vs. Hot Smash (1987) is a futuristic, air-hockey-like arcade sports game built around a top-down court. Each player moves a paddle to intercept a fast-moving ball and send it past the opposing defender into the goal. Rebounds off the arena's walls make accurate positioning and anticipation more important than a straightforward head-on exchange. Its competitive, reflex-driven rules produce short, frantic rallies reminiscent of electronic table hockey.

games.title: Mahjong Hourouki Part 1 - Seisyun Hen
games.description: Mahjong Hourouki Part 1: Seisyun Hen is a 1987 Japanese arcade mahjong title, subtitled roughly Adolescence. It lets the player select opponents and compete in traditional mahjong matches, with adult-oriented presentation placing it within the large market of late-1980s Japanese mahjong cabinets. The Part 1 subtitle identifies it as the opening installment of a themed series rather than an action-oriented variation on mahjong.

games.title: House Mannequin Roppongi Live hen
games.description: House Mannequin: Roppongi Live Hen is a 1987 adult-oriented Japanese mahjong game from Nichibutsu and a follow-up to House Mannequin. It retains the series' card-and-tile entertainment format while changing its setting to a Roppongi nightlife theme, reflected in the Live Hen subtitle. The title is an example of Nichibutsu's extensive line of character-driven mahjong arcade machines rather than a conventional action or puzzle game.

games.title: House Mannequin
games.description: House Mannequin is a 1987 Nichibutsu mahjong arcade game, released in Japan with an adult-themed presentation. As in the company's other tabletop titles of the period, the central activity is competing in Japanese mahjong matches rather than navigating an action playfield. It precedes the related Roppongi Live Hen edition released later the same year.

games.title: Hard Times
games.description:
Hard Times is a 1994 Italian arcade shooting game by Playmark, built as an unauthorized reworking of TAD Corporation's Blood Bros. Its Prohibition-era gangster theme recasts the shooting-gallery action of the original: players move a targeting sight across the scene, fire at enemies appearing among the scenery and contend with escalating waves of attacks. Two players can participate in the mobster firefights.

The game is also a preservation curiosity. Many of its original circuit boards were reportedly converted into Playmark's later puzzle game Hot Mind, contributing to Hard Times' relative rarity compared with the better-known shooter it imitates.

games.title: Hyper Street Fighter II: The Anniversary Edition

variants.title: Hyper Street Fighter II: The Anniversary Edition (USA 040202)
Hyper Street Fighter II: The Anniversary Edition (Asia 040202)
Hyper Street Fighter II: The Anniversary Edition (Japan 040202)
Hyper Street Fighter II: The Anniversary Edition (Japan 040123)
Hyper Street Fighter II: The Anniversary Edition (Japan 031222)

games.description:
Hyper Street Fighter II: The Anniversary Edition is Capcom's 2004 arcade celebration of the Street Fighter II lineage. Based on Super Street Fighter II Turbo, it offers the remarkable ability to choose not just a fighter but that character's version from one of five major Street Fighter II editions. A World Warrior, Champion Edition, Turbo, Super or Super Turbo incarnation can face opponents drawn from different points in the series' history.

Those choices are more than cosmetic. They preserve differences in character speed, move properties, special attacks and balance, allowing historically impossible matchups between older and newer interpretations of the roster. The familiar six-button fighting system and best-of-three contests remain the foundation, but the version-selection screen becomes a strategic decision of its own.

Issued for the fifteenth-anniversary celebration of Street Fighter, the arcade release was among the final titles for Capcom's CPS-2 hardware. As both a playable retrospective and an unusual competitive experiment, it turns the revisions of one influential fighting game into part of the game itself.

games.title: Hot Shots Tennis
games.description:
Hot Shots Tennis is a 1990 arcade tennis game developed by Incredible Technologies and released through Strata, unrelated to Sony's much later console game of the same name. The matches use a vertically split screen, giving each competitor a dedicated view of the court. A selection of 32 opponents provides a gradual rise in playing skill from beginner to expert.

Players position their athletes with a joystick and select hard or soft shots with two buttons; pressing them together produces a lob. Directional input also helps place serves. The split-screen presentation makes this a distinctive attempt to give both competitors a clear court perspective in an arcade sports game.

games.title: Hatch Catch
games.description: Hatch Catch is a Korean arcade puzzle game from 1995 in which players fire colored blocks toward a field of existing pieces. Linking three or more blocks of the same color makes the connected group disappear; clearing the remaining blocks completes the stage. As the arrangement becomes more crowded, the player must create useful combinations without sealing off future shots. The game provides a fixed sequence of 50 stages, making it a compact variation on the familiar color-matching projectile puzzle.

games.title: Hunchback
games.description:
Hunchback is Century Electronics' 1983 platform arcade game, loosely inspired by Victor Hugo's The Hunchback of Notre-Dame. Players guide Quasimodo across a succession of fixed castle-wall screens to rescue Esmeralda, running, jumping and grabbing swinging ropes to cross gaps. Spears, arrows, fireballs and other hazards require precise timing, while a knight climbing the wall creates a time limit on each section.

Rather than scrolling continuously, Hunchback presents a chain of short obstacle courses, each with its own trick. Crossing a section and ringing the bell at the far side becomes a compact test of learned timing before the next hazard appears. Its demanding rope swings and narrowly judged jumps helped make it memorable among early British computer players as well as arcade audiences.

The character reportedly began as a Robin Hood concept before being reworked into Quasimodo, explaining the green costume and the prevalence of arrows. Ocean later produced widely known home-computer conversions, broadening the game's reputation well beyond its arcade release.

games.title: Hunchback Olympic
games.description: Hunchback Olympic is a 1984 sports-game spin-off starring the protagonist of Hunchback. Instead of scaling castle walls, the familiar character competes in a selection of Olympic-style sporting events, with the aim of meeting qualifying requirements and progressing through the contests. It was also marketed as Herbie at the Olympics and offered as a conversion kit for Donkey Kong and Donkey Kong Jr. arcade boards, an interesting example of small publishers repurposing existing cabinets for new games.

games.title: Hustle
games.description:
Gremlin's Hustle, released in 1977, is a formative maze game in the lineage that later became known as Snake. Each player steers a continuously moving arrow across a rectangular arena, leaving a trail that becomes an obstacle. Numbered targets appear at changing positions, rewarding anyone quick enough to reach them without colliding with a wall, a trail or an opponent.

A round runs against a short time limit, so survival and aggressive point collection are always in tension. The trail can be used defensively to block an opponent or inadvertently trap its own owner. Building on Gremlin's earlier Blockade concept, Hustle made the growing-tail mechanic into a more overtly competitive scoring game. Its arcade promotion even included traveling challengers who offered cash prizes to players who could beat them.

games.title: Video Hustler

variants.title: Video Pool (bootleg on Moon Cresta hardware)

games.description:
Video Hustler is Konami's 1981 overhead billiards-inspired arcade game, distributed in North America by Dynamo as Lil' Hustler. The playfield resembles a green pool table, but the numbered pieces and shooting action have a distinctly stylized, puck-like quality rather than attempting a complete simulation of cue sports. Players aim shots to send the numbered objects toward pockets and build a score.

With simple graphics and little musical accompaniment, the emphasis falls on estimating angles, collisions and the next position of the pieces. It is an early example of a video game borrowing the geometry and calculated shots of billiards, and it also circulated under unauthorized names including The Billiards and Video Pool.

games.title: Heaven's Gate
games.description:
Heaven's Gate is a 1996 three-dimensional fighting game developed by Racdym and published by Atlus. Players choose from eight initially available fighters, each with a distinct combat style, and battle through one-on-one matches using 3D polygonal characters. The game offers both arcade progression and head-to-head play, with additional fighters available beyond the starting roster.

Originally developed under the name Ultimate Domain, it was an early attempt by both companies to enter a genre dominated by Virtua Fighter and Tekken. A proposed Sega Model 2 origin gave way to the final arcade hardware, and a PlayStation version followed. Its greatest historical interest is as an ambitious, relatively obscure entry in the first wave of 3D fighting games.

games.title: High Voltage
games.description:
High Voltage is a 1985 Japanese space shooter that stages combat from a forward-facing, simulated 3D perspective. The player pilots a starship sent to suppress an uprising on the planet Regit in the year 3030. Missions begin in space and continue toward the planet's surface, where different threats confront the craft.

Rather than moving a small ship through a standard side-scrolling playfield, the game draws opponents and scenery as targets ahead of the viewer. Its perspective and space-to-surface progression distinguish it from the many conventional two-dimensional shooters of the mid-1980s.

games.title: Heavy Metal
games.description:
Heavy Metal is a 1985 Sega overhead tank shooter in which the player's armored vehicle advances through vertically scrolling enemy territory. The tank can move around the playfield while attacking foes ahead, but the terrain scrolls continuously, preventing a leisurely approach to each threat. A radar display at the side of the screen warns of approaching targets.

Four collectible upgrades provide extra speed, stronger shots, missiles and temporary protection. The campaign spans four stages, and a single unprotected hit is fatal. Its combination of forward pressure, tactical movement and a military setting is an early ancestor of later arcade tank-action games.

games.title: Heavy Smash
games.description:
Heavy Smash is Data East's 1993 science-fiction sports game, imagining a brutal future version of handball. Armored athletes from a variety of national teams fight for control of a ball inside an arena, scoring goals while using tackles and even ranged attacks to disrupt their opponents. The teams have distinctive uniforms, including elaborate armor designs, and each possesses a powerful special shot.

Strong attacks require a power gauge to be built up, so the decision to spend a special move becomes part of the contest. Its combination of passing, goalkeeping and almost combat-game levels of contact makes Heavy Smash a particularly unusual entry in Data East's arcade sports catalogue.

games.title: Heavy Unit
games.description:
Heavy Unit is Kaneko's 1988 horizontally scrolling space shooter, originally published by Taito. The player defends the human colony of Le Tau from an alien assault, traveling through stages packed with mechanical creatures, dangerous terrain and large bosses. Like many shooters of its era, it requires careful collection of weapon and speed upgrades, but its defining gimmick is the ability to transform the player's craft into a humanoid battle robot.

The ship form uses more conventional forward fire, while the larger robot gains powerful alternative weapons, including a laser and tracking projectiles. The increased size of the robot makes it an easier target, producing a constant trade-off between attack power and maneuverability. Mid-stage and end-stage bosses punctuate the six-stage journey.

Its large sprites, imaginative biomechanical enemies and transformation system gave Heavy Unit an identity of its own alongside better-known late-1980s shooters. Versions later appeared on the PC Engine and Mega Drive, but the arcade original remains notable for the risk-versus-power choice built into every transformation.

games.title: Heavyweight Champ
games.description:
Heavyweight Champ is Sega's 1987 boxing arcade game, named after the company's much earlier 1976 boxing experiment but using a very different style of video presentation. The player fights through a series of opponents as the boxer Kid Crusher, aiming to climb the rankings and win the heavyweight title.

The cabinet's distinctive physical boxing controls provide a more tactile connection to throwing punches than an ordinary joystick-and-buttons fighting game. The focus on judging distance, responding to an opponent and landing blows makes it a notable bridge between early mechanical-feeling boxing attractions and later character-driven fighting games.

games.title: High Way Race
games.description:
High Way Race is Taito's 1983 overhead driving game, taking players through four courses identified with Asia, America, Africa and Europe. The player's car accelerates automatically, so the principal task is steering through traffic and hazards, preserving fuel and staying on the road as the scenery scrolls toward the bottom of the screen.

Fuel exhaustion can end the run, but so can failing a crucial jump onto a platform. Although the cabinet uses a joystick with multiple directions, normal steering is essentially left and right, giving the game an accessible but demanding arcade-racing rhythm.

games.title: Hydra
games.description:
Hydra is Atari Games' 1990 armed-watercraft racing game, built around fast-moving missions rather than conventional laps. The player pilots a powerful speedboat or hovercraft along narrow waterways to deliver secret cargo, threading past enemy vessels, mines, floating logs and other obstacles. A forward-firing gun lets the craft fight back, while a limited boost resource can launch it briefly into the air to clear danger or reach bonuses.

Fuel continuously runs down, making refills as important as avoiding enemy fire. Money and useful items can be collected en route to each destination. Its dramatic chase perspective and specialized arcade controls give Hydra something of the sensation of a high-speed action film played from the pilot's seat, an aquatic counterpart to Atari's other spectacle-driven driving cabinets.

games.title: Taisen Quiz HYHOO
games.description: Hayaoshi Taisen Quiz HYHOO is a 1987 Japanese competitive quiz game developed by Nichibutsu, released in July of that year. 'Hayaoshi' means answering quickly, and the machine emphasizes rapid responses in a head-to-head trivia format rather than leisurely single-player questioning. It uses three answer buttons and belongs to Nichibutsu's adult-themed arcade line, where quiz play was often paired with character illustrations. The compact controls and Japanese-language questions make it a distinctly regional example of the quiz-game boom.

games.title: Taisen Quiz HYHOO 2
games.description: Hayaoshi Taisen Quiz HYHOO 2 is Nichibutsu's follow-up to its competitive Japanese trivia game, released in November 1987 only a few months after the original. It retains the rapid-answer, opposing-player quiz format and three-button input arrangement, with an adult-themed visual presentation. The unusually short gap between the two games reflects how quiz titles could be refreshed for arcade operators without requiring entirely new kinds of controls or hardware.

games.title: Hyper Athlete
games.description:
Hyper Athlete is Konami's 1996 3D revival of its influential Track & Field and Hyper Sports formula, released in Japanese arcades and closely related to the PlayStation game International Track & Field. Up to four athletes can represent national teams in eleven events, including the 100-meter dash, hurdles, swimming, long jump, high jump, shot put, javelin, hammer, discus, triple jump and pole vault.

The classic three-button athletic controls return: players rapidly alternate two run buttons to build speed or power, then use the action button to time jumps, throws and other techniques. Qualification targets create pressure even in solo play, while persistent record tables encourage repeat attempts. With fully polygonal athletes and much more elaborate presentation, it updates one of Konami's quintessential button-mashing arcade series for the mid-1990s.

games.title: Hypernoid
games.description: Hypernoid is a brick-breaking ball-and-paddle arcade game developed by M. Priewe (NeoHomeBrew) for the Neo Geo MVS platform in 2021, featuring power-ups, multi-ball hazards, and boss encounters.

games.title: Hyper Pacman
games.description:
Hyper Pacman is SemiCom's 1995 Korean reimagining of the Pac-Man maze formula. Players guide a yellow or pink character around perspective-drawn mazes, gathering the necessary items while escaping ghosts. The game borrows the ability to leap over pursuers from Namco's Pac-Mania but adds an array of more aggressive equipment and secrets.

Collectible shoes permit jumps or improve speed, a shield affords protection and a laser helmet allows the player to shoot at enemies. These tools change the familiar cat-and-mouse relationship: instead of relying only on power pellets, a skilled player can take the offensive for limited periods. Secret food and bonus opportunities encourage exploration of the game's 30 mazes. Although its name and characters echo Namco's famous creation, Hyper Pacman is an unofficial arcade offshoot rather than part of the licensed series.

games.title: Hyper Sports
games.description:
Konami's Hyper Sports (1984), called Hyper Olympic '84 in Japan, is the sequel to the enormously successful Track & Field. It replaces the original events with seven disciplines: freestyle swimming, skeet shooting, the long horse vault, archery, triple jump, weightlifting and pole vault. Each event demands its own combination of rapid button pressing and precisely timed action, and players must meet qualification targets to progress.

The familiar two run or GO buttons and one action button make even complicated sports understandable at a glance. Swimming calls for frantic speed and timely turns, shooting and archery test coordination and aiming, and events such as the pole vault reward knowing when to release a carefully built-up effort. Alternating between these physical rhythms is the game's central appeal, particularly when several players take turns competing for better records.

The Japanese version carried a license associated with the 1984 Olympic Games, while the international release used the Hyper Sports name. Less of a mass-market phenomenon than its predecessor, it nevertheless extended the distinctive arcade sporting formula that made Konami's button-mashing athletics games a lasting fixture of the 1980s.

games.title: Hyperdrive
games.description:
Hyperdrive is Midway's 1998 futuristic 3D racing game, in which players pilot hovering spacecraft around tracks suspended in space. Unlike traditional automobile racers, the ships can alter their height above the roadway. Flying close to the surface produces greater speed, while rising above it can help overtake rivals or negotiate awkward traffic.

Four selectable craft offer different handling characteristics, and the game features three tracks with increasing difficulty, from Orbital Speedway to Deep Space. Its dedicated sit-down arcade presentation and unusual vertical racing mechanic make Hyperdrive an ambitious but relatively obscure entry in the post-Wipeout wave of anti-gravity racing games.

games.title: Hyper Duel
games.description:
Hyper Duel is Technosoft's 1993 horizontally scrolling shooter, distributed in Japanese arcades by Taito. It puts players in control of experimental Buster Gear fighters on a mission involving a stolen prototype and hostile forces. The central innovation is transformation: at any point, a craft can change from a nimble spaceship into a larger humanoid robot, each form with different weapons, firing patterns and handling.

Three selectable pilots provide different equipment, while collectible upgrades strengthen weapons and add supporting units that fly alongside the player. The robot is particularly powerful but presents a larger target, demanding a more deliberate approach to crowded scenes. Across seven stages, the game mixes dense mechanical enemies with huge boss encounters.

Developed by the studio famous for the Thunder Force series, Hyper Duel combines that lineage's fast shooting with a memorable transforming-mecha identity. Its later Sega Saturn conversion became especially sought after by import shooter enthusiasts, but the arcade original already displays the game's exceptionally elaborate sprite work.

games.title: Mahjong Hyper Reaction 2
games.description: Mahjong Hyper Reaction 2 is Sammy's 1997 follow-up to its animated adult mahjong game. Set around a stylish bar atmosphere, it pits the player in one-on-one Japanese mahjong contests against four illustrated female opponents. Winning matches advances the encounters and unlocks further character animations. The sequel emphasizes polished anime-style presentation rather than altering mahjong's underlying tile-and-hand rules.

games.title: Mahjong Hyper Reaction
games.description: Mahjong Hyper Reaction is a 1995 Japanese adult mahjong arcade game from Sammy. Players compete at Japanese mahjong against animated female characters, with the game's principal distinguishing feature being the unusually elaborate illustrations and motion sequences used to present opponents and victories. Its conventional mahjong competition is framed as a character-oriented arcade experience, and it was followed by Mahjong Hyper Reaction 2 in 1997.

games.title: Ibara
games.description:
Ibara is Cave's 2005 vertically scrolling bullet-hell shooter, shaped by the influence of Raizing's Battle Garegga. Set in a fantastical industrial age of steam machinery and eccentric military engineering, it sends a small fighter against Professor Teresa Rose and her formidable female guardians. The playfield fills with destructive machinery, spectacular boss craft and bursts of enemy fire, but scoring demands more than simply surviving.

Destroyed enemies release medals that can be collected in increasingly valuable chains. Weapon pickups, special bomb attacks and careful control of rank, the game's adaptive difficulty, reward players who understand the relationship between aggression and survival. Rather than the luminous fantasy projectiles associated with some other Cave shooters, Ibara uses a dense mechanical look, sometimes making the deadliest bullets deliberately hard to distinguish from the wreckage.

The project was directed by Shinobu Yagawa, whose earlier Raizing work is evident in its weapons, medal system and punishing challenge. Ibara is consequently both a major Cave release and a striking continuation of a distinctive strand of Japanese arcade shooting design.

games.title: Ibara Kuro Black Label

variants.title: Ibara Kuro Black Label (2006/02/06. MASTER VER.)
Ibara Kuro Black Label (2006/02/06 MASTER VER.)

games.description:
Ibara Kuro: Black Label is Cave's revised 2006 edition of its 2005 vertical shooter. The same steampunk battle against Professor Rose's forces returns, but the Black Label revision rebalances the systems and changes how players approach weapons, scoring and survival. Its mechanics are intended to provide a distinct experience rather than merely a harder setting for the original.

The game retains dense mechanical stages, formidable multi-part bosses, bombs and the emphasis on chaining valuable medals. Black Label was produced in very limited numbers, reportedly around a hundred boards, making it a particularly prized edition among arcade shooter collectors.

games.title: Ibara Kuro Black Label (Color Sat)

variants.title: Ibara Kuro Black Label (2006-02-06. MASTER VER. COLOR SAT)

modifications.description: Increases color saturation across stage backgrounds and sprites for improved bullet visibility.

games.description: Ibara Kuro Black Label (Color Sat) is a graphic palette hack by ArcCabView for Cave's 2006 vertical shoot-'em-up Ibara Kuro: Black Label, boosting color saturation to improve visual contrast and enemy bullet visibility.

games.title: Ibara (Color Sat)

modifications.description: Increases color saturation across stage backgrounds and sprites for improved bullet visibility.

games.description: Ibara (Color Sat) is a graphic palette hack by ArcCabView for Cave's 2005 vertical shoot-'em-up Ibara, adjusting background and sprite color saturation for clearer contrast.

games.title: Vs. Ice Climber
games.description:
Vs. Ice Climber is Nintendo's arcade edition of the 1980s mountain-climbing platform game, released for its NES-derived Vs. System. Popo and Nana climb tiers of icy platforms with small mallets, smashing openings overhead, jumping between ledges and avoiding roaming enemies. Each mountain culminates in an upper bonus area where the climbers can gather vegetables before trying to reach the passing condor.

The deceptively simple controls are made difficult by the characters' momentum and the need to strike ice from below, often while the ceiling is occupied by creatures or moving obstacles. Two-player action combines cooperation with the temptation to climb faster than a partner. Compared with the familiar Famicom/NES release, the Vs. edition adds or changes enemies and graphics, hidden bonuses, a super-bonus stage, stage selection and extended music. Those modifications make the coin-operated release more than a straightforward copy of the home game.

games.title: Vs. Ice Climber Dual
games.description: Vs. Ice Climber Dual is the Japanese dual-system arcade configuration of Nintendo's mountain-climbing platform game. The core action remains the same: Popo and Nana smash through overhead ice with mallets, leap between ledges, collect vegetables and avoid enemies while ascending the mountain toward the condor. Its identification as a Dual version reflects the dual-cabinet Vs. System arrangement, allowing play on paired screens and more participants than a single-screen setup. It should not be confused with an entirely new sequel or a mechanically unrelated game.

games.title: Puzzle & Action: Ichidant-R
games.description:
Puzzle & Action: Ichidant-R is Sega's 1994 sequel to Tant-R, exchanging the first game's detective setting for a playful medieval world. The returning heroes are now comic knights trying to rescue a princess, with progress determined by a succession of short, self-contained mini-games rather than combat stages.

Its collection of roughly twenty tasks ranges from timing a button press to remembering patterns, making fast visual judgments or solving simple action puzzles. The mini-game selector cycles through choices, so even choosing the next challenge can require good timing. The game's charm comes from cartoon animation, surprising rules and the way a single cabinet continually changes what is expected of the player. It is a distinctive ancestor of the frantic multi-game party format popularized later by console series.

games.title: Idol no Himitsu
games.description: Idol no Himitsu, or Idol's Secret, is a 1989 Japanese medal mahjong game. It combines the traditional tile-based competition of Japanese mahjong with an idol-themed presentation and a betting-oriented arcade format. Its documented appeal lies in the combination of character imagery and tabletop play rather than an action-game control scheme.

games.title: Idol-Mahjong Housoukyoku
games.description: Idol-Mahjong Housoukyoku is a 1988 Japanese adult mahjong game associated with the television and entertainment world, its title meaning approximately Idol Mahjong Broadcasting Station. The player takes part in mahjong matches against illustrated female performers, with erotic reveal imagery tied to success. An early example of the idol-themed mahjong niche, it shows how Japanese arcade makers combined traditional tile play, celebrity-style presentation and adult rewards.

games.title: Indoor Soccer
games.description: Indoor Soccer is Universal's 1985 two-on-two football game, played on a compact, side-scrolling field rather than a conventional overhead stadium. The small teams compete for possession, shoot at goal and use sliding challenges to disrupt opponents, with crowd noise adding to the atmosphere. Its unusual twin-eight-way-joystick cabinet gives the sport a distinctive physical control scheme. Released in March 1985, it was Universal's last wholly original arcade video game and one of the company's rare excursions into sports.

games.title: Iemoto
games.description: Iemoto is a 1987 adult-themed Japanese mahjong game from Nichibutsu. Rather than presenting mahjong as an abstract tabletop contest, it frames the matches around a melodramatic rescue story in which the player must defeat a succession of mercenary opponents to save captive women. The gameplay remains based on Japanese mahjong hands, with victories advancing the character-driven scenario. Its title means roughly Head of a School or Master of a House.

games.title: IGMO
games.description:
IGMO is a 1984 arcade action-maze game published by Epos. The hero, Igmo, must rescue Princess Iggy from the dragon Sintar, navigating a hazardous fantasy landscape under time pressure. He can fire in eight directions to defeat creatures such as Octoids, Spidoids and Crustoids, and must position or shoot floating Bergs to build a route across a river.

The journey ends in a confrontation with Sintar, whose fiery projectiles must be dodged while the player lands repeated shots. Rescuing the princess starts another, harder round. Its combination of multidirectional shooting, route creation and a fantasy rescue objective makes IGMO an unusual hybrid of maze and action game.

games.title: Ikari Warriors
games.description:
Ikari Warriors is SNK's landmark 1986 vertically scrolling run-and-gun arcade game, published in many Western markets by Tradewest. Inspired by the popularity of 1980s commando action films, it sends two heavily armed soldiers through jungles, rivers and enemy military installations to reach the village of Ikari. Infantry, tanks, bunkers and helicopters attack as players advance, using machine guns and grenades to clear a path.

Its defining controls are rotary joysticks that allow each soldier to move in one direction while aiming in another. Combined with simultaneous cooperative play, this makes the game far more flexible than contemporary shooters in which movement and firing direction were linked. Players can seize enemy tanks, but those vehicles consume fuel and may explode, forcing a well-timed escape. Ammunition and power-up supplies must also be managed during the long campaign.

Ikari Warriors became one of SNK's first major international arcade hits and helped establish rotary-control military shooters as a distinct genre. The soldiers later became identified with Ralf Jones and Clark Still, recurring characters in SNK's wider catalogue, while the arcade game's tense two-player teamwork remained its strongest legacy.

games.title: Ikari III - The Rescue
games.description:
Ikari III: The Rescue is SNK's 1989 continuation of the Ikari Warriors series, but it changes the action dramatically. Instead of primarily firing through ranks of enemies, its two commandos fight through hostile territory using fists, kicks and other hand-to-hand attacks as they attempt to rescue a kidnapped hostage. Guns can be acquired from defeated enemies, but ammunition is limited, making close combat the normal way to survive.

The overhead battlefield still scrolls through military encounters and includes vehicles and heavily armed enemies, preserving the original series' atmosphere. By shifting the focus toward brawling, Ikari III stands apart from the rotary-joystick shooting that made its predecessors famous.

games.title: Ikki
games.description:
Ikki is Sunsoft's unusual 1985 arcade action game about a peasant uprising in feudal Japan. Instead of commanding an army, players control the farmer Gonbe and, with a second player, his companion Tago, as they struggle against ninjas and other hostile forces. The action is viewed from above across garden-like maze areas, with a map and scattered objectives guiding the player's movement.

The main weapon is a thrown sickle that automatically seeks a nearby enemy, an unusual arrangement that makes movement and evasion more important than manually lining up shots. Players navigate obstacles, gather items and pursue the stage goal while avoiding being surrounded. The idea of mounting a great rebellion with only one or two farmers gives the entire game a deliberately comic flavor.

Known to many Japanese players through its later Famicom version, Ikki became a cult curiosity for both its premise and its demanding, sometimes awkward play. The arcade original remains a fascinating contrast to the heroic military shooters that dominated action-game design during the same period.

games.title: Imago
games.description: Imago is Acom's 1983 vertical shooter, combining the descending segmented enemies of Centipede with the aggressive formations of Galaga. A small player craft moves across the bottom portion of a vertical screen and fires at insect-like chains moving through a field of obstacles. Hitting a middle segment can break a chain into separate threats, while other enemies break away to dive toward the player. The eight-way joystick allows limited vertical evasive movement as well as horizontal steering, making the crowded lower playfield a central part of the challenge.

games.title: Imekura Mahjong
games.description:
Imekura Mahjong is a 1994 Japanese adult mahjong game built around footage and photographs of six live-action actresses rather than illustrated characters. The player competes in Japanese mahjong hands, trying to avoid exhausting their betting funds while causing opponents to lose theirs.

Winning hands unlocks progressively more revealing scenes, including still photographs and short, low-frame-rate video sequences. In contrast to many animated strip-mahjong games, Imekura's use of digitized live-action material is the distinguishing feature of its presentation.

games.title: Image Fight
games.description:
Image Fight is Irem's 1988 vertically scrolling shooter, best known for turning the early stages of the game into a graded combat-training simulation. Piloting the OF-1 fighter, the player battles through five simulated environments before the real mission begins. At the end of each training stage, the game assesses the proportion of enemies destroyed; an average kill rate below 90 percent forces the player into an extra Penalty Area before progressing.

The fighter can vary its movement speed and attach different auxiliary weapon units, adding a rich layer of tactical choices to the precision shooting. Certain attached guns can even be launched forward as powerful, returning weapons. Enemy patterns demand both aggressive destruction and careful control of the ship's position, especially when the scoring system penalizes missed targets.

Released after Irem's R-Type, Image Fight shares that studio's taste for elaborate mechanical enemies and punishing stage design, but its upward-scrolling format, variable speed and unusual performance examination give it a strongly individual identity. It became a respected challenge among arcade shooter specialists and was later adapted to several home platforms.

games.title: I'm Sorry
games.description:
I'm Sorry, released in Japan in 1985 as Gonbee no I'm Sorry, is a bizarre satirical maze game from Coreland and Sega. Its protagonist is a caricature of former Japanese prime minister Kakuei Tanaka, and the title plays on the similarity between the English words I'm sorry and the Japanese term for prime minister, sori. The objective is to gather gold bars from each stage and bring them to a designated building, an unmistakable joke about political greed.

The hero can carry only ten bars at a time, so later stages require multiple trips through dangerous streets and walkways. Enemies are caricatures of contemporary celebrities and public figures, including a moonwalking pop star and famous wrestlers, while conveyor belts, rolling barrels and other obstacles complicate each run. Punching and jumping help clear a path.

Its strange combination of cartoon slapstick, recognizably political satire and straightforward collection-maze gameplay makes I'm Sorry one of the most distinctive Japanese arcade oddities of the mid-1980s.

games.title: Indian Battle
games.description:
Indian Battle is Taito's 1980 Western-themed fixed shooter, presenting the period's stereotyped cowboys-versus-Indians scenario on a vertical screen. The player moves a cowboy horizontally along the bottom and fires upward at enemies who retaliate with arrows, tomahawks and rocks. Different targets yield different scores, with mounted riders and condors worth more than ordinary enemies.

Every third stage changes pace with a lasso bonus round, challenging the player to rope passing targets for additional points. Its combination of fixed-screen shooting, variable-value enemies and a periodic skill interlude makes it a curious early attempt to extend the Space Invaders formula beyond science-fiction imagery.

games.title: Danny Sullivan's Indy Heat
games.description:
Danny Sullivan's Indy Heat is Leland's 1991 overhead racing game, endorsed by the American IndyCar driver whose name appears in the title. Up to three arcade players compete against each other and computer racers on a series of twisting CART-inspired circuits, while Sullivan himself appears as a regular opponent. The view keeps the entire racing struggle close and immediately readable.

The cars can crash, catch fire and run short of fuel, so visits to the pits matter almost as much as steering skill.
