Prize money earned from finishing positions can be spent on better acceleration, tires, brakes, turbo reserves and pit crews. Closely related in design to Leland's Super Off Road, Indy Heat combines crowd-friendly multiplayer racing with the pleasure of gradually upgrading a car over a season.

games.title: Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom

variants.title: Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom (set 1)
Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom (set 2)
Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom (set 3)
Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom (set 4)
Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom (German)

games.description:
Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom is Atari Games' 1985 arcade adaptation of the 1984 film, starring the archaeologist on a mission to free enslaved children and recover the Sankara Stones from the Thuggee cult. Using an eight-way joystick and a whip button, players explore dangerous mine chambers, fight guards and snakes, and break open cages to rescue prisoners. Three selectable starting difficulty levels make the campaign accessible to different players.

The adventure moves through distinct sequences inspired by the movie. Mine exploration involves ledges, elevators and conveyors; a frantic mine-cart chase demands choosing the correct tracks; and the temple finale centers on recovering the sacred stones and escaping the cult leader Mola Ram. The constantly shifting objectives make it more varied than a typical licensed arcade platformer.

The game was also a technical showcase for Atari's System 1 hardware, being the first title on that platform to use digitized speech. Recognizable film dialogue and music associated with John Williams help connect the compact arcade stages to the original movie's atmosphere.

games.title: Inferno
games.description:
Inferno is Williams' 1984 isometric-style maze shooter, played across tiered arenas filled with monsters. The player moves through the maze while aiming shots in different directions, but simply destroying an enemy is not always enough. Each defeated creature releases a dark soul that races toward a monstrous mouth; if it reaches the exit, a tougher enemy is regenerated. Touching the fleeing soul before it escapes prevents that return.

The separate movement and firing controls support frantic multidirectional combat, while stairways and narrow passages make the arena feel closer to a hostile labyrinth than an open shooting gallery. This soul-catching mechanic gives Inferno an unusual second objective layered over its relentless monster combat.

games.title: Insector
games.description:
Insector is an unreleased 1982 Gottlieb arcade prototype designed by Tim Skelly, reportedly surviving in only one or two original units. The player controls an animated can of insect spray, destroying waves of bugs and collecting jewels scattered around the screen. Its arena-based action was Skelly's own response to the frenetic design of Robotron: 2084.

An especially unusual feature is the three-letter code entered at the start of a game. The letters seed the game's pseudo-random generator, allowing a player to reproduce the same enemy sequence deliberately or choose a different one for a fresh challenge. This makes Insector a fascinating example of a prototype exploring replayability and reproducible difficulty long before such options became commonplace.

games.title: Insector X
games.description:
Insector X is Hot-B's 1989 horizontally scrolling shooter, released in arcades by Taito. In its fanciful insect world, a miniature armored hero must defeat huge mechanized bugs and an invading army of cybernetic creatures. A colorful mixture of plant life, enormous insects and mechanical bosses gives the stages a distinctly whimsical look.

Two attack buttons control the upgradeable main gun and a separate selection of special or secondary weapons. The player weaves through airborne insects and shots while collecting improvements that make survival in later stages possible. Insector X was later adapted for the Famicom and Mega Drive, but the arcade version established its peculiar combination of cute scenery and military-style shooting.

games.title: International Cup '94
games.description:
International Cup '94 is a 1994 soccer arcade game from Taito, released on the F3 hardware platform. Players compete in fast-paced football matches, controlling a team on the pitch rather than managing a league from menus. Its brisk arcade pace and national-team competition reflect the surge of soccer games around the 1994 World Cup.

The title circulated under regional names, including Hat Trick Hero '94 in parts of North America. It belongs to Taito's line of accessible arcade football games, in which direct control and quick matches take priority over detailed sports simulation.

games.title: In The Hunt
games.description:
In the Hunt is Irem's lavishly animated 1993 horizontally scrolling submarine shooter, originally titled Kaitei Daisensou in Japan. Players command the Granvia, an advanced submarine sent to stop the Dark Anarchy Society after the group has devastated much of the planet. Its battles unfold underwater and across the surface, with torpedoes, depth charges and other weapons used against submarines, warships, mechanical creatures and enormous installations.

Unlike a shooter that forces constant forward movement, the Granvia can control its own pace through portions of a stage, allowing more deliberate positioning and attack. Different weapons are effective against targets above, below or ahead of the craft, and the stages continually shift between confined passages, open waters and spectacular set-piece encounters. The destructible scenery and large bosses create a remarkably cinematic sense of scale.

Several artists and developers associated with this project later worked on Metal Slug, and its lush pixel animation, mechanical designs and playful visual details anticipate that series. In the Hunt stands as one of the most visually distinctive submarine-themed arcade shooters ever made.

games.title: Intrepid
games.description:
Intrepid is Nova Games' 1983 espionage maze game, casting the player as a secret agent infiltrating an embassy to recover stolen plans. The agent searches rooms across multiple floors, using stairs and an elevator while avoiding guards and a strict time limit. Instead of simply collecting points, the player must locate a sequence of useful objects, including a key, a combination and an identification card needed to open and access the vault.

Other equipment provides tactical advantages: a disguise helps pass a sentry, a map reveals room contents, running shoes improve speed, a wrench can sabotage the elevator and an umbrella can enable escape from the roof. Successfully retrieving the plans and getting away completes the mission, which becomes harder on subsequent attempts. Its item-dependent progression makes Intrepid an unusually elaborate early arcade stealth-and-exploration game.

games.title: Intergirl
games.description: Intergirl is a little-known 1995 Korean adult-oriented arcade game from Barko, derived from the earlier Dragon Punch rock-paper-scissors game. Rather than being an entirely original action puzzler, it repackages the competitive hand-sign format with changed artwork and adult-themed visual presentation. Its significance is primarily as an unauthorized regional reworking of an established Japanese amusement-game concept.

games.title: Karaoke Quiz Intro Don Don!

variants.title: Karaoke Quiz Intro Don Don! (J 960213 V1.000)

games.description: Karaoke Quiz Intro Don Don! is a 1996 Japanese music-quiz game developed by Success and published by Sunsoft for Sega's ST-V (Titan Video) arcade system. Rather than focusing on general trivia, its questions are built around popular songs and karaoke culture, asking players to recognize or respond to musical material. Joystick-and-button controls support quiz responses, and the cartridge-based ST-V hardware gives it a richer audiovisual presentation than most earlier coin-operated quiz machines. It was released in Japan in 1996, with preserved cartridge builds dated February 13.

games.title: Intersecti
games.description:
Intersecti is the provisional name of an unidentified arcade circuit board preserved in MAME, rather than a confirmed commercial title. In a May 2006 message to the MAME development mailing list, Chris Hardy reported that the PCB had no identifying markings and that \"Intersecti\" was the only readable text in its sound ROM. A daughterboard carried the marking \"Serai-Padova-1\". After disassembling program ROMs labelled \"1911\", Hardy suspected that additional code might be hidden inside an epoxy-encapsulated module, but had not yet connected the board to test that possibility.

The preliminary MAME driver describes a Z80-based board with a 256×512-pixel raster display, but one ROM remained undumped and the controls were not documented. The original gameplay, manufacturer, and release date therefore remain unknown.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.
Original developer and publisher are not established.

games.title: Quiz & Variety Sukusuku Inufuku
games.description:
Quiz & Variety Sukusuku Inufuku is Video System's 1998 Japanese quiz game, mixing trivia with the care of a bizarre little virtual pet. Players answer questions and take part in varied short challenges while raising an Inufuku, a round, white creature that combines the appearance of several familiar pets. Progress in the quiz and variety-game portions is tied to the character's growth, giving the score-chasing action a gentle pet-raising framework.

The cheerful, eccentric design makes Inufuku stand apart from the straightforward multiple-choice quiz machines common in Japanese arcades. It was among Video System's last arcade releases, adding historical interest to an already unusual hybrid of trivia and virtual-pet simulation.

games.title: Space Invaders II
games.description:
Space Invaders II is Midway's 1980 American arcade sequel built around simultaneous two-player competition, not to be confused with Taito's separate Space Invaders Part II, marketed in North America as Space Invaders Deluxe. Its cocktail-table layout lets two players defend against descending alien formations at the same time. They can cooperate against the invaders, but are also free to shoot one another and potentially gain an advantage by stealing the rival's remaining ships.

The familiar laser cannons, moving formations and enemy fire are therefore transformed by an unpredictable human opponent. Midway reportedly developed the game in-house without Taito's authorization, using modified Space Invaders Deluxe hardware and separate sound circuitry for each player. It is a fascinating early experiment in adding direct player-versus-player conflict to a hugely successful single-player shooting formula.

games.title: Space Invaders / Space Invaders M
games.description:
Space Invaders, designed by Tomohiro Nishikado and released by Taito in Japan in 1978, is one of the foundational video games of the arcade era. A lone laser cannon defends Earth against eleven columns of descending aliens, moving horizontally along the bottom of a fixed screen and firing upward. The invaders advance left and right in formation, dropping closer after each reversal, while four destructible shields provide temporary cover and a mystery saucer periodically crosses overhead for bonus points.

Its deceptively straightforward rules produce a rising tension that was startling for the time. As enemies are destroyed, the remaining formation moves faster and its rhythmic marching sounds accelerate, making the last few invaders unexpectedly dangerous. Players can shoot holes through their own defensive barriers, so protection gradually becomes a set of openings and risks to manage. The game made high-score competition a central attraction, encouraging repeated attempts to survive another increasingly difficult wave.

Distributed in North America by Midway, Space Invaders became an international commercial phenomenon and helped establish video games as a major amusement industry. Its alien designs, sound pulse, defensive bunkers and descending-formation structure were imitated by countless successors. The slowdown-and-speedup effect originally arose from the way the hardware handled fewer on-screen enemies, but became one of the game's most famous dramatic features. Few arcade titles have had a comparable influence on both game design and popular culture.

games.title: Space Invaders Part II
games.description:
Space Invaders Part II (1979) is Taito's direct follow-up to the arcade phenomenon that defined the fixed-screen shooter. Designer Tomohiro Nishikado returned to the original formula of a horizontally moving laser base, destructible defensive shelters, and ranks of aliens that descend faster as their numbers dwindle. This time, however, certain invaders divide into smaller targets when shot, flashing UFOs require precise timing, and flying saucers can drop reinforcements to prolong a wave.

Part II also introduced brief comic intermissions between rounds, in which a surviving alien makes its escape, and expanded high-score recognition with player initials. It was produced partly to make use of spare Space Invaders hardware, yet its new enemy behavior and playful presentation made it more than a routine revision. Midway distributed the game in North America as Space Invaders Deluxe in 1980, with a lower point award for the flashing saucer. The attract mode of that version still displays the Space Invaders Part II name, a memorable trace of its Japanese origin.

games.title: Invasion
games.description:
Invasion: The Abductors is a 1999 science-fiction arcade shooter developed by Play Mechanix and published by Midway on its Zeus hardware. Its premise casts Earth's population as the subject of a long-running alien experiment: the extraterrestrial visitors return to harvest humanity, abducting and mutating people while attacking cities and landmarks. Players tackle four missions to stop the invasion.

The game supports two-player action and uses Midway's distinctive high-resolution 3D arcade technology rather than the 2D fixed-screen format associated with older games called Invasion. It is a comparatively obscure late-1990s Midway release, notable for taking an alien-invasion theme into an elaborate mission-based arcade shooting setting.

games.title: Invinco / Deep Scan
games.description:
Invinco / Deep Scan combines two Sega VIC Dual games on one arcade board. Invinco is Sega's inventive 1979 response to Space Invaders: players fire upward from the bottom of the screen at alien ranks whose members can disappear, tumble, withstand repeated hits, or explode and take nearby invaders with them. Its unusual targets demand more careful shot timing than the familiar marching formations suggest.

Deep Scan changes the pace completely, putting the player in charge of a surface vessel attacking submarines with depth charges. The pairing represents Sega's early practice of offering contrasting games in a single coin-operated cabinet, allowing operators to combine an alien shooter with a naval action game.

games.title: Invinco / Head On 2
games.description:
Invinco / Head On 2 is a dual-game Sega VIC Dual arcade release that pairs two different tests of timing. In Invinco, a cannon fires at Space Invaders-style formations containing blinking, rolling, armored, and explosive enemies, making individual targets behave differently rather than simply marching in lockstep.

Head On 2 instead puts the player in a car circling a compact network of lanes, collecting dots while avoiding oncoming computer-controlled cars. Lanes can be changed only at designated junctions, so the player must anticipate collisions and manage speed. The contrasting shooter and maze-driving formats make this a particularly revealing example of Sega's early multi-game arcade hardware.

games.title: Invinco
games.description:
Sega's Invinco (1979) looks at first like another Space Invaders imitator, but its enemies are unusually varied for the period. The player's cannon moves across the bottom of a vertical screen and fires at formations containing aliens that blink out of sight, roll to change their profile, survive multiple hits, or explode and destroy their neighbors. Different enemy types award different scores, rewarding players who learn when to fire and where to aim.

After a formation is cleared, a zigzagging 'sky chariot' attacks; later stages send progressively more of these enemies. Released on Sega's VIC Dual hardware and also offered in combination cabinets with Head On 2 or Deep Scan, Invinco shows how quickly developers began extending the fixed-shooter design established by Taito in 1978.

games.title: Invader's Revenge
games.description:
Invader's Revenge is a British variation on Space Invaders by Zenitone-Microsec, associated with early-1980s arcade conversions of Midway's original hardware. Instead of simply preventing aliens from reaching the ground, the player must protect a finite fuel supply. Six attackers appear in each wave, and individual aliens break formation to steal fuel or drop bombs that destroy it. Some damaged invaders even fall toward the player's ship, turning an accurate shot into a new hazard.

After seven waves, the player must negotiate a docking sequence to refuel. Its combination of fuel defense, varied alien formations, and a periodic docking challenge gives Invader's Revenge a distinct rhythm. Original conversions used an additional sound board for music and effects, making it a distinctive regional offshoot of the Space Invaders boom.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: In Your Face
games.description:
In Your Face is an unreleased 1991 Jaleco basketball game preserved as an arcade prototype. Its half-court street-basketball matches support one-on-one and two-on-two play, emphasizing close-quarters competition rather than a full-court sports simulation. The game uses joystick controls with three action buttons on Jaleco's Mega System 1 hardware.

It closely resembles the style of Jaleco's earlier NES basketball title Hoops, making it an interesting example of a console-era sports idea being reworked for arcade play. Its prototype status is central to its history: the game did not receive a normal commercial arcade launch.

games.title: IPM Invader
games.description:
IPM Invader (1979) is an early Japanese Space Invaders rival from IPM, the company soon renamed Irem. It retains the defining ingredients of Taito's hit: a cannon moving horizontally beneath advancing alien rows, protective obstacles, enemy fire, and bonus saucers. Unlike the original monochrome cabinet with colored overlays, IPM Invader used a color display and its own 6502-based hardware.

Its variations include a 'coffee break' intermission after every third wave. With the capsule option enabled, UFOs drop objects that eventually hatch into more invaders, countering strategies that depend on clearing narrow channels through the enemy formation. The game is particularly significant as part of Irem's earliest move into arcade video games, years before the company became famous for more ambitious shooters and action titles.

games.title: IQ-Block
games.description:
IQ-Block is a 1993 falling-block puzzle game from Taiwan's International Games System (IGS). Instead of simply making solid horizontal lines, players organize descending numbered blocks into matching sets or numerical runs to remove them and score points. The format adds a number-combination problem to the familiar demand for quick placement.

Running on compact Z80-based arcade hardware, IQ-Block supports two-player play and reflects IGS's early focus on accessible puzzle and amusement games. Later related sets appeared on different hardware, including versions associated with gambling-oriented adaptations, but the original stands as a straightforward number-matching arcade puzzle.

games.title: I, Robot
games.description:
Atari's I, Robot, designed by Dave Theurer and produced in 1983, is one of the most technically audacious arcade games of its era. Often cited as the first commercial arcade game to render filled, shaded 3D polygons in real time, it abandoned the line-vector appearance of Atari's earlier 3D experiments. Its story follows Unhappy Interface Robot #1984, a rebellious servant defying the giant surveillance eye of the authoritarian Big Brother.

The player moves across suspended geometric platforms, changing red squares to blue to weaken the eye's defenses. Jumping is dangerous whenever the eye is open, and birds, moving hazards, and other enemies complicate the route. Between platform stages, the robot flies through 3D space, shooting or dodging obstacles. Most unusually, the player can change the camera viewpoint: closer views increase the score multiplier but reduce visibility. Later enemies even attack the camera itself.

I, Robot also includes Doodle City, a separate mode for experimenting with polygon artwork. Despite these innovations, its unfamiliar controls and unconventional action failed to attract a broad arcade audience, and relatively few cabinets were produced. Its reputation has since risen dramatically among collectors and historians as a striking early step toward polygon-based video games.

games.title: Iron
games.description:
Iron is an unauthorized 1996 arcade adaptation of Iron Commando, the 1994 Super Nintendo beat-'em-up developed by Arcade Zone. Rather than being an independently designed arcade fighter, it runs a modified version of the console game on pirate hardware derived from the Super Nintendo architecture.

The underlying game is a side-scrolling brawler in which players advance through enemy-filled stages using punches, kicks, and weapons. Its significance in an arcade collection lies in the hardware conversion: the original console software was repackaged for coin-operated use, with ROM data-line scrambling rather than an entirely new arcade engine. It is a revealing artifact of the 1990s market for illicit console-to-arcade conversions.

games.title: Choutetsu Brikin'ger - Ironclad
games.description:
Choutetsu Brikin'ger, also known as Ironclad, is a 1996 horizontally scrolling shooter by Saurus set against the mechanical forces of the Iron Mask Republic. The player pilots a warship assisted by a powerful companion unit, the Iron Clad, which can be attached to the craft or launched into enemies with a charged attack. Multiple upgradeable shot types, close-range weapons, and a bomb attack give the game an unusually broad arsenal.

Its layered landscapes and perspective effects lend the action a pseudo-3D appearance, while selectable stage routes encourage repeat plays. Ironclad is best known as a Neo Geo CD release, making the preserved MVS arcade prototype especially interesting: it documents a seldom-seen cartridge version of a shooter that originally became available to players through a different branch of the Neo Geo family.

games.title: Iron Fortress
games.description:
Iron Fortress is a 1998 top-down tank action game from Eolith. Players choose from a group of military characters and maneuver an armed tank around city-like arenas, destroying hostile armored vehicles while defending a base. The action combines multidirectional shooting with stage-by-stage threats rather than the continuous movement of a conventional scrolling shooter.

Its resemblance to earlier arcade tank games such as Tank Force is immediately apparent, but its own stage layouts, weapon behavior, and pacing distinguish it. Iron Fortress is a relatively obscure example of the compact, mission-oriented action games still appearing in arcades toward the end of the 1990s.

games.title: Iron Horse
games.description:
Konami's Iron Horse (1986), released in Japan as Dai Ressya Goutou, is a fast-moving Wild West action platformer set aboard a train. The player fights through railcars and across their roofs, using ladders to move between levels while confronting armed cowboys and collecting money. Weapons include a pistol, a whip, and close-range attacks, forcing the player to adjust tactics to each enemy's distance.

The constantly moving train supplies a strong visual identity, and the vertical routes make each carriage more than a simple corridor. Its brisk platform combat and lively western-style music capture Konami's mid-1980s knack for turning a single unusual setting into a complete arcade action game. An unauthorized version circulated under the title Far West.

games.title: The Irritating Maze / Ultra Denryu Iraira Bou
games.description:
The Irritating Maze, known in Japan as Ultra Denryu Iraira Bou, is a 1997 Neo Geo arcade game based on a Japanese television challenge involving a metal wand and an electrified maze. Rather than fighting or collecting points in the traditional sense, players use a trackball to guide an object through narrow, winding passages without touching their boundaries. Tight corners, moving obstacles, and time pressure turn precise hand movement into the entire challenge.

Created by SNK and Saurus, the game is especially notable for its dedicated trackball controls, an unusual requirement for Neo Geo MVS hardware. Its connection to Japanese variety television and its deliberately aggravating precision make it one of the platform's strangest releases.

games.title: Itazura Tenshi
games.description:
Itazura Tenshi is a 1984 Japanese arcade action game developed by Alice and published by Nichibutsu. Players guide a small angel through a scrolling star field, connecting points of light to complete constellations while avoiding or attacking hostile creatures. Its objective mixes the movement and shooting of an arcade action game with a pattern-completion puzzle.

The game's romantic fairy-tale theme, in which an angel seeks the affection of another, gives it a softer identity than the military shooters common at the time. Released only in Japan originally, it later reached a wider audience through Hamster's Arcade Archives reissue in 2022.

games.title: Ixion
games.description:
Ixion is a Sega arcade prototype from 1983 built around the company's Zaxxon-era hardware. Players maneuver through a shooter-like playfield and collect letter symbols while confronting enemies and crystals; gathering the required letters leads to a special KAILO round. In this sequence, the KAILO ball repairs tiles while the opposing OLIAK ball destroys them, introducing a distinctive playfield-maintenance objective.

Reportedly prepared for a location test but never placed into broad production, Ixion survives as one of Sega's more obscure early-1980s experiments. Its combination of shooting, letter collection, and tile restoration sets it apart from the straightforward space shooters with which its hardware is associated.

games.title: Jack the Giantkiller
games.description:
Jack the Giantkiller is a 1982 Cinematronics platform adventure based on the fairy tale Jack and the Beanstalk. Players guide Jack upward through a sequence of obstacle-filled scenes, climb the giant beanstalk, infiltrate the giant's castle, collect treasures, and try to escape alive. The screens introduce different hazards and movement challenges, and later rounds gradually incorporate more of the game's set pieces.

Although contemporary with Donkey Kong, Jack the Giantkiller places more emphasis on progressing through a fairy-tale journey than mastering one repeating construction-site layout. It was also distributed in Japan under the title Treasure Hunt. Its multiple distinct scenes and storybook premise make it a memorable, if less celebrated, example of early arcade platform design.

games.title: Jackal
games.description:
Konami's Jackal (1986), known as Top Gunner in North American arcades, is an overhead military run-and-gun built around a heavily armed jeep. One or two players drive deep into enemy territory, firing a forward-facing machine gun and a directional grenade launcher while dodging soldiers, tanks, gun emplacements, and other defenses. The mission is not merely to reach the end of each battlefield: players are also encouraged to break open prisoner compounds and rescue captured soldiers.

Freed prisoners can be collected by the jeep and delivered to rescue helicopters, while weapon upgrades improve its secondary attack. Terrain and enemy placement demand a balance of driving, aiming, and rescue planning, especially in cooperative play. The scrolling battlefields culminate in large defensive encounters that give the campaign a satisfying forward momentum.

Jackal became one of Konami's best-loved mid-1980s vehicle shooters, and its combination of accessible controls with a humanitarian rescue objective gave it an identity distinct from the company's contemporary on-foot action games. Its later home conversions, especially on Nintendo systems, helped extend that reputation.

games.title: Jackpot Pool
games.description: Jackpot Pool is an Italian video-poker machine released in 1997 by Electronic Projects. Although its name evokes billiards, the documented game is a pool-themed gambling/card title rather than a cue-sport simulation. It was distributed in Italian variants, including a bootleg set, and is primarily operated through gambling controls rather than aiming a cue or navigating a playfield. Its unusual theme sets it apart from the more common fruit, royal-card and casino imagery used by contemporary Italian poker machines.

games.title: Jack Rabbit
games.description:
Jack Rabbit is a 1984 isometric action platformer from Italian manufacturer Zaccaria. Players guide a hungry rabbit through a succession of stages, collecting carrots while avoiding pits, snakes, bombs, and a pair of pursuing weasels. The game begins near Jack's house before introducing different environments, including a scrolling desert section, with hazards that alter the route to the next carrot.

Its angled view and changing scenery give it a different feel from the more straightforward side-on platform games of the period. The uncommon premise, lively pursuit mechanics, and Zaccaria's distinctive arcade hardware make Jack Rabbit a particularly recognizable European curiosity.

games.title: Jail Break
games.description:
Jail Break is Konami's 1986 run-and-gun game, released in Japan as Manhattan 24th Precinct. A mass prison escape has thrown the city into chaos, and the player takes the role of an armed police officer fighting through streets, public spaces, and the approach to the prison to rescue hostages and restore order. Enemies attack from several directions, demanding constant movement and careful use of the gun.

Rescuing innocent bystanders is more than a matter of score: civilians provide access to stronger weapons such as tear gas and a bazooka, while accidentally shooting them can strip the player of valuable equipment. The contrast between dangerous convicts and people who must be protected gives the game a sharper aiming challenge than an ordinary shoot-everything action title. Its distinctive synthesized speech and weapon-selection system reinforce Konami's mid-1980s arcade style.

games.title: Vs. Ninja Jajamaru Kun
games.description:
Vs. Ninja Jajamaru Kun is Jaleco's 1985 arcade adaptation of its Famicom action platformer, starring the mischievous ninja Jajamaru on a mission to rescue Princess Sakura from the villain Damazu-Dayuu. Players jump between the floors of compact, horizontally arranged stages, avoiding enemy attacks and striking opponents with shuriken. Each stage must be cleared before the next group of increasingly troublesome foes appears.

The game builds on the earlier Ninja-Kid tradition but uses its own characters and side-scrolling stage design. Presented on Nintendo's Vs. System, this version shows how a popular home-console platform game could be adapted to the competitive, credit-driven rhythm of the arcade.

games.title: Mahjong Janjan Baribari
games.description:
Mahjong Janjan Baribari is a 1992 Japanese medal-mahjong game associated with Nichibutsu, Yubis, and AV Japan. It belongs to the adult-oriented mahjong amusement market, where traditional tile-based play was combined with the presentation and reward systems of specialized coin-operated cabinets.

Rather than an action game, its core attraction is mahjong competition in a dedicated arcade environment. Its comparatively obscure distribution makes it a document of Japan's early-1990s mahjong and medal-game scene.

games.title: Lovely Pop Mahjong JangJang Shimasho
games.description:
Lovely Pop Mahjong JangJang Shimasho is a 1996 Japanese strip-mahjong game by Visco. Its opponents are the members of an all-female pop group called VisKiss, turning ordinary riichi-mahjong encounters into a lighthearted music-themed progression. Winning matches reveals elaborate animated scenes and opens bonus minigames that award additional points.

Those points can be spent in an in-game shop on special items that influence later mahjong rounds. The combination of character animation, minigames, and purchasable advantages gives the game considerably more structure than a simple sequence of one-off mahjong opponents. It was released exclusively in Japan.

games.title: Lovely Pop Mahjong JangJang Shimasho 2
games.description:
Lovely Pop Mahjong JangJang Shimasho 2 is Visco's Japanese arcade follow-up from 2000. It retains the first game's combination of mahjong matches, reward minigames, and a shop where earned points can be exchanged for advantageous items, but introduces a new four-member female band, Tinkerbell, as the central cast.

Compared with the original game's extensive animation, the sequel relies more heavily on still illustrations with camera movement and close-up presentation. The revised cast and visual treatment give this late arcade mahjong release a distinct identity despite its familiar underlying rules.

games.title: Jyanshin Densetsu - Quest of Jongmaster
games.description:
Jyanshin Densetsu: Quest of Jongmaster is a 1994 Aicom game for the Neo Geo MVS that turns mahjong into the combat system of a fantasy role-playing adventure. The heroine, Chi Fou, travels through towns and dungeons, meets characters, buys equipment, and gains experience and money while trying to defeat monsters released into the world. Instead of sword fights, encounters are resolved through mahjong contests, sometimes enhanced by special tiles or useful items.

The top-down exploration, character growth, and fantasy setting create a genuine quest structure around an otherwise familiar tabletop game. It is one of the Neo Geo's more eccentric genre combinations, and an interesting counterpart to other Japanese experiments with RPG-style mahjong adventures.

games.title: Jong Tou Ki
games.description:
Jong Tou Ki, also catalogued as Jantouki, is a 1990 adult-oriented Japanese mahjong game from Dynax. Players compete in riichi-mahjong matches against a succession of illustrated female opponents, with character scenes serving as rewards for success.

Its title is associated with a campus-themed mahjong narrative, placing it within the wave of character-focused mahjong cabinets that were popular in Japan around the turn of the decade. The game is notable primarily as part of Dynax's extensive specialization in arcade mahjong rather than for a radically different tile game.

games.title: Jackie Chan - The Kung-Fu Master
games.description:
The Kung-Fu Master Jackie Chan is a 1995 fighting game developed by Kaneko with the participation of Hong Kong action star Jackie Chan. It uses digitized performers rather than traditional hand-drawn sprites, giving its martial-arts fights the appearance of live-action choreography. The cast includes performers associated with Chan's films, and the original version features different versions of Jackie Chan as formidable boss opponents.

Matches use four-button attacks and special moves, while lively character animations and humorous presentation reflect the celebrity at the center of the project. Its heavily protected arcade hardware, unusual licensed cast, and digitized look make it a distinctive alternative to the anime-style fighters and motion-captured combat games that dominated the mid-1990s.

games.title: Jackie Chan in Fists of Fire
games.description:
Jackie Chan in Fists of Fire is Kaneko's revised 1995 edition of The Kung-Fu Master Jackie Chan. It retains the original's digitized martial artists and movie-star humor, but substantially develops the fighting system. Desperation attacks, a more elaborate combo system with on-screen combo records, and an escape mechanic that rewards rapid input give matches greater depth.

The update also makes the three previously boss-only versions of Jackie Chan playable, enlarging the selectable roster to nine and revising character balance. Rather than a wholly new sequel, Fists of Fire is a heavily enhanced version of the same unusual celebrity fighting game, and the edition most often remembered by fighting-game enthusiasts.

games.title: Jumping Cross
games.description:
Jumping Cross is a 1984 SNK motocross game viewed from an elevated, vertically oriented perspective. Players ride around off-road courses against rival motorcycles, negotiating obstacles and using jumps to clear raised sections of the track. The objective is to complete the route within the allotted time while maintaining enough speed to stay ahead of the competition.

Its combination of racing, course hazards, and carefully timed jumps recalls the emerging style of motocross videogames, but within an arcade format built for short, demanding runs. It is one of SNK's lesser-known experiments with sports and driving games before the company's later Neo Geo identity.

games.title: Judge Dredd
games.description:
Judge Dredd is a rail-shooting arcade game released by Acclaim in the late 1990s, developed by Gremlin Interactive and based on the long-running British comic rather than the 1995 film. Its story sends the feared lawman into Mega-City One to confront criminals who have taken hostages, including the mayor. The player progresses along a predetermined route through pre-rendered environments, firing at enemies that appear during each encounter.

The game spans a series of short stages and emphasizes fast target recognition and accuracy. Although its commercial release and revisions are sometimes catalogued under different years, it should not be confused with Midway's unrelated 1993 Judge Dredd beat-'em-up prototype. They share the licensed character but have completely different designs.

games.title: Judge Dredd
games.description:
Midway's Judge Dredd is an unreleased arcade beat-'em-up prototype developed in the early 1990s, years before the similarly named Gremlin/Acclaim shooting game. Drawing on the British comic-book lawman and the rising popularity of licensed arcade action, it places Judge Dredd in side-scrolling battles against criminals in Mega-City One.

The concept sought to combine the character-driven violence of Mortal Kombat with the cooperative brawling approach of games such as Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles. It never reached full commercial production, making the preserved prototype an intriguing record of Midway's attempts to develop another major licensed action franchise.

games.title: Return of the Jedi
games.description:
Atari's Return of the Jedi (1984) recreates the climax of the third Star Wars film through colorful, isometric scrolling action. Rather than using the wireframe graphics of Atari's 1983 Star Wars arcade game, it employs a raster-based perspective with smoothed scenery and sprites. The player alternates between Endor and space, piloting a speeder bike through the forest, flying the Millennium Falcon past Imperial fighters, and navigating dangerous approaches to the Death Star.

The game uses steering and firing controls to negotiate obstacles while shooting hostile units, with film-inspired set pieces linked into an arcade sequence that ultimately leads to the Death Star's destruction. Changing environments prevent the action from becoming a single repeated shooting pattern, even though each scenario is designed for quick arcade play.

Return of the Jedi is historically unusual because Atari released it before its own arcade adaptation of The Empire Strikes Back, reversing the middle and final films' release order. It also illustrates Atari's shift from the spectacular vector cockpit of its original Star Wars machine toward more colorful, accessible scrolling graphics.

games.title: Jin
games.description:
Jin is an obscure early-1980s arcade territory-capture game by Falcon, built as a conversion of Williams' Defender hardware. Its design follows Taito's Qix: the player works to claim portions of a playfield while avoiding threats that can interrupt an unfinished move. The focus is on gradually carving away safe territory rather than destroying enemies with conventional projectiles.

The game is remembered largely for its slow pace, austere graphics, and conspicuously reused Defender-style sound effects. Its preservation offers a glimpse of small operators adapting familiar arcade boards to support competing games.

games.title: Jitsuryoku!! Pro Yakyuu
games.description:
Jitsuryoku!! Pro Yakyuu is a Japanese arcade baseball game published by Jaleco in 1989 and associated with developer TOSE. It brings a traditionally console-friendly sport to a joystick-and-button cabinet, focusing on baseball competition rather than fantasy action or comedic minigames.

Its Japanese-only presentation and relatively obscure arcade distribution make it a small but interesting part of Jaleco's sports-game catalogue. The title translates approximately as 'Real Ability!! Pro Baseball'.

games.title: Jitsuroku Maru-chi Mahjong
games.description:
Jitsuroku Maru-chi Mahjong: Sugoku H na Kokuhaku Hen is a 1993 Japanese adult-themed mahjong game by Windom. It uses character illustrations and confession-themed presentation around competitive mahjong play, following the mature-oriented format prevalent in dedicated Japanese arcade mahjong cabinets.

The attraction lies in progressing through tile-based matches and character encounters rather than in any action-game mechanics. Its distinctly Japanese presentation makes it a representative, relatively obscure entry in the early-1990s mahjong arcade market.

games.title: Jumping Jack
games.description:
Jumping Jack is a 1984 arcade platform game from Universal in which players navigate compact obstacle courses, leaping between positions, avoiding hazards, and picking up bonus items for points. Its challenge is based on movement and timing, using a four-way joystick and two buttons rather than an elaborate weapon system.

This is the Universal arcade game, not the unrelated 1983 home-computer platformer of the same name published by Imagine Software. Its modest scale and collectible-driven stages are characteristic of the short-form platform games that filled arcades between the Donkey Kong boom and the arrival of larger scrolling adventures.

games.title: Jan Jan Paradise 2
games.description:
Jan Jan Paradise 2 is a 1997 mahjong game for Kaneko's Super Nova hardware, developed by Electro Design. The game features a cast of twelve illustrated characters who can serve as the player's chosen representative or as opponents. In a notable improvement over the first Jan Jan Paradise, the entire character roster is available for selection rather than a small randomly presented subset.

Winning mahjong matches unlocks additional adult-oriented character artwork and animated sequences. Its expanded selection system gives players more direct control over the order of encounters, a meaningful difference in a genre otherwise dominated by familiar tile-game rules.

games.title: Jan Jan Paradise
games.description:
Jan Jan Paradise is a 1996 Japanese strip-mahjong game by Electro Design for Kaneko's Super Nova arcade system. It offers twelve character portraits, but begins by presenting the player with a random selection of three possible protagonists. Subsequent opponents are also chosen from limited rotating groups, giving repeated playthroughs different character sequences.

Each defeated opponent reveals a progression of illustrations culminating in an animated adult-oriented scene. Eight of its characters also appear in Kaneko's Gals Panic S, linking this mahjong title to the company's better-known territory-capture puzzle series.

games.title: J. J. Squawkers
games.description:
J. J. Squawkers is an eccentric 1993 side-scrolling action platformer developed by Athena and distributed by Able. One or two players control the bird-like brothers Ani and Ototo as they try to restore peace to their village after its inhabitants are kidnapped or turned hostile. The heroes fire projectiles at an astonishing assortment of creatures while jumping across vividly illustrated stages and collecting helpful power-ups.

Its imaginative enemy designs, bright hand-drawn artwork, and unpredictable scenery distinguish it from more conventional run-and-gun games. Although relatively rare in arcades, J. J. Squawkers has acquired a cult following among players who enjoy visually extravagant, offbeat Japanese platformers.

games.title: Jumping Break
games.description:
Jumping Break is a 1999 arcade paddle-and-ball game by F2 System that modifies the familiar Breakout formula. Players move a character along the bottom of the screen to rebound a ball into the objects above, gradually destroying them and clearing the stage. Unlike a stationary paddle, the character can jump to intercept the ball at a higher point.

This small change gives the player more active control over difficult returns and turns an established genre into a more kinetic action game. Its late-1990s release shows that simple single-screen ball-and-paddle concepts still had room for experimentation long after the original breakout-game boom.

games.title: Jockey Grand Prix
games.description:
Jockey Grand Prix is a 2001 horse-racing betting game developed through a collaboration between BrezzaSoft and Sun Amusement for SNK's Neo Geo MVS arcade hardware. In contrast to the system's familiar fighting games, players do not control a racer: they select a horse, place a bet, and watch the result, with winnings handled through a payout mechanism on compatible cabinets. Its emphasis is on wagering rather than driving or action gameplay.

The game was released as an MVS cartridge but never received a conventional Neo Geo AES home-console edition. That makes it a conspicuous oddity in the Neo Geo library, demonstrating how the versatile arcade platform was also used for specialist amusement and betting machines.

games.title: Joe & Mac Returns
games.description:
Joe & Mac Returns is Data East's 1994 follow-up to Caveman Ninja, but it abandons the first game's side-scrolling journey in favor of compact single-screen platform arenas. The cavemen Joe and Mac jump between ledges and strike enemies with their clubs, trapping or dispatching the creatures needed to clear each stage. Two-player simultaneous play adds the familiar cooperative arcade appeal.

The structure is much closer to Snow Bros. than to the original Joe & Mac, with each arena becoming a short puzzle of movement, enemy positioning, and efficient attacks. Its prehistoric humor and recognizable heroes provide continuity with the earlier game, while the revised format gives the sequel a distinct place in Data East's catalogue.

games.title: Mahjong Jogakuen
games.description:
Mahjong Jogakuen: Karada Kensa-hen is a Japanese adult mahjong title from Windom, believed to date from the early 1990s. It combines tile-based mahjong competition with digitized photographic images of women rather than relying entirely on traditional anime artwork.

The photographic presentation is its principal distinguishing characteristic, reflecting the period when inexpensive digitization began changing the look of mature-themed Japanese arcade games. Its precise release date and many gameplay particulars remain poorly documented.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Joinem
games.description: Joinem is a compact maze-action arcade game developed by Global Corporation in 1983. The player negotiates single-screen labyrinths from an overhead view, moving through narrow corridors and avoiding threats as the maze challenge develops. Its up-to-two-player arrangement uses alternating turns rather than simultaneous cooperative play. The game's simple, direct controls and vertical monitor put it in the same broad early-1980s tradition as maze-action favorites, while its relatively obscure distribution has left few surviving accounts of its individual stages.

games.title: JoJo's Venture / JoJo no Kimyouna Bouken

variants.title: JoJo's Venture / JoJo no Kimyouna Bouken (Japan, 981202)
JoJo's Venture / JoJo no Kimyouna Bouken (Japan, 990108)

games.description:
JoJo's Venture is Capcom's 1998 one-on-one fighting game based on Hirohiko Araki's manga JoJo's Bizarre Adventure, specifically the Stardust Crusaders story arc. Built for the powerful CPS-III system, it combines fluid anime-style character animation with the series' flamboyant poses, unusual personalities, and supernatural 'Stand' abilities. Fighters such as Jotaro Kujo and Dio can summon their Stands to change attack properties, extend combos, and control space in ways unavailable to ordinary fighters.

The Stand system is the game's central innovation. Switching between normal and Stand-assisted fighting introduces a second layer of tactics, while comic-panel-style presentation and character-specific moves celebrate the source material. JoJo's Venture was also the starting point for the expanded Heritage for the Future edition released the following year.

Although less universally known than Street Fighter III, it became a cult favorite among fighting-game enthusiasts for its unusual mechanics, elaborate animation, and remarkably faithful adaptation of Araki's visual imagination.

games.title: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure: Heritage for the Future / JoJo no Kimyouna Bouken: Miraie no Isan

variants.title: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure: Heritage for the Future / JoJo no Kimyouna Bouken: Miraie no Isan (Japan, 990913, NCD)
JoJo's Bizarre Adventure: Heritage for the Future / JoJo no Kimyouna Bouken: Miraie no Isan (Japan, 990913)

games.description:
JoJo's Bizarre Adventure: Heritage for the Future is Capcom's 1999 revision of JoJo's Venture, still based on the Stardust Crusaders arc of Hirohiko Araki's manga. The distinctive Stand system remains the foundation: players can call forth supernatural companions, alter their available attacks, and combine character and Stand actions in complex offensive sequences.

This edition expands and rebalances the roster, bringing additional manga characters and new matchups to the CPS-III fighter. Its unusually specialized tactics, detailed animation, and faithful characterization helped it outlast its original arcade run as a competitive cult favorite. Heritage for the Future is an enhanced game in its own right, not simply another regional name for the 1998 original.

games.title: Jolly Card
games.description:
Jolly Card is a 1985 Austrian video-poker game associated with TAB-Austria and subsequently circulated through Fun World and numerous other manufacturers and bootleggers. Its core appeal is the familiar draw-poker cycle: deal a hand, select cards to hold, replace the rest and evaluate the result against the machine's payout table. A row of dedicated hold buttons makes the play accessible without a joystick.

Few European coin-operated card games acquired such a tangled family of revisions. Austrian, Croatian, Italian, Bulgarian and other derivatives modified graphics, denominations, languages and operating rules. Some adaptations even used timed credits rather than ordinary wagers. The game's wide bootleg afterlife makes Jolly Card an important reference point for the history of European video-poker cabinets.

games.title: Jolly Jogger
games.description:
Jolly Jogger is a 1982 Taito maze game in which a would-be jogger tries to cover the streets of a small city while three pursuing bullies interfere. The player traces routes around city blocks, making strategic use of special locations or items that can frighten the pursuers and temporarily turn the tables.

Its compact urban maze and chase mechanics place it in the broad Pac-Man family, but the jogging premise and ability to reverse the pursuit give it a distinct comic personality. The game also uses unusual bitmap display hardware layered onto circuitry related to Galaxian-style machines.

games.title: Mahjong Block Jongbou
games.description:
Mahjong Block Jongbou is a 1987 SNK arcade puzzle game that crosses Breakout with Japanese mahjong. Players use a rotary-controlled paddle to keep a ball in motion, breaking blocks decorated with mahjong tiles. Rather than relying exclusively on clearing the screen, they can also collect falling tiles to complete a valid mahjong hand and finish the stage that way.

The combination demands two kinds of planning: precise ball control and awareness of the combinations needed for a winning hand. The Japanese arcade release includes adult-oriented reward illustrations, which were removed from the later Famicom conversion. Jongbou is a distinctive example of arcade designers merging an established paddle game with a traditional tabletop pastime.

games.title: Mahjong Block Jongbou 2
games.description:
Mahjong Block Jongbou 2, also known as Jongbou Sono 2, is SNK's 1987 follow-up to its Breakout-and-mahjong hybrid. Players continue to rebound a ball into tile-bearing blocks, either clearing the board or assembling mahjong combinations from the pieces they collect.

The sequel preserves the original's basic mechanics while adding more direct competition, including play against a computer opponent or another player, as well as offensive power-ups. These changes give the familiar brick-breaking and tile-collection loop a more confrontational character. It remained an arcade-only follow-up rather than following its predecessor to the Famicom.

games.title: Joshi Volleyball
games.description:
Joshi Volleyball is a 1983 arcade volleyball game from Taito, with a title that translates as 'Women's Volleyball'. It presents the sport as a joystick-controlled contest in which players position their team and time their actions to send the ball over the net and score against the opposing side.

The game is notable as an early attempt to bring women's team volleyball to a coin-operated sports cabinet, well before more elaborate multi-sport arcade machines became commonplace. Its Japanese release and specialized hardware have made it a relatively uncommon entry in Taito's 1980s catalogue.

games.title: Journey
games.description:
Journey is Bally Midway's exuberant 1983 arcade tribute to the American rock band of the same name. The game's improbable story has aliens stealing the group's musical instruments, forcing Steve Perry, Neal Schon, Jonathan Cain, Ross Valory, and Steve Smith to travel across five worlds to recover them. Each musician has a different short action challenge, and the characters' heads are based on digitized photographs of the real band members.

The stages vary in format, mixing movement, combat, and collection rather than repeating a single shooter mechanic. Once the instruments are recovered, the band performs a concert while the player, now controlling a roadie, fights off obsessive fans trying to storm the stage. Real Journey music, including a tape playback of 'Separate Ways (Worlds Apart)' during the concert sequence, was a major part of the cabinet's attraction.

Developed to capitalize on Journey's early-1980s popularity, the game was rushed to align with the band's Frontiers-era publicity. Its combination of genuine band imagery, licensed music, and surreal arcade play made it one of the era's most unusual celebrity tie-ins, more memorable for its ambition and presentation than for conventional action-game design.

games.title: Joust
games.description:
Joust (1982), designed by John Newcomer for Williams Electronics, is one of the defining original arcade games of the early 1980s. Players ride flying ostriches through suspended platforms, defeating enemy knights mounted on buzzards. Combat depends on altitude rather than a conventional attack button: when two riders collide, the one with the higher lance wins. The two-way joystick steers the mount, while a flap button controls lift, making every fight a contest of momentum, height, and timing.

Defeated enemies leave eggs that must be collected before they hatch into new threats. Later waves introduce tougher riders, lava hazards, and the terrifying pterodactyl, whose deadly appearances turn slow play into a gamble. Two players can cooperate to clear waves but can also knock one another out of the air, creating an unusually entertaining mixture of teamwork and rivalry.

Its simple controls conceal demanding aerial physics, and the game helped establish a durable style of single-screen competitive action. With its unmistakable ostriches, resonant sound effects, and wonderfully strange medieval fantasy, Joust became one of Williams' most celebrated arcade classics and inspired a sequel, many conversions, and decades of imitations.

games.title: Joust 2 - Survival of the Fittest
games.description:
Joust 2: Survival of the Fittest is Williams' ambitious 1986 sequel to Joust, created for vertical-screen arcade cabinets. Its familiar foundation remains: players flap a flying mount to gain altitude and defeat enemy riders by striking them from above, then collect their eggs before they hatch. The new game adds more elaborate stages, stronger adversaries, and a broader variety of obstacles.

Its defining addition is the ability to transform between a nimble ostrich and a heavier flying Pegasus, changing the mount's handling and the tactics available in combat. The taller playfield and more complicated enemy patterns make Joust 2 a more demanding, less immediately approachable game than its predecessor.

Designer John Newcomer returned for the sequel, but it arrived after the arcade market's early-1980s peak and never achieved the original's fame. It remains a fascinating effort to expand a minimalist action classic into a richer, more elaborate challenge.

games.title: Joyful Road
games.description:
Joyful Road, released outside Japan as Munch Mobile, is SNK's wonderfully eccentric 1983 top-down driving game. Instead of piloting an ordinary racing car, the player steers a cheerful anthropomorphic vehicle with long mechanical arms extending from its windows. The goal is to follow a scrolling road, avoid traffic and roadside hazards, grab food and other bonus objects, and eventually park safely in a garage.

The controls require unusual coordination: driving the car is only half the task, because the player must also operate its arms to pick up useful items, including fuel needed to continue the journey. Collecting food and depositing litter add comic complications to the simple act of staying on the road.

Its colorful character design and simultaneous steering-and-grabbing challenge make Joyful Road one of SNK's strangest early arcade games. Beneath the playful exterior is a demanding coordination exercise unlike conventional racing or driving titles.

games.title: Puzzled / Joy Joy Kid
games.description:
Puzzled, released in Japan as Joy Joy Kid, is a 1990 SNK falling-block puzzle game for the Neo Geo system. Its story follows children attempting to save their villages by climbing a tall, obstacle-filled tower. Players guide descending shapes into place, clearing rows to keep the playfield open and advance the characters upward through successive floors.

Unlike the competitive focus of many later arcade block puzzles, Puzzled presents a longer single-player ascent with distinctive backgrounds and characters. It was an early example of SNK using the Neo Geo hardware for something other than fighting and shooting, giving the platform a whimsical, vertically structured variation on the Tetris formula.

games.title: Jurassic Park
games.description:
Jurassic Park is Sega's 1994 arcade shooting game based on Steven Spielberg's dinosaur film. One or two players ride through Isla Nublar in a guided vehicle, aiming at dinosaurs that emerge from the jungle, run alongside the road, or charge directly at the camera. The encounters include familiar creatures such as velociraptors and a Tyrannosaurus rex, with the player's quick reactions determining whether the expedition survives.

Developed by Sega AM3, the game combines scaled two-dimensional sprites with three-dimensional environmental effects to produce a convincing sense of depth and movement. Its large vehicle-themed cabinet reinforces the illusion of a dangerous safari. Although inspired by the film's world, the game takes the freedom needed for nonstop arcade action, making it a characteristic example of Sega's spectacular 1990s attraction-style shooters.

games.title: Jurassic Park

variants.title: Jurassic Park (bootleg of Mega Drive version)

games.description:
This Jurassic Park set is an unauthorized arcade conversion of Sega's 1993 Mega Drive/Genesis platform game, not the better-known 1994 Sega rail shooter. The underlying console game is a side-scrolling adventure through dinosaur-infested environments, with platforming, obstacles, and attacks against hostile creatures.

The coin-operated bootleg reproduces a home-console design on conversion hardware rather than using the original arcade Jurassic Park engine. Preserving it separately matters because the shared license and name conceal two fundamentally different games: one a console-derived action platformer, the other a purpose-built arcade shooting attraction.

games.title: Jr. Pac-Man
games.description:
Jr. Pac-Man (1983) is Bally Midway's ambitious continuation of the maze-chase series, developed by General Computer Corporation, the team behind Ms. Pac-Man. The player guides Pac-Man's young son through mazes that are much wider than the visible screen, with the playfield scrolling horizontally to follow him. There are no side escape tunnels, removing one of the dependable ways of fleeing ghosts in earlier games.

The roaming bonus prizes are unusually disruptive: as they travel around the maze, they transform ordinary dots into larger pieces of food that are worth more points but take longer to eat. They can also destroy power pellets, turning a tempting bonus into a threat to the player's survival. The result is a more demanding style of route planning in which familiar territory changes during play.

Its huge mazes and altered bonus behavior make Jr. Pac-Man one of the most distinctive classic Pac-Man derivatives. It was not an official Namco-designed sequel, and its place in the series reflects the unusual licensing and development arrangements surrounding Pac-Man's enormous American popularity.

games.title: Joryuu Syougi Kyoushitsu
games.description:
Joryuu Syougi Kyoushitsu is a 1997 Japanese arcade shogi game published by Visco for SSV hardware. Its extended title identifies professional female shogi champion Ichiyo Shimizu as its supervisor, giving the game an instructional or classroom-oriented identity rather than presenting shogi solely as a competitive board game.

Players engage with the rules and strategy of Japanese chess through a coin-operated digital board. Its subject and female-professional endorsement make it a rare exception to the action and mahjong games usually associated with Japanese arcade cabinets of the late 1990s.

games.title: Jatre Specter
games.description:
Jatre Specter is a 1979 Space Invaders-derived arcade set associated with Jatre and preserved in AdvanceMAME as a distinct version of Taito's original shooter. The player slides a laser cannon left and right beneath the alien formation, firing at advancing ranks while using defensive barriers to survive incoming shots. Each surviving invader accelerates the threat as the formation thins, while occasional saucers offer a scoring opportunity.

This set belongs to the early wave of regional Space Invaders adaptations rather than to Taito's later Space Invaders Part II sequel. Its documented identity is primarily the Jatre-associated ROM version; any substantial changes to the original game's rules are not firmly established.

games.title: Jump Bug
games.description:
Jump Bug is a pioneering 1981 scrolling arcade action game developed by Alpha Denshi and distributed in different markets by Sega and Rock-Ola. Players control a small Volkswagen Beetle-like car that moves through constantly changing landscapes by bouncing from platforms and clouds. The car can fire at hostile creatures, leap over gaps, and collect money bags and jewels while the scenery carries the action through cities, deserts, and other environments.

The player's jumps are central to both survival and scoring, distinguishing Jump Bug from the strictly ground-bound vehicle shooters of its day. Its continuous side-scrolling journey predates several better-known examples of the form, including Moon Patrol, and helped demonstrate how platform jumping could work beyond the confines of a single static screen.

Although less famous than Nintendo's and Konami's early platform hits, Jump Bug is an important transitional arcade game, combining vehicle action, shooting, collectible rewards, and horizontally scrolling levels at a remarkably early date.

games.title: Jump Coaster
games.description:
Jump Coaster is a 1983 Kaneko platform game in which a caped hero tries to rescue his girlfriend while racing through amusement-park-like hazards. Players jump around compact scenes, gather bags of gold, and avoid creatures and moving roller-coaster cars. Each round is divided into two different scenes that must be cleared before play continues.

The game's appeal lies in tight timing and unusual moving obstacles rather than a complicated combat system. Its curious mixture of rescue adventure and amusement-ride peril makes it one of Kaneko's more idiosyncratic early arcade platformers.

games.title: Jump Jump
games.description:
Jump Jump is a 1999 Korean arcade platform game from dgPIX Entertainment with an unusual inversion of the genre's central control. Instead of pressing a button to jump upward, the player guides a character falling down the screen, steering left and right to land on safe platforms and avoid dangerous ones. The descending playfield turns a familiar run-and-jump challenge into a test of reading platforms ahead and making quick lateral corrections.

Certain special 'Show Time' platforms trigger adult photographic rewards, tying the platform action to the mature-themed amusement market in which dgPIX specialized. Its unusual mechanics and limited circulation make it more than a routine late-1990s platformer, and an original arcade board was documented by preservationists before the game entered emulation.

games.title: Jump Kids
games.description:
Jump Kids is a 1993 single-screen platform action game by Comad that closely resembles Snow Bros. and Data East's Tumble Pop. Players control a cartoonish child with oversized hands, grabbing or slapping enemies and hurling them into others to clear an arena. Every defeated group leads to another stage, with several themed sets of levels to choose from.

The game is particularly notable for its derivative origins: portions of its code and design appear to have been taken from Tumble Pop. Its colorful presentation and simple enemy-throwing mechanic make it playable as an arena-clearing platformer while also marking it as a characteristic example of the era's unofficial arcade borrowing.

games.title: Jump Kun
games.description: Jump Kun is an unreleased 1984 arcade platform-game prototype developed by Kaneko. It is a straightforward run-and-jump design using a four-way joystick and two buttons, with provision for two players taking alternating turns. Although it never reached a normal commercial release, the preserved build gives a glimpse of the sort of compact, character-led platform games that Japanese studios were exploring in the period between Donkey Kong and the later, more elaborate side-scrollers.

games.title: Jumping Pop
games.description:
Jumping Pop is a 2001 Korean single-screen platform game by ESD, closely related in play style and assets to Data East's Tumble Pop. The player controls a monster hunter carrying a powerful vacuum device, sucking up enemies such as mummies and skeletons and then firing the captured creatures at their companions. Holding an enemy inside the vacuum for too long is dangerous, because the machine can explode.

Clearing each arena leads to the next screen, and themed groups of stages culminate in boss encounters. Beneath its bright visual makeover are many elements familiar from Tumble Pop, including reused graphics, making Jumping Pop as interesting for its unofficial reworking of an earlier game as for its energetic arcade action.

games.title: Jump Shot
games.description:
Jump Shot is a 1985 Bally Midway one-on-one basketball game designed as a conversion kit for Pac-Man-era cabinets. The player controls a small basketball figure against a computer opponent or another player, using a joystick and a shooting or blocking action to compete for possession and score baskets before the timer expires.

Instead of attempting to simulate a whole basketball team, Jump Shot strips the sport down to short, direct duels with quick transitions between attack and defense. Its use of hardware descended from Pac-Man is a reminder of how operators extended the lives of established arcade machines with inexpensive conversion games.

games.title: Jungle King
games.description:
Jungle King, released by Taito in 1982 and later reworked as Jungle Hunt, is a landmark early scrolling platform adventure. Its Tarzan-like hero attempts to rescue a captive woman through four distinct action sequences: swinging from vine to vine over the jungle, swimming through a river full of crocodiles, jumping over rolling rocks, and finally reaching the captors' camp. Each stage demands a different rhythm, shifting from precise jumping to underwater avoidance and combat.

The moving jungle backgrounds helped popularize layered parallax scrolling at a time when most platform games still used static screens. Equally striking was the game's decision to make several short, varied episodes form one continuous adventure, anticipating the cinematic stage progression of later action games.

The original Jungle King presentation featured a hero closely resembling Tarzan and an accompanying yell. After a rights dispute, Taito changed the character and presentation for Jungle Hunt; a later variation, Pirate Pete, altered the theme again. Preserving Jungle King therefore captures an important early version of a historically influential arcade game.

games.title: Jungler
games.description:
Jungler is a 1981 Konami maze combat game that replaces the usual human hero with a snake-like vehicle made of linked segments. Players steer through twisting passages while trying to defeat several similar computer-controlled creatures. Both the player's craft and its enemies can fire projectiles that shorten their targets, and head-on collisions are decided by the relative lengths of the two opponents.

This creates a constantly changing balance of power: an initially dangerous long enemy can become vulnerable after losing enough sections, while a damaged player has to avoid direct contact. With its distinctive moving chains and tactical maze battles, Jungler is an inventive alternative to the dot-collecting games that dominated the maze genre at the start of the 1980s.

games.title: Juno First
games.description:
Juno First (1983) is a fast, unusual Konami space shooter shown from a tilted overhead perspective. Unlike fixed shooters whose enemies remain in neat formations, its alien attackers move freely through a scrolling field. The player's craft can maneuver in several directions, including forward and backward, and must eliminate a specified number of enemies before the wave can end.

Enemy forms become more dangerous if they survive too long, rewarding decisive attacks. A radar display warns of threats beyond the immediate screen, while collectible capsules and special maneuvers add scoring and survival opportunities. The unusual perspective, ability to reverse direction, and pressure to hunt specific targets make Juno First feel more like a dynamic chase than an ordinary Galaxian descendant.

Its combination of free movement and structured waves has earned it a lasting cult reputation among early-1980s shooter fans, despite being less widely recognized than Konami's larger arcade hits.

games.title: Jyangokushi: Haoh no Saihai
games.description:
Jyangokushi: Haoh no Saihai is a 1999 Capcom mahjong game for the CPS-II arcade system. Its title plays on Sangokushi, the Japanese name for the Romance of the Three Kingdoms tradition, placing competitive mahjong within the imagery of China's legendary rival warlords.

Players take part in tile-based matches rather than the sword battles usually associated with the Three Kingdoms setting. As a late CPS-II release, it is an unusual entry in a hardware catalogue better known for Street Fighter, Marvel superheroes, and arcade shooters.

games.title: Far East of Eden - Kabuki Klash / Tengai Makyou - Shin Den
games.description:
Far East of Eden: Kabuki Klash, known in Japan as Tengai Makyou: Shin Den, is Hudson's 1995 one-on-one fighting game for the Neo Geo MVS. It draws its characters and setting from the popular Tengai Makyou role-playing series, translating the franchise's exaggerated, mythical version of Japan into colorful fighting-game arenas. Players select from an eccentric roster of heroes and duel with weapons, special attacks, and animated supers.

Matches resemble the weapon-based action of Samurai Shodown, but the game adds bonus items that appear during combat and can alter the flow of a round. Its bold character design, comic energy, and RPG connections distinguish it from the more serious martial-arts fighters of the period. It remains one of the few Tengai Makyou titles to receive a release outside Japan.

games.title: Kabuki-Z
games.description:
Kabuki-Z is a 1988 side-scrolling samurai action game published by Taito. Players wield a katana against human and supernatural opponents in a sequence of five levels, advancing through hostile scenery toward a dangerous boss at the end of each stage. Combat emphasizes close-range slashing rather than projectile-based shooting.

The game is remembered for its unusually bloody presentation, including theatrical finishing sequences after boss fights. Its mixture of historical costume drama, monsters, and violent swordplay makes it a distinctive late-1980s Japanese arcade brawler.

games.title: Kageki
games.description:
Kageki is a 1988 boxing-themed one-on-one fighting game developed by Kaneko and published by Taito and Romstar in different regions. The player is a street fighter taking on a gang of bizarrely caricatured opponents, eventually confronting its leader. Each contest is settled by knocking the rival down three times, making endurance and spacing more important than a single successful hit.

Its exaggerated faces, comical knockdowns, and unusual sampled voices give Kageki a personality far removed from serious martial-arts simulations. It also stands apart from later combo-heavy fighting games: the focus is on reading the opponent, choosing when to strike, and surviving a string of eccentric challengers.

games.title: Kageki
games.description:
This 1992 hack of Kageki is a modified ROM version of Kaneko's 1988 street-boxing game, rather than a true sequel. The underlying fights still pit the player's boxer against a series of gang members, with victory requiring repeated knockdowns.

The preserved hack is based on Japanese-region program material but changes the displayed year and uses altered English text in parts of the game. Documentation does not establish a new roster or substantially different combat system, so its interest lies chiefly in the localized program changes and the history of unofficial arcade ROM revisions.

games.title: Mahjong Kaguyahime
games.description:
Mahjong Kaguyahime is a 1988 Japanese medal-mahjong game by Miki Syouji, built around the legendary Princess Kaguya. Players combine traditional mahjong competition with wagering credits or medals, and the game's adult-oriented visual rewards depend in part on the size of the bet.

The mixture of folklore imagery, mahjong, and wager-sensitive character scenes places it squarely in Japan's specialized late-1980s medal-game market. It is not a conventional action or puzzle title, but a distinct form of gambling-oriented mahjong cabinet.

games.title: Mahjong Kaguyahime Sono2
games.description:
Mahjong Kaguyahime Sono2 is the 1989 sequel to Miki Syouji's Princess Kaguya-themed medal-mahjong game. It retains the combination of Japanese mahjong hands, credit or medal betting, and adult-oriented illustrated rewards, extending a formula in which the amount wagered can influence the presentation of character scenes.

The sequel belongs to the specialized betting-cabinet tradition rather than the action-oriented arcade market. Its surviving versions also document the adjustable payout and wagering features that distinguished medal mahjong from ordinary head-to-head mahjong games.

games.title: Kaiser Knuckle
games.description:
Kaiser Knuckle, released outside Japan as Global Champion, is Taito's 1994 entry in the Street Fighter II-era arcade fighting boom. Built on the Taito F3 system, it offers nine selectable fighters and three formidable bosses, with six attack buttons dividing punches and kicks by strength. Players battle through one-on-one matches using special moves, combinations, and carefully timed counterattacks.

The game stands out for its dramatic stage presentation: some arenas change as the fight progresses, with background elements breaking apart under the impact of combat. Its fast action and very demanding computer opponents, particularly the notorious final boss General, have given it an enduring reputation among fighting-game collectors.

Taito also experimented with a revised edition called Dan-Ku-Ga, but it never received a conventional arcade release. Kaiser Knuckle remains an appealing snapshot of how companies outside Capcom and SNK tried to develop their own distinctive competitive fighters during the genre's commercial peak.

games.title: Kaitei Takara Sagashi
games.description:
Kaitei Takara Sagashi, meaning 'Underwater Treasure Hunt', is a 1980 monochrome arcade action game published by Namco. The player operates a small boat at the surface, lowers a diver toward treasure on the seabed, and then tries to return safely while avoiding fish. Horizontal movement and harpoon attacks help the diver survive during descent and ascent, but collecting treasure also requires precise positioning.

Its play is built around short, dangerous trips between ship and seabed rather than around clearing waves of enemies. The project began as a third-party prototype before Namco acquired and extensively rewrote it, making it a revealing example of the company's experimental arcade output immediately before its color-video hits became famous.

games.title: Mahjong Kakumei
games.description:
