Mahjong Kakumei, or Mahjong Revolution, is a 1990 Japanese arcade mahjong game published by Jaleco. It belongs to the character-focused, adult-oriented mahjong tradition, combining conventional tile-based play with illustrated opponents and a presentation inspired by Japanese manga.

The game is part of Jaleco's less widely known tabletop output and was followed by Mahjong Kakumei 2: Princess League in 1992. Its interest lies primarily in this corner of the Japanese arcade market, where dedicated mahjong cabinets offered a very different experience from the action games that dominated international exports.

games.title: Mahjong Kakumei 2 - Princess League
games.description:
Mahjong Kakumei 2: Princess League is Jaleco's 1992 follow-up to Mahjong Kakumei. It is another Japanese arcade mahjong game, retaining the series' focus on competitive tile play and adult-oriented illustrated character presentation while introducing the Princess League subtitle.

Like its predecessor, it belongs to the specialized domestic mahjong-cabinet market rather than the broader action arcade scene. Detailed differences in its scoring systems or match rules are not reliably documented, so it is best understood as a distinct sequel rather than assigned unverified new mechanics.

games.title: Masked Riders Club Battle Race
games.description:
Masked Riders Club: Battle Race is a 1993 Banpresto motorcycle action-racing game based on the long-running Kamen Rider television franchise. Players select from ten masked heroes, each with different motorcycle performance and a distinctive close-range weapon, then race through nine vertically scrolling courses featuring industrial streets, beaches, snowfields, and other hazards.

The motorcycle advances automatically, so players must steer around traffic and obstacles, strike enemies that block the way, and use jumps or speed-boosting sections to maintain momentum. Collisions drain a fuel meter, and completing a course quickly rewards extra points. Two-player competition divides the playfield so rival riders can race side by side and interfere with each other's progress.

The combination of recognizable Kamen Rider characters, scrolling obstacle courses, and melee attacks makes it a distinctive licensed arcade racer rather than a conventional lap-based motorcycle simulation.

games.title: Kamikaze Cabbie
games.description:
Kamikaze Cabbie, known in Japan as Yellow Cab, is Data East's 1984 maze-driving game about operating a taxi in a busy city. From a top-down perspective, the player drives through streets to collect a passenger and deliver the fare to the requested destination. The cab must contend with traffic, police vehicles, and other obstacles while watching a fuel gauge that diminishes over time and after collisions.

Fuel can be replenished at service stations, so choosing an efficient route is as important as driving quickly. Fares and tips reward successful deliveries, while crashing into certain vehicles can also earn points. The urban delivery objective and open network of roads make Kamikaze Cabbie a striking precursor to later arcade games built around fast, chaotic taxi driving.

games.title: Kanatsuen no Onna
games.description:
Kanatsuen no Onna is a 1988 adult-themed medal-mahjong game from Panac, released in Japan. It combines mahjong play with wagering features and photographic or illustrated reward scenes depicting women, following the familiar formula of specialized mature-audience mahjong cabinets.

Its name refers to the Kanazuen district of Gifu, giving the game a specifically Japanese adult-entertainment setting. The title is mainly of interest as a preserved example of the medal-mahjong market rather than as a widely distributed international arcade release.

games.title: Kangaroo
games.description:
Kangaroo is a 1982 platform game developed by Sun Electronics and distributed in North America by Atari. The player controls a mother kangaroo wearing boxing gloves, desperately climbing platforms to rescue her joey from mischievous monkeys. She must jump over gaps, climb ladders, dodge thrown apples, and punch monkeys or their projectiles while collecting fruit for bonus points.

Its distinctive control scheme uses the joystick to jump rather than dedicating a button to the action, while a separate button throws punches. The vertically arranged stages and changing hazards create a rescue adventure that resembles Donkey Kong in broad outline but has a much more whimsical theme and its own movement rhythm.

Kangaroo was popular enough to inspire appearances in the Saturday Supercade animated television series. Its bright cartoon visuals and combination of punching, climbing, and jumping made it one of the memorable animal-character platform games of the early arcade era.

games.title: Kaos
games.description:
Kaos is a 1981 single-screen action game from GamePlan featuring a tiny character trying to catch dollar signs before they reach the bottom of a vertically arranged maze. Any missed money changes into dangerous dragons, creating a steadily increasing threat. Reaching the top can transform the protagonist into a dragon-fighting king, reversing the balance of danger.

Its unusual money-to-monster mechanic turns a collection task into a race against escalating hazards. Kaos is also historically notable as GamePlan's first internally designed video game, with both hardware and software developed by the company.

games.title: Karate Blazers
games.description:
Karate Blazers is a 1991 side-scrolling beat-'em-up by Video System, distributed in some regions by Tecmo. Up to four players choose from martial artists Mark, Glen, Akira, and Gil, then battle through streets and other hostile environments to recover stolen secret scrolls and rescue their master's daughter. The characters rely on punches, kicks, throws, and individually tailored special attacks.

As in Final Fight, enemies attack from both sides in crowded arenas, but the four-player cooperative format gives Karate Blazers its own energetic pace. Powerful crowd-clearing techniques can cost the player health, making their timing particularly important during large encounters. Its busy action and distinctive martial-arts cast make it a well-regarded cult entry in the early-1990s brawler genre.

games.title: The Karate Tournament
games.description:
The Karate Tournament, fully titled Chatan Yara Kuushanku: The Karate Tournament, is a 1992 one-on-one martial-arts game by Mitchell Corporation. Rather than presenting fantastic fighters throwing fireballs, it emphasizes competitive karate and a structured progression through skill grades. Players choose a starting level, from white to brown or black belt, and take on increasingly difficult opponents to improve their rank.

The simple two-button fighting system places the emphasis on reach, timing, and landing clean techniques. Its use of traditional belt classifications and formal match presentation gives it a distinctive identity among the increasingly theatrical arcade fighting games of the early 1990s.

games.title: Karian Cross
games.description:
Karian Cross is a 1996 competitive falling-block puzzle game by Deniam. Players arrange descending colored pieces so that three or more matching objects touch, causing them to disappear and opening room for further combinations. Chain reactions and larger clears send unwanted blocks to an opponent's field, making quick planning and tactical pressure equally important.

The design is reminiscent of Puyo Puyo and Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo, but with its own simple three-color matching rhythm. It is a lesser-known entry in the period's crowded arcade puzzle market, especially suited to head-to-head play.

games.title: Karnov
games.description:
Karnov is Data East's 1987 action platform game starring Jinborov Karnovski, a muscular, fire-breathing strongman with an unforgettable bald head and handlebar mustache. Players travel through side-scrolling landscapes filled with soldiers, monsters, traps, and giant bosses, using Karnov's ability to breathe fire to defeat enemies. The journey also includes ladders, hidden objects, and collectible items that provide new tactical options.

Part of the challenge lies in choosing when to use special equipment such as boomerangs, bombs, and temporary flight or climbing aids. Carefully searching each level reveals bonuses and useful items, giving the game an exploration component beyond its combat. The North American arcade version also differs from the Japanese original in enemy placement and certain hazards, making regional versions interesting to compare.

Karnov became one of Data East's best-known characters, later appearing in other company games and even returning as a fighting-game boss. Its bizarre mixture of circus strongman, fantasy enemies, and relentless arcade difficulty has made it an enduring cult classic.

games.title: Karnov (Neo-Geo port)
games.description: Karnov (Neo-Geo port) is a 2025 homebrew port of Data East's 1987 side-scrolling action-platformer Karnov to the Neo Geo MVS hardware created by iq132.

games.title: Karnov's Revenge / Fighter's History Dynamite
games.description:
Karnov's Revenge, known in Japan as Fighter's History Dynamite, is Data East's 1994 Neo Geo fighting game and the sequel to Fighter's History. Despite its title, it is not a platform-game sequel to Karnov; the fire-breathing strongman appears here as a powerful fighter among a varied international cast. The new Neo Geo version uses four attack buttons rather than the six-button layout of its predecessor.

Its distinctive mechanic is the weak-point system. Each fighter has a specific piece of clothing or equipment that can be struck repeatedly; enough successful hits cause the weak point to break away and leave the character temporarily stunned. This rewards targeting a recognizable body area rather than simply pursuing long combos.

With new fighters, revised balance, colorful character animation, and memorable characters such as Mizoguchi and Karnov, Fighter's History Dynamite became the better-known entry in Data East's fighting series. It combines conventional early-1990s one-on-one combat with a wonderfully strange approach to character vulnerability.

games.title: Ninja Kazan
games.description:
Ninja Kazan is Jaleco's 1988 side-scrolling action adventure, released in Japan as Iga Ninjutsuden. Players control the ninja Kazan as he battles hostile warriors and monsters through varied stages, using a sword and an expanding arsenal of shuriken, chains, and other projectile weapons. Magical scrolls provide stronger special attacks, while collectible items can improve survival.

The game combines precise platform jumps with demanding enemy encounters, and its different weapons make the approach to each stage more flexible than a simple sword-only action title. The historical-ninja atmosphere and supernatural foes place it within the late-1980s wave of elaborate Japanese arcade platform adventures.

games.title: Knuckle Bash
games.description:
Knuckle Bash is a 1993 Toaplan beat-'em-up that trades the company's famous shooting-game spaceships for professional wrestlers battling a corrupt organization. Players choose from an eccentric cast of fighters and punch, kick, and throw their way through hostile urban and wrestling-themed stages. Up to two players can cooperate, combining attacks against crowds of gang members and oversized bosses.

Its exaggerated wrestling poses, comic portraits, and offbeat opponents give the game a cheerful identity distinct from more serious street brawlers. Later stages and additional playable characters broaden the action beyond the starting trio. Knuckle Bash has become a cult favorite partly because it represents an unusual genre for Toaplan, a studio much better known for shooters such as Truxton and Batsugun.

games.title: Knuckle Bash 2
games.description:
Knuckle Bash 2 is an unauthorized 1999 arcade hack marketed as a sequel to Toaplan's 1993 wrestling-themed beat-'em-up. It preserves the original game's core side-scrolling battles, but changes the title screen, rearranges the order of levels, and allows the football-player character to be selected from the start.

The bootleg also uses altered sound hardware, substituting an OKI sound chip for the original YM2151-based arrangement. Rather than introducing a fully new campaign or engine, it repackages and modifies Knuckle Bash, making it a revealing example of how arcade bootlegs could be advertised as sequels.

games.title: Karate Champ
games.description:
Karate Champ, developed by Technos Japan and published by Data East in 1984, is one of the foundational one-on-one fighting games. Its most recognizable feature is the unusual dual-joystick control scheme: instead of moving with one stick and attacking with buttons, players combine directions on two sticks to execute punches, kicks, evasions, and other karate techniques. The fighter's actions therefore depend on deliberate combinations rather than memorized button sequences.

Matches are judged according to karate-style scoring, with clean techniques earning points and the contest interrupted by a referee. Different versions emphasize training challenges, tournament progression, and direct competition, while interludes can include tests such as breaking objects or confronting a charging bull. The North American version has English speech and some presentation differences from the Japanese Karate Dou.

Karate Champ helped establish the template of two characters facing one another in a structured martial-arts contest, years before Street Fighter and its imitators popularized the genre worldwide. Its measured, score-based combat remains strikingly different from the life-bar and combo systems that later came to dominate arcade fighting games.

games.title: Dead Eye
games.description: Dead Eye is a Konami light-gun shooter built for the company's PlayStation-derived GV arcade system, with a 1996 copyright and a Japanese commercial release reported in February 1997. One or two players aim their guns directly at the screen and fire at on-screen targets, using light-gun controls rather than a joystick. Its CD-based sound and PlayStation-family hardware reflect Konami's mid-1990s move toward console-related arcade technology. The surviving set carries Konami's GV054 game identifier, and its emulation has historically required separate disc data.

games.title: King of Dynast Gear
games.description:
King of Dynast Gear (1999) is an unauthorized hardware conversion of Dyna Gear, a dinosaur-themed run-and-gun platform game originally developed by Sammy. Its story sends time patrolman Roger back 65 million years after a clash with the villain Gustaf, who has turned the local dinosaurs into dangerous combat creatures. One or two players fight through side-scrolling prehistoric landscapes, jumping between platforms and shooting hostile beasts.

The distinctive feature of this version is not a new adventure but its electronics: EZ Graphics recreated the game on an E1-32XT-based board rather than the original arcade hardware. It is an unusual example of a late-1990s arcade bootleg that changed the underlying platform while retaining the recognizable game.

games.title: Dramatic Adventure Quiz Keith & Lucy
games.description: Dramatic Adventure Quiz: Keith & Lucy is a Japanese quiz game released by Visco in 1993 for the SSV arcade system. Its questions are presented within a science-fiction adventure about two cybernetic police officers opposing a powerful organization. Up to two players answer multiple-choice questions with four-button controls, advancing through the story by giving correct responses. The theatrical setting distinguishes it from straightforward arcade trivia compilations, although its Japanese-language questions make it less approachable to players unfamiliar with the language.

games.title: Ken-Go
games.description:
Ken-Go, released internationally as Lightning Swords, is a 1991 side-scrolling sword-fighting game published by Irem and developed by Nanao. Set in feudal Japan, it follows the samurai brothers Blue Dragon and Red Dragon through five stages of armed enemies. Two players can cooperate, moving and jumping through side-on scenes while cutting down attackers.

Its central mechanic is a charged sword slash: holding the attack button builds power through several levels before releasing a more forceful blow. Jumping is controlled by pushing the joystick upward, making the handling rather different from a conventional two-button beat-'em-up. The emphasis on timing powerful strikes gives this relatively obscure arcade title a deliberate rhythm.

games.title: Ketsui Kizuna Jigoku Tachi
games.description:
Ketsui: Kizuna Jigoku Tachi is one of Cave's most respected bullet-hell shooters, released in Japanese arcades in January 2003 on IGS's PGM hardware. Against a backdrop of environmental catastrophe and profiteering warfare, its pilots attack the arms manufacturer EVAC through five vertically scrolling stages packed with tanks, helicopters, naval vessels and elaborate bosses. Players choose between the slower, wide-firing Tiger Schwert and the faster, concentrated-fire Panzer Jäger, each equipped with a lock-on attack.

Ketsui's defining feature is its aggressive scoring system. Destroying enemies at close range with regular fire awards chips numbered from one to five; collecting a valuable chip starts a brief window during which lock-on kills can produce more chips of that value. Because lock-on attacks also expend part of the accumulated multiplier, high scores demand a continual balance between proximity, shot type and rapid boss destruction. Surviving the first five stages under strict conditions unlocks far harder second loops, including an exceptionally demanding encounter with the true final boss, Evaccaneer DOOM.

Its dense mechanical military designs, relentless bullet patterns and unusually risk-reward-driven scoring made Ketsui a favorite among expert shooter players. The game later received a Nintendo DS boss-rush adaptation and console releases, helping preserve a title long associated with the Japanese arcade scene.

games.title: Ketsui: Kizuna Jigoku Tachi (IKD 2007 Special - 2007 Cave Matsuri Version)

variants.title: Ketsui Kizuna Jigoku Tachi (IKD 2007 Special - 2007 Cave Matsuri Version)

games.description: Ketsui: Kizuna Jigoku Tachi (IKD 2007 Special) is a special event version of Cave's 2003 vertical bullet-hell shoot-'em-up Ketsui directed by Tsuneki Ikeda (IKD) and exhibited at the 2007 Cave Matsuri festival.

games.title: The King of Fighters 2003

variants.title: The King of Fighters 2003 (Japan, JAMMA PCB)

games.description:
The King of Fighters 2003 is SNK Playmore's final mainline King of Fighters release for the Neo Geo, and this set represents the Japanese dedicated JAMMA PCB edition rather than the usual interchangeable MVS cartridge. Its tournament introduces Ash Crimson and launches the Tales of Ash storyline, while familiar SNK combatants return to confront a new threat surrounding the Orochi seal.

The major change is Multi-Shift combat. Instead of waiting for a teammate to be knocked out, players can switch among three fighters during a single round, including through attacking tag changes. Each team also designates a tactical leader with access to a powerful Leader Super Special Move. The faster, more fluid system makes KOF 2003 a turning point between the series' classic Neo Geo era and its later installments, while the dedicated-board release provides a distinctive piece of its arcade hardware history.

games.title: Kick
games.description:
Midway's Kick (1981), subsequently retitled Kick Man, is a wonderfully peculiar arcade action game starring a unicycle-riding clown. As balloons drop from the top of the screen, the clown moves sideways to catch them on his hat, building a precarious stack. A dedicated kick button saves a missed balloon by booting it back upward before it hits the ground. Pac-Man and the familiar ghosts occasionally join the falling objects, adding a playful connection to Midway's licensed Namco hits.

The original upright cabinet used a trackball and illuminated kick buttons, making it particularly physical to play. Its design evolved from an unreleased late-1970s black-and-white project called Catch 40. The later Kick Man branding largely changed the title rather than the underlying game, leaving a distinctive early example of Midway experimenting beyond conventional shooters and maze chases.

games.title: Kick Boy
games.description: Kick Boy (1983) is an altered release of the Japanese arcade game Dacholer. Its original ostrich protagonist is replaced by a baseball-cap-wearing boy, and the action takes place around a harbor. The player must kick soccer balls toward pursuing dogs and other creatures, using the bouncing projectiles to clear a path while avoiding contact with enemies. Without a ball nearby, the hero is vulnerable, making the positioning and reuse of each projectile central to survival. Its relationship to Dacholer makes it more interesting as a redesigned version of an unusual single-screen action game than as a wholly independent concept.

games.title: Kicker
games.description:
Kicker is the 1985 international release of Konami's Shao-Lin's Road, a side-view martial-arts platform fighter related to the success of Yie Ar Kung-Fu. Players guide Lee through multi-tier arenas, jumping between platforms and kicking the Triad enemies entering from doorways. Each stage requires a specified number of defeats, with a stronger opponent interrupting the regular onslaught.

Defeated enemies may leave magical energy that can be collected and thrown as an attack, an important advantage against tougher foes. Unlike a conventional one-on-one fighting game, Kicker combines constant movement, crowd control and vertical platform positioning, showing Konami's early experiments with the arcade beat-'em-up formula.

games.title: Kick Goal
games.description: Kick Goal is a 1995 five-a-side soccer game from TCH. Rather than recreating the full eleven-player field, it concentrates the action into smaller teams and compact matches. Players direct their footballers with an eight-way joystick and three action buttons, combining ball movement, passing and shooting in a brisk arcade format. Its reduced team size is the key distinction from the many full-team soccer games released during the same decade.

games.title: Kick and Run
games.description:
Taito's Kick and Run (1986) is a lively arcade soccer game built around cooperative and competitive play. The scrolling field and animated, cartoon-like footballers make matches easy to follow, while players try to pass, tackle and score before the clock expires. The original cabinet was especially unusual for pairing joysticks with foot pedals used to kick the ball.

Up to four players could participate, with two people controlling the same side in cooperative matches or competing against each other. That combination of physical kicking controls and shared-team play makes Kick and Run a distinctive example of arcades turning an ordinary team sport into a social cabinet experience.

games.title: Kick Off
games.description: Kick Off: Jaleco Cup is Jaleco's 1988 arcade soccer game, released in Japan on Mega System 1 hardware. Players select from 20 national teams and compete in eleven-a-side matches governed by familiar football rules. Each match runs on a short three-minute arcade clock, so attacking quickly and converting chances is essential. The horizontal scrolling presentation and straightforward joystick-and-two-button controls distinguish this coin-operated title from the later, unrelated home-computer series also called Kick Off.

games.title: Kick Rider
games.description: Kick Rider (1984) is a motorcycle road-racing game with a top-down view and a deliberately combative twist. The player rides against a timer, overtaking other motorcycles while avoiding cars and roadside hazards. Rival riders kick sideways to push the player's bike off course, but the player can retaliate using the attack button together with the steering direction. Races begin from a traffic-light start and reward both speed and careful positioning, since getting trapped between nearby bikes can be more dangerous than the road itself.

games.title: Kid Niki - Radical Ninja
games.description:
Kid Niki: Radical Ninja is Irem's 1986 side-scrolling platform action game, released in Japan as Kaiketsu Yanchamaru. Its young ninja hero bursts out of training after learning that the Stone Wizard has kidnapped Princess Margo, then sets off across feudal-Japan-inspired landscapes. He jumps over hazards and strikes enemies with an unmistakable spinning sword, gathering bells and other bonuses as he advances toward increasingly extravagant bosses.

The colorful art, expressive enemies and large spinning weapon give the game a deliberately playful personality rather than the serious atmosphere of most ninja adventures. The Japanese and international versions even give the hero different hairstyles. Popular home-computer and console adaptations helped establish Kid Niki as one of Irem's more recognizable arcade characters of the mid-1980s.

games.title: Meikyu Jima
games.description: Meikyu Jima is the Japanese arcade puzzle game that became better known internationally as Kickle Cubicle. Players guide Kickle through single-screen frozen islands, using his freezing breath to turn enemies into ice blocks. These blocks can be kicked into position to bridge water or open routes toward the red Dream Bags needed to complete each stage. This particular set is identified as a pirate version of the original Japanese game, rather than a separate sequel. Its interest lies in preserving an unauthorized edition of Irem's distinctive combination of sliding-block logic and maze movement.

games.title: KiKi KaiKai
games.description:
KiKi KaiKai (1986) is Taito's charming but demanding overhead action shooter, starring Sayo-chan, a young Shinto shrine maiden. When the Seven Lucky Gods are kidnapped by supernatural creatures, she travels through haunted grounds and other eerie settings to recover them. Movement is multidirectional, and her two complementary attacks are thrown paper talismans and a close-range purification rod, useful for striking enemies that crowd too near.

Rather than relying on a spaceship or military theme, the game draws its distinctive enemy designs from Japanese folklore, with ghosts, demons and mischievous spirits filling the screen. Its combination of precise dodging, quick aiming and instantly recognizable heroine became the foundation for the later Pocky & Rocky series. KiKi KaiKai remains a notable early example of a scrolling shooter built around a character on foot.

games.title: Kick Start Wheelie King
games.description:
Kick Start: Wheelie King is a 1984 Taito motorcycle racer presented from behind the rider. The objective is to travel as far as possible against a strict time limit while weaving around other bikes, barrels and road edges. Steering is handled with a horizontal joystick, while the cabinet offers selectable control schemes for acceleration and gear changes. Taking a crash costs valuable seconds, so shifting down before difficult bends is as important as maintaining speed.

Despite the Wheelie King subtitle, the arcade game does not actually provide a wheelie maneuver. Arriving before Sega's Hang-On, it represents a comparatively early attempt to bring fast, road-level motorcycle action to video arcades.

games.title: The Killing Blade
games.description:
The Killing Blade is a 1998-era weapon-based fighting game from Taiwanese developer IGS, running on the PGM arcade system. Set in a fictionalized China scarred by Mongol invasion, its tournament gathers martial artists from rival sects, leading toward confrontations with the Twin Tartars and Lord Wizard. Players choose from a roster of armed fighters and battle one-on-one with the familiar four-button arcade fighting layout.

The game's period costumes, Chinese martial-arts imagery and elaborate special attacks distinguish it from Japanese and American fighting series of the time. Its original release was followed years later by The Killing Blade Plus, an uncommon example of a regional arcade fighting game receiving a substantial later edition.

games.title: The Killing Blade Plus / Ao Jian Kuang Dao Jiaqiang Ban

variants.title: The Killing Blade Plus / Ao Jian Kuang Dao Jiaqiang Ban (China, ver. 300)

games.description: The Killing Blade Plus, also called Ao Jian Kuang Dao Jiaqiang Ban, is IGS's 2005 revisiting of its late-1990s weapon-based fighting game. It returns to the turbulent Chinese martial-arts setting of the original, with fighters representing competing sects and clashes built around armed techniques, special moves and four-button controls. This is a later edition rather than the initial PGM release; the supplied sources establish that distinction but do not specify a reliable move-by-move list of balance or roster changes. Its existence illustrates the unusually long life of IGS's locally popular fighting properties.

games.title: Killer Comet
games.description: Killer Comet (1980) is an early space shooter produced by Game Plan and associated with Centuri. A small player-controlled space pod must survive among drifting alien creatures, bombs and a pursuing comet. The player can maneuver around the screen but fires upward, making positioning vital when enemies approach from awkward angles. Losing contact with the monsters, their projectiles or the glowing comet requires constant evasive movement. Its mixture of free movement and directional shooting gives it a different feel from the fixed-gun alien-invasion games that dominated the period.

games.title: King & Balloon
games.description:
Namco's King & Balloon (1980) is an inventive fixed-screen shooter descended from Galaxian. Instead of defending only the player character, the gun crew on the castle wall must protect a king wandering along the bottom of the screen. Enemy balloons descend to capture him, and players must shoot down the kidnappers before they carry him away. A destroyed cannon can be replaced, but losing the king repeatedly brings the game to an end.

The cabinet's remarkable novelty was its early use of synthesized speech. The king shouts for help while being abducted and comments on events, giving the rescue action a comic urgency absent from most contemporary shooters. The North American release used different voice recordings from the Japanese game, a rare localization detail for an arcade title from this period.

games.title: King of Boxer
games.description:
King of Boxer, released in 1985 and known internationally as Ring King, is a humorous arcade boxing simulation developed by Woodplace. Viewed from an elevated angle, bouts allow players to jab, throw body blows, dodge and guard while wearing down an opponent's stamina. A succession of increasingly strong boxers stands between the newcomer and the championship, and training opportunities between fights help prepare for tougher matches.

The game mixes recognizable boxing tactics with exaggerated knockdowns and cartoonish opponents, making it memorable as both a sports simulation and an arcade spectacle. Its broad range of attacks and the need to manage endurance distinguish it from simpler one-button boxing games of the early 1980s.

games.title: Killer Instinct
games.description:
Rare's Killer Instinct (1994), distributed in arcades by Midway under Nintendo license, brought lavish computer-rendered characters and aggressive combo mechanics to the one-on-one fighting boom. Its story revolves around the mysterious Ultratech corporation, whose tournament assembles an unlikely roster including the alien Glacius, the werewolf Sabrewulf and the skeletal swordsman Spinal. Six attack buttons provide light, medium and heavy punches and kicks, with fighters attempting to exhaust an opponent's two consecutive life bars.

The game is best remembered for long, rhythmic combos assembled through openers, automatic doubles, linkers and spectacular enders. A defender can interrupt a sequence with a correctly timed combo breaker, preventing offense from becoming completely one-sided. The announcer's exuberant calls and elaborate finishing attacks gave Killer Instinct its unmistakable personality.

A major technical showcase, the arcade machine combined a powerful custom Nintendo/Rare board with hard-disk storage and pre-rendered visual assets. Its mix of digitized-looking 3D artwork, rock-influenced soundtrack and unusual fighting rules made it a defining non-Capcom alternative in mid-1990s arcades.

games.title: Killer Instinct 2
games.description:
Killer Instinct 2 is Rare's arcade sequel to its influential combo-focused fighter, appearing in 1996 after the first game's 1994 success. Orchid's defeat of Eyedol opens a time portal that leaves returning combatants stranded in the distant past and releases the demon Gargos. New fighters such as Tusk, Maya and Kim Wu join established favorites, with rivalries and character-specific endings expanding the supernatural story.

The sequel retains six-button fighting, two life bars and the characteristic chain of combo openers, linkers, auto-doubles and breakers, but revises moves and expands options for pressure and counterplay. Like its predecessor, the cabinet uses a hard disk to accommodate the extensive audio and pre-rendered presentation. The Nintendo 64 title Killer Instinct Gold later adapted this game, though the original arcade version has its own place in the series' history.

games.title: Killer Instinct
games.description: This Killer Instinct bootleg is an unauthorized arcade conversion based on the Super Nintendo version of Rare's 1994 fighting game, not a standard copy of the original hard-disk arcade board. It retains the recognizable Ultratech tournament, six-button combat and elaborate combo system, but comes from the console adaptation's technical lineage rather than the original machine's graphics and storage hardware. For arcade historians, its significance lies in showing how operators and bootleg manufacturers repurposed a popular home version for coin-operated play.

games.title: Killer Instinct
games.description: Killer Instinct (prototype) preserves a pre-release development version of Rare's 1994 fighting game, identified in historical arcade records as software version 4.7 rather than one of the familiar commercial revisions. Like the finished arcade hit, it pits Ultratech's eccentric combatants against one another in six-button matches focused on long combinations and correctly timed combo breakers. This set is valuable as a surviving snapshot of the game's development. The supplied material does not establish which specific moves, audiovisual assets or balance settings differ, so it should not be treated as a documented alternate ruleset.

games.title: Kirameki Star Road
games.description: Kirameki Star Road is Taito's 1997 Japanese music-identification quiz game for its F3 arcade system. Rather than answering general-knowledge questions, players act as talent scouts promoting one of three aspiring female idols. Short excerpts of popular songs are played, and the player must identify the correct title or performer from multiple choices before time runs out. The idol-development framing, character scenes and musical emphasis give this quiz game a distinctive identity, especially for players familiar with Japanese pop culture.

games.title: Ryuusei Janshi Kirara Star
games.description: Ryuusei Janshi Kirara Star is a 1996 Japanese mahjong game by Jaleco, presented as a colorful science-fiction anime adventure. The player competes against a small cast of female opponents in successive mahjong matches, with animated story and adult-oriented reward scenes between rounds. An unusual twist is that modest winning hands may award time for an optional quiz sequence rather than immediately advancing a character scene. That combination of competitive tile play, bonus questions and elaborate animation sets it apart from more conventional strip-mahjong cabinets.

games.title: Kisekae Hanafuda
games.description: Kisekae Hanafuda is a Japanese arcade card game released by I'Max in December 1995. It is built around hanafuda, the traditional Japanese matching-card game, and uses a dress-up theme suggested by its title, which means roughly Dress-up Hanafuda. The available sources establish its card-game identity and release context but do not document enough of its special rules to claim that it substantially changes the underlying hanafuda format.

games.title: Kisekae Mahjong
games.description: Kisekae Mahjong is a 1995 Japanese arcade mahjong game developed by I'Max for its Multi Amenity Cassette System. The title means Dress-up Mahjong, and the presentation uses anime-style characters and costume-changing rewards as an incentive to win hands. Beneath that themed presentation it belongs to the Japanese arcade tradition of competitive mahjong, with the emphasis on completing scoring hands rather than reflex-based action.

games.title: Kitten Kaboodle
games.description:
Kitten Kaboodle, known in Japan as Nyan Nyan Panic, is Konami's 1988 overhead maze-action game starring an adventurous cat. Each level hides four keys needed to progress, while enemies and movable blocks complicate the search. Players can jump obstacles and kick blocks into approaching foes, sometimes uncovering a key or collectible in the process. Aligning three matching special blocks activates useful effects such as wiping out enemies or granting temporary protection.

The resulting game combines light combat, environmental puzzles and the pleasure of uncovering secrets. Its cute artwork conceals a demanding game of careful block placement and route planning, making it an overlooked entry in Konami's late-1980s arcade catalog.

games.title: Pro Mahjong Kiwame
games.description: Pro Mahjong Kiwame is a 1994 Japanese arcade mahjong title designed around a conventional four-player table. One human player faces three computer-controlled opponents in games emphasizing standard mahjong decisions, hand-building and tile discards. Rather than introducing an action-game gimmick, it focuses on the competitive structure of the tabletop original. The Kiwame name, implying mastery, later continued in an updated Sega ST-V edition.

games.title: Pro Mahjong Kiwame S
games.description: Pro Mahjong Kiwame S is the 1995 Sega ST-V follow-up to Pro Mahjong Kiwame, bringing the Japanese mahjong series to arcade hardware closely related to the Sega Saturn. Its core attraction remains the strategic tile game: players assemble scoring hands while weighing discards and opponents' visible tiles. The S edition is notable chiefly as a platform update to the earlier release and part of the brief period when Sega's Saturn-derived arcade board hosted both action games and tabletop adaptations.

games.title: Kizuna Encounter - Super Tag Battle / Fu'un Super Tag Battle
games.description:
Kizuna Encounter: Super Tag Battle is SNK's 1996 Neo Geo sequel to Savage Reign, set in the futuristic Jipang City. Instead of selecting one fighter, players form two-character teams from an eccentric roster of armed and unarmed combatants, then challenge rivals and the powerful boss King Leo. Its large sprites, colorful urban arenas and unusual weapons provide a distinct alternative to SNK's better-known King of Fighters formula.

The defining rule is the tag system. A teammate can be brought into the fight when the active character reaches the designated tag area, adding positional tactics beyond normal attacks and special moves. Losing either team member can cost the match, so conserving health and choosing when to switch is essential. The game's reputation was further enhanced by the extraordinary rarity of its original European Neo Geo home-cartridge release.

games.title: Klax
games.description:
Klax, developed by Atari Games and released in arcades in 1990, is one of the best-known puzzle games to emerge from the post-Tetris boom. Colored tiles tumble down a conveyor belt toward a paddle controlled by the player. The tiles must be caught and dropped into a five-column well to form same-colored rows, columns or diagonals called Klaxes. Successive waves demand particular combinations, such as vertical stacks, diagonal lines or multiple simultaneous clears, while dropped tiles accumulate as costly mistakes.

Unlike a conventional falling-block game, Klax gives players the chance to catch several tiles before placing them, toss one back up the belt and accelerate approaching pieces. Mastery depends on visualizing patterns while juggling the relentless flow of incoming tiles. Its distinctive clattering sound, cheering crowds and colorful three-dimensional conveyor made it immediately recognizable in an arcade.

Designed by Mark Stephen Pierce and programmed by Dave Akers, the project was completed quickly after Atari's Tetris-related legal troubles. It was converted to an extraordinary range of home systems, cementing its reputation as a defining early-1990s arcade puzzler.

games.title: KlonDike+
games.description: KlonDike+ is a 1999 arcade adaptation of solitaire-style card play, described in its surviving records as similar to Klondike and FreeCell. Its appeal is arranging cards through a deliberate sequence of legal moves rather than defeating an opponent or reacting to arcade hazards. The unusual title and coin-operated presentation make it an example of traditional patience games appearing on arcade hardware, although the available descriptions do not establish a complete ruleset for this particular implementation.

games.title: Knuckle Heads
games.description:
Namco's Knuckle Heads is a weapon-based fighting game released in 1993 during the arcade genre's post-Street Fighter II expansion. Framed as an international televised competition, it offers six fighters from different countries, each with distinctive weapons, special techniques and home-town stages. Players attack with standard strikes and a dedicated jump control rather than relying entirely on the joystick for aerial movement.

Its chief novelty is the ability to fight with as many as four people simultaneously, creating chaotic multiplayer encounters very different from the standard two-player duel. With its game-show presentation, varied arenas and crowd-oriented combat, Knuckle Heads represents Namco experimenting with a fighting-game format before its later 3D successes.

games.title: Knuckle Joe
games.description: Knuckle Joe (1985) is a side-scrolling street fighter licensed for distribution by Taito. Players guide the title character across a succession of enemy-filled stages, using punches, kicks, jumps and a combined-button guard to survive. Boss battles interrupt the regular brawling, while motorcycle bonus sections offer a change of pace by letting Joe attack hostile riders on the road. An unauthorized version circulated as Bone Crusher, reflecting the game’s presence outside its original arcade release.

games.title: Knightmare
games.description:
Knightmare is an unreleased 1983 arcade maze/action prototype developed by Gottlieb, preserved in an unfinished state. It uses an unusual pair of two-way joysticks plus two buttons, rather than the more conventional single-stick platform or shooter layout. Its horizontal display and Gottlieb hardware place it near the company's other early-1980s experiments, such as Q*bert and Krull, although the surviving documentation does not establish a complete set of objectives or stages.

This prototype is unrelated to Konami's 1986 MSX shooter Knightmare, despite the identical English title. Confusing the two would wrongly import the MSX game's fantasy hero, scrolling stages, and weapon systems into an entirely different arcade project.

games.title: Knights of the Round
games.description:
Knights of the Round is Capcom's 1991 medieval fantasy beat-'em-up, inspired by the legends of King Arthur. One to three players take the roles of Arthur, Lancelot and Percival as they fight across seven stages in search of the Holy Grail. Each knight has a distinct balance of speed, reach and strength, and combat emphasizes sword attacks, blocking and careful responses to heavily armored opponents.

Its signature innovation is a light role-playing progression system. Points and treasure provide experience, and leveling up changes a fighter's armor, weapons and appearance while making the character more powerful. That visible transformation gives the game a sense of adventure beyond the usual arcade brawler. Together with large sprites, memorable bosses and cooperative play, it helped establish Capcom's reputation for ambitious fantasy-themed fighting games.

games.title: Knight's Chance
games.description: Knight's Chance is a collection of four medieval fantasy-themed casino and pub games developed and published by Neobitz (Jeff Kurtz) for the Neo Geo MVS and AES platforms in 2014.

games.title: Kotoba no Puzzle Mojipittan

variants.title: Kotoba no Puzzle Mojipittan (Japan, KPM1 Ver.A)

games.description:
Kotoba no Puzzle: Mojipittan is Namco's 2001 Japanese word-puzzle game, which launched a successful series on the System 10 arcade board. Players place individual hiragana tiles on a grid to build valid Japanese words, gaining points when a placement creates several words at once. Unlike Scrabble, the vocabulary is formed through a more immediate tile-placement system, with spatial arrangement and compound word discovery driving the puzzle.

Its cheerful presentation hides a surprisingly deep challenge: a single well-chosen syllable can complete multiple intersecting words, producing satisfying chains of discoveries. The idea later moved to home consoles and handhelds, but the arcade original remains the starting point for Namco's distinctive language-based puzzle franchise.

games.title: The King of Dragons
games.description:
The King of Dragons is Capcom's 1991 fantasy side-scrolling beat-'em-up, set in a monster-infested kingdom threatened by the dragon Gildiss. Players choose from five character classes, including a fighter, cleric, elf, wizard and dwarf, then battle their way through 16 mostly short stages. Three-player cooperative action, ranged magical attacks, swords and shields give the party a varied tactical feel.

A simple experience system gradually strengthens the heroes, while improved weapons and equipment appear as the quest progresses. The unusually frequent boss encounters include dragons and other fantasy creatures, making progress feel like a condensed tabletop adventure. The game foreshadowed the richer role-playing elements of Capcom's later Dungeons & Dragons arcade beat-'em-ups.

games.title: Kodure Ookami
games.description:
Kozure Ookami (1987), sometimes romanized Kodure Ookami, is Nichibutsu's Japanese arcade adaptation of the manga Lone Wolf and Cub. Players control the wandering swordsman Ogami Itto as he fights through side-scrolling encounters with assassins while caring for his young son. Swordplay and close combat are joined by a wonderfully outlandish special weapon: the child's carriage can become a cannon, turning a familiar image from the source material into a powerful arcade attack.

The game also mixes shooting elements with its brawling, and destructible background objects can conceal useful bonuses. Its licensed manga setting and improbable baby-carriage weapon make it an unusual footnote in the history of Japanese action arcade games.

games.title: The King of Fighters 2000
games.description:
The King of Fighters 2000 continued SNK's NESTS storyline as the company's last KOF installment produced before its original bankruptcy. K' and his allies again face a shadowy conspiracy, while a sprawling cast of returning fighters and newcomers, including Ramon and Vanessa, competes in teams. Matches retain the series' four-button punches and kicks and demanding special-move combinations.

Its major contribution is an expanded Striker system. Teams consist of three active fighters and one assist character, and alternative Strikers open up unusual combination attacks, escapes and juggle possibilities. The emphasis on inventive assists gives KOF 2000 a particularly experimental feel compared with both the earlier three-person tournament games and the more traditional dream-match installments.

games.title: The King of Fighters 2001

variants.title: Crouching Tiger Hidden Dragon 2003 Super Plus (The King of Fighters 2001 bootleg)
Crouching Tiger Hidden Dragon 2003 (The King of Fighters 2001 bootleg)

games.description:
The King of Fighters 2001 is the concluding chapter of the NESTS story arc and the first mainline game released after SNK's original financial collapse, developed with South Korean company Eolith's involvement. The tournament brings K' and other established fighters into conflict with the organization and its leaders, culminating in a confrontation with Igniz. Returning combatants share the roster with newcomers including Angel, May Lee and K9999.

The four-person team system becomes unusually flexible: players choose how many members fight directly and how many act as Strikers. A team with more active fighters has fewer available assists, creating a strategic trade-off between endurance and combo potential. That configurable format, together with new move interactions and a distinctive presentation, gives the game a very different identity from the entries surrounding it.

games.title: The King of Fighters 2002

variants.title: The King of Fighters 10th Anniversary Extra Plus (The King of Fighters 2002 bootleg)
The King of Fighters 2002 Magic Plus (bootleg)
The King of Fighters 2002 Magic Plus II (bootleg)
The King of Fighters 2002 Plus (set 2, bootleg)
The King of Fighters 2002 Plus (set 1, bootleg)
The King of Fighters 10th Anniversary 2005 Unique (The King of Fighters 2002 bootleg)
The King Of Fighters 10th Anniversary (The King of Fighters 2002 bootleg)
The King of Fighters Special Edition 2004 (The King of Fighters 2002 bootleg)

games.description:
The King of Fighters 2002 is the series' second major dream-match installment, setting aside the ongoing storyline to bring together a large cast of familiar SNK fighters. Produced by Eolith and Playmore, it restores traditional three-character team battles without the Striker assists of KOF '99 through 2001. The four-button combat is deliberately fast and technical, rewarding close-range pressure, careful defense and intricate character-specific combos.

Its defining addition is the revamped MAX Mode, which allows players to spend power on extended offensive sequences and cancels, creating a demanding but expressive fighting system. KOF 2002 became an enduring competitive favorite, later inspiring updated releases and revisions. For players interested chiefly in mechanics rather than story, it is one of the Neo Geo series' most celebrated entries.

games.title: The King of Fighters 2003

variants.title: The King of Fighters 2003 (World / US, MVS)
The King of Fighters 2004 Plus / Hero (The King of Fighters 2003 bootleg)
The King of Fighters 2004 Ultra Plus (The King of Fighters 2003 bootleg)

games.description:
The King of Fighters 2003 is SNK Playmore's final mainline King of Fighters game for the Neo Geo, closing the platform's long association with the franchise. It begins the Tales of Ash storyline, introducing the enigmatic Ash Crimson alongside other new fighters such as Duo Lon and Shen Woo. Its tournament also reconnects with the mythology of the Orochi saga and features different routes to the final bosses.

The central innovation is the Multi-Shift system: three fighters form a team, but players can exchange the active character during a match rather than waiting for a knockout. Quick changes and attacking switch-ins create new combo and pressure opportunities. Each team also appoints a leader whose exclusive Leader Super Special Move consumes substantial power. The greater speed and freer team rotation make KOF 2003 a clear transitional chapter between the traditional Neo Geo installments and KOF XI.

games.title: The King of Fighters '94
games.description:
The King of Fighters '94 is one of SNK's most influential arcade releases and the beginning of a fighting-game franchise that ran far beyond the Neo Geo's commercial heyday. Its conceit was unusually ambitious: fighters from Fatal Fury, Art of Fighting, Ikari Warriors and Psycho Soldier share a single tournament, joined by new characters led by Kyo Kusanagi. The mysterious organizer Rugal Bernstein awaits the surviving team at the conclusion of the competition.

Instead of choosing one fighter, players select a fixed national team of three and fight a succession of one-on-one rounds until every opposing team member is defeated. Its four-button layout combines light and strong punches and kicks, while chargeable power meters, evasion and team assistance add tactical depth. Although later entries allowed customizable teams, the original's predetermined trios were central to its crossover identity.

Released in 1994, the game transformed SNK's separate fighting properties into a shared universe and established the annual KOF tradition. Its team-based format, distinctive characters and intricate rivalries became foundations for one of arcade fighting's longest-running series.

games.title: The King of Fighters '95
games.description:
The King of Fighters '95 refines SNK's team-based fighting format and marks a crucial step in the series' development. The most famous newcomer is Iori Yagami, Kyo Kusanagi's flame-wielding rival, whose introduction gives the saga one of its enduring character conflicts. Rugal returns as the tournament's organizer, while the roster again mixes original fighters with familiar faces from SNK's other games.

Unlike the fixed national teams of KOF '94, the new Team Edit option lets players assemble custom three-character lineups. Revised evasion, counterattack and power-gauge behavior expand the combat possibilities without losing the four-button foundation. The change to free-form team selection became a defining feature of nearly every later installment.

games.title: The King of Fighters '96
games.description:
The King of Fighters '96 is the third entry in SNK's flagship team-fighting series and a major turning point in its look and feel. The conflict between Kyo Kusanagi and Iori Yagami develops into the supernatural Orochi storyline, with the mysterious Goenitz serving as the principal antagonist. The roster introduces or restores important fighters, including Leona Heidern, while redesigned character animations and striking backgrounds give the game a more cohesive visual identity.

Combat also receives extensive changes. The earlier evasive dodge is replaced by forward and backward rolls, running becomes more fluid, and many characters gain new techniques suited to close-range combinations. These revisions established a faster, more mobile template for the series, making KOF '96 one of its most consequential mechanical transitions.

games.title: The King of Fighters '97

variants.title: King of Gladiator (The King of Fighters '97 bootleg)

games.description:
The King of Fighters '97 brings SNK's Orochi saga to a dramatic conclusion. Kyo Kusanagi, Iori Yagami and Chizuru Kagura confront the threat of the ancient entity Orochi, while character relationships and particular team choices affect the encounters and endings. The large cast includes the New Faces Team, whose members play an important role in the unfolding story.

Players can select between two fighting systems before assembling their three-person team. Advanced mode emphasizes running, rolling and a stock-based power gauge, while Extra mode preserves older-style dodging, charging and movement. This choice gives the game two distinct tempos and makes matchup decisions especially important. Its energetic soundtrack, character-driven endings and climactic supernatural boss battles helped make KOF '97 one of the series' best-loved narrative installments.

games.title: The King of Fighters '98 - The Slugfest / King of Fighters '98 - dream match never ends

variants.title: The King of Fighters '98 - The Slugfest / King of Fighters '98 - dream match never ends
The King of Fighters '98 - The Slugfest / King of Fighters '98 - dream match never ends (Korean board)
The King of Fighters '98 - The Slugfest / King of Fighters '98 - dream match never ends (not encrypted)

games.description:
The King of Fighters '98, called The Slugfest internationally and Dream Match Never Ends in Japan, is SNK's celebrated 1998 all-star fighting game. Abandoning the previous entry's plot, it reunites a broad roster from the early King of Fighters tournaments, including characters who would otherwise be absent for story reasons. The focus shifts entirely to one-on-one technique within three-member teams, with no need to follow the Orochi saga.

Like KOF '97, it offers Advanced and Extra styles with different movement and power-gauge rules, but the roster, moves and match balance are extensively revised. Fast footsies, tightly timed combinations and a wealth of character-specific strategies made it a long-standing favorite of competitive players. Its popularity ultimately led SNK to revisit the game with The King of Fighters '98 Ultimate Match a decade later.

games.title: The King of Fighters '98: Ultimate Match HERO

variants.title: The King of Fighters '98: Ultimate Match HERO (China, V100, 09-08-23)

games.description:
The King of Fighters '98: Ultimate Match HERO is the 2009 Chinese arcade edition of SNK Playmore's expanded KOF '98 remake, released on IGS's PGM2 hardware in cooperation with New Channel. It is not the original 1998 Neo Geo game or the 2008 Taito Type X version: this set is a distinct later arcade hardware adaptation of Ultimate Match.

Ultimate Match restores fighters missing from the original dream match, including Geese Howard, Kasumi Todoh and Eiji Kisaragi, and adds alternate character versions and substantial balance changes. Its Ultimate fighting style lets players combine selected traits of the familiar Advanced and Extra systems, customizing elements such as movement and power-gauge behavior. The HERO release is particularly interesting for carrying this large, traditionally styled 2D fighter onto a newer cartridge-based Chinese arcade platform.

games.title: The King of Fighters '99 - Millennium Battle

variants.title: The King of Fighters '99 - Millennium Battle (set 1)
The King of Fighters '99 - Millennium Battle (set 2)
The King of Fighters '99 - Millennium Battle (earlier)
The King of Fighters '99 - Millennium Battle (not encrypted)
The King of Fighters '99 - Millennium Battle (prototype)

games.description:
The King of Fighters '99: Millennium Battle opens SNK's NESTS storyline, moving the spotlight from Kyo Kusanagi to the mysterious new fighter K'. A secret tournament exposes a cloning conspiracy, while returning SNK characters encounter new opponents including Maxima and the formidable Krizalid. The series' distinctive four-button fighting remains intact, but team composition changes radically.

Instead of three participants, players select four characters: three active combatants and a fourth who acts as a Striker. The Striker can be summoned a limited number of times to perform an assisting attack, interrupting opponents or extending combinations. This new layer of team strategy gave the series a different feel and launched three consecutive games built around the NESTS conspiracy.

games.title: Koi Koi Shimasho 2 - Super Real Hanafuda

variants.title: Koi Koi Shimasho 2 - Super Real Hanafuda (Japan)

games.description: Koi Koi Shimasho 2: Super Real Hanafuda is a 1997 Japanese arcade card game by Visco. It uses the traditional Koi-Koi form of hanafuda, in which players collect matching cards to complete valuable combinations and decide whether to stop or continue a hand for greater rewards. The sequel adds an adult-oriented presentation with eight illustrated opponents, character dialogue and animated reward scenes. It is a distinctly Japanese example of familiar tabletop rules adapted into a coin-operated character-collection game.

games.title: Mahjong Koi no Magic Potion
games.description: Mahjong Koi no Magic Potion is a 1992 adult-themed Japanese arcade mahjong game from Nichibutsu. The player competes in mahjong against illustrated female opponents, attempting to form winning tile combinations while progressing through a lighthearted romantic-fantasy presentation. The title, meaning roughly Mahjong: Magic Potion of Love, reflects the whimsical framing rather than a separate action mechanic. It belongs to Nichibutsu's extensive lineup of character-driven mahjong cabinets from the early 1990s.

games.title: Konami GT
games.description:
Konami GT is the international PCB release of Konami's 1985 racing game RF2: Red Fighter, originally associated with the company's unusual Bubble System hardware. Players steer a sports car along a winding road, overtaking traffic and reaching checkpoints before the fuel supply runs out. Collecting fuel items extends the journey, while a turbo or high-gear setting increases speed at the expense of faster consumption and greater collision risk.

The car is steered with a rotary controller, with additional controls for driving functions. Unlike the original Bubble System cartridge, the Konami GT release runs from a conventional circuit board and omits the Bubble System's characteristic warm-up sequence. That hardware difference makes the set more than a simple overseas title change.

games.title: Baby Phoenix/GV System
games.description:
Konami's GV System, also known as Baby Phoenix, is a mid-1990s arcade platform built around technology closely related to Sony's original PlayStation. Introduced as an arcade system in 1995, it used a Konami-specific BIOS, dedicated arcade interfaces, and, for several games, CD-ROM drives. This AdvanceMAME entry represents the hardware BIOS, not a standalone game.

The platform supported a surprisingly varied catalog, including Hyper Athlete, Jikkyou Powerful Pro Yakyuu '96, Susume! Taisen Puzzle-Dama, Nagano Winter Olympics '98, and The Simpsons Bowling. Particular cabinets could require specialized peripherals, such as a trackball interface for The Simpsons Bowling or additional sensor and printer boards for Tokimeki Memorial: Oshiete Your Heart. GV is a revealing example of console-derived 3D-era technology being adapted for the practical demands of arcades and other amusement installations.

games.title: System GX
games.description:
Konami System GX is a versatile 2D arcade hardware family introduced in 1994, designed to handle a broad range of games using shared electronics and interchangeable program boards. Its main processor is a Motorola 68EC020, with dedicated graphics hardware providing multiple scrolling layers, sprites, line scrolling, and effects such as transparency. The platform was offered in several board configurations, allowing Konami to adapt the basic architecture to different cabinet and gameplay requirements. This AdvanceMAME entry is the system BIOS rather than a playable title.

GX powered some of Konami's most visually elaborate mid-1990s arcade releases, including Gokujou Parodius (Fantastic Journey), Salamander 2, Sexy Parodius, TwinBee Yahho!, and the fighting game Dragoon Might. Its colorful sprite work and layered visual effects mark a late high point of dedicated 2D arcade engineering at a time when the industry was rapidly moving toward polygonal hardware.

games.title: Kono e Tako
games.description: Kono e Tako is a 2003 arcade action puzzle developed by Mitchell for Namco System 10 hardware and distributed in Japan by Capcom. An octopus occupies the middle of the playing field while barrels advance inward from either side. Players manipulate the octopus to suck up barrels and spit them back out, arranging matching objects before the field becomes overcrowded. This unusual two-sided pressure and the octopus's inhale-and-launch action give the game a different rhythm from ordinary falling-block puzzles.

games.title: KO Punch
games.description:
Sega's KO Punch (1981), also known in Japan as Knockout Punch, is an early hybrid of video-game graphics and a physical strength-testing machine. Rather than controlling a boxer with a joystick, the player watches an opponent on a vertical monitor and strikes a real punching ball when the onscreen boxer drops his guard. The display measures the strength of the blow and determines whether it scores a knockout. Sega promoted it as the industry's first punching-power tester to use a television monitor.

Players can challenge seven boxing weight classes, ranging from flyweight to heavyweight, with three attempts per play. A successful knockout allows the contestant to tackle a higher class, while a failed punch requires another attempt. Released in Japan in October 1981, it combined the appeal of a traditional arcade test-of-strength attraction with animated video feedback several years before Nintendo's Punch-Out!! brought a very different approach to boxing into the arcade.

games.title: Mahjong-zukino Korinai Menmen
games.description: Mahjong-zukino Korinai Menmen is a 1988 Japanese mahjong game developed by Nichibutsu, one of the most prolific producers of coin-operated mahjong titles. Its matches use the familiar tile-drawing and hand-building structure of Japanese mahjong, presented with lighthearted cartoon female characters and adult-oriented interludes. The game's appeal lies in a character-driven presentation of an established table game rather than a new type of arcade action.

games.title: Koro Koro Quest
games.description:
Koro Koro Quest is an unusual Japanese children's medal game produced by Takumi and cataloged as a 1999 release. Its whimsical fantasy presentation disguises a simple game of chance as a miniature role-playing adventure: a hero faces enemies across three encounters, with battles resolved by rolling two dice. Beating an enemy's roll wins the encounter, while matching numbers can trigger a powerful special attack. In some near-miss situations, a fairy intervenes and the player can rapidly press a button in an attempt to improve a die.

Players who survive the early battles reach a Demon King encounter offering a larger medal reward. Despite the RPG-style artwork and battle scenes, it is fundamentally a token-wagering amusement machine rather than a conventional adventure game. It uses hardware related to Cave's arcade boards, and its surviving two-button software offers a glimpse of a specialized Japanese arcade format rarely seen outside its original market.

games.title: Ah Eikou no Koshien
games.description:
Ah Eikou no Koshien is a lively Japanese baseball game by Taito, named after the prestigious national high-school baseball tournament. Teams play recognizably conventional baseball, but pitching and batting include a chargeable stamina mechanic. Holding a charge can produce a more powerful throw or swing, while exhausting a player's energy affects both performance and comically exaggerated character animations.

The mix of real baseball rules, cartoon artwork and over-the-top actions makes it closer to arcade sports comedy than a sober simulation. Its Koshien theme gives it a specific cultural setting familiar to Japanese baseball fans.

games.title: Kyuukyoku no Othello
games.description: Kyuukyoku no Othello is a 1990 Japanese arcade adaptation of Othello, also known as Reversi, by Success. Players place black or white discs on an eight-by-eight board and flip opposing pieces trapped between their own, competing to control more of the board by the end. The cabinet supports players taking turns against the computer rather than directly competing in a simultaneous two-person mode. The title translates roughly as Ultimate Othello, emphasizing a familiar strategic board game in coin-operated form.

games.title: King of the Monsters
games.description:
King of the Monsters is SNK's 1991 Neo Geo giant-monster wrestling game, an affectionate fusion of Japanese kaiju cinema and professional wrestling. Players choose one of six enormous creatures, including reptilian and insect-like beasts, and fight across miniature Japanese cities. Buildings, highways and other scenery are crushed during the struggle, but victory requires overpowering the opponent and completing a wrestling-style three-count pin.

The combat is deliberately more physical than most fighting games, involving grappling, throws and power struggles as well as attacks. Two players can cooperate against computer monsters or battle each other, and the single-player campaign escalates through repeated confrontations. The ability to demolish a city while fighting a rival monster made it one of the Neo Geo's most memorable early spectacles.

games.title: King of the Monsters 2 - The Next Thing
games.description:
King of the Monsters 2: The Next Thing is SNK's 1992 sequel to its kaiju wrestling hit. Rather than concentrating only on arena duels, it blends monster combat with side-scrolling action stages in which the selected creature destroys lesser enemies before reaching a giant boss. Three playable monsters remain available, including the returning Geon, Astro Guy and Woo, now facing an extraterrestrial threat across locations around the world.

Its gameplay keeps the enormous grapples and exaggerated attacks of the original while adding a more traditional progression through hostile environments. Cooperative play and spectacular monster-versus-monster confrontations remain central, but the shift from wrestling arenas to a staged action adventure gives this sequel a markedly different identity.

games.title: The Koukouyakyuh
games.description: The Koukou Yakyuu is a 1985 Japanese baseball game by Alpha Denshi, centered on high-school rather than professional teams. Using joystick-and-button controls, players take part in baseball contests featuring the sport's familiar exchange of pitching, batting and fielding. Its high-school setting reflects the popularity of Japanese school baseball, particularly the national Koshien tradition. The surviving documentation does not establish unusual rules or special techniques beyond that sporting premise.

games.title: Knights of Valour / Sangoku Senki

variants.title: Knights of Valour / Sangoku Senki (ver. 100, Japanese Board)
Knights of Valour Plus / Sangoku Senki Plus (ver. 119)
Knights of Valour Plus / Sangoku Senki Plus (alt ver. 119)
Knights of Valour Super Heroes / Sanguo Zhan Ji Fengyun Zaiqi / Sangoku Senki Super Heroes (ver. 104, CN)

games.description:
Knights of Valour, released by IGS in 1999 on its PGM hardware, is a Chinese historical-fantasy beat-'em-up inspired by Romance of the Three Kingdoms. Players choose renowned warriors such as Guan Yu, Zhang Fei and Zhao Yun, then move through side-scrolling battlefields crowded with soldiers, officers and spectacular bosses. Swords, spears, special attacks and collectible equipment give the combat more variety than a typical two-button brawler.

The game became a major arcade property in East Asia and attracted numerous sequels, official revisions and unofficial modifications. Its lavish sprite art, cooperative fighting and folklore-inflected interpretation of the Three Kingdoms made it one of IGS's defining franchises, often compared with Capcom's Dungeons & Dragons beat-'em-ups.

games.title: Knights of Valour 2

variants.title: Knights of Valour 2 Plus - Nine Dragons

games.description:
Knights of Valour 2 is IGS's 2000 follow-up to its popular Three Kingdoms arcade beat-'em-up. Up to four players control a larger group of historical heroes, traveling through side-scrolling stages filled with armed soldiers and commanders. The characters have fighting-game-inspired special moves and long combination attacks, while different weapons and items can alter their approach to combat.

More elaborate story scenes and branching routes deepen the original game's structure, allowing decisions to affect later encounters and the route through the campaign. With its dramatic bosses, extensive move lists and fast cooperative battles, Knights of Valour 2 is one of the most ambitious late-era 2D beat-'em-ups from outside Japan.

games.title: Knights of Valour 2 New Legend / Sanguo Zhan Ji 2 Guang Sao Yu Jun

variants.title: Knights of Valour 2 New Legend / Sanguo Zhan Ji 2 Guang Sao Yu Jun (V302, Oversea)

games.description: Knights of Valour 2: New Legend, known in Chinese as Sanguo Zhan Ji 2 Guang Sao Yu Jun, is a 2008 continuation of IGS's Three Kingdoms beat-'em-up franchise. It returns to the weapon-wielding heroes and side-scrolling battles of Knights of Valour 2, emphasizing combinations, special techniques and cooperative combat against large groups of soldiers and commanders. This title represents a later release in the series rather than the original 2000 version. Although its name establishes it as a New Legend edition, the available material does not reliably identify each individual gameplay or roster change.

games.title: Knights of Valour 3 / Sanguo Zhan Ji 3

variants.title: Knights of Valour 3 / Sanguo Zhan Ji 3 (V104, China, Hong Kong, Taiwan)

games.description:
Knights of Valour 3 is IGS's 2011 continuation of the long-running Three Kingdoms beat-'em-up series, released on PGM2 hardware. The game again turns the warriors and battles of Romance of the Three Kingdoms into cooperative side-scrolling action, with selectable heroes fighting soldiers and imposing commanders using weapons, special moves and elaborate combinations.

Its significance lies in bringing the franchise's distinctive sprite-driven combat to a newer generation of IGS arcade equipment, years after many competing beat-'em-up series had left coin-operated machines. It demonstrates the lasting regional popularity of cooperative historical-fantasy brawlers.

games.title: Knights of Valour Super Heroes Plus / Sanguo Zhan Ji Luanshi Xiaoxiong

variants.title: Knights of Valour Super Heroes Plus / Sanguo Zhan Ji Luanshi Xiaoxiong (ver. 101)

games.description: Knights of Valour: Super Heroes Plus is a 2004 IGS release expanding the Super Heroes branch of the company's Three Kingdoms arcade beat-'em-ups. As in the main series, players guide famous Chinese warriors across side-scrolling battlefields, chaining weapon strikes and special attacks while confronting armies and dramatic bosses. This is an official later PGM edition, not simply the original 1999 Knights of Valour cartridge. The supplied record establishes its separate release history but does not provide enough verified specifics to attribute particular character, speed or balance modifications to this set.

games.title: Knights of Valour Super Heroes / Sanguo Zhan Ji Fengyun Zaiqi / Sangoku Senki Super Heroes

variants.title: Knights of Valour Super Heroes / Sanguo Zhan Ji Fengyun Zaiqi / Sangoku Senki Super Heroes (SANGO EX+) (ver. 201 'Yitong Zhongyuan', China)

games.description: Knights of Valour: Super Heroes is an IGS PGM entry in the Three Kingdoms beat-'em-up series, also identified by its Chinese subtitle Fengyun Zaiqi and the Japanese name Sangoku Senki Super Heroes. Players fight through historical-fantasy battlefields as armed heroes, using joystick movement, four-button actions and character-specific special attacks to cut through groups of enemies. The set is associated with a 2004 regional release and the alternate title Yi Tong Zhong Yuan. It is notable as a separately documented Super Heroes edition, although reliable details of its precise differences from other versions are limited.

games.title: Kram
games.description: Kram is a 1982 maze-action arcade game in which the player controls a small character navigating arenas full of pursuers. Rather than simply running away, Kram can construct walls to block enemies and reshape the paths through the maze. A separate action button destroys previously built barriers, letting the player open an escape route or change the defensive arrangement. Coins scattered across the stage provide points, turning the pursuit into a balancing act between collecting rewards and managing the maze itself.

games.title: Kozmik Kroozr
games.description:
Kozmik Kroozr is Midway's imaginative 1982 science-fiction shooter, starring the tiny astronaut Kapt. Krooz'r. The goal is not to destroy every alien in sight but to guide the character into a rotating mothership at the top of the screen while dodging hostile craft. The ship can only be boarded when its tractor beam becomes available, forcing players to survive and maneuver while waiting for the right opening.

An unusual rotary controller supports multidirectional aiming, while a protective shield can deflect incoming fire. Every fifth round offers a space-junk collection bonus. Originally developed under the title Mother-ship, the game was revised into a more comic, colorful form, making it one of Midway's stranger early-1980s arcade experiments.

games.title: Krull
games.description:
Krull is Gottlieb's 1983 arcade adaptation of the fantasy film, starring Prince Colwyn on a quest to rescue Princess Lyssa from the Beast. Rather than repeat one action mechanic, it strings together distinct challenges inspired by the story: collecting the pieces of a magical glaive, navigating dangerous terrain, fighting Slayers, discovering the route to the Black Fortress and confronting the final enemy. The screen designs and objectives change significantly as the journey progresses.

The cabinet uses two eight-way joysticks, one to move Colwyn and the other to direct his returning glaive weapons. This twin-stick arrangement makes combat unusually flexible, allowing players to run in one direction while attacking in another. The changing scenarios and unconventional weapon controls make Krull an ambitious licensed arcade game, even though its structure differs substantially from the film's sequence of events.

games.title: Krazy Bowl
games.description:
Krazy Bowl is American Sammy's 1994 ten-pin bowling game, playable with a trackball or joystick and suitable for turn-taking multiplayer competition. Regulation mode follows ordinary bowling, challenging players to accumulate strikes and spares over a standard game. The alternative Sweeper mode changes the arrangement and number of pins from frame to frame, rewarding precise placement and unusual spare conversions.

The physical rolling input and short, easy-to-understand turns suit a coin-operated bowling cabinet, while the nonstandard pin layouts give experienced players a second challenge beyond straightforward score chasing.

games.title: Kusayakyuu
games.description: Kusayakyuu, released by Taito in 1985, is a Japanese baseball arcade game whose title means roughly Sandlot Baseball. Its focus is informal ballplaying rather than the prestige of a professional league, with joystick-and-button controls used to take part in baseball competition. It is an obscure sports release from the period when Japanese manufacturers were rapidly experimenting with coin-operated interpretations of local sporting pastimes. The available historical descriptions do not establish a distinctive scoring system or unusual rule changes.

games.title: Kung-Fu Master
games.description:
Kung-Fu Master, developed by Irem and released internationally in 1984, is one of the foundational side-scrolling beat-'em-ups.
