In Japan it appeared as Spartan X, linking it to the Jackie Chan film Wheels on Meals, though the arcade game's rescue mission has its own structure. Players control Thomas, who fights through five floors of a hostile temple to rescue Sylvia from the villain Mr. X. Endless waves of grabbing thugs, knife throwers, small attackers and supernatural hazards stand between Thomas and a boss guarding each stairway.

The controls are simple but expressive: a four-way joystick handles walking, jumping and crouching, while separate punch and kick buttons offer different attack ranges. Punches are powerful but short-reaching, whereas kicks provide more space against crowds. Each floor advances toward its boss under time pressure, and clearing the final floor restarts the challenge at higher difficulty.

Designed under Takashi Nishiyama's direction, Kung-Fu Master became a major model for the action genre, influencing the later development of scrolling brawlers and martial-arts platform games. Its frantic combination of crowd control, stage bosses and rescue-story progression remains instantly recognizable.

games.title: Kung-Fu Taikun
games.description: Kung-Fu Taikun is an unusual 1984 Seibu Kaihatsu arcade game mixing platform movement with puzzle-like action and martial-arts imagery. Its horizontal playfield is controlled with a two-way joystick and action inputs, and the original cabinet notably supported a microphone, an uncommon feature for an early-1980s video game. Its combination of platform fighting and puzzle matching makes it distinct from the more familiar side-scrolling Kung-Fu Master, despite their similar names.

games.title: Kuri Kinton
games.description:
Kuri Kinton is a 1988 Taito side-scrolling martial-arts action game starring a special police agent who infiltrates a terrorist base to rescue a kidnapped family. The hero runs, jumps, punches and kicks through underground passages and fortified areas, following directional indicators while confronting waves of soldiers and martial artists. Stage bosses have visible health meters, and later fights demand increasingly careful positioning and attack timing.

The combat includes flying kicks and other techniques beyond basic strikes, mixing conventional beat-'em-up action with hazards and the occasional non-linear passage. Its exaggerated martial-arts presentation and bizarre opponents make it an appealing obscurity among Taito's late-1980s arcade releases.

games.title: Kurukuru Fever
games.description:
Kurukuru Fever is a 2003 Japanese falling-block puzzle game released for Seta's Nintendo 64-derived Aleck64 arcade system. Pairs of fruit blocks drop into a playfield, where groups of four matching fruits disappear in familiar chain-reaction fashion. Each animal character favors a particular fruit, however, and clearing that type triggers an unusual reversal: the entire board flips over and the match requirements become progressively smaller.

This gravity-changing mechanic turns ordinary stacking plans upside down, rewarding players who can anticipate how blocks will settle after a flip. Its unusual hardware and inventive variation on the Puyo Puyo formula make Kurukuru Fever a noteworthy late arcade puzzle game.

games.title: Kuzmich-Egorych
games.description: Kuzmich-Egorych is an obscure Russian unauthorized adaptation of Nintendo's Mario Bros., credited to Nippel and reportedly running on heavily modified Apple II-derived hardware. Like its inspiration, it belongs to the single-screen platform-action tradition in which characters move between elevated platforms while dealing with enemies. The game's principal historical interest is the improbable hardware conversion and its place among regionally produced arcade bootlegs. Its precise release date and the extent of any gameplay alterations remain undocumented.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Kyros
games.description:
Kyros, originally released in Japan as Kyros no Yakata, is a 1986-1987 vertically scrolling action brawler published by Alpha Denshi. A young hero named Mac enters Kyros's monster-filled mansion to rescue children trapped inside mirrors. Players fight enemies with bare hands and collectible weapons while exploring branching routes through the building, sometimes choosing different passages before reaching a stage boss.

Breaking mirrors frees prisoners, and various power-ups can attack enemies or alter the route. The setting combines haunted-house imagery with hand-to-hand combat, making Kyros an unconventional mixture of supernatural adventure and overhead beat-'em-up action.

games.title: Kyuukai Douchuuki
games.description:
Kyuukai Douchuuki is a 1990 Namco baseball game for System 2 hardware, and an unexpected spin-off of the company's fantasy action game Yokai Douchuuki. It borrows the broadly accessible style of Namco's World Stadium baseball titles but expands the selection into an international and fantastical collection of teams. Players can face conventional Japanese clubs alongside fanciful leagues and teams inspired by different countries and creatures.

Its cartoon-styled baseball action follows the essential pitching, batting and fielding cycle, while the huge selection of teams and cameos from Yokai Douchuuki give it a personality unlike an ordinary licensed sports simulation. The game is remembered as a playful fusion of Namco's sports and character-game traditions.

games.title: Last Striker / Kyuukyoku no Striker
games.description: Last Striker, known in Japan as Kyuukyoku no Striker, is a 1989 arcade soccer game with a manga-inspired cartoon presentation. Players control their footballers with a joystick and action buttons, competing in stylized matches rather than attempting a realistic simulation. Its expressive visual style is its clearest documented distinction from the more conventional soccer titles of the period; surviving sources offer little reliable information about specialized techniques or tournament modes.

games.title: Lady Bug
games.description:
Lady Bug is Universal's influential 1981 maze-chase game, released during the arcade craze following Pac-Man. Players guide a colorful ladybird through a maze, collecting flowers, hearts and letters while avoiding enemy insects. The central novelty is a set of rotating doors that change position when the player passes through them. Enemies cannot manipulate these doors, so a skilled player can steer pursuers into dead ends, create temporary escape corridors and deliberately reshape the chase.

The maze border also acts as a timer that triggers the appearance of additional enemies. Collectible letters spell EXTRA for an extra life or SPECIAL for a further bonus, adding risk to the search for valuable items. Although often compared with Pac-Man, Lady Bug's moving walls create a much more tactical style of maze navigation and helped it develop a lasting reputation among early arcade enthusiasts.

games.title: Lady Frog
games.description: Lady Frog is a 1990 arcade variation on Frogger created by Mondial Games. Players guide a frog through hazardous crossings, first avoiding vehicles on the way across a road and river, then tackling less conventional environments such as the floors of a building. Wasps, moving balls and other obstacles broaden the familiar pattern of carefully timed hops. Between stages, a short shooting-gallery bonus challenges players to hit flying hearts. The changing settings and bonus rounds distinguish it from a straightforward imitation of Konami's classic.

games.title: Lady Killer
games.description:
Lady Killer, originally released as Moeyo Gonta!!, is a 1993 adult-themed action puzzle game built around uncovering a hidden illustration. The player controls a diver in a pool-like playfield, moving and surfacing through covered sections to reveal portions of the background while avoiding hazards and hostile water skiers. Previously cleared spaces restrict subsequent movement, so choosing when and where to surface becomes a spatial puzzle rather than a simple tracing exercise.

The game later received a closely related sequel, Party Time: Gonta the Diver II. Its aquatic reveal mechanic makes it an unusual alternative to the Qix-inspired outline puzzles common in adult-oriented arcades.

games.title: Lady Master of Kung Fu

variants.title: Lady Master of Kung Fu (set 1, newer)
Lady Master of Kung Fu (set 2, older)

games.description: Lady Master of Kung Fu is a 1985 arcade action game starring a female martial artist armed with punches, kicks and nunchaku. Rather than following a single horizontal road, the heroine moves through a multi-floor building, using elevators to reach new areas and entering rooms to fight powerful opponents for rewards. The mixture of platform movement, room exploration and close-range combat makes it an early and unusual female-led martial-arts game.

games.title: Laguna Racer
games.description: Laguna Racer is a 1977 black-and-white driving game from Midway, representing the era before sprite-filled color racing cabinets became standard. Players steer a car down a winding roadway, accelerating with a pedal and selecting high or low gear while trying to travel as far as possible before time expires. Distance serves as the score, and meeting a specified threshold can extend the driving time. The steering wheel, accelerator and gear lever give this early microprocessor-based racer a physical feel distinct from later joystick-controlled driving games.

games.title: Land Breaker (World) / Miss Tang Ja Ru Gi

variants.title: Land Breaker (World) / Miss Tang Ja Ru Gi (Korea) (pcb ver 3.02)
Land Breaker (World) / Miss Tang Ja Ru Gi (Korea) (pcb ver 3.03) (AT89c52 protected)

games.description:
Land Breaker, also known by the Korean title Miss Tang Jjareugi, is a late-1990s territory-clearing arcade puzzle game with adult-oriented backgrounds. It resembles Qix and Gals Panic in its goal of revealing concealed images, but replaces the usual border-following character with a device that can move freely inside the active playfield. One button rotates the device between horizontal and vertical orientations, while another fires a laser line outward in both directions.

A successful cut divides the field, revealing any section that contains no enemy balls. Sections still containing hazards remain dangerous, so players can use repeated cuts to isolate and corral enemies before clearing them. The combination of freely positioned laser cuts and moving hazards gives the familiar picture-reveal formula an unexpectedly tactical structure.

games.title: Landing Gear
games.description:
Landing Gear is Taito's mid-1990s aircraft-landing simulator, following the tradition of the company's earlier Top Landing. The cockpit-style controls let players bank and pitch an aircraft while adjusting engine power, with instrumentation and a textured 3D landscape providing the illusion of real flight. Success depends on approaching the runway at a manageable speed and angle, then touching down safely rather than simply reaching a finish line.

Beginner and Expert classes offer different challenges, and progression brings access to larger or more demanding aircraft. Its emphasis on procedures, approach alignment and smooth landings makes it a distinctive arcade experience alongside the period's more action-oriented flight games.

games.title: Land Maker
games.description:
Land Maker is Taito's 1998 competitive puzzle game, created for the F3 system. Viewed from an isometric angle, its colorful blocks are fired into the field to connect matching colors and construct building-like formations. Larger combinations send stronger attacks to the rival's board, increasing the pressure as the blocks creep toward a losing position. Several playable characters and themed effects make the competition look closer to a whimsical strategy battle than a conventional tile puzzle.

Although its presentation recalls Puzzle Bobble, Land Maker relies on planning connections and timing chains rather than popping hanging bubble clusters. Its unusual architectural theme and versus-only arcade format give it a distinct identity among the late-1990s puzzle games.

games.title: Laser Battle
games.description: Laser Battle is a 1981 space-action game released in Europe by Zaccaria and distributed in the United States as Lazarian by Bally Midway. Players control a spaceship across a series of hostile missions, rescuing stranded craft while firing at meteorites, aliens, flying eyes and defensive emplacements. The need to protect or recover other vessels adds an objective beyond simply surviving waves of projectiles. The alternate Lazarian title reflects regional distribution of the same unusual multi-stage shooter.

games.title: Lasso
games.description: Lasso is a 1982 SNK arcade action game built around a cowboy's rope rather than a conventional gun. The rancher must round up wandering livestock with his lasso while keeping dangerous animals at bay. Stages involve catching sheep and cattle and fending off attacking wolves and other hazards, with an introductory practice area teaching players the rope's timing. This mixture of herding and defensive action gives Lasso a playful rural theme rarely encountered in early arcade games.

games.title: Last Blade / Bakumatsu Roman - Gekka no Kenshi, The

variants.title: Last Blade / Bakumatsu Roman - Gekka no Kenshi, The (set 1)
Last Blade / Bakumatsu Roman - Gekka no Kenshi, The (set 2)
The Last Soldier (Korean release of The Last Blade)

games.description:
The Last Blade is SNK's 1997 Neo Geo weapons-based fighting game set during Japan's turbulent Bakumatsu era. Combining supernatural fantasy with late-Edo-period atmosphere, it introduces swordsmen and other warriors whose disputes revolve around the boundary between life and death. Painterly stages, detailed character animation and a haunting soundtrack give the game a more restrained, elegiac identity than the company's Samurai Shodown series.

Its signature mechanic is the choice between Power and Speed styles. Power favors strong blows and devastating techniques, while Speed enables rapid chains of attacks, allowing the same character to be approached in two different ways. Precise deflections also reward players who read an opponent's timing. The resulting blend of cinematic presentation and exacting swordplay made The Last Blade a cult favorite among 2D fighting enthusiasts.

games.title: Last Blade 2 / Bakumatsu Roman - Dai Ni Maku Gekka no Kenshi, The
games.description:
The Last Blade 2 is SNK's 1998 sequel to its atmospheric Bakumatsu-era weapons fighter, and one of the Neo Geo's most visually admired titles. The conflict over the boundary between the living and spirit worlds continues, bringing back familiar swordsmen while adding new characters and expanding the roster. Its detailed backgrounds, melancholy music and elaborate character animations create a distinctive historical-fantasy mood.

The original game's Power and Speed combat styles return, alongside a new EX style that combines characteristics of both. Players again rely on carefully timed strikes, counters and deflections, with separate styles offering different combo routes and offensive priorities. The richer mechanics and somber presentation helped establish The Last Blade 2 as an enduring competitive and artistic highlight of SNK's late-1990s arcade output.

games.title: The Last Day
games.description:
The Last Day is a 1990 vertically scrolling shoot-'em-up from South Korean developer Dooyong. Piloting a small aircraft, the player crosses changing landscapes, including forests, waterways, cities and recognizable landmarks, while attacking enemy planes, tanks, artillery and boats. A powered-up main gun and limited screen-clearing bombs provide the means to survive increasingly crowded assaults.

Its conventional aerial-shooter design is a useful example of Dooyong's move from producing unauthorized arcade games to developing original titles. The game also circulated under the Korean title Chulgyeok D-Day, and relatively few boards reached Japan.

games.title: Last Duel
games.description:
Capcom's Last Duel: Inter Planet War 2012 (1988) is an unusual vertically scrolling shooter built around two distinct types of stage. The player fights an invasion of the planet Mu by the Galden forces, alternating between a ground vehicle on dangerous roads and a spacecraft battling enemies in the air. The rescue of the abducted Queen Sheeta provides the science-fiction premise.

The car can leap over holes, obstacles and enemies, while the spacecraft performs a temporary invulnerability roll. Weapons include lasers, twin shots, wider spreads and side-firing options, with speed upgrades reserved for the flight sections. Road stages impose a time limit until the boss is reached, adding urgency absent from the airborne missions. The alternating driving and shooting mechanics distinguish Last Duel from Capcom's more conventional 1980s scrolling shooters; it later received several home-computer conversions.

games.title: Last Fighting
games.description: Last Fighting (2000) is a maze-based action game by Taiwanese developer Subsino, modeled on the arena-bombing formula of Bomberman rather than on one-on-one fighting games. Characters navigate enclosed playfields and fight around the maze's obstacles. The game is also notable to arcade preservationists for its unusual Hitachi H8-based hardware, blitter graphics and serial protection device. Its emulation history includes problems with excessively fast movement and timers, so the behavior of some emulated versions may differ from the original board.

games.title: Last Fortress - Toride
games.description:
Metro's Last Fortress - Toride (1994) is an arcade mahjong-solitaire puzzle game. Rather than playing a conventional four-person mahjong match, the player works through layouts of matching tiles, clearing them from the playfield using a joystick and a single selection button. The Japanese subtitle Toride means "fortress," fitting the game's tile-clearing premise.

The game circulated in multiple regional versions. Alongside the ordinary Japanese release, an adult-themed Chinese edition reveals erotic pictures as boards are cleared; a German-language edition also exists. Those variants should not be confused with entirely different mahjong games, since the central challenge remains a tile-matching solitaire puzzle.

games.title: Last Hope

variants.title: Last Hope (bootleg AES to MVS conversion, no coin support)
variants.version: (bootleg AES to MVS conversion, no coin support)

games.description:
Last Hope is a horizontally scrolling science-fiction shooter by German independent studio NG:DEV.TEAM, originally released for the Neo Geo AES in 2006 and subsequently issued on Neo Geo CD and Dreamcast. Piloting the Z-42 Warpstar, the player ventures into enemy territory to stop a hostile fleet from reaching Earth. Its deliberate pace and demanding bullet patterns appeal to fans of classic tactical shooters.

A distinctive scoring system rewards two related skills: absorbing enemy bullets to increase one multiplier and destroying consecutive targets with a charged beam to build another. This AdvanceMAME set is specifically an unofficial conversion of the AES cartridge to Neo Geo MVS format, without conventional coin support; it should not be mistaken for a standard coin-operated release. A later revision, Last Hope: Pink Bullets, revised aspects of the game's difficulty and balance.

games.title: Last KM
games.description:
Last KM is a surviving prototype of an unconventional 1995 cycling arcade game, developed by Zeus Software for Spain's Gaelco. Its original installation used two interconnected exercise bicycles: players pedaled physically to race each other toward the finish, making the hardware part of the athletic challenge. The game ran on a modified version of Gaelco's Biomechanical Toy board, with scenery derived partly from photographed locations around San Sebastián.

Although tested in an arcade location in Barcelona, Last KM was never commercially released. Programmer Ricardo Puerto eventually helped Spanish preservation group RetroAcción recover the working prototype. The surviving software even contains a rendition of Giorgio Moroder's "Chase" as temporary, unlicensed music, an intriguing trace of the game's unfinished commercial status.

games.title: Last Mission
games.description:
Data East's Last Mission (1986) is a multidirectional overhead space shooter in which an exiled pilot is sent against an alien enemy in a desperate effort to restore his honor. Unlike a conventional vertically scrolling shooter, the craft can travel around the battlefield and change its facing direction, giving the action a more free-ranging feel reminiscent of Time Pilot.

The pilot must maneuver through enemies, collect weapon-strengthening items and make calculated use of limited smart bombs. Its combination of eight-directional movement, directional firing and a hostile science-fiction setting gives Last Mission a distinct identity within Data East's mid-1980s arcade catalog. Japanese and American revisions are preserved, and its original protection microcontroller became an important part of later emulation research.

games.title: The Last Starfighter
games.description:
Atari's The Last Starfighter is a remarkable unfinished 1984 arcade prototype based on the science-fiction film in which a gifted arcade player becomes an interstellar defender. Rather than directly flying a spacecraft, the player operates the weapons and swiveling gunner's station of the Gunstar. Battles require careful aiming, managing laser energy and monitoring a hull-temperature gauge: sustained enemy hits consume a limited coolant supply, and running out can destroy the ship.

Two side lasers can be fired independently or together, while the special Death Blossom attack unleashes a devastating burst across the screen. The prototype used solid, filled 3D polygon graphics, a Motorola 68000 processor and a mathematical coprocessor, at a time when most arcade 3D games relied on wireframe vectors. A controller derived from Atari's Star Wars cabinet was used during development.

The project was canceled before public release, reportedly when it was roughly three-quarters complete. Its high projected cabinet cost and Atari's financial pressures contributed to the decision. As a preserved prototype it offers a fascinating glimpse of an ambitious 3D arcade game that never reached commercial arcades.

games.title: Last Survivor
games.description:
Sega's Last Survivor (1989) is a rare early example of first-person maze combat, released in Japan on the powerful Sega X Board. Players move through corridors, turn their view using rotary controls and fight monsters and other armed opponents. Each participant begins with a key but needs four to escape; defeating rivals and collecting their keys turns the maze into a race to reach the exit.

Money earned from defeating enemies can be spent at in-maze shops on weapons, speed and protective equipment. Map terminals reveal the level layout and the locations of opponents, adding an element of hunting and evasion. The split viewpoints and simulated 3D corridors were unusually ambitious for their time.

For many years the game was extraordinarily difficult to preserve. A working PCB finally surfaced in 2012, allowing its protected FD1094 processor and program to be documented before battery-backed encryption data could be lost. That rescue is a major part of the title's modern reputation among Sega collectors.

games.title: Lazer Command
games.description:
Lazer Command (1976), by Meadows Games, is an early two-player tactical tank battle played across a symmetrical overhead maze. Each side starts with 15 tanks, but only one can be directly controlled at a time. Players drive through the corridors, fire on opposing tanks and attempt to destroy the enemy's entire force before the timer expires.

Losing a tank does not immediately end a turn: the player moves a small selection marker to another surviving vehicle, and may abandon a tank voluntarily to switch positions. This simple rule creates a surprisingly strategic contest of positioning, attrition and baiting opponents. The original cabinet featured a monochrome monitor with green and yellow color overlays and distinctive handle-style controls. It is effectively a head-to-head game rather than a single-player tank shooter.

games.title: Libero Grande
games.description:
Namco's Libero Grande (1997) takes an unusually personal approach to arcade soccer. Instead of switching control automatically to whichever teammate is near the ball, the player selects a star footballer and controls that one athlete throughout the match. Movement off the ball, finding space and coordinating with computer-controlled teammates therefore become as important as passing and shooting.

Players choose national teams and star characters modeled on real international footballers, with altered names such as Zenon Zadkine for Zinedine Zidane. The System 12 hardware provides polygonal stadiums, while two-player competition can use a divided view. Released on PlayStation in 1998, Libero Grande anticipated the dedicated single-player career modes that would later become familiar in major football franchises.

games.title: League Bowling
games.description:
League Bowling (1990) brings colorful ten-pin bowling to SNK's Neo Geo hardware, remaining the platform's only dedicated bowling title. Players choose a right- or left-handed bowler, select a ball weight and then adjust placement, spin, direction and power. Successful shots depend on timing the on-screen gauges rather than simply pressing a button at maximum force.

Three scoring systems give it variety: Regulation follows ordinary ten-pin rules, Strike 90 rewards strikes with extra points, and Flash introduces changing bonus values. Up to four people can take part, with two bowlers appearing simultaneously on a divided screen. Cartoon reactions and lively presentation make it a particularly accessible early Neo Geo sports game.

games.title: Lode Runner
games.description:
Irem's 1984 arcade adaptation of Lode Runner brings Doug Smith's influential 1983 computer puzzle-platform game to coin-operated machines. As a treasure hunter infiltrating the Bungeling Empire, the player gathers every piece of gold on a screen of platforms, ladders and ropes while evading patrolling guards. The signature mechanic is digging temporary holes in the floor, trapping pursuers or creating routes through otherwise inaccessible passages.

Unlike the original computer release, famous for its 150 puzzles and built-in editor, Irem's arcade edition uses a selected and adapted set of stages suited to arcade play. Its two digging buttons, one for each side, make rapid decisions essential. The conversion was successful enough to inspire three further Irem arcade installments, each reorganizing the puzzles and eventually introducing cooperative play.

games.title: Lode Runner II - The Bungeling Strikes Back
games.description:
Lode Runner II: The Bungeling Strikes Back (1984) is Irem's second arcade version of the pioneering puzzle-platform game. The player still collects all the gold in each fixed-screen maze, climbs ladders and ropes, and digs temporary traps to outwit guards. Successful play depends on planning escape routes and exploiting the enemies' pursuit behavior rather than overpowering them.

This installment supplies a new selection of 30 stages, including some drawn from the original computer game, and makes cosmetic changes to the guards. Its appeal lies in the substantially different puzzle layouts, which challenge players already comfortable with the first arcade Lode Runner.

games.title: Lode Runner III - The Golden Labyrinth

variants.title: Lode Runner III - The Golden Labyrinth
Lode Runner III - Majin No Fukkatsu

games.description:
Lode Runner III: The Golden Labyrinth (1985) continues Irem's arcade adaptation of Doug Smith's puzzle-platform formula. A lone runner must collect the gold in each room, avoid the guards and escape using ladders, ropes and temporary holes dug through the floor.

Like the second arcade installment, it offers a selection of 30 stages rather than the full computer game's original level set. The revised maze arrangements are the chief attraction: mastering the guards' movement and digging at the right moment matters far more than quick reflexes alone. It was also released in Japan under the title Majin no Fukkatsu.

games.title: Lode Runner IV - Teikoku Karano Dasshutsu
games.description:
Lode Runner IV: Teikoku Karano Dasshutsu (1986) is the fourth and final Irem arcade installment of the classic gold-collecting puzzle-platform series. The familiar challenge remains: navigate platforms and ladders, dodge guards, and dig temporary holes to trap enemies or open a path to every gold piece.

Its major addition is a genuine two-player cooperative mode, featuring 18 stages designed for partners to solve together. Coordinated movement and digging make it meaningfully different from the preceding arcade releases, which chiefly distinguished themselves through their stage selections. The regular single-player puzzle course is also present.

games.title: Lethal Enforcers II: Gun Fighters

variants.title: Lethal Enforcers II: Gun Fighters (ver EAA)
Lethal Enforcers II: Gun Fighters (ver JAA)
Lethal Enforcers II: Gun Fighters (ver UAA)

games.description:
Konami's Lethal Enforcers II: Gun Fighters (1994) takes the digitized-photography light-gun formula of its predecessor into an American Western setting. As a sheriff in 1873, the player shoots bandits through five scenarios, including a bank robbery, saloon confrontation, train holdup and criminal hideout. The game is effectively a prequel to the modern police action of the first Lethal Enforcers.

Precise shooting is vital because innocent civilians and fellow lawmen frequently appear amid the outlaws. Weapons can be improved during the campaign, but shooting the wrong target damages the player's standing and can result in demotion. Two-player light-gun action, theatrical Western settings and photographic actors give this sequel an identity distinct from the urban crime scenes of the original.

games.title: Led Storm Rally 2011
games.description:
Led Storm Rally 2011 is the earlier, futuristic version of Capcom's arcade road-racing game that eventually became Mad Gear and LED Storm. This 1988 design uses an overhead, vertically scrolling view as the player races along hazardous elevated highways, avoids rival vehicles and leaps obstacles. Its signature feature is the Storm 11 vehicle, which can transform between a car and a motorcycle rather than selecting from the three vehicles of the later commercial revision.

The different vehicle system, science-fiction presentation and course design make this more than a mere regional title change. Long regarded as an unreleased developmental version, Rally 2011 was subsequently preserved and became accessible through arcade collections, offering a glimpse of Capcom's ideas before the 1989 redesign.

games.title: Legend
games.description:
Legend (1986) is a rare side-scrolling action game by Coreland/Kyugo in which a young armored commander battles invaders threatening a kingdom. Combat combines direct attacks and evasive jumping with the ability to recruit soldiers, using money to win enemies over to the player's side. Weapons and equipment collected along the way expand the options available during the march across enemy territory.

Its emphasis on assembling a fighting force rather than simply punching through opponents is an unusual twist on the early beat-'em-up formula. Developed in Japan with Sega involvement, the game saw limited arcade distribution and should not be confused with the unrelated Super Nintendo beat-'em-up of the same name.

games.title: Legend of Success Joe / Ashitano Joe Densetsu
games.description:
Legend of Success Joe, known in Japan as Ashita no Joe Densetsu (1991), is a Neo Geo boxing and beat-'em-up game based on the influential Ashita no Joe manga and anime. Players follow streetwise boxer Joe Yabuki from a rough childhood toward the professional ring, moving between alleyway fights, training-related action and formal boxing matches.

Rather than presenting a conventional tournament of selectable fighters, it uses its licensed story to tie together different forms of combat. The game was developed by Wave Corporation for the Neo Geo, making it an early example of a third-party production for SNK's platform. Its distinctly mixed action format is as memorable as its connection to a celebrated Japanese sporting drama.

games.title: Legend
games.description:
This 1996 Legend is an unauthorized coin-operated conversion of the Super Nintendo beat-'em-up, not a revision of the unrelated 1986 Sega/Coreland arcade game. It brings the console game's fantasy-themed, side-scrolling combat to an arcade PCB, with players fighting through groups of armed enemies and bosses using close-range attacks and jumping maneuvers.

The main historical interest is the conversion itself: a home-console game repackaged for coin-operated use without an official arcade release. Its distinctive origin and hardware adaptation explain why it appears separately in AdvanceMAME's listings.

games.title: Legion - Spinner-87
games.description:
Legion - Spinner-87 is a 1987 vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter from Nichibutsu, originally issued in Japan as Choutoki Meikyuu Legion. Piloting a combat craft against the Dark Empire, the player fires at airborne and ground enemies while rescuing or collecting soldiers and engineers. These allies can improve weapons, provide bombs and temporarily accompany the ship in combat.

Certain points allow a choice between shorter and longer routes, adding variety to the journey toward the enemy's capital ship. The emphasis on recruiting support personnel gives Legion a distinctive progression system within the crowded late-1980s shooter field. The preserved world release is identified as Spinner-87.

games.title: Legionnaire
games.description:
Legionnaire (1992) is a side-scrolling street-fighting game from TAD Corporation and Seibu Kaihatsu. Three vigilantes, Frank, Chris and Alfred, battle a criminal syndicate that has kidnapped Judy, fighting through urban stages using punches, jumps and combinations of close-range attacks. Each character has a different visual style, and the game supports cooperative action.

Its straightforward rescue story is told through the gritty, early-1990s arcade beat-'em-up format, with groups of enemies and tougher encounters punctuating the route through the city. Released in Japan as Saishu Kakutou Kizoku Legionnaire, it is a cult alternative to more famous team brawlers of the same period.

games.title: LeMans 24
games.description:
Sega's LeMans 24 (1997) is a polygonal endurance-racing arcade game inspired by the famous French 24 Hours of Le Mans. Cars from major manufacturers compete over circuits associated with the event, with the action compressing a prolonged contest into an accessible arcade driving experience. Day-to-night lighting changes evoke the real race's exhausting passage of time.

Running on Sega Model 3 hardware, the game combines fast 3D graphics with licensed-style sports-car competition and an emphasis on managing speed through demanding corners. Its endurance-race identity made it a distinctive alternative to Sega's better-known Daytona and rally arcade series.

games.title: Lemmings
games.description:
This unreleased arcade prototype adapts Psygnosis's celebrated Lemmings, the 1991 puzzle game in which a stream of tiny creatures walks toward danger unless the player assigns them useful tasks. Builders construct bridges, diggers and miners remove obstacles, blockers redirect the crowd and floaters descend safely. The goal is to guide enough lemmings to the exit before the level's population is lost.

The Data East arcade adaptation translates the computer game's point-and-click strategy to coin-op controls, and surviving accounts describe an unusual two-player mode and a speed-up function that later influenced Lemmings 2. Its prototype status is important: although the game is fully recognizable, it was never a standard commercial arcade release.

games.title: Mahjong Lemon Angel
games.description:
Mahjong Lemon Angel (1990) is a Japanese adult-oriented mahjong game based on the late-night anime series Lemon Angel. The player participates in a school-romance scenario and chooses among three familiar characters, Tomo, Erika and Miki, as opponents. Winning mahjong hands advances the encounters and unlocks illustrated reward sequences.

The arcade version uses betting points and awards lemons for victories; these can be spent on helpful items. Its mixture of conventional mahjong competition, anime licensing and unlockable imagery places it firmly within the Japanese adult mahjong arcade tradition rather than among general-purpose action or puzzle titles.

games.title: Leprechaun
games.description:
Leprechaun (1982) is a simple forest maze chase designed for younger players. A small explorer runs across the screen to collect a leprechaun's pot of gold, which appears in different positions, while the mischievous owner pursues him. Reaching the pot starts the next stage; being caught costs a life.

Licensed from Tong Electronic, the game appeared in Enter-Tech's child-oriented Moppet Video cabinet line, with a smaller, approachable arcade presentation. A standard-cabinet version also circulated under the name Pot of Gold. Its unusually gentle difficulty reflects the intended audience.

games.title: Lethal Enforcers
games.description:
Lethal Enforcers (1992) is Konami's influential light-gun crime shooter, notable for using digitized photographs of actors and locations rather than traditional cartoon sprites. Playing a law-enforcement officer pursuing organized criminals, one or two players move through shooting-gallery scenarios involving bank robberies, hostage crises and other urban emergencies. The action advances automatically while players aim and fire at armed suspects.

The standard revolver can be replaced with stronger weapons, but civilians and fellow officers must be spared. Shooting innocent targets results in penalties, while carefully timed reloads and accurate fire are crucial to survival. Its intense photographic look helped make the game a prominent arcade attraction and contributed to debate about realistic violence in video games.

Lethal Enforcers was widely converted to home systems, often bundled with Konami's distinctive Justifier light gun. Its commercial impact led directly to the Western-themed prequel Lethal Enforcers II.

games.title: Lethal Justice
games.description:
Lethal Justice is a 1996 light-gun shooting game produced by The Game Room in the United States. Players aim at on-screen targets in a succession of gun-game scenes, using a straightforward point-and-shoot interface. The cabinet supports two players, and the preserved Version 2.3 software runs on Texas Instruments TMS34010-based video hardware.

Much less widely documented than Konami's Lethal Enforcers, it survives as an unusual American entry in the mid-1990s arcade gun-game market. The game even includes a background tribute to Landerland Coin-op Laundry.

games.title: Lethal Thunder
games.description:
Irem's Lethal Thunder (1991), released in Japan as Thunder Blaster, is a vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter with an unusual emphasis on rapid button presses. Rather than simply holding the firing button, players can mash it to increase their weapon's output, making the intensity of their attacks part of the control challenge.

The ship battles swarms of airborne enemies and large bosses, collecting alternate weapons along the way. Two-player cooperative play adds to the frantic feel. This distinctive firing mechanic is what most clearly separates Lethal Thunder from more conventional shooters of the period.

games.title: Levers
games.description:
Levers (1983) is a single-screen platform game from Rock-Ola, running on modified Galaxian-derived hardware. The player guides a small red-clad character across a collection of seesaw-like platforms, trying to gather all 18 flowers scattered around the stage. Falling off the bottom of the screen or colliding with a large rolling marble costs a life.

Its teetering platforms and distinctive flower-collecting objective make it an unusual experiment in early-1980s arcade platform design. It was also the last video game released by the Rock-Ola Manufacturing Corporation.

games.title: Laser Ghost
games.description:
Sega's Laser Ghost (1990) is a horror-themed shooting gallery inspired by the ghost-hunting films of the era. Up to three players take the roles of Bill, Max and Carol, using the cabinet's mounted guns to fight supernatural creatures and rescue a young girl abducted by a demon. The camera moves through haunted settings as ghosts, monsters and other threats appear from all directions.

Each gun offers ordinary shots and limited-use special attacks, requiring players to decide when a large concentration of enemies justifies using their strongest weapons. The dedicated three-gun cabinet and eerie theme make Laser Ghost an appealing departure from the military shooting games that dominated many arcades.

games.title: Lightning Fighters
games.description:
Lightning Fighters (1990), known in Japan as Trigon, is Konami's vertically scrolling shooter featuring powerful weapons and spectacular oversized enemy machines. Pilots battle through ten stages against aircraft, ground defenses and bosses, collecting upgrades that change their firepower into a broad laser or a fiery, serpent-shaped attack.

Its cooperative system is more than a second ship on screen: two players can use a special combined weapon, and the rules for bombs and respawning differ between solo and cooperative play. This makes the Japanese Trigon and the international Lightning Fighters particularly interesting to compare, and rewards players who master both the unconventional weapons and the stage patterns.

games.title: Long Hu Bang
games.description:
Long Hu Bang is a 1995 Chinese-language mahjong medal game from Taiwan's International Games System (IGS). Rather than a tile-matching solitaire puzzle, it is a video adaptation of competitive mahjong, built around completing hands and the betting and payout settings typical of Asian medal machines. It runs on IGS's Motorola 68000-based arcade hardware with a wide horizontal display.

The game is particularly notable for its regional editions. The Hong Kong release is known as Daai Baan Sing, while the Japanese version is titled Mahjong Ryukobou. Their shared underlying game and the protection circuitry of IGS's hardware made this family an interesting preservation and emulation project.

games.title: Liberation
games.description:
Liberation (1984), also released as Dual Assault, is a Data East overhead action game combining aerial combat with ground-level rescue missions. The player first flies a helicopter over an enemy-held landscape, attacking targets and searching for villages. After landing, the action changes to a ground vehicle such as a tank, which must fight through the settlement and free prisoners.

Its movement is less rigid than the automatic scrolling of many contemporary shooters, encouraging exploration as well as continuous fire. The alternating helicopter and land missions help distinguish this relatively obscure Data East game from straightforward military shoot-'em-ups.

games.title: Liberator
games.description:
Atari's Liberator (1982) turns the familiar Missile Command premise inside out. Instead of defending cities against incoming missiles, players command four spacecraft positioned at the corners of the screen and attack enemy installations on a rotating planet. A trackball moves the targeting cursor, and the nearest surviving spacecraft fires toward it when the player presses the shot button.

Threats include ships encountered during hyperspace sequences and hostile forces capable of destroying the player's corner vessels. A separate shield button offers limited protection, making each lost spacecraft a serious tactical setback. The rotating planet and awkward angles demand careful choice of firing positions.

Based on the Atari Force comic-book property, Liberator was also an unusually limited commercial production, with only around 762 machines manufactured. Its distinctive premise and control scheme have helped it become a collector's curiosity.

games.title: Libble Rabble
games.description:
Namco's Libble Rabble (1983) is an inventive action-puzzle game designed by Pac-Man creator Toru Iwatani. The player controls two arrow-shaped characters, the red Libble and blue Rabble, independently with a pair of joysticks. A line stretched between them catches on pegs, allowing players to draw closed loops around small Mushlin creatures, enemies and hidden treasures.

The central challenge is using two hands at once to shape loops quickly under a time limit. Small, deliberate captures can be worth more than indiscriminate sweeps, and the board's arrangement of pegs becomes a tool for planning paths. Although often compared to Qix, Libble Rabble's dual controls and rope-wrapping mechanic feel very different.

It was among Namco's earliest games built around a Motorola 68000 processor and remains one of its most distinctive early-1980s experiments.

games.title: Linky Pipe
games.description:
Linky Pipe is a competitive falling-piece puzzle game developed by South Korea's Eolith and released in late 1997, although some arcade databases list it under 1998. Pairs of pipe sections descend into a well, and players must rotate and position them to connect pipe ends into working runs. Successful connections build combinations and fill the opponent's water meter; the aim is to fill the rival meter before your own overflows.

Its unusual three-button scheme distinguishes it from more familiar block puzzlers. One button rotates the entire falling pair, while the other two rotate the individual halves independently. A special cursor-like piece occasionally lets players remove an unwanted pipe segment from a selected column. The intricate controls and pipe management create a notably demanding variation on the head-to-head falling-block formula, running on Eolith's Hyperstone-based arcade hardware.

games.title: Liquid Kids
games.description:
Liquid Kids, released in Japan as Mizubaku Daibouken (1990), is one of Taito's most charming scrolling platform games. The hero Hipopo is a small hippo-like creature who journeys through Woody Lake to rescue his girlfriend Tamasun and other inhabitants from the Fire Demon. Instead of conventional bullets, Hipopo throws large water bubbles that burst and wash enemies away.

Water also interacts with the environment, letting players discover routes, set off chain reactions and turn ordinary movement into inventive attacks. Bright backgrounds, expressive enemies and varied stage layouts give the adventure a personality reminiscent of Bubble Bobble while offering a larger, scrolling world. Originally an arcade release, it was later adapted to home platforms including the PC Engine and Saturn.

games.title: Little Robin
games.description:
Little Robin is a colorful early-1990s Spanish arcade platform game from TCH, released around 1993-94. Up to two players control small, Robin Hood-like characters through single-screen, multi-level arenas populated by fantasy enemies including gnomes, knights and dragons. The action is centered on clearing these opponents from platforms, in the broad tradition of Snow Bros. and other arena-based elimination games.

With its three-button controls, cartoon fantasy setting and modest distribution, Little Robin is an interesting example of Spanish developers producing original arcade software after the international boom in small-screen platform action.

games.title: Live Gal
games.description: Live Gal is a Japanese adult-themed mahjong game released by Central Denshi in May 1987. Players compete in traditional hand-building mahjong rather than matching identical tiles in the solitaire style, with photographic rewards providing the game's adult-oriented attraction. Arcade medal-game conventions distinguish it from a straightforward home mahjong simulation. Its horizontal display, Z80 processor and AY-3-8910 sound hardware are typical of the specialized Japanese mahjong cabinets of its period.

games.title: Lizard Wizard
games.description:
Lizard Wizard (1985) is an unusual single-screen science-fiction rescue shooter developed by Techstar. The player controls a flying ranger on the dangerous planet Zyfus, shooting rocks thrown from an erupting volcano before they turn into fire that helps hostile dragon-like lizards. Freed prisoners must be rescued and carried or guided to safety, rather than simply left to escape unaided.

Different rounds introduce new hazards, including creatures that must be destroyed before they reach the surface. Mixing target shooting with the responsibility to save civilians gives this rare Pac-Man-hardware-derived game more variety than its simple visual presentation suggests.

games.title: The Legend of Kage
games.description:
The Legend of Kage is Taito's mid-1980s ninja action game, originally released in Japanese arcades in 1984 and widely known from its subsequent home versions. Playing the young ninja Kage, the player must rescue Princess Kiri from a warlord's forces, fighting through forests, defensive walls and castle interiors against enemy ninjas and samurai.

Kage's spectacularly high jumps are the game's defining feature: the character can spring across much of the screen, hurl an unlimited supply of throwing stars and slash nearby enemies with a short sword. Stages evoke a rapidly changing Japanese landscape, and rescuing the princess does not necessarily mean the adventure is over. Its fast, airborne combat helped establish a style of cinematic ninja action that later arcade and console games would expand upon.

games.title: Lunar Lander
games.description:
Atari's Lunar Lander (1979) is a landmark of arcade space-flight simulation and the company's first vector-graphics arcade video game. Displayed in sharp monochrome lines, a small spacecraft descends toward the Moon's jagged surface. The player must rotate the craft and use a variable thrust lever to control horizontal drift and vertical speed, aiming for the narrow flat landing zones marked with different score multipliers.

The physics make inertia, fuel conservation and descent speed central to every attempt. A seemingly gentle approach can still end in disaster if the lander is tilted or moving too quickly at touchdown. Fuel acts as both a limited resource and a form of continued play, since additional credits can replenish it.

By translating a once-mainframe-style simulation into a physical arcade cabinet with an unusually tactile throttle, Lunar Lander helped demonstrate that video games could be about precise control and physical judgment rather than reflex shooting alone. Atari reused its vector hardware soon afterward for Asteroids.

games.title: Lock'n'Chase
games.description:
Lock'n'Chase (1981) is Data East's take on the maze-chase boom sparked by Pac-Man. The player controls a thief raiding a bank vault, collecting coins and valuables scattered through corridors while four police officers converge from different directions. Once the valuables are gathered, the thief must reach the exit to escape.

The distinctive twist is a limited ability to close doors behind the thief, temporarily blocking paths and allowing the player to manipulate the pursuing officers. This adds a tactical element absent from straightforward dot collection: a well-timed barrier can create an escape route, while an ill-judged one can trap the player. Its robbery theme and movable maze barriers make it one of the more characterful early Pac-Man contemporaries.

games.title: Locked 'n Loaded
games.description:
Data East's Locked 'n Loaded (1994) is a light-gun action game about an anti-terrorist strike team operating across the world. Players shoot their way through six missions that can be selected in different orders, each containing multiple locations and a tougher boss confrontation. Enemy attacks must be answered quickly, while inaccurate fire and sustained damage deplete the team's limited health.

Its emphasis on mission selection and varied scenery gives some structure to an otherwise direct two-player shooting-gallery experience. The game represents Data East's mid-1990s attempt to compete in a light-gun genre dominated by Konami and Sega.

games.title: Lock-On
games.description:
Tatsumi's Lock-On (1986) is an early cockpit-view aerial combat game built around sophisticated sprite scaling and screen rotation. At the controls of a futuristic jet fighter, the player flies across simulated landscapes, attacks enemy aircraft and ground targets, and survives increasingly difficult combat missions.

Its large, fast-moving sprite imagery creates the illusion of banking and diving through 3D space at a time when most arcade flight shooters still relied on fixed or scrolling overhead viewpoints. Licensed to Data East for American distribution, Lock-On is a notable stepping stone in the evolution of immersive arcade flight action.

games.title: Lock On
games.description:
Philko's Lock On (1991) is a horizontally scrolling aircraft shooter, entirely separate from Tatsumi's 1986 cockpit-view game of the same name. The player pilots a military aircraft through side-scrolling combat, attacking waves of airborne and ground enemies in a style reminiscent of Capcom's Carrier Air Wing.

The South Korean production is also noteworthy for its unusual technical origins: it runs on cloned Sega System 16-type hardware, reflecting the period when some regional manufacturers adapted existing arcade technology and visual assets for new titles.

games.title: Loco-Motion
games.description:
Loco-Motion (1982), developed by Konami and known in Japan as Guttang Gottong, turns the sliding-tile puzzle into a frantic railway-management game. A small locomotive moves continuously around a grid of track sections. By sliding neighboring squares into the single empty space, the player must connect rails ahead of the train and prevent it from reaching a dead end.

The challenge grows as the train accelerates and unexpected hazards complicate the route. Its clever combination of a familiar mechanical puzzle with continuous arcade pressure makes Loco-Motion an early standout among action-puzzle hybrids. It was distributed internationally through partners including Sega and Centuri.

games.title: Lode Runner - The Dig Fight

variants.title: Lode Runner - The Dig Fight (ver. B)
Lode Runner - The Dig Fight (ver. A)

games.description:
Lode Runner: The Dig Fight (2000) is Psikyo's late arcade revival of the classic Lode Runner formula. The player navigates platform mazes, digs temporary holes, evades pursuing guards and collects treasure, but the familiar puzzle design has been reworked for a newer generation of arcade hardware.

In addition to fresh stages and updated presentation, this Japanese release offers a two-player mode, making it a rare turn-of-the-millennium return to an action-puzzle concept closely associated with 1980s computers and Irem's arcade conversions.

games.title: Line of Fire / Bakudan Yarou

variants.title: Line of Fire / Bakudan Yarou (World, FD1094 317-0136)
Line of Fire / Bakudan Yarou (Japan, FD1094 317-0134)
Line of Fire / Bakudan Yarou (US, FD1094 317-0135)

games.description:
Sega's Line of Fire (1989), subtitled Bakudan Yarou in Japan, is an intense military light-gun shooter in which two commandos attempt to escape an enemy complex after discovering a heavily armed vehicle. Players man the vehicle's automatic weapons and fire at soldiers, gun emplacements, vehicles and other hazards while the viewpoint drives forward through hostile territory.

Its cabinet employed two mounted positional guns and was sold in both upright and sit-down versions. Fast sprite scaling gives the ride a convincing sense of forward motion, making Line of Fire feel partly like an on-rails vehicle chase rather than a traditional stationary shooting gallery. Cooperative play reinforces the image of two soldiers fighting from the same machine.

games.title: Logger
games.description:
Logger (1982) is a rare Donkey Kong-inspired platform game produced on Century Electronics' CVS arcade system. The player is a lumberjack whose axe and tools have been taken by an enormous blue bird. To retrieve them, he climbs across a series of platforms and ladders while jumping over rolling logs and other obstacles.

Its premise, stacked-screen playfield and obstacle-dodging make its debt to Nintendo's early platform hit clear, but its lumberjack-and-bird scenario and unusual hardware give it a separate place among the many regional Donkey Kong imitations.

games.title: Logic Pro 2
games.description:
Logic Pro 2 (1997) is Deniam's arcade take on the logic of Minesweeper. Players investigate a grid one square at a time, uncovering safe cells while using nearby-number clues to deduce the positions of hidden bombs. A mistake can end the attempt, so the challenge lies in interpreting the numbers and exposing the remaining safe territory efficiently.

Bright arcade presentation and joystick controls turn the familiar computer puzzle into a score-conscious coin-operated game. Despite its name, it has no connection to Apple's music-production software.

games.title: Logic Pro
games.description:
Logic Pro (1996), developed by Deniam and also released in Korea as Croquis, adapts Minesweeper-style deductive puzzles to the arcade. The player reveals cells on a concealed grid, reading numbers that indicate nearby bombs and using those clues to work out which squares can be safely opened. Progress requires careful logical inference rather than fast action.

Its compact joystick-and-button control scheme and colorful presentation show how a computer puzzle could be reformulated for arcade play. The title is unrelated to the digital audio workstation of the same name.

games.title: Legend of Hero Tonma
games.description:
Irem's Legend of Hero Tonma (1989) is a bright, whimsical side-scrolling platform adventure starring a small caped hero on a mission to rescue a princess. Tonma jumps across platforms, avoids elaborate traps and fires magical projectiles at enemies ranging from little creatures to oversized bosses. Weapons can be powered up to handle the increasingly difficult stages.

The game pairs cheerful cartoon graphics with the demanding enemy placement and precision jumping characteristic of late-1980s Irem arcades. Its combination of magic attacks, boss battles and fantasy scenery later reached a wider audience through a PC Engine conversion.

games.title: Legend of Makai
games.description:
Legend of Makai (1988), known in Japan as Makai Densetsu, is a fantasy action-adventure platformer developed by NMK and published by Jaleco. A young swordsman ventures through interconnected hostile areas to rescue a princess from an evil wizard. Rather than merely moving left to right, the hero explores, confronts monsters and visits shops that sell equipment, weapons and magic items.

The ability to buy upgrades and choose how to progress gives the game a more exploratory feel than a typical arcade platform shooter. Its swordplay, branching movement and light role-playing elements make it a distinctive example of the arcade action-adventure experiments of the late 1980s.

games.title: Looping
games.description:
Looping (1982) is an eccentric aviation action game in which a small aircraft can perform complete 360-degree turns. Players steer and accelerate through connected areas filled with balloons, enemy fire, rockets and environmental hazards, destroying obstacles and finding the way to a final docking station.

Its main challenge is learning the aircraft's circular movement and delicate momentum rather than simply pointing a weapon forward. The unusual up/down steering control allows inverted flight and looping maneuvers that feel different from ordinary scrolling shooters. Created in Europe and published in North America by Venture Line, Looping remains an early example of inventive arcade flight controls.

games.title: Looptris
games.description: Looptris is a homebrew falling-block puzzle game developed by Blastar for the Neo Geo MVS platform and released in December 2021.

games.title: Looptris Plus
games.description: Looptris Plus is an expanded 2022 edition of Blastar's Neo Geo falling-block puzzle game Looptris, adding new modes and presentation refinements.

games.title: Lord of Gun
games.description:
Lord of Gun (1994) is an IGS light-gun shooter with brightly animated monsters instead of the photographed criminals favored by many contemporary gun games. One or two players travel through a sequence of ten stages, aiming at enemies that rush onto the screen and shooting their way toward large end-of-stage bosses.

Hostages and other targets complicate the action, requiring players to distinguish immediate threats from characters they should protect. Its colorful fantasy presentation and relatively long series of stages make it an interesting East Asian alternative to Lethal Enforcers and other Western-style shooting galleries.

games.title: Lost Tomb
games.description:
Lost Tomb (1982-83) is Stern Electronics' overhead exploration shooter set in a labyrinthine ancient pyramid. The player searches its many chambers for treasure and passages toward an eventual escape, while shooting mummies, scorpions and spiders. Two joysticks separate movement from firing direction, permitting evasive maneuvers while attacking threats from another angle.

There are dozens of rooms across multiple pyramid levels, with time pressure, hidden dangers and limited-use whips adding to the tension. Unlike a fixed-screen shooting gallery, Lost Tomb requires players to remember routes, judge when to fight and decide how much treasure is worth the risk. Its dual-stick controls foreshadow later multidirectional action games.

games.title: The Lost World
games.description:
Sega's The Lost World: Jurassic Park (1997) is a spectacular two-player rail shooter based on the film. As members of a rescue expedition on Isla Sorna, players search for Ian Malcolm and Sarah Harding while surviving attacks from dinosaurs. The camera carries them through prehistoric environments as raptors and other creatures charge, and the players use tranquilizer guns to stop them.

Running on Sega Model 3 hardware, the game showcased detailed 3D dinosaurs, fast animation and large-scale cinematic set pieces. A dedicated gun cabinet made encounters feel immediate, especially when an enormous dinosaur filled the screen. Its lavish visual presentation helped establish it as a memorable successor to Sega's earlier Jurassic Park gun game.

games.title: Lot Lot
games.description:
Lot Lot (1985) is a peculiar Japanese puzzle game built around moving small balls through connected compartments. The player controls two pointers, one directly and one following the first after a short delay. Pressing the action button swaps the contents of the compartments indicated by the pointers, allowing balls to be redirected toward scoring pits.

The challenge is to guide the balls away from the zero-point or losing exit and into pits worth 10, 30 or 50 points, meeting each round's score target. Because the delayed second pointer is never quite where the player is concentrating, success demands planning several actions in advance. Developed with Tokuma Shoten involvement and distributed in arcades by Irem, Lot Lot is a distinctive early example of real-time logic puzzles.

games.title: Lotto Fun 2
games.description:
Lotto Fun 2 is a 1993 follow-up to H.A.R. Management's mechanical lottery-style redemption game. The attraction is built around selecting numbers and hoping the correct ping-pong balls are drawn or enter the target, with prizes dispensed as tickets according to the result. The player interacts with the game using a joystick and buttons, but the lottery outcome, not fast reactions, is central to the experience.

This sequel uses considerably more capable electronics than the 1987 original, including a Motorola 68000-based main system and BSMT2000 digital audio hardware. Its place in arcade history is as a ticket-redemption attraction, not a conventional action game, illustrating how electronic displays and physical prize mechanisms could be combined in a single cabinet.

games.title: Lotto Fun
games.description:
Lotto Fun is a 1987 lottery-themed redemption machine from H.A.R. Management, built around the spectacle of ping-pong balls circulating in a blower. Players choose lottery numbers and hope the appropriate balls land in the scoring slot; the outcome determines the ticket reward. Its eight-way joystick and screen provide an electronic interface to an attraction that also depends on physical lottery equipment.

Promotional material advertised operator-selectable Choose 3, Choose 4, and Choose 6 games, along with ticket or token payout arrangements. Its Motorola 6809-based electronics and simple on-screen presentation reflect the late-1980s crossover between arcade video technology and prize-redemption amusements. Lotto Fun 2 followed in 1993.

games.title: Lover Boy
games.description:
Lover Boy (1983) is a rare adult-themed Japanese maze game from G.T. Enterprise. It borrows the basic overhead chase structure of Pac-Man but replaces the usual food collection with the pursuit of women across a city maze while avoiding police and a pursuing dog. The game includes explicit sexual scenes and sexual assault as part of its premise.

Its content makes it a particularly controversial and disturbing artifact of the early Japanese adult arcade market rather than a typical family-oriented maze game. An unauthorized version circulated under the name Triki Triki.

games.title: Logic Pro Adventure
games.description:
Logic Pro Adventure (1999) is a colorful puzzle game by Deniam, released through Amuse World in Japan. Instead of presenting isolated puzzles, it sends the player across a world map to solve nonogram-style picture-logic challenges. Colored gems indicate the size and difficulty of each puzzle, while completed boards award gems needed for progression.

The adventure offers an unusually large collection of puzzles, with a goal of obtaining 50 gems of each type before confronting a final boss puzzle. Its cartoon backgrounds and map-based structure make it a substantial departure from the straightforward minesweeping of the earlier Logic Pro games.

games.title: Lunar Rescue
games.description:
Taito's Lunar Rescue (1979) builds on the success of Space Invaders with a more elaborate mission: rescuing stranded astronauts from the Moon. A small lander leaves its mothership at the top of the screen, threads through horizontally moving asteroids and uses limited thrust to touch down safely on a landing pad. After collecting an astronaut, it must return upward, firing at hostile saucers on the way back.

The game cleverly alternates two control challenges. The descent rewards careful fuel management and precise positioning, while the ascent demands accurate shooting and avoidance. The limited landing sites create increasing pressure as rescue operations continue.

Developed by a team led by Space Invaders creator Tomohiro Nishikado, Lunar Rescue is an early example of mixing physics-based landing with arcade shooting. It also circulated under such names as Galaxy Rescue and Destination Earth.

games.title: Last Resort
games.description:
Last Resort (1992) is a demanding horizontally scrolling shooter for SNK's Neo Geo, drawing inspiration from classics such as R-Type. In a future where a computer-controlled defense system has turned against humanity, the player pilots a compact cyber jet through a devastated technological world, confronting waves of robotic enemies and enormous mechanical bosses.

The game's defining weapon is an indestructible detachable drone. It can absorb small bullets, fire in different directions and be launched toward enemies with a charged attack before returning to the player's ship. Learning to position and exploit this device is essential to mastering the game's unforgiving encounters. Five stages repeat on a second, harder loop.

Its opening cityscape famously recalls the dystopian Neo-Tokyo of the anime film Akira, and its dark backgrounds, detailed mechanical art and exacting difficulty have made Last Resort a cult favorite among Neo Geo shooter enthusiasts.

games.title: Land Sea Air Squad / Riku Kai Kuu Saizensen

variants.title: Land Sea Air Squad / Riku Kai Kuu Saizensen
Storming Party / Riku Kai Kuu Saizensen

games.description:
Land Sea Air Squad (1986), also released as Storming Party, is Taito's overhead military run-and-gun game. A lone sergeant fights through dense enemy territory using a machine gun and grenades, in the general style of Commando. What sets it apart is the ability to commandeer vehicles: tanks, helicopters and speedboats allow the player to cross land, air and water sections more quickly while surviving more damage than an exposed infantryman.

The blend of foot combat and vehicle changes gives the stages a broader battlefield feel, and special events such as passing trains add variety. The Japanese title Riku Kai Kuu Saizensen literally emphasizes the land, sea and air fronts of the campaign.

games.title: Little Casino 2
games.description:
Little Casino II (1984) is Digital Controls' follow-up to its compact casino-themed amusement machine. It offers an operator-configurable menu of card, dice, and betting games. Its documented software options include blackjack, poker, craps, horse racing, and slots, while a contemporary owner's manual also describes a configuration with high-low card play. The games share a small illuminated button panel, with players choosing a game, placing point wagers, and making decisions appropriate to the selected rules.

The hardware was intended for countertop or bar-top installation rather than a conventional joystick arcade cabinet. Operators could adjust coinage, the number of hands, available games, and other settings. Several program revisions survive, including versions 17.0, 18.1, and 30.0, providing a snapshot of how the same cabinet was updated for different amusement locations.

games.title: Little Casino
games.description:
Digital Controls' Little Casino (1982) translates the atmosphere of a small casino into an amusement-oriented tabletop video machine. Its documented game selection includes blackjack, high-low cards, poker, and a dice game. Instead of navigating an action playfield, the player chooses a game and makes betting decisions using illuminated buttons. Winnings and losses are tracked as points rather than cash, giving familiar card and dice rules the quick, repeatable structure of a coin-operated arcade session.

The cabinet was designed for bars and other locations with limited floor space. Its red backlit buttons flash during the attract sequence and illuminate to show the available actions during play, a practical solution to sharing one control panel among several games. This early multi-game format helps explain the appeal of countertop gambling-themed amusements before touchscreen casino terminals became commonplace.

games.title: Lucky 8 Lines
games.description:
Lucky 8 Lines is Falcon's 1989 licensed version of Wing's New Lucky 8 Lines, a video-slot design that evaluates winning symbol arrangements across eight lines. It replaces the single central payline of a traditional slot with a grid-based gambling display, giving a spin several opportunities to register a result. Four primary buttons and separate betting-control modes are documented for the machine.

The series spawned an unusually large collection of board revisions, encrypted versions and regional modifications. A non-coin model also existed, illustrating the movement of eight-liner software between cash gambling and other amusement settings.

games.title: Lucky & Wild
games.description:
Lucky & Wild (1992) is one of Namco's most distinctive arcade action games, combining a driving chase with simultaneous light-gun shooting. Inspired by buddy-cop films, it casts players as two flamboyant lawmen pursuing criminals across highways and city streets. One player operates the steering wheel and accelerator while also firing a mounted or handheld gun; a partner can concentrate on shooting from the passenger seat.

The split responsibilities make cooperative play chaotic in the best possible way: the driver must avoid traffic, negotiate corners and keep enemies within range, while both players shoot hostile vehicles and attackers. The arcade cabinet's physical combination of wheel, pedals and guns is essential to its appeal.

A fast-moving soundtrack, theatrical crashes and exaggerated characters help Lucky & Wild capture the energy of an action-movie car chase. Few arcade games have reproduced its particular blend of team-based driving and shooting.

games.title: Lucky Today
games.description:
Lucky Today is a 1980 electronic fruit machine by Sigma, notable for running on hardware derived from Namco's Galaxian shooter. Rather than moving a ship, players insert credits, use the two-way control to set a bet and press the start button to run a slot-machine round. Its vertically oriented CRT and limited controls retain the physical character of an early arcade cabinet while serving a gambling game.

Its later unauthorized counterpart, Chewing Gum, closely follows the same program. Lucky Today is an instructive example of arcade electronics being reused for gambling machines just as dedicated video slots were beginning to spread.

games.title: Lupin III
games.description:
Lupin III (1980) is an early Taito maze-and-chase game licensed from the long-running Japanese manga and anime about gentleman thief Arsène Lupin III. The player guides Lupin around a fixed-screen layout, trying to steal bags of money from the upper part of the screen and bring them safely to the bottom while avoiding pursuing guards.

Lupin can carry only a limited number of bags at a time, so a successful run requires repeated journeys across dangerous routes. Simple four-directional movement and shifting enemy positions create a tense game of timing and escape. Its use of a popular television and manga character also makes it an early example of arcade games built around established Japanese entertainment licenses.

games.title: Lovely Cards
games.description:
Lovely Cards is a 1985 card-game release from Tehkan, the Japanese company later known as Tecmo. It is closely related to Lovely Poker but was presented as an amusement-only gambling-style game rather than a direct cash-payout version. Play centers on electronic poker hands selected through a dedicated gambling-control panel, with adult-oriented imagery providing part of the game's presentation.

The game is historically interesting for its relationship to the betting-labelled Lovely Poker program and for the existence of encrypted software sets. The original Z80-based hardware also reflects how modest 1980s arcade technology could support card games alongside more conventional action titles.

games.title: Las Vegas Girl
games.description:
Las Vegas Girl (1994) is an adult-themed falling-block puzzle game by Comad, based closely on the formula of Columns. Colored pieces descend into a vertical well, and the player arranges matching elements to clear them before the playfield fills. The scoring and survival challenge is framed by a casino-style presentation.

The game's main distinguishing feature is its erotic photo backgrounds, which were aimed at adult arcade venues. Beneath that presentation is a straightforward match-and-clear puzzle rather than a casino gambling simulation.

games.title: Legendary Wings
games.description:
Legendary Wings (1986), called Ares no Tsubasa in Japan, is Capcom's imaginative fusion of vertical shooting and side-scrolling platform action. Players control winged warriors sent by the god Ares to stop DARK, a once-beneficial supercomputer that has turned against humanity. The adventure combines mythological imagery with futuristic enemies and towering mechanical defenses.

During flight sections, the heroes move across a vertically scrolling battlefield and fire at airborne threats. Other sections switch to side-view movement through dangerous interiors, with jumping and attacks suited to a platform game. Two-player cooperative play and the changing action styles give the arcade game an unusual rhythm.

A later Nintendo Entertainment System version rearranged aspects of the original experience, making the coin-operated game particularly interesting to compare. Legendary Wings is remembered for its striking mixture of classical mythology, science-fiction machinery and Capcom's early shooter design.

games.title: M-4
games.description:
M-4 (1977) is an early Midway tank-combat arcade game. Players control armored vehicles from opposing sides of an overhead battlefield, aiming and firing at rival tanks and other military targets. The controls use a vertically moving joystick and firing buttons rather than the elaborate steering systems of later vehicle simulators.

Its blocky monochrome graphics and forceful electronic battle noises reflect the transitional period when dedicated video cabinets were replacing electromechanical combat amusements. M-4 is chiefly notable as a straightforward competitive military shooter from the first generation of microprocessor-based arcade games.

games.title: Mission 660
games.description:
Mission 660 (1986), released in Japan as The Alphax Z, is a vertically scrolling space shooter developed by Woodplace and distributed by Taito. Defending a threatened space colony, the player pilots a fighter through formations of attacking ships, punctuated by larger enemies that require sustained fire to defeat.

Collecting power-star items strengthens the ship's weapons, while the game's enemy roster includes some unexpectedly whimsical creatures, such as flying cats, mice and skull-like attackers. This mix of conventional science-fiction combat and oddball enemy designs gives the otherwise straightforward shooter a memorable identity.

games.title: M-79 Ambush
games.description:
M-79 Ambush (1977) is an early Ramtek shooting-gallery game built around the sight and sound of a battlefield. The player aims a simulated M-79 grenade launcher at passing tanks, motorcycles and other hostile vehicles, trying to destroy them as they move across the screen. Friendly United Nations trucks must be spared.

Destroyed targets leave wreckage behind, gradually changing the battlefield. Its simple aiming mechanism and military target-recognition challenge recall electromechanical shooting galleries, making M-79 Ambush an interesting bridge between older gun amusements and fully electronic arcade shooters.

games.title: Mace: The Dark Age

variants.title: Mace: The Dark Age (boot ROM 1.0ce, HDD 1.0b)

games.description:
Mace: The Dark Age (1996) is Atari Games' dark-fantasy 3D fighting game, later converted to the Nintendo 64.
