Warriors armed with swords, axes and other brutal weapons battle in polygonal arenas, each seeking power connected to the legendary Mace of Tanis and the sorcerer Asmodeus. The roster favors distinct fighting styles and exaggerated medieval-fantasy character designs.

Combat mixes weapon strikes, special moves, combinations and gruesome finishing attacks. Certain stages contain environmental hazards that can punish fighters caught near the edge of the arena, while the fully 3D presentation separates it from the sprite-based Mortal Kombat games that influenced its style.

Mace illustrates the mid-1990s arcade industry's rush to bring mature, spectacle-heavy one-on-one fighters into polygonal 3D, and remains a distinctive Atari entry in a genre dominated by Japanese studios.

games.title: M.A.C.H. 3
games.description:
M.A.C.H. 3 (1983) is Gottlieb/Mylstar's pioneering LaserDisc aerial combat game. Real aerial footage recorded onto disc provides the scenery, while computer-generated aircraft, targeting sights and enemies are overlaid on top. Players choose between Fighter and Bomber missions, attacking airborne or ground targets while steering to avoid hazards and incoming fire.

The mixture of live-action footage and simple animated graphics created an unusually convincing sensation of flying low over real terrain. A joystick and separate gun and bomb buttons keep the action direct despite the technically sophisticated presentation.

Released during the brief boom in LaserDisc arcade games, M.A.C.H. 3 demonstrated that filmed imagery could be used for more than branching cartoon adventures. It remains one of the most distinctive shooting games of the format.

games.title: Mach Breakers
games.description:
Mach Breakers (1995), subtitled Numan Athletics 2, is Namco's flamboyant sequel to Numan Athletics. Up to four players compete as superhuman athletes in a series of wildly exaggerated sporting contests, choosing from seven characters with differing speed and power. Challenges replace ordinary athletics with feats of strength, unusual races and spectacular tests of accuracy or reflexes.

The three-button control scheme makes each event a miniature contest of timing, rapid presses or careful aiming. The variation between disciplines keeps multiplayer sessions lively and gives different characters opportunities to excel. Released on Namco's NB-series hardware, Mach Breakers is a cult favorite for players who enjoy competitive arcade minigame collections rather than traditional sports simulations.

games.title: Macho Mouse
games.description:
Macho Mouse (1982) is a brightly colored maze game from Techstar, starring a mouse trying to make its way through a network of corridors while avoiding cats. Moving through the maze changes the playfield's appearance, and the player can jump to stun pursuing cats temporarily rather than relying solely on escape routes.

Its lighthearted animal characters and special defensive jump make it a lesser-known contemporary of the early maze-chase boom, using modified hardware related to Round-Up.

games.title: Vs. Mach Rider (Endurance Course Version)

variants.title: Vs. Mach Rider (Japan, Fighting Course Version)

games.description:
Vs. Mach Rider (Endurance Course Version) brings Nintendo's 1985 futuristic motorcycle combat game to the Vs. System arcade platform. Set in the year 2112 after hostile forces have invaded Earth, the player races a high-performance motorcycle through dangerous sectors while fighting armed enemy riders. Traffic, track obstacles and enemy attacks demand quick lane changes, acceleration and accurate shooting.

The Endurance Course emphasizes surviving a sustained series of road sections, combining combat with the challenge of keeping the bike under control at high speed. The original home game also featured other modes, so the arcade edition's specific course configuration matters when comparing versions. Its mixture of post-apocalyptic motorcycle racing and vehicular gunplay is unusual among Nintendo's mid-1980s arcade releases.

games.title: Super Spacefortress Macross / Chou-Jikuu Yousai Macross
games.description:
Super Spacefortress Macross (1992) is Banpresto's vertically scrolling arcade shooter based on the animated film Macross: Do You Remember Love?. Players pilot VF-1 Valkyrie fighters into battles against the giant Zentradi forces, reenacting recognizable scenes from the film. The selectable pilots include Max Jenius and, during two-player play, Hikaru Ichijyo.

Collecting transformation items changes the Valkyrie's combat mode. The fighter configuration uses spreading fire, GERWALK emphasizes a concentrated beam, and Battroid employs homing attacks; additional power-ups strengthen these weapons. Bombs, boss fights and bonus pickups such as character dolls add to the scoring challenge.

The appeal lies in bringing the transforming mecha, space battles and familiar characters of Macross into a conventional but colorful 1990s arcade shooter. It should not be confused with the mechanically different scoring-based Macross II.

games.title: Super Spacefortress Macross II / Chou-Jikuu Yousai Macross II
games.description:
Super Spacefortress Macross II (1993) is Banpresto's arcade shoot-'em-up based on the original video animation Macross II: Lovers Again, set decades after the original series. The player fights the invading Marduk forces through vertically scrolling space battles and animated-mecha combat.

Rather than relying only on survival or defeating a stage boss, each stage gives the player a required score that must be reached before a fixed time limit expires. Shooting down enemies and collecting bonuses contribute to the target, and the clock continues to matter even if the major enemies are defeated early. Cooperative two-player games combine both players' scores, while a competitive option lets them race for points on a selected stage.

This score-driven design gives Macross II a different rhythm from Banpresto's first Macross shooter, making aggressive play and efficient point collection as important as careful dodging.

games.title: Macross Plus
games.description:
Macross Plus (1996) is a vertically scrolling arcade shooter based on the anime's experimental-fighter storyline. Players can choose among recognizable aircraft and pilots, including Isamu Dyson in the YF-19, Guld Bowman in the YF-21 and a VF-11 pilot. Each fighter takes part in battles against airborne enemies and heavy targets amid familiar Macross technology.

The weapon system combines standard shots, bombs and missile attacks, with homing behavior helping to clear formations. Power-ups increase the aircraft's effectiveness, while the distinctive roster and high-energy combat place the game firmly in the tradition of anime-themed arcade shooters. It is separate from the earlier Macross and Macross II coin-op games rather than a simple update to either one.

games.title: Multi Amenity Cassette System BIOS
games.description:
The Multi Amenity Cassette System was a mid-1990s Japanese arcade platform associated with I'Max and built around Seta's ST0016 hardware. Rather than representing a playable game, this BIOS supplies the system software for interchangeable titles. Its small library was oriented toward Japanese tabletop and novelty entertainment, including Kisekae Mahjong, Kisekae Hanafuda, and the later Yu-Jan. The hardware's dedicated mahjong-style inputs reflect the specialized cabinets for which it was intended.

The MACS BIOS is a reminder that cartridge-based arcade systems did not serve only action games and fighting games. In this case, the same general idea of reusable hardware supported a comparatively obscure group of Japanese amusement titles, preserved in emulation through a shared system ROM.

games.title: Mad Alien
games.description:
Mad Alien (1980) is Data East's curious combination of alien shooter and road-combat game. The player drives a police car fitted with a gun along a vertically scrolling highway, firing at alien riders arranged in formations ahead. Individual enemies sometimes peel away to attack, borrowing an idea from Galaxian.

Each round alternates between formation shooting and a faster chase involving cars and motorcycles. The player's gun permits only one shot on screen at a time, while collisions cost lives. Some scenes take place inside dark tunnels, where only the portion of road illuminated by the headlights remains visible. This mixture of shooting, changing scenery and automotive hazards distinguishes Mad Alien from the fixed-screen invader games that inspired it.

games.title: Mad Ball V2.0
games.description:
Mad Ball V2.0 (1998) is a South Korean Breakout-style arcade game from Yun Sung, using photographs of swimsuit models as stage backgrounds. The player steers a paddle to keep a ball in play and smash rows of blocks, much as in Arkanoid. As the board clears, enemies and unusual targets become exposed against the picture behind them.

Power-ups modify the ball or paddle, and the paddle can also gain a gun to shoot blocks and enemies directly. This added attack option provides another way to break through difficult arrangements. The adult-oriented photo presentation distinguishes it from the more family-friendly block-breakers on which the game is based.

games.title: Mad Crasher
games.description:
Mad Crasher (1984) is SNK's unusual diagonally scrolling futuristic road shooter. The player drives a high-speed vehicle along elevated highways shown from an isometric perspective, avoiding gaps, colliding with rivals and shooting enemies while negotiating a twisting roadway. Jumping is especially important, both for surviving missing sections of road and for reaching bonuses.

Its angled viewpoint and parallax-scrolling scenery create an impressive sense of movement for a mid-1980s game. Released in Japan in December 1984, Mad Crasher is an early illustration of SNK experimenting with pseudo-3D action before its later arcade successes.

games.title: Mad Donna
games.description:
Mad Donna (1995) is an adult-oriented maze-chase game by Tuning Electronic, borrowing the basic structure of Pac-Man. The player moves through single-screen labyrinths, clearing the required items while avoiding opponents and obstacles. Completing stages reveals photographic images of women, with successive rounds unlocking more of each picture.

Its conventional maze play is chiefly distinguished by the erotic reward system and by the low-budget adult arcade market for which it was created. Multiple software sets are preserved.

games.title: Mad Gear
games.description:
Mad Gear (1989) is Capcom's fast-paced vertically scrolling combat racer, also distributed internationally as LED Storm. Players choose a vehicle and race along dangerous elevated highways, dodging traffic, pushing opponents off the road and jumping gaps or landing directly on rival cars. Forks offer alternate paths, while bonuses replenish energy or strengthen the car's ability to ram opponents. Falling off the highway triggers a recovery winch that must be guided back to the roadway.

Nine stages lead through futuristic cities, forests, deserts, tunnels and other hazardous settings. Its rough-and-tumble vehicle combat recalls Data East's Bump 'n' Jump, but its branching roads and detailed Capcom presentation give it a different personality. The title Mad Gear was later reused for the criminal gang in Final Fight.

This commercial release is distinct from the earlier Rally 2011 LED Storm prototype, which featured a transformable car/motorcycle in place of the finished game's vehicle selection.

games.title: Mad Motor
games.description:
Mad Motor is an unreleased late-1980s side-scrolling motorcycle action game developed by Mitchell. The player rides through highways, cities and other landscapes, attacking enemies on bikes, in cars and even on airborne craft. Boss encounters range from heavily armed vehicles to absurd, oversized characters.

Its standout feature is the ability to transform the rider and machine into a much bulkier fighter mounted on a small tricycle-like vehicle, changing the look and force of combat. Although it was never a regular commercial arcade release, the surviving prototype reveals a colorful and peculiar attempt to mix a motorcycle chase with beat-'em-up mechanics.

games.title: Mad Shark
games.description:
Mad Shark (1993) is a vertically scrolling shooter developed by MOSS and published by Allumer. Piloting a fighter aircraft, players battle enemy planes, ground installations and large bosses, collecting weapon upgrades that provide wider gunfire, homing attacks or missiles. Limited bombs offer an emergency answer to crowded patterns of enemy bullets.

The game is closely related in spirit to Seibu Kaihatsu's Raiden, reflecting MOSS's origins among former Seibu staff. Its energetic military science-fiction style and challenging weapon-management choices make it a solid early-1990s shooter. Mad Shark was MOSS's first title, preceding the studio's later work on the Raiden franchise.

games.title: Booby Kids
games.description:
Booby Kids (Magnet System) is a Spanish arcade conversion of Nichibutsu's 1987 action game Kid no Hore Hore Daisakusen, adapted for EFO/Cedar's disk-based Magnet System. The player guides a small character through overhead maze-like stages, dealing with hostile creatures by digging holes or traps and letting the enemies fall into them. Timing and positioning are more important than firing conventional projectiles.

The conversion is historically interesting because Magnet System operators could change games by replacing magnetic media rather than an entire arcade board. It is distinct from the later Nintendo console adaptation also known as Booby Kids, even though they share the same original premise.

games.title: The Burning Cavern
games.description: The Burning Cavern is a 1987 action shooter created by EFO SA and Cedar for Spain's Magnet System, an uncommon arcade platform that distributed games on interchangeable floppy disks. It is classified as a walking shooter, using an eight-direction joystick and three action buttons, with support for two players taking turns. Its distinctive historical importance lies in the medium as much as the action: the game survives as a disk image from Magnet System hardware rather than as an ordinary fixed-ROM board. Modern preservation work recovered matching reads of its aging, unusually demanding disk format.

games.title: A Day In Space
games.description: A Day in Space is a 1987 space-themed action game made by Spain's EFO S.A. and Cedar for the floppy-disk-based Magnet System. Descriptions identify it as a side-scrolling shooter with maze-like passages, hazards and items to collect. Two people can play in turns rather than cooperatively. The surviving disk carries a March 31, 1987 date; preservation work was unusually delicate because aging media produced inconsistent reads, although the discrepancies were largely confined to later disk areas.

games.title: Exzisus
games.description:
This is the Spanish Magnet System conversion of Taito's 1987 horizontal shooter Exzisus, distributed by EFO S.A. and Cedar as disk revision EX 1.0. The underlying game follows a flying humanoid robot across four hostile planets. It can fire forward and drop missiles, send bird- and dog-like robot companions at enemies, and collect an A power-up to become a faster spacecraft that can absorb an additional hit. Bosses include the gigantic Gold Moai and a mechanical yeti.

Unlike Taito's original multi-CPU arcade board, this edition runs on the Magnet System's Z80-based hardware and loads from a floppy disk. An improved preservation dump corrected graphical corruption in the first stage. Its interest lies both in the unusual transformations and in the rare Spanish hardware adaptation, rather than in a new sequel to Exzisus.

games.title: Paris Dakar
games.description: Paris Dakar is a little-known motorcycle racing game developed by EFO S.A. for Spain's floppy-based Magnet System in 1987. Contemporary recollections describe five stages: three races reminiscent of Sega's Enduro Racer, followed by two unusual dune sections in which the rider climbs and descends while dodging falling motorcycle and jeep parts. The intended cabinet could use motorcycle handlebars instead of an ordinary joystick. No conclusive record establishes whether the game reached commercial distribution or remained a prototype, making its surviving disk an important document of an ambitious Spanish arcade platform.

games.title: Time Scanner
games.description:
Time Scanner (TS 2.0) is the 1987 Magnet System floppy-disk conversion of Sega's video pinball game. A ball travels through vertically extended tables, with flippers in different sections and scrolling that follows the ball downward. Three initially selectable tables, Volcano, Ruins and Saqqarah, have distinctive objectives involving named lanes, targets and special holes; clearing them unlocks a final stage with Breakout-style bricks.

Developed for Spanish operators by EFO S.A. and Cedar, this conversion brings a game originally issued on dedicated Sega hardware to the interchangeable Magnet System. The version is historically interesting as one of several adaptations documented through surviving, difficult-to-preserve magnetic disks.

games.title: War Mission
games.description:
War Mission is an original 1987 vertically scrolling aircraft shooter from EFO S.A. and Cedar, created specifically for the Spanish Magnet System rather than converted from another company's arcade board. The player flies through formations of enemy aircraft, dodges projectiles and collects star-marked weapon improvements. Its strikingly large collision area, occasional shots appearing without visible enemies and restrictive on-screen bullet limit give it an unusually unforgiving character. In particular, spreading shots with a three-star upgrade can actually leave the player unable to fire again at close range until previous bullets disappear.

Unlike many Magnet System titles, War Mission loads its program from disk at startup instead of repeatedly pausing for level data. It was an important discovery for arcade preservationists, who recovered usable game code from deteriorating floppy media. Two software revisions are known, and two-player operation is available through service settings, although disabled by default.

games.title: Xain'd Sleena
games.description:
This is EFO S.A. and Cedar's 1987 Magnet System conversion of Technos Japan's Xain'd Sleena, a 1986 action game known in North America as Solar Warrior. Players guide the space warrior Xain through the liberation of five planets, mixing run-and-gun platforming with interplanetary shooting sequences. Xain can crouch, perform a double jump, gather replacement weapons and fight a major boss before escaping each doomed base in a spaceship.

The original combines separately themed planets with space-flight interludes, an uncommon structure for its period. The SC 3.0 Magnet version is notable for translating that elaborate action game onto EFO's floppy-disk arcade system. The archived set was initially classified as a prototype; its gameplay should not be mistaken for a newly designed 1987 sequel.

games.title: Magical Drop II
games.description:
Data East's Magical Drop II (1996) brought its frantic color-matching puzzle formula to SNK's Neo Geo MVS. A small character at the bottom of the playfield catches clusters of colored drops and throws them back into descending columns. Aligning at least three of one color clears them, while rapid successive clears or cascading chains push the rival's pieces downward. Unlike puzzles built around slowly rotating falling shapes, the emphasis is on extremely fast rearrangement and aggressive timing.

The cast takes its identities from Tarot cards, and different characters affect the opponent's board with different attack patterns. The sequel adds rainbow drops and permits normal and special drops to be matched together; the Japanese edition also includes a separate set of predetermined logic puzzles. Its lively animation, competitive two-player design and soundtrack by Data East's Gamadelic team helped establish the series as a favorite among Neo Geo puzzle-game players.

games.title: Magical Drop III
games.description:
Magical Drop III is Data East's 1997 culmination of the Neo Geo puzzle series, retaining the explosive pace of catching colored drops at the bottom of the screen and returning them to form groups of three or more. The player wins by arranging swift combinations and chains that force an opponent's columns downward. A third button introduces fresh rows on demand, allowing experienced players to set up longer attacks rather than simply waiting for the board to descend.

Its expanded roster draws from the 22 major Tarot arcana, with character-specific attack patterns and hidden fighters. Alongside conventional versus play and solo challenges, Magical Journey turns the contest into a board-game-style race against the Empress, punctuated by short minigames. Colorful animation, distinctive character designs and unusually technical high-speed competition made it a standout of the late Neo Geo era. It was also Data East's final arcade release before the company left the coin-operated market.

games.title: Magical Error wo Sagase
games.description: Magical Error wo Sagase (1994), from Technosoft and Jaleco, is a timed spot-the-difference game with a distinctive visual twist: the two illustrations are mirrored rather than presented in the same orientation. One or two players scan the images and indicate the mismatching detail using joystick-and-button controls. Incorrect selections drain the remaining time, so careless guessing is costly. Each stage contains five picture challenges, followed by a bonus game that can replenish the clock. Its emphasis on visual comparison and quick decisions sets it apart from the match-three puzzle games that dominated many mid-1990s arcades.

games.title: Magic's 10
games.description:
Magic's 10 is a 1995 Italian video gambling game by A.W.P. Games, built around poker-style card play on a 68000-based arcade board. Five dedicated buttons provide the compact control scheme expected of an electronic card cabinet. Several preserved program revisions, including versions 16.15, 16.45 and 16.55, testify to continued software adjustments after its introduction.

The original board used additional control hardware that initially complicated emulation, an unusual technical detail for an otherwise straightforward-looking coin-op. Its later companion, Magic's 10 2, continued the same Italian poker-machine line.

games.title: Magic's 10 2
games.description:
Magic's 10 2 is a 1997 video-poker game from Italy's ABM Games and a follow-up to A.W.P. Games' Magic's 10. As with its predecessor, play is organized around button-selected poker gambling rather than moving an on-screen character. It retains a horizontal display and a Motorola 68000-based hardware family, with revisions including version 1.1 and an early beta program.

The close relationship between the two games is preserved in their shared hardware and emulation history. This sequel represents the continuing market for dedicated Italian poker machines during the late 1990s.

games.title: Magicball Fighting
games.description: Magicball Fighting is a 1994 Korean arcade baseball game by SemiCom, the first entry in a four-game sports lineage later continued by Wonder League Star, Wonder League '96 and MuHanSeungBu. It presents baseball in a colorful coin-op format, with two-player support and an eight-way joystick plus three action buttons. SemiCom operated under several trading names, including Jeil and Mijin, a reason these baseball titles sometimes appear under different corporate credits. As the earliest game in the sequence, Magicball Fighting is an interesting example of South Korea's domestic arcade sports development before the studio's better-documented follow-ups.

games.title: Magic Bubble
games.description:
Magic Bubble is a late-1990s Korean bubble-shooting puzzle game from Yun Sung, closely modeled on Taito's Puzzle Bobble series. Players aim colored bubbles into the mass hanging above the playfield, clearing groups of three or more before the formation reaches the bottom. Two-player competition turns efficient clearing into a race against an opponent. The arcade program also exists in an adult-themed edition.

Although some databases give an earlier date, the preserved game is identified as a modification of Puzzle Bobble 4, released in 1997, so a 1998-or-later origin is more credible. Reports describe nearly identical stage arrangements but altered bubble graphics, music and backgrounds, with imagery borrowed from unrelated games. It is best understood as an unofficial reworking, not a new installment in Taito's series.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Magic Card II
games.description:
Magic Card II is a 1996 Impera electronic poker/card-gambling machine in the Austrian tradition of Jolly Card and Royal Card. It uses a seven-button control panel and 65C02-family hardware with a horizontal CRT, putting wager, hold and deal functions at the player's fingertips rather than using a joystick.

The surviving sets include a Bulgarian-language release and heavily modified boards. Emulator research has found that even some versions long assumed to be original were altered to varying degrees, making the boundary between official revisions and local hacks particularly difficult to establish for this title.

games.title: Magic Sticks
games.description:
Magic Sticks is a 1995 Playmark coin-op from Italy that combines a simple, single-button interaction with chance-based credit rewards. Unlike a standard draw-poker machine, it is catalogued as a miscellaneous gambling game, and its precise stick-selection or prize rules are poorly recorded; it should not be described as ordinary video poker merely because of its gambling classification.

The machine is visually and technically distinct from many of Playmark's other releases, using a Motorola 68000 processor, OKI sampled audio and a 320-by-240 horizontal display. Surviving photographs of its dedicated PCB and in-game instruction screens have helped document this relatively uncommon title.

games.title: Magic Purple
games.description: Magic Purple (1996) is a Korean side-scrolling platform action game by Unico Electronics, featuring cartoonish duck-like heroes who can punch and shoot their way through enemies. Its brightly colored characters recall Sega's Dynamite Dux, though it is a separate arcade release. Players gather bonus items as they advance through the stages. The preserved board is especially notable because it was a long-sought, previously poorly documented title: collectors recovered a surviving PCB and helped add it to emulation archives years after its creation. Some item names do not match their graphics, a curious sign of possible late development changes.

games.title: Magix / Rock
games.description: Magix, also known as Rock, is a 1995 falling-block puzzle game with adult-themed presentation. The player arranges descending shapes on a fixed playfield, borrowing the basic visual vocabulary of Tetris-style arcade puzzles rather than a conventional scrolling action format. The game circulated in multiple board or copyright variants, including a bootleg lacking the original copyright message. Its primary historical interest is as one of the many small-scale mid-1990s puzzle releases that combined straightforward block manipulation with mature material.

games.title: Magician Lord
games.description:
Magician Lord was one of the original showcase games for SNK's Neo Geo system in 1990. Players control Elta, a young magician fighting through the fantasy realm of Cadacis to recover eight mystical books and prevent the resurrection of the destructive god Az Atorse. The game is a scrolling action-platformer, with jumps, projectiles, ladders, traps and enormous bosses that fill much of the screen. Its elaborate hand-drawn fantasy art and detailed animations helped demonstrate what SNK's expensive new arcade platform could do.

Its defining mechanic is magical transformation. Collecting the right combinations of elemental orbs changes Elta into powerful forms such as the Dragon Warrior, Shinobi, Samurai and Waterman, each with different attacks or movement abilities. A hit can revert an empowered form, making the pursuit and preservation of transformations central to surviving the lengthy stages.

Known for its imposing boss designs and punishing difficulty, Magician Lord became an early Neo Geo signature title despite later criticism of its rigid controls and relentless enemy attacks. Its status as a launch-era MVS/AES game preserves a snapshot of the platform's initial ambition: dramatic, arcade-sized fantasy action rather than the fighting games that would eventually define the hardware.

games.title: Mag Max
games.description:
Nichibutsu's Mag Max (1985) is a horizontally scrolling shooter built around a memorable modular spacecraft. Players begin with a small flying craft and can collect separate pieces to assemble the towering Mag Max robot. The completed machine has more formidable attacks and a much larger silhouette, but lost components can leave the player reduced to a smaller, more vulnerable form. A giant three-headed mechanical dragon, Babylon, is among its most recognizable enemies.

Rather than remaining on a single flight path, the player can move between the surface and underground sections of the scrolling battlefield through transporters. The change of altitude alters the terrain, threats and view of the landscape, while the search for missing robot parts creates an ongoing reason to change routes. This unusual combination of a transforming hero and linked playfields gives Mag Max an identity well beyond a standard 1985 spaceship shooter.

games.title: Magical Spot
games.description: Universal's Magical Spot (1980) is a fixed-screen space shooter in which the player's ship must prevent insect-like invaders from overrunning the playfield. A large craft above drops wriggling larvae, which can survive shots and descend through rows of objects before forming cocoons. If too many hatch, dangerous adult moths emerge and descend on the player. Unlike the simple one-hit invaders of many contemporary games, the creatures' different life stages force the player to prioritize threats before the screen becomes crowded. Magical Spot is a distinctive early example of an arcade shooter built around evolving enemy behavior.

games.title: Magical Spot II
games.description: Magical Spot II is Universal's 1980 revision of its insect-themed fixed-screen shooter. As in the original, the player fires at creatures released from an overhead alien craft, trying to destroy larvae before they develop into more aggressive flying threats. It retains the original's unusual insect life-cycle theme and basic shooting rhythm rather than introducing a different genre. The changes are comparatively modest, to the point that contemporary cabinets were not always clearly marked as a sequel. A Magical Spot II machine can even be glimpsed in the 1982 film Rocky III.

games.title: Tokoro San no MahMahjan
games.description: Tokoro San no MahMahjan is a Japanese mahjong arcade game released by Sega in December 1992 on its System 24 hardware. Rather than relying on generic opponents, it prominently features television entertainer and comedian George (Joji) Tokoro, whose name and likeness give the game its character. Players engage in Japanese-style mahjong against computer opposition, using a dedicated mahjong input layout. Its celebrity theme makes it an unusual example of an early-1990s Japanese arcade adapting a familiar tabletop pastime into a personality-driven game.

games.title: Tokoro San no MahMahjan 2
games.description: Tokoro San no MahMahjan 2, released by Sega in Japan in May 1994, continues the celebrity-branded mahjong game introduced two years earlier. Once again, television comedian George (Joji) Tokoro is the public face of a computerized Japanese mahjong competition. The sequel, sometimes subtitled Tokoro's Cup, retains the emphasis on traditional tile-based play rather than action mechanics. Running on Sega's System 24 family, it offers a useful glimpse into the niche for licensed, personality-led tabletop games in Japanese amusement centers.

games.title: Mahou Daisakusen
games.description:
Mahou Daisakusen, released internationally as Sorcer Striker, is Raizing's 1993 debut vertically scrolling shooter. Its setting replaces conventional fighter jets with a wild mixture of sorcery, machines, knights and goblin armies. Four selectable characters, including the swordsman Gain and the young witch Chitta, attack the mechanized forces of a goblin empire through six stages packed with aerial targets, ground threats and sprawling bosses. Each pilot has a distinctive attack configuration, and weapon items build up a steadily more destructive offense.

Developed by a team with roots in Compile's shoot-'em-up tradition, it became the first game in Raizing's Mahou Daisakusen line, followed by Kingdom Grandprix and Dimahoo. Its fantasy-industrial artwork, eccentric enemies and relentlessly escalating formations distinguish it from the military shooters of its era. The Japanese title literally evokes a grand magical military operation, a fitting description of its playful fantasy warfare.

games.title: Mahjong Kyoretsuden
games.description: Mahjong Kyoretsuden is one of SNK's earliest Neo Geo releases, appearing on the MVS in Japan in 1990. It presents Japanese riichi mahjong in a contemporary setting of mahjong parlors, with human opponents rather than fantasy monsters. An unusual character-creation feature lets the player assemble a face from several facial elements and enter a name before competing. This attempt to personalize a traditional tabletop contest makes the game a curiosity in the Neo Geo launch library, better known for action and fighting games than dedicated mahjong titles.

games.title: Maikobana
games.description: Maikobana is a 1990 Japanese arcade adaptation of hanafuda, the traditional card game played with illustrated flower cards. Produced by Nichibutsu, it combines ordinary card-matching and scoring rules with adult-themed reward illustrations featuring Japanese women. Rather than using action-game controls, players select cards and hands through a purpose-built tabletop interface. It represents a large, largely Japan-only branch of arcade entertainment in which familiar card games were packaged with character art and mature themes.

games.title: The Main Event

variants.title: The Main Event (4 Players ver. Y)
The Main Event (2 Players ver. X)
The Main Event (4 Players ver. F)
Ring no Ohja (Japan 2 Players ver. N)

games.description:
Konami's The Main Event (1988), known in Japan as Ring no Ohja, brings televised professional wrestling to a lively tag-team arcade format. Players choose two wrestlers from a roster of eight and fight through successive bouts, switching partners as the match demands. Grapples, strikes and tag tactics are accompanied by a noisy ringside presentation that evokes a professional wrestling broadcast. Certain overseas versions allow freer team selection than the original Japanese single-player setup.

Designed for multiplayer cabinets, the game supports versions with up to four participants and emphasizes the chaotic pace of tag wrestling over a solitary one-on-one championship ladder. It should not be confused with SNK's unrelated 1984 boxing game Main Event.

games.title: Main Event
games.description: SNK's Main Event (1984) is an arcade boxing game, unrelated to Konami's later wrestling game of the same name. From an angled, almost isometric view of the ring, the player faces a succession of boxers with different fighting styles. Punching consumes stamina, while taking hits reduces the boxer's power more severely; managing this meter is essential because a depleted fighter is knocked out. The unusual perspective and constant trade-off between aggression and endurance give it a distinctive feel among the era's boxing games.

games.title: Mahjong Studio 101
games.description: Mahjong Studio 101 is a Japanese gambling-style mahjong title released by Dynax in October 1988. It dresses traditional mahjong play in a movie-studio theme, rather than presenting the tiles as an abstract board game. The cabinet uses a dedicated mahjong keyboard, whose separate tile and action keys reflect the specialized control panels common in Japanese mahjong arcades. Its medal-game presentation and studio motif make it a representative example of Dynax's themed mahjong releases.

games.title: Major Title 2
games.description:
Irem's Major Title 2 (1992), released overseas as The Irem Skins Game, expands its arcade golf predecessor into a more varied contest. Up to four players select golfers with contrasting strengths, such as power hitting or precision, then play tournament, match, stroke or skins formats on two courses. The view changes from behind the golfer before the swing to a bird's-eye tracking shot once the ball is struck. Players set power beforehand and adjust a swing meter for trajectory and spin rather than working through a conventional multi-click simulation.

Its expressive sprites and accessible but nuanced ball control foreshadow the style of Neo Turf Masters. Several developers from Irem later formed Nazca, the studio behind that celebrated 1996 Neo Geo golf game, making Major Title 2 a fascinating link in arcade golf history.

games.title: Major Title
games.description:
Major Title is Irem's 1990 arcade golf game, casting the player in the final round of a major tournament with the objective of finishing eighteen holes atop the leaderboard. It blends a behind-the-golfer setup view with an overhead perspective that follows the ball in flight. Instead of the standard timed three-click swing, players select shot strength separately and use a vertical meter to determine launch angle and spin; changing stance can add draw or fade.

The simplified control system creates quick-paced golf while still rewarding judgement of distance, lie and green conditions. It supports multiplayer competition and led to the expanded 1992 sequel Major Title 2, also known overseas as The Irem Skins Game.

games.title: Mallet Madness
games.description: Mallet Madness is a 1999 video redemption attraction controlled with a physical handheld mallet rather than a joystick. The player strikes targets represented on screen, translating an old-fashioned fairground smashing game into a succession of animated challenges. Four selectable minigames include rescuing pirate captains from sharks and clearing crocodiles so people can cross a damaged bridge. Developed for dedicated Rapid Fire amusement hardware, its mixture of tactile controls and short, immediately understandable objectives was designed for the redemption-arcade floor rather than prolonged console-style play.

games.title: Malzak
games.description: Malzak is an exceptionally obscure early-1980s horizontally scrolling shooter produced in New Zealand by Kitronix. It has the feel of Konami's Scramble, with a spacecraft flying past hostile terrain and attacking threats along the route, but examination of the surviving program shows that it was not simply a copied Scramble ROM set. The game has its own implementation, making it a rare example of locally developed New Zealand arcade software. Two known variants, Malzak and Malzak II, survive, and their emulation required considerable investigation of the unusual Signetics video circuitry and stored game settings.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Mang-Chi
games.description: Mang-Chi is a 2000 Korean tile-matching puzzle game by Afega, built in the tradition of Columns and other falling-block arcades. Players arrange colored or illustrated pieces to create groups of matching symbols and clear room on the board. Its Korean name translates as 'hammer', and another version circulated as Hammer Boy. Related in style to the adult puzzle game Honey Dolls but without that game's mature presentation, Mang-Chi is an example of Afega's small, locally focused arcade catalog.

games.title: Mania Challenge
games.description:
Mania Challenge is Technos Japan's 1986 follow-up to Mat Mania, expanding the televised-wrestling formula with direct two-player competition. In the original game the player fought a ladder of theatrical wrestlers; this revision names its main grappler Dynamite Tommy and introduces Hurricane Joe as an equally capable second-player character. Throws, kicks, punches and turnbuckle action retain the deliberately exaggerated arcade wrestling style.

The roster is revised from Mat Mania and the presentation identifies its fictional wrestling circuit as the Taito Wrestling Federation. The ability for two friends to compete directly, rather than merely take alternating runs at the same computer opponents, is the edition's defining addition.

games.title: Maniac Square
games.description: Maniac Square is a 1996 puzzle game from the Spanish arcade studio Gaelco. It uses falling pairs of colored pieces that can be rotated and arranged into horizontal, vertical or diagonal matches of at least three. Occasional star pieces act as wildcards. The main pressure comes from a countdown timer: completing a required number of matches advances the goal meter and replenishes play time, so a steady stream of quick clears matters as much as large combinations. The brisk, simple design fits Gaelco's tradition of accessible, distinctly European coin-operated games.

games.title: Many Block
games.description: Many Block is an obscure 1991 block-puzzle project associated with UPL and the Korean company Bee-Oh. It originated from an unreleased UPL design called Jewels, which did not pass location testing; the recovered material is described as a late prototype rather than a successful commercial launch. The preserved game supports two players and uses eight-direction joysticks with two buttons on vertical-screen NMK-style hardware. Its chief interest is the unusual development trail from a Japanese company's abandoned puzzle game to a Korean-associated version, although surviving descriptions do not reliably document the precise block-clearing rules.

games.title: Mappy
games.description:
Namco's Mappy (1983) is a whimsical but surprisingly tactical platform game starring a police mouse reclaiming stolen household valuables from a mansion occupied by cats. Mappy runs along horizontal floors, bouncing between them on trampolines, while smaller Meowky cats and their leader Goro patrol the rooms. Unlike most platform heroes, Mappy cannot simply jump at will. Movement between stories depends on timed rebounds, and excessive use of the same trampoline causes it to break.

Doors are the game's signature weapon. Swinging one into a pursuing cat briefly stuns it, while special microwave doors send a wave across an entire corridor. Bells and trapdoors offer additional opportunities to outwit the pursuers. Recovering stolen stereos, televisions and paintings in a carefully chosen order increases scoring opportunities, as do occasional bonus rounds.

Its playful cartoon animation and memorable soundtrack helped Mappy become an enduring favorite in Japan, even though it achieved less recognition in North America. The combination of spatial planning, risk-reward scoring and precise timing gives the seemingly simple cat-and-mouse chase lasting depth.

games.title: Marble Madness
games.description:
Atari Games' Marble Madness (1984), designed by Mark Cerny, is one of the arcade's great experiments in turning a physical sensation into a video game. Using a trackball, players roll a glass marble through six intricate, isometric race courses filled with narrow bridges, ramps, moving hazards and enemies. The goal is not to defeat opponents but to reach each finish line before time expires. Leftover seconds carry into later races, while two simultaneous players can compete for faster finishes and time bonuses.

Momentum is everything. The marble must be nudged, accelerated and slowed with precision, and a careless turn can send it tumbling off an edge. The courses make memorable use of surreal architecture, hostile black marbles, moving obstacles and sudden changes in elevation, creating a game that feels closer to manipulating a real object than controlling a conventional sprite.

Marble Madness was the first game on Atari's System 1 platform and an early arcade showcase for richly layered synthesized stereo sound. Its distinctive angular visuals, trackball control and Brad Fuller and Hal Canon soundtrack have made it a landmark of mid-1980s arcade design and a widely ported cult classic.

games.title: Marble Madness II
games.description:
Marble Madness II, also known as Marble Man, is Atari Games' unreleased 1991 sequel to the trackball classic. It retains the challenge of guiding a rolling marble through isometric courses but greatly expands the journey, with numerous courses and three bonus rounds, new hazards, animated enemies and settings including an underwater section. The sequel gives the marble a more overtly cartoonish personality and introduces additional power-up abilities.

Atari built prototypes and tested the game but did not proceed with a commercial release. Surviving versions also reflect experiments with different controls after the distinctive trackball of the first game. Long known largely through photographs and collector accounts, Marble Madness II is a rare chance to see how Atari attempted to transform a celebrated 1984 design for the arcade market of the early 1990s.

games.title: Marine Boy
games.description: Marine Boy is a 1982 underwater action game from Orca. The player guides a swimmer through an ocean inhabited by hostile fish, firing at threats while helping dolphins and rescuing mermaids. Reaching a mermaid within a clam shell marks the goal of a stage. Its blend of swimming movement, shooting and rescues distinguishes it from the spaceship-based shooters that dominated the early arcade years. The aquatic setting also requires the player to navigate around creatures rather than merely hold position at the bottom of a screen.

games.title: Marine Date
games.description: Taito's Marine Date (1981) is an unusual underwater obstacle game whose hero is a red octopus determined to reunite with his yellow octopus sweetheart. A trackball controls the motion of the octopus as he bounces through a maze of coral, walls and hostile sharks. The challenge is to reach the waiting partner with a limited number of shots or movements before his energy is exhausted. An ink attack provides a means of dealing with a threatening shark. Its playful romantic premise and indirect, billiards-like navigation make it an early arcade curiosity rather than a conventional maze chase.

games.title: Mariner
games.description: Mariner (1981), also distributed as 800 Fathoms, is a scrolling submarine shooter from Amenip/Nova Games. A submarine fights through underwater passages, launching torpedoes at enemies in its path and missiles toward other threats. The horizontal voyage passes through five areas with changing terrain and increasingly crowded hazards, culminating in confrontations with large enemy submarines. Restricted passages become especially dangerous when the landscape encroaches on the craft. Its combination of scrolling, dual weapons and undersea scenery predates the more elaborate submarine shooters that followed later in the decade.

games.title: Mario Bros.
games.description:
Nintendo's Mario Bros. (1983), created under Shigeru Miyamoto's direction, transformed the hero of Donkey Kong into a plumber and introduced his brother Luigi. The two investigate sewers invaded by Shellcreepers, Sidesteppers and Fighterflies, clearing each single-screen phase of pests. The crucial rule is that enemies cannot normally be defeated by landing directly on them. Instead, the brothers jump into platforms from below to overturn a creature, then kick it while it lies helpless. Crabs require repeated hits, while flies must be struck at the right moment.

A central POW block flips enemies across the screen, and the left and right boundaries wrap around, creating tactical escapes and surprise encounters. Two players can cooperate to clear the sewers or mischievously interfere with each other, a deliberate part of the game's appeal. Periodic bonus rounds reward the collection of scattered coins, while later waves become faster and more crowded.

Mario Bros. established Luigi, the brothers' plumbing identity and many of the conventions associated with the franchise, even though its fixed-screen structure differs greatly from 1985's Super Mario Bros. Its rhythmic bump-and-kick combat and simultaneously competitive and cooperative play made it one of Nintendo's defining early arcade games.

games.title: Markham
games.description: Markham is a 1983 horizontal shooter from Sun Electronics in which a fighter aircraft is sent against hostile installations in Antarctica. Alongside conventional forward fire, the player can use missiles and adjust the angle of attack, making it possible to reach targets approaching from awkward positions. Its low-flying combat over research bases and other ground installations creates a different rhythm from fixed-direction side-scrollers. The ability to tilt the firing line is the game's most distinctive tactical feature, requiring attention to enemy placement as well as collision avoidance.

games.title: Mars
games.description: Mars is a 1981 scrolling space shooter from Artic, clearly belonging to the same early genre as Scramble. The player pilots a small satellite-shaped ship above a horizontally moving planetary landscape and attacks ground installations and airborne enemies. Its chief control distinction is the ability to fire in eight directions, allowing the craft to target threats that are not directly ahead. The mixture of shifting terrain, enemy formations and directional gunnery makes Mars an interesting contemporary variation on the emerging scrolling-shooter formula.

games.title: Martial Masters
games.description:
Martial Masters, known in Chinese as Xing Yi Quan, is IGS's lavishly animated one-on-one fighting game for the PolyGame Master arcade system. Set amid the turmoil at the end of China's Qing dynasty, it draws heavily on Chinese martial arts traditions, mixing stylized historical fighters, exaggerated techniques and fluid hand-drawn action. Players choose from a diverse cast and use throws, aerial attacks, special moves and elaborate super attacks in fast-moving two-dimensional duels.

Its combo system rewards precise sequences and includes special pressure techniques and quick recovery options after knockdowns. The unusually expressive animation, with sweeping clothing and clearly differentiated fighting styles, is the game's major attraction. Often compared with Capcom's Street Fighter III for its visual craftsmanship, Martial Masters became a cult favorite among enthusiasts of lesser-known arcade fighting systems.

games.title: Maru-Chan de Goo!
games.description: Maru-Chan de Goo! is a 1997 Japanese Sega ST-V party game built around the licensed Maru-chan instant-noodle mascot. Rather than following a single long campaign, it pits two players against one another in short, ramen-themed minigames. The bright promotional style and quick competitions reflect the Japanese amusement industry's appetite for branded attractions during the late 1990s. Its cartridge-based Titan Video hardware shares much of its architecture with Sega's Saturn, making it a striking example of a consumer-oriented advertising character appearing in a dedicated arcade game.

games.title: Super Marukin-Ban
games.description: Super Marukin-Ban is a 1990 Japanese adult-themed mahjong game associated with Yuga. It uses the familiar framework of one-player mahjong against computer-controlled opponents, with illustrations of women supplying the presentation and reward scenes. Known in Japanese as Mahjong Super Marukin-ban, it belongs to the extensive local market for mature mahjong cabinets, where traditional tile strategy was blended with provocative artwork. The gameplay is fundamentally tabletop mahjong rather than a reflex-based puzzle or action game.

games.title: Chibi Marukochan Deluxe Quiz
games.description: Chibi Maruko-chan Deluxe Quiz is Takara's 1995 Japanese Neo Geo MVS trivia game based on the popular manga and anime about the schoolgirl Maruko. Styled as a colorful quiz and variety show, it lets players assemble a small team with Maruko and two selected supporting characters, each contributing different attributes. Questions and character interludes make familiarity with the series and Japanese language important. Unlike action-heavy Neo Geo releases, this title is primarily a celebration of a licensed television property through a traditional arcade quiz format.

games.title: Marvin's Maze
games.description: Marvin's Maze is SNK's 1983 maze action game about collecting dots while escaping or destroying hostile Robonoids. It offers two ways to clear a maze: gather every dot or destroy the required number of robots shown on the screen. The player's weapons are equally versatile, since enemies can be shot directly or dropped through sections of flooring activated by the game's 'Trick' mechanism. This makes traps and route planning just as valuable as accurate firing. Released in Japan under the title ACW, Marvin's Maze is a creative variation on the Pac-Man-era maze formula.

games.title: Marvel Land
games.description:
Namco's Marvel Land (1989) is a colorful side-scrolling platform adventure set inside a fantasy amusement park. Players guide Prince Paco, known as Talmit in some English versions, on a quest to free Princess Luxie and the park's guardians from the evil Mole King. Stages traverse fairground attractions, twisting pathways and boss arenas, with power-ups such as winged boots and other magical aids changing the hero's movement and attacks.

The game makes unusually inventive use of its theme, including parade-style sequences, rides and nods to Namco's own characters. Although its jumping and exploration invite comparisons with Super Mario Bros., the spectacle of a magical theme park, varied stage layouts and whimsical sprite art establish a personality of its own. It is a particularly charming example of what Namco's System 2 hardware could deliver outside its better-known driving and shooting games.

games.title: Master Boy
games.description: Master Boy is Gaelco's 1991 Spanish arcade quiz game, succeeding an earlier 1987 title with a more graphical presentation. One or two players answer a succession of true-or-false questions after selecting a subject such as science, geography, history, music or sport. Questions are further divided into difficulty tiers including Junior, Senior, Master and group play. Its Spanish-language educational and pop-culture focus gave it a regional identity unlike the often Japanese-only quiz games of the period. This is a documented question-and-answer game, not an undocumented gambling or trivia cabinet.

games.title: Master of Weapon
games.description:
Taito's Master of Weapon (1989) is a vertical-scrolling shooter set on a devastated future Earth. After nuclear catastrophe, a reconstruction computer called the God System turns against humanity, and the player pilots a combat craft to stop its machines. The ship begins with a forward photon cannon and ground-directed bombs. Collecting P icons increases the cannon's spread, while marked supply capsules offer other weapons; even the ship's exhaust can harm close pursuers.

The game's grim science-fiction setting and varied mechanical enemies give it a character distinct from Taito's brighter shooters. A preserved early prototype, named Yukiwo after its programmer, provides a rare view into its development before it acquired the final Master of Weapon title.

games.title: Master's Fury
games.description: Master's Fury is a 1996 Korean one-on-one fighting game and follow-up to Dragon Master. It offers ten playable combatants, each with a separate assortment of martial-arts strikes and special attacks, in a format influenced by Street Fighter II and Fatal Fury. Players move through international matchups against computer opponents or challenge a second player. The surviving PCB was labeled Dragon Master '96, connecting the sequel directly to its predecessor. Its recovery and later emulation improvements helped preserve a relatively little-known corner of Korea's mid-1990s fighting-game scene.

games.title: The Masters of Kin
games.description: The Masters of Kin is a late-1980s side-scrolling fantasy beat-'em-up in which the warrior Zorg pursues the sorcerer Zangar after his wife is kidnapped. He advances through monster-filled medieval landscapes, attacking with his sword and facing hostile creatures on the way to Zangar's castle. The game mixes mythological storytelling with simple arcade combat and continuous side-scrolling progression. Its rough presentation and obscure history mark it as an unusual, independently produced alternative to the better-known fantasy action games of the period.

games.title: Match It II
games.description: Match It II, released in Japan as Shisensho II in 1993, is Irem's sequel to its popular solitaire tile-matching puzzle. Players remove pairs of identical illustrated tiles from a crowded board, but a pair is valid only if the two can be linked by a path containing no more than two right-angle turns. Finding pairs therefore involves looking several moves ahead, since an apparently easy match can block a better route later. Decorative artwork and additional options build on the original Shisensho's quiet but exacting challenge. It is a game of spatial deduction rather than falling-piece reflexes.

games.title: The Mating Game
games.description:
The Mating Game is a British single-player skill-with-prizes video amusement title produced by Barcrest, probably around 1996, for the company's MPU4 Video platform. This was a coin-operated prize-machine environment rather than a conventional joystick-driven action arcade system. The hardware paired an MPU4 controller based on the Motorola 6809 with a separate Motorola 68000 video subsystem, and this title used additional OKI sampled-sound hardware. Modern MAME maps a trackball and four color-coded buttons, labeled Left Red, Left Yellow, Right Yellow, and Right Red.

MAME 0.106 catalogued two editions, Datapak and Standard, both of which were then marked non-working. The documented ROM differences include changes disabling the data logger in the Standard set. Although the game's prize-machine classification and controls are known, surviving driver notes do not establish its precise questions, challenges, scoring, or payout rules.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Mat Mania
games.description:
Mat Mania, released in Japan as Exciting Hour, is Technos Japan's 1985 professional wrestling arcade game, published in North America by Taito. Its televised presentation features a hyperactive announcer and a sequence of flamboyant opponents as the player battles toward the championship. Each wrestler has distinctive tactics, from brawling to acrobatic maneuvers, and the player must master punches, kicks, grapples, throws and attacks from the ropes to pin opponents.

The game's exaggerated personalities and readable wrestling moves gave early arcade wrestling a sense of televised drama uncommon at the time. Its commercial success led to the 1986 revision Mania Challenge, which added competitive two-player wrestling. Alongside Technos's earlier Tag Team Wrestling, Mat Mania helped establish the vocabulary for later arcade wrestling games.

games.title: Matrimelee / Shin Gouketsuji Ichizoku Toukon
games.description:
Matrimelee, the 2002 Neo Geo installment of Atlus's Power Instinct/Gouketsuji fighting series, is an exuberant parody of the traditional one-on-one tournament. The eccentric Gouketsuji clan holds a contest connected to a royal marriage, bringing together returning oddballs, fresh challengers and a number of guest fighters. Its animated combat mixes familiar special moves and combos with bizarre transformations, slapstick humor and an irreverent tone far removed from more solemn martial-arts games.

Developed by Noise Factory, it makes lively use of the Neo Geo's aging hardware with expressive sprites, energetic music and crowd-pleasing visual gags. The bizarre roster and deliberately eccentric personality make Matrimelee a cult favorite among players seeking a fighting game beyond the usual Street Fighter and King of Fighters conventions.

games.title: Mausuke no Ojama the World

variants.title: Mausuke no Ojama the World (J 960314 V1.000)

games.description: Mausuke no Ojama the World is a 1996 Japanese competitive puzzle game from Data East, released on Sega's ST-V arcade hardware. It presents a character-led falling-piece contest starring Mausuke, a large-mouthed mascot reflected in the game's mouth-shaped pieces. Two players can compete as the board fills and carefully arranged matches clear space while disrupting the rival's progress. Sometimes identified overseas as Kiss Off, it is a quirky example of the character-focused puzzle boom of the mid-1990s, with unusual artwork and an arcade platform closely related to the Sega Saturn.

games.title: Max-A-Flex
games.description:
Exidy's Max-A-Flex was an unusually direct attempt to turn home-computer software into a commercial arcade platform in 1984. The cabinet contained an Atari 600XL computer and accepted standard Atari 8-bit cartridges, allowing operators to change games without replacing the machine's main electronics. Its original selection comprised Boulder Dash, Astro Chase, Flip & Flop, and Bristles, all published by First Star Software. A conventional eight-way joystick and single action button provided the arcade controls.

The defining feature was a separate coin-operated timer. Credits bought playing time rather than lives: an on-screen countdown and warning sounds urged players to insert more coins, and the controls stopped responding when time expired, even if lives remained. The game itself could continue running in the background until another credit was added. This ingenious but awkward arrangement makes Max-A-Flex an early precursor to the more familiar multi-game, time-based arcade systems that followed later in the decade.

games.title: Maximum Force v1.05
games.description:
Maximum Force is Atari Games' 1997 light-gun rail shooter, created by Mesa Logic as a follow-up to its work on Area 51. Players aim and fire at armed terrorists as prerecorded, digitized video environments sweep the screen, reloading by shooting off-screen. The missions move through hostile locations and reward both quick target identification and accuracy, while carelessly shooting civilians incurs penalties. A second gun allows cooperative play.

The game combines a grounded counterterrorist theme with exaggerated arcade action and hidden targets. The AdvanceMAME set identified as v1.05 represents a specific software revision; a no-gore version and earlier revisions are also documented. Its filmed scenery and direct gun controls typify the mid-1990s revival of the arcade shooting gallery.

games.title: Max RPM
games.description:
Bally Midway's Max RPM (1986) is a two-player driving game built around an unusual vertically split monitor. Each player gets an independent view of the road, complete with a rear-view mirror, while racing through drag-strip, city and country-road sections. The dedicated cabinet supplies steering wheels, accelerator pedals and four-position gearshifts, making it a more physical driving experience than joystick-operated racers. A computer opponent fills the other lane when playing alone.

The separate views can depict both cars when they approach one another, increasing the sense of a shared race despite the split display. The combination of manual shifting and direct head-to-head competition distinguishes Max RPM from most contemporary arcade racers.

games.title: Maya
games.description: Maya (1994) is an adult-themed solitaire tile-matching game, commonly associated with Promat. Players remove pairs of mahjong-style tiles from a stacked arrangement, uncovering background illustrations as the board clears. Rather than simulating a full competitive mahjong match, the game uses the spatial matching format found in Shanghai-style solitaire. Preservation notes identify its code and layout as closely derived from Dynax's Dragon Punch/Sports Match, with replacement artwork. That connection makes it another example of how frequently mid-1990s arcade puzzle programs were adapted for different markets and presentations.

games.title: Mayday
games.description:
Mayday, also styled Mayday!!, is an early-1980s scrolling spacecraft shooter from Hoei. The ship travels across a hostile planetary landscape, firing both forward and backward at waves of attackers. An eight-way joystick changes position and speed, while a dedicated Mayday button briefly slows the action, giving the player a chance to escape dangerous formations. The fast scrolling and rescue-free combat recall the slightly earlier Defender.

Its broad resemblance to Defender caused Williams to regard it as an infringement, and the resulting dispute reportedly ended production. The emergency slow-motion control and bidirectional fire nevertheless give Mayday a recognizable identity beyond its contemporary inspirations.

games.title: Mayhem 2002
games.description: Mayhem 2002 is Cinematronics' 1985 futuristic arena sport, combining elements of soccer, roller derby and full-contact combat. Players chase a ball around the playfield, jostle rivals with elbows and attempt to deliver the ball into whichever of four goals is currently illuminated. It can be thrown from a distance or carried toward the goal, and successful scores add points. The shifting active target ensures that possession alone is not enough: players must track the open goal while keeping opponents away from the ball. Its odd hybrid of sports and arena fighting stands apart from conventional arcade simulations.

games.title: Mayjinsen
games.description: Mayjinsen is a 1994 Japanese arcade shogi game by Seta, devoted to the traditional strategy game often called Japanese chess. Players compete on a nine-by-nine board, moving differentiated pieces and using the distinctive shogi rule that captured pieces can later be dropped back into play. Presented as a rapid-fire championship, it appeared on Seta hardware associated with the ST-0016 graphics system. The game belongs to a niche in which traditional tabletop competition was made available in coin-operated cabinets rather than home computers.

games.title: Mayjinsen 2
games.description: Mayjinsen 2 is Seta's late-1994 sequel to its arcade shogi title, continuing the Japanese chess competition on the company's specialized arcade hardware. As in traditional shogi, victory requires mating the opposing king, with captured pieces available for redeployment under shogi's distinctive drop rules. The game is a digital treatment of an established board game rather than a new action or puzzle format. Its presence alongside the first Mayjinsen illustrates the long Japanese arcade tradition of electronic shogi and mahjong play.

games.title: Kikiippatsu Mayumi-chan
games.description: Kikiippatsu Mayumi-chan is a 1988 Japanese mahjong arcade game from Victory, with a presentation centered on a group of cheerleaders. Its principal play follows traditional Japanese mahjong conventions, while a password system allows aspects of a player's progress to be preserved between sessions. The title, loosely evoking Mayumi-chan in a moment of danger, combines familiar tile-based strategy with the character art and novelty features common to Japanese tabletop arcade machines in the late 1980s.

games.title: Amazing Maze
games.description:
Midway's Amazing Maze (1976) is an early competitive video maze game, built around a deceptively simple contest: two players begin at opposite sides of a newly generated labyrinth and race to reach one another's starting position. A brief preview gives both participants a chance to inspect the walls before moving their geometric markers with joysticks. In single-player games, the machine supplies an opponent; the winner earns the point for that maze.

Its randomly changing layouts put memory, route planning and quick decision-making ahead of combat. Released years before Pac-Man established the familiar maze-chase template, Amazing Maze is a valuable example of how early arcade developers used simple graphics and direct human competition to create a tense, replayable game.

games.title: Maze Invaders
games.description:
Maze Invaders is an unreleased Atari maze-action prototype from 1981, field-tested in 1982. Players work through shifting mazes to collect fruit while avoiding hostile creatures. Walls and passages move, so familiar routes can change unexpectedly, and the player's weapon can destroy certain enemies while only stunning others. The mixture of maze collecting and shooting suggests an experimental alternative to the successful fixed-layout maze games of the period.

The project failed its location tests and did not become a production cabinet; only a very small number of machines are reported to survive. Its later recovery makes it a particularly interesting look at Atari's abandoned early-1980s experiments.

games.title: Mazer Blazer
games.description: Stern's Mazer Blazer (1983) is an arcade shooting-gallery game with a striking two-handed electronic gun controller. The player fires into a maze to stop waves of cosmic attackers from reaching a vulnerable base. Enemy creatures follow paths through differently colored zones that influence their scoring value, and numerous alien types change the rhythm of each round. Shooting flashing blocks can raise a force field and delay an advance, adding a small tactical element to the otherwise rapid target shooting. Its large physical gun and maze-defense premise make it one of the more unusual shooting attractions of the early 1980s.

games.title: Mazinger Z
games.description:
Mazinger Z is a 1994 vertical-scrolling shooter by Banpresto based on Go Nagai's enormously influential giant-robot manga and anime. Players choose one of three famous super robots, Mazinger Z, Great Mazinger or Grendizer, and fly into battles against successive waves of mechanical enemies. Each robot can use a normal ranged weapon, a close-range energy attack and a powerful special move, producing a blend of conventional shooter patterns and close-up mecha combat.

The appeal lies in controlling recognizable anime machines rather than anonymous fighter craft, supported by oversized robotic enemies and attacks that evoke the original television series. It is an uncommon case of a licensed anime property receiving a dedicated arcade scrolling shooter rather than a fighting or adventure game.

games.title: Magical Cat Adventure
games.description:
Magical Cat Adventure is a 1993 Japanese side-scrolling platform game from Wintechno, starring a mischievous magical cat who battles through forests, caves, ships, castles and other fantasy settings. The hero jumps between ledges, avoids traps and fights enemies using an assortment of weapons found in chests, ranging from simple projectiles to more spectacular magical attacks. The colorful, expressive sprite art and plentiful scenery give the game the feel of a cartoon adventure.

The export release differs from the Japanese version, known as Catt, in its storytelling, animations, graphics and difficulty balance. Those regional differences make it more than a straightforward renamed edition, and they are of particular interest to arcade preservationists.

games.title: Multi Champ Deluxe
games.description: Multi Champ Deluxe is a Korean compilation-style arcade game from ESD, appearing around 1999-2000. Players choose from six short games modeled on familiar arcade and tabletop formats: a maze chase in the style of Pac-Man, falling-block puzzles reminiscent of Columns and Tetris, a Pang-like shooting challenge, Shanghai tile matching and card solitaire. Adult-themed character rewards tie the otherwise separate games together. Its charm and historical interest lie in the attempt to package a miniature multi-genre arcade collection on one board rather than create a wholly new play mechanic.

games.title: Mahjong Campus Hunting
games.description: Mahjong Campus Hunting is a 1990 Japanese adult-themed mahjong game developed by Dynax. It presents mahjong contests against illustrated female opponents in a campus-themed setting, using the tile selections and strategic decisions of Japanese arcade mahjong rather than reflex-based action. The game belongs to Dynax's extensive series of mature tabletop titles, a specialized but commercially significant segment of the Japanese amusement market. Its appeal is rooted in conventional mahjong rules coupled with character-driven presentation.

games.title: Miss Mahjong Contest
games.description: Miss Mahjong Contest in Yakuman Daigaku is a 1989 adult-themed Japanese mahjong game by Nichibutsu. The conceit is a beauty competition decided at the mahjong table: players face female rivals in tile-based contests, with illustrated reward scenes supplying the pageant atmosphere. Standard Japanese mahjong tactics remain the central activity, while the framing gives the game a recognizable identity among the many mature mahjong titles of the era. The playful combination of a campus setting and a beauty contest is characteristic of Nichibutsu's late-1980s arcade catalog.

games.title: Derby Quiz My Dream Horse
games.description: Derby Quiz: My Dream Horse is a 1998 Japanese horse-racing trivia game from Namco, released on its System 12 arcade hardware. It centers its questions and presentation on the world of thoroughbred racing rather than offering a conventional driving or horse-racing simulation. Players select answers using dedicated buttons, with knowledge of Japanese racing culture and written Japanese essential to progressing. Its distinctive subject makes it a rare example of a specialist quiz game on hardware otherwise famous for visually elaborate fighting games such as Tekken 3.

games.title: Mechanized Attack
games.description:
SNK's Mechanized Attack (1989) is a gun-controlled arcade action game in which players assault a tropical island occupied by a secret army of cyborgs. Shooting begins with an approach over water against gunboats, helicopters and a battleship, then moves inland through escalating encounters. What initially look like human or animal adversaries reveal mechanical bodies when damaged, giving the invasion a distinctive science-fiction twist. Certain points let players choose their route through the campaign.

The original cabinet's direct aiming and rapid-fire shooting distinguish it from ordinary joystick scrolling games. A Nintendo Entertainment System adaptation followed in 1990, with support for the NES Zapper, but the arcade edition is the primary gun-game experience.

games.title: Meadows Lanes
games.description: Meadows Lanes is a 1977 black-and-white arcade bowling game for one or two players. A bowler near the bottom of the screen can be moved laterally before delivering the ball. Players influence the shot's speed and hook, attempting to knock down the pins and accumulate the best score over ten frames. Its minimal screen presentation concentrates on the fundamentals of bowling, timing and lane position. As an early electronic sports simulation, it illustrates how developers translated a familiar physical pastime into simple arcade controls before color sports games became common.

games.title: Mega Blast
games.description:
Mega Blast (1989) is Taito's energetic multi-directional scrolling shooter, built around a spacecraft surrounded by four gun turrets. Rather than relying solely on a forward cannon, the player can fire across different angles and upgrade individual turrets by collecting power-up orbs. The landscape generally moves horizontally but sometimes shifts into vertical scrolling, forcing players to adapt their positioning and firing patterns. Two players can fight through the invasion together.

A particularly playful feature is its array of minibosses and enemies that resemble characters and machines from other Taito games. Beneath its science-fiction exterior, Mega Blast serves as a colorful tribute to the company's arcade history, with weapon management and multidirectional fire supplying the distinctive challenge.

games.title: Megadon
games.description:
Megadon (1982), developed by Epos and licensed to Photar, is a curious maze-based space shooter. The player's small ship navigates enclosed arenas, firing ion bombs at the so-called Cosmic Infidels while avoiding dangerous walls and other creatures. Missed shots ricochet around the maze and can eventually strike the player, making accuracy as important as quick reflexes. Some enemies require multiple hits, and a dwindling fuel supply discourages hesitation.

Contemporary advertising promoted its large number of increasingly difficult maze layouts. The unusual danger of one's own bouncing projectiles gives Megadon a memorable risk-reward mechanic very different from straightforward fixed-screen shooting.

games.title: Mega Man - The Power Battle

variants.title: Mega Man - The Power Battle (CPS1 Asia 951006)
Mega Man: The Power Battle (CPS2, USA 951006, SAMPLE Version)
Mega Man: The Power Battle (CPS2, USA 950926, SAMPLE Version)
Mega Man: The Power Battle (CPS2, USA 950925, SAMPLE Version)

games.description:
Mega Man: The Power Battle (1995) adapts Capcom's platform-shooter hero to the arcades in a distinctive boss-rush format. Instead of negotiating long stages, players choose Mega Man, Proto Man or Bass and immediately confront Robot Masters drawn from the console series. Three different routes offer sets of six opponents, each with its own attack patterns and weaknesses. Winning a duel grants a defeated boss's weapon, which can then be used against later adversaries, before the campaign culminates in the confrontation with Dr. Wily.

Built for Capcom's CPS-2 platform, it preserves the familiar jumping, charged shots and special-weapon strategy in compact, arcade-friendly encounters. Two players can cooperate, turning traditionally solitary Mega Man battles into shared tests of timing. Its colorful animation and rearranged boss themes made it a welcome celebration of the original series.

games.title: Mega Man 2: The Power Fighters
games.description:
Mega Man 2: The Power Fighters (1996) refines Capcom's arcade boss-battle formula, with Mega Man, Proto Man and Bass joined by the powerful robot Duo. Two players can cooperate as they fight Robot Masters, collect defeated enemies' weapons and work toward a final confrontation with Dr. Wily. Each character has different attributes and moves, while selectable story paths give the campaign varied goals and boss selections.

The sequel's larger cast, more expressive animation and additional combat options turn the concept into a spirited mixture of classic Mega Man action and fighting-game presentation.
