Rather than a conventional platform adventure, it is a sequence of concentrated boss encounters whose shared-screen cooperative play is its defining arcade feature.

games.title: Mega Play BIOS
games.description:
Sega's Mega Play was a cartridge-based arcade system derived from the Mega Drive/Genesis and introduced in the early 1990s. Like the earlier Mega-Tech, it brought console-related software into commercial amusement cabinets, but its business model was different: coins purchased ordinary game credits, and play ended through the game's own game-over rules rather than when a common timer expired. The JAMMA-compatible system provided four cartridge slots and used special arcade cartridges that could not simply be played on a domestic Mega Drive.

Mega Play was restricted to Mega Drive-derived titles rather than also supporting Master System software. Its BIOS coordinated the arcade-specific cartridge and credit functions, making this entry a system component rather than a standalone game. The hardware illustrates Sega's shift from selling timed demonstrations of console games to offering console-derived games as conventional coin-operated attractions.

games.title: Megatack
games.description:
Megatack (1980) is an unusual fixed-screen space shooter featuring a small Spacepod confronted by alternating waves of monsters and expanding rings. The Spacepod can fire upward and diagonally to either side, though rapidly tapping the firing control changes the pattern of shots. Enemies descend from above and can become especially dangerous once they reach the player's level. In the alternating ring rounds, larger rings split into additional targets when hit, forcing careful target selection and timing.

With its distinctive three-way firing and two very different enemy patterns, Megatack stands apart from the endless orderly formations of Space Invaders. Surviving instruction material also documents operator-selectable starting lives, reflecting the tuning available on early arcade machines.

games.title: Mega-Tech BIOS
games.description:
Sega's Mega-Tech, introduced in 1989, transformed the Mega Drive/Genesis into a multi-game arcade attraction at a time when the console was still relatively new. Developed by Sega's European operation, it used interchangeable cartridges and could run specially prepared Mega Drive games as well as a smaller selection of Master System titles. Players inserted coins to purchase a limited amount of time, then selected a game and could move between available titles while that time remained.

A distinctive feature was its dual-monitor arrangement. One screen displayed the game while the other showed the selection menu, instructions, and a running timer. The system was therefore as much a public showcase for Sega's home software as an arcade platform in its own right. The later Mega Play system adopted a more conventional credit-and-game-over structure, making the difference between the two BIOS sets historically significant.

games.title: Mega Zone
games.description:
Konami's Mega Zone (1983) is an overhead scrolling shooter in which the player pilots an amphibious rocket tank through heavily fortified territory. A single weapon can destroy both air and ground threats, while occasional forks in the route allow a choice of paths and enemy formations. Gathering power-energy pods eventually summons a MEG item that combines the tank with another machine, enlarging it and substantially increasing firepower.

The campaign builds toward an assault on the fortress command tower, whose mechanical defenses must be attacked at vulnerable moments. Combining Xevious-like aerial combat with a transforming ground vehicle and branching routes, Mega Zone is an inventive early scrolling shooter from Konami's pre-Gradius period.

games.title: Megumi Rescue
games.description:
Megumi Rescue is an unreleased 1987 Sega System E arcade prototype built around an ingenious firefighting action puzzle. Two firefighters carry a rescue sheet along the street while a third bounces on it toward the windows of a burning building. The player must position the sheet correctly and send the airborne rescuer into openings to save trapped people, while avoiding flames and other dangers. The action has some of the timing and ricochet qualities of a ball-and-paddle game but a completely different theme.

The arcade version reportedly failed its location test, yet the concept survived in a 1988 Sega Master System release. Its recovery as an arcade prototype offers a rare look at a Sega game that reached home players only after its intended coin-operated debut was abandoned.

games.title: Meijinsen
games.description: Meijinsen is a 1986 Japanese arcade adaptation of shogi, Japan's traditional chess-like strategy game. Opponents move their differentiated pieces across a nine-by-nine board and can reintroduce captured pieces into play, a rule that distinguishes shogi from Western chess. The title refers to a shogi championship, and the cabinet offers a computer opponent rather than an action-based campaign. Its surviving hardware and revisions document the era when Japanese manufacturers brought specialized board-game simulations into video arcades.

games.title: Meosis Magic
games.description:
Meosis Magic is a Japanese medal-machine game by Sammy, preserved in a 1990s arcade set. It belongs to the country's coin-operated medal and video-slot scene, where cabinet credits and token payouts are integral to the attraction rather than a conventional score attack. The game uses a two-way joystick and five buttons on hardware driven by a NEC V60-class CPU, a distinctive configuration for a gambling-style machine.

The available records establish its medal-game identity and controls but not the exact symbols, bonuses or payout combinations, so those details should not be assumed from other Sammy machines.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Mercs
games.description:
Mercs is Capcom's 1990 run-and-gun action game and the arcade successor to Commando, known in Japan as Senjo no Ookami II. Three soldiers of the Wolf Force unit fight through a fictional African conflict to rescue a kidnapped former president. Viewed from above, players move in eight directions while firing at enemy troops, vehicles and fortified positions. The arcade version's standout feature is simultaneous three-player cooperation, turning the relentless enemy formations into a noisy team assault.

The soldiers can collect stronger weapons, deploy screen-clearing special attacks and commandeer military hardware at particular points. Large enemy tanks, armored vehicles and other bosses punctuate its multi-stage campaign, while Capcom's CPS-1 hardware supports rich terrain details and numerous moving combatants.

With its direct controls, spectacular explosions and compact stages, Mercs represents the mature form of Capcom's 1980s military shooter formula. It is one of the best-known arcade examples of three-player cooperative run-and-gun action and remains distinct from the substantially altered Sega Genesis and home-computer versions.

games.title: Merlins Money Maze
games.description: Merlin's Money Maze is a little-known single-player maze game made by Zilec-Zenitone in 1986. The player navigates a maze with a four-direction joystick rather than playing a shooter or a falling-block puzzle. Released during the period when Zilec was producing small-run British coin-operated games, it survives mainly through arcade ROM preservation and brief catalogue records; detailed information about its level objectives and scoring rules remains scarce.

games.title: Mermaid
games.description: Mermaid (1982) is an unusual boating and windsurfing arcade game developed by Sanritsu and distributed in North America by Rock-Ola. The player guides a small one-masted craft from harbor to harbor through stretches of hazardous water, avoiding obstacles while negotiating the course. Its focus on boat handling rather than shooting gives the game a rare nautical sporting theme for its era. The game circulated under different distribution arrangements, helping this modest, unconventional arcade title reach markets outside Japan.

games.title: Meta Fox
games.description: Meta Fox is Seta's 1989 vertically scrolling military shooter, placing the player in a blue aircraft against enemy fighters, helicopters, tanks, ships and gun emplacements. The plane has unlimited standard fire and a supply of powerful bombs for clearing dangerous clusters. P-marked items strengthen its weapons, while additional power-ups can improve its offensive capabilities. The mixture of air and ground targets keeps the action busy as the battlefield continuously advances. Its straightforward approach and vivid enemy variety make it a characteristic late-1980s alternative to the better-known shooters from Capcom and Toaplan.

games.title: Metal Black
games.description:
Taito's Metal Black (1991) is a visually striking horizontal shooter in which pilot John Ford takes a prototype Black Fly fighter into battle against the alien Nemesis forces. Earth has already suffered catastrophic defeat, and the remaining hope lies in harnessing energy particles called Newalone. Collecting these particles raises the ship's firepower and charges a powerful beam attack, but the same resource is also sought by major enemies. Boss fights become spectacular beam duels in which each side tries to overpower the other.

Unlike shooters built around interchangeable weapon pickups and screen-clearing bombs, Metal Black focuses on this single escalating energy system. Deciding whether to maintain a strong regular shot or expend gathered Newalone in a dramatic beam strike provides the central tactical choice. The six-stage journey is filled with surreal imagery, haunting music by Zuntata and unsettling glimpses of humanity's collapse.

Originally conceived in relation to Taito's Gun Frontier and sometimes regarded as an unofficial continuation of its ideas, Metal Black became a cult favorite for its dark science-fiction atmosphere, elaborate parallax effects and unconventional weapon mechanic. It is widely remembered as one of Taito's most artistically distinctive shooters.

games.title: Metamorphic Force
games.description:
Metamorphic Force is Konami's 1993 side-scrolling beat-'em-up with a shape-shifting twist. Four warriors answer a goddess's call to defeat a resurrected evil king, fighting through monster-filled fantasy stages in the familiar belt-scrolling style of Final Fight. Each hero can collect a golden statue to transform into a powerful anthropomorphic beast, dramatically changing attacks and combat strength. A lion, wolf, bear and minotaur-like form give the quartet distinctive personalities and fighting styles.

The transformations and large animated enemies are the major attraction, while cooperative play lets friends unleash their animal forms together. Its vivid graphics, forceful soundtrack and fantastical rather than urban setting make Metamorphic Force one of Konami's more memorable late-period arcade brawlers.

games.title: Metal Clash
games.description: Metal Clash is Data East's unusual 1985 robot-combat game, blending elements of a fighting game and a fixed-screen shooter. Players pilot a flying mechanical fighter called Saiber, destroying minor robots before confronting larger alien machines. Punches, kicks and aerial movement replace the usual focus on gunfire, and certain flying enemies can restore energy when destroyed. The result is a succession of science-fiction duels and skirmishes rather than a conventional one-on-one martial-arts tournament. Its combination of mecha characters, close-range attacks and an early arcade fighting structure makes it a distinctive curiosity of the mid-1980s.

games.title: Metal Hawk
games.description:
Namco's Metal Hawk (1988) is a spectacular helicopter combat game played on a cabinet with an analog flight stick. The player pilots an attack helicopter over a large battlefield, racing to score enough points before the timer expires. Guns destroy airborne targets while missiles strike tanks, vessels and other ground or sea installations. The helicopter can maneuver around the battlefield and change altitude, revealing more of the terrain below.

The game's striking presentation comes from Namco's scaling and rotation technology, which gives the ground a sense of depth as the helicopter swoops over it. The effect evokes a cross between the strategic overhead action of Assault and Sega's arcade flight shooters. Its specialized controls and demanding hardware made it an ambitious attraction, and its combination of aerial freedom with timed target hunting remains highly distinctive.

games.title: Metal Saver
games.description:
Metal Saver is a 1994 Korean single-screen platform action game from First Amusement, built around the enemy-clearing formula popularized by Snow Bros. and Bubble Bobble. Players select Hanbit, a martial artist, or Narae, a gun-wielding girl, and use their different attacks to eliminate every enemy before advancing to the next stage. The two characters can also fight together in cooperative play, and periodic boss encounters include an oversized spider.

The game is an interesting artifact of Korea's mid-1990s arcade industry. Its 68000-based board closely resembles that of Final Tetris, and early MAME researchers noted similarities between its protection circuitry and later Semicom games, although a direct company relationship has not been established.

games.title: Metamoqester
games.description:
Metamoqester, released by Banpresto in 1995 and developed by Pandorabox, is an unusual boss-rush fighting game that replaces conventional one-on-one tournaments with cooperative battles against enormous monsters. One or two players choose from three heroes and attack elaborately animated creatures with weak, medium, and strong strikes, plus a fourth button for shooting or throwing a weapon. Its spectacle and team-based approach recall Konami's Monster Maulers more than Street Fighter II.

Released in Japan as Oni: The Ninja Master, it draws on Pandorabox's In'nin role-playing game setting. The floating symbols seen in its introduction use Siddham script, traditionally associated with Buddhist Sanskrit texts. Running on early Cave-developed arcade hardware, it remains a distinctive experiment in the fighting genre.

games.title: Metro-Cross
games.description:
Namco's Metro-Cross (1985) turns a futuristic obstacle course into a race against the clock. Its helmeted hero, the Runner, dashes through 32 side-scrolling rounds, weaving around moving barriers, collapsing floor panels, bouncing tires, and other hazards. Rather than simply pressing a button to run, players use an eight-way joystick to regulate speed and shift between lanes while a separate button makes the Runner jump. Reaching the finish line in time is essential: expiration of the countdown results in the Runner being electrocuted and an immediate game over.

The course design rewards learning how obstacles and useful objects interact. Green slippery zones slow progress, springboards can launch the Runner forward, and skateboards provide both speed and protection from slippery tiles. Drink cans are especially versatile: kicking one can award points or a speed boost, while jumping onto it briefly freezes the timer. Every fourth round offers extra time based on what was saved in the previous three.

With its tilted perspective, distinctive orange-clad protagonist, and emphasis on momentum instead of combat, Metro-Cross stands apart from conventional 1980s platform games. It ran on hardware related to Namco's Pac-Land system and later appeared on the Famicom and several European home computers.

games.title: Astro Chase
games.description:
Astro Chase is the Exidy Max-A-Flex arcade presentation of First Star Software's 1982 Atari 8-bit space shooter, programmed by Fernando Herrera. Players pilot a small ship across a freely scrolling star map, defending Earth against 16 incoming Mega-Mines. Alien saucers continuously harass the ship, but destroying the mines before even one reaches the planet is the real objective; a mine reaching Earth ends the defense in catastrophe. Clearing all the mines advances to a new stage, with increasingly demanding enemy opposition.

The arcade version is notable for its origin on a home computer rather than dedicated coin-op hardware. Exidy's Max-A-Flex system adapted Atari computer technology to an arcade cabinet, bringing a small selection of First Star titles into amusement venues. The game's animated launch sequence and relentless rendition of the 1812 Overture lend personality to its otherwise uncompromising survival challenge.

games.title: Boulder Dash
games.description:
Boulder Dash, created by Peter Liepa and Chris Gray and published by First Star Software in 1984, reached arcades through Exidy's Max-A-Flex system. Players guide Rockford through underground caves, digging away earth and collecting enough diamonds to unlock the exit before time expires. Rocks obey simple but dangerous gravity: undermine a boulder and it falls, potentially crushing Rockford or an enemy. Mastering these predictable interactions is central to solving each cave.

The game combines reflexes with spatial puzzles, as fireflies, butterflies, and amoebas complicate routes through the mines. Dropping a boulder on certain enemies can transform them into diamonds, turning a threat into a resource. With 16 cave layouts and selectable difficulty levels, Boulder Dash helped establish the enduring rocks-and-diamonds puzzle genre. The Max-A-Flex cartridge preserves an early example of a home-computer hit crossing into coin-operated play.

games.title: Bristles
games.description:
Bristles is a 1983 action-platform game by Fernando Herrera, adapted from the Atari 8-bit computer to Exidy's Max-A-Flex arcade system. As Peter the Painter, players traverse the floors of a cutaway building and try to paint every room before the clock runs out. Ladders and elevators connect floors, but an empty elevator shaft can send Peter tumbling to the basement.

Its playful household hazards are unusually specific: flying paint cans knock Peter down, wandering buckets steal brushes, and Brenda the Brat leaves fresh handprints on newly painted walls. Candy canes can distract Brenda, while a paint mixer can briefly trap the pursuing Bucket Chucker. Later buildings introduce steam pipes and limited paint supplies, adding route planning to the frantic painting challenge.

games.title: Flip & Flop
games.description:
Flip & Flop is an isometric tile-marking platform game created by Jim Nangano for First Star Software in 1983 and made available as an Exidy Max-A-Flex arcade cartridge. Its stages alternate between Flip, a kangaroo bounding over raised platforms, and a monkey who moves along the undersides of the structures. The objective is to pass across every marked square while avoiding pursuit and the dangerous edges of the playfield.

A zookeeper chases Flip, while a moving net threatens the upside-down character. Sticky tiles can temporarily hold these pursuers, making them useful for planning safe routes. Stages grow more intricate, eventually asking players to mark certain squares twice, and brief circus scenes punctuate the progression. The alternating upright and inverted movement gives the game a memorable twist on Q*bert-style spatial puzzles.

games.title: Monster Farm Jump
games.description:
Monster Farm Jump is a 2001 Tecmo arcade platform game based on the Monster Farm franchise, known internationally as Monster Rancher. Players choose from four recognizable creatures, including Golem, and guide them along elevated three-dimensional courses. The challenge is to jump forward or backward between sections, collect items, avoid gaps, and reach the end of each course without falling.

Running on PlayStation-derived Sony ZN arcade hardware, the game translates the series' monster characters into a reflex-oriented obstacle course rather than its usual creature-raising format. It was released in Japan, where Monster Farm had also become an animated television franchise.

games.title: Mahjong Fun Club - Idol Saizensen
games.description: Mahjong Fun Club: Idol Saizensen is a 1989 Japanese adult-oriented mahjong game from Video System. Players face female opponents in mahjong matches, with pin-up-style images awarded for victories. An unusual waiter character provides items during play, adding a service-themed presentation to the familiar competitive mahjong format. Its subtitle refers to the Japanese entertainment-industry concept of an 'idol,' rather than a conventional sports or combat theme.

games.title: Mahjong Gakuen
games.description:
Mahjong Gakuen (1988), released under the Yuga label, is a Japanese adult mahjong game associated with Capcom's early arcade development. It pits players against female opponents in traditional mahjong matches, then presents progressively more explicit reward scenes. A dedicated interaction button distinguished it from many contemporaries by letting players affect the post-match animation.

The artwork is credited in contemporary histories to Akira 'Akiman' Yasuda, who later became famous for Capcom's fighting-game illustrations. Its unusually elaborate presentation attracted considerable attention in Japanese arcades; elements of its graphics were subsequently adapted for the Western-market poker game Poker Ladies. A related version is known as Chi-Toitsu.

games.title: Mahjong Gakuen 2 Gakuen-chou no Fukushuu
games.description:
Mahjong Gakuen 2: Gakuen-chou no Fukushuu, meaning 'Revenge of the Academy Head,' is the 1989 sequel to the adult Japanese mahjong title Mahjong Gakuen. Players compete in head-to-head tile matches against female characters, with increasingly revealing illustrations serving as the reward for success. The game retains its predecessor's provocative school-themed identity rather than moving to conventional arcade action.

The series also became notable for a controversial PC Engine adaptation, Mahjong Gakuen: Touma Soushirou Toujou, whose explicit first release was withdrawn and replaced with a censored version. That episode reflects the unusual boundary between adult arcade mahjong and mainstream console publishing in late-1980s Japan.

games.title: Magical Date EX / Magical Date - sotsugyou kokuhaku daisakusen

variants.title: Magical Date EX / Magical Date - sotsugyou kokuhaku daisakusen (Ver 2.01J)
Magical Date / Magical Date - dokidoki kokuhaku daisakusen (Ver 2.02J)

games.description:
Magical Date EX is Taito's expanded 1997 version of Magical Date, a romance-themed arcade mini-game collection. Instead of a conventional action campaign, players pursue a relationship with one of three girls, choosing outings and completing small skill challenges to raise affection. Failure costs lives; success improves the relationship, leading toward a confession at a Christmas party. The original Magical Date featured 17 mini-games, with the EX release representing a distinct arcade revision.

Built for Taito's PlayStation-derived FX-1 system, the series offers a striking example of Japanese arcade developers combining dating-simulation storytelling with the rapid, replayable tests familiar from party games. Its two Japanese sets are titled Magical Date EX: Sotsugyou Kokuhaku Daisakusen and Magical Date: Dokidoki Kokuhaku Daisakusen.

games.title: Magical Crystals
games.description:
Magical Crystals is a colorful 1991 fantasy action game by Kaneko, played from a diagonal, slightly overhead perspective. One or two players control young wizards who navigate floating platforms, evade enemies, and free fairies trapped in crystals. The heroes can jump over gaps and attacks and launch rebounding magic projectiles; holding the attack button produces a stronger shot. Timing movement is as important as fighting, since falling from a platform costs a life.

Its compact stages combine collectible objectives, enemies, and occasional boss confrontations, giving it a character somewhere between maze action and platform shooting. Kaneko also licensed the game to Atlus, and several Japanese and international arcade revisions are preserved.

games.title: Gionbana
games.description: Gionbana is a 1989 Nichibutsu adult-themed arcade game based on hanafuda, Japan's traditional illustrated playing cards, rather than mahjong despite using a mahjong-style control panel. Players compete in card matches against female opponents, with revealing illustrations awarded after victories. Its name evokes Kyoto's Gion entertainment district, giving this compact gambling-card format a distinctly Japanese setting.

games.title: Mahjong G-MEN'89
games.description: Mahjong G-MEN '89: Satsusareta OL is a 1989 Nichibutsu mahjong game wrapped in a detective-story premise. Players take the part of an investigator pursuing clues surrounding the murder of an office worker, confronting female characters through one-on-one mahjong matches. The crime-drama framing and adult rewards distinguish it from the studio's more straightforward strip-mahjong releases. The subtitle refers to a 'murdered office lady,' using a common Japanese abbreviation for a female office worker.

games.title: Atari Mini Golf
games.description: Atari Mini Golf is an unreleased 1978 black-and-white prototype devoted to miniature golf. Instead of the large simulated courses found in later golf games, it presents putting as a compact coin-op challenge on simple gray-scale layouts. Its preservation is significant chiefly because the game never reached normal commercial production, making it a glimpse of Atari experimenting with sports-themed amusement concepts during the late 1970s.

games.title: Major Havoc
games.description:
Atari's Major Havoc (1983), designed by Owen Rubin with level work from the young Mark Cerny, is one of the company's most ambitious color-vector arcade games. In a galaxy littered with autonomous defenses from the fallen Vaxxian Empire, the player controls Major Rex Havoc on a mission to destroy enemy space stations and rescue humanity's remnants. Each mission blends very different activities: shooting through a fleet of robot defenders, guiding a spacecraft onto a station, and entering a platform maze to find the reactor and escape before it explodes.

The platform sections use a distinctive horizontal roller controller, with buttons to jump and activate a limited-use shield. Players must time their movements around force fields, hostile robots, and other hazards, navigating increasingly intricate stations in search of their cores. The crisp vector graphics allow smooth rotation and spectacular explosions, while the shifting play styles create an unusually cinematic arcade rhythm.

Major Havoc was developed near the end of Atari's classic vector era, and the production game never included the narrative conclusion Rubin had envisioned. Its idiosyncratic combination of space combat, precision platforming, and exploration earned it a devoted cult following. Decades later, enthusiasts worked with Rubin to expand the original game into Major Havoc: The Promised End.

games.title: Major Havoc - The Promised End

modifications.description: Adds new mission stages, enemy encounters, and a final boss ending sequence to Atari's vector arcade game Major Havoc.

games.description: Major Havoc - The Promised End is an extensive homebrew expansion hack by JMA for Atari's 1983 vector arcade game Major Havoc, introducing new levels, gameplay mechanics, and an ending mission sequence.

games.title: Mahjong Hourouki Gaiden
games.description: Mahjong Hourouki Gaiden is a 1987 Japanese mahjong game by Home Data, loosely connected to the Mahjong Hourouki fiction about itinerant gamblers. Rather than relying on static screens, it features conspicuous animated sequences during its matches. Its focus on the atmosphere of professional or wandering mahjong play makes it a period curiosity among Home Data's early tile-game releases.

games.title: Mahjong Housoukyoku Honbanchuu
games.description: Mahjong Housoukyoku Honbanchuu is a 1994 Japanese mahjong release by Nichibutsu, presented around the theme of a television broadcast in progress. It uses a dedicated mahjong keyboard and frames its tile competition as a live entertainment program. The title roughly means 'Mahjong Broadcasting Station: On the Air'; a related two-player release circulated as Zoku Mahjong Housoukyoku.

games.title: M.I.A. - Missing in Action
games.description:
M.I.A.: Missing in Action is Konami's 1989 side-scrolling military action game and a spiritual successor to Green Beret, known in the West as Rush'n Attack. One or two special-forces soldiers infiltrate heavily guarded enemy territory, fighting through soldiers, vehicles, and fortifications to rescue prisoners of war. The soldiers begin armed with knives, but can acquire additional firepower as they progress through multi-level combat areas linked by platforms and ladders.

The campaign builds toward a prison-camp rescue, followed by the dangerous job of escorting freed captives to an extraction helicopter. With its simultaneous cooperative play, cinematic combat scenarios, and emphasis on close-range attacks amid enemy gunfire, M.I.A. extends the tough, fast-moving formula of its predecessor while reflecting the popularity of 1980s commando films.

games.title: Midnight Run: Road Fighter 2

variants.title: Midnight Run: Road Fighter 2 (EAA, Euro v1.11)

games.description:
Midnight Run: Road Fighter 2 is a 1995 Konami arcade racing game that revives the name of the company's 1984 top-down racer in a three-dimensional, street-racing format. Players drive powerful road cars through nighttime routes, weaving through traffic and fighting for position under time pressure. A distinctive driving feature is the ability to switch between automatic and manual transmission during a race, giving players a way to adjust how directly they manage speed and acceleration.

The arcade title was followed by a PlayStation conversion in 1997, marketed simply as Midnight Run in Europe. Its combination of contemporary 3D graphics and the Road Fighter lineage makes it a notable mid-1990s reinvention of an earlier Konami racing property.

games.title: Midnight Resistance
games.description:
Midnight Resistance is Data East's 1989 run-and-gun action game, built around a pair of commandos fighting the armies of the villainous King Crimson to rescue their kidnapped relatives. Across nine scrolling stages, players climb platforms, shoot soldiers and vehicles, and confront oversized bosses. Its defining physical feature is a rotary joystick: players can move in one direction while twisting the stick to aim their weapon in another, making positioning and independent targeting essential.

Defeated enemies drop keys that can be spent in weapon shops between stages, allowing players to purchase stronger guns and other upgrades. The late-game rescue sequence also uses keys to free family members, and the ending varies with how many are saved. Large enemy machines, tightly packed firefights, and unusual rotary controls made Midnight Resistance a memorable arcade favorite, with later home-computer and console adaptations.

games.title: Money Puzzle Exchanger / Money Idol Exchanger
games.description:
Money Puzzle Exchanger, known in Japan as Money Idol Exchanger, is Face's 1997 Neo Geo MVS puzzle game built around Japanese coin denominations. Coins drop into a vertical playfield, and players grab, carry, and throw them into matching groups. Rather than simply clearing three identical symbols, groups combine according to monetary value, such as five one-yen coins turning into a five-yen coin. Larger combinations eventually disappear, rewarding players who plan chains of exchanges.

The action has the speed and head-to-head tension of Magical Drop, but its arithmetic-based merging rules give it an identity of its own. A cast of brightly drawn, transformation-heroine-style characters and energetic music add to its eccentric charm. It was the last arcade game developed by Face and is especially prized by fans of competitive puzzle games.

games.title: Mighty Guy
games.description: Mighty Guy is a 1986 Nichibutsu overhead action game in which a lone martial-arts fighter confronts waves of armed soldiers without using firearms. Players move through enemy-filled areas and rely on close-range fighting skills rather than the guns typical of military arcade shooters. Its forward-driving combat and battleground presentation invite comparison with Ikari Warriors, but the hand-to-hand emphasis gives this obscure release a markedly different rhythm.

games.title: Vs. Mighty Bomb Jack
games.description:
Vs. Mighty Bomb Jack is Tecmo's 1986 arcade adaptation of the Famicom platform game Mighty Bomb Jack, presented on Nintendo's Vs. System hardware. Players guide Jack through interconnected rooms, collecting bombs and treasure while avoiding monsters and looking for hidden passages. The large stages mix nimble jumps with route-finding and secrets, building on the earlier arcade game Bomb Jack.

The Vs. edition rearranges some secret passages, removes certain warp locations, and adds a two-player option. Those changes make it more than a straight arcade display of the console original, rewarding players who already know the home version with slightly different paths to discover.

games.title: Mikie
games.description:
Mikie is Konami's 1984 comic maze-action game about a student trying to collect hearts that form a message from his girlfriend. Each scene plays out in a different part of the school, from classrooms and corridors to the cafeteria, as Mikie moves around desks and furniture while avoiding teachers, the janitor, and other authority figures. Players can headbutt or otherwise stun pursuers, but must keep moving as the hazards grow more frantic.

The game's slapstick presentation is one of its strongest features, reinforced by a jaunty licensed pop-song soundtrack. Its Japanese version, Shinnyuushain Tooru-kun, instead casts the hero as a new office employee; the international edition alters the scenery and characters to create the school setting. That substantial regional reworking makes Mikie an especially interesting example of 1980s arcade localization.

games.title: Millipede
games.description:
Millipede (1982) is Atari's sequel to Centipede, taking the garden-defense shooter into a faster, more crowded direction. Using a trackball to maneuver an archer across the lower playfield and a button to fire, players blast a segmented millipede as it descends through mushrooms and flowers. Destroying a segment splits the creature, creating additional threats that must be managed before they reach the player's area.

The sequel introduces a larger collection of pests, including beetles, earwigs, mosquitoes, inchworms, and swarms of bees, each altering the field or forcing quick changes in target priority. DDT bombs can be shot to release insect-killing clouds, enabling risky but lucrative chain reactions. The whole design is tuned for constant movement and moment-to-moment triage rather than memorizing a single attack pattern.

Although its predecessor remains more widely recognized, Millipede is celebrated among trackball enthusiasts for its greater variety and intensity. Its finely balanced mixture of precise control, enemy behavior, and explosive opportunities makes it one of Atari's strongest early-1980s score-attack games.

games.title: Mighty Monkey

variants.title: Mighty Monkey (bootleg on Super Cobra hardware)

games.description: Mighty Monkey is a 1982 arcade action game starring a monkey hero inspired by Sun Wukong, the Monkey King of Chinese folklore. Players negotiate enemy-packed scenes and can activate a transformation that turns the hero into a dragon-like head. In this form the character cannot shoot, but can swallow certain enemy fireballs, making the power a defensive alternative to ordinary attacks. Bootleg hardware adaptations of the game also appeared on boards associated with Scramble and Super Cobra.

games.title: Minnasanno Okagesamadesu
games.description:
Minasan no Okagesama Desu! Dai Sugoroku Taikai is a 1990 Neo Geo MVS mahjong game that mixes tile competition with a dice-driven board game. Players advance around a sugoroku track between matches, and the squares they land on can affect the next encounter or determine who they face. Its oddball characters and comic presentation are based on the popular Japanese television variety show featuring the comedy duo Tunnels.

Rather than offering a sequence of isolated mahjong opponents, the game uses board progression to introduce randomness and shifting circumstances. It stands out as one of the more unconventional early Neo Geo releases, particularly for its strongly Japanese television references.

games.title: Minefield
games.description:
Minefield is Stern's 1983 horizontally scrolling tank shooter, set during a hazardous crossing of a desert toward an enemy fortress. Players steer a battle tank through a parallax-scrolling landscape, fire at ground vehicles and aircraft, and avoid the mines scattered across the route. Missiles collected on the ground can be used against fortified targets, giving the action a second layer of attack planning beyond ordinary gunfire.

Its detailed desert backdrop and mix of air, surface, and mine threats give the game a distinct battlefield atmosphere. The journey ultimately culminates at the heavily defended installation that the tank has been sent to destroy.

games.title: Minesweeper (4-Player)
games.description:
Minesweeper (4-Player) is a multiplayer version of Amutech's 1977 grid-based boat game, closely related in concept to Gremlin's Blockade. Each player steers a small craft around a fixed screen, continuously leaving behind an impassable line of mines. The challenge is to outlast rivals without running into another boat's trail, one's own trail, or the edge of the arena.

Unlike the later Windows logic puzzle of the same name, this is a real-time competitive light-cycle game. The four-player configuration expands a simple two-person contest into a more crowded test of anticipation and turning space.

games.title: Minesweeper
games.description:
Amutech's Minesweeper (1977) is an early competitive maze game in which two players steer boats around an invisible grid, depositing a continuous trail of mines behind them. A collision with the arena boundary or any mine trail loses the round, so success depends on anticipating the opponent's route and gradually fencing them into a smaller area. Its play closely resembles Gremlin's influential Blockade, substituting boats and naval mines for the original's abstract line-tracing contest.

The game needs a human opponent for meaningful play; an unattended boat simply travels until it crashes. Despite sharing a name with the later computer puzzle genre, it has entirely different real-time mechanics.

games.title: Inferno
games.description: Inferno is a 1978-era Meadows arcade game that combines angled-view maze exploration with four-direction shooting. Players move through a compact perspective maze, destroying enemies and then racing to collect the dark souls they release before those souls can reach a monster's mouth. This second objective makes a successful shot only the beginning of the challenge: the player must also expose themselves to danger to capture the escaping prize. Its unusual three-point visual perspective and pursuit mechanic set it apart from contemporary fixed-screen shooters.

games.title: Mini Golf
games.description: Mini Golf is Bally/Sente's 1985 coin-operated take on miniature golf. Players putt their way around 18 colorful, compact holes decorated with miniature-course obstacles, including loops and a waterfall. The challenge comes from choosing the correct direction and strength to guide the ball around each trick layout with as few strokes as possible. Its cheerful animation and novelty hazards give it the feel of a mechanical seaside putting attraction translated to a video screen.

games.title: Minivader
games.description: Minivader is a tiny 1990 Taito fixed-screen shooter modeled on the company's original Space Invaders. Players move a cannon across the bottom of the screen and fire at descending rows of aliens, reducing the formation before the attackers reach the ground. Its stripped-down presentation is deliberate: Minivader was supplied as a simple test board for arcade cabinets, making it useful for checking a monitor and controls rather than demonstrating Taito's newest hardware. Its existence is a charming reminder that even diagnostic equipment could contain a playable game.

games.title: Mirax
games.description: Mirax is a 1985 pseudo-3D space shooter from Current Technologies, built around a forward-moving view over a hostile landscape. Players pilot a spacecraft toward Mirax City, where the Alpha Centauri Empire is assembling a devastating super-laser installation. Enemy aircraft and ground targets approach across the scaling landscape, requiring continuous shooting and evasive movement as the city draws nearer. The use of simulated sprite scaling gives the action a striking sense of depth for an obscure mid-1980s release.

games.title: Mirai Ninja
games.description:
Mirai Ninja is Namco's 1988 Japanese side-scrolling action game, featuring a futuristic ninja fighting through a mechanical fortress. Players guide the armored hero across platforms and through enemy-filled corridors, using a sword at close range and throwing shuriken at more distant targets. Running, jumping, and crouching must be timed carefully as the game introduces traps, robotic opponents, and large bosses over its 12-stage adventure.

Its visual design belongs to the same science-fantasy world as the live-action film Mirai Ninja, directed by Keita Amemiya and produced with Namco's involvement. Running on Namco System 2 hardware, it brings the film's cybernetic samurai imagery into a demanding arcade action format and remains relatively little known outside Japan.

games.title: Mission Craft
games.description:
Mission Craft is an unofficial Korean vertical shooter released by Sun Amusement in 2000. Although the action follows the familiar pattern of a scrolling shoot-'em-up, its presentation borrows heavily from unrelated PC and console games: backgrounds and interface elements evoke StarCraft, music is taken from Warcraft II, and explosions and other effects recall contemporary Japanese action titles. The result is a conspicuous collage of recognizable assets rather than an authorized Blizzard adaptation.

One or two players fight through waves of airborne threats with the rapid pacing associated with Psikyo-style arcade shooters. Its eclectic appropriation of famous game material makes Mission Craft a notable example of the unlicensed arcade market around the turn of the millennium.

games.title: Missile Command
games.description:
Atari's Missile Command (1980) is one of the landmark arcade games of the Cold War. Designed by Dave Theurer, it asks players to defend six cities from an escalating barrage of missiles, bombers, and satellites. A trackball moves the targeting cursor, while three separate buttons fire counter-missiles from the left, center, or right battery. Each shot blooms into an expanding explosion that destroys enemy weapons entering the blast radius, making anticipation more important than raw firing speed.

Ammunition is limited, and enemy warheads may split into multiple targets as they descend. Choosing which city to protect, where to place overlapping explosions, and when to use the faster center battery is essential to survival. Once every city is destroyed, the game ends with the chilling message 'THE END' rather than a conventional victory scene.

Missile Command was a major commercial and cultural success, spawning home conversions, imitations, and later reinterpretations. Its threat of unavoidable nuclear devastation was unusually stark for an arcade game of its day, and Theurer later described the anxious dreams he experienced while working on it. Few games express the tension between a simple control scheme and overwhelming consequences so effectively.

games.title: Miss World 2002
games.description: Miss World 2002 is a 2002 adult-oriented Qix-style territory-capture game by Comad. Players guide a tracing cursor around a playfield, enclosing sections of the screen while avoiding moving hazards. As territory is claimed, a concealed photographic image is gradually revealed. The release continues the formula of Comad's earlier Miss World games, emphasizing adult photographs rather than the illustrated characters of Gals Panic.

games.title: Miss World '96
games.description:
Miss World '96 is a 1996 Korean adult-oriented puzzle game by Comad, closely patterned after Kaneko's Gals Panic and the older arcade game Qix. Players steer a cursor across a rectangular playfield, drawing lines to claim territory while avoiding wandering enemies. Completing sufficiently large areas uncovers photographs of female models, with different reward images depending on performance.

The game became notorious for using the 'Miss World' name without authorization from the international beauty-pageant organization. Its reliance on photographic rewards, rather than cartoon portraits, makes its place in the 1990s adult territory-capture boom especially clear.

games.title: Wakakusamonogatari Mahjong Yonshimai
games.description: Wakakusa Monogatari Mahjong Yonshimai is a 1996 Japanese adult mahjong game centered on four sisters, very loosely borrowing the Japanese title of Little Women. Players challenge the sisters in riichi-style mahjong, earning points and unlocking animated reward scenes after successful matches. The illustrated character presentation and occasional bonus games distinguish it from more utilitarian tile-game cabinets.

games.title: Mahjong Angels - Comic Theater Vol.2
games.description: Mahjong Angels: Comic Theater Vol. 2 is a 1991 Dynax arcade mahjong game that presents its opponents and events in a comic-book style. Traditional Japanese tile matches are accompanied by short narrative and humorous illustrated sequences, giving the play a serialized 'comic theater' identity instead of a purely abstract score contest. It is an example of Dynax packaging the familiar mahjong format around character-driven entertainment.

games.title: Mahjong Camera Kozou
games.description: Mahjong Camera Kozou is a 1988 Japanese adult mahjong title from Miki Syouji, built around a camera and travel theme. Players compete in mahjong matches against women portrayed as being in remote locations, unlocking revealing photographic scenes when they win. Its photographic presentation reflects the late-1980s move by Japanese mahjong machines away from simple illustrated reward screens toward more elaborate visual attractions.

games.title: Mahjong Camera Kozou
games.description: This 1989 Mahjong Camera Kozou set preserves another version of Miki Syouji's camera-themed adult mahjong game. As in the 1988 release, players face women in tile matches and earn revealing photographs associated with distant destinations as rewards. The separate ROM set records a later arcade configuration of the same unusual travel-and-photography concept; the available historical documentation does not establish any further rule changes.

games.title: Mahjong Chuukanejyo
games.description: Mahjong Chuukanejyo, also catalogued as Mahjong Zhong Hua Er Nu, is a Dynax medal-mahjong game released for the Chinese market in June 1998. It adapts competitive mahjong to an arcade setting with betting conventions, rather than the tile-pair removal of mahjong solitaire. Its regional title and release distinguish it from Dynax's many Japanese adult-mahjong productions, illustrating the company's expansion of its specialized mahjong hardware and software into other Asian markets.

games.title: Mahjong Clinic
games.description: Mahjong Clinic is a 1988 Japanese adult mahjong game by Home Data with a hospital-and-nurses theme. Players challenge stylized female medical staff to tile matches, with suggestive reward scenes following victories. The clinic framing gives this otherwise conventional strip-mahjong setup a recognizable identity within Home Data's late-1980s series of thematic mahjong releases.

games.title: Mahjong The Dai Chuuka Ken

variants.title: Mahjong The Dai Chuuka Ken (China, v. D111)

games.description: Mahjong The Dai Chuuka Ken is a Japanese medal-mahjong game from Dynax, released in August 1995. Built for the betting-oriented mahjong arcade market, it presents competitive mahjong in a Chinese-themed package. It belongs to Dynax's extensive line of dedicated video mahjong machines, which used specialized control schemes and operator-adjustable wagering features rather than conventional action-game joysticks.

games.title: Mahjong Derringer
games.description: Mahjong Derringer is a 1989 Japanese adult-themed mahjong game from Dynax, released in June of that year. Its name refers to the compact derringer pistol, although the game is a competitive mahjong title, not a shooting game. The production is remembered chiefly as one of Dynax's more provocative late-1980s adult mahjong releases, mixing the conventional tile-hand competition of the genre with deliberately sensational presentation.

games.title: Mahjong Dial Q2
games.description: Mahjong Dial Q2 is a 1991 Japanese arcade mahjong game from Dynax that adds short bonus mini-games to the main tile competition. These interludes award random items that can influence subsequent play, introducing an element of chance beyond the deal itself. The game's emphasis on bonus prizes makes it more than a bare sequence of mahjong hands, while its 'Dial Q2' title references the premium-rate telephone services familiar in Japan at the time.

games.title: Mahjong Diplomat
games.description:
Mahjong Diplomat is a 1987 Japanese mahjong title from Dynax, released in July of that year and preserved in AdvanceMAME in a betting-capable version. It uses a dedicated mahjong keyboard rather than a joystick, with individual tile-selection and command buttons suited to the decisions of Japanese mahjong. Players work with tile combinations and calls in head-to-head mahjong play; the betting hardware also offers configurable wager and payout settings.

Its horizontal, relatively low-resolution display and Z80-based board place it among the specialized Japanese tabletop machines of the late 1980s. The betting variant is particularly notable because it preserves the commercial settings and controls of a machine designed for a different arcade environment from conventional action cabinets.

games.title: Mahjong Erotica Golf
games.description: Mahjong Erotica Golf is a 1994 Japanese adult mahjong game associated with Fujic and AV Japan. It combines head-to-head tile matches with a novelty golf presentation: successful play is tied to progress around a simulated course, while digitized photographs of female opponents provide the adult reward element. The improbable pairing of golf imagery and mahjong strategy gives this niche release its particular character.

games.title: Mahjong Electron Base
games.description: Mahjong Electron Base is a 1993 Dynax betting-style mahjong game distinguished by its strict scoring arrangements and 'Three Tiles Exchange' feature. Players face six female opponents and can use the exchange option to alter a hand before play continues. Special visual effects accompany announced riichi and winning hands, while the soundtrack and character illustrations make the presentation more elaborate than an ordinary electronic tabletop mahjong machine.

games.title: Mahjong Focus
games.description: Mahjong Focus is a 1989 Nichibutsu adult mahjong game structured around travel to different locations. Instead of a single static group of opponents, players visit a succession of places to challenge new characters at Japanese mahjong. Also known as Nozokimeguri Mahjong Peep Show, it uses its sightseeing framework to connect the adult reward scenes and tile matches.

games.title: Mahjong Friday
games.description: Mahjong Friday is a 1989 Dynax adult mahjong game whose reward system revolves around photography. Winning against female opponents allows the player to take provocative snapshots, making the camera imagery a central part of its appeal. The cabinet belongs to the late-1980s Japanese strip-mahjong tradition, but distinguishes itself through the idea of collecting pictures of defeated opponents.

games.title: Mahjong Gottsu ee-kanji
games.description: Mahjong Gottsu ee-kanji is a 1991 Nichibutsu Japanese adult mahjong game that adds purchasable bonus items to normal tile matches. Players can spend resources on timely assistance during a hand, introducing decisions about when an advantage is worth buying. Its female opponents and reward scenes follow the studio's familiar adult-mahjong format, while the item economy provides an extra strategic layer. It is related to the medal-game variant Mahjong Bakuhatsu Junjouden.

games.title: Medal Mahjong Gottsu ee-kanji
games.description: Medal Mahjong Gottsu ee-kanji is the medal-based version of Nichibutsu's 1991 adult mahjong release, also associated with the title Mahjong Bakuhatsu Junjouden. Unlike the standard amusement presentation, this version is designed around medal-style wagering and payouts during Japanese mahjong matches. The separate arcade set documents how the same theme was adapted for the country's coin-and-medal amusement market.

games.title: Mahjong G-Taste
games.description: Mahjong G-Taste is a 2002 Psikyo arcade mahjong game based on the Japanese adult manga G-Taste. It replaces the genre's usual original female cast with characters and artwork connected to the licensed series, using Japanese mahjong matches as its principal interactive element. As a late example of commercial adult mahjong in arcades, it also illustrates Psikyo's range beyond the scrolling shooters for which the company is best known.

games.title: Mahjong Hourouki Okite
games.description: Mahjong Hourouki Okite is a 1988 Home Data mahjong game that places players among rough-looking gamblers and gangsters rather than the glamorous female opponents common in the genre. It is part of the studio's Mahjong Hourouki line, inspired by stories of wandering mahjong players and the underworld surrounding high-stakes games. Its hard-boiled characterization gives the tile competition a more disreputable gambling-den atmosphere.

games.title: Mahjong If
games.description: Mahjong If...? is a 1990 Dynax arcade mahjong game built around Japanese competitive mahjong rather than tile-matching solitaire. The title's question-mark motif distinguishes its presentation, while the underlying game follows the specialized, often betting-oriented format of late-1980s and early-1990s Japanese mahjong cabinets. The surviving ROM family includes several numbered revisions, notably variants identified as 2921 and 2931, which were preserved separately because of their differing program sets.

games.title: Mahjong Ikaga Desu ka
games.description: Mahjong Ikaga Desu ka is an unusual Japanese mahjong title by Mitchell, released in 1991 with the subtitle 'A Pleasure Trip of Two Nights and Three Days.' Its encounters unfold around a bus-stop and excursion motif rather than a conventional tournament setting. The combination of everyday travel scenery and mahjong competition makes the game a distinctive, if obscure, entry in Mitchell's arcade catalog.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Mahjong Kinjirareta Asobi
games.description: Mahjong Kinjirareta Asobi is a 1991 adult mahjong game from Home Data, published with a subtitle referring to a forbidden game and a teacher's desires. Players challenge female characters in Japanese tile matches, with suggestive reward scenes forming part of the progression. Its risqué school-related framing places it firmly within the adult thematic mahjong games that were popular in Japanese arcades in the early 1990s.

games.title: Mahjong Kyou Jidai
games.description: Mahjong Kyou Jidai, roughly translated as Mahjong Mania Time, is a 1986 Japanese arcade mahjong game by Sanritsu. It concentrates on competitive mahjong hands with the adult-oriented presentation common to its market. A conspicuous English slogan on its title screen advertises it as an exciting mahjong game, an amusing period detail. Players make the usual tile-hand decisions of competitive mahjong through a four-button arcade control scheme, rather than navigating an action-game playfield.

games.title: Mahjong Koi Uranai
games.description: Mahjong Koi Uranai, released by Nichibutsu in 1992, combines Japanese mahjong with romance fortune-telling. A fortune-teller character provides the narrative device for encounters with female opponents, and victories lead to revealing scenes. The game uses its prediction-of-love theme to organize a familiar adult-mahjong formula, rather than presenting the matches as an ordinary competitive tournament.

games.title: Mahjong Kojinkyouju
games.description: Mahjong Kojinkyouju is a 1989 Home Data adult mahjong game whose title translates as 'Private Lesson Mahjong.' Instead of a cartoon fantasy cast, the game features a digitized Japanese woman presented as a private tutor. Players engage her in mahjong matches, with the tutor premise lending a knowingly suggestive tone to the photographic presentation. The use of captured imagery makes it stand apart from more traditional hand-drawn mahjong releases of the period.

games.title: Mahjong La Man
games.description: Mahjong La Man is a 1993 adult mahjong release associated with Nichibutsu and AV Japan. Players compete against female opponents in Japanese tile matches, with strip-style reward scenes following victories. It belongs to the studio's collaboration-heavy period of photographic and adult-themed mahjong games, and is chiefly notable today as an uncommon Japanese arcade release.

games.title: Major League
games.description:
Major League is Sega's 1985 baseball arcade game, bringing a full diamond contest to a cabinet with more elaborate physical controls than most sports games of its era. Players pitch, bat, run bases, and field using a trackball, a dial, and dedicated buttons, giving the action an unusually hands-on character. The combined controls reward accurate timing and deliberate decisions rather than simple directional joystick play.

The game's title screen carries a 1985 copyright, although Japanese arcade records place its release in early 1986. It is unrelated to the later Famicom game based on the American baseball film of the same name.

games.title: Mahjong Jikken Love Story
games.description: Mahjong Jikken Love Story is a 1991 Nichibutsu adult mahjong game framed as a romantic science experiment. Players use a fictional mahjong computer to help construct an ideal woman, with tile-game victories advancing the unusual laboratory-themed scenario. It is related to Nichibutsu's Lady Maker, bringing that premise to an amusement arcade format. The combination of comic pseudo-science and adult matchmaking imagery gives the release an identity beyond its mahjong rules.

games.title: Mahjong The Mysterious World
games.description: Mahjong The Mysterious World, also known as Mahjong Sekai no Shinpi, is a 1994 Dynax medal-mahjong game. It packages head-to-head Japanese mahjong in a themed presentation while retaining the wagering-style conventions of dedicated mahjong machines. An optional 'Gal Mode' is documented in the operator settings, reflecting the adult-oriented material often tucked into this genre. Preserved versions include more than one Japanese set and a Taiwanese-language relative, Maque Caihui Ying.

games.title: Mahjong Nanpa Story
games.description: Mahjong Nanpa Story is a 1989 adult mahjong game from Brooks set against a seaside-resort backdrop. Players encounter women during a beach-holiday scenario and compete against them in Japanese tile matches, with revealing scenes awarded for success. Its relaxed summer setting and character encounters differentiate it from the urban detective and school-themed mahjong games of the same period.

games.title: Mahjong Natsu Monogatari
games.description: Mahjong Natsu Monogatari, or Mahjong Summer Story, is a 1989 Video System adult mahjong game featuring a lineup modeled on popular Japanese entertainment idols. Players progress through five stages of tile competition, each associated with a different female celebrity likeness. The game's emphasis on recognizable contemporary personalities offers a snapshot of late-1980s Japanese idol culture as it intersected with coin-operated adult entertainment.

games.title: Mahjong Quest
games.description: Mahjong Quest is a fantasy-themed Japanese mahjong game developed by Whiteboard and Santos and released around 1990-91. It presents tile matches within an RPG-like adventure setting, allowing players to obtain power-ups as they progress rather than treating each match as an isolated contest. The combination of mahjong rules, fantasy presentation, and special abilities makes it an unusual genre hybrid.

games.title: Mahjong Reach Ippatsu
games.description: Mahjong Reach Ippatsu is a late Japanese gambling-mahjong release by Dynax, dated December 1998. Its title highlights two recognizable riichi-mahjong concepts: declaring riichi when a hand is ready, and ippatsu, the bonus associated with winning shortly afterward under the required conditions. It belongs to the medal-oriented branch of arcade mahjong, using the familiar tile-hand rules as the basis for a specialist coin-operated game. More than one Japanese program revision has been preserved.

games.title: Mahjong Shikaku
games.description:
Mahjong Shikaku is a 1988 adult mahjong game in which a date repeatedly turns into a series of tile-game confrontations. After entering a name, the player attempts to reach a hotel with a girlfriend, but other women interrupt the journey and demand mahjong matches. Progress through the successive locations depends on winning these encounters, and victories produce adult reward scenes.

The elaborate date narrative distinguishes it from strip-mahjong machines with no story beyond choosing an opponent. Its title is a pun on 'assassin,' and the artwork incorporates playful references to well-known Japanese anime character designs.

games.title: Mahjong Sisters
games.description:
Mahjong Sisters is Toaplan's 1986 adult mahjong game, an unusual departure for a studio later celebrated for demanding scrolling shooters. Players choose from three sisters and compete in Japanese mahjong, gaining revealing reward scenes by winning hands. There are also additional chances to remove clothing through a tenpai-based guessing challenge or a game of yakyuken, a rock-paper-scissors variant associated with strip games. Losing a hand can reverse the player's progress as a sister puts clothing back on.

Its mixture of traditional tile strategy and interactive reward contests shows how adult mahjong cabinets experimented with play beyond the core rules. The game is especially noteworthy within Toaplan's catalog because so much of the company's reputation rests on action titles such as Truxton and Batsugun.

games.title: Mahjong Uranai Densetsu
games.description: Mahjong Uranai Densetsu is a 1992 Nichibutsu adult mahjong game with a fortune-telling motif. Players compete against female characters in Japanese mahjong, with lingerie-themed illustrations unlocked after victories. Its title translates approximately to 'Mahjong Fortune-Telling Legend,' and its presentation follows the period trend of giving strip-mahjong contests a recognizable supernatural or romantic theme.

games.title: Mahjong-yougo no Kisotairyoku
games.description: Mahjong-yougo no Kisotairyoku is a quirky 1989 Home Data mahjong game remembered for its deliberately odd character presentation. An intense-looking male host and a digitized delivery girl on roller skates accompany the tile competition, producing a visual style very different from the conventional fantasy heroines of adult mahjong. The title plays on the idea of elementary mahjong terminology, but the eccentric on-screen cast is its clearest distinguishing feature.

games.title: Mahjong Yuugi
games.description: Mahjong Yuugi is a 1990 Japanese arcade mahjong game from Visco, presented with bright, cute character art. Small girl characters appear as attendants who throw the dice for the player, adding a playful touch to the conventional Japanese mahjong setup. The title means roughly 'Mahjong Pastimes,' matching the game's lighthearted treatment of a familiar tabletop contest.

games.title: Mahjong Channel Zoom In
games.description: Mahjong Channel Zoom In is a Jaleco video-mahjong title released in Japanese arcades in March 1991, despite the 1990 copyright date on its title screen. It uses a dedicated mahjong control arrangement rather than a joystick, with two-player input hardware documented in its emulation profile. Its appearance in Japanese operator rankings at the time shows that it was a contemporary commercial mahjong release, not simply a title known from later ROM dumps.

games.title: Mortal Kombat
games.description:
Mortal Kombat (1992) is Midway's landmark one-on-one fighting game, created by Ed Boon, John Tobias, and their team as a darker, digitized alternative to the hand-drawn style popularized by Street Fighter II. Seven selectable fighters, including Liu Kang, Johnny Cage, Sonya Blade, Scorpion, and Sub-Zero, enter a supernatural martial-arts tournament controlled by the sorcerer Shang Tsung. Matches follow a best-of-three-round structure, with distinctive high and low punch and kick buttons plus a separate block button.

The game's defining spectacle is its use of actors recorded and converted into digital sprites, lending the characters an unusually photographic look. Special moves range from fireballs to Scorpion's spear and Sub-Zero's freezing projectile. After winning a match, a player may perform a secret Fatality, a gruesome finishing move revealed by the announcer's famous command to 'Finish Him!' Hidden characters, secret fights, and the four-armed champion Goro helped turn the game's mysteries into arcade folklore.

Mortal Kombat became a commercial phenomenon and one of the central games in the early-1990s debate over violence in video games. Its home release was promoted as 'Mortal Monday,' and controversies surrounding games like this contributed to the creation of the American ESRB ratings system. The original remains an important milestone for digitized graphics, arcade competition, and the growth of the fighting-game genre.

games.title: Mortal Kombat II
games.description:
Mortal Kombat II (1993) expands Midway's digitized fighting formula into a larger and faster supernatural contest. The action moves to Outworld, where Shao Kahn's forces lure Earth's champions into another deadly tournament. Twelve selectable fighters include returning favorites Liu Kang, Scorpion, and Sub-Zero alongside Kitana, Mileena, Jax, Kung Lao, and Baraka. Players again fight best-of-three-round matches using high and low attacks, a dedicated block button, and character-specific special moves.

Compared with the first game, movement and attacks are more fluid, combos are easier to assemble, and new techniques introduce more tactical variety. Every fighter has multiple elaborate Fatalities, while secret finishers such as Babalities and Friendships provide deliberately absurd alternatives to outright violence. Additional hidden opponents and stage-specific secrets made experimentation and rumor-sharing major parts of the arcade experience.

Often regarded as one of the series' high points, Mortal Kombat II refined its predecessor without abandoning its distinctive personality. Its dark fantasy backgrounds, atmospheric music, and instantly recognizable cast made it one of the most prominent competitive arcade games of the decade. It was also an early showcase for Midway's DCS digital sound system.

games.title: Mortal Kombat 3
games.description:
Mortal Kombat 3, released to arcades in 1995 with a 1994 copyright, is Midway's third major entry in its digitized fighting series. The story drops the traditional tournament format: Shao Kahn has invaded Earthrealm, forcing its surviving warriors to fight back against his forces. New characters such as Sindel, Stryker, Kabal, and the cybernetic ninjas join returning favorites in battles across urban streets, subways, and other modern environments.

The major gameplay addition is a dedicated Run button and a stamina meter, allowing players to rush forward and pressure opponents rather than relying entirely on careful defensive spacing. Preset chain combinations, often nicknamed 'dial-a-combos,' enable sequences of strikes, while uppercuts in some arenas knock fighters through ceilings into new stages. The game also adds Animalities, returning Fatalities, and pre-fight Kombat Kodes that can modify versus matches.

Mortal Kombat 3 accelerated the series' pace and expanded its competitive systems, although its altered roster proved divisive. Midway quickly followed it with Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3, which restored popular missing fighters and further revised the balance. Together these editions became a central part of 1990s arcade fighting culture.

games.title: Mortal Kombat 3

variants.title: Mortal Kombat 3 (scrambled bootleg of Mega Drive version)

games.description:
This 1996 unauthorized Mortal Kombat 3 arcade board is not a conversion of Midway's original arcade program. Instead, it runs a modified, scrambled version of the Sega Mega Drive/Genesis adaptation of Mortal Kombat 3 on hardware derived from Sega's 16-bit console. The result has the reduced resolution, animation, and sound characteristics of the home version, even though it is operated with arcade controls and coins.

Players still engage in one-on-one fights using the third game's Run mechanic, special moves, and chain combinations. One distinguishing change is that the hidden ninja Smoke can be selected immediately alongside the regular cast. The board is an especially interesting example of the 1990s practice of repackaging home-console software as an unofficial coin-operated game.

games.title: Mortal Kombat 4
games.description:
Mortal Kombat 4 (1997) brought Midway's violent fighting series into real-time 3D polygon graphics while retaining much of the timing and attack language of its 2D predecessors. The story introduces the fallen Elder God Shinnok as a new central threat, with veterans such as Liu Kang, Raiden, Scorpion, and Sub-Zero joined by characters including Quan Chi, Fujin, and Tanya. The game continues the familiar best-of-three-round fighting structure, complete with brutal Fatalities and a dedicated block button.

Its new systems include a sidestep maneuver that lets fighters move around attacks in depth and the ability to draw weapons for additional moves. Fighters can also pick up objects in certain arenas and throw them at opponents. These changes make three-dimensional positioning and weapon use part of the contest without transforming the game into a fully free-roaming 3D fighter.

Mortal Kombat 4 marks a major technical turning point for the franchise, with polygonal characters replacing the digitized actors of the first three arcade games. It was also the last mainline Mortal Kombat created specifically for arcades before the series concentrated on home consoles.

games.title: Mahjong Keibaou
games.description: Mahjong Keibaou is a 1993 Nichibutsu adult mahjong game built around a horse-racing theme. Players challenge computer opponents in Japanese mahjong while the presentation borrows imagery from racetracks and betting culture. Its combination of tile strategy and racing spectacle reflects the industry's tendency to package mahjong play in familiar Japanese leisure and gambling settings.

games.title: Mahjong THE LADY HUNTER
games.description:
Mahjong The Lady Hunter is a 1990 Nichibutsu adult mahjong game styled as a comic-book superhero adventure. The masked hero is an affectionate Batman parody, complete with a chest emblem based on Nichibutsu's owl logo and an owl-shaped throwing weapon used when declaring riichi. Rather than defeating criminals through hand-to-hand combat, he confronts glamorous female thieves across the mahjong table.

Its exaggerated comic panels and costumed characters give the game an unusually playful personality. The superhero motif is reflected in small touches throughout the tile matches, turning an otherwise familiar adult mahjong game into a sustained genre spoof.

games.title: Maikobana
games.description: Maikobana is a 1990 Nichibutsu video hanafuda game, built around the traditional Japanese flower-card pastime rather than mahjong tiles. Its adult-oriented presentation uses geisha or dancing-girl imagery as a reward theme, while this particular arcade version is configured for medal-based wagering. It is a niche example of the ways established Japanese card games were adapted into early electronic amusement and betting cabinets.

games.title: Mars Matrix: Hyper Solid Shooting
games.description:
Mars Matrix: Hyper Solid Shooting is a 2000 vertically scrolling bullet-hell shooter developed by Takumi and published by Capcom for its CPS-2 arcade hardware. Set against a rebellion on a colonized Mars, it puts players in heavily armed Mosquito fighters facing dense formations of enemy aircraft, mechanical defenses, and huge bosses. The screen quickly fills with bullets, but the game's signature mechanic turns that danger into an opportunity rather than only something to evade.

Holding the main attack control activates a field that absorbs enemy fire, then hurls the captured shots back in a devastating counterattack. Destroyed targets release experience cubes, and catching them quickly builds chains that increase both scoring potential and the ship's power. With essentially one primary action button used for several distinct functions, success depends on precise timing, aggressive bullet collection, and knowing when to switch between offense and defense.

Following Takumi's Giga Wing, Mars Matrix further explores the idea of weaponizing enemy projectiles. Its extreme score multipliers can push the arcade score toward a 12-digit ceiling, and its intricate scoring system made it a favorite among high-level shoot-'em-up players. A later Dreamcast conversion added its own enhancements, but the original arcade version remains celebrated for its concentrated, high-risk design.

games.title: Monster Maulers
games.description:
Monster Maulers is Konami's 1993 monster-fighting arcade game, released in Japan as Kyukyoku Sentai Dadandarn. Players choose one of three members of the Ultimate Task Force, Kotetsu, Anne, or Eagle, and travel around the world battling giant creatures sent by the villainous Happy Droppers. Rather than clearing streets full of ordinary enemies, the game centers on large, individual boss encounters, blending the controls of a fighting game with the spectacle of a beat-'em-up.

Each hero has a distinct set of attacks and special techniques, and two-player cooperative battles allow teammates to perform additional combined maneuvers. Some of the monsters are references to enemies from other Konami franchises, including Gradius-related games. The exaggerated superhero costumes, bombastic presentation, and Japanese theme-song tradition evoke Super Sentai television series. Its unusual cooperative boss-fighting structure also makes it a close relative of Banpresto's later Metamoqester.

games.title: Marchen Maze
games.description:
Märchen Maze is Namco's 1988 isometric action game inspired by Alice in Wonderland. Players guide Alice through nine strange, floating worlds of narrow paths and platforms, using a bubble blower to push enemies over the edges. Holding the attack button produces larger bubbles, while jumping and careful movement help Alice avoid marbles and other projectiles that can knock her into the void.

The fairy-tale visual design disguises a demanding positional combat game: opponents are often more effectively defeated by pushing them off a platform than by simply attacking them head-on. Collectible power-ups and increasingly elaborate paths add to the challenge. Its oblique perspective and storybook atmosphere make Märchen Maze one of Namco's more distinctive late-1980s arcade experiments.

games.title: Medal Mahjong Circuit no Mehyou
games.description: Medal Mahjong Circuit no Mehyou is a 1992 Japanese mahjong game developed in association with Kawakusu and Nichibutsu. It combines adult mahjong opponents with race-car and motor-racing imagery, presenting tile matches through a Grand Prix theme. This medal version incorporates wagers and payouts, with bets limited to three credits per hand, distinguishing it from standard amusement-only mahjong machines.

games.title: Medal Mahjong Moukari Bancho

variants.title: Medal Mahjong Moukari Bancho (2007/06/05 MASTER VER.)

games.description:
Medal Mahjong Moukari Bancho is a 2007 Japanese mahjong-themed medal game from Cave, produced under an AMI licence. Unlike Cave's better-known bullet-heavy shooters, it belongs to the amusement-center medal market and presents a tabletop mahjong format rather than real-time shooting action. The preserved 5 June 2007 master program runs on Cave's SH-3-based CV1000 hardware, also associated with the company's late-period arcade releases.

Its unusual position in Cave's catalogue is more firmly documented than its detailed rules or medal awards, and the emulated program has historically been marked preliminary. It is therefore best understood as a rare Cave-developed gambling/tabletop title, not a conventional shooting game.

games.title: Minky Monkey
games.description:
Minky Monkey is an early arcade game from Technos, bearing a 1982 copyright and released in Japan in 1983. Players guide a small red-clad boy through platform-like screens, collecting fruit and carrying it to a designated empty space to complete a message. Its layout and character animation have a family resemblance to the climbing-and-collecting action of Donkey Kong Jr., but the fruit-delivery objective supplies its own puzzle-like goal.

Produced with Roller Tron, Minky Monkey is historically important as Technos's first game, preceding the company's later successes with Karate Champ, Double Dragon, and the Kunio-kun series.

games.title: Monkey Mole Panic
games.description:
Monkey Mole Panic is a 1992 video adaptation of the traditional whack-a-mole amusement game, developed by East Technology and licensed through Nakanihon. The screen shows a grid of nine holes from which monkeys or moles suddenly appear. Instead of swinging a physical mallet, players strike them by pressing one of nine large dedicated cabinet buttons, each mapped to a corresponding hole.

The result is a fast test of reaction time and hand-eye coordination, while preserving the immediately understandable appeal of a mechanical fairground attraction. Its unusual control panel is central to the experience and cannot be adequately represented by an ordinary two-button arcade joystick.

games.title: Muchi Muchi Pork!
games.description:
Muchi Muchi Pork! is Cave's 2007 vertically scrolling bullet-hell shooter, distinguished by an exuberant parody of food, pigs, and anime heroines.
