Three women transformed into pig-themed fighters by the villain General Pork Fillet pilot flying motorbikes through five stages packed with enemy aircraft and dense projectile patterns. Its colorful, comic appearance contrasts with the demanding dodging and scoring systems associated with Cave's shooters.

The special 'lard attack' and a stream of collectible pig-head medals turn combat into a balancing act between survival and building points. As in many Cave games, players are rewarded for aggressive positioning and understanding how enemy destruction influences collectible items. A second loop can be reached by clearing the initial game without losing a life, giving expert players a substantially tougher challenge.

Distributed by AMI, Muchi Muchi Pork! became a cult favorite for its oddball aesthetic and elaborate score play. It was later paired with Pink Sweets in an Xbox 360 compilation, helping preserve one of Cave's most eccentric late-period arcade releases.

games.title: Mutant Night
games.description:
Mutant Night is a 1987 UPL action-platform shooter starring Mutron-kun, a small white creature with a large eye. Players move across scrolling landscapes and attack bizarre enemies with bubbles while jumping between platforms and avoiding incoming fire. Repeated taps of the jump button allow Mutron-kun to rise or float for longer, turning aerial movement into a central part of the game.

Shooting small pods releases colored power-up orbs that may enlarge the character into an invulnerable giant, create duplicate creatures, strengthen the projectile attack, or grant bonus points. Its strange character designs, unpredictable transformations, and mixture of shooting with precise jumps make it an unusual cult title from UPL's arcade catalog.

games.title: Maze of Flott
games.description:
Maze of Flott is a 1989 Taito arcade maze-action game in which players drive a small car around a sprawling, colorful city. The objective is to search streets and connected buildings for keys that open the way forward, while collecting fuel and avoiding other cars and dangerous obstacles. Entering buildings shifts the action into winding, corridor-like interiors, so success requires both driving dexterity and route planning.

The unusual combination of a vehicle, urban exploration, and key-collecting puzzles distinguishes Maze of Flott from straightforward racing games. Its Japan-only release has made it a relatively obscure entry in Taito's late-1980s catalog.

games.title: Moguchan
games.description: Moguchan, also known as Mogu Chan, is an obscure 1982 Japanese vertical-screen platform and maze game associated with Orca and an Eastern Commerce license. Players guide a character around the stage to collect scattered fruit while avoiding hostile mole-like creatures. The ROM set is sometimes identified as a bootleg, but the precise nature of that designation is uncertain. Its simple fruit-gathering objective and unusual enemies typify the small, experimental character-driven arcade games of the early 1980s.

games.title: Mogura Desse
games.description: Mogura Desse is an unusual 1991 Konami program that uses a simple whack-a-mole game as a factory test for arcade cabinet controls. Moles appear on screen and the player responds with the corresponding joystick or button inputs; the straightforward action helps technicians check whether the hardware registers movement and presses correctly. Designed for up to four players rather than an ordinary commercial release, it is primarily a piece of arcade service history. Its playable presentation turns a functional diagnostic board into a minor Konami curiosity.

games.title: Mole Attack
games.description: Mole Attack is a 1982 video adaptation of the fairground whack-a-mole game, manufactured by Yachiyo Electronics. Nine holes correspond to nine separate pushbuttons, and the player's task is to strike each emerging mole before it disappears. Unlike a joystick-driven action game, success depends on fast visual recognition and finding the matching button. The red king mole awards a mystery bonus, while waiting until an ordinary mole has emerged farther can increase its value. Mistiming a hit until a mole shows its tail instead costs points. The game's physical nine-button arrangement gives it much of the appeal of its mechanical inspiration.

games.title: Momoko 120%
games.description:
Jaleco's Momoko 120% (1986) is a delightfully eccentric Japanese platform game that tells a character's entire life story through a succession of escape sequences. Momoko must climb burning multistory buildings, using ladders, escalators and trampolines while shooting hostile creatures and staying ahead of a fire rising from below. Hidden doors lead to obstacle-based bonus challenges or shortcuts. Reaching the roof and jumping aboard an airship completes a stage; in subsequent levels Momoko grows from a small child into an adult, culminating in a wedding and a new generation of Momoko.

The game has an especially curious licensing history. It was originally conceived around the anime Urusei Yatsura, but the arcade characters were changed when that license was not secured. Nevertheless, an arrangement of the anime's opening song, 'Lum's Love Song,' remained as background music. The Famicom adaptation *Urusei Yatsura: Lum's Wedding Bell* did use the licensed characters, making the two versions an unusual pair.

games.title: Monster Bash
games.description:
Sega's Monster Bash (1982) is an early horror-themed platform game starring Little Red, also known as Bashman. Across three distinct screens, he pursues Dracula through a haunted mansion, Frankenstein's monster through a castle, and the elusive Chameleon Man through a graveyard. The player climbs between floors, uses passageways and zaps lesser creatures, but each principal monster can only be defeated after lighting candles, energizing a magic sword and collecting its temporary SuperZap power.

Each setting adds its own tactical complication. Wolfmen in Frankenstein's castle can duck under shots, while Chameleon Man blends into the background until Little Red triggers a color-changing spot to reveal him. Its shifting objectives, cartoon-monster cast and elaborate sound hardware distinguish it from the simpler single-screen climbing games of its time. AdvanceMAME also recognizes a two-board hardware version of the original game.

games.title: Monster Zero
games.description: Monster Zero is an unusual 1982 science-fiction shooter from Nihon Game. Rather than simply clearing waves for points, the player must raise ten flags during each stage by shooting enemies. Completing the flag objective advances the game through a six-stage cycle; surviving all six begins a tougher cycle. The game uses an eight-way joystick and a firing button, with a colorful playfield built on hardware derived from the Galaxian family. Its complicated protection circuitry long made accurate emulation difficult, adding a second kind of challenge for preservationists beyond its arcade gameplay.

games.title: Monte Carlo
games.description:
Atari's Monte Carlo is an early overhead racing game, released in 1980, in which a Grand Prix car travels along a scrolling roadway filled with bends, narrow sections and roadside scenery. The player selects one of eight tracks of increasing difficulty and steers with a rotary control while monitoring speed, fuel and score. Four computer-controlled cars create moving hazards: collisions may cause spins or crashes, and the rivals can even lose control themselves.

Unlike later racing games built around perspective scaling, Monte Carlo presents its action from directly above, letting the player read the track's shape as it scrolls by. Engine revs, squealing tires and crash noises come from discrete analog sound circuits. Produced in relatively small numbers, it represents Atari's experimentation with dedicated racing controls before the genre's early-1980s boom.

games.title: Money Money
games.description:
Money Money (1983) is an Italian arcade adventure by Zaccaria that changes its style of play from scene to scene. The player gathers bags of cash in a maze, leaps between rooftops to collect more money, swims among islands while avoiding sharks and crocodiles, and finally drives a jeep over gaps and around falling hazards. Hostile pursuers and spiders complicate the earlier stages, although a collected potion briefly allows the player to defeat them by contact. Reaching home converts the amassed wealth into a bonus before the game cycles at higher difficulty.

Its variety is matched by a memorable sound presentation. Money Money uses synthesized speech to announce the beginning of the hunt and the driving sequence, and celebrates success with the familiar 'I'm in the Money' refrain. The unusual combination of maze chase, platforming, swimming and driving makes it a distinctive product of Italy's early arcade industry.

games.title: Monza GP
games.description: Monza GP is a 1981 overhead racing game associated with Olympia and Leante Games. Players steer a small car through a scrolling roadway whose environments include urban stretches, slippery sections, tunnels and bottlenecks. Passing traffic and occasional emergency vehicles pose collision hazards, while a timer and extra-car awards reward sustained driving. The original cabinet used a steering wheel, accelerator and two-speed gear control, along with separate seven-segment score displays. Its style and compact racing cabinet clearly belong to the early wave of games influenced by Sega's Monaco GP, although Monza GP uses its own hardware.

games.title: Wild West C.O.W.-Boys of Moo Mesa

variants.title: Wild West C.O.W.-Boys of Moo Mesa (ver EA)
Wild West C.O.W.-Boys of Moo Mesa (ver AA)
Wild West C.O.W.-Boys of Moo Mesa (bootleg ver AA)
Wild West C.O.W.-Boys of Moo Mesa (ver UA)

games.description:
Konami's Wild West C.O.W.-Boys of Moo Mesa (1992) turns Ryan Brown's animated television western into a colorful side-scrolling run-and-gun game. Up to four players take the roles of Marshal Moo Montana, the Dakota Dude, the Cowlorado Kid and arcade newcomer Buffalo Bull, battling the forces of corrupt Sheriff Terrorbull. Players move across seven stages, shooting enemies, avoiding environmental hazards and confronting a boss at the end of each stage. Different pickups improve gunfire or provide special attacks, including screen-clearing thunderbolts, while sarsaparilla restores health.

Although its cartoon artwork suggests a children's adventure, the game has the busy enemy patterns, cooperative chaos and detailed animation associated with Konami's early-1990s licensed arcade hits. Shooting chickens to reveal helpful items is one of its playful touches. The AdvanceMAME family includes regional program revisions and a bootleg board set.

games.title: Moon Alien Part 2
games.description: Moon Alien Part 2 is Nichibutsu's 1980 variation on Namco's Galaxian, running on related arcade hardware. The player steers a ship horizontally along the foot of a vertically oriented screen and fires upward at rows of alien craft. Enemies peel away from formation into diving attacks, making the timing of each shot and the avoidance of collisions central to survival. Its interest lies less in a new ruleset than in its place among the many early commercial reinterpretations of Galaxian. An older ROM revision and the related Super GX release are preserved alongside it.

games.title: Moon Cresta
games.description:
Nichibutsu's Moon Cresta (1980), developed by Jorudan, gave the fixed-screen space shooter one of its earliest genuine risk-and-reward power-up systems. The player's spacecraft consists of three separable sections, initially flown one at a time while waves of strange aliens cross and dive through the screen. Survive long enough and a timed docking challenge allows one section to join another, increasing firepower from a single shot to three and eventually five simultaneous shots. The larger combined craft is also harder to protect, and a failed docking maneuver can destroy a valuable section.

Enemies vary dramatically, from splitting eye-shaped creatures to fast-moving formations and meteors. Because the standard attackers do not fire, their erratic movement and collisions create the danger. Docking requires lining up ship sections with the two-way joystick and controlling descent with the fire/thrust button, turning what would otherwise be a short pause into a tense skill test.

A hit arcade export, Moon Cresta circulated under regional names including Eagle and inspired an exceptionally large family of licensed versions and bootlegs. Its multi-part ship design and active docking sequence remain its defining contributions to early shooter history.

games.title: Moon Quasar
games.description: Moon Quasar (1980) is Nichibutsu's expanded follow-up to Moon Cresta, retaining the original game's wave-based shooting and three-part spacecraft while introducing a fuel-management twist. A decreasing fuel counter appears on screen, and special refueling sequences periodically interrupt the attack waves. During these sequences, the player maneuvers surviving spacecraft sections toward a passing mothership, creating a docking challenge in the opposite direction from Moon Cresta's familiar ship assembly. Successfully managing both combat and replenishment adds another layer of pressure to the original's precision movement. Like its predecessor, it uses Galaxian-derived hardware and a two-way joystick with a combined fire and maneuvering button.

games.title: Moonwar
games.description: Stern Electronics' Moon War (1981), also listed as Moonwar, is a horizontally scrolling, multidirectional shooter centered on defending lunar supply bases. The player steers a spacecraft with a rotary wheel, uses thrust to change speed, and fires on hostile attackers while traveling across the Moon's surface. Dedicated controls raise a defensive shield and perform a rapid direction-reversing hyper-flip. Fuel and shield resources must be replenished at friendly bases, giving the action a survival objective beyond enemy destruction. Its unusual steering-and-button control panel is a major part of the experience, demanding more than the left-right movement of contemporary space shooters.

games.title: Moon War
games.description: Moon War (prototype on Frenzy hardware) is a preserved developmental version of Stern's 1981 lunar shooter rather than a separate sequel. It retains the concept of piloting a spacecraft across a scrolling lunar landscape, defending supply bases, fighting attackers and managing fuel. A rotary steering control and separate action buttons handle movement, firing and defensive maneuvers. Its chief historical interest is the prototype implementation on hardware associated with Stern's Frenzy, documenting a different technical route for the game before the familiar production version. Differences in exact stage content are not established by the available documentation.

games.title: More More
games.description: More More is a 1999 Korean arcade collection of 17 quick-fire skill minigames from SemiCom and Exit. At each round, the player chooses among four or five currently available challenges and must meet the selected game's objective to continue. Strong performances receive an 'Excellent' grade, and earning four such grades awards an extra life. With an eight-way joystick and three buttons, it emphasizes rapidly adapting to new instructions rather than mastering one long campaign. Its format belongs to the competitive, party-style minigame boom of late-1990s arcades.

games.title: More More Plus
games.description: More More Plus (1999) expands SemiCom and Exit's minigame formula from 17 challenges to 20, updates the presentation and changes the selection system. Instead of choosing from a limited rotating group, players can pick any of the 20 games, creating more freedom to favor familiar challenges or experiment with unfamiliar ones. Each short event must be completed successfully to continue, and four 'Excellent' results award an extra life. The sequel preserves the original's fast, joystick-and-button arcade tests while making its larger collection more immediately accessible.

games.title: Mortal Race
games.description:
Mortal Race is an unreleased 1995 arcade racing prototype from the Spanish company New Dream Games. Preserved by MAME researchers decades later, it shares part of its development lineage with Top Driving but is a separate game, not merely another ROM revision. Its top-down racing action emphasizes rally-style driving and negotiating elaborate course features more heavily than direct competition with other cars.

The game's unusual history emerged when a Mortal Race title logo was discovered inside Top Driving's ROMs, even though that game never displayed it. A genuine Mortal Race board was subsequently found, revealing different hardware, an additional vehicle and tracks, and a design closer to a rally challenge. This makes it a particularly interesting example of an arcade game whose changing design can be traced through surviving prototypes and code.

games.title: Mosaic
games.description: Mosaic is a 1990 falling-block puzzle game developed by Space, with a later licensed version associated with Fuuki. It draws on the arcade popularity of Tetris-style descending-piece challenges, but with its own colorful cartoon presentation, including an incongruous large purple duck visible in contemporary gameplay material. The vertical puzzle action uses a joystick and two buttons and supports alternating players. It has no connection to the identically named 2019 narrative game by Krillbite.

games.title: Mosaic
games.description: F2 System's Mosaic (1999) is a timed picture-assembly puzzle game built around swapping misplaced tiles. Players select one part of a scrambled image and then another to exchange their positions, gradually restoring the complete picture before time runs out. A framing story concerns an angel expelled from a heavenly kingdom who must solve the king's puzzles to return. The game supports two players and uses an eight-way joystick with three buttons. Despite sharing its name with Space's 1990 arcade puzzle title, this Korean F2 System release is a distinct game, and it should not be confused with the unrelated modern adventure of the same name.

games.title: Syougi No Tatsujin - Master of Syougi
games.description: Master of Syougi (1995), also called Syougi no Tatsujin, is ADK's Neo Geo adaptation of shogi, the Japanese strategy board game often compared with chess. Players move differently ranked pieces across a nine-by-nine board, aiming to checkmate the opposing king; captured pieces can later be dropped back into play, a defining shogi rule. In the single-player tournament, opponents are represented by digitized portraits, while two players can compete against each other locally. Its presence on SNK's cartridge-based arcade platform is a reminder that the Neo Geo catalogue extended beyond fighting games and shooters.

games.title: Moto Frenzy

variants.title: Moto Frenzy (Mini Deluxe Field Test Version)

games.description: Atari Games' Moto Frenzy (1992) is a motorcycle-racing arcade attraction designed around a physical ride-on machine. Its simulated bike can lean, pivot and perform wheelies, while independent motors provide movement and feedback corresponding to control inputs and track events. Courses vary in scenery and hazards, with an Arctic stage even featuring attacking polar bears. Handlebar-based controls and a moving seat make the cabinet a central part of the experience. Two machines could be linked for head-to-head racing, distinguishing Moto Frenzy from ordinary joystick-driven motorcycle games.

games.title: Motos
games.description:
Namco's Motos (1985) reimagines the arena battle as a contest of shoving rather than shooting. The player pilots a small bumper craft around floating platforms, attempting to knock every hostile space bug over the edge without being pushed off in return. Some stages contain gaps and precarious shapes, forcing careful positioning rather than blind charges. Collected Power Parts increase the force of collisions, while Jump Parts allow the craft to hop over danger.

Across 62 rounds, the combination of movement, momentum and changing arena geometry creates a compact arcade puzzle with a surprising amount of tactical depth. Motos was among Namco's final eight-bit games for a vertically oriented display, using hardware descended from the Super Pac-Man family.

games.title: Mouja
games.description:
Mouja (1996) is a competitive falling-block puzzle game by Etona in which pairs of yen coins descend into a playing well. Rather than matching colors, players make change: arranging coins to equal a higher denomination combines them into a more valuable piece, and bringing two 500-yen coins together makes them disappear. Careful placement can trigger long chains when newly created coins fall into further combinations.

The game resembles Puyo Puyo in its descending-pair structure and Money Puzzle Exchanger in its arithmetic theme, but the emphasis on incrementally converting denominations gives each chain a distinctive logic. Opponent play adds another layer of pressure, rewarding quick calculations and efficient use of limited space.

games.title: Mouse Attack
games.description: Mouse Attack is a mid-1990s video redemption game produced by The Game Room. Mice appear to steal pieces of cheese, and the player tries to stop them by striking the on-screen targets with a mallet-style input. The goal is a quick reaction and successful defense of the cheese rather than a conventional sequence of fighting-game matches, despite some arcade database genre labels. Its origins in ticket-redemption amusement machines explain the straightforward, physical interaction.

games.title: Mouser
games.description: UPL's Mouser (1983), distributed in North America by Cosmos, is a single-screen climbing game about a cat trying to reach its sweetheart at the top of a seven-story building. The cat gathers ladder parts while chasing harmless blue mice and avoiding dangerous pink ones, thrown objects and a roaming dog. Floors, gaps and ladders make each screen a timing puzzle, with fish and money offering additional points. The structure recalls Donkey Kong, but the mixture of friendly targets, hostile mice and a cat protagonist gives Mouser its own mischievous character.

games.title: Bio-hazard Battle (Mega Play)
games.description: Bio-Hazard Battle (Mega Play) is Sega's 1993 coin-operated adaptation of its Mega Drive shooter, known in Japan as Crying. Four selectable craft fly through organic, alien-infested landscapes, destroying mutated lifeforms while changing weapons through colored pickups. A separate floating attack unit can help shield the ship or extend its firepower, lending the otherwise traditional horizontally scrolling stages a defensive element. The Mega Play version runs on Genesis-derived arcade hardware with coin-based credits and special program revisions, rather than being an ordinary unmodified home cartridge.

games.title: Columns III (Mega Play)
games.description: Columns III: Revenge of Columns (Mega Play) brings Sega's competitive 1993 falling-jewel puzzle to coin-operated hardware. The player rotates descending columns of three gems, making matches of three or more identical colors horizontally, vertically or diagonally. Unlike the first Columns, the emphasis is on duels: successful matches build attacks that disrupt an opponent's well, while the single-player mode presents a succession of computer challengers. Sega's Mega Play release converts the home-console contest to arcade credit-based play, making head-to-head speed and tactical gem placement the main attractions.

games.title: Golden Axe II (Mega Play)
games.description: Golden Axe II (Mega Play) is the coin-operated Sega Mega Drive version of the 1991 fantasy beat-'em-up, not the separate arcade sequel The Revenge of Death Adder. Ax Battler, Tyris Flare and Gilius Thunderhead return to fight the sorcerer Dark Guld, combining sword or axe attacks with distinct forms of elemental magic. Players battle through side-scrolling stages, collect magic books from enemies and use powerful screen-wide spells against crowds and bosses. This 1993 Mega Play adaptation modifies the Genesis game for credit-based arcade operation, preserving its familiar three-hero adventure in a dedicated coin-op format.

games.title: Grand Slam (Mega Play)
games.description: Grand Slam (Mega Play) is Sega's 1993 arcade tennis game on Mega Drive-derived hardware, related to the console title Grand Slam: The Tennis Tournament '92. Players control a tennis competitor from a courtside view, positioning for serves and returns and trying to place shots beyond an opponent's reach. The game is built around complete tennis exchanges rather than the abbreviated button-mashing of a party minigame. Its Mega Play cartridge is a comparatively obscure member of Sega's small collection of coin-operated Genesis adaptations.

games.title: Gunstar Heroes (Mega Play)
games.description:
Gunstar Heroes (Mega Play) brings Treasure's celebrated 1993 Genesis debut to Sega's coin-operated platform. Gunstar Red and Gunstar Blue fight an empire seeking four powerful gems, running, jumping and firing through wildly varied stages with mechanical bosses and set-piece encounters. Players combine two of four fundamental weapon types into different firing patterns, and can supplement shooting with throws and close-range attacks.

The original became famous for its elastic animation, huge multipart bosses and an almost constant stream of new ideas. The Mega Play edition adapts that action to coin-based arcade credits and revised game code, making this a particularly noteworthy example of a home-console showcase returning to arcades on related hardware.

games.title: Mazin Wars / Mazin Saga (Mega Play)
games.description: Mazin Wars / Mazin Saga (Mega Play) is Sega's 1993 arcade adaptation of the Genesis action game based on Go Nagai's Mazinger mythology. The player controls a powered fighter battling mutants and hostile machines through side-scrolling stages, with combat occasionally shifting into large-scale clashes against imposing mechanical opponents. An eight-way joystick and three buttons provide attacking, jumping and a special attack or guard action; double-tapping a direction performs a dash. Unlike a general-purpose Genesis cartridge, this is a dedicated Mega Play conversion with a coin-operated interface and its own arcade program.

games.title: Shinobi III (Mega Play)
games.description: Shinobi III: Return of the Ninja Master (Mega Play) takes Sega's acclaimed 1993 Genesis ninja platformer into the arcade. Joe Musashi runs, leaps and double-jumps through forests, military installations and other elaborate stages, dispatching foes with shuriken, sword strikes and limited ninjutsu powers. Horseback and surfing sequences interrupt the platform combat, while aggressive bosses reward learning their patterns. Its fast movement and fluid animation made Shinobi III one of the defining late-era 16-bit action games. This dedicated Mega Play release adapts the experience to Sega's coin-operated, Genesis-based arcade board rather than simply playing a stock home cartridge.

games.title: Sonic The Hedgehog 2 (Mega Play)
games.description:
Sonic the Hedgehog 2 (Mega Play) is Sega's 1993 arcade conversion of the 1992 Mega Drive sequel. Sonic races through loop-filled side-scrolling courses, collects rings for protection and uses the new Spin Dash to accelerate from a standstill. The original sequel introduced Miles 'Tails' Prower and expanded Sonic's design with faster levels, elaborate machinery and high-speed boss battles.

The Mega Play cartridge is a purpose-built arcade revision, subject to coin-based credits and stricter progression than a home-console session. It belongs to Sega's small family of Mega Play conversions, which often shortened or altered Genesis games to suit arcade play; it is distinct from the time-rental Mega-Tech release.

games.title: Sonic The Hedgehog (Mega Play)
games.description:
Sonic the Hedgehog (Mega Play) is a heavily revised 1993 arcade version of Sega's foundational 1991 Mega Drive platformer. The core action remains instantly recognizable: Sonic sprints through hills, springs, loops and industrial stages, collecting rings and freeing animals from Doctor Robotnik's machines. A hit only costs rings when Sonic has some in reserve, encouraging daring movement and rapid recovery.

Unlike the standard Genesis game, this Mega Play version cuts the zone selection down to a shorter route through Green Hill, Spring Yard, Star Light, Scrap Brain and Final Zone, imposes severe stage timers and removes functional bonus stages. The special-stage rings no longer provide access to Chaos Emeralds, and extra-life monitors do not behave as in the home release. These changes make the cartridge a genuine arcade remix rather than just Sonic running in a cabinet.

games.title: Streets of Rage II (Mega Play)
games.description: Streets of Rage II (Mega Play) adapts Sega's 1992 Genesis beat-'em-up to its coin-operated Mega Play system. Axel Stone and Blaze Fielding return to confront the crime boss Mr. X after Adam Hunter is kidnapped; newcomers Max Thunder and Skate add very different fighting styles. Players battle through urban stages using combinations, throws, weapons and character-specific special attacks, with two-player cooperation at the center of the action. The home original was celebrated for its large sprites, varied move sets and Yuzo Koshiro's club-influenced soundtrack. The Mega Play cartridge preserves the street-fighting premise in dedicated arcade software governed by credits rather than ordinary home-console play.

games.title: Tecmo World Cup (Mega Play)
games.description: Tecmo World Cup (Mega Play) is a 1993 soccer game distributed by Sega as a cartridge for its Mega Play arcade system. Teams compete in joystick-controlled football matches, attempting to pass, shoot and score while defending against opposing attacks. Its place in the catalogue is notable because Mega Play concentrated on Genesis-style action and puzzle conversions, making a sports title a less common offering. The cartridge uses Sega's coin-operated Mega Play hardware; the available material does not establish a distinct set of advanced rules or changes beyond its arcade presentation.

games.title: Mighty! Pang
games.description:
Mighty! Pang (2000) is Mitchell's fourth entry in the bubble-bursting Pang series, released on Capcom's CPS-II hardware. The familiar premise remains intact: a small character moves across a single-screen arena, firing vertically to split large bouncing bubbles into progressively smaller ones until every bubble is gone. Shots, walls and obstacles must be managed carefully because even a tiny surviving bubble can end a life.

This installment adopts a markedly different, more cartoon-like visual style and organizes its action into three modes. Tour mode offers a structured journey of 57 stages, while Panic and Expert provide alternate tests of speed and precision. Ice floors, destructive blocks and other inherited hazards complicate the apparently simple shooting. Its Japanese-only arcade release makes it one of the less familiar chapters of a series otherwise widely distributed around the world.

games.title: Moon Patrol
games.description:
Moon Patrol (1982), developed by Irem and distributed in North America by Williams, is an influential horizontally scrolling arcade shooter in which the player drives a patrol buggy across a perilous lunar frontier. The vehicle rolls automatically toward the right, but the player can vary its speed, jump craters and rocks, and fire simultaneously forward at ground hazards and upward at attacking spacecraft. Alien bombs sometimes create new craters, so the terrain itself can change while a difficult jump is already being planned. Checkpoint markers reward progress through the Beginner and Champion courses.

Moon Patrol is especially famous for its multilayer parallax backgrounds: distant mountains and nearer scenery scroll at different speeds, creating a striking impression of depth on relatively modest hardware. Its smooth mix of jumping, shooting and anticipation became a model for later vehicle-based action games. The bouncy soundtrack, lunar setting and precise rhythm of hazards help explain its enduring status as an early-1980s arcade classic.

games.title: Mad Planets
games.description:
Gottlieb's Mad Planets (1983) is a frantic arena shooter with one of the period's most distinctive control schemes. A flight-style joystick moves the spacecraft around the playfield, while a separate rotary control aims its gun independently. New planets emerge near the center and grow rapidly; destroying them before they reach full size awards valuable bonuses. If a planet matures, its orbiting moons must first be destroyed, at which point the now enraged 'mad planet' pursues the player with increasing speed. Stranded astronauts and roaming comets add further decisions and hazards.

The resulting action feels like a cross between Robotron's multidirectional combat and an astronomical demolition exercise. The ability to move in one direction while firing in another makes skillful circling essential, and a mishandled grown planet can suddenly dominate the screen. Though less commercially famous than Gottlieb's Q*bert, Mad Planets has earned a strong cult following for the precision and aggression of its controls.

games.title: Magical Pumpkin: Puroland de Daibouken
games.description: Magical Pumpkin: Puroland de Daibouken is a Japanese children's arcade ride released in 1996 and associated with Capcom and Sanrio's Puroland theme park. The specialized three-seat cabinet combines a physical ride with a video-based, on-rails driving adventure featuring Sanrio characters. Young riders can steer through a colorful course, but the experience is deliberately gentle, with no conventional win-or-lose condition. This makes it closer to an interactive attraction than a competitive driving game. Its unusual ride hardware and Japan-only distribution are more important to its history than high scores or elaborate mechanics.

games.title: Moonquake
games.description:
Moonquake is an unreleased 1987 Bally Sente arcade prototype built on an unusual system based on Amiga 500 hardware with an expanded Ensoniq sound design. The player guides a robot through a slowly moving field of floating, block-like asteroids, jumping between safe surfaces in a manner reminiscent of Q*bert. Landing on a block cracks it; returning to a damaged block can make it crumble and fall away, while gaps and other obstacles threaten the character.

Former Sente executive Roger Hector recalled that programmer Bob Smith developed the game and suggested it was left unfinished amid the company's impending shutdown. The surviving prototype is therefore a rare glimpse of a project that never reached commercial arcades, as well as an early experiment in using home-computer-derived hardware for a coin-operated game.

games.title: Mr. Dig
games.description: Mr. Dig is a 2000 Korean arcade puzzle game by Sun that closely imitates Namco's Mr. Driller. The player guides a small digger through stacked colored blocks, clearing a downward path toward a depth target while gathering air capsules to prevent suffocation. Large groups of unsupported blocks can collapse after digging, so reckless excavation risks being crushed. The arcade game offers depth challenges such as 500 and 1,000 meters and adds extra block arrangements to the familiar formula. It is unrelated to the identically named 1984 home-computer game that imitates Mr. Do!, an easy source of confusion in automatic game databases.

games.title: Mr. Do!
games.description:
Universal's Mr. Do! (1982) is a landmark single-screen maze game in which a clown tunnels through earth to harvest cherries while monsters hunt him. Unlike Pac-Man's fixed corridors, the entire landscape can be excavated, allowing the player to create escape routes or dangerous dead ends. Mr. Do throws a bouncing power ball that returns after hitting an enemy, and can also drop heavy apples onto pursuers by excavating the soil beneath them. A screen may be cleared by collecting every cherry, defeating the enemies, spelling EXTRA or discovering a diamond.

The combination of destructible terrain, weapons and multiple completion routes gives Mr. Do! an unusually flexible tactical vocabulary for its era. Apples can be used both as traps and as obstacles, while pursuing monsters eventually gain the ability to dig after the clown. The original became a popular fixture in arcades and inspired a succession of Universal sequels, including Mr. Do's Castle and Do! Run Run.

games.title: Mr. Driller
games.description:
Namco's Mr. Driller (1999) combines the immediate appeal of a digging game with the chain reactions of a falling-block puzzler. Players control Susumu Hori, the son of Dig Dug's Taizo Hori, and drill downward through immense columns of multicolored blocks. When matching blocks touch, they merge and may disappear in groups; unsupported stacks then fall, crushing anyone beneath them. Meanwhile an air gauge continually drains, forcing the player to balance rapid descent with detours for oxygen capsules.

The game is playable with exceptionally simple directional and drill controls, but its cascades create intricate decisions about where to dig, when to shelter and which columns to destabilize. Levels measured in hundreds of meters become a race against both physics and oxygen. Mr. Driller launched a distinctive Namco puzzle series, inheriting the underground theme of Dig Dug while inventing a considerably faster and more strategic form of arcade excavation.

games.title: Mr Driller 2
games.description: Mr. Driller 2 (2000) expands Namco's colorful subterranean puzzle series with more block configurations, additional stages and simultaneous two-player play. Susumu Hori returns alongside Anna Hottenmeyer, both racing down through collapsing stacks of colored blocks while a constantly shrinking air supply forces risky decisions. Drilling through one group may cause whole sections above to fall, rewarding advance planning but punishing careless moves. The sequel retains the original game's accessible one-button drilling and adds a competitive dimension, making its speed-and-survival formula especially well suited to arcades.

games.title: Mr. Driller G
games.description:
Mr. Driller G (2001) is the third major arcade installment in Namco's digging puzzle series and a substantial expansion of its cast and modes. Six characters are available, including Susumu Hori, Anna Hottenmeyer, Susumu's father Taizo (the original Dig Dug), Ataru, Puchi the dog and the robot Holinger-Z. Each descends through layers of colored blocks, triggering collapses while hunting oxygen capsules before the air meter empties.

Story sequences and the threat posed by Dr. Manhole's Ankoku Drillers give G a more developed narrative than its predecessors. Race and survival-style competitions broaden the familiar depth challenges, and character choice can influence the balance of versus matches. It is an ambitious continuation of a puzzle design that turns a single drilling action into a chain-reaction survival game.

games.title: The Amazing Adventures of Mr. F. Lea
games.description:
The Amazing Adventures of Mr. F. Lea (1982) is a peculiar four-part arcade game from Pacific Novelty, starring a flea determined to reach an inviting dog's back. Players choose among four compact challenges that borrow recognizably from Frogger, Donkey Kong and Jungle Hunt: crossing lawnmower-filled terrain, negotiating a dog's body and tail, and jumping past obstacles to reach the destination. Completing all four scenes advances the game to another cycle.

The cabinet's playful audio is unusually elaborate, using arrangements of familiar classical and popular tunes for individual stages and transitions. It was Pacific Novelty's final arcade video game and received a very limited release, making its inventive, if derivative, minigame structure a curiosity among collectors.

games.title: Mr. Goemon
games.description:
Konami's Mr. Goemon (1986) is the arcade origin of the long-running Ganbare Goemon series, loosely inspired by the legendary Japanese outlaw Ishikawa Goemon. In this side-scrolling platform adventure, Goemon pushes through streets and rooftops filled with hostile pursuers, striking with a pipe, throwing objects or jumping onto enemies. Some foes can grab the character, requiring frantic movement to break free, and tougher enemies attack with projectiles. The player must travel toward the right-hand end of each stage while surviving the obstacles.

Its caricatured Edo-period setting, mischievous hero and comic action established many of the personality traits that later flourished in Konami's console Goemon games. Unlike those larger adventures, the original is a focused, demanding arcade platformer built around a four-way joystick and two buttons.

games.title: Mr. Jong
games.description:
Mr. Jong (1983) is a distinctive Japanese action-puzzle game by Kiwako and Sanritsu that mixes maze navigation with mahjong tiles. Players move Mr. Jong around the playfield, pushing tiles into a collection area at the top to assemble valid mahjong combinations while escaping pursuing ogres. A tile can also be shoved into an ogre to crush it, and a special power tile briefly makes enemies vulnerable to contact.

The game's export versions, BlockBuster and Crazy Blocks, retain the maze-chase concept but replace the mahjong imagery with more familiar Western symbols, with changes to the tile-matching rules. It is not a Mr. Do! clone despite occasional catalogue descriptions to that effect: its sliding blocks, tile combinations and enemy encounters make it an unusual hybrid of mahjong puzzle and Pengo-like action.

games.title: Mr. Kougar
games.description: Mr. Kougar is an early-1980s platform game attributed to ATW USA, in which the player clears every dot scattered across moving platforms while dodging creatures called Banalets. A two-way joystick and one button govern movement and jumping, making the shifting platforms themselves a central hazard. Touching an egg grants temporary invulnerability and releases a fairy that travels upward, potentially destroying enemies it encounters. The unusual twist is that the fairy may instead free another Banalet, adding a further pursuer to the stage. Bootleg variants, including Troopy, reflect the game's scattered distribution.

games.title: Mahjong Rokumeikan
games.description: Mahjong Rokumeikan is a 1988 Japanese adult-themed mahjong title whose visual rewards feature women. Its name invokes the Rokumeikan, the famous Western-style reception hall built in Tokyo in the nineteenth century and associated with Japan's Meiji-era Westernization. Beneath that cultural reference is the familiar Japanese arcade format of competitive mahjong, where completing tile hands rather than matching pairs forms the central play.

games.title: Mrs. Dynamite
games.description: Mrs. Dynamite (1982) is an early maze-action game by Universal. The player races through a labyrinth, avoiding roaming monsters and collecting dynamite that can be deployed against pursuers. Safe movement and timed use of the explosives are the keys to surviving the enclosed playfield. Its simple one-button controls and emphasis on turning picked-up explosives into defensive opportunities make it a compact example of the creative maze-game variations that followed the success of Pac-Man.

games.title: Mr. TNT
games.description: Mr. TNT (1983), a licensed reissue of Techstar's Gorkans, is a grid-based arcade action puzzler. A small character moves along narrow blue pathways, collecting scattered caches of explosives while avoiding moving, lit fuses. Crucially, the grid disappears along traveled routes, progressively removing safe corridors and forcing players to plan a path before escape options vanish. The character and hazards can effectively dismantle the playfield as they move, so success depends less on pure speed than on anticipating which connections must remain available. It runs on hardware derived from Namco's Pac-Man design.

games.title: Mister Viking
games.description: Sega's Mister Viking (1984) is a vertically scrolling action shooter that replaces the usual spacecraft with a Norse warrior searching for his people's lost treasure. The Viking moves around the landscape with an eight-way joystick, fighting enemies that approach on foot or in flight from multiple directions. Shooting and close-range attacks are supplemented by power-ups occasionally delivered by a Viking ship. Its unusual mixture of mythological imagery and multidirectional shooting makes the game stand out from the contemporary military and outer-space shooters built around similar scrolling technology.

games.title: Miss Bingo
games.description: Miss Bingo (1994) is Min Corporation's expanded version of its earlier adult-oriented puzzle game Miss Puzzle. Players slide tiles to create horizontal, vertical or diagonal groups of three or more identical symbols, causing cleared spaces to fill as the remaining pieces settle. Additional tiles continually enter the playfield, so careless moves can cause the board to overflow. The revision updates the graphics and adds a split-screen two-player mode. As in its predecessor, successful puzzle play is linked to revealing photographic background images; the arcade mechanics remain those of a timed matching-and-survival challenge.

games.title: Mahjong Scout Man
games.description: Mahjong Scout Man is an adult-oriented Japanese mahjong game produced by AV Japan and released in March 1994. It is distinguished by digitized imagery, used to give its presentation a photographic look instead of relying entirely on drawn characters. The original Japanese subtitle alludes to infiltration of an adult-video filming scene, linking its mahjong contests to the adult-entertainment theme that defines the game.

games.title: Mouse Shooter GoGo
games.description: Mouse Shooter GoGo (1995) is a single-screen action-puzzle game in which the player guides a mouse around the arena while throwing colored balls into groups of the same color. Matching balls disappear, gradually clearing the arrangement, but moving balls can also strike the mouse and force a restart. The ball currently being carried doubles as a shield against incoming hazards. One button throws the ball, while another locks the direction of the throw, creating a balance between rapid movement and carefully aimed matches. Its unusual free-roaming character distinguishes it from more conventional stationary-launcher bubble puzzles.

games.title: Mobile Suit Gundam
games.description:
Mobile Suit Gundam (1993), developed by Allumer and published by Banpresto, is a one-on-one fighting game built around the iconic mecha of the Gundam franchise. Players select from ten mobile suits and battle against other machines in side-view arenas, combining close-range attacks with the ranged weapons associated with the series. Rather than commanding military units on a strategy map, the game puts the player directly in control of a single giant robot.

Its arcade release in Japan includes both Japanese and English display options. An updated successor, Mobile Suit Gundam: EX Revue, appeared in 1994 with revisions to the fighting formula. The original is an early example of a major anime property being interpreted through the arcade fighting-game boom.

games.title: Marvel Super Heroes
games.description:
Capcom's Marvel Super Heroes (1995) is a fast, highly animated CPS-II fighting game loosely inspired by Marvel's Infinity Gauntlet comic storyline. Ten selectable heroes and villains, including Spider-Man, Wolverine, Iron Man, Captain America, Magneto and Doctor Doom, battle in one-on-one matches with six-button controls, special moves, aerial attacks and devastating super combos. Thanos's pursuit of the Infinity Gems supplies the tournament's central conflict.

The Infinity Gems are more than background lore. During a match, players can collect and activate gems for temporary advantages involving speed, power, defense and character-specific effects, opening up tactics that differ from a conventional Street Fighter duel. The gigantic sprites and exaggerated attacks build on X-Men: Children of the Atom and helped establish Capcom's particularly kinetic approach to Marvel characters. Marvel Super Heroes became a key stepping stone toward the later Marvel versus Capcom crossover series.

games.title: Moon Shuttle
games.description:
Moon Shuttle (1981), developed by Nichibutsu and distributed in North America by Taito, alternates between two distinctly different shooting challenges. First, the player guides a spacecraft through a dense asteroid belt, blasting gaps through rocks and accelerating through the resulting openings. Clearing that hazardous passage leads to combat against waves of alien craft that swoop in from several directions and fire on the ship. The pattern then repeats with greater difficulty.

The asteroid runs reward quick passage but punish misjudged gaps, while the alien encounters emphasize precise aiming and survival. Its use of speech samples and an unusual option to add credits during play for additional lives distinguish it from the many straightforward Galaxian-style shooters produced around the same time.

games.title: Marvel Super Heroes Vs. Street Fighter

variants.title: Marvel Super Heroes Vs. Street Fighter (Europe 970625)
Marvel Super Heroes Vs. Street Fighter (Asia 970625)
Marvel Super Heroes Vs. Street Fighter (Asia 970620)
Marvel Super Heroes Vs. Street Fighter (Brazil 970827)
Marvel Super Heroes Vs. Street Fighter (Brazil 970625)
Marvel Super Heroes Vs. Street Fighter (Hispanic 970625)
Marvel Super Heroes Vs. Street Fighter (Japan 970707)
Marvel Super Heroes Vs. Street Fighter (Japan 970702)
Marvel Super Heroes Vs. Street Fighter (Japan 970625)
Marvel Super Heroes Vs. Street Fighter (USA 970827)
Marvel Super Heroes Vs. Street Fighter (USA 970625)

games.description:
Marvel Super Heroes vs. Street Fighter (1997) continues Capcom's CPS-II crossover fighting series by pairing Marvel comic characters with the cast of Street Fighter. Instead of controlling one fighter per match, players assemble teams of two and swap between partners during combat. The off-screen character can recover some health, while Variable Attacks, counters and combined super moves turn team management into a key part of the fight. Spectacular aerial combos, screen-filling projectiles and a six-button layout carry forward the fast style established by X-Men vs. Street Fighter.

The roster mixes icons such as Spider-Man, Wolverine and Captain America with Ryu, Chun-Li and other Capcom fighters, and the game includes humorous character interactions and flamboyant super attacks. It is the second major Marvel/Capcom crossover fighter and an important link in the evolution of the tag-team format later associated with Marvel vs. Capcom.

games.title: Metal Soldier Isaac II
games.description:
Taito's Metal Soldier Isaac II (1985) is an overhead action shooter in which the player pilots a transforming combat robot through enemy-filled stages. In its humanoid form Isaac attacks with a Wind Blaster and a powerful returning Shuttle Punch that can pierce multiple targets. After taking enough damage, the robot's body is destroyed and the remaining fighter craft continues the battle, equipped with aerial fire and a ground-attack bomb. Destroying an armor dock can allow the fighter to recover its robot body. The objective includes eliminating enemy installations before confronting a major base at the stage's end.

Despite its numeral, Isaac II was not preceded by a commercially released game: a substantially different prototype called Metal Soldier Isaac led to the finished title. The attract-mode music was also later rearranged for the first stage of Taito's Darius, giving this relatively obscure game a lasting place in the company's musical history.

games.title: Mahjong Satsujin Jiken
games.description: Mahjong Satsujin Jiken, or Mahjong Murder Case, is a 1988 adult mahjong game from Nichibutsu. Despite its crime-mystery title, the central activity is competitive Japanese mahjong, with female character imagery typical of Nichibutsu's late-1980s releases. The game is a useful illustration of how arcade mahjong developers wrapped familiar tile-hand play in increasingly elaborate narrative and visual themes to differentiate cabinets.

games.title: Monster Slider
games.description:
Monster Slider (1997) is a competitive falling-block puzzle game developed by DATT Japan and converted for arcades by Visco from an earlier Sega Saturn release. Colored blocks drop in pairs, and groups of three or more matching pieces disappear, setting up the usual possibilities for chain reactions. Its defining innovation is a playfield that tilts: pieces slide toward the lower side under gravity, and the player can reverse the tilt to rearrange stacks or produce new matches.

This ability to move blocks after they have landed gives the familiar versus-puzzle formula a distinctive tactical twist. The arcade conversion redesigns its monster characters with a softer appearance and focuses on story and two-player competition, dropping the Saturn edition's endless mode.

games.title: Metal Slug - Super Vehicle-001
games.description:
Metal Slug: Super Vehicle-001 (1996) is Nazca's acclaimed debut entry in SNK's run-and-gun series, renowned for its extraordinary pixel animation and affectionate parody of military action. Soldiers Marco Rossi and Tarma Roving fight General Morden's forces through six side-scrolling missions, using pistols, grenades and rescued prisoners' weapon upgrades. Heavy machine guns, flamethrowers and other weapons change the rhythm of firefights, while the titular Metal Slug tank provides heavy armor, a cannon and the ability to crush enemies under its treads.

Its frantic cooperative action is filled with details that reward observation: soldiers panic, vehicles shed components, buildings crumble, and rescued hostages celebrate their freedom. The game was developed by veterans of Irem's GunForce and In the Hunt, and its meticulous hand-drawn animation helped establish a visual identity that subsequent installments retained for years. Metal Slug became one of the Neo Geo MVS platform's signature series and a benchmark for arcade sprite art.

games.title: Metal Slug 2 - Super Vehicle-001/II
games.description:
Metal Slug 2: Super Vehicle-001/II (1998) reunites Marco Rossi and Tarma Roving against General Morden, now supported by an increasingly bizarre coalition of adversaries. New playable soldiers Eri Kasamoto and Fio Germi expand the roster, and the campaign moves through deserts, cities, ruins and other elaborate environments. Players still run, jump and shoot through enemy forces while rescuing prisoners and boarding powerful vehicles, but new transformations can leave characters overweight or even mummified, changing their abilities and appearance.

The sequel increases the original's comic absurdity and eventually reveals an extraterrestrial threat. It is also notorious for severe slowdown when many sprites fill the screen. SNK's later Metal Slug X revisited much of the same material with rebalanced action and improved performance, making the two versions particularly interesting to compare.

games.title: Metal Slug 3
games.description:
Metal Slug 3 (2000) is one of SNK's most ambitious Neo Geo run-and-gun games, expanding the series far beyond a straightforward military campaign. Marco, Tarma, Eri and Fio battle soldiers, giant crustaceans, zombies, strange beasts and aliens through five enormous missions. A major innovation is the branching route system: players can take different paths through several stages, encountering alternative hazards, enemies and vehicles. Familiar guns and grenades are joined by an extravagant assortment of Slugs, including underwater and airborne machines.

The adventure continually changes its tone, from tropical beaches and underwater ruins to scenes of science-fiction horror and a spectacular final assault. Zombie transformations and other comedic effects preserve the series' taste for visual surprises even during its most difficult battles. The enormous last mission, intricate bosses and exceptional hand-drawn animation have helped make Metal Slug 3 a fan favorite and a high-water mark of Neo Geo sprite craftsmanship.

games.title: Metal Slug 6
games.description: Metal Slug 6 is an unofficial bootleg hack of Metal Slug 3 for Neo Geo hardware, not the separately developed official Metal Slug 6 released years later on Sammy's Atomiswave system. It retains the underlying missions, enemies and side-scrolling run-and-gun action of Metal Slug 3, but alters the program to provide additional tricks and character or weapon manipulation. In this edition, the fourth button can cycle to a different character while walking; pressing it together with fire can switch to a random weapon, including unusually powerful weapons. These modifications turn a familiar campaign into a novelty variation and explain why this set is grouped with Metal Slug 3 rather than with the official sixth installment.

games.title: Metal Slug 4
games.description:
Metal Slug 4 (2002), developed by Mega Enterprise and Noise Factory for SNK's Neo Geo hardware, sends the series' commandos against the computer-terrorist organization Amadeus. Marco Rossi and Fio Germi are joined by new fighters Trevor Spacey and Nadia Cassel, replacing two members of the preceding game's playable cast. The familiar side-scrolling missions combine soldiers, armored vehicles and large mechanical bosses with several new rides and weapons, including a dual machine gun.

The most notable mechanical addition is a timed combo-scoring system: collecting emblems starts a window in which continued enemy defeats build a bonus that can be cashed out by surviving. This gives experienced players an added incentive to press forward aggressively rather than merely staying alive. The game retains the series' explosive artwork and slapstick violence while reflecting the transition of Metal Slug development after SNK's original era.

games.title: Metal Slug 5
games.description:
Metal Slug 5 (2003) is a late Neo Geo entry developed by Noise Factory and SNK Playmore. When a secret disc relating to the Metal Slug project is stolen, Marco, Tarma, Eri and Fio investigate the Ptolemaic Army, an organization mixing advanced military technology with archaeological intrigue. Across five missions, they fight soldiers, machinery and enormous bosses with the series' familiar mix of accurate shooting and frantic evasive movement.

A new sliding move allows characters to advance low to the ground while firing, adding a small but useful option to the traditional jump-and-shoot controls. Several distinctive vehicles appear, particularly the transformable Slug Gunner robot, alongside underwater and aerial machines. Its darker presentation and emphasis on mechanical enemies give Metal Slug 5 a somewhat different atmosphere from the alien and zombie spectacles of Metal Slug 3.

games.title: Metal Slug X - Super Vehicle-001
games.description:
Metal Slug X (1999) is SNK's extensive revision of Metal Slug 2, using its familiar characters, plot and stages as the foundation for a more varied, faster-running arcade campaign. Marco, Tarma, Eri and Fio again battle Morden's army and its strange allies, rescuing hostages and collecting ever-more-destructive weapons along the way. Compared with its predecessor, enemy placements, bosses, item locations, backgrounds and available weaponry have been reworked, and new encounters appear in earlier stages.

Metal Slug 2's notorious slowdown is substantially reduced, although not eliminated, while the revised balance makes familiar routes less predictable. X is therefore much more than a simple bug-fix release: it is an alternate arrangement of an entire run-and-gun adventure, and for many players the definitive way to experience the second game's ideas.

games.title: Mushihime-Sama Matsuri Ver 1.5
games.description: Mushihime-Sama Matsuri Ver 1.5 is a special festival edition of Cave's vertical shoot-'em-up Mushihime-Sama produced for the May 2011 Cave Matsuri event on Cave CV1000 hardware, reworking the original game with Ver 1.5 scoring and bullet patterns.

games.title: Ms. Pac-Man

variants.title: Ms. Pacman Champion Edition / Super Zola Pac Gal

games.description:
Ms. Pac-Man, released in North American arcades by Midway in 1982, is one of the most beloved maze games ever made. The title character must clear every pellet from a labyrinth while evading Blinky, Pinky, Inky and Sue. Eating a power pellet temporarily turns the ghosts vulnerable, allowing a rapid chain of captures for escalating points, while bonus fruit roams the maze. Unlike the original Pac-Man's single repeated maze layout, Ms. Pac-Man cycles among four different designs, with changing colors, moving fruit and less predictable ghost movement.

The game began not inside Namco but as an enhancement kit called Crazy Otto, created by General Computer Corporation. A licensing arrangement with Midway transformed that project into an official Pac-Man follow-up, complete with new character art and intermission scenes about Pac-Man and Ms. Pac-Man's romance. Its enormous arcade popularity helped make its heroine one of gaming's most recognizable figures. It remains a model of how relatively modest changes to movement patterns and maze variety can refresh a classic design without losing its simplicity.

games.title: Ms. Pac-Man Twin
games.description: Ms. Pac-Man Twin (1992) is an unauthorized Argentine adaptation of Ms. Pac-Man that makes a striking change to the familiar maze-chase formula: two people can play simultaneously rather than alternating turns. Players guide their characters through pellet-filled mazes while evading ghosts and chasing power-pellet scoring opportunities. Its cooperative or competing simultaneous movement creates situations absent from the original single-character design. The set was produced without permission from Namco or General Computer Corporation and circulated principally in Argentina, making it an unusual regional modification of an arcade landmark.

games.title: Miss Puzzle
games.description: Miss Puzzle (1994) is an adult-oriented tile-matching arcade game by Min Corporation. Instead of dropping pieces into a well, the player slides existing tiles around a grid, attempting to line up three or more identical symbols horizontally, vertically or diagonally. Removed tiles cause others to shift into the empty spaces, while new pieces continue to appear, creating a race to prevent the screen from filling. A stage timer and periodic bonus phases add pressure. Successful clearing gradually uncovers a photographic illustration behind the tiles. The later Miss Bingo reused the basic mechanics with revised graphics and optional split-screen competition.

games.title: Monsters World
games.description: Monsters World (1994) is an unauthorized reworking of Mitchell's Super Pang, distributed under the TCH name. Its central play is the familiar bubble-clearing challenge: a character moves along the bottom of a single-screen arena, firing upward to split bouncing hazards into smaller pieces until the screen is clear. The main alteration is visual, replacing Super Pang's colored bubbles with horror-themed skulls, pumpkins and monster faces. It is best understood as a bootleg reskin of an existing arcade design rather than a separately invented shooter, and its resemblance to the source game is precisely what makes it an interesting curiosity.

games.title: Magic Sword - Heroic Fantasy
games.description:
Magic Sword: Heroic Fantasy (1990) is Capcom's ambitious side-scrolling fantasy action game, built around an ascent through a tower of fifty floors to defeat the evil influence of the Black Orb. Players fight with swords and ranged magical energy, collect treasure and keys, avoid traps and race toward each floor's exit. Cages release one of several possible companions, including knights, ninjas, wizards and archers, each bringing different attacks or utility. Only one ally travels with the hero at a time, so choosing whom to rescue becomes an important tactical decision.

A recharging magic meter determines the strength of the hero's ranged attack, rewarding measured strikes over mindless button pressing. Companions fight automatically in response to the player's actions, creating a distinctive two-character rhythm even in a one-player game. Its varied floors, elaborate sprite work and treasure-filled exploration connect the arcade immediacy of Black Tiger with a more elaborate fantasy adventure structure.

games.title: After Burner
games.description:
After Burner (Mega-Tech) brings Sega's celebrated jet-combat spectacle to the coin-operated Mega-Tech platform using a home-system adaptation of the arcade concept. The player pilots an F-14 Tomcat against waves of enemy aircraft, weaving through fast-moving environments and using cannon fire and homing missiles to destroy targets. The original 1987 After Burner was renowned for Yu Suzuki's sprite-scaling technology and deluxe moving cabinets, which made its simulated aerial maneuvers a major arcade attraction.

This cartridge should not be confused with that dedicated arcade machine: Mega-Tech used Sega's console-derived hardware and charged for timed access to selectable cartridges. It preserves the recognizable aircraft and high-speed shooter premise in a substantially different technical and physical format.

games.title: Arrow Flash
games.description:
Arrow Flash (Mega-Tech) is Sega's coin-operated presentation of its 1990 Mega Drive side-scrolling shooter. The player pilots a transforming craft through horizontally scrolling stages packed with alien enemies, projectiles and bosses. At any moment, the ship can change between a conventional fighter and a humanoid robot, with different weapon behavior and movement characteristics. A limited Arrow Flash attack provides a powerful emergency offensive or defensive option, while collected modules expand the ship's firepower.

The transformation system distinguishes Arrow Flash from most contemporary space shooters, as each form is useful in different attack patterns. On Mega-Tech the Genesis-derived game appears in a multi-cartridge arcade cabinet with timed, coin-funded play, rather than on a purpose-built shooter board.

games.title: Alien Storm (Mega-Tech
games.description:
Alien Storm (Mega-Tech) is Sega's coin-operated release of the Mega Drive adaptation of its 1990 arcade action game. The Alien Busters, a small band of eccentric specialists, fend off an invasion using close-range energy weapons, limited special attacks and occasional rapid-fire shooting sequences. Each character has a different visual style, and missions mix side-scrolling street combat with fast shooting encounters.

Although the title originated as a dedicated arcade game, this Mega-Tech cartridge is based on the console version, not a direct reproduction of the original multi-player arcade board. Its multi-game cabinet and timed credit system offer a different way to experience Sega's deliberately strange blend of Golden Axe-style brawling and science-fiction shooting.

games.title: Astro Warrior
games.description:
Astro Warrior (Mega-Tech) is the arcade-cabinet version of Sega's 1986 Master System vertically scrolling shooter. The player flies the Astro Raider through three stages of attacking spacecraft and mechanical defenses, shooting enemies and gathering power-ups before confronting a boss at each stage's end. Destroying particular ground targets can reveal supplies, and collected support craft or weapon upgrades strengthen the ship's normally modest firepower.

It is a straightforward example of Sega's early home-console shooting design, with a repeated three-stage loop and increasing enemy pressure. The Mega-Tech release places this Master System game inside Sega's timed, coin-operated multi-cartridge system, illustrating how the platform accommodated both 8-bit and Mega Drive software.

games.title: Alien Syndrome
games.description:
Alien Syndrome (Mega-Tech) adapts Sega's 1987 science-fiction rescue shooter through the Master System version rather than running the original dedicated arcade board. Players control Rick and Mary as they explore alien-infested stations, fire at grotesque creatures and free captured comrades. Once enough prisoners are rescued, the exit opens, but the team must reach it before a time bomb detonates; a large alien boss typically blocks progress. Different weapons found around the complex improve the odds of survival.

The scrolling maze layout makes route planning and finding hostages as important as marksmanship. This Mega-Tech cartridge presents the home-system interpretation on Sega's timed, coin-funded arcade hardware, a distinct lineage from the original arcade release.

games.title: Bonanza Bros.
games.description:
Bonanza Bros. (Mega-Tech) presents Sega's eccentric 1991 stealth-platform game in a coin-operated cabinet using the Mega Drive version. Brothers Robo and Mobo infiltrate guarded buildings to steal a list of valuables and escape before time expires. Their movement combines running, hiding behind doors and walls, and stunning pursuing guards, while split-screen two-player play allows the brothers to tackle a stage together. The cartoon characters and toy-like architecture make the caper feel like a slapstick heist rather than a conventional combat game.

Originally created for Sega's dedicated arcade hardware, Bonanza Bros. reached Mega-Tech through its home-console conversion. That matters when comparing layouts and presentation: the multi-cartridge Mega-Tech board offers timed play, not the same experience as the original stand-alone coin-op machine.

games.title: Altered Beast
games.description:
Altered Beast (Mega-Tech) is Sega's time-metered arcade-cabinet version of the Mega Drive conversion of its 1988 mythological beat-'em-up. Resurrected by Zeus, a warrior advances through monster-filled stages to rescue Athena. Defeating special white wolves releases Spirit Balls, and collecting enough transforms the hero first into a muscular fighter and then into a powerful beast, such as a werewolf or dragon, with a new attack repertoire. A battle against the stage boss follows each transformation.

The original arcade game became a symbol of Sega's late-1980s spectacle, and the Genesis version was famously bundled with the console in its early years. Mega-Tech returned that home adaptation to a coin-operated setting, but its hardware and time-based pricing should not be confused with the original arcade release's dedicated system.

games.title: Columns
games.description:
Columns (Mega-Tech) is Sega's arcade presentation of the jewel-matching puzzle game that became one of the Mega Drive's best-known early titles. Vertical columns of three colored gems fall into a rectangular well; the player moves them, cycles the order of the gems and tries to line up three or more matching colors vertically, horizontally or diagonally. Successful clears may produce chain reactions as unsupported gems fall into new combinations.

Its slower, more deliberate rhythm contrasts with Tetris, emphasizing visual pattern recognition in several directions. On the Mega-Tech system, the console version is offered as a selectable cartridge with coin-funded timed play. This is distinct from Sega's other dedicated Columns arcade boards, a useful distinction for arcade hardware historians.

games.title: Crack Down
games.description:
Crack Down (Mega-Tech) brings Sega's tactical 1990 action game to the arcade through its Mega Drive conversion. Two agents, Ben and Andy, infiltrate enemy compounds from an overhead perspective and must plant bombs at marked points before time runs out, then escape. Guards and robotic enemies patrol corridors, making cover and careful movement important; machine guns, heavier weapons and emergency smart bombs help players fight their way through.

The emphasis on placing explosives at prescribed locations gives Crack Down a different rhythm from an ordinary run-and-gun shooter. Its Mega-Tech cartridge is based on the home-console version of a game that also had a stand-alone arcade release, and was operated in Sega's multi-game, time-metered cabinet.

games.title: Cyber Police ESWAT: Enhanced Special Weapons and Tactics

variants.title: Cyber Police ESWAT: Enhanced Special Weapons and Tactics (Mega-Tech)

games.description:
ESWAT: City Under Siege (Mega-Tech), listed as Cyber Police ESWAT, is Sega's Genesis-based reimagining of its 1989 arcade police shooter. The player begins as a lightly equipped police officer combating organized crime; after earning a promotion, the hero gains an armored ESWAT suit equipped with far stronger weapons and jet-assisted movement. The side-scrolling stages combine platform jumps, gunfire, environmental traps and mechanized bosses.

Despite sharing a title and theme with the original arcade Cyber Police ESWAT, the Mega Drive game has substantially different stage design and progression. The Mega-Tech version uses this console incarnation in a coin-operated, timed-play cabinet, so it should not be mistaken for the original arcade game's board or its prisoner-capture structure.

games.title: Fire Shark
games.description:
Fire Shark (Mega-Tech) is Sega's coin-operated Mega Drive version of Toaplan's military-themed vertical shooter, known in Japan as Same! Same! Same! The player pilots a biplane against waves of tanks, aircraft, warships and artillery, weaving through gunfire while collecting speed increases and weapon upgrades. Distinctive weapons include a broad, twisting flame attack capable of covering large portions of the screen.

The action is built around tight enemy formations and relentless pressure, carrying forward the design tradition of Toaplan's earlier Flying Shark. Although the title originated as a dedicated 1989 arcade game, this Mega-Tech cartridge runs the console adaptation under Sega's timed multi-game cabinet system rather than the original arcade code.

games.title: Golden Axe
games.description:
Golden Axe (Mega-Tech) is the Mega Drive adaptation of Sega's influential 1989 fantasy beat-'em-up, offered in a coin-operated Mega-Tech cabinet. Ax Battler, Tyris Flare and Gilius Thunderhead seek revenge on the tyrant Death Adder, fighting through side-scrolling environments with weapons, throws and screen-wide magic spells. Each hero has a different elemental specialty, and stealing magic potions from small thieves builds the power of the next spell. Players can also ride fantastic beasts whose attacks help clear crowds.

The original Golden Axe helped define cooperative fantasy brawling in arcades, and the popular Mega Drive conversion brought its distinctive combat home. The Mega-Tech release is based on that conversion, with timed credit-based access; it must not be confused with the original dedicated arcade PCB or with Golden Axe II.

games.title: Golden Axe II
games.description:
Golden Axe II (Mega-Tech) is the time-based arcade-cabinet presentation of Sega's 1991 Mega Drive sequel to Golden Axe. Ax Battler, Tyris Flare and Gilius Thunderhead return to confront Dark Guld, a new villain who has seized the magical Golden Axe. Players advance through fantasy landscapes defeating groups of enemies with close-range weapons, throws and elemental spells, and gather magic books to power stronger attacks. Returning rideable creatures offer additional ways to control large crowds.

Although visually and mechanically close to the first game, Golden Axe II is specifically a Genesis sequel, not the later dedicated arcade game Golden Axe: The Revenge of Death Adder. Mega-Tech's coin-operated timer further distinguishes this edition from both home cartridges and Sega's separate Mega Play conversion.

games.title: Great Golf
games.description: Great Golf (Mega-Tech) is a Sega Master System golf game distributed for the company's multi-cartridge coin-operated platform. Viewed from a golfing perspective, players select clubs, aim shots and judge power in an attempt to complete a course with as few strokes as possible. Hazards, approach shots and putting reward careful control rather than reflexes. The title is associated with the later Master System Great Golf, also called Masters Golf in Japan, and should not automatically be conflated with the earlier Sega game bearing the same English name. As a Mega-Tech cartridge, it was played in a cabinet charging for timed access instead of using a dedicated golf arcade board.

games.title: Ghouls'n Ghosts
games.description:
Ghouls'n Ghosts (Mega-Tech) is Sega's coin-operated presentation of the Mega Drive conversion of Capcom's brutal 1988 platform shooter. Knight Arthur battles through cemeteries, burning villages and demonic fortresses to rescue Princess Prin-Prin. He runs, jumps and throws weapons in several directions, but a single hit strips away his armor and leaves him fighting in his underwear; another hit costs a life. Treasure chests and upgraded armor can unlock new equipment and powerful magic.

The series is famous for its demanding enemy placement and for requiring a second complete playthrough to reach the true ending with the necessary special weapon. The Mega Drive version was a notable early console showcase, and the Mega-Tech cartridge makes that adaptation available through timed arcade play, not the original Capcom CPS hardware.

games.title: Great Soccer
games.description: Great Soccer (Mega-Tech) is Sega's coin-operated presentation of its Master System football game, also known as World Soccer in several regions. Players guide an international team through matches, passing, dribbling, tackling and shooting while trying to create chances and defend their own goal. Team selection and the contrast between offense and defense supply the core of its accessible sports simulation. Its Mega-Tech cartridge was distributed in 1989, although the underlying Master System title had appeared earlier. It belongs to Sega's unusual selection of 8-bit console games playable in a timed, multi-cartridge arcade cabinet.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Kid Chameleon
games.description:
Kid Chameleon (Mega-Tech) is the 1992 Mega Drive platform adventure presented in Sega's timed coin-operated cabinet. The hero, Casey, enters a virtual-reality game and discovers magical helmets that transform him into characters with different powers, ranging from agile fighters to armored or fantastical forms. The player races through obstacle-filled side-scrolling stages, using each transformation to reach secrets, defeat enemies or survive otherwise impassable hazards. Hidden teleporters can redirect the route through a maze of more than a hundred levels.

Its enormous interconnected stage structure and emphasis on experimenting with helmets made Kid Chameleon a particularly ambitious Genesis platformer. The Mega-Tech cartridge preserves that console-oriented design inside an arcade rental system rather than converting it into a conventional short-credit arcade game.

games.title: Last Battle
games.description:
