Last Battle (Mega-Tech) is Sega's coin-operated Mega Drive release of a 1989 side-scrolling martial-arts action game. The player controls Aarzak, battling hostile fighters with punches, kicks and jumps as he travels between stages and confronts stronger opponents. A power meter fills as enemies are defeated, eventually allowing a more formidable combat state. Routes and confrontations alternate between crowd fights and challenging individual opponents.

The game's Japanese original, Hokuto no Ken: Shin Seikimatsu Kyuseishu Densetsu, was based on Fist of the North Star. The international Last Battle replaced the licensed characters and altered its presentation. The Mega-Tech entry is this console version operated through Sega's timed arcade multi-game system, not a separate original arcade brawler.

games.title: Moonwalker
games.description:
Michael Jackson's Moonwalker (Mega-Tech) is the Mega Drive version of Sega's 1990 game based on the film Moonwalker, offered in a time-metered arcade cabinet. Controlling a suited Michael Jackson, the player explores side-scrolling stages, defeats pursuers through dance-inspired attacks and searches for kidnapped children. Rescuing all the children opens the way to the stage's final encounter. In some stages, freeing a particular child first can trigger a falling star that transforms Jackson into a laser-firing robot. The soundtrack draws on recognizable Jackson songs.

Crucially, this is not the separate three-player isometric Moonwalker arcade game, in which contact with Bubbles the chimpanzee activates the robotic transformation. Sega developed distinct arcade and console adaptations of the film; Mega-Tech uses the latter, making its stage design and gameplay fundamentally different from the dedicated arcade cabinet.

games.title: Mystic Defender
games.description:
Mystic Defender (Mega-Tech) presents Sega's 1989 Mega Drive supernatural platform adventure in a coin-operated cabinet. The player controls Joe Yamato, known as Kujaku in the Japanese original, on a mission to stop the sorcerer Zao and rescue Alexandra. Monsters and traps fill the side-scrolling stages, but Joe fights primarily through charged magical attacks rather than conventional weapons. Additional spells provide straight shots, long-reaching flames and ricocheting projectiles, making weapon choice important when confronting different enemy patterns.

The game is related to the earlier SpellCaster and to the Kujaku Oh manga and anime, although international releases changed characters and names. Its Mega-Tech cartridge brings the Genesis version into Sega's timed multi-game arcade format.

games.title: Parlour Games
games.description: Parlour Games (Mega-Tech) is Sega's coin-operated release of a Master System collection of traditional indoor games. The cartridge offers billiards, darts and World Bingo, each controlled through menu and aiming inputs rather than the movement conventions of an action game. Billiards includes several rule variants, while the darts selection features formats such as 301, 501 and Around the Clock. World Bingo combines bingo-style number matching with slot-machine imagery. The collection illustrates Mega-Tech's broader library of console-derived diversions, offering a casual alternative to the platform games and shooters that dominated its other cartridges.

games.title: The Revenge of Shinobi
games.description:
The Revenge of Shinobi (Mega-Tech) is Sega's coin-operated presentation of its influential 1989 Mega Drive ninja action game. Joe Musashi seeks revenge on the Neo Zeed organization, advancing through side-scrolling stages with shuriken, close-range sword strikes, high somersault jumps and limited ninjutsu powers. Leaping between upper and lower routes is often essential, and each region culminates in a memorable boss. The soundtrack by Yuzo Koshiro became one of the Mega Drive's early musical showcases.

The original home release is also remembered for pop-culture-inspired enemies that were revised in later editions for licensing reasons. Mega-Tech uses a console-derived program in a timed multi-cartridge arcade machine, not the original Shinobi arcade hardware, making it a distinct stage in the series' history.

games.title: Super Hang-On
games.description:
Super Hang-On (Mega-Tech) brings Sega's celebrated motorcycle racer to a coin-operated multi-game cabinet through its Mega Drive adaptation. The action is viewed from behind the bike as the player threads through traffic, takes tight bends and races to reach checkpoints before time runs out. Turbo speed becomes available once the motorcycle has accelerated sufficiently, rewarding confident riding while making collisions increasingly costly. The underlying Super Hang-On design offers routes inspired by different continents and demands precise control at very high speed.

The original 1987 arcade game became famous for its specialized motorcycle cabinets and fast pseudo-3D road presentation. Mega-Tech instead runs the home-console version with ordinary controls and a timed credit system, so it is important not to confuse this cartridge with Sega's dedicated riding machine.

games.title: Space Harrier II
games.description:
Space Harrier II (Mega-Tech) is the timed arcade presentation of Sega's 1988 Mega Drive launch-era rail shooter, a direct sequel to Space Harrier. The hero flies and runs across a rapidly approaching checkerboard landscape, blasting bizarre enemies and weaving around incoming attacks. Huge bosses punctuate 13 stages, and the character's movement across the screen is the main defense against the relentless forward rush of obstacles and projectiles.

The game's bright fantasy scenery, shouted voice samples and scaling-style effects evoke Sega's celebrated arcade original, but Space Harrier II was initially designed for the Mega Drive rather than for the earlier dedicated arcade board. Its Mega-Tech release makes this home-console sequel a coin-operated title, offering a useful example of Sega transferring console software back into the amusement market.

games.title: Shinobi
games.description:
Shinobi on Sega's Mega-Tech arcade system is based on the Sega Master System conversion, not the original 1987 System 16 arcade program. Joe Musashi still battles the Zeed organization through side-scrolling ninja missions, throwing shuriken, fighting at close range and moving between platforms as he searches for kidnapped children. The Master System adaptation, however, changes several important rules: Joe has a health gauge instead of dying to a single strike, and rescuing hostages is optional but rewards the player with health and weapon improvements.

Special first-person bonus rounds can award ninjutsu techniques, making successful hostage rescues valuable even when they are not required to finish a stage. Mega-Tech hardware runs this Master System game in its compatible mode, adding a separate instruction display and coin-purchased playing time. This distinction makes the cartridge a historically interesting variant of Sega's influential ninja action game rather than a direct reproduction of the original coin-op.

games.title: Super Monaco GP
games.description:
Super Monaco GP on Sega's Mega-Tech system is the Mega Drive-based adaptation of Sega's celebrated Formula One racing game. From a cockpit-like forward view, players steer through tight bends, overtake rival cars and fight for a competitive finishing position. The Mega Drive version broadened the original arcade concept with a World Championship campaign, allowing drivers to compete across international circuits and advance to stronger teams.

Sega's 1989 dedicated arcade original became famous for its steering-wheel cabinet, gear-selection hardware and demanding Monaco qualifying session. The Mega-Tech cartridge should not be confused with that elaborate Sega X Board installation: it brings a console-style racing experience to a timed, coin-operated multi-game cabinet, illustrating how Sega reused its home library in amusement venues.

games.title: Sonic The Hedgehog 2
games.description:
Sonic the Hedgehog 2 is Sega's 1992 speed-focused platform sequel, presented here in its Mega-Tech arcade cartridge edition. Sonic and his new companion Miles 'Tails' Prower race through sprawling side-scrolling zones of slopes, springs, loops and hazards to stop Dr. Robotnik's plans for the Death Egg. The Spin Dash lets Sonic accelerate from a standstill, while collectible rings protect him from ordinary damage.

The game adds spectacular half-pipe special stages for collecting Chaos Emeralds, competitive split-screen play and the ability for a second player to control Tails in the main adventure. Sega's Mega-Tech version substantially retains the Mega Drive game, including its options and two-player features, but incorporates the arcade system's credit-funded overall play timer and separate score display. This distinguishes it from the more heavily modified Mega Play version, which removes several console features.

games.title: Sonic The Hedgehog
games.description:
Sonic the Hedgehog, Sega's breakthrough 1991 Mega Drive platform game, also appeared as a Mega-Tech arcade cartridge. Sonic races across the rolling Green Hill Zone, the flooded Labyrinth Zone and other visually distinctive environments, gathering golden rings while freeing animals imprisoned in Dr. Robotnik's robots. Momentum, branching routes, springs and loop-the-loops encourage players to combine careful platforming with bursts of speed.

Rings act as an unusually forgiving form of protection: a hit scatters them, giving Sonic a chance to recover some before another hit becomes fatal. Giant rings at the ends of certain acts lead to rotating special stages where players can seek Chaos Emeralds. The Mega-Tech release preserves the essence of the original Mega Drive game but makes it playable in a coin-operated, time-limited format; AdvanceMAME also distinguishes two Mega-Tech cartridge sets. It is not the shortened, rebalanced Mega Play conversion.

Sonic's mixture of expressive animation, fast scrolling and accessible controls made him Sega's international mascot and a defining figure of the 16-bit console era. Its arcade appearance is a revealing example of the traffic between home-console design and amusement hardware in the early 1990s.

games.title: Super Thunder Blade
games.description:
Super Thunder Blade is the 1988 Mega Drive helicopter shooter, presented on Sega's Mega-Tech arcade system. Following the arcade Thunder Blade, it sends an attack helicopter through four military missions, blasting enemy aircraft and installations with a rapid-fire gun and homing missiles. Its main sections use a behind-the-helicopter perspective, with the aircraft weaving around buildings, cave walls and incoming fire; boss confrontations switch to an overhead viewpoint.

A distinctive air-brake control slows forward motion, making it possible to dodge obstacles or line up targets more carefully. Although inspired by Sega's striking arcade hardware, Super Thunder Blade is its own Mega Drive game rather than a direct reproduction of the original moving-cabinet experience. On Mega-Tech it becomes a timed, credit-operated attraction.

games.title: Joe Montana II: Sports Talk Football

variants.title: Joe Montana II: Sports Talk Football (Mega-Tech)

games.description:
Joe Montana II: Sports Talk Football is a 1991 Sega Mega Drive American football game also distributed for the Mega-Tech arcade system. Players choose offensive and defensive plays, pass or run the ball and compete in full football matches, with a broad selection of teams and a playbook of more than 50 plays. The side-on field view zooms in on active plays, and two players can compete or cooperate.

Its defining feature is synthesized play-by-play commentary that reacts to the action, an ambitious presentation technique on cartridge hardware in 1991. The original also offers exhibition and league play. In Mega-Tech cabinets, the console-derived game runs within Sega's coin-operated, time-controlled environment rather than in a dedicated football arcade machine.

games.title: Tetris
games.description:
Tetris for Sega's Mega-Tech is a rare arcade release of the Mega Drive adaptation of Alexey Pajitnov's falling-block puzzle. Players rotate and position seven four-square shapes in a ten-column well, completing horizontal rows to clear them before the rising stack reaches the top. As the descent speed increases, anticipation and efficient placement become essential; clearing four rows at once earns a particularly valuable 'Tetris'.

This cartridge has a notable history distinct from both Atari Games' 1989 arcade Tetris and Sega's earlier System 16 arcade version. Sega's planned Mega Drive retail release was cancelled amid disputes over console publishing rights, but its game survived in the Mega-Tech coin-operated format. The resulting cartridge is an unusual piece of Tetris licensing history and an uncommon way to experience Sega's home-system interpretation of the classic puzzle.

games.title: Thunder Force II MD
games.description:
Thunder Force II MD is Technosoft's 1989 Mega Drive adaptation of its X68000 shooter, available on Sega's Mega-Tech arcade hardware. It alternates between overhead, freely navigable battlefield sections, where players must locate and destroy enemy bases, and fast horizontal scrolling sections that culminate in imposing bosses. This unusual two-perspective structure bridges the exploratory original Thunder Force and the more straightforward side-scrolling sequels.

Players collect and switch between different weapon types, including the series' signature homing Hunter shots, and can acquire rotating CRAW support pods that provide extra firepower and intercept some incoming bullets. Weapons lost on destruction add a tactical cost to careless flying. The 'MD' suffix identifies the Mega Drive adaptation, while the Mega-Tech cabinet adds timed coin-operated play to what was originally a console release.

games.title: Arnold Palmer Tournament Golf
games.description:
Arnold Palmer Tournament Golf is Sega's 1989 Mega Drive golf simulation presented as a Mega-Tech arcade cartridge. Players select clubs, adjust aim and shot shape, and operate a three-step swing meter to determine power and ball flight. A caddy offers advice on distances and the lie, while putting requires a closer view of the green and a different judgment of direction and strength.

The game offers practice rounds and an extended tournament involving courses associated with the United States, Japan and Britain. Better performance can improve the golfer's abilities and unlock higher-quality clubs. Its branding is a localization curiosity: the Japanese original featured golfer Naomichi Ozaki, whereas Arnold Palmer's name was used for Western marketing, without making Palmer a playable character in the game. Mega-Tech's timed arcade presentation sets this cartridge apart from the standalone home release.

games.title: Tommy Lasorda Baseball
games.description:
Tommy Lasorda Baseball is a Sega Mega Drive baseball game also issued for the Mega-Tech cartridge arcade system in 1989. The game combines batting, pitching, fielding and base running with team management: players select from 26 city-based clubs, whose athlete names and statistics are fictional, and consider the strengths and stamina of their batters and pitchers. Matches can be played individually or as part of a longer season leading toward the championship.

Pitch selection and timing at the plate are complemented by fielding decisions and adjustable conditions such as wind and defensive errors. The console edition's password-based season progression illustrates the title's home-game origins, while Mega-Tech provides a coin-operated presentation with a timed session. Manager Tommy Lasorda's endorsement supplied a recognizable baseball name to Sega's early 16-bit sports library.

games.title: World Championship Soccer
games.description:
World Championship Soccer is Sega's overhead-view football game, adapted to the Mega-Tech arcade system from the early Mega Drive library. Players select a national side, then pass, dribble, shoot and slide-tackle their way through brisk matches. Teams have differing ratings for speed, skill, defending and goalkeeping, but the rules are deliberately simplified, emphasizing immediate action instead of fouls and tactical management.

The game became closely associated with the 1990 World Cup, appearing in Europe as World Cup Italia '90, although this Mega Drive-derived title should not be confused with similarly named 8-bit conversions. The Mega-Tech release places its console-style international competition in Sega's multi-cartridge, timed arcade format.

games.title: Magical Tetris Challenge
games.description:
Magical Tetris Challenge is Capcom's 1998 competitive puzzle game that combines Disney characters with the familiar falling-block mechanics of Tetris. Mickey Mouse, Minnie Mouse, Donald Duck and Goofy face opponents in storybook-style contests, fitting rotating shapes together to complete lines while trying to disrupt the other player's board. Alongside the seven classic tetrominoes, special pieces of unusual sizes and shapes create sudden changes of fortune.

The approachable Disney presentation disguises a combative variation of a puzzle classic, with careful line clearing used both to survive and to overwhelm rivals. Its arcade release on Seta's Aleck64 hardware makes it part of the late-1990s trend toward familiar licensed characters in competitive puzzle games. Capcom later brought the concept to home systems including the Nintendo 64.

games.title: Martial Champion
games.description:
Martial Champion is Konami's 1993 one-on-one fighting game, developed during the surge of arcade brawlers following Street Fighter II. Ten international combatants compete in best-of-three-round matches, with a roster spanning martial artists, soldiers and weapon-wielding specialists. Its colorful stages and unusually tall leaps give many encounters a distinctive rhythm.

Rather than the customary three strengths of punches and kicks, its controls emphasize high, middle and low attacks. Some fighters can be disarmed, allowing their weapons to be taken and used by opponents, a striking departure from conventional unarmed tournament fighters. Although overshadowed by bigger genre franchises, Martial Champion is an interesting Konami experiment with range, spacing and weapon ownership.

games.title: Mouse Trap
games.description:
Mouse Trap, released by Exidy in 1981, is a maze-chase game that transforms the familiar pellet-collecting formula into a battle of improvisation. Players guide a mouse through corridors, gathering cheese while cats patrol the passages. Three dedicated color-coded buttons open and close corresponding doors, letting skilled players reroute pursuit and reshape the maze moment by moment.

Bones collected in the maze allow the mouse to become a dog temporarily and chase down the cats for bonus points, but a marauding hawk threatens either form. The central teleport box provides a risky escape to a random corner. Mouse Trap stands out among early Pac-Man-inspired games for making the maze itself an active player-controlled tool rather than a fixed obstacle course.

games.title: Mega Twins
games.description:
Mega Twins, known in Japan as Chiki Chiki Boys, is Capcom's 1990 colorful fantasy platform action game. Two young princely survivors travel through the ruined kingdom of Alurea in search of the legendary Dragon Blue Eyes stone, hoping to reverse the devastation wrought by monsters. One or two players jump, climb walls, slash enemies with magic swords and use limited screen-clearing spells while navigating lively side-scrolling stages.

The blue twin favors stronger sword attacks, while the red twin can carry more magical power. Hidden treasure chests supply coins, health and upgrades, rewarding exploration beyond the direct route. Its playful character designs and cooperative swordplay make Mega Twins one of Capcom's appealing, less widely remembered arcade platformers of the early 1990s.

games.title: Mug Smashers
games.description:
Mug Smashers is a 1990 side-scrolling beat-'em-up in which Axel and his friend Miles fight through the streets of San Francisco to rescue Axel's kidnapped sister, police officer Sheila, from the criminal Mad Dog. Players advance through crowds of street thugs using punches, kicks and jumping attacks, occasionally turning discarded weapons such as knives, wrenches or firearms against the opposition.

The game follows the multi-plane street-fighting formula popularized by Double Dragon and Final Fight, but stands out for its camp character designs, exaggerated enemies and unusually scrappy presentation. It was developed with involvement from Britain's 3-D Games, and its sound effects and music have been identified as borrowing from The Combatribes.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Multi Champ
games.description:
Multi Champ is a Korean multi-event arcade game developed by Excellent Soft Design (ESD), whose first coin-operated release appeared in 1998. Rather than offering one continuous campaign, it assembles a selection of compact, competitive mini-games in which quick reactions and simple joystick-and-button controls matter more than long-term memorization. Its colorful, cartoon-style presentation and support for one or two players make it suitable for short arcade sessions.

Different board revisions and regional versions circulated, including Korean and World sets. Multi Champ is historically notable as the debut of ESD, a small developer that went on to make other distinctive Korean arcade games.

games.title: Muroge Monaco
games.description:
Muroge Monaco is an early-1980s electronic casino-card game from an unidentified manufacturer. It uses a button-only control panel and an unusually simple Motorola 6802-based board, reflecting the primitive but specialized hardware common to the first generation of video gambling cabinets. Related program sets include a possible bootleg and a rethemed Las Vegas, Nevada version.

Its sparse presentation and one-bit delta-sigma sound hardware have made the underlying board more thoroughly documented than its precise betting rules. The closely related revisions are a useful example of early gambling software being repackaged for different markets.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.
Original developer and publisher are not established.

games.title: Mushihime-Sama
games.description:
Mushihime-Sama, Cave's 2004 'Insect Princess' shooter, follows Princess Reco riding the golden beetle Kiniro into a forest of enormous insects. The game turns this organic fantasy setting into a classic Cave 'bullet hell' challenge: five vertically scrolling stages fill with dense, carefully patterned projectile barrages, ending in elaborate insect bosses. Players maneuver through narrow gaps, build firepower with options and upgrades, and reserve bombs for especially dangerous moments.

Its three modes offer notably different experiences. Original favors fast aimed enemy shots, Maniac emphasizes elaborate patterns and a demanding scoring system, and the initially hidden Ultra pushes bullet density and difficulty to extremes. Players also select shot types that alter the balance between coverage and concentrated attack.

The combination of intricate enemy animation, woodland imagery, Manabu Namiki's music and precision-focused scoring made Mushihime-Sama one of Cave's defining mid-2000s releases. It later gained revisions and home conversions, but the original arcade game remains a key work in the modern manic-shooter tradition.

games.title: Puzzle! Mushihime-Tama
games.description:
Puzzle! Mushihime-Tama is Cave's 2005 arcade puzzle spin-off of Mushihime-Sama, using the same insect-fantasy characters on Cave's CV1000 hardware. Princess Reco launches colored stones into a packed playfield, clearing groups of three or more matching pieces to open a passage for a trapped Kojuu creature. The task mixes quick targeting with careful management of how the remaining stones are supported and arranged.

Every fifth stage introduces a different challenge: players must repeatedly strike a marked point on a boss with stones to keep it from escaping. Closely related in spirit to Cave's earlier Puzzle Uo Poko, the game replaces the original shooter's streams of bullets with colorful, increasingly intricate rescue puzzles.

games.title: Musoubana
games.description:
Musoubana is a 1995 Japanese adult-oriented hanafuda game developed by Yubis and published by Nichibutsu. Its progression is built around matches against five illustrated opponents, with each opponent requiring victories across three rounds of traditional flower-card play. Winning grants points that can be spent on assistance items in later rounds, adding a limited resource-management element to the card game.

Between opponents, a memory-matching bonus game offers opportunities for additional points. The game's adult reward illustrations reflect a particular strand of Japanese arcade and medal-game entertainment rather than the action-oriented video game market.

games.title: Mustache Boy
games.description:
Mustache Boy is a 1987 overhead maze-action game in which a small mustachioed character races across a grid of tiles to change every tile to the required color. Wandering enemies interrupt the route, so the player must plot an efficient path, leap over hazards and trigger special tiles that can eliminate pursuers.

Collectible balloons yield points and bonuses, while the ability to jump across gaps makes the board feel more like a platforming maze than a simple Pac-Man clone. Clearing all the tiles completes the round, and the game supports one or two players.

games.title: US AAF Mustang
games.description:
US AAF Mustang is a 1990 horizontally scrolling World War II shooter developed by NMK and published by UPL. Players pilot a P-51 Mustang through battles against Japanese and German forces, sweeping across coastal, jungle and European battlefields. Waves of fighter aircraft, ground emplacements and enormous bomber bosses demand continuous movement and fire.

The plane's forward shots can be upgraded, while separate ground attacks help clear targets below. The action is particularly memorable for richly layered parallax backgrounds, dramatic aircraft explosions and a campaign that crosses several theaters of war. It is a polished example of the early-1990s military shoot-'em-up, also known through its home conversion as Fire Mustang.

games.title: Mutant Fighter
games.description:
Mutant Fighter, called Death Brade in Japan, is Data East's 1991 fantasy wrestling game. Instead of conventional martial artists, players select from a roster including Hercules, an Amazon, a minotaur, a golem and a dragon, then grapple in one-on-one bouts against other mythological fighters. Throws, suplexes and wrestling-style attacks matter as much as ordinary strikes, with each combatant differing in speed, power and defense.

Its mixture of sword-and-sorcery imagery and professional-wrestling mechanics gives it a distinctive identity among the Street Fighter II era's arcade combat games. It also features an unusually theatrical set of opponents, including legendary beasts and supernatural bosses.

games.title: Mutation Nation
games.description:
Mutation Nation is SNK's 1992 Neo Geo side-scrolling beat-'em-up set in a city overrun by victims of grotesque genetic experiments. Ricky and Johnny fight their way through six districts of mutated gang members, monsters and mechanical enemies, using fists, kicks, jumping strikes and throws to survive. Two players can join forces in an adventure defined by colorful, exaggerated creature animation.

Rather than relying on discarded street weapons, the game distributes elemental power spheres that activate different special attacks. Players must decide when to save or spend these abilities, especially against large bosses. Its heavy-impact animation and comic-book body horror place it among the more individualistic early Neo Geo action games.

games.title: MVP
games.description:
M.V.P. is Sega's 1990 baseball arcade game for the System 16B platform, with a 1989 copyright date. Players compete through conventional innings, selecting pitches and controlling batting and fielding with a joystick and three buttons. Its available game formats include a pennant-race final involving Japanese professional teams and an all-star contest.

Sega emphasized immediate, dramatic sports action: powerful pitches can vary in speed and force, fielders attempt spectacular diving catches, and home runs or outstanding defensive plays receive close-up replays. The game shows Sega experimenting with television-style presentation in baseball before many of its better-known home-console sports titles.

games.title: Marvel Vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes

variants.title: Marvel Vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes (Europe 980123)
Marvel Vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes (Asia 980123)
Marvel Vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes (Asia 980112)
Marvel Vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes (Brazil 980123)
Marvel Vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes (Hispanic 980123)
Marvel Vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes (Japan 980123)
Marvel Vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes (Japan 980112)
Marvel Vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes (Japan 980123) (Single PCB)
Marvel Vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes (Europe 980112)
Marvel Vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes (USA 980123)
Marvel Vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes (USA 971222)

games.description:
Marvel vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes is Capcom's 1998 crossover fighting spectacle, pairing Marvel Comics icons with characters from Street Fighter, Mega Man and other Capcom series. Players assemble two-character teams, switching partners during combat while performing elaborate combos, aerial launches and screen-filling super moves. A third, randomly assigned special guest character can be called in for a limited number of assist attacks.

The game expands the tag-team structure introduced in X-Men vs. Street Fighter and Marvel Super Heroes vs. Street Fighter. Its most theatrical mechanic is the Variable Cross, which temporarily allows both members of a team to attack together, often creating spectacular combinations. The battle against the merged Professor X/Magneto villain Onslaught provides its climactic encounter.

Built on Capcom's CPS-2 hardware, the game became a staple of late-1990s competitive arcades for its fluid animation, oversized character roster and flamboyant comic-book presentation. It helped establish the crossover formula that would later reach an even wider audience with Marvel vs. Capcom 2.

games.title: Michael Jackson's Moonwalker
games.description:
Michael Jackson's Moonwalker is Sega's 1990 arcade action game based loosely on Jackson's film and musical persona. Up to three players control versions of the singer in white 'Smooth Criminal' suits, exploring isometric stages while rescuing kidnapped children from the criminal Mr. Big. Instead of conventional punches or firearms, Jackson attacks enemies with bursts of magic, and holding the attack button strengthens the blast.

The game's most unforgettable move is Dance Magic: Jackson starts a choreographed routine that forces surrounding enemies to dance along before collapsing, turning a screen-clearing attack into a miniature music video. The chimpanzee Bubbles can also trigger a transformation into a heavily armed robot.

Different from the side-scrolling home-console Moonwalker, Sega's System 18 arcade version makes spectacular use of digitized Jackson music, synchronized dance animations and cooperative play. Its unlikely mixture of celebrity licensing, child-rescue objectives and surreal combat remains one of the strangest recognizable arcade adaptations of a pop star.

games.title: Mighty Warriors
games.description:
Mighty Warriors is a 1990 one-on-one arcade fighting game developed by Electronic Devices. Players select stylized martial artists and compete in head-to-head bouts, using joystick movement, strikes and special techniques to wear down an opponent. A distinctive gimmick allows fighters to transform or mutate temporarily during combat, changing the appearance and possibilities of a match.

Released in the early wave of arcade fighting experiments before Street Fighter II's dominance, it is a relatively obscure example of the genre's fascination with unusual character powers.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: MX5000
games.description:
MX5000, titled Flak Attack in Japan, is Konami's 1987 vertically scrolling military shooter. Players pilot a fighter aircraft against the forces of the Tesaris Empire, attacking planes, helicopters, tanks, ships and ground installations. The campaign moves through plains, volcanoes, ocean, tundra and an enemy base, with separate forward-firing weapons and bombs for targets beneath the aircraft.

Destroying enemies fills distinct Plane and Tank power gauges, earning upgrades that include more powerful laser fire, improved bombing patterns and speed boosts. This dual progression gives the player another reason to engage both aerial and ground threats instead of merely surviving them. The game's mixed battlefields and varied target types make it an interesting Konami alternative to the spacecraft-oriented Gradius formula.

games.title: Kosodate Quiz My Angel
games.description:
Kosodate Quiz: My Angel is Namco's 1996 Japanese arcade quiz game that turns trivia into a miniature parenting simulation. One or two players take the roles of a girl's parents, guiding her from birth into adulthood. Each timed multiple-choice question tests general knowledge: correct answers earn child-support funds, especially when given quickly, while mistakes consume the family's limited hearts.

Between quiz rounds, players make decisions about the child's upbringing and spend the earned resources on activities or choices that influence her personality and future. This interplay between straightforward four-answer trivia and branching family outcomes gives the game a recognizable identity beyond a standard Japanese quiz cabinet.

games.title: Kosodate Quiz My Angel 2
games.description:
Kosodate Quiz: My Angel 2 is Namco's 1997 follow-up to its parenting-themed quiz game. Players work through four-choice trivia questions while watching an illustrated daughter grow up, with their performance contributing to the simulated upbringing and its eventual outcome. The premise turns a succession of short quiz challenges into a lighthearted life story.

The sequel continues the original's combination of Japanese cultural trivia and character-focused presentation, making it an unusual example of quiz arcade design that builds a continuing narrative around a player's answers.

games.title: Kosodate Quiz My Angel 3
games.description:
Kosodate Quiz My Angel 3 is Namco's third arcade entry in its unusual child-raising trivia series, released in Japan in 1998. Instead of treating questions as an isolated test of general knowledge, the series frames success as the task of bringing up a daughter. Players answer multiple-choice questions to earn the resources needed for her upbringing, while the child's growth and life choices give the quiz a long-term goal. The combination of domestic-life simulation and trivia made My Angel distinct from more conventional Japanese arcade quiz machines.

This third installment follows the 1996 original and its 1997 sequel, and runs on Namco System 11 hardware. It uses four answer buttons and supports two players, continuing the series' approachable, character-driven presentation at a time when most high-profile arcade releases were action or fighting games.

games.title: Virtual Mahjong 2 - My Fair Lady

variants.title: Virtual Mahjong 2 - My Fair Lady (J 980608 V1.000)

games.description:
Virtual Mahjong II: My Fair Lady is Micronet's 1998 adult-oriented mahjong game for Sega's ST-V arcade hardware. The game centers on four-sided Japanese mahjong matches against a computer opponent named Aya. Victories unlock fully rendered 3D reward scenes showing Aya in different cosplay outfits, a distinctive presentation feature carried over from the original Virtual Mahjong.

Unlike many rival strip-mahjong games built around a roster of illustrated opponents, this sequel concentrates on a single character and a range of three-dimensional scenes. It was also released for the Sega Saturn, reflecting the close relationship between ST-V arcade boards and Sega's home console.

games.title: My Hero
games.description:
My Hero, known in Japan as Seishun Scandal, is Sega's 1985 side-scrolling street-fighting platform game. When a gang member kidnaps the hero's girlfriend, the player pursues him through a city street, a ninja-infested area and other increasingly improbable locations. Punches, kicks and jumps dispatch attackers, while carefully timed leaps are essential for avoiding obstacles and projectiles.

The arcade adventure cycles through three increasingly difficult stages, and a rescued bystander can temporarily fight alongside the hero. Its uncompromising one-hit vulnerability and densely arranged hazards give it a demanding rhythm quite different from later, slower-paced beat-'em-ups. Sega subsequently adapted the game for the Master System.

games.title: Mystic Marathon
games.description:
Mystic Marathon is Williams' 1984 fantasy racing game, an arcade oddity in which a small elf-like Benkin competes with six computer-controlled rivals across magical islands. Players run, jump and swim through winding courses, seeking a top-three finish to qualify for the next race. Success depends on selecting fast routes while avoiding apple-throwing trees, sinkholes, lightning, monsters and other time-wasting hazards.

Caves, boats and other magical shortcuts can dramatically improve a race, while an overview display helps track the positions of competitors. Instead of the usual lives-based combat, the game creates tension through route planning and the unforgiving cost of even a brief delay. Its hybrid of platforming and race strategy remains distinctive within Williams' arcade catalog.

games.title: Mystic Riders
games.description:
Mystic Riders, known in Japan as Mahou Keibitai Gun Hohki, is Irem's 1992 side-scrolling fantasy shooter. Players control young witches riding flying broomsticks through colorful environments full of strange monsters and magical machinery. The broomstick serves both as transportation and a weapon: it can be launched as a spinning attack in multiple directions, complementing the regular stream of magic shots.

The game supports cooperative play and mixes lively character animation with demanding enemy formations across six stages. Its whimsical setting offers a striking contrast to the military and science-fiction imagery that dominated contemporary horizontal shooters.

games.title: Mysterious Stones - Dr. John's Adventure

variants.title: Mysterious Stones - Dr. Kick in Adventure

games.description:
Mysterious Stones: Dr. John's Adventure is Technos Japan's 1984 overhead action game, released in Japan as Dr. Kick's Adventure. An explorer searches ancient temples and archaeological sites for valuable artifacts, breaking open stones to uncover their contents while trying to avoid or defeat hostile guardians. The player moves across compact, densely populated screens, using attacks to clear a path and reveal treasure.

Its archaeological treasure hunt combines maze movement, simple combat and the risk of spending too long searching dangerous rooms. The game's quirky setting and emphasis on examining objects distinguish it from more conventional early-1980s shooters.

games.title: Mystic Warriors
games.description:
Mystic Warriors is Konami's 1993 cooperative ninja action game, a spiritual successor to Sunset Riders. Up to four players choose from a team of fighters opposing the authoritarian SKULL organization, running through layered side-scrolling stages and attacking enemies with endless shuriken or close-range blades. Jumps between platforms, slides and dangerous boss confrontations make the combat highly mobile.

Players can break open containers for weapon enhancements, and a life meter allows several hits before defeat. After the initial character selection, one hero is kidnapped, giving the remaining team a personal rescue mission. Konami's vivid backgrounds, large animated bosses and elaborate action sequences make it a memorable late-era 2D arcade production.

games.title: Nagano Winter Olympics '98
games.description:
Nagano Winter Olympics '98 is Konami's licensed multi-event sports arcade game, drawing on the 1998 Winter Olympic Games in Japan. Competitors tackle events such as speed skating, skiing, luge, bobsleigh, snowboard disciplines and curling, each requiring different timing, steering or button technique. Players can select individual Olympic contests or take part in an extended multi-event championship.

The arcade game belongs to Konami's Track & Field and Hyper Sports tradition, adapting its accessible, short-form competitive events to winter disciplines. Rapid shifts between precision, rhythm and speed make it particularly suitable for head-to-head play in an amusement setting.

games.title: NAM-1975
games.description:
NAM-1975 is one of the Neo Geo's original 1990 launch-era games, a military shooting gallery that borrows the camera and aiming conventions of Cabal. Set against a fictionalized backdrop of the Vietnam War, it follows soldiers Silver and Brown as they rescue captives and uncover a scientist's plan to build a devastating superweapon. The action moves through six stages of enemy troops, vehicles, helicopters and enormous bosses.

Players move a character along the foreground while directing a separate gun sight into the battlefield. Fire holds the soldier in place for precise aiming, while a rolling dodge provides a crucial moment of invulnerability. Temporary machine guns and flamethrowers supplement standard weaponry, and two players can coordinate attacks.

Its large sprites, dramatic character portraits and sampled audio advertised the Neo Geo MVS's power at the platform's debut. The game's punishing difficulty and stylized action place it between traditional shooting galleries and the cinematic combat games that followed.

games.title: Namennayo
games.description:
Namennayo is a 1982 overhead obstacle-avoidance game based on Japan's Nameneko craze, featuring cats dressed and posed as rebellious youths. The player steers a cat riding a small motorcycle along a course, dodging hazards and collecting fish. Rather than fighting enemies with projectiles, the challenge comes from positioning, steering and reacting to obstacles in the path.

Its greatest historical curiosity is the character license: Nameneko's costumed real-cat photographs were a popular novelty in early-1980s Japan, giving this otherwise simple action game an unmistakable period identity.

games.title: Name That Tune
games.description:
Name That Tune is Bally Sente's 1986 arcade adaptation of the television music quiz. Players listen to melodies and identify songs through multiple-choice answers, with the presentation built around on-screen text and a small animated hand playing piano notes. The quiz format recreates the appeal of recognizing a tune after hearing only a brief fragment.

Much of the game's cartridge space is devoted to the music itself, resulting in unusually restrained animation compared with other mid-1980s arcade releases. It is a distinctive example of an amusement machine centered on sound recognition rather than dexterity.

games.title: Naname de Magic!
games.description:
Naname de Magic! is a 1994 Japanese competitive falling-piece puzzle game by Atlus. Instead of eliminating ordinary horizontal rows, players arrange matching elemental symbols along diagonal lines to trigger attacks against an opponent. The emphasis on diagonal patterns gives familiar stacking and color-matching decisions a different geometry.

Its super-deformed fantasy fighters, animated reactions and escalating head-to-head pressure reflect the same arcade-puzzle trend that produced games such as Puyo Puyo. The diagonal-matching rule is what sets this relatively obscure title apart from its better-known contemporaries.

games.title: Narc
games.description:
NARC is Williams' 1988 run-and-gun crime thriller, starring narcotics officers Max Force and Hit Man on a campaign against Mr. Big's drug empire. Players advance through side-scrolling streets, junkyards and hideouts, confronting dealers, guard dogs, vehicles and grotesquely caricatured criminals. Machine guns, rockets and the option to arrest some suspects create a peculiar mixture of police action and relentless arcade violence.

Its enormous digitized-looking characters, graphic explosions and notorious drug-war imagery made it one of the most provocative coin-ops of its period. Evidence and money collected during stages contribute to scoring, and two players can cooperate against the waves of opponents.

Running on Williams' powerful arcade hardware, NARC helped establish the studio's taste for loud, spectacular digitized presentation, a direction later pushed much further by Mortal Kombat. Its violence and exaggerated anti-drug message remain central to its historical reputation.

games.title: Nastar
games.description:
Nastar, called Rastan Saga II in Japan, is Taito's 1988 sequel to Rastan. Players guide a barbarian warrior through six side-scrolling rounds, cutting down monsters while scaling platforms and facing dangerous bosses in a fantasy world threatened by evil forces. Sword attacks can be directed at different heights, and different weapons and special attacks provide alternatives to simple close-range slashing.

The game keeps the original's heroic-fantasy premise but changes its visual style and movement, making it a notably different action experience from the first Rastan. Its dramatic enemy designs and imposing castle settings preserve the series' sword-and-sorcery identity.

games.title: NATO Defense
games.description:
NATO Defense is Pacific Novelty's 1982 maze-action game, putting the player in control of a tank clearing mines from cities threatened by enemy armor. Movement through maze-like streets removes mines, while shells can destroy opposing tanks or certain wall sections. Ammunition is limited, requiring visits to supply dumps, so players must balance thorough mine clearing with the need to defend themselves.

The cabinets featured an unusual prerecorded cassette loop of simulated military radio chatter, adding atmosphere independently of the game's electronic effects. Alternate maze revisions also circulated, making it a curious intersection of Pac-Man-style route planning and early combat simulation.

games.title: Naughty Boy
games.description:
Naughty Boy, developed by Jaleco in 1982, is a scrolling maze-action game about a boy attacking monster-occupied fortresses with thrown stones. Players move up through winding terrain, avoiding creatures and obstacles while holding the fire button to control how far stones travel. Reaching the fortress is not enough: its targets must be destroyed before the round is cleared.

The game occasionally switches to a hot-air-balloon bonus sequence, in which the boy drops rocks onto a monster below while a fuel gauge counts down. Released in Japan and distributed in North America by Cinematronics, Naughty Boy was one of Jaleco's earliest internally developed arcade video games.

games.title: Navarone
games.description:
Navarone is a 1980 monochrome fixed-screen shooter from Namco. The player commands a small warship moving around the edge of an enemy-held island, firing inward to remove dots and mines while dodging shots from invulnerable coastal guns. A skull at the island's center offers an additional target when gaps appear in its defenses. Clearing the island before time runs out awards a bonus and advances to the next round.

Unlike the usual fixed shooter with a ship confined to the bottom of the screen, Navarone lets players move around the island perimeter, changing the direction from which targets are attacked. One of Namco's final black-and-white arcade titles, it takes its name from the wartime adventure The Guns of Navarone.

games.title: SportStation: NBA Showtime NBA on NBC Gold Edition (ver 3.0, Feb 18 2000) / NFL Blitz 2000 Gold Edition
games.description:
SportStation: NBA Showtime NBA on NBC Gold Edition / NFL Blitz 2000 Gold Edition is Midway's 2000 dual-game arcade platform, allowing players to select either of two extravagant professional-sports attractions in one cabinet. NBA Showtime offers frantic two-on-two basketball with real NBA players, towering slam dunks and the familiar 'on fire' shooting streak. NFL Blitz 2000 Gold presents fast, heavily simplified American football defined by violent tackles, spectacular passes and unrestrained scoring.

Both games favor immediate competition, big 3D spectacle and participation by up to four players over strict sports realism. The SportStation conversion hardware was offered as a way for operators to provide both basketball and football without dedicating separate machines. This set represents the 2000 Gold revisions, not a standalone NBA basketball title.

games.title: NBA Hangtime
games.description:
NBA Hangtime is Midway's 1996 continuation of the flamboyant two-on-two basketball formula that made NBA Jam famous. Licensed NBA athletes perform improbable dunks, shove opponents aside and race between baskets in games built for up to four human players. Beyond the familiar turbo-powered action and 'on fire' shooting streaks, Hangtime adds spin moves, alley-oops and spectacular double dunks that can ignite an entire team.

The major new feature is Create Player, allowing users to design and develop their own basketball star with adjustable physical characteristics and attributes. Success against successive NBA teams earns upgrades, giving the arcade game a sense of progression beyond individual matches. Hangtime preserved Midway's style after the NBA Jam name moved to another publisher, and remains one of the most fully featured entries in the series.

games.title: NBA Jam
games.description:
NBA Jam is Midway's landmark 1993 two-on-two basketball game, designed by Mark Turmell and famous for turning an officially licensed professional sport into an over-the-top arcade spectacle. Digitized portraits of NBA stars race around a compact court, launch themselves into impossible slam dunks and knock opponents over with little regard for ordinary basketball rules. With up to four participants, every possession can become a chaotic rivalry between friends.

Its most famous mechanic is being 'on fire': three consecutive baskets by one player trigger flaming shots, improved shooting ability and unlimited turbo until the streak is broken. A booming announcer, exaggerated physics, hidden characters and secret button codes reinforce the game's sense of showmanship. Defense is just as direct as offense, as players steal, block and shove their way toward the basket.

A huge commercial success, NBA Jam revitalized the arcade sports genre and became a 1990s pop-culture phenomenon. Tim Kitzrow's exuberant commentary, including 'He's on fire!', helped define its identity. Numerous home conversions and later sequels followed, but the original cabinet remains a prime example of arcade design favoring immediacy, competition and spectacle over simulation.

games.title: NBA Jam Extreme
games.description:
NBA Jam Extreme is Acclaim's 1996 attempt to reinvent the basketball series after acquiring the NBA Jam name from Midway. Matches retain the familiar two-on-two format, exaggerated dunks and fast-paced competition, but the court and players are rendered in full 3D rather than the earlier games' digitized 2D style. Players select NBA teams, control the ball with a joystick and combine passes, shots and physical defense in short, showy games.

The new Extreme control offers an amplified version of the traditional turbo-powered action, while broadcaster Marv Albert supplies commentary in place of NBA Jam's original announcer. Its 3D redesign makes it a fascinating contrast with Midway's competing NBA Hangtime, which stayed closer to the visual and mechanical style of the classic series.

games.title: SportStation: NBA Showtime NBA on NBC (ver 2.1, Sep 22 1999) / NFL Blitz 2000 Gold Edition

variants.title: SportStation: NBA Showtime NBA on NBC (ver 2.1, Sep 22 1999) / NFL Blitz 2000 Gold Edition (ver 1.5, Sep 22 1999)
variants.version: (ver 2.1, Sep 22 1999) / NFL Blitz 2000 Gold Edition (ver 1.5, Sep 22 1999)

games.description:
SportStation: NBA Showtime NBA on NBC / NFL Blitz 2000 Gold Edition is Midway's 1999 dual-game amusement platform. From a game-selection menu, arcade visitors can choose either the company's 3D two-on-two basketball extravaganza or its aggressively simplified NFL football action. NBA Showtime emphasizes giant dunks, long-range shots and 'on fire' streaks, while NFL Blitz prioritizes dramatic passes, ferocious tackles and rapid scoring over the subtleties of regulation football.

The combined cabinet accommodates multiplayer competition and uses Midway's Vegas-era graphics technology for both sports. Unlike a simple revision of one title, this SportStation set is a paired release that lets an operator offer two established arcade hits on the same hardware; later versions updated its NBA component to the Gold Edition.

games.title: NBA Play By Play
games.description:
NBA Play By Play is Konami's 1998 licensed basketball game, bringing a broadcast-style view of the court to arcade competition. Players select among the NBA's 29 teams of the period and take part in matches that can lead through the playoffs to the NBA Finals. Up to four participants can control opposing sides, passing, dribbling, shooting and fighting for rebounds.

Konami's earlier NBA Give 'n Go used a different camera presentation, while Play By Play favors a more television-like sideline perspective. Special offensive actions include alley-oops, fake dunks, double-clutch shots, fadeaways and rebound dunks, lending variety to its relatively conventional full-court basketball framework.

games.title: NBA Showtime NBA on NBC

variants.title: NBA Showtime NBA on NBC (ver 2.0, Apr 25 1999)

games.description:
NBA Showtime: NBA on NBC is Midway's 1999 return to the extravagant two-on-two basketball style of NBA Jam, now presented with fully 3D players and courts. Official NBA team rosters and the NBC television license combine with familiar superhuman dunks, turbo-charged movement and running commentary. Up to four players can participate, with two athletes from each team competing at a time.

The game preserves the celebrated 'on fire' system: three unanswered successful shots empower a player to score more easily and challenge opponents with fewer restrictions. It also introduces a personal-foul limit for shoving, adding a small tactical cost to the series' traditionally rough defending. NBC-style graphics and sounds make the matches feel like a deliberately exaggerated television broadcast.

Showtime is a significant transition in Midway's basketball lineage, translating the explosive 2D gameplay of NBA Jam and NBA Hangtime to contemporary 3D arcade hardware. It was later paired with NFL Blitz 2000 in Midway's SportStation combination cabinets.

games.title: Ninja Baseball Bat Man
games.description:
Ninja Baseball Bat Man, released by Irem in 1993 and known in Japan as Yakyuu Kakutou League-Man, is one of the arcade era's most eccentric four-player beat-'em-ups. A team of robotic baseball heroes travels across the United States to recover artifacts stolen from the Baseball Hall of Fame. Enemies take the form of animated bats, balls, gloves and other baseball-themed absurdities, producing a surreal combination of sports imagery and cartoon violence.

Each hero has a distinctive fighting style, with combos, throws, slides and dash attacks available against large crowds. Players can collect food, baseball-themed weapons and special items, while some attacks become available when health is critically low. The oversized bosses and wildly animated stages give the game an identity unlike more conventional street brawlers.

Though less commercially prominent than many contemporary four-player fighters, Ninja Baseball Bat Man developed a strong cult following for its imaginative artwork, intricate moves and cooperative chaos. Its visual inventiveness makes it a notable late entry in Irem's arcade action catalog.

games.title: Ninja Combat
games.description:
Ninja Combat is an early Neo Geo action game released by Alpha Denshi and SNK in 1990. Two ninja heroes, Joe and Hayabusa, battle the Kage Ichizoku clan after a mysterious fortress appears in the city. Players move through scrolling streets and enemy strongholds, hurling shuriken, collecting more powerful weapons and using special techniques against gangs of ninjas and supernatural foes.

The game supports cooperative play and mixes forward-moving action with weapon pickups such as swords, axes and nunchaku. Its large character sprites and dramatic enemy designs exemplify the ambitious but sometimes awkward experiments of the Neo Geo's first year. The result sits between traditional ninja beat-'em-ups and projectile-heavy action games.

games.title: Ninja Commando
games.description:
Ninja Commando is Alpha Denshi's 1992 Neo Geo overhead run-and-gun game. Three ninjas pursue the villain Spider, whose time-travel schemes threaten to alter history. As the action scrolls upward through successive historical settings, players dodge swarms of enemies, unleash ranged attacks and confront bosses drawn from the game's fanciful interpretation of the past.

Each playable ninja has different capabilities and can perform powerful ninpo techniques using fighting-game-like directional commands. The game recalls Alpha Denshi's earlier Time Soldiers in its time-hopping premise but replaces the military theme with spectacular ninja weaponry and exaggerated special effects. Cooperative play adds to its fast, crowded arcade pacing.

games.title: Namco Classics Collection Vol.1
games.description:
Namco Classics Collection Vol. 1 is a 1995 arcade compilation built for Namco's ND-1 hardware. It collects Galaga, Xevious and Mappy, three influential early-1980s releases, with Super Xevious available through the Xevious selection. Alongside the familiar originals are newly created 'Arrangement' versions of the principal games, giving visitors a reason to revisit old favorites rather than simply replay their original ROMs.

Galaga Arrangement expands the fixed-screen alien shooter with new enemy formations and stages; Xevious Arrangement rebuilds the vertically scrolling aerial campaign with revised areas and bosses; and Mappy Arrangement updates the cat-and-mouse platform chase with fresh layouts and presentation. The arrangements add modernized graphics, sound and other mechanical changes while preserving each game's recognizable identity.

Appearing at a time when 3D graphics were reshaping arcades, this collection was an unusually thoughtful celebration of Namco's early history. It also anticipated the widespread appeal of classic-game compilations and arcade remixes.

games.title: Namco Classics Collection Vol.2
games.description:
Namco Classics Collection Vol. 2 followed in 1996, revisiting another group of arcade landmarks on Namco's ND-1 system. Players can choose Pac-Man, Rally-X and Dig Dug in versions designed to preserve their core gameplay, with New Rally-X available from the Rally-X menu. Every principal game also has an Arrangement counterpart with redesigned graphics, music, enemies and stages.

Pac-Man Arrangement turns the maze-chase classic into a sequence of varied, increasingly elaborate arenas; Dig Dug Arrangement expands tunneling and enemy-pumping action; and Rally-X Arrangement revisits flag collection and pursuit through mazes. Most arrangements introduce simultaneous multiplayer, although Rally-X Arrangement remains a single-player game. The original Rally-X titles are reformatted for a vertical screen, an important distinction from their earlier horizontal-monitor cabinets.

Together with Vol. 1, it represents Namco's early attempt to create new arcade experiences from its back catalog rather than offering only literal reissues. Its Arrangement games became cult favorites in their own right.

games.title: Nebulas Ray
games.description:
NebulasRay is Namco's 1994 vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter, set amid a rebellion against the militaristic Master Force. Players pilot a Fighting Ray starfighter through six stages of enemy ships, armored installations and giant bosses, using forward guns and a limited supply of bombs to survive. Two-player cooperative play lets pilots confront the unusually detailed battlefield together.

Weapon capsules provide upgrades and special attacks, some temporary and others retained until the player's ship is destroyed. The game is particularly remembered for its richly rendered, model-like enemies and layered scrolling backgrounds, which give its otherwise traditional shooting action an almost pre-rendered three-dimensional appearance. It is one of Namco's standout late-period 2D shooters.

games.title: Neck-n-Neck
games.description:
Neck-n-Neck is a 1992 horse-racing redemption game created by Incredible Technologies for Bundra Games. Players choose among six horses, then time button presses to jump over fences during a race. A poorly judged jump slows the horse, so success depends on rhythm and reacting to obstacles rather than steering around a track.

The game was designed for an amusement and ticket-redemption setting, with winnings affecting ticket rewards. Its minimal controls and immediately legible contest set it apart from the more elaborate racing simulations of the period.

games.title: Rettou Juudan Nekkyoku Janshi - Higashi Nippon Hen

variants.title: Rettou Juudan Nekkyoku Janshi - Higashi Nippon Hen (Japan)

games.description: Rettou Juudan Nekkyoku Janshi: Higashi Nippon Hen is a 1988 Japanese adult-themed mahjong game whose title describes a passionate mahjong player's journey across eastern Japan. Its travel motif connects a succession of mahjong encounters to different locations, replacing a purely abstract series of matches with a geographical theme. The game is an example of the late-1980s fashion for dressing competitive mahjong in character-driven adventures and provocative imagery.

games.title: Nemesis
games.description:
Nemesis is the international title of Konami's 1985 horizontal shooter Gradius, one of the most influential games in the genre. Players pilot the Vic Viper through hostile space and organic environments, dodging enemies and terrain while hunting the glowing cores of giant mechanical bosses. The stages feature elaborate enemy formations, volcanic hazards and the memorable combination of free movement with relentlessly advancing scenery.

The defining innovation is its selectable power-up meter. Destroying selected enemy groups produces capsules that advance a cursor through upgrades such as Speed Up, Missile, Double, Laser and Option. Activating the meter purchases the highlighted upgrade, forcing players to decide whether to take an immediate improvement or wait for more powerful equipment. The floating Options follow the ship's movements and copy its fire, rewarding carefully chosen positions during a fight.

Gradius established systems, visual motifs and a difficulty philosophy that shaped countless subsequent shooters, including Konami's own long-running Gradius and Salamander series. Its combination of weapon planning, memorization and precision flying makes Nemesis far more than a simple succession of shooting stages. Regional Nemesis editions include differences from the Japanese Gradius original, but retain the essential landmark design.

games.title: Nemo
games.description:
Nemo is Capcom's 1990 arcade platform-action game inspired by Winsor McCay's Little Nemo in Slumberland and the animated film adaptation. Young Nemo and his companion Flip travel through a fantastical dream kingdom filled with hostile toys, surreal landscapes and larger-than-life bosses. The first player controls Nemo with a magical scepter, while the second can join as Flip with a cane.

The pair jump between platforms, climb ladders and walls, and defeat enemies with their weapons, thrown objects or by landing on foes. Seven stages lead deeper into Slumberland and its escalating nightmare. The arcade game differs substantially from Capcom's home-console Little Nemo: The Dream Master, making it a distinct adaptation of the same fantasy property rather than a direct conversion.

games.title: SD Gundam Neo Battling
games.description:
SD Gundam Neo Battling is Banpresto's 1992 Japanese vertically scrolling shooter featuring super-deformed versions of Mobile Suit Gundam robots. Players select a Gundam from a roster of mobile suits and fly through enemy formations, attacking other mecha in a brightly colored, overhead-view battle. The selected unit influences weapon behavior and performance.

An eight-way joystick controls movement, while a single attack button provides the main weapon and can be held to charge a stronger strike. Cooperative two-player action and the recognizable chibi Gundam designs give the game an approachable appearance despite its busy shooter mechanics. It was among the earliest Gundam-themed arcade shooters.

games.title: Neo Bomberman
games.description:
Neo Bomberman is a 1997 Neo Geo MVS installment in Hudson's long-running Bomberman series, developed by Produce! and built around explosive maze action. Players traverse grid-based arenas, plant bombs and escape their cross-shaped blasts while destroying enemies and breakable blocks. Hidden items increase movement speed, blast reach and bomb capacity, or grant special abilities such as remote detonation.

The game offers both a stage-based adventure and competitive battles, making it a natural fit for the Neo Geo's multiplayer arcade environment. Rideable creatures and colorful, animated monsters add variety to the familiar task of trapping opponents while avoiding one's own explosives. It is notable as an arcade-focused Neo Geo entry rather than a conversion of the contemporary home-console Bomberman games.

games.title: Neo-Geo Cup '98 - The Road to the Victory
games.description:
Neo-Geo Cup '98: The Road to the Victory is SNK's 1998 World Cup-themed football game and an updated successor to Super Sidekicks 3. Players select national teams and compete in fast, arcade-style matches with quick passing, shooting and defensive tackles. Its tournament progression resembles qualification and the group stages of the 1998 FIFA World Cup, including opponents inspired by actual national-team matchups.

The game favors immediate joystick-driven competition over detailed team management, with dramatic close-up scoring sequences and the familiar colorful presentation of SNK's football series. Despite its World Cup imagery, it is not an officially licensed FIFA simulation; its identity rests on the Neo Geo's established arcade soccer action.

games.title: Neo Drift Out - New Technology
games.description:
Neo Drift Out: New Technology is Visco's 1996 isometric rally racing game for the Neo Geo. Drivers choose among rally versions of the Mitsubishi Lancer, Subaru Impreza and Toyota Celica, each with different handling, speed and durability. From an elevated three-quarter view, the player powerslides through hairpins, avoids roadside hazards and races the clock across several terrain types.

After a practice run, the campaign proceeds through six timed stages with changing road surfaces and obstacles, including water, ice and barriers. The sharp turns and tight countdown reward smooth control more than simply holding the accelerator. Its compact courses and brisk, instantly readable visuals make it one of the Neo Geo's most satisfying arcade racing curiosities.

games.title: Neo-Geo
games.description:
SNK's Neo-Geo Multi Video System, launched in 1990, became one of the most enduring arcade platforms ever made. Its interchangeable ROM cartridges allowed an operator to install several games in one cabinet, with MVS boards available in one-, two-, four-, and six-slot configurations. Players could select among the installed titles, while operators could refresh a cabinet's lineup simply by replacing cartridges and artwork. That flexibility gave arcades an economical way to offer a changing selection of games without repeatedly purchasing entire machines.

The system combined a 12 MHz Motorola 68000 processor, a Z80 sound CPU, and Yamaha's YM2610 audio hardware with exceptionally strong sprite-based 2D graphics. SNK marketed the machine as a 24-bit system, although that label referred to its overall architecture rather than a single 24-bit CPU. A distinctive companion was the Neo-Geo AES home system, which delivered essentially the same games and hardware performance at a premium price. Compatible memory-card features even allowed supported games to carry progress between home and arcade play.

The MVS became closely associated with Fatal Fury, Samurai Shodown, The King of Fighters, Metal Slug, and many other fighting and action titles. Although 3D graphics transformed the wider industry, developers continued to exploit the Neo-Geo's large animated sprites, detailed pixel art, and expressive sound for more than a decade. Commercial software releases lasted into 2004, giving the platform an extraordinary fourteen-year life and an influence that far outstripped its original hardware specifications.

games.title: Neo Mr. Do!
games.description:
Neo Mr. Do! is a 1996 Neo Geo update of Universal's classic Mr. Do! maze game. A colorful clown-like character digs paths through the ground, collecting fruit while avoiding monsters that can pursue him along the tunnels or force new paths of their own. Fruit collected in uninterrupted groups increases the scoring reward, encouraging risky routes through crowded areas.

The player's bouncing power ball can eliminate enemies, but it must return before being thrown again. Dropping large objects onto monsters provides another way to survive, and clever use of the terrain is as important as reflexes. The game preserves the original's distinctive mixture of digging, collecting and enemy manipulation with brighter graphics and new audiovisual presentation.

games.title: Neo Pang
games.description: Neo Pang is a 2010 homebrew arcade action game by CeL for the Neo Geo platform inspired by Mitchell's classic balloon-popping game Pang.

games.title: Neo Pong
games.description: Neo Pong is an early homebrew ball-and-paddle game developed by Neodev for the Neo Geo platform in 2002.

games.title: Mahjong Neruton Haikujirada
games.description: Mahjong Neruton Haikujiradan is a 1990 Dynax arcade mahjong game inspired by the Japanese matchmaking television show Nelton Benikujiradan. The program, associated with the comedy duo Tunnels, popularized the term neruton for group matchmaking parties, and characters linked to the show appear in the game. It therefore mixes conventional competitive mahjong with a very particular piece of late-1980s Japanese television culture. Released in November 1990, the game is notable for borrowing the look and recognition of a contemporary entertainment phenomenon.

games.title: Nettoh Quiz Champion
games.description:
Nettoh Quiz Champion is a colorful Japanese arcade trivia game released by Nakanihon in April 1995 and developed by Dynax. One or two contestants answer Japanese-language quiz questions using four answer buttons instead of a joystick. Cartoon presenters, exuberant graphics, and competitive quiz-show staging give it the feel of a television game show, while promotional artwork depicts quiz confrontations and a map-like progression screen.

The title is sometimes rendered Nettou Quiz Champion and roughly evokes a fiercely contested quiz championship. It ran on Motorola 68000-based hardware and later appeared in a Korean-language version titled Se Gye Hweng Dan Ultra Champion. That localization is particularly noteworthy for a game whose central challenge is language-dependent general knowledge rather than reflexes.

games.title: Net Wars
games.description:
Net Wars is a 1983 maze shooter developed by Orca and also distributed under license by Esco Trading. The player steers a small craft freely through an enclosed network of corridors, firing at hostile ships while trying not to collide with enemies or the maze's boundaries. The fixed-screen perspective and compact labyrinth make movement and positioning as important as shooting.

Its emphasis on navigating a hazardous network separates it from the more straightforward space-invader formations typical of early arcade shooters.

games.title: New Fantasia
games.description:
New Fantasia is a 1995 adult-oriented territory-capture arcade game by Comad and New Japan System. Its play resembles Taito's Qix and Kaneko's Gals Panic: players move along the boundaries of a field and trace lines to claim areas, revealing portions of a concealed digitized photograph. Enemies roaming the active playfield can interrupt unfinished lines, making each excursion away from safety a calculated risk.

A countdown timer adds pressure to divide and claim enough territory before the round ends. The title is part of a prolific Korean series of adult-themed Qix derivatives, distinguished mainly by its photographic reveal presentation rather than a radically new underlying puzzle system.

games.title: News
games.description:
News is a 1993 Korean-style competitive falling-piece puzzle game credited to Poby and Virus. Despite its title, it is not about journalism: the core game closely imitates Puyo Puyo, with colored pieces dropping into a playfield and disappearing when players build matching groups. Planning chain reactions and preserving space become increasingly important as pieces accumulate.

The game has a conspicuous illustrated woman as its background and uses voice snippets during play. Its borrowings make News an unusual example of the wave of unauthorized or loosely imitative arcade puzzle games that followed Puyo Puyo's success.

games.title: New Sinbad 7
games.description:
New Sinbad 7 is a 1982 maze shooter by Artic Electronics, also associated with ATW, inspired by Sinbad's legendary voyages. The player moves through a monster-filled city labyrinth surrounding a palace. Shooting enemies removes parts of the palace walls, eventually opening a route to a key or treasure at the center.

Collecting a key opens another voyage challenge, including screens in which the player must shoot blocks while some break free and move dangerously around the arena. Different enemy types, a timer and a strict limit on simultaneous shots make the game unexpectedly demanding. Its mixture of maze exploration and changing shooting challenges distinguishes it from the many simple fixed-screen shooters of the period.

games.title: New Cross Pang
games.description:
New Cross Pang is a 1999 Korean arcade puzzle game from F2 System, also associated with the title Toads' Raid. Colored balls accumulate on a playfield, and players must bring matching colors together to make groups disappear. The story casts this color-clearing task as an effort to stop a kingdom from being overrun by mushroom-like invaders.

Successive rounds increase the required number of cleared groups, turning a simple matching rule into a race against a crowded board. The game's bright fantasy presentation reflects the popularity of fast color-matching arcade puzzles in the 1990s.

games.title: NFL Football
games.description:
NFL Football is Bally Midway's pioneering 1983 laserdisc sports game, which combines real professional-football footage with interactive play selection. Instead of controlling animated athletes directly, players act much like coaches, choosing offensive or defensive calls from a playbook and watching corresponding recorded action unfold. The video material drew on a Los Angeles Raiders versus San Diego Chargers game.

A computer interprets the choices and selects suitable clips, providing an unusually realistic visual presentation for an era when most football games used simple sprites. This makes NFL Football more a tactical, video-assisted decision game than a conventional joystick sports simulation. Its use of filmed footage is an early example of the ambitious, often experimental possibilities arcade operators saw in laserdisc technology.

games.title: Nekketsu Grand-Prix Gal
games.description: Nekketsu Grand-Prix Gal is a 1991 Nichibutsu adult mahjong game built around a motor-racing theme. Despite the words Grand Prix in its title, this is not a driving game: the player competes in mahjong while the imagery and presentation borrow from racing culture. Released in Japan in July 1991, it shows how Nichibutsu used topical themes to differentiate its many specialized mahjong titles.

games.title: NeoGeo 2-Player Tetris
games.description: NeoGeo 2-Player Tetris is a homebrew two-player falling-block puzzle game developed by Crim and Stephen for the Neo Geo platform in 2008.

games.title: New Hidden Catch (World) / New Tul Lin Gu Lim Chat Ki '98

variants.title: New Hidden Catch (World) / New Tul Lin Gu Lim Chat Ki '98 (Korea) (pcb ver 3.02)
variants.version: (World) / New Tul Lin Gu Lim Chat Ki '98 (Korea) (pcb ver 3.02)

games.description:
New Hidden Catch, also known as New Tul Lin Gu Lim Chat Ki '98, is a 1999 picture-comparison puzzle game from Eolith. Two nearly identical illustrations appear side by side, and the player must quickly locate small visual differences between them. Every successful identification advances the round or contributes to the score, while the clock keeps the pressure on.

Its gameplay is closer to a spot-the-difference book than a traditional action game, making visual observation and rapid selection its central skills. The bright illustrations and compact challenges suit brief arcade sessions and head-to-head competition.

games.title: Nibbler
games.description:
Nibbler is Rock-Ola's 1982 maze game, combining the pellet-eating structure of Pac-Man with the self-avoidance challenge of Snake. Players steer a serpent through a fixed maze, devouring food while its body grows longer with every pickup. Each turn affects the future path of the trailing body, so a route that looks harmless now can become an inescapable trap moments later.

Unlike Pac-Man, there are no pursuing monsters. The player's main enemy is the snake itself: colliding with its body costs a life. Clearing all food advances to a harder maze, and longer runs demand carefully planned loops that leave enough room for movement.

Nibbler became famous for its enormous scores and for the quest to reach one billion points, a feat associated with arcade champion Tim McVey in 1984. The long-play endurance challenge gave this apparently simple maze game a place in competitive arcade history, later revisited in documentaries about classic high-score chasing.

games.title: Night Love
games.description:
Night Love is a Japanese adult-themed mahjong game released by Central Denshi in 1986.
