It belongs to the era of dedicated mahjong arcade cabinets rather than joystick-controlled action games: players select and discard tiles and issue mahjong commands using a multi-key control panel while competing against the computer. Its adult-oriented presentation places it alongside the numerous character-driven mahjong titles produced for Japanese amusement venues during the mid-1980s.

The preserved set bears the date code 860705, corresponding to July 5, 1986. It runs on Z80-based hardware with AY-3-8910 sound and a digital-to-analog audio channel, and uses a wide horizontal display. The game is historically interesting as part of the extensive, often region-specific mahjong arcade market that mainstream histories of the period tend to overlook.

games.title: Night Striker
games.description:
Night Striker is Taito's 1989 sprite-scaling action shooter, placing the player in an armored flying car racing through nighttime cities, tunnels and industrial districts. A terrorist organization has kidnapped a scientist and his daughter, and the player must destroy attacking aircraft, trucks and mechanical enemies while avoiding scenery at high speed. The behind-the-vehicle viewpoint creates a convincing impression of diving into the screen.

The car can move across the play area and fire straight ahead, while a shield gauge absorbs damage and is replenished between stages. Large bosses punctuate the action, and branching route choices after each victory lead through different combinations of the game's 21 stages. A single run visits only part of the complete stage network, adding variety and replay value.

Its neon-lit visual style, elaborate scaling effects and soundtrack helped distinguish Night Striker from Sega's Space Harrier and other contemporaneous rail shooters. The game is an atmospheric late-1980s example of using 2D sprites to evoke a fast-moving three-dimensional world.

games.title: Ninja Clowns
games.description:
Ninja Clowns is Strata's bizarre 1991 side-scrolling beat-'em-up in which one or two circus clowns battle an assortment of rival performers and urban misfits. In addition to punches and kicks, the heroes fight with slapstick equipment including spring-loaded boxing gloves, soda-water bottles and cream pies. The comic tone extends to enemies, bosses and unexpected bonus sequences.

The goal is to work through crowded stages to confront the villainous clown Twisto. Its uneasy combination of martial-arts combat and circus humor makes it one of the more unusual, and most visually eccentric, street-fighting games of the early 1990s.

games.title: The Ninja Kids
games.description:
The Ninja Kids is Taito's 1990 four-player side-scrolling action game, in which a team of ninja puppets confronts a cult attempting to summon Satan. Everything, from the heroes to their enemies, looks like an animated stage puppet, giving the game's violent supernatural battles an oddly comedic character.

Four ninjas have distinct weapons and fighting styles: Hanzo favors a sword, Sasuke uses a chain-and-sickle, Akame attacks with shuriken and Genta wields a heavy three-section staff. Elemental ninjutsu techniques give each character additional offensive options, while cooperative play lets the group tackle large crowds and bosses together. Its puppet-theater presentation and varied fighters make it an overlooked but highly distinctive Taito beat-'em-up.

games.title: Ninja-Kid II
games.description:
Ninja-Kid II, released by UPL in 1987 as Ninja-kun Ashura no Shou and known in North America as Rad Action, expands the original Ninja-kun's single-screen platform action into more varied, sometimes scrolling stages. The small ninja jumps between platforms, hurls shuriken at roaming enemies and uses acrobatic movement to survive increasingly crowded encounters.

Power-up scrolls grant temporary enhanced attacks, and different scenes introduce new terrain and enemies rather than simply repeating the same fortress layout. The sequel preserves the first game's lively arcade simplicity while placing greater emphasis on movement, exploration and changing stage designs.

games.title: Ninjakun Majou no Bouken
games.description:
Ninjakun Majou no Bouken is UPL's 1984 vertical-platform arcade game, an early appearance of the diminutive ninja Ninja-kun. The hero climbs mountains and castle platforms, defeating all enemies on a screen with shuriken before moving to the next area. Jumping onto enemies can stun them, creating an opening for a carefully aimed attack.

The three principal stage patterns repeat with increasing difficulty, while collected scrolls add points and special items can open bonus opportunities. Its compact multi-level arenas and constant upward movement helped establish the style later expanded in Ninja-Kid II.

games.title: Ninja Master's - haoh-ninpo-cho
games.description:
Ninja Master's: Haoh Ninpou Chou is ADK's 1996 Neo Geo one-on-one fighting game, set in a stylized world of rival ninja warriors and feudal combatants. Ten playable characters bring different movement, attack ranges and special techniques to best-of-three-round matches.

Its defining mechanic is the ability to draw or sheathe a character's weapon during combat, changing the available attacks and combo possibilities. A super meter adds further tactical decisions, while the detailed character sprites and fast combo system reward experimentation. It is one of the Neo Geo's more intricate and underappreciated fighting games.

games.title: The Ninja Warriors
games.description:
The Ninja Warriors is Taito's 1987 side-scrolling action game, remembered especially for its enormous triple-monitor panoramic arcade cabinet. Two robot ninjas, Kunoichi and Ninja, infiltrate a military dictatorship to defeat the tyrant Banglar. Players move across a wide, continuously scrolling battlefield, fighting soldiers and machines with short-range blades and a limited supply of throwing shuriken.

Damage gradually tears away the heroes' clothing to reveal the machinery beneath, a memorable visual indication of their synthetic nature. The wide aspect ratio allows enemies to approach across a broad battlefield, making positioning and weapon conservation unusually important. Cooperative play lets the two ninja robots fight side by side.

Taito's elaborate cabinet, detailed backgrounds and atmospheric soundtrack made The Ninja Warriors a showpiece of late-1980s arcade presentation. It became an enduring cult favorite and inspired later reinterpretations, but the original's panoramic display remains central to its identity.

games.title: Ninja Emaki
games.description:
Ninja Emaki is Nichibutsu's 1986 overhead ninja run-and-gun game, also known as Youma Ninpou Chou. Players control Shinbei on a quest to rescue a princess from supernatural enemies, moving through scrolling landscapes and firing arrows at attackers. Picked-up scrolls temporarily grant powerful magical weapons with different attack patterns, helping against dense enemy formations and demanding bosses.

The first areas resemble a vertical shooter, but later stages place greater emphasis on moving through the terrain on foot. Japanese and international versions differ in how much damage the hero can take. The set associated with the alternate Ninja Emaki name includes a bootleg conversion of Nichibutsu's original game.

games.title: Nightmare in the Dark
games.description:
Nightmare in the Dark is a 2000 Neo Geo platform-action game from Eleven and Gavaking, following a lonely gravekeeper investigating stolen corpses. Each compact cemetery stage is filled with zombies, ghosts, goblins and other supernatural threats. Instead of simply destroying enemies with projectiles, players repeatedly strike them with fire until they become large flaming balls that can be pushed into other monsters.

The resulting chain reactions clear groups of enemies and release treasure, creating a rewarding rhythm reminiscent of Snow Bros. and Tumble Pop. Five themed stages, each with several rounds, offer escalating challenges and colorful boss fights. Its elaborate sprite animation and lighthearted horror atmosphere made it a late Neo Geo cult favorite.

games.title: Night Driver
games.description:
Night Driver is Atari's pioneering 1976 first-person driving game, placing players behind a simulated steering wheel on a dark, winding road. The road itself is nearly invisible; rows of bright roadside markers suggest its shape and create the illusion of forward movement. Steering, accelerating and shifting gears keep the car between the markers as the corners become sharper and the clock counts down.

The arcade cabinet used a steering wheel, accelerator pedal and gear selector, making physical driving controls a large part of the experience. Players could select courses of varying difficulty, and crashes cost valuable time rather than ending the game immediately. Its sparse monochrome graphics nevertheless create a surprisingly effective sensation of driving into the distance.

Night Driver is a landmark in the development of first-person racing games and one of the clearest early examples of pseudo-three-dimensional road graphics. The visual trick of constructing a road from advancing perspective markers influenced a long line of later driving games, even as their graphics became far more sophisticated.

games.title: Nitro Ball
games.description:
Nitro Ball, released by Data East in 1992, is a furious overhead run-and-gun game with an unexpected pinball twist. Players charge through themed arenas while shooting enemies, dodging incoming attacks and ricocheting objects into targets, bumpers and other scoring devices. The battlefields resemble giant pinball tables, where hitting the right object can create chain reactions, bonuses and useful power-ups.

Its five stages mix settings and enemy types, including zombies and science-fiction monsters, with a style of action reminiscent of Smash T.V. The combination of overhead-shooter intensity and elaborate pinball scoring makes Nitro Ball one of Data East's more inventive arcade experiments.

games.title: Niyanpai
games.description:
Niyanpai, also known as Nyanpai: Musume Pai, is a 1996 Japanese solitaire-mahjong puzzle game from Nichibutsu. Rather than playing a conventional four-player mahjong match, players work to complete a specified tile hand by identifying and matching tiles. The challenge lies in recognizing combinations and choosing moves that advance the required pattern.

The game features character-oriented Japanese presentation and simple joystick-and-button controls. Released late in Nichibutsu's long association with arcade mahjong, it offers a tile-puzzle variation on the genre rather than a standard competitive mahjong simulation.

games.title: Multi 5 / New Multi Game 5
games.description:
Multi 5, also titled New Multi Game 5, is a late-1990s Korean multi-game arcade package collecting five distinct attractions on one board. Tong Boy is a platform-action game built around ideas from Donkey Kong and its sequels, while Bubble Gum imitates Puzzle Bobble's colored-bubble matching. Cross Point follows the falling-gem formula of Columns, Box Logic draws on Logic Pro, and Rocktris offers a Tetris-like falling-block challenge.

Tong Boy contains 49 rounds, with its final stages taking inspiration from Donkey Kong 3. Cross Point and Rocktris include adult photographic backgrounds, giving the compilation a mixed-audience identity typical of some independent Korean arcade releases. The package is an unusual example of combining familiar but unrelated game formats into a single low-cost coin-operated board.

games.title: Naughty Mouse
games.description:
Naughty Mouse is a 1981 single-screen platform game by Amenip, also associated with the name Woodpecker. Its unlikely hero must climb from his house at the bottom of the screen to his girlfriend's home at the top, using ladders and a jump button to escape brightly colored woodpeckers hatching from giant eggs. Some ladders become electrified after use, turning a safe route upward into a deadly return path. Reaching the top converts unused time into bonus points.

The game runs on hardware derived from Namco's Pac-Man system, an example of how early arcade boards were adapted for entirely different genres. The surviving Naughty Mouse sets and the related Woodpecker version differ in colors and stage arrangements.

games.title: Nekketsu Mahjong Sengen! AFTER 5
games.description: Nekketsu Mahjong Sengen! AFTER 5 is a Japanese adult-themed mahjong game released by Video System in January 1991. Its after-work setting brings a cast of businesswomen together for one-on-one Japanese mahjong matches, with anime illustrations and revealing scenes awarded for victories. Played through a dedicated mahjong control panel rather than an ordinary arcade joystick, it belongs to the strip-mahjong genre that flourished in Japanese amusement centers in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

games.title: Noah's Ark
games.description:
Noah's Ark is a 1983 children's arcade game from Enter-Tech's Moppet Video line, not the unrelated 1992 Nintendo Entertainment System platformer. The player guides Noah around a compact playfield, shepherding pairs of animals aboard the ark before the rising floodwater overtakes them. Each stage requires a minimum number of rescued pairs, making quick movement and careful animal collection more important than combat.

Built with young players in mind, it was the third Moppet Video title after Desert Race and made more extensive use of the system's hardware than its predecessors. Its biblical rescue premise and small dedicated cabinets make it an unusual example of early arcade entertainment intended specifically for children.

games.title: Noboranka
games.description:
This Game Electronics bootleg of Noboranka reproduces Coreland's unusual 1986 climbing shooter, distributed in Japan by Data East and known overseas as Zippy Bug. Playing as a small insect hero, the player climbs a towering tree, shoots hostile bugs, and tries to rescue a kidnapped princess. Destroyed enemies can drop fruit for points or dangerous skulls, while collectible items provide temporary protection and other advantages.

A particularly distinctive mechanic is limited flight: taking to the air consumes letters from an 'I Love You' indicator, which gradually refills. This pirate version runs on Sega System 1-derived hardware; its bootleg status should not be confused with a separate original game.

games.title: No Man's Land
games.description:
Universal's No Man's Land (1980), known in Japan as Sengoku no Jieitai, is an overhead tank-combat game built around a deceptively simple battlefield. An eight-way joystick steers the player's tank, whose gun fires in its direction of travel. Enemy tanks are either already moving or sitting dormant, often across a river accessible only by bridges. Destroying an active opponent awakens another parked tank, so eliminating the more valuable stationary targets calls for careful routing under fire.

The changing number and speed of enemy vehicles make each successive screen more demanding, accompanied by an increasingly urgent soundtrack. Gottlieb licensed No Man's Land for American distribution in December 1980, marking the veteran pinball manufacturer's first venture into arcade video games.

games.title: Nostradamus
games.description:
Nostradamus is a 1993 vertically scrolling shooter by Face, presenting a science-fiction catastrophe in which two pilots fight to save a devastated Earth. Dalas and Joanna fly different craft through nine stages, and their standard weapons favor different strategies: Dalas gains a broader pattern that curls behind his ship, while Joanna concentrates fire forward. Their contrasting handling and firing patterns give the two-player action a genuine tactical choice.

The signature Energy Boost Accelerator, or EBA, can be fitted in blue or red form. Holding the fire button charges a protective energy barrier behind the craft; releasing it unleashes a powerful attack. The blue Plasmic Wave projects a long laser, while the red Phoenix Wave spreads fiery destruction across the front of the ship. Switching colors, collecting crystals and choosing when to charge the shield are central to surviving its elaborate enemies and bosses.

games.title: Nostromo
games.description: Nostromo is a little-documented shooting game preserved from a bootleg board built around hardware associated with Sega's Head On. Its relationship to the similarly obscure Star Trek arcade bootleg is uncertain: the two games are closely related, but surviving evidence does not establish securely which came first or whether both derive from a lost original. That uncertainty, together with incomplete information about its sound hardware, makes Nostromo an example of how difficult it can be to reconstruct the lineage of early unauthorized arcade boards.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Nouryoku Koujou Iinkai
games.description:
Nouryoku Koujou Iinkai, released by Tecmo in Japan in 1995, is a quiz and brain-training arcade game whose name translates roughly as 'Brainpower Improvement Committee'. Rather than offering a single conventional trivia test, it runs players through a succession of different short question-and-answer challenges. Correct answers earn points, while mistakes and hesitation drain a life meter. At the end of each round, performance determines how much energy is restored, followed by a timed bonus challenge.

Its eight-round structure puts equal emphasis on accuracy and response speed. It is an unusual example of a Japanese arcade quiz game built around linked minigames rather than a straightforward question list.

games.title: Nova 2001
games.description:
Nova 2001 is UPL's 1983 single-screen, multidirectional space shooter. Instead of remaining at the bottom of the display like a traditional Space Invaders ship, the player's craft can roam the arena and fire in eight directions. Distinctive alien formations enter from all sides, making positioning, anticipation and escape routes as important as shooting. Collectible upgrades strengthen the ship, and limited bombs can clear an otherwise overwhelming screen.

The game is an appealing transitional design between fixed shooters and later free-roaming arena combat. Its sequel, Ark Area, appeared in Japanese arcades in 1988. AdvanceMAME includes regional Nova 2001 sets, including a Japanese revision associated with a correction to the original game's unreliable coin-handling behavior.

games.title: New Rally X
games.description:
New Rally-X is Namco's 1981 revision of Rally-X, the overhead maze-driving game in which a blue car must collect ten flags while outrunning aggressive red vehicles. The car never stops moving, so players steer around bends and boulders while consulting a radar display for the positions of flags and pursuers. A button lays a cloud of smoke that temporarily disables following cars, but each use consumes precious fuel. Scoring rewards smart collection order: taking the Special Flag early doubles the value of subsequent flags, while the new Lucky Flag awards a bonus based on remaining fuel.

Namco redesigned the mazes, reduced the number of enemy cars in early rounds, improved the graphics and introduced a longer, catchier musical theme. These changes made New Rally-X considerably more approachable than its notoriously punishing predecessor. In Japan it became even more popular than Rally-X; in North America, Midway chiefly offered it as an upgrade kit for existing cabinets. The balancing changes and Lucky Flag make it much more than a simple graphical revision.

games.title: Neratte Chu
games.description: Neratte Chu is a 1996 puzzle game by Seta, released in Japan in May of that year. It is a two-player-capable toss-style puzzle game, with players using an eight-direction joystick and three buttons rather than the typical one-button falling-block setup. The title runs on Seta's unusual ST0016-based hardware, a compact system handling both graphics and sound. Detailed descriptions of its scoring and object-matching rules are scarce, so its distinctiveness is better established by its control layout and hardware than by speculative claims about puzzle mechanics.

games.title: Night Slashers
games.description:
Night Slashers is Data East's horror-themed side-scrolling beat 'em up, released in arcades in 1993 despite the later year sometimes associated with its ROM sets. Up to three players choose from Jake White, a cybernetically enhanced American hunter; Christopher Pal, a European vampire fighter; and Zhao Hong Hua, an Asian martial artist versed in mystic techniques. They battle zombies, mutants, vampires, werewolves and other monsters on their way to stopping the undead ruler King Zarutz.

Its three-button controls support attacks, jumps and special techniques, with more elaborate combinations than the standard Final Fight formula. The grisly enemy designs, dramatic bosses and deliberately outrageous horror imagery give the game a distinctive personality. Regional versions also differ in their presentation of blood and violence: the Japanese release retains red blood and additional graphic details that were toned down or made adjustable for overseas markets.

games.title: New! Super Mario Bros.
games.description: New! Super Mario Bros. is a 2020 homebrew side-scrolling platformer demo created by OzzyOuzo for the Neo Geo platform.

games.title: Ninja Spirit
games.description:
Ninja Spirit, known in Japan as Saigo no Nindou, is Irem's spectacularly difficult 1988 side-scrolling ninja action game. The hero Tsukikage travels through war-torn landscapes, swamps, temples and cliffs, fighting soldiers, demons and huge bosses across seven stages. His arsenal includes a sword, shuriken and other specialized weapons, each useful against different threats; the action is notable for the sheer number of enemies and projectiles it can put on the screen.

Its most memorable power-up produces shadow doubles that follow the ninja's movements and duplicate his attacks, allowing a skilled player to cover large sections of the screen with overlapping weapons. The ability to leap, climb and attack in multiple directions gives the combat unusual mobility for its era. Admired for detailed artwork and responsive controls, Ninja Spirit remains a cult favorite partly because its unforgiving later stages demand mastery of the shadow system.

games.title: Nintendo Super System BIOS
games.description:
Nintendo's Super System adapted Super Nintendo Entertainment System hardware for early-1990s arcade cabinets. Its interchangeable game boards offered modified versions of familiar Super NES releases, including Super Mario World, F-Zero, Super Tennis, and ActRaiser. The games retained their console-derived play styles, but the cabinet imposed a paid time limit rather than allowing unrestricted home-console sessions.

The Super System followed the general philosophy of Nintendo's earlier PlayChoice-10: let arcade visitors sample several home-console experiences through one coin-operated machine. This BIOS supports the arcade system's operating functions, not a separate playable title, and documents Nintendo's continuing effort to bridge its domestic console business and amusement-machine heritage.

games.title: Act Raiser
games.description:
ActRaiser on the Nintendo Super System is a specially adapted arcade edition of Quintet's acclaimed Super Nintendo game. In the home original, a divine protagonist alternates between side-scrolling action and an overhead civilization-building simulation. The coin-operated Nintendo Super System version removes the settlement-management portions, concentrating instead on the action sequences in which the Master animates a warrior statue to fight monsters and confront enormous bosses.

That change makes this more than a straightforward SNES cartridge in an arcade cabinet. The Nintendo Super System itself let operators install console-derived games in a timed, coin-operated format, and ActRaiser is one of the clearest examples of a game altered to suit shorter arcade sessions.

games.title: The Addams Family
games.description:
The Addams Family for the Nintendo Super System is the coin-operated presentation of Ocean's 1992 Super Nintendo platform adventure, based on the 1991 film. As Gomez Addams, players explore the family's sprawling, trap-filled mansion to rescue Morticia, Pugsley, Wednesday and the other missing relatives. Hidden rooms, platforms, hostile creatures and collectible bonuses encourage exploration rather than a straight run to the exit.

Its unusual arcade setting comes from Nintendo's Super System hardware, which presented specially packaged SNES games in a cabinet with a paid time allowance. It should not be confused with an independently developed arcade version of the movie.

games.title: David Crane's Amazing Tennis

variants.title: David Crane's Amazing Tennis (Nintendo Super System)

games.description:
David Crane's Amazing Tennis arrived on the Nintendo Super System in 1992 as a coin-operated version of the Super Nintendo tennis simulation. Matches are seen from behind the near-side player, emphasizing the timing and placement of shots rather than an overhead court view. Players can select grass, clay or hard courts, compete in exhibitions or tournaments, and choose among fictional opponents with different strengths.

The game supports a broad selection of tennis strokes, including lobs, volleys, slices and drop shots, as well as hard and soft serves. Its comparatively detailed shot selection stands out among the simpler sports games offered on Nintendo's timed arcade hardware.

games.title: Contra 3: The Alien Wars

variants.title: Contra 3: The Alien Wars (Nintendo Super System)

games.description:
Contra III: The Alien Wars brings Konami's 1992 Super Nintendo run-and-gun blockbuster to Nintendo's coin-operated Super System. Commandos Bill Rizer and Lance Bean battle an alien invasion with a succession of frantic side-scrolling missions, oversized bosses and weapon pickups. Their arsenal includes interchangeable guns and limited screen-clearing bombs, while some stages shift to a rotating overhead perspective that made striking use of the Super Nintendo's hardware.

Cooperative two-player action and the combination of fast shooting, acrobatic jumps and memorable boss encounters made Contra III a major early SNES showcase. The Nintendo Super System edition retains its console-derived identity while placing the action within an arcade cabinet's timed-play format.

games.title: F-Zero
games.description:
F-Zero is Nintendo's futuristic racing game, presented here in its Nintendo Super System arcade incarnation. Players choose from four hovercraft with different acceleration, grip and durability, then compete on twisting circuits suspended high above the ground. Sliding zones, magnets, barriers and rival vehicles make surviving at extreme speed as important as finishing in a good position. The racer also has an energy meter that can be replenished at designated track sections.

Originally a launch-era Super Nintendo title, F-Zero became a celebrated demonstration of the console's Mode 7 scaling and rotation effects, which make its flat course layouts appear to rush beneath the player's vehicle. Its arcade appearance is notable because the Super System reused console technology rather than employing a separate specialist racing board.

games.title: Lethal Weapon
games.description:
Lethal Weapon for the Nintendo Super System is the coin-operated version of Ocean's 1992 action-platform game inspired by the first three films. Players select detectives Martin Riggs or Roger Murtaugh, whose different abilities affect combat and movement. From police headquarters they choose missions set in such places as docks and sewers, searching interconnected platforms and ladders for objectives under tight time limits.

The game mixes gun battles with exploration, and its selectable mission order gives it a less linear structure than many movie-license platformers. The Super System adaptation brings this SNES game into Nintendo's timed, multi-cartridge arcade environment.

games.title: NCAA Basketball
games.description:
NCAA Basketball is a 1992 collegiate basketball game from Sculptured Software, offered as a Nintendo Super System cartridge. Players select college teams for exhibitions or tournament-style play, controlling passing, shooting and defense on a court shown in a behind-the-player, pseudo-3D perspective. The rotating and scaling court presentation exploits the Super Nintendo's Mode 7 capabilities, giving the game a visual identity unlike many flat, side-on basketball simulations.

In AdvanceMAME this is the coin-operated Super System release, not a separate game engineered for conventional arcade basketball hardware.

games.title: Robocop 3
games.description:
RoboCop 3 is the Nintendo Super System edition of Ocean's 1992 Super Nintendo action game, based on the film in which Omni Consumer Products attempts to displace residents of Detroit. Players control the armored RoboCop through hostile urban areas, shooting enemies, avoiding hazards and pushing through side-scrolling platform stages.

This arcade cartridge uses the SNES-style platform action rather than the quite different polygonal driving and combat sequences found in some contemporary computer versions of RoboCop 3. Its appearance in Nintendo's Super System line reflects the period when selected console releases were repackaged for timed arcade play.

games.title: Skins Game
games.description:
Skins Game is the Nintendo Super System version of Irem's 1992 golf game, related to Major Title and the arcade release known as The Irem Skins Game. Players select a golfer and manage club choice, aim and swing timing while negotiating fairways, bunkers and greens. The 'skins' scoring format places special value on winning individual holes rather than simply accumulating the lowest total over a round.

This is an Irem golf game adapted to Nintendo's coin-operated Super Nintendo hardware, not the unrelated Midway golf games sometimes incorrectly attached to the same title in game databases.

games.title: Super Mario World
games.description:
Super Mario World reached arcades as a Nintendo Super System cartridge following its landmark 1990 Super Nintendo debut. Mario and Luigi explore Dinosaur Land to rescue Princess Peach and the captured Yoshis from Bowser. The game's interconnected levels introduce the rideable Yoshi, hidden exits leading to alternative routes and the Cape Feather, whose flight mechanics reward practice and experimentation. The spin jump and richly varied enemies add further layers to the established Super Mario formula.

Designed by Nintendo's EAD team under Shigeru Miyamoto, Super Mario World became one of the defining 16-bit platform games, renowned for its expansive map and inventive level design. The Super System edition is historically unusual because it puts a long-form home-console adventure into a coin-operated, time-limited environment rather than building a new arcade Mario game from scratch.

games.title: Super Soccer
games.description:
Super Soccer, known in Japan as Super Formation Soccer, is Human Entertainment's 1991 Super Nintendo football game offered in a Nintendo Super System cabinet. The action uses a distinctive view looking up the length of the pitch from behind the attacking team, with Mode 7 effects creating a convincing sense of depth. Players select national sides, pass and shoot through exhibition matches or a tournament, and manage tactical positioning as play switches between attack and defense.

The arcade adaptation makes a number of small interface changes compared with the home version, including removal of some goalkeeper and lineup options. It is a rare example of a console football game appearing on Nintendo's official coin-operated SNES-based platform.

games.title: Super Tennis
games.description:
Super Tennis is a 1991 Super Nintendo tennis game brought to the Nintendo Super System. Developed by Tose, it presents fast, colorful tennis with a behind-the-court viewpoint and a selection of fictional professional players. Players compete in singles or doubles, choose shots with different speed and spin, and can work through a world circuit rather than playing only isolated exhibition matches.

Its precise timing, positioning and variety of shot types helped distinguish it among early 16-bit sports games. The arcade release uses Nintendo's Super System hardware, whose coin-operated time allowance transforms the familiar home-game experience into a short-session attraction.

games.title: Night Stocker
games.description:
Night Stocker is a 1986 Bally Sente arcade game that combines vehicle steering with light-gun shooting, an unusual physical-control arrangement for its time. A moving first-person view carries the player's vehicle across an alien landscape toward a robot fortress, while enemies stream forward and must be shot with a separate gun. The car travels automatically, leaving the driver to steer around hazards and manage a limited ammunition supply.

A shield gauge absorbs damage and can be replenished by collecting crystals; the on-screen distance counter tracks progress toward the next fortress. This science-fiction follow-up to Bally Sente's Stocker puts simultaneous driving and aiming at the center of the challenge, making its mixed control system its chief historical curiosity.

games.title: N-Sub
games.description:
N-Sub is a 1980 Sega fixed-screen naval shooter in which the player pilots a submarine against attacking surface vessels and enemy subs in the Cobalt Blue Sea. An eight-way joystick maneuvers the craft, and two separate firing buttons launch torpedoes vertically toward ships or horizontally toward submarines. Holding a fire button produces a short burst, allowing accurate timing against formations that also attack with missiles, torpedoes and depth charges.

One of Sega's early VIC Dual games, N-Sub predates the widespread standardization of shooter controls and is distinctive for its dual-direction weapon system. Successive enemy fleets increase the pressure, turning its simple underwater battlefield into a demanding test of positioning and projectile timing.

games.title: Mahjong Nerae! Top Star
games.description: Mahjong Nerae! Top Star is a Japanese mahjong arcade game released in March 1990, built around a show-business theme. Its extended title translates approximately as 'Aim High! Top Star: Show Business World Survival Mahjong'. It is part of the late-1980s and early-1990s Japanese tradition of character-driven, single-player mahjong games, with the entertainment-industry setting providing the identity behind its mahjong matches.

games.title: Numan Athletics
games.description:
Numan Athletics is Namco's 1993 futuristic answer to button-mashing arcade track-and-field games. Up to four superhuman athletes, called Numans, compete in eight absurdly exaggerated events that turn sporting feats into science-fiction spectacles. Challenges include running faster than a high-performance car, stopping incoming missiles and throwing huge objects across impossible distances. Each event has its own button sequence and qualification target, with three action buttons used in different ways to build speed, time attacks or control movement.

Its exaggerated character animation, announcer, changing international venues and competitive multiplayer setup turn a familiar Olympic-game structure into a colorful comic-book contest. It later received an arcade sequel, Mach Breakers: Numan Athletics 2, continuing the theme of superpowered competitors rather than realistic sports simulation.

games.title: Number Crash
games.description:
Number Crash is an unusual 1983 single-screen platform game by Universal. Instead of simply collecting objects, the player navigates shelves and platforms to retrieve numbered pieces and arrange them in a scoring box. The final number sequence affects the bonus, so sets and ordered runs can be far more valuable than a random collection. A four-way joystick and jump button govern movement around the playfield while the clock imposes pressure.

Its mixture of arcade platform timing and number-sequence planning makes it a curious departure from the more conventional climbing and maze games of its era.

games.title: Vs. Platoon
games.description:
Vs. Platoon is a 1987 Nintendo Vs. System arcade adaptation of the action game based on Oliver Stone's Vietnam War film. The player works through jungle patrols, enemy encounters and connected areas, moving across side-scrolling terrain and completing objectives such as finding equipment or destroying a bridge. Its action is more mission-oriented than a straightforward run-and-gun game, with exploration and survival interspersed with combat.

This edition is part of Nintendo's Vs. arcade line, which brought selected Nintendo Entertainment System games to coin-operated cabinets. The film license and multiple mission objectives distinguish it from the better-known fantasy and platform titles on the same system.

games.title: Night Warriors: Darkstalkers' Revenge

variants.title: Vampire Hunter: Darkstalkers' Revenge (Japan 950307 stop version)

games.description:
Night Warriors: Darkstalkers' Revenge is Capcom's 1995 sequel to Darkstalkers, known in Japan as Vampire Hunter. Its roster assembles fourteen fantastic fighters drawn from horror legends and folklore, including vampire Demitri, succubus Morrigan, werewolf Jon Talbain and newcomers Donovan Baine and Hsien-Ko. Beneath its animated monster designs lies a fast six-button fighting game built on Capcom's CPS-2 hardware.

The sequel expands the original's combat with chain combinations, improved special-move management and the ability to stock super-meter energy for later use. Its elaborate sprite animation, theatrical transformations and spectacular supernatural attacks made it a standout among mid-1990s arcade fighters. The new characters also bring a different perspective to the series, as Donovan and Hsien-Ko are monster hunters confronting the Darkstalkers themselves.

games.title: N.Y. Captor
games.description:
N.Y. Captor is a 1985 Taito shooting-gallery game in which a police marksman must shoot terrorists without harming their hostages or other innocent bystanders. The player aims a light gun at targets appearing across urban scenes, making recognition and precision just as important as speed. It is one of Taito's earliest dedicated gun-controlled arcade releases, predating the company's better-known Operation Wolf.

The game also hides small cameos from Chack'n Pop, including Chack'n and a Monsta. An unauthorized version circulated under the title Colt.

games.title: New York New York
games.description:
New York! New York! is Universal's 1980 fixed-screen alien-invasion shooter, set against a recognizable skyline and the Statue of Liberty. The player operates a ground-based cannon while waves of enemy craft sweep across the sky and fire missiles. Destroying the requisite wave brings out a UFO, whose defeat leads to a faster and more hazardous repetition of the attack.

Gottlieb licensed the game for American distribution in 1981. A later Japanese revision, Waga Seishun no Arcadia, replaced the New York backdrop with Captain Harlock imagery to capitalize on the popularity of the space-pirate anime, an unusual example of an arcade game changing its apparent theme while retaining largely the same action.

games.title: New Zero Team
games.description:
New Zero Team is a 1997 rerelease of Seibu Kaihatsu's cooperative 1993 beat 'em up Zero Team, represented here by an alternative ROM set. The action follows a team of four fighters battling through side-scrolling urban stages, combining punches, kicks, throws and powerful emergency attacks against groups of enemies. Weapons and scenery objects can be picked up and used during fights.

The New Zero Team revision changes aspects of the original game's progression and balancing; versions of this rerelease also appeared on Seibu's V33-based hardware. This set is a variation of that revived arcade brawler, not an independent sequel.

games.title: New Zero Team

variants.title: New Zero Team (V33 SYSTEM TYPE_B hardware)
New Zero Team (V33 SYSTEM TYPE_B hardware, Zhongguo Shantou Yihuang license)

games.description:
New Zero Team is Seibu Kaihatsu's 1997 revival of its 1993 side-scrolling brawler Zero Team. Players choose members of a four-person combat squad, each with individual fighting moves, then battle kidnappers and other criminals through urban stages. The combat mixes throws, jumping attacks, special moves and improvised weapons such as crates, barrels and heavier arms dropped by enemies.

The rerelease is particularly interesting for its updated game balance and changed early-stage order, as well as its appearance on NEC V33-based arcade boards rather than only the original hardware. Its later commercial circulation in East Asia helped keep Seibu's relatively obscure cooperative fighter alive after the first Zero Team release.

games.title: Ironman Stewart's Super Off-Road
games.description:
Ivan 'Ironman' Stewart's Super Off-Road is Leland's 1989 top-down truck racer, designed around the immediate chaos of three-player competition. Each player has a dedicated steering wheel and accelerator button, sending miniature off-road trucks around compact stadium circuits filled with bumps, mud, jumps and tight bends. The computer-controlled truck bears the identity of real off-road racing champion Ivan Stewart, whose endorsement helped establish the game's theme.

Money earned from race results buys upgrades to tires, suspension, acceleration and top speed, while limited nitro boosts can turn a close finish into a win. The cabinet's multiple steering wheels, striking overhead tracks and upgrade economy made Super Off-Road a fixture of early-1990s arcades and helped inspire a long line of similarly frantic multiplayer racing games.

games.title: Off Road Challenge
games.description:
Off Road Challenge is Midway's 1997 arcade truck racer and a later entry in the series that began with Ivan Stewart's Super Off-Road. Unlike the original's tiny overhead stadiums, this game puts players behind rugged trucks on sprawling three-dimensional courses through deserts, mountain roads and city surroundings. Tracks feature changing surfaces, jumps, shortcuts and collisions, demanding a balance between aggressive driving and vehicle control.

Races award money that can be spent at a Speed Shop to improve the truck's acceleration, suspension and other performance characteristics. Nitro pickups and protective items add another arcade layer, while the choice of visible and secret trucks gives players different handling styles.

games.title: Ironman Stewart's Super Off-Road Track Pack
games.description:
Ivan 'Ironman' Stewart's Super Off-Road Track Pack is an expansion kit for Leland's popular three-player overhead truck racer. It keeps the original's steering-wheel racing, rough terrain, cash prizes, nitro boosts and purchasable vehicle upgrades but replaces the familiar courses with eight new tracks. These include Shortcut, Cut-off Pass, Pig Bog, Rio Trio, Leapin' Lizards, Redoubt About, Boulder Hill and Volcano Valley.

Rather than inventing new mechanics, the Track Pack renews the game's competitive appeal with fresh corner sequences, hazards and shortcuts, giving experienced players new layouts to master on existing Super Off-Road cabinets.

games.title: Off the Wall
games.description:
Atari Games' Off the Wall (1991) is an inventive multiplayer reworking of Breakout. One to three players control paddles around the edges of a square arena, bouncing a ball through elaborate formations of bricks toward an exit. Instead of merely clearing the screen, a player can end a round by sending the ball into the exit, often earning points for the blocks left intact. Some blocks move, resist damage or drop replacements, and the physics allow players to impart spin to the ball.

Pickups can enlarge the paddle, slow the ball, catch it or add a shooting weapon, while prolonged rallies may generate extra balls. Multiplayer adds the unusual complication that a ball's color, determined by the paddle last touching it, affects who scores. The result is a surprisingly strategic, abstract-art take on the paddle-and-ball genre, distinct from Bally Sente's unrelated 1984 game of the same name.

games.title: Oh My God!
games.description:
Oh My God! is Atlus's eccentric 1993 falling-block puzzle game. Instead of rotating ordinary two- or three-piece columns, the player guides a descending, snake-like chain of colored balls around the screen. When the chain lands, its balls become part of the stack, and matching three or more of a color horizontally, vertically or diagonally clears them. Long matches and chain reactions are rewarded, and clever players can even complete a match while pieces are still falling.

Increasing chain length, more colors and a faster descent gradually complicate the puzzle. The odd combination of snake-style steering and Columns-like matching gives Oh My God! a distinct identity among the many competitive puzzle games of the early 1990s.

games.title: Oishii Puzzle Ha Irimasenka
games.description:
Oishii Puzzle Ha Irimasenka is a 1993 Sunsoft puzzle collection featuring characters from the Hebereke series. It offers several kinds of visual and word puzzles, including crosswords, jigsaws, spotting differences between pictures and searching crowded scenes for hidden figures. The changing activities make it more like a colorful arcade party challenge than a single-rule falling-block game.

The Japanese title can be translated approximately as 'Would You Like a Delicious Puzzle?' An unauthorized English-language version was distributed as Triple Fun.

games.title: Ojanko Yakata 2bankan
games.description: Ojanko Yakata 2bankan, released by Video System in Japan in February 1987, continues the company's school-themed Japanese mahjong line. Players face computer-controlled opponents at a dedicated mahjong panel, with the high-school setting and character presentation providing the identity for otherwise traditional Japanese tile-matching and scoring play. Its title identifies it as a second Ojanko Yakata installment, preceding the later Ojanko High School.

games.title: Ojanko Club
games.description: Ojanko Club is a Japanese mahjong arcade game released by Video System in June 1986. Its title means roughly 'Mahjong Girl Club', and it is an early entry in the company's series of character-themed mahjong titles. The game centers on mahjong play rather than joystick action, illustrating the specialized cabinet and control-panel culture of Japanese mahjong arcades in the mid-1980s.

games.title: Ojanko High School
games.description:
Ojanko High School is a 1988 Japanese strip-mahjong game from Video System, placing its mahjong contests in a fictional school. The roster mixes female students with several comic male opponents and a character named Soh Takeko, who later reappeared in the developer's Aero Fighters series. Winning matches progresses through the cast and unlocks mature-themed character scenes.

Its crossover references are especially notable: characters from Video System's Rabbit Punch (Rabio Lepus) appear in altered roles, including the Rabbit King as the principal. That makes this obscure mahjong title a small but revealing part of Video System's interconnected arcade history.

games.title: Ojanko Yakata
games.description: Ojanko Yakata is a Japanese, school-themed mahjong game released by Video System in December 1986. Players compete in traditional mahjong matches presented through a cast of illustrated characters, combining the specialized mahjong-panel format with the character-driven style that would become common in late-1980s Japanese amusement centers. The game belongs to Video System's early Ojanko line and was followed soon afterward by Ojanko Yakata 2bankan.

games.title: Ojousan
games.description: Ojousan, released by Nichibutsu in Japan in December 1987, is an adult-themed Japanese mahjong game. Its title means 'Young Lady', and computer-opponent matches are accompanied by female character illustrations and mature rewards. Surviving ROM sets include a normal version and a distinct BET-labeled version, reflecting the variety of arcade mahjong formats circulating in Japan at the time.

games.title: Oriental Legend Special / Xi You Shi E Zhuan Super

variants.title: Oriental Legend Special / Xi You Shi E Zhuan Super (Korea 101)
Oriental Legend Special / Xi You Shi E Zhuan Super (100)
Oriental Legend Special / Xi You Shi E Zhuan Super (100 alt)
Oriental Legend Special / Xi You Shi E Zhuan Super (ver. 103, China, Tencent) (unprotected)

games.description:
Oriental Legend Special, also known as Xi You Shi E Zhuan Super, is IGS's 1998 enhanced version of its popular Journey to the West-inspired arcade brawler. Tang-era monk San Zang travels toward India for Buddhist scriptures, protected by martial-arts disciples who fight demons and supernatural enemies. Players move through side-scrolling stages, combining ordinary attacks with character-specific special techniques and magic.

This revision adds fighting skills and rebalances existing ones rather than merely repackaging the original Oriental Legend. Its colorful mythical cast, elaborate move system and cooperative combat make it representative of IGS's distinctive PGM-era beat 'em ups, which often borrowed ideas from both arcade fighters and action role-playing games.

games.title: Oriental Legend 2 (Korea) / Xiyou Shi E Zhuan Qunmoluanwu

variants.title: Oriental Legend 2 (Korea) / Xiyou Shi E Zhuan Qunmoluanwu (World, China, Japan, Hong Kong, Taiwan) (ver. 205) [Oriental Ex]
variants.version: (Korea) / Xiyou Shi E Zhuan Qunmoluanwu (World, China, Japan, Hong Kong, Taiwan) (ver. 205) [Oriental Ex]

games.description:
Oriental Legend Special Plus, also titled Xi You Shi E Zhuan Qunmoluanwu and marketed in Korea as Oriental Legend 2, is a 2004 expansion of IGS's Journey to the West-themed brawling series. It continues the side-scrolling fight against demons from the original Oriental Legend while enlarging the playable roster from five characters to eleven. A distinctive new transformation ability allows selected fighters to assume the forms of other characters, greatly expanding the available combat techniques.

Despite the Korean title, this is a PGM-generation enhancement of Oriental Legend Special, not the later PGM2 game also called Oriental Legend 2. The overlap in naming has made the series' arcade releases unusually easy to confuse.

games.title: Oli-Boo-Chu
games.description:
Oli-Boo-Chu is the overseas title of Irem and GDI's 1981 maze game Punching Kid. The player guides a small, round-bodied character through a maze, chasing mice toward their holes and catching them for points while avoiding much larger lizard-like creatures. Rather than reproducing Pac-Man's dot-clearing loop, the game emphasizes pursuing mobile targets, timing encounters and exploiting the mouse holes for extra scoring opportunities.

Its odd combination of cartoon animals and maze pursuit is characteristic of the experimental period immediately following Pac-Man's success, when arcade designers tried many alternatives to simple pellet collection.

games.title: Omega Fighter
games.description:
Omega Fighter is UPL's inventive 1989 vertically scrolling shooter, set almost entirely against the surface and defenses of one gigantic enemy spacecraft. Instead of flying over unrelated landscapes, the player's small fighter dismantles successive sections of an immense alien battle cruiser as the mission progresses. Two main weapon types provide contrasting tactics: an increasingly powerful but short-ranged Ion Laser and a wider shot that covers more of the screen.

The scoring system particularly rewards aggressive, close-range kills, encouraging players to take risks that conventional shooters would discourage. Special items and bombs provide emergency options, while the enemy carrier's machinery and bosses give the stages a coherent visual identity. A revised Omega Fighter Special set also exists, making this an especially interesting cult title for shooter enthusiasts.

games.title: Omega Race
games.description:
Omega Race is Bally Midway's 1981 vector-graphics space shooter, built around a futuristic combat arena enclosed by an electrified boundary. Players rotate a small spacecraft with a spinner, use a separate thrust control to accelerate and fire at hostile drone ships, commanders and mines. Momentum persists when the thruster is released, so lining up a shot means planning a route as well as aiming. Enemy formations and hazards grow increasingly dangerous as the score climbs.

The game uses bright vector outlines rather than the raster sprites common in many contemporary arcades, and its dedicated spinner control gives the ship exceptionally smooth rotation. A compact but demanding blend of Asteroids-style inertia and arena combat, Omega Race is also notable as Midway's only original vector-display arcade video game.

games.title: Omotesandou
games.description:
Omotesandou is a 1989 Japanese tabletop arcade game from Anime Tec, identified by its original ROM date code 890215. Its preserved controls include a dedicated hanafuda, or Japanese flower-card, button layout, and historical emulator notes associate it with hana-awase-style play. Rather than using a joystick, players select cards and game commands through the specialized control panel, reflecting the established design of Japanese card-game cabinets.

The game runs on a Z80 with AY-3-8910 and DAC audio and presents its graphics on a wide horizontal screen. Documentation of its particular scoring rules and progression remains limited, but its distinctive flower-card inputs make it a useful example of the variety hidden within arcade databases' broad 'tabletop' category.

games.title: One Shot One Kill
games.description:
One Shot One Kill is an obscure 1996 Korean light-gun arcade shooter developed by Promat, with possible European distribution by Playmark. One or two players aim directly at targets in a succession of shooting stages, using gun controllers rather than conventional joysticks. The game's urban sequence includes an appearance by Korean pop musician Seo Taiji, an unexpected period detail in this little-known release.

Its dedicated gun interface and support for simultaneous players place it in the lineage of arcade shooting galleries, though its specific stages and rules are much less thoroughly documented than those of better-known light-gun games.

games.title: One + Two
games.description: One + Two is a 1997 arcade puzzle game by Barko, built around matching tiles in a playfield with an adult-themed visual presentation. It belongs to the competitive Japanese and Korean arcade puzzle tradition of the period, using an eight-way joystick and three buttons rather than a conventional mahjong panel. Surviving descriptions identify it as a tile-matching game; more detailed information about its exact match rules is not well documented.

games.title: Onna Sansirou - Typhoon Gal
games.description:
Onna Sansirou: Typhoon Gal is Taito's unusual 1985 martial-arts arcade game, starring Yuki, a young woman who takes on rival fighters in a sequence of judo-themed bouts. Unlike the later Street Fighter model, the game unfolds as an action contest against successive opponents, with punches, kicks, jumps, headbutts and throws used to defeat challengers. Opponents range from ordinary martial artists to powerful dojo masters, and mastering the throw system is essential to winning.

Known internationally as Typhoon Gal, it predates the explosion of one-on-one fighting games and is noteworthy for its female martial-artist protagonist and physical, grappling-oriented action. Its characterful animation and dojo setting give it an identity distinct from more conventional belt-scrolling beat 'em ups.

games.title: OOPArts
games.description:
OOPArts is an unreleased 1992 arcade prototype created by Success for Sega's System C-2 hardware. Its basic design is a brick-breaking game in the tradition of Arkanoid, with a ball used to eliminate targets across successive playfields. The surviving emulated version is specifically identified as a joystick-modified build, so its control scheme should not be assumed to represent a finished commercial cabinet.

Because the game never reached ordinary arcade distribution, it is chiefly of interest as a preserved experiment in the early-1990s revival of paddle-and-ball games. The existence of a working prototype offers a glimpse of a Sega-compatible title that otherwise would have remained obscure.

games.title: Opa Opa
games.description:
Opa Opa is Sega's 1987 arcade maze game, also known as Fantasy Zone: The Maze. Instead of the side-scrolling shooting associated with Fantasy Zone, it sends the tiny winged hero through overhead mazes to collect dots while avoiding pursuing enemies. Each world contains three regular mazes followed by a timed bonus round in which the player gathers coins. Enemy-generating areas create additional pressure, so moving quickly and preventing new threats from appearing are central to success.

Built on Sega's System E hardware, Opa Opa is an unusual genre experiment for a series otherwise defined by colorful scrolling shooters. An unprotected early hardware revision was also preserved, alongside the more familiar encrypted arcade version.

games.title: Konami's Open Golf Championship
games.description:
Konami's Open Golf Championship is a 1994 arcade golf simulation, released in Japan as Golfing Greats 2. It follows Konami's earlier Golfing Greats with a presentation centered on course selection, shot planning and accuracy. Players aim their shots, select the appropriate club and judge strength and timing while working around the familiar hazards of fairways, bunkers and greens.

Its comparatively traditional sporting focus contrasts with the exaggerated fantasy courses of some later arcade golf games. The Japan and overseas titles refer to the same entry in Konami's arcade golf line.

games.title: 2 On 2 Open Ice Challenge
games.description:
NHL Open Ice: 2 on 2 Challenge is Midway's 1995 hockey counterpart to NBA Jam, replacing detailed simulation with spectacular hits, fast breakaways and two-on-two scoring races. Four players can compete simultaneously, controlling real NHL teams and players from the mid-1990s season. The action is enlivened by a 'hot' meter that rewards successful checks, steals and goals with a temporary performance boost, turning momentum shifts into crowd-pleasing spectacles.

Pat Foley provides the energetic commentary, while the NHL and NHLPA licenses supply recognizable athletes, uniforms and team identities. Big-head options, hidden characters and exaggerated physical play make this one of the most distinctive sports entries in Midway's arcade lineup.

games.title: Operation Wolf
games.description:
Operation Wolf is Taito's influential 1987 light-gun shooter, in which special-forces soldier Roy Adams fights through enemy territory to rescue hostages. The large on-screen gun controller doubles as a machine gun and grenade launcher: sustained fire cuts down troops, while explosive rounds are vital against armored vehicles and helicopters. Six scrolling missions require players to conserve ammunition, shoot supply crates and manage damage while ultimately protecting prisoners during their escape.

The original arcade cabinet's imposing mounted weapon, physical recoil and cinematic explosions made Operation Wolf a landmark shooting-gallery attraction. It helped popularize the modern scrolling light-gun shooter and was widely converted to home computers and consoles. Its hostage-protection sequences make indiscriminate firing dangerous, adding a tactical constraint to the otherwise relentless action.

games.title: Operation Wolf 3
games.description:
Operation Wolf 3 is Taito's 1994 light-gun shooter developed by East Technology, a very loose follow-up to Operation Wolf and Operation Thunderbolt. Two counterterrorist agents, Hornet and Queen Bee, assault the SKULL organization after terrorists seize an island equipped with nuclear missiles. The five stages move through a factory, freeway, devastated city and enemy headquarters before a final missile confrontation, using digitized characters and backgrounds rather than the earlier games' traditional sprite artwork.

An unusual ammunition system permits continuous automatic fire but gradually reduces its rate as a meter empties; releasing the trigger rapidly restores it. Players can also collect heavier weapons and grenades, and occasional shooting-gallery bonus rounds offer extra points. The result is faster and more visually grounded than its predecessors, though its connection to the series is largely thematic.

games.title: Orange Club - Maruhi Kagai Jugyou
games.description:
Orange Club: Maruhi Kagai Jugyou is a Japanese adult mahjong game released by Daiichi Denshi in February 1988. Its subtitle means 'Secret Extracurricular Lesson', reflecting the game's school-themed presentation. Players compete in one-on-one Japanese mahjong against a cast of eight illustrated women, with successive victories unlocking a series of revealing scenes for each opponent.

A related BET version circulated under the separate title VIP Club: Maruhi Ippatsu Kaihou, illustrating how manufacturers repackaged adult mahjong games for different Japanese cabinet and scoring formats.

games.title: Orbit
games.description:
Orbit is Atari's 1978 two-player space-combat game, one of the company's early attempts to bring the computer-game tradition of Spacewar! into coin-operated form. Two players pilot rival spacecraft and try to destroy each other with projectiles. A broad bank of physical switches lets competitors select different levels of inertia, projectile speed, gravity and arena behavior, changing the feel of a match from straightforward dogfighting to a demanding orbital duel.

Certain settings add gravity effects or boundary rebounds, while optional space stations can allow damaged ships to return to the fight. The controls and configurable rule sets are the real attraction: Orbit is less a single scripted arcade challenge than a customizable contest between two human pilots.

games.title: Orbite
games.description:
Orbite is an unfinished space-shooter prototype developed by Italian manufacturer Model Racing around 1979. It was never commercially released, and the surviving code lacks essential finished-game features, including complete scoring and audio routines. The prototype is only partly playable, so it is best understood as preserved development material rather than a lost, fully functional arcade release.

Its survival is exceptional: the original assembler source was recovered from floppy disks belonging to a former Model Racing developer, allowing the incomplete game to be reconstructed and documented.

games.title: Orbitron
games.description: Orbitron is a little-known 1982 space-defense shooter developed by Comsoft and distributed under license by Signatron USA. The player controls a defender on a vertically oriented single-screen playfield, using a joystick and fire button to protect a planet from incoming hostile spacecraft. Its straightforward premise recalls the early wave of arcade alien-attack games, while the preserved version runs on Galaxian-derived hardware.

games.title: Orbs
games.description:
Orbs is a 1994 sliding-puzzle arcade prototype associated with American Sammy. Its challenge is built around rearranging pieces on a fixed playfield rather than fighting enemies or navigating a scrolling world. The preserved ROMs bear handwritten prototype labels dated October 7, 1994, and much of the available program space appears unused, suggesting a game that never reached an ordinary mass-produced release.

Its historical appeal lies largely in that surviving work-in-progress build, which offers a rare view of a mid-1990s arcade puzzle project outside the era's mainstream falling-block formula.

games.title: Ordyne
games.description:
Ordyne is Namco's 1988 horizontally scrolling 'cute 'em up', distinguished by its playful cartoon art and a surprisingly elaborate economy. Scientist Yuichiro Tomari and his assistant Sunday Chin fly through fanciful worlds to rescue Tomari's kidnapped fiancée from Dr. Kubota. Defeated enemies leave crystals that can be spent in in-game shops on weapons, upgrades and extra lives, encouraging players to think about which purchases will best help them survive the next stretch.

Bonus shooting games provide further chances to build up currency, while simultaneous two-player action adds to the chaos. Running on Namco's System 2 hardware, Ordyne combines the technical polish of late-1980s arcade shooters with a lighter tone and shopping mechanics more usually associated with role-playing games.

games.title: Oriental Legend 2
games.description:
Oriental Legend 2 is IGS's 2007 PGM2 side-scrolling action game, returning to the supernatural battles of the Chinese epic Journey to the West. Players select mythological heroes and battle demons through layered stages using martial-arts combinations, special techniques, equipment and defensive blocking. The combat system is unusually elaborate for a coin-operated beat 'em up, rewarding familiarity with each character's moves and the tactical use of collected items.

An optional electronic-card system allows players to preserve progress and equipment between sessions, an unusual bridge between classic arcade brawling and persistent character development. This later PGM2 game must be distinguished from the earlier Oriental Legend Special Plus, which was also called Oriental Legend 2 in Korea.

games.title: Oriental Legend / Xi Yo Gi Shi Re Zuang

variants.title: Oriental Legend / Xi Yo Gi Shi Re Zuang (ver. 126)
Oriental Legend / Xi Yo Gi Shi Re Zuang (ver. 105, Korean Board)
Oriental Legend / Xi Yo Gi Shi Re Zuang (ver. 111, Chinese Board)
Oriental Legend / Xi Yo Gi Shi Re Zuang (ver. 112, Chinese Board)
Oriental Legend / Xi Yo Gi Shi Re Zuang (ver. 112)

games.description:
Oriental Legend, also called Xi You Shi E Zhuan, is IGS's 1997 cooperative beat 'em up inspired by the Chinese novel Journey to the West. During the Tang dynasty, the monk San Zang journeys toward India to obtain sacred Buddhist scriptures, while his disciples fend off demon armies and supernatural creatures. The playable cast draws from familiar mythical heroes including Sun Wukong, the Monkey King, and fights through colorful side-scrolling environments filled with enemies and bosses.

Its deep collection of character-specific attacks, special moves and magic makes Oriental Legend more intricate than many conventional arcade brawlers. The game helped establish the identity of IGS's PolyGame Master platform, and later received expanded editions with additional fighters and abilities.

games.title: OutRunners
games.description:
OutRunners is Sega's exuberant 1992 sequel to the Out Run tradition of high-speed road trips. Players choose from eight wildly different cars, each with distinctive handling and personality, then race along branching routes through vivid international scenery. Like the original Out Run, each checkpoint extends the timer and every fork in the road leads to a different stage, making route choice part of the game's replay value.

Its major innovation is direct multiplayer competition. Twin-seat cabinets permit head-to-head racing, and linked machines can support larger contests, bringing an intensely social element to Sega's panoramic driving formula. The colorful vehicles, lively soundtrack and frequent changes of scenery make it a memorable late-era expression of the company's sprite-scaling arcade racers.

games.title: Psycho-Nics Oscar
games.description:
Psycho-Nics Oscar is Data East's 1987 side-scrolling robot shooter, set in a future city overrun by hostile machines. The player controls a humanoid combat mech, advancing through industrial terrain while shooting enemies, jumping hazards and facing large mechanical bosses. Its signature power-up system resembles Gradius: collecting capsules advances a selector across a row of upgrades, and a separate button activates the highlighted enhancement.

This choice between taking an immediate improvement and saving toward a later, more powerful one adds strategy to otherwise relentless run-and-gun action. Oscar's robotic protagonist, multi-button controls and intricate mechanical enemies made it a notable influence on later home-computer action games, including the Turrican style of platform shooting.

games.title: Osman
games.description:
Osman, called Cannon Dancer in Japan, is a 1996 arcade platform-action game developed by Mitchell Corporation with a striking resemblance to Capcom's Strider. The acrobatic hero Kirin battles soldiers, machines and fantastic bosses across a futuristic setting, attacking primarily with swift kicks rather than a sword. He can cling to walls and ceilings, leap between surfaces and unleash limited screen-clearing attacks, giving combat an unusually fluid, athletic rhythm.

Collecting power-ups creates phantom afterimages that follow and duplicate Kirin's movements, multiplying the reach of his attacks. Several of its creators had worked on Strider, but the game's surreal imagery, martial-arts focus and bizarre set pieces give it an identity of its own. An uncommon late-1990s arcade title, Osman became a sought-after cult favorite long before modern rereleases introduced it to a wider audience.

games.title: Disco Mahjong Otachidai no Okite
games.description: Disco Mahjong Otachidai no Okite is a 1995 Japanese mahjong game by Sphinx, presenting its tile-based contests against a discotheque and nightlife backdrop. Players participate in mahjong matches through a specialized mahjong interface, with the club setting providing the game's theme and character presentation. The title is often rendered as 'Disco Mahjong: Law of the Stage', and it represents a late example of the themed Japanese arcade mahjong games popular during the previous decade.

games.title: Othello Shiyouyo
games.description:
Othello Shiyouyo, meaning 'Let's Play Othello', is a 1998 Japanese arcade adaptation of the Othello/Reversi board game by Success and Itsui. Running on Sega's Saturn-derived ST-V hardware, it turns the familiar contest of placing black and white discs into an illustrated game with anime-style characters and multiple play modes. The aim remains to trap and flip the opponent's discs between your own, finishing with a greater share of the board.

Its ST-V cartridge format is a good example of late-1990s arcade hardware being used for board-game adaptations as well as faster action titles.

games.title: Othello Derby
games.description:
Othello Derby is a 1995 Japanese arcade game that wraps the classic Othello/Reversi board game in a horse-racing theme. The player chooses a black or white horse, representing the color of their pieces, and faces a series of increasingly difficult computer opponents. During each 'race', play switches to the Othello board: placing a piece must trap opposing discs in a straight line so they can be flipped.

A strict ten-second move timer prevents lengthy deliberation, with the game making a move automatically if time expires. Winning the board-game contest advances the player's horse to the next opponent, an entertainingly odd blend of abstract strategy and arcade racing presentation.

games.title: Operation Thunderbolt
games.description:
Operation Thunderbolt is Taito's 1988 sequel to Operation Wolf, expanding the military light-gun format to simultaneous two-player combat. Roy Adams returns with fellow operative Hardy Jones to rescue passengers from a hijacked airliner whose hostages have been dispersed across hostile territory. Players fight through eight missions, shooting soldiers, jeeps, helicopters and armored vehicles while conserving ammunition and using grenades against tougher targets.

Unlike the original's mostly side-scrolling presentation, Operation Thunderbolt introduces sequences that move into the screen, including assaults from vehicles and boats. Hostage-rescue stages still punish careless shooting, while gun pickups and supply crates can reverse a desperate situation. The increased spectacle and cooperative light-gun controls made it a natural successor to Taito's influential original.

games.title: Otona no Mahjong
games.description: Otona no Mahjong, meaning 'Adult Mahjong', is a 1988 Japanese arcade mahjong game released by Apple. Its setting is an upscale hotel, where the familiar Japanese tile game is presented in a mature-themed amusement format. Like other Japanese mahjong cabinets of its period, it uses a dedicated mahjong control panel rather than ordinary platform-game controls. The hotel motif and adult presentation distinguish it from the many school- and club-themed mahjong releases of the same era.

games.title: Off the Wall
games.description:
Bally Sente's Off the Wall (1984) is a two-player arcade racquetball game, entirely unrelated to Atari's 1991 brick-breaker of the same name. Each competitor controls a character on one side of a central net, moving with a two-way joystick and rotating the racket arm using a trackball-style control. Players try to place the ball where the opponent cannot return it, with rallies decided by missed shots, excessive bounces and other court violations.

The first player to eleven points wins, and solo play is possible against computer opponents at different skill levels. Hitting a small target at the top of the net temporarily increases its height, adding an extra tactical wrinkle. Its unconventional combination of character movement and racket rotation is the game's most distinctive feature.

games.title: Outfoxies
games.description:
The Outfoxies is Namco's remarkable 1995 arena-combat game, sometimes catalogued with a 1994 development year. Seven eccentric assassins, including a wheelchair-bound scientist, a chimpanzee and a pair of murderous twins, are pitted against one another by a mysterious employer. Instead of fighting on a flat stage, competitors run, climb and leap across elaborate multi-level arenas, grabbing guns, explosives, swords and improvised weapons to empty the opponent's life bar.

The environments are almost characters in themselves: moving machinery, destructible scenery, dangerous platforms and dramatic changes in arena layout force combatants to improvise constantly. The camera zooms to follow the action, allowing duels to spread across large stages. Long before platform fighters became a major genre, The Outfoxies experimented with the same mixture of free movement, environmental hazards and item-driven combat, earning an enduring cult reputation.

games.title: Out Run
games.description:
Out Run is Sega's landmark 1986 driving game, created under the direction of Yu Suzuki and celebrated for making arcade racing feel like a glamorous holiday rather than a formal motorsport event. Players take the wheel of a red Ferrari Testarossa convertible, accompanied by a passenger, and race through sunlit coastal roads, forests and mountain scenery against a demanding time limit. Traffic, sharp curves and sudden hills require anticipation, while forks in the road let players choose a route through a branching network of fifteen stages to one of several endings.

Out Run's dedicated sprite-scaling hardware created a remarkably smooth impression of speed, particularly in its deluxe moving cabinets. Just as memorable was the selectable in-car radio, with Hiroshi Kawaguchi's 'Magical Sound Shower', 'Passing Breeze' and 'Splash Wave' becoming iconic arcade music. Its combination of scenic spectacle, branching routes and relaxed, luxurious fantasy influenced decades of racing games and remains one of Sega's defining arcade achievements.

games.title: Out Zone
games.description:
Out Zone is Toaplan's 1990 vertically scrolling run-and-gun shooter, blending the perspective of a shoot 'em up with the freedom of a soldier moving on foot. Two cyborg mercenaries are sent to stop an alien invasion through seven hostile stages. Players dodge swarms of projectiles, cross dangerous terrain and confront large bosses while selecting between a directional weapon that fires where the soldier faces and a powerful forward-only spread shot.

A constantly draining energy meter makes movement and item collection urgent even when no enemy is nearby. Power-ups increase firepower, while 'E' items restore energy and weapon-change pickups alter the available firing pattern. Hidden cameos from other Toaplan games, including Zero Wing and Flying Shark, reward exploration, making Out Zone both a demanding shooter and a playful celebration of the developer's arcade catalog.

games.title: Over Drive
games.description:
Over Drive is Konami's 1990 high-speed arcade driving game, released outside Japan. Viewed from behind the car in a rapidly advancing pseudo-3D roadway, it challenges players to reach successive checkpoints before the time expires. Steering through traffic and bends while maintaining speed is central to both survival and scoring, with faster driving rewarded more generously.

Its emphasis on an intense, short driving sprint rather than an elaborate championship makes it a comparatively obscure but distinctive entry among Konami's early-1990s racers.

games.title: Over Top
games.description:
Over Top is ADK's 1996 overhead rally racer for the Neo Geo, developed in the tradition of the studio's earlier Thrash Rally. Rather than confining players to one vehicle type, it offers sports cars, motorcycles, vans and heavy off-road machines with different acceleration and handling. Players race through connected landscapes with changing weather and road surfaces, looking for shortcuts while trying to reach each checkpoint before the timer runs out.

A course map and directional warnings help players anticipate turns at speed, but choosing when to cut across rough ground remains a constant gamble. The range of vehicles and compact, detailed overhead scenery give Over Top an unmistakably arcade feel, even as its course progression evokes a long-distance rally.

games.title: Ozma Wars
games.description:
Ozma Wars is a pioneering 1979 fixed-screen space shooter from Shin Nihon Kikaku, the company that became SNK. The player defends against successive waves of alien craft, meteors and other hazards while a moving starfield creates the impression of travel through space. Unlike Space Invaders, the craft does not have a fixed number of lives. Instead, its energy reserve continuously runs down and falls sharply after a hit, making even quiet moments costly. Periodically a friendly mothership docks with the fighter and replenishes its energy.

As one of SNK's first arcade video games, Ozma Wars is important both for the company's history and for its unusually early use of a persistent energy meter. Often sold on or adapted from Space Invaders-era hardware, it also shows how quickly arcade shooters were experimenting with stage variety and survival systems after the initial invasion-game boom.

games.title: Ozon I
games.description:
Ozon I is a 1983 Italian arcade shooter by Proma that places the player in charge of a mobile anti-aircraft gun. Enemy planes cross a vertically oriented battlefield, dropping bombs and firing missiles at friendly tanks below.
