Track & Field on PlayChoice-10 is the NES adaptation of Konami's pioneering Olympic-style sports game, known in Japan as Hyper Olympic. Competitors tackle events such as sprints, long jump, javelin, hurdles and other athletics disciplines, building speed through repeated button presses before timing an action precisely to jump or throw.

The mixture of frantic button tapping and exact timing created a distinctive arcade spectator sport and made the original 1983 coin-op famous. The NES release adjusts the event presentation for its controller and display, and the PlayChoice cartridge brings that home conversion back to a coin-operated setting.

games.title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles
games.description:
Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (1989) on PlayChoice-10 is Konami's NES action-adventure, not the same game as the four-player arcade beat-'em-up. Players switch among Leonardo, Michelangelo, Donatello and Raphael while searching for April O'Neil and confronting Shredder's forces. Each Turtle has a different weapon and attack range, and the adventure moves between an overhead city map and difficult side-view action stages.

The game is remembered for its challenging platforming, resource management and notorious underwater bomb-disarming sequence. Because injured or captured Turtles can become unavailable, choosing which hero tackles a hazard matters. Its unconventional structure makes it an important distinction for anyone comparing the console and arcade branches of the TMNT franchise.

games.title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles II: The Arcade Game

variants.title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles II: The Arcade Game (PlayChoice-10)

games.description:
Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles II: The Arcade Game is Konami's NES adaptation of the celebrated 1989 Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles coin-op brawler, available on PlayChoice-10. Players choose a Turtle and fight waves of Foot Soldiers, robots and recognizable villains using simple jump, attack and special-move controls. Two-player cooperative play reproduces much of the lively appeal of the original arcade action.

The NES cartridge changes the artwork, stage layouts and number of simultaneous players to fit its hardware, and adds material not found in the original arcade version. It is therefore a distinct home conversion, even though its title explicitly celebrates its coin-operated inspiration.

games.title: Trojan
games.description:
Trojan on PlayChoice-10 is Capcom's NES version of its 1986 post-apocalyptic action game, known in Japan as Tatakai no Banka. The hero crosses a ruined landscape armed with a sword and shield, fighting soldiers and bosses while learning when to strike, block or leap over attacks. Enemies with longer weapons and different defenses force the player to adapt rather than simply attack continuously.

The home conversion alters parts of the structure and includes additional modes compared with the original arcade release. Its deliberate, weapon-based combat occupies an interesting position between early martial-arts games and later side-scrolling action adventures.

games.title: Volley Ball
games.description:
Volleyball is Nintendo's 1986 NES sports game, made available in arcades on PlayChoice-10. Players control a six-person volleyball team, selecting men's or women's competition and national teams before entering matches. Serves, passes, sets, blocks and spikes are represented through short, timing-sensitive button actions.

The view keeps both sides of the court visible, and the emphasis is on correctly positioning players and judging the trajectory of each rally. Its relatively complete team-sport rules make it a distinctive early console simulation rather than a purely reflex-based volleying minigame.

games.title: Nintendo World Cup
games.description:
Nintendo World Cup (1990), a Technos Japan soccer game on PlayChoice-10, is a gloriously unruly interpretation of football. Each side fields six super-deformed players, and the user controls one while issuing basic commands to teammates. Passing and shooting are important, but the rules largely ignore offsides and fouls, so hard tackles and dramatic special shots become part of the spectacle.

Matches are fast, physical and often comically destructive, with exhausted opponents sometimes left sprawled on the ground. The game was localized from Nekketsu High School Dodgeball Club: Soccer Story, part of Technos's Kunio-kun series; the international editions replace the Japanese school teams with national sides. Its blend of sports strategy and beat-'em-up energy makes it one of the more unconventional PlayChoice offerings.

games.title: Wild Gunman
games.description:
Wild Gunman on PlayChoice-10 is the 1984 NES light-gun game inspired by Nintendo's earlier 1974 electro-mechanical Western shooting attraction. Using a Zapper-style gun, the player faces cartoon outlaws in a series of quick-draw contests. The crucial rule is to wait for the explicit fire signal before shooting; drawing too early loses the duel regardless of accuracy.

Other scenarios introduce multiple opponents or shooting-gallery encounters in a saloon setting. With its emphasis on reflexes and timing, Wild Gunman turns a simple screen-and-gun interaction into a miniature Western standoff. The PlayChoice cartridge is the electronic NES interpretation, not the original projected-film amusement machine.

games.title: Yo! Noid
games.description:
Yo! Noid (1990) is a Capcom-published NES platform game based on the red-suited advertising mascot of Domino's Pizza, available through Nintendo's PlayChoice-10. Players guide the Noid across New York-themed stages, defeating enemies with a yo-yo and avoiding hazards that can cost a life instantly. The levels mix running jumps with obstacles and boss encounters that frequently use a different style of competition.

The game is a localized reworking of the Japanese title Kamen no Ninja Hanamaru, with the protagonist and presentation changed to fit the American advertising character. That unusual origin makes Yo! Noid a memorable intersection of console platform design, fast-food marketing and arcade distribution.

games.title: Pocket Gal
games.description:
Pocket Gal (1987) is Data East's adult-oriented arcade billiards game, closely related to the company's earlier Side Pocket. Players aim a cue ball around a small pool table, adjusting the strength and spin of each stroke to pocket a set of balls. Shots and attempts are limited, so a missed opportunity or scratch can be more serious than merely conceding position to an opponent.

The game blends its compact pool puzzles with bonus challenges and illustrated female characters whose outfits change as stages are cleared. It was distributed in several licensed and bootleg forms and later followed by Pocket Gal Deluxe. Its combination of arcade pool physics, shot economy and cheeky presentation gave it a more recognizable identity than an ordinary billiards simulation.

games.title: Print Club
games.description:
Print Club (1995), created by Atlus in collaboration with Sega, is a landmark Japanese arcade photo-sticker booth rather than a conventional videogame. Customers pay to pose for a camera, choose decorative frames or graphic embellishments on a screen and receive a small sheet of printed stickers showing their photographs. The original service popularized a format in which the amusement itself was making and sharing a personalized memento.

The early machines became enormously popular among Japanese teenagers, particularly schoolgirls, and helped create the purikura culture of collecting and exchanging decorated photo stickers. The small printed pictures also offered a different social use for arcade technology: the result could be taken away, shown to friends and attached to notebooks or other personal possessions. The name purikura derives from the shortened Japanese pronunciation of Print Club.

Although it appears in emulator software lists because of its Sega-based electronics, Print Club is historically more significant as an arcade social phenomenon than as a game with scores or stages. An emulation environment cannot fully reproduce the original experience without its camera, printer and physical booth.

games.title: Puzzle Club
games.description:
Puzzle Club (2000) is Yun Sung's adult-oriented arcade compilation containing six distinct puzzle games rather than a single set of rules. Magic Eye challenges players to find differences between pictures; Box Logic uses nonogram-style grids; Mad Ball is a Breakout-inspired paddle game; Magic Bubble follows Puzzle Bobble; Bogle Puyo imitates Puyo Puyo; and Rocktris draws on Tetris.

Several of the modes reveal adult photographic backgrounds during play, while others emphasize more conventional puzzle challenges. The compilation's heavy borrowing from successful puzzle franchises is central to its identity, making it a revealing example of late-1990s and early-2000s arcade multi-game boards built from familiar formulas.

games.title: Power Drift
games.description:
Sega's Power Drift (1988), designed by Yu Suzuki, is a spectacular arcade racing game that treats its twisting courses like giant roller coasters. Players choose a cartoonish driver and race a small car across one of five circuits, each containing five stages. To move on, they must finish a four-lap race in at least third place. Elevated turns, sudden drops, off-road excursions and dramatic changes of perspective make every stage a test of timing and steering rather than straightforward highway driving.

The game uses Sega's powerful Y Board sprite hardware, which scales and rotates huge numbers of objects to simulate a three-dimensional world long before textured polygon racers became standard. The viewpoint tilts with the bends, while some dedicated moving cabinets physically jolt and lean, enhancing the sensation of a violent ride. Expert players who win all five races in a circuit can unlock special challenges featuring vehicles associated with other Sega games, including After Burner and Super Hang-On.

Power Drift was both a commercial success and a notable technical step beyond earlier Sega sprite racers such as Out Run. Its colorful, deliberately exaggerated tracks and convincing speed make it one of the clearest demonstrations of how far late-1980s sprite-scaling arcade graphics could be pushed.

games.title: Power Drift - Link Version

variants.title: Power Drift - Link Version (Japan, Rev A)

games.description:
Power Drift: Link Version (1988) is a distinct linked-cabinet edition of Sega's celebrated Y Board racing game. Its driving fundamentals remain those of the original: choose a driver, race along gravity-defying courses full of bends and dips, and finish high enough to qualify for the next stage. Scaled and rotated sprites create the impression of a twisting 3D track, backed by the steering wheel, pedals and optional motion-cabinet experience.

What separates this edition is its support for linked installations, intended to let multiple arcade machines participate in a connected racing setup rather than simply running isolated games. The link-specific hardware and program differences warrant its separate identity in MAME-derived catalogs. Link communication itself may not be fully supported in emulation, so the historical multiplayer capability should not be assumed available in every AdvanceMAME configuration.

games.title: Peek-a-Boo!
games.description:
Peek-a-Boo! (1993) is Jaleco's adult-themed take on the Breakout and Arkanoid formula. The player moves a paddle horizontally across the bottom of the playfield, bouncing a ball upward to destroy an arrangement of bricks. Missing the ball costs a chance, while completing each stage reveals a photographic image of an adult model.

The straightforward ball-and-paddle action is designed around clearing patterns efficiently and anticipating rebounds. Its image-reveal rewards place it among the many Japanese arcade games that combined established puzzle or action mechanics with mature content during the early 1990s.

games.title: Peggle
games.description:
Peggle (1991), created by Incredible Technologies and released by Strata, is an arcade skill game that has no connection to PopCap's much later game of the same name. A small bouncing character falls through a playfield of colored pegs, and the player's task is to direct its path so it strikes as many targets as possible before landing in one of several cups at the bottom. Some pegs need repeated hits, while the cups can award extra points, time or another bounce.

Rather than launching balls from a cannon, players manipulate the playfield by rotating pegs and shifting the receiving cups, with joystick and trackball control versions known to exist. The unusual blend of pinball-like rebounds and deliberate board manipulation makes it a distinctive entry in Incredible Technologies' early-1990s catalog.

games.title: Penguin Brothers
games.description:
Penguin Brothers (2000) is a charming single-screen platform-action game by Subsino, featuring blue and pink penguins that can play cooperatively or competitively. The penguins place or throw bombs to destroy enemies, break obstacles and reveal hidden rewards. Defeating every enemy produces a key, which must then be collected and carried to the exit, frequently through a second section of the stage.

A distinctive mechanic is the presence of rotating platforms: characters can cling underneath a platform and rotate it to reach a higher or lower level. Bomb explosions can also injure the penguins, so cooperative players have to coordinate their attacks rather than simply covering the screen with explosives. With its bright designs and mixture of Bubble Bobble-style stage clearing and Bomberman-style bombs, Penguin Brothers became a late-era arcade cult favorite. Regional variants include A-Blast and Hong Tian Lei.

games.title: Penfan Girls - Step1. Mild Mind
games.description: Eolith's Penfan Girls: Step1. Mild Mind is a Korean arcade puzzle game carrying a 1999 copyright, although its Korean release is recorded in March 2000. Rather than clearing falling blocks, players choose geometric pieces, rotate them, and fit them into vacant spaces on the playfield. Its measured, shape-fitting challenge and adult-themed presentation make it an unusual member of Eolith's arcade catalogue. The game is also notable for its rarity: the surviving arcade boards were scarcely documented before collectors brought them to the attention of the emulation community.

games.title: Pengo
games.description:
Pengo is a 1982 maze-action classic developed by Coreland and published by Sega. Its hero is a little red penguin trapped among ice blocks and hostile Sno-Bees. With a four-way joystick and a single push button, players send blocks sliding through the maze to crush enemies, or break blocks that cannot move. Some ice blocks conceal Sno-Bee eggs, which can be destroyed before they hatch, while surviving creatures rearrange the maze by breaking ice as they pursue Pengo.

The playfield is more than scenery. Pushing against an outer wall briefly stuns nearby Sno-Bees, allowing Pengo to run them over. Three indestructible diamond blocks can be aligned horizontally or vertically for a large bonus, with a higher reward for a line away from the walls. Fast clears earn time bonuses, and after every second round a charming penguin intermission interrupts the action. The 16 rounds eventually repeat with rising pressure.

Pengo became an enduring example of character-driven early-1980s arcade design, mixing the immediacy of a maze chase with the satisfaction of turning the environment into a weapon. Japanese editions are particularly remembered for their use of the melody 'Popcorn'; export revisions replaced the tune and altered some timing. Sega's penguin later found a home on several domestic systems, while the original inspired numerous imitators and bootlegs, including Penta.

games.title: Pepper II
games.description:
Exidy's Pepper II (1982) reimagines the territory-capturing idea of Amidar as a four-screen maze chase. Players control Pepper, an angel who runs along the edges of rectangular areas, leaving a zipper trail behind. Completing a closed loop fills the enclosed space and awards points, but retracing an unfinished path unzips it. All four interconnected mazes must be filled before a level is complete.

Roaming Eyes pursue Pepper, while the Whippersnapper follows and undoes unfinished zipper trails. Enclosing a pitchfork temporarily turns the angel into a devil who can chase down the Eyes; a changing central symbol can instead eliminate the Whippersnapper when captured at the right moment. Prizes, route planning, and carefully timed power-ups give the deceptively simple game real tactical depth. Despite the numeral in its title, there was never a Pepper I. A ColecoVision conversion later introduced the game to home players.

games.title: The Percussor
games.description: Orca's The Percussor (1981) is an unusual space-themed shooter that combines fixed-screen battles with movement between horizontally connected combat areas. Players pilot an aircraft with eight-way movement, firing forward-facing guns and missiles against saucers, helicopters, and other airborne threats. The central task is to destroy a series of enemy ground bases, which must be hit with missiles rather than ordinary gunfire. Dodging bombs and pursuing missiles while lining up an attack on each fortified position gives the game a different rhythm from the fixed formations of contemporary alien shooters. Some arcade documentation identifies the surviving board as a possible bootleg.

games.title: Perestroika Girls
games.description:
Perestroika Girls is a 1994 adult-themed territory-capture puzzle game published by Promat and also licensed to Fuuki. Its underlying design follows Taito's Super Qix closely: players move along the edge of a playfield and draw lines into open territory to claim areas of an obscured picture. Completing enough of the screen reveals a full illustration and advances to the next stage.

The game adds moving hearts to collect for points and gems that can confer shields, increased speed, or time-stopping effects. Players can reverse along a partly drawn line, but lingering too long invites a pursuing flame. Clearing more than 80 percent of a picture reveals the stage's adult illustration. Its close technical relationship to Super Qix, including substantial reused code according to arcade preservation notes, makes it particularly interesting as a derivative of Taito's influential formula.

games.title: Performan
games.description:
Performan is a 1985 single-screen action game developed by Toaplan and released through Data East. Players guide a small robot around an overhead arena, attacking enemies with a returning 'Perfor-Boomerang' and digging into the ground to avoid danger or reposition. Enemies can also burrow, so disappearing underground is not always a safe escape.

Explosive meca-stones scattered around the field can be pushed or detonated with boomerangs, creating opportunities to eliminate several opponents in one blast for higher scores. Explosions can also stun the player, making careful placement essential. Collectible gifts, temporary invincibility, and bonuses leading toward extra lives reward deliberate play. Produced early in Toaplan's history, Performan shows the studio experimenting with maze-action mechanics before becoming especially associated with scrolling shooters.

games.title: Peter Pack-Rat
games.description:
Peter Pack-Rat is a colorful Atari Games platform adventure, released in 1985 on the interchangeable Atari System 1 hardware despite displaying a 1984 copyright. Players control Peter, a resourceful rat who scampers through a junkyard, sewer, and tree, gathering watches, bottles, cans, and other shiny objects to carry home to his nest. Completing a delivery list clears the stage, while later visits introduce more items, enemies, and altered shortcuts.

Peter can jump, climb, and throw collected objects at a memorable gang of animal adversaries, including a bulldog, cat, snake, spider, and owl. Stunned flying animals can even be ridden briefly to reach otherwise awkward platforms. The arcade cabinet's unusual control arrangement combines an eight-way joystick with a jump control on its handle and conveniently placed throw buttons.

Programmed by Peter Thompson, with artwork by Debbie Hayes and music by Brad Fuller, the game is celebrated for its lively animation and distinctive soundtrack. It was made in comparatively small numbers as complete cabinets, with additional Atari System 1 conversion kits extending its reach. Its playful personalities and demanding object-management challenge have made it a cult favorite among Atari arcade collectors.

games.title: Pettan Pyuu
games.description:
Sun Electronics' Pettan Pyuu (1984) is a deceptively tricky overhead action-puzzle game starring a small robot named Pettan. Players negotiate compact mazes of floor tiles and red barriers while using four kinds of square plates to flatten or fling away troublesome bugs. Each plate type responds differently to the direction from which it is approached, turning apparently simple enemy encounters into positioning puzzles.

Touching a bug or being struck by a moving plate costs a life, while efficient routes and fewer activated tiles can improve the score. Encounters with Pettan's girlfriend and special bonus sequences provide lighter interruptions. Originally a Japanese exclusive, with a planned overseas title BanBam never commercially realized, it finally reached Western audiences through Arcade Archives decades later. Its designer, Koji Kenjo, would go on to create the Custom Robo series.

games.title: Psychic Force 2012
games.description:
Psychic Force 2012 is Taito's 1998 sequel to its unconventional psychic-combat fighting game. Instead of standing on a flat arena floor, fighters hover freely inside enclosed three-dimensional battlegrounds, maneuvering in any direction while launching elemental projectiles, rushing in for close attacks, and throwing up defensive barriers. The roster and story expand the conflict between factions of psychically gifted people, with new fighters and updated visual effects.

The combat system revolves around balancing health and psychic energy. The Psycho Gauge powers offensive and defensive techniques, while quick dashes, barrier-breaking attacks, and wall-recovery counters create a contest of spacing and timing unlike conventional one-on-one fighters. Hyper Charge trades health for greater offensive potential, adding another calculated risk.

Its arcade incarnation is particularly notable for running on Taito's rare Wolf System, a PC-derived platform incorporating Pentium hardware and 3D acceleration. The game subsequently reached the Dreamcast, received a modified PlayStation adaptation as Psychic Force 2, and later appeared in Taito's Psychic Force Complete compilation. Its fully airborne battles remain among the more distinctive experiments of the late-1990s 3D fighting boom.

games.title: Pocket Gals V.I.P
games.description: Pocket Gals V.I.P. is a late-1990s adult-themed arcade billiards game continuing the Pocket Gal line. Players aim and take shots around a virtual pool table, clearing successive layouts while receiving illustrated pin-up rewards for progress. Its appeal lies in combining straightforward cue-sport rules with a short, score-driven arcade progression rather than a full-scale pool simulation. The surviving versions include sets with different regional presentation and artwork, making it a curious late entry in the arcade tradition of adult billiards games.

games.title: PGM (Polygame Master) System BIOS
games.description:
The PolyGame Master, or PGM, was introduced by Taiwanese manufacturer IGS in 1997 as a cartridge-based arcade platform competing in the same market as SNK's Neo-Geo MVS. Its interchangeable game boards let operators reuse a common motherboard across a range of releases. Early titles included Oriental Legend, followed by games such as The Killing Blade, Knights of Valour, Martial Masters, and Demon Front. The system became particularly associated with side-scrolling action games inspired by Chinese history, martial arts, and popular folklore.

PGM hardware centered on a Motorola 68000 processor with a Z80-driven ICS2115 sample-based sound system. Its graphics circuitry supported scrolling tile layers, large sprites, and sprite scaling, all useful for crowded brawlers and vividly animated fighting games. Some cartridges added ARM-based protection hardware, an important complication for later emulation. This BIOS contains the shared system software rather than a playable game, and represents an influential regional alternative to the better-known Japanese cartridge arcade platforms.

games.title: Pleasure Goal / Futsal - 5 on 5 Mini Soccer
games.description:
Pleasure Goal, subtitled Futsal: 5 on 5 Mini Soccer, is a 1996 Neo Geo sports game that trades regulation football for quick, compact five-a-side matches. Players choose from 16 national teams and compete on smaller pitches viewed from above, passing, dribbling, and shooting in a brisk arcade interpretation of indoor soccer. Shorter distances and frequent changes of possession encourage constant attacking play.

Its detailed pre-rendered sprites and different stadium settings give the matches a distinctive look, while the simplified rules and immediate joystick-and-button controls make it easy to pick up. Known as Futsal in Japan, Pleasure Goal is an overlooked alternative to the era's more conventional eleven-a-side football games on the Neo Geo.

games.title: Phantom II
games.description:
Midway's Phantom II (1979) is an early vertically scrolling air-combat shooter in which players pilot a Phantom jet through skies crowded with enemy aircraft. The eight-way joystick steers the plane as it continuously advances, while a firing button destroys targets for points. Opponents can lurk behind cloud cover, making the game's radar display a vital way of locating concealed threats; shooting enemies while radar is active can earn additional points.

Unlike later shooters built around a stock of lives, Phantom II uses timed play that can be extended through scoring. When the plane is shot down, its pilot ejects and parachutes to safety before a replacement jet enters. The combination of forward scrolling, concealed enemies, and a radar mechanic makes it an interesting transitional design between the earliest fixed shooters and the aerial action games that followed.

games.title: Phelios
games.description:
Namco's Phelios, copyrighted 1988 and released in Japanese arcades in 1989, turns Greek mythology into a theatrical vertically scrolling shooter. Players guide Apollo on the winged horse Pegasus through seven dangerous regions to rescue Artemis from Typhon. Rather than piloting a conventional spacecraft, Apollo attacks with a magical sword that launches small projectiles when tapped or a much stronger blast when the fire button is held and released.

Charging attacks while weaving around harpies, monsters, and elaborate bosses is the game's defining rhythm. Weapon enhancements add more options, while dramatic between-stage artwork advances the mythological rescue story. The game runs on Namco System 2 hardware, helping it deliver richly layered backgrounds, large enemies, and striking visual effects. Its mixture of fantasy imagery and charge-shot combat distinguishes it from the military and science-fiction shooters that dominated the period, and a later Mega Drive port brought it to home audiences.

games.title: Phoenix
games.description:
Phoenix (1980), developed by Amstar and widely distributed by Centuri and other licensees, is one of the most recognizable fixed-screen shooters of the period. Players move a laser-armed ship left and right beneath waves of alien birds, shooting at diving attackers while conserving a temporary protective shield. The five-stage cycle begins with small bird formations, escalates to large phoenixes whose damaged wings can regenerate, and culminates in a battle against a fortified alien mothership.

The climax is unusually elaborate for its time: players must shoot through the mothership's moving defenses and outer hull to strike the alien commander inside. The shield can save the ship from collision or enemy fire, but its short duration and recharge delay demand careful timing. Later waves loop with growing difficulty, making consistent positioning as important as reflexes.

Phoenix helped establish multi-stage progression and memorable boss encounters in early arcade shooters, standing apart from games built entirely around identical repeating formations. Its booming effects and distinctive musical cues were part of its appeal. Licensed conversions, notably Atari's 2600 version, helped preserve its reputation, while various alternate boards and unauthorized adaptations became part of its arcade history.

games.title: Photo Y2K

variants.title: Real and Fake / Photo Y2K (ver. 102, Japan Board)

games.description: IGS's Photo Y2K (1999) is a timed spot-the-difference puzzle game. Two near-identical pictures appear side by side, and players must identify five altered details before the clock expires. Incorrect guesses are punished with lost chances, so quick visual comparison matters more than random clicking. Its straightforward picture-based challenges make it a markedly different experience from the tile-matching and falling-block games common in late-1990s arcades. Some sets are known under the alternative title Real and Fake.

games.title: Phozon
games.description:
Phozon is Namco's unusual 1983 abstract puzzle-action game about assembling molecules rather than fighting enemies. Players steer a small particle called the Chemic around a playfield, collecting moving colored Moleks and attaching them in the specific arrangement shown in a central target diagram. Completing the required shape advances the round, but an incorrect attachment can make the formation unwieldy and force risky maneuvering.

A roaming enemy called the Atomic pursues the Chemic, turning what might otherwise be a tranquil geometric puzzle into a game of evasive movement and rapid spatial planning. Rotating and arranging the growing structure without being caught requires the player to think several moves ahead. Phozon is especially memorable for its scientific imagery, oddball character designs, and bold departure from Namco's better-known maze chases and shooters.

games.title: Phraze Craze
games.description: Merit's Phraze Craze (1986) is a coin-operated word-guessing game in the style of a televised phrase-and-letter contest. A hidden saying or phrase is presented under a topic heading, and players select letters in an attempt to complete it. A spinning wheel determines the points available for correct letters, while wrong guesses or unlucky 'ZAP' and 'ZILCH' results end a turn. The game offers a cerebral, button-driven alternative to reflex-heavy arcade entertainment and was also sold in cabinets configured for multiple players.

games.title: Phraze Craze (Sex Kit)
games.description: Phraze Craze (Sex Kit) is Merit's adult-topic conversion of the 1986 word-guessing arcade game. It retains the original contest format: players spin for point values and reveal letters to solve concealed phrases, with failed guesses and unfavorable wheel outcomes costing turns. The distinguishing feature is its sex-themed phrase material, distributed as a kit rather than a completely new game. The adult question categories could be controlled through operator settings, reflecting the bar and amusement-venue market for which Merit's trivia machines were designed.

games.title: Pickin'
games.description: Pickin' is a 1983 single-screen puzzle game by French developer Valadon Automation. Players maneuver colored blocks around a maze and attempt to place each one into its matching colored corral. Moving the pieces is complicated by hostile hazards called the Disrupter and the Killer, so a successful solution depends on planning safe routes as well as arranging the blocks correctly. Its focus on sorting and positioning objects, rather than shooting or collecting dots, gives this early arcade puzzler a distinctive identity.

games.title: Pig Newton
games.description: Pig Newton is an unusual 1983 Sega arcade platform game based on Malcolm Hancock's cartoon pig character. The action takes place around an apple tree, where wolves threaten to chop it down. Players control the pig as he climbs and moves through the tree, dropping apples onto the wolves below to drive them away. The whimsical premise turns a simple platform setting into a game of timing attacks against threats beneath the hero. It was developed for Sega's G80 hardware and never became a widely distributed arcade success, making surviving versions especially interesting to collectors of obscure Sega games.

games.title: Pigout
games.description:
Leland's Pigout: Dine Like a Swine (1990) is a comic maze-platform game supporting up to three players at once. The players guide differently colored pigs around elaborate multi-level playfields, eating food and drinking beverages while avoiding a butcher and hungry wolves. Cans and other thrown objects can stun pursuing enemies, providing an emergency escape when the animals are cornered.

Players also search for jars of jam needed to advance, while each new stage rearranges the action in a different setting, from sewers and construction sites to bookstores and factories. Its combination of Pac-Man-style collection, ladders, throwable defenses, and simultaneous three-player chaos makes Pigout a lively late entry in the arcade maze genre.

games.title: Pigskin 621AD
games.description:
Pigskin 621AD is a 1990 Midway sports game that turns American football into a rough-and-tumble medieval contest. Teams of five compete to carry a ball across the opposing goal line, but the field is littered with logs, pits, bushes, and other hazards that can interfere with a drive. Players can punch and tackle opponents as well as pass the ball, and the result feels closer to a brawler crossed with a sports game than to a conventional football simulation.

The odd historical setting, deliberately exaggerated physical contact, and accessible competitive play gave Pigskin its cult following. A player controls the active ball carrier or defender while teammates provide support, and learning to exploit the field's obstacles is as useful as executing clean passes. Its irreverent style makes it a distinctive footnote in Midway's tradition of arcade sports games that prize spectacle over realism.

games.title: Pinbo
games.description: Jaleco's Pinbo (1984) adapts pinball to a video screen with flippers, bumpers, and scoring targets, while adding hazards that would be impossible on a conventional table. Enemies can move across the playfield and interfere with the ball, so keeping a rally alive requires more than simply watching its trajectory. Hitting the appropriate targets to spell 'JALECO' earns access to a bonus round. The result is an early example of digital pinball using arcade-style characters and special objectives to go beyond the mechanics of a mechanical table.

games.title: Ping Pong
games.description:
Konami's Ping Pong (1985) is a streamlined table-tennis game built around timing and choosing the right stroke. The action is viewed from an angled perspective, with the competitors represented mainly by their hands and paddles. Bats automatically track the moving ball, leaving players to judge when to use topspin, backspin, or a powerful smash. Matches use table-tennis-style scoring, and computer opponents become more demanding as players progress.

Its straightforward design hides subtle choices about rally length, spin, and shot placement. A particularly charming touch is the presence of the penguin from Konami's Antarctic Adventure, later known as Pentarou, as a spectator and in the introduction. Alongside its arcade success, Ping Pong became familiar to home-computer and console players through Konami's conversions.

games.title: Pink Sweets: Ibara Sorekara

variants.title: Pink Sweets: Ibara Sorekara (2006/04/06 MASTER VER....)
Pink Sweets: Ibara Sorekara (2006/04/06 MASTER VER...)
Pink Sweets: Ibara Sorekara (2006/04/06 MASTER VER.)
Pink Sweets: Suicide Club (2017/10/31 SUICIDECLUB VER., bootleg)
Pink Sweets: Ibara Sorekara (2006/xx/xx MASTER VER.)

games.description:
Pink Sweets: Ibara Sorekara is Cave's 2006 follow-up to Ibara, transforming its rose-themed enemies and characters into a deliberately eccentric, pastel-colored bullet-hell shooter. The bosses from the earlier game become playable pilots, battling waves of food-named enemies and enormous mechanical opponents. Its most distinctive combat feature is a combined shot-and-barrier system, which makes defensive timing as important as shooting accurately.

Although its colors and character voices create a whimsical atmosphere, Pink Sweets is notorious among shooting-game enthusiasts for its demanding difficulty. Early arcade revisions also contained a widely discussed extra-life exploit: after building a sufficiently large reserve, the life counter could effectively stop falling below a certain point. The contrast between cute presentation, intricate scoring and survival mechanics, and punishing play makes it a singular entry in Cave's catalogue. It later appeared on Xbox 360 alongside Muchi Muchi Pork!.

games.title: Pipe Dream
games.description:
Pipe Dream is Video System's 1990 arcade adaptation of the pipe-laying puzzle game also known as Pipe Mania. Players receive a succession of randomly ordered pipe segments and must fit them onto a square grid before a stream of green liquid, known as 'flooz', reaches the unfinished route. Straight sections, elbows, and crossovers must be used in their supplied orientation, forcing players to plan around awkward pieces rather than simply rotate a perfect solution.

The goal is to carry the flooz through at least the required length of connected pipe, with extra points for longer, more efficient networks. A small delay before the liquid begins moving offers preparation time, but once it starts, every mistake becomes urgent. Its blend of construction, spatial reasoning, and real-time pressure made the original computer game a success and translated effectively to the coin-operated puzzle market.

games.title: Pipeline
games.description: Pipeline is a 1990 single-player sliding-style puzzle arcade game by South Korea's Daehyun Electronics. It uses a horizontal display and joystick-driven controls with action buttons, rather than the overhead action-adventure format of the unrelated 1988 BBC Micro game with the same name. The preserved arcade hardware combines Z80 processors with an M68705 controller and a Yamaha YM2203 sound chip. Contemporary documentation identifies its puzzle category, but not enough verified step-by-step rules survive to justify a more specific account of the tile mechanics.

games.title: Pipi & Bibis / Whoopee!!
games.description:
Pipi & Bibis, also known in Japan as Whoopee!!, is Toaplan's cheeky 1992 single-screen platform game about two saboteurs infiltrating buildings. One or two players climb ladders and cross platforms, planting timed charges on the computer terminals scattered around each floor. Once the final bomb is in place, the entire stage enters a frantic escape sequence: the heroes must reach the exit before the building erupts.

Scientists and security agents patrol the corridors, and touching them costs a life. A handheld stun weapon briefly knocks enemies down, buying time to finish the job or cross a dangerous passage. Between stages, the adult-themed game reveals parts of pin-up illustrations, a conspicuous contrast with its colorful platform action. The sequence of placing explosives and then racing for safety gives Pipi & Bibis a memorable tempo, quite different from Toaplan's better-known scrolling shooters.

games.title: The Pirates of Dark Water

variants.title: The Pirates of Dark Water (SNES bootleg)

games.description: The Pirates of Dark Water is an unauthorized arcade adaptation of the Super Nintendo game based on the animated fantasy television series. Produced by Conny Co. in the mid-1990s, it brings the console title's side-scrolling action to bootleg coin-operated hardware rather than presenting a separately designed arcade release. Players fight through fantasy locations populated by enemies from the source adventure. Its interest lies primarily in the conversion itself, an example of a console game repackaged for arcade operation without an official license.

games.title: Pirates
games.description:
Pirates is a 1994 arcade shooting game by Spanish developer NIX, built around a pirate treasure hunt rather than a conventional space or military setting. Two seafarers are sent to recover three pieces of a map from islands including Shetland, La Isabela, and Papeete before sailing to the location of the hidden treasure. From a third-person shooting viewpoint, players fire at rival pirates and scenery, throw bombs, and slide to evade incoming attacks.

Stages end when the enemy meter is emptied or a boss is defeated, while repeated hits on a passing witch or other creatures can yield bonuses. The game's hardware and program design were closely derived from TAD's Blood Bros., making Pirates a fascinating example of a little-known European company adapting a successful gallery-shooter formula to a new theme.

games.title: Pirate Treasure
games.description: Pirate Treasure (1982) by Tong Electronic is an overhead maze-and-collection game in which a red pirate ship cruises among islands in search of points and treasure. Larger islands yield larger rewards when visited, but a hostile black pirate vessel patrols the playfield and can create dangerous active volcanoes on already raided islands. Colliding with the rival ship or a volcano destroys the player's boat. A roaming treasure chest adds an extra objective, especially when the rival ship moves it to another island. The simple four-direction movement conceals a game of route selection and risk management.

games.title: Pisces
games.description: Pisces is an early-1980s fixed-screen shooter by Subelectro, with licensed and bootleg versions also circulated under names such as Omni. Players control a spacecraft at the bottom of the screen and shoot down formations of aliens sweeping in from the sides. Each wave introduces new enemy patterns, and completing a stage sends the ship onward to the next encounter. Its straightforward combination of lateral movement, rapid fire, and changing attack formations places it firmly in the post-Galaxian school of arcade space combat.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Pistol Daimyo no Bouken
games.description:
Namco's Pistol Daimyo no Bouken (1990) is a wildly eccentric horizontally scrolling shooter starring a diminutive feudal lord with a cannon mounted on his head and fans strapped to his feet. Originally introduced as an enemy in Bravoman (Beraboh Man), Pistol Daimyo becomes the hero of his own adventure through surreal Japanese landscapes packed with folklore-inspired creatures and bizarre bosses.

Players steer the airborne character while the scenery scrolls relentlessly past. Tapping fire shoots a small cannonball, but holding and releasing the button charges a much stronger projectile, making good timing crucial against resilient enemies. Breaking special vases reveals collectible Hanafuda cards that can lead to bonus opportunities. The game's absurd humor, theatrical enemies, and unusual choice of protagonist make it one of Namco's most distinctive Japan-only arcade shooters.

games.title: Pitapat Puzzle
games.description:
Pitapat Puzzle is a 1997 Korean arcade puzzle game from F2 System that emphasizes hands-on manipulation of colored marbles. Players move a small carrier around the playfield, picking up and dropping marbles to connect groups of three or more of the same color. Clearing a group also breaks adjacent boxes, which can release additional marbles and set off a chain reaction.

A separate button feeds more pieces into the field, adding a tactical choice between extending the current arrangement and triggering a new opportunity. Clearing the entire board can yield a substantial bonus under the right conditions. Its compact controls, destructible obstacles, and chain-building mechanics distinguish it from the straightforward falling-pair design of many contemporary arcade puzzle games.

games.title: Pit Boss
games.description:
Merit Industries' The Pit Boss (1983) was an early example of the multi-game bar-top casino machine. Rather than having a joystick-driven playfield, it offers several compact betting games selected from the same cabinet: Joker Poker, blackjack, Off to the Races horse betting, and a fourth option that varies by program revision, either a craps-like dice game or Super Slots. Players manage wagers and make selections through dedicated buttons, with each game delivering a different rhythm of decisions and chance.

Its countertop and cocktail configurations suited bars and lounges, where a small collection of familiar casino games could attract repeated short sessions. Numerous surviving program sets and related titles such as Player's Choice and Dealer's Choice show how Merit adapted the same general hardware and menu concept over time.

games.title: Pitfall II
games.description:
Sega's Pitfall II (1985) brings Activision's jungle-exploration hero Pitfall Harry to the arcade in a considerably reworked version of the familiar adventure. Harry explores connected platforms, climbs ladders, swings and jumps across hazards, and searches for valuable objects while avoiding dangerous animals and other obstacles. The arcade adaptation introduces its own stage structure, enemies, and visual design rather than merely reproducing the Atari home game.

Its appeal is the combination of precise platform movement and exploration: players have to learn which routes are safe while retrieving items and progressing through the jungle environment. The title is historically notable as Sega's coin-operated treatment of a character created by David Crane at Activision, an unusual crossover between the console and arcade worlds of the mid-1980s.

games.title: Pit Fighter
games.description:
Atari Games' Pit-Fighter (1990) is a brutal underground fighting game remembered for its early use of digitized actors. Players select one of three combatants, wrestler Buzz, kickboxer Ty, or martial artist Kato, and enter an illegal fight circuit against increasingly formidable opponents. Up to three people can cooperate on the same screen, using punches, kicks, powerful special attacks, and objects found around the arena to survive each match.

The fighters occupy a spacious scrolling stage rather than the fixed plane of later one-on-one fighting games. Crowds jostle around the participants, weapons can be grabbed, and periodic Grudge Matches turn cooperative partners against one another. The ability to zoom the camera as the characters move was especially striking in 1990.

Pit-Fighter's animation and rough presentation have aged differently from its technological ambition, but its photographed characters, theatrical violence, and three-player cooperative combat were influential steps toward the digitized spectacle that would later become synonymous with Mortal Kombat. It remains an unmistakable artifact of the early arcade fighting-game boom.

games.title: Pit & Run
games.description:
Taito's Pit & Run (1984) is an overhead racing game with a strong emphasis on fuel management. Players steer a small car against nine computer opponents along compact courses, keeping enough speed to finish each trial while watching a steadily falling fuel gauge. Driving into a GVS service station replenishes the tank, and slippery sections of the track demand careful steering.

Later trials introduce a turbo upgrade that increases performance but consumes fuel much more quickly, forcing a trade-off between speed and the need for another pit stop. Its mixture of arcade racing, route choice, and refueling strategy gives Pit & Run a character distinct from pure time-trial games of the period.

games.title: Pachinko Gindama Shoubu
games.description: Pachinko Gindama Shoubu is a 1998 Japanese video-pachinko game from Nakanihon and Dynax. Instead of using a real pachinko playfield, it recreates the ball-launching amusement on a CRT screen. A paddle-style control adjusts the action, with two additional buttons, bringing the feel of a pachinko parlor to a conventional arcade video cabinet. The title, roughly Silver Ball Match, refers to the small metal balls central to pachinko and reflects the overlap between Japanese medal amusement and traditional video games.

games.title: Pachinko Gindama Shoubu DX
games.description: Pachinko Gindama Shoubu DX is the deluxe companion to Nakanihon and Dynax's 1998 video-pachinko game, released in Japan in April of that year, one month after the regular edition. It translates pachinko's ball-launching and prize-chance format into a video cabinet rather than a physical field of pins. This DX edition uses a paddle controller with a single action button, a slightly different input arrangement from the original game's two buttons.

games.title: Poker Ladies
games.description:
Poker Ladies is a 1989 adult-oriented arcade video-poker game released by Mitchell, with an American edition licensed to Leprechaun. Players form paying poker hands to build a point total for each of nine women. Reaching the required threshold unlocks a suggestive character interaction sequence, after which the game advances through its cast. The hold-card buttons, Deal control and Cancel control make poker selection and progression the central activities rather than reflex action.

The artwork has a notable pedigree: Capcom artist Akira Yasuda, later famous for his Street Fighter II character designs, originally created much of it for Mahjong Gakuen. Capcom adapted that material from mahjong into poker for wider international distribution under the Mitchell name. The Leprechaun edition changes the number of hands available, and censored and uncensored bootlegs also survive. This unusual mix of recycled artwork, adult bonus scenes and straightforward card play makes Poker Ladies a distinctive late-1980s curiosity.

games.title: PK Scramble
games.description: PK Scramble is a 1993 Japanese arcade football game by Cosmo Electronics devoted entirely to the penalty shootout. Players select a team and attempt to score from the spot by choosing a shooting direction and timing the kick, then respond to opposing attempts by defending the goal. By stripping away normal midfield play, the game concentrates on anticipation and reading an opponent rather than passing or tactical positioning. It is a small but distinctive variation on the era's more expansive arcade soccer simulations.

games.title: Pocket Gal Deluxe
games.description:
Data East's Pocket Gal Deluxe, copyrighted 1992 and released in Japan in 1993, is a colorful adult-themed billiards game. Players line up shots on a virtual pool table, using English and occasional jump shots to pocket balls, earn points, and advance through four stages associated with different illustrated women. Trick-shot opportunities interrupt the normal sequence of frames, and two-player matches are decided over multiple games.

Compared with the original Pocket Gal, the Deluxe edition refreshes the audiovisual presentation while retaining the mixture of recognizable cue-sport mechanics and pin-up rewards. Its jazzy soundtrack and arcade-focused scoring make it an accessible, if distinctly period-specific, entry in Data East's billiards series.

games.title: Penguin-Kun Wars
games.description:
Penguin-Kun Wars (1985) is UPL's delightfully odd take on a sporting contest called 'Dojiball'. Two animal competitors stand at opposite ends of a rectangular table, each starting with five balls. Players roll balls toward their opponent in an attempt to leave all ten on the other side, while catching and returning balls that come back. A round can also end on time, in which case the side with fewer balls wins.

The penguin hero faces a succession of animal rivals, including a bear, panda, koala, and beaver, each giving the simple contest a fresh personality. Positioning, timing, and controlling the flow of multiple balls are more important than complicated controls. Its easy-to-understand rules made it particularly well suited to quick arcade challenges, and the concept later received home conversions and revised versions.

games.title: PlayBall!
games.description:
PlayBall! is a rare 1983 Williams arcade prototype that turns baseball imagery into an inventive multi-ball paddle game. Players control a round, glove-wearing character who moves left and right along the bottom of a crowded stadium and can wrap around from one side of the screen to the other. Balls of several sports fall from the stands; the hero must bounce them upward repeatedly until they are caught and removed, while dangerous bowling balls must be avoided. Collecting bases and falling snacks earns additional points.

Later rounds introduce a baseball bat for smashing bowling balls, and a limited time-out ability temporarily freezes the action. Its lively speech, oddball humor, and deceptively hectic juggling of multiple balls separate it from ordinary Breakout clones. The game never received a commercial release, and programmer Larry DeMar has said that only a single original machine existed.

games.title: PlayChoice-10 BIOS
games.description:
Nintendo's PlayChoice-10, introduced in 1986, was a coin-operated showcase for Nintendo Entertainment System games. One machine could hold up to ten interchangeable game boards, with selections ranging from Super Mario Bros. and The Legend of Zelda to many other NES favorites. Unlike a normal arcade game that ends when the player loses all lives, PlayChoice-10 sold a limited amount of play time. A player could browse the installed titles, read instructions, switch games, and add more coins to extend the session.

The familiar two-monitor cabinet placed menus, help text, and time information on one screen while the second displayed gameplay, although single-monitor versions also existed. Its shared BIOS managed game selection, credit timing, and the distinctive dual-screen presentation. The PlayChoice-10 is important less for exclusive game design than for showing how Nintendo repackaged its successful home-console library for arcades, years before multi-game systems became commonplace.

games.title: Power Instinct Legends
games.description:
Power Instinct Legends, released in Japan as Gouketsuji Gaiden: Saikyou Densetsu and internationally as Gogetsuji Legends, is Atlus and Cave's 1995 follow-up to Power Instinct 2. It expands the series' eccentric, family-feud fighting roster into paired battles: players select two characters for a team, but unlike later tag-team fighters, they do not freely switch characters in the middle of a bout. The starting roster features a mixture of returning relatives, transformed personalities, and new challengers.

The series' peculiar humor, exaggerated facial expressions, double jumps, rushing attacks, and character transformations remain central to its identity. It adds tactical variety through team composition and its two-character match structure, while preserving the fast, chaotic feel of earlier Power Instinct games. Its unusual cast and lively presentation make it one of the more distinctive alternatives to the major mid-1990s fighting franchises.

games.title: Pleiads
games.description:
Tehkan's Pleiads (1981), distributed in North America by Centuri, expands the early space-shooter formula into a four-part cycle of distinct encounters. Players defend an Earth city from transforming Martian invaders, battle new formations of flying enemies, and eventually navigate a hazardous landing sequence. The ship moves horizontally along the bottom of the screen and can fire upward, while a special warp action provides an unpredictable escape from danger.

The successive stages feature different enemy behaviors rather than simply increasing the speed of the same pattern. Walking invaders build barriers across the city, birdlike ships dive from above, and other foes require carefully aimed hits. This variety gives Pleiads a close relationship to the influential Phoenix without simply copying its five-wave structure.

Originally developed before Tehkan became Tecmo, Pleiads stands among the company's earliest notable arcade releases. Its name appears as 'Pleiads' in the game but was often expanded to 'Pleiades' on North American cabinet artwork, a small historical curiosity that survives in collector documentation.

games.title: Play Girls
games.description: Play Girls is a 1992 adult-themed block-breaking arcade game by Hot-B. Players guide a horizontal paddle at the bottom of a playfield, bouncing a ball into clusters of bricks and chests to clear each stage. As blocks disappear, illustrations of women become visible behind the action, providing the game's pin-up reward structure. Its rules draw directly on the familiar Arkanoid style, with the emphasis on keeping the ball in play and controlling rebounds. The title also spawned unauthorized and retitled hardware adaptations, including LA Girl, that changed the background art while keeping the basic stage layouts.

games.title: Play Girls 2
games.description: Play Girls 2 is a 1993 adult-themed arcade shooter by Hot-B, and a change of genre from the original Play Girls block-breaker. Instead of directing a paddle, players steer a character with an eight-way joystick and use two buttons to attack through stages filled with enemies and hazards. The game retains the series' suggestive artwork, but places more emphasis on direct action and dodging than on clearing bricks. Running on Taito L-System-derived hardware, it survives in Japanese, European, and bootleg sets that document the title's varied distribution.

games.title: Plotting
games.description:
Taito's Plotting (1989), known as Flipull in Japan, is an inventive action puzzle game built around ricocheting symbol-marked blocks. Players face a formation of tiles and fire a single tile toward the stack. Matching symbols disappear, but when the shot reaches a different symbol, that unmatched tile rebounds to become the next projectile. Clearing the field therefore depends on choosing the right target for the piece currently in hand.

As the stack shrinks, blocked angles and awkward symbols can leave the player with no productive shot, rewarding the ability to plan several exchanges ahead. Its unusual 'shoot one, receive another' mechanic distinguishes Plotting from conventional falling-block puzzle games. The idea was accessible enough to inspire numerous home-computer and console adaptations, including releases on the Famicom and Game Boy.

games.title: Plasma Sword
games.description:
Plasma Sword: Nightmare of Bilstein is Capcom's 1998 science-fiction fighting game and the sequel to Star Gladiator. Characters armed with futuristic melee weapons battle in three-dimensional arenas, with sidesteps and dashes making positioning as important as timing an attack. The returning hero Hayato Kanzaki confronts the threat of Bilstein's apparent return, while a larger cast adds new combat styles and rivalries.

The sequel replaces the original Plasma Combo system with a super-move gauge that can store multiple levels of energy for powerful Plasma Strikes. Each fighter also has a distinctive Plasma Field technique that temporarily catches an opponent in a special attack with character-dependent effects. These additions give matches a spectacular flavor without abandoning the weapon clashes and evasive movement of the original. Developed for Capcom's PlayStation-derived ZN-2 arcade board and later ported to Dreamcast, Plasma Sword is a colorful representative of the late-1990s 3D fighting boom.

games.title: Plump Pop
games.description:
Plump Pop is Taito's 1987 reinterpretation of the classic Circus trampoline game, recast with a family of cartoon animals. Players choose cats, dogs, or pigs and move two parents carrying a trampoline. Their child bounces skyward to burst balloons and hit enemies, then must be caught and launched again. A dial controls the parents' position, while a button can increase the strength of a bounce.

Its campaign alternates enemy-clearing stages with fruit-catching bonuses and boss encounters. Power-ups can increase the trampoline's width or strengthen attacks, but failing to catch a bouncing child costs a life. The mix of careful paddle positioning, split-second catching, and whimsical character animation makes Plump Pop a distinctive bridge between early trampoline games and later arcade action-puzzle designs.

games.title: Plus Alpha
games.description:
Plus Alpha is a 1989 Jaleco vertically scrolling shooter with a distinctly cheerful anime-inspired style. The heroines Selia and Rumy travel through seven fantasy countries, battling enemies over flower fields, oceans, snowfields, deserts, and other colorful landscapes. Players choose among three craft with differing characteristics and collect enhancements that alter the size and trajectory of their projectiles. Each stage ends with a large boss encounter.

Compared with the demanding military shooters of its day, Plus Alpha is remembered for its approachable difficulty, bright designs, and whimsical enemies reminiscent of Konami's TwinBee. Originally a Japanese arcade title, it has enjoyed a second life through modern retro reissues, introducing its inventive scenery and lighter tone to a broader audience.

games.title: Polygonet Commanders
games.description: Polygonet Commanders is a 1993 Konami first-person tank combat game and an early example of the company's polygonal arcade experiments. Players operate a tank through stark, flat-shaded 3D battlefields, steering with twin controls that represent its left and right treads. Each stage demands the destruction of a target number of enemy vehicles before time expires, with successful attacks adding time to the clock. The combination of independent-track steering, turret aiming, and sparse polygon graphics makes it a distinctive ancestor of later 3D vehicle shooters.

games.title: Croupier
games.description:
Croupier is a 1997 video roulette title from Italian arcade manufacturer Playmark. Rather than offering an action challenge, it presents the casino game's central decision: choosing roulette wagers before the wheel determines the outcome. The machine was built around a horizontal display and a joystick-and-button control layout, adapting a familiar table game to a coin-operated video cabinet.

The title is sometimes catalogued as Croupier (Playmark Roulette) to distinguish it from other arcade games with similar names. Its Motorola 68000-based hardware and OKI sample playback connect it technologically to Playmark's other mid-1990s amusement products, even though its subject matter is conventional casino roulette.

games.title: Pnickies
games.description:
Pnickies is Capcom's 1994 arcade falling-block puzzle game, built around brightly colored jelly pieces and carefully engineered chain reactions. Pairs of pieces descend into a well, but groups of ordinary matching colors do not vanish automatically. To remove a connected group, players must incorporate two star-marked pieces of the same color, making the positioning of those special blocks central to every move.

When a group disappears, the pieces above it fall and may create new combinations, so elaborate chains reward advance planning. The simple presentation conceals a more deliberate strategy than the immediate four-in-a-row clearing of many rival puzzle games. Pnickies is also notable as an unusual puzzle entry in Capcom's 1990s arcade line-up.

games.title: Paint & Puzzle
games.description: Paint & Puzzle is a 1993 puzzle-redemption game from Century Vending that uses a gun-style pointing device to interact with a sliding-tile picture puzzle. Rather than manipulating a joystick-controlled character, players select portions of an image and move them into the correct arrangement, working against the limits of a coin-operated session. Its unusual light-gun interface shows how amusement manufacturers adapted familiar tabletop and picture puzzles into accessible arcade attractions.

games.title: Pochi and Nyaa
games.description:
Pochi and Nyaa is Aiky's 2003 competitive puzzle game for the Neo Geo, created by developers associated with Compile and distributed by Taito. Colored cat-and-dog pieces fall in pairs into separate wells, where players can rotate and stack them. Unlike Puyo Puyo, adjacent pieces of one color do not vanish merely because enough have accumulated: the player chooses when to activate a group using a special trigger piece.

That freedom turns the game into a battle of careful construction and timing. Large connected arrangements can be prepared before a trigger causes a dramatic chain reaction, sending nuisance pieces to an opponent's field. Its charming animal cast and flexible combo system give it a personality of its own. Released near the end of the Neo Geo MVS's commercial life, Pochi and Nyaa is remembered as one of the platform's last original third-party arcade titles.

games.title: Pocket Racer
games.description:
Pocket Racer is Namco's 1996 Japan-only arcade racing game, a comic, super-deformed spin-off of Ridge Racer. Cars have exaggerated proportions and race around lively circuits with a lighter, toy-like atmosphere than the main series. The underlying challenge still involves choosing a line through corners, controlling speed, and outmaneuvering rival cars, but the bright presentation makes it an approachable contrast to Namco's more realistic racers.

Built on System 11 hardware closely related to the original PlayStation, Pocket Racer demonstrates how Namco reused its 3D driving technology for a smaller, characterful arcade concept. Its limited release and unusual place in the Ridge Racer family make it especially interesting to collectors.

games.title: Poitto!
games.description: Poitto! is a 1993 competitive puzzle game developed by Metro and published by Able. Players arrange falling bottles of different colors, attempting to connect at least three of the same color horizontally, vertically, or diagonally to make them vanish. Creating larger groups and consecutive clears helps build points and increase the pressure in a head-to-head match. Its colorful bottles and accessible matching rules place it among the many Japanese arcade puzzlers developed in the wake of the falling-block boom.

games.title: Poizone
games.description:
Poizone is Eterna's 1991 ecological maze-action game and an inventive variation on Sega's Pengo. Players guide a penguin named Zozo through 50 contaminated stages, using movable blocks to clear dangerous material while evading monsters. The objective is to destroy at least 90 percent of each stage's toxic blocks before the timer expires, rather than simply eliminating the enemies.

Eight kinds of toxic block demand different treatment: some must be struck from a particular direction, while others must be pushed away. Mishandling one can cost a life, so recognizing each block's behavior matters as much as dexterity. Power pills help with dangerous encounters, and diamonds offer scoring bonuses. This shift from combat to careful decontamination gives Poizone a distinctive puzzle identity despite its familiar maze mechanics.

games.title: Pokio
games.description: Pokio is a 1994 Dutch electronic gambling game distributed on BFM/ELAM game-card hardware. It uses a single-player, six-button control panel and a horizontal video display, with surviving sets identified by their Dutch game-card numbers. The program belongs to the European video-slot and card-gambling machine market rather than the joystick-based arcade industry. The exact poker or slot rules have not been sufficiently documented to distinguish it more specifically from related BFM/ELAM gambling titles.

games.title: Poker Dice
games.description:
Poker Dice is an unusual 1991 coin-operated dice game from Strata and Incredible Technologies. It replaces the cards of ordinary poker with dice-based poker combinations, presenting a gambling-style game on a vertically oriented screen operated entirely through six buttons. Its hardware belongs to Incredible Technologies' 8-bit arcade family, which also powered sports and novelty releases such as Golden Tee Golf and Slick Shot.

The game was distinctive enough to attract notice in contemporary trade reporting. A 1991 arcade-industry review praised its graphics and described it as compelling but difficult for beginners to understand. That reaction captures its unusual place in the era's coin-op market: a specialized dice-and-poker concept offered alongside the far more common sports, fighting, and action machines.

games.title: Polaris
games.description:
Polaris is a 1980 submarine-combat shooter developed by Taito, reversing the usual perspective of an aerial space invaders game. Players maneuver a submarine below the waterline, launching torpedoes and firing at enemy submarines, boats, aircraft, and underwater obstacles. Attacks arrive from above and below, while depth charges and mines make every safe route temporary.

The changing waves require players to manage both horizontal positioning and depth, avoiding the seabed while aiming shots through a busy ocean. Its military theme and layered air-and-sea threats give the game a different rhythm from contemporary alien shooters. Polaris is an interesting early example of Taito's attempts to broaden the fixed-screen shooter beyond spaceships and extraterrestrial enemies.

games.title: Pole Position
games.description:
Namco's Pole Position (1982), distributed in North America by Atari, is a landmark in arcade racing. Players take the wheel of a Formula One-style car at Fuji Speedway and must first complete a qualifying lap quickly enough to earn a place on the starting grid. Successful qualifiers then enter a timed race, overtaking opponents, avoiding roadside hazards, and trying to finish as high as possible before the clock runs out. A steering wheel, accelerator pedal, and gear selector help create the sensation of driving a real racing machine.

Its convincing behind-the-car viewpoint, fast-scaling roadside scenery, and demanding cornering gave the game a sense of speed that was revolutionary in 1982. Racing is not only about holding the accelerator: careless contact with another car or a trackside object can destroy the vehicle and waste valuable seconds. Qualifying performance matters because a better grid position improves the player's prospects in the race.

Pole Position was an enormous commercial success and helped establish the template for modern arcade driving games, including its use of a preparatory qualifying session and a recognizable real-world circuit. Its appeal was heightened by dedicated sit-down cabinets and promotional advertising along the racetrack. The game became one of the most influential racing titles of the decade and spawned a direct sequel the following year.

games.title: Pole Position II
games.description:
Pole Position II (1983) builds on Namco's enormously successful Formula One arcade racer without abandoning its approachable structure. Players first qualify in a time trial, then compete against traffic and the clock in a race whose success depends on clean lines, timely overtakes, and avoiding spectacular crashes. The major addition is a choice of four circuits instead of one: Fuji, Suzuka, Seaside, and the simpler Test course.

Each layout brings different corners and surroundings, creating new challenges for players who mastered the original Fuji Speedway. The familiar steering wheel, accelerator, and two-speed gear selector return, as do the vivid scaling graphics and fast behind-the-car perspective. A commercially successful sequel in its own right, Pole Position II extended the life of the original arcade hardware through conversion kits and was later included with the Atari 7800 home console.

games.title: Police Trainer
games.description:
Police Trainer is a 1996 light-gun arcade game from P&P Marketing that turns marksmanship drills into a sequence of competitive tests. Rather than following a continuous story, players undertake separate exercises involving timed targets, accuracy, reaction speed, and the need to distinguish dangerous objects from innocuous ones. Passing each exam requires meeting its score or completion conditions, with limited mistakes allowed before the attempt is lost.

The arcade's gun controls make the game immediately accessible, but achieving reliable high scores demands quick target recognition and disciplined shooting. Its modular challenge structure made it especially suitable for repeat competition and for comparing scores with another player. Police Trainer helped establish a recognizably arcade-style approach to firearms training simulations and eventually received a sequel.

games.title: Pollux
games.description:
Pollux is a 1991 vertically scrolling space shooter by Korean developer Dooyong, published by Atlus in parts of Asia. Players pilot a fighter against enemy spacecraft, fixed gun emplacements, and large bosses while advancing toward a hostile computer controlling a future space installation. It follows the established power-up-heavy shooter style, with collectibles that increase firepower, speed, or provide limited-use bombs.

Several weapons behave very differently, including straight laser bursts, wide-spreading shots, rearward fire, and homing missiles. Choosing the right enhancement for upcoming enemies is an important part of survival, especially as the screen fills with threats. Two-player cooperative play and the abundance of weapon icons give Pollux a familiar but distinctive place among the early-1990s Korean scrolling shooters.

games.title: Poly-Net Warriors
games.description:
Poly-Net Warriors is a Japan-only Konami arcade combat game from 1993 and one of the company's early experiments with polygonal 3D. From a first-person viewpoint, players control brightly colored robots in enclosed arenas, launching bouncing energy balls at opponents while dodging their return fire. Matches are timed, and defeating rival robots requires both accurate shooting and movement through the arena.

The game supports battles against themed computer-controlled teams as well as linked multiplayer competition. Its playful robot designs contrast with the austere geometry of the environments, producing a look unlike Konami's familiar sprite-based arcade hits. Poly-Net Warriors is notable less as a conventional scrolling shooter than as a curious early step toward 3D arena action.

games.title: Poly-Play
games.description:
Poly-Play is an extraordinary piece of arcade history: a 1985 multi-game cabinet produced by VEB Polytechnik in Karl-Marx-Stadt, East Germany. Built within the German Democratic Republic's state-run electronics industry, it offered a selection of compact games rather than one continuous adventure. Titles include Hase und Wolf, a Pac-Man-like chase, Hirschjagd, a deer-hunting action game, and other diversions involving racing, shooting, and simple puzzles.

Its games use direct, easy-to-understand controls and modest graphics suited to the hardware available in the Eastern Bloc. The cabinet is significant because commercial arcade machines from East Germany were exceptionally rare, and Poly-Play is widely regarded as the country's only domestically developed arcade video-game platform of its kind. Roughly two thousand units have been reported as manufactured, making surviving machines important artifacts of gaming behind the Iron Curtain.

games.title: Poly-Play
games.description:
Poly-Play (ZRE-PP) is a later, 1989-associated version of the East German Poly-Play multi-game arcade system. Like the original 1985 cabinet, it offers a menu of small action and puzzle diversions, including the maze chase Hase und Wolf, the shooting game Hirschjagd, and other simple contests involving driving, memory, or target shooting. The focus is on short, straightforward games that can be selected from a common machine.

This separate AdvanceMAME entry documents the later ZRE-PP software and hardware lineage, including a known Czech-language set, rather than a newly invented game franchise. Together with the earlier version, it preserves a rare example of coin-operated video-game design within the former German Democratic Republic.

games.title: Tobe! Polystars
games.description:
Tobe! Polystars is Konami's colorful 1997 scrolling shooter and the first released game for the company's unusual M2 arcade hardware. Players control the police officers Poly and Stan on a campaign to liberate planet Polygon from an invading organization. The action mixes recognizable TwinBee and Parodius influences with polygon-based characters, playful scenery, and boss battles at the end of each of seven stages.

Different control-style selections let players tailor their approach before starting, while weapon and special-attack choices bring variety to the shooting. The visual blend of 3D geometry and bright cartoon designs makes it stand out from both traditional sprite shooters and the more realistic 3D games of its time. Never officially ported to home consoles, Polystars has become a sought-after curiosity for fans of Konami and obscure arcade hardware.

games.title: Mahjong Pon Chin Kan
games.description: Mahjong Pon Chin Kan is a 1991 Japanese mahjong game developed by Visco. Players compete through conventional mahjong hands, with the game's adult-themed presentation supplemented by mahjong-related quiz questions that can award bonus items. The combination of tile play and quiz rewards sets it apart slightly from simpler single-purpose mahjong cabinets, while keeping it firmly within the Japanese arcade mahjong tradition.

games.title: Ponpoko
games.description:
Ponpoko is a 1982 single-screen platform game by Sigma Enterprises starring a tanuki, the raccoon dog of Japanese folklore. Players climb ladders, jump between ledges, and collect all the food scattered around each level before the hunger meter runs out. Moving caterpillar-like creatures and dangerous snakes patrol the maze, while hidden hazards and deep drops make careless shortcuts dangerous.

Mystery pots add a gamble to the collection route: some contain helpful bonuses, but others release a snake directly into the player's path. Later stages rearrange the platforms and introduce more hazards, steadily increasing the importance of memorizing safe routes. Ponpoko's appealing animal protagonist and combination of climbing, gathering, and precise jumps place it among the early character-driven platform games that followed Donkey Kong.

games.title: Pontoon
games.description:
Sega's Pontoon is a 1989 arcade adaptation of the blackjack-family card game, released in Japan on Sega System 18 hardware. The aim is to build a hand close to twenty-one without exceeding it, making decisions around the cards dealt rather than shooting or platforming. Unlike many small gambling-game boards, this version runs on Sega's comparatively sophisticated 68000-based arcade system, with a Z80 sound processor and Yamaha audio hardware.
