The cabinet supports two players using eight-way joysticks and three buttons apiece. Its use of System 18 makes it a curious outlier in Sega's late-1980s arcade catalogue, and it should not be confused with Tehkan's unrelated 1985 coin-operated Pontoon machine.

games.title: Pontoon
games.description:
Pontoon is a 1985 blackjack-style gambling card game by Tehkan, the Japanese company later known as Tecmo. A single player uses a five-button control panel to wager on card hands and decide whether to draw additional cards or stand, aiming for a stronger total than the dealer without exceeding the game's limit. It is a dealer-versus-player card machine, not a puzzle or an action game.

The horizontal-screen hardware uses a Z80 processor and AY-3-8910 sound chip. Its original coin-operated design included a payout hopper, a detail that distinguishes it from point-only casino amusements and historically complicated its early emulation after winning hands.

games.title: Poolshark
games.description:
Atari's Poolshark (1977) is an early arcade interpretation of pocket billiards with a simple but unconventional control scheme. Rather than aiming a cue stick, players directly steer the cue ball with a joystick and try to sink as many of the fifteen other balls as possible within a thirty-second round. Each successful pot scores a point, and clearing the table earns a short bonus period. Pocketing the cue ball itself ends the round immediately.

The emphasis on rapid scoring instead of conventional pool rules makes Poolshark more of a fast arcade challenge than a careful simulation. One or two players can compete across successive timed turns, making it an interesting example of Atari's sports experiments before realistic digital billiards became practical.

games.title: Poosho Poosho
games.description:
Poosho Poosho is a 1999 Korean block-breaking game by F2 System, following the studio's Jumping Break. Players guide a character along the bottom of the screen, bouncing a magical ball upward to destroy barriers and other targets. Unlike a stationary paddle, the character can jump to intercept the ball at a higher position, adding an unusual layer of timing to familiar Breakout-style play.

Its cartoon story follows characters transformed into red and blue slime creatures who must overcome magical obstacles and rescue their companions from a dragon. The combination of platform-like movement, bouncing-ball control, and bright fantasy graphics gives it an identity beyond a straightforward Arkanoid clone.

games.title: Pooyan
games.description:
Konami's Pooyan (1982) is a charming fixed-screen shooter with one of the period's most imaginative premises. Mama Pig rides a gondola up and down a cliff, firing arrows to burst the balloons carrying a pack of hungry wolves. The wolves have kidnapped her piglets, and each round is a desperate attempt to stop more enemies from reaching their destination. The controls are remarkably simple: move vertically with a two-way stick and fire horizontally at the right moment.

The game alternates between wolves descending toward the ground and wolves floating upward to a high ledge. Those that reach safety can create new danger, so players must prioritize targets rather than simply fire at the nearest balloon. A supply of meat can lure wolves together for large bonus scores, while falling rocks and other hazards punish predictable movement.

Pooyan is remembered for its cartoon storytelling, expressive animation, and use of familiar melodies, including classical and traditional tunes. Its easy-to-grasp setup disguises a demanding exercise in trajectory prediction, and its unusually domestic hero gives it a personality quite unlike the space battles that dominated many earlier arcade shooters. The game also appeared on several home systems and in unauthorized forms such as Pootan.

games.title: Pop Bingo
games.description: Pop Bingo is a 1996 Korean competitive puzzle game from Dooyong that merges colored-ball matching with a bingo board. Building on the visual style of Snow Pop, it introduces letter-marked balls whose removal fills spaces on a separate bingo card. The objective is not merely to clear the playfield, but to complete a line on the card before the opponent can do the same. Adult photographs appear as inter-stage rewards, creating a curious contrast with the otherwise cute puzzle presentation.

games.title: Pop 'n Bounce / Gapporin
games.description:
Pop 'n Bounce, titled Gapporin in Japan, is Video System's 1997 Neo Geo block-breaker with an emphasis on moving creatures rather than static bricks. Players use a paddle and ball to eliminate enemies arranged around the arena, but different targets have their own behavior: some are protected by eggs, others withstand ordinary hits, and some combine into larger creatures. Power-ups can supply extra attacks, while indestructible obstacles complicate the ball's path.

Collecting the letters of 'ATTACK' triggers a useful multi-ball effect, producing a burst of fast-moving action. Its characterful creatures and varied target reactions make it feel livelier than a conventional Breakout clone. The game appeared in arcades on the Neo Geo MVS but did not receive an official AES home-cartridge release.

games.title: Popeye
games.description:
Nintendo's Popeye (1982) is a classic single-screen platform game built around the characters of the famous comic strip and cartoons. Players guide Popeye around a multi-level stage collecting items dropped by Olive Oyl while staying clear of Brutus, the Sea Hag, and other threats. Depending on the stage, the collectibles are hearts, musical notes, or letters spelling 'HELP'. Unlike Donkey Kong, Popeye cannot jump: the four-way joystick moves him along stairs and ladders, and his action button delivers a punch.

Brutus is dangerous across several platform levels, so players must use the environment intelligently. Popeye can punch certain projectiles and, once per stage, eat a can of spinach that briefly gives him the power to knock Brutus away. Three different layouts recur with increasing difficulty, mixing route planning and quick reactions.

The game occupies a notable place in Nintendo's early arcade history, following the company's successful character-platform experiments. It was designed by Shigeru Miyamoto and Genyo Takeda and went on to receive home conversions, most famously for the Famicom/NES. Its recognizable characters, melodic theme, and distinctive no-jump action give it a lasting identity among the early-1980s classics.

games.title: Pop Flamer
games.description: Pop Flamer (hack?) is an alternate, possibly modified arcade set of Jaleco's 1982 maze-action game. The underlying play remains the same: players guide a mouse through compact mazes, popping balloons while using a limited-fuel flamethrower to repel frogs and other monsters. The fire weapon has to be conserved, and the stage's balloon-clearing goal demands movement through dangerous corridors. The precise alterations in this set are not reliably documented, so it is best regarded as a variant of Pop Flamer rather than a distinct game with invented new mechanics.

games.title: Pop Flamer
games.description:
Pop Flamer is a 1982 maze-action game by Jaleco in which a small mouse runs around a compact playfield trying to burst all the balloons. Frogs and other hostile creatures obstruct the route, and the mouse can hold them off with a flamethrower. Fuel is limited, so repeatedly firing at everything in sight is not a sustainable strategy.

Clearing every balloon completes the stage, but safely reaching them means threading through moving enemies and deciding when to use fire rather than simply dodging. The combination of a cute animal hero, maze navigation, and a scarce defensive resource makes Pop Flamer an interesting contemporary of Pengo and the early character-action boom.

games.title: Pop'n Pop
games.description:
Taito's Pop'n Pop (1997) mixes the appeal of Puzzle Bobble with a Space Invaders-like screen of advancing colored balloons. Players move a character along the bottom and fire balloons upward, creating groups of at least three matching colors to clear them before the descending mass reaches the danger line. Chain reactions and precise placement make large clearances possible, while different character choices lend the game a cheerful atmosphere.

The cast includes characters drawn from Taito's earlier arcade games, turning the puzzle action into a small celebration of the company's history. Its familiar color-matching concept is altered by the moving formation of targets, creating a more direct, shooter-like pressure than in the static arrangements of Puzzle Bobble. It is an appealing late-1990s example of Taito revisiting established arcade ideas in a new combination.

games.title: Popper
games.description: Popper is a 1983 arcade action-puzzle game by Omori, strongly reminiscent of Q*bert. Players control a rabbit moving across a stepped, geometric arrangement of cubes, changing their colors by landing on them while keeping clear of moving hazards. The goal is to transform the required tiles without being caught or falling off the playing area. Its bouncing protagonist and color-changing playfield belong to the wave of experimental platform-puzzle games that followed Q*bert's success.

games.title: Pop's Pop's
games.description: Pop's Pop's is a 1999 Korean music-quiz arcade game developed by Afega. Rather than relying on general-knowledge questions, it plays a musical excerpt and asks competitors to identify or select the correct song title. The format turns recognition of popular tunes into a timed arcade challenge and can be played in a competitive setting. Though its music library and regional question sets are not extensively documented, its sound-based identification mechanic is clear, making it a distinctive alternative to standard text-only quiz cabinets.

games.title: Porky
games.description: Porky is a quirky 1985 driving-and-shooting arcade game developed by Shinkai and published by Magic Electronics. Players steer a large pig through a cityscape full of potholes while fighting back against wolves with a distinctly unconventional weapon: flying sausages. Falling bombs and barbecue forks add further hazards, while airborne piglets can be rescued for bonus points. The game combines simple lateral driving controls with rapid shooting and occasional jumps, all wrapped in deliberately ridiculous cartoon imagery.

games.title: Portraits
games.description:
Portraits is an unusual 1983 photo-safari arcade game from Olympia. Players aim an in-game camera at different animals and try to capture the required assortment of wildlife without allowing the creatures to damage their equipment. The game's real novelty comes after a high score: on equipped cabinets, lights above the monitor signal a built-in black-and-white camera that can photograph the player and incorporate the image into the attract display.

This blend of basic arcade target play with a physical photography feature makes Portraits an especially curious early attempt at personalizing the arcade experience, long before camera-based attractions became common.

games.title: Poto Poto
games.description:
Poto Poto is a 1994 Sega head-to-head puzzle game built around hexagonal pieces that interlock into honeycomb-like formations. Players control a small cart and release colored pieces onto the playfield, attempting to assemble matching groups. Clearing a group can detach pieces supported by it, causing large sections of the formation to fall and creating opportunities for cascading attacks.

The competitive objective is to keep one's own arrangement under control while sending trouble to an opponent's side. Its unusual hexagonal geometry forces players to consider diagonal connections and structural support rather than the rectangular columns used in many falling-block rivals. The cheerful presentation and slightly unpredictable collapses make Poto Poto a distinctive entry in Sega's early-1990s arcade puzzle catalogue.

games.title: Pound for Pound
games.description: Pound for Pound is a 1990 boxing game by Irem shown from an overhead perspective, with large fighters who circle and strike one another in the ring. Players use a trackball to move and position their boxer and buttons to attack, trying to create openings while avoiding an opponent's punches. A succession of tougher rivals stands between the player and the championship. Its substantial character graphics, unusual viewpoint, and demanding controls make it an uncommon alternative to more conventional side-view boxing games.

games.title: P.O.W. - Prisoners of War
games.description:
P.O.W.: Prisoners of War is SNK's 1988 side-scrolling beat-'em-up, known in Japan as Datsugoku: Prisoners of War. One or two soldiers break out of captivity and fight through four stages on their way to destroying an enemy base and escaping by helicopter. The journey begins in a prison camp and continues through warehouses, jungle terrain, and heavily defended military positions, with guards, armed enemies, and vehicles blocking the route.

Players use an eight-way joystick and separate attack buttons to punch, kick, jump, and combine moves into more powerful strikes. Weapons taken from enemies can turn an encounter around, but close-quarters positioning is crucial when soldiers crowd the screen. Cooperative play lets two prisoners fight side by side, while the constant advances of the camera maintain a relentless pace.

Released as the belt-scrolling brawler was becoming a major arcade genre, P.O.W. helped establish SNK's appetite for military-themed action. Its blunt combat and rescue narrative were later adapted into an NES game with significant differences, leaving the arcade original as the faster, more direct cooperative experience.

games.title: Power Balls
games.description:
Power Balls is a 1994 Playmark block-breaking game that shifts the familiar paddle-and-ball action sideways. Players select a character with particular strengths and face objects arranged to the right of the screen, hitting a ball into them and returning it whenever it rebounds. Missing the return costs a life, while clearing the obstacles opens the next stage. Special boss encounters periodically replace the ordinary targets and must be struck repeatedly.

Its left-to-right court, playable characters, and bosses give the game a different rhythm from traditional bottom-paddle games such as Arkanoid. Power Balls was also offered as a conversion kit for existing Super Slam cabinets, demonstrating the arcade industry's interest in reusing established hardware.

games.title: Power Drive
games.description:
Bally Midway's Power Drive (1986) turns monster-truck competition into a physical, button-bashing arcade sports game. Instead of driving a truck around a continuous racecourse, up to three players compete in separate events inspired by arena monster-truck shows, including speed runs, car crushing, high jumps, and sled pulling. Repeatedly pressing the controls powers the heavy vehicles through each contest, making the game as much a test of frantic input rhythm as of racing judgment.

Its side-view presentation, oversized tires, and intentionally exaggerated competitions gave it a distinctive niche among 1980s driving games. Designed to appeal to fans of track-and-field button-mashing games, Power Drive transforms mechanical horsepower into an energetic arcade contest.

games.title: Gouketsuji Ichizoku
games.description:
Gouketsuji Ichizoku, released internationally as Power Instinct, is Atlus's 1993 one-on-one fighting game about an eccentric family's struggle for control of the Gouketsuji clan. Eight selectable fighters enter a tournament packed with extravagant moves and deliberately absurd character designs. The four-button system offers weak and strong punches and kicks, while running, double jumping, and attacks performed in motion distinguish its pace from some contemporaries.

Its best-known innovation is the transformation mechanic: the elderly fighter Otane Gouketsuji can temporarily become a younger version of herself through a special technique, altering her appearance and combat options. The idea arose from the development team's unusually playful character designs and became a defining feature of the series.

Power Instinct arrived during the post-Street Fighter II fighting-game boom, but stood apart through its music, Japanese humor, exaggerated personalities, and unusual mobility. It inspired several sequels, including Power Instinct 2 and Power Instinct Legends, and later received Super Famicom and Mega Drive conversions. The original remains a cult favorite for players who appreciate fighting games that take their combat seriously without taking their characters seriously.

games.title: Power Play
games.description: Power Play is a 1985 Cinematronics arcade soccer game that reduces the sport to a compact two-on-two contest. Each side consists of a field player and a goalkeeper, with the computer managing the keepers and, in solo play, the opposing team. Players steer their footballer around the pitch and try to create scoring opportunities with quick, direct attacks rather than elaborate team tactics. The minimalist format gives Power Play a brisk, competitive style that suited short coin-operated matches.

games.title: Pang Pang Car
games.description:
Pang Pang Car is a 1999 top-down driving-and-collection game by Icarus with adult-themed stage rewards. Players choose one of four cars and race around scrolling urban environments gathering tokens while hostile vehicles try to intercept them. An on-screen radar marks both remaining collectibles and pursuing opponents, helping the driver plan a route through the streets.

Each vehicle has weapons that can destroy rival cars or open access to otherwise blocked parts of a stage. Clearing an area reveals a digitized pin-up photograph, with further portions unlocked through continued progress. The combination of open-map collection, vehicle combat, and picture rewards makes Pang Pang Car more of a maze-action game on wheels than a conventional racer.

games.title: Ping-Pong King
games.description: Ping-Pong King is a 1985 table-tennis arcade game by Taito. Players take part in compact rallies, returning the ball across a virtual table and attempting to beat the opponent through well-timed strokes and shot placement. Although the cabinet supports two players, its play options use alternating turns rather than a simultaneous head-to-head contest. It is a relatively obscure example of the mid-1980s boom in arcade recreations of familiar sports.

games.title: Ping Pong Masters '93
games.description: Ping Pong Masters '93 is an Italian table-tennis arcade game developed by Electronic Devices in 1993. It turns fast exchanges of a small ball into a compact head-to-head sports contest, with support for one or two players. A four-direction joystick and three buttons provide a more elaborate input scheme than the paddle knob associated with the earliest arcade tennis games. Its dual Z80 processors, YM2413 music chip and horizontal raster display reflect the modest, independently developed European coin-op hardware of the early 1990s.

games.title: Planet Probe
games.description:
Planet Probe is an exceptionally rare 1985 shooter associated with the Kyugo/Orca development circle. A small spacecraft explores an alien world on a vertically oriented screen, while the landscape scrolls horizontally in layered, pseudo-3D perspective. The pilot can fire both at airborne enemies and at installations in the background, creating an unusual combination of upward shooting and attacks directed into the scenery. The journey passes deserts, volcanic terrain, oceans, and futuristic settlements. There are no conventional weapon power-ups, but hidden bonus targets reward experimentation.

Its history is almost as remarkable as its gameplay. For years, reports of Planet Probe came largely from Italian arcade players, and its existence was questioned until a deteriorating circuit board surfaced in Italy in 2012 and was successfully preserved. Its hardware closely resembles that of Vastar. Among its eccentric secrets are a silhouetted bicycle scene reminiscent of E.T. and a memorable high-score tune that one former player was able to reconstruct from memory more than two decades later. The known game appears to recycle its environments rather than lead to a conventional final ending.

games.title: Poka Poka Satan
games.description:
Poka Poka Satan is an unusual 1996 Japanese children's arcade game by Kato Seisakujo, built around a physical whack-a-mole concept rather than ordinary joysticks. Players protect a princess from swarms of mischievous, often winged creatures by striking the enemies as they appear. Its elaborate cabinet has three monitors: a display for the action and two horizontal, touch-sensitive play surfaces struck with plastic hammers. In two-player mode each participant takes one hammer and screen; solo play involves both surfaces.

The game contains three distinct stages, with patterns of enemies demanding rapid recognition and accurate strikes. Behind the custom cabinet is first-generation Cave arcade technology, adapted to drive the unusual dual playfield arrangement. It is a distinctive example of a children's physical-interaction game surviving through emulation of what would otherwise be a difficult cabinet to reproduce.

games.title: Prehistoric Isle in 1930
games.description:
Prehistoric Isle in 1930 is SNK's 1989 horizontally scrolling shooter set around the mysterious disappearance of ships near the Bahamas. Two reconnaissance biplanes investigate the uncharted Greenhell Isle, only to discover a world of dinosaurs, giant prehistoric animals, and other hostile creatures. Across five stages, players fly through dense formations of airborne and ground-based enemies before facing enormous bosses. The vivid prehistoric setting distinguishes it from the military and science-fiction shooters that dominated contemporary arcades.

Its signature mechanism is a weapon satellite, or 'option', obtained by shooting dinosaur eggs and collecting their power-ups. The option can be rotated around the biplane, and its position changes the weapon it fires: forward flame attacks, ricocheting projectiles, bombs, energy waves, or mines behind the aircraft. Choosing the best position for an approaching threat is more important than simply collecting stronger firepower. Speed upgrades help the relatively vulnerable aircraft survive, while even small prehistoric humans can become dangerous if they cling to the plane.

Known in Japan as Genshi-Tou 1930's, the game combines the tactical satellite idea popularized by R-Type with SNK's own elaborate animation and eccentric creature designs. Its development team included contributors who would work on later Neo Geo projects. A very different sequel, featuring modern helicopters, arrived ten years later.

games.title: Prehistoric Isle 2
games.description:
Prehistoric Isle 2, released for the Neo Geo MVS in 1999, revisits SNK's dinosaur-filled shooter series with contemporary military helicopters in place of the original game's 1930s biplanes. Developed by Saurus and Yumekobo and published by SNK, it sends players through six side-scrolling stages against rampaging prehistoric creatures, including dinosaurs capable of firing fantastical energy attacks. The two selectable helicopters have different firing patterns and bomb attacks, providing a choice between concentrated and spread-oriented offense.

A major new element is the rescue of civilians stranded amid the carnage. Collecting and protecting survivors provides scoring opportunities and rewards, while power-ups enhance the helicopter's weapons. Skilled players can build impressive score multipliers by combining maximum firepower with chains of destroyed enemies, and can earn bonuses for carrying rescued people to the end of a stage. The game's detailed, pre-rendered-looking sprites and enormous bosses reflect late-1990s Neo Geo spectacle. Unlike its predecessor, it was released for the arcade MVS system without a contemporary Neo Geo AES cartridge.

games.title: Princess Clara Daisakusen
games.description:
Princess Clara Daisakusen, better known in Japan as Purikura Daisakusen, is a colorful 1996 isometric action shooter from Atlus for Sega's ST-V arcade system. Its heroine, Kurara (Clara), first appeared in the Power Instinct fighting games. Here she sets out to rescue her abducted sister after the mechanical Scrap Empire invades the magical Miracle World. Three playable characters, Kurara, Kirara, and Grey, fight through the fantasy setting from a diagonal overhead viewpoint.

Players can fire magic at a distance, strike nearby enemies with a hammer-like attack, and use a companion called a Pure Egg to launch bombs. Defeating enemies in different ways releases rescued animals or gems, which influence the Pure Egg's evolving abilities. Its character-switching fantasy action, cheerful artwork, and elaborate evolution system make it a notably different showcase for ST-V hardware than the platform's many fighting-game conversions.

games.title: Prime Goal EX
games.description:
Prime Goal EX is Namco's Japanese-only 1996 arcade soccer game for its PlayStation-derived System 11 hardware. Building on J-League Soccer V-Shoot, it presents the Japanese professional league with fourteen clubs, adding Kashiwa Reysol and Cerezo Osaka to the twelve teams featured in its predecessor. The team rosters reflect the mid-1990s league, and colorful club mascots help give the game a distinctly Japanese sporting identity.

Players maneuver footballers with an eight-way joystick and use action buttons to pass, shoot, and challenge for the ball. An arcade-style match presentation emphasizes quick play over a detailed simulation, and a newspaper-like results screen follows the final whistle. The English commentary was recorded in Japan by Nigel Chisholm, who later recalled performing it with a deliberately American-sounding accent despite being English. It captures the wave of J-League enthusiasm that inspired several Japanese arcade and console soccer series in the period.

games.title: Primal Rage 2
games.description:
Primal Rage II is Atari Games' unfinished follow-up to its 1994 dinosaur fighting hit. Developed during the mid-1990s and tested only in very small numbers, it abandons the original's all-monster playable cast in favor of human-like 'Avatars' who can transform into the familiar prehistoric gods. The proposed roster also included a sabre-toothed beast, Slash Fang, while the skeletal dragon Necrosan was intended as a major antagonist. The surviving version uses a six-button fighting layout and PlayStation-derived arcade hardware with a hard disk.

Unlike an ordinary unreleased prototype known only from photographs, Primal Rage II has a remarkable preservation history. A handful of test cabinets appeared in California, surviving boards were later demonstrated to collectors, and extensive emulation efforts eventually made its partially finished battles accessible. Atari cancelled the project before commercial release, so this AdvanceMAME entry is a rare test build rather than a completed sequel. Its mechanics and presentation are consequently best understood as a glimpse into a development path that Atari never finalized.

games.title: Primal Rage
games.description:
Primal Rage is Atari Games' 1994 head-to-head fighter in which prehistoric monsters, worshipped as gods, battle for control of a post-apocalyptic Earth renamed Urth. Its seven combatants include two enormous tyrannosaurs, dinosaur-like predators, and giant apes, each with a distinctive assortment of special attacks and gruesome finishing moves. The characters were animated using photographed stop-motion models, giving their movements a weight and texture quite different from traditional hand-drawn fighting-game sprites.

Matches take place in each monster's domain, with small human worshippers wandering around the foreground. The beasts can devour these followers to recover health, turning otherwise decorative bystanders into a tactical resource. Special-move commands were also unusual: in the original scheme, players held attack buttons while entering joystick motions, rather than simply performing a motion and then pressing a button. Later arcade revisions refined the inputs and added conveniences, while hidden encounters and peculiar mini-games offered rewards for experimentation.

Arriving during the mid-1990s fighting-game boom, Primal Rage stood out through its monstrous cast, dark humor, and deliberately outrageous violence. The franchise expanded into home ports, toys, and other merchandise, while a planned sequel was cancelled. Even with its controversial content and unconventional controls, the arcade original remains a distinctive rival to the human martial artists of Street Fighter and Mortal Kombat.

games.title: Premier Soccer
games.description: Premier Soccer is a 1993 association-football arcade game from Konami, played with an eight-way joystick and two action buttons. Players control a team of footballers in brisk, head-to-head matches, moving the active player across the field to intercept the ball, build attacks, and score goals. Its compact control scheme favors immediate arcade competition over the complexity of a management or simulation game. Released in the period when Konami was establishing a significant reputation for sports games, it ran on dedicated 68000-based hardware and supported two-player matches. A curious detail in the game's presentation is that its Northern Ireland identification uses the flag of the Republic of Ireland.

games.title: Professor PacMan
games.description:
Professor Pac-Man is Bally Midway's highly unusual 1983 attempt to take the Pac-Man franchise into the world of trivia. Instead of navigating a maze, one or two players answer multiple-choice questions about patterns, memory, observations, and general knowledge. The familiar yellow character acts as a schoolmaster and an animated timer, eating a line of pellets while participants choose among three answers. Correct responses are worth more points the sooner they are entered, and players can earn bonus questions and recover lost lives through good performance.

The question set contains hundreds of puzzles, including visual-recognition tasks based on grids, objects, and occasional Pac-Man imagery. Two-player games reward whichever contestant responds correctly first, turning the format into a competitive quiz. Midway planned multiple editions for different audiences and periodic replacement question sets, but these ambitions did not materialize.

Professor Pac-Man is remembered less as a successful game than as a strange commercial footnote. Only about 400 cabinets were manufactured, and many were reportedly returned and converted to other games. Its abandonment of maze-chase play alienated audiences expecting another Pac-Man action game, yet the surviving machines document an especially adventurous moment in the early arcade industry.

games.title: Progear
games.description:
Progear, released in Japan as Progear no Arashi in 2001, is Cave's first horizontally scrolling bullet-hell shooter. Published by Capcom for CPS-2 arcade hardware, it takes place in a richly illustrated steampunk kingdom where young pilots fight against the oppressive, mechanically armed Metoruin sages. Players select a pilot and aircraft as well as a supporting gunner, producing different combinations of speed, firing patterns, and offensive capabilities. Five stages send the small aircraft through dense clouds of projectiles, armored formations, and enormous industrial bosses.

Its central feature is a scoring system built around transforming enemy bullets into collectible jewels. Shooting enemies under the right conditions while using the focused gunner attack can generate spectacular showers of gems, rewarding careful positioning and the decision to risk grazing dangerous patterns rather than simply evade them. Different combinations of pilots and gunners alter both play style and character relationships.

Progear is particularly striking for combining Cave's exacting, pattern-driven shooting design with richly detailed side-scrolling scenery instead of its customary vertical format. It became a cult favorite among specialist shooter players, who prize its difficult survival routes and intricate high-score strategies. The artwork, elaborate machinery, and children's resistance narrative give it a distinctive identity within Capcom's late CPS-2 catalog.

games.title: Progress
games.description: Progress is a 1984 overhead tank shooter from Chuo in which a heavily armed vehicle drives through scrolling battlefields while enemies attack from the air and ground. The tank has forward-firing guns as well as guided missiles aimed with a movable crosshair; a separate control can lock the missile target. Jeeps, turrets, helicopters, boats, and concealed threats demand different responses, while incoming fire and collisions threaten the player's limited supply of tanks. A first hit can leave the vehicle burning, with another hit finishing it. Reaching the end of a course earns a bonus and leads to tougher opposition. Its multiple weapons and independently aimed ordnance make Progress more involved than many of its early-1980s tank-shooter contemporaries.

games.title: Progressive Music Trivia
games.description: Progressive Music Trivia is a 1985 North American coin-operated trivia game developed by Enerdyne Technologies and published by PGD. Instead of mixing unrelated general-knowledge subjects, its questions focus on music, turning players' knowledge of songs and performers into the main challenge. Four answer buttons and a vertically oriented display place it squarely in the mid-1980s arcade quiz boom, when dedicated question-and-answer machines competed alongside action games for floor space.

games.title: Prop Cycle
games.description:
Prop Cycle is Namco's whimsical 1996 flying game, famous for its extraordinary pedal-powered arcade cabinet. Players sit at what resembles an exercise bicycle, pedaling to keep a fantastical flying machine in motion and steering by moving its handlebars. Pulling and pushing the bars changes altitude, while turning them banks the craft. The objective is to burst balloons scattered across floating landscapes before the time limit expires, gathering enough points to rescue the fantastical land of Solitar from its airborne predicament.

Unlike a typical racing game, Prop Cycle is about finding efficient three-dimensional routes through the air. Players must combine physical effort, altitude control, and quick steering to fly through clusters of balloons without losing momentum. The landscapes include floating islands and picturesque fantasy architecture, rendered on Namco's System 22 3D arcade hardware.

The physical cabinet is inseparable from the game's identity: pedaling is not merely decorative but a direct part of maintaining flight. At a time when Japanese arcade manufacturers were experimenting with elaborate motion and sports machines, Prop Cycle offered an unusually gentle, imaginative challenge based on coordination rather than combat.

games.title: Pro Soccer
games.description: Pro Soccer is an early overhead-view football game from Data East, released in 1983 on the DECO Cassette System and later as a dedicated arcade board. The field scrolls vertically, with one goal at each end, and players move their footballers to pass, shoot, defend, and try to outscore the opposing team. Its top-down perspective and straightforward ball control contrast with later television-style football games. The title is unrelated to the 1990s home-computer and console game sometimes called Pro Soccer, which was derived from Kick Off 2.

games.title: Pro Sports - Bowling, Tennis, and Golf
games.description: Pro Sports: Bowling, Tennis, and Golf is a 1983 multi-sport arcade release from Data East. Rather than concentrating on a single sporting event, it combines three of the company's early recreations of familiar sports in one arcade package, allowing players to switch between ten-pin bowling, racket play, and golf. The collection reflects Data East's experimentation with multi-game coin-operated hardware at a time when many sports titles were still distributed individually on its interchangeable DECO Cassette System. Its appeal lies in offering several distinct forms of sports play within the limitations of early-1980s arcade graphics and controls.

games.title: Pro Tennis
games.description: Pro Tennis is Data East's 1982 arcade interpretation of singles tennis, originally issued as cartridge DT-122 for the DECO Cassette System and later distributed as a standalone game. The court is shown at a diagonal from behind one player's end, and a joystick and two buttons provide the basic movement and stroke controls. Players exchange shots across the net, attempting to place the ball beyond the opponent's reach while following the structure of a tennis match. An early example of Data East's arcade sports catalog, it was subsequently included as one of the three sporting events in Pro Sports: Bowling, Tennis, and Golf.

games.title: Party Time: Gonta the Diver II / Ganbare! Gonta!! 2

variants.title: Party Time: Gonta the Diver II / Ganbare! Gonta!! 2 (World Release)
Ganbare! Gonta!! 2 / Party Time: Gonta the Diver II (Japan Release)

games.description: Party Time: Gonta the Diver II, known in Japan as Ganbare! Gonta!! 2, is Mitchell's 1995 follow-up to Moeyo Gonta!!, the game also known as Lady Killer. It is a vertically oriented, adult-themed puzzle game built around turning or flipping tiles to complete picture-based challenges, controlled with an eight-way joystick and three buttons. The artwork and playful presentation are an important part of its identity, with completed puzzles progressing the presentation. The World and Japanese releases share the same underlying game, although their titles differ. It is an unusual puzzle entry in Mitchell's catalog, quite separate from the company's more famous Puzz Loop games.

games.title: Bishoujo Janshi Pretty Sailor 18-kin
games.description: Bishoujo Janshi Pretty Sailor 18-kin is a 1994 Japanese adult mahjong game from Sphinx that trades on the imagery of magical-girl anime. Its characters resemble the heroines of Sailor Moon, although this is an unofficial parody rather than a licensed adaptation. Players compete in Japanese mahjong against the game's female opponents, with victories unlocking adult-themed scenes. The '18-kin' in the title explicitly marks the game as intended for adults. It belongs to the substantial strand of 1990s Japanese arcade mahjong games that combined a traditional tile game with anime character artwork.

games.title: Bishoujo Janshi Pretty Sailor 2
games.description: Bishoujo Janshi Pretty Sailor 2 is Sphinx's second adult-themed magical-girl mahjong game, released in Japan in 1994. Like its predecessor, it uses the visual language of Sailor Moon without being an official adaptation. This edition centers on a winged demon challenger playing mahjong against the Sailor-inspired heroines, with explicit reward scenes following victories. Its principal interest is as a continuation of a specific Japanese arcade subgenre: competitive mahjong presented through unlicensed anime parody and mature imagery.

games.title: PS Arcade 95
games.description:
PS Arcade 95 is the historical BIOS-set name used in older MAME and AdvanceMAME releases for Eighting/Raizing's PlayStation-derived arcade hardware, subsequently identified in newer MAME versions as the Eighting/Raizing ZN-1 system. Instead of describing one game, this entry supplies the shared firmware used by a Sony-based board adapted for dedicated coin-operated cabinets. Its PlayStation-family graphics and processing hardware was supplemented by arcade-specific sound and interface components.

Games associated with this platform include Beastorizer, better known as the original Bloody Roar, and Raizing's later shooter Brave Blade. The BIOS's changing name in MAME history is a useful clue for emulator users: the older psarc95 designation and the later coh1002e designation refer to the same Eighting/Raizing hardware family, not to two separate arcade games.

games.title: Power Spikes
games.description:
Power Spikes is Video System's 1991 arcade volleyball game, a successor in spirit to the company's Super Volleyball series. Players control a national team in fast-paced indoor matches, positioning athletes to receive serves, set up attacks, and deliver spikes past the opposing side. A compact two-button control scheme supports timing-based attacks and defensive reactions, while the action alternates between team movement and dramatic close-up presentations of powerful hits.

Different regional editions emphasize different national-team selections, with the Japanese version particularly associated with Japan's volleyball team. The game helped establish Video System's enduring association with arcade volleyball, paving the way for the more extravagant Neo Geo sequel Power Spikes II.

games.title: Power Spikes II
games.description:
Power Spikes II is the 1994 Neo Geo MVS continuation of Video System's arcade volleyball series. Where the first Power Spikes was recognizable indoor volleyball, this sequel adds a flamboyant science-fiction 'Hyper League' with armored athletes and spectacular special attacks. Players control teams in five-on-five matches, receiving, setting, blocking, and spiking the ball while choosing how and when to use enhanced moves. Teams and player abilities differ, giving matches a more exaggerated character than a straightforward sports simulation.

The game also retains a conventional volleyball flavor alongside its futuristic competition, making it appealing to both fans of the earlier series and players looking for an unusual arcade sports spectacle. It remains one of the very few volleyball titles on SNK's Neo Geo hardware, and the series' most extravagant entry.

games.title: Mahjong Panic Stadium
games.description: Mahjong Panic Stadium is a 1990 Japanese arcade mahjong game from Nichibutsu that gives the traditional tile game an unlikely baseball theme. Players compete in mahjong while the surrounding presentation draws on the imagery of a ballpark and sports competition. It also belongs to Nichibutsu's adult-oriented mahjong line, incorporating mature character artwork. The unusual combination of mahjong, baseball, and adult themes makes it a period curiosity rather than a conventional baseball simulation.

games.title: Power Surge
games.description: Power Surge is a 1988 arcade maze game from Innovative Concepts in Entertainment in which the player controls an electrical spark navigating a circuit-like playfield. Resistors and hostile sparks act as obstacles or targets, and the objective is to eliminate threats and complete the circuit to reach the next level. Its abstract electrical theme makes it visually and mechanically distinct from the character-based mazes more common in the genre. The concept also appeared in redemption-machine form, where successful play could be rewarded with prizes rather than only an on-screen score.

games.title: Psychic 5
games.description:
Psychic 5 is a 1987 platform-action game developed by NMK for Jaleco that has become a cult favorite for its intricate movement and hidden rewards. Across eight tall, maze-like stages, players guide a group of five psychically gifted characters, beginning with children Naoki and Akiko, through rooms filled with enemies, doors, and secrets. Each character has different abilities, affecting movement speed, jumping, attacking, and exploration. Players can switch characters at special locations, letting them choose the best skills for the next obstacle.

Its controls allow unusually expressive movement: players can jump, swing a hammer or another character-specific weapon, and slow their descent by hovering. Defeating the evil Satan at the end of a stage is only part of the challenge; finding hidden bonuses and learning the layout of each labyrinth gives the game its depth. The combination of character switching, vertical exploration, and precise physics makes it more demanding than its cheerful appearance suggests.

Psychic 5 never became a major international arcade franchise, but its distinctive blend of action and exploration inspired a devoted following. Several ideas and characters later appeared in Jaleco's Famicom game Esper Boukentai, and a much later remake, Psychic 5 Eternal, renewed interest in the original.

games.title: Psycho Soldier
games.description:
Psycho Soldier is SNK's 1987 side-scrolling action game starring Athena Asamiya and Sie Kensou, teenage psychic fighters battling mutants in a ruined world. Unlike the earlier Athena, its heroine is a modern descendant of that game's protagonist. The arcade game supports two simultaneous players, who advance through destructible environments while unleashing psychic energy blasts and fighting grotesque monsters.

A distinctive energy system powers the heroes' attacks and defensive abilities. Collectible spheres orbit the character to block threats, then can be fired at enemies at the cost of consuming them. With enough psychic energy, stronger attacks and temporary transformations become available. Breaking scenery reveals supplies and hidden items, encouraging exploration even as the stages scroll onward.

Psycho Soldier is especially remembered for its fully sung theme song, an exceptional feature in a 1987 arcade game. Athena and Kensou later became recurring members of SNK's The King of Fighters cast, and the song itself was revisited in several of those games. The combination of a vocal soundtrack, anime-inspired heroes, and cooperative action gives it an important place in SNK history.

games.title: Psychic Force
games.description:
Psychic Force is Taito's unusual mid-1990s fighting game in which opponents hover freely within a cubic arena rather than standing on the ground. The combatants, called Psychiccers, wield elemental and supernatural powers, and matches are fought in full three-dimensional-looking space while retaining a fundamentally two-dimensional fighting structure. Players can move vertically and horizontally, fire energy attacks, defend with barriers, and slam opponents against the arena walls for additional damage. This makes spacing, momentum, and wall positioning as important as conventional fighting-game combinations.

The characters' supernatural abilities and personal conflicts are central to the presentation, with each fighter representing a different style of ranged and close combat. Initially developed on Taito's PlayStation-derived FX-1 hardware, the game attracted a cult following in Japan despite limited Western commercial success. Its revised arcade edition, Psychic Force EX, adjusted the balance and made the hidden boss Keith readily selectable, while a later sequel expanded the series' distinctive airborne-duel concept.

games.title: Psychic Force EX
games.description:
Psychic Force EX is Taito's enhanced 1996 revision of its airborne arena fighter Psychic Force. As in the original, two psychic-powered characters hover inside a bounded, cube-shaped battlefield, attacking with elemental techniques, energy projectiles, barriers, and blows that can send an opponent crashing into a wall. Rather than a wholly new sequel, EX refines the original combat system and revises character balance.

The most visible change is that Keith Evans, previously a secret boss character, is directly selectable without a special code. Other changes adjust the cost and effectiveness of defensive barriers, the use of psychic energy, and the balance between offensive and defensive tactics. It is therefore a meaningful alternate ruleset for experienced players, not merely another regional version or a cosmetic ROM revision.

games.title: Point Blank
games.description:
Point Blank, released in Japan as GunBullet, is Namco's 1994 light-gun game that replaces a continuous shooting adventure with a succession of short, inventive target-shooting challenges. One or two players use physical pistols to pop balloons, hit cardboard targets, avoid bystanders, protect the cartoon protagonists Dr. Don and Dr. Dan, and complete accuracy or speed tests. Each event has its own success condition, often requiring a certain number of hits before a brief timer expires, so players must read the instructions and react immediately.

A range of difficulty settings turns the same basic gun-handling skills into very different tests. Sometimes the objective is to shoot as rapidly as possible; elsewhere, a single mistaken shot can ruin a perfect run. Two-player competition is particularly effective because both players aim at the same colorful screen under pressure to score first or avoid penalties.

With its comical presentation and largely nonviolent targets, Point Blank offered a welcome alternative to the gritty police and military light-gun shooters of the era. Its rapid-fire mini-game format proved popular enough to support arcade sequels and home versions, and Dr. Don and Dr. Dan became recognizable mascots of the series.

games.title: Point Blank 2
games.description:
Point Blank 2, released in Japan as Gunbarl, is Namco's 1999 continuation of its comic light-gun shooting series. Players once again wield pistols to tackle a rapidly changing selection of miniature challenges: hitting specified targets, shooting quickly and accurately, and avoiding forbidden objects while racing the clock. Familiar characters Dr. Don and Dr. Dan return to accompany the slapstick shooting contests.

The sequel expands the event library to more than seventy challenges, with courses arranged around different difficulty levels and variable stage selections. As in the original, the appeal lies in the way each short scenario asks for a different shooting skill, especially when two players compete side by side. It is an expansion of Point Blank's carnival-shooting formula rather than a traditional on-rails action shooter.

games.title: Parallel Turn
games.description: Parallel Turn is Jaleco's 1984 winter-sports arcade game presented from an overhead perspective with vertical scrolling. Rather than depicting only downhill skiing, it combines six events: Ski Lift, Slalom, Ski Jump, Biathlon, Dog Sled, and Downhill. Each changes the immediate sporting challenge, while rapid button presses are used to build speed. Its mixture of obstacle avoidance, timing, and varied winter activities reflects the early arcade enthusiasm for multi-event sports games.

games.title: Power Up Baseball
games.description:
Power Up Baseball is a never-commercially-released 1996 baseball game created through a partnership between Midway and Incredible Technologies. Conceived as a baseball counterpart to NBA Jam, it mixes recognizable baseball action with digitized players, exaggerated animation, and exuberant commentary from broadcaster Ken 'Hawk' Harrelson. Special test cabinets incorporated trackballs, connecting its physical controls to Incredible Technologies' experience with Golden Tee Golf. Approximately fifteen machines were reportedly built for testing.

The game's history took an unexpected turn decades later when archived development materials were recovered and a playable version was reconstructed for preservation. Its existence reveals how Midway attempted to translate its hugely successful arcade-sports formula from basketball to baseball. The surviving version represents an unfinished, location-tested experiment rather than a polished retail release.

games.title: Puchi Carat
games.description:
Puchi Carat is Taito's 1997 hybrid of block-breaking action and competitive falling-block puzzle play. Players move a paddle to bounce a ball upward into clusters of suspended gemstones. Destroying a supporting gem can disconnect an entire group from the ceiling and cause it to fall, turning carefully aimed shots into large scoring opportunities. New rows of gems descend over time, so survival depends on removing dangerous formations before they fill the playfield.

The game retains the immediate physical feel of Breakout and Arkanoid while borrowing the chain-reaction tactics of color-matching puzzle games. Special flashing gems can clear larger sections, and head-to-head play transforms quick shots and clever disconnections into a contest of pressure and reaction. Its cheerful character art and colorful jewel graphics help it stand apart from Taito's more conventional paddle games.

games.title: PuckMan
games.description:
PuckMan is the original Japanese name and release of Namco's Pac-Man, the landmark 1980 maze-chase arcade game designed by Toru Iwatani. The player guides a yellow, circular character through a fixed maze, eating every dot while avoiding four colored ghosts with distinct movement behavior. Large power pellets briefly turn the ghosts vulnerable, allowing the player to chase and eat them for increasing bonus points. Fruit rewards, side tunnels, and changes in ghost speed add depth to an apparently simple objective.

The game was created partly to attract audiences beyond the military and space-shooter themes that dominated late-1970s arcades. Its bright characters, nonviolent premise, memorable sounds, and short comic intermissions helped establish personality-driven video games as a mass-market phenomenon. The American name Pac-Man replaced PuckMan for Midway's release, and that revised title became world-famous.

Pac-Man's ghost behavior and scoring routes turned it into a competitive classic, while its infamous level-256 split-screen overflow became one of arcade history's best-known bugs. Although this set may be grouped differently in some emulator metadata, PuckMan itself is Namco's authentic Japanese original, not an unauthorized bootleg. It inspired countless sequels, imitations, and adaptations and remains one of the medium's most recognizable works.

games.title: Puckman Pockimon
games.description:
Puckman Pockimon is an unlicensed Korean maze game released by Genie in 2000 that combines characters from Namco's Pac-Man and Nintendo's Pokémon. One player controls Pac-Man and the other Pikachu, guiding them through mazes filled with pellets, ghosts, and Pokémon-themed hazards. Both characters can play simultaneously, giving the normally solitary Pac-Man formula a cooperative twist. Portals between parts of the mazes add another navigational complication.

The game borrows heavily from the sound and design vocabulary of Pac-Man and Ms. Pac-Man, despite running on hardware related to Sega's System C2. Its unlikely mixture of two unrelated franchises, digitized pictures shown between rounds, and unauthorized use of familiar graphics make it a striking example of the unofficial crossover games that circulated in some late arcade markets.

games.title: PuLiRuLa
games.description:
PuLiRuLa is Taito's surreal 1991 side-scrolling beat 'em up, starring Zac and Mel in the fantastical land of Radishland. An evil force has stolen the keys that control the flow of time, transforming peaceful creatures into strange monsters. The heroes travel through bizarre landscapes, fighting enemies with magical attacks and retrieving the keys to restore each area's normality. Defeated foes often turn into harmless animals, which players can collect for bonus points.

The combat is straightforward, but the game's identity rests in its extravagant visual imagination. Psychedelic backgrounds, enormous creatures, unnerving human figures, and unexpected transformations give it a dreamlike atmosphere quite unlike Capcom's urban brawlers. Two players can cooperate, making progress through the strange environments while facing increasingly elaborate stage bosses. PuLiRuLa became a cult favorite for its whimsical yet occasionally disturbing Japanese character art.

games.title: Pulsar
games.description:
Pulsar is a maze-and-shooting arcade game released by Gremlin/Sega around 1980-81. The player drives a small tank through a top-down maze, collecting colored keys and carrying each one to the matching lock to open the way onward. The maze is not static: barriers and force fields periodically change its available routes, while roaming enemies fire when they line up with the player along a clear horizontal or vertical path.

Success depends on remembering where locks are located, recognizing safe corridors as the layout shifts, and using the tank's gun to clear immediate threats. The combination of collecting objectives and responding to a changing maze makes Pulsar an early alternative to pure maze-chase or shooting games. It was designed and programmed by Larry Clague and Mike Hendricks.

games.title: Pulstar
games.description:
Pulstar is Aicom's visually spectacular 1995 horizontal shooter for SNK's Neo Geo system, and one of the platform's clearest responses to Irem's R-Type. Piloting the Dino246 spacecraft, players face eight demanding stages of alien machinery, biological monsters, narrow passages, and enormous bosses. A forward-mounted protective pod helps absorb threats, while collectible equipment expands the ship's attacking and defensive possibilities. Charging the main weapon for powerful shots is essential when heavy enemies approach.

Pulstar is famously unforgiving. Enemy patterns and environmental hazards reward memorization, and losing a life can force the player to rebuild a carefully developed arsenal. Its demanding checkpoints make learning each stage as important as reflexes. The game's elaborate scenery and animated enemies were created using pre-rendered imagery, giving the Neo Geo a polished appearance that recalled contemporary computer-generated graphics.

Although its resemblance to R-Type is unmistakable, Pulstar's gloomy science-fiction atmosphere and technical showmanship won it a following among shoot-'em-up specialists. Staff connections and the same general production lineage would later contribute to Blazing Star, which adopted a more accessible and spectacular approach to Neo Geo shooting.

games.title: Punch-Out!!
games.description:
Punch-Out!! is Nintendo's landmark 1984 boxing arcade game and the starting point of one of its most recognizable sports series. Players fight six increasingly eccentric opponents, including Glass Joe, Bald Bull, and Mr. Sandman, by watching their movements for openings, dodging punches, guarding, and answering with carefully timed blows. The protagonist is shown from behind as a green-haired, partially transparent wireframe, an ingenious way to keep the opponent visible in a close-up boxing game.

The original cabinet used two monitors stacked vertically. The lower screen displayed the fight, while the upper screen presented portraits, scores, the round timer, and other status information. A special control allowed more powerful uppercuts alongside ordinary left and right punches. Each opponent had unique animations and tactics, and mastering the visual cues behind their attacks was the real key to progress.

Punch-Out!! was a major commercial success and helped establish Nintendo's talent for character-rich arcade games. Its exaggerated boxers and striking dual-screen presentation predated the better-known NES adaptation, which reimagined the series around Little Mac. The arcade game also marked an early Nintendo assignment for composer Koji Kondo, later celebrated for his work on Super Mario Bros. and The Legend of Zelda.

games.title: The Punisher
games.description:
The Punisher is Capcom's 1993 Marvel Comics beat 'em up, starring Frank Castle and S.H.I.E.L.D. operative Nick Fury in a relentless campaign against the Kingpin's criminal empire. One or two players advance through city streets, docks, criminal hideouts, and other locations, fighting gangs of thugs and memorable bosses. It follows the broad model of Final Fight but makes especially extensive use of weapons, including guns, knives, baseball bats, and improvised objects.

The heroes can combine punches and throws into elaborate attacks, seize opponents, and turn the surrounding environment against enemies. Firearms periodically become available or are drawn automatically during certain encounters, giving the action a distinctive comic-book gunplay element absent from most contemporary brawlers. The game's presentation uses bold visual effects and comic-style flourishes to echo the source material.

Often ranked among Capcom's strongest arcade beat 'em ups, The Punisher is notable for tight controls, fast pacing, and an unusually elaborate assortment of combat options. It is also an early example of Capcom's collaboration with Marvel before the company's better-known superhero fighting games.

games.title: Punk Shot
games.description:
Punk Shot is Konami's 1990 street-basketball game in which the Ramblers and Slammers settle their rivalry on rough urban courts. Up to four players can compete in teams of two, moving their characters with joysticks to pass, shoot, steal, and block. The rules are recognizably those of basketball, but the presentation is deliberately unruly: players confront aggressive opponents and absurd disruptions rather than a carefully officiated professional game.

The action is quick and exaggerated, with dramatic leaps and chaotic movement encouraging head-to-head play. Its back-alley atmosphere and four-player cabinet distinguish Punk Shot from conventional basketball simulations and place it among Konami's more playful arcade sports experiments.

games.title: Pururun
games.description:
Pururun is a 1995 puzzle game developed by Metro and published by Banpresto. Its playfield is filled with round, two-colored blobs, each with both an outer color and an inner color. Connecting four or more blobs of the same visible color causes them to pop, but the remaining material changes to the inner color, opening new opportunities for chain reactions. Players must create these reactions to guide the game's cheerful heroes, Pipi and Moko, toward their goal.

Unlike simpler color-matching games, a successful move can transform the board rather than merely remove pieces. Planning around both visible and hidden colors gives the puzzles an extra layer of strategy, while its cute characters and bright animation contrast with the demanding combinations required later in the game.

games.title: Pushman
games.description:
Pushman is a 1990 puzzle-platform game from Korean developer Comad in which a small hero must move boxes through a series of compact rooms to fill holes and reach an exit. The challenge is complicated by moving enemies, hazards, and a strict time limit; some situations require collecting power-ups or choosing the order in which obstacles are moved. Each room becomes a test of spatial planning under arcade pressure rather than a simple race to the opposite side.

The game has an unusual production footnote: portions of its soundtrack draw on music from Jaleco's Psychic 5, including material associated with Akiko's stages. It is one of the more distinctive Korean puzzle-action titles of its period, mixing block-pushing logic with the demands of a traditional arcade platform game.

games.title: Puyo Puyo
games.description:
Puyo Puyo is Compile's classic competitive falling-block puzzle game, popularized by Sega's 1992 arcade version. Pairs of colored, jelly-like creatures fall into a vertical well and can be shifted or rotated before landing. Connecting four or more Puyos of the same color makes them disappear; unsupported Puyos then fall, potentially setting off further clears. Creating multi-stage chain reactions is the key to high scores and to attacking an opponent with nuisance Puyos that clutter their field.

The arcade version gave the formula a strong head-to-head identity through a cast drawn from Compile's Madou Monogatari fantasy games, led by spellcaster Arle Nadja. Each rival appears with expressive dialogue and distinct character art, making a puzzle contest feel like a sequence of humorous duels. Successful attacks are represented by comical magical spells rather than simply abstract score penalties.

Originally introduced in a simpler form on Japanese home computers, Puyo Puyo became one of the most influential multiplayer puzzle franchises after its arcade breakthrough. The apparently modest four-piece matching rule creates remarkable strategic depth through chains, counterattacks, and timing, inspiring countless sequels and competitive tournaments.

games.title: Puyo Puyo 2
games.description:
Puyo Puyo 2, commonly called Puyo Puyo Tsu, is Compile's hugely influential 1994 follow-up to Puyo Puyo. As before, players drop pairs of colored blobs into a well, clear groups of four or more, and build chains to flood an opponent's screen with nuisance Puyos. The central innovation is the ability to offset incoming attacks: a player can counter with a chain of their own, reducing or cancelling the nuisance pieces that would otherwise fall. The new rule transforms the pace and tactics of competitive play by making defense and retaliation part of the same system.

The sequel also expands the roster of colorful fantasy opponents and varies the progression through its character encounters. Its tight controls and carefully balanced chain-and-counter mechanics made it a standard for serious Puyo competition, and much of the series' later competitive identity was established here.

games.title: Puyo Puyo Sun
games.description:
Puyo Puyo Sun is Compile's 1996 third main arcade entry in its colorful falling-block puzzle series. Players still rotate falling pairs of Puyos, connect at least four of a color, and create chains to attack opponents with nuisance pieces. The major addition is the special Sun Puyo, which enters play during the exchange or cancellation of attacks and can greatly amplify the value of chains that clear it. Managing these new pieces adds an extra tactical layer to the counterattack system introduced in Puyo Puyo 2.

The game wraps the formula in a humorous summer setting, with a dangerously enlarged sun and multiple story routes featuring characters from the series' fantasy cast. Its Japanese title plays on 'san', meaning three, and the English word 'sun'. The addition of Sun Puyos makes this an experimental entry rather than a straightforward replacement for the enduring competitive rules of Puyo Puyo 2.

games.title: Puyo Puyo Sun (English translation)

modifications.description: Translates all 24 story cutscenes, 69 character win quotes, menus, character select, rule demonstrations, and endings into English.

games.description: Puyo Puyo Sun (English translation) is an English localization patch by Zanac for Compile's 1996 Sega ST-V falling-piece puzzle game Puyo Puyo Sun. Building upon the Puyo Nexus community translation and adding translations for ST-V arcade-exclusive content, it localizes all 24 story cutscenes across Arle, Draco, and Schezo's courses, all 69 character win quotes, the secret Carbuncle final stage, menus, in-game chain graphics, and endings into English.

games.title: Puzzle Club
games.description:
Puzzle Club is an unreleased Namco puzzle game from 1990, preserved from prototype code for the System 1 arcade platform. Players slide animated picture tiles so that every horizontal row displays matching symbols before the timer runs out. A completed row locks into place and shifts to the bottom, requiring the remaining rows to be solved with progressively less freedom. Finishing the arrangement completes a stage and awards points.

Two visual modes give the same basic idea quite different appearances. A child-friendly 'Pacman Story' mode uses animated Pac-Man characters, while an adult-oriented 'Floor Exercise' mode uses slot-machine symbols and includes a bonus picture puzzle. Despite being substantially complete, Puzzle Club never received a normal arcade release and lacks a finished title screen. It is a rare glimpse of Namco experimenting with timed spatial puzzles outside its better-known action series.

games.title: Taisen Puzzle-dama
games.description:
Taisen Puzzle-dama is Konami's 1994 competitive falling-block puzzle game, released outside Japan as Crazy Cross. Pairs of colored balls descend into a well, and matching three or more of the same color clears them. Successful clears and chain reactions send trapped balls to the opponent's playfield, where they arrive encased in blocks. Breaking these blocks can release new balls and trigger counter-combinations, so attacks can also provide an opportunity for retaliation.

The game emphasizes head-to-head contests against either human players or a succession of colorful computer-controlled characters. Its locked-ball mechanic gives it a distinctive strategy despite the obvious resemblance to Puyo Puyo, and it became the beginning of Konami's own Taisen Puzzle-dama series.

games.title: Puzzle Star
games.description:
Puzzle Star is a 1999 puzzle game from International Games System for the PGM arcade hardware. Each stage presents a stack of assorted icons and a target number of three-of-a-kind matches to complete within a time limit. Players take symbols from the left edge of rows and place them in a small selection area, trying to assemble matching trios. An unsuccessful combination returns symbols to the stack, creating further complications for later choices.

Special star symbols can earn additional time when used correctly, and a limited ability to return a selected icon allows the player to recover from occasional mistakes. Unlike falling-block puzzlers, Puzzle Star is a planning game about selecting from an existing arrangement, balancing the immediate match against the effect on the remaining board.

games.title: Puzzle De Pon!
games.description:
Puzzle De Pon! is Visco's 1995 Neo Geo MVS puzzle game, built around the familiar mechanics of Taito's Puzzle Bobble but with a different objective. Players aim and fire colored bubbles upward, matching groups of three or more to make them disappear. Rather than simply clearing the entire board, they must free a special target plate by removing all the bubbles attached to it. Once the plate drops, the stage is complete.

The arcade game contains 39 stages whose layouts and hanging targets become steadily more difficult. Zodiac-themed milestones add a distinctive structure to the progression. Licensed use of Puzzle Bobble's fundamental concept, coupled with its plate-dropping objective, makes Puzzle De Pon! a recognizable but genuinely different Neo Geo puzzle challenge.

games.title: Puzzle King
games.description:
Puzzle King: Dance & Puzzle is a 1998 Korean puzzle arcade game from Eolith, running on the company's Hyperstone-based 32-bit hardware. It supports two players with eight-direction joysticks and two buttons, and combines a match/toss-style puzzle format with dance-themed presentation. The credits even identify motion-capture and dance-direction staff, an unusually elaborate production detail for an arcade puzzler.

This is the original Eolith game preserved under the ROM name puzzlekg. It should not be confused with an entirely different Puzzle King compilation released by K1 Soft and HAN System in the early 2000s, which repackaged games including Snow Bros. and unofficial Pac-Man derivatives.

games.title: Puzzli
games.description: Puzzli is a 1995 aquatic-themed puzzle game developed by Metro and released by Banpresto. Rows of colorful sea creatures appear in a vertical playfield, and players must arrange three or more matching creatures so they can be caught and removed. If the accumulating creatures descend past the safe area, the game ends. Its underwater presentation and fishing motif give a playful identity to a straightforward color-matching puzzle formula.

games.title: Puzzli 2
games.description: Puzzli 2 is the 1999 sequel to Metro's underwater matching game, released on IGS's PolyGame Master arcade system. The player again works to bring three fish of the same type together near the water's surface, catching them to clear the stage. Uncaught fish accumulate below, and allowing the pile to cross the danger line ends the attempt. The game supports solo stage-clearing and two-player competition, retaining the original's fishing imagery while bringing the series to more powerful late-1990s arcade hardware.

games.title: Puzz Loop
games.description:
Puzz Loop is Mitchell Corporation's 1998 arcade puzzle game that established the now-familiar formula of shooting colored marbles into a moving chain. A stream of balls winds along a track toward a central hole, and the player rotates a launcher to fire additional balls into it. Connecting three or more marbles of the same color removes them; well-placed shots can separate a long chain and start cascading reactions as gaps close. The challenge is to destroy the entire approaching sequence before it reaches the endpoint.

Its rotating cannon, moving target, and time pressure make Puzz Loop fundamentally different from static-grid matching games such as Puyo Puyo. Anticipating the chain's motion and planning shots several marbles ahead are the keys to survival. Released internationally under the name Ballistic on some platforms, it was an influential early example of the marble-chain puzzle genre, preceding the better-known Zuma games that later popularized similar mechanics.

games.title: Puzznic
games.description:
Puzznic is Taito's 1989 arcade puzzle game, built around arranging symbol-marked blocks so identical pieces touch and disappear. Players move a cursor over a block and slide it horizontally, after which gravity causes unsupported pieces to fall. What begins as a simple matching exercise quickly becomes a series of intricate spatial problems involving obstacles, platforms, restricted movement, and the order in which blocks are removed.

The arcade game offers branching puzzle selections, allowing players to choose alternative routes when a particular layout proves difficult. The original Japanese arcade presentation also includes adult-themed rewards, an aspect that was removed from many home conversions. Puzznic became a popular multi-platform puzzle title because its basic rules were easy to understand while the later stages demanded careful planning rather than reflexes.

games.title: Taito Power Goal
games.description:
Taito Power Goal is the European title of Taito's 1994 arcade football game Hat Trick Hero '95, part of the series that began with Football Champ and Hat Trick Hero. Teams representing different nations compete in fast, exaggerated matches, with arcade-style player movement and straightforward passing, shooting, and tackling controls. The game prioritizes goals, physical challenges, and dramatic attacking play over the detailed tactics of a football simulation.

Running on Taito's F3 hardware, this edition continues the colorful presentation and playful excess of the earlier series while refreshing the football action for mid-1990s arcades. The Power Goal name identifies the European release rather than a wholly unrelated sports game.

games.title: Power Instinct 2
games.description:
Power Instinct 2 is Atlus's eccentric 1994 one-on-one fighting game, known in Japan as Gouketsuji Ichizoku 2. The members of the wealthy, deeply dysfunctional Gouketsuji family assemble for another tournament after the disappearance of its previous winner, Otane. The playable roster expands to thirteen characters, including new fighters alongside returning favorites such as the elderly sisters Otane and Oume, who can transform into younger versions of themselves during combat.

The fighting uses familiar special moves, throws, and character-specific techniques, but the game's individuality lies in its gleefully strange cast, slapstick animation, and bizarre transformations. Characters range from martial artists and musicians to extravagant caricatures, and each has distinctive attacks and personal motivations. Its unusual sense of humor and transformative mechanics made Power Instinct one of the more recognizable outsiders to the Street Fighter-dominated arcade fighting scene.

games.title: Photo Y2K 2
games.description: Photo Y2K 2, also known as Real or Fake 2, is a 2001 picture-comparison puzzle game from Taiwan's International Games System. Each round displays two photographs of swimsuit models with a small number of deliberate differences. Players move a cursor over the images with a joystick and identify the altered areas before the timer expires. The challenge is careful visual inspection under time pressure, rather than matching falling tiles or solving abstract patterns. Its photographic material and straightforward spot-the-difference mechanics place it within a popular line of East Asian arcade observation games.

games.title: Pyramid
games.description: Pyramid is a 1996 BFM/ELAM video-slot machine for the Dutch market, preserved on game card 95-750-898. Its Egyptian-sounding name refers to this later electronic gambling game, not Sankyo's unrelated 1970s Breakout-style arcade title of the same name. It runs on 6809-family hardware with a horizontal display and a compact joystick/button arrangement. The documented experience is slot-machine gambling; surviving references do not establish any particular pyramid-themed bonus rules.

games.title: Puzzle De Bowling
games.description: Puzzle De Bowling is a 1999 Japanese puzzle game that reimagines the color-matching action of Puzzle Bobble as a game of bowling. Players launch balls upward into arrangements of colored pins, aiming to connect and clear groups of at least three matching pins. Precise angles and combinations can earn bowling-themed bonuses for strikes, spares, doubles, and turkeys. A power gauge builds as pins are removed, adding another reason to plan efficient shots. Its scoring terminology and pin graphics give an otherwise familiar bubble-shooting formula a distinctive sports twist.

games.title: Puzzle Break
games.description: Puzzle Break is SemiCom's 1997 arcade puzzle-action game, combining a paddle-and-ball mechanic with blocks that advance from above. Players maneuver a paddle to deflect bouncing balls toward the descending formation, breaking blocks before the playfield becomes overwhelmed. It resembles a variation on the block-breaking tradition of Breakout, with the added pressure of a moving mass of targets rather than a static wall. One or two players can tackle its timed, reaction-driven rounds.

games.title: Puzz Loop 2
games.description:
Puzz Loop 2 is Mitchell Corporation's 2001 arcade follow-up to the influential marble-chain puzzle game, published for Capcom's CPS-2 system. Players rotate a central launcher and fire colored balls into a moving chain, trying to create groups of three or more before the advancing marbles reach the end of their track. Removing well-placed groups can pull other balls together and produce chain reactions, rewarding careful aim and anticipation of the moving formation.

The sequel's most important expansion is a dedicated two-player versus mode, allowing opponents to test their accuracy and chain-making skill directly. It retains the simple, instantly readable appeal of the original while providing more reasons to master fast, efficient marble clearing.

games.title: Quiz & Dragons
games.description:
Quiz & Dragons: Capcom Quiz Game is a 1992 arcade title that merges trivia questions with fantasy board-game and role-playing elements.
