Players choose an adventurer and travel across a branching map by dice rolls, facing monsters and other encounters represented by multiple-choice questions. Correct responses advance the quest and defeat enemies; wrong answers cost precious health. Its fantasy characters, monsters, and illustrated map turn a quiz session into an adventure rather than a succession of unrelated question screens.

Different characters offer their own abilities, and the original game allows solo play or cooperation. The Japanese re-release changes aspects of progression, including more direct control over dice rolls and additional experience mechanics. Quiz & Dragons is notable for being a quiz game with a fully developed adventure structure, especially unusual for a Capcom CPS-1 arcade release.

games.title: QB-3
games.description:
QB-3 is an unreleased 1982 color-vector arcade shooter developed by Rock-Ola. The player guides a tiny figure around the faces of a rotating cube, blasting enemies that occupy the surfaces and collecting dollar-sign bonuses. When the character walks beyond the edge of one face, the cube rotates to reveal another, changing the direction and arrangement of the threats. This unusual shifting playfield makes navigation part of the challenge rather than merely an obstacle between the player and the targets.

The game reached an advanced prototype stage but was never commercially launched. Its rare surviving code preserves a creative attempt to combine vector graphics, shooting, and a rotating three-dimensional illusion at a time when most arcade shooters still used fixed or simply scrolling screens.

games.title: Q*bert
games.description:
Q*bert is Gottlieb's seminal 1982 arcade action-puzzle game, built around a pyramid of colorful cubes shown from an isometric perspective. Players guide the round, long-nosed Q*bert with a diagonally mounted four-way joystick, hopping from cube to cube to change every top surface to the required color. The goal sounds simple, but enemies appear from above and along the pyramid's edges, forcing quick changes of route. Leaping off the structure usually costs a life, while limited flying-disc escapes can carry Q*bert away from danger.

Enemies have distinct personalities and behavior. Coily begins as a bouncing ball before becoming a pursuing snake, while other creatures reverse progress by changing cube colors or block paths. Later rounds require repeated visits to certain cubes, turning the pyramid into a demanding exercise in route planning and timing. Q*bert's garbled speech, cartoon expressions, and famous swearing symbols make the hazards feel like a slapstick comedy.

Created by programmer Warren Davis, artist Jeff Lee, and sound designer David Thiel, Q*bert was a major arcade hit and an unusually characterful game for its era. Its abstract Escher-like pyramid, diagonal controls, memorable sound effects, and merchandising made it one of the icons of the early-1980s arcade boom. Unlike a straightforward platform game, its real challenge comes from transforming the entire playfield while staying ahead of multiple pursuers.

games.title: Q*bert's Qubes
games.description:
Q*bert's Qubes is Mylstar's 1983 sequel to Q*bert, replacing the original pyramid's simple color-changing tiles with rotating, three-sided cubes. As Q*bert hops between the 25 cubes of a diamond-shaped playfield, each move rotates the cube he leaves behind. The challenge is to line up the colors on the visible faces with a target cube and then create horizontal, vertical, or diagonal lines of matching cubes, much like tic-tac-toe. Completing the required number of lines advances the round.

The game keeps the diagonal joystick movement and bizarre enemies of the original, but demands much more planning because a hop changes the state of the board in a different way depending on direction. Characters such as Meltniks, a rat, and purple pursuers interfere with attempts to complete lines, while helpful pickups can temporarily slow or freeze enemies. Its complex spatial puzzle made it a less immediate game than Q*bert, but an intriguing continuation for players who wanted more than another pyramid of colored tiles.

games.title: Quiz Crayon Shinchan
games.description: Quiz Crayon Shin-chan is a 1993 Japanese arcade quiz game from Taito based on Yoshito Usui's popular comedy manga and animated television series. The familiar young troublemaker Shinnosuke Nohara gives the trivia format a recognizable character identity instead of the anonymous presentation of many quiz cabinets. Released in August 1993, the game uses a five-button quiz control arrangement, placing a contemporary television phenomenon in Taito's coin-operated lineup.

games.title: Crayon Shinchan Orato Asobo
games.description: Crayon Shinchan: Ora to Asobo is a 1993 Japanese arcade collection of short mini-games based on the irreverent manga and anime character Shinnosuke Nohara. Rather than following a single action format, it moves between simple challenges such as quizzes and tug-of-war contests, using the familiar cartoon cast and humorous presentation to hold the collection together. The controls are straightforward enough for quick arcade sessions, and the varied activities emphasize timing, simple decisions, and playful competition. It is a distinctly family-oriented companion to the many more conventional arcade quiz games produced in Japan during the early 1990s.

games.title: Quiz Do Re Mi Fa Grand Prix
games.series: Quiz Do Re Mi Fa Grand Prix

variants.title: Quiz Do Re Mi Fa Grand Prix (Japan)

games.description: Quiz Do Re Mi Fa Grand Prix is Konami's 1994 Japanese arcade quiz game organized around popular music and musical recognition. Instead of relying exclusively on written general-knowledge questions, it challenges contestants with music-themed trivia, including identifying songs from short introductions or opening phrases. The focus on recognizable tunes and contemporary Japanese entertainment makes it a particularly period-specific quiz title, with much of its challenge dependent on familiarity with the music of its original audience.

games.title: Quiz Do Re Mi Fa Grand Prix2 - Shin-Kyoku Nyuukadayo
games.series: Quiz Do Re Mi Fa Grand Prix

variants.title: Quiz Do Re Mi Fa Grand Prix2 - Shin-Kyoku Nyuukadayo (Japan)

games.description: Quiz Do Re Mi Fa Grand Prix 2: Shin-Kyoku Nyuukadayo is Konami's 1995 continuation of its Japanese music-trivia arcade game. It retains the emphasis on music knowledge and audio-based questions while introducing a refreshed selection of songs and entertainment topics. The subtitle refers to the arrival of new songs, highlighting the way this type of arcade quiz depended on up-to-date material rather than a fixed set of timeless questions. It is an expansion of the music-quiz format rather than a conventional rhythm-action game.

games.title: Quiz Gakumon no Susume

variants.title: Quiz Gakumon no Susume (Japan ver. JA2 Type L)

games.description: Quiz Gakumon no Susume is a Japanese arcade trivia game released by Konami in 1993. Its title can be rendered as 'Quiz: Get That Scholarship', and its presentation casts the player as a student working through an academic setting. Questions are delivered by different teachers, turning a series of multiple-choice challenges into a lighthearted examination of the player's knowledge. The classroom theme gives this otherwise traditional question-and-answer game an identifiable setting, fitting the period's Japanese arcade boom in elaborate, character-driven quizzes.

games.title: Quiz Ghost Hunter
games.description: Quiz Ghost Hunter is a 1994 Japanese arcade trivia game published by Sega and developed by C.P. Brain. It gives the question-and-answer format a supernatural, ghost-hunting theme and runs on Sega's high-resolution System 24 hardware, normally associated with a very different mix of action and arcade releases. The game was issued in Japan in September 1994; preserved versions include a ROM-based board variant.

games.title: Qix
games.description:
Qix is Taito America's groundbreaking 1981 action-puzzle game, designed by Randy and Sandy Pfeiffer. The playfield is a large, empty rectangle patrolled by the strange, unpredictable Qix, a moving mass of abstract lines. The player controls a marker that travels along the boundary and draws new lines into the unclaimed area. When a line reconnects safely to an existing border, part of the playfield is enclosed and filled. Capturing the required proportion of the screen completes the level.

Two buttons offer different drawing speeds, with slower, riskier lines yielding a greater reward. The Qix must never touch an unfinished line, and moving enemies known as Sparx patrol the boundaries. As more territory is captured, the space available for maneuvering shrinks and the dangers become harder to manage. Deciding when to draw one large region or several smaller ones is the heart of its strategy.

Qix was a striking departure from the theme-driven arcade hits of its day, relying on geometry, territory control, and tension rather than recognizable characters or combat. Its concept inspired a long lineage of 'draw to claim the screen' games and was widely adapted for home systems. The title is pronounced 'Kicks', an idiosyncratic detail that suits its abstract design.

games.title: Quiz Jinsei Gekijoh
games.description: Quiz Jinsei Gekijoh is Taito's 1993 Japanese arcade blend of trivia and a board-game-like journey through human life. Its title means roughly 'Quiz Human Life Theatre', and progression uses a sugoroku-style board whose spaces represent episodes along the characters' life paths. Successful quiz answers move the player through the unfolding sequence, turning general-knowledge questions into events within a comic simulation of life's milestones. The combination of a personal-life theme and board-game structure gives it a more narrative identity than a straightforward collection of unrelated trivia questions.

games.title: Quiz-Mahjong Hayaku Yatteyo!
games.description: Quiz-Mahjong Hayaku Yatteyo! is a 1991 Nichibutsu arcade hybrid of Japanese mahjong, trivia, and board-game progression. Players move along a virtual board and encounter different challenges depending on where they land, sometimes playing mahjong and sometimes answering quiz questions. The game is also part of Nichibutsu's adult-oriented mahjong catalog, using its characteristic anime-style female character illustrations as part of the presentation. The alternation between tile-based play and question-and-answer tests makes it more varied than a standard one-on-one mahjong game.

games.title: Quiz Nanairo Dreams: Nijiirochou no Kiseki

variants.title: Quiz Nanairo Dreams: Nijiirochou no Kiseki (Japan 960826)

games.description:
Quiz Nanairo Dreams: Nijiirochou no Kiseki is Capcom's unusual 1996 CPS-2 game that combines a trivia quiz with a romantic adventure. Players move through a board-game-like fantasy world, answering questions to progress the story and strengthen relationships with a cast of heroines. Correct answers not only help the journey continue but also improve the characters' affection, making knowledge and performance central to the game's dating-simulation structure.

The broader objective is to befriend the heroines, obtain seven magical crystals, and confront an evil threat. Multiple routes and relationship scenes give the game more replay value than a fixed sequence of quizzes. Its cheerful character art and story-heavy presentation made it an especially distinctive Capcom arcade release; one heroine, Saki, later appeared as an assist character in Marvel vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes.

games.title: Quintoon
games.description: Quintoon's Dutch edition is a 1993 single-player BFM/ELAM electronic redemption and slot-style machine, distributed as game-card programs 95-750-243 and 95-750-136. It uses a five-button panel and a horizontal video display driven by Motorola 6809-family electronics. This set is specifically the Dutch regional version, distinct from the separately preserved UK Quintoon program. Although the exact prize combinations are not documented, the localized software and hardware illustrate the regional tailoring of European amusement machines.

games.title: Quiz Rouka Ni Tattenasai
games.description: Quiz Rouka Ni Tattenasai! is a Sega System 24 quiz adventure released in Japan in December 1991, despite the later year sometimes attached to its database entry. A sequel to Quiz Shukudai wo Wasuremashita!, it strands its characters in the past and sends them searching for the missing components of a time machine. Progress depends on answering four-choice questions, with the selection of questions influenced by the birthday entered at the beginning. The cast includes the eccentric Doctor Doc and a robot named Scooter. Sega's own records describe support for up to four simultaneous players, making this a particularly sociable example of Japan's story-driven arcade quiz games.

games.title: Quiz Sangokushi
games.description: Quiz Sangokushi: Chiryaku no Hasha is a 1991 Japanese trivia game built around the wars and rivalries of the Three Kingdoms era. The title refers to a 'champion of ingenuity', and its illustrations draw on the characters and atmosphere of the famous Chinese historical saga. Players encounter quiz questions within this war-themed presentation rather than simply working through a neutral question bank. Its historical imagery also connects it to Jangokushi: Haou no Saihai, a mahjong title that reused some of the same character sprites.

games.title: Quiz Syukudai wo Wasuremashita
games.description: Quiz Syukudai wo Wasuremashita, or 'Quiz: I Forgot My Homework', is a 1991 Japanese arcade game from Sega that mixes trivia with a school-themed adventure. In its comic story, an adult couple are transformed into children by the eccentric Dr. Tenma and must overcome a sequence of school rivals and quiz challenges to recover their normal lives. The board-game-like progression and cartoon story turn question answering into a series of encounters, rather than an impersonal test of general knowledge. Released for Sega's System 24 platform, it represents the early-1990s Japanese fascination with narrative quiz machines.

games.title: Quiz Theater - 3tsu no Monogatari
games.description:
Quiz Theater: 3tsu no Monogatari, or Three Stories, is a 1994 Taito quiz game released on the F3 cartridge system. Its theatrical, story-oriented presentation extends a series begun by Hot-B, and its design reflects the movement of former Hot-B staff into Taito after that company's collapse. Supporting four participants and four answer buttons, it brings a multi-player trivia contest to hardware more widely recognized for colorful action and puzzle titles.

The game was released in Japan in November 1994. Its music gained a later archival release through Taito's Zuntata label, which included material from the game on the limited Zuntata Rare Selection: Impromptu album in 2000. That soundtrack preservation is a notable part of the legacy of an otherwise relatively little-known quiz title.

games.title: Quiz Tonosama no Yabou
games.description:
Quiz Tonosama no Yabou is Capcom's 1991 Japanese historical trivia game set during the Sengoku period. Players take the role of a feudal warlord, attempting to expand their territory by defeating rival lords in quiz battles. Each attempt to conquer a province leads to questions that can cover a broad range of subjects, including general knowledge, popular culture, and entertainment rather than only Japanese history.

By making the map of Japan and its rival daimyo the framework for question-and-answer encounters, the game turns traditional quiz success into a form of territorial strategy. The result is a distinctive hybrid of historical parody and the competitive arcade trivia format.

games.title: Quiz Tonosama no Yabou 2 Zenkoku-ban
games.description: Quiz Tonosama no Yabou 2: Zenkoku-ban is Capcom's 1995 sequel to its feudal-Japan strategy quiz game. It once again presents the player as a lord seeking control of the country, with trivia contests standing in for battles against rival provinces and commanders. The 'Zenkoku-ban' subtitle identifies the nationwide edition, broadening the territorial ambition of the original's Sengoku-era setting. Like its predecessor, the appeal is the humorous contrast between the grand business of unifying Japan and the very modern knowledge needed to win quiz encounters.

games.title: Quiz Torimonochou
games.description:
Quiz Torimonochou is Taito's 1990 Japanese arcade trivia adventure, framed as a comic period drama involving the lords Heihachi and Nariyoshi. Players progress through a sequence of rounds by selecting answers to four-choice questions with dedicated buttons, earning points for quick correct responses and losing life markers for mistakes. Its story and presentation evoke a historical arrest-and-investigation tale rather than a conventional television game show.

The game is particularly challenging to players unfamiliar with Japanese, because success depends on reading kanji, hiragana, and katakana. It was released on Taito F2 hardware and later converted for the Sharp X68000, making it a noteworthy example of an arcade quiz deeply rooted in its domestic language and cultural context.

games.title: Quantum
games.description:
Quantum is Atari's extraordinarily inventive 1982 color-vector arcade game, developed by General Computer Corporation. Players use a trackball to control a glowing probe, which leaves a trail behind as it races around the screen. Completing a loop captures the atomic particles caught inside, with each enclosure awarding points or eliminating targets. A stage ends when all required nuclei have been trapped. Touching hazardous particles or bonds destroys the probe, so the challenge is to draw large, efficient loops at high speed without crossing danger.

The abstract science theme is given visual life through bright vector lines, orbiting particles, and unpredictable movement. There are no conventional fire buttons: the entire game is built around guiding a moving point with the trackball and closing its trail. Different types of particles and active bonds complicate the geometry, rewarding quick reactions and confident movement rather than cautious exploration.

Quantum was developed during Atari's collaboration with GCC, the company behind the famous Super Missile Attack enhancement for Missile Command. Designer Betty Ryan played a leading role, an important early example of a woman designing a major arcade game. The machine was also unusual for letting passersby interact with the attract mode and for allowing players to draw their initials with the trackball. Its limited production and distinctive controls have made it one of Atari's most sought-after vector-game curiosities.

games.title: Quadro Quiz II
games.description: Quadro Quiz II is a German-language trivia arcade game released by Status Games in 1985. Players answer questions across a range of subjects using four dedicated selection buttons rather than action controls. It belongs to the European question-and-answer cabinet tradition of the mid-1980s, when localized language and subject matter were important parts of a quiz machine's appeal.

games.title: Quarterback
games.description:
Quarterback is a 1987 American-football arcade game from Leland Corporation, offering play against the computer or another player. On offense, the player chooses a play and maneuvers the quarterback to find an opening for a run or a pass. Defensive play involves anticipating the opponent's strategy and stopping the ball carrier before the offense gains ground. Its joystick-driven action and play selection give it a mixture of tactical football decisions and immediate arcade movement.

The game emerged from the company that continued the arcade work of Cinematronics under Leland's ownership. Multiple board and cabinet revisions were produced, including a cocktail version, showing how the company adapted its sports games to different arcade installations.

games.title: Quartet
games.description:
Quartet is Sega's 1986 side-scrolling run-and-gun platform game designed for up to four simultaneous players. Players select from Joe, Mary, Lee, and Edgar, a team of differently colored heroes fighting through a sprawling space base overrun by robots. Each stage is a maze of platforms, doors, and enemies, and progression requires defeating a boss, collecting its key, and finding the level's exit. Weapons and other bonuses appear along the way, including jet packs that make the many elevated passages easier to navigate.

The original large cabinet's four-player support was its defining feature, turning the game into a chaotic cooperative expedition as the group scattered across the scrolling levels. Its soundtrack by Sega's arcade sound team became particularly well regarded, and the game's blend of platform exploration and shooting gave it a character quite different from contemporary single-screen arena games.

Quartet later received a more compact two-player adaptation, Quartet 2, which retains the basic stages and gameplay but changes the cabinet and player arrangement. The original remains one of Sega's memorable experiments in multiplayer cooperative arcade action before the later boom in four-player beat 'em ups.

games.title: Quartet 2
games.description:
Quartet 2 is Sega's 1986 two-player adaptation of the four-player arcade game Quartet. Players guide armed heroes through a side-scrolling space base, collecting weapons and occasional jet packs, destroying robots, and defeating stage bosses to obtain the keys needed to reach each exit. Despite the numeral in its title, it is not a wholly new story-driven sequel: it largely repackages the Quartet gameplay for smaller two-player cabinets.

The most important difference is the reduction from four simultaneous players to two, changing the cooperative experience and making the game practical for ordinary upright installations. The Japanese Quartet 2 version preserved here represents that alternate cabinet configuration and regional release.

games.title: Quasar
games.description:
Quasar is a pioneering 1980 arcade space shooter from the Italian manufacturer Zaccaria, one of the company's earliest original video games. Its structure is unusual for the period: a complete cycle passes through four different forms of play rather than repeating a single enemy formation. The opening phase resembles Space Invaders, with the ship moving along the bottom of the screen to shoot descending UFOs. A second phase opens up movement across the playfield against formations of hostile spacecraft, with fuel becoming an additional concern.

A third phase asks the player to follow a tractor beam toward the quasar while avoiding meteors. In the final confrontation, the ship stays at the center and rotates to fire at surrounding targets. Surviving all four phases restarts the sequence at a higher difficulty. This mixture of fixed shooting, free movement, navigation, and a rotating defense phase was ambitious for an early raster arcade game.

Produced by a company better known for pinball machines, Quasar is an important piece of Italy's own arcade-development history. Its successive variations on space combat make it an interesting contrast to the more standardized wave-based shooters dominating the start of the 1980s.

games.title: Quester
games.description:
Quester is Namco's 1987 Japanese block-breaking game, created in the wake of the enormous success of Taito's Arkanoid. Players use a rotary controller to slide a paddle across the bottom of the screen, bouncing a ball into colorful brick formations and trying to destroy them without allowing the ball to fall. Certain blocks reveal power-ups that widen the paddle, change the ball's behavior, or provide other advantages, while unusual stage arrangements demand accurate angle control.

The game comprises dozens of rounds and makes extensive use of Namco-themed imagery. Some brick patterns depict recognizable figures or spacecraft from earlier Namco hits, including Pac-Man and Galaxian, giving the game the feel of a lighthearted celebration of the company's history. Its spinner-driven controls and precise ricochet play make it a polished, if relatively obscure, counterpart to Arkanoid.

games.title: Quintoon
games.description: Quintoon is a 1993 British BFM electronic redemption and slot-style game, represented here by UK game-card software. Designed for a dedicated button-controlled cabinet, it uses 6809-based electronics and a horizontal screen. Its nine-button controls in the supplied older profile distinguish this UK set from the Dutch Quintoon entry, which is preserved separately with different regional game cards. The game belongs to BFM's family of pub and amusement gambling machines; its exact prize sequence is not reliably documented.

games.title: Quiz
games.description: Quiz is a 1986 Italian-language trivia machine associated with Elettronolo, preserved in AdvanceMAME through an Italian bootleg of its second revision. Players work through numbered rounds of general-knowledge questions, selecting one of three numbered answers with dedicated buttons before the on-screen countdown expires. Surviving screens include cinema questions, with the running score and remaining seconds displayed alongside the choices. The Z80-based board and its later revised question sets make it a small but distinctive example of the locally produced quiz cabinets that circulated outside the major Japanese and American arcade markets.

games.title: Miyasu Nonki no Quiz 18-Kin
games.description: Miyasu Nonki no Quiz 18-Kin is a 1992 Japanese adult-oriented quiz game built around illustrations associated with manga artist Nonki Miyasu. Players answer trivia questions through dedicated buttons, with the correct responses advancing a presentation of humorous and erotic character artwork. The '18-kin' in the title identifies the game as intended for adults, marking it as part of Japan's niche market for mature coin-operated quiz and mahjong machines. Its defining feature is the connection between a conventional quiz format and the specific visual style of its credited artist.

games.title: Quiz
games.description: Quiz, revision 2.11, is an Italian-language quiz arcade program documented as a 1991 update to a board originally made in 1986. The revised software introduced new question categories while retaining the earlier machine's five-button quiz interface. Its history is particularly unusual because the original 1986 game survives in emulation as a bootleg, whereas the 2.11 revision was recovered from an original manufactured PCB. The ROM name quiz211 identifies this later software revision, not a separate quiz franchise.

games.title: Quiz 365
games.description: Quiz 365 is a 1994 Japanese arcade trivia game from Nakanihon, presented as a spoof television quiz program. Its title refers to a daily quiz-show format, and its staging draws on Japanese broadcast conventions, even substituting the name 'HNK' for the familiar public broadcaster NHK. Mock program breaks and sponsor announcements reinforce the impression of participating in an eccentric television production. The emphasis on a television-show atmosphere distinguishes it from more simply presented question-and-answer machines, although its appeal is strongly tied to the language and popular culture of its original Japanese audience.

games.title: Quiz Channel Question
games.description: Quiz Channel Question is a 1993 quiz arcade game associated with KM Korea, with Japanese and other East Asian regional program variants preserved. Players use four answer buttons on a conventional quiz cabinet, while the different versions reflect the importance of language and regional question banks in arcade trivia games. An oddity in its implementation is an internal clock that fails to handle years after 1999 properly; a documented example displays 1906 in place of 2006.

games.title: Quiz Meitantei Neo & Geo - Quiz Daisousa Sen part 2
games.description:
SNK's Quiz Meitantei Neo & Geo: Quiz Daisousa Sen Part 2 (1992) reunites private detectives Neo McDonald and Geo Kentucky in a Japanese-language quiz adventure for the Neo Geo. Instead of simply answering isolated trivia questions, players investigate mysteries, speak with characters and overcome quiz challenges to move the story forward. Two scenarios can be selected at the outset: a time-travel mystery called Love Over Time and an alien-conspiracy case called Client from Space.

The sequel expands its predecessor's quiz repertoire with a bingo challenge requiring three correct answers in a row, timed yes-or-no questions, slot-machine-style question selection and picture-comparison puzzles. It also adds question categories while dropping the original game's competitive Sugoroku board-game mode. The combination of detective melodrama and varied quiz formats is an unusually story-driven use of SNK's fighting-game-oriented Neo Geo hardware.

games.title: Quiz Daisousa Sen - The Last Count Down
games.description:
Quiz Daisousa Sen: The Last Count Down is a 1991 Neo Geo quiz adventure that introduced SNK's private investigators Neo McDonald and Geo Kentucky. The two detectives become entangled in comic-book-style mysteries, and players solve their problems not by fighting but by answering Japanese-language trivia questions. Story mode offers distinct investigative scenarios, including a missing-dog case that escalates into an international criminal conspiracy.

Alongside the story is a two-player Sugoroku mode, a board-game contest involving a treasure hunt and rival adventurers. Quiz challenges vary in presentation, including special stages in which correct answers help the detectives advance through an action scene or climb a tower. Its blend of branching adventures, cartoon storytelling and trivia led to a direct sequel, Quiz Meitantei Neo & Geo, in 1992.

games.title: Quiz DNA no Hanran
games.description: Quiz DNA no Hanran (1992), developed by Face for Japanese arcades, is a fast-paced two-player trivia game whose title roughly means 'Revolt of DNA.' Players use four answer buttons to respond to questions written in Japanese, sometimes facing brief sequences of several questions in quick succession. Its distinctive visual presentation mixes quiz screens with surreal, science-fiction-flavored imagery, setting it apart from more conventional televised-game-show imitations.

games.title: Quiz F-1 1,2finish
games.description: Irem's Quiz F-1 1,2finish (1992) recasts a Formula One championship as a trivia competition. Players select a racing team and qualify by answering rapid true-or-false questions; accuracy and speed influence their starting positions. The subsequent race unfolds as a season of sixteen Grands Prix in which correct answers advance the car and mistakes cost positions. Rather than requiring conventional steering skill, the game transforms the pressure of motor racing into a battle of knowledge and quick responses, with a joystick and four answer buttons on Irem arcade hardware.

games.title: Quiz H.Q.
games.description:
Quiz H.Q. is Taito's 1990 Japanese-only quiz spin-off of its car-chase hit Chase H.Q. Detectives Tony Gibson and Raymond Broady return, but apprehending criminals now depends on answering four-choice questions against the clock. Correct answers bring their sports cars closer to fleeing suspects; mistakes deplete a supply of wrench-shaped life markers. Both players can participate, with Tony driving the familiar black Porsche and Broady the red Nissan 300ZX associated with S.C.I.

The stages retain an elaborate police-chase framing. Gas-station stops offer chances to replenish lives, while bar visits introduce matching-card bonuses. At the end of a chase, the viewpoint switches to a pursuit sequence where each right answer makes the police ram the criminal's vehicle. Arrests lead to a bonus target-shooting quiz. This odd but imaginative hybrid exemplifies Taito's early-1990s habit of adapting established action series to Japan's popular quiz-game format.

games.title: Moriguchi Hiroko no Quiz de Hyuu!Hyuu!

variants.title: Moriguchi Hiroko no Quiz de Hyuu!Hyuu! (Ver 2.2J 1995/05/25)

games.description: Moriguchi Hiroko no Quiz de Hyuu!Hyuu! is a 1995 quiz game for Taito's F3 system built around Japanese singer and television personality Hiroko Moriguchi. Its defining feature is the presentation: the attract sequence imitates a real Japanese television program, complete with announcer, studio-show theatrics and a mock sponsorship credit naming Taito. Up to four participants can answer questions, making it a distinctly social alternative to the publisher's action games. The title's 'hyuu-hyuu' is an enthusiastic Japanese sound expression, reinforcing the atmosphere of a lively televised quiz show.

games.title: Quiz King of Fighters
games.description:
Quiz King of Fighters (1995) turns SNK's famous fighting-game characters into contestants in a comic quiz adventure. When Yuri Sakazaki is kidnapped, players choose one of six heroes from three SNK series: Ryo and Robert from Art of Fighting, Terry and Mai from Fatal Fury, or Haohmaru and Nakoruru from Samurai Shodown. A branching board-game map determines encounters, and rolling a die moves the chosen fighter toward quiz duels with familiar opponents.

Wrong answers reduce the character's health, replacing punches and special moves with the pressure of timed trivia. Cameos from across SNK's fighting universes provide much of the appeal. Released on Neo Geo hardware and later adapted for the Korean market, it is an unusual crossover in which knowing the answers matters more than executing combos.

games.title: Quiz Mekurumeku Story
games.description: Quiz Mekurumeku Story is a Sega quiz-and-board-game hybrid released in Japanese arcades in May 1993, although its title screen carries a 1992 copyright. Up to four players guide children who have become lost in a land of quizzes and must find their way home by answering questions. Each prescribed run of correct answers earns opportunities to turn over panels on a 7-by-7 board. Panels can produce different effects, and enclosing panels of one color between matching colors changes their ownership, adding a territory-control element to the trivia competition. The player with the most panels can enter an additional spot-the-difference adventure. Its mixture of narrative, quizzes, and tactical panel flipping gives it a distinctive place among Sega's System 24 releases.

games.title: Quiz Bisyoujo Senshi Sailor Moon - Chiryoku Tairyoku Toki no Un
games.description:
Quiz Bisyoujo Senshi Sailor Moon: Chiryoku Tairyoku Toki no Un (1997) combines Banpresto's Sailor Moon license with a Japanese quiz board game. After choosing a Sailor Guardian, the player rolls a virtual die to move across a map, meets monsters and bosses from the series, and answers questions to resolve encounters. Between quiz sessions the game returns to the map for another roll, creating a rhythm closer to an animated tabletop adventure than to a conventional action game.

Character art, voice clips, music and animated scenes give the production the atmosphere of the television series. Released in Japan for one or two players, it is particularly notable as a late-1990s character-licensed arcade quiz with an elaborate audiovisual presentation.

games.title: Quizmaster
games.description:
Quizmaster is a German-language arcade trivia game dating to 1985, credited to Löwen Spielautomaten in surviving emulator records and to Coinmaster in historical listings. Players respond to on-screen questions through a button-only control panel, making knowledge of the German question bank more important than reflexes. The machine uses a Z80 processor, an AY-3-8910 sound chip, and a horizontal display.

Its history intersects with the emergence of Britain's skill-with-prize quiz machines: Coinmaster's Quizmaster was an early title in that field. The precise relationship between the preserved German version and British prize-paying equipment, including whether the German installation paid prizes, is not firmly documented. That uncertainty is worth preserving rather than treating every surviving Quizmaster set as the same commercial machine.

games.title: Quiz Panicuru Fantasy
games.description: Quiz Panicuru Fantasy is an early-1990s Japanese quiz game from NMK, wrapping multiple-choice trivia in a fantasy-themed presentation. Four answer buttons form the central control interface. A separate Medal Quiz Panicuru Roulette edition was subsequently preserved as a related variation, showing that the concept was adapted for the Japanese medal-machine market as well as conventional video-quiz play.

games.title: Nettou! Gekitou! Quiztou!!
games.description:
Namco's Nettou! Gekitou! Quiztou!! (1993), roughly 'Hot Battle! Fierce Battle! Quiz Island!!', is a four-player Japanese trivia contest built around territorial conquest. Each competitor begins in a different corner of a 36-square island and captures adjacent areas by clearing multiple-choice question stages. Special squares offer picture questions, alternative answer formats, time bonuses or a choice of question categories.

The game becomes especially competitive when a player enters territory already held by another participant or a computer-controlled rival. Ownership is contested through a demanding eight-question challenge whose answers share a common keyword, and a single mistake can repel the invader. After the island is conquered, an enormous subterranean demon presents a final quiz. The mixture of board-game tactics, cartoon enemies and simultaneous four-player rivalry makes it one of Namco's more elaborate quiz releases.

games.title: Quiz TV Gassyuukoku Q&Q
games.description: Quiz TV Gassyuukoku Q&Q is a 1992 Japanese trivia game from Dynax that borrows the look and atmosphere of a television quiz program. One or two participants select answers using dedicated four-button controls as the game presents Japanese-language questions. Its game-show framing and local subject matter place it firmly within the boom in domestic Japanese arcade quiz titles of the early 1990s.

games.title: Qwak
games.description:
Atari's Qwak (1982) is an unreleased animated sliding-block puzzle prototype, not the unrelated 1974 Atari duck-shooting game Qwak!. It adapts the classic fifteen-puzzle idea, rearranging pieces within a confined grid to complete an arrangement, and runs on Atari's 6502-based color raster hardware. The prototype is notable for using moving-object graphics for text rather than treating all lettering as static background artwork.

Atari reportedly evaluated a touch-screen interface during development, but focus-group players preferred a conventional joystick or buttons. The game never received a commercial arcade release; its surviving prototype ROMs were dumped in 1998. It offers a glimpse of Atari experimenting with puzzle gameplay and alternative controls well before touch-screen arcade games became commonplace.

games.title: Quiz Chikyu Bouei Gun
games.description: Quiz Chikyu Bouei Gun, meaning Quiz Earth Defense Force, is a Taito quiz game for the F2 arcade system. Despite its 1991 copyright, Japanese arcade records date its release to February 1992. Its title provides a science-fiction or military-flavored frame for a two-player question-and-answer game operated with five selection buttons. The music is credited to Yoshiro Horie, linking this relatively obscure quiz release with Taito's broader arcade sound production.

games.title: Quiz Kokology 2
games.description: Tecmo's Quiz Kokology 2 (1993) is a Japanese quiz and personality game built around 'kokology,' a form of playful self-discovery derived from the idea of studying the mind. Instead of relying solely on right-or-wrong factual knowledge, it asks players to consider imaginary situations and interpretive choices, then offers readings of what those choices may reveal about personality, relationships and attitudes. Following the 1992 original, the sequel keeps the approachable four-answer format and treats the arcade cabinet as a lighthearted personality-test machine rather than a conventional sports or action contest.

games.title: Quiz Kokology
games.description:
Quiz Kokology: Quiz & Shinri Game (1992) is Tecmo's unusual Japanese arcade blend of trivia and personality testing. The title refers to 'kokology,' a playful approach to understanding the mind through hypothetical situations. Players answer questions about imagined scenes and everyday choices, and the game interprets those responses as clues to personality and relationships rather than judging every response as an ordinary correct-or-incorrect fact.

Its cheerful visuals even represent players as bees, an eccentric touch for a psychology-themed cabinet. A sequel appeared in 1993, making this a small but distinctive branch of Japan's arcade quiz-game boom.

games.title: Quiz Quest - Hime to Yuusha no Monogatari

variants.title: Quiz Quest - Hime to Yuusha no Monogatari (Japan)

games.description: Quiz Quest: Hime to Yuusha no Monogatari is Taito's 1991 Japanese arcade quiz adventure, with a title meaning 'Story of the Princess and the Hero.' It replaces the usual television quiz setting with a fantasy role-playing framework: the player takes the role of a hero, and answering questions correctly defeats monsters encountered along the journey. Japanese-language multiple-choice challenges therefore serve as the substitute for conventional combat, giving the game a distinctive blend of fantasy adventure and trivia. The production runs on Taito's F2 hardware and uses five-button quiz controls.

games.title: Quiz Sekai wa SHOW by shobai

variants.title: Quiz Sekai wa SHOW by shobai (Japan)

games.description: Quiz Sekai wa SHOW by shobai brings a Japanese television quiz program to Taito's arcade hardware. Released in the early 1990s, it models its atmosphere on the popular show Sekai wa SHOW by Shobai!!, turning questions about subjects familiar to contemporary Japanese audiences into a coin-operated competition. Players use four answer buttons to respond to trivia, while the television-show license provides its principal identity. Its appeal is closely tied to the program and cultural knowledge of the period, making it a particularly local example of the Japanese quiz boom.

games.title: R2D Tank
games.description: R2D Tank is a top-down tank action game developed by Sigma and released under license by Venture Line around 1981. The player drives a tank across a single-screen battlefield, collecting dots for points while firing at enemy armored vehicles. Destroyed enemies are replaced by new attackers, and later stages increase the pressure. Red mine-like objects are both hazards and targets, since they can be cleared with the tank's gun. Its compact design combines maze-like movement with the continuous pursuit of an early arcade shooter.

games.title: Raiden II New / Raiden DX

variants.title: Raiden II New / Raiden DX (newer V33 PCB) (Raiden DX EEPROM)
Raiden II New / Raiden DX (newer V33 PCB) (Raiden II EEPROM)

games.description:
Raiden II New / Raiden DX is a 1996 reissue of Seibu Kaihatsu's vertically scrolling shooters on a newer V33-based arcade board. Depending on its EEPROM configuration, the board operates as a revised Raiden II or Raiden DX. The familiar Fighting Thunder craft still shoots through waves of tanks, aircraft and large bosses, using selectable weapons, missiles and screen-clearing bombs.

Unlike an ordinary ROM revision, this release changes the audiovisual experience and the campaign sequence. Raiden II New uses a rearranged stage order, omits some inter-stage material and replaces the original soundtrack with short sampled loops. Collectors prize the board as an unusual official hardware variation, even though its sound is much less celebrated than that of the original games.

games.title: Rabbit
games.description:
Rabbit (1997) is a colorful two-dimensional fighting game developed by Aorn and published in arcades with a roster inspired by animals of the Chinese zodiac. Its eight selectable fighters include the rabbit-themed Wu Ling, tiger-like Rex and fox-like Yu-Lan. Each martial artist is accompanied by an animal spirit whose supernatural abilities can be invoked in combat.

Fights use four buttons for light and heavy punches and kicks, alongside a spirit gauge that governs special attacks. The deliberately cartoonish art and spectacular spirit animations give Rabbit a very different look from the darker martial-arts games of its day. It was among Aorn's final productions before the studio closed.

games.title: Rabio Lepus
games.description:
Rabio Lepus (1987), released in North America as Rabbit Punch, is Video System's whimsical horizontally scrolling shooter starring rocket-powered robot rabbits. When monsters kidnap the royal family of Bunnyland, Rabio and Lepus fly through six stages packed with mechanical animals, surreal hazards and large bosses. The rabbits' basic gunfire is unlimited, but stronger homing missiles have to be replenished.

Unusually for a shooter, the protagonists can also deliver a close-range punch, useful against nearby enemies and objects. Carrot containers and other items supply rewards, extra missiles or protection, while the colorful fantasy imagery constantly contrasts with the game's demanding action. The title became a cult favorite, and one of its rabbit heroes later appeared as a hidden character in Aero Fighters 3.

games.title: Raccoon World
games.description: Raccoon World is a 1998 Korean arcade platform game by Eolith featuring a cartoon raccoon named Naudoya. Players run and jump through brightly colored side-view stages, gathering fruit while negotiating bombs, enemies and other hazards. Its cheerful presentation and straightforward two-button controls recall an earlier generation of coin-op platformers, making it an unusual release at a time when three-dimensional action games dominated new arcade hardware.

games.title: Race Drivin'
games.description:
Atari Games' Race Drivin' (1990) is the ambitious sequel to Hard Drivin', continuing the studio's attempt to make an arcade driving game behave like a real automobile rather than a simple speed challenge. Its flat-shaded polygon environments are navigated with a steering wheel, accelerator, brake, clutch, gear shifter and ignition key, while force feedback adds physical resistance to the steering. Drivers race against checkpoints and the clock while learning how different cars behave at speed.

Alongside the original stunt circuit, Race Drivin' introduces a Super Stunt track packed with improbable corkscrews, jumps and a full pipe, plus an autocross course suited to practicing lines and handling. A recorded best lap can serve as a virtual pace car, and linked cabinets permit competition. The combination of serious simulated physics with outrageous stunt architecture makes it one of the most distinctive driving cabinets of the early polygon era.

games.title: Racing Hero
games.description:
Sega's Racing Hero (1989) merges the motorcycle thrills of Hang-On with the branching road trip of Out Run. Seen from behind the rider, players accelerate through traffic on an international motorbike race, dodging cars, trucks, other motorcycles and roadside obstacles before the checkpoint timer expires. Collisions cause spectacular spills and waste precious seconds.

At the end of a stage, a route-selection screen allows players to choose the next destination, creating several possible paths through the game. Running on Sega's powerful X Board hardware, Racing Hero favors rapid sprite-scaled spectacle over realistic motorcycle simulation and stands as a lesser-known relative of the company's celebrated deluxe racing games.

games.title: Racin' Force
games.description:
Racin' Force (1994) is Konami's unusual three-dimensional sports-car racer, offering four courses ranging from fast circuits to a winding country road. Players compete against computer-controlled rivals while trying to reach checkpoints before the clock runs down, with linked cabinets supporting multiplayer races. The driving view and track surfaces have an angular, distinctive appearance because the game incorporates voxel-style rendering into its three-dimensional scenery.

The course selection, changing light conditions and emphasis on quick reaction give it the structure of a traditional arcade racer, but its graphics technology make it an intriguing outlier among Konami's mid-1990s hardware experiments.

games.title: Racing Beat
games.description: Racing Beat is a 1991 Formula One-style racing game from Taito running on the high-powered Taito Z system. Players drive from a forward-looking racing perspective, using a steering wheel and gear controls to negotiate a circuit and compete against other cars. Unlike many arcade racers that merely ask players to survive a checkpoint timer, Racing Beat includes a pit-stop feature activated from the gear-lever controls, borrowing an element of real motor racing strategy. Its cabinet presentation and racing display evoke contemporary linked-cabinet Formula One games such as Namco's Final Lap.

games.title: Racing Jam
games.description:
Konami's Racing Jam (1997/1998) is an arcade driving game that combines the excitement of a racing cabinet with the car selection and mechanical tuning associated with home driving simulations. Players choose from a large roster of cars and tackle several distinct events, including circuit races, time trials, twisting uphill and downhill roads, and gymkhana-style maneuvering tests. Adjustments to engine performance and suspension let players tailor a car to the event.

The game also has an unusual development history: initially intended to showcase Konami's advanced Cobra hardware, it ultimately appeared on the Hornet platform. A subsequent Chapter 2 release expanded the original. Racing Jam remains a striking example of Japanese arcades absorbing the late-1990s enthusiasm for car collecting and tuning.

games.title: Rack 'em Up
games.description: Konami's Rack 'em Up (1987), known in Japan as The Hustler, is a top-down billiards game offering nine-ball and rotation pool. Players line up shots, judge angles and attempt to sink the required balls using joystick and button controls rather than a physical cue. The table-focused presentation makes positioning the cue ball and planning successive shots central to success. Released at the height of Japan's arcade sports-game experimentation, it offers a relatively measured alternative to Konami's faster action titles.

games.title: Rack + Roll
games.description: Rack + Roll, also released as Hex Pool, is a 1986 arcade billiards puzzle by Shinkai, licensed to Status Games in North America. Instead of facing a computer opponent across a conventional match, the player tries to clear the table by pocketing the balls and saving the eight ball for last. Shot accuracy matters because three misses end the game. Its unusual cabinet ancestry and solitary, score-oriented interpretation of pool distinguish it from later versus billiards simulations.

games.title: Radar Scope
games.description:
Nintendo's Radar Scope (1980) is a space shooter that combines Galaxian-like diving enemy formations with a striking pseudo-three-dimensional view. The player defends the Sonic Spaceport against 48 Gamma Raiders, firing along a receding perspective grid as enemy craft break formation, swoop toward the foreground and threaten the base. Targets destroyed close to the player's position earn more points, encouraging risky last-second shooting.

Although technologically ambitious, Radar Scope failed to meet Nintendo of America's sales expectations. Large quantities of unsold cabinets became a serious financial problem for the company's young American operation. Nintendo responded by repurposing the hardware for Donkey Kong (1981), turning a failed shooter into a crucial stepping stone in the company's arcade history. That unexpected connection has made Radar Scope far more historically significant than its modest commercial success suggests.

games.title: Radar Zone
games.description: Radar Zone (1982), also distributed as Outline, is a grid-based territory-capture game from Century Electronics. The player travels along the lines of a geometric playfield and tries to enclose rectangles, claiming the points displayed inside them. Moving sparks patrol the grid edges, turning each attempt to close an area into a timing challenge. The balance between taking a safe short route and trying to capture a large region gives the simple maze design its tension. Radar Zone ran on Century's Convertible Video System and survives in several variants.

games.title: Radikal Bikers
games.description:
Gaelco's Radikal Bikers (1998) turns the daily business of pizza delivery into a frantic scooter race through stylized Italian cities. Riding an Italjet Dragster, players weave between cars and street obstacles, discover shortcuts, and try to deliver a pizza before a rival courier and the countdown timer. The colorful graphics exaggerate speed and traffic chaos rather than pursuing realistic simulation.

The three principal courses are named after pizzas: Margherita in Milan, Capricciosa in Rome and Diabola in Naples, representing increasing difficulty. Pickups provide temporary turbo acceleration, points or the ability to kick vehicles out of the way. Its lighthearted premise, competitive cabinet play and distinctly Mediterranean scenery made Radikal Bikers one of Spanish studio Gaelco's most recognizable arcade games.

games.title: Rad Mobile
games.description:
Rad Mobile (1990/1991) is a landmark Sega driving game that sends the player racing from Los Angeles toward New York in a first-person cross-country competition. The sports car must overtake rivals and avoid traffic, police and roadside hazards while reaching checkpoints before time runs out. Rain, darkness, fog and banking turns affect visibility and the view from the cockpit; players are expected to switch on the windshield wipers and headlights when conditions demand it.

The game inaugurated Sega's 32-bit System 32 arcade platform and helped advance the company's sprite-scaling approach to three-dimensional driving. It also contains a small but famous piece of company history: a Sonic the Hedgehog ornament dangles from the rear-view mirror, one of the character's first public appearances. Later adapted to Sega Saturn as Gale Racer, Rad Mobile combines technological showmanship with memorable interactive weather effects.

games.title: Rad Rally
games.description: Rad Rally (1991) is Sega's follow-up to Rad Mobile, retaining its fast first-person road racing while shifting from a transcontinental journey to a choice of four courses: Sunset, Rain, Night and Mountain. Drivers race through changing visibility conditions and busy traffic, now with a functional rear-view mirror to help track approaching competitors. Operators could also connect cabinets for head-to-head racing. The result is a more compact, competition-focused variation on the System 32 driving formula.

games.title: Radical Radial
games.description:
Radical Radial (1982) is an inventive scrolling action game in which the player controls a living wheel that can accelerate, slow down, jump and shoot. Its alternating courses combine two genres: in an alien landscape, the wheel fires at attackers and leaps over rocks; on a busy highway, it dodges unpredictable traffic, oil slicks and disabled vehicles. Emergency vehicles can send other cars skidding across the road, adding to the chaos.

After the combat and traffic sections comes a bonus course focused on gathering points. The absurd hero and constant switch between shooting and evasive driving give Radical Radial an identity far stranger than that of a conventional space shooter.

games.title: Rafflesia
games.description:
Rafflesia (1986) is a vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter developed by Coreland for Sega arcade hardware. Piloting a spacecraft through eerie alien sectors, players destroy waves of enemies before confronting large bosses, eventually challenging the entity called Rafflesia. Two forward-firing weapons are available, but using the stronger attack drains a limited energy reserve. Falling 'tears of Rafflesia' replenish that energy, so collecting them is essential to maintaining heavy firepower.

Its unsettling biological imagery and resource-dependent attack distinguish it from many straightforward mid-1980s shooters. The title shares its name with a genus of enormous parasitic flowering plants.

games.title: Ragnagard / Shin-Oh-Ken
games.description:
Ragnagard, released in Japan as Shin-Oh-Ken (1996), is a Neo Geo fighting game by Saurus built around deities and legendary figures from Japanese mythology. Its characters are modeled as prerendered, three-dimensional-looking sprites, giving the action an unusual visual texture compared with SNK's hand-drawn fighters. The roster features elemental powers and imposing mythical adversaries.

The defining mechanic is an Aerial Battle System that allows fighters to launch themselves upward, air-dash and continue combos above the ground. Players charge elemental power gauges to perform special techniques, with stronger desperation attacks available under critical health conditions. Its distinctive art and aerial mobility make it a curious experiment within the crowded 1990s arcade fighting genre.

games.title: Raiden
games.description:
Seibu Kaihatsu's Raiden (1990) became one of the defining vertically scrolling shooters of the decade. Set during an alien invasion of Earth, it puts one or two pilots in Fighting Thunder strike aircraft and sends them through eight punishing stages packed with tanks, gun emplacements, aircraft and massive bosses. The core weapons have distinct identities: the red spread shot covers wide areas, while the blue laser concentrates damage. Missile upgrades add further firepower, and a limited supply of bombs can rescue players from otherwise hopeless situations.

Raiden is admired for its carefully arranged enemy patterns, substantial challenge and cooperative play, which rewards learning where threats will emerge. Scoring bonuses and hidden secrets encourage repeated runs even after the stages become familiar. Developed under financial pressure after Seibu's earlier Dynamite Duke underperformed, it unexpectedly sold thousands of arcade boards and founded a long-running series. The powerful red-and-blue weapon choice became a recognizable hallmark of the Raiden name.

games.title: Raiden II
games.description:
Raiden II (1993) expands Seibu Kaihatsu's hit vertical shooter with bigger enemies, more elaborate destruction and a striking new weapon: the Bend Plasma. This purple energy beam curves and twists toward targets, following them as they move, while the traditional red spread shot and focused blue laser return. Two kinds of missiles and the newly introduced cluster bomb add further tactical choices.

Across eight stages, players battle relentless ground defenses, swarming aircraft and gigantic machines. Two-player cooperation remains important, with shots fired into a partner's craft able to create powerful additional projectiles. Its meticulously animated enemy explosions and spectacular purple beam became visual signatures of the series. Raiden II was followed by the more experimental Raiden DX and later reached home players through The Raiden Project compilation.

games.title: Raiden DX
games.description:
Raiden DX (1994) is Seibu Kaihatsu's substantial reworking of Raiden II rather than a simple change in difficulty. It preserves the familiar red spread shot, blue laser, purple Bend Plasma, missiles and bombs, but reorganizes the experience into three selectable missions: a short Training course, the medium-length Alpha mission and the extended, demanding Bravo mission.

Beyond these routes, DX adds numerous hidden scoring opportunities and ranks performance at the end of stages, rewarding skilled play and experimentation. The different routes give experienced players reasons to return without merely repeating Raiden II's eight-level campaign. For fans of Seibu's exacting shoot-'em-up design, it is one of the most replayable variations on the original Raiden formula.

games.title: Raiders
games.description:
Raiders is a 1983 space shooter for Century Electronics' Convertible Video System (CVS) arcade hardware. The player pilots a craft able to move vertically as well as horizontally, firing lasers and dropping bombs against descending alien formations. Its progression includes a large mothership with three vulnerable ports and a docking sequence, so the action extends beyond simply clearing repeated waves of small enemies.

Century's CVS hardware was designed to let operators convert a cabinet from one game to another, making Raiders part of an early attempt at a reusable arcade platform. The two-button, eight-direction control scheme supports the game's combination of movement, bombs and directed fire. It is a relatively obscure contemporary of the better-known Astro Fighter and Astro Blaster school of vertically oriented science-fiction shooters.

games.title: Raiders5
games.description:
Raiders5 (1985) is an unusual maze shooter by UPL, released in Japan through Taito. Players guide a small spacecraft through enclosed labyrinths full of pursuing aliens, searching for the way out while destroying walls to create new routes. Breakable targets serve both as scoring opportunities and as obstacles that must be cleared to open an exit.

Shots can temporarily stun enemies into harmless forms, letting the player move past or reposition them, while power-ups provide stronger ways to eliminate threats. By combining destructible mazes with combat and route planning, Raiders5 offers a distinctive twist on the familiar arcade maze-chase formula.

games.title: Raimais
games.description:
Taito's Raimais (1988) is a fast maze-chase game from Arkanoid designer Akira Fujita. Players control Rika Midorikawa, a young woman trying to rescue her kidnapped brother, as she drives a futuristic three-wheeled vehicle through interconnected labyrinths. Each stage requires collecting the scattered dots and finding an exit while evading hostile vehicles and other threats. A dedicated turbo button supplies bursts of speed, while a second button activates collected items such as lasers.

The game contains a long sequence of mazes, boss encounters and route choices, with the Japanese version offering a more developed story. Power-ups and the high-speed vehicle transform the Pac-Man-like premise into something closer to a dangerous futuristic road trip. Raimais also received a Famicom Disk System adaptation under the name Youmais.

games.title: Rainbow Islands
games.description:
Rainbow Islands: The Story of Bubble Bobble 2 (1987) is one of Taito's most imaginative arcade platform games. Formerly trapped as dragons in Bubble Bobble, Bubby and Bobby are now human boys ascending a series of colorful islands to defeat the Dark Shadow. Unlike the first game's fixed screens, each round scrolls upward as the player climbs toward the summit. The danger is constant: linger too long and rising water will swallow the stage from below.

The heroes' magical rainbows are extraordinarily versatile. They can strike enemies, form temporary stairways, collect items and collapse onto foes when jumped upon. Shoes, potions and other pickups enhance speed and rainbow-making ability, while learning how to stack and shatter rainbows is central to high-level play. Collecting colored diamonds in the correct circumstances also unlocks special rewards and secret endings.

Designed with deceptively simple controls but deep mechanical possibilities, Rainbow Islands became a major arcade favorite and was widely converted to home computers and consoles. Its combination of inventive traversal, memorable music, treasure hunting and escalating pressure helped establish Taito's reputation for playful, technically intricate platform games.

games.title: Rainbow Islands
games.description:
Rainbow Islands Extra is Taito's revised edition of the 1987 platform classic, represented separately from the original game in AdvanceMAME. Its fundamental mechanics remain intact: Bubby and Bobby climb vertically scrolling islands using magical rainbows as weapons, platforms and item collectors, racing ahead of rising floodwater.

The Extra edition reshuffles stage content and boss encounters, producing different challenges for players who already know the standard routes. Because enemy placement and progression are changed rather than the controls, the familiar techniques of chaining rainbows, collecting diamonds and seeking secret rewards still apply. It is best regarded as an alternate, harder campaign for one of Taito's most celebrated arcade games.

games.title: Rally Bike / Dash Yarou
games.description:
Rally Bike, released in Japan as Dash Yarou (1988), is Toaplan's demanding overhead motorcycle racer. Players weave through traffic and rival bikes on long scrolling routes through American locations, trying to finish ahead of a required number of opponents. Speed alone is not enough: fuel steadily runs down, crashes waste precious reserves, and stopping at a service area costs valuable positions.

The game forces constant trade-offs between aggressive overtaking and keeping enough fuel to reach the finish. The crowded roads, sudden hazards and unforgiving collision rules make Rally Bike feel closer to an endurance challenge than a carefree arcade sprint. It later received home conversions, but its tough, precise road racing remains distinctly Toaplan.

games.title: Rally X
games.description:
Namco's Rally-X (1980) is a landmark maze-chase game in which a blue car races through a scrolling road network collecting ten flags while evading pursuing red vehicles. Enemy cars are faster than the player's, making route planning essential. A limited fuel supply doubles as a resource for laying smoke screens, which temporarily disable pursuers, and stationary rocks complicate escape routes. A small radar display reveals the positions of flags and enemies beyond the visible portion of the maze.

The game helped establish features that became familiar in later arcade action games, including a scrolling maze, overhead radar and special challenge rounds. Although its success was overshadowed by Namco's Pac-Man, Rally-X developed a lasting following and inspired New Rally-X in 1981. Its deceptively simple car-and-flag premise rewards map awareness and careful use of the smoke button rather than pure reaction speed.

games.title: Rambo III
games.description:
Taito's Rambo III (1989) is an arcade shooting game based on the Sylvester Stallone action film. Players direct an on-screen aiming cursor across scenes of Soviet-occupied Afghanistan, blasting armed soldiers, vehicles and installations while advancing through successive combat encounters. Despite the film license, the arcade version emphasizes continuous shooting and spectacular set pieces rather than narrative detail.

Rambo and Colonel Trautman are represented in the two-player action, and tanks and other heavily armed enemies provide major confrontations. Its crosshair-based controls and densely populated battlefields distinguish it from the unrelated side-scrolling and overhead home-console adaptations of the same movie.

games.title: Rampage
games.description:
Rampage (1986) is Bally Midway's gleeful reversal of the traditional arcade hero fantasy: up to three players control monsters whose sole ambition is to destroy cities. George the giant ape, Lizzie the reptile and Ralph the wolf climb skyscrapers, smash windows, pulverize buildings and devour anything edible they discover. Military helicopters, tanks, police and soldiers try to stop the demolition, but the monsters can even punch and injure one another.

Each building crumbles as its structural sections are destroyed, creating a satisfying cycle of climbing, punching and watching the city collapse. Food restores health, while toxic objects and falls can inflict damage. When a monster's health runs out, the creature shrinks back into a vulnerable human. The game strings together dozens of cities over many in-game days, making destruction itself the attraction.

Inspired by giant-monster movies such as King Kong and Godzilla, Rampage became a memorable three-player arcade favorite and a frequent subject of home conversions. Its humorous animations and cooperative-but-competitive chaos produced a formula that sustained sequels and later film adaptations.

games.title: Rampart
games.description:
Atari Games' Rampart (1990) is a pioneering hybrid of strategy, action and spatial puzzle-solving. Each round cycles through three interlocking tasks: assemble irregular wall sections to enclose a castle, position cannons inside the defenses, then aim and fire at invading ships or rival players' fortresses. When the bombardment ends, the player has only moments to rebuild damaged walls before the next attack. A castle left unenclosed cannot be defended, so even a strong offensive position can collapse through poor repair work.

The building phase resembles an urgent game of Tetris played across an irregular battlefield, while the combat phase recalls Missile Command. Arcade cabinets commonly used trackballs for rapid cursor control, and multiplayer matches turn the construction puzzle into a direct competition for territory. Its tightly coupled cycle of building defenses and repelling attackers is often cited as an early ancestor of the tower-defense genre.

games.title: Rapid Hero
games.description:
Rapid Hero (1994), also known in an international version as Arcadia, is a vertical-scrolling shooter from NMK. Players select between two aircraft with different firing patterns, one concentrating damage straight ahead and the other spreading shots across a wider area. Collectible upgrades provide stronger weapons, auxiliary fire and guided attacks, while large mechanical enemies dominate the screen.

The stages make dramatic use of aerial perspective, with enemy craft appearing through clouds and enormous warships filling the scrolling playfield. Created by developers associated with Thunder Dragon 2, Rapid Hero preserves NMK's interest in formidable military machinery and densely staged battles.

games.title: Rapid Fire
games.description:
Rapid Fire (1998) is a competitive light-gun shooting game from HanaHo that emphasizes quick recognition and accurate aim rather than a continuous military storyline. One or two players tackle a succession of short target-shooting scenes, striking the required objects before the timer expires and avoiding mistakes that hurt their performance. The scenes move through different historical and fantasy settings, from pirates to post-apocalyptic action.

Its many miniature challenges and increasing difficulty make it closer to a shooting-gallery contest than a conventional on-rails adventure. The accessible presentation and emphasis on head-to-head scoring were designed for repeat arcade play.

games.title: Rastan
games.description:
Rastan Saga, known outside Japan as Rastan (1987), is Taito's celebrated sword-and-sorcery action platformer. A muscular barbarian crosses six dangerous stages of rocky wilderness, caverns and fortresses, battling skeletons, demons, monsters and huge bosses. An eight-way joystick and separate attack and jump buttons let players slash in different directions, leap over traps and attack while airborne.

The hero begins with a sword but can find axes, maces and other weapons, as well as armor, shields, jewelry and health-restoring items. Many improvements are temporary, making it important to use each pickup before it disappears. Ledges, collapsing surfaces and deadly environmental traps are as threatening as the enemies, while the game's music and fantasy imagery build a distinctive atmosphere.

Rastan was a major arcade success and received numerous home conversions. Its heavy-hitting combat, dramatic scenery and imposing soundtrack helped define the barbarian-action style of late-1980s arcade gaming.

games.title: Rave Racer
games.description:
Namco's Rave Racer (1995) is the third arcade installment in the Ridge Racer family, introducing new courses, improved handling and a more energetic visual and musical identity. Drivers still rely on controlled high-speed drifting to negotiate corners and pass rivals before timed checkpoints expire. In addition to returning tracks from earlier games, new urban and mountain roads add more varied scenery and challenging bends.

Built on Namco System 22 hardware, Rave Racer improves force-feedback steering, car models and roadside detail, while linked cabinets support extensive multiplayer races. Its soundtrack emphasizes high-energy electronic dance music, making it as much a showcase of mid-1990s arcade style as a technically polished driving game.

games.title: Ray Storm
games.description:
RayStorm (1996) is Taito's spectacular polygonal successor to the sprite-based RayForce. Players pilot an R-Gray spacecraft through vertically oriented battles that sweep across land, space and heavily defended installations. The action remains on a two-dimensional plane, but the camera and enemies move through elaborate three-dimensional environments, creating dramatic perspective shifts and enormous mechanical bosses.

The key weapon is a lock-on laser: holding the targeting control marks enemies, often on a lower visual plane, before unleashing homing energy strikes. Different ship configurations vary their firepower and lock-on behavior, while concentrated targeting can yield substantial scoring rewards. The combination of layered shooting mechanics and a cinematic camera makes the game immediately recognizable.

Although its story is not a direct continuation of RayForce, RayStorm became an important part of Taito's Ray trilogy and reached home audiences through versions for the PlayStation and other platforms. Its blend of technical spectacle, aggressive enemy patterns and distinctive music made it a standout of the transition from sprite-based shooters to polygonal arcade graphics.

games.title: Razzmatazz
games.description: Razzmatazz (1983) is an obscure Sega shooting-gallery game that appears to have remained at the arcade testing stage. Its play involves aiming at animal targets, including ducks and polar bears, rather than battling the spacecraft or soldiers typical of contemporary shooters. Built with hardware related to Sega's Zaxxon, it survives as an unusual experiment in light-gun-style arcade entertainment, with no widely released home version.

games.title: Real Bout Fatal Fury / Real Bout Garou Densetsu
games.description:
Real Bout Fatal Fury (1995) reshapes SNK's Fatal Fury fighting series with faster combos, a new power gauge and an emphasis on aggressive positioning. Sixteen fighters battle in South Town, including Terry Bogard, Geese Howard and returning favorites. The four-button layout now dedicates separate controls to punch, kick, strong attack and movement between the foreground and background evasive planes.

The game introduces ring-outs, letting fighters win by knocking an opponent beyond the edge of certain stages, while its escalating power gauge unlocks stronger techniques and desperation attacks. Chain combinations are easier to perform than in earlier Fatal Fury titles, making fights fluid and dangerous at close range. As the first Real Bout installment, it established the basis for several of SNK's most refined later Neo Geo fighters.

games.title: Real Bout Fatal Fury 2 - The Newcomers / Real Bout Garou Densetsu 2 - the newcomers

variants.title: Real Bout Fatal Fury 2 - The Newcomers / Real Bout Garou Densetsu 2 - the newcomers (set 1)
Real Bout Fatal Fury 2 - The Newcomers / Real Bout Garou Densetsu 2 - the newcomers (set 2)
Real Bout Fatal Fury 2 - The Newcomers (Korean release)

games.description:
Real Bout Fatal Fury 2: The Newcomers (1998) is SNK's final major Neo Geo installment in the Real Bout branch of Fatal Fury. It reunites the established South Town cast while adding boxer Rick Strowd and kung-fu fighter Li Xiangfei, alongside the appearance of the young challenger Alfred. Familiar characters have new or revised moves and fresh stage art.

The fighting system returns to a primary battle lane with a secondary sway lane for dodging, although some stages restrict combat to a single plane. Breakable scenery and some of the more elaborate rules of Real Bout Special are removed, favoring quick, direct exchanges and advanced combination play. With its large roster and polished four-button controls, it is a fitting conclusion to the late-1990s Real Bout trilogy.

games.title: Real Bout Fatal Fury Special / Real Bout Garou Densetsu Special
games.description:
Real Bout Fatal Fury Special, released in 1997 with a 1996 copyright, is SNK's expanded follow-up to the first Real Bout Fatal Fury. The roster grows to nineteen selectable fighters, bringing back characters such as Tung Fu Rue, Cheng Sinzan, Laurence Blood and Wolfgang Krauser. Entirely revised backgrounds and character presentation give the game a more lavish look.

The battle system alters how fighters shift between foreground and background planes, while the original's ring-out rules give way to stage-edge interactions that can leave an opponent stunned. The accessible chain-combo system and powerful special attacks remain, but new balance and defensive opportunities reward experienced players. Its bright animation, character themes and enormous cast make it one of the Neo Geo's most characterful late-era two-dimensional fighters.

games.title: Vs. Atari R.B.I. Baseball
games.description:
Vs. Atari R.B.I. Baseball is the Nintendo Vs. System arcade version of the early R.B.I. Baseball game, bringing a surprisingly detailed baseball contest to coin-operated play. Players choose from ten teams with lineups modeled on real major-league players and compete against the computer or a second human. Batting, pitching, stealing bases and positioning fielders are handled with an eight-way stick and two buttons, balancing quick execution with the tactical decisions of a baseball manager.

Different players have recognizable statistical strengths, so choosing pitchers, substitutions and the right hitting approach matters. This accessible but strategic adaptation helped lay the groundwork for the long-running R.B.I. Baseball name.

games.title: Real Battle Mahjong King
games.description: Real Battle Mahjong King, also known as Shizhan Majiang Wang, is a 1998 medal-mahjong game from GMS. The January 1998 release date is better documented than the 1995 date sometimes assigned to the ROM set. It presents competitive mahjong on a horizontal screen using an unusually minimal two-direction joystick and two-button layout, rather than the many-key panel of most Japanese mahjong machines. The preserved version is identified as program revision 8.8 and is a small but distinctive part of the late-1990s Japanese mahjong arcade catalogue.

games.title: Royal Casino
games.description:
Royal Casino is a 1984 Dyna Electronics video-gambling machine using a Z80 processor, AY-3-8910 audio and a five-button panel. Its reel-and-symbol presentation belongs to the early eight-line video-slot tradition, a style that would become common in later Cherry Master-type cabinets.
