Instead of a physical wheel or action-game controls, the cabinet presents gambling results directly on a horizontal monitor.

Preserved hardware includes distinct larger and smaller PCB layouts, as well as the related Casino Winner program. The board variations show how the same core slot design could be repackaged at a time when video gambling hardware was still changing rapidly.

games.title: Rail Chase
games.description:
Sega's Rail Chase (1991) is a spectacular on-rails light-gun shooter inspired by cliff-hanging adventure films. One or two players ride a runaway mine cart through caves, ruins and hazardous outdoor routes while gunmen, vehicles and traps attack from all directions. The cart moves automatically, leaving players free to shoot enemies, break obstacles and keep pursuing bosses from catching up.

At track junctions, players can shoot direction signs to choose different routes, making each escape slightly different. A visible damage indicator tracks the punishment the cart is taking, while set pieces include collapsing structures and giant boulder chases reminiscent of Indiana Jones. With its moving viewpoint and constant stream of cinematic hazards, Rail Chase anticipates Sega's later emphasis on fast-paced, spectacle-driven gun games.

games.title: Raiden Fighters
games.description:
Raiden Fighters (1996) is Seibu Kaihatsu's faster, more score-driven offshoot of its Raiden shooting series. Instead of piloting only the traditional Fighting Thunder craft, players choose from several military aircraft with different movement speeds, shot patterns and special weapons. Short, intense vertically scrolling stages pit the squadron against overwhelming formations of tanks, fighters and elaborate mechanical bosses.

The game shifts the emphasis toward chaining destruction, collecting medals and uncovering hidden scoring opportunities. Bombs remain essential for survival, but learning enemy appearances and optimizing the sequence of kills becomes a major part of expert play. Built for Seibu's SPI hardware, Raiden Fighters launched a trilogy celebrated by dedicated shoot-'em-up players for its speed and depth.

games.title: Raiden Fighters 2

variants.title: Raiden Fighters 2 (Asia, Dream Island license, SPI)

games.description:
Raiden Fighters 2: Operation Hell Dive (1997) greatly expands Seibu Kaihatsu's score-focused vertical shooter with a larger selection of aircraft. The roster includes machines with distinct shot spreads, laser systems and movement characteristics, including the recognizable Fighting Thunder from Raiden II. Players fight through dense waves of modern military hardware, using ordinary fire, charged attacks and bombs to survive.

In addition to medals and hidden bonuses, cooperative play can unlock a powerful Hybrid Attack when the two players coordinate their weapons. The fast pacing and unusually varied ships invite experimentation with different scoring routes and survival strategies. It is a substantial sequel rather than a simple extension of the original Raiden Fighters.

games.title: Reactor
games.description:
Reactor (1982) is one of the arcade era's strangest and most inventive action games. Designed by Tim Skelly for Gottlieb, it puts the player inside an unstable nuclear reactor where dangerous particles ricochet around an arena surrounding a growing, lethal central core. Instead of simply shooting them, the player steers a small craft with a trackball and uses momentum to knock hostile particles into the deadly outer walls. A decoy button can lure attackers away, while energy management becomes crucial as the reactor heats up.

The action feels like a combination of pinball, physics puzzle and survival game. Every collision changes the flow of the arena, and as the reactor core expands the available space shrinks. Reactor was notably one of the first arcade games to place its programmer's name prominently on the title screen. Its unusual mechanical design and swirling visual effects have secured it a lasting cult reputation.

games.title: Reaktor
games.description: Reaktor (1987) is a late example of the classic bat-and-ball arcade format, developed by Zilec. A player moves a paddle back and forth at the bottom of the screen, rebounds a ball upward and tries to clear formations of bricks without allowing the ball to escape. The game focuses on precise positioning and reading the ball's changing angle, putting it in the broad Breakout and Arkanoid tradition rather than the nuclear-reactor action of Gottlieb's similarly named Reactor.

games.title: Billiard Academy Real Break
games.description: Billiard Academy Real Break (1998) is a Japanese-style top-down pool game offering pocket-billiards and nine-ball play. Players aim and take shots around a conventional billiards table in either solo or alternating-turn versus modes, trying to meet the score target for each match. Its adult-oriented presentation adds a cheering female character and reward scenes after successful games, making it a hybrid of straightforward digital billiards and the visual-novel-style incentives common in some Japanese arcade titles of the period.

games.title: Rebus
games.description: Rebus is a 1995 Italian arcade puzzle game from Microhard, built on hardware closely related to Gaelco's Splash! and Microhard's The Return of Lady Frog. Despite descriptions that associate it with pub trivia, its arcade configuration points to an adult-oriented, picture-based puzzle: the machine includes adjustable settings for the displayed girls and a 'Paint Mode', alongside difficulty and lives. Players use an eight-way joystick and two buttons. Its 68000-based board also uses a Z80 for sound, and its unusual software and protection routines have made it a distinctive part of the Splash! hardware family in MAME.

games.title: Recalhorn
games.description:
Recalhorn is a nearly finished but unreleased Taito F3 platform-game prototype from 1994. Players guide a young boy and his white animal companion through colorful side-scrolling fantasy stages, jumping on enemies, collecting fruit and using a magical horn to overcome hazards. Rescued animals become summonable helpers, each with a different ability useful for reaching difficult places or defeating enemies. Summoning a particular mount requires the right collected coins.

Boss fights conclude the larger sections of the adventure, while a heart-based health system makes exploration more forgiving than in many older arcade platformers. Its polished animation, imaginative mounts and extensive level design make Recalhorn a particularly interesting example of a commercially unreleased game preserved through emulation.

games.title: Recordbreaker
games.description:
Recordbreaker (1988), also known in Japan as Go for the Gold, is Taito's ten-event arcade sports competition. Players attempt to beat qualifying marks in disciplines such as the 100-meter sprint, hurdles, long and triple jump, pole vault, swimming, weightlifting, horizontal bar, shot put and relay racing. Events can be attempted in different orders, but failure to qualify can end the competition.

Its four-button controls demand rapid tapping for speed and well-timed presses for jumping, throwing, breathing or passing a relay baton. The varied tests of rhythm, timing and stamina recall Konami's Track & Field, but the broader event list gives Recordbreaker its own athletic identity.

games.title: Red Alert
games.description:
Red Alert (1981), developed by Irem and released internationally with GDI involvement, is an early fixed-screen anti-aircraft shooter. Players move a ground-based cannon left and right, firing upward at waves of fighters and bombers before they can destroy the defended city. Stages change the attack patterns and scenery, with landmarks indicating different locations around the world.

One of its most memorable features is a spoken mission briefing that warns of approaching enemies, an unusually prominent use of synthesized speech for its period. Red Alert builds tension through the need to intercept multiple targets before their bombs reach the ground, making each volley a question of timing rather than unrestricted movement.

games.title: Red Baron
games.description:
Atari's Red Baron (1980/1981) is an early first-person combat flight simulator that puts players in the cockpit of a World War I biplane. Rendered in crisp monochrome vector graphics, the battlefield shows rolling terrain, enemy aircraft, observation balloons and ground defenses in simulated three dimensions. An analog joystick controls pitch and direction while a trigger fires the machine gun; sustained firing can overheat the weapon.

The action alternates between dogfights and attacks on ground targets, with enemy planes maneuvering more aggressively as the game continues. Developed around hardware related to Atari's Battlezone, Red Baron was a striking demonstration of how vector graphics could suggest an open three-dimensional world. Its physical flight controls and distinctive visual style set it apart from the fixed-screen shooters that still dominated arcades.

games.title: Red Clash
games.description: Red Clash (1981) is an early vertically oriented space shooter developed by Kaneko and published by Tehkan. Players control a blue spacecraft confronting waves of red enemy ships and projectiles, aiming to survive increasingly crowded attack patterns while collecting points. Its simple single-fire-button controls and direct arcade design reflect the transition from Space Invaders-style fixed shooters toward more elaborate formation-based space battles. The game's Kaneko origins are visible in surviving high-score graphics.

games.title: Redline Racer
games.description:
Redline Racer (1987) is an overhead-view car racing game from Cinematronics, distributed by Tradewest. Players steer around a series of sixteen winding circuits, racing against rival vehicles in a format reminiscent of Atari's Sprint games. The two-player edition allows direct competition using dedicated steering controls.

Though it was not a major arcade hit, Redline Racer has an interesting legacy: its technology and racing approach helped form the basis of the later and much more successful Ivan 'Ironman' Stewart's Super Off Road.

games.title: Red Robin
games.description: Red Robin (1986) is an obscure side-scrolling platform game developed by Italian company Elettronolo. Using horizontal movement and two action buttons, the player navigates a colorful succession of platforms and obstacles, collecting jewelry and other valuables while avoiding hazards. Its straightforward run-and-jump design recalls the mid-1980s arcade and home-computer platformers that preceded the genre's move toward more elaborate character-driven adventures.

games.title: Defend the Terra Attack on the Red UFO

variants.title: Defend the Terra Attack on the Red UFO

games.description:
Defend the Terra Attack on the Red UFO (1981) is an early Japanese space shooter from Uko, closely related in style and hardware to Namco's Galaxian. Players slide a ship along the bottom of the screen and fire upward at formations of small flying saucers, eventually confronting a larger mothership. The action relies on timing shots and avoiding incoming attacks rather than on power-ups or complex weapon systems.

The game also circulated in an unauthorized version known as Exodus. Its survival on Galaxian-family hardware illustrates how the success of late-1970s fixed-screen shooters encouraged a wave of derivative and converted arcade boards.

games.title: Regulus
games.description:
Regulus (1983) is a top-down tank shooter built for Sega's System 1 arcade hardware. The player's tank advances through a vertically scrolling battlefield, moving in eight directions while firing forward and launching bombs to hit targets farther up the screen. Enemy tanks, installations and environmental obstacles force constant maneuvering.

Using two different attacks gives Regulus a more tactical rhythm than many early tank games, since aiming ahead and positioning the vehicle are as important as avoiding enemy fire. Its scrolling battlefield is an early example of the military-vehicle format that would grow more elaborate in later arcade shooters.

games.title: Reikai Doushi
games.description:
Reikai Doushi: Chinese Exorcist (1988), also known as The Last Apostle Puppetshow, is an eccentric one-on-one fighting game by Home Data. The player controls a Chinese exorcist battling a succession of supernatural opponents, including hopping vampires known as jiangshi or kyonshi. The combat unfolds from a side view, but the fighters look like animated puppets rather than conventional hand-drawn sprites.

The game used imagery based on physical doll-like figures, giving its characters a distinctive stop-motion appearance years before prerendered fighters became fashionable. Arenas also have an unusual wraparound or teleporting edge behavior. Originally conceived with more adult-oriented content before its direction changed, Reikai Doushi remains a remarkable early experiment in unusual fighting-game presentation.

games.title: Relief Pitcher
games.description:
Relief Pitcher (1992) is Atari Games' baseball arcade game, notable for letting players experience either a complete game or the pressure of entering a series of contests as a relief pitcher. Pitchers can be configured by throwing arm, delivery style and specialty pitch, while three-button controls select fastballs, breaking balls and other throws. Batters choose between normal swings, power hits and bunts, and the joystick governs placement and fielding.

The game avoids licensing real baseball teams, instead offering fictional city selections and extensive statistics. A play-by-play announcer reinforces the ballpark atmosphere. Although Atari had developed an earlier game with the same name for System 1 hardware, this released version is a separate design rather than a finished edition of the abandoned 1986 prototype.

games.title: Relief Pitcher
games.description:
Relief Pitcher is an unreleased Atari Games baseball prototype developed for the company's System 1 arcade hardware around 1986. Unlike Atari's commercially released 1992 game of the same name, it was built around a different control system and gameplay. Two Hall-effect joysticks handled the action, while buttons were used for throwing, batting and rapidly tapping to make players run faster around the bases or in the outfield.

The prototype supported competition against another player or the computer but apparently never progressed beyond limited testing. Its survival is an interesting reminder that familiar arcade titles sometimes conceal abandoned earlier designs with little in common beyond their names.

games.title: Mahjong Ren-ai Club
games.description: Mahjong Ren-ai Club (1993) is a Japanese arcade mahjong game by Fujic centered on matches against selectable female opponents. Rather than using Mahjong solitaire's tile-matching rules, it follows the competitive tabletop tradition associated with Japanese mahjong cabinets. Its adult-oriented character presentation places it among the many romance-themed mahjong games that were popular in Japanese amusement venues during the early 1990s.

games.title: Renegade
games.description:
Renegade (1986) is a pivotal arcade beat-'em-up by Technos Japan and designer Yoshihisa Kishimoto. Instead of moving on a single horizontal plane, the player fights through open street areas, walking toward or away from the screen while punching, kicking, grappling and knocking enemies down. The hero must survive confrontations with groups of thugs, armed bikers and dangerous gang leaders, learning when to strike and when to escape being surrounded.

The original Japanese game, Nekketsu Kouha Kunio-kun, follows school tough Kunio as he defends his friend Hiroshi from rival gangs. For Western audiences, Technos dramatically redrew the setting and characters into a gritty American street-rescue story. The combat was influenced in part by Kishimoto's own experiences and martial-arts cinema.

Its multidirectional brawling, gangs of simultaneous attackers and repeated boss confrontations helped establish the structure of the side-scrolling beat-'em-up, anticipating Technos' own Double Dragon. Renegade is an essential milestone in the evolution of arcade hand-to-hand combat.

games.title: Renju Kizoku
games.description:
Renju Kizoku (1994), developed by Visco, is an arcade adaptation of renju, the competitive Japanese five-in-a-row board game. Players take turns placing black and white stones on a grid, seeking to complete an unbroken line of five horizontally, vertically or diagonally. Unlike casual gomoku, formal renju rules restrict certain powerful patterns for the first player, adding a layer of tactical balance.

The game's emphasis on reading threats several moves ahead makes it a quiet strategic alternative to the action-heavy Neo Geo-era arcade catalog. Its full Japanese title, Kira Kira Gomoku Narabe Renju Kizoku, appeared in arcades around 1995 despite a 1994 copyright.

games.title: Rescue Raider
games.description:
Rescue Raider (1987) is a top-down twin-stick vehicle shooter from Bally Sente, and one of the last games released for the company's SAC-I arcade system. Players drive an armored rescue vehicle through hostile multi-screen territories, collecting classified documents that reveal the positions of hostages, fuel, weapons and other objectives on a radar map. Escaping with rescued personnel and sufficient fuel is as important as eliminating the enemy.

The left joystick moves the vehicle, while the right fires independently in eight directions; a separate button cycles available special weapons. This control system makes combat flexible but demanding, especially when navigating narrow routes under fire. Its combination of exploration, resource management and Robotron-like shooting makes it one of Bally Sente's more ambitious action games.

games.title: Rescue
games.description:
Stern's Rescue (1982) is a pioneering twin-stick helicopter game in which the player flies above hostile seas to save paratroopers stranded in the water. The pilot must hover low enough to lower a rescue ladder, allow survivors to climb aboard and deliver them to an island. Enemy helicopters, submarines and ships fire at the aircraft, while hungry sharks threaten swimmers who remain in the water too long.

Two joysticks separate movement from eight-directional firing, giving the game fast, independent combat controls. The helicopter must also avoid hitting parachutists with its rotors or skimming the surface too closely. Several layers of scrolling clouds and scenery create a convincing impression of depth, an impressive visual technique for the period.

Rescue is remembered as an inventive early mixture of combat shooting and civilian extraction, with a demanding rhythm that rewards careful flying as much as aggressive firepower.

games.title: Return of the Invaders
games.description:
Return of the Invaders (1985) is Taito's full-color revival of the Space Invaders formula, developed with work by UPL. The player again moves a cannon along the bottom of a fixed screen, protecting it with defensive barriers and shooting down advancing alien formations. This time the invaders do far more than march left and right: they circle, dive toward the cannon, deflect incoming shots and appear in imaginative new patterns.

Destroying flying saucers can release weapon upgrades, while challenge stages interrupt the main battles with different scoring tests. The result preserves the simple rhythm of the 1978 original but fills it with features borrowed from the more elaborate shooters that had appeared since. Originally developed under the working title Space Invaders Part 3, it forms an important bridge between the classic series and the more radical updates that followed.

games.title: Revenger '84
games.description:
Revenger '84 is an unusual science-fiction shooter released by Epos Corporation in 1984, with Magic Electronics also credited on surviving material. Instead of presenting space combat as a succession of anonymous waves, it gives the player a specific mission: navigate a galactic map, reach the intruder base in sector E9, and destroy it. Success transports the fighter to another galaxy, where the game warns that the laws of physics are different. A four-way joystick and two buttons control the action on a vertically oriented screen.

That changing-physics premise is the game's most memorable feature, giving its galactic journey a more experimental character than many contemporary shooters. AdvanceMAME preserves the game through ROM sets identified as newer and older revisions; the distinction reflects surviving PCB and ROM revisions rather than a separate sequel.

games.title: Revolution X
games.description:
Revolution X (1994) is Midway's outrageous three-player shooting game built around the rock band Aerosmith. In a dystopian future, the authoritarian New Order Nation has outlawed youth culture and kidnapped the band. Players man mounted machine guns and blast through waves of soldiers, helicopters, security devices and military hardware while searching for Aerosmith's missing members.

Like Midway's Terminator 2 arcade shooter, the action moves automatically through elaborate digitized environments, with players aiming and firing at everything from enemies to destructible scenery. Hidden objects and rescue opportunities affect the outcome, while CD-quality music and video appearances by the band provide the central attraction. Its mixture of celebrity licensing, campy rebellion and relentless gunfire makes it an unmistakable product of the 1990s arcade spectacle era.

games.title: Rezon
games.description:
Rezon (1991) is Allumer's extremely demanding horizontally scrolling shooter, heavily influenced by Irem's R-Type. Players pilot a spacecraft through six stages filled with mechanical enemies, tight corridors and heavily armored bosses. A pair of small support units, known as Arms, travel with the ship and provide additional firepower. Their firing angles change with the player's movements, allowing attacks to be directed into spaces the main cannon cannot easily cover.

Mastering these auxiliary weapons and memorizing enemy patterns are essential because the difficulty is unforgiving. Although its visual design and relentless challenge recall its famous inspiration, Rezon's shifting support-fire system gives it a mechanical identity of its own. It was one of the first games to bear the Allumer name prominently.

games.title: Raiden Fighters Jet
games.description:
Raiden Fighters Jet (1998) is Seibu Kaihatsu's third and final game in the original Raiden Fighters trilogy. It retains the series' fleet of specialized aircraft, dense vertical shooting, secret bonuses and powerful cooperative Hybrid Attack, but reorganizes the campaign around performance. Rather than following a fixed sequence, players earn advancement through successive mission levels based on how well they play, eventually reaching the demanding real combat phases.

The shifting progression rewards survival, efficient enemy destruction and score-oriented techniques, making each route feel like a test of mastery. Modes aimed at different skill levels and an energetic rave-influenced soundtrack distinguish Jet from its predecessors. Its layered scoring systems and uncompromising speed have made it a favorite among expert arcade-shooter enthusiasts.

games.title: Ribbit!
games.description:
Ribbit! (1991) is Sega's playful frog-themed action game and an unofficial spiritual successor to Frogger. One or two players guide frogs around single-screen environments, eating a required number of harmless insects, such as ants and dragonflies, while avoiding spiders, rodents and other dangerous creatures. The goal is to clear the stage before the timer expires, rather than merely cross the road to a safe destination.

Environments change every few rounds, moving between locations such as beaches, factories and waterways. River stages revisit Frogger's familiar floating logs and turtles, but the focus on collecting food gives Ribbit! its own structure. Cooperative play and brightly colored graphics make it a curious late arcade reinterpretation of a much older classic.

games.title: Ridge Racer 2
games.description:
Ridge Racer 2 (1994) is Namco's refined multiplayer edition of its breakthrough arcade racing game. The high-speed road racing and exaggerated drifting of the original remain central: players slide through corners to maintain momentum, weave past traffic and reach checkpoints before their time expires. Additional music tracks, remixes and small gameplay improvements refresh the experience without fundamentally changing the original circuit.

Its most important addition is support for linked cabinets, allowing up to eight racers to compete simultaneously using multiple two-seat units. Built on Namco's System 22 polygon hardware, Ridge Racer 2 helped transform an already impressive solo racing attraction into a social arcade spectacle and paved the way for the more extensive Rave Racer.

games.title: Ridge Racer
games.description:
Ridge Racer (1993) is one of the defining arcade racing games of the early three-dimensional era. Namco's System 22 hardware renders a richly textured coastal road, colorful rival cars and sweeping bends at a speed that was startling in contemporary arcades. The player starts behind the pack, tries to overtake competitors and reaches successive checkpoints while the timer counts down. Its signature technique is power sliding: deliberately breaking traction to drift through tight corners without losing much speed.

Although the arcade original centers on one main circuit with variations, mastering its corners and rival traffic gives it considerable replay value. A force-feedback steering wheel, accelerator, brake and dramatic cabinet presentation reinforce the sense of speed, while the propulsive electronic soundtrack established a sound closely associated with the series.

Ridge Racer became an emblem of Namco's 3D expertise and gained wider fame through its 1994 PlayStation launch-era conversion. Its stylized, accessible drifting philosophy influenced countless later arcade racers and helped establish polygonal racing as a central attraction of the 1990s.

games.title: Riding Hero
games.description:
Riding Hero (1990) is an ambitious Neo Geo motorcycle racing game by SNK that combines arcade-speed competition with an unusual role-playing mode. In World Grand Prix mode, players select a bike and compete on international circuits against skilled rivals. In the RPG mode, a young rider explores locations, talks to people, buys a motorcycle and enters races to earn money and pursue the prestigious Suzuka 8 Hours event.

The motorcycle action is viewed from behind the bike and emphasizes steering, overtaking and track knowledge. Riding Hero was also the first Neo Geo title to support a dedicated Multi Play link connection, enabling two compatible cabinets or systems to race directly against one another. Its mix of racing simulation, adventure progression and early linked-cabinet technology makes it a distinctive entry in SNK's launch-era library.

games.title: Riding Fight
games.description:
Riding Fight (1992) is Taito's unusual futuristic beat-'em-up that takes place entirely on high-speed hoverboards. Players control bounty hunters Burn Bowie and Keith Jager as they pursue the Death Serpent crime organization through city streets and hazardous tracks. The viewpoint races forward automatically while enemies approach on hoverboards, motorcycles and other vehicles, forcing the heroes to punch, kick, jump and dodge obstacles without ever stopping.

Defeated enemies can drop weapons or restorative items, and large bosses cap the stages. Its fusion of racing-game perspective and direct hand-to-hand combat looks unlike most contemporary side-scrolling brawlers. Developed for Taito's powerful F3 hardware, the game also features graphics work associated with Natsume and VAP.

games.title: Riddle of Pythagoras
games.description:
Riddle of Pythagoras, known in Japan as Pythagoras no Nazo, is a late-1980s Sega arcade ball-and-paddle game. Players move a bat horizontally along the bottom of the screen, using it to bounce a ball into blocks above and clear the playfield while keeping the ball in play. Its dial-based steering and familiar brick-breaking objective place it near the Arkanoid tradition.

Developed with Nasco and related studios on Sega's System E hardware, the game received a Japanese arcade release around the turn of 1986 and 1987. Its unusual mathematical title gives a familiar paddle-game format a curious identity.

games.title: Rim Rockin' Basketball
games.description:
Rim Rockin' Basketball (1991) is a four-player arcade basketball game developed by Incredible Technologies and released by Strata. Rather than treating basketball as an exaggerated dunking contest, it offers a more conventional team game with passing, dribbling, shooting and positional play. Each player can control members of a five-person team, making teamwork and choosing open shots central to winning.

Its competitive four-player setup and straightforward joystick-and-button controls made it well suited to arcade groups, while the emphasis on organized basketball distinguishes it from the increasingly spectacular sports games that became fashionable later in the decade.

games.title: Ring of Destruction: Slammasters II

variants.title: Super Muscle Bomber: The International Blowout (Japan 940831)
Super Muscle Bomber: The International Blowout (Japan 940808)

games.description:
Capcom's Ring of Destruction: Slammasters II (1994), released in Japan as Super Muscle Bomber: The International Blowout, transforms the studio's wrestling series into a conventional one-on-one fighting game. Instead of the original Saturday Night Slam Masters' pinfalls and spacious wrestling ring, matches take place on side-view stages and are won by exhausting the opponent's health. Its five-button arrangement offers light and heavy punches, light and heavy kicks, and a dedicated grab, combining street-fighting combos with elaborate wrestling throws.

The roster brings back established personalities such as Mike Haggar and Biff Slamkovich and introduces newcomers including Victor Ortega, Black Widow, Rip Saber, and The Wraith. The oversized characters retain designs associated with Tetsuo Hara, the artist of Fist of the North Star. Running on Capcom's CPS-2 hardware with QSound audio, it is a distinctive midpoint between a flamboyant pro-wrestling spectacle and the studio's more technical fighting games. Japanese and export releases also use different character names.

games.title: Ring Rage
games.description:
Taito's Ring Rage (1992) is a colorful professional-wrestling game built around an eccentric roster of eight grapplers, including K.O. Joe, Yasha the Ninja Warrior, Gunboat Rodie, and B.B. Scorpion. Each wrestler has a characteristic appearance, fighting approach, and special attacks. Players compete in conventional ring bouts as well as tag-team tournaments, Royal Rumble-style contests, and survival matches, with up to four participants supported.

The action extends beyond an ordinary wrestling ring to settings such as cage matches, warehouses, and junkyards. Its exaggerated characters and rough-and-tumble presentation distinguish it from straightforward sports simulations. The arcade version runs on Taito's F3 hardware, and surviving versions include Japanese and export program revisions.

games.title: Riot
games.description:
Riot (1992) is a third-person shooting-gallery game developed by Tecmo and published by NMK. Its play resembles Cabal, with one or two commandos aiming a cursor at enemies while dodging incoming attacks, but adds an unusual two-plane shooting system. Separate fire controls target enemies in the foreground or the background, so players must continually judge which layer contains the immediate threat.

Across six rounds, the protagonists battle soldiers, helicopters, vehicles, and increasingly bizarre enemies in ruined streets, jungles, train rooftops, and industrial facilities. Destroyed targets and airborne bonus objects can yield equipment such as a flamethrower, shotgun, or grenade launcher. The campaign's unexpected shift from military action to supernatural bosses gives this otherwise methodical gallery shooter a particularly strange identity.

games.title: Riot City
games.description:
Riot City is a 1991 side-scrolling beat-'em-up developed by Westone and published by Sega on System 16B hardware. Two detectives, Paul and Bobby, confront the M.I.D. drug syndicate after its members kidnap Paul's girlfriend. The pursuit takes them across the decrepit Riot Island, through apartments, a hospital, a factory, and a casino. Paul is the more balanced fighter, while Bobby is a slower but harder-hitting brawler.

Much of the game follows the structure of Capcom's Final Fight: players advance from left to right, clear crowds of thugs, and defeat a boss before moving to the next stage. Unlike its inspiration, Riot City does not let the heroes wield discarded weapons, keeping combat focused on punches, kicks, and close-quarters techniques. Its close resemblance to Final Fight makes it an interesting example of the arcade beat-'em-up boom.

games.title: Rip Cord
games.description:
Rip Cord (1979) is a black-and-white parachuting game designed by Arlan Granger for Exidy. A plane crosses the sky above a landscape dotted with landing targets, and the player must choose when to jump, avoid hostile helicopters, and guide a parachutist toward a safe touchdown. Successful play demands a careful balance between an early parachute deployment and a dangerously fast free fall.

Its cabinet used an unusually physical control: a triangular D-ring handle that the player pulled to open the parachute. Once the canopy is deployed, a paddle steers the falling character horizontally. Presented at the 1978 AMOA trade show and released in early 1979, Rip Cord is an inventive contemporary of Atari's Sky Diver, notable for turning a real parachuting gesture into an arcade input.

games.title: Rip Off
games.description:
Cinematronics' Rip Off (1980), designed by Tim Skelly, is a black-and-white vector shooter in which survival depends on protecting a shared resource rather than keeping a limited stock of lives. Eight fuel canisters sit in the middle of the screen while hostile 'pirate' vehicles arrive from the edges, try to latch onto them, and drag them away. Players steer and rotate their tank-like craft, firing at invaders or ramming them before the stockpile disappears.

One or two players can defend the same canisters simultaneously, with independent movement and firing controls. Destroyed player vehicles return to the field, but lost fuel does not: the game ends only when the enemy has stolen every canister. Faster attackers, armed enemies, and changing formations gradually force more sophisticated defensive positioning.

Rip Off is especially important for its unusually complete cooperative design and enemy craft that appear to coordinate their attacks. Although sometimes advertised as the first cooperative video game, earlier cooperative arcade games existed; its lasting innovation was making two independently controlled ships defend the same vulnerable objective. A Vectrex version followed in 1982.

games.title: Ripper Ribbit
games.description:
Ripper Ribbit (1997) is a single-player arcade redemption game from LAI Games starring a hungry cartoon frog. Instead of shooting conventional enemies, the player aims at insects around a colorful pond, using the frog's tongue to catch suitable targets before the timer expires. Hazardous insects and missed opportunities make target selection and quick reactions important, while special bugs can award additional points or tickets.

The game combines a shooting-gallery style of aiming with a lighthearted insect-catching theme. Its TMS34010-based electronics and straightforward one-button interaction reflect its purpose as a short, accessible skill-and-ticket attraction rather than a traditional multistage action game.

games.title: Risky Challenge
games.description:
Risky Challenge (1993), known in Japan as Gussun Oyoyo, is Irem's unusual combination of falling-block puzzle and platform adventure. Treasure hunters Vic and Vinnie are trapped in a collapsing underground dungeon and must escape by making use of blocks dropping into each room. Rather than simply matching colors, players arrange the falling pieces to form steps, bridges, and safe paths so that the small adventurers can climb toward the exit.

The challenge comes from anticipating how new blocks will alter the terrain while the characters navigate hazards and rising danger. Its cooperative possibilities and animated, comical heroes give the game a personality unlike ordinary block-stacking puzzles. The concept proved popular enough in Japan to launch the Gussun Oyoyo series and receive console adaptations.

games.title: Roller Jammer
games.description:
Roller Jammer is a 1984 roller-skating action racer developed by Alice and published by Nichibutsu. The player first tackles a training course, collecting flags, then races along narrow scrolling paths crowded with rival skaters. Winning requires overtaking a prescribed number of competitors while staying on the track and using punches to knock opponents out of the way.

Passing rivals awards points and extra time, making aggressive skating as important as clean movement. The combination of a racing timer, physical jostling, and roller-derby imagery sets it apart from typical vehicle racers. The game reached North American arcades in 1985 and received a modern Arcade Archives release.

games.title: Real Mahjong Haihai
games.description:
Real Mahjong Haihai (1985) is an early Japanese adult-oriented mahjong game from Alba. It uses the hand-building, drawing, and discarding conventions of Japanese riichi mahjong, presenting head-to-head matches against female computer opponents. Winning games advances the presentation and reveals risqué character artwork, a reward structure that became familiar in Japan's specialist arcade mahjong market.

Released in November 1985, the game helped establish Alba's Real Mahjong Haihai line. AdvanceMAME also includes a betting-oriented variant, reflecting the different commercial formats in which Japanese mahjong machines were sold.

games.title: Real Mahjong Haihai Jinji Idou Hen

variants.title: Real Mahjong Haihai Jinji Idou Hen (Japan)

games.description:
Real Mahjong Haihai Jinji Idou Hen (1986) is Alba's follow-up to its 1985 adult mahjong game. The Japanese subtitle refers to a personnel reshuffle, signaling a new installment with different featured opponents rather than a wholesale change of genre. Players continue to compete in Japanese-style mahjong, building winning hands against computerized rivals and unlocking revealing illustrations as rewards.

The game belongs to the early wave of dedicated Japanese mahjong arcade titles and uses hardware closely related to its predecessor, including a Z80 processor and sampled speech capabilities. Its appeal is centered on tile strategy and character presentation rather than reflex-based action.

games.title: Real Mahjong Haihai Seichouhen
games.description:
Real Mahjong Haihai Seichouhen is a 1986 Japanese adult mahjong title released by Visco as part of the Real Mahjong Haihai series. The subtitle can be read as 'Growing Up Chapter'. Like the other entries, it revolves around competitive Japanese mahjong and a character-driven presentation in which successful play unlocks more revealing imagery.

Issued in Japan in December 1986, it preserves the series' combination of traditional tile-game rules and risqué arcade rewards. It is particularly notable as a continuation published under the Visco name rather than Alba, the company associated with the original game.

games.title: Rampage: World Tour
games.description:
Rampage: World Tour (1997) brings Midway's city-destroying arcade classic back after an eleven-year absence. George the gorilla, Lizzie the lizard, and Ralph the wolf once again scale skyscrapers, punch walls until buildings collapse, and eat civilians to restore health while the military responds with soldiers, helicopters, and aircraft. Up to three people can play at once, turning each city into a chaotic mixture of cooperation and competition for destruction bonuses.

The sequel expands the journey far beyond the original game's North American cities, with recognizable international locations and landmarks. Players can influence their route by collecting World Tour flags, and radioactive waste temporarily transforms a monster into the even more destructive V.E.R.N. A new kick action joins the familiar climbing, jumping, and punching.

Original Rampage designers Brian Colin and Jeff Nauman returned for World Tour, preserving the humor and deliberate absurdity of the 1986 hit while providing more varied scenery, bigger sprites, and a much longer itinerary. The result was a successful 1990s revival of one of arcade gaming's most recognizable multiplayer concepts.

games.title: Road Blasters
games.description:
Atari Games' RoadBlasters (1987) blends a high-speed road race with vehicular combat. Players drive an armed sports car through a sequence of fifty rallies, blasting enemy vehicles and roadside turrets while dodging traffic and collecting fuel. The central resource is gasoline rather than a conventional health bar: collisions and time spent on the road consume fuel, and reaching the next checkpoint before the tank empties is essential.

A special support aircraft occasionally drops weapon upgrades, including additional firepower or temporary defensive equipment. The arcade cabinet's steering wheel, accelerator, and weapon controls give the action a tactile, driving-game feel, while digitized perspective scaling makes the road rush toward the player. Its distinctive red sports car and mixture of shooting and racing inspired several home conversions.

games.title: Road Burners
games.description:
Road Burners (1999) is a motorcycle racing arcade game from Atari Games, built around a physically tilting bike-style control unit. Players lean into turns while racing through traffic on courses inspired by real locations, including Washington, D.C., and Las Vegas. Passing checkpoints adds time, so the immediate challenge is to maintain speed and travel as far as possible before the clock expires.

The linked-cabinet option allows riders to compete directly, emphasizing the social spectacle of arcade motorcycle racing. Its distinctive attraction is the use of body movement to steer, rather than relying solely on a wheel or joystick.

games.title: Road Fighter
games.description:
Konami's Road Fighter (1984) is a fast, top-down road-racing game in which the player must reach each stage's destination without running out of fuel. The small sports car darts through dense traffic, avoiding ordinary drivers and unpredictable lane-changing vehicles while collecting special fuel pickups. Touching a rival car can send the player's vehicle into a spin, and recovery demands a quick steering correction before the car strikes the roadside.

Different road surfaces and scenery, from coastal highways to bridges and forest roads, gradually raise the difficulty. Players can shift between low and high gear to manage acceleration and top speed. Its clear overhead viewpoint, punishing collision system, and relentless fuel pressure made Road Fighter an enduring early Konami driving game, followed by several related titles and home adaptations.

games.title: Road Riot 4WD
games.description:
Road Riot 4WD (1991) is Atari Games' off-road racing and combat title starring weapon-equipped four-wheel-drive buggies. Instead of racing on tidy asphalt circuits, competitors charge through rugged courses filled with bends, obstacles, and aggressive rivals. A mounted gun lets the player attack other vehicles while steering and managing speed over difficult terrain.

The game offers a series of increasingly demanding tracks, with the competition escalating beyond the opening course into a broader racing challenge. Its combination of steering-wheel arcade hardware, exaggerated dune-buggy physics, and automotive gunplay gives Road Riot a different character from Atari's earlier RoadBlasters.

games.title: Road Runner
games.description:
Atari Games' Road Runner (1985) turns the Warner Bros. cartoons into a fast, comical chase. Players control the Road Runner as Wile E. Coyote pursues him across scrolling desert highways, collecting birdseed to keep his strength up while avoiding traffic, cliffs, and elaborate ACME traps. The chase is not simply about outrunning the coyote: eating enough seed and anticipating hazards are necessary to stay alive.

Road Runner's speed and cartoon animation contrast with Wile E. Coyote's increasingly desperate contraptions. The game translates familiar gags from the animated shorts into hazards the player can read and exploit, making it an unusual licensed arcade action game from Atari's mid-1980s catalog.

games.title: Robby Roto
games.description:
The Adventures of Robby Roto! (1981) is a Bally Midway maze game about a small digging robot searching an underground mine. Players tunnel through dirt to reach trapped miners and scattered treasures, opening pathways while trying to escape the creatures roaming the excavation. Because each cleared section changes the map, the player is effectively building the maze while exploring it.

Robby can exploit the terrain to approach valuables, avoid danger, and reach the exit, but the available time and enemy movements keep the mission urgent. Its combination of digging, rescue objectives, and overhead maze navigation anticipates elements later associated with other underground arcade games, while retaining its own cheerful visual style.

games.title: Robo Army
games.description:
SNK's Robo Army (1991) is a side-scrolling beat-'em-up for the Neo Geo starring two cybernetic fighters, Maxima and Rocky. After escaping the control of a scientist known as Jeed, they fight through Neo-Detroit to destroy his robot army. Each player controls a different hero, although their basic moves are similar, and a two-player team can tackle the six-stage campaign together.

The fighters punch, kick, jump, and unleash energy attacks, but the game's signature touch is its destructive combat: defeated robotic enemies can leave behind parts that serve as improvised weapons. The heroes can also temporarily transform into heavily armored vehicles, turning a brawl into a brief rampage. Large mechanical bosses, metallic sound effects, and a relentlessly industrial setting make Robo Army a characteristic early Neo Geo action spectacle.

games.title: Robocop
games.description:
Data East's RoboCop (1988) adapts the 1987 science-fiction film as a side-scrolling blend of shooting and beat-'em-up action. Players guide the armored Detroit police officer through crime-ridden streets, warehouses, and other hostile locations, confronting armed gangs and the forces behind Omni Consumer Products. RoboCop can strike enemies at close range or fire his pistol and acquired weapons, with action punctuated by challenges inspired by scenes from the film.

The recognizable metallic walk, digitized speech, and imposing ED-209 encounter helped translate the movie's atmosphere to the arcade. Data East developed the coin-op game under a sublicense from Ocean Software, which later brought adaptations to home computers. Its substantial success helped make RoboCop one of the most widely recognized film-licensed arcade games of the late 1980s.

games.title: Robocop 2
games.description:
RoboCop 2 (1991) is Data East's arcade sequel to its 1988 movie adaptation. The cyborg policeman returns to Detroit to fight the drug trade surrounding the dangerous substance Nuke and confront the criminal Cain, whose fate in the film leads to the creation of RoboCop 2. The game is primarily a side-scrolling shooter, with RoboCop advancing through enemy-filled streets and industrial scenes while firing at threats from several directions.

Compared with the first arcade RoboCop, this installment gives more emphasis to gunfire and less to deliberate platform action. Its stages, bosses, and presentation borrow from the 1990 film while taking considerable liberties with the order of events, creating a distinct arcade interpretation rather than a scene-for-scene retelling.

games.title: Atomic Robo-kid
games.description:
Atomic Robo-Kid (1988) is an eccentric horizontally scrolling shooter from UPL. The player controls a squat, heavily armed robotic hero sent to reclaim the devastated colony of Terra-12 from mutant alien invaders. Robo-Kid can fly, hover in place, and move on foot through environments that combine open passages with tight caverns, collecting weapons and upgrades along the way.

The game's huge, sometimes screen-filling bosses are a major attraction, and several stages offer branching paths rather than one strictly linear route. Dueling enemy robots and colorful, grotesque creatures add variety to its prolonged campaign. Its peculiar character design, exploratory pacing, and elaborate enemies separate it from the sleek spaceship shooters that dominated the genre.

games.title: Robot Bowl
games.description:
Robot Bowl (1977) is Exidy's monochrome arcade interpretation of ten-pin bowling. Seen from above, a mechanical-looking bowler steps toward the foul line while players choose the direction and timing of a throw. Buttons allow the ball's path to be adjusted and, crucially, curved left or right after release, making hooks an important way to hit difficult pin formations.

The game follows familiar bowling scoring rules and supports one or two participants. Designed and programmed by Edward Valeau and Howell Ivey, it reflects a period when arcade manufacturers were looking for recognizable sports activities that could work with simple on-screen animation and dedicated controls.

games.title: Robotron
games.description:
Robotron: 2084 (1982) is one of the foundational twin-stick arcade shooters. Designed by Eugene Jarvis and Larry DeMar for Williams, it places a lone human survivor in single-screen arenas filled with murderous robots. The left joystick moves the hero in eight directions while the right joystick fires independently, allowing players to retreat and attack at the same time. Each wave begins in apparent chaos and rapidly becomes a demanding exercise in movement, positioning, and target prioritization.

The robots are not interchangeable cannon fodder. Grunts charge the player, Hulks are nearly indestructible, and Enforcers and other specialists create overlapping threats. Rescuing the last human family members earns escalating score bonuses, but the temptation to collect them often leads straight into danger. There is no scrolling or hiding; survival depends on reading the whole arena and carving out space.

Robotron's ferocious pace, piercing electronic sounds, dense sprite action, and distinctive dual-joystick controls influenced generations of arena shooters. It remains a landmark of arcade game design because its basic rules are instantly understandable yet reward tremendous skill. The subtitle 2084 evokes a dystopian future in which humanity's own machines have turned against it.

games.title: Robo Wres 2001
games.description:
Robo Wres 2001 (1986) is Sega's futuristic take on professional wrestling, replacing human athletes with six mechanical contestants supposedly representing different countries. Seen from an elevated viewpoint, each match takes place inside a wrestling ring where robots can move in multiple directions, grapple, and unleash individual special moves. Three attack buttons produce different techniques according to the fighters' position and distance.

The player must win a sequence of bouts to claim the championship, with defeated robots reduced to scrap. Built on hardware related to Sega's earlier Appoooh, it retains the recognizable spectacle of wrestling while exchanging body slams between people for collisions between oversized machines.

games.title: Rock Climber
games.description:
Rock Climber (1981) is a climbing action game released by Taito with a control scheme reminiscent of Crazy Climber. The player scales a steep rock face using two joysticks, one for each arm, coordinating hand movements to ascend while avoiding wildlife and other hazards. Monkeys, birds, and bears threaten to knock the climber off the cliff, while a radar display tracks positions on the rock face.

Rather than scaling an urban skyscraper, the game turns the same demanding hand-over-hand movement into an outdoor mountaineering challenge. It is an obscure early example of specialized dual-joystick arcade controls, implemented on electronics related to Namco's Galaxian hardware.

games.title: Rock'n Tread
games.description:
Rock'n Tread (1999) is Jaleco's Japan-only arcade rhythm game, built around matching musical prompts with precisely timed button presses. Notes and rhythm cues advance across the display, and accuracy determines the player's performance and score. Its music-game presentation draws on the late-1990s arcade boom popularized by Konami's beatmania.

Rock'n Tread became the opening entry in a short-lived series of closely related releases, including multiple sequels and a two-player variant. The series is also remembered for a legal dispute in which Konami challenged Jaleco over similarities to beatmania, contributing to the games' removal from circulation.

games.title: Rock'n Tread 2
games.description:
Rock'n Tread 2 (1999) continues Jaleco's arcade music-game series only months after the original. As in its predecessor, players follow on-screen musical prompts and attempt to hit the corresponding inputs in time, accumulating points for accurate rhythm and timing. It is a single-player performance game rather than a conventional action title.

Released exclusively in Japan, this sequel belongs to Jaleco's concentrated attempt to enter the arcade rhythm market at the end of the 1990s. It retains the Rock'n Tread identity while offering another installment in the series' rapidly expanding song-based format.

games.title: Rock'n 3
games.description:
Rock'n 3 (1999) is the third main installment in Jaleco's Japanese arcade rhythm-game line. Players respond to scrolling musical notes and timing prompts, pressing the appropriate controls in step with the music to build a high score. Its emphasis is on tempo recognition and repeated performances of individual songs, not exploration or combat.

Released in December 1999, it followed Rock'n Tread and Rock'n Tread 2 in quick succession. The cabinet and gameplay belong to the same short-lived rhythm-game family that Jaleco developed during the height of Japan's music-arcade craze.

games.title: Rock'n 4
games.description:
Rock'n 4 is a rare 2000 entry in Jaleco's Japanese rhythm-game series, represented in emulation by a prototype arcade version. Instead of steering a character through stages, the player follows timed musical cues using performance-oriented inputs. The Rock'n games employed a pick-like switch and a foot pedal, emulated through ordinary button inputs, to evoke instrumental playing.

As the last arcade installment in a series that began with Rock'n Tread in 1999, it is an unusual survival from Jaleco's brief engagement with the music-game market. Its prototype status is important: the preserved game should not be mistaken for a widely distributed mainstream arcade release.

games.title: Rock'n MegaSession
games.description:
Rock'n MegaSession (1999) is a two-player-capable offshoot of Jaleco's Rock'n Tread rhythm-game series. Players respond to musical timing cues rather than controlling conventional on-screen characters, attempting to synchronize their inputs with the soundtrack and earn high performance scores. The possibility of two simultaneous performers distinguishes it from the solo-focused early Rock'n Tread titles.

The game was released only in Japan, during a burst of Jaleco rhythm-game releases in 1999. Its dual-player format reflects the appeal of music cabinets as public, social performances as much as individual score challenges.

games.title: Rock 'n Rage
games.description:
Konami's Rock 'n Rage (1986), known in Japan as Koi no Hotrock, combines a rock-music premise with an overhead, freely scrolling action adventure. After the band's singer Sheena is kidnapped by a strange force, bandmates John and Rick travel through five different historical periods to rescue her. One or two players fight enemies, search for the route onward, and confront a boss at each era's conclusion.

Breaking pots may reveal score bonuses or musical-note weapons that permit ranged attacks, while special characters can supply temporary protection. The time-travel theme provides a changing collection of enemies and settings, and the soundtrack includes a recognizable arrangement of 'Rock Me Amadeus'. Its mix of pop-culture humor, cooperative brawling, and historical fantasy gives this relatively obscure Konami game a distinctive personality.

games.title: MTV Rock-N-Roll Trivia
games.description:
MTV Rock-N-Roll Trivia (Part 2) is a 1986 arcade quiz game from Triumph Software that tests players' knowledge of rock music and music-video culture. Its questions draw on performers, songs, and popular-music history, particularly material associated with the 1960s through the early MTV years. The 'Part 2' designation identifies a second question set rather than a different action game.

It is an example of the brief period when licensed music-video branding could provide the central theme for a coin-operated trivia machine. The challenge depends on recognizing facts about music culture rather than reflex-based controls.

games.title: Roc'n Rope
games.description:
Konami's Roc'n Rope (1983) is an inventive climbing platform game designed by Tokuro Fujiwara, who later worked on several major Capcom titles. Players guide an archaeologist up precarious ledges to reach a legendary phoenix, firing a harpoon rope into platforms above and climbing toward the next foothold. Dinosaurs and cavemen patrol the route, and there is no ordinary attack for disposing of them.

A flashlight can briefly stun enemies, while careful use of the climbing rope may leave pursuers vulnerable to a fall. Collectible feathers and eggs offer bonuses or temporary protection. The game's four layouts include open cliffs, caverns, and moving platforms, all of which demand deliberate route planning. Its harpoon-based locomotion is the defining feature, turning traversal itself into the principal puzzle.

games.title: Rod-Land
games.description:
Rod-Land (1990) is Jaleco's charming single-screen platform game starring two fairies, Tam and Rit, on a mission to rescue their kidnapped mother. Each fairy carries a magic rod that captures monsters inside a glowing field; repeatedly slamming the trapped creature against the ground defeats it and may release bonuses. Its bright graphics, whimsical enemies, and cooperative two-player option invite comparisons with Bubble Bobble, but its movement rules are strikingly different.

The fairies cannot jump. Instead, they climb existing ladders and conjure one temporary ladder at a time to reach higher platforms or escape danger. Moving that ladder can also strand an approaching monster, turning its placement into a tactical tool. The arcade game includes an additional adventure after the first quest, involving an ominous pyramid. This blend of combat, clever route-making, and storybook presentation makes Rod-Land a distinctive favorite among single-screen arcade platformers.

games.title: Rohga Armor Force
games.description:
Rohga: Armor Force, also known as Wolf Fang, is Data East's 1991-era follow-up to Vapor Trail, replacing aircraft with heavily armed walking combat machines. One or two players pilot mechs through horizontally scrolling battlefields, firing on enemy vehicles, helicopters, and enormous mechanical bosses. Unlike a normal spaceship, the mech can land on platforms, hover, and exploit changes in terrain height, giving combat a platform-game dimension.

Players can choose one of several preset machines or assemble a custom suit from modular parts, trading speed, weaponry, and defensive characteristics. The original Japanese version offers route selections and story sequences that were curtailed in some export versions. With its elaborate mechanical sprites and customizable hardware, Rohga is one of Data East's more unusual arcade shooters.

games.title: The Return of Ishtar
games.description:
The Return of Ishtar (1986) is Namco's ambitious arcade sequel to The Tower of Druaga. Rather than repeating the earlier game's single-character dungeon climbing, it requires two players to work together as the warrior Gil and the priestess Ki. Gil handles close combat while Ki uses magical spells, and the partners navigate interconnected rooms, defeat monsters, and solve the dungeon's challenges by combining their complementary skills.

Its structure is closer to a cooperative action role-playing adventure than a conventional score-chasing arcade game. It dispenses with a typical score counter and uses a password system so players can resume progress, both unusual choices for a mid-1980s coin-op title. The mandatory partnership, sprawling interconnected setting, and reliance on discovering spell effects make it a fascinating experiment in arcade adventure design.

games.title: Rolling Crush
games.description:
Rolling Crush (1999) is a Korean puzzle game developed by SemiCom that follows the marble-shooting formula associated with Mitchell's Puzz Loop. Players aim colored balls toward a moving chain and try to form matching groups before the advancing line reaches its dangerous endpoint. Aiming accurately and setting up successive matches are more important than speed alone.

Its arcade revisions include releases under different licensing arrangements, with changes to visual presentation and menus. Rolling Crush illustrates how quickly the rotating-chain puzzle format spread beyond its original creators in the late 1990s.

games.title: The Return of Lady Frog
games.description:
The Return of Lady Frog (1993) is an adult-themed arcade puzzle game from Microhard built around uncovering photographs hidden beneath a grid. The player places bombs to clear small groups of covered squares, gradually exposing the background image. Gray barriers can be destroyed, but moving balloons can absorb explosions and frustrate attempts to clear the field; separate rocket attacks are needed to deal with them.

Despite its title, it is not a straightforward sequel to the earlier Lady Frog. Its mechanics and hardware have more in common with contemporary adult image-reveal puzzle games such as Splash!, making it a curious example of the borrowing and reworking common in smaller arcade releases.

games.title: Rollergames
games.description:
Konami's Rollergames (1991) recreates the televised roller-derby spectacle rather than using the side-scrolling beat-'em-up format of the unrelated NES adaptation. Two players can compete in a rink where teams of skaters and their managers are based on the television program. The action emphasizes racing around the track, maneuvering past opponents, and the physical clashes that made the show distinctive.

The arcade game includes power-up icons, at least in the Japanese release, that can temporarily speed a skater up, enable a spinning attack, or hinder opponents. Its combination of licensed personalities, sporting competition, and arcade exaggeration makes it an unusual Konami sports title from the early 1990s.

games.title: Rolling Crash / Moon Base
games.description:
Rolling Crash / Moon Base (1979) is a Nichibutsu two-in-one arcade release pairing a driving maze game with a Space Invaders-style shooting game. In Rolling Crash, the player steers a car around a figure-eight network of lanes, collecting dots while enemy cars attempt to ram it. Collisions at lane-changing points can shove the player's car into another lane, and collecting dots momentarily affects vehicle speed.

The companion Moon Base is a fixed-screen alien shooter. The combined board is a useful snapshot of the late-1970s arcade market, when manufacturers experimented with offering multiple familiar play styles from one machine. Rolling Crash's interconnected figure-eight course is its most distinctive departure from earlier car-and-dot games such as Head On.

games.title: Rompers
games.description:
Namco's Rompers (1989) is a deceptively cute single-screen maze action game about Chap, a straw-hatted gardener trying to rescue his girlfriend Rumina. Across 61 gardens, Chap must collect every key while avoiding bizarre creatures. His only direct defense is to push heavy stone walls over, crushing enemies on the other side, but many of them soon hatch from eggs and return to the chase.

The layouts demand careful planning because walls are simultaneously obstacles, weapons, and routes to safety. A time limit adds further pressure: when it expires, a fast, invulnerable vampire named Tsukaima joins the pursuit. Designed by Akira Usukura, also associated with Splatterhouse, Rompers balances comical animation with unusually demanding puzzle-like movement. It was initially a Japan-only arcade release and later appeared in Namco's Museum compilations.

games.title: Rong Rong
games.description:
Rong Rong (1994) is a mahjong-solitaire puzzle game from Nakanihon, also known as Puzzle Game Rong Rong. Unlike traditional competitive mahjong, play involves removing pairs of matching tiles from layered arrangements, in the manner of Shanghai. The game offers several distinct modes: a story-oriented Rong Rong course, a competitive two-player battle mode, and an adult-themed 'Sexy Girls' mode.

In the latter, clearing the board gradually reveals model photographs, with additional mini-games between stages. Battle mode splits the screen so two players can race to solve comparable tile layouts. These variations make Rong Rong more than a simple fixed-board tile-matching game, even though its basic rules remain rooted in mahjong solitaire.

games.title: Rotary Fighter
games.description:
Rotary Fighter (1979) is a Japanese fixed-screen shooter from Kansai Seiki Seisakusho, also known as Kasco. It is closely modeled on Taito's Space Invaders: rows of descending aliens must be destroyed with a horizontally moving gun before they reach the bottom of the screen. The graphics differ slightly, but the central rhythm of shooting through formations while avoiding enemy fire remains recognizable.

Released during the extraordinary Space Invaders boom, it illustrates the wave of imitation products that appeared throughout Japanese arcades in 1978 and 1979. Kasco itself ceased operations in 1980 as that market contracted.

games.title: Rage of the Dragons
games.description:
Rage of the Dragons (2002) is a Neo Geo fighting game developed through a collaboration involving Mexico's Evoga and Japan's Noise Factory, with publishing by Playmore. Its central idea is a two-character tag team: each player chooses a pair of fighters and can switch between them during a match, allowing the resting partner to regain some health. Partner attacks and coordinated combinations reward players for thinking beyond the abilities of a single character.

A special meter charges as fighters land attacks and can be spent on stronger techniques and counters. The game's cast, dramatic visual style, and loose thematic connections to Double Dragon give it a distinctive identity among the Neo Geo's later fighting games. Released near the end of the platform's commercial life, it has since gained renewed attention through modern reissues.

games.title: Rough Racer
games.description:
Rough Racer (1990) is a top-down racing game released by Sega on System 24 hardware, closely related in spirit to Atari's Sprint series. One to four drivers compete on compact, brightly colored circuits, fighting to finish at least third in order to progress. Courses change theme and layout, demanding quick adjustments to tight turns and the movements of computer-controlled rivals.

The game features ten tracks and emphasizes the immediacy of multiplayer cabinet racing rather than realistic simulation. Its overhead viewpoint and arcade rules make it an interesting counterpart to Sega's better-known behind-the-car racers, such as Out Run and Power Drift.

games.title: Rougien
games.description:
Rougien (1982) is a vertically scrolling space shooter from Sanritsu with an unusual hero: a NASA-style space shuttle. Armed with a forward-firing weapon, the shuttle fights through waves of aliens, missiles, and defensive installations to reach the monstrous Space Devil Rougien, whose giant mouth-like form dominates the final confrontation. The boss is vulnerable only during brief flashing moments, so the player must time shots rather than simply fire continuously.

The game's combination of an ordinary-looking shuttle, alien attack formations, and a surreal final enemy gives it a distinct character among early 1980s space shooters.

games.title: Round-Up
games.description:
Round-Up (1981), also released by Taito as Fitter, is a maze-and-puzzle game with a more elaborate objective than simply collecting dots. Players guide a small white robot through passages patrolled by enemy creatures, capture a red robot to change color, and then touch one of nine white circles in the maze's center to turn it red. Each successful conversion resets the player's position, requiring the sequence to be repeated while avoiding the pursuers.

After all nine circles are converted, a separate puzzle phase presents a pattern of colored squares that must be reproduced by rotating rows or columns of a central cube. This unexpected switch from pursuit to pattern manipulation gives Round-Up a distinctive two-part rhythm. The American release was distributed by Centuri, while the Fitter name was used in Japan.

games.title: Round Up 5 - Super Delta Force
games.description:
Round Up 5: Super Delta Force (1989) is Tatsumi's high-speed driving pursuit game, strongly influenced by Out Run and Chase H.Q. The player is a police officer tracking five escaping criminals across a series of highways. Branching roads determine which fugitive will be pursued, while traffic, curves, and roadside collisions threaten to consume the strict time limit.

After catching a suspect, the player must first deal with an escorting gang of bikers before repeatedly ramming the fleeing vehicle to make an arrest. Limited speed boosts help close the distance but must be conserved for difficult stretches. The combination of branching routes, exaggerated chase sequences, and two-part missions gives the game its own twist on the late-1980s arcade pursuit formula.

games.title: Route 16
games.description:
Route 16 (1981), developed by Tehkan and Sun Electronics, is a car-based maze game in which sixteen interconnected rooms form a single larger landscape. Inside each room, a close-up view shows the player's red car navigating narrow passages, collecting money bags, and avoiding pursuing vehicles. Leaving a room switches to an overview map displaying all sixteen sectors and the general locations of the cars and remaining prizes.

This change of scale is the game's defining feature: players must plan routes across the overall map while reacting quickly to dangers within individual mazes. Fuel limits add urgency, while flags can briefly reverse the usual balance of power and let the player disable pursuers. Route 16 preceded the home-console revision Route-16 Turbo and is an inventive early hybrid of driving and maze strategy.

games.title: Royal Card
games.description:
Royal Card is a 1991 video-poker machine by TAB-Austria, closely associated with the Central European family of Jolly Card-style gambling cabinets. It presents card hands on a horizontal screen and relies on dedicated deal/hold buttons for the familiar choose-and-replace rhythm of video poker. Its 65SC02 processor and AY-3-8910 audio circuitry underline the economical design of these single-purpose machines.

A remarkable number of regional adaptations and bootlegs later appeared, including Polish, German and Greek sets with encrypted graphics or revised rules. Some clandestine installations even concealed the poker game behind a separate multigame interface. That complicated lineage makes Royal Card more than a routine poker program: it is a window into Europe's highly varied 1990s video-gambling trade.

games.title: Royal Mahjong
games.description:
Royal Mahjong is an early Japanese two-player-style mahjong machine represented in AdvanceMAME by a bootleg of Nichibutsu's original game. It implements mahjong hand-building and scoring in a gambling-oriented cabinet format, where wagers are made in credits and winning hands can pay out additional credits rather than merely increasing an arcade score.

Its importance is primarily historical, as an example of the early transition from electronic mahjong to dedicated betting-style arcade machines. The preserved set should be distinguished from ordinary competitive, score-based mahjong games.

games.title: River Patrol
games.description:
River Patrol (1981) is a top-down river-navigation game by Orca, here represented by an unauthorized bootleg version. Players pilot a small boat upstream through a twisting jungle river, trying to rescue people struggling in the water. Rocks, crocodiles, and the riverbanks threaten to wreck the craft, while increasingly narrow passages demand precise steering.

The boat is continually influenced by the current: accelerating pushes it upstream, but easing off the throttle allows it to drift backward. The need to rescue swimmers while preserving forward progress gives the game an unusual balance between careful navigation and urgency. Its original design later evolved into The Bounty, which introduced altered graphics and shooting elements.

games.title: Rough Ranger
games.description:
Rough Ranger (1988), also distributed as Super Ranger, is a side-scrolling action shooter by South Korea's SunA Electronics. One or two players fight through a guarded military base to rescue a kidnapped woman, shooting armed soldiers, changing between upper and lower platforms, and navigating the doorways from which enemies emerge. Both its layout and the behavior of its masked gunmen owe an obvious debt to Namco's Rolling Thunder.

Unlike its single-player inspiration, Rough Ranger supports simultaneous two-person action, letting partners cover different approaches to the same danger. It is an interesting early example of a Korean-developed arcade game adapting an established Japanese spy-shooter formula to cooperative play.

games.title: Road Riot's Revenge
games.description:
Road Riot's Revenge is an unreleased Atari Games off-road racing prototype developed in 1993 and preserved in revisions dated 1994. A follow-up to Road Riot 4WD, it puts the player behind the wheel of an armed truck on racing courses crowded with rival vehicles. Guns and missiles can be used to hinder competitors, combining rough-terrain driving with vehicle combat.

Steering and pedal controls anchor the action in the arcade racing tradition, while its experimental status explains why it is much less familiar than Atari's released driving games. The preserved versions provide a glimpse of a series extension that never reached ordinary commercial production.

games.title: Radiant Silvergun
games.description:
Radiant Silvergun (1998) is Treasure's celebrated vertically scrolling shooter, originally created for Sega's ST-V arcade hardware and later adapted for the closely related Sega Saturn. Instead of collecting conventional weapon power-ups, the player begins with an entire arsenal: three basic shot types that can be combined into additional attacks, plus a close-range sword. Choosing the right weapon for each formation matters as much as reflexes, because enemies, terrain, and enormous multi-part bosses are designed around specific tactical possibilities.

The scoring system rewards destroying long sequences of enemies of the same color. These chains also help strengthen weapons over the course of a run, creating an unusually close link between high-score strategy and survival. The sword can absorb certain projectiles and charge a devastating area attack, while dismantling bosses piece by piece awards additional rewards. The result is a meticulously structured game in which careful planning can be as valuable as evasive skill.

Radiant Silvergun marked a major shift for Treasure, previously best known for console action games. Its small development team created it first for the arcade despite uncertainty about the genre's commercial prospects, and animated scenes were produced with assistance from Gonzo. Long treasured by import enthusiasts, it helped establish the reputation that later surrounded Treasure's Ikaruga and remains one of the most influential late-1990s shooters.

games.title: R-Shark
games.description:
R-Shark (1995) is a vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter from South Korea's Dooyong. The player takes the role of an interstellar bounty hunter who can choose among eight wanted criminals to pursue, with the selected targets forming major boss encounters. The spacecraft begins with a modest forward gun and homing-missile support, but can acquire stronger lasers and other weapons, upgrade its firepower, and unleash special attacks.

The selectable quarry gives this otherwise traditional upward-scrolling shooter a distinctive mission structure. Its colorful mechanical enemies and weapon effects reflect Dooyong's participation in the mid-1990s arcade shooting market, far removed from the similarly named R-Type series.

games.title: Rolling Thunder 2
games.description:
Rolling Thunder 2 (1990) is Namco's colorful sequel to its influential spy-themed run-and-gun game. The secret agents return to fight the terrorist organization Geldra across urban and exotic settings, with the player guiding a hero between upper and lower platforms, firing limited ammunition at masked soldiers, and entering marked doors to find fresh supplies or heavier weapons.

The most important improvement is simultaneous two-player play: one agent is Leila, now the main single-player protagonist, while the second player controls a male partner. Together they can cover one another against enemies arriving from different heights and doorways. Larger, more vibrant scenery and improved audiovisual presentation make the familiar calculated gunplay feel more elaborate, while retaining the original's demanding rhythm of shooting, ducking, and choosing when to advance.

games.title: Rolling Thunder
games.description:
Namco's Rolling Thunder (1986) is a defining early side-scrolling spy-action game. Players control secret agent Albatross, sent to infiltrate the terrorist organization Geldra and rescue the captured operative Leila Blitz. Levels are built around two heights connected by jumps and drops, with colored doorways concealing enemies, ammunition, and occasional improved weapons. The protagonist begins with a pistol whose ammunition is limited, so every shot and every opportunity to restock matters.
