The hooded enemy soldiers, known as Maskers, emerge from doors and punish careless advances. Some rooms yield a machine gun, but its ammunition also runs out. Survival requires stopping to read enemy patterns, ducking under attacks, and choosing the safest path between platforms rather than holding the fire button and running blindly.

Rolling Thunder's distinctive combination of cinematic espionage, stylish sprite animation, and methodical shooting influenced later action games including Shinobi. Licensed to Atari Games for the American market, it was followed by arcade and console sequels and remains one of Namco's best-known departures from its earlier maze and shooting games.

games.title: Romar Triv
games.description: Romar Triv is an obscure French-language Canadian trivia arcade game distributed by Romar, described in contemporary game records as a head-to-head quiz. It is especially noteworthy as a conversion kit for Intrepid circuit boards, repurposing action-game hardware for a question-and-answer format. Its question ROMs use an unconventional address-reading arrangement, a quirk shared with Super Triv that complicated the game's eventual emulation. The surviving documentation establishes its language, quiz format, four-button inputs and hardware ancestry, but not a detailed scoring or category system.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: R-Type
games.description:
Irem's R-Type (1987) is one of the most influential horizontal shooters ever made. Players pilot the R-9 Arrowhead against the grotesque alien Bydo empire, navigating eight meticulously constructed stages filled with enemy formations, moving machinery, and enormous bosses. The ship's basic gun can be supplemented by a powerful Wave Cannon that grows stronger while the fire button is held, making the timing of charged shots crucial to surviving encounters.

Its revolutionary weapon is the Force, an indestructible orange pod that can be attached to the front or rear of the ship or launched independently. Used as a shield, battering ram, or remote gun platform, the Force turns combat into a positional puzzle: its placement can completely change the safest solution to a stage. Weapon pickups alter its firing characteristics, while small satellite bits add further defensive possibilities. Careful memorization and deliberate movement matter more than constant aggression.

R-Type debuted on Irem's M72 hardware and became famous for detailed biomechanical artwork influenced by science-fiction cinema and H. R. Giger. The Force's design has been linked to the movement of dung beetles. Commercial success, numerous home conversions, and a long-running series cemented its position as a genre landmark, inspiring countless shooters built around detachable weapons, charged attacks, and intricate level design.

games.title: R-Type II
games.description:
R-Type II (1989) continues Irem's struggle against the Bydo with a new R-9 variant, more elaborate machinery, and six punishing side-scrolling stages. The player retains the familiar combination of a chargeable Wave Cannon and detachable Force pod, now with additional weapon choices and new types of laser fire. Attaching the Force to different sides of the ship remains central to navigating cramped formations and protecting vulnerable angles.

The sequel is notorious for its demanding stage layouts, especially the narrow passages and fast-moving hazards that require careful memorization. Compared with the original, the visual effects are richer and the enemy patterns more aggressive, making it a natural continuation for experienced R-Type players rather than a gentle introduction to the series.

games.title: R-Type Leo
games.description:
R-Type Leo (1992) is an unusually free-flowing entry in Irem's famous shooter series. It retains the side-scrolling science-fiction atmosphere and elaborate bosses, but breaks with the original R-Type's slow, defensive strategy. Instead of the traditional detachable Force, the player relies on two auxiliary 'Psy Bits' that can seek out nearby enemies, and the overall pace is faster and more action-oriented.

Its weapon system, colorful mechanical environments, and two-player simultaneous support give it a character closer to conventional early-1990s shooters than its predecessors. Its vibrant art and relatively approachable rhythm have earned it a special place among R-Type fans, even though the altered mechanics make it something of an outlier within the series.

games.title: Rumba Lumber
games.description:
Rumba Lumber is a prehistoric single-screen action game from Taito, released in Japan in 1985 despite its 1984 copyright date. The player controls a caveman who cuts down trees with an axe while trying to trap a flying pterodactyl within a small enclosure of remaining trees. The problem is not simply to clear the forest: removing the wrong tree can leave the dinosaur too much room to escape and reduce the final bonus.

Rolling stone wheels can knock down trees or temporarily stop other creatures, including a tyrannosaur and a mole. The stages introduce hazards such as a river, regrowing mushrooms, and an erupting volcano. Its unusual combination of tree-cutting, territory control, and enemy avoidance recalls elements of Timber, Qix, and Dig Dug without duplicating any of them.

games.title: Runaway
games.description:
Runaway is an unreleased Atari arcade prototype field-tested in 1982. The player drives a runaway railway engine through a scrolling track network, collecting mailbags, taking on extra railcars, rescuing people, and avoiding hostile locomotives. Track switches, changes of direction, and jumps over obstacles add a layer of navigation to the usual arcade chase.

The game includes drawbridges, between-stage bonus choices, and selectable skill levels, demonstrating how much of its design had been developed before cancellation. After its limited 1982 field test, the prototype resurfaced publicly at the California Extreme exhibition in 1998. It is an intriguing example of an Atari project preserved despite never entering normal arcade production.

games.title: Run and Gun
games.description:
Konami's Run and Gun (1993), released in Japan as Slam Dunk: B-Ball Show Time, is a fast five-on-five arcade basketball game that favors spectacular offense over detailed simulation. Viewed from one end of the court, players execute passes, steals, rebounds, and dramatic slam dunks with minimal rule interruptions. Apart from the shot clock and boundaries, most of the complexities of professional basketball are stripped away to keep play continuous.

Some cabinets used an unusual dual-monitor arrangement to show opposing ends of the court from complementary perspectives, making the physical setup part of the attraction. The game predates Konami's licensed NBA Give 'n Go and stands as the opening installment in the company's Run and Gun basketball series.

games.title: Run and Gun 2
games.description:
Run and Gun 2 (1996) expands Konami's arcade basketball formula with improved graphics on System GX hardware and more elaborate moves. Five-on-five teams race up and down the court, executing passes, fast breaks, dunks, and defensive maneuvers in an intentionally streamlined version of the sport. New techniques include alley-oops, spins, and stronger options for blocking opponents and controlling possession.

The game supports solo play and multiplayer competition or cooperation on the same team, preserving the original's emphasis on quick, crowd-pleasing action. Its detailed player animation and more varied maneuvers make it a substantial follow-up rather than simply a roster update.

games.title: Rushing Beat Shura
games.description:
Rushing Beat Shura is an unauthorized arcade conversion of Jaleco's Super Famicom beat-'em-up, preserved as a 1997 bootleg. The game retains the console title's side-scrolling street fights, in which one or two players battle through groups of enemies using punches, kicks, throws, and character-specific techniques. Its arcade identity comes from the conversion of home-console software for coin-operated use, not from a separately developed official Jaleco sequel.

The preserved hardware uses Super Nintendo-derived components, including the Ricoh 5A22 processor, an important distinction from purpose-built arcade beat-'em-up boards. As a result, its appearance and fundamental gameplay are those of the console original, while its commercial format is that of an illicit arcade adaptation.

games.title: Rushing Heroes
games.description:
Rushing Heroes (1996) is Konami's 3D American football arcade game. Players select from teams with different ratings for passing, rushing, blocking, and tackling, then choose plays and attempt to outmaneuver the opposing defense. Running, passing, and kicking options reproduce the tactical structure of football, while animated players and spoken commentary give the matches an accessible televised-sport presentation.

Its large rendered athletes and perspective view distinguish it from older sprite-based football games. The focus is on immediate competition and satisfying offensive plays rather than the management depth of a home-console sports simulation.

games.title: Rival Schools
games.description:
Rival Schools: United by Fate (1997) is Capcom's exuberant 3D fighting game set among competing Japanese high schools. Its cast includes students, teachers, athletes, and martial artists whose personal stories intersect across a stylized schoolyard mystery. Each player selects a team of two characters, although fights are conducted one fighter at a time. The partner can be called in for spectacular 'Team Up' techniques that add a cooperative flourish to ordinary one-on-one combat.

Built on PlayStation-derived arcade hardware, Rival Schools combines polygonal fighters with bold anime character designs and highly expressive animations. A straightforward four-button system of two punches and two kicks makes the basics approachable, while launchers, aerial exchanges, and partner choices create depth. Its blend of school comedy, character relationships, and over-the-top fighting helped the game develop a lasting cult following and led to the sequel Project Justice.

games.title: Rygar
games.description:
Tecmo's Rygar (1986), originally titled Argos no Senshi in Japan, is a demanding side-scrolling action platformer about a legendary warrior battling through hostile lands to defeat the ruler Ligar. Its signature weapon is the Diskarmor, a spiked circular blade attached to a chain that shoots forward and returns like a lethal yo-yo. Players can jump, crouch, climb ropes, and use special maneuvers to negotiate complicated landscapes packed with monsters.

The combat system rewards mastery of reach, timing, and movement. Hidden bonuses and equipment upgrades provide help during the long adventure, but the pace remains uncompromising. Rygar became one of Tecmo's signature early arcade games and inspired several very different home adaptations, most famously the NES version with its more exploration-oriented design.

games.title: Gourmet Battle Quiz Ryohrioh CooKing
games.description:
Gourmet Battle Quiz Ryohrioh CooKing (1998) is a Japan-only quiz game by Visco centered on food and cooking knowledge. One or two players participate in a culinary contest by answering questions rather than fighting enemies or moving through conventional action stages. Its exaggerated cooking-competition theme recalls the televised Japanese phenomenon Iron Chef.

The arcade game's novelty lies in turning a specialized topic, cuisine and culinary trivia, into a head-to-head coin-operated challenge. Its dependence on Japanese-language questions also helps explain why it remained a regional curiosity.

games.title: VS Mahjong Otome Ryouran
games.description:
VS Mahjong Otome Ryouran (1998) is an adult-themed Japanese mahjong game for Kaneko's Super Nova arcade platform. Players compete in mahjong matches against selectable illustrated female characters, with anime-style sequences and revealing presentation providing the rewards for successful play. Unlike traditional fixed-panel mahjong machines, this title uses joystick-based controls.

Developed by Electro Design and published by Kaneko, it reflects the late-1990s transition of adult mahjong toward more elaborate character graphics. The cast also draws on models associated with Kaneko's Gals Panic S2.

games.title: Ryu Jin
games.description:
Ryu Jin (1993), whose name means 'Dragon God', is a vertically scrolling shoot-'em-up developed by East Technology and published by Taito for Japanese arcades. One or two players pilot a combat craft through airborne enemy formations, collecting armament upgrades and confronting increasingly dangerous opposition. The game follows the fast, forward-scrolling style of early-1990s Japanese shooters, with cooperative play allowing two pilots to cover more of the screen.

Its Japan-only distribution and limited documentation make it a comparatively obscure entry in Taito's publishing catalog, but the basic shooting-game format and two-player option are well established.

games.title: RyuKyu
games.description:
RyuKyu (1990) is a card-based puzzle game developed by Success for Sega's System 16 arcade hardware. Known in some home versions as Solitaire Poker, it asks players to place cards into a five-by-five grid and form poker hands along rows, columns, and diagonals. Each combination earns points according to its value, and the player must reach a target score to progress to the next round.

Unlike ordinary poker, there is no betting contest with an opponent: the challenge is spatial planning, balancing several potential hands before the board fills. This unusual mixture of solitaire, pattern construction, and poker rankings gives RyuKyu a distinct identity among Sega's early-1990s puzzle releases.

games.title: Strikers 1945
games.description:
Psikyo's Strikers 1945 (1995) is a landmark vertically scrolling shooter that imagines a new global conflict immediately after World War II. Players select from six distinct propeller-driven aircraft, each equipped with its own primary weapon, charge attack, and screen-clearing bomb. Their mission is to defeat the secret military organization CANY, whose supposedly conventional weapons gradually give way to gigantic robots and science-fiction machinery.

The first four stages appear in a variable order, helping each run feel different, while the later stages demand mastery of increasingly dense bullet patterns. Gold bars and other bonuses reward precise timing and risk-taking. Strikers 1945 helped establish the brisk, disciplined shooting style for which Psikyo became famous: short bursts of dangerous enemy fire, fast-moving bullets, and bosses whose attack sequences require repeated practice.

games.title: Strikers 1945 II
games.description:
Strikers 1945 II (1997) refines Psikyo's celebrated military-fantasy shooter with more elaborate stages, smoother presentation, and a new selection of six aircraft. Following the defeat of CANY in the first game, the FGR faction uses stolen technology to renew the threat of global war. Players again choose an aircraft with distinctive weapons, a charged special shot, and emergency bombs, then fight through a mixture of familiar wartime settings and extravagant mechanical enemies.

The first four areas appear in varying order, with the remaining stages arranged as a more demanding finale. Psikyo's characteristic fast bullet patterns and sudden close-range attacks reward learning enemy behavior, while score-minded players can collect gold bars at favorable moments for higher rewards. It remains one of the studio's most polished and accessible traditional vertical shooters.

games.title: Strikers 1945 III (World) / Strikers 1999
games.description:
Strikers 1945 III, released in Japan as Strikers 1999 (1999), moves Psikyo's famous shooting series from postwar propeller fighters to modern jet aircraft. A mysterious invasion of nanomachines turns the world's military equipment against humanity, prompting an international team of pilots to launch a counterattack. Players select aircraft inspired by modern combat jets, each with distinctive firepower, charged weapons, and bombs.

Its vertical-scrolling stages retain the series' fast-moving enemy bullets, intimidating bosses, and alternating early-stage order, but the setting introduces advanced aircraft and futuristic threats on a much larger scale. The secret aircraft and demanding second loop add incentives for expert players. Strikers 1999 is a particularly vivid example of Psikyo's ability to wrap rigorous, pattern-based arcade shooting around an extravagantly implausible military story.

games.title: Strikers 1945 Plus
games.description:
Strikers 1945 Plus (1999) is Psikyo's Neo Geo adaptation and reimagining of its Strikers 1945 formula, published by SNK for MVS cabinets. Although the action still scrolls vertically, the game is framed for the Neo Geo's horizontal display. Players select from six World War II-era aircraft, plus a hidden fighter, and battle through eight stages filled with mechanical war machines and overwhelming firepower.

The aircraft have unique normal attacks and charged supershots, while bombs summon supporting aircraft that protect the player as they attack. Randomized ordering for the opening stages and a much harder second loop preserve the replay value of the arcade originals. Rather than a simple conversion of Strikers 1945 II, Plus mixes familiar enemies and stage ideas with revised presentation and mechanics specifically suited to the Neo Geo.

games.title: Saboten Bombers
games.description:
Saboten Bombers (1992) is a colorful single-screen platform game developed by NMK and published by Tecmo. Players control two animated cacti, Wanpi and Tsuupi, clearing each stage of pests by throwing bouncing bombs. The weapons ricochet around platforms before exploding, making trajectories hard to predict; the explosions can also hurt the player who threw them.

Across more than fifty stages, the two-player cooperative action mixes the charm of Bubble Bobble with the volatility of an arena full of explosives. Bonus items and cake pieces provide rewards, while a separate versus mode allows competitive play. Its deceptively simple objective becomes increasingly tactical as the screens fill with enemies, bomb blasts, and awkward escape routes.

games.title: Sadari
games.description:
Sadari (1993) is an adult-themed falling-block puzzle game developed by Dooyong and published by NTC. Players arrange colored pieces into lines of three or more matching blocks, clearing space on the board and scoring points as new blocks continue to arrive. Special power-up pieces can alter the field, rewarding players who plan combinations rather than merely eliminate isolated matches.

Its puzzle mechanics follow the match-three tradition established by games such as Columns, while its risqué imagery reflects a separate branch of the early-1990s Korean arcade market. The game is more about board management and pattern recognition than the action suggested by many of Dooyong's better-known shooting titles.

games.title: Safari
games.description:
Safari (1977) is a black-and-white hunting action game released by Gremlin Industries and licensed to Taito for Japanese distribution. Players guide a hunter around a single-screen wilderness, aiming a rifle at approaching lions, snakes, wild boars, and vultures. The unusual two-joystick arrangement divides movement and firing direction, demanding that players position the hunter while aiming at threats coming from different angles.

Rounds last a limited amount of time, and being caught by an animal costs precious seconds while the hunter recovers. The large monochrome animal sprites are unusually expressive for such early hardware. Scoring enough points can earn extended play, giving skilled players another reason to balance aggressive hunting against avoiding contact.

games.title: Safari Rally
games.description:
Safari Rally (1979) is an early SNK maze-driving game. Players guide a car through a network of lanes, collecting dots while avoiding rival vehicles that attempt to collide with it. The patterns of enemy cars and traffic grow more complicated as sections of the maze are cleared, turning what initially seems like a straightforward drive into a careful exercise in route choice.

Its single-screen, overhead design belongs to the brief vogue for car-and-dot maze games around the end of the 1970s, before arcade driving games moved toward more elaborate scrolling roads and simulated depth.

games.title: Pretty Soldier Sailor Moon
games.description:
Pretty Soldier Sailor Moon (1995) is a side-scrolling beat-'em-up developed by Gazelle and published by Banpresto, based on the hugely popular manga and anime franchise. Players choose from Sailor Moon, Mercury, Mars, Jupiter, and Venus, each bringing distinctive attacks and special moves to the fight against waves of supernatural enemies. One or two players advance through five stages, punching, kicking, throwing opponents, and confronting bosses drawn from the series' magical-girl world.

The game pairs colorful animation and recognizable character designs with the stage-by-stage structure of Final Fight. Gazelle's staff included developers associated with the celebrated Toaplan arcade tradition, and the game's dramatic effects and highly detailed sprites show that pedigree. It remains a notable licensed arcade adaptation because it gives each of the five heroines a substantial active role rather than relegating the series to a conventional puzzle or quiz format.

games.title: Mahjong Sailor Wars
games.description:
Mahjong Sailor Wars (1993) is a Japanese adult-themed mahjong game by Nichibutsu, presented as a spin-off of the Mahjong Triple Wars line. Its opponents are anime-style sailor-uniform heroines, and victorious mahjong play unlocks revealing character scenes. Despite the borrowed magical-girl imagery, the core challenge is forming winning hands under Japanese mahjong rules rather than controlling characters in action combat.

The game belongs to Nichibutsu's substantial catalog of character-focused mahjong machines. A separate Sailor Wars-R variant adapted the theme to a betting or medal-machine format.

games.title: Salamander
games.description:
Konami's Salamander (1986), released in North America as Life Force, is a spectacular spin-off of Gradius. It follows the Vic Viper and the new Lord British spacecraft through six stages that alternate between horizontal and vertical scrolling. The ships fight through biological interiors, volcanic landscapes, and hostile mechanical structures, confronting bosses of extraordinary scale. Two players can cooperate simultaneously, a major attraction compared with the original Gradius.

The initial Salamander release replaces Gradius's selectable power meter with straightforward weapon pickups, producing faster and more immediate action. Obstacles grow or change shape as players approach, and the game's combination of organic imagery and mechanical hazards creates an exceptionally memorable visual identity. Different regional and later Japanese Life Force versions also vary in presentation and power-up behavior.

Salamander was influential for its mixture of scrolling directions, cooperative play, and carefully choreographed set pieces. Its unforgettable first stage, where living tissue seems to close around the players, helped make it a classic of 1980s shooting-game design and a lasting branch of the Gradius family.

games.title: Salamander 2
games.description:
Salamander 2 (1996) revives Konami's biological science-fiction shooter a decade after the original. Once again the Vic Viper and Lord British spacecraft fight through six stages that mix horizontal and vertical scrolling, dodging alien organisms, mechanical defenses, and huge boss creatures. The colorful two-dimensional artwork is enhanced by three-dimensional effects, giving the familiar grotesque environments a new sense of depth.

The simplified item-based weapon system returns, with several weapons capable of temporary higher-power upgrades. Two-player simultaneous action remains a central feature. Salamander 2 does not radically reinvent its predecessor, but its elaborate stage transformations and modernized audiovisual presentation make it a carefully crafted late arcade sequel to one of Konami's signature shooters.

games.title: Samurai Shodown V Special / Samurai Spirits Zero Special

variants.title: Samurai Shodown V Special / Samurai Spirits Zero Special (set 1, uncensored)
Samurai Shodown V Special / Samurai Spirits Zero Special (set 2, censored)
Samurai Shodown V Special / Samurai Spirits Zero Special (set 3, less censored)

games.description:
Samurai Shodown V Special (2004), known in Japan as Samurai Spirits Zero Special, is the final official Samurai Shodown release for SNK's original Neo Geo hardware. It builds on Samurai Shodown V with a larger playable roster, adding major bosses such as Amakusa, Zankuro, Gaoh, and Mizuki to the existing fighters. The familiar weapon-based duels retain their emphasis on spacing, punishing counters, and the danger of a single powerful slash.

This version is especially remembered for its brutal finishing moves and the controversy surrounding censorship of certain home-cartridge releases. Different revisions altered how much violence was shown, and replacement cartridges were issued in response to complaints about the original release. As a competitively focused revision rather than an entirely new numbered episode, V Special is often treated as the most complete late-era Neo Geo expression of the series' high-damage sword-fighting formula.

games.title: Samurai Shodown / Samurai Spirits
games.description:
SNK's Samurai Shodown (1993), called Samurai Spirits in Japan, reshaped the one-on-one fighting genre by making weapons and measured spacing more important than long strings of punches. Set in a stylized late-eighteenth-century world, it brings together swordfighters, ninjas, and other combatants, including Haohmaru, Nakoruru, and Galford, in a supernatural struggle culminating in a confrontation with Amakusa. Its roster of twelve selectable fighters offers dramatically different attack ranges and fighting rhythms.

The game emphasizes slow, dangerous blows that can remove a huge amount of health. Fighters may be disarmed, forcing them to improvise until their weapons are recovered, while a rage gauge boosts the danger of an angry opponent. SNK's zooming camera, striking sprite work, and soundtrack incorporating traditional Japanese instruments give the duels a cinematic sense of scale.

Samurai Shodown became one of the Neo Geo's defining successes and provided a compelling alternative to Street Fighter II's unarmed martial arts. Its weighty attacks, distinctive feudal-fantasy setting, and memorable characters established a major fighting-game franchise that continued for decades.

games.title: Samurai Shodown II / Shin Samurai Spirits - Haohmaru jigokuhen
games.description:
Samurai Shodown II (1994), known in Japan as Shin Samurai Spirits, expands SNK's acclaimed weapon-based fighter with a larger cast, more expressive animation, and refinements to nearly every part of combat. Returning favorites are joined by new fighters with distinctive blades and techniques, bringing the roster to fifteen. Duels remain built around the threat of powerful attacks, careful spacing, and sudden reversals rather than lengthy combos.

A more elaborate rage and special-move system can unleash devastating attacks, including techniques that temporarily break an opponent's weapon. New evasive maneuvers, richer stages, and playful hidden details add depth without losing the original's identity. Widely admired for its balance of spectacle and technical combat, Samurai Shodown II is often regarded as one of the high points of SNK's classic Neo Geo fighting catalog.

games.title: Samurai Shodown III / Samurai Spirits - Zankurou Musouken

variants.title: Samurai Shodown III / Samurai Spirits - Zankurou Musouken (set 1)
Fighters Swords (Korean release of Samurai Shodown III)
Samurai Shodown III / Samurai Spirits - Zankurou Musouken (set 2)

games.description:
Samurai Shodown III: Blades of Blood (1995) takes SNK's sword-fighting series in a darker, more severe direction. Its redesigned roster and somber stages revolve around the threat of the murderous swordsman Zankuro. Several lighter characters from earlier games disappear, while the returning fighters are redrawn in a more serious style. Players choose between Slash and Bust versions of each warrior, allowing different move sets and approaches to combat.

The controls shift toward three levels of sword attack plus a kick button, and matches reward sharp timing, decisive counters, and knowledge of each character's capabilities. Compared with Samurai Shodown II, the atmosphere is more ominous and the battles can be brutally short. This willingness to revise both mechanics and tone gives the third installment its own strong identity.

games.title: Samurai Shodown IV - Amakusa's Revenge / Samurai Spirits - Amakusa Kourin
games.description:
Samurai Shodown IV: Amakusa's Revenge (1996) returns to the supernatural conflict surrounding Amakusa while developing the aggressive combat style introduced by Samurai Shodown III. Its seventeen playable warriors can still be selected in Slash or Bust forms, altering their techniques and personalities. The action is faster and more combo-oriented than the first two games, yet the risk of a heavy weapon strike remains central.

A new combination attack initiated with the C and D buttons offers extended offense, while unusual systems include intentionally forfeiting a round to regain a tactical advantage in the next. Some defensive mechanics from the previous game were removed, leading to a more committed style of play. Detailed character animation, elaborate backgrounds, and multiple endings make this a memorable late-1990s Neo Geo fighter.

games.title: Samurai Shodown V / Samurai Spirits Zero

variants.title: Samurai Shodown V / Samurai Spirits Zero (set 1)
Samurai Shodown V / Samurai Spirits Zero (bootleg)
Samurai Shodown V / Samurai Spirits Zero (set 2)

games.description:
Samurai Shodown V (2003), titled Samurai Spirits Zero in Japan, returns SNK's weapon-based fighting series to its feudal-era roots. Developed by Yuki Enterprise, it serves as a prequel to the original game and features a large cast of returning favorites and new warriors. Haohmaru, Nakoruru, and other familiar characters fight alongside new figures in a story of unrest surrounding the general Gaoh.

Its combat emphasizes measured sword strikes, defensive judgment, and explosive moments of high damage. New and revised special systems change how fighters manage their rage and opportunities for reversal. The game was developed during SNK's revival and is significant as one of the last major fighting titles produced for the original Neo Geo platform. It was subsequently revised into Samurai Shodown V Special.

games.title: Samurai
games.description:
Samurai (1980), also known as Samurai Goyō, is an early Sega arcade action game set in a stylized historical Japan. The player controls a lone swordsman inside an arena, moving between enemies and striking with a blade that can be held at different heights. Guards attack directly while other opponents launch projectiles and use weapons such as hooked ropes, creating a primitive but demanding form of crowd combat.

After the player defeats enough ordinary opponents, a stronger officer appears to challenge the samurai in a duel. The game's separation of common enemies and boss encounters was unusual for its time. Released on Sega's VIC Dual hardware, Samurai is an important precursor to later sword-fighting action games, not to be confused with an unrelated Odyssey² game sometimes described under the same name.

games.title: Samurai Aces
games.description:
Samurai Aces (1993), known in Japan as Sengoku Ace, is the first arcade game developed by Psikyo. It reimagines feudal Japan as a wild mixture of military technology, fantasy monsters, and anachronistic flying machines. Players choose from six very different pilots, each with an individual aircraft, shot pattern, bomb attack, and personality, then fly through vertically scrolling stages to confront an evil cult and its bizarre mechanical creations.

Its colorful bosses transform and unfold into unexpected shapes, anticipating the extravagant machinery of Psikyo's later Strikers games. Two-player cooperative play and different character combinations add variety, while numerous endings reward experimentation. Samurai Aces is an important early statement of the studio's distinctive mix of fast arcade shooting, dramatic set pieces, and playful fantasy storytelling.

games.title: Sando-R
games.description:
Sando-R (1995), released outside Japan as Treasure Hunt: Puzzle & Action, is Sega's third entry in the Tanto-R series of timed mini-game collections. Running on the Saturn-derived ST-V arcade platform, it places one or two players in a colorful, three-dimensional cartoon adventure where each step is resolved through a short challenge. The twenty-two mini-games combine observation, quick reactions, puzzle solving, and other simple tasks under strict time limits.

Success depends on understanding a new rule almost immediately, then completing it before time runs out. The game turns arcade play into a series of unpredictable contests rather than a single continuous action system. Its whimsical visuals and competitive cooperative possibilities make it an inventive example of Sega's party-style arcade design.

games.title: Sand Scorpion
games.description:
Sand Scorpion, also known as Sasori, is a 1992 vertically scrolling shooter developed by Sankindo and published by Face. One or two players fly through airborne enemy formations and heavily defended areas, using upgraded weapons to survive attacks from all sides. The action follows the traditional arcade shooting pattern of moving upward through stages, collecting useful equipment, and confronting larger enemies.

Its combination of cooperative play and elaborate weapon effects places it among the lesser-known Japanese vertical shooters of the early 1990s. The name Sasori means 'scorpion' in Japanese.

games.title: Sarge
games.description:
Sarge (1985) is Bally Midway's unusual military action game in which up to two players command combat vehicles against both enemy forces and one another. The player begins with a tank but can also deploy helicopters, switching between different tactical possibilities during the battle. Its separate movement controls and firing inputs give the action a physical, multi-joystick feel closer to an arcade combat simulator than a simple overhead shooter.

Destroying enemy vehicles and surviving engagements earns promotions. Designed with contributions from artist Brian Colin and programmer Jeff Nauman, who later worked together on Rampage, Sarge was an early example of an arcade game allowing players to field different types of vehicles within the same conflict. Its competitive and cooperative possibilities gave it an unusual degree of tactical flexibility for the era.

games.title: Taisen Tanto-R Sashissu!!
games.description:
Taisen Tanto-R Sashissu!! is Sega's fourth Tanto-R mini-game collection, officially released in Japanese arcades in February 1998 on the Saturn-derived ST-V platform. Unlike earlier cooperative-leaning entries, its twelve mini-games are designed as direct head-to-head contests. Players choose from six characters and compete in quick challenges involving memory, striking with a paper fan, air hockey, and other tests of timing and observation.

The winner of each contest takes money from the loser; reaching the required sum clears a stage, while running out of funds ends the game. This competitive wager-like structure gives Sashissu a clearer two-player rivalry than the series' earlier collections. A Korean version was distributed as DaeJeon! SanJeon SuJeon.

games.title: Sasuke vs. Commander
games.description:
Sasuke vs. Commander is a 1980 fixed-screen shooter published by SNK and developed by Tose, reportedly its first game. Rather than imitating the space battles of contemporary shooters, it follows a blue-clad ninja defending a Japanese castle. Sasuke moves horizontally along the bottom of the screen and throws kunai at red and green ninjas leaping between trees. Their shuriken are dangerous, but so are the bodies of defeated enemies, which tumble down and must be dodged.

Regular waves alternate with timed 'Magic Bonus' encounters against eight distinctive commanders. Each announces a magical technique before attacking, and faster victories award larger bonuses. After the complete sequence, the stages repeat. The unusual emphasis on individual bosses makes it an early example of a shooter built around recurring boss battles, well before that structure became commonplace.

A Japanese arcade success, Sasuke vs. Commander also illustrates SNK's early experimentation outside conventional science-fiction themes. It retains an especially memorable game-over gag: the defeated hero runs away, trips over a rock and falls flat.

games.title: Satan of Saturn
games.description:
Satan of Saturn is a 1981 fixed-screen space shooter developed by SNK and distributed in North America by Taito under the name Zarzon. Inspired by Space Invaders but organized into four different screens, it sends the player's ship on a campaign toward Saturn, confronting attacking rockets, UFOs and the creatures called Satans. The craft moves left and right at the bottom of the vertically oriented display, with the player firing upward and aiming to survive successive enemy formations.

Comets and dragonfly-like targets provide additional scoring opportunities, while reaching the designated score threshold awards an extra ship. The changing screens and variety of targets help distinguish it from a straightforward Invaders imitation. Its alternate Western title is worth noting when comparing arcade sets or original cabinet artwork.

games.title: Saturn
games.description: Saturn is a relatively obscure 1983 vertical shooter developed by Britain's Zilec Electronics and distributed by Jaleco. The player pilots a spacecraft defending Saturn against approaching aliens, star-shaped hazards and brightly colored ringed planets. Play continues as an arcade endurance challenge rather than a story-driven campaign. The game uses an eight-way joystick and two buttons, and its Z80-based hardware represents the less familiar British-developed side of Jaleco's early arcade catalogue.

games.title: Sauro
games.description:
Sauro is a 1987 horizontally scrolling submarine shooter from Spanish developer Tecfri. Players guide a submarine through waters filled with hostile vessels, depth charges and mines, using an eight-way joystick and two buttons to navigate and attack. Fuel pickups are important for survival, while triple-shot weapons, missiles and shields offer relief from the increasingly crowded attack patterns. A powerful enemy submarine waits at the end of each section.

The game's preservation history has revealed numerous board revisions and licensed editions. Particularly intriguing is a Tecfri board titled Sea Wolf, an apparently earlier or experimental version that lets players begin at any of five stages, unlike the ordinary Sauro releases. It is an unusual European take on the scrolling arcade shooter.

games.title: Savage Reign / Fu'un Mokushiroku - kakutou sousei
games.description:
Savage Reign, released by SNK for the Neo Geo in 1995 as Fu'un Mokushiroku, is a weapon-based one-on-one fighter set in a futuristic version of South Town known as Jipang City. A mysterious champion, King Leo, challenges the world's fighters to a tournament promising wealth and glory. The eccentric cast combines martial arts with unconventional weapons and larger-than-life character designs.

Matches take place on two levels of the arena, between which fighters can leap using a dedicated button. Alongside punches and kicks, characters can strike with or throw their weapons, mixing close combat with ranged pressure. Holding attack buttons produces stronger blows, while the camera zooms during close encounters. These mechanics borrow ideas from Samurai Shodown and Fatal Fury but combine them in a distinctive way. Its cult following and unusual fighting system led to the 1996 follow-up Kizuna Encounter, which expanded the concept into tag-team combat.

games.title: Super Bagman
games.description:
Super Bagman is Valadon Automation's 1984 sequel to the French arcade platform game Bagman, licensed to Stern Electronics for North American distribution. The striped-suit convict returns to a sprawling mine to steal sacks of gold and deliver them to a wheelbarrow at the surface. Carrying a bag slows him down, making every ladder, passage and encounter with pursuing guards a small logistical puzzle. The three-screen mine contains moving carts, lifts, an escalator and obstructing walls.

This sequel substantially broadens the original formula with pistols, bombs and pickaxes that can stun guards or open blocked passages. Heavy blue treasure bags are especially valuable, and rescuing another convict from a dungeon can earn an extra life. Environmental tricks, such as dropping a gold bag onto a guard climbing below, reward planning as much as reflexes. Digitized speech and the complicated, interconnected layout give Super Bagman a character quite unlike most single-screen platform games of its period.

games.title: Super Champion Baseball
games.description: Super Champion Baseball is Alpha Denshi's 1989 arcade baseball game, published in North America by SNK. It is the third entry in the Champion Baseball line, following Champion Baseball and Champion Baseball Part-2: Pair Play from 1983. The game revisits the sport with revised graphics and play on more capable Motorola 68000-based hardware, using an eight-way joystick and three buttons for its baseball controls. Two players are supported. Although less famous than Alpha Denshi's later Neo Geo sports games, it forms a useful link between the company's early baseball machines and its more advanced late-1980s arcade work.

games.title: Super Basketball
games.description:
Konami's Super Basketball (1984) turns basketball into an urgent arcade scoring challenge rather than a full simulation of a match. The player's team is always attacking and starts behind on points, with a short clock in which to overtake the computer-controlled opposition. Passing, dribbling and shooting each have their own button, and scoring from beyond the three-point line is worth more than a close-range basket. Turnovers and poor decisions waste precious seconds as increasingly skilled teams stand in the way.

The game progresses from lower-level opponents toward tougher championship competition. Precise shot timing, court positioning and quick passing matter more than elaborate plays, and bonus shooting sequences add variety between matches. Released before Konami's better-known Double Dribble, Super Basketball is an early example of the company's sports-arcade design, already emphasizing brisk controls, recognizable basketball rules and constant pressure from the clock.

games.title: Space Battle
games.description: Space Battle is a 1980 fixed-screen shooter by Hoei, running on hardware derived from Namco's Galaxian system. The player's craft operates near the bottom of the screen, firing at alien ships arriving in different attack patterns. Below the craft sit five space bases that enemy attackers attempt to bomb; clearing a wave while preserving as many bases as possible earns additional points. Speech synthesis adds a distinctive element to this early Japanese shooter. Despite sharing its title with other games, Hoei's Space Battle is a separate arcade production with its own base-defense objective.

games.title: Super Bishi Bashi Championship
games.description:
Super Bishi Bashi Championship is Konami's exuberant compilation of short, competitive mini-games, presented in an updated 1998 arcade edition. Players compete by hammering three large colored buttons to perform absurdly simple tasks at frantic speed. The games range from rhythm and reaction tests to comical contests such as enlarging a dancer's hairstyle or propelling a bodybuilder toward food. Most rounds last only moments, putting the emphasis on instantly readable rules, timing and crowd reactions.

The original three-player version of Super Bishi Bashi Champ appeared in Japan in 1996; the later JAA revision is a two-player release, although three-player variants also exist. The series is full of Konami in-jokes, including a Gradius-style 'Speed Up' cue and a cameo by a Parodius character. Its huge variety and party atmosphere make it a particularly distinctive alternative to conventional arcade fighting games.

games.title: Sonic Blast Man TURBO 2
games.description:
Sonic Blast Man TURBO 2, also preserved as Sonic Blast Man II Special Turbo, is an unauthorized coin-operated conversion of Taito's Super Nintendo beat-'em-up Sonic Blast Man II. It retains the console game's side-scrolling superhero action, in which the protagonists fight through enemies using punches, kicks and special moves, but adapts the software for arcade coin inputs and a modified control panel.

The bootleg is especially notable for its hardware: rather than using an official Nintendo arcade platform, it ran on a custom board assembled around Super Nintendo-compatible technology. Its makers encrypted the game data, relocated the start-up code and added protection checks and coin-handling routines. Recovering a playable version for emulation required both decryption and repairs to SNES graphics emulation, making this one of the more technically curious console-to-arcade bootlegs.

games.title: Sonic Blast Man
games.description:
Sonic Blast Man is an unusual Taito arcade attraction carrying a 1990 copyright and released in Japan in early 1991. Instead of controlling a side-scrolling hero with a joystick, players physically punch a large padded target, with the machine measuring the force and translating it into the superhero's on-screen feats. Scenarios include striking an attacker and dealing with gigantic threats. Players get three punches per challenge, with both their highest impact and combined power recorded.

The memorable physical interface also caused controversy. After reports of injuries to players' arms and wrists, Taito recalled American machines in 1995; in 1996 the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission announced a $50,000 civil penalty related to alleged failures to report incidents. The later Super Nintendo Sonic Blast Man has a substantially different side-scrolling combat system, preserving the punching challenges only in adapted form. The original is therefore best understood as a distinctive physical arcade machine, not the console beat-'em-up.

games.title: Super Bobble Bobble
games.description:
Super Bobble Bobble is an unauthorized arcade variant of Taito's Bubble Bobble, issued by Datsu Electronics. It keeps the central two-player platform-puzzle loop: Bub and Bob blow bubbles to trap enemies on single-screen stages, then burst the bubbles to eliminate them and collect falling bonus items. Careful jumping and cooperation are essential as the screens become more crowded.

This bootleg has identifiable gameplay differences rather than simply a changed title. Its settings include an option controlling monster speed, and several enemies that normally throw stones, fireballs or bottles no longer use those projectiles. The Space Invader-like enemy still fires its laser. It also provides access to the alternate 'Super Bubble Bobble' stage sequence. These changes make its difficulty and enemy behavior noticeably different from the official Taito board.

games.title: Space Bomber
games.description:
Space Bomber is Psikyo's offbeat 1998 fixed-screen shooter, a comic reinvention of Space Invaders built around capturing opponents rather than merely shooting them. The player's spacecraft can maneuver freely and use a grappling device to seize up to three enemies. Captured creatures can then be deployed as weapons, with different targets producing very different attacks and tactical possibilities. Ordinary shooting and power-ups remain useful, but deciding which enemies to capture adds an unusual layer of strategy.

Its bizarre parade of flying animals, oversized objects and visual jokes contrasts with Psikyo's more serious military shooters. The relentless formations, boss encounters and playful weapon combinations give Space Bomber a personality of its own, especially in cooperative play.

games.title: Strike Bowling
games.description: Strike Bowling is a 1982 Taito bowling game controlled with a trackball, allowing the player to direct a ball down the lane and attempt strikes and spares. Up to two players can compete through the familiar sequence of bowling frames. Its presentation is notably playful: a strike brings a congratulatory display accompanied by a line of dancing cheerleaders. Built around an Intel 8080 CPU at a time when Taito was moving to newer hardware, it is an entertaining snapshot of the company's early sports arcade design.

games.title: Super Breakout
games.description:
Atari's Super Breakout (1978) expands the paddle-and-ball concept established by the influential 1976 Breakout. Players turn a rotary paddle controller to bounce the ball into a wall of destructible bricks, scoring points while preventing it from falling off the bottom. The attraction is the simple but exacting relationship between paddle position, rebound angle and an increasingly unforgiving ball trajectory.

The sequel adds three memorable variations. In Double, the player controls two vertically separated paddles and eventually has two balls to manage. Cavity hides additional balls within pockets in the brick formation, releasing them into play when those compartments are breached. Progressive makes the wall advance steadily toward the paddle, turning the game into a race against the descending bricks. These modes transform Breakout's basic mechanic without obscuring its elegant simplicity, and helped establish the multi-ball and moving-wall ideas later explored by many brick-breaking games.

games.title: Super Bubble Bobble

variants.title: Super Bubble Bobble (Sun Mixing, Mega Drive clone hardware)

games.description:
Super Bubble Bobble is a 1996 unlicensed arcade adaptation published by Sun Mixing on hardware derived from the Sega Mega Drive. It is closely related to the unauthorized Mega Drive game Super Bubble Bobble MD rather than to Taito's official Bubble Bobble boards. Players guide two small dragon-like characters, Bub and Cororon, through single-screen stages, blowing bubbles to catch enemies and clearing each round by bursting them.

The arcade conversion retains the console game's recognizable graphics and stage layouts but dispenses with its wider selection of novelty characters; its two playable characters are assigned to the first and second players. It also uses round selection in place of the console version's character-selection arrangement. The unusual hardware and unauthorized origin make this a separate curiosity from the similarly named Super Bobble Bobble bootleg of the original Taito arcade game.

games.title: Space Bugger
games.description: Space Bugger is a 1981 shooter by Game-A-Tron that rotates the Space Invaders formula into a confrontation on two fronts. The player's craft occupies the middle of the screen, with alien formations approaching from both left and right. It must fire in either direction while sheltering behind barriers on both sides. As in Space Invaders, repeated enemy fire and the player's own shots progressively wear away the cover. The distinctive double-sided layout makes staying safe a matter of watching both flanks instead of just the sky overhead.

games.title: Scandal Mahjong
games.description: Scandal Mahjong is a 1989 Japanese adult mahjong game by Nichibutsu. It uses conventional mahjong competition as the basis for a single-player series of matches against female opponents, with adult-oriented illustrations forming part of its presentation. The arcade release also exists in a separate betting or medal-oriented edition, a distinction reflected in the preserved game sets. It belongs to Nichibutsu's extensive late-1980s line of mahjong machines rather than to the action games for which the company's earlier arcade catalogue is better known.

games.title: Success Joe
games.description:
Success Joe, also known as Ashita no Joe, is a 1990 arcade action game based on the influential Japanese boxing manga and anime Tomorrow's Joe. Players control Joe Yabuki as he develops from a street fighter into a boxer, following a progression that mixes side-view fights in alleyways with actual boxing-ring contests. This structure makes it a hybrid of beat-'em-up and boxing game rather than a conventional one-on-one sports simulation.

The license gives it a recognizable dramatic setting drawn from one of Japan's best-known sports stories. Its narrative roots are particularly significant in Japan, where the manga's portrayal of Joe and his rival Toru Rikiishi became a cultural phenomenon. The arcade game translates that rise through the boxing world into direct joystick-and-button combat.

games.title: Super Cup Finals
games.description: Super Cup Finals is a 1993 Taito football game for its F3 arcade hardware. The action is shown from an angled, perspective view of the pitch, and players can compete against the computer or another person. Kicking and shooting options depend on a player's position relative to the ball, giving the compact arcade controls several distinct outcomes. The cabinet's dial-based input and multi-button layout distinguish it from the joystick-only football games of the era. Although less celebrated than Taito's other sports titles, it offers a brisk, competitive interpretation of association football.

games.title: Space Chaser
games.description:
Space Chaser is Taito's early maze-chase game, released around 1979-1980. The player steers a small rocket around a network of corridors, collecting every dot while avoiding hostile rockets that relentlessly pursue it. A limited supply of fuel enables a temporary speed boost, but using it recklessly can leave the player without an escape when an enemy comes up behind on a straight passage.

Unlike later maze games whose protagonists eat their pursuers, Space Chaser revolves around route planning and speed management. Cornering at the right moment can break a pursuer's approach, while long corridors are particularly hazardous. Its spacecraft theme and pressure from a limited boost make it a distinct early branch of the maze-action genre.

games.title: Schmeiser Robo
games.description:
Schmeiser Robo is a 1993 two-dimensional fighting game built around pilots battling inside humanoid machines called Walkers. Players choose from eight distinct characters and robots, then fight best-of-three-round duels against computer opponents or a second player. Despite its heavy mechanical theme, the combat follows fighting-game conventions, with separate punch, kick and guard buttons.

It adds techniques such as air guarding, counterattacks and guard cancels, giving its machine battles a more technical rhythm than their oversized appearance suggests. Each Walker has a different visual identity, and a powerful non-playable boss, Z'Hell, awaits in the tournament. It remains a relatively obscure example of the early-1990s rush to innovate in one-on-one arcade fighters.

games.title: Special Criminal Investigation
games.description:
Special Criminal Investigation, commonly abbreviated S.C.I., is Taito's 1989 sequel to the high-speed police pursuit game Chase H.Q. Detectives Tony Gibson and Raymond Broady return, now riding in a red Nissan 300ZX sports car to intercept dangerous criminals before time runs out. The familiar third-person, behind-the-car perspective puts players on busy highways filled with traffic and obstacles, demanding quick reactions and careful use of limited time.

The major addition is armed pursuit. Instead of relying only on collisions to stop a suspect's car, players can fire from their vehicle while using a nitrous boost to gain speed and catch the target. The arcade control layouts vary, but combine steering, acceleration, braking, gear changes and separate attack functions. The mix of a racing game's forward momentum with the spectacle of an action movie makes S.C.I. more aggressive than its predecessor and a memorable entry in Taito's late-1980s driving catalogue.

games.title: Scion
games.description: Scion is a 1984 vertically scrolling shooter that combines aerial combat with attacks on installations below. Players pilot a craft over a succession of defended areas, shooting enemy aircraft while destroying the large interconnected ground structures that occupy the landscape. Clearing those installations is required to progress to the next scene, so simply surviving the flying enemies is not enough. Its eight-way movement and two-button control setup give the player more freedom than the fixed-screen invader shooters of the preceding decade.

games.title: Super Cobra
games.description:
Super Cobra is Konami's 1981 side-scrolling shooter and a direct successor to Scramble. Piloting a helicopter-like craft, players navigate an increasingly treacherous series of caves and outdoor sections, firing forward and dropping bombs onto enemies and ground targets. Collisions with rocks, installations or incoming fire are fatal, and fuel steadily drains until replenished by destroying fuel tanks. At the end of the course the player must seize a valuable prize and escape.

The game expands Scramble's obstacle-course structure with more numerous and varied sections, including narrow passageways that require very precise flight. Constant terrain awareness is as important as shooting, while the fuel gauge ensures that evasion alone cannot sustain a run. Super Cobra became a recognizable early-1980s arcade favorite and was adapted for numerous home systems, helping establish the horizontal shoot-'em-up as a long-running genre.

games.title: Super Contra
games.description:
Super Contra is Konami's 1988 arcade sequel to Contra, continuing the two-player run-and-gun campaign against an alien infestation. Commandos Bill Rizer and Lance Bean fight through hostile bases and grotesque biological strongholds, blasting soldiers, machines and enormous alien bosses. Players move and jump through side-scrolling sections with an eight-way gun while also encountering overhead stages that change how movement and firing are handled.

The sequel intensifies the original's arcade formula with denser enemy attacks, larger creatures and a revised selection of upgradable weapons. Grabbing the right weapon capsule can transform the flow of a stage, while losing a life strips away a valuable advantage. Fast cooperative play and spectacular boss designs remain central to its appeal.

Although the home-console adaptation is widely known as Super C, the arcade Super Contra has its own stage construction and presentation. Together with Contra, it helped define Konami's punishing but accessible cooperative action style.

games.title: Scorpion
games.description:
Scorpion is a 1982 vertically oriented space shooter developed by I.G.R. for Italian arcade manufacturer Zaccaria. Players control a spacecraft with guns and a limited stock of missiles through five distinct sections populated by huge spiders, webs and scorpions. The opening area scrolls horizontally as spiders descend and leave obstructing strands, while a later encounter features a web-spinning enemy that attempts to trap the craft inside a growing spiral. Eight-way movement and directional firing are essential for escaping these formations.

Other stages pit the player against a giant scorpion, a twisting maze with fuel refills and an enormous black widow protected by webbing. The largest creatures require correctly placed missiles rather than ordinary gunfire. The stages repeat at greater difficulty after a completed circuit, with the final section appearing from the second loop onward. Its insect-themed encounters and changing objectives make Scorpion more elaborate than its relatively obscure reputation suggests. A bootleg version was also adapted to Moon Cresta hardware.

games.title: Scooter Shooter
games.description: Scooter Shooter is a 1985 Konami action shooter with an unusual competitive structure. Two riders on small flying scooters start from opposite sides of a horizontally scrolling playfield and advance toward the center, battling enemies along the route. The game can pit a player against the computer or another human opponent, combining shooter mechanics with head-to-head competition. Its split-screen presentation gives the race toward the middle a different feel from Konami's more familiar solo scrolling shooters.

games.title: Scramble
games.description:
Scramble is Konami's landmark 1981 horizontally scrolling shooter, distributed in North America by Stern. The player pilots a rocket-powered aircraft through six consecutive hostile areas, firing straight ahead and dropping bombs onto targets below. Enemy rockets, UFOs, narrow caves and the terrain itself pose constant dangers. A fuel meter steadily falls throughout the mission, forcing the pilot to bomb ground-based fuel tanks to stay airborne. The final objective is to destroy an enemy base before the course begins again.

Its linked, visually different stages were a major departure from shooters built around a repeating fixed screen. The simultaneous need to steer through an obstacle course, shoot moving threats and maintain fuel created a demanding but highly influential formula. Scramble also used distinctive audiovisual cues and increasingly severe terrain to make progress easy to recognize.

A major early commercial success, it helped establish the multi-stage horizontal shooter and inspired numerous imitators, conversions and unauthorized hardware adaptations. Konami soon expanded its ideas in Super Cobra, while Scramble's fuel-management and forward-scrolling structure became important reference points for later arcade action games.

games.title: Scrambled Egg
games.description:
Scrambled Egg is a 1983 maze-action game developed by Technos Japan, later revised for overseas release as Eggs. Players steer a small creature through a field of eggs and wandering enemies. Kicking an egg sends it moving across the playfield, and repeated collisions eventually crack it open to release a chick. All chicks must be hatched and collected to clear the stage, but enemies can interfere by repairing damaged eggs or poisoning the newly freed chicks.

The player's projectile can temporarily stun enemies, while well-aimed eggs can knock them out. Chain reactions between eggs add a puzzle element to the chase-game format. As one of Technos Japan's early releases, it predates the studio's later fame for Double Dragon and the Kunio-kun series, and its egg-pushing concept also foreshadows ideas revisited in Mysterious Stones.

games.title: Screw Loose
games.description:
Screw Loose is an unreleased 1983 arcade prototype featuring Robop, a small blue robot moving across a perspective grid. Using twin eight-way joysticks, players steer Robop independently of his firing direction, blasting enemies and gathering such objects as hamburgers, nuts and atoms. Collecting the required items lights the bulbs around the field, and illuminating them all advances to the next stage.

An insect-like 'Inchworm' adds the game's strangest hazard by stealing Robop's detachable hands. The player must recover them before they disappear off the playfield, while also avoiding the deadly Cherry Bomb. Its unusual combination of twin-stick shooting, collection objectives and cartoon mechanical hazards makes Screw Loose a fascinating glimpse at an arcade design that never received a normal commercial release.

games.title: Stadium Cross
games.description:
Stadium Cross is a 1992 Sega motocross racer developed by AM1 for System Multi 32 arcade hardware. Players race off-road motorcycles around stadium courses, taking high jumps, leaning through corners and performing wheelies while competing for position. The behind-the-bike viewpoint and emphasis on aerial landings make it a different experience from Sega's car-racing games of the same period.

Its original attraction included motorcycle-shaped controls that could tilt from side to side and forward or backward, strengthening the sensation of riding a dirt bike over jumps. Linked cabinets could accommodate up to eight racers, turning the game into a noisy multiplayer stadium event. The distinctive physical controller and unusual networked racing format are important parts of its arcade identity.

games.title: Scud Race
games.description:
Scud Race, released by Sega in 1996 and known in North America as Sega Super GT, is a visually striking arcade racer built around the Sega Model 3 platform. Based on the era's GT racing scene, it offers licensed high-performance cars including the Ferrari F40, McLaren F1, Porsche 911 and Dodge Viper. Players race from a behind-the-car view through four strikingly different circuits, ranging from relatively accessible daytime and nighttime routes to more demanding layouts.

The technology was a major attraction: elaborate 3D scenery, smooth high-speed driving and intricately modeled cars showcased Sega's leap beyond its Model 2 racers. Twin and deluxe cabinets could be linked for multiplayer competition, while operators could configure longer endurance-style sessions. Its handling is firmly arcade-focused, rewarding memorization of corners and skillful use of speed rather than strict simulation.

Although it never received a conventional home-console port, Scud Race became a cult favorite among Sega racing enthusiasts and a notable showcase for the company's late-1990s arcade hardware.

games.title: Scud Hammer
games.description:
Scud Hammer is Jaleco's eccentric 1994 arcade redemption attraction based on the Japanese game of rock-paper-scissors, or janken. Players choose a cartoon opponent and strike the cabinet's rock, paper or scissors input pads with a dedicated hammer. Winning a throw provides a brief opportunity to pound a head-shaped target, translating physical blows into damage on the on-screen opponent's face.

The goal is to fill the opponent's damage gauge and score a knockout over a small series of rounds. Its mixture of fast decisions, physical force and comic retaliation makes it closer to a whack-a-mole machine than to a conventional joystick game. The original purpose-built cabinet, with its hammer and targets, is central to understanding the game.

games.title: Scud Race Plus
games.description:
Scud Race Plus is Sega's 1997 revision of its Model 3 GT racing game Scud Race, released primarily in Japan. It preserves the original's fast handling, four licensed supercars and richly detailed circuits while adding options aimed at dedicated players. A new Super Beginner Reverse course can be selected through a Start-button command, a Time Attack mode offers focused lap competition, and additional vehicle choices are available on the new course through hidden selections.

Like the original, it supports linked racing cabinets and is known as Sega Super GT Plus when configured for the American region. Rather than being a wholly new sequel, this is a refined and somewhat elusive arcade update that rewards players willing to discover its extra content.

games.title: Super Derby
games.description: Super Derby is a 1996 horse-racing betting game from Italian arcade manufacturer Playmark. Rather than steering a horse, the player chooses wagers and watches a simulated field of numbered horses race toward the finish, with the contest shown from an overhead view. The cabinet uses a four-way joystick and two buttons, while a Motorola 68000 drives the colorful race presentation. The result is closer to a computerized betting attraction than a conventional racing game, and surviving revisions include the v.07.03 and v.10.04 program versions.

games.title: SD Fighters
games.description: SD Fighters is a Korean one-on-one fighting game released by SemiCom in 1996. Its roster consists of eight super-deformed, or 'SD', characters, whose oversized heads and compact bodies give its battles a playful appearance. Combat is organized around an eight-way joystick and three attack buttons, an arrangement more reminiscent of some contemporary 3D fighters than of Street Fighter's six-button layout. SemiCom later revisited the concept with Cute Fighter, which expanded the cast and introduced additional stages.

games.title: SD Gundam Psycho Salamander no Kyoui
games.description:
SD Gundam Psycho Salamander no Kyoui is a 1991 Japanese arcade action shooter based on the Super Deformed Gundam characters. A squat, stylized Gundam advances through horizontally scrolling stages packed with enemy mobile suits and other mechanical threats. Some sections are fought on foot with jumping and close-range action, while others allow the machine to fly, changing the feel of combat.

Players use ranged weapons and a sword, collecting upgrades such as cannons, machine guns and protective shields. Equipment can also be adjusted between stages, making weapon choice part of the progression. Simultaneous two-player action and the blend of platform and shooter stages set it apart from a straightforward Gundam-themed scrolling shooter.

games.title: SDI - Strategic Defense Initiative

variants.title: SDI - Strategic Defense Initiative (Europe, System 16A, FD1089B 317-0027)

games.description:
SDI: Strategic Defense Initiative is Sega's 1987 arcade shooter inspired by the Cold War-era concept of orbital missile defense. The player pilots a defensive spacecraft while attempting to intercept incoming missiles, satellites and other threats before they reach their targets. Unusually, movement and aiming are independent: a joystick moves the craft, while a trackball positions the weapon's crosshair, and a button fires at the selected point.

The mission alternates defensive stages, in which projectiles must be stopped before reaching Earth, with offensive missions that require attacking hostile installations and vehicles. The simultaneous demands of steering, targeting and monitoring multiple threats make its controls more intricate than those of most shooters of its period. The political and technological premise also gives SDI an unmistakably late-1980s identity, echoing the contemporary Strategic Defense Initiative rather than inventing a purely fictional alien war.

games.title: Super Dodge Ball / Kunio no Nekketsu Toukyuu Densetsu
games.description:
Super Dodge Ball, released for SNK's Neo Geo in 1996 as Kunio no Nekketsu Toukyuu Densetsu, revives Technos Japan's energetic Kunio-kun sports series. Teams of three compete to knock out their opponents by hurling a dodgeball across a divided court. Each character has a health gauge, and players can use the captain's special throws, elaborate directional inputs and team maneuvers to overwhelm the opposition. Defeated on-court players can continue supporting their team from outside the opposing side of the court.

Compared with the earlier Super Dodge Ball, this version adds fighting-game-style command moves, counters, special passes and a powerful attack fueled by a team gauge. The colorful animation and exaggerated impacts make every exchange feel like a miniature martial-arts confrontation. Historically, it is poignant as one of Technos Japan's last arcade productions before the company closed in 1996.

games.title: DoDonPachi SaiDaiOuJou (hack)

modifications.description: Modifies DoDonPachi SaiDaiOuJou gameplay parameters on Cave CV1000-D hardware.

games.description: DoDonPachi SaiDaiOuJou (hack) is a 2021 modified build of Cave's vertical bullet-hell shoot-'em-up DoDonPachi SaiDaiOuJou.

games.title: DoDonPachi SaiDaiOuJou & Knuckles

modifications.description: Rebalances scoring, hyper gauge mechanics, and stage routing in DoDonPachi SaiDaiOuJou.

games.description: DoDonPachi SaiDaiOuJou & Knuckles is a 2021 gameplay and balance modification of Cave's vertical bullet-hell shoot-'em-up DoDonPachi SaiDaiOuJou created by CaveDwellers.

games.title: DoDonPachi SaiDaiOuJou Saya Type B

modifications.description: Adds a playable Saya configuration in DoDonPachi SaiDaiOuJou.

games.description: DoDonPachi SaiDaiOuJou Saya Type B is a 2022 character modification of Cave's vertical bullet-hell shoot-'em-up DoDonPachi SaiDaiOuJou featuring a playable Saya Type B variant.

games.title: Super Doubles Tennis
games.description: Super Doubles Tennis is a 1983 Data East arcade tennis game built specifically around doubles rather than conventional singles play. Four tennis players appear on the court, two on each side of the net. The human player controls one member of a pair while the computer directs the partner when playing alone, and the contest follows the familiar objective of returning shots and placing the ball beyond the opponents' reach. The doubles format makes court coverage and coordination with a partner central to the game's appeal.

games.title: Space Dungeon
games.description:
Space Dungeon is a 1982 Taito arcade shooter designed by Rex Battenberg, blending the immediate action of a twin-stick shooter with the exploration of a maze game. Each level is a six-by-six grid of connected rooms containing enemies, laser defenses and valuable treasure. Players enter through one room and eventually seek the 'Collect Bonus' exit, gathering as much loot as possible along the way. A map at the top of the display reveals explored rooms and helps plan a route through the complex.

The control scheme is an essential part of the experience: one eight-way joystick moves the spacecraft, while a second aims and fires its laser independently. Dangerous creatures include a competing thief that steals treasure but can be made to drop its haul when shot. If the player's craft is destroyed, the treasure it was carrying is left behind, creating a risky incentive to return and recover it. Visiting every room also grants a substantial exploration bonus.

Released in the same era as Robotron: 2084, Space Dungeon is an early and distinctive example of twin-stick movement and shooting, but its room-by-room structure and treasure-collection decisions give it a more methodical feel. It later received a home conversion for the Atari 5200.

games.title: Sea Bass Fishing
games.description: Sea Bass Fishing is a 1998 arcade fishing game by A Wave, distributed by Able. Instead of relying on combat or racing reflexes, players choose bait or lures and try to land as many large sea bass as possible before the session timer expires. The game turns the timing and selection of tackle into a score-focused challenge, reflecting the popularity of specialized fishing attractions in Japanese arcades during the late 1990s.

games.title: SAR - Search And Rescue
games.description:
SAR: Search and Rescue is SNK's 1989 top-down run-and-gun shooter, following a rescue mission to investigate a missing spacecraft on a dangerous alien world. One or two operatives advance through hostile corridors and outdoor areas, shooting monstrous creatures and collecting stronger weapons as the expedition grows more perilous. The overhead view and relentless forward progression recall SNK's Ikari Warriors and Guerrilla War, although SAR replaces military enemies with science-fiction horrors.

Its mixture of cooperative action, increasingly grotesque opponents and changing environments gives it a darker tone than the company's earlier commando shooters. The goal is not merely to survive the enemy waves, but to discover what happened to the lost expedition.

games.title: Search Eye
games.description: Search Eye is a 1999 visual-search puzzle game developed and published by Korean company Yun Sung. Rather than relying on falling blocks or match-three mechanics, players study illustrated scenes and identify concealed objects or specified targets. The game contains 70 levels, with the challenge coming from observation and rapid recognition of details. Its hidden-object format makes it an unusual arcade puzzle title from the end of the 1990s.

games.title: Super Earth Invasion
games.description:
Super Earth Invasion is an unauthorized variant of Taito's foundational 1978 shooter Space Invaders. Its playfield retains the recognizable structure: a laser cannon moves along the bottom of a fixed screen, firing into rows of aliens that march sideways and descend toward the ground. Enemy missiles and the gradual erosion of protective bunkers force the player to keep changing position, while the surviving invaders accelerate as their numbers fall.

The title represents one of the many unofficial adaptations produced during the worldwide Space Invaders boom. It is valuable as an example of how rapidly the original design spread through copied or modified arcade hardware, although the available documentation does not establish substantial new game mechanics unique to this release.

games.title: Sea Wolf
games.description:
Sea Wolf is Midway's influential 1976 submarine-shooting arcade game, designed around a real periscope-style controller. The player looks through the viewer, swings it left or right to aim a crosshair and presses a thumb button to launch torpedoes at ships passing across the surface. Different targets move at different speeds, with nimble patrol boats particularly difficult to hit. Floating mines can intercept torpedoes, and a limited supply of shots must reload before the player can fire again.

The game is a timed high-score challenge rather than a voyage through levels. Its cabinet blends screen graphics with physical optical effects: lights and reflected indicators inside the periscope give the player information about explosions and reloading. This combination made the sensation of aiming the weapon as important as the action on the monitor.

Sea Wolf was a video-game successor to earlier electromechanical submarine attractions, particularly Midway's Sea Devil and the tradition established by Sega's Periscope. Its commercial success demonstrated the appeal of dedicated, immersive controls at a time when the arcade industry was only beginning to move beyond electromechanical machinery.

games.title: Sea Wolf II
games.description:
Sea Wolf II is Midway's 1978 follow-up to its successful periscope-controlled submarine shooter. Players peer through large rotating periscopes, aim at ships racing across the surface and fire torpedoes using thumb buttons, trying to sink as many targets as possible before time expires. Mines drifting between the submarine and its targets can intercept shots, while a brief reload delay after a volley creates a rhythm of aiming and conserving ammunition.

The key attraction is competitive two-player play, with separate periscopes and targeting crosshairs allowing simultaneous attacks. Sea Wolf II also moves the original concept into color video graphics while preserving the physical indicators and reflected effects that made its predecessor's cabinet distinctive.
