It is an instructive example of late-1970s arcade designers refining an already successful specialized controller instead of replacing it with a generic joystick.

games.title: Second Love
games.description: Second Love is a 1986 Japanese adult mahjong game by Nichibutsu. The player takes part in mahjong matches presented with romance-themed, adult-oriented artwork. Listed in some arcade catalogues as a medal game, it belongs to Nichibutsu's extensive mahjong lineup and illustrates the company's shift toward dedicated mahjong entertainment alongside its more conventional arcade releases. Detailed rule variations and progression for this particular title are not well documented.

games.title: Section Z
games.description:
Section Z is Capcom's 1985 science-fiction shooter, sending a lone space ranger into the alien fortress Balangool to defeat the controlling intelligence known as L-Brain. Unlike a straightforward one-way scrolling game, the station is divided into alphabetically labeled sections connected through a branching network of corridors. Players navigate these areas, shooting enemies to the left or right and choosing routes through the complex in search of its final sector.

Directional firing is a defining mechanic: the protagonist can turn to attack either side of the screen while moving through sections that scroll horizontally or vertically. Weapon upgrades such as stronger lasers, spread attacks and shields help deal with dense alien defenses. Its branching routes and changing screen directions reward spatial awareness and experimentation as much as reflexes.

Section Z is also historically interesting because its later Nintendo Entertainment System adaptation significantly redesigned the arcade game. The original remains a distinctive mid-1980s Capcom shooter built around navigating an interconnected space station rather than simply surviving a fixed succession of stages.

games.title: Sega Ninja
games.description:
Sega Ninja, known in Japan as Ninja Princess, is Sega's 1985 overhead run-and-gun game starring a female ninja fighting to reclaim territory from hostile forces. She advances through scrolling landscapes while throwing knives or upgraded shuriken at samurai, ninjas, animals and stage bosses. The eight-way joystick allows flexible movement and attacks, while temporary invisibility can help survive particularly dangerous encounters.

Most stages scroll vertically, though the game varies its presentation and obstacles over the campaign. The heroine and feudal-Japanese setting give it a different identity from the military shooters popular at the time. It was later adapted to home computers and consoles, often with a reduced level count or altered content.

games.title: Seicross
games.description:
Seicross, originally released in Japanese arcades as Sector Zone, is Nichibutsu's 1984 hybrid of shooter and futuristic racing game. The player rides a hovering motorcycle through a side-scrolling hostile landscape, ramming rival riders, shooting threats and collecting stranded people for points. Energy replenishments are important for keeping the vehicle in action, while rough ground and approaching obstacles force constant movement.

The action alternates between areas emphasizing hostile riders and more hazardous terrain, eventually confronting the memorable Dinosaur Tanks. These bizarre mechanical enemies launch their heads after being destroyed, an unexpected threat even after the main body has fallen. The course then loops with increased difficulty. Seicross stands out for treating speed, collisions, rescue and shooting as equally important parts of its arcade formula.

games.title: Seiha
games.description: Seiha is a 1987 Japanese mahjong game by Nichibutsu, featuring a lineup of eight female opponents. Its appeal rests on one-on-one mahjong competition framed by character portraits and adult-oriented presentation. The game belongs to Nichibutsu's prolific late-1980s collection of dedicated mahjong arcade machines; specific rule variations beyond the standard mahjong premise are not clearly documented.

games.title: Sel Feena
games.description:
Sel Feena is a 1991 maze-action game developed by East Technology. Players move around enclosed arenas containing wandering enemies, chests and special floor squares. Its central trick is to hurl a chest at a foe, trapping it inside, then throw the occupied chest onto a marked square to release collectible coins. Hesitation is risky because trapped enemies can eventually escape.

When no chest is at hand, a stun shot offers a temporary defense, while a wider stun blast can stop nearby pursuers in an emergency. The combination of enemy trapping, positional puzzles and quick item collection creates a different challenge from simply defeating everything on screen.

games.title: MuHanSeungBu
games.description: MuHanSeungBu is a 1997 Korean arcade baseball game from SemiCom, also associated with DMD. Known in English listings as SemiCom Baseball, it presents competitive baseball using an eight-way joystick and three buttons, with support for two players. The title appeared after SemiCom's Wonder League baseball releases, and belongs to a distinctive local line of Korean sports arcade games. Its 68000-based hardware and colorful horizontal display place it among the technically more elaborate baseball cabinets of the late 1990s, although detailed rules unique to this entry are sparsely documented.

games.title: Sengeki Striker
games.description:
Sengeki Striker is a 1997 vertically scrolling shoot-'em-up released on Kaneko's Super Nova arcade hardware. The player's craft attacks with a main gun supported by up to four auxiliary units called Gambits. Laser Gambits concentrate fire forward, while Vulcan Gambits use rapid shots and can adjust their aim toward enemies. Collecting upgrades strengthens the central weapon and expands the available escort units.

A limited stock of bombs gives players a fast way to clear hostile fire and damage clustered enemies. Deciding how to build the Gambit formation, and when to sacrifice a bomb to escape a dense pattern, provides the tactical interest beneath its conventional scrolling-shooter appearance.

games.title: Sengoku Mahjong
games.description: Sengoku Mahjong is a 1991 Japanese mahjong game set against the historical backdrop of the country's Sengoku, or Warring States, period. Instead of armies meeting on a battlefield, rival warlords compete through mahjong hands as the player seeks to overcome opposing figures. The historical theme distinguishes it from the romance and adult-oriented imagery that dominated many contemporary arcade mahjong releases. It was distributed as a medal-style mahjong game rather than a conventional action title.

games.title: Sengoku / Sengoku Denshou
games.description:
Sengoku is SNK's 1991 Neo Geo side-scrolling beat-'em-up, also titled Sengoku Denshou. Two modern warriors confront the spectral armies of a defeated feudal warlord who has returned centuries after his death. City streets and buildings give way to supernatural landscapes as the heroes face samurai, demons and other figures from Japanese folklore. The scrolling backgrounds and sudden transitions between the modern and spirit worlds give the adventure an unmistakably theatrical style.

Its signature mechanic is the ability to summon spirit forms and transform temporarily into different fighters, including a swordsman, an armored wolf and a ninja. Each has distinctive attacks and movement, rewarding players who choose the right form for the enemies ahead. Weapon pickups and cooperative play enrich the usual punching-and-kicking progression. Sengoku became a recognizable early Neo Geo action series, more memorable for its supernatural transformations and atmosphere than for strict realism.

games.title: Sengoku 2 / Sengoku Denshou 2
games.description:
Sengoku 2 is SNK's 1993 Neo Geo sequel to Sengoku, bringing back the war against the resurrected Mad Shogun. This time, the villain's interference reaches across different historical eras, and players pursue his forces through locations that shift dramatically in time and appearance. The supernatural imagery and cooperative side-scrolling action remain central to the series.

Combat is redesigned around swords carried as standard equipment, allowing broad horizontal attacks, vertical slashes and different defensive maneuvers. Combinations of buttons enable dodges, blocks and special techniques, while jumps and powerful weapon strikes are necessary against the game's varied opponents. The time-traveling premise and more elaborate swordplay make this sequel substantially more than a simple collection of new stages.

games.title: Sengoku 3
games.description:
Sengoku 3 is the 2001 concluding entry in SNK's Neo Geo supernatural beat-'em-up trilogy, developed by Noise Factory. A new group of warriors battles possessed fighters and malevolent spirits across a selection of international locations. Players can initially choose from four characters, with additional characters becoming available as the story develops. The stages can be tackled through a branching selection rather than only in a fixed linear order.

Its major distinction is a deep combination-based fighting system. Separate attacks, directional special moves, launchers, juggles and powerful techniques allow skilled players to sustain elaborate chains against groups of enemies. This makes the game feel closer to a traditional tournament fighter than either of its predecessors, while retaining cooperative brawling and the series' occult atmosphere. Frequently admired for its animation and combat mechanics, Sengoku 3 is a standout late-era Neo Geo beat-'em-up.

games.title: Senjyo
games.description:
Senjyo is a 1983 arcade shooter by Tehkan, later known as Tecmo, built around a pseudo-three-dimensional battlefield. The player operates a tank-mounted gun and aims through a crosshair at enemy machines approaching from the horizon. The tank remains at a fixed position while its gun tracks threats, and a specified number of targets must be destroyed to advance to the next round.

The perspective scaling and receding ground give the illusion of looking across a wide landscape, making target acquisition more important than free movement. Senjyo's radar-like presentation and unusual aiming controls help distinguish it from the vertically scrolling shooters and fixed alien formations common in its period.

games.title: Sen-Know
games.description: Sen-Know is a Japan-only 1999 action-puzzle game by Kouyousha and Kaneko for the Kaneko Super Nova system. Its title can be translated as 'brainwashing'. The gameplay applies falling-piece pressure to a pipe-connection puzzle in the tradition of Pipe Dream: the player must organize incoming pieces into useful connections rather than merely stack matching colors. Its combination of planning and urgency makes it a relatively obscure but distinctive late-1990s arcade puzzler.

games.title: Senkyu
games.description:
Senkyu, also known as Battle Balls, is a 1995 puzzle game by Seibu Kaihatsu in which colored spheres fall into a vertical playfield in rotating groups of three. Players turn each cluster while it descends, trying to arrange four or more balls of the same color into a connected group. Matching spheres disappear and those above fall into the spaces they leave, potentially setting off valuable chain reactions.

The game includes score-focused single-player play, puzzles and competitive battles. Unlike the rigid blocks of Tetris, its round pieces and cascading formations create a fluid sense of movement, encouraging players to anticipate where balls will settle. It is an accessible but highly strategic entry from a developer better known for arcade shooters.

games.title: Sente Diagnostic Cartridge
games.description:
The Sente Diagnostic Cartridge is a 1984 maintenance utility for Bally/Sente's interchangeable-cartridge arcade hardware. It was designed to test the components of a cabinet rather than to provide ordinary gameplay, making it an important example of the specialized service software supplied with modular arcade systems.

The underlying board used a Motorola 6809-family main CPU, a Z80 in its audio subsystem, and CEM3394 analogue synthesizer chips. The diagnostic cartridge could be used to check board functions, including sound hardware, from the arcade installation itself. As a preserved utility, it offers insight into the practical repair and reliability concerns of professional coin-operated machines.

games.title: Sex Triv
games.description: Sex Triv is a 1985 adult-themed arcade quiz game published by Status Games. It challenges players with questions about sexuality, relationships and related popular culture, organized under four tongue-in-cheek categories: Ensexlopedia, Sensual Knowledge, Erotic Facts and Sexperts Only. Correct answers earn points, making knowledge rather than reflexes the basis of the competition. Its unusual subject matter reflects the adult-oriented trivia machines found in some mid-1980s bars and amusement locations.

games.title: Sexual Trivia
games.description: Sexual Trivia is an adults-only quiz game produced in 1985 by the American company Kinky Kit and Game Co. It tests players with English-language questions drawn from multiple sex- and relationship-themed categories, using a bank of buttons rather than a joystick for its responses. Contemporary promotional material advertised thousands of questions and several cabinet formats, including upright and tabletop models. AdvanceMAME preserves two sets of version 1.02SB, and the emulated hardware includes support for a ticket dispenser. Its subject matter and amusement-machine presentation distinguish it from the more conventional general-knowledge trivia games of the period.

games.title: Sexy Parodius
games.description:
Sexy Parodius is Konami's 1996 horizontal shoot-'em-up and a mischievous continuation of its Gradius-parody series. Players choose from an eccentric collection of ships and characters, ranging from familiar Konami craft to cartoon animals and absurd novelty fighters. Each has its own weapon style, while the traditional power-up system lets players improve speed, firepower, shields and supporting options. Enemies and bosses parody Konami games and popular culture with relentless visual jokes.

A key change from earlier Parodius games is the mission system: each stage sets an extra objective, such as collecting enough items or destroying a specific target. Success or failure can alter the route through later stages, so clearing the screen of threats is no longer the only measure of performance. The whimsical presentation disguises precise movement and genuinely demanding shooting patterns.

With its outrageous animation, musical quotations and increasingly surreal encounters, Sexy Parodius is an inventive example of Konami turning its own long-running shooter traditions into comedy without abandoning the mechanical precision that made those games popular.

games.title: Street Fighter
games.description:
Street Fighter is Capcom's 1987 one-on-one fighting game and the origin of one of arcade gaming's most influential franchises. Players take the role of the martial artist Ryu, traveling through a world tournament to defeat ten challengers across Japan, the United States, England, China and Thailand. A second player can join as Ken, but the other fighters are opponents rather than selectable characters. The journey culminates in a difficult battle against the Muay Thai champion Sagat.

The game establishes many features that later became standards: a best-of-three-round match structure, health meters, timed combat and special techniques entered through joystick motions. Ryu's Hadoken projectile, Shoryuken rising punch and Tatsumaki spinning kick already appear here, although they are harder to execute than in later games. Early deluxe cabinets famously used large pressure-sensitive punch and kick pads; more common revisions adopted the six-button layout that would become synonymous with the series.

Street Fighter did not immediately transform arcades, and its controls can feel awkward compared with later entries. Its historical significance is enormous nonetheless: it introduced Ryu, Ken, Sagat and the core vocabulary that Street Fighter II would refine into the modern competitive fighting-game template.

games.title: Street Fighter II - The World Warrior

variants.title: Street Fighter II - The World Warrior (World 910522)
Street Fighter II - The World Warrior (World 910214)
Street Fighter II - The World Warrior (Japan 911210)
Street Fighter II - The World Warrior (Japan 910214)
Street Fighter II - The World Warrior (Japan 910306)
Street Fighter II - The World Warrior (US 910206)
Street Fighter II - The World Warrior (US 910214)
Street Fighter II - The World Warrior (US 910318)
Street Fighter II - The World Warrior (US 910228)
Street Fighter II - The World Warrior (US 910411)
Street Fighter II - The World Warrior (US 910522)
Street Fighter II - The World Warrior (US 911101)

games.description:
Street Fighter II: The World Warrior is Capcom's landmark 1991 fighting game, a defining release of the arcade industry's early-1990s resurgence. Eight selectable fighters from different countries, including Ryu, Ken, Chun-Li, Guile, Blanka and Zangief, compete in one-on-one matches before confronting four computer-controlled bosses. Each combatant has a distinctive fighting style, special moves, personality and stage, and each victory brings the player closer to the tournament's final opponent, M. Bison.

Its six-button control system distinguishes light, medium and heavy punches and kicks, while carefully designed joystick motions trigger fireballs, rising attacks and command grabs. Normal attacks can be linked or canceled into combinations, creating a vast tactical space built from spacing, timing, blocking and matchup knowledge. Compared with its 1987 predecessor, the game's responsive movement, readable animation and sharply differentiated characters made matches both approachable and remarkably deep. The ability for a challenger to interrupt a single-player game and face another person was central to its popularity.

Street Fighter II became a worldwide arcade phenomenon, generating long queues, local rivalries, countless console adaptations and a flood of competing fighting games. Its music, stages, catchphrases and character designs became part of popular culture, while later updates such as Champion Edition and Hyper Fighting established the practice of revising and rebalancing competitive arcade fighters. Few games have had a comparable influence on how arcade competition is organized and played.

games.title: San Francisco Rush 2049
games.description:
San Francisco Rush 2049 is Atari Games' 1999 futuristic installment in the Rush arcade racing series, set in a stylized San Francisco decades beyond the present. Players race high-performance cars through elevated roadways, giant jumps and routes filled with spectacular hazards. The physics emphasize momentum and dramatic aerial stunts, allowing spectacular crashes and risky shortcuts as important parts of the experience.

The defining novelty is the ability to deploy wings while airborne, letting racers adjust their vehicle's flight and land difficult jumps more precisely. Stunt-oriented play complements the conventional races, rewarding drivers who master tricks and aerial control. Its richly imagined future city and exaggerated track design take the Rush formula further from ordinary street racing while preserving the series' unusually physical handling.

games.title: San Francisco Rush 2049: Special Edition
games.description:
San Francisco Rush 2049: Special Edition is a 2003 arcade update of Atari Games' futuristic San Francisco racing game, released after the original company's arcade operations had ended. It retains the high-speed tracks, hidden shortcuts, spectacular jumps and airborne control wings that define Rush 2049, but expands the game with two additional circuits, ten new cars and new shortcuts.

The update has an unusual history. Midway's planned Rush 2049 Tournament Edition remained unfinished when its arcade division closed, and equipment supplier Betson adapted that material into Special Edition, unlocking the extra courses and removing the unfinished tournament-network features. Some of its additions also appeared in the Dreamcast game. The result is a rare example of a third party rescuing and extending a late-period American arcade racer rather than simply repackaging it.

games.title: Street Fighter II' - Champion Edition

variants.title: Street Fighter II' - Champion Edition (Accelerator Pt.II)
Street Fighter II' - Champion Edition (Rainbow set 1)
Street Fighter II' - Champion Edition (Rainbow set 2)
Street Fighter II' - Champion Edition (Red Wave)

games.description:
Street Fighter II': Champion Edition is Capcom's major 1992 update to Street Fighter II: The World Warrior. For the first time, the four boss characters, Balrog, Vega, Sagat and M. Bison, are selectable, expanding the playable cast from eight to twelve. Both competitors can also choose the same fighter, opening mirror matches that were impossible in the original release. Alternative costume colors distinguish identical characters, and many moves and matchups were adjusted for competitive balance.

The underlying six-button combat remains familiar, but the speed, animation details and revised techniques reward players willing to relearn their favorite character. Champion Edition also refined the competitive structure at a time when Street Fighter II machines were often surrounded by challengers waiting for their turn.

Its success proved that a widely installed arcade fighting game could sustain interest through a substantial official revision. The expanded character selection and mirror-match support became essential features of later fighting games, while the update's popularity helped inspire the subsequent Hyper Fighting revision and a large ecosystem of unofficial modifications.

games.title: Street Fighter II' - Hyper Fighting

variants.title: Street Fighter II' Turbo - Hyper Fighting (Japan 921209)

games.description: Street Fighter II' - Hyper Fighting (released in Japan as Street Fighter II' Turbo - Hyper Fighting) is Capcom's 1992 competitive update to Street Fighter II': Champion Edition on CPS-1 hardware, increasing game speed and adding new special moves across the twelve-character roster.

games.title: Street Fighter Alpha: Warriors' Dreams
games.description:
Street Fighter Alpha: Warriors' Dreams is Capcom's 1995 return to the Street Fighter universe with a fresh visual and mechanical identity. Known in Japan as Street Fighter Zero, it takes place earlier in the series chronology and uses more anime-inspired character animation than Street Fighter II. Ryu, Ken and Chun-Li are joined by returning fighters such as Adon and Birdie, plus characters connected to Final Fight and other Capcom properties, including Guy and Sodom.

Alpha introduces a three-level Super Combo meter, allowing players to save energy for more powerful attacks or use smaller portions earlier. Air blocking, Alpha Counters and chain-combo possibilities add new defensive and offensive choices. These systems make matches feel more fluid and exploratory while retaining the series' familiar six-button fundamentals and special-move inputs.

Running on CPS-II hardware, Alpha successfully launched a parallel Street Fighter line distinct from the incremental revisions of Street Fighter II. Its prequel setting, energetic soundtrack and redesigned cast laid the foundations for Alpha 2 and Alpha 3, both of which would substantially expand the combat system.

games.title: Street Fighter Alpha 2
games.description:
Street Fighter Alpha 2, released by Capcom in 1996 and called Street Fighter Zero 2 in Japan, greatly expands the ideas of Alpha: Warriors' Dreams. It revisits the series' pre-Street Fighter II setting with a larger cast, new stages, revised character stories and returning favorites including Dhalsim, Zangief and Gen. The anime-inspired graphics and expressive animation give the roster a distinct identity beside the more familiar World Warrior designs.

Its central innovation is the Custom Combo system, known as Original Combo in Japan. By spending Super Combo gauge, players can temporarily string together attacks and special moves in combinations not normally possible, creating new opportunities for pressure and damage. Alpha Counters, air blocking and the multi-level Super Combo system remain, but the earlier game's comparatively simple chain combos are displaced by a more flexible, demanding mechanic.

Alpha 2 became a major competitive entry in its own right, appreciated for a system that rewards both strong fundamentals and creative combo construction. It also deepened the series' stories and provided the basis for the later Street Fighter Zero 2 Alpha update.

games.title: Street Fighter Alpha 3
games.description:
Street Fighter Alpha 3 is Capcom's 1998 culmination of the Alpha subseries, known in Japan as Street Fighter Zero 3. It assembles an expansive cast drawn from Street Fighter, Final Fight and earlier Alpha games, adding such characters as Cody, Karin and Rainbow Mika alongside returning favorites. Its colorful animation, large move lists and elaborate stages give the game a particularly celebratory feeling while preserving the series' earlier narrative setting.

The defining change is the choice of three fighting styles, or 'ISMs', before a match. A-ISM/Z-ISM offers the familiar multi-level Super Combo system, X-ISM uses a more traditional high-damage style with a single powerful super attack, and V-ISM replaces ordinary supers with flexible custom combinations. The styles alter more than meter behavior, encouraging different tactics and even different matchups for the same character. Additional modes and dramatic encounters broaden the arcade experience.

The complex V-ISM system became especially notable in competitive play, where elaborate custom combos reward precise execution and matchup knowledge. Alpha 3 remains one of Capcom's richest CPS-II fighters, balancing a large roster and playful presentation against a remarkably technical rule set.

games.title: Super Football Champ
games.description:
Super Football Champ is Taito's 1996 arcade soccer game, a successor within the Football Champ and Hat Trick Hero family. Played from a view of the pitch, it emphasizes quick passing, shooting and combinations that bring out the players' special abilities. Its six-button controls allow more varied actions than the simple two-button football games of earlier years, while colorful polygon-based graphics distinguish its presentation from the series' older sprite-based releases.

The game appeared on Taito's FX-1A hardware and was subsequently adapted for the PlayStation. Its tournament-style competition is designed for brisk matches against the computer or another player, retaining the direct arcade feel of the company's popular football games while updating the graphics and control possibilities.

games.title: Street Fighter EX
games.description:
Street Fighter EX is the 1996 fighting-game collaboration between Capcom and Arika, introducing the series to polygonal 3D graphics on PlayStation-derived arcade hardware. Although its arenas and characters are modeled in three dimensions, the combat remains fundamentally a two-dimensional duel, preserving familiar joystick motions, six attack buttons and traditional Street Fighter spacing. Series regulars such as Ryu and Ken appear alongside an original cast that includes Kairi, Hokuto, Skullomania and Doctrine Dark.

The game introduces Guard Breaks, which can punish passive defense, and Super Cancels, allowing one Super Combo to flow into another for extravagant attack sequences. The three-level super gauge encourages players to decide between saving resources and using them to extend pressure or damage.

Street Fighter EX was a conspicuous departure from Capcom's hand-drawn arcade fighters, and its new characters gained a following of their own. While it never supplanted the mainline series, the game established a distinct branch of Street Fighter design that Arika expanded in EX Plus and EX2.

games.title: Street Fighter EX 2
games.description:
Street Fighter EX2 is Arika and Capcom's 1998 sequel to the polygonal Street Fighter EX line. The characters and arenas are three-dimensional, but matches continue to take place mainly along a classic two-dimensional fighting plane. Returning mechanics include Guard Breaks and the ability to cancel one Super Combo into another, giving players strong offensive options beyond ordinary special moves.

The major addition is the Excel Combo system, which temporarily allows players to connect a flexible sequence of normal and special attacks, rewarding planning and fast execution. A revised cast introduces new personalities alongside familiar Street Fighter veterans and Arika's original fighters. EX2 is especially interesting as an attempt to maintain the timing and strategic fundamentals of a 2D fighter while taking advantage of the increasingly sophisticated visuals of late-1990s 3D arcade hardware.

games.title: Street Fighter EX 2 Plus
games.description:
Street Fighter EX2 Plus is the expanded 1999 arcade revision of Arika and Capcom's polygonal fighter Street Fighter EX2. Its most conspicuous addition is a reshuffled and larger roster: Sagat joins the EX series, returning characters such as M. Bison, Pullum Purna and Darun Mister are restored, and newcomers Vulcano Rosso and Area contribute unusual fighting styles. Nanase becomes a regular playable character, while Hayate is absent from this arcade version.

The combat continues to combine Street Fighter's six-button, largely two-dimensional rules with 3D characters and arenas. Guard Breaks and Super Cancels return, while the Excel Combo system is loosened to allow repeated attacks in sequences that were restricted in the original EX2. A new Meteor Combo class gives each fighter at least one extravagant super attack that consumes a fully stocked three-level meter. These additions make Plus considerably more than a cosmetic update and generally the most comprehensive arcade version of EX2.

games.title: Street Fighter EX Plus
games.description:
Street Fighter EX Plus is Arika and Capcom's 1997 expanded edition of the first polygonal Street Fighter EX. The original game mixes traditional six-button, side-on Street Fighter combat with 3D characters and arenas, preserving familiar special-move inputs while adding Guard Breaks and chains of Super Cancels.

The Plus update makes previously hidden or time-released fighters readily available and adds further secret characters, including Evil Ryu, Bloody Hokuto and the experimental Cycloid Beta and Gamma fighters. This greatly broadens its character selection without replacing the underlying combat rules. It is the more feature-rich arcade edition of the original EX and a direct precursor to the redesigned EX2 system.

games.title: Street Fighter III: New Generation
games.description:
Street Fighter III: New Generation is Capcom's ambitious 1997 sequel to Street Fighter II, built for the powerful CPS-III arcade system. Rather than simply reassembling the old cast, it introduces a largely new roster headed by Alex, a powerful New York fighter, alongside characters such as Dudley, Ibuki, Elena, Yun and Yang. Ryu and Ken return as familiar anchors, while the mysterious Gill serves as the final opponent. The exceptionally fluid, hand-drawn animation marks one of the series' greatest visual advances.

The defining new mechanic is parrying: by pressing toward an incoming attack at the correct moment, players can deflect it without taking normal block damage and immediately look for a counterattack. This transforms the flow of defense, allowing bold reactions to fireballs, jump attacks and even carefully timed sequences of multiple hits. Dashes, high jumps and new offensive techniques further distance the game from Street Fighter II while retaining the six-button control system.

Initially, the unfamiliar cast and demanding defensive mechanics divided some players, but the foundations laid by New Generation became hugely influential. Subsequent Street Fighter III revisions deepened the parry system and established one of the most technically admired branches of Capcom fighting games.

games.title: Street Fighter III 2nd Impact: Giant Attack

variants.title: Street Fighter III 2nd Impact: Giant Attack (Japan, 970930)

games.description:
Street Fighter III 2nd Impact: Giant Attack is Capcom's 1997 update to New Generation, retaining the spectacular CPS-III animation while reshaping the roster and combat rules. Yun and Yang become distinct fighters with different moves, while Hugo, Urien and returning series villain Akuma expand the cast. The gigantic Hugo and imposing Urien help explain the subtitle, and the revised stages and character moves make the update feel considerably more complete.

Its innovations include EX Special Moves, powered-up techniques purchased with part of the Super Art gauge, and throw escapes. Personal Actions let fighters perform character-specific gestures that can also provide useful benefits, while a bonus challenge has Sean throw basketballs for the player to parry. These additions reward technical knowledge and provide more ways to spend resources and turn defense into offense.

Although later overshadowed by 3rd Strike, 2nd Impact is an important transitional entry. It is also notable for offering an unusual widescreen display mode on CPS-III hardware, a rare feature among contemporary competitive fighters.

games.title: Street Fighter III 3rd Strike: Fight for the Future

variants.title: Street Fighter III 3rd Strike: Fight for the Future (USA, 990512)
Street Fighter III 3rd Strike: Fight for the Future (USA, 990608)

games.description:
Street Fighter III 3rd Strike: Fight for the Future is Capcom's definitive 1999 revision of Street Fighter III and one of the most celebrated competitive two-dimensional fighting games ever made. The roster expands with Chun-Li, Makoto, Remy, Q and Twelve, while the returning fighters receive new moves, stages and balancing changes. The detailed sprite animation of CPS-III, jazzy hip-hop-influenced soundtrack and striking stage backgrounds give it a distinctive identity among late-1990s arcade games.

Its combat revolves around exact spacing, fast attacks, selective use of Super Arts and, above all, the parry system. A precisely timed forward input can deflect attacks without normal block stun, creating opportunities for breathtaking reversals, but failed attempts expose the player to punishment. Air parries, red parries during block strings, throw techniques and character-specific movement make the interactions exceptionally rich. The choice of Super Art also changes each fighter's tactical options and available meter.

Initially less commercially dominant than Street Fighter II, 3rd Strike became a long-lived tournament favorite. Its cultural legacy includes Daigo Umehara's extraordinary sequence of parries against Justin Wong at EVO 2004, often remembered as 'Evo Moment 37', which helped introduce competitive fighting games to a new online audience. The game remains a reference point for mastery, animation and high-level arcade competition.

games.title: Street Fighter III 3rd Strike: Fight for the Future (4rd Arrange Edition 2013)

modifications.description: Rebalances character frame data, hitboxes, juggle properties, and Super Arts across the roster.

games.description: Street Fighter III 3rd Strike: Fight for the Future (4rd Arrange Edition 2013) is a community balance and gameplay arrangement hack of Capcom's 1999 CPS-3 fighting game Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike, modifying move properties, juggle potential, and Super Art behavior across the cast.

games.title: Sport Fishing 2
games.description:
Sport Fishing 2 is Sega's 1995 arcade fishing attraction, developed by Ryobi as a sequel to the earlier Sport Fishing. Its purpose-built rod controller is central to the experience: players cast and reel while the apparatus imitates the force of a fish pulling on the line. The game offers fishing grounds in the Caribbean and Pacific and a range of marine species to pursue, turning deep-sea fishing into a tactile score-focused competition.

The unusual physical controller places Sport Fishing 2 among Sega's specialist arcade simulations, where manipulating a dedicated device is at least as important as what appears on screen. It is quite different from a conventional joystick-controlled sports game.

games.title: Straight Flush
games.description:
Straight Flush is a 1979 paddle-and-ball game that reworks Breakout with the visual language of playing cards. Players bounce a ball upward to remove targets shaped like hearts, diamonds, clubs and spades instead of conventional bricks. Special cards set diagonally in the upper corners can be flipped to reveal sequences that award bonuses.

A flying witch may enter the playfield after a bonus has been earned, introducing a moving obstacle that makes rebounds harder to predict. As in Breakout, losing the ball past the paddle costs a life, and play continues until the supply is exhausted. The card imagery and unexpected hazards give Straight Flush a distinct personality within the crowded late-1970s brick-breaker genre.

games.title: Street Football
games.description:
Street Football is a 1986 arcade interpretation of American football played on a small city street rather than a regulation field. The action uses an angled perspective and three-player teams, with the blue team facing a red opponent controlled by the computer or another person. The goal is to outscore the opposition during a brief six-minute contest.

Players control the ball carrier with the cabinet's directional control and can throw passes to a highlighted teammate. A timing gauge helps determine the height and execution of a throw, making successful passing dependent on both positioning and release timing. The compact teams and street setting turn football into a quick, informal arcade contest.

games.title: Sea Fighter Poseidon
games.description:
Sea Fighter Poseidon is a 1984 Taito underwater action game in which a diver rides a powered sea scooter on a mission to rescue captured companions. Players maneuver through enemy-filled water, firing torpedoes at hostile divers and vehicles while keeping an eye on the scooter's fuel supply. The number of hostages to rescue increases as the stages progress, and collecting everyone is required to finish a level.

The scooter is both a weapon and a risk: it can explode after collisions, enemy attacks or fuel exhaustion. The diver can abandon it to avoid immediate danger, but swimming without the vehicle leaves the character more vulnerable. This vehicle-management twist gives the rescue mission a different rhythm from more conventional scrolling underwater shooters.

games.title: San Francisco Rush
games.description:
San Francisco Rush is Atari Games' 1996 arcade racing game, famous for recreating the hills of San Francisco as enormous opportunities for jumps, shortcuts and spectacular crashes. Players choose high-powered cars and race through city streets, steep descents and winding highways, where mastering the road surface and knowing where to cut across the scenery matter as much as sheer speed.

Its driving model emphasizes weight, suspension and exaggerated but convincing momentum, making airborne landings and collisions feel consequential. The game invites experimentation with hidden routes and alternative approaches to corners rather than demanding a single perfect racing line. This combination of accessible racing and unpredictable physics defined the Rush series and helped make it a memorable North American arcade favorite.

games.title: San Francisco Rush: The Rock
games.description:
San Francisco Rush: The Rock, subtitled Alcatraz Edition, is the expanded 1997 version of Atari Games' San Francisco Rush. It retains the original game's distinctive weighty driving physics, exaggerated jumps and dramatic crash sequences, while adding four courses inspired by the Alcatraz area alongside the original tracks. Additional shortcuts and music invite returning players to investigate every corner of the new layouts.

A mirrored-course option offers another challenge even after the standard routes are mastered. The Rock builds on what made Rush popular: racing fast is important, but discovering unexpected routes and learning to control a vehicle hurtling through the air are just as satisfying.

games.title: Street Fighter: The Movie
games.description:
Street Fighter: The Movie is an unusual 1995 arcade fighting game developed by Incredible Technologies for Capcom, based on the 1994 live-action film. Instead of Capcom's hand-drawn sprites, the fighters are digitized from filmed performers, including actors associated with the movie's cast. Familiar characters such as Ryu, Ken, Guile, Chun-Li and M. Bison appear in a visual style closer to Mortal Kombat than to Street Fighter II, although the six-button controls and directional special moves remain recognizably Capcom-inspired.

Its combat experiments with lengthy aerial juggles and the ability to cancel special moves into other specials, producing unusually aggressive combinations. Several characters also gain new techniques not seen in the main Street Fighter games. These mechanics make the arcade edition substantially different from a simple photographic reskin.

The separately developed home-console game called Street Fighter: The Movie is not a direct port of this arcade version. The coin-operated release remains a curious collision of Hollywood licensing, digitized-fighter fashion and Capcom's established competitive fighting formula.

games.title: SF-X
games.description: SF-X, short for Space Fighter-X and also released as Skelagon, is a 1983 horizontally scrolling space shooter developed by Nihon Game and distributed under the Nichibutsu name. One or two players pilot a spacecraft through enemy-filled stages, moving in eight directions and firing with a two-button control layout. Its layered star and color backgrounds, speech-capable sound hardware and elaborate circuit board reflect the period's rapid experimentation with scrolling shoot-'em-ups. Although obscure today, it is a distinct Japanese shooter rather than a variant of Sega's similarly named SF series.

games.title: Street Fighter Zero 2 Alpha
games.description:
Street Fighter Zero 2 Alpha is Capcom's revised 1996 Japanese arcade edition of Street Fighter Alpha 2. It retains the game's anime-styled roster, three-level Super Combo meter, air blocking and Alpha Counters, but adjusts character balance and provides extra move and character variations. Classic-style versions of several Street Fighter II veterans, including Ryu, Ken, Chun-Li, Sagat and M. Bison, appear alongside the expanded cast.

The Custom Combo system is altered so that its activation and meter requirements differ from the original Zero 2, making resource management and combo planning noticeably different. The revision also features additions such as Survival and Dramatic Battle options and new techniques for certain characters. It was mainly an arcade release in Japan and selected other regions, while much of the content reached Western audiences through home versions of Alpha 2.

For players already familiar with Alpha 2, Zero 2 Alpha is an interesting alternative ruleset and a reminder that Capcom continued refining its popular CPS-II fighting games between major sequels.

games.title: Super Gem Fighter: Mini Mix
games.description:
Super Gem Fighter: Mini Mix is Capcom's 1997 comic fighting game, called Pocket Fighter in Japan, that recasts characters from Street Fighter, Darkstalkers and Red Earth as tiny, big-headed caricatures. Ryu, Chun-Li, Morrigan, Felicia and other familiar faces battle through colorful stages filled with slapstick animations, absurd costumes and jokes about their original games. Despite the intentionally silly appearance, the matches use a coherent one-on-one fighting system built around compact, approachable controls.

Collecting colored gems during a bout powers up individual special moves, making gem acquisition part of the tactical contest. Elemental orbs can afflict opponents with unusual effects, while long attack strings trigger extravagant costume changes and exaggerated visual gags. The simplified three-button design makes it easier to enjoy than most six-button Capcom fighters, but skilled players can still exploit timing and combination attacks.

Its cheerful crossover roster and playful mechanics make Super Gem Fighter a genuine fighting game rather than a novelty minigame. It also forms a natural companion to Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo, another Capcom title that uses super-deformed versions of familiar fighters.

games.title: Gladiator 1984
games.description: Gladiator 1984 is a 1984 SNK arcade action game centered on riding and obstacle avoidance rather than arena sword fighting. The player advances on horseback or in a chariot, steering around hazards and jumping obstacles that appear along the route. Its simple racing-like progression and period setting distinguish it from SNK's more familiar shooters of the time. The game is an obscure early example of the company's experimentation with different action formats before its later Neo Geo success.

games.title: Super Masters Golf

variants.title: Jumbo Ozaki Super Masters Golf (World, FD1094 317-0058-05c)
Jumbo Ozaki Super Masters Golf (Japan, FD1094 317-0058-05b)

games.description: Super Masters Golf is a 1989 Sega golf simulation for the company's System 24 arcade hardware. Also distributed as Jumbo Ozaki Super Masters Golf, it carries the name of Japanese professional golfer Masashi 'Jumbo' Ozaki. One or two players use an eight-way joystick and action buttons to play a coin-operated version of the sport. Its unusually high-resolution System 24 display and floppy-disk-based software distinguish it from simpler contemporary arcade golf games; separate World and Japanese board revisions are preserved.

games.title: Steel Gunner
games.description:
Namco's Steel Gunner is a 1990 light-gun action game starring Neo Arc police officers Garcia and Cliff, who operate heavily armed Gargoyle suits against the terrorist organization STURM. Two players can fight together through four scripted acts, tracking enemy robots as the scenery scrolls in different directions. The guns have unlimited machine-gun ammunition, while a second control launches a scarce, screen-clearing missile. Shooting innocent bystanders costs health, but protecting them can help players survive.

The scenery is unusually destructible, with windows, barrels and other objects responding to gunfire. Giant mechanical bosses punctuate the campaign, and an accuracy rating at the end of each act adds an element of marksmanship to the spectacle. One of Namco's early major gun-based arcade productions, Steel Gunner established a short-lived series known for its oversized enemies and animated, cinematic presentation.

games.title: Steel Gunner 2
games.description:
Steel Gunner 2 brings Garcia and Cliff back to defend Neo Arc City from Vanguard's invading mechanical forces. This Namco System 2 light-gun sequel expands the original's shooting-gallery formula into six acts, taking the two officers from city streets and underground passages to the enemy's immense spacecraft. Players sweep their gun sights across moving scenes, destroy cyborgs and robots with unlimited gunfire, and reserve limited missiles for crowded encounters. Hitting civilians still drains health.

The sequel emphasizes spectacular sprite scaling, breakable background objects, pseudo-3D movement and large multi-part boss battles. A night-vision sequence and a timed self-destruct confrontation help distinguish it from its predecessor. The arcade release was also marketed as a conversion kit for Taito's Operation Thunderbolt cabinets, an unusual practical link between competing manufacturers' gun games.

games.title: Shackled
games.description: Shackled is Data East's 1986 US release of the dungeon action game known in Japan as Breywood. Played from an overhead perspective, it sends Kevin through maze-like prison levels to unlock cells and rescue captured companions. Freed prisoners follow him and help attack monsters, but the challenge is to guide them safely to the exit while locating keys, treasure and useful weapons. Grenades, boomerangs and other power-ups expand the player's options, while secret passages lead to hidden areas. With two-player cooperation and a rescue objective, it offers a distinctive variation on the dungeon-crawling action popularized by Gauntlet.

games.title: Shadow Force
games.description:
Shadow Force is an ambitious 1993 side-scrolling beat-'em-up from Technos Japan, featuring four selectable heroes battling Dr. Wong and his organization. Its standout mechanic is the ability to possess ordinary enemies: by approaching an opponent and using the transformation control, a player can take over that fighter and use its own attacks. This makes the large and varied enemy roster part of the player's combat toolkit.

The fighting system is far more elaborate than that of a typical brawler, with high and low punches and kicks, jumping, blocking and combination moves. Players can choose the order of the opening stages, and one-on-one fights between action stages introduce a tournament-style element. Multiple endings further reward experimentation. The game's unusual mix of cooperative brawling, possession and fighting-game mechanics makes it one of Technos's most distinctive late arcade productions.

games.title: Shadowland
games.description:
Shadowland is the English-language version of Namco's 1987 arcade platform adventure Yōkai Dōchūki. Its mischievous young hero, Tarosuke, must journey through a Japanese supernatural underworld filled with ghosts, demons and other creatures before his fate is decided. Across five stages he jumps between platforms, attacks with spiritual energy, gathers money for shops and searches for concealed routes. Charging his energy shots adds a tactical element to the simple movement and combat.

Boss encounters feature a summoned spirit that can fly and fire at powerful oni guardians. Rather than ending with a single predetermined victory, the game judges Tarosuke's behavior and awards one of five outcomes, ranging from damnation to a place in heaven. Its Buddhist folklore, unusual moral conclusion and colorful imagery made it a distinctive early showcase for Namco's System 1 hardware.

games.title: Shadow Warriors
games.description:
Shadow Warriors is the European title of Tecmo's 1988 arcade beat-'em-up Ninja Gaiden, released in Japan as Ninja Ryūkenden. One or two players control differently colored ninjas traveling across an exaggerated version of the United States to confront the sinister Bladedamus. Streets, train cars and enemy hideouts are filled with gangsters, wrestlers and other imposing opponents. The ninjas use combinations of punches, kicks and aerial throws, and can smash scenery to uncover weapons and restorative items.

Its memorable control scheme includes a special button mounted on the joystick for grabbing overhead bars and moving along them. Wall backflips, hanging kicks and a temporarily acquired sword expand the move set beyond the usual arcade brawler. Although it launched the Ninja Gaiden name, this cooperative arcade game is substantially different from the cinematic, precision-platforming NES game developed around the same time. Its combination of theatrical presentation and acrobatic movement helped distinguish it in the late-1980s beat-'em-up boom.

games.title: Shanghai II
games.description: Shanghai II is a Japanese arcade continuation of the mahjong-tile solitaire game. The player studies a layered arrangement of tiles and removes matching pairs that are free to slide out from the left or right. Because blocked tiles cannot be selected, a successful solution depends on opening access to buried pieces rather than simply choosing the first available match. This edition offers several animal-themed board layouts, along with features such as hints and undoing moves. The familiar tabletop rules become a timed, score-oriented arcade puzzle challenge.

games.title: Shanghai III
games.description: Shanghai III is a 1993 arcade mahjong-solitaire game developed by Success and Kuusoukagaku and published by Sunsoft under license from Activision. Players remove matching pairs from a stack of traditional mahjong tiles, but only tiles with at least one unobstructed side can be selected. The puzzle ends in victory when every tile is cleared, or in failure when no legal matches remain. Twelve layouts can be approached in different orders, while time limits, assistance items and between-round bonus challenges give the coin-operated format a stronger progression structure. The game also supports competitive play between two people.

games.title: Shanghai
games.description:
Sunsoft's 1988 arcade adaptation of Shanghai brought Activision's influential 1986 mahjong-solitaire puzzle into amusement centers. A layered arrangement of 144 tiles must be cleared by selecting identical pairs, with the crucial restriction that each selected tile must have an exposed side and cannot be trapped beneath another. Flowers and seasons have special matching rules. The challenge is to plan ahead so promising early removals do not leave inaccessible pieces at the end.

Although it uses mahjong tiles, Shanghai is a solitary pattern-removal puzzle rather than the four-player gambling or competitive game of mahjong. Its simple rules, enormous number of possible tile arrangements and easily understood visual design made it particularly suited to quick arcade sessions and inspired numerous follow-up releases.

games.title: Shanghai Kid
games.description:
Shanghai Kid is a pioneering 1985 one-on-one martial-arts fighting game developed by Nihon Game, later associated with Culture Brain, and known in Japan as Hokuha Syourin Hiryū no Ken. A Shaolin fighter faces a succession of opponents in tournament bouts, using an eight-way joystick and separate punch and kick buttons. Attacks must be directed toward openings in an opponent's guard, and careless strikes can be blocked or countered.

Particularly notable is its 'RUSH!' sequence, which rewards a well-timed chain of blows with a combination attack. Together with special techniques, audible calls and distinct fighting styles, this anticipated elements that would become widespread in later versus fighters. It is an early and historically interesting link between martial-arts action games and the more technical arcade fighting genre.

games.title: Limited Edition Hang-On
games.description: Limited Edition Hang-On is Sega's 1991 revised presentation of Super Hang-On. The player races a motorcycle from a behind-the-bike viewpoint, weaving through traffic, negotiating bends and reaching checkpoints before the clock expires. The familiar turbo system permits a burst of speed beyond the normal maximum once the bike is traveling fast enough. Unlike a mere cabinet reissue, this edition redraws the courses across its Africa, Asia, Americas and Europe routes to make them more forgiving. It was also sold in a striking blue full-size motorcycle cabinet modeled on the original Hang-On's tilting ride-on machine.

games.title: Super Hang-On

variants.title: Super Hang-On (mini ride-on, Rev A, FD1089B 317-0034)
differences: Hardware configuration: mini ride-on, Rev A, FD1089B 317-0034.

games.description:
Sega's Super Hang-On (1987) followed the hugely influential Hang-On with a faster, longer and more varied arcade motorcycle racer. Viewed from behind the bike, each race is a continuous dash between checkpoints through twisting roads and streams of slower traffic. Riders can choose among four continent-themed courses, from the short African route to the demanding European marathon. Reaching the bike's normal top speed unlocks turbo acceleration, pushing it to around 324 km/h and making disciplined cornering essential to beating the timer.

Super Hang-On retains the sensation of leaning a real motorcycle into bends, particularly in its ride-on cabinet, while Sega's sprite-scaling technology creates dramatic changes in speed and scenery. Its selectable music and elaborate courses helped sustain Sega's reputation for spectacular dedicated-cabinet driving games during the late 1980s.

games.title: Super Hang-On
games.description: This Super Hang-On set is an unauthorized upgrade or conversion for Sega's earlier Hang-On hardware, rather than a standard protected Super Hang-On board. It preserves the recognizable behind-the-motorcycle checkpoint racing, including high-speed traffic avoidance and turbo acceleration, while representing a different and historically interesting way operators could run the later game. For collectors and emulator users, its significance lies primarily in the bootleg hardware conversion, not in a separately documented new racing campaign.

games.title: Shanghai - The Great Wall / Shanghai Triple Threat

variants.title: Shanghai - The Great Wall / Shanghai Triple Threat (JUE 950623 V1.005)

games.description: Shanghai: The Great Wall, also known as Shanghai Triple Threat, is a 1995 mahjong-solitaire puzzle game released on Sega's ST-V arcade system. Drawing on the long-running Shanghai series, it challenges players to clear intricate arrangements of mahjong tiles by selecting matching pairs with free sides. The deceptively simple matching rule makes the order of removal crucial: opening one layer can expose useful pairs, while a poorly planned choice may strand tiles underneath the stack. It is a later, visually more elaborate arcade entry in Sunsoft's adaptations of Activision's tile-matching formula.

games.title: Shark Attack
games.description:
Shark Attack is a 1981 arcade action game developed by Pacific Novelty and also known during development as Deep Death. Instead of hunting sea creatures, the player controls a shark that must devour incoming scuba divers while avoiding their spearguns. An eight-way joystick steers the shark, while separate buttons bite and provide a short thrust of speed. Waves of increasingly dangerous divers make the predator's movements and timing central to survival.

The cabinet was unusual for its prerecorded cassette soundtrack, which played a loop of divers' alarmed voices and reactions to the shark. That theatrical audio presentation, together with its reversal of the usual human-versus-monster role, makes Shark Attack a memorable curiosity of the early arcade era.

games.title: Space Harrier
games.description:
Space Harrier is Yu Suzuki's landmark 1985 Sega arcade rail shooter, immediately recognizable for its brightly colored fantasy landscapes, impossible architecture and enormous creatures. The player controls a flying, cannon-toting hero racing forward through the Fantasy Zone, dodging obstacles and shooting enemies that rapidly grow in size as they approach. A flight-style analog controller moves the Harrier around the screen, with quick reactions needed to evade projectiles, columns and oncoming monsters.

Sega's 'Super Scaler' sprite technology gives the game its remarkable sense of speed and depth, with twisting landscapes and huge animated bosses making each stage feel like a ride through a surreal world. Deluxe versions used a moving cockpit to reinforce the sensation of flight, while Hiroshi Kawaguchi's energetic soundtrack became an arcade favorite. Space Harrier was a defining showcase for Sega's mid-1980s hardware, helped shape the rail-shooter genre and influenced many later pseudo-3D action games.

games.title: Shadow Dancer
games.description:
Shadow Dancer is Sega's 1989 arcade follow-up to Shinobi and one of the early games built for the System 18 platform. It once again features a ninja infiltrating enemy-held areas, but adds a loyal attack dog that can be commanded to pin or distract foes. The hero throws shuriken, fights at close range, rescues captives and employs limited ninja magic while surviving the game's unforgiving encounters.

The canine companion changes the rhythm of play: sending the dog first creates an opening against guarded opponents, but leaving it exposed can temporarily remove this tactical advantage. Shadow Dancer retains Shinobi's side-scrolling action and dramatic stage bosses while establishing a distinctive identity through cooperation between ninja and dog. The later home-console Shadow Dancer games differ considerably from the arcade original.

games.title: Sheriff
games.description:
Sheriff is Nintendo's 1979 Western-themed multidirectional shooter, also distributed in North America as Bandido. A lone sheriff stands amid a ring of advancing bandits and must shoot them before their gunfire reaches him. Its unusual twin-control arrangement separates movement from aiming: one eight-way control moves the sheriff, while another chooses the direction of fire, allowing the player to shoot independently of travel.

This early example of independent movement and aiming anticipated the twin-stick ideas later made famous by Robotron: 2084. Sheriff is also historically associated with Nintendo designer Shigeru Miyamoto's early arcade work and remains a notable bridge between simple fixed-screen shooters and more flexible arena combat games.

games.title: Shienryu
games.description: Shienryu is a 1997 vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter developed by Warashi and released on Sega's ST-V arcade hardware. Players pilot a fighter against dense waves of aircraft, ground defenses and imposing mechanical bosses, gathering weapon upgrades to improve their chances. Its fast-moving enemy formations and large bursts of projectiles favor careful positioning and timely use of special attacks. The arcade game shares the sturdy, sprite-heavy presentation of the Sega Saturn architecture, to which it was later ported, and stands as a lesser-known example of the late-1990s Japanese scrolling-shooter tradition.

games.title: Super High Impact
games.description: Super High Impact is Midway's 1991 arcade American-football game, an exaggerated follow-up to High Impact Football. Two teams race through compact, full-contact matches played from an overhead field view, with a joystick and action button directing the selected player. Rather than aiming for a strict simulation of professional football, the game emphasizes quick plays, huge tackles and aggressive defensive hits. Its blunt arcade presentation and physical comedy anticipate the faster, more theatrical American-football games for which Midway later became famous.

games.title: Shinobi
games.description:
Shinobi is Sega's influential 1987 side-scrolling ninja action game, starring Joe Musashi on a mission to rescue kidnapped children from the Zeed criminal organization. Each stage is divided into short sections packed with armed guards, sword fighters and other enemies. Musashi throws shuriken, attacks at close range, jumps between platforms and upper walkways, and can unleash a powerful ninja-magic attack once per stage. Rescuing the hostages is as important as reaching the exit, and the end of each mission brings a distinctive boss fight.

The game's deliberate pacing rewards positioning and precision more than indiscriminate fighting. Bonus rounds switch to a dramatic first-person view as approaching ninjas must be stopped with shuriken. Shinobi became one of Sega's signature late-1980s arcade properties and launched a long-running series, with its cinematic ninja theme, rescue mechanics and combination of shooting and close combat proving especially influential.

games.title: Shippu Mahou Daisakusen
games.description:
Shippū Mahō Daisakusen, released internationally as Kingdom Grandprix, is Raizing's unusual 1994 sequel to Mahō Daisakusen. It combines vertically scrolling fantasy shooting with a race: players fight airborne enemies while also trying to pass rival competitors and reach the finish ahead of them. Different flying characters have distinct weapons, and accurate attacks help clear the path while missed opportunities can cost race positions.

The result is an arcade hybrid in which surviving bullets is only part of the challenge; maintaining speed and managing the traffic of rival racers can be equally important. Its whimsical flying craft, colorful medieval-fantasy world and unusual combination of shooter scoring with finishing order make it one of Raizing's more inventive early releases.

games.title: Shanghai Matekibuyuu
games.description: Shanghai Matekibuyuu, known outside Japan as Shanghai: True Valor, is a later entry in the Shanghai mahjong-solitaire series. It presents patterned stacks of traditional mahjong tiles and asks players to remove them in matching pairs, selecting only pieces that are not covered or blocked on both sides. Although the rules are easy to understand, clearing the board requires planning around hidden and inaccessible tiles. Its late-1990s presentation updates the familiar formula for arcade hardware and a contemporary home-console adaptation.

games.title: Shocking
games.description: Shocking is a 1997 overhead action-adventure game by Yun Sung that combines monster battles with small maze and puzzle challenges. The player moves from room to room, fighting creatures and working out how to proceed through each enclosed area. Rather than presenting a continuous scrolling battlefield, the game relies on individual rooms with their own obstacles and objectives. Its mixture of combat, exploration and environmental problem-solving distinguishes it from a conventional arcade run-and-gun shooter.

games.title: Shock Troopers - 2nd Squad
games.description:
Shock Troopers: 2nd Squad is Saurus's 1998 Neo Geo run-and-gun sequel, replacing the original cast with four new commandos and more elaborate visual effects. From an overhead, diagonally scrolling viewpoint, players fight through enemy soldiers, vehicles and large bosses using a mixture of gunfire, evasive movement and limited special attacks. The selectable characters differ in their weapons and fighting styles, providing variety across repeated campaigns.

Compared with the first Shock Troopers, this sequel emphasizes larger, more detailed sprites and a revised set of missions. Its brisk two-player cooperation and plentiful on-screen destruction recall classic arcade military shooters while making full use of the Neo Geo's colorful sprite hardware.

games.title: Shock Troopers
games.description:
Shock Troopers is a 1997 Neo Geo run-and-gun game developed by Saurus and published by SNK. Players battle a terrorist army across forests, mountains and military installations, selecting either a single commando or a team of three fighters who can be switched during play. Its eight-character roster offers varied weapons and special attacks, while a dodge roll lets skilled players escape dense fire without simply retreating.

Branching routes give the campaign replay value, and two players can cooperate against swarms of troops, armored vehicles and giant bosses. The combination of character selection, route choice, rolling evasions and fast-paced overhead shooting made Shock Troopers a standout late-1990s Neo Geo action title.

games.title: Shogun Warriors
games.description: Shogun Warriors is Kaneko's 1992 one-on-one fighting game, titled Fujisan Buster in Japan. Fighters drawn from exaggerated Japanese and international stereotypes battle in side-view arenas, using punches, kicks and character-specific special techniques. It belongs to the wave of arcade versus fighters that followed Street Fighter II, but is especially memorable for its bizarre character designs and flamboyant attacks. Rather than a standard martial-arts tournament aesthetic, it embraces colorful fantasy and absurdity, making it a curious example of the genre's early-1990s experimentation.

games.title: Satan's Hollow
games.description:
Bally Midway's Satan's Hollow is a distinctive early-1980s fixed-screen shooter that turns a battle against flying gargoyles into a confrontation with the Devil. The player moves a rocket launcher horizontally, firing at descending monsters and activating a rechargeable shield when attacks become overwhelming. Destroyed enemies produce sections of a bridge that must be carried across a river of lava at the edge of the screen. Once the bridge is complete, the player can cross over to battle Satan himself.

This bridge-building objective gives the usual formation-shooting action a welcome strategic wrinkle: players must decide when to collect and deliver a section rather than keep shooting. Defeating Satan upgrades the launcher, after which an even longer crossing must be assembled. Its theatrical infernal theme and unusual progression made Satan's Hollow an inventive entry in Midway's classic shooter catalog.

games.title: Shoot the Bull
games.description: Shoot the Bull is Bally Midway's 1985 electronic darts game, built around a trackball used to aim at a dartboard and a button used to throw. Up to four participants can play several recognizable variations, including a bullseye challenge, Black Out, 301 and Poison 301 Pro. In the 301 games, competitors must reduce their score to exactly zero, with the finishing throw subject to special rules. Its straightforward sports premise makes it an unusual arcade conversion kit for hardware related to Pac-Man rather than a reflex-based action game.

games.title: Shooting Gallery
games.description: Shooting Gallery is a 1984 light-gun arcade game developed by Seatongrove in Britain and published by the Italian manufacturer Zaccaria. Players aim a gun at on-screen shooting-gallery targets rather than moving a character with a joystick; the original machine also includes adjustable timing settings. The game is a relatively uncommon example of an early-1980s shooting conversion built around Signetics S2650 and Intel 8035 hardware. Its preservation history is notable because proper gun inputs and game ROMs had to be identified before it became playable in MAME.

games.title: Shoot Out
games.description:
Data East's Shoot Out (1985) takes the appearance of a shooting gallery and turns it into a tense joystick-controlled gunfight. The player aims in eight directions and fires at criminals who emerge from behind walls, windows and scenery, while a separate button allows a jump to evade incoming bullets. Crouching and angling shots are important because enemies appear at different heights. Civilians occasionally enter the scene and must not be hit.

An optional target-practice area introduces the controls before a campaign of increasingly difficult stages, each demanding accurate fire and quick reactions. Its combination of static foreground shooting, movable aim and acrobatic dodging gives Shoot Out a distinct rhythm compared with contemporary light-gun games.

games.title: Must Shoot TV
games.description:
Must Shoot TV is an unreleased light-gun prototype developed by Incredible Technologies during the late 1990s. Its premise casts the player as Chuck, a disgruntled employee of the fictional ITS Cable company, taking out his frustrations on television programming. A mock channel guide leads into timed shooting-gallery scenes that parody broadcasts and home-shopping advertisements, with targets hit by aiming a gun at the screen. The prototype supports one or two competing players and survives in a test build rather than a documented commercial release.

Preserved on Incredible Technologies' 32-bit arcade hardware, it remained largely unknown until MAME 0.226 added the recovered prototype in October 2020. Its unusual television-satire setting makes it a particularly curious example of an arcade game that never reached the market.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Shougi
games.description: Shougi is a 1980 arcade adaptation of Japanese chess by Alpha Denshi, one of the company's earliest video games. Two players take turns moving pieces on a grid-based board, aiming to capture the opposing king. Unlike Western chess, captured pieces can be returned to play under the rules of shogi, making control of the board and the timing of piece drops essential to the strategy. Its coin-operated tabletop presentation illustrates how early arcade designers experimented with translating traditional board games to video screens.

games.title: Showdown
games.description:
Exidy's Showdown (1988) is an unusual Western-themed light-gun game in which the gun is used to play poker rather than shoot outlaws. Sitting at a card table with saloon characters Tex (called Doc in some versions), Dolly, and Rawhide, the player aims the cabinet-mounted gun at playing cards and fires to make selections. This turns an otherwise familiar card game into a distinctive piece of physical arcade interaction, closer to a shooting-gallery novelty than conventional button-operated video poker.

Running on Exidy's 440 hardware, Showdown was released in October 1988, toward the end of the company's run of light-gun arcade titles. Its credited designers and programmers were Larry Hutcherson, Vic Tolomei, and Ken Nicholson. AdvanceMAME's version 5.0 set represents a later program revision, with version 4.0 also known to survive.

games.title: Sea Hunter Penguin
games.description:
Sea Hunter Penguin is an obscure 1995 single-screen platform game attributed to WSAC Systems. Its side-on action takes place across several narrow, staggered platforms populated by brightly colored cartoon creatures and objects. The player moves a small humanoid character through this crowded playfield using an eight-way joystick and three buttons, with a timer and round indicator at the top of the screen. Despite the title, it is not simply a remake of Sega's Pengo.

The game's surviving PCB reveals an unusual history: its code and hardware are derived from Dragon Punch, and an internal program label dates the revision to February 20, 1995. One color PROM in the board recovered for emulation was damaged, complicating the reproduction of some palette effects. These preservation problems, together with its strikingly eccentric presentation, make Sea Hunter Penguin a notable rarity among mid-1990s platform games.

games.title: Shrike Avenger
games.description: Shrike Avenger is a rare 1986 Bally/Sente prototype built around an ambitious first-person aerial-combat simulator. Players pilot a combat craft from a cockpit perspective using a flight stick and multiple action buttons, while a specialized enclosed cabinet was designed to move with the action. It ran on the unique SAC-II hardware and was never produced in normal commercial quantities. With only a small group of prototype machines built, it stands as an early attempt to combine arcade video simulation with physical motion, foreshadowing the elaborate ride-based flight cabinets that would become more common later.

games.title: Shooting Master
games.description: Shooting Master is Sega's gun-controlled arcade shooter in which the player attempts to rescue Princess Iris from a criminal syndicate. The action follows a series of scripted scenes, beginning with a city-street pursuit and continuing through locations including a forest and a warehouse. The player fires at pursuing gangsters while avoiding hits to the princess, whose safety directly affects the game. Its dedicated recoiling light-gun cabinet was designed to give each shot a physical impact, making the hardware an important part of the experience.

games.title: Shot Rider
games.description: Shot Rider is a 1985 motorcycle racing game by Seibu Kaihatsu. The rider races along a scrolling road, steering around hazardous bends, other vehicles and competing motorcycles. Unlike a purely clean time trial, contact and aggressive positioning are part of the challenge: opponents can be knocked aside, but collisions also threaten to unseat the player. The result is an arcade road race that blends speed management with a rough-and-tumble struggle for space among traffic.

games.title: Shuffleboard
games.description: Midway's Shuffleboard (1978) brings the traditional tabletop game to a black-and-white video screen. One or two players use a large trackball to slide pucks down a rectangular playing surface, trying to stop them in areas worth the most points. Later throws can strike earlier pucks and push them out of scoring positions, so touch and placement are as important as raw speed. The substantial trackball control provides a tactile substitute for the real game's sliding motion and makes this an interesting example of an early coin-operated sports simulation.

games.title: Shuffleshot
games.description: Shuffleshot is Incredible Technologies' arcade take on shuffleboard, using a trackball to control the speed and placement of pucks sliding toward marked scoring zones. Up to four players compete over a sequence of turns, trying to place their shots accurately while knocking rivals away from valuable positions. Its compact rounds and direct physical controls make it well suited to competitive play in bars and amusement centers. The game belongs to the same family of accessible trackball sports games as Incredible Technologies' golf and bowling releases.

games.title: Shuttle Invader
games.description: Shuttle Invader is an early Japanese Space Invaders-style game produced by Omori Electric. The player moves a cannon horizontally at the foot of the screen, firing upward at rows of descending alien shuttles while using defensive cover against their attacks. It follows the familiar fixed-screen survival and score-chasing formula rather than adding a new setting or story. The original black-and-white display was supplemented by colored screen overlays, a common technique for giving early monochrome arcade games a brighter appearance.

games.title: Shuuz
games.description:
Shuuz is Atari Games' 1990 arcade simulation of horseshoes, starring a cast of comic characters and a running stream of background gags. The trackball determines the power and angle of each throw as players try to land horseshoes close to a stake or loop them around it for a ringer. Different playable throwers have individual handling characteristics, so accurate pitching requires more finesse than simply rolling the trackball as hard as possible.

The humor is as prominent as the sport: farm animals, spectators, advertising planes and other distractions animate the rural playing field. Its blend of straightforward competition and exaggerated cartoon presentation made Shuuz an unusual alternative to the era's more conventional arcade sports games.

games.title: Super Invader Attack
games.description: Super Invader Attack is an unauthorized variation of Taito's Space Invaders, related to Zaccaria's The Invaders. A gun at the bottom of the screen moves from side to side, firing upward at descending rows of attackers while avoiding their return shots. As in the 1978 original, the shrinking alien formation becomes more urgent as enemies are destroyed. Its principal historical interest is as one of the many hardware and software adaptations that sprang up around the enormous popularity of Space Invaders.

games.title: Sichuan II
games.description: Sichuan II is an unauthorized version of the tile-matching puzzle also seen as Shisensho: Joshiryo-hen and Match It.
