Instead of removing stacked pairs as in Shanghai, the player clears a flat arrangement by selecting two identical tiles that can be connected by an unobstructed path according to the game's matching rules. The board must be emptied before time runs out. AdvanceMAME's Sichuan II entry preserves a variant identified as a possible hack, while the related Match It release removed the Japanese game's erotic interludes. Its appeal is in finding the right sequence of matching connections before the board becomes blocked.

games.title: Sichuan II
games.description: This second Sichuan II set is another version of the same tile-connection puzzle, catalogued as a possible hack. Players must remove matching tiles from a flat board by finding pairs that can be joined through the available empty space, working toward a completely cleared layout before the timer expires. The closely related Match It and Shisensho: Joshiryo-hen releases share the underlying matching-game concept. The precise gameplay differences between the two Sichuan II sets are not well documented, so this set is best understood as an alternate preserved version rather than a confirmed redesign.

games.title: Side Arms - Hyper Dyne
games.description:
Side Arms: Hyper Dyne is Capcom's 1986 scrolling science-fiction shooter, starring two armored pilots fighting the invading Bozon forces. The distinctive side-view combat suits can fire both left and right, with separate attack buttons covering enemies approaching from either direction and another button changing the selected weapon. Shooting floating upgrade symbols cycles through possible bonuses, rewarding players who hold off collecting an item until it displays the equipment they want.

The weapon system includes spread fire, heavy lasers and additional support fire, while two-player cooperation provides another unusual feature: with the right special item, the pilots can combine their suits into a more powerful unit. The mixture of horizontal and occasional vertical scrolling, mechanical enemies and versatile fire directions helped distinguish Side Arms from the crowded mid-1980s shooter field.

games.title: Side By Side
games.description: Side By Side is Taito's 1996 polygonal arcade driving game centered on Japanese mountain-pass racing. Drivers navigate narrow roads packed with sharp bends, relying on braking, cornering rhythm and controlled slides rather than the wide open circuits common to many racing games. Its 3D graphics and recognizable Japanese road-car atmosphere brought the growing touge racing culture into amusement centers. Side By Side was the starting point of Taito's series that would later continue under the Battle Gear name.

games.title: Side By Side 2
games.description: Side By Side 2, also known as Side By Side 2 Evoluzione, is Taito's 1997 continuation of its Japanese mountain-road racing series. The game retains the behind-the-car polygonal viewpoint and its focus on demanding downhill-style roads, where hairpin corners and close barriers reward careful speed control and drifting technique. Building on the original's road-car competition, it offers a more developed version of the touge racing formula. This series went on to form the foundation for Taito's later Battle Gear arcade games.

games.title: Side Pocket
games.description:
Side Pocket is Data East's 1986 arcade pool game, replacing a simulated professional table with a score-based challenge. The player lines up shots, sets their strength and tries to pocket balls efficiently enough to reach target scores and advance to more difficult rounds. Consecutive successful shots and balls sunk in numerical order earn bonuses, while specially marked pockets can trigger extra rewards. Missing too often or scratching has consequences in the solo mode.

Two-player options include competitive pool and nine-ball, giving the game a different pace from ordinary high-score play. Its combination of billiards fundamentals and arcade-specific scoring made Side Pocket a durable favorite that was subsequently adapted for home systems.

games.title: Side Track
games.description: Side Track, also spelled Side Trak, is an early black-and-white railway maze game from Exidy. The player controls a train moving around interconnected tracks and must collect waiting passengers without colliding head-on with a hostile computer-controlled locomotive. A four-way control changes the route at junctions, while a speed button permits a short burst of acceleration. Each completed circuit adds another car to the player's train, making navigation progressively more demanding. Its combination of track switching, pursuit and a growing vehicle predates several later maze games built around collecting objects while avoiding an opponent.

games.title: Silent Dragon
games.description: Silent Dragon is Taito's 1992 side-scrolling beat-'em-up about a group of fighters confronting the mutant forces of the villainous Dr. Bio. Players choose from several brawlers and advance through streets and enemy hideouts, punching, kicking and using their characters' individual fighting moves against gangs and hulking bosses. It follows the cooperative, multi-character style established by late-1980s arcade brawlers, with a deliberately exaggerated science-fiction backdrop and substantial boss encounters.

games.title: The Legend of Silkroad
games.description: The Legend of Silkroad is a side-scrolling fantasy beat-'em-up that follows warriors from Korea, China and Mongolia on a journey across a mythologized Silk Road. The three playable heroes, Munmoo, Sochun and Jamuka, have different fighting styles and can unleash both physical attacks and magical techniques. Players defeat groups of human and supernatural enemies, collect food to restore health, and acquire magic stones to power stronger attacks. A lengthy route with hidden stages, combined with two-player cooperation, makes it a particularly ambitious example of the fantasy-themed arcade brawler.

games.title: Silk Worm
games.description:
Tecmo's Silk Worm (1988) gives cooperative shooting a clever asymmetrical twist: one player pilots a helicopter while the other drives an armed jeep. The helicopter can rise above obstacles and attack from the air, whereas the jeep remains on the ground and must jump hazards while firing into enemy formations. Both move across the same horizontally scrolling battlefields, facing aircraft, tanks, gun emplacements and enormous combined mechanical bosses.

The different vehicles create complementary but unequal challenges, and neither can simply imitate the other's tactics. Weapon upgrades, shield items and relentless enemy assaults make the action intense even when playing solo. This unusual land-and-air partnership became the game's signature and helped Silk Worm stand apart from conventional two-player shooters.

games.title: Simpsons Bowling
games.description: Simpsons Bowling is Konami's 2000 3D bowling game based on the animated television series. Players select familiar residents of Springfield, including Homer, Marge, Bart, Mr. Burns and Krusty, and roll through cartoon-styled bowling matches. A trackball controls the throw while the bowlers' different power, accuracy and curve characteristics influence results. Alongside traditional bowling is a spare-conversion challenge, and up to four people can take turns. Its character animations and sitcom humor turn an accessible physical sport into a lively licensed arcade attraction.

games.title: The Simpsons
games.description:
Konami's The Simpsons is a 1991 arcade beat-'em-up that lets up to four players become Homer, Marge, Bart and Lisa on a frantic rescue mission. After Smithers kidnaps Maggie, the family fights through Springfield landmarks from Krustyland and Moe's Tavern to Mr. Burns's power plant. Each character uses a signature weapon or fighting style: Homer's fists, Marge's vacuum cleaner, Bart's skateboard and Lisa's jump rope. The simple jump-and-attack controls make it easy for newcomers to join the battle.

A particularly charming feature is the set of team attacks, which allow pairs of family members to combine their abilities, while background cameos reward fans of the television show. Large, expressive sprites reproduce the series' early visual style, and both two-player and four-player cabinet editions appeared. The Simpsons remains one of the most fondly remembered licensed cooperative arcade games of its era.

games.title: Sindbad Mystery
games.description: Sindbad Mystery is Sega's 1983 maze-puzzle game starring a cartoon version of Sinbad the sailor. The player explores enclosed mazes, gathering question-mark symbols that gradually reveal clues on a treasure map while dodging roaming enemies. Once the treasure's position is known, Sinbad must reach the correct location and dig it up with the action button. Finding it before time runs out earns a bonus and advances to another island. The mix of map deduction, maze navigation and light action makes it rather different from Sega's better-known purely reflex-based arcade games.

games.title: Sinistar
games.description: This prototype version of Williams' Sinistar preserves a developmental form of the 1983 multidirectional space shooter. The player mines drifting planetoids for crystals that become homing Sinibombs, while red Worker ships gather the same material to assemble the enormous Sinistar. Once the creature is complete, its pursuit turns the level into a desperate battle to survive and destroy it. The prototype is valuable chiefly as a separate preserved build of a major Williams arcade game; the supplied documentation does not establish specific gameplay changes from the final release.

games.title: Sinistar
games.description:
Williams' Sinistar (1983) is a furious multidirectional space shooter built around one of the most memorable villains of the golden arcade age. The player flies freely through an asteroid field, shooting planetoids to uncover crystals that are converted into homing Sinibombs. Meanwhile, enemy Worker ships collect the same crystals to build Sinistar, a gigantic mechanical skull, while Warrior ships harass the player. Once assembled, Sinistar comes roaring after the ship, and only a well-stocked supply of bombs can destroy it.

The game uses a distinctive 49-way optical joystick to give the ship fine directional control and produce dramatic acceleration. Its digitized speech, particularly Sinistar's threatening taunts, became a landmark of arcade sound design. The combination of resource gathering, competing enemy construction and terrifying pursuit makes Sinistar far more than a routine space shooter and one of Williams' most enduring classics.

games.title: Sukeban Jansi Ryuko
games.description: Sukeban Janshi Ryuko is a Japan-only Sega System 16 mahjong game developed by Whiteboard and released around 1988-1989. The heroine confronts an evil group through matches of Japanese mahjong rather than conventional action combat. Players must build winning hands while managing the normal rules of the tile game, and special features include a temporary ESP ability for viewing an opponent's concealed tiles. Its combination of mahjong competition, character-driven presentation and adult-oriented material is typical of a particular niche of late-1980s Japanese arcade software.

games.title: Skill Trek
games.description:
Skill Trek is an early-1990s Barcrest pub quiz/amusement-with-prizes game running on the company's MPU4 Video hardware. Unlike a pure reel-spinning slot, it is catalogued as a skill or question-based attraction, blending the British tradition of prize machines with a screen-based interface. It uses a horizontal display and the MPU4's paired processor arrangement rather than a dedicated arcade action board.

The surviving version 1.1 sets document a machine aimed at the British pub market, although their detailed question flow and prize rules are not clearly established. It is therefore best distinguished by its skill-machine format and Barcrest platform rather than by unsupported claims about particular challenges.

games.title: Super Kaneko Nova System BIOS
games.description:
Super Kaneko Nova System BIOS is the startup firmware for Kaneko's cartridge-based arcade platform, introduced in 1996. Commonly abbreviated SKNS, the hardware used a Hitachi SH-2 RISC processor with custom graphics circuitry and Yamaha YMZ280B sample playback. Its reusable motherboard and removable program boards offered operators a modular alternative to replacing an entire arcade system.

The BIOS existed in regional forms for Japan, North America, Europe, Asia, and Korea, reflecting the territory configuration of the original boards. Hardware documentation identifies the region data as residing in a dedicated ROM on the motherboard. The BIOS set therefore preserves more than a generic boot image: its variants also document how the same physical platform was configured for different markets.

games.title: Skull Fang
games.description: Skull Fang is Data East's 1996 vertical air-combat shooter on the company's MLC arcade system. Players choose among four combat aircraft with different speed, protection and weapon characteristics and launch sorties against heavily armed enemy formations. Its unusual chase mode allows the pilot to vary the scrolling speed with a throttle-like system rather than simply follow a fixed battlefield, while a conventional automatic-scroll mode is also available. Collectible weapon upgrades, bombs and specialized maneuvers add depth to its high-speed airborne battles. The blend of shoot-'em-up action and adjustable-speed pursuit gives Skull Fang a different feel from Data East's earlier military shooters.

games.title: Skull & Crossbones
games.description:
Skull & Crossbones is Atari Games' 1989 swashbuckling arcade action game in which two pirates attempt to recover their stolen treasure from an evil wizard. Players fight through ships, beaches, castles and supernatural enemy strongholds using swordplay, punches and additional weapons. Rather than simply attacking constantly, a pirate can parry and time blows in a fencing-like combat system. Hidden treasure and other booty gathered during a level can be traded for useful equipment.

A second player can join the expedition, combining pirate adventure with cooperative combat. Its eclectic opponents, including skeletons, ninjas and mythological creatures, give the action a playful fantasy quality. The varied locations and treasure economy distinguish Skull & Crossbones from more conventional side-scrolling beat-'em-ups.

games.title: Sky Adventure
games.description: Sky Adventure is SNK's 1989 vertically scrolling shooter in which pilots oppose the forces of Colonel Claud. Players select among several aircraft and fly over changing landscapes, engaging enemy planes, ground installations and strange fantasy-inspired adversaries. Different planes carry different armaments, and the game allows aircraft choices between acts. Scoring is evaluated on an act-by-act basis, with strong performance rewarding the player with extra resources. Its varied enemies and unusual setting make it a colorful alternative to more straightforward military flying games.

games.title: Sky Alert
games.description: Sky Alert is a vertically scrolling arcade shooter created by Metro and released in Japan in 1992. Two aircraft types provide different weapon configurations: one combines focused laser fire with broader missile options, while the other offers spread guns and heavy secondary attacks. Players can switch between their aircraft's primary attack styles and use bombs when enemy formations become overwhelming. The core challenge is to navigate waves of fighters and ground threats while selecting the weapon pattern best suited to each encounter. It was among Metro's earliest arcade productions.

games.title: Sky Army
games.description: Sky Army is an early-1980s horizontally scrolling helicopter shooter by Shoei. The player flies a red helicopter through a war zone, destroying enemy aircraft, ground troops and military targets while avoiding hostile fire. Missions include attacking bridges and fighting over waterways where submarines and other defenses appear. Its combination of aerial dogfights and attacks on ground infrastructure gives the action a broader battlefield than a simple fixed-screen shooter.

games.title: Sky Base
games.description: Sky Base is a little-documented 1982 space shooter from Omori Electric. The player controls a spacecraft that moves horizontally across the bottom of the screen in a fixed-screen shooting arrangement. The surviving descriptions establish this basic arcade format but provide little reliable information about the enemy patterns or any distinctive scoring rules. It is chiefly of interest as one of Omori's comparatively obscure early arcade releases.

games.title: Sky Bumper
games.description: Sky Bumper is a 1982 arcade flight shooter by Venture Line. Players steer a small airplane over a night-time city, destroying enemy helicopters and shooting gateways that lead to new areas. The craft can perform loops, while contact with certain boundaries makes it ricochet rather than simply crash, giving the game its bumper-like movement gimmick. Navigating the gates without colliding with hazards is as important as firing accurately. Its distinctive bouncing flight behavior helps set it apart from more conventional horizontal shooters.

games.title: Sky Chuter
games.description: Irem's Sky Chuter (1980) is an early fixed-screen shooting game in which a horizontally moving missile launcher must defend against attacking aircraft. Planes enter from either side of the sky, dive toward the player's position and drop dangerous parachute bombs. The player fires upward to destroy the aircraft and intercept their threats before being hit. Eliminating the last plane advances the game to a new enemy pattern. Its two-direction movement and single fire button make it a simple, demanding example of early Japanese arcade shooting design.

games.title: Sky Diver
games.description: Sky Diver is Atari's 1978 arcade game about timing a parachute jump. A plane passes over the screen and the player chooses when the skydiver leaps, how long to free-fall and when to open the parachute. After deployment, horizontal steering helps guide the parachutist toward a narrow landing area. Delaying the parachute increases the potential score but leaves less room for correction and risks a failed landing. The game turns a simple action into a compact risk-versus-reward challenge and is a characteristic example of Atari's early sports-themed arcade experiments.

games.title: Sky Fox
games.description:
Sky Fox, known in Japan as Exerizer, is Jaleco's 1987 fixed-screen space shooter. Unlike the more restrictive movement of Space Invaders, the player's craft can maneuver in eight directions while confronting a succession of distinct enemy waves. A slow but unlimited standard weapon is supplemented by faster laser fire that consumes energy; collecting dropped upgrades replenishes that resource and improves the ship.

Its encounters range from formations of small aliens to strange fantasy-like enemies, asteroids and huge bosses, with sprite scaling adding a sense of depth to some attacks. The changing stages recall Gorf rather than a single endlessly repeated formation, making Sky Fox an unusual hybrid of old-school shooting and more elaborate late-1980s spectacle.

games.title: Sky Kid
games.description:
Namco's Sky Kid (1985) is a whimsical side-scrolling combat game featuring cartoon biplanes and a surprisingly demanding bombing mission. One or two players pilot the Red Baron and Blue Max, flying across enemy territory, shooting at aircraft and ground targets, and picking up a bomb en route to destroy a designated objective. The plane travels across the landscape while the player controls its position on screen, and a dedicated loop button provides a crucial evasive maneuver.

Unlike ordinary shooters where simply destroying enemies is enough, a successful mission depends on reaching the target with the bomb and landing safely afterward. The loop can even help recover from certain dangerous situations, while the exaggerated characters and lively music give the wartime premise a playful tone. Sky Kid became one of Namco's most distinctive mid-1980s arcade shooters and led to an expanded sequel.

games.title: Sky Kid Deluxe
games.description:
Sky Kid Deluxe is Namco's 1986 expanded follow-up to its cartoon biplane shooter. Players once again fly the Red Baron and Blue Max across side-scrolling battlefields, collecting a bomb for a designated target while fighting aircraft and avoiding ground fire. A dedicated loop maneuver offers a tactical way to evade danger or regain control.

The Deluxe edition adds new mission sequences, including winter scenery and snow effects, along with new characters and a battle report between missions. Rather than changing the fundamental bombing-and-landing objective, it broadens the original's presentation and stage variety, making it a worthwhile companion to Sky Kid rather than a completely different game.

games.title: Sky Lancer
games.description: Sky Lancer is a 1983 arcade shooter developed by Orca. The player controls an astronaut who fights incoming aliens from a vertically oriented playfield using joystick movement and a single firing button. The game's surviving descriptions are brief, but establish its space-combat premise and straightforward shooting controls. A licensed version distributed by Esco Trading is also known, making this a small but documented entry in Orca's early-1980s arcade catalog.

games.title: Sky Love
games.description: Sky Love is an early Japanese arcade shooter released by Omori Electric in December 1979. It uses a vertically mounted display and the simple control scheme typical of the immediate post-Space Invaders era: a two-direction joystick and a single firing button. Progress is organized into numbered waves, with a display that can be mistaken for a player-number indicator. The game supports alternating players and represents one of the lesser-known fixed-screen shooting experiments of the late 1970s, using Intel 8080-era electronics and an SN76477 sound generator.

games.title: Sky Raider
games.description: Sky Raider is a 1978 Atari bombing game viewed over a vertically scrolling landscape. Rather than piloting a visible fighter through enemy fire, the player uses an analog flight control to move an aiming sight over bridges, factories, aircraft and other targets below, then releases bombs to score points. Nothing shoots back, so the central challenge is precision and selecting valuable targets before the timer expires. Its smoothly scrolling scenery and first-person bomber viewpoint made it an ambitious departure from fixed-screen arcade shooting at the end of the 1970s.

games.title: Sky Robo
games.description: Sky Robo, released in Japan as Tatakae! Big Fighter, is Nichibutsu's 1989 side-scrolling space shooter with a transforming craft. The player normally controls an agile spacecraft firing forward, but can change into a larger robot that attacks in multiple directions at the cost of maneuverability. Switching between these modes is essential when confronting enemies above, below or directly ahead, while weapons can be improved with power-ups. Large bosses punctuate the stages, and a recognizable enemy from Nichibutsu's earlier Terra Cresta makes an appearance. It is one of the company's last traditional action-game productions before its arcade catalog became heavily focused on mahjong.

games.title: Sky Skipper
games.description:
Sky Skipper is Nintendo's unusual 1981 rescue game in which a biplane pilot must save animals and members of a royal family imprisoned by gorillas. Each stage is a maze-like landscape: the player drops a bomb to stun the gorilla guarding a cage, then swoops down to collect the captives before their jailer recovers. Fuel is limited and restored by making rescues, while collisions with the environment or enemies cost a life.

Unlike a standard shooter, victory depends on timing, navigating confined spaces and gathering everyone before running out of fuel. Its playful premise and unusual rescue mechanics are notable in Nintendo's early arcade history. The original game received only limited distribution, adding to its reputation as a collector's curiosity.

games.title: Sky Smasher
games.description: Sky Smasher is a 1990 vertically scrolling military-style shooter by Nihon System. One or two players pilot aircraft through waves of enemies and increasingly demanding bullet patterns, relying on constant movement and accurate shooting to survive. Its horizontally arranged two-player cooperation and detailed late-era sprite graphics place it in the familiar tradition of arcade aerial shooters. The game is particularly remembered by genre enthusiasts for its high difficulty rather than for an extensively documented storyline or experimental control system.

games.title: Sky Soldiers
games.description:
Sky Soldiers is a 1988 vertical shooter developed by Alpha Denshi, with an unusual time-travel campaign. The player's fighter moves through battles set in different historical periods, from the two world wars to later conflicts, before returning to a futuristic space station. Stages end in boss battles, and the changing time periods bring a diverse collection of enemy aircraft and defenses.

At the start of a stage, players configure their ship's limited bomb armament, choosing among missiles, fireballs, homing attacks and more powerful explosives. These weapons must be conserved because resupply is restricted, while the standard gun provides continuous fire. The shifting historical settings and loadout decisions add a distinctive tactical flavor to the familiar vertically scrolling action.

games.title: Saturday Night Slam Masters

variants.title: Muscle Bomber Duo - Ultimate Team Battle (World 931206)
Muscle Bomber Duo - Heat Up Warriors (Japan 931206)

games.description:
Saturday Night Slam Masters is Capcom's 1993 professional-wrestling arcade game, known in Japan as Muscle Bomber: The Body Explosion. It combines the characterful presentation of a fighting game with the rules of professional wrestling: powerful strikes and throws wear down an opponent, but a match generally ends only when a wrestler secures a three-count pin or a submission. Players choose from a roster of larger-than-life competitors, each with special maneuvers and a signature finishing move.

Its two main formats offer one-on-one championship play and tag-team battles, with up to four players participating. Character illustrations by Tetsuo Hara, renowned for Fist of the North Star, give the roster an especially muscular look, while Final Fight's Mike Haggar appears as a playable wrestler. The mixture of spectacular grapples, arcade accessibility and Capcom character design made Slam Masters a distinctive sports-and-fighting hybrid.

games.title: Slap Fight
games.description:
Slap Fight is Toaplan's 1986 vertically scrolling shooter, also released in North America as Alcon. Piloting a small spacecraft above an enemy-controlled world, the player attacks ground installations and hostile formations while working toward powerful weapon upgrades. Its defining mechanic is a selection-based upgrade system: collecting stars moves a cursor through a sequence of improvements, but the player must decide when to activate the highlighted choice. Speed, added wing guns, wider shots and other equipment compete for limited upgrade opportunities.

Growing the ship's firepower can also make its silhouette larger and more vulnerable, turning progression into a balance between offensive power and survival. The game's cleanly arranged enemy patterns and exacting difficulty are characteristic of Toaplan's early shooter design. Slap Fight helped establish the studio's influential approach to weapon systems before later successes such as Twin Cobra and Truxton.

games.title: Slap Shot
games.description: Slap Shot is Taito's 1994 arcade air-hockey game, not the unrelated Sega Master System ice-hockey title of the same name. Players control paddles on a tabletop-style rink, striking a puck toward the opposing goal while defending their own end. Fast rebounds off the sides and special powered shots create a more exaggerated contest than conventional tabletop hockey. Its compact arena, direct joystick controls and focus on sudden reversals of play make it a fast competitive sports diversion.

games.title: Slap Shooter
games.description: Slap Shooter is a 1986 ice-hockey game released by Sega for Japanese arcades on the System E hardware. It adapts the basic competition of hockey to joystick play, with players maneuvering across the rink to gain possession of the puck, attack the opposing goal and defend their own. Its relatively modest arcade release makes it a lesser-known example of Sega experimenting with traditional sports during the mid-1980s.

games.title: Slick Shot
games.description:
Slick Shot is a 1990 billiards arcade machine from Grand Products, closely associated with the company that became Incredible Technologies. Unlike ordinary video pool games, it combines an on-screen table with a short physical cueing surface: the player strikes a real ball with a real cue, and infrared sensors calculate its speed and direction as it enters the cabinet. The measured shot is then reproduced in the electronic pool game.

Players can choose between the game's own shot-based challenge and nine-ball rules. The mechanical and digital parts form a single control system, making Slick Shot an unusual hybrid of bar-room billiards and arcade simulation. Its specialized cabinet is as central to the experience as the software itself.

games.title: Slipstream
games.description:
Slipstream is Capcom's 1995 Formula One-style racer developed for Sega's System Multi 32 hardware. Drivers select among several single-seat racing cars with different handling and acceleration, then tackle courses inspired by Grand Prix venues including Monaco, Japan, Germany and Australia. The action uses smoothly scaled road and vehicle sprites rather than the polygons increasingly common in mid-1990s racing games.

Its signature feature is a turbo meter that gradually fills and periodically produces a speed boost, encouraging the player to preserve momentum through corners and make the most of brief bursts on the straights. Several competition formats, including individual races and a championship, add replay value. As a late release on Sega's sprite-scaling Multi 32 system, Slipstream represents an interesting technological endpoint for this style of arcade racer.

games.title: Slither
games.description:
Slither is an unusual 1982 arcade shooter from Century II and GDI, controlled with a trackball rather than a conventional joystick. The player moves a blaster around an arena while shooting segmented snakes that slither through vegetation. The attacks grow more complex as different-colored snakes arrive, while other creatures, including pterodactyls and mutant gorillas, add hazards and change the terrain. Clearing waves quickly preserves a decreasing bonus, but survival grows harder as the snakes begin pursuing the player directly.

Its freely maneuvered trackball weapon, organic enemies and shifting arena make Slither feel quite unlike a typical fixed-screen alien shooter. It is a particularly curious early attempt at blending multidirectional aiming with maze-like enemy movement.

games.title: Sliver
games.description:
Sliver is a 1996 adult-oriented puzzle game by Hollow Corp, combining tile-based puzzle play with photographic imagery. It uses an eight-way joystick and three buttons, and supports alternating two-player sessions. Its unusual hardware is more historically distinctive than its puzzle design: the PCB carries a pair of Zoran JPEG-decoder chips to decompress pictures stored in the ROMs.

Early MAME implementations displayed the photographic backgrounds through a substitute set of already-decoded images. Later emulation reproduced the actual JPEG decoding, including visible compression artifacts in the original pictures. That makes Sliver an unexpected example of dedicated image-compression hardware in a comparatively obscure coin-operated game.

games.title: Slots
games.description:
Slots is a 1995 Dutch-market video-slot game from BFM/ELAM, preserved as game card 95-750-368. Its four-button, horizontal-screen cabinet offers electronic slot gambling rather than the joystick-based play of mainstream arcades. It belongs to a group of closely related programs sold in different European jurisdictions.

The regional history is part of the story: BFM/ELAM slot cabinets became familiar sights in Belgian bars around the turn of the millennium, before changes to gambling restrictions curtailed cash-awarding operation. This set is specifically the Dutch program and should not be conflated with the Belgian cash or token variants.

games.title: Solar Assault DR2
games.description:
Solar Assault DR2 is Konami's 1997 revised 3D arcade shoot-'em-up in the Gradius universe. Unlike the series' familiar side-scrolling games, it sends the player racing into the screen along a forward-moving course, maneuvering in both horizontal and vertical directions to dodge hazards. Players choose between iconic ships such as the Vic Viper and Lord British, collect power capsules and improve weapons through the recognizable Gradius upgrade system. Speed control is important for negotiating the scrolling environment, and an enemy hit can still be fatal unless a protective shield is active.

The DR2 revision expands the original Solar Assault with additional stage content, including the Fierce Blaze stage, while preserving its cinematic rail-shooter presentation. Its combination of traditional Gradius ship upgrades with 3D movement makes it one of the series' more unusual arcade spin-offs.

games.title: Solite Spirits
games.description:
Solite Spirits is a 1999 Korean vertically scrolling shooter developed by Team Muhaha and published by Promat, later reworked and released as 1945k III. Drawing heavily on Psikyo's Strikers 1945 games, it offers a selection of modern fighter aircraft, each with its own normal weapons, charged attack and bomb effect. Holding the fire button spends a rechargeable gauge on a stronger attack, while power-up items improve the regular shot and its supporting weapons.

The original version contains six stages and differs from the later 1945k III releases in stage content, weapon tuning and other balance details. As the earlier form of a better-known unofficial Strikers-style shooter, Solite Spirits offers a valuable look at the game's development rather than simply being another name for the finished revision.

games.title: Slots
games.description:
Slots (Belgian Cash) is BFM/ELAM's 1996 Belgian cash-paying video-slot program, represented by game cards including 95-750-938 and 95-752-008. Its four-button gambling panel and 6809-family electronics provide the straightforward wager-and-result operation of a dedicated video fruit machine.

The cash designation matters: BFM/ELAM also sold visually related Dutch and Belgian token versions, whose software and intended payout arrangements were different. Such cabinets were once widespread in Belgian bars, though later regulations substantially changed where and how cash-paying machines could operate.

games.title: Slots
games.description:
Slots (Belgian Token) is a 1996 BFM/ELAM video-slot variant intended for token-oriented operation rather than the Belgian Cash edition's monetary payouts. The preserved game-card programs include 95-750-943 and later related revisions. A horizontal video display and four-button panel keep play in the familiar electronic fruit-machine format.

Its chief historical interest is the distinction between otherwise similar cash and token configurations. Regional legislation and prize handling were important reasons for European machine manufacturers to issue multiple software versions of the same slot concept.

games.title: Pro Cycle Tele Cardioline

variants.title: Pro Cycle Tele Cardioline (Salter Fitness Bike V.1.0, Checksum 02AB)

games.description:
Pro Cycle Tele Cardioline is a distinctive interactive cycling program developed by Spanish arcade specialist Gaelco for Salter Fitness's commercial exercise bikes. Rather than accepting coins for a conventional arcade race, the original equipment turned a real workout into an on-screen cycling challenge. Riders could follow a course alone or compete against a computer-controlled cyclist, with the display showing their progress alongside information such as distance, speed, power, and calories. Before a stage, the user could select its duration, the opponent's difficulty, and a route profile with different numbers and gradients of climbs.

Gaelco's artists based the animated athletes on footage recorded with real performers, giving the program a visual style closely related to the company's 1990s arcade games. When run in an emulator, its specialized bike inputs are represented by three buttons: acceleration and gear changes through seven ratios. Salter's director later recalled that the original idea was inspired by the detailed race information shown during a Tour de France broadcast. Although the hardware belongs to the late-1990s Cardioline family, the preserved checksum-02AB software revision is dated January 2000.

games.title: Pro Stepper Tele Cardioline

variants.title: Pro Stepper Tele Cardioline (Salter Fitness Stepper V.1.0, Checksum F208)

games.description:
Pro Stepper Tele Cardioline is Gaelco's interactive fitness program for Salter's commercial stepper machines, part of the same Cardioline range as Pro Cycle. Instead of showing cyclists, this version depicts athletes running, using animation derived from filmed performers. The screen transforms a stepping workout into a route-based sporting challenge, combining the animated exercise with progress indicators and the course and opponent options of the Cardioline software. It was designed for gyms, not as a conventional coin-operated arcade cabinet.

The game runs on Gaelco hardware built around a Motorola 68000 processor, although the original stepper installation did not have audio output. The preserved F208 revision is dated April 1997. Its existence is an unusual reminder that arcade developers' graphic techniques and game design were also used in professional fitness equipment during the 1990s.

games.title: Sly Spy
games.description:
Sly Spy is Data East's 1989 arcade action game, also known as Secret Agent outside North America. Its tuxedo-clad secret agent confronts a terrorist organization through a rapid sequence of stages that openly evoke James Bond movies. The game shifts between running gun battles, parachuting combat, a motorcycle chase and underwater shooting, with a different rhythm and hazards in each section. When armed, the spy shoots his way past guards and machinery; without a gun, he must rely on kicks and other close-range attacks.

The changing perspectives, cinematic entrances and extravagant bosses give Sly Spy the feeling of an entire spy thriller compressed into a short arcade experience. The game borrows recognizable ideas from other action hits but builds a distinctive identity through its relentless changes of scene and gleefully over-the-top espionage imagery.

games.title: Smash T.V.
games.description:
Smash T.V. is Williams' 1990 arena shooter designed by Eugene Jarvis and Mark Turmell, combining the frantic twin-stick movement of Robotron: 2084 with a satirical vision of violent television entertainment. One joystick moves the contestant while the other fires in eight directions, allowing the player to run away from danger while shooting back into a dense crowd. Each single-screen arena fills with robots, mutants and gunmen entering through surrounding doors, while prizes, cash and temporary weapon upgrades tempt players into risky positions.

Clearing a room opens exits into different parts of a larger stage, with hidden keys eventually offering access to the extravagant Pleasure Dome bonus area. Giant bosses, a relentless announcer and the gleeful promise of consumer prizes turn the violence into dark comedy. Two-player cooperation and exquisitely immediate controls made Smash T.V. an enduring arcade favorite and a defining update of the classic multidirectional shooter.

games.title: Vs. Stroke & Match Golf
games.description: Vs. Stroke & Match Golf is Nintendo's 1984 arcade adaptation of the Famicom game Golf, produced for the Nintendo Vs. System. Using a joystick and action buttons, players select a club, aim the shot and time their swing to move the ball through an 18-hole course. Stroke play rewards a low total number of shots, while match play compares players hole by hole against an opponent. Arcade-specific credit and swing allowances adapt the familiar home-game rules to coin-operated play. Its simple overhead course view and timing-based swing system helped establish a straightforward template for early video-game golf.

games.title: Super Monaco GP

games.description:
Super Monaco GP is Sega's spectacular 1989 Formula One-style arcade racer, a successor in spirit to the company's Monaco GP games. From a low cockpit viewpoint, the player first completes a timed qualifying lap to determine a starting position, then races against a field of nineteen opponents on a fictional circuit inspired by Monaco. Staying above a constantly tightening position requirement is essential: dropping too far down the order ends the run even before the race distance is complete. Drivers can choose between automatic and manual gearboxes, with the seven-speed option rewarding those who can manage rapid shifts.

Sega's X Board hardware powers its fast, smoothly scaled scenery and close-quarters competition, while dedicated cabinets used elaborate steering and driving controls. Finishing near the front unlocks a further challenge in wet conditions, adding to the game's demanding arcade progression. Super Monaco GP became one of Sega's major late-1980s driving showcases and later inspired substantially expanded console adaptations.

games.title: Super Miss World
games.description: Super Miss World is a 1996 adult-oriented puzzle game from South Korean developer Comad, following the territory of Qix and Kaneko's Gals Panic. Players guide a cursor around the screen, drawing lines that partition the playfield; enclosing sufficient territory clears the stage and uncovers a photograph concealed beneath the background. The emphasis is on claiming areas efficiently rather than simply moving to a destination. Running on Comad's EXPRO02-based hardware, it belongs to the wave of Korean arcade puzzle games built around photographic reveal mechanics.

games.title: Super Major League
games.description: Sega's Super Major League (1995) is an arcade baseball game for the ST-V Titan Video system, a cartridge-based platform closely related to the Sega Saturn. A successor in name and theme to Sega's 1985 Major League, it delivers two-player baseball using joystick movement and six-button controls. The game was released in Japan as Final Arch and exported under the Super Major League title. Its differing regional presentations make it an interesting example of Sega adapting a sports title for ST-V's international arcade market.

games.title: Snake Pit
games.description:
Snake Pit (1984) is a Bally/Sente action game starring Outback Jack, a whip-wielding adventurer making his way through a temple filled with snakes, scorpions, moving creatures, traps and lethal pits. Its striking control arrangement separates movement, handled by a trackball, from the direction of his whip, handled by a four-way joystick. Clearing the creatures in a chamber opens the way forward, while the hazards increasingly demand precise positioning and quick attacks.

The game has a defined 28-wave adventure rather than an endlessly repeating maze. At its midpoint, Jack discovers the Golden Amulet of Alaron, which can provide temporary protection during later waves but will not save him from every hazard. Large enemies, laser-firing statues and other surprises make Snake Pit one of Bally/Sente's more elaborate early arcade experiments.

games.title: Snacks'n Jaxson
games.description:
Snacks'n Jaxson is a bizarre 1984 Bally/Sente game in which Jaxson De Box, a clown with an extendable neck, tries to eat food floating around his dining table. Players use a trackball to steer his head toward desirable snacks and a button to sneeze away unwanted objects. At the same time they must keep his bouncing, detached nose in play; letting it smash through the window costs a life.

Breakfast, lunch, dinner and midnight-snack courses bring different food patterns, with bonus events involving such activities as juggling and catching objects. Its combination of food collection, ball bouncing and two simultaneous concerns makes the game difficult to classify and unmistakably characteristic of Bally/Sente's experimental SAC-I library.

games.title: Snap Jack
games.description: Universal's Snap Jack (1982) is an unusual side-scrolling action game combining maze-style dot collection with the pace of a shooter. Players guide a long-legged, stretching cartoon character across hilly landscapes and tunnels, collecting dots while jumping past dangerous sea creatures, large fish and objects such as boots and kettles carried by overhead conveyors. The constantly changing terrain rewards careful timing as much as rapid movement. Its whimsical obstacles and hybrid of Pac-Man-style collecting with Scramble-like scrolling set it apart from more conventional platform games of the period.

games.title: Snapper
games.description: Snapper (1990) is a Korean maze game by Philko based on the classic growing-snake idea rather than the unrelated British home-computer game with the same name. Players steer a hungry snake around enclosed stages, collecting balls that lengthen its body. The task is to gather the required objects and reach the exit without running into the snake's own tail or hostile creatures. Increasingly cramped paths turn each additional segment into a hazard, giving the game a spatial-planning challenge beneath its simple arcade controls. Its hardware is related to that used by Philko's Atomic Point rather than being a conventional Sega System 16 board.

games.title: Snow Board Championship
games.description:
Gaelco's Snow Board Championship, released in the mid-1990s, turns downhill snowboarding into a fast, overhead-view arcade racing game. Players choose a rider associated with Europe, Japan or the United States, then steer through bends, hazards and gates while trying to beat a course's time limit. Beginner and Championship play offer several tracks, including tight slalom sections and opportunities for jumps or bonus-scoring stunts. A speed-boost control helps recover momentum after a collision, and two players can compete for times in alternating runs.

The Spanish-developed game is also notable for the protection hardware that complicated its emulation for years. Researchers eventually determined how its data-transforming device worked, allowing the previously broken controls, text and sounds to function correctly.

games.title: Snow Bros. 2 - With New Elves / Otenki Paradise
games.description:
Snow Bros. 2: With New Elves, known in Japan as Otenki Paradise ('Weather Paradise'), is Toaplan's 1994 follow-up to its popular single-screen platform game. Up to four players cooperate across six worlds, clearing rooms of enemies and defeating bosses on their way to rescue a kidnapped princess. The familiar method of covering foes with snow and launching them as bouncing projectiles returns, but the sequel introduces new playable heroes with different elemental-style attacks instead of simply repeating Nick and Tom's abilities.

Defeated enemies leave bonuses and changing letter tokens; completing the word EXTRA awards a life and skips to the next stage. Its bright cartoon visuals, expanded multiplayer action and unusually playful enemies contrast with the intense shooting games for which Toaplan was chiefly known. Released shortly before the company's closure, it became one of its last original arcade productions.

games.title: Snow Bros. - Nick & Tom
games.description:
Snow Bros.: Nick & Tom (1990) is Toaplan's beloved fixed-screen platform game in the tradition of Bubble Bobble. One or two players control snowman brothers Nick and Tom, climbing through 50 compact stages to rescue two kidnapped princesses. Rather than defeating enemies with direct shots, they must bury them under layers of snow, turn them into giant snowballs, then kick those balls across the platforms. A rolling enemy can knock out others and trigger spectacular chains, with especially large bonuses for clearing a screen using a single launch.

Colored potions change movement speed, throwing range or snow power, while a green potion temporarily transforms the brothers into floating, enemy-clearing balloons. Every tenth stage brings a boss. Linger too long and an invincible pumpkin-headed pursuer arrives, eventually summoning deadly ghosts to force the action forward. Secret bonus events, including collecting letters to spell SNOW, reward attentive players.

Widely distributed internationally by Romstar, Snow Bros. became a cult arcade favorite and inspired several ports, a 1994 sequel and later revivals. Its unusually small, JAMMA-compatible conversion board also made it a common sight in generic cabinets, while Korean licensed versions and bootlegs such as The Winter Bobble expanded its arcade footprint.

games.title: Soccer Brawl
games.description:
Soccer Brawl is SNK's futuristic take on association football, released on the Neo Geo in 1992. Teams of cybernetically enhanced players represent eight countries in five-a-side matches staged in Osaka's SNK Stadium or the metallic Super Dome in San Francisco. The action is presented from an angled side view, and there is little concern for ordinary football discipline: players tackle, punch, slide and use devastating charged shots that can knock opponents aside.

Two-button attacking and passing controls make it immediately accessible, while the power gauge encourages players to choose between quick plays and dangerous long-range strikes. The pitch's surrounding barriers can rebound shots back into play, adding an arena-sports twist. Its exaggerated physical combat and science-fiction equipment make it a distinctive early Neo Geo sports title.

games.title: Atari Soccer
games.description:
Atari Soccer (1980) is an early overhead-view football arcade game designed for two or four people around a shared cabinet. Each side fields two controlled players, with computer players filling vacant positions when fewer than four people participate. Rather than joysticks, players use large trackballs to race about the pitch and buttons to kick the ball; the side scoring the most goals before the timer expires wins.

Its physical appeal comes from the substantial 4.5-inch trackballs also found in Atari's Football and Basketball machines, which turn running and quick changes of direction into a vigorous hands-on contest. Programmed by Dave Theurer, later celebrated for Missile Command and Tempest, the black-and-white game also appeared in a special French cabinet under the name Coupe du Monde.

games.title: Soccer Superstars
games.description:
Konami's Soccer Superstars (1994) is a four-player arcade football game running on the company's powerful GX hardware. The pitch is viewed from above at an angle, with the playing field rotating as the action moves, creating an unusual television-like presentation. Players steer their footballers with joysticks and use three action buttons for passes, shots and match play, either against the machine or in shared multiplayer contests.

Its high-resolution graphics, rotating playfield and distinctive crowd presentation were ambitious for the period; some cabinets and hardware configurations also supported dual-screen output. Often discussed alongside Konami's later International Superstar Soccer games, Soccer Superstars represents a transitional era when arcade football was experimenting with more elaborate graphics and camera handling.

games.title: Sokonuke Taisen Game
games.description: Sokonuke Taisen Game (1995) is a Japan-only, two-player party-action game released by Sammy and credited to developer Sekarabe. Instead of a conventional platform adventure, it offers a procession of strange short challenges, including inflating balloons and transforming into dragons. Players must perform the tasks while dealing with comic but dangerous hazards such as buzzsaws and bombs, sometimes protecting a companion as well as themselves. With one-button and joystick controls and colorful cartoon graphics, its appeal comes from the absurdity and frantic timing of its competitive mini-games.

games.title: Soukyugurentai / Terra Diver
games.description:
Soukyugurentai, internationally titled Terra Diver, is a 1996 vertically scrolling shooter developed by Raizing for Sega's ST-V arcade system. Its unusual horizontal-monitor presentation gives the game generous room for its elaborate military-science-fiction scenery and dense attack patterns. Players pilot one of several distinct aircraft, using conventional forward shots, screen-clearing bombs and a special laser system that can lock onto multiple targets. Switching laser modes changes how enemies are acquired and attacked, adding a layer of tactics to its rapid shooting and dodging.

The targeting reticles and layered, near-future visual design became its signature, while the characteristic Raizing blend of demanding enemy formations and resource management appealed to dedicated shooting-game fans. It subsequently received Japanese Sega Saturn and PlayStation conversions.

games.title: Solar Fox
games.description:
Solar Fox is Bally/Midway's 1981 maze-action game that replaces Pac-Man's pursuing ghosts with cannons mounted on the four sides of a rectangular arena. Players pilot a spacecraft around a matrix of solar cells and must collect every cell by flying over it. Meanwhile, moving perimeter sentinels launch projectiles across the playfield, forcing constant changes of course. The ship has no conventional gun; the challenge is to cross the field quickly without running into fire.

Two movement speeds and escalating cell arrangements make the task more than a simple collection exercise. Completing a grid swiftly awards bonuses and can skip stages, rewarding players who optimize their routes. The result is an unusually elegant fusion of maze navigation, shooting-game pressure and score chasing.

games.title: Solar Quest
games.description:
Cinematronics' Solar Quest (1981) is a vector-display space shooter combining Asteroids-style movement with the gravitational danger of a sun at the center of the screen. The player rotates, thrusts, shoots and occasionally uses hyperspace to reposition while waves of hostile ships converge. The ship also carries limited nuclear weapons, which can be detonated after launch to destroy multiple enemies.

Destroyed alien ships leave survivors drifting toward the star. Players can collect them for rescue bonuses, but retrieving them means approaching the same lethal gravity well they are trying to avoid. This rescue-versus-survival tension is its defining twist. Solar Quest was later adapted for the Vectrex, where its crisp vector artwork found a natural home.

games.title: Soldam
games.description:
Jaleco's Soldam (1992) is a falling-block puzzle game that mixes color matching with rules reminiscent of Reversi. Each piece is a rotatable square of four fruit symbols, and placing matching colors across a horizontal, vertical or diagonal line can recolor the pieces between them. A row vanishes only when all of its fruits are the same color, so clearing the board depends on setting up transformations rather than merely grouping identical pieces.

Special letter pieces can spell EXTRA and summon a fairy to clear fruit, while obstructing pieces and enemy interference complicate long stages. A rising level of pressure steadily reduces room for mistakes. Its distinctive flip-and-clear mechanic makes it an inventive alternative to the more familiar Tetris and Puyo Puyo formulas.

games.title: Sol Divide - The Sword Of Darkness
games.description:
Sol Divide: The Sword of Darkness (1997) is one of Psikyo's most unusual arcade shooters, set in a fantasy world of warriors, monsters and sorcery rather than aircraft and machinery. Three playable heroes, Kashon, Vorg and Tyora, have differing strengths in ranged attacks, close combat and magic. Although the scenery scrolls horizontally and the characters can fly, merely shooting from a distance is often ineffective: players must approach enemies, execute melee combinations and collect spells to survive the large bosses.

Magic consumes a limited resource that can be replenished through fighting and pickups, and different spells provide tactical advantages against the game's supernatural enemies. The hybrid of shoot-'em-up positioning, brawler-style attacks and light role-playing progression earned Sol Divide a reputation as a divisive but singular entry in Psikyo's catalog.

games.title: Solitary Fighter
games.description:
Solitary Fighter (1991) is Taito's follow-up to Violence Fight, a gritty arena-fighting game that precedes the standardized one-on-one fighting-game formula of the 1990s. Players choose from six brawlers competing in an underground tournament, moving freely around enclosed arenas rather than remaining on a single horizontal fighting line. Punch, kick and jump buttons can be combined for stronger attacks, while objects on the stage can be picked up and thrown.

The rough-and-tumble fights are deliberately chaotic: opponents may receive help from knife-wielding bystanders and improvised weapons can change a match. Its unusual free-movement combat places it closer to Pit-Fighter and street-brawling games than to Street Fighter II.

games.title: Solomon's Key
games.description:
Solomon's Key (1986) is Tecmo's demanding combination of puzzle-solving and platform action. Players control the young wizard Dana across a sequence of single-screen chambers, collecting a key and reaching the exit before time runs out. Dana's wand can create or destroy stone blocks, turning each level into a puzzle of building stairs, opening passages, protecting against monsters and occasionally trapping enemies. Jumping, timing and careful spatial planning matter as much as knowing the correct solution.

The chambers conceal valuable treasures, magical items and optional secrets, while an apparently straightforward route can hide several possible solutions. Constant enemy pressure and a strict timer make experimentation risky. A celebrated cult favorite with numerous home conversions, Solomon's Key stands apart for making the environment itself the player's main tool rather than relying on conventional weapons.

games.title: Solvalou
games.description:
Namco's Solvalou (1991) revisits the universe of Xevious from a striking first-person perspective. Instead of looking down on the legendary Solvalou fighter, players see the planet's surface and approaching enemies directly ahead. The craft follows a forward-moving route while the player steers to dodge incoming fire, uses guns against aerial threats and drops bombs on installations on the ground. Familiar Xevious enemy designs and the imposing Andor Genesis mothership link the action to the original.

Built for Namco's advanced 3D arcade hardware, the game replaces Xevious's crisp overhead patterns with sweeping landscapes and a sense of flight. It remains a fascinating experiment in transforming one of the most recognizable vertically scrolling shooters into an immersive rail-shooting experience.

games.title: SegaSonic The Hedgehog
games.description:
SegaSonic the Hedgehog (1993) is an isometric arcade action game starring Sonic, Mighty the Armadillo and Ray the Flying Squirrel. Captured by Dr. Eggman on his dangerous island, the three must escape a succession of collapsing bridges, runaway machinery, spikes and other traps. Rather than using the normal Sonic jump-and-spin controls, the cabinet supplies a trackball for each player, making fast rolling movement and precise changes of direction the central skills. Up to three people can tackle the stages together.

The viewpoint and physical control invite comparisons with Marble Madness, but the frantic pace, collecting rings and familiar Sonic characters give it a distinct identity. Developed for Sega's System 32 hardware, it remained an arcade exclusive for decades and is particularly notable for introducing Mighty and Ray, who later resurfaced in other Sonic games.

games.title: Sonic The Hedgehog 2

variants.title: Sonic The Hedgehog 2 (bootleg of Mega Drive version)

games.description: This arcade version of Sonic the Hedgehog 2 is an unauthorized conversion of Sega's Mega Drive/Genesis platform game rather than a purpose-built SegaSonic title. Sonic races through scrolling zones, collects rings, frees trapped animals and fights Dr. Robotnik's machines, with high-speed loops and the original console-style stage layouts providing the main attractions. The bootleg board alters the experience for coin operation: Sonic's on-screen life icon becomes a coin counter, the original two-player option is absent and DIP switches can adjust the timer and number of lives. It is an interesting example of console software being repackaged for an unofficial arcade market.

games.title: Sonic The Hedgehog 3

variants.title: Sonic The Hedgehog 3 (bootleg of Mega Drive version)

games.description: Sonic the Hedgehog 3 in this set is an unauthorized arcade-board adaptation of Sega's Mega Drive/Genesis platform game, not an official arcade sequel. Its underlying adventure follows Sonic and Tails through the fast-moving stages of Angel Island, with Knuckles appearing as a rival, rings to collect and Dr. Robotnik's machines to defeat. The bootleg retains the recognizable console gameplay but provides operator-adjustable settings, including a time limit and number of lives, to suit coin-operated play. Because the precise conversion differs from an official Sega arcade release, its significance is chiefly as a rare example of a pirate arcade port of a major home-console hit.

games.title: Sonic Boom
games.description: Sega's Sonic Boom (1987) is a vertically scrolling combat-aircraft shooter unrelated to the much later Sonic the Hedgehog franchise of the same name. Players pilot a jet through six stages of enemy fighters, ground defenses, vehicles and large bosses, collecting weapon improvements from defeated formations. Additional escort craft strengthen the aircraft's firepower, while limited bombs offer a way to survive especially crowded attacks. Its mix of modern military targets, steady vertical scrolling and escalating boss encounters places it among Sega's late-1980s arcade shooting games.

games.title: Waku Waku Sonic Patrol Car
games.description: Waku Waku Sonic Patrol Car (1991) is a Sega kiddie-ride attraction built around a short interactive Sonic the Hedgehog driving adventure. Here Sonic is a police officer taking his patrol car through city traffic when Dr. Eggman begins causing trouble. Players steer with a real wheel, use the siren and make Sonic jump from the car to confront Eggman, while the cabinet rocks in response to the onscreen action. Unlike Sega's standard video arcade games, it was designed as a brief, approachable ride for younger visitors. Its combination of physical motion, steering-wheel play and early Sonic character animation makes it an unusual artifact of the mascot's initial popularity.

games.title: Aero Fighters 2 / Sonic Wings 2
games.description:
Aero Fighters 2, also called Sonic Wings 2 (1994), brings Video System's fast vertically scrolling shooting series to the Neo Geo MVS. Players choose pilots from several countries, each with a distinctive fighter, personality and weapon spread, then fly through international landscapes filled with aircraft, tanks, ships and oversized bosses. Collecting power-ups strengthens the guns, while a limited stock of bombs clears the screen or inflicts heavy damage.

Two players can fight cooperatively, and the colorful selection of eccentric pilots and surprising bosses lends personality to an otherwise demanding traditional shooter. The Neo Geo's large sprites and detailed scenery helped make it a memorable continuation of the series beyond its original dedicated arcade hardware.

games.title: Aero Fighters 3 / Sonic Wings 3
games.description:
Aero Fighters 3 / Sonic Wings 3 is Video System's 1995 Neo Geo sequel, retaining the series' rapid vertically scrolling combat but exchanging modern jets for an eccentric selection of historic and unusual aircraft. Players select from ten standard craft and can unlock two secret pilots, each bringing distinctive weapons, bombs and behavior. Battles travel between countries and increasingly bizarre locations, with changing routes and enemies that make repeated runs less predictable.

Weapon power-ups, limited bombs and two-player cooperation remain central, but the new aircraft lineup and wonderfully strange characters push the series' offbeat humor further. The combination of compact stages, sudden boss appearances and branching progression gives this entry its own flavor rather than merely repeating Aero Fighters 2.

games.title: Son of Phoenix
games.description: Son of Phoenix is an unauthorized version of the 1985 shooter Repulse, also encountered under the title '99: The Last War. Players move a defending spacecraft along the bottom of a fixed screen, shooting successive waves of robotic invaders and descending alien craft. Later waves end in confrontations with large enemy ships, and a limited-energy shield can absorb attacks at the cost of its charge. Helpful craft occasionally deliver weapon or other bonuses. The Son of Phoenix name describes the bootleg identity of the arcade set; the underlying game design belongs to Sega and Kyugo's Repulse lineage rather than to a separate Phoenix sequel.

games.title: Son Son
games.description:
SonSon is Capcom's 1984 side-scrolling action game inspired by the Chinese classic Journey to the West. One or two players guide SonSon and TonTon across six stacked lanes while the scenery continually scrolls toward them. The characters can switch levels, slow their forward motion and shoot approaching foes, while collecting food and bonuses along the route to rescue their friends. Enemies, gaps and barriers force quick lane decisions instead of the usual unrestricted jumping of platform games.

Its compact, almost board-game-like six-tier layout and whimsical figures from Asian folklore give it an unmistakable early-Capcom appearance. Although simple in structure, SonSon combines shooting, rhythmic movement and cooperative positioning in ways that anticipate some of the studio's later arcade action games.

games.title: SOS
games.description: SOS is an early monochrome fixed shooter from Namco, released around 1979-1980. Players move a fighter plane left and right along the bottom of the screen, firing single shots at diving enemy aircraft. Its distinguishing feature is the recurring SOS alarm: an arrow directs the player toward one side of the screen, and reaching that position before the signal ends awards points and removes some of the attackers that have slipped past. The combination of shooting accuracy and urgent side-to-side movement makes SOS an interesting variation on the basic Space Invaders-era formula. It belongs to Namco's early black-and-white arcade output before its larger color-screen successes.

games.title: Sotsugyo Shousho
games.description: Sotsugyo Shousho, meaning 'Graduation Certificate', is a Japanese collection of competitive arcade minigames developed by Mitchell and published by Atlus in November 1995. Up to two players take part using eight-way joysticks and three action buttons, with play organized around short individual challenges rather than one continuous adventure. The game runs on Data East-derived 68000 graphics hardware with a HuC6280 sound CPU, a comparatively sophisticated setup for a niche minigame release. A Korean edition appeared in 1996 under the name Jor-eop Jeungmyeongseo, preserving the unusual school-themed title in translation.

games.title: Soul Calibur
games.description:
Soulcalibur (1998) is Namco's landmark 3D weapon-fighting sequel to Soul Edge, originally released for System 12 arcade hardware. A roster of warriors drawn from different cultures pursues the cursed sword Soul Edge, fighting with swords, staffs, nunchaku and other distinct weapons. Each combatant has a large set of attacks, throws and defensive options, with victories depending on spacing, timing and knowing when to counterattack or sidestep.

Its breakthrough is the Eight-Way Run system: players can move smoothly in all directions around their opponents, turning the third dimension into an integral part of a fight rather than an occasional evasive maneuver. Guard impacts, ring-outs and character-specific weapon reach reward thoughtful use of the arena as well as fast reactions. The combination made Soulcalibur one of the most influential 3D fighting games of its generation.

The 1999 Dreamcast conversion became especially celebrated for improving on the arcade visuals and adding extensive home features, helping the title reach a much wider audience. The arcade original remains important as the game that established the Soulcalibur identity and refined the weapon-based fighting formula begun by Soul Edge.

games.title: Soul Edge Ver. II
games.description:
Soul Edge Ver. II (1996) is Namco's revised arcade edition of the original Soul Edge, the weapon-based 3D fighting game that launched the series later known as Soulcalibur. Set against a mythic sixteenth-century backdrop, it follows warriors such as Mitsurugi, Taki and Sophitia as they search for a powerful, malevolent sword. Unlike contemporary bare-handed fighters, each character's weapon shapes their reach, timing, offensive options and defensive strategy. Fighters can sidestep, block, strike and attempt to knock an opponent out of the ring.

The Ver. II update expands the playable roster and refines the presentation of the earlier arcade release, with additional selectable characters and improved graphics. Soul Edge's blend of cinematic character stories, dramatic weapon clashes and three-dimensional positioning laid the foundations for Namco's much more famous Soulcalibur sequel.

games.title: Space Beam
games.description: Irem's Space Beam (1979) is an early fixed-screen shooting duel in which the player's cannon faces a computer-controlled adversary across a field of alien ships. Players move left and right along the bottom of the screen and fire upward through the intervening targets, gradually clearing away the cover that protects both sides. The opposing cannon shoots back from above, and laser range depends on a visible fuel supply. Destroying targets creates opportunities but also exposes the player to increasingly direct fire. This tactical struggle over the remaining cover gives Space Beam a different rhythm from formation-based invader shooters.

games.title: Space Duel
games.description:
Atari's Space Duel (1982) builds on Asteroids and Asteroids Deluxe with a vivid color vector display and an unusually strong emphasis on two-player action. Players rotate, thrust and fire as they destroy geometric targets, hostile craft and mines in a wraparound space arena. Instead of ordinary rocks, the screen fills with colored shapes that break into smaller, more dangerous fragments.

The key innovation is a choice of competitive or cooperative play. In team mode, two independent ships are connected by a flexible filament, making movement and survival a joint challenge; other options allow players to control different craft or space-station configurations. Its striking vector graphics, alternative play modes and distinctive linked-ship concept make Space Duel a notable late example of Atari's original vector-shooter lineage.

games.title: Space Cruiser
games.description: Space Cruiser (1981) is a Taito space shooter organized as a sequence of changing encounters rather than a single repeating alien formation. Piloting the title ship, players defend Earth from UFOs and missiles, navigate asteroid threats and confront space stations, enemy bases and other increasingly dangerous targets. The craft moves from side to side while firing upward, with each sector introducing a new situation on the way to the alien home world. A mission map links the encounters and gives the game a sense of progression. One of the earliest games on Taito's SJ System, Space Cruiser shows the company experimenting with a more structured space campaign.

games.title: Space Invaders DX (US) v2.1
games.description:
Space Invaders DX (1994) is Taito's anniversary-minded reworking of its legendary 1978 shooter. Its normal mode recreates the original alien formations, descending rows and protective bases in several display styles, including monochrome, simulated colored overlays and full-color presentation. Rather than reinventing the core game, it lets players revisit its different historical visual appearances on newer hardware.

Two extra modes expand the formula. Versus mode divides the screen for simultaneous competition, with special colored invaders causing beneficial or troublesome effects when shot. Parody mode replaces the familiar invaders with humorous imagery and references to other Taito games. The combination makes DX both a preservation-minded celebration of Space Invaders and a playful multiplayer remix.

games.title: Space Firebird
games.description:
Nintendo's Space Firebird (1980) is an energetic fixed-screen shooter that replaces marching alien ranks with deadly, swooping space birds. Players steer a spacecraft along the bottom of the display, firing at gulls, eagles and stronger emperor birds that dive in elaborate looping formations. Different bird types take different numbers of hits, and their attacks can scatter shots in several directions. A special warp maneuver provides an escape from particularly dangerous swoops.

Its unpredictable-looking formations and multi-hit enemies distinguished it from Nintendo's earlier Space Fever and other straightforward Space Invaders derivatives. Released during Nintendo's first years in the dedicated video arcade business, Space Firebird helped establish the company's growing taste for distinctive enemy behavior and colorful action.

games.title: Space Fever
games.description:
Space Fever (1979) is Nintendo's early answer to the enormous success of Taito's Space Invaders. Players operate a laser cannon at the bottom of the screen, shooting descending ranks of aliens while sheltering behind eroding barriers. The enemies become increasingly threatening as their numbers thin, and an occasional high-value flying craft offers bonus points.

Nintendo altered the familiar formula through three selectable variations. One splits the invading force into two independently moving groups; another adds new rows as the attack develops; the third plays closer to the original Space Invaders. Its unusual alien artwork, altered sound and multiple modes reveal a company still experimenting with the fixed-shooter format before Donkey Kong transformed its arcade fortunes.

games.title: Space Fortress
games.description: Space Fortress (1981) is a Century Electronics shooter built around three different space-defense scenarios. In one, the player rotates and thrusts a ship through an Asteroids-like battle against flashing alien objects. Another places a fortress at the center of the playfield, requiring protection against attackers and dangerous tractor beams. A third switches to a more conventional bottom-of-screen defense against diving enemies. The abrupt changes in viewpoint and objectives make the game an unusual mixture of the major shooting styles of its era, preserved as part of Century's interchangeable CVS arcade system.

games.title: Space Guerrilla
games.description: Space Guerrilla is a 1979 arcade defense shooter by Omori Electric in which players control an anti-aircraft vehicle protecting a city from an alien attack. Hostile spacecraft sweep overhead in waves, firing on the ground and sometimes diving directly toward the defending position. The player aims and fires to destroy the invaders before they overwhelm the city's defenses. The changes in enemy flight patterns and sudden kamikaze assaults provide the central difficulty. An early Japanese fixed shooter, it combines the basic invader-defense premise with a more active sense of an aerial raid.

games.title: Space Gun
games.description:
Taito's Space Gun (1990) is a violent science-fiction light-gun shooter that sends one or two rescue operatives into a space installation overrun by grotesque aliens. The action advances automatically from room to room as players aim cabinet-mounted guns at attacking creatures, machinery and hazards, while trying to rescue surviving human hostages. A variety of special ammunition, including explosive, freezing and incendiary effects, offers alternatives to ordinary shots.

The game's dark, monster-filled environments draw openly on the atmosphere of cinematic space horror. Its large sprites, dramatic enemy transformations and cooperative shooting made it a memorable early-1990s counterpart to Taito's more colorful Operation Wolf style of gun games.

games.title: Space Intruder
games.description: Space Intruder (1980) is Shoei's variation on the Space Invaders formula. The player moves a cannon or tank horizontally at the bottom of the screen, firing at rows of aliens moving back and forth as they descend toward Earth. Flying saucers offer extra points, while successful shooting gradually changes the pace and density of the attack. Closely resembling the Space Invaders Part II generation of shooters, it illustrates how quickly Taito's original design was adapted by other Japanese arcade manufacturers.

games.title: Space Launcher
games.description: Nintendo's Space Launcher (1979) is an early space-action game that anticipates the lane-crossing structure later made famous by Frogger. Players guide an unarmed mining vessel upward through moving hazards and hostile craft toward valuable lunar docking stations. After collecting ore or reaching a high-scoring dock, the craft must travel safely back toward Earth, repeating the trip to clear the remaining objectives. Ships encountered at close range can trigger a protective shield, but enemy fire remains dangerous. Its emphasis on navigating traffic and making return journeys is quite different from the stationary shooting games that dominated the period.

games.title: Space Odyssey
games.description: Space Odyssey (1981) is Sega's multidirectional scrolling science-fiction shooter, licensed to Gremlin for American distribution. Players direct a continuously moving spacecraft through a series of seven-sector rounds, destroying attacking UFOs with shots and bombs while avoiding indestructible meteors. Some sectors scroll horizontally and others vertically, requiring adaptation to different attack patterns.
