Speed and distance traveled contribute to end-of-round bonuses, while black holes temporarily disable the craft and force risky escapes. The stage-to-stage variety and emphasis on flying fast distinguish it from the more static shooters of its time.

games.title: Space Seeker
games.description:
Taito's Space Seeker (1981) is a hybrid of shooter and light strategy game built around a map of a planet under invasion. Players select which threatened location to defend, then enter one of two different action sequences. Enemy bases lead to side-scrolling battles with both forward shots and bombs; enemy fleets become first-person shooting encounters in which targets rush toward the player's guns.

Because hostile positions can attack friendly bases even while the player is deciding where to fly, the order of engagement matters. The alternating viewpoints and tactical map make Space Seeker an unusually ambitious design for the early 1980s, predating many more familiar games that combined strategic selection with arcade shooting.

games.title: Space Trek
games.description: Space Trek (1980) is a Sega VIC Dual shooter in which the player's ship moves freely around a single-screen battlefield, fighting successive groups of aliens. The craft can fire in combat and deploy a temporary force barrier that repels collisions but uses a limited energy supply and restricts movement. Different rounds shift the action from battles against blue alien formations in space to attacks near an enemy base and other scenarios. The barrier adds a useful defensive tradeoff to the straightforward shooting, while the changing stages give this relatively obscure early Sega game more variety than its simple graphics suggest.

games.title: Space Wars
games.description:
Space Wars (1977) is Cinematronics' pioneering vector-display adaptation of the space-combat concept from the early computer game Spacewar! Two players pilot small spacecraft in a shared arena, rotating, thrusting and firing at one another while navigating the gravity of a central sun and, in some settings, a drifting meteor. Hyperspace can save a ship from danger but relocates it unpredictably. The first pilot to win the required number of engagements claims the match.

Several selectable conditions alter gravity and other hazards, allowing the players to choose very different duels. Its crisp black-and-white vector graphics, distinctive five-button controls and direct competitive format make it one of the defining arcade bridges between university computer games and commercial coin-operated video games.

games.title: Space Zap
games.description:
Space Zap (1980) is a Bally/Midway fixed shooter built around an elegantly simple defensive challenge. A laser base sits in the center of the screen while mines, alien ships and orbiting attackers approach from above, below, left and right. Four direction buttons instantly point the gun toward a threat, and a fifth fires, making quick recognition and hand coordination essential.

The base cannot flee, so every approaching object must be destroyed before it arrives. As the attack accelerates, survival becomes a frantic sequence of directional choices rather than conventional joystick movement. Its distinctive control layout and minimal presentation make Space Zap a particularly pure early arcade test of reflexes.

games.title: Space Fury
games.description:
Space Fury (1981) is Sega/Gremlin's colorful vector-display shoot-'em-up, notable for an alien commander who taunts the player with synthesized speech between rounds. The player controls a ship using separate rotate, thrust and fire buttons, destroying hostile spacecraft before they can assemble into more dangerous formations. At the beginning of several rounds, one of a set of weapon modules can be chosen, producing different firing patterns such as spread shots, rear fire or concentrated forward fire.

The combination of speech, expressive enemy portraits and tactical weapon selection gives the game a character beyond its simple arena combat. Running on Sega's G80 vector hardware, Space Fury stands alongside the period's other attempts to develop Asteroids-style action into a more theatrical arcade experience.

games.title: Space Walk
games.description: Midway's Space Walk (1978) is a black-and-white action game that recasts the bouncing-figure mechanic of Circus or Clowns as a contest between astronauts in space. A figure leaps from a platform and must be caught or redirected using a movable springboard, with the goal of striking targets overhead. Well-aimed launches can transform the astronaut into a controllable rocket for extra points. One player can face the machine, or two players can compete from opposing sides. The spatial timing and seesaw-like platform action place Space Walk among the inventive paddle-game variations of the late 1970s.

games.title: Super Pang
games.description:
Super Pang, known in North America as Super Buster Bros. (1990), is Mitchell's sequel to the popular Pang / Buster Bros. Players move along compact, single-screen stages, launching vertical harpoons at bouncing balloons. A hit splits a large balloon into two smaller ones, and the resulting fragments must be cleared without allowing any to touch the characters. Ladders, platforms and changing hazards complicate the familiar task, while different weapons and bonuses help control crowded screens.

Tour mode takes one or two players through an extended journey of stages, while Panic mode concentrates on a relentless succession of bubbles and the challenge of survival. With its intuitive rules, high-risk positioning and cooperative play, Super Pang refines one of the most distinctive arcade action-puzzle formulas of its era.

games.title: Spark Man
games.description: Spark Man (1989) is a side-scrolling action game from Korean developer SunA Electronics. Players control an armored, robot-like hero moving through stages filled with gunmen and other hostile creatures, attacking with a basic weapon as well as stronger, limited-ammunition pickups. The hero can also strike at close range with a kick, while stage-ending confrontations demand surviving and clearing groups of enemies. Its gritty futuristic look and run-and-gun progression invite comparison with RoboCop. The game spans nine levels and represents the lesser-known Korean arcade action titles of the late 1980s.

games.title: Sparkz
games.description: Sparkz is an unreleased 1992 Atari Games puzzle prototype combining ideas from pipe-connecting games and falling-block puzzles. Players arrange pieces to form a continuous electrical path from one side of the playfield to the other. Completing a connection sends a spark across the board, contributing to the construction of a cartoon monster in a scientist's laboratory. The puzzle depends on planning routes before available space becomes crowded, rather than simply eliminating identical blocks. Preserved as a prototype, Sparkz offers a glimpse at an inventive, experimentally themed arcade puzzle game that never received a regular commercial release.

games.title: Spatter
games.description:
Spatter (1984), called Sanrin San-Chan in Japan, is a charming Sega maze-chase game starring a small child riding a tricycle. The player pedals around elevated paths collecting flowers while dodging toy vehicles, robots and other pursuers. Many walkways have two lanes separated by a springy barrier; bouncing against it can push enemies aside or create a way past an approaching obstacle.

Between the overhead mazes, bonus scenes change to a side-on platform view, where the hero tries to reach a girl and deliver the flowers while avoiding hazards. The bright toy-like setting, unusual tricycle protagonist and alternating screen styles give Spatter a personality quite different from the period's more conventional maze games.

games.title: Super Pinball Action
games.description: Super Pinball Action (1991) is Tecmo's digital pinball sequel to Tehkan's earlier Pinball Action. Rather than merely presenting one abstract table, it supplies four differently themed boards, including carnival, border, monster and adult-oriented imagery, each with its own targets and scoring objectives. The player uses flipper-style controls to keep the ball alive, activate features and rack up points. Its colorful art and detailed board mechanisms aim to evoke a physical pinball machine while taking advantage of video-game animation and changing displays. The game belongs to the early period of arcade video pinball, when traditional table play was being reinterpreted with increasingly elaborate graphics.

games.title: Space Encounters
games.description:
Space Encounters (1980) is Midway's first-person space shooter built around a moving trench or canyon reminiscent of the Death Star attack in Star Wars. The player pilots an assault craft down the corridor, aiming at approaching ships and avoiding fire, canyon walls and the drifting debris left by destroyed enemies. The view's rushing floor and walls create a striking pseudo-3D impression on an otherwise simple monochrome display.

A countdown adds another unusual twist: while time remains, collisions spin the craft out of the channel and cost valuable seconds; once that protection expires, an impact ends the run. The combination of simulated forward motion, mounting debris and a finite survival window gives Space Encounters a compelling early example of arcade cockpit-style action.

games.title: Space Force
games.description: Space Force (1980) is a Venture Line space shooter closely modeled on Atari's Asteroids. Players navigate a spacecraft through a field of large rocks, shooting them into smaller fragments while evading the resulting debris and the attacks of roaming UFOs. The wraparound arena, thrust-based movement and steadily multiplying hazards keep the challenge focused on controlling the ship while clearing the screen. It is a straightforward example of how the success of Asteroids inspired similar vector-style and raster space shooters from other arcade manufacturers.

games.title: Special Forces II
games.description: Special Forces II is a 1985 side-scrolling action game in the vein of Kung-Fu Master, built around an anti-terrorist commando theme. The player advances through hostile territory while fighting armed enemies in close-quarters encounters. Its emphasis on constant forward movement and repeated combat links it to the mid-1980s wave of martial-arts and rescue-themed arcade games. Documentation on this particular edition is limited, so its specific stages and differences from the earlier Special Forces are not securely established.

games.title: Space Invaders '95: The Attack Of Lunar Loonies

variants.title: Space Invaders '95: The Attack Of Lunar Loonies (Ver 2.5O 1995/06/14)
Space Invaders '95: The Attack Of Lunar Loonies (Ver 2.5A 1995/06/14)

games.description:
Space Invaders '95: The Attack of Lunar Loonies is Taito's exuberant 1995 reinterpretation of its seminal fixed shooter. Rather than controlling a conventional laser cannon, players choose among whimsical heroes, including a dog riding in a refuse bin and a girl piloting a robot, and shoot down equally absurd formations of pigs, chickens and other cartoon invaders. The familiar horizontal movement and descending enemy ranks remain, but colorful attacks, bosses and character-specific effects refresh the formula.

Running on Taito's F3 hardware, its bright anime-inspired graphics and jokes make it a genuine 'cute-'em-up' rather than a straight remake. It demonstrates how Space Invaders could be transformed into a playful character game while retaining its instantly recognizable underlying mechanics.

games.title: Space King 2
games.description: Space King 2 (1979) is Leijac's follow-up to Space King and a close relative of Taito's Space Invaders Part II. Players move a laser cannon across the bottom of the screen, firing upward at lines of invaders that move horizontally and slowly advance toward the ground. The attraction is the familiar battle of attrition against a formation that becomes increasingly dangerous as it thins. Its modest alterations and direct imitation of the Space Invaders formula illustrate the intense competition among manufacturers during the first years of the fixed-shooter boom.

games.title: Space Laser
games.description: Space Laser (1980) is Taito's release of a fixed-screen shooting duel closely related to Irem's Space Beam and Leijac's Space War. The player operates a laser cannon beneath a field of moving ships that can serve as both targets and cover, attempting to hit the opposing weapon at the top of the screen before it fires back. As the intermediate ships disappear, both sides become more exposed. The game's straightforward left-right movement and shooting place emphasis on aim, timing and exploiting gaps through the shifting defensive screen.

games.title: Special Forces
games.description: Special Forces, also titled Special Forces: Kung-Fu Commando, is a 1985 action game developed by Senko Industries. Players guide a heavily armed commando on a side-scrolling mission to fight terrorists and rescue hostages from a captured embassy. Gunfire is used against armed attackers and incoming grenades, while other sections emphasize close-range, martial-arts combat. The combination of shooting and hand-to-hand fighting recalls Irem's Kung-Fu Master but exchanges its martial-arts tournament atmosphere for an exaggerated contemporary rescue mission.

games.title: Space Lords
games.description:
Space Lords (1992) is Atari Games' ambitious first-person space-combat game, built around linked multiplayer cabinets and cooperative crews. One player pilots a spacecraft, controlling movement, weapons and evasive hyperspace jumps, while a second can act as gunner. The ship's energy can be redistributed among speed, agility, firepower and shields, giving encounters a strategic dimension beyond simply shooting faster.

A large mission sequence pits crews against different alien factions, while multiplayer configurations allow rival ships and teams to compete. The special cabinet controls, linked-machine possibilities and separate pilot and gunner roles made Space Lords an unusual attempt to bring the social appeal of multiplayer simulations into the arcade.

games.title: Space Position
games.description: Space Position (1986) is a futuristic overhead racing game developed by Nasco and published by Sega. Cars race through a stylized future city, with the camera usually keeping competing vehicles together in one view. When the racers become too widely separated, the screen splits to follow them independently, an unusual solution to the problem of displaying head-to-head racing. Players must negotiate traffic and hazards while managing fuel, using wheelies and jumps to avoid obstacles. Its changing camera arrangement and science-fiction setting distinguish it from conventional circuit racers of the mid-1980s.

games.title: Speed Ball
games.description:
Speed Ball: Contest at Neonworld is an unreleased Williams arcade sports prototype dated 1985, not the similarly named pinball game made by Tecfri. It stages a futuristic ball sport that has been described in contemporary retrospective coverage as resembling robot soccer. Players try to direct play and score against an opposing side, using an unusual combination of a trackball, joystick and action button. Its fast, arena-based competition was an attempt to turn an invented future sport into an accessible arcade contest.

The prototype runs on Williams' 6809-era hardware and supports two-player competition. Surviving ROMs were added to emulation years after its cancellation, allowing players to experience a design that never received an ordinary arcade release. Its distinctive input arrangement and neon-futurist presentation set it apart from both conventional soccer games and the other Speed Ball titles of the period.

games.title: Speed Coin
games.description: Speed Coin is an unreleased 1984 Stern Electronics arcade prototype based on a simple physical puzzle: guide a rolling coin down a tilting platform and drop it through the hole at the bottom without breaking it. Players shift the platform's angle with the controls, trying to finish as rapidly as possible. Completion times determine score multipliers, so success depends not only on reaching the goal but on doing so smoothly and quickly. The unusual premise and short competitive runs give the game the feel of a mechanical skill toy translated into video form.

games.title: Super Dodge Ball
games.description:
Super Dodge Ball (1987), known in Japan as Nekketsu Kōkō Dodgeball Bu, is Technos Japan's energetic team sports game featuring the hot-blooded schoolboy characters later associated with the Kunio-kun series. Players command a team whose members occupy both their own half of the court and the sidelines behind their opponents. Throwing the ball, catching it and knocking rival players out are the basic objectives, but different characters have powerful special shots that turn an ordinary gym contest into comic mayhem.

The Japanese version follows Nekketsu High School against domestic and overseas rivals, while the international release changes team identities and national matchups. Fast passes, positioning and the timing of special throws make the competition surprisingly tactical. The game's exaggerated animation and competitive two-player play helped establish the distinctive character of Technos's subsequent sports spin-offs.

games.title: Speak & Rescue
games.description: Speak & Rescue is Sun Electronics' 1980 space shooter, closely related to Stratovox and Space Echo. Players operate a defending craft at the bottom of the screen, shooting at invading alien formations while trying to prevent the attackers from carrying away people on the ground. The rescue objective gives purpose to otherwise familiar fixed-screen shooting. The game is particularly associated with early synthesized speech: human cries for help and other voice effects add urgency to the abductions. Regional and bootleg versions appeared under different titles, preserving an early example of arcade developers using speech to make a simple shooting scenario more dramatic.

games.title: Spectrum 2000
games.description: Spectrum 2000 (2000) is a Korean vertically scrolling shooter by Yona Tech, released late in the arcade shoot-'em-up era. Players choose from five fighter jets with differing attributes and weapons, then battle successive waves of airborne and ground-based opposition. Collecting power-ups strengthens or transforms the selected jet, creating opportunities to build a more formidable weapon configuration during a run. It supports both single-player and cooperative shooting, favoring the familiar arcade combination of rapid enemy formations, constant dodging and heavily armed aircraft.

games.title: Spectar
games.description:
Spectar (1980) is Exidy's sequel to Targ, turning its distinctive car-combat maze into a more elaborate collection-and-survival challenge. The player drives the Whummel through a grid of streets, shooting hostile Rammers and dangerous Spectars while navigating new obstacles that break up the once-regular layout. Glowing stars or gems scattered around the maze provide an alternative route to clearing a level, but enemies continually emerge from spawning pods.

The result blends the chase-and-shoot format of Targ with an early form of Pac-Man-like collecting. Brighter scenery, more varied maze structures and the ever-present risk of being cornered make Spectar a notable step in the development of early maze-action games.

games.title: Speed Attack!
games.description: Speed Attack! is a 1984 Japanese competitive playing-card game by Seta Kikaku, not the sports or shooting game its name might suggest. The screen arranges ordinary playing cards into separate groups around a central playing area and keeps a visible score, while up to two players use dedicated button banks to make their selections. It runs on a compact Z80-based board identified as CB-0. The game's unusual multiplexed key-matrix input circuitry was a particular challenge when its controls were reconstructed for emulation.

games.title: Speed Ball
games.description: Speed Ball (1987) is a video pinball game from Spanish manufacturer Tecfri. Players operate a simulated pinball table, attempting to keep the ball in play and accumulate points by striking targets with flippers rather than steering a character through an arena. The overhead table presentation reflects the arcade industry's interest in reproducing traditional amusement machines on video hardware. This title is distinct from Williams' unrelated, unreleased 1985 prototype Speed Ball: Contest at Neonworld.

games.title: Speed Freak
games.description:
Speed Freak (1979) is Vectorbeam's pioneering monochrome vector racing game, one of the earliest arcade attempts to portray driving from a first-person, behind-the-wheel viewpoint. Players race down a winding road, passing traffic and roadside hazards including trees, hitchhikers, cows and cacti. The challenge is to cover as much distance as possible at high speed before the timer expires, steering around obstacles and recovering from inevitable crashes.

Collisions can produce dramatic effects, including a shattered windshield or a car exploding into flying parts, but they do not immediately end the run. The angular wireframe road and rapid forward motion were impressive for the period. Speed Freak is a revealing precursor to later cockpit racers, emphasizing the sensation of speed over detailed race rules.

games.title: Speed Racer
games.description: Speed Racer (1995) is Namco's arcade racing adaptation of the Japanese anime known internationally by the same name. Players drive Speed's famous Mach 5 against rival cars, aiming to finish the course while weaving through traffic and avoiding hazards. The vehicle's distinctive gadgets help overcome obstacles, bringing a recognizable element of the cartoon to the racing action. Unlike the unrelated console game Rad Racer, this is a purpose-built Namco arcade title using advanced 3D hardware. Its anime license and gadget-equipped car give it a different personality from the more conventional racing simulators of the period.

games.title: Speed Spin
games.description: Speed Spin (1994) is a table-tennis arcade game that focuses on fast, short rallies rather than complex simulation. Players use joystick-based controls to position their paddles and return the ball across the table, trying to outplay opponents through placement and timing. Two modes provide different goals: a Tour progression and a World Championship competition. The game's bright presentation and immediate sports action made it an unusual alternative to the football, basketball and racing games that dominated mid-1990s arcade sports cabinets.

games.title: Speed Up
games.description:
Gaelco's Speed Up (1996) is a polygonal arcade racing game built around elimination rather than simply crossing the finish line first. Up to eight drivers can compete through linked cabinets, choosing from cars with different performance characteristics and courses rated Beginner, Advanced or Expert. After each lap, the last-place driver is removed; the contest continues until only the winner remains.

The elimination rule changes racing tactics by making every intermediate lap potentially decisive. In single-player mode, computer-controlled rivals fill the field, while linked cabinets turn the game into a larger arcade competition. Its colorful 3D presentation and fast handling reflect the influence of Ridge Racer, but its knockout format gives Speed Up a distinctive identity.

games.title: Super Eagle Shot
games.description: Super Eagle Shot (1994) is a golf arcade game developed by Seta, using joystick and three-button controls to bring course play to coin-operated hardware. Players compete over a sequence of holes, attempting to finish with the lowest stroke count while managing the familiar demands of direction and shot selection. The game supports multiplayer competition and even provides an operator option for an extra hole on par play. Running on Seta's specialized ST0016-based hardware, it is a comparatively obscure example of the company's mid-1990s sports catalog.

games.title: Spelunker II
games.description:
Spelunker II: 23 no Kagi (1986) is Irem's arcade sequel to Spelunker, sending treasure hunters into another sprawling underground world filled with dangerous creatures, secret passages and traps. The game retains the original's fragile protagonist, careful jumps, rope climbing and the hunt for keys, while adding more elaborate environments and exploration. Players traverse caves in multiple directions, using equipment and explosives to clear obstacles and find routes to the next area.

Its Japanese subtitle refers to '23 Keys', emphasizing the puzzle-like search through the subterranean levels. With an expanded adventure structure and a different fantasy setting, it is more than a straightforward set of replacement stages, while preserving the deliberate, hazard-conscious movement associated with the series.

games.title: Spelunker
games.description:
Spelunker (1985) is Irem's arcade adaptation of the influential cave-exploration platform game. Players guide a fragile adventurer ever deeper into underground passages, seeking keys, treasure and a route toward a legendary subterranean destination. The caves are packed with ladders, ropes, lifts, mine carts, bats, ghosts and lethal environmental hazards. An air supply imposes time pressure, and even small errors in movement can bring the expedition to an abrupt end.

Bombs, flares and other equipment help negotiate the labyrinth, but exploration requires careful management of routes and resources. The arcade version's scrolling caverns and demanding controls give it a distinctive identity beside the better-known home editions. Its reputation for punishing falls and precision jumping made Spelunker a long-lived cult favorite, especially in Japan.

games.title: Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo
games.description:
Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo (1996) is Capcom's ingenious competitive falling-gem puzzle game featuring miniature versions of characters from Street Fighter and Darkstalkers. Pairs of colored gems drop into each player's well. Matching colors alone will not clear them: a corresponding Crash Gem must touch the group to break it. Building large rectangular Power Gems and triggering chains sends Counter Gems into an opponent's field, turning careful preparation into a sudden offensive attack.

Every character has a distinctive counter-gem drop pattern, so matchups influence strategy even though the core controls remain simple. Between exchanges, animated Capcom fighters act out miniature battles that mirror the players' progress. Beneath the playful presentation lies a remarkably deep duel of timing, board management and calculated risk.

Originally built for CPS-2 arcade hardware, Puzzle Fighter became a competitive cult classic and inspired numerous console versions and later reinterpretations. Its smart balance of accessibility and advanced gem-building tactics makes it one of Capcom's most enduring departures from traditional fighting games.

games.title: Super Puzzle Fighter 2 X'

modifications.description: Backports the X' mode character drop-pattern rebalances and gem-attack adjustments from Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo HD Remix to the CPS-2 arcade version.

games.description: Super Puzzle Fighter 2 X' (X Prime) is a 2021 balance hack of Capcom's 1996 CPS-2 falling-gem puzzle game Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo created by Kaito Sinclaire. It recreates the rebalanced X' mode from Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo HD Remix on original arcade hardware, adjusting attack drop patterns and character balance.

games.title: Spider
games.description: Spider (1994) is a Spanish Qix-style territory-capture puzzle game with an adult-themed photographic presentation. The player moves a cursor across a playfield and draws lines to enclose areas, progressively revealing an image while trying to avoid losing the cursor. Unlike straightforward Qix variants, each drawing action is limited by a web-power supply, so claiming large regions requires careful planning. Bonus rounds switch the objective to quickly encircling numbers. The alternative Buena Vision edition omits the nudity, reflecting the different presentations available for this obscure arcade release.

games.title: Spiders
games.description: Spiders (1981) is a Sigma fixed-screen shooter in which the player's spacecraft fights an onslaught of crawling and descending spiders. The ship moves horizontally along the bottom of the screen and fires upward, but there is more to watch than the enemies themselves: the spiders weave an expanding web that must also be shot away. If the web reaches the player's position or too many attackers escape, the game becomes increasingly dangerous. Its moving web structure gives an otherwise familiar early-1980s shooting format a distinct and memorable threat.

games.title: Spider-Man: The Videogame
games.description:
Spider-Man: The Videogame (1991) is Sega's colorful four-player superhero beat-'em-up, featuring Spider-Man, Black Cat, Hawkeye and Namor the Sub-Mariner. The heroes join forces against a collection of Marvel villains, including Venom, Doctor Octopus, the Green Goblin and Doctor Doom. Each character brings different attacks and special abilities, allowing cooperative teams to divide enemies and handle crowded fights.

Its most memorable design choice is the changing scale of the action. Many sections begin as large-sprite, street-level brawls, then zoom outward into smaller-sprite platform stages where the heroes explore larger environments and climb or jump through hazards. Built for Sega System 32 hardware, the game uses that transition to offer more variety than a conventional side-scrolling beat-'em-up. Its comic-book presentation and four-hero cooperation have made it a favorite among Marvel arcade collectors.

games.title: Spikeout Final Edition
games.description:
Spikeout Final Edition (1999) is Sega's expanded revision of the 3D arcade brawler Spikeout: Digital Battle Online. Players choose street fighters and battle through a city infested with rival gangs, using punches, throws, charged attacks and teamwork to defeat crowds and bosses. Linked Sega Model 3 cabinets allow as many as four people to cooperate, and the players can select routes through a sprawling network of urban areas.

Final Edition expands the original game from three main stages to five, introduces new routes and bonus missions, adjusts character balance and offers a special three-minute Rush mode. These changes make it more than a cosmetic update: the larger campaign and additional cooperative opportunities became the preferred version for many dedicated Spikeout players.

games.title: Spikeout
games.description:
Spikeout: Digital Battle Online (1998) is Sega's ambitious 3D beat-'em-up for the Model 3 arcade system. Rather than fighting through a narrow side-scrolling corridor, players explore a fully modeled city, clearing gangs from streets, shops and other detailed environments. Combos, grapples, jumping throws and powerful charged attacks offer multiple ways to handle enemies. Each of the game's three main stages contains a network of areas and branching routes, rewarding repeat exploration.

Its standout innovation is multiplayer through linked cabinets, allowing up to four people to join a cooperative fight and use coordinated tactics against larger groups and bosses. The emphasis on open environments and team-based action gave Spikeout a loyal following despite its limited distribution. Sega later expanded the concept with Spikeout Final Edition.

games.title: Spiker
games.description: Spiker (1986) is Bally/Sente's arcade volleyball game, featuring one-on-one matches played with a joystick-based control scheme. The player positions a character on the court, returns the ball over the net and tries to outmaneuver the opposing athlete through the timing and placement of shots. Its fluid character animation was a notable part of the presentation. Available for both single-player competition and two-player matches, Spiker adds an athletic sports title to the eclectic library of Bally/Sente's SAC-I arcade hardware.

games.title: Spinal Breakers
games.description:
Spinal Breakers (1990) is a post-apocalyptic shooting game from Video System that follows the conventions of Cabal-style gallery shooters. Players control time-traveling soldiers, moving their characters in the foreground while aiming a separate gun cursor into the scenery to destroy waves of enemies. The heroes can roll to evade shots and use limited grenades to clear a crowded screen, while the primary machine gun has unlimited ammunition.

Its story involves artificial humanoids called Hildroids who revolt and spread their influence through different historical periods. The campaign moves through settings ranging from wartime Europe and ancient civilizations to feudal Japan, mixing grotesque enemies with unusual scenery and boss fights. The combination of foreground dodging and independent aiming makes it a distinctive two-player alternative to more conventional scrolling shooters.

games.title: Spin Master / Miracle Adventure
games.description:
Spin Master, also known as Miracle Adventure (1993), is Data East's lively two-player platform action game for the Neo Geo. Treasure hunters Johnny and Tom set out to rescue their friend Mary from the Mad Doctor while searching for fragments of a valuable treasure map. Players leap across scrolling stages, attack with yo-yos or other weapons found in chests, and use slides and special moves to deal with crowds of comical enemies.

Enormous cartoon bosses and constantly changing scenery give the adventure a theatrical look, with lively animations that take good advantage of the Neo Geo's sprite capabilities. Its quick movement, weapon variety and cooperative play make it one of the system's most approachable action-platform games.

games.title: Splash!
games.description:
Splash! (1992) is an adult-oriented arcade action-puzzle game developed by OMK Software and published by Gaelco. The player maneuvers a paintbrush-like cursor across a single-screen board, wiping away colored covering to reveal an illustration underneath. Progress is measured by the percentage uncovered, but moving bubbles threaten the cursor and collisions cost lives. A limited supply of shots can destroy bubbles, forcing players to decide when to clear a hazard and when to dodge it.

The combination of territory-revealing action, time pressure and limited defensive ammunition distinguishes Splash! from standard Qix-style line-drawing games. Regional editions, including Painted Lady, use different presentations of its mature imagery.

games.title: Splat!
games.description: Splat! (1982) is an unusual arcade food-fight game in which players choose a cartoon competitor and attempt to hit an opponent with falling food. A central dispenser feeds objects onto conveyor belts; as the food drops, contestants must catch it before throwing it across the playfield. Successful direct hits temporarily incapacitate an opponent, and replacement heads effectively supply additional chances to continue the fight. Its competitive, slapstick premise and emphasis on catching and throwing moving objects set it apart from the spaceship and maze games common in arcades of the period.

games.title: Splatter House
games.description:
Splatterhouse (1988) is Namco's landmark horror-themed side-scrolling beat-'em-up. A young man named Rick awakens in the sinister West Mansion wearing a mysterious Terror Mask that grants him unnatural strength. His girlfriend Jennifer has disappeared, and the only way to find her is to fight through grotesque creatures, lethal traps and monstrous bosses lurking in the mansion. Rick punches, kicks and uses improvised weapons such as planks, cleavers and shotguns, although careless fighting can be brutally punished.

The game stands out for its cinematic horror imagery, disturbing creature designs and relentless atmosphere, drawing heavily on slasher films and supernatural cinema. Detailed animations and dramatic sound effects made its violence unusually graphic for a late-1980s arcade game. Despite the straightforward combat system, careful positioning and learning enemy patterns are essential to survival.

Splatterhouse became a cult classic, inspired multiple sequels and remains one of Namco's most recognizable departures from its brighter arcade catalog. Its masked protagonist, grisly settings and blending of action with horror helped establish an aesthetic later explored by many other games.

games.title: Splendor Blast
games.description: Splendor Blast (1985) is Alpha Denshi's unusual blend of futuristic racing and shooting. Players pilot a spacecraft around pseudo-3D interplanetary courses, weaving past rival vehicles and sharp bends while collecting energy and ammunition. Some sections emphasize pure high-speed navigation, while others introduce hostile creatures and targets that can be destroyed with the craft's weapons. A fuel gauge acts as both a survival resource and a limit on how long the craft can remain in the race. Its fusion of arcade driving, science-fiction obstacles and combat predates many better-known vehicle-combat hybrids.

games.title: Splendor Blast II
games.description: Splendor Blast II (1985) is a rare Alpha Denshi arcade game blending pseudo-3D space racing with combat. Players steer a futuristic spacecraft through curving interplanetary routes, avoiding other vehicles and obstacles while using weapons against targets that appear during the journey. Fuel and energy pickups are important for maintaining the run, making collisions costly beyond the immediate loss of speed. Like the closely related Splendor Blast, it combines the perspective and forward motion of an early racing game with the hazards and shooting of a space-action title. Documentation of precise changes between the two releases is limited.

games.title: Super Punch-Out!!
games.description:
Super Punch-Out!! (1984) is Nintendo's expanded arcade boxing game, following the original Punch-Out!! with a new lineup of extravagant opponents. Players view their own green-haired boxer from behind, his body rendered as a transparent wireframe so the opponent's punches remain visible. The action centers on reading tells, choosing high or low attacks, blocking and dodging, then exploiting the brief moments when a rival is vulnerable. The challengers include Bear Hugger, Dragon Chan, Vodka Drunkenski, Great Tiger and Super Macho Man, each with a recognizable style and special attacks.

A new evasive maneuver allows the boxer to duck, essential against some of the more spectacular attacks, including Dragon Chan's leaping kick. Like its predecessor, the arcade cabinet uses two monitors to display the fight and supporting information. Its exaggerated opponents, pattern-based bouts and distinctive viewpoint helped make Punch-Out!! one of Nintendo's most recognizable sports-action series.

games.title: Super Cross II
games.description: Super Cross II (1986) is a Japanese motocross arcade racer from GM Shoji. One or two players compete on off-road motorcycle courses, steering through the track and attempting to finish ahead of rivals. Its emphasis on motocross rather than road racing gives it a different setting from the car-oriented arcade racers of the period. It is a relatively obscure mid-1980s coin-op sports title, preserved in multiple Japanese program sets; detailed documentation of its individual tracks and scoring systems is limited.

games.title: Springer
games.description: Springer (1982) is Orca's whimsical platform game starring a hopping rabbit who ascends through a sky filled with clouds. Players bounce upward from platform to platform, collecting eggs and other bonus objects on the way to the sun at the top of the screen. Eggs can hatch into dragons, which the rabbit can kick for points, while a decreasing bonus counter encourages rapid climbing. Each successful ascent leads to another, more challenging layout. Its cheerful character, vertical progression and simple jump-and-collect action distinguish it from the period's darker shooters.

games.title: Sprint 1
games.description:
Atari's Sprint 1 (1978) is a single-player overhead racing game descended from Sprint 2. Players steer a small car around a series of compact tracks, trying to complete as many laps as possible against a timer while avoiding computer-driven vehicles and other hazards. A real steering wheel, accelerator and four-speed gear selector give the simple top-down graphics a convincing physical driving interface.

The computer-controlled cars follow the racing course but can interfere with the player, and collisions cause temporary loss of control. At the end of the run, performance is rated according to the driver's score, with sufficiently strong results earning extra time. Sprint 1 retains the immediate mechanical appeal of Atari's early driving cabinets while packaging it for solo play.

games.title: Sprint 4
games.description:
Atari's Sprint 4 (1977) expanded the top-down racing of Sprint 2 into a four-driver contest. Each participant had a steering wheel, accelerator and four-position gear shifter, while computer-controlled traffic filled any empty places. Drivers raced for distance and points on a selection of ten circuits, competing against both the timer and one another. At the end, the machine rated each performance as "Granny", "Rookie" or "Pro".

Its large, four-sided cocktail-style cabinet made multiplayer competition the attraction, with drivers gathered around the same display. The game's simple overhead graphics concealed a surprisingly demanding combination of steering, shifting and collision avoidance. Surviving boards also document revisions with slightly different car-sprite sizes, a small but distinctive detail in Atari's early racing history.

games.title: Sprint 8
games.description:
Sprint 8 pushed Atari's 1977 overhead racing series to an unusual extreme: eight people could race at once around the same circuit. The giant cocktail-style cabinet accommodated two driving stations on each side, complete with individual steering wheels, four-position gear shifters, accelerator pedals and, unlike the earlier Sprint games, brakes. Computer drivers occupied unused positions, keeping the track crowded even with fewer than eight human racers.

The four selectable courses were more elaborate than those in Sprint 4, and the higher-resolution display helped distinguish the chaos of eight simultaneously moving cars. Like its predecessors, Sprint 8 rewarded distance covered during a timed race and rated drivers from "Granny" to "Pro". A special board variation offered tag-and-chase play, making this exceptionally large cabinet a landmark of early local multiplayer arcade design.

games.title: S.P.Y. - Special Project Y

variants.title: S.P.Y. - Special Project Y (World ver. N)
S.P.Y. - Special Project Y (US ver. M)

games.description:
Konami's S.P.Y.: Special Project Y (1989) is a James Bond-flavored action game in which one or two agents infiltrate an island stronghold to foil a villain's nuclear plot. Rather than committing to a single format, the adventure shifts between an over-the-shoulder jetpack attack, side-scrolling hand-to-hand combat and forward-moving shooting sequences. One moment the agents are dodging gliders and a large helicopter above the ocean; the next they are fighting guards through the enemy base.

An eight-way joystick and two action buttons cover the game's changing situations, with discarded firearms, weapon upgrades and screen-clearing explosives helping the agents survive. Its cinematic spy-film opening and succession of different perspectives give S.P.Y. an unusual identity among Konami's late-1980s action games.

games.title: Spy Hunter
games.description:
Bally Midway's Spy Hunter (1983) turned the fantasy of a gadget-equipped secret-agent car into one of the defining arcade driving shooters. From a vertically scrolling overhead view, players guide the G-6155 Interceptor through traffic, destroying hostile vehicles while sparing civilian cars and motorcycles. Enemies range from armored Road Lords and tire-slashing Switch Blades to shotgun-carrying Enforcers and a bomb-dropping helicopter. Hitting civilians temporarily suspends scoring, so reckless fire has a cost.

The unforgettable weapon-supply system lets the player drive up a moving van's ramp and emerge with oil slicks, smoke screens or surface-to-air missiles. Certain routes pass through boathouses that transform the Interceptor into a speedboat, changing the combat without breaking the chase. The physical cabinet featured an aircraft-style steering yoke with weapon buttons, a gear lever, an accelerator pedal and illuminated indicators for the available equipment.

Designed by George Gomez, Spy Hunter was originally conceived with a James Bond connection, but instead used the infectious Peter Gunn theme after licensing plans changed. Its weapon van, transforming vehicle and distinctive controls became arcade icons. A major American commercial hit, it inspired numerous home conversions and a long-running franchise.

games.title: Spy Hunter 2
games.description:
Spy Hunter II (1987) brought Bally Midway's armed road battles back to the arcade, but made a dramatic change in perspective. Instead of the original game's overhead scrolling view, the action unfolds from behind each player's car, with a shared monitor divided into two driving displays. A second driver can join cooperatively, and each station has its own steering controls, accelerator and gear shifter.

Players use machine guns and acquire additional weapons from supply trucks while fending off motorcycles, explosive attacks and airborne enemies. An escort objective involving a courier provides bonuses for reaching the weapon vans safely, while radar displays help locate threats. The follow-up retained the Peter Gunn music but never matched its predecessor's popularity; its unusual split-screen presentation and different handling remain the defining features of this much less common sequel.

games.title: Faster, Harder, More Challenging Q*bert
games.description:
Faster, Harder, More Challenging Q*bert is Mylstar's unreleased 1983 experiment with a tougher follow-up to the enormously popular Q*bert. Warren Davis revisited the familiar isometric pyramid, where Q*bert must hop across blocks to change their colors while avoiding Coily, dangerous balls and other pursuers. The four-way joystick is mounted diagonally, so each direction corresponds to a hop along the pyramid.

This prototype does more than accelerate the original action. Blocks can shift position, a new Coily-like adversary called Q*bertha joins the pursuit, and bonus rounds appear after selected levels. Although the project never entered normal arcade production, its preserved ROM makes it a particularly valuable glimpse of a canceled sequel and the design ideas being considered after Q*bert's breakout success.

games.title: Super Qix
games.description:
Taito's Super Qix (1987) updates the territory-capturing puzzle action of Qix. Players move a marker along safe boundaries and draw lines across a dangerous playfield; closing off an area claims it and gradually reveals a concealed picture. Enemy movement makes every excursion away from the border a calculated risk, and a sufficient percentage of the screen must be captured to advance through the game's sixteen rounds.

Unlike the spare original, Super Qix adds rewards that appear after sections are enclosed, including speed boosts, shields, temporary enemy freezes and score bonuses. Letter pickups can produce additional rewards, and claiming unusually large portions of the board earns extra points. The result combines Qix's tense risk-versus-reward drawing mechanic with a more colorful, power-up-driven arcade structure.

games.title: Squash
games.description: Gaelco's Squash (1992) translates the enclosed-court racket sport into a lively two-player arcade contest. Viewed on a side-on court, opponents pursue a rapidly rebounding ball and try to place shots their rival cannot return. An eight-way joystick and two buttons provide movement and shot control, creating quick rallies in which anticipation and positioning matter more than elaborate simulation. Its unusually specific sporting subject makes it a distinctive entry in Gaelco's early-1990s arcade catalog.

games.title: Space Raider
games.description: Universal's Space Raider (1982) is a vertically scrolling space shooter in which the player battles waves of alien craft from a top-down viewpoint. A four-way joystick moves the ship while a single fire button handles its weapons. With constant movement through a hostile space battlefield, the game follows the more mobile shooter tradition associated with titles such as Juno First rather than the static formations of the original Space Invaders.

games.title: Sega Rally 2
games.description:
Sega Rally 2 (1998) brought Sega's influential rally-driving series to the Model 3 arcade hardware, with greatly expanded polygonal scenery, more detailed cars and an emphasis on sliding through corners at speed. Drivers tackle different surfaces and weather conditions, adapting their braking and steering to gravel, dirt and tarmac. Cars inspired by actual rally machinery, together with force-feedback steering, pedals and a handbrake on suitable cabinets, made the experience feel more physical than a conventional arcade racer.

The sequel built upon Sega Rally Championship's celebrated drift-friendly handling and time-extended course progression. Its deluxe and linked twin cabinets added a social, competitive dimension, while the impressive Model 3 presentation made Sega Rally 2 a late-1990s showcase for Sega's dedicated racing hardware.

games.title: Sega Rally 2 DX
games.description:
Sega Rally 2 DX is the deluxe-cabinet version of Sega's Model 3 rally racer. It retains the original game's high-speed course competition, mixed driving surfaces and precision cornering, but was designed for a large sit-down installation with a roughly 50-inch projection display. The deluxe controls included force-feedback steering and a separate handbrake, encouraging dramatic slides around tight hairpins.

This is a cabinet and software variation rather than a distinct sequel. Early DX releases are documented with small visual and vehicle-behavior differences from later twin-cabinet software, and deluxe installations could be linked for multiplayer racing. Its enormous projected image was a major part of the arcade experience that distinguished this edition from the standard upright game.

games.title: Super Real Darwin
games.description:
Data East's Super Real Darwin (1987) is a vertically scrolling shoot-'em-up built around an unusual biological evolution system. As the player's small spacecraft collects upgrades, it mutates into progressively different shapes rather than simply receiving a bigger gun. The changing body of the craft is both a visual spectacle and a way of communicating its current firepower and capabilities.

A sequel to Darwin 4078, the game sends its evolving fighter through alien forces and large bosses in a science-fiction conflict involving the life energy known as Evol. The combination of experimental-looking enemy design, transformation-based progression and conventional precision shooting sets Super Real Darwin apart from more straightforward military-themed shooters of its era.

games.title: S.R.D. Mission
games.description:
S.R.D. Mission (1986) is a vertically scrolling rescue-and-shoot game in which a spacecraft attacks an alien-occupied space station while evacuating stranded personnel. Players use separate attacks against aerial enemies and ground installations, blasting through enemy formations as the scenery moves steadily downward. People in suits appear amid the fighting and must be collected by flying over them rather than shot.

Some rescued personnel provide weapon improvements, creating a reason to search the screen carefully even under heavy fire. Its mixture of air-to-air shooting, ground bombing and noncombatant rescue gives this comparatively obscure shooter a tactical concern beyond simply destroying everything in sight. A bootleg version was also circulated as F-X.

games.title: Sunset Riders

variants.title: Sunset Riders (scrambled bootleg of Mega Drive version)

games.description:
This edition of Sunset Riders is an unofficial arcade conversion of the Sega Mega Drive/Genesis game, not a revision of Konami's original arcade board. It preserves the Wild West bounty-hunting theme, with gunmen pursuing outlaws through side-scrolling stages, shooting enemies, jumping over hazards and confronting wanted bosses. The arcade hardware runs a scrambled adaptation of the console software rather than the original Konami arcade program.

The distinction matters because the Mega Drive adaptation has its own presentation and content choices; players should not expect a perfect reproduction of the four-player coin-op original. In AdvanceMAME, this set is most interesting as an example of a pirate cabinet built from commercially released home-console code.

games.title: Super Real Mahjong Part 2
games.description:
Super Real Mahjong Part II (1987) helped define Seta's Japanese series of anime-styled arcade mahjong games. Players face a computer-controlled opponent in traditional Japanese mahjong, choosing discards and calls to assemble winning hands. Success advances a sequence of animated adult-themed rewards, while lost hands can reverse that progress.

This entry is notable for its single featured opponent, its series-defining animated presentation and its unforgiving structure: the player must preserve enough in-game funds to continue, with no normal continue option. Beneath the fan-service presentation is a tile-based game requiring familiarity with riichi mahjong rather than a simple matching puzzle.

games.title: Super Real Mahjong Part 3
games.description:
Seta's Super Real Mahjong Part III (1988) continues the series' Japanese mahjong play and elaborate hand-drawn animated rewards. Players first compete against Kasumi Serizawa and later face her older sister Miki, winning hands to advance through each character's sequences and losing ground when the opponent wins. Its tile selection and hand-building follow conventional Japanese mahjong rules.

Part III introduced continues to the series and was the last installment to display animated representations of the player's hands. Those changes make it a useful midpoint between the relatively simple presentation of Part II and the larger, more cinematic productions that followed.

games.title: Super Real Mahjong PIV

variants.title: Super Real Mahjong PIV (Japan, older set)

games.description:
Super Real Mahjong PIV (1993) is Seta's fourth major anime-themed mahjong arcade release. It presents one-on-one Japanese mahjong matches against a series of female characters, with successful hands unlocking animated scenes and losses delaying progress. The emphasis remains on constructing legal winning hands and managing the tactical decisions of actual mahjong, rather than matching loose tiles as in Shanghai.

Compared with earlier entries, Part IV greatly expands the character animation and story presentation, while abandoning the on-screen animated hands previously seen during play. Its larger roster and more developed visual sequences reflect the series' move toward lavish multimedia presentation during the 1990s.

games.title: Super Real Mahjong P5
games.description:
Super Real Mahjong P5 (1994) carries Seta's Japanese mahjong series into another elaborate set of animated character encounters. Players challenge three opponents, advancing through their individual sequences by winning conventional mahjong hands. Defeats can undo progress, and running out of playing funds ends the session.

The appeal of this installment lies in the contrast between methodical tile strategy and its increasingly polished anime-style animation. Its custom Seta-based audiovisual hardware also distinguishes it technically from the earliest games in the series.

games.title: Super Real Mahjong P6
games.description:
Super Real Mahjong P6 is Seta's mid-1990s continuation of its Japanese one-on-one mahjong series, featuring a new cast and increasingly elaborate anime-style interludes. Players must form valid winning hands, decide when to call or discard tiles, and progress through character encounters; the adult-themed presentation remains a reward for successful play rather than replacing the mahjong rules.

The game uses different hardware from Part V, combining a Motorola 68000 with Seta's NILE graphics and sound technology. That hardware shift makes it one of the series' more distinctive later arcade entries, both in its artwork and its preserved board design.

games.title: Super Real Mahjong P7
games.description:
Super Real Mahjong P7 (1997) is a late entry in Seta's long-running series of Japanese mahjong games with elaborate animated storytelling. Players choose among three character-centered story routes and play successive one-on-one mahjong matches. The opponents' order and accompanying scenes vary with the selected route, offering narrative variety without changing the fundamentals of hand-building and tile strategy.

Unlike several earlier installments, Part 7 avoids special gameplay items that would give the player artificial advantages. Its unusually substantial anime-style cutscenes and straightforward emphasis on mahjong make it one of the series' most presentation-heavy arcade releases.

games.title: Sunset Riders / Super Street Fighter II - The New Challengers

variants.title: Sunset Riders / Super Street Fighter II - The New Challengers (scrambled bootleg of Mega Drive versions)

games.description:
This unusual two-game pirate arcade board combines scrambled Mega Drive versions of Sunset Riders and Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers. It should not be mistaken for a Konami/Capcom collaboration or a pairing of their original arcade ROMs. Instead, commercially released console games were adapted to unauthorized coin-operated hardware.

Sunset Riders supplies side-scrolling Western bounty-hunting and gunfights, while Super Street Fighter II provides one-on-one martial-arts matches featuring the expanded roster of sixteen fighters. The set's historical interest lies in the way home-console software was repackaged for arcade use, with the compromises and technical peculiarities of such bootleg conversions.

games.title: The Speed Rumbler
games.description:
Capcom's The Speed Rumbler (1986) mixes driving and run-and-gun action in a dangerous high-speed rescue mission. Super Joe races through hostile territory in an armored car, shooting enemy vehicles and attempting to save prisoners held by the Zapper organization. The scrolling stages are packed with roadblocks, enemy gunfire and opportunities to switch between vehicle action and fighting on foot when the car is destroyed or abandoned.

Rescuing captives and collecting upgrades improves the chance of surviving six demanding stages. The game stands out among mid-1980s shooters because its forward-driving momentum and vehicle-versus-infantry situations make each encounter feel less predictable than a standard scrolling shoot-'em-up.

games.title: Silent Scope
games.description:
Konami's Silent Scope (1999 in arcades, with versions dated 2000) made the physical act of sniping its central attraction. The player uses a large mounted rifle to eliminate terrorists and protect hostages, but the cabinet's defining feature is its real optical-style scope: a small display within the sight shows a magnified view of the area being aimed at on the main monitor. Carefully lining up a distant target is therefore a physical task, not merely moving an on-screen cursor.

The story follows a sniper trying to rescue the kidnapped U.S. presidential family, with missions featuring rooftops, moving targets and tense hostage situations. Story, practice and timed play reward accuracy and quick recognition, while delays and misses give enemies opportunities to shoot back. Its distinctive dual-view rifle made Silent Scope one of the most memorable specialist light-gun experiences of its generation.

games.title: Silent Scope 2
games.description:
Silent Scope 2 (2000), also known as Dark Silhouette, Fatal Judgment or Innocent Sweeper depending on region, continues Konami's sniper-focused arcade series. Players once again aim a mounted rifle with a magnifying scope display, picking off distant enemies while trying to avoid collateral damage and survive retaliatory fire.

The sequel introduces two playable operatives, Jackal and Falcon, whose viewpoints offer different angles on the anti-terrorist storyline. Its emphasis remains on precision, identifying threats quickly and choosing the correct target under pressure, while the specialized cabinet retains the unusual hands-on sniper experience of the original Silent Scope.

games.title: Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers

variants.title: Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers (World 931005)
Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers (Asia 931005)
Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers (Asia 930914)
Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers (Hispanic 930911)
Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers (Japan 931005)
Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers (Japan 930911)
Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers (Japan 930910)
Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers (World 930911)
Super Street Fighter II: The Tournament Battle (World 931119)
Super Street Fighter II: The Tournament Battle (Asia 931005)
Super Street Fighter II: The Tournament Battle (Hispanic 931005)
Super Street Fighter II: The Tournament Battle (Japan 931005)
Super Street Fighter II: The Tournament Battle (Japan 930911)
Super Street Fighter II: The Tournament Battle (World 930911)
Super Street Fighter II: The Tournament Battle (USA 930911)
Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers (USA 930911)
Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers Super 2 (USA 930911)
Super Street Fighter II X: Grand Master Challenge (Japan 940311)
Super Street Fighter II X: Grand Master Challenge (Japan 940223)
Super Street Fighter II X: Grand Master Challenge (Japan 940223 rent version)

games.description:
Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers (1993) is Capcom's major revision of the Street Fighter II formula and the first game released on its CPS-II arcade platform. The roster expands to sixteen fighters with the arrival of Cammy, Fei Long, T. Hawk and Dee Jay, joining the twelve returning world warriors. One-on-one bouts still revolve around directional special moves, six-button attacks, spacing, throws and punishing an opponent's mistakes.

The new hardware brought redrawn character artwork, refreshed stages and voices, a new musical presentation and substantial balance adjustments. It also refined the distinct fighting styles that had made Street Fighter II a global competitive phenomenon. The pace differs from the preceding Hyper Fighting and the later Super Turbo, making The New Challengers a separate snapshot of the series' evolution.

Its combination of four additional characters and a new arcade system was a major moment in 1990s fighting-game history, and its roster became the foundation of subsequent Street Fighter II editions.

games.title: Super Street Fighter II - The New Challengers

variants.title: Super Street Fighter II - The New Challengers (scrambled bootleg of Mega Drive version)

games.description:
This Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers set is an unauthorized arcade conversion of the Japanese Sega Mega Drive version, rather than Capcom's original CPS-II release. The essential game is still a one-on-one fighter with sixteen selectable world warriors, six-button attacks and signature special moves, including the four newcomers Cammy, Fei Long, T. Hawk and Dee Jay.

The scrambled console-derived board is historically distinct from the CPS-II original, with the graphics, sound and software characteristics of a home conversion adapted for coin-operated play. For collectors and emulator users, it illustrates the unusual trade in bootleg arcade machines built around repurposed Mega Drive games.

games.title: See See Find Out
games.description:
Icarus's See See Find Out (1999) blends a spot-the-difference puzzle with the urgency of a whack-a-mole attraction. Two nearly identical pictures appear side by side, and players must recognize the mismatched details and strike their locations before the timer expires. The game can be attempted solo or as a competitive two-player challenge.

Its real appeal is the rapid transition from visual inspection to physical action: noticing a tiny change is only half the problem, because the player must mark it quickly and accurately. That combination makes this obscure Korean arcade title more active than a conventional picture-comparison puzzle.

games.title: Super Shanghai Dragon's Eye
games.description:
Super Shanghai Dragon's Eye (1992) is a tile-clearing puzzle game based on the Shanghai family of solitaire mahjong games. Players remove matching pairs of free tiles from intricate layered arrangements, planning several moves ahead to avoid blocking the pairs needed later. A board that seems simple at first can become unsolvable through careless removal choices.

The Dragon's Eye concept adds a distinctive variation to the familiar tile-matching formula, while selectable formations and animated tile sets give the game replay value. Unlike the Super Real Mahjong series, this is a spatial matching puzzle, not a simulated four-player mahjong contest.

games.title: Sharpshooter
games.description:
Sharpshooter (1998), by P & P Marketing, is a competitive light-gun target game built around a series of themed shooting challenges. The two players use separate red and blue optical guns, aiming at matching colored targets or other specified objects while avoiding incorrect hits. Challenges range across circus tricks, alien encounters, haunted castles, Western scenes and pirate settings before the final Ultimate Challenge.

Each short event demands fast recognition and precision: hitting appropriate targets raises a progress indicator, while mistakes cost ground. Rather than staging a continuous firefight, Sharpshooter turns quick, varied tests of observation and marksmanship into its core arcade competition.

games.title: Super Space Invaders '91

variants.title: Majestic Twelve - The Space Invaders Part IV (Japan)

games.description:
Taito's Super Space Invaders '91, also released as Majestic Twelve: The Space Invaders Part IV, is a colorful 1990 reinvention of its foundational fixed-screen shooter. The player moves a cannon along the bottom of the screen, destroying descending alien formations before they reach the defenses. The classic marching rhythm survives, but new enemy patterns, backgrounds and power-ups make the action much less austere.

Shooting the familiar flying saucer can now release equipment such as a protective shield, increased firing power or a temporary freeze effect. One of the most distinctive interruptions is the cattle-rescue bonus round, in which players shoot at saucers attempting to abduct cows. It combines deliberate nostalgia for the original Space Invaders with the playful excess of a much later arcade era.

games.title: Super Sidekicks / Tokuten Ou
games.description:
SNK's Super Sidekicks (1992), known in Japan as Tokuten Ou, brought accessible international soccer to the Neo Geo MVS. Players select one of twelve national teams and attempt to win the SNK Cup through group matches and knockout rounds. The action takes place on a scrolling pitch with large sprites, dramatic shots and simplified controls that favor quick passing, tackling and attacking over strict simulation.

The competing nations are differentiated principally by formations rather than intricate player statistics. With its brisk pace, animated celebrations and immediate two-player appeal, Super Sidekicks became the foundation of SNK's best-known arcade football series.

games.title: Super Sidekicks 2 - The World Championship / Tokuten Ou 2 - real fight football
games.description:
Super Sidekicks 2: The World Championship (1994), also called Tokuten Ou 2 in Japan, expands SNK's Neo Geo soccer series beyond the first game's compact national-team tournament. Larger international competition, improved animation and more varied match presentation give the sequel the atmosphere of a World Cup event.

Players still control their team through straightforward joystick-and-button football, building attacks, tackling and timing shots without complicated simulation commands. The greater visual detail and more dramatic treatment of decisive scoring opportunities helped establish the sequel as a favorite among fans of fast arcade soccer.

games.title: Super Sidekicks 3 - The Next Glory / Tokuten Ou 3 - eikoue no michi
games.description:
SNK's Super Sidekicks 3: The Next Glory (1995) broadens its Neo Geo football series to a large international field of national teams and several competition modes. Matches retain the immediate overhead-to-oblique arcade presentation of earlier installments, with rapid passing, tackling and spectacular close-range attacks.

A wider selection of teams and tournaments is the headline change, while enhanced animation and dynamic camera angles make the action more theatrical. It remains an accessible competitive soccer game rather than a detailed sports simulation, particularly suited to quick head-to-head arcade sessions.

games.title: Ultimate 11 - The SNK Football Championship / Tokuten Ou - Honoo no Libero, The
games.description:
Ultimate 11: The SNK Football Championship (1996), known in Japan as Tokuten Ou: Honoo no Libero, is the fourth major entry in SNK's Super Sidekicks line. It continues the series' colorful Neo Geo approach to international soccer with fast-running matches, national teams, accessible attacking controls and tournament competition.

Building on Super Sidekicks 3, Ultimate 11 emphasizes exaggerated movement, quick counterattacks and dramatic match presentation rather than realistic tactical depth. It is best understood as the final arcade-era refinement of the Super Sidekicks style, despite carrying a different English title.

games.title: Swinging Singles
games.description:
Swinging Singles (1983) is an obscure adult-oriented maze game from Entertainment Limited. The player steers a car through gridded streets, avoiding police and other obstacles while trying to locate a key and reach a destination within the maze. Success triggers a brief sexually suggestive reward sequence.

Its basic play is a route-finding and avoidance challenge rather than a driving simulation, with the risqué theme providing the novelty that distinguished it from more conventional maze games of the period.

games.title: Super Slam
games.description:
Super Slam (1993) is an arcade tennis game built for quick singles or doubles matches, with as many as four people taking part. Players move their athletes around the court and time racket swings to send the ball past an opponent, making shot placement and reaction speed the core skills.

The arcade format imposes a time limit on solo play against the computer, with additional credits required to continue after time expires. Its emphasis is on accessible competitive tennis rather than the detailed rules and pacing of a simulation.

games.title: S.S. Mission
games.description:
Comad's S.S. Mission (1992) is a vertically scrolling helicopter shooter in which the player attacks an alien invasion from above. The aircraft faces waves of hostile ships, ground defenses and large end-of-stage bosses while the screen moves steadily through each battlefield.

Helicopter-shaped pickups improve the main weapons, and a limited supply of screen-clearing bombs offers an emergency escape when enemy fire becomes overwhelming. With an eight-way joystick and two action buttons, S.S. Mission follows a direct, power-up-driven style of early-1990s shoot-'em-up.

games.title: Superior Soldiers
games.description:
Superior Soldiers (1993), also known as Perfect Soldiers in Japan, is Irem's futuristic one-on-one fighting game set after a catastrophe has transformed humanity. Seven selectable combatants use extraordinary powers, martial-arts techniques and special attacks in battles framed by a dark science-fiction storyline.

Its larger-than-life character designs and force-powered combat reflect the wave of experimental fighters that followed Street Fighter II. The North American Superior Soldiers release also has presentation differences from the Japanese Perfect Soldiers, making the two regional versions interesting to compare beyond their different titles.

games.title: SegaSonic Bros
games.description:
SegaSonic Bros. is an unreleased 1992 Sega puzzle-game prototype starring Sonic-themed characters rather than the familiar platforming hero's usual running adventures. Developed for Sega's System C2 arcade hardware, it experiments with a falling-block puzzle format intended for competitive coin-operated play.

Designed by Fukio Mitsuji, known for Bubble Bobble and Puzzle Bobble, its falling pieces are groups of four colored, curled-up Sonic characters. Players rotate the clusters and try to surround a Sonic of one color with characters of another matching color to clear them, an unusual rule that demands more planning than ordinary color matching. The game failed its location tests and never reached commercial production; a surviving board later brought it back to public attention.

games.title: Syusse Oozumou
games.description:
Syusse Oozumou (1984) is a Japanese arcade sumo wrestling game centered on the pursuit of professional success. Players guide a wrestler through bouts against progressively stronger opponents, trying to push rivals out of the circular ring or force them to touch the ground.

The encounters revolve around positioning, pressure and the timing of pushes and throws. Its subject matter is unusual in early arcade sports games, presenting the traditional progression toward sumo's highest ranks as a compact series of competitive matches.

games.title: Space Attack / Head On
games.description:
Space Attack / Head On is a late-1970s Sega/Gremlin dual-game arcade release pairing two quite different early arcade designs. Space Attack is a fixed-screen alien shooter inspired by Space Invaders, with the player defending the bottom of the screen against descending enemies and a bonus saucer after a wave is cleared.

Head On instead places a car in a top-down circuit maze where the aim is to collect dots while avoiding an oncoming rival vehicle. Offering both modes in one cabinet illustrates an early arcade approach to providing variety before multi-game systems became commonplace.

games.title: Space Attack
games.description:
Sega's Space Attack (1979) is an early fixed-screen shooter built on the VIC Dual arcade platform and closely modeled on the Space Invaders formula. A movable gun at the bottom of the screen fires into ranks of alien ships, with timing and careful positioning needed as the formation approaches.

A distinctive bonus sequence follows a cleared alien wave, when a saucer travels downward and can be shot for an extra reward. Its similarity to Sega's Alpha Fighter places it among the many closely related reinterpretations of Taito's breakthrough shooter produced during the original invasion-game boom.

games.title: Super Speed Race
games.description:
Taito's Super Speed Race (1979) is an early overhead-view driving game with a vertically scrolling roadway. Players steer a racing car through traffic on a largely straight course, using a physical steering wheel, accelerator and gearshift while trying to maintain speed without colliding with other vehicles.

Colorful roadside scenery provides motion and context, while a separate speedometer and high-score display were part of the original cabinet's appeal. The game belongs to Taito's long-running Speed Race lineage, which helped establish the basic visual language of top-down arcade motoring.

games.title: Scramble Spirits
games.description:
Sega's Scramble Spirits (1988) is a vertically scrolling military shooter in which a propeller-driven fighter battles enemy aircraft, ships and ground installations. The main plane has separate attacks for aerial and ground targets, making players choose their shots as successive layers of danger pass beneath them.

A central mechanic is recruiting up to two companion fighters. These escorts can be assigned to support aerial combat or attack low-altitude targets, giving the player some control over the shape of the formation and its firepower. The game's large sprites, dramatic zooming effects and detailed music make it a distinctive showcase of Sega's late-1980s arcade technology.

games.title: Super Sprint
games.description:
Super Sprint (1986) revived Atari's overhead racing tradition with colorful tracks, faster action and up to three competitors around a single monitor. Each participant uses a steering wheel and accelerator to race small cars around circuits that fit entirely on screen. Early layouts are straightforward, but later tracks introduce narrow bridges, obstacles and increasingly treacherous corners.

Collectible wrenches add an important layer of progression. After gathering enough, drivers can upgrade their cars' acceleration, traction or top speed, making races about more than merely surviving the next turn. This combination of compact races, physical steering wheels and persistent improvements made Super Sprint a standout multiplayer arcade racer.

Released during Atari Games' mid-1980s resurgence, it proved that the simple top-down formula of the original Sprint series could still draw crowds when supplemented with modern presentation and rewarding progression.

games.title: Sunset Riders
games.description:
Konami's Sunset Riders (1991) is a lavish Wild West run-and-gun game that sends four bounty hunters after a succession of notorious outlaws. Steve and Billy fight with revolvers, while Bob and Cormano use longer firearms. Players move, jump and fire in eight directions through saloons, frontier towns, railway scenes and horseback chases, with wanted posters introducing the villains awaiting at the end of each stage.

Gun upgrades let players fire rapidly or carry a second weapon, while cash bonuses and hidden supplies reward exploration. The action is full of theatrical interruptions, including gunfights across moving trains, stampeding animals and colorful boss introductions. Depending on the cabinet, two or four players can fight side by side, a major part of its appeal.

The game's cartoon presentation, comic dialogue and energetic soundtrack turned the Western setting into a distinctive counterpart to Konami's contemporary action hits such as Contra. It remains one of the company's most recognizable cooperative arcade shooters.

games.title: Super Speed Race Junior
games.description:
Taito's Super Speed Race Junior (1985) is a late entry in its long-running series of vertically scrolling road games.
