The player steers a red car through city streets while avoiding other traffic, staying on the road and responding to crossings along the route. Pedestrians can pass over zebra crossings, and a train may occupy a level crossing, turning the simple racing course into a test of observation and timing.

The overhead perspective and steering-wheel-based controls connect it directly to the Speed Race tradition, but the added road hazards give this Japanese release a livelier, more urban character than its earliest predecessors.

games.title: Steep Slope Sliders
games.description:
Steep Slope Sliders (1998) is a colorful snowboarding game developed by Cave for Sega's ST-V-derived arcade hardware. Players select a rider, descend courses in settings such as Japan, Italy and Canada, and attempt either fast times or impressive trick scores. Beyond conventional downhill runs, freestyle events include half-pipes and snowboarding parks.

Its trick-oriented controls, stylized boarders and the option to race against a recorded ghost distinguish it from a simple slalom game. The arcade release is also notable for using Sega Saturn-related technology in a sports title published by Capcom.

games.title: Super Stingray
games.description:
Alpha Denshi's Super Stingray (1986) is an overhead tank shooter with a somewhat tactical pace. Players maneuver a combat vehicle across hostile terrain, destroying enemy tanks and defenses on the way toward fortified enemy positions. The action combines dodging incoming fire with choosing safe routes through the battlefield.

Its tank-versus-fortress premise and deliberate movement separate it from the more common aircraft-based shooters of its era, even though it uses the familiar eight-way joystick and two-button arcade control scheme.

games.title: Space Stranger
games.description:
Space Stranger (1978), produced by Yachiyo Electronics, is a Japanese imitation of the emerging Space Invaders formula. Players move a cannon left and right beneath a formation of aliens, firing upward while avoiding enemy shots and trying to eliminate the attackers before they descend too far.

Built around Intel 8080-era hardware and a simple monochrome presentation, the game is historically interesting as part of the rapid wave of locally produced invasion shooters that followed Taito's original success.

games.title: Super Strike Bowling
games.description:
Super Strike Bowling (1990) is a specialized physical-control version of Strata Bowling. Instead of relying solely on a trackball, its conversion kit uses a miniature bowling lane and a real ball as the player's input, turning the bowling release into part of the arcade attraction.

The underlying game simulates ten-pin bowling, with the player trying to direct each roll toward the pins and build a score through strikes and spares. Its distinctive small-scale alley makes Super Strike noteworthy as a hybrid of video game and mechanical amusement equipment.

games.title: Space Stranger 2
games.description:
Space Stranger 2 (1979) is Yachiyo Electronics' follow-up to its early Space Invaders-style shooter. The basic challenge remains defending the bottom of a fixed screen with a horizontally moving gun, firing upward at advancing aliens while dodging their attacks.

This revision changes the arrangement of the enemy formation and introduces variations within the familiar invasion-game structure. Its historical interest lies in the rapid experimentation surrounding the enormous popularity of fixed-screen alien shooters in the late 1970s.

games.title: Space Tactics
games.description:
Sega's Space Tactics (1981) is a particularly unusual arcade defense shooter. Players protect a set of ground bases against alien formations seen in a forward-looking, pseudo-3D space view. A laser cannon and limited defensive shields help repel attackers, while the bases themselves can contribute powerful shots.

Its extraordinary cabinet is the real attraction: instead of merely moving a crosshair across a fixed picture, the machine physically moves its monitor assembly in response to the player's aiming controls. This mechanical movement creates the sensation of looking around a much larger battlefield. Few arcade shooters combine electronic action and moving hardware so directly, making Space Tactics a remarkable curiosity from the era before widespread polygonal 3D.

games.title: Stadium Hero
games.description: Data East's Stadium Hero (1988) is a Japanese arcade baseball game designed around quick contests rather than a lengthy statistical simulation. Players control batting, pitching and fielding with a joystick and action buttons, attempting to outscore the opposing side over successive innings. Cartoon-like athletic presentation and direct timing-based input make it approachable as a head-to-head sports game.

games.title: Stadium Hero 96
games.description:
Stadium Hero '96 (1996) revisits Data East's arcade baseball formula with updated character graphics and a more colorful, exaggerated presentation. One or two players can compete in baseball matches or pursue a championship in tournament play, alternating between pitching, batting and defensive action.

Running on Data East's MLC hardware, the game belongs to the mid-1990s tradition of fast, cartoon-styled arcade sports titles rather than a fully detailed baseball management simulation.

games.title: Stagger I
games.description:
Afega's Stagger I (1998) is a vertically scrolling shooter spread across twelve stages of attacks on enemy vehicles, installations and giant bosses. Players steer a fighter through hostile terrain, collecting improvements to increase the rate and strength of their fire. A chargeable special attack provides extra offensive power when the fire button is held, while larger bombs help clear emergencies.

Its unusual two-player distinction gives each side a different special-weapon effect, including large sweeping projectiles for one player and a bomber-like attack that can block shots for the other. The result is a hard-driving late-1990s shooter with a few mechanical quirks beyond its straightforward appearance.

games.title: Stakes Winner / Stakes Winner - GI kinzen seihae no michi
games.description:
Saurus's Stakes Winner (1995) puts horse racing on SNK's Neo Geo hardware, letting players act as jockeys instead of wagering spectators. Eight selectable horses have different ratings for speed, strength and stamina, so each race requires managing a mount's strengths rather than simply holding down the acceleration button.

Players guide their horse around crowded tracks, decide when to push for extra speed and conserve energy for the finish. Bonus events can improve a horse's performance between races, introducing some progression to the competition. Its animated animals and accessible controls make it an unusual sports title in the Neo Geo arcade library.

games.title: Stakes Winner 2
games.description:
Stakes Winner 2 (1996) expands Saurus's Neo Geo horse-racing game with more jockey contests and a refined stamina-based riding system. Players choose horses with differing speed, burst and endurance characteristics, then navigate crowded tracks while trying to time their effort for the finishing stretch.

Repeated acceleration maintains pace but consumes energy, while using the crop creates a stronger burst at an even greater stamina cost. That risk-versus-reward management, together with steering and tactical positioning, makes the races about more than sheer button-mashing.

games.title: Super Tank Attack
games.description:
Super Tank Attack, also known as Battle Tank, is a 1992 MicroProse arcade prototype built around first-person armored-vehicle combat. Players control a tank from a simulated forward view, engaging computer-controlled enemies or competing against another human driver. It was an attempt to bring a more simulation-oriented style of battlefield action to coin-operated hardware.

The project never reached normal commercial production. MicroProse's arcade division changed ownership, and the tank game was canceled, leaving a small number of prototype machines and surviving documentation. Its status as an abandoned arcade experiment is more certain than many of the details claimed in later secondhand gameplay summaries.

games.title: Starblade
games.description:
Namco's Starblade (1991) is a pioneering real-time polygonal rail shooter in which players man the gun turret of a spacecraft during an assault on a gigantic enemy installation. The ship follows a predetermined route through formations of hostile fighters, armored structures and space debris while the player aims independently and shoots threats before they can retaliate. Its battles culminate in a dramatic attack on the enemy's massive Red Eye weapon.

Running on Namco's System 21 polygon hardware, Starblade delivered a sense of cinematic scale that was still rare in arcades at the time. The original cabinet used a yoke-style gun controller and a curved reflective viewing arrangement to amplify the image's apparent depth, while force feedback in the seat added to the sensation of being aboard a spacecraft.

Its ambitious presentation helped establish an arcade vocabulary of scripted 3D space battles that later games would explore with more advanced technology. Starblade remains a milestone in the transition from sprite-based shooters to immersive polygonal spectacles.

games.title: Star Castle
games.description:
Star Castle (1980) is Cinematronics' vector-graphics space shooter built around a beautifully simple objective: destroy the central cannon hidden behind three rotating rings of energy barriers. The player's small ship can rotate, thrust and fire around an open field, gradually blasting gaps in the rings while evading shots from the center and dangerous moving mines.

The outer defenses rotate in opposite directions, so opening a clear path to the cannon is only temporary. Staying near the center improves the chance of a decisive hit but also increases the danger, creating a tense balance of patience and aggression. The glowing vector graphics give the circular fortress a clarity that suits the design perfectly.

Developed during the golden age of arcade space shooters, Star Castle became a lasting cult favorite. Its central target, three nested defensive rings and pursuit by enemy sparks form a remarkably readable challenge whose difficulty grows naturally with the player's skill.

games.title: Star Cruiser
games.description:
RamTek's Star Cruiser (1977) is a two-player space-combat game descended from the Spacewar tradition. Each pilot steers a small craft through an open playfield and tries to shoot down the opponent. Objects leaving one edge of the screen reappear on the opposite side, letting both ships and projectiles loop around the arena.

Unlike many other Spacewar derivatives, its original control stations used steering wheels and accelerator pedals. The absence of a central gravitational star produces a relatively direct dogfight focused on maneuvering, aim and anticipating an opponent's route.

games.title: Star Fighter
games.description:
SunA's Star Fighter (1990) is a vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter for one or two players. The pilots attack enemy spacecraft, tanks, fixed gun emplacements and large bosses while collecting upgrades dropped by destroyed targets. Available pickups include additional side weapons, brief protective shields, speed increases and extra bombs.

One unusual feature is a changeable weapon pickup that cycles through numbered possibilities as it is shot, allowing skilled players to select a preferred attack pattern rather than simply grabbing the first power-up they see. This gives the otherwise traditional scrolling combat a small element of planning.

games.title: Star Fire 2
games.description:
Star Fire 2 is Exidy's 1979 revision of Star Fire, an early first-person space-combat arcade game. Players pilot a fighter through a forward-looking starfield, steering toward enemy spacecraft and firing lasers while avoiding incoming attacks. The gameplay remains very close to the original rather than introducing an entirely new mission.

The most meaningful changes involve clearer graphics and an improved high-score entry and display system. That is historically notable because Star Fire had pioneered the ability to enter initials beside a high score; Star Fire 2 refined one of the arcade features that soon became standard across the industry.

games.title: Star Fire
games.description:
Exidy's Star Fire (1979) is a first-person color space shooter created by programmer David Rolfe with artwork by Ted Michon and Susan Ogg. Players view the battlefield from their cockpit, steer their fighter toward approaching ships and fire laser weapons while dodging hostile attacks. Its imagery deliberately evokes the space battles of Star Wars, though the finished arcade game was released without that license.

The original machine was an elaborate sit-down environmental cabinet that surrounded the player with the spectacle of space combat. Star Fire's forward-looking perspective, full-color raster effects and rapid-fire battles were technically ambitious for their time.

Its greatest historical distinction may be the personalized high-score table. Star Fire is widely credited as the first arcade video game to let players enter their initials beside their scores, a feature that would become central to arcade competition for decades. That innovation makes the game significant far beyond its space-shooter mechanics.

games.title: Star Force
games.description:
Tecmo's Star Force (1984), originally associated with the Tehkan name, is a relentlessly paced vertical-scrolling space shooter. Players pilot the Final Star through enemy formations and hostile structures, firing forward while weaving between shots and pursuing high scores. Each successive area is identified by a Greek-letter name, and powerful targets punctuate the journey.

The game is especially remembered for its elaborate hidden bonus objects and score opportunities, which reward experienced players for recognizing patterns and discovering when to fire at seemingly empty portions of the scenery. Its difficulty rises through dense, fast-moving formations rather than an elaborate inventory of selectable weapons.

Star Force became an influential Japanese arcade and console shooter, particularly after Hudson's home versions helped popularize rapid-fire play and score chasing. Its stark, speedy action established a style that remained recognizable in the later Star Soldier family.

games.title: Stargate
games.description:
Stargate (1981), also known as Defender II, is Williams' challenging sequel to Defender. Players again patrol a horizontally scrolling alien world in a ship capable of moving in either direction, rescuing humanoids before Landers carry them away and transform them into deadly Mutants. The screen can reverse direction, so awareness of the radar and threats on both sides is essential.

The sequel adds new alien types, a limited invisibility device and the titular Stargate. Passing through this portal can teleport the ship to a human in danger, while entering with rescued humanoids can yield additional strategic rewards, including rapid advancement through waves. The extra mechanics deepen an already demanding six-button control system.

Designed in the tradition of Eugene Jarvis's famously unforgiving arcade shooters, Stargate prizes multitasking: shooting enemy ships is never enough if the population below is being abducted. Its frantic pace and sophisticated rescue rules make it one of the great high-skill games of the early 1980s.

games.title: Star Gladiator
games.description:
Capcom's Star Gladiator (1996) is a weapons-based 3D fighting game set in a far-future universe of interplanetary conflict and mysterious Plasma Power. Combatants wield swords and other distinctive weapons in one-on-one arenas, using directional movement, guarded attacks and flashy special techniques to overcome opponents.

Built for Capcom's PlayStation-derived ZN arcade hardware, the game explores a different style of fighting from the company's established Street Fighter series. Its science-fiction cast includes the swordsman Hayato and the villainous Dr. Bilstein, with an emphasis on cinematic flourishes and exaggerated weapon effects. It later led to the sequel Plasma Sword.

games.title: Star Guards
games.description:
Star Guards (1987) is Bally Midway's three-player multidirectional shooter starring flying robot warriors. Each participant uses twin eight-way joysticks, one to move and the other to fire, allowing independent movement and aiming. The robots battle enemies across a network of planets or stars while collecting energy and trying to defeat each area's leaders.

Capturing successive locations grants new robot identities and special abilities, including defensive and projectile-based powers. The combination of three simultaneous players, dual-stick controls and a campaign-like star map gives Star Guards an unusual structure compared with the company's better-known single-screen shooters.

games.title: Star Hawk
games.description:
Cinematronics' Star Hawk (1979) is a monochrome vector-graphics shooter that depicts a stream of enemy craft approaching through a simulated 3D space corridor. Instead of flying freely, players steer a gunsight around the display and shoot hostile ships before they pass or inflict penalties.

The timed challenge becomes increasingly difficult as enemy movement speeds up. Certain targets are particularly important because allowing them to escape can subtract points, making target prioritization as important as rapid firing. Its crisp wireframe display and direct arcade controls place Star Hawk among the earliest attempts to create depth and motion with vector graphics.

games.title: Star Jacker
games.description:
Sega's Star Jacker (1983) is a vertically scrolling shooter with a memorable formation-based twist. Rather than controlling a single craft, the player initially leads three starfighters moving in a line, each following the path of the ship in front and contributing firepower. A larger squadron deals more damage but is also harder to steer through narrow gaps in enemy fire.

Separate weapons attack aerial targets and installations on the ground, recalling the two-layer combat of Xevious. When a fighter is destroyed, the formation shrinks, and the run ends when the last ship is lost. Its unusual system turns the surviving size of the squadron into a visible measure of both strength and vulnerability.

games.title: Vs. Star Luster
games.description:
Vs. Star Luster is Namco's 1985 space-combat game adapted from the Famicom for Nintendo's VS. arcade system. Inspired by cockpit-style space simulators such as Star Raiders, it places the player behind a forward-looking view of space rather than the overhead perspective common to contemporary shooters.

Players navigate between sectors, locate enemy forces and protect friendly bases, using cockpit instruments and a strategic map to understand a battlefield that cannot all be seen at once. Its combination of navigation and first-person dogfighting is more demanding than a simple score-based space shooter, and the arcade release preserves an unusual example of a home-console space simulation repackaged for coin-operated play.

games.title: Starship 1
games.description:
Atari's Starship 1 (1977) is an early first-person space-combat game in which the player defends the Federation from hostile craft while traveling through star and asteroid fields. A flight-style yoke moves the view and aiming reticle, allowing the player to track enemy ships and fire the main weapons. Speed controls and a limited supply of additional attacks add decisions beyond simply holding the trigger.

The monochrome screen, cockpit-like controls and use of analog mechanisms helped create a sense of piloting well before fully three-dimensional graphics became possible in mainstream arcade machines. The concept was later reinterpreted for Atari's home console under the name Star Ship.

games.title: Star Soldier: Vanishing Earth
games.description:
Star Soldier: Vanishing Earth (1998) brought Hudson's established vertically scrolling shooter series to the Nintendo 64 and to Seta's closely related Aleck64 arcade hardware. Players choose among three ships with distinct built-in weapons and pilot them through enemy formations, defensive installations and large bosses.

Unlike earlier series entries in which weapon pickups could change a ship's primary armament, each selected craft retains its own fighting style. Special Ex-Arms supply limited high-impact attacks, adding another decision to the usual movement, shooting and bomb management. The arcade version is particularly interesting as a rare coin-operated appearance of a franchise most closely associated with home systems.

games.title: Starspinner
games.description:
Starspinner is an early-1980s electronic slot machine attributed to ACE, with a Dutch-language set preserved for arcade emulation. It uses a Z80-based board and a vertically presented gambling display rather than a mechanical reel assembly. Operator settings include coin values, payout percentage and whether credits are cleared on reset, showing how the cabinet could be configured for different venues.

The surviving evidence does not establish special symbols or bonus modes, but its regional program and dedicated slot hardware make it an example of the first wave of video fruit machines in European amusement locations.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Star Sweep
games.description:
Star Sweep (1997) is a Japanese falling-block puzzle game by Axela, distributed in arcades with Namco's involvement. Red, yellow and blue pieces descend into a vertical playfield, often carrying star symbols at one or both ends. Rather than merely matching blocks by color, the player must join compatible stars to clear pieces from the screen.

Successive clearances can be linked into rewarding combos, and a full field ends the game if the player cannot recover quickly enough. Its story mode presents a succession of puzzle opponents across an island, while separate challenges emphasize scoring, survival or fast clearing. The combination of falling pieces and star-matching rules gives it a personality distinct from both Tetris and Columns.

games.title: Star Trek
games.description:
Sega's Star Trek (1982) is a color vector-graphics space-combat game that puts the player in command of the starship Enterprise. Klingon vessels and other threats appear around the ship, while the captain uses phasers, photon torpedoes and warp travel to protect Federation space and defend starbases.

The display is divided into three functional areas: a tactical scanner shows local space from above, a forward viewer presents enemies approaching in simulated depth, and a status panel tracks shields, weapons and warp energy. Steering, turning and firing require attention to all three views, while digitized speech and familiar Star Trek terminology strengthen the atmosphere.

Its distinctive control panel and mixture of strategic radar awareness with first-person shooting make it an ambitious licensed arcade adaptation, rather than simply a generic space game with the Enterprise's name attached.

games.title: Star Trigon
games.description:
Namco's Star Trigon (2002) is a charming one-button arcade action puzzle about rescuing stranded aliens in space. The player's astronaut automatically revolves around small planets, and pressing the button at the right instant launches them toward another world. Successful jumps trace lines between planets, and completing a triangle traps and rescues any drifting aliens inside it.

The challenge comes from timing jumps, conserving the character's limited air supply and deciding which triangular routes will capture the most creatures. Its simple control scheme conceals a surprisingly intricate spatial puzzle, giving Star Trigon a distinctive identity among Namco's early-2000s arcade games.

games.title: Star Wars
games.description:
Atari's Star Wars (1983) is one of the great vector-graphics arcade spectacles, recreating the climactic assault on the Death Star from the original 1977 film. Players take the role of Luke Skywalker in his X-wing, flying through a first-person sequence of TIE fighter combat, low-altitude attacks on the station's surface and a final run down the trench toward the thermal exhaust port. The game's glowing color vectors give its starfields, towers and huge structures a striking sense of speed and depth.

The special yoke controller moves the ship's aiming reticle, and four triggers fire the X-wing's lasers. Incoming shots can be destroyed, but collisions and enemy hits drain a limited supply of deflector shields. The goal is to survive all three phases and hit the exhaust port, after which the assault begins again at greater difficulty. Digitized dialogue from the film and the familiar orchestral music greatly enhance the illusion of taking part in the movie.

Developed under Atari's vector-graphics expertise, Star Wars was a major commercial and critical success and became one of the most beloved licensed arcade games ever made. Its trench run remains an enduring example of how carefully staged gameplay can turn relatively simple 3D graphics into a cinematic experience.

games.title: Triv Two
games.description: Triv Two is a 1984 quiz arcade game from Status Games, following the company's earlier Triv-Quiz format. Players answer multiple-choice questions drawn from interchangeable question sets, with subject matter including television, sports, entertainment and miscellaneous knowledge. The series' central idea is to combine trivia knowledge with score management: questions lead to point totals and the possibility of earning a place on the machine's high-score table. Four pushbuttons provide the input, making the game especially suited to bars and other locations where a joystick-driven action game was not the only attraction. A separate vertical-screen configuration of Triv Two also survives.

games.title: Triv Four
games.description: Triv Four is a mid-1980s entry in Status Games' Triv-Quiz family, continuing its question-and-score arcade format. The player is presented with a trivia question, chooses how much of the current score to risk, and selects an answer from the displayed alternatives. The underlying Triv-Quiz format includes subject areas such as sports, entertainment and world facts, with higher scores rewarding sustained correct answers. Triv Four uses four selection buttons rather than a joystick, and belongs to a series whose principal differences between editions lie in the question material and hardware revisions rather than reflex-based action.

games.title: Saint Dragon
games.description:
Jaleco's Saint Dragon (1989) is a horizontal-scrolling shooter with an unusual protagonist: a mechanical dragon rebelling against a conquering army of cyborg monsters. Players guide the serpentine creature through five stages of hostile machinery, enemy craft and towering bosses, firing forward while maneuvering around dangerous terrain.

Its signature mechanic is the armored tail, which trails the dragon's movements and can be positioned to absorb incoming attacks. Weapon pickups offer lasers, bombs, projectiles and temporary maximum-power modes, but survival depends as much on twisting the tail into a shield as on aggressive shooting. That body-based defense system gives Saint Dragon a memorable silhouette and a distinctive tactical rhythm.

games.title: Steal See
games.description:
Steal See (2000), developed by Moov Generation and published by Eolith, is a Korean arcade puzzle game centered on gradually exposing concealed images. Its main Steal See mode asks players to reveal portions of a hidden picture, while the alternative Get Land mode follows a territory-capturing style reminiscent of Qix and Gals Panic.

The emphasis on unveiling artwork through puzzle actions places it among the picture-reveal games that found an audience in late-1990s and early-2000s amusement centers. The two play modes distinguish it from titles built around only one form of image-reveal puzzle.

games.title: Steel Talons
games.description:
Atari Games' Steel Talons (1991) brought 3D polygonal helicopter combat to an imposing two-player arcade cockpit. Pilots fly an attack helicopter across mountainous and desert landscapes, using a cannon, rockets and guided missiles to destroy designated targets before time runs out. The simulation-like controls include a flight stick, collective lever and rudder pedals, with a separate mode offering more demanding helicopter handling.

The cabinet supports solo missions, two-player cooperation and competitive helicopter duels. Radar and cockpit indicators help locate enemies while the game's terrain and horizon continuously shift with the aircraft's movements. Speakers and physical feedback built into the seats further emphasize the sensation of controlling a heavy combat machine.

Its complex controls and large cabinet made Steel Talons a specialized attraction rather than a conventional joystick shooter. The game remains an impressive example of Atari's attempt to bring realistic-feeling polygonal vehicle simulation into the coin-op market.

games.title: Steel Talons
games.description:
This prototype version of Steel Talons preserves a development-stage build of Atari Games' 1991 polygonal helicopter combat simulator. The underlying concept is the same as the released game: fly an armed attack helicopter over three-dimensional terrain, locate mission targets and engage them with guns, rockets and guided missiles.

The main historical value of this set is its pre-release status, allowing researchers to compare software from the development process with the final arcade revisions. Without a documented feature-by-feature comparison, it should not be assumed to contain different missions or control rules simply because it is labeled a prototype.

games.title: Steel Worker
games.description:
Taito's Steel Worker (1980) is an unusual construction-site puzzle game in which the player must keep an automatically walking laborer from falling to his death. Rather than directly moving the worker, the player selects and places sections of scaffolding ahead of him, building horizontal paths, diagonals and stairways to bridge gaps between platforms.

As the worker advances, elevators and other site hazards complicate the route. A limited-use reversal command can send him back in the other direction when the current path becomes unsafe. The challenge lies in planning a bridge while the character keeps moving, creating a striking early example of indirect-control puzzle design.

games.title: Stepping Stage
games.description:
Jaleco's Stepping Stage Special (1999) is a Japanese arcade rhythm game built around dancing on a floor controller in time with music. Like other late-1990s dance attractions, it asks players to respond to rhythmic visual cues with accurately timed physical steps, turning a song into a score-based movement challenge.

The installation used an unusually elaborate multi-screen audiovisual setup and additional PC-based video hardware alongside its arcade processors. Its distinctive cabinet and presentation make it an interesting, comparatively rare contemporary of the dance-game boom led by Dance Dance Revolution, even though surviving emulation does not always reproduce the full original installation.

games.title: Strike Gunner S.T.G
games.description:
Strike Gunner S.T.G. (1991) is a vertically scrolling military shooter in which a high-tech aircraft battles enemy helicopters, jets, turrets and huge mechanized bosses. Its primary cannon has unlimited ammunition and grows stronger with upgrades, but the game's most distinctive feature is the special-weapon selection made before each stage.

A broad arsenal of secondary attacks offers different tactical advantages, yet each special weapon can be chosen only once during a complete run. Deciding when to deploy a particularly useful weapon introduces a layer of planning to the intense, formation-heavy shooting. The arcade original later served as the basis for a Super Nintendo conversion.

games.title: Stinger
games.description:
Seibu Denshi's Stinger (1983) is an early horizontally scrolling space shooter presented on a vertically oriented monitor. Players guide a fighter through a hostile space fortress, destroying alien ships and avoiding the hazards of the surrounding structures.

An unusual defensive aid called Bongo can be activated to attack enemies for a short period, supplementing the ship's regular firepower. The scrolling direction and unconventional screen layout give this relatively obscure Seibu release a distinctive appearance among early-1980s shooters.

games.title: Stack Columns
games.description:
Sega's Stack Columns (1994) is a competitive variation of its familiar falling-gem puzzle series. Players rotate descending three-gem columns and match colors to clear the field, with longer combinations producing more valuable chains. The emphasis shifts from solitary survival toward attacks that disrupt an opponent's playfield.

Its defining system is the Stack, a pressure-building attack meter influenced by Columns III. Successful combinations raise the available attack strength, and activating it pushes the rival's gems upward, potentially causing an immediate defeat. That tension between clearing safely and saving a stronger attack gives Stack Columns its own strategic identity within the series.

games.title: Steel Force
games.developer: Electronic Devices Italy / Ecogames S.L. Spain
games.publisher: Electronic Devices Italy / Ecogames S.L. Spain
games.description:
Steel Force (1994) is a top-down science-fiction action game in which one or two Federation soldiers fight through maze-like space-station environments infested with hostile forces. With an eight-way joystick and dedicated action buttons, players move through corridors, shoot enemies and search for each stage's exit before the time limit expires.

Ammunition, health packs and weapon upgrades are scattered around the maps, rewarding exploration but creating pressure to keep moving. Its combination of dense gunfights and maze navigation recalls computer action games such as Alien Breed, adapted to a faster, more direct arcade format.

games.title: Storm Blade
games.description:
Visco's Storm Blade (1996) is a vertically scrolling military shooter featuring an eclectic selection of aircraft and pilots. Choices include an F-14 Tomcat, a MiG-29, a Harrier and even a specially modified World War II-era Zero, each associated with its own weapon style. One or two players fight through attacks by aircraft, tanks, ships and heavily armored bosses.

Standard power-ups improve the main guns, stronger pickups provide larger jumps in firepower, and limited super bombs can clear crowded sections of the battlefield. Storm Blade's mixture of modern military equipment, exaggerated character choices and energetic screen-filling action gives it a playful personality.

games.title: Stocker
games.description:
Bally/Sente's Stocker (1984) is an overhead driving game about racing a car across the southern United States from Florida toward California. Instead of a closed circuit, players follow a winding network of roads, intersections and detours, choosing routes while steering through traffic and avoiding accidents. The timer is represented by a shrinking fuel supply, and reaching gas stations is essential for extending the journey.

Police cars are a special hazard because being stopped or ticketed costs valuable progress or points. The freedom to take shortcuts and even cut across unsuitable terrain makes Stocker more exploratory than a typical racing cabinet. Its combination of route choice, fuel management and fast steering offers an unusual road-trip structure for a mid-1980s arcade game.

games.title: Super Toffy
games.description:
Super Toffy (1994) is a revised action-puzzle game derived from Toffy and, further back, Dangerous Dungeons. Players move through compact platform-like stages, collecting the required treasures while avoiding monsters and navigating the level layout. The game demands careful path planning as well as quick movement around hazards.

Compared with its predecessors, Super Toffy rearranges many levels, adds new between-stage artwork and introduces a pickup that temporarily freezes enemies. Score-based extra lives give skilled players a little more room for error. Its value as a distinct release lies in these changes, not simply in a new title screen.

games.title: Stompin'
games.description:
Bally/Sente's Stompin' (1986) transforms a bug-defense game into a full-body arcade attraction. Insects and other creatures approach a stock of food at the center of the screen, and the player must physically step on corresponding sections of a floor-mounted pressure pad to squash the attackers. Simply seeing the correct target is not enough; reacting with the correct foot movement is the challenge.

Different environments introduce a variety of critters, while helpful creatures must be spared. A limited screen-clearing zapper supplies emergency assistance when too many pests close in. Its enormous floor controller makes Stompin' an early and memorable precursor to later rhythm and dance games built around bodily movement.

games.title: Stone Ball
games.description:
Stone Ball (1994), from Art & Magic, is a riotous prehistoric sports game that mixes soccer, hockey and combat. Teams of cavemen armed with oversized clubs try to drive a stone ball into the opposing cave, but the rules happily permit rough tackles, fights and power-up attacks.

Two-on-two matches can involve up to four human players, with different villages supplying colorful teams. Speed and power bonuses, together with attacks that can burn or bury opponents, turn each contest into a chaotic struggle for possession. Its exaggerated animation and deliberately unruly rules are the main attraction rather than conventional sporting realism.

games.title: Koutetsu Yousai Strahl
games.description:
UPL's Koutetsu Yousai Strahl (1992) is a horizontally scrolling shooter in which an advanced jet fighter confronts the forces of a mad scientist who has seized a gigantic airborne fortress. Players fly through six stages featuring jungles, stormy skies, cityscapes and heavily defended mechanical installations.

Its outstanding feature is the weapon-selection hangar before each mission. Players can configure a primary gun, a support weapon and bombs, choosing among lasers, twin shots, homing missiles and defensive options. Support weapons can be directed into different firing angles, allowing attacks against enemies that approach from awkward positions. The planning between stages and the distinctive industrial artwork make Strahl one of UPL's more elaborate late shooters.

games.title: Strata Bowling
games.description:
Strata Bowling (1990), developed by Incredible Technologies and published by Strata, is a trackball-controlled ten-pin bowling game following the tradition of Capcom Bowling. Players roll toward the pins by sweeping the trackball, turning the speed and direction of their hand movement into the virtual ball's delivery.

Beyond ordinary scoring, this follow-up adds alternate rule sets such as Flash and Strike or Die, along with updated animations and a memorable sung theme. Its immediate physical controls make it a natural fit for quick bar and amusement-center competition; the related Super Strike variant replaced the trackball with a miniature physical bowling alley.

games.title: Strategy X
games.description:
Konami's Strategy X (1981), distributed by Stern in North America, is a vertically scrolling tank combat game with a strong emphasis on negotiating hostile terrain. Players advance through successive zones filled with rotating gun turrets, jeeps, enemy tanks and barriers while firing at threats ahead of them. The final objective is to penetrate an enemy base and destroy its central target.

Walls can block progress, explosive objects may clear nearby defenses, and colored terrain presents additional danger. With each section introducing different obstacles and attack patterns, Strategy X is more varied than its simple overhead tank graphics first suggest. It is a notable early Konami example of a shooter organized around distinct combat zones and an explicit mission objective.

games.title: Raiga - Strato Fighter
games.description:
Tecmo's Raiga: Strato Fighter (1991) is a horizontally scrolling space shooter set during a futuristic invasion of Earth. Players pilot the Raiga fighter through enemy fleets, large warships and massive bosses, collecting weapons and upgrades from destroyed carriers.

Its defining maneuver is the ability to turn the spacecraft around and fire backward, allowing attacks against enemies approaching from behind rather than forcing the player to face forward at all times. Optional support weapons, including different Auto Guard systems, further expand the available firepower. This combination of directional shooting and selectable equipment gives Raiga a distinctive tactical edge over more conventional side-scrolling shooters.

games.title: Streaking
games.description:
Streaking is a mischievous 1981 maze game by Shoei, built on Galaxian-derived hardware. The player guides an unclothed woman through city streets, collecting food and articles of clothing while avoiding pursuing police officers. Gathering her outfit is central to the game's comic premise, and portals at the maze's corners offer a quick escape from danger.

Its Pac-Man-like chase mechanics are dressed up with an unusually risqué theme for an early arcade game. Streaking also makes a fleeting appearance on screen in the 1983 comedy film Joysticks.

games.title: Street Smart
games.description:
Street Smart is SNK's 1989 arena fighting game, released before the one-on-one fighting boom of the early 1990s. Players choose between two martial artists and travel between street-fighting venues, facing a succession of tough opponents. Unlike later versus fighters confined to a single plane, combatants can move freely up and down as well as left and right within the arena, using punches, kicks and jumps to wear down their opponents.

The arcade game's distinctive two-player mode is cooperative rather than a conventional head-to-head tournament: partners battle enemies together, with occasional grudge matches between the human fighters for bonuses. Its combination of free-moving combat, simple attack strings and crowd-lined arenas puts it at an interesting point between belt-scrolling brawlers and SNK's later fighting games. The Mega Drive adaptation changed the structure and added features not found in the coin-op original.

games.title: Street Hoop / Street Slam / Dunk Dream
games.description:
Street Hoop, known as Street Slam in North America and Dunk Dream in Japan, is Data East's fast, stylish 1994 three-on-three basketball game for the Neo Geo MVS. Ten international teams compete in the Japanese and European versions, while the American release emphasizes city-based teams. Each team has different ratings for speed, defense, three-point shooting and dunking, giving the compact roster recognizable strengths.

The action uses accessible shoot, pass, block and steal controls, with high lob passes setting up spectacular alley-oop dunks. A super-shot meter builds as a team scores, eventually enabling gravity-defying power dunks. Colorful oversized players, energetic music and exaggerated aerial moves make this feel more like street-court spectacle than a strict simulation. Its short arcade matches are particularly suited to two-player competition.

games.title: Strider
games.description:
Capcom's Strider (1989), released in Japan as Strider Hiryū, is a landmark cinematic action-platform game that introduced many arcade players to the acrobatic ninja Hiryu. Set in a dystopian future controlled by Grandmaster Meio, it sends Hiryu across Soviet territory, a huge airborne battleship, the Amazon and eventually Meio's orbital stronghold. Developed for Capcom's CPS-1 hardware and created alongside a manga project with Moto Kikaku, the game stood out for its sweeping environments, enormous bosses and strikingly varied music.

Hiryu attacks with the Cypher, a blindingly fast plasma blade, and can run, slide, somersault, cling to walls and traverse ceilings. Rather than simply moving from left to right, players must master momentum and climbing to negotiate vertical passages, moving machinery and enemies approaching from every direction. Power-ups extend his blade, restore health or summon robot companions, including a mechanical tiger and hawk.

Memorable encounters, from the colossal mechanical gorilla to a council of Soviet figures that merges into a serpentine monster, helped establish Strider's surreal visual identity. Multilingual speech, fluid animation and the famous Mega Drive conversion reinforced its reputation; Hiryu later returned in sequels and Capcom crossover games. The arcade sets preserved in AdvanceMAME include regional versions whose title presentation and voice samples differ.

games.title: Strider 2
games.description:
Strider 2 is Capcom's official 1999 arcade sequel to its celebrated ninja action game, arriving a decade after the original. On Sony ZN-based hardware it blends crisply animated 2D characters with polygonal backgrounds, giving Hiryu a more cinematic battlefield while preserving the side-scrolling pace. Its five missions include assaults in Hong Kong, Germany and Antarctica, followed by a return to the battleship Balrog and Grandmaster Meio's Third Moon fortress. The initial missions can be tackled in different orders.

Hiryu still wields his Cypher blade and climbs walls and ceilings, but his move set now includes dashes, double jumps, backflips and the aerial Savage Slash. Collectible Boost charges let him temporarily unleash plasma waves, making offensive timing as important as platform navigation. Boss battles receive particular emphasis, and the rival Strider Hien adds a further connection to the game's expanded storyline.

This is distinct from U.S. Gold's unrelated Strider II/Strider Returns for home computers and consoles. Capcom's arcade sequel was later adapted for the original PlayStation, and remains notable for translating the first game's free-flowing swordplay into an era dominated by 3D graphics.

games.title: Super Triv
games.description: Super Triv is a mid-1980s arcade trivia game by Hara Industries, known in both English-question and French-question versions. Players use four buttons to respond to questions stored on dedicated ROMs. Its most unusual feature is technical rather than visual: the game accesses its question data through indirect ROM addressing, a method also found in Romar Triv and initially troublesome for emulator authors. The preserved English edition eventually became playable after its program ROM mapping was corrected. It is a particularly obscure example of specialist quiz hardware designed for the amusement trade.

games.title: Strike Fighter
games.description:
Sega's Strike Fighter (1991) is a fast jet-combat shooter descended from After Burner and G-LOC: Air Battle. The player flies a fighter through formations of hostile aircraft, evading incoming fire while attacking with a cannon and lock-on missiles. Its viewpoint and sprite-scaling presentation recall Sega's spectacular late-1980s cockpit games, but the action also builds on G-LOC's more direct combat structure. Missiles are not limited by a finite ammunition supply.

Released in Japanese arcades as a conversion for G-LOC hardware, Strike Fighter later provided the basis for the home game After Burner III on the FM Towns and Sega CD. It is an intriguing bridge between the exuberant After Burner style and Sega's later combat-flight titles.

games.title: Strike Force
games.description:
Strike Force is Midway's 1991 spiritual continuation of Defender and Stargate, upgrading their hectic horizontal shooting for two simultaneous players. A reptilian Saurian invasion threatens human colonies across an entire star system. Players pilot fighters over planetary surfaces, shoot down alien craft, rescue colonists before they are abducted and mutated, and eventually attack the enemy megaship Apocalypse. Unlike Defender's fixed wave progression, a strategic map lets players decide which threatened planet to visit next.

The fighters can switch into heavily armed turrets, and in cooperative play one player's turret can attach to the other's ship, allowing independent aiming from a shared vehicle. Specialized weapons, deployable marines and supply purchases expand the familiar rescue-and-shoot formula. Cleared planets can come under renewed attack, making it necessary to balance further conquest against defending the worlds already saved.

Running on Midway's Y-Unit hardware, Strike Force is much more elaborate than its minimalist ancestors. It remained relatively uncommon in arcades and never received a contemporary home conversion. The preserved Saurian Front prototype shows an earlier stage of the game's development.

games.title: Strike Zone Baseball
games.description:
Strike Zone Baseball is Leland's 1988 arcade interpretation of American baseball, emphasizing hands-on batting and pitching rather than purely managerial choices. The player can choose from numerous teams and play matches or concentrate on hitting in a home-run derby mode. Batting uses on-screen gauges to control the timing and direction of the swing, while pitchers and fielders are handled through the game's dedicated controls.

The production was an unusually demanding project for its small development team; contemporary credits indicate that D. Christianson and J. Hubber spent roughly nine months making it, including a period of unpaid work to finish the game. The arcade version should not be confused with the separate computer adaptation associated with Orel Hershiser.

games.title: Strength & Skill
games.description:
Strength & Skill is a 1984 multi-event arcade sports contest from Sun Electronics, released in Japan as The Guiness. Rather than concentrating on a single sport, it challenges players to set records across six eccentric disciplines, including sawing a log, driving a pile, running up a slope, throwing rings, spinning a disc and skateboarding. Each activity calls for a different combination of joystick positioning and rapid or precisely timed button presses.

The two-player competition and short tests of speed, timing and coordination recall the early arcade fascination with record-setting athletic challenges. Its deliberately odd selection of events makes it more distinctive than the generic sports label suggests.

games.title: Street Drivin'
games.description:
Street Drivin' is an unreleased 1993 Atari Games driving prototype and a follow-up to Hard Drivin' and Race Drivin'. It retains their first-person approach to polygonal driving and physical steering, pedal and gear controls, while adding a new course and a police car. The goal remains to negotiate a demanding three-dimensional road layout rather than to simply weave through traffic in a sprite-based racer.

Because it never reached a regular commercial release, the surviving ROM is primarily of historical interest. Its complicated control calibration also reflects the specialized driving cabinets for which Atari's simulation-oriented racers were designed.

games.title: Street Heat
games.description: Street Heat is a 1985 arcade driving-and-shooting game from Epos. Viewed from behind a police cruiser, the player navigates busy roads and winding stretches while firing at criminal vehicles. Avoiding traffic and roadside obstacles is as important as landing shots, since collisions cost precious time and interrupt the pursuit. The combination of a road-racing viewpoint and an armed police car makes it a lesser-known precursor to the later arcade tradition of high-speed pursuit games.

games.title: Super Trivia Master
games.description: Super Trivia Master is Enerdyne Technologies' 1986 follow-up to Trivia Master, developed for the bar and amusement market. It is a question-and-answer competition supporting as many as four participants, using dedicated buttons for responses rather than arcade movement controls. Its appeal rests on comparing knowledge and scores across players, with questions supplied from ROMs and presented on a conventional raster monitor. The sequel remains closely associated with the earlier Enerdyne quiz hardware, making the pair an interesting snapshot of the trivia-cabinet boom of the mid-1980s.

games.title: S.T.U.N. Runner
games.description:
S.T.U.N. Runner (Spread Tunnel Underground Network Runner) is Atari Games' spectacular 1989 hybrid of futuristic racing and shooting. The player pilots a high-speed craft through enclosed tunnels, steep banked turns and exposed sections of track at speeds supposedly exceeding 900 mph. The objective is to reach each checkpoint before time expires while avoiding barriers, enemy machines and hazards that threaten to slow the vehicle down.

Weapons allow the craft to blast obstructions and rivals; limited shockwave attacks clear an especially dangerous stretch, while boost strips grant bursts of speed and brief protection. Players learn to ride the walls of the tunnels to preserve momentum and take turns efficiently. Rather than relying solely on flat sprites, the game uses polygonal environments and vehicles rendered by technology descended from Atari's Hard Drivin' system.

Its distinctive sit-down cabinet, vivid neon imagery and relentless sensation of acceleration make S.T.U.N. Runner a memorable transition between the sprite-scaling racing era and the fuller 3D arcade racers of the 1990s. The hardware-intensive original has a very different presence from its numerous home adaptations.

games.title: ST-V Bios
games.description:
ST-V BIOS is the firmware for Sega's Titan Video arcade platform, introduced in 1995 and closely related to the Sega Saturn home console. The system used two Hitachi SH-2 RISC processors, with VDP1 handling sprites and textured polygons and VDP2 providing multiple scrolling and rotating background planes. A Motorola 68000 and Yamaha SCSP sound chip supported its audio capabilities.

Where the Saturn normally used optical discs, the arcade platform relied on interchangeable ROM cartridges and cabinet-specific interfaces. The common hardware architecture let Sega reuse much of its console-era technology while tailoring startup, region settings, and operator functions to amusement centers. Multiple BIOS revisions exist for different territories and production periods, making this set part of the historical record of Sega's mid-1990s hardware strategy.

games.title: Subroc-3D
games.description:
Sega's Subroc-3D (1982) is one of the most historically important attempts to give arcade players genuine stereoscopic depth. Developed with Matsushita, it places the player's eyes against a special periscope-like viewing unit that delivers alternating images to each eye. The result is a three-dimensional sea-and-air combat spectacle rather than the flat perspective tricks usually called '3D' at the time.

Players aim through the viewer at approaching ships and aircraft, using elevation and horizontal movement to line up targets and fire. The scenery shifts between ocean and sky, with changes of lighting and background reinforcing the sense of distance. Its elaborate optical cabinet, custom hardware and stereo presentation made it unusually ambitious for 1982, although faithfully reproducing the original depth effect requires more than displaying its images on an ordinary flat monitor.

games.title: Subs
games.description:
Subs is Atari's late-1970s submarine-combat arcade game, notable for a purpose-built two-monitor cabinet with separate control stations. Each player steers a submarine and fires torpedoes at the other, but the opponent's vessel is normally hidden from direct view. Instead, players must infer its position from a small sonar display, briefly revealed silhouettes and the path of incoming torpedoes.

Steering wheels and torpedo buttons make the encounter feel like a stripped-down naval duel. The contest is won by scoring more hits within the time limit, and a computer opponent can take the second position when only one person plays. Its dual-screen arrangement was an early and ambitious example of using specialized arcade hardware to create a form of competitive play that a shared display could not easily provide.

games.title: Super Casino
games.description: Super Casino is a 1984 electronic casino game from Data Amusement, played on an upright, portrait-oriented CRT. Its simple two-way joystick and single-button panel are unusual for a gambling cabinet, more closely resembling the controls of early action games. The Z80-based machine belongs to the period when arcade operators were experimenting with video replacements for electromechanical casino attractions. Its exact betting choices are not documented well enough to assign it to a specific card or reel game.

games.title: Idol Janshi Su-Chi-Pie Special
games.description: Idol Janshi Su-Chi-Pie Special is a 1993 Jaleco arcade mahjong game built around the popular Su-Chi-Pie character series. Players face a cast of anime-styled female opponents in Japanese riichi mahjong matches, with character portraits, dialogue and suggestive reward scenes adding personality to what is fundamentally a tile-based game. The arcade release draws on the series' earlier home-console success and reflects a distinctive Japanese tradition of character-driven mahjong cabinets. Knowledge of mahjong hands and calls, rather than reflexes, determines success.

games.title: Suikoenbu
games.description:
Suikoenbu, known internationally as Outlaws of the Lost Dynasty, is Data East's 1995 one-on-one fighting game inspired by the Chinese classic Water Margin. Eleven warriors gather around the legendary Liangshan marshes to battle for supremacy. Running on Sega's ST-V cartridge system, it features colorful hand-drawn martial artists, elaborate special-attack effects and a fantasy-historical setting very different from contemporary urban fighting tournaments.

Weapons play a key role: combatants can fight with blades and other arms, but may be left to continue unarmed when their weapon gauge is exhausted. The combination of weapon management and familiar special-move combat gives the matches their own rhythm. Data East followed the game with Suikoenbu: Fuuun Saiki, making this one of the company's last distinctive attempts to establish a fighting-game franchise.

games.title: Sundance
games.description:
Sundance is Cinematronics' unusual 1979 vector-graphics action puzzler, designed by Tim Skelly. Two angled grids appear to float in space, while tiny suns ricochet between them. The player opens holes in the lower grid to catch the suns as they bounce through, earning points by predicting where they will land. A well-aimed nova can also be fired from a hole to intercept a sun rather than waiting for the next bounce.

The grids draw closer together as play continues, reducing the time available to react. Its luminous pseudo-3D geometry and button-based hole selection make it unlike conventional maze or shooting games. The original hardware, extensively adapted from the Space Wars vector platform, was also unusually fragile, contributing to the rarity of surviving cabinets.

games.title: Super Burger Time
games.description:
Super Burger Time is Data East's 1990 arcade sequel to BurgerTime, returning chef Peter Pepper to a world of gigantic hamburgers and hostile walking food. The goal is to build each burger by crossing its stacked ingredients on platforms and ladders, causing bread, meat and vegetables to fall onto the serving plates below. Enemies prowl the stages and can interrupt the chef before he completes an order.

This sequel adds more elaborate scenery, larger characters and direct attacks and special items, making the cooking chase more action-oriented than the 1982 original. Two chefs can play simultaneously, sharing the screen as they race to finish the oversized meals. It retains the ingenious dropping-ingredient chain reactions that made BurgerTime memorable, while giving players a wider range of ways to survive its crowded kitchens.

games.title: Super Draw Poker
games.description:
Super Draw Poker is a 1983 electronic draw-poker game from Stern, produced under licence from Valadon Automation. It follows the established video-poker format, using dedicated buttons to select cards and play hands rather than joystick movement. With a ten-button panel and portrait screen, the machine was built for a specialized gambling environment rather than a conventional action-game cabinet.

Surviving sets include an alternative program and a bootleg board, while emulator researchers have documented the payout control and reconstructed the appropriate poker input layout. Its Stern connection is particularly interesting because the company was also prominent in pinball and arcade action games.

games.title: Superbike
games.description: Superbike is a 1983 Century Electronics action game that blends motorcycle stunt riding with side-scrolling shooting. Rather than competing in a conventional road race, the player guides a bike through an obstacle-filled course, jumping over gaps, trees and other hazards while earning points and using weapons. Its rhythm of accelerating, leaping and avoiding collisions is reminiscent of Moon Patrol, but presented as an eccentric stunt-bike adventure on Century's CVS hardware.

games.title: Super Bond
games.description:
Super Bond, also known as Agent Super Bond, is a mid-1980s action-maze game built from the ideas and hardware of Stern's Lost Tomb. The player moves through a succession of interconnected rooms, shooting attackers, collecting necessary objects and trying to locate the exit while avoiding deadly hazards. Its secret-agent and hostage-rescue imagery gives the familiar labyrinth exploration a loose spy-film flavor.

As an unauthorized reworking rather than a wholly new design, its interest lies in the alternate theme and conversion history as much as its gameplay. It retains the dense single-screen rooms and tactical movement associated with Lost Tomb.

games.title: Super Bug
games.description:
Super Bug is a pioneering 1977 Atari/Kee Games driving game that puts the player behind the wheel of a small yellow Volkswagen-style Beetle in a constantly scrolling overhead city. The road can turn in several directions, and the player must steer through corners, avoid curbs, traffic and oil slicks, and cover as much distance as possible before the fuel timer runs out. A steering wheel, accelerator and gear selector give it a more physical feel than joystick-controlled racers.

Its black-and-white screen uses a colored overlay to make the car appear yellow. Programmed by Wendi Allen, credited at the time as Howard Delman, Super Bug was an important early example of a scrolling playfield and helped lay the groundwork for Atari's Fire Truck. Its combination of open-looking roads and real driving controls was remarkably forward-thinking for the mid-1970s.

games.title: Super Chase - Criminal Termination
games.description:
Super Chase: Criminal Termination is Taito's 1992 arcade continuation of Chase H.Q. and Special Criminal Investigation, turning the pursuit of fleeing suspects into a frantic first-person driving experience. Tony Gibson and his partner receive briefings from dispatcher Nancy before chasing criminal vehicles through fast-moving traffic. Unlike the earlier behind-the-car games, the viewpoint looks out from the pursuing vehicle, emphasizing the sensation of speed and sudden collisions.

The player steers, accelerates, changes gears and uses limited turbo boosts to catch each suspect before the timer expires. Different missions feature different pursuit vehicles, including a powerful truck, while the final capture still depends on repeatedly ramming the target. Large raster-scaling effects and dedicated driving controls make the original coin-op cabinet a considerably more physical experience than its later home adaptation.

games.title: Superman
games.description:
Taito's Superman, released in late 1988 and widely associated with its 1989 Japanese launch, is a cooperative arcade action game starring DC Comics' Man of Steel. Superman fights across American cities and into alien territory to stop the invading Emperor Zaas. A second player can join as a red-costumed Superman, giving the game an unusual two-hero presentation rather than a conventional superhero-and-sidekick pairing.

The action alternates between multi-directional beat-'em-up sections, where Superman punches enemies, throws objects and uses charged energy attacks, and flying shoot-'em-up sequences. Colored crystals replenish health or enhance attacks, and stages switch between city streets and aerial combat. The game's audio draws on John Williams' famous Superman film theme, connecting the coin-op adventure to the character's big-screen identity.

Its mixture of ground combat and airborne shooting makes it a distinctive licensed action game from the pre-fighting-game arcade era. Although the stages can be straightforward, the ability to fly and fight cooperatively captures much of Superman's larger-than-life appeal.

games.title: Super Pac-Man
games.description:
Super Pac-Man is Namco's 1982 official successor to the arcade phenomenon Pac-Man, designed by Toru Iwatani. Rather than clearing rows of small dots, players must eat all the food and prizes hidden behind locked gates. Keys placed around the maze open selected doors, sometimes far from the key itself, creating a new navigational challenge while Blinky, Pinky, Inky and Clyde continue their pursuit.

Traditional power pellets still turn the ghosts vulnerable, but the defining addition is the Super Power pellet. It transforms Pac-Man into an oversized, temporarily invulnerable character who can break through locked gates. A separate speed button allows him to race through the maze while super-powered. Bonus rounds and changing key-door relationships reward planning as well as quick reactions, distinguishing the game from the direct chase of its predecessor.

As Namco's own sequel following the separately developed Ms. Pac-Man, Super Pac-Man is an important, if divisive, branch of the series. Its larger sprites, gates, keys and transformation mechanic are among the boldest changes made to Pac-Man's original arcade formula.

games.title: The Super Spy
games.description:
The Super Spy is SNK's strikingly unusual 1990 Neo Geo action game, combining first-person brawling, gunplay and light role-playing progression. Playing CIA operative Roy Heart, the player infiltrates a skyscraper occupied by terrorists, moving through corridors and elevators, entering rooms, freeing hostages and fighting increasingly dangerous guards. Enemies appear at arm's length, with the hero's fists or weapons visible in the foreground.

Combat mixes punches, kicks, knives and firearms with blocking and careful positioning; gun ammunition and knife condition make weapons finite resources. Hostages supply medical aid, equipment or useful information, while defeating enemies raises experience levels and improves combat strength. Its close-up fights resemble a first-person interpretation of Punch-Out!! crossed with a corridor-based beat-'em-up, making it one of the Neo Geo's most distinctive early releases.

games.title: Super Tank
games.description:
Super Tank is a 1981 overhead tank shooter created by Germany's Video Games GmbH and licensed in other markets. Up to two players maneuver armored vehicles across a field of mines, bushes and enemy tanks, shooting threats while looking for protective diamond bonuses. Clearing the preliminary battlefield leads to a boss encounter against the enormous Super Tank, whose vulnerable point is its gun.

The two-part structure, first clearing hazards and then tackling a single oversized enemy, gives it a recognizable progression uncommon in very early tank games. It was one of the few known original coin-operated games created by the German manufacturer, which also produced Looping.

games.title: Super Triv II
games.description: Super Triv II is a 1986 English-language trivia game from Status Games, part of the company's line of Triv Quiz machines. Its spare, text-focused screen presents a question with three labeled answers and a clearly displayed point value. Players answer through dedicated cabinet buttons, building a score by getting questions right; the game also displays speed bonuses, rewarding quick knowledge as well as correct choices. Subjects range across popular culture and general knowledge. Beneath its uncomplicated presentation is a distinctly arcade-like contest for ever-higher point totals.

games.title: Super Triv III
games.description: Super Triv III, released by Status Games in 1988, continues the company's button-operated, score-based trivia series. English-language questions appear one at a time with three possible answers, a current point value, and the player's running total. Correct answers are confirmed on-screen, and the question selection includes entertainment and film knowledge. Like Super Triv II, it uses an Intel 8085-family processor and an AY-3-8910 sound chip, retaining a simple text-first presentation rather than elaborate animation. This later entry preserves the familiar question-and-answer format, presenting a fresh round of trivia competition without introducing an elaborate action-game component.

games.title: Super-X
games.description:
Super-X is a 1994 vertically scrolling shooter developed by South Korea's Dooyong and distributed in versions associated with Mitchell and N.T.C. Across seven repeating stages, the player pilots a small fighter through dense waves of enemy craft and ground targets, firing a main weapon and conserving screen-clearing bombs. Weapon pickups offer a broad red spread, a blue lightning-style beam or concentrated green fire.

At maximum weapon strength, the fighter enters a temporary Super Power state that unleashes an especially heavy barrage; a dedicated pickup can activate it instantly. Its aggressive pacing, upgrade system and visual style place it firmly in the Raiden school of arcade shoot-'em-ups, while the cycling power surge gives it a mechanic of its own.

games.title: Super Lup Lup Puzzle / Zhuan Zhuan Puzzle

variants.title: Super Lup Lup Puzzle / Zhuan Zhuan Puzzle (version 4.0 / 990518)
Lup Lup Puzzle / Zhuan Zhuan Puzzle (version 3.0 / 990128)
Lup Lup Puzzle / Zhuan Zhuan Puzzle (version 2.9 / 990108)

games.description:
Super Lup Lup Puzzle, also known as Zhuan Zhuan Puzzle, is Omega System's 1999 marble-matching arcade game and an unofficial variation on Mitchell's Puzz Loop. A chain of colored balls snakes along a spiral toward a central goal, while the player rotates a cannon at the center and shoots additional balls into the line. Three or more matching colors disappear, buying time and sometimes creating chain reactions, while occasional special pieces temporarily slow the advancing marbles.

The aim is to remove every ball before the chain reaches the goal. Operators could choose between ordinary picture backgrounds and more risqué photographic rewards through the game's settings, a conspicuous difference from its puzzle-game inspiration. The rapid aiming and color-matching require a different kind of planning from falling-block contests such as Puyo Puyo.

games.title: Super Model
games.description:
Super Model is Comad's 1994 picture-revealing arcade puzzle game, a comparatively restrained reworking of the adult Qix-style New Fantasia. Players draw boundaries across a covered playfield to expose photographs of models, trying to uncover a required percentage before time runs out while avoiding moving enemies. Revealing enough of the image is not the only challenge: an on-screen gauge can shift the hidden picture toward a monster image, forcing careful management of when and where to draw.

This tension between claiming territory and preserving the desired photograph provides an extra layer beyond a straightforward Qix clone. Super Model is notable for replacing the more explicit images associated with some games in its family.

games.title: Super Model II
games.description: Super Model II is a 1997 Comad territory-capture puzzle game in the style of Qix and the Korean Fantasia series. Players trace lines to section off a playfield and reveal a picture beneath it, avoiding enemies while the uncovered area grows. Its adult-themed photographic rewards and straightforward joystick-and-button controls make it part of the large 1990s arcade family of picture-revealing action puzzles rather than a conventional tile or block puzzler.

games.title: Super Nudger II
games.description:
Super Nudger II is a 1989 Coinmaster British prize-machine hybrid, combining the chance-based format of a fruit machine with quiz questions. Rather than relying only on reel outcomes, the player can improve the result through question-answering, bringing skill-based play into a conventional pub-gambling environment. Four buttons provide the simple panel control for the electronic game.

The preserved release is identified as program P173, version 5.21. Its mixture of quiz and fruit-machine ideas makes it more distinctive than a standard slot, although the exact relationship between correct answers, nudges and prizes is not fully documented in surviving references.

games.title: Super Glob
games.description:
Super Glob is a 1983 Epos maze-platform game related to The Glob and Beastie Feastie. Players guide a voracious little creature through multi-level corridors, riding elevators and crossing side passages to eat the food scattered around each stage. Hostile animals patrol the pathways and can contest control of the elevators, forcing the player to improvise escape routes.

The hero can cling to ceilings and drop onto pursuers, turning an ordinary chase into a game about vertical positioning and timing. Clearing the snacks completes a level, with the stages growing more crowded and demanding as play continues. This Super Glob release is chiefly distinguished from its close relatives by its naming and distribution history.

games.title: Super Crown Golf
games.description:
Super Crowns Golf is Nasco's 1989 arcade golf game, the third installment following Crowns Golf and Crowns Golf in Hawaii. Players choose shots and try to play the course while accounting for wind and the varying difficulty of putting and approaching the green. The cabinet combines buttons and directional inputs with a rotary controller, giving shot adjustment a tactile feel.

The game's settings include an indoor practice option and adjustable wind conditions, indicating an emphasis on repeatable shot practice as well as competitive play. It is a relatively rare example of golf remaining part of the late-1980s coin-operated sports market.

games.title: Super League
games.description:
Super League is Sega's 1987 System 16 baseball game, distinguished by specialized arcade controls that mimic aspects of batting and pitching. At the plate the player operates a small batter-shaped lever to adjust the bat's height, then times the swing against pitches that vary in speed and elevation. Pitching uses a trackball and buttons to select height and curve, making the contest unusually physical and immediate.

Close plays receive enlarged cinematic views, adding drama to tight decisions on the bases. The game helped establish the baseball lineage that Sega continued with Tommy Lasorda Baseball on the Mega Drive, but the original arcade machine's mechanical batting control and trackball pitching are distinctive features not reproduced by ordinary home gamepads.

games.title: Super Locomotive
games.description:
Super Locomotive is Sega's charmingly unusual 1982 railway action game. Players drive a steam train from station to station, switching tracks to avoid oncoming locomotives, red signals and road vehicles at crossings. The scrolling upper view shows the train moving through the railway, while an accompanying track diagram helps anticipate dangers ahead.

The locomotive can fire at airborne threats and activate a temporary protective barrier, but both defenses consume energy that must be restored by collecting supplies. Its mixture of route planning, fast reactions and light shooting is very different from conventional racing games. A famous element of its original arcade presentation is its use of a melody derived from Yellow Magic Orchestra's Rydeen.

games.title: Vs. Super Mario Bros.
games.description:
Vs. Super Mario Bros. is Nintendo's 1986 coin-operated adaptation of the Famicom/NES landmark, designed for the company's Vs. System arcade hardware. Mario or Luigi runs and jumps through the Mushroom Kingdom, defeating enemies by landing on them, collecting coins and power-ups, entering pipes and reaching the flagpole at each stage's exit. Its instantly recognizable controls and carefully staged platform obstacles made the original game a worldwide phenomenon.

The arcade version is deliberately tougher than the home game: several layouts are reworked, power-ups and warp opportunities are reduced, and new stages introduce especially demanding obstacles. Some of these stage designs subsequently appeared in Japan's Super Mario Bros. 2, known internationally as The Lost Levels. This is not simply an NES ROM in a cabinet, but a distinct arrangement of the classic adventure crafted for coin-operated play.

games.title: Super Rider
games.description: Super Rider is a 1983 side-scrolling motorcycle action game by Venture Line, also distributed under license by Taito. The rider races over broken bridges, gaps and roadside obstructions, timing jumps to clear hazards and keep moving along the course. Its emphasis is on surviving a series of stunt-like obstacles rather than completing laps against rival motorcycles, placing it closer to an action platform game on wheels than a conventional racing simulator.

games.title: Super Slams
games.description: Super Slams, released in Japan as From TV Animation Slam Dunk: Super Slams, is a 1995 arcade basketball game from Banpresto based on Takehiko Inoue's hugely popular Slam Dunk manga and anime. Four selectable teams compete in lively, stylized matches featuring familiar character designs and exaggerated athletic moves. The licensed presentation and accessible controls favor the dramatic spirit of the series over a detailed basketball simulation, making it a notable anime-related sports release from the mid-1990s.

games.title: Super Trio
games.description:
Super Trio is a bright 1994 Korean run-and-gun platform game by Game Ace. One or two players choose among three cartoon animals, Jake the mouse, Tomi the cat and Brudo the dog, and work through scrolling stages packed with monsters, hazards and useful items. All three heroes share the same abilities, so selection is largely a matter of personality rather than differing move sets.
