Players jump between platforms, shoot enemies, collect food for health and follow direction signs toward each stage's exit and boss encounter. Its playful art recalls early console mascots, but the steady stream of projectiles and cooperative action gives it the rhythm of an arcade shooter.

games.title: Vs. Super Xevious
games.description:
Vs. Super Xevious is Nintendo's Vs. System arcade release of Namco's Super Xevious: Gump no Nazo, part of the influential Xevious line of vertical shooters. Players pilot the Solvalou above enemy territory, using separate attacks against airborne craft and ground installations. The constantly scrolling battlefield mixes aerial formations with concealed ground targets, preserving the dual-layer shooting concept that distinguished the original Xevious.

This particular set is a Vs. System adaptation rather than the standard 1982 Xevious coin-op, and should be understood as a different branch of the series with its own stage and challenge structure.

games.title: Surprise Attack
games.description:
Surprise Attack is Konami's 1990 science-fiction run-and-gun platform game, directed by Castlevania creator Hitoshi Akamatsu. In the year 2031, the operative Red Thunderbolt infiltrates a moon-based installation occupied by terrorists, fighting through corridors and defense systems to locate and disarm planted bombs. Its side-scrolling gunplay and elevated walkways resemble Rolling Thunder and Shinobi, but the setting grows more unusual as the mission progresses.

Later stages exploit the station's artificial gravity, allowing the action to shift across floors, walls and ceilings. This turns even familiar jumping and shooting into a spatial puzzle as the player tries to reach the next bomb before time runs out. The shifting gravity and urgent bomb-disposal objectives make Surprise Attack a distinctive entry in Konami's arcade action catalogue.

games.title: Surf Planet
games.description:
Surf Planet is a 1997 three-dimensional snowboarding arcade game from Gaelco, despite the misleadingly tropical title. Players choose a rider and descend mountain courses such as Mount Cook, Mont Blanc, Mount McKinley and Lake Tahoe, racing against other snowboarders while passing checkpoints to extend the timer. The behind-the-rider view emphasizes high-speed turns, ramps and collisions with competitors.

A standing cabinet with a dedicated control lever contributes to the sensation of shifting balance on a board, and linked cabinets allow competitive racing. Stunts and shortcuts add to the challenge, while the game's rock soundtrack supplies the attitude of late-1990s extreme-sports entertainment.

games.title: Survival Arts
games.description:
Survival Arts is a 1993 fighting game developed by Scarab and published by Sammy, part of the wave of digitized martial-arts games that followed Mortal Kombat. Eight eccentric warriors compete in a tournament of brutal one-on-one fights, with photographed actors converted into animated sprites and an emphasis on grisly finishing attacks. Its lurid costumes, oversized weapons and bloody effects distinguish it from the cleaner cartoon aesthetic of many Japanese fighters.

Players use standard joystick-based movement, attacks and character-specific special techniques to defeat successive rivals. Planned Super Nintendo and Mega Drive ports never reached release, leaving the arcade original as the main way to experience this peculiar Mortal Kombat contemporary. The game also has a small historical connection to Scarab's later action title Dyna Gear, which reused background figures from one of its stages.

games.title: Survival
games.description:
Survival is a rare 1982 overhead maze shooter from Rock-Ola with an unusual microscopic theme. The player controls a blue cell traveling through a network of veins and membranes, firing medicine at viruses and shooting away sections of the maze itself. Obstacles can be removed, but destroying the wrong elements changes how the remaining enemies behave, so reckless shooting is not always helpful.

Progress involves clearing the cellular labyrinth, manipulating the viruses and reaching the next stage before the increasingly crowded environment becomes fatal. Its abstract setting and destructible pathways make it notably different from Rock-Ola's better-known Nibbler.

games.title: Susume! Taisen Puzzle-Dama
games.description:
Susume! Taisen Puzzle-Dama is a 1996 Konami competitive falling-ball puzzle game in the Taisen Puzzle-Dama series. Pairs of colored balls descend into each player's well, and groups of three or more large balls disappear when connected. Smaller encased balls cannot be removed directly: they must first be transformed by clearing adjacent large balls, creating opportunities for explosive chain reactions.

Clearing combinations sends nuisance pieces to the opponent, so careful setup matters as much as keeping the well from filling. Colorful anime-styled characters and lively reactions turn its abstract matching rules into a cheerful head-to-head contest. It is closely related to Puyo Puyo in competitive spirit, but the conversion of small balls into large ones provides a different tactical rhythm.

games.title: Suzuka 8 Hours 2
games.description:
Suzuka 8 Hours 2 is Namco's 1993 motorcycle racing follow-up on System 2 hardware. The player races against the clock and computer-controlled riders from a fast behind-the-bike perspective, weaving through traffic and avoiding crashes that squander precious seconds. In addition to the Japanese Suzuka circuit, this edition provides other tracks, including Green Hill, Bayside and a mountain course, broadening the original game's limited selection.

The arcade presentation centers on motorcycle-style controls rather than a typical steering wheel, making weight transfer and cornering feel physically involving. It retains the first game's endurance-racing identity while offering more varied scenery and race routes.

games.title: Suzuka 8 Hours
games.description:
Suzuka 8 Hours is Namco's 1992 motorcycle arcade racer based on the famous Japanese endurance event at Suzuka Circuit. Instead of attempting an eight-hour simulation, players race a short series of timed laps, negotiating bends and overtaking other motorcycles without crashing. Contact with barriers or other riders throws the racer from the bike and costs the time needed to finish.

The behind-the-bike view and dedicated motorcycle-shaped riding controls are central to its appeal. As the race advances, the scenery moves from daylight toward evening, evoking the changing conditions of the real event. Its popularity led directly to Suzuka 8 Hours 2 the following year.

games.title: Watashiha Suzumechan
games.description: Watashiha Suzumechan, whose title translates as 'I Am Suzume-chan', is a Japanese adult-themed mahjong game released by Dyna Electronics in 1986. It presents the traditional tile game in an anime-styled amusement setting, with illustrated character imagery and a gambling-oriented format. Rather than a tile-matching puzzle, its underlying attraction is mahjong itself: drawing and discarding tiles to build a winning hand. The game's compact Z80-based hardware, square video display, and Japanese-only release mark it as a product of the busy mid-1980s market for specialized mahjong arcade cabinets.

games.title: SvC Chaos - SNK vs Capcom

variants.title: SvC Chaos - SNK vs Capcom Plus (set 1, bootleg)
SvC Chaos - SNK vs Capcom Plus (set 2, bootleg)
SvC Chaos - SNK vs Capcom Super Plus (bootleg)

games.description:
SVC Chaos: SNK vs. Capcom is SNK Playmore's 2003 crossover fighting game, bringing characters from the two rival arcade companies together on Neo Geo hardware. Fighters from The King of Fighters, Fatal Fury and Samurai Shodown meet Street Fighter regulars and less expected Capcom figures, with character-specific exchanges before matches celebrating the franchises' histories. The game uses one-on-one rounds rather than team battles.

Its four-button controls, evasive movement and cancel-based offense are closer to SNK's King of Fighters tradition than to Capcom vs. SNK's selectable groove system. A power gauge enables super moves and powerful Exceed attacks, while the Front Grand Step adds a distinctive forward-movement option. The roster's unusual matchups, austere backgrounds and dark character art give this crossover a personality unlike Capcom's more exuberant versus titles.

SVC Chaos was a late major release for the original Neo Geo arcade platform. Its presence in arcades and on later home systems demonstrates how enduring both companies' fighting-game characters had become by the early 2000s.

games.title: SvC Chaos - SNK vs Capcom

variants.title: SvC Chaos - SNK vs Capcom (JAMMA PCB)
SVC Chaos - SNK vs CAPCOM (JAMMA PCB, set 2)

games.description:
SVC Chaos: SNK vs. Capcom (PCB version) is the dedicated arcade-board edition of SNK Playmore's 2003 Neo Geo crossover fighter. The underlying contest is the same as the MVS cartridge release: familiar SNK and Capcom combatants battle in one-on-one matches using four attack buttons, special-move cancels, a super-power gauge and devastating Exceed techniques. Brief character-specific dialogue makes the unexpected matchups part of the attraction.

What distinguishes this set in AdvanceMAME is its board configuration rather than a separate game design. It documents the dedicated-PCB form of a title more commonly associated with Neo Geo MVS cartridges, while preserving the same late-era SNK fighting style and roster.

games.title: Super Visual Football: European Sega Cup

variants.title: Super Visual Football: European Sega Cup

games.description:
Super Visual Football: European Sega Cup is Sega's 1994 European arcade football game on System 32 hardware. It is a regional form of the Japanese J.League 1994, whose licensed Japanese club competition was adapted for different markets. Players control footballers on the pitch with an eight-way joystick and three action buttons, passing, shooting and challenging opponents in quick arcade matches.

The game emphasizes direct play rather than detailed team management. It is especially notable as a regional conversion of Sega's Japanese league football title, with the identity of the competition changed for European arcades.

games.title: S.V.G. - Spectral vs Generation / Sheng Mo Shiji

variants.title: S.V.G. - Spectral vs Generation / Sheng Mo Shiji (M68k label V200) (ARM label V200, ROM 10/11/05 S.V.G V201)
variants.version: (M68k label V200) (ARM label V200, ROM 10/11/05 S.V.G V201)

games.description:
S.V.G.: Spectral vs Generation is a 2005 crossover fighting game created by Idea Factory for IGS's PGM arcade system. Its cast comes from Idea Factory's fantasy role-playing properties Spectral Force and Generation of Chaos, bringing swordfighters, magic users and other familiar characters into one-on-one combat. Players choose among a roster of warriors with individual weapons, special moves and fighting styles, competing in best-of-three battles.

The title is unusual for adapting characters from turn-based fantasy RPGs into a conventional 2D fighting format rather than drawing from an existing arcade franchise. Later PlayStation 2 and PSP versions helped give this relatively obscure PGM release a wider audience.

games.title: Super Volleyball
games.description:
Super Volleyball is Video System's 1989 arcade simulation of international indoor volleyball. Players choose among national teams and coordinate the classic sequence of receiving, setting and spiking the ball across the net. Timing matters on both sides: a well-prepared attack can score decisively, while properly positioned front-row players can leap to block a rival's spike.

The sport's back-and-forth rhythm translates naturally to two-player competition, with little downtime between points. Super Volleyball became one of the better-known arcade treatments of the sport and was adapted for several home systems, where its precise timing and tactical ball placement remained the main attraction.

games.title: Star Wars Arcade
games.description:
Star Wars Arcade is Sega's 1993 polygonal space-combat game, bringing the original trilogy's battles to the Model 1 arcade era. Players fly Rebel starfighters through an asteroid field and against TIE fighters, strike at an Imperial capital ship and attempt the climactic assault on the Death Star. The stages use rapidly moving three-dimensional scenery and cinematic viewpoints to create the feeling of participating in the films' space battles.

Its two-person cabinet has a particularly clever cooperative arrangement: one player pilots and fires forward, while a second acts as a gunner who can aim independently across the screen. That division of labor makes the experience different from Atari's classic 1983 Star Wars vector shooter, even though both share the thrill of attacking the Death Star. Sega's powerful Model 1 hardware was crucial to its fully polygonal presentation.

games.title: SWAT
games.description:
SWAT is a 1984 abstract action shooter developed by Coreland for Sega's System 1 hardware, not a conventional police or military combat game. Players steer small armed agents around a playfield split into blue and purple tunnel sections, trying to prevent strange aliens from completing pathways between the bottom and top of the screen. Enemy Blockers extend the tunnels, while other creatures chase the players or attack from the completed structures.

Shots can destroy vulnerable sections, and the agents can push some tunnel pieces out of alignment to break a dangerous connection. Smart bombs clear nearby enemies but require careful positioning. The distinctive tunnel-building battle gives SWAT a strong puzzle-like element alongside its frantic shooting.

games.title: SWAT Police
games.description: SWAT Police is a 2001 arcade action shooter by South Korean company ESD. Players take the roles of police officers Cruise and James in a horizontally scrolling succession of firefights against armed criminals. Although it resembles a shooting-gallery game, aiming and movement are handled with a joystick and action buttons rather than a light gun. Two players can join forces, turning the confrontations into cooperative gunplay instead of a solitary target-shooting exercise.

games.title: Super World Court
games.description:
Super World Court is Namco's 1992 arcade tennis game, expanding the World Court line with a larger selectable roster and colorful venues. Players can contest singles or doubles matches using an eight-way joystick and shot buttons, positioning themselves on the court to return serves, approach the net and place winners. Up to four competitors can participate in doubles on suitable cabinets.

Courts include American hard court, French clay, British grass and a whimsical Namco-themed location with a Pac-Man cameo. The mixture of recognizable tennis rules and a playful presentation makes it an accessible bridge between straightforward early sports simulations and later arcade tennis games.

games.title: Swimmer
games.description:
Swimmer is a 1982 vertically scrolling action game by Tehkan, later known as Tecmo. The player guides a swimmer through hazardous waters, gathering floating fruit for points while dodging hostile wildlife and other obstacles on the route to a treasure island. A dedicated dive action lets the character duck beneath threats, turning vertical timing into the central survival skill.

Its unusual aquatic setting and mixture of sideways swimming, quick dives and collectible power-ups distinguish it from the era's crowded field of land-based maze games and space shooters. The deceptively simple course becomes steadily more treacherous as the screen scrolls onward.

games.title: Super World Stadium
games.description:
Super World Stadium is Namco's early-1990s arcade baseball series entry, translating Japanese professional-style baseball into a fast, approachable coin-op game. Batters position themselves in the box and time their swings, while pitchers choose deliveries and fielders handle the ball after contact. Bunting, base stealing and defensive decisions give the game more depth than a simple hitting contest.

Its colorful player sprites, compact matches and familiar Namco sports presentation set the pattern for numerous yearly Super World Stadium updates. This original release is the foundation of a long-running series whose later editions updated the season identity while preserving the core arcade baseball mechanics.

games.title: Super World Stadium '92
games.description:
Super World Stadium '92 is Namco's 1992 seasonal edition of its colorful arcade baseball series. Players pitch, bat, field and run bases in full matches, choosing a lineup and trying to outscore the opposing team. Hitting depends on placing the batter and timing the swing, while bunts, steals and strategic pitching add variety beyond simply swinging for home runs.

Rather than reinventing the series, the '92 edition continues its quick-playing Japanese baseball formula with a contemporary season presentation. It remains a useful snapshot of Namco's early annual approach to sports games.

games.title: Super World Stadium '93
games.description:
Super World Stadium '93 is Namco's 1993 follow-up in its series of arcade baseball games. A match proceeds through pitching, batting, fielding and base running, with players using the joystick to position the batter and action buttons to swing, bunt or attempt steals. The bright sprite graphics and brisk play make the rules of baseball accessible within a coin-operated format.

As an annual edition it retains the established Super World Stadium mechanics while reflecting the series' progression through successive Japanese baseball seasons. The pleasure lies in quick tactical decisions at the plate and in the field rather than in complex front-office management.

games.title: Super World Stadium '95
games.description:
Super World Stadium '95 continues Namco's long-running arcade baseball series with a 1995-season presentation and the familiar balance of accessible action and baseball tactics. Players control both the offensive and defensive sides of a full match: choose pitches, time swings, field batted balls and send runners toward the next base. Careful batting position and well-timed bunts can be just as useful as a powerful hit.

The game's colorful, slightly exaggerated visuals suit a coin-operated contest, while the yearly edition structure made it a continuing attraction for fans of Japanese baseball.

games.title: Super World Stadium '96
games.description:
Super World Stadium '96 is Namco's 1996 arcade baseball installment, carrying forward the series' fast innings and approachable controls. The player handles batting, pitching, fielding and base running, trying to exploit pitch selection and batting timing to manufacture runs. Bunting and stealing bases keep the contest from becoming a simple home-run competition.

The dated title marks another annual season iteration rather than a separate kind of baseball game. It offers a mid-1990s version of Namco's recognizable, colorful ballpark presentation and competitive two-player sports action.

games.title: Super World Stadium '97
games.description:
Super World Stadium '97 is a 1997 installment in Namco's established coin-operated baseball series. Players contest innings by pitching, striking the ball, fielding and advancing runners, with direct joystick-and-button control over important plays. Shot placement, the timing of a swing and decisions about stealing or sacrificing bases all contribute to scoring.

The annual release continues the series' bright arcade treatment of Japanese baseball, favoring a rapid, readable match over a painstaking statistical simulation. It belongs to the late-1990s run of seasonal Super World Stadium updates.

games.title: Super World Stadium '98
games.description:
Super World Stadium '98 is Namco's Japan-only 1998 arcade baseball entry. It belongs to the company's yearly line of sports games, in which players directly handle batting, pitching and fielding while using bunts, base-running choices and well-timed swings to build an advantage. The familiar Super World Stadium formula emphasizes colorful ballpark action and short competitive matches rather than a detailed baseball management simulation.

As the 1998 installment, its primary historical distinction is its place in the sequence of seasonal revisions to Namco's arcade baseball series.

games.title: Super World Stadium '99
games.description:
Super World Stadium '99 is Namco's 1999 seasonal update of the arcade baseball series. Batting involves selecting a position in the box and timing the swing, while pitching, fielding and base-running controls turn each inning into a mixture of reflexes and tactical choices. Bunting and attempted steals can change the course of a close game.

The release preserves the familiar colorful presentation and approachable full-match structure of earlier Super World Stadium games, documenting the series' continued life in Japanese arcades toward the end of the decade.

games.title: Star Wars Trilogy
games.description:
Star Wars Trilogy Arcade is Sega's lavish 1998 Model 3 shooting attraction based on the three original Star Wars films. The player relives famous sequences, including the Death Star attack, the battle of Hoth and the forest battle on Endor, using a joystick-controlled targeting reticle to destroy Imperial ships, walkers and other threats. The arcade cabinet's large display, music and voice samples are designed to make the journey feel like an interactive collection of film set pieces.

Special event prompts occasionally allow actions outside ordinary shooting, and boss confrontations include encounters with Darth Vader and Boba Fett. The missions vary between spacecraft combat, vehicle-based battles and on-foot action, making the game broader than a single continuous rail shooter.

Sega's powerful Model 3 graphics hardware gives the scenes sweeping polygonal environments and dense action, while recognizable sound and settings provide much of the emotional impact. The game is remembered as one of the major licensed arcade spectacles of the late 1990s, and one never given a straightforward contemporary home conversion.

games.title: Pachinko Sexy Reaction 2
games.description:
Pachinko Sexy Reaction 2 is the 1999 follow-up to the Japanese arcade pachinko simulation, again combining ball-launching play with adult-oriented anime reward scenes. Players try to complete challenges on several themed pachinko tables, using their outcomes to advance through a total of sixteen rounds. The new game expands the setting to locations including a swimming pool, zoo and beach, and later offers alternate routes through funfair, city, restaurant or cinema-themed stages.

Like the first game, its core action centers on manipulating the flow of balls through a pachinko machine rather than controlling a traditional platform-game character. The branching stage structure and greater number of rounds distinguish this sequel from its predecessor.

games.title: Pachinko Sexy Reaction
games.description:
Pachinko Sexy Reaction is a 1998 Japanese arcade simulation of pachinko with risqué anime presentation. Players launch metal balls into pinball-like pachinko layouts, trying to achieve the objectives of five different machines. Each table has its own arrangement and rules, with some incorporating slot-machine-style elements alongside the main ball-launching action.

Success unlocks increasingly revealing illustrations of one of five anime heroines, making the reward scenes a major part of the game's identity. Its combination of pachinko mechanics and adult-oriented visual rewards places it within a distinctly Japanese branch of late-1990s amusement games.

games.title: Syvalion
games.description:
Syvalion is Taito's 1988 multi-directional action shooter built around an extraordinary control scheme: the player steers a golden mechanical dragon with a trackball and incinerates robotic enemies with its breath. Rather than simply following a fixed horizontal route, the dragon winds through enclosed labyrinths, passing obstacles and taking on massive bosses at the end of stages.

Fire breath is limited by an energy gauge that must be replenished, forcing a balance between attacking and maneuvering. The game's branching routes and changing stage layouts add variety to repeat attempts. Its distinctive dragon protagonist, large animated machinery and tactile trackball movement make Syvalion one of Taito's most inventive late-1980s action games.

games.title: Super Zaxxon
games.description:
Super Zaxxon is Sega's 1982 follow-up to its groundbreaking isometric shooter Zaxxon, retaining the striking diagonal viewpoint while making the challenge faster and more punishing. Players pilot a spacecraft through heavily defended fortresses, dodging walls, gun emplacements and enemy fighters. The craft can climb and dive as well as move laterally, and its shadow and on-screen altitude indicator help the player judge whether it will clear obstacles or strike targets.

Fuel drains continuously and must be replenished by destroying fuel tanks, so the player has to balance cautious flying with attacking ground installations. A stretch of outer-space combat separates the fortress sections, and a mechanical enemy waits at the end. Super Zaxxon is more than a simple graphical revision: altered terrain and aggressive enemy placement put greater demands on players already accustomed to the unusual perspective.

The original Zaxxon's simulated depth was a landmark of early-1980s arcade design. Super Zaxxon extends that idea into a tougher specialist sequel, retaining an unmistakable visual identity in an era when most shooters still scrolled purely vertically or horizontally.

games.title: Tac/Scan
games.description:
Tac/Scan is Sega's distinctive 1982 vector-graphics shoot-'em-up, controlled with a rotary dial and played on a vertically oriented monitor. Instead of piloting a lone craft, the player commands a formation of seven fighters that fire together, creating broad salvos against enemy squadrons. Individual ships can be lost, and replacements can be collected, making the surviving formation itself an important resource.

The action rotates through several different perspectives: a conventional advancing armada, a more dramatic pseudo-3D attack, and a space-warp tunnel that demands careful dodging. Maintaining enough ships to survive later encounters is as important as scoring hits. Its vibrant vector effects, stereo sound and unusual squadron system make it one of Sega's most inventive early shooters.

games.title: Tactician
games.description:
Tactician is an early-1980s shooter developed by Konami and licensed to Sega that adds a defensive construction phase to familiar fixed-screen alien combat. The player controls a small ship near the bottom of the display, with some freedom to move vertically as well as horizontally. Before each wave, the player can place small barrier elements around the field, creating obstacles intended to disrupt the approaching enemies.

Once the attack begins, the ship must shoot the invaders and navigate around the positions established earlier. The result is an unusual combination of shooter reflexes and advance planning: protective walls can help, but an awkward arrangement may also restrict movement. This simple but distinctive idea sets Tactician apart from straightforward Space Invaders imitators.

games.title: Tail to Nose - Great Championship
games.description:
Tail to Nose: Great Championship is a 1989 overhead Formula One-style racing game by Video System, released in Japan as Super Formula: Chijou Saisoku no Battle. From its vertically scrolling, bird's-eye view, players guide a single-seater around winding racing circuits, timing turns and overtaking rival cars while trying to maintain speed. The teams, drivers and sponsors evoke the 1988 Formula One season, though their names were altered rather than officially licensed.

Its clear top-down perspective favors racing lines and precision over the cockpit spectacle of contemporary pseudo-3D racers. Tail to Nose began a line of Video System Formula racing games that continued with the F-1 Grand Prix series, making it a significant early entry in the developer's motorsport catalogue.

games.title: Tailgunner
games.description:
Tailgunner is Vectorbeam's 1979 black-and-white vector shooter with a wonderfully unconventional point of view. Rather than flying toward enemies, the player mans the rear gun of a large spacecraft and watches hostile fighters approach from behind. Groups of attackers rush across the screen, and the gunner moves crosshairs to shoot them before they slip out of range.

The battlefield's moving starfield emphasizes the reversed perspective, while a limited defensive shield provides an emergency way to survive threatening formations. The crisp vector lines and viewpoint make Tailgunner feel almost like an early three-dimensional targeting simulator. It is also historically notable as one of the distinctive releases associated with the short-lived Vectorbeam operation and Cinematronics' vector-arcade lineage.

games.title: Taito FX1
games.description:
Taito FX1 is the BIOS for Taito's arcade platform based on Sony ZN-1 PlayStation-derived hardware, introduced around 1995. It combines Sony's MIPS processor and 3D graphics circuitry with Taito-designed ROM boards, sound devices, and cabinet connections. Like other ZN-derived systems, the firmware is specific to the manufacturer's hardware configuration rather than interchangeable with every Sony arcade board.

Two principal FX-1 sound-board arrangements are documented. One uses a Z80 with a Yamaha YM2610 synthesizer, while another employs Taito-associated Zoom sound hardware with a dedicated sample processor. These variations demonstrate how Taito adapted a common 3D-capable foundation to different production requirements. This entry holds the FX-1 startup code, not a self-contained program.

games.title: Taito GNET
games.description:
Taito G-NET is a Sony ZN-2-derived arcade system introduced around 1998, using PlayStation-family processing and graphics alongside a distinctive removable-media arrangement. Its hardware comprises a Sony motherboard, a Taito board containing sound and flash-storage circuitry, and a separate interface for protected PCMCIA-format cards. Optional boards could add communication or save-data functions.

G-NET's boot process is particularly unusual. Its firmware checks the inserted card and compares it with data already held in onboard flash memory. When the stored contents do not match, the machine updates its flash memory from the card before restarting. This approach combined operator-friendly media changes with security and a local cache, making the BIOS and its flash-handling behavior central to the system's operation.

games.title: Taiwan Mahjong
games.description: Taiwan Mahjong is a 1988 Japanese medal mahjong game from Miki Syouji, preserved in AdvanceMAME in its December 8, 1988 betting version. It uses a horizontal screen and presents a coin-operated version of the traditional tile game, in which players work toward a winning hand rather than clearing a puzzle board. The '[BET]' designation reflects its wagering-oriented arcade format. The surviving hardware uses a Z80 processor, AY-3-8910 sound and a digital-to-analog audio channel, a relatively modest setup for a game built around table play instead of animated action.

games.title: Talbot
games.description:
Talbot is a quirky 1982 maze game by Volt Electronics. The player is a small rabbit breeder whose animals have escaped into a field of corridors, and the goal is to gather them before thieves can make off with them. A loyal hunting dog accompanies the farmer and can be directed to help guard or trap troublemakers, adding an unusual companion-management element to the chase.

The maze must be crossed under time pressure while collecting food or milk to replenish energy and avoiding the thieves' attacks. Rather than simply eating every object in a maze, Talbot asks the player to protect and recover moving animals, giving the familiar early-1980s chase format a distinctive rural theme.

games.title: Tangram Q
games.description:
Tangram Q is an obscure 1983 SNK arcade puzzle game inspired by the traditional Chinese tangram. The aim is to assemble a target silhouette from a selection of geometric pieces before the timer expires. Its vertically oriented display and simple left-right joystick and button interface adapt a tabletop shape-recognition challenge to a coin-operated format.

Instead of testing shooting accuracy or speed of movement, Tangram Q rewards visual reasoning: the player must recognize how separate pieces fit together to reproduce the given figure. Its unusual subject makes it an early example of an arcade game centered on a traditional spatial puzzle.

games.title: Tang Tang
games.description:
Tang Tang is a 2000 action-puzzle platform game that takes much of its inspiration from Tecmo's Solomon's Key. One or two players select cartoon space heroes known as the Tangibles and negotiate single-screen stages, creating and removing blocks to build stairs, seal off enemies or reach otherwise inaccessible areas. Collecting the required energy crystals opens the exit portal to the next level.

A limited supply of projectile attacks offers protection against monsters, but success depends more on arranging platforms and planning routes than on shooting everything in sight. Boss encounters punctuate the progression. The block-building mechanic turns each stage into a small improvisational puzzle, especially when a second player joins the action.

games.title: Tank 8
games.description:
Tank 8 is Kee Games' remarkable 1976 eight-player combat arcade game, one of the earliest coin-ops designed around a large group competing simultaneously. Eight small tanks share a single overhead battlefield filled with walls and mines. Each player uses dedicated directional controls to maneuver and fire shells at the others, with hits scoring points and explosions turning the crowded arena into chaotic competition.

Operators can select free-for-all combat or team play, in which players cooperate against tanks assigned to the opposite side. Accommodating eight people at once required a distinctive oversized cabinet and an unusually social setup for the era. Tank 8 expanded the head-to-head ideas of Atari's earlier Tank into a genuine multiplayer arena years before such experiences became common.

games.title: Tank Battalion
games.description:
Tank Battalion is Namco's 1980 overhead tank shooter and an important ancestor of Battle City and Tank Force. The player defends an eagle-marked headquarters inside a maze of destructible brick walls while enemy tanks enter from above. Each round requires destroying twenty opponents, but the game ends immediately if an invader reaches and shoots the base, even when the player still has lives remaining.

The player can blast gaps through walls to create shorter routes or firing lanes, though a badly placed shot can also expose the headquarters to attack. As different enemy patterns and maze layouts appear, the best defense becomes a balance between intercepting threats and preserving the cover around the base. Its simple defensive premise would be refined and popularized in later Namco tank games.

games.title: Tank Busters
games.description: Tank Busters is Valadon Automation's 1985 overhead maze shooter. The player drives an armed tank through a town laid out as connected streets and obstacles, searching for enemy bases to destroy. Fuel is limited, so collecting refills along the route is essential while navigating toward the remaining targets and fending off threats. The combination of exploration, target hunting and a constantly draining fuel supply makes it more of a tactical action maze than a straight battlefield duel.

games.title: Tank Force
games.description:
Tank Force is Namco's 1991 return to the base-defense formula pioneered by Tank Battalion and popularized by Battle City. Players maneuver small tanks through top-down mazes, protecting an eagle-marked headquarters while destroying incoming enemies. Different enemy vehicles have distinct movement and attack patterns, and walls can be blown apart to create new firing lanes or expose the base to danger.

A large assortment of pickups supplies stronger shots, shields, explosions and other temporary advantages, greatly expanding the original game's tactical possibilities. Two players can cooperate on a standard upright cabinet, while certain configurations allow four simultaneous players. Its cheerful graphics and increasingly busy arenas make Tank Force both a nostalgic sequel and a highly enjoyable cooperative arcade game.

games.title: Puzzle & Action: Tant-R
games.description:
Puzzle & Action: Tant-R is Sega's 1992 collection of rapid-fire mini-games and the first entry in its popular Puzzle & Action series. Starring the detectives Robo and Mobo from Bonanza Bros., it presents a succession of timed challenges instead of one continuous type of action. Players may need to count objects, remember patterns, identify the correct picture or solve a brief visual puzzle before the clock runs out.

Each stage offers a rotating selection of mini-games, and players must clear enough challenges to advance. The unpredictable changes of task and the pressure of a short timer are the main attraction, especially with friends sharing the controls. Tant-R helped establish a durable arcade format in which observation, quick thinking and party-game competition take precedence over traditional shooting or platforming.

games.title: Tao Taido
games.description:
Tao Taido is Video System's unusual 1993 fighting game about eight martial artists seeking the secrets of a legendary combat discipline. It follows the familiar side-on tournament format, with distinctive fighters, special techniques and a succession of increasingly difficult opponents, but uses an unusually compact two-button attack scheme. The game also features an unconventional cooperative two-player option rather than being limited to ordinary competitive matches.

Its eccentric character art and experimental control ideas set it apart from the more standardized fighters that followed Street Fighter II. Malcolm, one of its combatants, later made a cameo-like return as a pilot in Video System's Aero Fighters 3.

games.title: Tapper
games.description:
Tapper is Bally Midway's 1983 arcade classic about the impossible demands of running a crowded bar. Players control a bartender at four parallel serving counters, sliding full mugs toward approaching customers and collecting the returning empties before they fall and break. Patrons who reach the bartender without service cost a life, so success requires an increasingly frantic rhythm of pouring, changing lanes and catching glasses.

The cabinet is a major part of its history: it was designed to evoke a real bar, with a brass-colored foot rail, drink-holder details and a dedicated beer-tap-shaped controller instead of an ordinary firing button. Different stages depict rowdy customers in varied drinking establishments, while bonus rounds challenge the player to identify the one unshaken can after a shuffle.

Tapper was originally associated with Budweiser branding, an unusual promotional arrangement for an arcade game. A later alcohol-free version, Root Beer Tapper, substituted a more family-friendly theme while preserving the ingenious service mechanics. The distinctive controller, humorous animations and mounting multitasking pressure have made Tapper an enduring arcade favorite.

games.title: Targ
games.description:
Targ is Exidy's 1980 maze shooter, set in a grid of streets called Crystal City. The player steers a small green vehicle named the Wummel around blocks of buildings, firing at aggressive red Targ craft that try to ram it. Unlike many space shooters, most of these enemies have no guns: their threat comes from cornering the player in the network of narrow streets.

Occasionally a faster, blue Spectar smuggler appears and can be destroyed for extra points. Clearing a wave of Targs advances the game to a tougher pattern, making route selection and shooting lanes increasingly important. Targ's combination of a geometric urban maze and roaming attackers was an early contribution to the maze-shooter genre, and its world was revisited in Exidy's Spectar.

games.title: Target Hits
games.description:
Target Hits is a 1994 light-gun arcade game by Gaelco organized around several shooting-gallery challenges rather than a conventional scrolling adventure. One mode is a target range where moving targets must be hit accurately without shooting skulls; missed targets and mistakes cost lives. Other scenes use different themes and target arrangements, requiring quick recognition as well as steady aim.

One or two players can compete for scores and accuracy, with results displayed after each section. Its attraction is the variety of short, skill-based light-gun tests, emphasizing precision and reaction time over a long narrative campaign.

games.title: Tarzan
games.description:
Tarzan is a 1999 electronic gambling/medal machine from International Games System (IGS), not an adaptation of Disney's Tarzan platform game released in the same year. The original program belongs to IGS's Asian video-slot catalogue, with a button-driven gambling interface and a horizontal display. Different preserved revisions include V107 and V109C; later dumps document additional program variants.

The cabinet's Z80-family technology and medal-machine classification place it firmly in the late-1990s amusement-gambling market. Detailed reel and bonus rules are not reliably described in the available archival records, so similarities to the unrelated Disney game should not be inferred.

games.title: Time Attacker
games.description:
Time Attacker is a little-known Shonan paddle-and-ball arcade game from the early 1980s, built around the basic premise of breaking colored brick formations before time runs out. The player moves a paddle along the bottom of the screen, bouncing a ball back toward rows of red and green blocks. Hitting blocks removes them, while missing the return wastes valuable time or a life.

The machine also provides configurable special hazards, including enemy appearances and oil zones, which complicate an otherwise minimalist Breakout-style contest. Its unusual timer-oriented rules and rotary paddle control make it an obscure variation on one of the arcade industry's foundational action-puzzle designs.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Tattoo Assassins
games.description:
Tattoo Assassins is a notorious unreleased 1994 fighting-game prototype developed by Data East Pinball as a proposed rival to Mortal Kombat. Its premise revolves around mystical ink that allows fighters' tattoos to become real weapons and creatures. Nine eccentric combatants battle one another using digitized actor sprites, special attacks and over-the-top finishing moves, with the absurdity deliberately pushed far beyond the more serious martial-arts tournaments of the time.

The project was associated with Back to the Future screenwriter Bob Gale and Data East executive Joe Kaminkow, and was developed under an aggressive deadline. A small number of prototypes were tested, but the game was cancelled before a commercial arcade release. Surviving versions show an extraordinary range of grotesque and joke finishing animations, providing a fascinating glimpse into the excesses of the early-1990s fighting-game boom.

games.title: Taxi Driver
games.description: Taxi Driver is a 1984 Japanese maze-driving arcade game released under the Graphic Techno EW name, a joint label associated with Seibu Lease and Vic Tokai. Rather than a behind-the-car racing simulation, it presents driving as a top-down, maze-oriented action challenge on a vertical screen. Players guide their vehicle with a four-way joystick and two buttons, taking turns in the two-player mode. The board is notably elaborate for such a modest-looking game, using three Z80 processors and a pair of AY-3-8910 sound chips. The title should not be confused with unrelated home-computer games or later taxi simulators.

games.title: Tazz-Mania
games.description:
Stern Electronics' Tazz-Mania (1982) combines the room-by-room combat of Berzerk with the frantic, open-area shooting associated with Robotron: 2084. Players move in eight directions, clearing stationary targets known as hoppers while shooting or evading different moving enemies. The exits open once the targets are destroyed, but the room's side walls steadily close inward, creating a constant choice between collecting points and escaping before being crushed.

Smart bombs eliminate threats and halt the walls, and periodic bonus rooms provide a chance to replenish supplies. Although related in spirit to Stern's earlier maze shooters, its changing enemy patterns and collapsing arenas make it a game of time management as much as marksmanship. AdvanceMAME also preserves different sets and a notable bootleg conversion using Galaxian-derived hardware.

games.title: The Block Kuzushi
games.description: The Block Kuzushi is a Japanese Breakout-style arcade game developed by Tamsoft and published by D3 Publisher in February 2000. Players maneuver a bat to keep a ball in play and clear arrangements of blocks, following the classic ball-and-paddle formula associated with Breakout and Arkanoid. Unusually for the genre, its Tecmo ZN-1 arcade-board implementation was designed to be playable with a joystick rather than relying on a dedicated paddle or spinner. It stands out as a late example of a simple arcade concept running on PlayStation-derived hardware, complete with polished audiovisual presentation.

games.title: Tecmo Bowl
games.description:
Tecmo Bowl (1987) is Tecmo's influential American-football arcade game, played on a distinctive wide cabinet with two adjacent monitors and support for as many as four participants. Players guide the fictional Wildcats or Bulldogs through fast, side-view football, choosing from a compact playbook of four offensive moves. On defense, anticipating the opponent's play can disrupt blocking and pass routes, while successful runs depend on finding openings and breaking tackles.

The original arcade release is quite different from the later, better-known Nintendo Entertainment System game: it has only two fictional teams, larger and more colorful graphics, and a four-player setup, whereas the home version added licensed real-player rosters. Tecmo Bowl's accessible blend of play calling and immediate action became the foundation for the enormously popular Tecmo Super Bowl series. Surviving arcade revisions include Japanese and international boards, as well as an early test-location prototype documented by preservationists.

games.title: Twin Bee Yahhoo!
games.description:
TwinBee Yahho! (1995), subtitled Fushigi no Kuni de Oabare!!, is Konami's colorful final arcade installment in the original TwinBee shooting trilogy. Players fly the cartoonish TwinBee and WinBee through whimsical vertically scrolling stages, blasting airborne enemies while bombing targets on the ground. Striking clouds releases bells whose changing colors award different upgrades, while rescue and cooperative attacks retain the series' playful two-player identity.

This installment adds substantial customization before the first stage: players choose a difficulty course, one of four charged attacks, and a control scheme separating or combining shots and bombs. Charged punches, duplicate-ship attacks and bursts in multiple directions encourage different play styles. Its expressive presentation includes voice acting and a vocal theme by Mariko Kouda, and it later appeared with Detana!! TwinBee on PlayStation and Saturn. Konami also prepared an English-language version called Magical TwinBee, although it did not receive a conventional international arcade launch.

games.title: Thunder Ceptor
games.description:
Namco's Thunder Ceptor (1986) puts players in the cockpit of a futuristic fighter rushing down a simulated three-dimensional corridor toward heavily armed enemies. An analog flight stick controls the craft with aircraft-style inverted vertical movement, while a pedal accelerates and separate weapons include a rapid-fire cannon and a limited stock of powerful bombs. A central radar, energy gauge and progress display help the pilot survive enemy formations and large battleships.

Its scaling perspective and mixed-processor hardware marked an ambitious technical experiment for Namco between its early sprite-based shooters and later polygonal games. The arcade release was Japan-only, and the later 3-D Thunder Ceptor II added a stereoscopic viewing system. The original's distinctive arcade flight controls and energetic soundtrack make it a particularly unusual entry in Namco's 1980s shooter catalog.

games.title: Taiwan Chess Legend
games.description:
Taiwan Chess Legend is a mid-1990s Uniwang tabletop and medal-oriented arcade game based on Chinese chess. The screen presents a board-game rather than a conventional action playfield, using dedicated gambling or selection controls on a horizontal display. It belongs to the Taiwanese amusement market, where familiar traditional tabletop games were frequently converted into coin-operated electronic attractions.

Although some secondary descriptions speculate about a particular Chinese-chess variant, the available sources do not securely establish whether this program uses full xiangqi or dark-chess rules. Its identity as an arcade chess title is clear; its exact rule set is less so.

games.title: Twin Cobra II
games.description:
Twin Cobra II, known in Japan as Kyukyoku Tiger II, is a 1995 vertically scrolling military shooter published by Taito for the F3 System. It continues the helicopter warfare of Toaplan's Twin Cobra, sending one or two aircraft through six stages of tanks, enemy planes and large bosses. Color-changing pickups provide a focused red shot, a wide blue spread or a player-specific green weapon, while bombs clear dangerous attack patterns. Collecting additional bomb icons with a full stock can produce an especially powerful Hyper Bomb.

The game's development began at Toaplan, but the company's closure in 1994 left the project unfinished. Former Toaplan staff completed it under the newly founded Takumi Corporation, making it the studio's first arcade release. Chaining increasingly valuable star pickups adds a scoring incentive beyond simple survival, and its more elaborate F3 graphics give this sequel a different feel from the 1987 original.

games.title: TouchDown Fever
games.description:
SNK's TouchDown Fever (1987) brings American football to a vertically scrolling, overhead arcade field, with room for up to four players. Players select formations, run or pass to advance the ball, attempt kicks and defend against opposing drives. The unusual controls borrow the rotating joystick approach associated with SNK's Ikari Warriors, allowing movement and facing direction to be managed separately for quick changes of play.

Its roster uses teams associated with NFL cities without an official league or player license, and the game emphasizes brisk arcade action over exhaustive simulation. It was followed by TouchDown Fever II and later adapted for the Nintendo Entertainment System. The rotating controls and upright field distinguish it from Tecmo Bowl, another well-known arcade football title of the same year.

games.title: Thunder Dragon
games.description:
Thunder Dragon is NMK's 1991 vertically scrolling helicopter shooter, distributed by Tecmo. One or two players pilot a futuristic attack helicopter across eight stages against military vehicles, aircraft and mechanical bosses. Numbered pickups upgrade the main gun with different shooting patterns, while a limited supply of bombs offers relief from crowded screens and enemy fire.

Its arcade hardware and revisions have an unusually complicated preservation history, including protected and unprotected original boards and bootlegs with altered sound hardware or audio borrowed from Raiden. Beneath those variations is a direct, demanding early-1990s shooter built around rapid weapon upgrades, precise movement and elaborate end-of-stage encounters.

games.title: Thunder Dragon 2
games.description:
Thunder Dragon 2 (1993) takes NMK's helicopter-shooter series in a deliberately eccentric direction. Instead of the original attack helicopter, the players choose contrasting aircraft, including an old-fashioned propeller plane and a faster modern-looking craft, each with different weapons and handling. The eight vertically scrolling stages combine ground targets, airborne enemies, colorful bullets and substantial bosses, with power-ups improving the fighters' attack capabilities.

Scoring tricks provide much of its personality: even the letters announcing a stage can be shot for points, and collectible objects become increasingly valuable when handled carefully. A loud, idiosyncratic spoken soundtrack and relentless pace distinguish it from the first Thunder Dragon. The game was also distributed under the alternate title Big Bang.

games.title: Team Hat Trick
games.description: Team Hat Trick is a rare Bally/Sente ice-hockey arcade game dated to 1985 and developed from the company's earlier Hat Trick. Its key change is support for four human players, giving each side more directly controlled skaters while preserving the compact overhead rink and fast pursuit of the puck. Players steer their skaters, shoot at goal and manage the slippery movement characteristic of the original. The four-player version was apparently not widely released commercially, making surviving cabinets and the preserved ROM especially significant to enthusiasts of Bally/Sente prototypes and unusual multiplayer sports games.

games.title: John Elway's Team Quarterback
games.description:
John Elway's Team Quarterback is Tradewest's late-1980s arcade football game, part of the family of releases associated with John Elway's Quarterback. It combines selectable offensive plays with direct control of passes, runs and kicks, using an unusual spring-loaded throwing joystick rather than an ordinary digital stick for the quarterback's passing action. Players take different positions at the cabinet according to whether they are playing offense or defense.

The arcade design predates and differs from the home conversions sold under the star quarterback's name. Its physical passing control and focus on timing distinguish it from simpler button-driven football games, and the Team Quarterback version reflects the attempt to adapt a recognizably American sport into a distinctive coin-operated attraction.

games.title: Technical Bowling
games.description: Technical Bowling is a Japanese bowling-themed arcade game released by Sega in December 1997 for the Saturn-derived ST-V hardware. Its cabinet uses a trackball and buttons rather than a conventional joystick, matching the physical gesture of aiming and delivering a bowling ball. The title was marketed in the Japanese medal-game sector, a reminder that Sega's ST-V platform supported amusement and redemption-oriented titles alongside conventional video games. Detailed rules and award mechanics are not well documented, so it is best understood as a specialized arcade bowling release rather than an established tournament-style simulation.

games.title: Techno Drive
games.description:
Namco's Techno Drive (1998) is an inventive arcade driving test disguised as a futuristic motoring adventure. Rather than racing against a fixed field of opponents, players travel back through time to improve humanity's driving skills by completing a succession of eccentric challenges. One exercise tests steering, another smooth braking or acceleration, and others require drifting, avoiding traffic or transporting a bowl of liquid without spilling it. Results receive letter grades and are printed by the cabinet at the end of the session.

The game divides its challenges into steering, pedal-control and combined driving tests, using a steering wheel, accelerator and brake in ways quite different from a traditional racing game. Its surreal visuals, lively techno soundtrack and short diagnostic mini-games showcase Namco's experimental approach to specialized arcade cabinets during the late 1990s.

games.title: Tech Romancer
games.description:
Tech Romancer, known in Japan as Choko Senki Kikaioh, is Capcom's 1998 3D fighting game built as a love letter to giant-robot anime. Players choose a mecha inspired by different eras and styles of Japanese robot animation, then battle opposing machines in arenas filled with destructible buildings. The action favors spectacular weapons, throws and special attacks rather than the subtle martial-arts exchanges of Capcom's Street Fighter series.

Smashing scenery can expose weapons and recovery items, while a Hero Mode power-up temporarily strengthens a machine's abilities. Distinct character stories, anime-style cutscenes and extravagant finishing attacks complete the television-mecha atmosphere. Released on Capcom's ZN-2 arcade hardware and later converted to Dreamcast, it remains a particularly imaginative alternative to conventional one-on-one fighters.

games.title: Tecmo World Cup Millennium
games.description:
Tecmo World Cup Millennium is a 2000 Japanese arcade soccer game developed by Tecmo, continuing the World Cup line that began in the late 1980s. One or two players compete in fast national-team football matches using joystick-and-button controls, and the series' emphasis on direct ball play makes it more of an arcade sports contest than a management simulation.

A particularly unusual hidden challenge awaits skilled players: completing the competition without losing a match or using another credit unlocks an extra match against a team of exaggerated, unusually tall or heavy opponents rendered in silver or gold. Running on PlayStation-derived arcade hardware, this late installment brings a characteristically whimsical bonus to Tecmo's enduring soccer formula.

games.title: TeddyBoy Blues
games.description:
Sega's TeddyBoy Blues (1985) is an unusual single-screen platform shooter starring a young hero with a tiny gun and an absurd menagerie of enemies. Numbers on doors indicate how many creatures will emerge; shooting them reduces them to collectible balls. If the balls are left alone, they turn into time-draining nuisances, so players must keep moving through the shifting maze while clearing each wave before the clock expires.

The arcade game is also remembered for its connection to the Japanese pop song Teddy Boy Blues, sung by Yoko Ishino, which supplied the musical identity and promotional tie-in. Its mixture of shooting, platform movement and frantic cleanup gives it a personality far removed from Sega's more conventional mid-1980s action games.

games.title: Tee'd Off
games.description: Tecmo's Tee'd Off (1986) is a top-down arcade golf game built around a multidirectional trackball. Players aim and control the strength of shots through a 22-hole course, judging distance and position while navigating the hazards of each green. The physical trackball gives drives, approaches and putting a directness that a joystick would struggle to reproduce. It is a relatively obscure example of a dedicated sporting cabinet from Tecmo, years before similarly trackball-driven golf became a major presence in bars and arcades.

games.title: Teeter Torture
games.description: Teeter Torture is an exceptionally rare early-1980s arcade prototype associated with Exidy hardware. The player moves a cannon back and forth along a seesaw and shoots falling hooked weights before they attach to either side. Every missed weight changes the board's balance, as does the cannon's own position; allowing either end to fall onto its dynamite plunger ends the attempt in an explosion. The unusual gravity-and-balance mechanic distinguishes it from conventional fixed shooters. For years only a single cabinet was publicly known, and appearances at California Extreme helped preserve awareness of the game.

games.title: Tehkan World Cup
games.description:
Tehkan World Cup (1985) is a landmark overhead soccer arcade game whose rapid pace is inseparable from its trackball controls. Rolling the ball steers a player across the scrolling pitch, while the kick button handles passing and shooting; the strength and direction of a movement give play a fluid, almost air-hockey-like rhythm. Throw-ins, corners and other familiar football situations are included, but matches are deliberately compressed for immediate coin-op competition.

The cabinet became particularly memorable in multiplayer play, where quick reactions and aggressive passing could produce goals within seconds of kickoff. Developed by Tehkan, later renamed Tecmo, it anticipated the company's subsequent football titles and the wider enthusiasm for accessible arcade soccer during the 1980s and 1990s.

games.title: Teki Paki
games.description:
Teki Paki, released by Toaplan in 1991, is a deceptively simple falling-block puzzle game. Groups of three colored pieces descend into a well; placing five or more connected blocks of the same color causes them to vanish. Because new pieces can merge with those already on the field, players aim to construct large combinations and cascading clears while keeping the stack from reaching the top.

Its spare rules make it easy to grasp, but arranging colors efficiently under increasing speed creates a demanding scoring challenge. A marked departure from Toaplan's famous shooters, Teki Paki shows the studio applying its arcade instincts to the growing competitive-puzzle genre.

games.title: Tekken
games.description:
Namco's Tekken (1994) helped bring three-dimensional martial-arts fighting into the mainstream arcade. Eight initially playable fighters enter the King of Iron Fist Tournament, with the Mishima family conflict gradually emerging as the series' central story. Its defining control scheme assigns separate buttons to left punch, right punch, left kick and right kick, allowing combinations of individual limbs to produce strings, throws and special moves.

Although its combat generally takes place along a two-dimensional line, fully modeled characters and moving camera angles make every bout feel distinct from earlier sprite-based fighters. Running on PlayStation-related Namco System 11 hardware, Tekken became an early showcase for the technical relationship between arcade games and Sony's new console. Its roster, recognizable fighting styles and four-limb controls established a formula that remained central to one of gaming's most enduring fighting series.

games.title: Tekken 2 Ver.B
games.description:
Tekken 2 (1995) expands Namco's early 3D fighting formula with a larger roster, new moves and a stronger focus on combinations and counterattacks. Each of the four attack buttons still corresponds to a fighter's left or right arm or leg, while the combat system adds moves such as reversals, back throws and elaborate throw sequences. The familiar King of Iron Fist Tournament now follows Kazuya Mishima's reign, bringing new family rivalries and supernatural themes into the story.

This AdvanceMAME entry identifies the Ver.B arcade revision, rather than merely the original Ver.A release. Tekken 2 was a major commercial and critical success in arcades and on PlayStation, cementing the series' identity through characters such as Jun Kazama, Lei Wulong and a growing collection of dramatically different fighting styles.

games.title: Tekken 3
games.description:
Tekken 3, launched in arcades in 1997 after its 1996 development and copyright period, is one of Namco's most important 3D fighting games. Its cast introduces a new generation, including Jin Kazama, Ling Xiaoyu and Hwoarang, while bringing back established veterans. Players still control four individual limbs, but the fighting system is faster and adds more practical sidestepping, letting competitors move around attacks rather than simply retreat along a straight line.

Smooth animations, refined juggles and striking character designs made Tekken 3 a defining competitive fighter of the late 1990s. The game ran on Namco System 12 and later became a blockbuster PlayStation release, where additional modes broadened its appeal. The arcade original remains important for its focused one-on-one combat and its pivotal role in the evolution of 3D fighting games.

games.title: Tekken Tag Tournament
games.description:
Tekken Tag Tournament (1999) turns Namco's four-button 3D fighting series into a team contest. Players choose two fighters and can switch between them mid-match, using substitutions to preserve a partner's health, sustain pressure or set up tandem attacks. Victory normally comes when either member of the opposing team is knocked out, making tag timing and team construction as important as individual combos.

As a celebratory crossover of the first three Tekken games, it reunites many characters irrespective of their positions in the storyline. The arcade version was developed for Namco System 12 hardware, before a visually enhanced PlayStation 2 launch edition helped establish the new console's fighting-game library. Its tag mechanics created a distinctive parallel branch of the Tekken franchise.

games.title: Tel Jan
games.description: Tel Jan is a 1999 Japanese arcade mahjong game released by Electro Design on Kaneko's Super Nova System. It presents tile-based mahjong competition with colorful character illustrations, belonging to the line of mahjong titles made for dedicated Japanese amusement venues. Unlike the system's action and fighting cartridges, this release focuses on a traditional tabletop game rendered electronically. The available historical descriptions do not establish enough specific rules or modes to distinguish it beyond its mahjong format and hardware.

games.title: Telephone Mahjong
games.description: Telephone Mahjong is a 1988 Japanese mahjong game from Nichibutsu, a company especially prolific in arcade adaptations of the tile game. Its theme combines mahjong matches with women shown talking on the telephone, giving the presentation a playful, adult-oriented character. It belongs to Nichibutsu's specialized mahjong catalog rather than its better-known action-game line, and is played as a tabletop tile competition rather than an action or reflex game. Surviving descriptions offer little reliable detail about its particular scoring options or progression.

games.title: Tempest
games.description:
Atari's Tempest (1981, with some early material carrying a 1980 date) is one of the great innovations of the vector-graphics arcade era. Designed by Dave Theurer, it places a claw-shaped blaster on the rim of a three-dimensional geometric well. Players spin a rotary controller around its edge, shooting enemies climbing upward through the lanes before they reach the rim. Different enemy types move, split or lay dangerous obstacles, and reaching the end of each wave sends the player hurtling through the cleared tunnel.

Its luminous color vectors, rapidly shifting tube shapes and exceptionally responsive spinner give it a sense of depth and velocity far beyond most contemporary shooters. A limited Superzapper can remove immediate threats, while skilled players learn to manage dangerous lanes instead of firing indiscriminately. Tempest's striking abstract presentation and escalating difficulty established it as a true arcade classic, inspiring later tube shooters and numerous reinterpretations.

games.title: Tengai / Sengoku Blade: Sengoku Ace Episode II
games.description:
Tengai, known in Japan as Sengoku Blade: Sengoku Ace Episode II, is Psikyo's 1996 side-scrolling follow-up to Sengoku Ace. Instead of piloting aircraft, players control an eccentric cast of flying warriors in a fantasy version of feudal Japan, fighting supernatural enemies, machines and grotesque bosses. Each character has distinctive shots, a powerful charged attack and a limited-use bomb, and two players can combine their abilities in cooperative play.

The switch from vertical to horizontal scrolling gives the series a fresh visual identity while retaining Psikyo's characteristic fast enemy patterns and short, intense boss battles. Its lavish character artwork, humorous dialogue and multiple story combinations make the cast as memorable as the shooting itself.

games.title: Tenkomori Shooting
games.description:
Tenkomori Shooting (1998) is Namco's playful collection of rapid-fire shooting challenges, structured like the studio's Point Blank mini-games but played with a joystick. Players guide a monkey up a tower, attempting one short mission on each floor and racing against a strict time limit. The scenarios parody many kinds of arcade shooter, ranging from spaceship battles and missile defense to cockroach extermination, ninjas and other absurd targets.

Different difficulty courses alter the number of floors to clear, while being hit often costs valuable time rather than immediately ending the mission. With a large selection of challenges, sudden shifts in perspective and affectionate nods to older arcade hits, the game is a compact celebration of shoot-'em-up history through Namco's mischievous late-1990s humor.

games.title: Tenth Degree
games.description:
Tenth Degree is an unfinished Atari 3D fighting-game project from 1998, previously developed under the name Juko Thread. Its anime-inspired fighters were designed for fast, one-on-one combat drawing on both Tekken-style movement and the immediacy of Street Fighter. The project involved veteran fighting-game designer James Goddard, and contemporary previews discussed varied martial-arts styles and possible experimental presentation features.

Although playable development versions were demonstrated, the game was never established as a normal commercial arcade release. Its preservation offers a glimpse of Atari's attempt to enter the increasingly competitive late-1990s polygonal fighting market.

games.title: The Eye of Typhoon (Tsunami Edition)

variants.title: The Eye of Typhoon (Tsunami Edition, beta 7, 2022-07-31)

games.description: The Eye of Typhoon (Tsunami Edition) is a homebrew Neo Geo port and enhancement by OzzyOuzo of Viccom's 1996 martial-arts fighting game The Eye of Typhoon, originally developed for the 3DO and PC.

games.title: Terminator 2 - Judgment Day
games.description:
Midway's Terminator 2: Judgment Day (1991) is a hugely successful two-player arcade machine-gun shooter produced alongside James Cameron's film. The players operate mounted light-gun-style weapons as reprogrammed T-800 Terminators, fighting Skynet's robotic armies in the future and then protecting John and Sarah Connor in the past. Stages scroll automatically through ruined battlefields, laboratories and recognizable film locations, demanding precise destruction of enemies while avoiding friendly targets.

The cabinet's hefty guns, digitized images of film performers and sampled dialogue made it a spectacular theatrical attraction. Some stages require defending human resistance fighters or destroying vital machinery rather than simply eliminating opponents, giving the shooting a welcome variety of objectives. Its combination of cinematic branding, cooperative firepower and elaborate presentation became a touchstone for licensed arcade games of the early 1990s.

games.title: Terra Cresta
games.description:
Nichibutsu's Terra Cresta (1985) is a distinctive vertically scrolling shooter and the spiritual successor to Moon Cresta. Players pilot the Wing Galibur over islands and enemy installations, shooting aircraft, ground defenses and giant threats while searching for numbered upgrade modules. Each recovered ship section docks with the main craft, enlarging it and adding weapons such as rear shots or stronger forward fire.

At any time the player can separate the collected sections into a temporary attack formation; with the full set assembled, a special transformation instead produces a powerful invulnerable phoenix. Deciding when to split the ship, and risking its increasingly large silhouette to gain greater firepower, creates an unusually tactical rhythm for a mid-1980s shooter. The game's combination mechanic became the signature of the continuing Cresta series.

games.title: Terra Force
games.description:
Terra Force (1987) is Nichibutsu's science-fiction shooter built around a striking change of viewpoint. Players pilot a spaceship across a vertically scrolling planetary surface, blasting hostile craft and structures before descending into underground passages presented as horizontally scrolling stages. The alternation between open-air attacks and more confined cave navigation forces a change in tactics as hazards and enemy formations vary.

Weapons and speed upgrades help overcome larger formations, while its mixed scrolling styles make it stand out among conventional vertical shooters. Terra Force is an interesting companion to Nichibutsu's Terra Cresta, but it is a distinct game with its own mission structure rather than a simple sequel.

games.title: Tetris

variants.title: Tetris (Japan, B-System, YM2203)
variants.version: (Japan, Taito B-System, Master of Weapon Conversion Kit)

games.description:
Sega's 1988 arcade version of Tetris helped turn Alexey Pajitnov's Soviet computer puzzle into a Japanese coin-op phenomenon. Players move and rotate tetrominoes as they fall into a rectangular well, creating complete horizontal lines that disappear to make space. Increasing speed turns an initially orderly construction puzzle into a test of foresight and precision, and the simple rules encourage fierce high-score competition.

Running on Sega System 16 hardware, this influential rendition became a cornerstone of the late-1980s arcade puzzle boom and was associated with the rise of Tetris as a global entertainment phenomenon. AdvanceMAME preserves several Japanese System 16 board revisions, encrypted sets and bootlegs. The arcade release should not be confused with later home editions, which introduced different visual styles, music, options and multiplayer rules.

games.title: Tetris Plus
games.description:
Tetris Plus is Jaleco's mid-1990s variation on the falling-block classic, featuring a puzzle adventure alongside standard Tetris play. In Puzzle Mode, a tiny professor explores a structure made from blocks, and players must clear lines to guide him safely toward the bottom and the exit before danger catches up. Placing tetrominoes becomes a matter not only of survival but also of manipulating the platform beneath a moving character.

The addition of a character, discrete stages and timed objectives makes Tetris Plus feel like a cross between traditional Tetris and an action puzzle. Its arcade version ran on Jaleco's Mega System 32 hardware and was later adapted to home platforms, helping extend the Tetris formula beyond endless score chasing.

games.title: Tetris Plus 2
games.description:
Tetris Plus 2 (1997) continues Jaleco's character-driven variation on Tetris. As in the original, players arrange falling tetrominoes and complete lines to reshape the ground beneath an on-screen explorer, trying to clear a path to the exit while avoiding traps and wasted moves. The sequel introduces the professor's faster-moving assistant as another playable character and adds new stage layouts and challenges.

Its blend of classic line clearing and a character navigating the evolving stack gives it a different rhythm from competitive Tetris. Several arcade hardware and regional versions have been preserved, including a Mega System 32 release.

games.title: Tetris
games.description:
This version of Tetris is Sega's 1988 Japanese arcade adaptation running on the company's more economical System E hardware, distinct from the better-known System 16 board sets. The rules remain the celebrated original puzzle: rotate and position falling four-square pieces to complete horizontal rows, clear space and survive increasing speed.

Its preservation is interesting chiefly for the hardware conversion, which brought the same hugely popular Soviet-designed concept to a different Sega arcade platform. Players will recognize the essentials immediately, but this is an identifiable board version rather than a generic entry standing for every edition of Tetris.

games.title: Tetris
games.description:
This unusual Tetris set is an unlicensed arcade adaptation attributed to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, with its exact production year uncertain. It preserves the central Tetris objective of fitting falling tetrominoes together and clearing complete horizontal rows, but runs on hardware derived from Taito's Arkanoid platform rather than Sega's familiar System 16 boards.

The preserved encrypted set is a curiosity of international arcade hardware reuse and the spread of Tetris through unofficial conversions. Its uncertain dating and manufacturing history make it important to distinguish it from Sega's licensed Japanese arcade versions.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: ThunderForce AC
games.description:
Thunder Force AC (1990) is the arcade adaptation of Technosoft's celebrated Mega Drive shooter Thunder Force III, published through Sega. Players pilot the FIRE LEO-03 Styx in fast horizontal-scrolling battles across alien worlds, switching between weapons to match the terrain and incoming threats. The standard forward and rear guns can be supplemented by specialized equipment such as the wall-piercing Wave, the ground-hugging Fire and the homing Hunter.

The arcade version rearranges and replaces some material from the home original, making it more than a direct hardware transplant. Its demanding stage design, enormous bosses and energetic soundtrack capture the appeal of Technosoft's shooter series while showing the less-common path of a successful home-console game moving into arcades.

games.title: Tetris the Absolute The Grand Master 2

variants.title: Tetris the Absolute The Grand Master 2
Tetris the Absolute The Grand Master 2 Plus

games.description:
Tetris the Absolute: The Grand Master 2 (2000) is Arika's formidable sequel to Tetris: The Grand Master, designed for the most accomplished players of the falling-block classic. Tetrominoes eventually appear directly at the bottom of the well at near-instantaneous gravity, requiring players to rotate and slide them during the brief delay before they lock. Clear speed, consistency and recovery ability affect the rank achieved, turning an ordinary Tetris session into a demanding examination.

The game adds new modes and refinements to the first Grand Master, including a cooperative-style doubles option, while the enhanced Grand Master 2 Plus revision introduces further challenges. Its intricate ranking system and extreme late-game speed have made it a central reference point for competitive Tetris mastery and high-level arcade play.

games.title: Tetris The Grand Master
games.description:
Arika's Tetris: The Grand Master (1998), published through Capcom, reimagines the falling-block classic as an arcade skill examination. Players still rotate tetrominoes into place to clear horizontal lines, but their performance earns martial-arts-style ranks that climb toward the coveted Grand Master title.
