Increasing gravity, strict time expectations and a final stretch of near-instantly falling blocks reward precise technique rather than casual survival.

The game's level progression and grading made high-speed finesse a discipline in its own right. Running on Capcom's PlayStation-derived ZN-2 hardware, it established the conventions later expanded by The Grand Master 2 and subsequent installments. For advanced players it is one of the defining attempts to make Tetris an exacting competitive arcade art.

games.title: Target Ball
games.description: Target Ball is a 1995 Korean arcade billiards game by Yun Sung. Presented from an overhead view, it combines cue-ball aiming and pocketing with an adult-oriented reward format: successful play advances through pin-up imagery, with a separate version featuring nudity. The joystick-and-button interface adapts billiards to ordinary video-game cabinet controls. Its pairing of pool mechanics with revealing pictures reflects a distinctive niche in Korean arcade production of the period.

games.title: Task Force Harrier
games.description:
Task Force Harrier is UPL's 1989 vertically scrolling combat-aircraft shooter. Piloting a Harrier fighter, players battle across enemy territory and must use different attacks against airborne opponents and ground-based vehicles or installations. Escort craft can be collected to boost firepower and arranged in different formations, adding a tactical choice to the usual dodging and shooting.

The game's military theme, alternating targets and adjustable support fighters set it apart from many single-weapon shooters of its era. Known in Japan as Task Force Harrier and overseas in several board variants, it is one of UPL's distinctive late-1980s action titles.

games.title: The Deep
games.description:
The Deep (1987), also released as Run Deep, is an underwater-themed arcade shooter in which a surface vessel attacks submarines, mines and strange aquatic enemies below. Players steer left and right while dropping depth charges that sink toward targets at different distances, making anticipation essential. Incoming missiles, torpedoes and mines threaten the boat, while supply capsules and other pickups provide extra weapons or useful temporary abilities.

The ship can also descend beneath the waves in certain situations, and successive screens present different assignments, such as destroying installations or recovering objects. This mixture of naval combat and mission-based progression gives the game more structure than a straightforward fixed-screen shooter.

games.title: The End
games.description:
Konami's The End (1980) is a fixed-screen space shooter in which alien insect craft attack not just the player's ship but three brick-built defensive positions. The invaders carry stolen blocks to the top of the playfield and gradually spell the word END. Players can lose through ordinary combat, but allowing the aliens to complete the word produces another distinctive defeat condition.

The result is an inventive variation on the Space Invaders formula: aiming at approaching enemies must be balanced against stopping the systematic theft of defensive bricks. Alternate arcade sets, including Omega and a Stern-distributed release, preserve this unusual early Konami design.

games.title: The Gladiator / Shen Jian Fu Mo Lu / Shen Jian Fengyun

variants.title: The Gladiator / Shen Jian Fu Mo Lu / Shen Jian Fengyun (M68k label V101) (ARM label V107, ROM 06/06/03 SHEN JIAN V107)
The Gladiator / Shen Jian Fu Mo Lu / Shen Jian Fengyun (M68k label V100) (ARM label V100, ROM 01/16/03 SHEN JIAN)

games.description:
The Gladiator, also known as Shen Jian Fu Mo Lu, is a 2003 Chinese fantasy action game developed by International Games System for its PolyGame Master arcade platform. Set around a cursed sacred sword and a conspiracy involving martial-arts clans, it features a cast of warriors drawn into a conflict filled with revenge, supernatural powers and elaborate weapon techniques. Players fight through side-scrolling encounters with enemies and formidable bosses in a richly illustrated martial-arts setting.

The game emphasizes flowing weapon attacks and the spectacle of Chinese wuxia storytelling, setting it apart from the urban brawlers more familiar to Western arcade audiences. Multiple program revisions have been preserved, reflecting the complicated arcade history of IGS's later PGM releases.

games.title: The Grid
games.description:
The Grid (2001 in some arcade catalogs, originally released around 2000) is Midway's ambitious multiplayer third-person arena shooter, framed as a violent futuristic television contest. Players run through 3D arenas, collect weapons and eliminate opponents to earn points and money. Its memorable control scheme combines a joystick for movement with a trackball for aiming, plus buttons for jumping and shooting, providing independent mobility and precision without a conventional PC mouse.

Multiple cabinets can be linked to support up to six players, and contestants can save progress and upgrades using an identifying number. Created by a team associated with Mortal Kombat, it even features guest appearances by fighters from that series. As one of Midway's final original coin-operated video games, The Grid captures an era when arcades were experimenting with networked multiplayer shooters in the shadow of the PC arena-game boom.

games.title: The Hand
games.description:
The Hand (1981), also known as Got-Ya in some releases, turns a Pac-Man-style dot maze into a contest of rock, paper and scissors. The player's character and pursuing enemies are represented by hands that can form one of the three gestures. Collecting all the dots completes a maze, but touching an opponent is safe only when the player's current sign beats the enemy's. Matching signs produce a draw, while losing the confrontation costs a life.

The familiar maze-chase formula acquires an extra layer of rapid gesture switching and pattern recognition. Its odd premise and economical presentation make it one of the more distinctive small arcade titles to emerge during the early-1980s maze-game boom.

games.title: The Mah-jong
games.description: The Mah-jong is a 1987 Japanese arcade mahjong game associated with Visco. Players compete in tile-based hands against selectable illustrated female opponents, with character reactions supplying the game's visual personality. Like many Japanese video-mahjong releases of the period, it brings a tabletop game into a specialized coin-operated format rather than emphasizing reflex-driven action. Specific rules, reward sequences and modes are poorly documented in the available historical sources.

games.title: The Pit
games.description:
The Pit (1982) is a tense underground exploration game developed by AW Electronics. An astronaut lands beside a dangerous excavation and must dig through tunnels to recover crystals and other treasure, then return safely to the spaceship. Falling rocks, hostile creatures, flying projectiles and acid make the journey hazardous, and an enemy tank above ground gradually destroys the terrain protecting the player's ship.

The escape route leads through the titular pit, whose retracting floor exposes a lethal creature beneath it. Unlike an ordinary maze chase, the game asks players to plan a route in and out while managing a disguised time limit and destructible terrain. Its subterranean digging and hazards are historically interesting precursors to ideas later explored by Boulder Dash and other action-puzzle games.

games.title: Thunder Heroes
games.description: Thunder Heroes is a 2001 side-scrolling fantasy beat-'em-up by Primetek Investments. It is closely based on the earlier Gaia Crusaders, retaining the fundamental structure of moving through enemy-filled stages and defeating groups of opponents with close-range attacks. The major distinction is its altered presentation and character graphics, making it effectively a reworked version of the parent game rather than an entirely new fighting system. For arcade preservation, its value lies in documenting an unusual later rebranding of a relatively obscure belt-scrolling brawler.

games.title: Thief
games.description:
Thief (1981) is a maze-chase arcade game by Pacific Novelty in which a criminal getaway car collects scattered dollar bills while being pursued by police cruisers. Golden dollar-sign pickups temporarily reverse the chase, allowing the player to ram the police for bonus points. Each completed maze advances the fugitive through increasingly grandiose criminal nicknames, from petty offenses toward Public Enemy No. 1.

The driving theme is deliberately close to Pac-Man, but the game's most remarkable feature is its sound: prerecorded police-radio chatter plays from a continuous-loop tape mechanism in the cabinet. The combination of frantic mazes, police pursuit and unusual audio hardware makes it a memorable oddity of the early arcade boom.

games.title: Thunder Blade
games.description:
Sega's Thunder Blade (1987) puts players at the controls of an attack helicopter in a spectacular blend of overhead scrolling and forward-looking pseudo-3D combat. Each mission alternates a top-down flight segment with an into-the-screen section, asking the pilot to shoot tanks, aircraft and fortified positions while weaving around skyscrapers, canyon walls and other scenery. Unlimited machine-gun fire and air-to-ground missiles keep the action moving even under dense attacks.

The large moving arcade cabinet, with its dedicated helicopter-style controls, was a major part of the attraction. Blending visual techniques associated with Sega's Super Scaler games with a rotating cockpit presentation, Thunder Blade became one of the company's most recognizable late-1980s showpieces. Its shifts in perspective remain unusual even among other military-themed shooters of the period.

games.title: Thunder Cross II
games.description:
Thunder Cross II (1991) is Konami's horizontally scrolling sequel to Thunder Cross, again sending a heavily armed starfighter across hostile planets and mechanical fortresses. Players collect upgrade capsules and deploy multiple option satellites above and below the ship, expanding the reach of its firepower against swarming enemies and large bosses. Different weapons and the vertical arrangement of the options reward careful positioning.

The sequel enhances the series' detailed 2D artwork, soundtrack and stage variety while retaining the classic Konami shooting philosophy of power-up management and memorized hazard patterns. Released primarily in Japan, it remains less widely known than Gradius or Parodius but is highly regarded among fans of the company's arcade shooters.

games.title: Thunder Zone
games.description:
Thunder Zone (1991), released in North America as Desert Assault, is Data East's isometric military action shooter built for cooperative play. Soldiers advance across diagonally scrolling battlefields, firing at enemy infantry, vehicles and fortified positions while using grenades and other weapons to clear dangerous areas. Large bosses and combat set pieces give the campaign a theatrical, war-movie quality.

The arcade game supports multiple players simultaneously, and the international variations are especially interesting for preserving its alternate Thunder Zone and Desert Assault identities. The unusual isometric viewpoint, outsized explosions and emphasis on teamwork distinguish it from more familiar top-down run-and-gun titles.

games.title: Thunder Hoop
games.description:
Thunder Hoop (1992) is a Spanish side-scrolling action-platform game by Gaelco. The player controls a genetically engineered young fighter who battles mutants and soldiers while pursuing the villainous Dr. Genbrain. Jumping between platforms, climbing ladders and shooting energy projectiles are central to progress, with tougher enemies and large bosses guarding the stages.

Its bright graphics and peculiar superhero premise give it a different flavor from contemporary Japanese arcade platformers. The game later received a sequel, TH Strikes Back, continuing the story with an older version of the hero.

games.title: TH Strikes Back

variants.title: TH Strikes Back (non North America, version 1.0, checksum 020EB356)

games.description:
TH Strikes Back (1994) is Gaelco's follow-up to Thunder Hoop, set roughly a decade after the original. The genetically enhanced hero has grown up and must once again battle the forces of Genbrain after an attack on the project responsible for his creation. Players traverse scrolling platform stages, fighting humans and monsters with energy attacks projected from the hero's fists.

A normal shot, a stronger special attack and the ability to defeat some foes by jumping on them give combat several approaches, while simultaneous two-player support makes the sequel more cooperative than the first game. Its comic-book science-fiction setting and unusual Spanish arcade provenance make it a distinctive mid-1990s platform shooter.

games.title: Thrill Drive
games.description:
Konami's Thrill Drive (1998) turns ordinary road travel into a frantic arcade driving game where surviving the course matters as much as speed. Players choose among different vehicle types, then race through congested roads in Japan, the United States or Europe, dodging traffic, hazards and sudden obstacles while reaching checkpoints before time runs out. Crashes consume time and hurt the player's driving assessment.

Rather than presenting conventional professional racing, the game leans into the escalating comedy and danger of reckless driving, accompanied by dramatic replays and rankings. It launched a series remembered for its chaotic road situations and exaggerated treatment of accidents.

games.title: Thunder Hurricane
games.description: Operation Thunder Hurricane is Konami's mid-1990s arcade shooting game built around a heavy machine-gun-style controller. Players use the mounted gun to fire into fast-moving on-screen action, emphasizing sustained aiming and reflexes rather than the single-shot pistol approach of many light-gun cabinets. Known in preserved software as Thunder Hurricane, it represents Konami's continued experimentation with elaborate dedicated-gun attractions. Detailed stage objectives and campaign structure are not well documented in the surviving descriptions.

games.title: ThunderJaws
games.description:
Atari Games' ThunderJaws (1990) is a two-player action shooter that switches between underwater swimming sequences and side-scrolling platform combat inside enemy installations. Secret agents infiltrate the base of the villainous Madame Q, battling armed divers, sharks, mutants and mechanical defenses while rescuing captives and collecting stronger weapons. A speargun handles the aquatic fights; on land, the agents leap across platforms and shoot their way through guarded complexes.

The repeated change from submerged movement to running-and-jumping gunplay gives each mission an unusual rhythm. Its mixture of outrageous comic-book villains, demanding enemies and cooperative shooting places it among Atari's more colorful late-era arcade action games.

games.title: Thunder & Lightning
games.description:
Thunder & Lightning (1990) is Seta's eccentric character-driven variation on Breakout. Instead of a plain paddle, a little hero named Mr. Chin carries a horizontal stick above his head and bounces a ball into blocks and moving obstacles. Keeping the ball in play is complicated by flying or traveling carriers that release power-ups, including longer paddles, the ability to catch and release the ball, extra lives and offensive weapons.

Its cartoon characters and animated distractions turn a traditional paddle puzzle into a more elaborate arcade spectacle. The game demonstrates how the Arkanoid boom continued inspiring visually inventive ball-and-paddle releases into the 1990s.

games.title: Thunder Cross
games.description:
Konami's Thunder Cross (1988) is a classic side-scrolling space shooter in the tradition of Gradius. Players fly a Thunder fighter through seven stages of mechanical enemies and imposing bosses, collecting power-ups that provide different weapons and as many as four satellite options. Unlike Gradius's fixed trailing option formation, the Thunder Cross options can be positioned in a vertical array above and below the ship, allowing their combined fire to sweep dangerous sections of the screen.

Vulcan, laser and ricocheting boomerang attacks offer different offensive strengths, and completing the game begins a tougher second loop. The detailed stages, forceful music and flexible option arrangement gave Thunder Cross a strong identity within Konami's celebrated arcade shooter catalog.

games.title: Thunder Fox
games.description:
Thunder Fox (1990) is Taito's two-player side-scrolling military action game starring agents Thunder and Fox, specialists sent to dismantle a global terrorist threat. The heroes fight at close range with knives and fists but can also seize guns, grenades and flamethrowers from enemies. Missions move through army installations, ships and other settings, occasionally changing pace with vehicle-based action.

The two protagonists have somewhat different fighting strengths, encouraging cooperative tactics rather than identical play. Its large sprites, lively combat and mixture of melee and ranged weapons make it an entertaining bridge between belt-scrolling brawlers and traditional run-and-gun games.

games.title: Tickee Tickats
games.description: Tickee Tickats is Raster Elite's 1994 arcade light-gun shooting and ticket-redemption game. It presents short marksmanship challenges in the style of later shooting galleries such as Point Blank, with successful play rewarded through the cabinet's ticket system rather than a lengthy narrative campaign. The combination of electronic targets, gun input and physical prize tickets places it within the arcade redemption market, a different environment from conventional high-score shooters.

games.title: Tic Tac Trivia
games.description:
Tic Tac Trivia is a 1985 countertop quiz game from Merit Industries that merges multiple-choice questions with a tic-tac-toe board. Players select positions in a three-by-three grid and earn the right to claim squares by answering trivia questions, turning general knowledge into a contest for lines and blocked moves. Categories range across familiar pub-quiz subjects such as sports and entertainment, and answers are chosen with dedicated cabinet buttons.

The game belongs to Merit's 6221 hardware family, alongside the Trivia Whiz series. Its question-ROM sets and later revisions provide a glimpse into the mid-1980s American bar-arcade market, where short social quiz games coexisted with action machines and video poker.

games.title: Tiger Heli
games.description:
Tiger-Heli (1985) is Toaplan's landmark vertically scrolling attack-helicopter shooter, published by Taito. Players fly over hostile territory, bombarding tanks, gunboats and emplacements with short-range gunfire while carefully conserving powerful bombs. The bombs can destroy enemies and hostile shots in a broad radius, and can even explode automatically if struck while still attached to the helicopter. Collectible support helicopters add firepower but must be protected from enemy attacks.

The game's slow, deliberate helicopter movement and dangerous ground targets established a distinct identity within an arcade genre otherwise dominated by spacecraft. As Toaplan's first shooting game, Tiger-Heli helped lay the foundations for the company's later classics, including Twin Cobra and Flying Shark, and for a generation of military-themed vertical shooters.

games.title: Tiger Road
games.description:
Tiger Road (1987), known in Japan as Tora e no Michi, is Capcom's martial-arts platform adventure starring Lee Wong, a monk sent to rescue children kidnapped by the sinister Ryu Ken Oh. Armed with an axe-like weapon, he leaps between platforms, fights monsters and bandits, and works through large scrolling stages with different routes and hazards. Training sequences and weapon upgrades periodically add new capabilities.

Its blend of mythical martial-arts imagery, energetic platforming and demanding boss encounters sets it apart from Capcom's more straightforward beat-'em-ups. The large stages and training trials give the action a sense of progression beyond simply surviving each screen.

games.title: Timber
games.description:
Bally Midway's Timber (1984) is a wonderfully peculiar competitive arcade game about two lumberjacks racing to meet a daily woodcutting quota. Players move around a clearing as trees spring up from the ground, then swing an axe left or right to fell them. Its two-joystick control scheme separates movement from chopping direction, demanding careful positioning as the timer ticks down. Bears throw beehives into the work area and falling trees can stun careless loggers.

In two-player games, the rival lumberjacks compete directly for the most productive shift, adding slapstick rivalry to the basic time-management challenge. Created during Bally Midway's experimental early-1980s period, Timber remains a distinctive alternative to conventional platform and maze games, with its unusual controls and comically industrial theme.

games.title: Time Crisis
games.description:
Namco's Time Crisis (1995) transformed arcade light-gun shooting through an ingenious cover mechanic. Armed with a recoil-simulating pistol, the player assumes the role of agent Richard Miller, storming a fortified castle to rescue the president's daughter. Pressing a foot pedal makes the agent stand up and fire; releasing it ducks behind cover, avoiding enemy shots while automatically reloading. The player must emerge, fire accurately and retreat without allowing the stage's time limit to expire.

Unlike earlier shooting galleries, surviving requires a rhythm of exposure and concealment rather than constant firing. Quick enemy reactions, cinematic camera moves and the satisfying pedal-and-gun combination made the dedicated cabinet especially memorable. Time Crisis became one of Namco's most enduring arcade series and established a control idea that defined the feel of its many sequels.

games.title: Time Crisis 2
games.description:
Time Crisis II (1997) expands Namco's cover-based light-gun formula into a cooperative two-player adventure. Agents Keith Martin and Robert Baxter pursue a conspiracy involving an orbital weapons system, rescuing their captured colleague while battling soldiers across trains, city streets and other cinematic locations. Each player has an individual gun and foot pedal: pressing the pedal exposes the agent to shoot, while releasing it takes cover and reloads.

The sequel's most important improvement is synchronized two-player action, with separate screens and viewpoints that let both participants see different aspects of the same scene. A flashing warning also identifies potentially lethal incoming attacks, sharpening the game's risk-and-reward timing. Large set pieces and cooperative cover play helped establish Time Crisis II as one of the signature light-gun attractions of its era.

games.title: Time Killers
games.description:
Time Killers (1992) is a deliberately outrageous weapon-based fighting game by Incredible Technologies and Strata. Its combatants come from different historical and fantastic eras, but the real novelty lies in its five attack buttons: left arm, right arm, left leg, right leg and head. Successful blows can sever limbs, leaving an opponent to struggle on with fewer attacks, while deadly decapitation moves can end a fight instantly.

Released during the boom following Street Fighter II, it sought attention through cartoonishly excessive violence, gory finishing moves and an unconventional control scheme. It became a cult curiosity rather than a major tournament standard, and its ideas later informed the equally lurid BloodStorm.

games.title: Time Limit
games.description: Time Limit is a 1983 arcade action-platform game from Chuo Co., Ltd. Players guide a police officer through a large multistory building in search of a planted bomb, racing against a countdown while gunmen and environmental hazards interfere. Ladders, lifts and escalators provide routes between floors, and the officer can shoot pursuers while avoiding rolling or swinging obstacles. Its combination of a vertically interconnected building and a strict bomb-disposal deadline gives this obscure title a recognizably early-1980s arcade tension.

games.title: Time Pilot
games.description:
Konami's Time Pilot (1982), designed by Yoshiki Okamoto, is one of the most imaginative multidirectional arcade shooters of its era. A futuristic jet travels through five periods of aviation history, fighting biplanes in 1910, World War II aircraft, modern fighters and eventually advanced enemies. The player craft stays near the center of the screen while the surrounding sky scrolls in the direction of travel, creating the illusion of unrestricted flight. A powerful enemy mothership appears after enough targets are destroyed, opening the way to the next era.

Parachuting pilots can be rescued for bonus points, and enemy formations encourage the player to maneuver rather than simply stay in one position. Its smooth eight-direction movement and chronological stage progression helped distinguish it from fixed-screen shooters. Time Pilot became an influential Konami classic, followed by Time Pilot '84 and adapted to numerous home systems.

games.title: Time Scanner
games.description:
Sega's Time Scanner (1987) is a computerized pinball game running on System 16 hardware. Instead of controlling a physical steel ball and flippers, players navigate elaborate vertically scrolling tables full of ramps, bumpers, targets and bonus features. The Volcano, Ruins and Saqqarah tables present different themed objectives, while a fourth stage with Breakout-like blocks opens after the others have been completed.

Each table is larger than a single screen, so the display scrolls to follow the ball between upper and lower sections with their own flippers. Time Scanner is an ambitious attempt to bring the variety and spectacle of a pinball machine to a video arcade cabinet, with its elaborate stages rewarding more than merely keeping the ball alive.

games.title: Time Soldiers
games.description:
Time Soldiers (1987), developed by Alpha Denshi and published internationally by SNK and Romstar, is a two-player overhead run-and-gun game with a time-traveling mission. Players search for captured comrades across prehistoric landscapes, ancient civilizations, world wars and futuristic battlefields. A rotary joystick lets each soldier move in one direction while aiming the gun independently, supporting precise attacks against enemies that approach from any side.

Special gates shift the team between historical eras, and clues identify the time period where a missing soldier is held. The campaign's varied scenery and boss monsters make it more adventurous than many military shooters. Known in Japan as Battle Field, it is a strong example of the rotary-control action games that followed Ikari Warriors.

games.title: Time's Up!
games.description: Time's Up! is a homebrew horizontal-scrolling shoot-'em-up developed and published by NGF Dev. Inc. for the Neo Geo platform in 2012.

games.title: Time Tunnel
games.description:
Taito's Time Tunnel (1982) is a highly unusual railroad maze game in which players control a locomotive by switching track junctions instead of steering it freely. The train must collect carriages, pick up passengers at stations and eventually deliver them to a space station, completing linked tasks across three distinct phases. Hazards such as other trains and alien creatures threaten the route, and the engine must reach refueling points before its limited fuel runs out.

Planning switch changes ahead of the train is the central challenge: a bad junction can send the locomotive away from its objective or directly into danger. Its combination of rail scheduling, maze navigation and surreal space-travel imagery makes Time Tunnel one of the more original early arcade puzzle-action games.

games.title: Tinkle Pit
games.description:
Namco's Tinkle Pit (1993) is a colorful maze-action game starring Pitt and Patti, two characters who attack enemies with unusual tethered Tinker Balls. Players drop a ball and extend a line while moving; releasing the control calls the ball back, allowing it to slam into enemies. Collectible popcorn adds a second attack that ricochets around walls, while clearing the creatures from each maze opens the next stage.

The game doubles as a nostalgic celebration of Namco history, filling its levels with cameo characters and objects from Pac-Man, Dig Dug, Xevious, Mappy and other classics. Its carefully timed ball-return mechanic offers a fresh alternative to direct-fire maze shooters, while its playful crossover presentation rewards longtime arcade fans.

games.title: The Tin Star
games.description:
The Tin Star is a 1983 Wild West shooting game from Taito. Players guide a frontier sheriff through encounters with outlaws in streets, saloons and other western settings, firing in multiple directions while ducking or hiding to avoid return shots. Shooting objects in the scenery can disrupt enemies, and bonus scenes include mounted duels that reward especially well-timed attacks.

Rather than a conventional Space Invaders-style formation shooter, the game stages compact gunfights around the sheriff's movements and defensive positioning. Its cartoon Western atmosphere and changes of location give it a distinctive identity among Taito's early action games.

games.title: The Invaders
games.description:
The Invaders is a rare 1978 Italian-made variation on Space Invaders, associated with arcade manufacturer Zaccaria. A gun at the bottom of the screen moves sideways and fires upward at descending ranks of hostile alien craft, while the player must avoid or destroy their shots before they reach the ground.

The basic formula is closely modeled on Taito's groundbreaking original, but the board uses Signetics 2650-family hardware rather than the customary Midway or Taito design. For collectors, this set documents how quickly the invasion-shooter craze spread into European-made machines and local hardware adaptations.

games.title: Title Fight
games.description:
Title Fight (1992) is Sega's boxing arcade game built around a distinctive dual-joystick control system. Each stick governs a fighter's arms and defensive responses, giving the player direct influence over punches, blocking and evasive moves during a bout. The action is displayed with unusual outlined, partly transparent character graphics intended to keep the fighters readable during close exchanges.

The physical two-stick interface is central to its appeal, distinguishing it from boxing games that reduce attacks to a few fixed punch buttons. It belongs to Sega's experimental early-1990s sports releases, where arcade hardware was used to recreate a sport's motions in an unconventional way.

games.title: Toukidenshou - Angel Eyes
games.description:
Toukidenshou: Angel Eyes (1996) is Tecmo's stylized two-dimensional fighting game with an entirely female cast. Eight playable women, ranging from a ninja and a biker to a schoolgirl and a character wielding a stuffed bear, are drawn into a supernatural tournament to select a new archangel. The visual presentation is unusual: some fighters use hand-drawn 2D artwork while others have a rendered appearance that resembles pre-rendered 3D sprites.

Fighting emphasizes fast movement, aerial attacks and extended combos, sometimes allowing a well-timed sequence to cause enormous damage. Its striking visual contrasts and high-powered combat have given the game a cult following as one of the more eccentric Japanese fighters of the late 1990s.

games.title: Tokimeki Memorial Taisen Puzzle-dama
games.description:
Tokimeki Memorial Taisen Puzzle-dama (1995) is Konami's competitive falling-block puzzle game featuring the cast of its popular dating simulation Tokimeki Memorial. Players choose a character and drop paired colored pieces into a grid, creating clusters of matching colors and setting off chain reactions to send trouble to the opposing playfield. Each victory is framed as a lively character encounter with animated reactions and personality.

Its mechanics build on Konami's Taisen Puzzle-dama system rather than plain Tetris, rewarding carefully staged combinations and tactical attacks. The unusual crossover of a romance-game cast with a two-player arcade puzzle contest makes it both a distinctive Konami spin-off and a snapshot of the series' mid-1990s popularity.

games.title: Vs. T.K.O. Boxing
games.description: Vs. T.K.O. Boxing is a 1987 boxing arcade game produced for Nintendo's VS. System, adapted from the ring action of Data East's Ring King. Players control a boxer through bouts against progressively stronger opponents, positioning for punches, defending themselves and aiming to win by knockout or decision. The VS. cabinet format brings a familiar console-era boxing design to coin-operated competition under an alternate title. Its significance lies mainly in this reworking and licensing history rather than an entirely separate set of fighting mechanics.

games.title: T-MEK
games.description:
Atari Games' T-MEK (1994) is a futuristic first-person arena combat game in which players pilot heavily armed hovering tanks known as MEKs. Competitors maneuver across large 3D landscapes, fire specialized weapons and try to destroy opposing vehicles before time or score limits are reached. Different machines have different combat capabilities, and computer opponents join battles even when fewer humans are present.

The cabinet was designed for competitive multiplayer, with as many as three linked two-player machines supporting six human combatants. Its surround-sound system and expansive enclosed battle arenas helped create the impression of a futuristic spectator sport. T-MEK stands as an ambitious early arcade interpretation of vehicular deathmatch play, blending ideas from Battlezone with the emerging 1990s enthusiasm for arena shooters.

games.title: Tokimeki Mahjong Paradise - Dear My Love
games.description: Tokimeki Mahjong Paradise: Dear My Love is a 1997 Japanese arcade mahjong game featuring colorful, voiced female characters and adult-oriented reward scenes. Players compete in mahjong hands, earning character interactions and purchasing useful game aids as they progress. Conversation prompts involving romantic or dating situations add a character-driven layer to the conventional tile-game structure. Despite its name, it should not be confused with Konami's Tokimeki Memorial puzzle spin-offs; it belongs to Japan's specialized video-mahjong tradition.

games.title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles

variants.title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (US 4 Players, set 1)
Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (US 4 Players, set 2)

games.description:
Konami's Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (1989) is one of the definitive four-player arcade beat-'em-ups, translating the popular animated series into a frantic cooperative adventure. Leonardo, Raphael, Donatello and Michelangelo fight through streets, sewers and enemy hideouts to rescue April O'Neil and Splinter from Shredder's forces. Each turtle has a recognizable weapon, and the battles feature familiar enemies such as Foot Soldiers, Bebop, Rocksteady and Krang.

The large four-player cabinet was part of the game's appeal, letting friends join forces in an accessible mix of jumping, striking, throwing and special attacks. Colorful cartoon sprites, voice samples and memorable music made the production feel like a playable television episode. It was a major arcade success, and its format helped define the cooperative licensed brawler of the early 1990s. Two-player and regionally renamed Teenage Mutant Hero Turtles versions also exist.

games.title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles - Turtles in Time

variants.title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles - Turtles in Time (4 Players ver UAA)
Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles - Turtles in Time (2 Players ver UDA)
Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles - Turtles in Time (4 Players ver ADA)

games.description:
Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Turtles in Time (1991) is Konami's celebrated sequel to its 1989 four-player brawler. When Shredder steals the Statue of Liberty, the four turtles pursue his forces through a comic-book journey spanning prehistoric times, pirate ships, the Old West and the future. Players battle Foot Soldiers and animated-series bosses using rapid weapon combos, throws and special attacks, with each turtle bringing his familiar signature weapon.

The game refines its predecessor with more detailed animations, richer sound and memorable techniques such as throwing enemies toward the screen. Two-player and four-player cabinets were produced, while the later Super Nintendo conversion altered the stages and features. Its inventive time-travel premise and cooperative spectacle have made Turtles in Time one of the most fondly remembered arcade beat-'em-ups.

games.title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles - Mutant Warriors

variants.title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles - Mutant Warriors (SNES bootleg)

games.description:
Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Warriors is a 1997 unofficial arcade conversion of the Super Nintendo version of Konami's Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Tournament Fighters. Rather than the cooperative scrolling action of Konami's arcade TMNT games, it is a one-on-one versus fighter in which the turtles and other characters from the franchise use punches, kicks and special moves in side-view arenas.

The original Japanese Super Famicom release was titled Mutant Warriors, and this pirate coin-op board runs adapted SNES software in an arcade cabinet. Its historical importance is therefore as an unauthorized console-to-arcade conversion, not as a lost original Konami fighting game. Its behavior and presentation reflect the underlying home-console game and the limitations of the bootleg hardware.

games.title: Thundercade / Twin Formation
games.description:
Thundercade (1987), also known as Twin Formation and Tokusyu Butai U.A.G., is Seta's vertically scrolling combat shooter with an unusual motorcycle protagonist. Players race through hostile territory on an armed bike fitted with sidecar guns, backed by aerial support, blasting tanks, soldiers and heavy weapons as the landscape scrolls downward. Military bases, forest regions and other environments culminate in large boss encounters, including a submarine and heavily fortified installations.

Its blend of ground-vehicle movement and vertically scrolling shoot-'em-up firepower sets it apart from the aircraft-themed shooters of the period. Sidecar equipment and relentless enemy waves give it a distinctive sense of armored assault.

games.title: The Next Space
games.description: The Next Space is a 1989 vertically scrolling shooter by SNK. Players steer a spacecraft through waves of alien enemies, firing a primary weapon and a separate secondary attack while dodging hostile shots. Red capsules release speed upgrades, while blue ones supply different auxiliary weapons, encouraging the pilot to adapt firepower to the dangers ahead. Its economical two-button design and straightforward power-up system place it among SNK's lesser-known late-1980s space shooters.

games.title: T.N.K. III
games.description:
T.N.K. III (1985), known as T.A.N.K. in Japan, is an influential early military action game by SNK. Players control a prototype tank sent behind enemy lines, fighting through hostile bases with a machine gun and powerful cannon while searching for upgrades. Its rotary joystick allows movement in one direction while turning the tank's turret independently, an innovative control scheme that later became a trademark of SNK's Ikari Warriors and related shooters.

The protagonist, Ralf Jones, subsequently became a familiar character in Ikari Warriors and The King of Fighters, making this obscure tank adventure an unlikely origin point for part of SNK's enduring character roster. Unofficial variants also converted the rotary input to more conventional joystick arrangements.

games.title: The NewZealand Story
games.description:
Taito's The NewZealand Story (1988) is an expansive and charming platform game starring Tiki, a small kiwi who escapes captivity and sets out to rescue friends imprisoned by the villainous leopard seal Wally. Each colorful level is a sprawling maze of platforms, doors and hazards, with a caged kiwi waiting at its end. Tiki attacks with arrows that can be replaced by bombs, lasers or bouncing fireballs, and can even hijack balloons, airships and UFOs to fly through otherwise unreachable passages.

Its friendly cartoon appearance masks demanding platforming, secret routes and bosses, and a time limit can summon an especially dangerous pursuer. The distinctive flying vehicles and inventive level layouts set it apart from contemporary mascot games. Popular home adaptations and its energetic soundtrack helped establish The NewZealand Story as a favorite of late-1980s arcade platform fans.

games.title: Tower of Druaga
games.description:
Namco's The Tower of Druaga (1984) is a pioneering fusion of arcade action, maze exploration and role-playing progression. Players guide the armored hero Gilgamesh through sixty floors of a monster-filled tower to rescue the priestess Ki and recover the Blue Crystal Rod. On each floor, the knight must find a key, reach the exit and survive slimes, wizards, knights and dragons, fighting with a sword and defending with a shield.

The real challenge lies in its secrets: hidden treasure chests appear only after performing particular actions, many of which are cryptic and some of which supply equipment needed to finish the game. Players in Japan famously pooled clues and exchanged discoveries, turning the tower into a collective puzzle rather than a simple reflex test. Its unusual blend of secrets, equipment and dungeon advancement profoundly influenced Japanese action role-playing games, including later titles such as The Legend of Zelda and the broader tradition of exploratory fantasy adventures.

games.title: Toffy
games.description: Toffy is a 1993 maze-action game by Midas in which the player digs and navigates through chambers to collect enough diamonds or strawberries to unlock the exit. Hostile creatures patrol the passages, but falling stones and bombs can be used to crush or destroy them, sometimes turning defeated enemies into valuable gems. The result resembles an action-puzzle dungeon: success depends on planning safe routes and manipulating the environment rather than attacking everything directly. Its collectible-based progression and falling-object hazards make it a modest but recognizable relative of Boulder Dash-style maze games.

games.title: Toggle
games.description:
Toggle is an unreleased Bally/Sente arcade prototype from 1985 that blends a tank duel with a territory-control puzzle. The player and computer opponent drive small tanks around a gridded arena, claiming squares simply by crossing over them. Shooting can temporarily disable the rival, but victory depends on owning more squares when the round ends, not just scoring hits.

Special pickups can reverse captured colors, claim an entire line or change vehicle speed, creating opportunities for dramatic turnarounds. Its combination of arcade shooting and spatial competition was unusual for the period, and the preserved prototype offers a glimpse of Bally/Sente's inventive but commercially uncertain experiments.

games.title: Toki
games.description:
Toki (1989) is TAD Corporation's memorable side-scrolling platform game about a warrior transformed into an ape by an evil sorcerer. To rescue his kidnapped beloved and recover his human form, Toki crosses jungles, caverns, underwater passages and icy fortresses, fighting bizarre monsters along the way. His main weapon is a stream of projectiles spat from his mouth, and pickups change the attack into more powerful patterns, flames or other effects.

The game's oversized, highly expressive sprites and grotesque bosses give it a comic fantasy look quite unlike most contemporary military action games. Precise jumps and carefully timed shots are necessary because enemies and hazards can quickly overwhelm the slow-moving hero. Known in Japan as JuJu Densetsu, Toki became a cult arcade favorite and spawned multiple home adaptations and later revivals.

games.title: Tokio / Scramble Formation
games.description:
Scramble Formation, released by Taito in 1986 and known as Tokio in English-language markets, is a vertically scrolling shooter set above recognizable districts of Tokyo. The player flies a red biplane past landmarks in Shinjuku, Akasaka, and Ginza, battling aircraft, tanks, and ships. Shooting down certain red planes lets the pilot recruit them as escorts, transforming a lone fighter into a small airborne squadron.

The game's signature mechanic is changing the formation of these wingmen. A narrow line can attack both air and ground targets, a spread formation concentrates on airborne enemies, and a cross-shaped arrangement specializes in ground attacks. The right formation is vital against the huge warships that periodically emerge from the clouds. Releasing the escorts as a sacrificial attack provides another emergency tactic. The original Japanese title and the alternate name Tokio are both represented in arcade ROM sets; even the on-screen language setting can change the displayed title.

games.title: Toki no Senshi - Chrono Soldier
games.description: Toki no Senshi: Chrono Soldier is an obscure 1987 Japanese vertically scrolling shooter from Sega, with a title meaning roughly 'Soldier of Time'. It runs on Sega System 2 hardware and uses an eight-way joystick with two action buttons. Its historical interest extends to its surviving arcade revisions: preservation work uncovered an encrypted MC-8123 version as well as an earlier version regarded as a possible prototype. Detailed, reliable accounts of its specific weapons and stage progression remain scarce.

games.title: Taisen Tokkae-dama
games.description:
Taisen Tokkae-dama (1996) is Konami's competitive ball-matching puzzle game, a spin-off of its Puzzle-Dama series on Konami GX hardware. Rather than merely rotating falling pairs, players manipulate colored balls rising from below, grabbing a ball and repositioning it to make groups of three or more matching colors. Cleared groups send extra balls to an opponent's field, turning quick rearrangements and chain reactions into direct attacks.

Its bright anime presentation and character selection place it among the competitive puzzle games popular in Japanese arcades during the mid-1990s. Depending on the cabinet arrangement, up to four players can participate. A hidden character-selection trick also exists: using the second button at the difficulty selection reveals three additional characters.

games.title: Tokyo Gal Zukan
games.description: Tokyo Gal Zukan is a 1989 adult-themed Japanese mahjong game from Nichibutsu, played with a dedicated mahjong-button panel rather than a joystick. Its presentation pairs conventional competitive mahjong with portraits of women from Tokyo. A related medal or betting-market edition was released as Tokimeki Bishoujo, making this title representative of Nichibutsu's extensive range of late-1980s mahjong cabinet variants.

games.title: Tokyo Wars
games.description:
Namco's Tokyo Wars (1996) turns downtown Tokyo into a 3D armored battlefield. Players join either the Green or White force and drive tanks through city streets or a dockside area, seeking out and destroying the opposing team's vehicles. Crushed cars, damaged roadside objects, and collapsing sections of scenery make the environments feel unusually physical for an arcade combat game. Tanks respawn after destruction, keeping the battle moving rather than ending an individual player's participation.

The custom sit-down cabinet uses a steering wheel, separate forward and reverse pedals, firing controls, and a switch between in-tank and external camera views. Up to eight players could compete on linked machines, either fighting one another or joining forces against computer-controlled tanks. Deluxe installations went further with pneumatic recoil synchronized to the main gun, an unusually elaborate piece of arcade feedback. Running on Namco's Super System 22 hardware, Tokyo Wars is remembered as much for the scale of its linked-cabinet battles as for its destructive urban spectacle.

games.title: Tom Tom Magic
games.description: Tom Tom Magic is a 1997 video-pinball arcade game produced by Hobbitron T.K. Trading. It presents pinball-style play on a conventional raster monitor rather than a physical pinball table, using an eight-way joystick and three buttons. The surviving game runs on NMK-derived 16-bit hardware with a Motorola 68000 processor and FM/sample-based sound. Although its exact scoring features are poorly documented, it is a distinctive example of digital pinball presented in an ordinary joystick-equipped arcade cabinet.

games.title: Tomahawk 777
games.description: Data East's Tomahawk 777 (1980) is an early fixed-screen shooter in which the player commands a submarine and fires upward at attacking targets above the water. Its simple four-way joystick and single firing button reflect the transitional period between early black-and-white shooting galleries and the more elaborate color arcade shooters that followed. The machine also circulated as Tomahawk Missile through ESI, and surviving Revision 1 and Revision 5 ROM sets preserve differences in its early production history.

games.title: TomCat
games.description:
TomCat is Atari's unfinished 1985 color-vector flight-simulator experiment and one of the company's last attempts to develop a new vector arcade game. The player could choose either a jet or a helicopter and fly across a spare wireframe landscape with a horizon, instrument display, and objects such as tanks and enemy helicopters. It was conceived as a demonstration of free-flight simulation rather than a conventional scrolling shooter.

The prototype has particular historical importance as a glimpse of the end of Atari's vector era. A developer demonstrated two linked TomCat units, but Atari's support for new XY-vector hardware had effectively evaporated. The project was canceled while the team was investigating alternate vector-generation hardware, and its developer moved on to the Hard Drivin' project. Its surviving prototype is consequently far more significant as an engineering artifact than as a finished commercial release.

games.title: Tondemo Crisis
games.description:
Tecmo's Tondemo Crisis (1999) is an arcade adaptation of the deliriously comic minigame adventure better known outside Japan as Incredible Crisis. The story follows the members of an ordinary Japanese family whose attempts to get home for their grandmother's birthday are derailed by increasingly absurd catastrophes. Rather than maintaining a single genre, the game moves through short action challenges, timing tests, vehicle sequences, and other quick-changing tasks linked by animated scenes.

Individual challenges demand different reflexes and control rhythms, while the narrative provides the running joke: even the simplest errand can spiral into a citywide disaster. The arcade version uses PlayStation-derived Sony ZN hardware, but it is important not to confuse its arcade-specific presentation and controls with every detail of the later home edition. The combination of slapstick animation and rapid-fire minigames makes Tondemo Crisis an unusual late-1990s arcade release.

games.title: Tonton
games.description: Tonton is a 1987 Japanese medal-style mahjong video game from Dynax. Its defining character is Tonton, a cartoon pig who challenges the player to a mahjong match. Played on a dedicated mahjong-button panel, it combines the familiar tile-based game with a playful mascot and the presentation conventions of Japan's medal amusement market. The BET-labeled ROM set reflects this particular arcade distribution format.

games.title: Toobin'
games.description:
Toobin' (1988) is one of Atari Games' most inventive late-1980s arcade action games. One or two players guide the inner-tube riders Bif and Jet down a surreal sequence of rivers, ranging from recognizable American waterways to prehistoric landscapes and the canals of Mars. They paddle around rocks, mines, wildlife, and hostile riverside characters, pass through scoring gates, and throw collectible soda cans at obstacles and enemies. Progress is a blend of river navigation, racing, and high-score strategy rather than a conventional finish-line contest.

The control panel has no joystick: each rider uses four paddling buttons to propel or turn the tube and a fifth to throw cans. Successive clean passes through gates increase the score multiplier; missed gates and punctured tubes undo those gains. Hidden six-packs provide unlimited ammunition, and a pursuing alligator discourages players from lingering in a safe spot. Different routes, warp whirlpools, and colorful bonus letters reward exploration as well as dexterity.

Designer Dennis Harper recalled that Toobin' began as a kayaking simulator, but its original rowing controller was difficult for test players to understand. The team transformed the river technology into an accessible button-driven game, building numerous courses with an in-house level editor. The original cabinet reinforced the watery theme with rotating drums behind the marquee to suggest a flowing waterfall. An American promotional contest even rewarded players who collected the letters spelling TOOBIN'.

games.title: Top Blade V
games.description: Top Blade V is a 2003 Korean arcade game by SonoKong and Expotato based on the Beyblade spinning-top craze. Instead of ordinary one-on-one martial arts combat, players select a character and an associated top, then compete to drive the rival top out of the arena. Its roster of twelve characters and joystick-based controls translate the toy's competitive premise into a videogame contest. The game runs on BrezzaSoft's Crystal System hardware and derives from a Windows release issued in late 2002.

games.title: Top Driving
games.description: Top Driving is a 1995 overhead-style racing game distributed by the Spanish company Proyesel, associated with the alternate title Mortal Race. Players compete on scrolling tracks against other vehicles using joystick-based steering and arcade-style acceleration. Its preservation history is unusually interesting: a separate version called Mortal Race, credited to New Dream Games, was later discovered on different hardware, with extra tracks and a stronger rally emphasis. Top Driving is therefore not merely a renamed ROM set, but a distinct commercial adaptation of a related racing design.

games.title: Vs. Top Gun
games.description:
Vs. Top Gun is Konami's 1987 arcade combat-flight shooter for Nintendo's Vs. System, adapted from the film-inspired game released on the NES. Seen from the cockpit of an F-14, the player engages hostile aircraft with machine-gun fire and missiles while monitoring radar, fuel, speed, and altitude. Missions include aerial dogfights and attacks on heavily defended targets, interrupted by demanding midair refueling and aircraft-carrier landing sequences.

The game is notable for translating the movie's fighter-pilot fantasy into a compact, technically ambitious arcade experience. Its cockpit viewpoint and sudden switches between combat, refueling, and landing give it a distinctive rhythm, although those same sequences helped establish its reputation for difficulty.

games.title: Top Gunner
games.description:
Top Gunner is Exidy's remarkable 1986 vector-graphics flight-combat game, unrelated to Konami's jeep-based Jackal, which also used the Top Gunner name in North America. Exidy's game puts the player in a simulated aircraft cockpit, fighting enemy helicopters and ships using a flight yoke, throttle, and firing controls. The cabinet was especially unusual: a cockpit-style motion seat moved in response to the simulated flight, creating a physical sensation of banking and combat.

Designed for Fifty 50's XCD-1 simulator hardware, Top Gunner evolved from Exidy's earlier Vertigo project. With Vic Tolomei handling much of the software, it represents one of the last commercial applications of color-vector graphics to an arcade flight simulator. Its specialized moving cabinet and vector display place it far outside the more familiar joystick-driven shooters of 1986.

games.title: Top Hunter - Roddy & Cathy
games.description:
Top Hunter: Roddy & Cathy is SNK's 1994 Neo Geo action-platformer starring two interplanetary bounty hunters battling the Klapton space pirates. Roddy and Cathy can extend their arms to grab opponents, hurl enemies into one another, manipulate switches, and interact with stage scenery. The adventure spans four themed planets, Forest, Ice, Wind, and Fire, with large bosses, hidden items, and changing routes.

Its cleverest feature is a two-plane playfield: the heroes can jump between foreground and background lanes to dodge attacks, reach objects, or corner enemies. Fighting-game-style special moves and rideable machines add further variety, while simultaneous two-player action makes the stages feel like a hybrid of beat 'em up and platformer. Developed by a team that included former Irem staff, Top Hunter also foreshadows the exaggerated animation and vehicle-based comedy later associated with SNK's Metal Slug games.

games.title: Top Landing
games.description:
Top Landing (1988) is Taito's arcade flight-landing simulator and the successor to Midnight Landing. Rather than emphasizing aerial combat, it challenges the player to bring an airliner safely onto the runway, balancing direction, speed, descent, and alignment during the final approach. Flights take place at airports associated with cities including Tokyo, Paris, San Francisco, and Sydney, with scenery rendered in an increasingly sophisticated 3D style.

Compared with the earlier simulator, Top Landing adds detailed daytime surroundings and a greater sense of flying over real terrain. Its dedicated cockpit-style controls made landing itself the central arcade skill test, an unusual premise in a market dominated by combat and racing games. It is often singled out as one of Taito's early ventures into polygonal 3D graphics.

games.title: Toppy & Rappy
games.description: Toppy & Rappy is a 1996 Korean arcade platform-action game from SemiCom, featuring a pair of cartoon protagonists who have matching abilities rather than distinct character classes. Players advance through side-view stages, defeat enemies, and collect money used to buy weapons and ammunition between stages. This shop-based progression distinguishes it from platform games in which defeated enemies simply drop immediate weapon upgrades. Its colorful but eclectic artwork and two-player setup reflect SemiCom's lesser-known strand of mid-1990s arcade development.

games.title: Top Racer
games.description:
Top Racer is an unauthorized arcade version of Namco's influential 1982 Formula One game Pole Position. The underlying race remains recognizable: the driver first attempts a timed qualifying lap at Fuji Speedway and then joins a race, steering around rival cars and roadside hazards while trying to beat the countdown. The cockpit-behind-car view, fast scaling road graphics, and qualification requirement all derive from the parent game.

Its significance lies in being a bootleg hardware and branding variant rather than an independently designed racer. Several Top Racer sets survive, allowing preservation projects to document the proliferation of unlicensed Pole Position-derived arcade boards.

games.title: Top Roller
games.description: Top Roller is an overhead-view roller-skating action race in which one or two players compete against the clock while trying to stay on the track. Rival skaters attempt to shove the player off course, and the route is littered with water crossings, street traffic, and even attacks from helicopters. Success depends on dodging or jumping past hazards while pushing competitors aside and maintaining forward progress. Its roller-skating premise gives this otherwise straightforward racing-platform hybrid a distinctive early-arcade personality.

games.title: Top Secret
games.description:
Exidy's Top Secret (1986) is a weapon-laden driving action game on the Exidy 440 hardware, not the Capcom platformer also known in Japan as Top Secret. The player drives a futuristic combat car along a hazardous roadway, steering and accelerating while shooting enemy vehicles and collecting ammunition. The scenery grows more elaborate as the route continues, eventually leading through an urban complex to a massive tank encounter.

The cabinet is memorable for its unusually crowded controls: a steering wheel, pedal, and eight illuminated buttons handling different weapons and functions, including missiles, oil, turbo, shields, and a special Top Secret action. A dedicated LED panel displays instrumentation such as speed and engine revolutions. It is an especially distinctive relative of Spy Hunter, using Exidy's shooter-oriented hardware for a vehicle-combat experience.

games.title: Top Shooter
games.description: Top Shooter is a 1995 basketball-themed arcade redemption game from Sun Mixing, built on modified, unlicensed Sega Mega Drive-compatible hardware. Players attempt to score baskets while opposing defenders obstruct their shots, with successful play contributing to a ticket-oriented scoring system. It occupies the unusual space between a conventional sports videogame and a prize-redemption machine, and its repurposed console-derived electronics are part of its historical interest.

games.title: Top Speed
games.description:
Top Speed, released in Japan as Full Throttle, is Taito's 1987 high-speed road racer. The player drives a red sports car through changing scenery and traffic, racing from checkpoint to checkpoint before the time limit expires. Like Sega's Out Run, it presents the road in a fast-moving behind-the-car perspective, with occasional forks offering alternative routes.

Its signature difference is a limited nitro boost supply that provides sudden bursts of acceleration, inviting risky passing maneuvers when the clock is running down. The combination of route choices, swerving traffic, and carefully timed boosts makes Top Speed a distinct entry in the late-1980s arcade racing boom.

games.title: Tora Tora
games.description: Tora Tora is an early Game Plan arcade shooter, preserved as a prototype from around 1980. The player operates a mobile anti-aircraft gun beneath a harbor containing sixteen vulnerable destroyers. Enemy aircraft fly overhead and drop bombs, sometimes diving toward the ships, while the gunner must shoot them down before the fleet is destroyed. The straightforward horizontal defense setup is notable for its focus on protecting a collection of targets rather than simply surviving incoming fire.

games.title: Toride II Adauchi Gaiden
games.description: Toride II: Adauchi Gaiden is a 1994 arcade mahjong-solitaire puzzle game from Metro, also known as Pai Toride II. Unlike competitive hand-based mahjong, it presents layered arrangements of tiles to be cleared by selecting matching, accessible pairs. The challenge comes from choosing an order that avoids leaving crucial tiles blocked, with progressively more involved layouts keeping the tile-removal puzzle engaging. It is part of the Japanese arcade tradition of adapting Shanghai-style solitary mahjong to coin-operated play.

games.title: Tornado Baseball / Ball Park
games.description: Tornado Baseball, also circulated as Ball Park, is a 1976 arcade baseball game associated with Dave Nutting Associates and Midway. Two human players face each other in a simplified match drawn with stick-figure athletes. The pitcher selects pitches and positions fielders with dedicated controls, while the batter times a swing; after part of an inning the players change roles and control positions. Its clear rules and short, operator-adjustable game length made it a practical coin-operated interpretation of baseball before more elaborate animated sports games appeared.

games.title: Torus
games.description: Torus is a 1996 color-matching puzzle game by Yun Sung built around stacks of colored rings. New rings descend into three columns, and the player manipulates a peg to take rings from beneath a column and transfer them elsewhere. Aligning matching colors across the same row clears the rings, freeing space for the next arrivals. Because new pieces keep dropping, the central problem is rearranging a crowded field without letting any column fill to the top. Its bottom-access ring transfers give it a very different feel from falling-block puzzles based on rotating pairs.

games.title: Toryumon
games.description:
Toryumon, also romanized Touryuumon and subtitled Gateway to Success, is a 1995 Japanese competitive puzzle game developed by JAMP and published by Sega. Pairs of yellow blocks fall into a pit, with some corners carrying blue quarter-circle markings. Joining four marked corners into a complete blue circle clears those blocks and can spread new markings to neighboring pieces, creating opportunities for chains. Successful clears also send nuisance blocks to the opposing player's field.

Running on the aging Sega System 16B platform, Toryumon is noteworthy as one of the final arcade releases for that long-lived hardware family. The distinctive corner-matching system offers a twist on the head-to-head falling-block puzzle format popular in the wake of Puyo Puyo.

games.title: Treasure of the Caribbean
games.description: Treasure of the Caribbean is a pirate-themed puzzle game originally developed by FACE Corporation for the Neo Geo in 1994 and later published in 2011 by N.C.I / Le Cortex.

games.title: Total Carnage
games.description:
Total Carnage (1992) is Midway's ferocious follow-up in spirit to Smash TV, created by much of the same development team. Captain Carnage and Major Mayhem invade the fictional nation of Kookistan to confront General Akhboob, a Gulf War-era caricature, and an army of soldiers, mutants, and war machines. The tone is deliberately outrageous: military satire, enormous bosses, frantic explosions, and countless enemies turn the rescue mission into an arcade spectacle.

Like Smash TV, it uses independent twin-stick controls: the left joystick moves the soldier, while the right fires in any of eight directions. Unlike its predecessor's single-screen arenas, Total Carnage adds expansive scrolling battlefields, branching routes, bombs, weapon pickups, and prisoners to rescue. Players can cooperate to survive the onslaught, and collecting a huge set of hidden keys unlocks the secret Pleasure Dome area.

The game is remembered for extending the twin-stick formula into a bigger, more openly satirical action campaign. Its aggressive difficulty, comic-book excess, and relentless enemy pressure make it a quintessential early-1990s Midway release.

games.title: Total Vice
games.description: Total Vice is a 1997 Konami arcade light-gun-style rail shooter built for the short-lived Konami M2 platform. Like Virtua Cop, it emphasizes reacting quickly to enemies that appear along a predetermined route, aiming and firing as the action moves from scene to scene. The game's obscure hardware is a major part of its identity: it was one of only a handful of Konami M2 arcade releases and received no conventional home-port equivalent, making original boards and emulation preservation especially important to its history.

games.title: Come Back Toto
games.description: Come Back Toto is a 1996 Korean arcade platform game from SoftClub that reworks the Snow Bros formula with different player and enemy artwork. As in the parent game, players fight through compact platform arenas, trapping and disposing of enemies to clear each stage rather than simply running to an exit. Its unusual character sprites give the familiar snowball-combat design a different personality. Although listed as a separate title, its closest historical context is as an unofficial derivative of Toaplan's Snow Bros.

games.title: Touche Me
games.description: Touche Me is an obscure adult-oriented maze game, likely produced around 1990 by an unidentified developer. The player guides a rabbit character called George Rabbit around the paths of a maze, attempting to cover or paint all the required routes while avoiding three pursuing enemies. The premise has some affinity with territory-marking maze games, but places its action in an eccentric cartoon setting involving a second character, Jessie, and a safe. It is also closely related in code and style to the arcade game Lady Frog.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.
Original developer and publisher are not established.

games.title: Touch & Go
games.description:
Touch & Go is Gaelco's 1995 beach-volleyball arcade game, presented from a side-on view of the sand court. Matches are played two against two, with players timing movement, passes, blocks, and attacks to keep the ball in play and outscore the opposing team. In a two-player cabinet, friends can cooperate as teammates or compete against one another with computer partners.

The game also supports linked cabinets for four-person matches, emphasizing the social side of volleyball. Its crisp, colorful animation and accessible sports controls give it a distinct identity within Gaelco's arcade catalog, better known for driving and action games.

games.title: Shin Nihon Pro Wrestling Toukon Retsuden 3 Arcade Edition

variants.title: Shin Nihon Pro Wrestling Toukon Retsuden 3 Arcade Edition (Japan, TR1/VER.A)

games.description: Shin Nihon Pro Wrestling Toukon Retsuden 3 Arcade Edition is a 1997 Japanese professional-wrestling game developed by Yuke's and TOMY and distributed by Namco on System 12 hardware. Based on New Japan Pro-Wrestling, it brings the Toukon Retsuden series' wrestler-versus-wrestler grappling competition into the arcade, with ring contests centered on strikes, holds, throws, and pinning an opponent. This arcade edition is an unusual example of a Japanese console-associated wrestling franchise appearing on dedicated coin-operated hardware.

games.title: Tournament Table
games.description:
Atari's Tournament Table (1978) is a dedicated multiplayer arcade table offering a collection of early paddle-and-ball sports games. Instead of a single fixed game, the machine lets players choose variants of Pong-style soccer, hockey, basketball, handball, and the four-player Quadrapong, alongside Breakout. Its selection of roughly a dozen variants encourages competition around the cabinet, with rotary controls used to position the on-screen paddles.

The game belongs to Atari's formative era, when the arcade market was moving from dedicated two-player ball games toward more varied programmable cabinets. It is also related in concept to Atari's Video Olympics for the VCS, although the coin-operated table was designed for communal play by as many as four people.

games.title: Turbo Out Run

variants.title: Turbo Out Run (Out Run upgrade, FD1094 317-0118)
differences: Hardware configuration: Out Run upgrade, FD1094 317-0118.

games.description:
Turbo Out Run (1989) is Sega's follow-up to the landmark Out Run, replacing the original's carefree route-choosing drive with a direct race across the United States. At the wheel of a Ferrari F40, the player speeds from New York toward Los Angeles, racing the clock and a computer-controlled rival in a Porsche 959. Checkpoints mark progress through a fixed cross-country course filled with traffic, changing scenery, and demanding bends.

The key addition is a turbo boost that delivers a burst of acceleration but must be managed as the engine heats up. Between sections, players can choose improvements to their car, shifting the experience toward competitive high-speed racing. Sega sold Turbo Out Run both as a dedicated machine and as an upgrade to existing Out Run hardware, making it a direct continuation of the earlier game's spectacular sprite-scaling road presentation.

games.title: Toy Land Adventure
games.description: Toy Land Adventure is a 2001 Korean stage-based platform action game from SemiCom. Its toy-world story concerns Mr. Monitor, a once-friendly resident who has become an evil monitor, and two toy heroes, a cat and a dog, attempting to stop him. The adventure contains six worlds and 54 stages, with enemies and environmental challenges encountered as the pair pushes toward their goal. Its colorful toybox setting and character-driven premise give it the feel of a late arcade-era cartoon platformer.

games.title: Toypop
games.description:
Toy Pop is Namco's charming 1986 maze-action game, with simultaneous two-player play starring the puppet Pino and the doll Acha. The characters move through toy-themed rooms known as 'boxes', opening presents and battling animated toys while searching for the four golden hearts needed to unlock the exit. Certain packages reveal weapon upgrades, and the right projectile must be used against enemies resistant to ordinary shots.

The adventure comprises 44 boxes and features appearances by the wizard Mahou before a final confrontation with the witch Majyo. Its compact, room-by-room structure blends the collecting pressure of a maze game with the tactics of a multidirectional shooter. Originally a Japan-only arcade release, Toy Pop later became more widely known through Namco Museum on the PlayStation.

games.title: Time Pilot '84
games.description:
Time Pilot '84: Further into Unknown World is Konami's 1984 science-fiction sequel to Time Pilot. The player pilots a constantly moving craft across a scrolling overhead battlefield, rotating freely to chase enemy formations. Instead of the original game's recognizable historical aerial eras, the sequel uses futuristic bases, metallic vehicles, and surreal changing landscapes. Defeating enough regular enemies summons a large guardian that must be destroyed to advance.

Its key tactical addition is a two-weapon system. Standard forward shots destroy vulnerable green targets, but armored silver enemies and stage bosses require homing missiles, fired after maneuvering into position to acquire a lock. The result is less about shooting continuously and more about switching targets and attack methods while flying at speed. Distributed extensively as a conversion kit, Time Pilot '84 also contains a small cameo by the biplane from the first Time Pilot.

games.title: Top Player's Golf
games.description:
Top Player's Golf (1990) was one of the early titles showcasing SNK's Neo Geo MVS and AES hardware. Players choose one of four golfers and compete on courses at two country clubs, managing club selection, aim, and the power and timing of each shot. Three modes offer different styles of competition, including Stroke Play, head-to-head Match Play, and Nassau-style contests with additional side challenges.

The game features digitized speech and optional caddie advice, giving its otherwise traditional golf simulation a distinctive arcade presentation. Although later eclipsed in Neo Geo enthusiasts' memories by Neo Turf Masters, Top Player's Golf remains significant as an early sports title for the platform and a snapshot of SNK's original launch-era lineup.

games.title: TPS
games.description:
TPS is the BIOS for Tecmo's PlayStation-derived arcade platform, introduced in 1997 and built around Sony ZN-1 hardware. The main board supplied MIPS processing, textured 3D graphics, and Sony audio facilities, while Tecmo used its own ROM and interface boards to adapt the platform to coin-operated cabinets.

The documented TPS family includes optional auxiliary Z80 and Yamaha YMZ280B sound circuitry, so configurations were not necessarily identical across production boards. The BIOS set preserves Tecmo's version of the shared startup firmware and its relationship to the board's protection and peripheral hardware. It is a system component rather than a standalone arcade release.

games.title: Track & Field
games.description:
Track & Field, originally released in Japan as Hyper Olympic, is Konami's landmark 1983 athletics game and one of the most influential sports titles of the arcade era. Up to four players compete across six events: 100-meter dash, long jump, javelin, 110-meter hurdles, hammer throw, and high jump. Competitors must meet qualifying standards to move forward, turning each event into a brief contest of speed, rhythm, and precision.

Its defining innovation was a control scheme built around two rapidly alternated run buttons and a third action button. Tapping quickly builds speed, while carefully timed presses determine jumps and throws. This deceptively simple arrangement inspired countless button-mashing sports games and became notorious for the punishment it inflicted on arcade control panels and players' fingers. Some machines were later fitted with trackball controls to reduce wear.

With its sports-announcer atmosphere, recognizable events, and infectious multiplayer competition, Track & Field became one of Konami's biggest early arcade successes. It helped establish a whole lineage of Olympic-style minigame competitions and is still a vivid reminder of how the physical controls of a cabinet could become the core of a videogame's appeal.

games.title: Trail Blazer
games.description:
Trail Blazer is a 1987 Coinmaster electronic quiz game, unrelated to the better-known 1986 home-computer racing game of the same name and also distinct from later mechanical fruit machines carrying the title. It uses a three-button panel and Coinmaster's characteristic compact video hardware. The program contains a question-and-answer component, but the surviving arcade dump lacks the original question data, leaving the complete quiz experience incompletely preserved.

That missing material is a significant part of the game's history: although its hardware and interface can be studied, the full original question catalogue cannot be reconstructed from the available set.

games.title: Thrash Rally
games.description:
Thrash Rally is Alpha Denshi's 1991 top-down rally racer for the Neo Geo, released by SNK. Drivers select vehicles with different handling, durability, acceleration, and top-speed characteristics before taking on rally stages set on varied terrain. The scrolling overhead viewpoint keeps the car central while tight bends, roadside barriers, and changing surfaces demand constant correction.

Players can compete in a World Rally Championship-style series or tackle a long-distance Paris-Dakar-inspired challenge. Each course is a race against the clock, rewarding efficient cornering and a willingness to push speed near the limits of control. Thrash Rally is a relatively early example of the compact, fast-moving overhead driving style later refined in games such as Neo Drift Out and Over Top.

games.title: Tranquillizer Gun
games.description:
Sega's Tranquillizer Gun (1980) is an unusual jungle maze game about capturing, rather than killing, wildlife. The player controls a hunter who shoots lions, gorillas, elephants, and snakes with a tranquilizer gun, then must carry each unconscious animal back to a truck.
