A sedated animal remains available for only a short time, so reaching it and returning safely becomes a logistical puzzle as well as a test of reflexes.

The hunter moves through paths cut into dense jungle, while the truck can travel around the outer boundary. Every successfully transported animal advances the collection goal, and capturing the required animals completes the round. This mixture of maze navigation, timed retrieval, and shooting makes Tranquillizer Gun a distinctive Sega title from the early fixed-screen arcade period.

games.title: Transformer
games.description:
Transformer is a Sega scrolling shooter from 1986 closely related to the Master System game TransBot, known in Japan as Astro Flash. The player pilots the transforming CA-214 fighter in a post-apocalyptic science-fiction setting, battling forces controlled by a hostile computer called DALAUS. Enemy waves attack as the background scrolls horizontally, and the craft can change between aircraft and robot forms.

The central weapon mechanic uses collectible question-mark icons to cycle through a range of temporary armaments, rewarding quick choices about how best to handle the next wave. The arcade version is a comparatively obscure member of Sega's mid-1980s shooter catalog, and should not be confused with an official game based on the Transformers toy license.

games.title: Trapeze / Trampoline
games.description: Trapeze is Exidy's 1978 ball-and-paddle game, conceived as a successor to Circus and released in Japan by Taito under the name Trampoline. The player uses a rotary paddle control to position the bouncing apparatus and keep acrobatic clowns airborne, directing them toward fixed targets such as stars and chairs. The action builds on the simple physical timing and rebound trajectories of early arcade paddle games. Exidy's own Trapeze version remained essentially an unreleased prototype, making Taito's Trampoline release an important part of the game's history.

games.title: Traverse USA / Zippy Race
games.description:
Traverse USA, also known as Zippy Race in Japan and MotoRace USA in other markets, is Irem's 1983 motorcycle racing game. The player travels across the United States from Los Angeles toward New York, weaving through traffic and obstacles while managing a limited fuel supply. Its stages alternate between an overhead highway view, where passing cars improves the rider's rank, and a behind-the-bike perspective as the next city approaches.

The route passes cities such as Las Vegas, Houston, St. Louis, and Chicago, and later stages bring faster motorcycle classes that are harder to control. The changing camera perspectives and cross-country progression were ambitious touches for a racing game of its era, giving the trip a sense of distance well beyond a single repeating circuit.

games.title: Tricky Doc
games.description: Tricky Doc is a 1987 platform game by Spanish developer Tecfri starring a scientist who has accidentally released his own experimental creatures. Across six stages, the professor pursues the escaped monsters through platforms, ladders, and obstacles, using a spray weapon to immobilize them. Jumping, ducking, and moving between levels of the screen are as important as attacking, because the creatures keep roaming while the scientist attempts to recapture or subdue them. Its eccentric laboratory premise marks it as one of Tecfri's distinctive European arcade productions.

games.title: Trick Trap
games.description:
Trick Trap, known in Japan as Labyrinth Runner, is Konami's 1987-88 overhead run-and-gun adventure. The Prince of Vegetaria sets out to rescue Princess Papaya from the Devil, fighting through forests, castle defenses, mazes, and other monster-filled areas. The player runs through scrolling passages, fires at enemies, and collects stronger weapons, including a laser, while limited time adds pressure to every encounter.

Bombs and a screen-clearing attack offer ways to escape crowded situations, but the game demands careful use of its available weapons and routes. Once the timer runs out, a relentless enemy pursues the player, making hesitation dangerous. Trick Trap belongs to Konami's wave of action-heavy late-1980s arcade releases, but its fantasy rescue setting and labyrinth layouts distinguish it from military shooters.

games.title: Trio The Punch - Never Forget Me...

variants.title: Trio The Punch - Never Forget Me... (World)
Trio The Punch - Never Forget Me... (Japan)

games.description:
Trio the Punch: Never Forget Me... is Data East's gloriously eccentric 1990 arcade action game. Players choose one of three fighters, the burly Santos, the ninja Kamakura-kun, or the swordsman Rosesub, each equipped with an improbable assortment of attacks and weapons. Across dozens of short, shifting stages, the objective is usually to defeat enough enemies to collect hearts and trigger a boss encounter. The scenery, opponents, and rules change abruptly, giving the game an unpredictable comic rhythm.

The real appeal lies in its surreal humor. Stages contain absurd character transformations, unexpected boss appearances, and bizarre prize lotteries between rounds that can help or hinder the player. Data East characters such as Karnov and Chelnov also make appearances. Rather than the polished consistency of a conventional beat 'em up, Trio the Punch offers a chaotic collection of arcade jokes, which has made it a beloved cult curiosity among players who enjoy the stranger corners of Japanese game design.

games.title: Triple Punch
games.description:
Triple Punch, also sold as Knock Out!!, is a 1982 maze-outline game in which the player controls a carpenter racing to complete a large grid of rectangular spaces. Moving along the boundaries paints each edge; enclosing a rectangle fills it and scores points. Unlike many single-screen territory games, the maze scrolls horizontally and wraps around, giving players a larger circuit to explore.

Several different enemies patrol the paths, including a gorilla, ghost, eraser, and fire. The eraser can undo incomplete work, while the carpenter can repel most foes with three quick punches, although the fire cannot be stopped. Completing multiple rectangles together increases the score bonus. Its mixture of path planning, enemy avoidance, and opportunistic punching gives this early arcade title a character of its own.

games.title: Mahjong Triple Wars
games.description: Mahjong Triple Wars is a 1989 Japanese mahjong game from Nichibutsu that frames its tile matches with fantasy role-playing elements. Rather than presenting only a succession of ordinary mahjong opponents, it introduces selectable characters, collectible or usable items, and bonuses associated with winning. The result reflects the late-1980s Japanese arcade trend of combining established mahjong rules with character progression and adult-oriented presentation.

games.title: Mahjong Triple Wars 2
games.description: Mahjong Triple Wars 2 is Nichibutsu's 1990 follow-up to its RPG-flavored arcade mahjong game. It retains the combination of traditional Japanese mahjong matches with fantasy-themed character and item systems, placing particular emphasis on bonus items that assist play. The sequel is part of the company's large catalog of adult-oriented mahjong cabinets, but its role-playing embellishments make it more than a bare tile-game conversion.

games.title: Triple Hunt
games.description:
Atari's Triple Hunt (1977), designed by Owen Rubin, is a three-in-one arcade shooting gallery controlled by a mounted gun. The operator could configure the cabinet for Hit the Bear, Witch Hunt, or Raccoon Hunt, each with different targets and scenery. Bears move through a woodland scene, while the haunted-house version fills windows and skies with ghosts, witches, and bats. Players try to score as many hits as possible before the timer expires.

The game is particularly notable for its physical presentation. The scenes used graphical overlays and masks in combination with electronic targets, giving greater depth than the primitive screen imagery alone could convey. Switching games required changing artwork and a cabinet setting, making Triple Hunt a hybrid of the traditional shooting-gallery attraction and a programmable video arcade machine.

games.title: Tri-Pool
games.description: Tri-Pool is a 1981 arcade billiards game from Noma offering three variations: straight pool, nine-ball, and snooker. The player uses an eight-way joystick to place a targeting marker and select where to strike the cue ball, with buttons controlling the shot and its strength. A limited supply of cue balls turns each visit to the table into a scoring challenge rather than a full-length simulation of club billiards. Its selection of cue-sports disciplines made it a versatile early video-pool machine.

games.title: Tri-Sports
games.description:
Tri-Sports is Bally Midway's 1989 trackball-controlled sports compilation, combining three distinct games on one arcade board. Power Strike offers several varieties of bowling, Pool Shark provides cue-sports modes including nine-ball and straight pool, and Mini Golf Deluxe adds putting puzzles and trickier miniature-golf layouts.

The trackball is the unifying feature, but it serves different purposes in each sport, from defining a bowl's release to aiming and controlling a billiards shot or putt. The package makes use of Midway's MCR-68 family of hardware with upgraded audio, and its variety gives players more reasons to return than a single-purpose sports cabinet.

games.title: Trivial Pursuit
games.description: Trivial Pursuit: Baby Boomer Edition is Bally/Sente's coin-operated adaptation of the famous trivia board game, with questions aimed at the Baby Boomer generation. Players choose on-screen personalities and navigate a board while answering questions, aiming to progress by demonstrating knowledge rather than reflexes. The edition uses Bally/Sente SAC-I hardware and shares the underlying gameplay format with other Trivial Pursuit arcade question sets; the subject matter is what sets this particular version apart.

games.title: Trivial Pursuit
games.description: Trivial Pursuit: Spanish Edition is a 1987 localized arcade version of Bally/Sente's adaptation of the popular board game. Players move around an on-screen game board and answer questions to advance, using joystick-and-button controls instead of cards and dice. Its defining feature is the Spanish-language question material, distinguishing it from the North American Genus and specialist editions while retaining the same basic trivia competition.

games.title: Trivial Pursuit
games.description: Trivial Pursuit: Genus I is the general-knowledge edition of Bally/Sente's 1984 arcade trivia game. It takes the familiar idea of navigating the Trivial Pursuit board and answering questions in different subjects, then translates the experience into a joystick-operated coin-op game. Players select on-screen characters and attempt to make progress through correct answers. The Genus I question set is the original broad-topic counterpart to the later Genus II and specialist arcade editions.

games.title: Trivial Pursuit
games.description: Trivial Pursuit: Genus II is Bally/Sente's alternate general-knowledge question set for its arcade version of the famous trivia board game. As in Genus I, players steer an on-screen character around a board, answering questions and competing through knowledge rather than physical skill. Its identity is defined by the revised Genus II question collection, extending the life of the same SAC-I hardware and basic gameplay.

games.title: Trivial Pursuit
games.description: Trivial Pursuit: All Star Sports Edition is Bally/Sente's sports-focused variant of its 1984 coin-operated trivia game. Players compete on the familiar board-style screen, progressing by answering questions, but the challenge here centers on sporting facts and history rather than the broad general-knowledge categories of Genus I and II. The special question set illustrates how Bally/Sente reused one arcade format for several different audiences.

games.title: Trivial Pursuit
games.description: Trivial Pursuit: Young Players Edition is a family-oriented variant of Bally/Sente's arcade adaptation of the trivia board game. Players navigate the board and answer questions in the same joystick-based format as the other releases, but the question collection is aimed at a younger audience. It is one of the specialist SAC-I arcade editions alongside the Genus, Baby Boomer, and All Star Sports versions.

games.title: Triv Quiz
games.description:
Triv-Quiz is an early-1980s arcade question-and-wager game from Status Games. Players begin with a bank of 10,000 points, read a question, and decide how much of their score to risk before choosing among three possible answers. Categories include Sports, Entertainment, World Facts, and an Expert Challenge, creating an appealing mix of knowledge testing and calculated risk.

Unlike simple multiple-choice cabinets, Triv-Quiz makes betting confidence part of every round: a difficult question can be profitable or disastrous depending on the player's wager. The machine also allowed operators to program their own advertising messages through its service menu, a reminder of how countertop and arcade quiz games were marketed to venues.

games.title: Tropical Angel
games.description:
Tropical Angel is Irem's unusual 1983 water-skiing arcade game. Players steer a female skier across a scrolling waterscape, weaving around rocks and other hazards while passing through pairs of flags before time expires. The accelerator must be held down to maintain speed, and the course becomes increasingly crowded with buoys, ramps, and even sharks.

A dedicated trick button makes the skier turn around and travel backward, temporarily sacrificing steering control in exchange for bonus points. This playful risk-reward mechanic distinguishes Tropical Angel from ordinary racing games, as a good run requires both precise gate navigation and judicious showboating.

games.title: Trog
games.description:
Trog (1990) is Bally Midway's prehistoric answer to Pac-Man, starring four cartoon dinosaurs, Rex, Bloop, Spike, and Gwen. The dinosaurs explore small islands in the land of Og, collecting every egg while avoiding the one-eyed cavemen known as Trogs. Unlike Pac-Man, the characters can punch their pursuers, knocking them backward or eventually off the island. Special pickups can transform the dinosaurs and temporarily turn them into fierce predators.

Up to four players can join the same game, giving the maze format a lively cooperative and competitive twist as they compete for eggs and survival. Each island has traps, different routes, and distinct enemy behavior. The game uses a bright clay-animation-inspired visual style, with expressive prehistoric characters that look more like stop-motion creatures than the abstract sprites of classic maze games.

Trog is also notable for its unusual development history. An earlier prototype, sometimes called BattleTrog, emphasized strategy and placing bones to influence the maze. The final arcade release abandoned much of that complexity in favor of more immediate action. This evolution helped give the game a distinctive place in Midway's catalog alongside its better-known shooters and fighting games.

games.title: Trojan
games.description:
Trojan, released in Japan as Tatakai no Banka, is Capcom's 1986 post-apocalyptic sword-fighting action game. Players control a warrior fighting through ruined streets, fortifications, and enemy-held territory to confront the ruler Achiless. Rather than simply attacking with bare hands, the hero carries both a sword and a shield, slashing at enemies while blocking projectiles and melee strikes.

The eight-way joystick handles movement, crouching, and jumping, with separate buttons for the sword and shield. Positioning the shield correctly is often as important as attacking, especially against knife throwers and powerful stage bosses. Directed by Takashi Nishiyama, Trojan builds on the side-scrolling martial-arts combat he explored in Kung-Fu Master, offering a more defensive and weapon-focused variation on the early beat 'em up.

games.title: Tron
games.description:
Tron (1982) is Bally Midway's celebrated arcade adaptation of Disney's groundbreaking science-fiction film. Rather than trying to compress the film into one kind of action game, it offers four distinct challenges set inside the computer world: Light Cycles, Battle Tanks, the Grid Bugs, and the MCP Cone. Players choose the order in which to attempt these domains within each stage, gradually advancing through the game's increasingly demanding phases.

The striking control panel combines an eight-way joystick with a trigger and a rotary spinner. In the tank and grid-bug sequences the dial aims shots independently of movement, while the Light Cycle challenge tests sharp turning and careful positioning to avoid lethal trails. The MCP sequence requires carving through a rotating barrier to reach the central target. This variety, together with fluorescent blue cabinet artwork and dramatic electronic sound, gave the game an identity inseparable from the film's neon-computer aesthetic.

Tron became a major arcade hit, selling roughly 10,000 cabinets and winning a contemporary coin-operated game award. It also has a fascinating production history: Midway considered several radically different prototypes before consolidating a set of minigames into the finished machine. The recognizable cabinet, unusual controls, and multiple gameplay styles helped make Tron one of the most enduring licensed arcade games of the early 1980s.

games.title: Trophy Hunting - Bear & Moose V1.0
games.description: Trophy Hunting: Bear & Moose (2002) is a competitive arcade hunting game built around two players selecting equipment and pursuing large game. Players can choose weapons such as a scoped revolver, bolt-action rifle, compound bow, or muzzleloader before hunting bears in settings including Colorado, Idaho, and Maine, or moose in Montana, Utah, and Alaska. The gun-based cabinet emphasizes aiming and target selection, with the different hunting locations and weapons providing variety between sessions.

games.title: Top Ranking Stars
games.description:
Top Ranking Stars, released internationally as Prime Time Fighter, is Taito's 1993 boxing game for the F3 arcade system. Rather than strictly following realistic weight divisions, it stages an all-weight-class championship with six internationally themed boxers. Each fighter has characteristic attacks and special moves, and matches can end by knockout or a points decision.

The game translates the tactics of a fighting game into the boxing ring, emphasizing spacing, quick combinations, and reading an opponent's attacks. Its distinctive roster and colorful Taito F3 graphics make it an interesting alternative to the more simulation-oriented boxing titles of the period.

games.title: Truck Kyosokyoku
games.description:
Truck Kyosokyoku, also known as Truck Kyousoukyoku: Ai to Kanashimi no Rodeo, is a 2000 Namco arcade racer developed by Metro and inspired by Japan's flamboyantly decorated dekotora trucks. Players select one of four massive, heavily ornamented vehicles and race through five stages under a strict time limit. Bright paintwork, elaborate lighting, and oversized truck bodies give the competition a very different flavor from conventional sports-car racing.

Running on Namco System 12 hardware, the game celebrates a uniquely Japanese vehicle culture in which working trucks become personal artistic statements. Its emphasis on keeping a bulky truck moving through traffic and reaching checkpoints is as much a novelty of theme as a driving challenge.

games.title: Truco-Tron
games.description: Truco-Tron is an Argentine arcade conversion of Truco, the traditional Spanish-deck card game built around bluffing and trick-taking. The player faces a computer opponent using a 40-card deck, with each hand decided over a maximum of three tricks. Calls and raises can increase the stakes, and a player can prevail either by taking the necessary tricks or by persuading the opponent to concede. Joystick-and-button prompts turn the negotiations of this popular regional game into an unusual arcade tabletop experience.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Truco Clemente
games.description: Truco Clemente (1991) is an Argentine arcade card game from Miky SRL that combines the rules of Truco with the famous comic-strip character Clemente, created by cartoonist Caloi. Players challenge Clemente in the traditional bluffing and trick-taking contest, choosing when to play cards, call raises, or accept the opponent's bets. The character's expressions and banter give a distinctly local personality to a game deeply associated with Argentine social life.

games.title: Truxton / Tatsujin
games.description:
Truxton, known in Japan as Tatsujin, is Toaplan's formidable 1988 vertically scrolling shooter, released by Taito and distributed in North America by Midway. The player pilots the Super Fighter against the invading Gidan forces, flying through fields of hostile spacecraft, fortified terrain, and enormous mechanical bosses. Relentless enemy patterns and the danger of losing carefully accumulated firepower make survival unusually tense.

The game features three memorable weapon styles, ranging from a concentrated forward attack to broad coverage and spectacular electrically charged fire. Collectible power-ups improve the chosen weapon, while a limited bomb supply provides a way to survive emergencies or crush major targets. The enormous skull-shaped bomb emblem became an enduring visual symbol of the series.

Truxton helped define Toaplan's brand of exacting arcade shooting: fast bullets, richly layered enemy formations, and high stakes when a life is lost. Its design strongly influenced the company's later shooters and earned a lasting reputation among players seeking the demanding end of the genre.

games.title: Truxton II / Tatsujin II / Tatsujin Oh

variants.title: Truxton II / Tatsujin II / Tatsujin Oh (Japan)

games.description:
Truxton II, released in Japan as Tatsujin Oh, is Toaplan's 1992 sequel to its punishing 1988 vertical shooter. The player again flies a lone advanced fighter through dense enemy formations, now displayed with more elaborate graphics, larger mechanical bosses, and sweeping stage environments. The campaign consists of six enormous areas that loop at progressively harder settings, making complete mastery a long-term challenge.

Weapon pickups switch among distinct fire patterns, including red area-fire bursts, a blue homing laser, and wide green projectiles. Further pickups increase power or speed, while special bombs can save the fighter during heavy assaults. The game's exacting enemy placement and tendency to punish lost power-ups have made it notorious even among experienced shoot-'em-up players. Truxton II represents Toaplan's increasingly elaborate early-1990s approach to the traditional scrolling shooter.

games.title: Trivia Challenge
games.description:
Trivia Challenge is a 1985 question-and-answer arcade game developed by Joyland under licence from Senko Industries. It presents quiz prompts on a vertical monitor and uses four buttons for responses rather than a joystick. Its electronics are derived from the same broad family as several Galaxian-era conversion games, making it a compact early example of trivia content running on adapted arcade hardware.

The principal preservation limitation is missing question ROM data. As a result, the surviving emulated program does not reproduce the full original quiz, and it would be misleading to claim a complete question selection or detailed progression scheme.

games.title: Trivia Genius
games.description: Trivia Genius is a 1985 quiz game from Enerdyne Technologies, preserved as a related version of the company's Trivia Master. It belongs to the same early wave of dedicated coin-operated trivia titles, presenting text-based questions and receiving answers through a panel of four buttons. Its importance within AdvanceMAME is partly archival: the game was eventually recognized as part of the Trivia Master hardware and ROM family rather than a completely unrelated design. Specific differences in its questions and rules are not sufficiently documented to describe it as a new kind of quiz game.

games.title: Trivia Master
games.description:
Trivia Master is a 1985 coin-operated quiz game developed by Enerdyne Technologies and distributed by PGD. It brings trivia competition to an arcade cabinet rather than a board game or television studio, using a color monitor and four-button answer selection. Questions held in ROM supply the challenge, while the results allow players to compare their knowledge and scores. The game belongs to the surge of bar-friendly quiz machines that offered a quieter alternative to action-oriented arcade titles.

Multiple ROM sets and a related edition named Trivia Genius have survived, reflecting the revisions and question variations common to this type of machine. Its follow-up, Super Trivia Master, appeared the next year and expanded the franchise's multiplayer appeal.

games.title: Trivia Quest
games.description:
Trivia Quest is a 1984 English-language quiz machine developed by Techstar and distributed under the Sunn name, an early entrant in the North American bar-trivia market. A single player answers multiple-choice questions using four dedicated buttons on a vertically oriented display. Its known question packs cover general knowledge and sports, with material ranging from conventional trivia to questions about baseball, football and hockey. The original hardware uses a Motorola 6809 processor and two AY-3-8910 sound chips.

Unusually, its question library was distributed across replaceable ROMs, allowing an operator to change the material without replacing the entire game. A 2026 analysis of the preserved ROMs recovered 489 question records, divided into 201 general-knowledge and 288 sports entries. Each question offers four choices, while the data also identifies Scholar and Genius difficulty levels. The question text was stored as ordinary ASCII, a revealing detail from the early days of electronic trivia before more elaborate compression and obfuscation became common.

games.title: Trivia ? Whiz
games.description: Trivia ? Whiz is Merit's 1985 countertop trivia game, presented here in its horizontal-screen configuration. Each credit provides a short series of multiple-choice questions, answered using the machine's colored selection buttons. Question packs cover subjects such as entertainment, sports and general knowledge, with some versions also including adult-oriented trivia. Success is measured through points and high scores rather than an action-game character's survival. The same Merit 6221-based hardware supported interchangeable question ROMs, and the horizontal edition is a good example of the compact trivia machines found in North American bars during the 1980s.

games.title: Trivia ? Whiz
games.description: Trivia ? Whiz Edition 2 is a revised 1985 question set for Merit's popular countertop quiz machine. It retains the original's rapid sequence of multiple-choice questions and button-based responses while supplying different ROM-based trivia content. Categories span familiar bar-quiz topics, with surviving alternative question ROMs including adult-oriented material. The game shares the Merit 6221 hardware and basic scoring structure of the earlier edition; its identity comes from its revised questions and program ROMs, not from a new graphical or action-game mechanic.

games.title: Trivia ? Whiz
games.description: Trivia ? Whiz Edition 4 is a later 1985 variation of Merit's compact quiz game, built around the same multiple-choice, button-operated format as the original. Its most recognizable addition is 'Strange But True', a true-or-false trivia category that broadens the usual selection of general knowledge, entertainment and sports questions. Different surviving ROM sets preserve alternative trivia material, including adult-themed questions, and the program appeared in both horizontal and vertical configurations. Edition 4 illustrates how Merit kept arcade quiz cabinets fresh by updating their question banks rather than replacing the underlying game.

games.title: Trivia ? Whiz
games.description: Trivia ? Whiz is Merit's mid-1980s trivia game in a vertical-screen cabinet configuration. The rules remain those of the countertop and horizontal editions: respond to multiple-choice questions using dedicated answer buttons and attempt to build a competitive score. ROM-based question banks allow the operator to vary the material, with general entertainment, sports and knowledge topics appearing across the series. This version is historically interesting because Merit adapted essentially the same quiz software and 6221 hardware to different cabinet and display layouts.

games.title: Pro Baseball Skill Tryout
games.description:
Pro Baseball Skill Tryout is Data East's 1985 Japanese arcade game based on the idea of a professional baseball entrance examination. Instead of playing a complete nine-inning match, competitors face a series of distinct baseball skill tests. These include long-distance throwing, base stealing, pitching, batting and fielding, each requiring different timing and control from the four-way joystick and two buttons. The variety of short challenges gives it a very different rhythm from traditional baseball simulations.

Released in Japanese arcades under the title Pro Yakyuu Nyuudan Test Tryout, it turns the pressure of an athletic recruitment test into a score-driven arcade competition. Its colorful, stylized presentation and energetic YM2203 soundtrack contrast with the demanding precision needed in the individual events. It remains a distinctive sports oddity in Data East's mid-1980s catalog.

games.title: Battle Arena Toshinden 2
games.description:
Battle Arena Toshinden 2 is a 1995 3D weapons-based fighting game developed by Tamsoft and distributed in arcades by Capcom on Sony's ZN-1 hardware. Returning fighters such as Eiji, Sofia, and Mondo bring swords, whips, spears, and other distinct fighting styles to enclosed arenas, joined by new contenders and secret characters. Matches are decided through striking, guarding, special moves, and ring-outs, with each character's weapon range shaping their tactics.

Unlike many polygonal fighters of its period, Toshinden emphasizes movement around an arena as well as along a single combat line. Players can sidestep and roll away from attacks, and this sequel adds a combo system, revised defensive movement, and an Overdrive meter. The game is historically notable for reversing the series' original home-console origin: Toshinden 2 appeared first in arcades before reaching the PlayStation, using hardware closely related to Sony's console.

games.title: Samurai Nihon-ichi
games.description:
Samurai Nihon-ichi is a mid-1980s Japanese side-scrolling sword-fighting game developed by Kaneko and published by Taito. The player guides a lone samurai through landscapes filled with hostile swordsmen, knife-throwing birds, tigers, and stage bosses. Rather than relying on one universal attack, the warrior has separate high and low sword swings, choosing the appropriate stroke for each approaching threat.

The four-way joystick controls running, crouching, and jumping, making spacing and defensive timing central to play. Its straightforward but demanding sword combat reflects the wave of martial-arts action games that followed Kung-Fu Master, with an especially strong feudal-Japanese theme.

games.title: Takeda Shingen
games.description:
Takeda Shingen, released internationally as Shingen Samurai-Fighter, is Jaleco's 1988 historical hack-and-slash arcade game. Players take the role of the Sengoku-era daimyo Takeda Shingen, battling soldiers and rival commanders in a side-scrolling campaign leading toward his famous adversary Uesugi Kenshin. Sword attacks, defensive movement, and power-ups support the close-range combat, and a second player can join the fight.

The game also breaks up its battlefield stages with mounted archery bonuses inspired by yabusame, in which Shingen aims at targets while riding a horse. This combination of beat 'em up fighting and historical Japanese imagery sets it apart from contemporary urban brawlers.

games.title: Turkey Shoot
games.description:
Turkey Shoot is Williams Electronics' eccentric 1984 light-gun arcade shooter. Set in an absurd near future, it casts the player as a 'Turkey Terminator' hunting violent, mutated humanoid turkeys that have overrun the streets. Using an aiming gun, grenades, and a limited-use gobble attack, the player must eliminate targets through increasingly crowded shooting-gallery stages. The comic enemy designs and deliberately ridiculous premise give the game a tone unlike a military gun shooter.

Its most famous feature is physical rather than electronic: the cabinet could blow actual turkey feathers into the space in front of the display at the end of a successful stage. That theatrical trick makes Turkey Shoot a memorable example of Williams' willingness to add surprising mechanical effects to a video arcade machine.

games.title: Thunder Strike
games.description: Thunder Strike is a 1991 side-view flying shooter from The Game Room, also issued in a licensed version associated with East Coast Coin Company. Players pilot through horizontally oriented combat using an eight-way joystick and three buttons, with two people supported in alternating turns. Its unusual technical ancestry is part of its appeal: the game runs on hardware associated with Technos' Double Dragon family, repurposed for scrolling shooting rather than street fighting. Surviving arcade sets include an older revision, documenting a small American shooter that is easy to overlook among more familiar early-1990s releases.

games.title: Table Tennis Champions
games.description: Table Tennis Champions is a 1995 arcade sports game from Gamart, released in June of that year. It recreates competitive table tennis on a horizontal screen, with up to two players using eight-way joysticks and three buttons to control play. Its relatively compact setup is built around a NEC V30 processor and sampled audio, instead of the more extravagant hardware increasingly found in mid-1990s arcades. The game represents a straightforward, rarely encountered attempt to bring the short exchanges and quick reactions of ping-pong to a coin-operated sports cabinet.

games.title: Mahjong
games.description:
T.T Mahjong is a 1981 Japanese arcade mahjong game distributed by Taito under license from Alpha Denshi's earlier Jongputer design. It belongs to the first generation of computerized mahjong cabinets, reproducing the familiar process of drawing, discarding, declaring combinations, and completing a winning hand against the machine. The controls use a specialized mahjong panel with individually labeled tile keys and buttons for calls such as Pon, Chi, Kan, Riichi, and Ron.

Its historical importance lies less in spectacle than in standardization. The dedicated multi-button interface and clearly displayed tile hand helped establish conventions that would persist across the huge Japanese arcade mahjong market for years afterward.

games.title: Tough Turf
games.description:
Tough Turf is a 1989 side-scrolling beat 'em up developed by Sunsoft and Sega, set in the warehouses, streets, sewers, and industrial districts of a gang-controlled city. One or two players guide office-worker-looking heroes through eight stages, fighting large groups of thugs before reaching the gang's hideout. Enemies attack with fists, bottles, and improvised weapons, while players can seize dropped pipes and other objects for their own use.

Separate punch, kick, and jump buttons allow several combinations of attacks and defensive responses. Its mix of weapon pickups and cooperative street fighting follows the late-1980s beat 'em up formula, but the unassuming protagonists and deliberately grimy urban locations give it a distinctive flavor.

games.title: Tube Panic
games.description:
Tube Panic is a strikingly experimental 1984 space shooter developed by Fujitek and published by Nichibutsu. Rather than using the flat scrolling viewpoint familiar from most contemporary shooters, it sends a spacecraft racing through pseudo-3D tunnels and rotating geometric environments. Enemy formations rush toward the player along the tunnel walls, and the view follows the ship as it navigates the structures. Other passages open into broad space-battle areas.

The fighter can adjust its travel speed, dodge obstacles, and fire a forward beam cannon. Energy management also matters, since the ship's power runs down and is replenished by successfully docking with its mothership at the end of an area. With its rotating tunnel effects and unusually dynamic camera presentation, Tube Panic is an important early arcade experiment in simulated three-dimensional shooting.

games.title: Tugboat
games.description:
Tugboat is an approachable 1982 river-navigation game from Enter-Tech's Moppet Video line, designed with younger arcade players in mind. The player guides a tugboat upstream through a winding channel, dodging floating logs and passing buoys while collecting points from lighthouses. Its control scheme is intentionally simple, with a two-way joystick and a horn button that sounds the boat's horn.

Later stages progressively increase the boat's speed and narrow the available waterway, making collision avoidance more difficult. The gentle boating theme and uncomplicated controls reflect the short-lived market for child-friendly dedicated arcade cabinets during the early 1980s.

games.title: Tumble Pop
games.description:
Tumble Pop is Data East's lively 1991 single-screen platform game about two ghost hunters cleaning up a world full of monsters. Players explore stages set in different countries and eventually outer space, using backpack vacuum cleaners to suck up enemies. Releasing the button fires the captured creatures back across the screen, where they ricochet into other monsters and set off satisfying chain reactions. A stage is cleared only when every enemy has been defeated.

The immediate appeal is in turning enemies into ammunition. Holding a group of monsters in the vacuum creates a powerful projectile, but keeping them trapped for too long is risky. Bonus letters spelling TUMBLE POP, hidden rewards, and boss rounds encourage careful play, while simultaneous two-player action makes the confined arenas chaotic in the best way.

Drawing on the compact-stage tradition of Bubble Bobble and Snow Bros, Tumble Pop became one of Data East's most recognizable platformers. Its globe-trotting cartoon style and vacuum mechanic were distinctive enough to help it stand apart in an already crowded genre.

games.title: Tunnel Hunt
games.description: Tunnel Hunt is an Atari arcade shooter developed in the late 1970s and later distributed by Centuri. The player pilots a futuristic spacecraft through a forward-moving tunnel, avoiding the walls while firing at enemy craft that appear ahead. The perspective creates the illusion of flying into the screen, making reactions to depth and approaching obstacles central to the challenge. As an early pseudo-3D shooter, Tunnel Hunt is an interesting bridge between simple fixed-screen space games and the more sophisticated cockpit-style action titles that followed.

games.title: Turbo
games.description:
Sega's Turbo (1981) was a major technical and commercial milestone in arcade racing. Players drive a Formula-style car along a roadway shown from behind the vehicle, passing traffic as the background shifts through city streets, winding countryside, coastal roads, tunnels, and changing weather conditions. Rather than demanding a perfect lap time, each round requires overtaking a quota of other vehicles before the timer expires.

The cabinet offers a steering wheel, accelerator pedal, and gear control. Rival cars weave across the road, and collisions threaten the player's progress, so threading through traffic is the essential skill. Turbo's vivid roadside scenery, changing times of day, and smoothly scaling objects created a much stronger impression of forward motion than most earlier racing machines. It was also available in an elaborate sit-down cockpit cabinet.

Designed by Steve Hanawa, Turbo helped popularize the third-person chase-camera presentation that became a staple of arcade racing. Its success encouraged the genre's progression toward ever more convincing pseudo-3D roads, culminating in the spectacular scaling racers of the mid-1980s. It remains one of Sega's foundational driving games.

games.title: Turbo Force
games.description:
Turbo Force is Video System's 1991 vertically scrolling shooter and a direct stylistic predecessor to the company's Sonic Wings series. Up to three players can simultaneously pilot unlikely flying combat vehicles, battling a futuristic army of aircraft, tanks, and giant mechanical opponents. Bright explosions, frequent boss confrontations, and densely packed enemy formations give the game the energetic rhythm of early-1990s Japanese shooters.

The ship's power can be improved with pickups, but firepower gradually declines even without taking damage, encouraging constant movement and collection. Instead of a conventional stock of bombs activated on demand, certain special pickups unleash a screen-wide attack immediately when collected. The three-player cooperative option and distinctive improvised aircraft make Turbo Force stand out among contemporary scrolling shooters.

games.title: Turbo Sub
games.description:
Turbo Sub is an unusual mid-1980s first-person arcade shooter from Entertainment Sciences. Set after an alien invasion, it puts the player at the controls of a futuristic submarine fighting hostile creatures and machines beneath the ocean surface. The forward-facing display creates a simulated 3D undersea journey, combining rapid movement through the environment with firing at threats ahead.

The game's dramatic cockpit viewpoint and science-fiction submarine premise distinguish it from both ordinary ship shooters and the space-flight games it otherwise resembles. Its arcade release remained relatively obscure, but a later Atari Lynx adaptation introduced the concept to a new audience.

games.title: Turbo Tag
games.description:
Turbo Tag is an unreleased 1985 Bally Midway prototype that turns demolition-derby driving into a frantic overhead-view chase. The player's car can ram other vehicles safely only while turbocharged; without turbo power, contact with an opponent costs a life. A red tag car can steal the turbo ability, abruptly changing the balance between hunter and hunted.

The player must hit other cars before they park, dodge bombs and gather bonus objects. Collecting a complete set of four special items opens a bonus round, while picking up the letters T-U-R-B-O ends the regular round. Its unusual combination of vehicle combat, collecting and risk management survives as an intriguing glimpse of a Bally Midway game that never reached commercial production.

games.title: Neo Turf Masters / Big Tournament Golf
games.description:
Neo Turf Masters, known in Japan as Big Tournament Golf, is a celebrated 1996 Neo Geo golf game from Nazca, the studio also responsible for Metal Slug. Six golfers, each with distinct strengths in driving, accuracy, recovery and putting, compete on four imaginative 18-hole courses set in the United States, Japan, Australia and Germany. Players can tackle stroke play alone or with a friend, or face each other in match play.

Its approachable swing system separates shot power from ball height, leaving hook and slice to dedicated controls rather than demanding a difficult timing sequence. That simplicity hides considerable depth: strong winds, hazardous bunkers and water, challenging greens and the contrasting golfers make course management important. Occasional longest-drive and closest-to-the-pin contests can award additional holes, a particularly arcade-minded reward for precise play.

The lush digitized-looking artwork, expressive character animations and exuberant presentation helped give Neo Turf Masters an enduring reputation far beyond the usual audience for golf games. Nazca included former Irem developers who had worked on Major Title 2, explaining some of the design lineage. Originally a Neo Geo MVS cartridge, it later appeared on the AES and Neo Geo CD and has been repeatedly reissued, sometimes under its Japanese title because of the 'Masters' trademark.

games.title: Turkey Hunting USA V1.0
games.description:
Turkey Hunting USA is a 2001 light-gun hunting game by Sammy USA. Rather than pursuing a single fixed course, players hunt turkeys across five American states: Florida, New Mexico, Montana, Pennsylvania and Kansas. Each location offers different weather conditions and a different level of difficulty. The choice of rifle, shotgun, power bow or muzzleloader changes the hunting equipment available to the player.

Bonus challenges test shooting accuracy, and perfect performances can unlock turkey calls or decoys. The game also tracks high rankings in individual states as part of its 'grand slam master' objective. It belongs to Sammy's series of specialized arcade hunting games, which also included Deer Hunting USA and Wing Shooting Championship.

games.title: Turnover
games.description:
Turnover is a 1990 British pub gambling/prize game by Barcrest, represented by version 2.3 and other MPU4 Video software revisions. It belongs to the company's video-based amusement-with-prizes line, replacing the presentation of a purely mechanical fruit machine with a display driven by the MPU4 platform. Its betting and prize-oriented cabinet format is distinct from ordinary joystick action games.

The surviving sets include 2.33 and other numbered variations, with alternative video ROMs preserved alongside them. The exact winning combinations are not securely documented, but the game's place in Barcrest's evolving pub-machine catalogue is well established.

games.title: Turtles
games.description:
Turtles is a 1981 Konami maze game distributed by Stern in North America. The player guides Mama Turtle through eight floors of a building, searching mystery boxes for kidnapped baby turtles. Finding a baby causes it to climb onto her back and reveals a home in one of the maze's corners. Mama must deliver each youngster individually while avoiding pursuing beetles; some mystery boxes release additional enemies instead of babies.

Mama's only defense is a limited supply of Bug Bombs, effectively mines that temporarily stun beetles and allow her to pass. Replacement bombs occasionally appear in the middle of the maze, so using them too freely can leave her vulnerable. Enemies become faster and more aggressive as play continues. After all eight floors, a brief rescue scene plays before the cycle starts again at higher difficulty.

The game's international history is especially unusual. Konami's earlier version, 600, used racing cars as enemies, required the babies to be collected before leaving each level and employed an energy meter for bombs. Stern's Turtles substantially altered those rules, while Sega distributed a related edition called Turpin. Its cartoon presentation and domestic-rescue premise distinguish it from the many maze chases released in the wake of Pac-Man.

games.title: Turtle Ship
games.description:
Turtle Ship is a 1988 Korean shooter developed by Philko and exported by Pacific Games. Its title refers to the historic Korean turtle ship, although the action follows a fantastical craft flying and travelling through hostile environments. The game mixes horizontally and vertically moving shooter sequences, confronting players with bats, insects, fish, seahorses, enemy ships, fixed guns and large bosses.

Three separate attack buttons control the main gun, missiles and a powerful thunder weapon. Destroyed enemies yield upgrades such as stronger frontal missiles, additional missiles, a three-way shot, a brief slowing effect and Super Thunder. Turtle Ship is also an unusual example of Korean arcade production drawing heavily on existing Japanese hardware and software: historical arcade documentation identifies it as a reworking of Capcom's Side Arms, with traces of that game reportedly still present in its code.

games.title: Tutankham
games.description:
Tutankham is a 1982 Konami action-maze game, also distributed in North America by Stern, that sends an explorer into the treasure-filled chambers of an Egyptian tomb. Narrow corridors are patrolled by snakes, bats and other deadly creatures. The player collects valuables, retrieves keys to open sealed passages and races toward the exit before the countdown expires. Since only one key can be carried at a time, navigating and retracing routes are important parts of the challenge.

Its defining twist is a laser weapon that fires only horizontally. The explorer can move vertically, but cannot shoot upward or downward, making the position of an approaching enemy crucial. Limited flash bombs destroy the threats currently on screen, while warp passages offer shortcuts unavailable to the monsters. Running out of time is particularly dangerous because the weapon stops functioning, and unused time contributes to the stage-end bonus.

Tutankham was a commercial and critical success at a time when maze games were experimenting with combat and exploration. Its strange truncated title has a story of its own: arcade histories recount that the planned name 'Tutankhamon' was shortened when the display layout changed to vertical orientation. The combination of action, key-hunting and weapon limitations gives it a distinctive identity among early-1980s arcade adventures.

games.title: Tut's Tomb
games.description: Tut's Tomb is a 1996 light-gun redemption game by Island Design, themed around the search for King Tutankhamun's tomb. It supports two players simultaneously, each shooting with a single-trigger gun controller. Rather than a conventional joystick adventure, this is a gun-based amusement-machine release built around targeting on a shared horizontal screen. It runs on TMS34010 graphics hardware associated with other Island Design gun and redemption titles. Available historical descriptions do not reliably document its individual targets, scoring rules or stage sequence.

games.title: Tecmo World Cup '98
games.description:
Tecmo World Cup '98 is Tecmo's 1998 international soccer game for Sega's ST-V arcade cartridge system, hardware closely related to the Sega Saturn. Two players can compete using an eight-way joystick and six-button controls, in another entry in Tecmo's long-running series of coin-operated football games.

The ST-V release has an unusual preservation history. A second version, Tecmo World Soccer '98, was later found with a different title screen and team names. MAME development also exposed protection and goalkeeper-related behavior that complicated emulation. Those details make this comparatively obscure soccer title noteworthy as a late-1990s ST-V release, although the surviving supplied documentation gives little reliable detail about its match rules or special moves.

games.title: Twin Action
games.description:
Twin Action is a 1995 Korean horizontal shooter from Afega, featuring twin heroes in a colorful, cartoon-like battlefield. Players steer with an eight-way joystick, firing multidirectional shots while maneuvering through crowded projectile patterns. Ground-directed bombs and a powerful screen-clearing special attack supplement the normal weaponry.

Beneath its playful appearance lies a highly derivative technical history. MAME developers discovered that Twin Action closely follows UPL's U.S. AAF Mustang, including copied elements of its NMK-based hardware and protection behavior. Its music also incorporates material from the Super Nintendo game Sonic Blast Man. The result is a distinctive example of the unauthorized adaptation and recycling found in some mid-1990s Korean arcade releases.

games.title: TwinBee
games.description:
TwinBee is Konami's influential 1985 vertically scrolling shooter and one of the formative examples of the 'cute 'em up'. Instead of grim military machinery, players fly smiling, anthropomorphic spacecraft through brightly colored landscapes, fighting whimsical aerial enemies and bombing targets on the ground. One player pilots TwinBee and a second can join simultaneously as the pink WinBee. Separate buttons fire at airborne and surface targets, expanding on the two-layer combat popularized by Xevious.

The signature mechanic is a system of bells hidden in clouds. Shooting a bell repeatedly sends it bouncing upward and changes its color; catching different colors grants speed boosts, enhanced firepower, protective barriers or extra firing images, while ordinary yellow bells reward precise collection with escalating scores. The ships can also lose their arms without immediately losing a life, disabling their ground bombs until a cartoon ambulance arrives to repair them. In cooperative play, the two spacecraft can join forces for special attacks.

TwinBee was the first game released on Konami's Bubble System arcade platform, which used magnetic bubble memory rather than ordinary ROM cartridges in its original form. It became a major Japanese franchise, inspiring sequels, home conversions, music releases and animated spin-offs. Its mix of scoring tricks, teamwork and lighthearted style helped establish an alternative to the increasingly militaristic shooter genre.

games.title: Twin Brats
games.description:
Twin Brats is a 1995 Italian maze game by Elettronica Video-Games, closely modeled on the arcade classic Lady Bug. The player guides a diaper-clad child through a top-down maze, collecting dots while escaping enemies and dangerous skull symbols. Rotating doors can be used to redirect movement, block an attacker or create a temporary safe route, so survival depends on manipulating the maze as well as running through it.

The game couples this familiar chase-and-collect formula with adult-themed intermission artwork, revealing images as levels are cleared. Several program versions survive. Beyond the changed presentation, its rotating-door mechanics make the Lady Bug connection much more specific than a general resemblance to Pac-Man.

games.title: Twin Cobra
games.description:
Twin Cobra is Toaplan's landmark 1987 helicopter shooter, released in Japan as Kyukyoku Tiger and distributed internationally with Taito involvement. Piloting an attack helicopter, players fight through a vertically scrolling campaign against tanks, gun emplacements, helicopters, warships and imposing bosses. It builds on Toaplan's earlier Tiger-Heli, making the action faster, denser and much more focused on mastering patterns of incoming fire.

The game's famous color-coded weapon pickups provide four very different attack styles, including a wide spread, a multi-directional attack and concentrated forward fire. Collecting speed upgrades and timing the limited, devastating bombs is essential when enemy formations threaten to surround the helicopter. Between sections the aircraft returns to a landing area, giving the campaign a distinctive military rhythm.

Twin Cobra became a touchstone for late-1980s vertically scrolling shooters and helped define Toaplan's precision-heavy approach, which influenced many later developers. The Japanese Kyukyoku Tiger and overseas Twin Cobra sets also differ in their multiplayer arrangements, making the regional variations more consequential than a changed title screen.

games.title: Twin Eagle II - The Rescue Mission
games.description:
Twin Eagle II: The Rescue Mission is Seta's 1994 sequel to its helicopter-based shooter. One or two players fly combat helicopters through three major stages, each divided into three combat areas. Before each stage, players choose their route through the available areas, a branching structure that lends the military campaign some variety.

Air-to-air gunfire is complemented by ground-targeting bombs against tanks, missile launchers, skyscrapers and other destructible scenery. Destroying certain buildings reveals trucks carrying weapon upgrades or score bonuses. The player can also launch a missile barrage to clear dangerous enemy formations and projectiles. Each area concludes with a boss, while the mix of scrolling landscapes and more isometric ground-combat sections gives the sequel a broader visual range than its predecessor.

games.title: Twin Eagle - Revenge Joe's Brother
games.description:
Twin Eagle: Revenge Joe's Brother is a 1988 vertically scrolling helicopter shooter developed by Seta and distributed in Japan by Taito. Players fly over land, sea and enemy bases, blasting planes, helicopters, tanks and anti-aircraft positions. Destroyed buildings may reveal hostages worth extra points, while weapon icons change the aircraft's firepower between machine guns, cannons, spread shots and missiles. Speed upgrades and screen-clearing bombs provide further tactical options.

The game stood out in its day for extensive use of digitized images and sampled sound, including a rock vocal track used during aerial battles. Its unusual mixture of photographic backgrounds, forceful music and punishing shooting action makes it readily identifiable. A sequel, Twin Eagle II, arrived in 1994.

games.title: Twin Falcons
games.description:
Twin Falcons is the overseas title of Philko's 1989 horizontal shooter Whizz. Players control a military aircraft and switch between weapons suited to airborne enemies and targets on land or sea. Destroyed formations release icons for adjustable speed, laser fire, manually fired triple shots, automatic spread shots and a wider five-projectile weapon.

The game is another example of Korean arcade releases built around reused Japanese technology. Historical accounts associate Whizz with boards originally intended for Capcom's Side Arms, giving the shooter a curious hardware pedigree alongside its conventional side-scrolling air-combat action.

games.title: Twin Hawk
games.description:
Twin Hawk, known in Japan as Daisenpu, is a 1989 vertically scrolling World War II-themed shooter from Toaplan. Players pilot a military aircraft over an increasingly hostile battlefield, firing at tanks, armored vehicles and fixed ground installations. Unusually for an aerial shooter, its enemies are concentrated on the ground rather than in opposing fighter formations. Rather than relying on a large collection of different guns, the game emphasizes the aircraft's basic firepower and the timing of supporting attacks.

Its defining feature is a formation of friendly escort planes summoned by a dedicated button. These allies arrive to bolster the player's fire and can be sacrificed in powerful attacks, creating a strategic choice between retaining protection and dealing immediate damage. The game uses Toaplan's familiar compact playfield and dense enemy arrangements but has its own identity thanks to this escort mechanic and its distinct military presentation.

games.title: Twinkle
games.description:
Twinkle is a 1997 Korean maze game published by Semicom and developed by Tirano. It follows Hyper Pacman, retaining its overhead dot-eating action while adding more gadgets and secrets. Players guide a round, cartoonish hero through 40 mazes, collecting pellets and avoiding pursuing enemies. Special pellets allow the character to eat enemies temporarily, echoing Pac-Man's classic reversal of the chase.

The assortment of pickups is more elaborate than in the original inspiration: bombs and laser helmets can destroy walls, vision goggles reveal hidden objects, speed boosts and jump shoes assist escapes, and fruit supplies bonus points. The resulting game combines traditional maze patterns with a steady succession of power-up-driven surprises.

games.title: Twinkle Tale

variants.title: Twinkle Tale (bootleg of Mega Drive version)

games.description:
Twinkle Tale is an unauthorized coin-operated adaptation of the 1992 Sega Mega Drive action shooter, found in arcades as a 1993 bootleg. The original game follows Saria, a young magician crossing the fantasy kingdom of Alpherion to rescue imprisoned wizards and recover magical gemstones. Its overhead run-and-gun stages mix linear enemy-filled routes with more open areas that reward exploration. Saria uses projectile attacks and consumable magic while fighting supernatural creatures and large bosses.

The version preserved in AdvanceMAME is not a separately designed arcade sequel. It runs the Mega Drive-derived game on modified console-style hardware with coin-operation circuitry. The conversion is historically interesting as an example of home-console software being repackaged for amusement centers without an authorized arcade release; emulation of the board's protection has also been documented as incomplete.

games.title: Twin Qix
games.description:
Twin Qix is a rare, unreleased 1995 Taito F3 prototype that revisits the line-drawing territory-capture formula of Qix. Players use a dial-based controller to venture out from safe borders, trace enclosing lines and claim sections of the playfield without being struck by roaming hazards. Building on the original concept, this sequel introduces a two-player mode, additional enemies and new power-ups.

Only a single Japanese prototype board has been reported, and the game never reached a normal commercial release. It is therefore a particularly uncommon glimpse of Taito experimenting with an established early-1980s puzzle-action design on newer arcade hardware.

games.title: Twins
games.description:
Twins is an adult-themed arcade puzzle game originally developed by the Spanish company Ecogames around 1993, with later licensed board versions appearing through Electronic Devices in 1994. It is a match-oriented puzzle played using an eight-way joystick and two buttons, with pin-up imagery providing the mature presentation. Its Spanish origin was established more firmly when preservation researchers recovered the original Ecogames board, after some later Italian versions had already become known in emulation.

The game also has a distinctive piece of borrowed audio history: tracks in its soundtrack were taken from Spanish Amstrad CPC games including Rock'n Roller, Clever & Smart II and Mad Mix Game. That combination of locally developed hardware, recycled computer-game music and later licensed editions makes Twins an unusual artifact of the early-1990s European arcade market.

games.title: Twinkle Star Sprites
games.description:
Twinkle Star Sprites is ADK's inventive 1996 Neo Geo shooter that turns scrolling combat into a competitive duel. Two players, or one player against the computer, occupy separate vertical playfields. Each clears waves of cartoon enemies with ordinary shots, charged attacks and limited bombs. Rather than simply racing for points, players aim to destroy enemies in connected groups, sending fireball hazards into the opponent's screen.

Those attacks can be shot back as counterattacks, reflected again as stronger attacks and even escalated into temporary boss encounters. Every chain is therefore both a scoring opportunity and a way to overwhelm a rival. A cast of whimsical fantasy characters, led in story mode by Load Ran and her companion Rabbicat, adds individual attack patterns and comic personality to the otherwise fiercely tactical action.

The unusual combination of a cute scrolling shooter and a versus puzzle game makes Twinkle Star Sprites one of the Neo Geo's most distinctive multiplayer titles. It was also among ADK's final releases for the platform and developed a lasting cult following thanks to the tension created by its escalating attack-and-reflect system.

games.title: Twin Squash
games.description:
Twin Squash is Sega's 1991 System C2 variation on competitive Breakout. Two players use their own ball-and-paddle playfields, clearing groups of bricks while watching a shared balance meter. Clearing four or more blocks at once can push blocks upward on the player's side while forcing the opponent's downward.

The match ends when a player's bricks reach the bottom of their playfield. Missing the ball does not immediately eliminate the player; instead, the blocks drop lower and become more threatening. That rule transforms a familiar brick-breaking game into a duel built around aggressive clearing, careful recovery and the pressure of the opponent's progress.

games.title: Two Tigers
games.description:
Two Tigers is a distinctive 1984 Bally Midway aerial-combat game, available in cooperative and head-to-head configurations. Rather than steering a plane with a conventional joystick, players use rotary-style controls to turn continually moving fighter aircraft while firing at other planes and dropping bombs on an enemy warship below. Downed enemy aircraft crash into the ship and damage it, while bombs and detonated naval mines can destroy further sections. Enough holes sink the vessel.

The cooperative mode emphasizes a joint campaign against successive ships. The alternative dogfight configuration pits the two pilots against each other. Unlike many shooters, a crashed aircraft can be replaced without a conventional finite life stock; the real pressure comes from failing to sink enough ships before they escape.

The game uses an unusual combination of aerial dogfighting and indirect destruction, rewarding players for turning enemy planes into weapons. Bally Midway also produced a conversion kit associated with Tron cabinets, and surviving versions differ in controls and presentation, adding interest for collectors of the company's MCR-era hardware.

games.title: Tecmo World Cup '94
games.description:
Tecmo World Cup '94 is a 1994 soccer arcade game that builds on Tecmo World Cup '90. Up to four players can compete in a fast, accessible tournament against national teams, with scrolling and zoom effects giving the matches a lively presentation. The emphasis is on quick attacking football rather than simulation: well-placed crosses followed by headers or bicycle kicks can be especially effective ways to score.

The game features a 16-team international competition and belongs to Tecmo's series of arcade football titles, later followed by releases such as Tecmo World Soccer '96 and Tecmo World Cup '98.

games.title: Tower & Shaft
games.description:
Tower & Shaft: Aleck Bordon no Fuyukai na Nakamatachi is a 2003 arcade platform game for Seta's Aleck64 hardware, derived from the Macintosh games NS-Tower and NS-Shaft. The hero, Aleck Bordon, explores two temples in search of treasures with divine powers, with each temple built around a different style of movement.

In Tower, Aleck moves sideways automatically while the player holds and releases a button to time jumps between platforms. In Shaft, the player steers horizontally while descending through a vertical obstacle course, trying to land on lower platforms without falling out of view or being caught by spikes descending from above. Story and endless modes give the compact, timing-based design both a set progression and a high-score challenge.

games.title: Tecmo World Soccer '96
games.description:
Tecmo World Soccer '96 is a 1996 Neo Geo soccer game centered on a brisk international tournament. Players choose from 32 national sides and fight through a seven-match World Cup-style campaign, where a loss ends the run and drawn games are settled with penalty shoot-outs. It is built around immediate joystick-and-button football action suitable for quick arcade matches.

Compared with earlier Tecmo soccer games, it adds more deliberate passing options, including crosses and forward passes to teammates, as well as feints and rush techniques. Its large selection of teams and accessible competitive play made it a recognizable part of the Neo Geo's varied sports library.

games.title: TX-1
games.description:
TX-1 is Tatsumi's ambitious 1983 Formula One-style driving game, famous for its enormous three-monitor panoramic cabinet. The three adjacent displays extend the road far into the driver's peripheral vision, while steering-wheel feedback, pedals and gear changes give the game a demanding, physical feel. Players race against the clock, passing slower traffic and controlling their speed carefully to avoid skids and collisions.

Its greatest design innovation is the branching road. At several junctions, players choose one route or another, creating different courses and influencing which of the final racing circuits they encounter. This idea would become a major part of later arcade racing design, most famously Sega's Out Run. Unlike a conventional linear checkpoint race, TX-1 rewards both precise driving and knowledge of alternate routes.

Built when arcade manufacturers were competing to make ever more elaborate cockpit machines, TX-1 became a notable commercial success in Japan and was licensed to Atari for North American distribution. Its three-screen presentation remains one of the most visually striking experiments of the early 1980s driving-game boom.

games.title: TX-1
games.description:
TX-1 is Tatsumi's 1983 three-screen Formula One-style racing game, represented here by a licensed Atari/Namco/Taito variant. Its giant panoramic display allows the driver to see traffic and approaching bends across three adjacent monitors. Steering-wheel feedback, throttle, braking and gear changes make cornering and overtaking more involved than in many contemporary racing games.

Races are checkpoint-based, but the road periodically forks and the player's chosen route determines the later stages. This branching structure anticipated the route selection made famous by Out Run. The licensed edition preserves the remarkable triple-monitor experience and arcade racing mechanics of Tatsumi's original TX-1 rather than constituting a separate game.

games.title: Tylz
games.description:
Tylz is an unreleased 1982 arcade prototype built around an isometric, scrolling tile-painting puzzle. The player guides a jester across a patterned playfield, changing black squares to purple either by walking over them or shooting them. Moving across an empty gap can create a black tile, which must then be colored in turn. Enemy soldiers and knights interfere as the player tries to complete the board.

A crown may occasionally appear and, when collected, advances the player several levels. Only a handful of prototype circuit boards are reported to have been built, making Tylz an obscure example of the experimental action-puzzle designs that appeared around the time of Q*bert.

games.title: Ultra Balloon
games.description:
Ultra Balloon is a 1996 Korean single-screen platform game from SunA that openly borrows the bubble-trapping formula of Taito's Bubble Bobble. Cartoonish heroes confront enemies on compact platforms, using bubbles to capture them before finishing them off and clearing the stage. Its brightly colored characters, playful animation and familiar level-by-level structure belong to the wave of Korean arcade games that reworked popular Japanese hits.

The game is also known for recycled audiovisual material: arcade histories have identified background art taken from the Sega Saturn title Clockwork Knight. It is best approached as an unlicensed, eccentric variation on a well-established action-platform formula rather than as an official Bubble Bobble installment.

games.title: Undercover Cops
games.description:
Undercover Cops is Irem's ferocious 1992 side-scrolling beat-'em-up set in a filthy, futuristic New York City. Three selectable agents, Bubba, Flame and Claude, are called in to overthrow the criminal mastermind Dr. Clayborn and his army. Up to three players can fight simultaneously through ruined streets, industrial zones and other hostile districts, facing ordinary gang members as well as bizarre mutants and heavily armed enemies.

Its combat follows the broad template of Final Fight but distinguishes itself through the extraordinary variety of improvised weapons. Players can pick up objects ranging from metal beams and stones to unusual pieces of street debris, and even use items such as fish against enemies. The backgrounds teem with unsettling details, exaggerated violence and grotesque enemy designs, including dangerous machinery that can crush a careless character.

Undercover Cops became a cult favorite for its outstanding pixel art and grimly comic dystopian atmosphere. Its lavish sprite animation and environmental detail are characteristic of Irem's early-1990s arcade work, giving it a personality far removed from a generic street-brawling game.

games.title: Mahjong Uchuu yori Ai wo komete

variants.title: Mahjong Uchuu yori Ai wo komete (Japan)

games.description: Mahjong Uchuu yori Ai wo Komete, roughly 'Mahjong: From Space with Love', is a 1989 Japanese adult-themed mahjong game. The premise places a group of women in danger from hostile space robots, using science-fiction imagery to frame matches of Japanese mahjong. Players make tile selections through a dedicated mahjong control panel rather than the joystick used by most action games. It is a representative example of the story-themed, character-driven mahjong machines popular in Japanese amusement centers during the late 1980s.

games.title: Ufo Senshi Yohko Chan
games.description:
UFO Senshi Yohko-chan is a 1988 Japanese overhead action-maze game starring a young alien heroine who descends from a UFO to defend a city. Players guide Yohko through streets and passages while avoiding or attacking monsters, robots, gargoyle-like creatures and armored opponents. She can fire a weapon and use a digging or hiding ability to evade pursuit, while collecting coins for points.

The colorful cartoon character and mixture of shooting, evasion and maze navigation give it a personality distinct from conventional space shooters. Its Japanese title translates roughly as 'UFO Soldier Yohko-chan'.

games.title: Ultimate Tennis
games.description:
Ultimate Tennis is Art & Magic's 1993 arcade tennis game, noted for the unusual depth effect of its smoothly scrolling court graphics. Players choose from six competitors with different abilities and take part in versions of the four Grand Slam tournaments: Wimbledon, the US Open, Roland Garros and the Australian Open. Two people can also play against each other, although doubles are not included.

The controls distinguish hard shots, soft shots and lobs, with combinations producing slices, topspin, drop shots and other more specialized strokes. A replay feature allows a successful rally to be watched again. Its responsive shot selection, dramatic court perspective and vivid animation helped the game stand out among early-1990s sports machines. Contemporary promotional accounts reported substantial worldwide arcade-board sales, including an unusually strong showing in Japan for a European-developed title.

games.title: Waku Waku Ultraman Racing
games.description:
Waku Waku Ultraman Racing is a 1996 Japanese Sega kiddie ride based on Tsuburaya Productions' Ultraman television franchise. Children sit on an Ultraman-shaped mechanical ride while watching and interacting with a screen-based race featuring Ultraman or Ultraseven against familiar kaiju and aliens, including Baltan. The course incorporates a confrontation with Baltan before the goal is reached.

Part of Sega's Waku Waku line of coin-operated rides, it combines moving amusement equipment with video-game imagery on modified System 16B-derived hardware. It is better understood as an interactive children's attraction than as a conventional stand-alone racing game or shooter.

games.title: Ultraman
games.description:
Ultraman is a 1991 arcade fighting game from Banpresto and Bandai based on the Japanese live-action superhero created by Tsuburaya Productions. Players control the giant silver-and-red defender of Earth in one-on-one battles against monsters drawn from the television series. Punches, kicks and throws weaken an enemy while a short energy timer evokes Ultraman's limited time on Earth.

An unusual finishing rule makes the combat more than a simple contest to empty a life bar. After reducing a monster's health to the FINISH state, the player must accumulate enough special energy to deliver a decisive final attack, such as Ultraman's famous Specium Ray. The game's appeal lies in reproducing televised giant-monster confrontations rather than the competitive tournament structure of later fighting games.

games.title: Ultra Maru-hi Mahjong
games.description: Ultra Maru-hi Mahjong is a 1993 Japanese adult-themed mahjong arcade game. Its title means approximately 'Ultra Secret Mahjong', and the available descriptions identify matches against female opponents as the central attraction. It belongs to the Japanese video-mahjong tradition, where human opponents, character illustrations and adult-themed rewards are presented around standard tile-game play. Surviving source descriptions do not establish additional rules or unusual mechanics specific to this release.

games.title: Ultra Tank
games.description:
Ultra Tank is a 1978 Atari arcade tank-combat game, continuing the company's early experiments with head-to-head vehicle battles. Two tanks maneuver around a top-down arena of obstacles, trying to shoot each other before the timer runs out. Depending on operator settings, the battlefield can contain barriers or land mines, and tanks can even be made invisible, radically changing the encounter.

The simple goal of earning more hits than the opponent is complicated by walls that block both movement and lines of fire. Ultra Tank belongs to the line of arcade tank games that began with Kee Games' Tank and helped establish the appeal of direct, local two-player competition before modern scrolling action games became common.

games.title: Ultra X Weapons / Ultra Keibitai
games.description:
Ultra X Weapons, called Ultra Keibitai in Japan, is a 1995 vertical shooter published by Banpresto and developed by Seta for the SSV arcade platform. It draws on the Ultraman universe, but puts the players in combat spacecraft rather than directly controlling the giant superhero. Players select from seven ships and fight through waves of alien craft, sub-bosses and giant monster bosses across seven stages; the first four stages can be chosen in different orders.

Weapons can be upgraded with collected items, while a special attack briefly summons an Ultraman to strike enemies across the screen. With simultaneous two-player support and three-button controls, the game combines conventional scrolling-shooter action with the kaiju spectacles of its source franchise. The export title and Japanese title are alternative names for the same game, and a separate pre-release review build is also documented.

games.title: Ultraman Club - Tatakae! Ultraman Kyoudai!!
games.description:
Ultraman Club: Tatakae! Ultraman Kyoudai!! is a 1992 arcade action game from Banpresto that turns Tsuburaya's giant heroes into small, super-deformed cartoon characters. Players select from eight versions of Ultraman and fight monsters in overhead, single-screen arenas. The immediate objective is to defeat every enemy on screen and advance to the next encounter.

Each character has a short-range attack that can be used freely and a stronger ranged attack with restricted ammunition.
