Fallen opponents leave bonuses, including extra lives and special attacks, rewarding aggressive but carefully controlled fighting. The subtitle translates roughly as 'Fight! Ultraman Brothers!'

games.title: Uncle Poo
games.description:
Uncle Poo is a bizarre 1983 Diatec maze game in which a comical elderly protagonist tries to escape a series of treasure-filled labyrinths. Players collect valuables and evade animal enemies as the maze becomes increasingly dangerous. Uncle Poo's unlikely weapon is flatulence, which can be used against pursuing creatures, while roller skates allow bursts of faster movement.

The game combines these comic abilities with a rising or advancing flood hazard that forces the player to keep progressing. Its outlandish protagonist and gross-out humor make it one of the more eccentric maze games of the early 1980s.

games.title: Under Fire
games.description:
Under Fire is a 1993 Taito shooting game in which one or two police operatives confront a violent gang called the Hoppers. Using mounted submachine-gun-style controllers, the players shoot through scenes of robberies and urban chaos, targeting armed criminals while avoiding civilians and fellow officers. Each player has a health meter, so careless shots and enemy attacks carry a cost.

The presentation combines digitized photographic imagery with animated gun battles in locations such as city streets, a convenience store and an amusement park. Its infrared gun system and recoil feedback distinguished the original cabinet from more conventional light-gun machines. Arriving in the wake of Konami's Lethal Enforcers, Under Fire is a particularly physical example of early-1990s police-themed arcade shooting, with a strong emphasis on accuracy and target discrimination.

games.title: UniWar S
games.description:
UniWar S is the overseas name of Irem's 1980 fixed-screen shooter Ginga Teikoku no Gyakushuu, loosely translated as 'The Galactic Empire Strikes Back'. Players steer a small yellow spacecraft left and right along the bottom of the screen, firing upward at successive alien formations. Different stages introduce distinct enemies and attack patterns rather than merely repeating the same wave.

A particularly nasty hazard is the 'space soldier': some destroyed enemies drop attackers that descend past the player's ship and then threaten it from below. This reversal complicates an otherwise familiar Galaxian-style shooting rhythm. The game belongs to the early generation of Japanese fixed shooters, when designers were adding multi-stage progression and unusual enemy behaviors to the Space Invaders formula.

games.title: Unknown Meyco Game
games.description:
The unidentified Meyco Games program preserved as unkmeyco is an early-1980s American electronic blackjack title, later associated with the Casino Black Jack software family. Its gambling format is the familiar contest against a dealer's hand, with decisions made through dedicated cabinet controls rather than arcade movement. The surviving ROM originated on Meyco's dedicated gambling electronics, related to the hardware used by Wild Arrow.

Because the original set name was simply 'unknown Meyco game' and later catalogues reorganized these programs, its identification should be treated as a provisional archival label rather than evidence of a separate named commercial release.
research_notes: Original game title is unknown.

games.title: U.N. Squadron
games.description:
U.N. Squadron is Capcom's 1989 side-scrolling jet fighter shooter, released in Japan as Area 88 and based on the manga and anime series of that name. Players fly combat missions over desert installations, naval forces and heavily defended military targets. Unlike many arcade shooters, the aircraft uses a life or damage gauge, so surviving a dangerous section is not simply a matter of avoiding a single fatal hit.

Players choose from pilots with different aircraft characteristics and earn money for destroying enemies. Funds can be spent on equipment such as additional missiles, bombs and other special weapons, bringing an element of loadout planning to the fast-moving battles. The side-scrolling structure, large bosses and demanding terrain make the game notably different from Capcom's familiar vertical 194X shooters.

The international U.N. Squadron edition removes the explicit Area 88 branding and some material found in the Japanese release, including a special mission. It remains one of Capcom's most recognizable late-1980s horizontal shooters and later inspired a separate, substantially redesigned Super Nintendo adaptation.

games.title: Untouchable
games.description:
Untouchable is a 1987 adult-oriented gambling and mahjong game from Dynax, preserved in the Japanese version 2.10 program. It uses a horizontal display and dedicated mahjong/gambling keys rather than a fighting-game joystick scheme. Operator settings include difficulty, stage progression, score thresholds and double-up difficulty, confirming its combination of tile-game progression and wagering mechanics.

Its August 1987 Japanese release places it among Dynax's early mahjong-gambling productions. It has no relationship to the unrelated late-1990s fighting game that sometimes appears in automatically collected descriptions under the same title.

games.title: Puzzle Uo Poko
games.description:
Puzzle Uo Poko is a 1998 Cave arcade puzzle game in which one or two cooperative players control cartoon cats on an underwater expedition. Each stage contains colored glass balls that must be removed by joining groups of three or more matching colors. Clearing the playfield allows the cats' tiny submarine to descend toward the next level, creating a playful adventure through 30 increasingly difficult stages.

Instead of dropping pieces from the top as in a typical falling-block puzzle, the player launches balls into the field from a side-mounted plunger. Pulling the plunger back farther changes the force and travel of the ball, making angle, timing and momentum central to successful matches. The combination of pinball-like physics, color matching and cooperative play gives Uo Poko a distinctive feel among late-1990s arcade puzzle games.

games.title: Up'n Down
games.description:
Up'n Down is Sega's 1983 pseudo-3D driving maze game, starring a tiny purple dune buggy on a winding, vertically scrolling road. The goal is to collect a set of colored flags scattered along branching routes before time runs out. Other vehicles, rocks and road hazards obstruct the narrow track, and the player can accelerate, slow down and choose a direction at intersections.

The buggy's most useful trick is jumping. Carefully timed leaps can clear road obstacles or pass over rival cars, turning the driving game into a mixture of racing, navigation and action-platform timing. Knowing when to switch lanes and how to recover a missed flag is as important as driving quickly.

With its toy-like vehicles and brightly colored, twisting roads, Up'n Down reflects Sega's early-1980s appetite for unusual arcade concepts. Its collection-based objectives make it quite different from a conventional racing game, even though it wraps those objectives in constant forward motion.

games.title: Up Scope
games.description:
Up Scope is a 1986 submarine-themed shooting game distributed by Grand Products. Looking through a periscope-like viewpoint, the player tries to destroy ships while watching for an enemy submarine hunter. If the hunter is not eliminated in time, the game shifts into a more dangerous encounter in which the opponent drops depth charges as the player prepares to fire a torpedo.

The cabinet is technologically unusual: the video portion uses a Commodore Amiga 500 computer motherboard with an additional EPROM board rather than a more typical dedicated arcade platform. That hybrid construction makes Up Scope an interesting example of home-computer technology pressed into coin-op service.

games.title: Up Your Alley
games.description:
Up Your Alley is a 1987 Cinematronics bowling arcade game closely related to the company's earlier Alley Master. Players bowl in a video-rendered lane, using stick-and-button controls to determine the delivery and compete for strikes and spares. The emphasis is on timing and repeatable shot placement rather than the physical mechanics of a real bowling alley.

Its naming history is unusual: 'Up Your Alley' was also used during Alley Master's development, and surviving arcade records refer to the later release as a reissue. The two versions are closely connected in the preservation history, with revisions to their parent-and-clone classification reflecting discoveries about the original hardware.

games.title: Urachacha Mudaeri
games.description:
Urachacha Mudaeri is a 2002 Korean multiplayer arcade party game from GamToU, built around a rapid succession of short, timing-based minigames. Up to three players compete by pressing colored buttons quickly or in the required order, much like Konami's Bishi Bashi series. Each challenge has its own simple rules and awards points for speed or accuracy.

Based on a Korean comic, its scenes frequently draw on the life of an office worker, turning everyday tasks and absurd situations into frantic button-mashing contests. The appeal is less about mastering one long game than about reacting instantly to the next unpredictable challenge.

games.title: Urashima Mahjong
games.description:
Otogizoushi Urashima Mahjong is a 1989 Japanese arcade mahjong game developed by UPL. Its name references both traditional illustrated Japanese stories and the folktale of Urashima Taro. Rather than offering an arcade action adaptation of the legend, it uses that literary framing for a mahjong game controlled through a dedicated tile-selection interface.

Its folkloric title and Japanese-market presentation place it among the character- and story-themed mahjong machines of the late 1980s. The surviving descriptive sources provide no reliable evidence of special rule variations beyond the underlying mahjong play.

games.title: U.S. Classic
games.description:
U.S. Classic is a 1989 golf game from Seta with an unusually direct trackball-based swing mechanic. Players view the hole from the tee, taking account of wind direction, wind speed and distance before selecting a club. The strength and direction of the trackball movement determine the shot, making physical control of the ball itself a central part of the challenge.

The game rewards good scoring with additional holes, encouraging players to reach par or better in a limited number of attempts. Licensed for distribution by Romstar and Taito in different markets, it offers a more tactile alternative to golf games built entirely around a timed button-press swing meter.

games.title: Games V18.2
games.description:
Games V18.2 is a 1989 version of U.S. Games' coin-operated multi-game software for countertop and upright amusement machines. Instead of offering one fixed arcade challenge, the system lets patrons choose among short bar-oriented activities, a format the company had developed through Super Duper Casino and Super Ten. Its established repertoire mixed card and dice games with trivia, word challenges, and simple arcade-style skill games, all operated through a small button panel rather than a joystick.

The V18.2 designation identifies a specific software revision, not a separate action game. In AdvanceMAME it belongs to the same family as the later Games V18.7C and V25.4X sets, making it useful for tracing the evolution of U.S. Games' multi-game cabinets at the end of the 1980s.

games.title: Games V18.7C
games.description:
Games V18.7C is a 1991 revision of U.S. Games' multi-game amusement platform, following the earlier V18.2 and V18.5 releases. It is a menu-driven collection intended for bar-top or upright machines rather than a single self-contained arcade game. The broader U.S. Games range combined casino-inspired card games with word puzzles, quizzes, and compact action or skill challenges, using a button-only control panel.

This V18.7C program is preserved as a separate ROM revision in the Games family, alongside later V21 and V25 releases. Its interest for arcade historians lies in documenting the continued updating of a multi-title cabinet that could offer a variety of diversions without requiring separate boards for every game.

games.title: Games V25.4X
games.description:
Games V25.4X is a 1992 U.S. Games multi-game release, one of the later preserved revisions of the company's countertop amusement software. Players choose from a menu of short games instead of following a single campaign. The product family was known for its mixture of poker- and blackjack-style diversions, trivia, word games, and simple reflex-based challenges such as brick-breaking, aimed at the American bar and leisure market. Operation centers on a row of selection and action buttons rather than conventional arcade joystick movement.

In AdvanceMAME, V25.4X acts as the parent version for several earlier Games revisions, including V18.2 and V18.7C. Its 6809-based electronics and modest 400-by-248-pixel display illustrate a parallel branch of arcade history in which commercial success came from updating compact, reusable multi-game machines rather than producing elaborate dedicated video-game cabinets.

games.title: Super Duper Casino
games.description:
Super Duper Casino is a 1987 multi-game amusement machine from the American manufacturer U.S. Games, offered for countertop and upright installations. Despite its casino-themed name, its original selection went well beyond simulated betting: a documented ten-game version combined Draw Poker, U.S. Blackjack and U.S. Craps with the paddle-based Brick-Break, the horse-and-chariot selection game U.S. Chariots, the phrase puzzle Wizard of Words, and two sets each of sexual and sports trivia. Players selected a game and interacted through a compact button panel, making it suited to bars and other locations where a full-size joystick cabinet was impractical.

Its versatility was a central selling point. Contemporary advertisements promoted conversion boards for existing countertop cabinets and allowed operators to enable or disable particular games to suit their customers. The preserved California V3.2 edition belongs to this early period of the U.S. Games line, which soon expanded into Super Ten and the successive Games software versions. A 1988 New Jersey regulatory bulletin even listed Super Duper Casino's ten titles while considering exceptions for amusement devices, an unusually precise contemporary record of what the machine offered.

games.title: Super Ten V8.3
games.description:
Super Ten V8.3 is a 1988 U.S. Games multi-game title designed for North American countertop and upright amusement machines. It belongs to the manufacturer's button-operated line of bar games, whose appeal came from offering a selection of short diversions on one machine rather than a single arcade experience. The related U.S. Games catalog mixed electronic card games, trivia, word challenges, and simple reflex-based games, creating something closer to a compact video amusement center than a conventional action cabinet.

The V8.3 suffix identifies the preserved software revision. AdvanceMAME also recognizes V8.2 and V8.3X variants, reflecting the frequent program updates characteristic of these machines. Super Ten appeared in February 1988, between the original Super Duper Casino and the later Games V18 and V25 releases.

games.title: Us vs. Them
games.description:
Us vs. Them is a 1984 laserdisc arcade shooter that blends filmed scenes with computer-generated gameplay graphics. The player pilots a spacecraft defending Earth against an alien invasion, with battles unfolding over recognizable locations including San Francisco, Chicago and Hollywood as well as forests, mountains and deserts. The action combines horizontal and vertical shooting sequences against incoming extraterrestrial forces.

Brief live-action interludes show frightened civilians and military commanders, lending the invasion story an unusually cinematic presentation for the period. Produced during the short-lived laserdisc arcade boom, Us vs. Them illustrates the ambition of developers who tried to merge interactive action with motion-picture spectacle well before full-motion video became common in home games.

games.title: Ultra Toukon Densetsu
games.description:
Ultra Toukon Densetsu is a 1993 Japanese beat-'em-up from Banpresto, presenting Tsuburaya's Ultraman heroes as squat, super-deformed characters. Players can choose Ultraman, Ultraseven or Ultraman Taro, then move through side-scrolling stages fighting gangs of monsters and other enemies from the franchise.

The combat uses close-range punches, jumping and dash attacks, with a charged move for delivering a stronger signature energy blow. The mixture of chibi character art and familiar Ultraman powers makes the game notably lighter in tone than the more realistic giant-monster battles of other Ultraman adaptations. The Japanese title translates roughly as 'Legend of Ultra Fighting Spirit'.

games.title: Valkyrie No Densetsu
games.description:
Valkyrie no Densetsu, or The Legend of Valkyrie, is Namco's lavish 1989 fantasy action-adventure for its System 2 arcade hardware. The player controls Valkyrie, a sword-wielding heroine fighting to save a magical world; a second player can join as her green, lizard-like companion Kurino Xandra. The camera follows the characters through overhead and angled environments packed with creatures, traps, jumps, branching paths and giant bosses.

Combat is based on ranged sword or trident attacks, but the heroes can also jump across gaps, collect money, purchase items and acquire magical abilities. Health and a depleting hourglass impose pressure on exploration, making it important to balance searching for helpful resources with moving onward. The elaborate stages frequently demand more than reflex shooting, rewarding familiarity with routes, hazards and secrets.

A follow-up to the Famicom's Valkyrie no Bouken, the arcade game is remembered for colorful fantasy artwork, imaginative enemies and impressive sprite scaling. It was initially a Japan-focused release and has become one of Namco's best-regarded arcade adventures, standing apart from the company's better-known shooters and racing games.

games.title: Valtric
games.description:
Valtric is a 1986 vertically scrolling shooter from Jaleco in which players control a hovering vehicle over a heavily defended landscape. The craft moves in eight directions and can aim its forward fire while also dropping bombs against ground targets. Walls and other obstacles constrain the route, so progress involves steering through the terrain rather than merely dodging enemy bullets.

An unusual jump or ascent action lets the vehicle rise over danger, while detachable 'option' units provide extra gunfire in directions determined by their positions. Weapon upgrades and large bosses punctuate the four major areas. Valtric combines the air-and-ground targeting of Xevious with maneuvering and companion-fire ideas more commonly associated with Gradius.

games.title: Vamp 1/2
games.description:
Vamp x 1/2 is a 1999 Korean scrolling beat-'em-up developed by Danbi System and distributed by F2 System, based on a Korean comic. A strange energy descends on the world, and four young heroes connected with wolf, bear, leopard and human clans set out to investigate. Players choose a fighter and battle through groups of enemies in broad side-scrolling stages.

Each hero has a distinctive set of close-range attacks and can transform into more powerful forms, gaining flashier moves as the action escalates. The arcade version substantially expands the animations and combat options of an earlier version of the game, making this a noteworthy example of Korean comic-book material finding its way into a coin-operated brawler. Some European machines use the alternative spelling Vamf x 1/2.

games.title: Vandyke
games.description:
Vandyke is a 1990 top-down action game from UPL featuring a barbarian warrior battling through fields crowded with monsters. The view resembles overhead run-and-gun games such as Ikari Warriors, but the hero's weapons are fantasy equipment rather than firearms. He starts with a sword and can collect alternatives such as boomerangs, bombs and long-reach flails.

Players push forward while dodging dangerous creatures, including giant insects and other fantastical enemies, and collecting items that increase attack power. Its mixture of close combat and projectile-like weapons gives it the feel of an overhead hack-and-slash adventure rather than a conventional scrolling shooter.

games.title: Vanguard II
games.description:
Vanguard II is SNK's 1984 sequel to the influential scrolling shooter Vanguard, but it radically changes the format. Instead of traveling through forced-scrolling tunnels while firing in four directions, the player pilots a spacecraft around a freely traversable, top-down battlefield. The task is to disable a large alien installation by destroying the power pods spread across its surface.

Airborne defenses must be shot directly, while surface installations are bombed with the help of a targeting sight. Once enough pods have been eliminated, the station's central core becomes vulnerable and can be destroyed to finish the stage. This change in perspective and objective makes Vanguard II an unusually independent sequel rather than a simple refinement of the original.

games.title: Vanguard
games.description:
Vanguard is SNK's influential 1981 science-fiction shooter, distributed in North America by Centuri. Piloting a small spacecraft, the player fights through a multi-part underground fortress occupied by the alien Gond. The path twists through horizontally, vertically and diagonally scrolling passages, forcing constant adjustment to terrain and approaching enemies. Fuel runs down during the journey and is replenished through combat, keeping the player under pressure to move and shoot.

Its celebrated control arrangement allows the ship to move independently while firing in any of the four cardinal directions using separate buttons. This makes encounters far more flexible than in earlier one-direction shooters. Temporary invulnerability pickups allow the player to ram through enemies or even tunnel walls, offering an aggressive escape from dangerous situations. Different regions of the fortress have distinct layouts and threats, culminating in a showdown with Gond.

Vanguard was an important early example of multi-directional shooting and varied scrolling within a single game. Its striking sound effects and musical cues, along with the demanding four-button attack scheme, helped establish SNK in Western arcades before the company's later Neo Geo fame.

games.title: Mahjong Vanilla Syndrome
games.description:
Mahjong Vanilla Syndrome is a 1991 Japanese adult-themed mahjong game with a light fantasy story. A young man opens a mysterious door in the forest and finds himself trapped in another dimension, where the bunny-eared guardian Vanilla challenges him to mahjong. Winning matches offers a route home and introduces additional female opponents who guard the strange realm.

The game provides a story mode with dialogue and sequential opponents as well as a battle mode that allows a more direct choice of rivals. Also known as Mahjong Final Bunny, it is an example of early-1990s Japanese video mahjong in which character illustrations and a whimsical narrative frame the traditional tile game.

games.title: Van-Van Car
games.description:
Van-Van Car is a 1983 Sanritsu maze game that turns Pac-Man-style dot chasing into a miniature vehicle battle. Viewed from above, the player steers a yellow car fitted with a spike on its nose, trying to burst balloons scattered around a compact maze. Three hostile cars patrol the passages and threaten to ram the player before all the balloons are collected.

The nose-mounted spike gives the vehicle a distinctive way to deal with hazards, but positioning and careful turning remain critical. Originally developed for hardware related to Pac-Man's, Van-Van Car shows how early arcade designers reused familiar maze technology while experimenting with different movement and objectives.

games.title: Vapor Trail - Hyper Offence Formation

variants.title: Vapor Trail - Hyper Offence Formation (World revision 1)

games.description:
Vapor Trail: Hyper Offence Formation is Data East's 1989 vertically scrolling jet fighter shooter, released in Japan as Kuuga: Operation Code Vapor Trail. The player fights a terrorist organization threatening New York, choosing from three aircraft with very different characteristics: the balanced Silph, heavily armed Valkyrie and agile Seylen. A second pilot can join for simultaneous cooperative play.

Weapon pickups range from powerful forward guns to homing missiles and other specialized attacks. Each jet can also activate a defensive shield, adding an important survival option when enemy fire becomes dense. The game changes its scrolling speed and direction for dramatic encounters, with enemy warplanes and gigantic bosses demanding different tactics from the available aircraft.

Its pounding rock soundtrack, bold parallax scenery and the choice of distinct planes give Vapor Trail a forceful arcade personality. The soundtrack and weapon selection made it a memorable alternative to the more numerous helicopter-themed vertical shooters of its era.

games.title: Vapor TRX
games.description:
Vapor TRX is a 1998 Atari Games futuristic racing machine in which the competitors pilot small rocket-powered craft rather than wheeled cars. Six vehicles race through four obstacle-filled courses featuring cities, canyons and other fantastical environments. Turbo pads provide sudden bursts of speed, while collectible weapons allow racers to attack opponents as well as outmaneuver them.

The game's emphasis is on aggressive, high-speed arcade competition rather than realistic driving technique. Running on Atari's late-1990s 3D hardware, it combines vehicle racing with combat and airborne maneuvering; both production and prototype software versions are preserved in arcade collections.

games.title: Varth - Operation Thunderstorm
games.description:
Varth: Operation Thunderstorm is Capcom's 1992 vertically scrolling shooter, an inventive extension of the company's long-running 194X tradition. The setting is a distant colony planet whose automated defenses have been turned against humanity by a rogue supercomputer. Players fly through 30 short stages fighting mechanized enemies, massive aircraft and ground defenses, collecting new weapons while trying to survive increasingly dense attacks.

The defining feature is a pair of support pods that accompany the player's ship. These satellites fire their own weapons and can block many incoming bullets, while different pod arrangements change which directions are protected. Choosing between a forward-focused formation and a surrounding defensive layout creates tactical decisions seldom found in the simpler 1942-style shooters. A supply of powerful bombs can rescue the player when the screen becomes too crowded.

Varth is remembered among Capcom shooter enthusiasts for its substantial campaign, responsive controls and unusual balance between offense and protection. The pods give it a very different rhythm from a standard one-hit-kill vertical shooter, encouraging players to learn enemy patterns and deliberately position their defenses.

games.title: Vasara
games.description:
Vasara is Visco's 2000 vertical shooter, combining the weaponry of a science-fiction shoot-'em-up with a fantasy version of Japan's Sengoku period. Players choose among three historical-inspired warriors riding flying machines, facing mechanical armies, armed commanders and elaborate bosses. The game's anime-style cutscenes and character designs reinforce its unusual fusion of feudal Japanese imagery and futuristic combat.

A normal shot handles distant targets, but holding the attack button produces a close-range melee strike that can also deflect incoming bullets. Bombs clear the screen in emergencies, while a special Vasara gauge allows a powerful charged attack when filled. Learning when to close in and slash rather than simply shoot makes the game stand apart from more traditional bullet-dodging shooters.

games.title: Vasara 2
games.description:
Vasara 2 is Visco's 2001 sequel, returning to an alternate Sengoku-era Japan filled with flying war machines and intense projectile patterns. The player chooses from four regular characters, with an additional hidden character, and battles a succession of enemy formations and imposing bosses. Its story again draws on the conflict surrounding Oda Nobunaga, mixing historical figures with fantastical technology.

The sequel expands the emphasis on dense bullet patterns and precision flying while retaining charged attacks and close-range combat. A striking rule is that direct collision with certain enemies repels the player's craft instead of immediately killing it, shifting the main survival challenge toward hostile projectiles. Released near the end of Visco's arcade activity, Vasara 2 is a notable late entry in the company's shooter catalog.

games.title: Vastar
games.description:
Vastar is a 1983 side-scrolling shooter set on a devastated future Earth, where a giant robot defends the planet against the Galaxy Empire. The player controls the flying Vastar robot, blasting alien formations over landscapes that include recognizable ruined monuments. The game's visual mix of robot combat and post-apocalyptic scenery gives it a distinctive early-1980s science-fiction atmosphere.

Vastar has a rechargeable protective shield, but its energy is finite. When exhausted, the robot transforms into a more vulnerable aircraft-like form that can continue firing but no longer benefits from the same defense. Reaching a base restores shield power and the robot's original configuration, making survival a matter of conserving protection between safe points. The game was completed around the collapse of its original developer, Orca, and was subsequently associated with Sesame Japan.

games.title: Vautour
games.description:
Vautour is an unauthorized variation of Phoenix, the influential 1980 fixed-screen shooter. Players move a small spacecraft horizontally along the bottom of the display, shooting descending waves of alien birds while using a temporary protective shield to survive attacks. The first stages feature smaller enemies diving from formations; later waves introduce eggs that hatch into large phoenixes whose vulnerable bodies must be hit precisely.

The cycle culminates in an enormous enemy mothership, where the player must open a path through its defenses and hit the alien commander. Vautour preserves the recognizable enemy structure and shield-based tactics of Phoenix. Its significance in AdvanceMAME lies primarily in documenting a bootleg edition of that arcade classic rather than an independently designed shooter.

games.title: U.S. Championship V'ball
games.description:
U.S. Championship V'Ball is Technos Japan's 1988 arcade beach-volleyball game, also published in North America by Taito. The story follows George and Michael, a pair of beach players seeking a large cash prize on the competitive circuit. Matches take place in stylized locations such as Daytona Beach, New York, Los Angeles and Hawaii, against increasingly skillful teams.

The game compresses volleyball into quick, action-heavy rallies involving digging, setting, spiking and defending the court. A single player controls a two-person team with assistance from the game, while multiplayer configurations allow cooperation or direct competition, with some versions supporting four players. Strong timing and positioning matter more than elaborate button combinations.

Its large, expressive character sprites, energetic music and exaggerated athletic action make V'Ball a characteristic Technos sports game. The title later gained wider recognition through the Nintendo Entertainment System adaptation Super Spike V'Ball, although the arcade original has its own presentation and pace.

games.title: VS Block Breaker
games.description:
VS Block Breaker is a 1997 Kaneko Super Nova arcade game, released in Japan as Saru-Kani-Hamu-Zou. Developed by MediaWorks, it reworks the Breakout formula with bright cartoon graphics and a comical animal theme. Players bounce a ball toward formations of blocks, trying to clear the playfield while keeping the ball in play.

The game includes animated jumping characters alongside its paddle-and-ball action, giving the familiar brick-breaking activity a playful presentation. Its Japanese title combines the names of a monkey, crab, hamster and elephant, matching the lighthearted tone of this lesser-known late-1990s arcade puzzle game.

games.title: Virtua Bowling
games.description:
Virtua Bowling is a 1996 arcade ten-pin bowling game from IGS that supports up to four participants. Players choose details such as bowler gender, handedness and ball weight, then position their character on the approach before setting the delivery angle and power. A short shot timer keeps the action moving, while curved throws add a further element of ball control.

Success is measured by the pins knocked down over a series of qualifying frames. Strong enough scores unlock later rounds and special challenges that demand particular pin-clearing results. Its selection of equipment and shot placement turns the familiar sport into a compact, competitive coin-op skill game.

games.title: Vicious Circle
games.description:
Vicious Circle is an unreleased 1996 fighting-game prototype from Atari Games, created during the arcade industry's fascination with Mortal Kombat and Killer Instinct. Nine extravagant competitors, including a ninja, biker, vampire, werewolf and shape-shifting metal fighter, enter a brutal tournament. The action uses pre-rendered-looking characters, combination attacks and violent finishing moves.

Its exaggerated fantasy roster, gruesome effects and cinematic finishers show Atari experimenting with the darker style of mid-1990s one-on-one fighting games. Because it never received a standard commercial release, Vicious Circle survives chiefly as an unusual prototype rather than as a title with an established competitive arcade scene.

games.title: Vendetta
games.description:
Vendetta is Konami's 1991 side-scrolling beat-'em-up and the successor to Crime Fighters. Members of the Cobras gang must rescue their kidnapped friend Kate from the rival Dead End Gang. Players choose from four fighters: former prizefighter Blood, wrestler Hawk, martial artist Boomer and ex-soldier Sledge. Depending on the arcade configuration, up to four players can battle together through city streets, industrial districts and enemy strongholds.

The combat differs from many contemporaries by separating punches and kicks into dedicated buttons, allowing ground attacks against fallen opponents and emphasizing physical, close-up brawling. The heroes can seize improvised weapons, including bats, chains and other objects found in the scenery, while enemy gangs attack in groups and force the players to watch both sides of the screen.

Vendetta is remembered for its chunky, expressive character animation, distinctive music and aggressive cooperative action. Regional releases differ in certain visual details and content, while the Japanese version carries the direct sequel title Crime Fighters 2. It remains one of Konami's best-regarded early-1990s beat-'em-ups.

games.title: Venom & Spider-Man - Separation Anxiety
games.description:
Venom & Spider-Man: Separation Anxiety is an unauthorized 1997 arcade conversion of the 1995 Super Nintendo beat-'em-up developed by Software Creations and originally published by Acclaim. Players control Spider-Man, Venom or both together as they battle street criminals and enemies connected with the Life Foundation's dangerous symbiote experiments. Its side-scrolling stages combine punches, jumps, web-related attacks and cooperative combat against bosses drawn from Marvel Comics.

The game follows the earlier Maximum Carnage and shares its comic-book brawling style. The version included in AdvanceMAME is specifically a coin-operated bootleg running SNES-derived hardware and software, not an original 1997 arcade production. Its existence illustrates the practice of converting popular home-console cartridges into unauthorized arcade machines.

games.title: Venture
games.description:
Venture is Exidy's influential 1981 dungeon-exploration arcade game, starring a tiny smile-faced adventurer named Winky. Armed with a bow, he enters a succession of monster-infested rooms to collect treasures. Between rooms, the game displays an overhead plan of the dungeon; approaching a doorway causes the view to zoom into a larger, detailed room, where Winky must fight guards and snatch the treasure before escaping.

Its biggest threat is the Hallmonster, an indestructible creature patrolling the corridors. Spending too long in a treasure room causes one to enter and hunt the player down, making speed just as important as clearing enemies. A distinctive joystick allows Winky to turn to aim without necessarily moving, while arrows and room layouts reward carefully judged attacks. Even defeated monsters can be dangerous until their remains disappear.

Released years before the better-known Gauntlet, Venture helped establish the appeal of arcade dungeon crawling with treasure collection, room-based combat and escalating pressure. Its zooming transitions and the constant threat of the Hallmonsters give the game a tense pace despite its playful, minimalist art.

games.title: Virtua Fighter
games.description:
Virtua Fighter is Sega AM2's groundbreaking 1993 martial-arts game, directed by Yu Suzuki and widely recognized as the first commercially successful 3D polygonal fighting game. Running on Sega's Model 1 arcade system, it presents eight fighters with different real-world-inspired disciplines, including Akira Yuki's Bajiquan, Pai and Lau Chan's Chinese martial arts, and Wolf Hawkfield's professional wrestling. The cast fights on polygonal stages with a three-dimensional visual presentation, although movement is largely restricted to a fighting plane.

The controls are deceptively simple: a joystick plus Punch, Kick and Guard. Different directions, timings, combinations and throws create a sophisticated combat system based on spacing, recovery and reading an opponent. A round can be won by knockout, time expiration or knocking the rival out of the ring. In single-player mode, the eight regular competitors lead to the mysterious final opponent Dural.

Virtua Fighter transformed the arcade fighting genre, demonstrating that polygonal characters could deliver readable, precise and deeply technical hand-to-hand combat. Its austere flat-shaded graphics may look primitive beside later sequels, but the emphasis on realistic styles, tactical guarding and ring positioning became defining features of the series. Its success helped launch an entire generation of 3D fighting games.

games.title: Virtua Fighter 3
games.description:
Virtua Fighter 3 is Sega AM2's technically ambitious 1996 sequel, developed for the powerful Model 3 arcade hardware. It adds two striking fighters to the established martial-arts roster: Aoi Umenokoji, an expert in Aiki-jujutsu, and the enormous sumo wrestler Taka-Arashi. High-resolution character models, fluid animation and richly detailed environments made it a major display of Sega's mid-1990s 3D graphics technology.

The most important gameplay change is a dedicated fourth button for dodging. Used with different joystick directions, it lets fighters step into or out of the screen to avoid attacks and create immediate counterattack opportunities. Stages also introduce genuine changes in elevation, including slopes, stairs and uneven moving surfaces. The terrain therefore becomes part of the strategy rather than simply decorative scenery.

Virtua Fighter 3 continued the series' reputation for exacting, technique-driven play. A related Team Battle edition allowed teams of fighters to compete, and the game's 3D stage design and evasion mechanics expanded the possibilities of arena-based martial arts beyond the simpler, flat-ring layouts of earlier entries.

games.title: V-Five
games.description:
V-Five is Toaplan's intense 1993 science-fiction vertical shooter, known internationally as Grind Stormer. Players pilot a high-performance space fighter through six stages packed with enemy formations, intricate bullet patterns and large mechanical bosses. Its fast action and escalating density make it a characteristic example of Toaplan's influence on the later bullet-hell school of shooters.

The most interesting distinction is between the two main regional styles of play. Japanese V-Five uses a Gradius-like power-up bar: collecting items advances a selection cursor, allowing the pilot to activate upgrades such as stronger weapons, speed or defensive systems at a chosen moment. Grind Stormer instead awards pickups more directly and includes a conventional stock of screen-clearing bombs. The stages are largely shared, but these different upgrade systems change how the entire game is approached.

This dual identity makes V-Five particularly rewarding to revisit. Beyond quick reactions, the Japanese rules demand advance planning about which weapon or support system to build next, while the overseas arrangement favors immediate adaptation to pickups appearing during combat.

games.title: Virtua Fighter Kids
games.description:
Virtua Fighter Kids is Sega's 1996 lighthearted reinterpretation of Virtua Fighter 2 for the Sega ST-V arcade platform. The familiar martial-arts cast has been redrawn as miniature, oversized-headed cartoon figures, with brisker music and an intentionally playful presentation. Beneath those visual changes, however, the game remains a genuine Virtua Fighter fighting game built around punches, kicks, guards and character-specific techniques.

The unusually cute character proportions make the combat look comic rather than intimidating, but many of the original fighters' recognizable moves and personal traits remain intact. It is an intriguing example of Sega adapting a technically advanced fighting series to the Saturn-related ST-V hardware while courting a broader and younger-looking audience.

games.title: Virtua Fighter Remix
games.description:
Virtua Fighter Remix is Sega's 1995 graphical and technical revision of the original Virtua Fighter, released on the Saturn-related ST-V arcade platform. It retains the original game's eight-character martial-arts tournament and its tightly focused Punch, Kick and Guard controls. Fighters still win by knockout, time decision or knocking their opponents out of the ring, with Dural waiting as the final challenger.

The primary changes are visual: texture-mapped characters and increased polygon detail replace the stark flat-shaded look associated with the 1993 Model 1 game. It also introduces a player-grade qualification feature derived from Virtua Fighter 2. Remix was closely connected with Sega's effort to improve the presentation of Virtua Fighter on Saturn hardware and is best regarded as an enhanced edition of the foundational game rather than a full sequel.

games.title: V Goal Soccer
games.description:
V Goal Soccer is a 1994 Tecmo arcade football game, released in several regional versions. It uses scrolling match action, joystick controls and a set of dedicated football buttons to present international soccer in a fast coin-operated format. Two players can compete directly, while the single-player game pits the user against computer-controlled teams.

The title belongs to the same Tecmo arcade soccer family as World Cup '94, and their hardware and preservation histories are closely intertwined. Its surviving descriptive sources do not establish a reliable list of special moves or tournament rules unique to V Goal Soccer, so the main distinction in the collection is the separately titled regional release rather than an invented set of gameplay innovations.

games.title: Vampire Hunter 2: Darkstalkers Revenge
games.description:
Vampire Hunter 2: Darkstalkers' Revenge is Capcom's 1997 Japanese CPS-2 fighting game, not a true sequel to Vampire Hunter but an alternate edition built from the Vampire Savior engine. It brings back the lineup associated with Night Warriors, including Donovan, Huitzil and Pyron, while removing newer Vampire Savior characters such as Jedah, Lilith, Q-Bee and B. B. Hood. The result is a familiar monster roster fighting within the faster, more elaborate third-generation Darkstalkers rule set.

Battles use Vampire Savior's unusual double-life-gauge format, where losing one life bar does not interrupt the match with a traditional new round. Characters employ fast chains, special attacks and super moves, and the revised stage colors and character behavior distinguish this edition from the earlier game with a similar name. Released alongside Vampire Savior 2, it is an important example of Capcom treating character selection and combat-system variations as separate arcade products.

games.title: Ace Driver: Victory Lap

variants.title: Ace Driver: Victory Lap (Rev. ADV2, World)

games.description:
Ace Driver: Victory Lap is Namco's 1996 3D Formula-style arcade racer and a follow-up to Ace Driver. Players take the wheel of highly stylized open-cockpit racing cars in a cockpit experience built around rapid cornering, overtaking and maintaining speed against rival drivers. The upgraded sequel adds vehicles and additional circuits beyond the first game's selection.

A new Championship mode links the available tracks into a consecutive series of races, rewarding consistent performance rather than success on only one course. Its elaborate dedicated driving presentation and fast polygonal graphics represent Namco's continuing development of serious-looking, but unmistakably arcade-paced, motor racing during the mid-1990s.

games.title: Victorious Nine
games.description:
Victorious Nine is a 1984 Taito arcade baseball game that turns a full nine-inning contest into accessible, score-oriented sports action. Players choose from a roster of baseball teams and alternate between batting and pitching, timing hits and directing the ball into the field while trying to advance runners and score. The opposing side takes over after the usual sequence of strikes and outs.

A joystick-and-button interface handles the action, with support for two players taking turns against each other. Its relatively simple batting and fielding presentation reflects an era when arcade baseball games were translating a complicated sport into short, instantly recognizable sequences of play.

games.title: Victory
games.description:
Victory is Exidy's 1982 multi-directional space shooter, designed by Vic Tolomei. Players pilot a small craft called the Battlestar over a planet threatened by alien forces that have established radar systems and dangerous quark silos. Enemy craft attack from the air and drop troops toward the ground, while the player tries to destroy hostile installations and prevent the invaders from releasing their most destructive weapons.

The controls are unusually elaborate for the period: a rotary controller aims the ship, while dedicated buttons handle thrust, laser fire, shields and a powerful Doomsday Device. Holding thrust longer builds speed, so precise control is needed to maneuver safely while attacking. Speech synthesis accompanies the action, making the machine particularly striking for an early-1980s shooter.

The game's complex custom hardware and unusual control scheme are part of its historical interest. Exidy later offered a conversion kit called Victor Banana, which transformed the serious science-fiction imagery into a comic theme while reusing the underlying game technology.

games.title: Victory
games.description:
Victory is Exidy's 1982 multi-directional shooter, represented here by the Comsoft-licensed edition of the original game. The player controls the Battlestar, a heavily armed spacecraft fighting an alien force that has occupied a planet and installed radar and quark silos. Enemy ships and paratroopers threaten the surface while the pilot destroys hostile targets and survives increasingly complicated attacks.

A rotary controller handles the craft's direction, with separate controls for thrust, firing, shields and a powerful Doomsday Device. Speech synthesis and layered electronic sound accompany the combat. The Comsoft release preserves the gameplay and distinctive controls of Exidy's Victory; it is a licensed version rather than an unrelated game bearing the same title.

games.title: Victory Road
games.description:
Victory Road is SNK's 1986 sequel to Ikari Warriors, known in Japan as Dogou Souken. Commandos Paul and Vince return, but the military war has become a supernatural adventure against aliens, mutants and monstrous bosses. The action still scrolls vertically, with up to two players fighting through waves of enemies while collecting increasingly extravagant weapons.

Like Ikari Warriors, the game uses an eight-way rotary joystick that lets the player move in one direction while aiming in another. Grenades, powerful firearms and destructible objects are central to progress, while protective armor can absorb limited damage. Secret weapon pickups hidden beneath rocks and short boss encounters behind special doors give the journey an exploratory quality missing from the original battlefield shooter.

The shift from military combat to bizarre science fiction, together with sampled voices and flamboyant enemy designs, gives Victory Road a memorable identity among run-and-gun games of the 1980s. Its unusual rotary control remains a defining part of the arcade experience.

games.title: Video Pinball
games.description:
Video Pinball is Atari's 1979 attempt to reproduce the feeling of a real pinball table using arcade video hardware. A simulated metal ball ricochets around bumpers, spinners and scoring targets while the player works two flippers and tries to keep it from draining. The physical cabinet adds special presentation features that make the video playfield appear beneath a decorative pinball backdrop.

Its controls evoke a mechanical machine: a plunger launches the ball, flipper controls act independently, and the player can nudge the game to alter the ball's movement. Excessive nudging causes a tilt, just as on a conventional pinball table. Special combinations, including repeated hits on the Atari logo, can award extra balls.

Video Pinball was an inventive hybrid at a time when video games and electromechanical amusements still shared the same arcade floor. Its mirrored cabinet artwork and tactile nudge system show how designers worked to preserve the ritual of pinball even as the ball and targets became electronic.

games.title: Video Vince and the Game Factory

variants.title: Video Vince and the Game Factory (prototype)

games.description:
Video Vince and the Game Factory is an unreleased 1984 Mylstar Electronics arcade prototype. It is a platform game starring Vince, who traverses levels trying to trap a variety of roaming creatures in cages. One of the enemies is notably reminiscent of Coily, the snake from Q*bert, a connection that fits Mylstar's broader lineage within the Gottlieb arcade business.

The surviving prototype uses an eight-way joystick and two buttons. Its small documented footprint and lack of a commercial launch make it an unusual example of an action-platform concept that never progressed beyond development boards.

games.title: Viewpoint
games.description:
Viewpoint is Sammy and Aicom's visually striking 1992 shooter for the Neo Geo MVS. Instead of the usual overhead or side-on presentation, its six stages unfold in an angled isometric perspective reminiscent of Zaxxon. The player pilots a compact spacecraft through twisting futuristic structures, dodging enemy formations, obstacles and gigantic mechanical bosses against finely shaded, intricately drawn scenery.

The main laser can be charged by holding the fire button, trading immediate shots for a heavier blast. Several spectacular special weapons supplement it, including a sweeping wall of fire, an expanding circular explosion and clusters of homing missiles. Learning the diagonal perspective and the exact routes through obstacles is central to survival, since gaps and bullets can be deceptively hard to judge from the angled viewpoint.

Viewpoint became a cult favorite for its distinctive artwork, powerful techno-influenced soundtrack and punishing difficulty. It was Sammy's only original Neo Geo MVS title and later received home conversions, but the arcade edition remains especially memorable as one of the platform's most unusual shooters.

games.title: Vigilante
games.description:
Vigilante is Irem's 1988 side-scrolling street brawler, a spiritual successor to the company's influential Kung-Fu Master. A lone fighter battles through urban streets, a junkyard, a bridge and a construction area to rescue his kidnapped girlfriend from a violent gang. Enemies attack from both directions using punches, grapples and weapons, while a tough boss guards the end of each of the five stages.

The hero can punch, kick, jump and crouch, and can sometimes pick up nunchaku for greater reach and damage. Taking a hit can knock the weapon away, forcing a return to bare-handed combat. The constantly arriving gang members reward steady forward movement, while chokeholds and armed attackers punish careless positioning.

Vigilante retains the accessible one-plane combat of Kung-Fu Master but replaces the martial-arts-movie temple with a gritty late-1980s urban setting. It illustrates an important transitional style of beat-'em-up just before games such as Double Dragon and Final Fight popularized broader, more freely navigable fighting arenas.

games.title: Vimana
games.description:
Vimana is Toaplan's 1991 vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter, in which the survivors of a devastated world fight back using mysterious ancient spacecraft. One or two players travel through enemy installations, dense formations and large bosses, collecting upgrades that strengthen the main guns and restore scarce special weapons. The game's title evokes the flying craft found in Indian mythology, giving its otherwise futuristic setting an unusual name and atmosphere.

Its distinctive attack system rewards both rapid tapping and deliberate charging. Repeated presses fire the main twin-shot weapon, while holding the fire button unleashes a wider, powerful multi-directional blast. The special Circle Bomb first surrounds the spacecraft and can then be sent after nearby enemies, offering a different kind of protection from a conventional instantaneous screen-clearing bomb.

Vimana arrived during Toaplan's highly productive period of precision shooters, but its charge shot and circulating bomb mechanic give it an individual rhythm. Rather than constantly switching between weapon types, players concentrate on mastering when to fire rapidly, when to build a stronger shot and when to release their limited special attacks.

games.title: Vindicators Part II
games.description:
Vindicators Part II is Atari Games' uncommon follow-up to its 1988 tank-combat shooter, released as a conversion kit for Gauntlet cabinets in 1989. Rather than a completely new adventure, it is a compact reworking of the original Vindicators. Its campaign keeps only ten of the original fourteen stations, changes aspects of the weapons, and removes the promotional contest stages and collectible contest stars. Approximately 400 conversion kits were reportedly manufactured.

One or two players guide futuristic tanks through hostile bases, destroying defensive turrets and enemy vehicles while collecting fuel and stars. Fuel steadily drains, making movement and combat a race against time; stars fund purchases of armor, speed, and heavier weaponry between stages. The distinctive dual-stick tank controls remain central to the experience. Its unusual conversion-kit history makes Part II more of an alternate, streamlined Vindicators than a conventional sequel.

games.title: Vindicators
games.description:
Atari Games' Vindicators (1988) is a cooperative, multidirectional tank shooter set in a galaxy under attack by the Tangent Empire. Players command SR-88 battle tanks through a series of fortified enemy stations, destroying hostile armor, gun emplacements, and flying attackers. Each level involves searching for a key to open the exit while surviving a steadily depleting fuel supply. Running dry leaves the tank almost immobile and starts a short countdown toward destruction.

The game combines arcade shooting with an unusually involved upgrade economy. Collectible stars can be spent between stages on speed, weapon strength, shields, homing missiles, and bombs; obtaining the right equipment becomes especially important for the heavily armored bosses. Its dedicated cabinet was shaped to resemble a tank, complete with decorative treads and four tank-style handles, giving two players independent twin-control movement and firing. Atari also created three special contest stages in early revisions, allowing qualifying players to compete for a promotional T-shirt.

Vindicators is remembered for its demanding fuel management and distinctive hardware as much as its firefights. A shortened follow-up, Vindicators Part II, later appeared as a Gauntlet conversion kit, while the original was adapted to several home systems, including an unlicensed Nintendo Entertainment System cartridge.

games.title: Violence Fight
games.description:
Taito's Violence Fight (1989) is an early one-on-one arcade brawler that uses the free movement of a belt-scrolling beat-'em-up rather than the fixed plane of later tournament fighters. In a fictional underground fighting circuit, players choose from four colorful bruisers, including Bad Blue, Lee Chen, Lick Joe, and Ben Smith, then face rivals in enclosed city arenas. Each match is contested over as many as three rounds, with two victories needed to advance.

An eight-way joystick lets fighters circle their opponents, while punch, kick, and jump buttons allow combinations, special strikes, knockdown throws, and even the use of crates and barrels as weapons. In an especially eccentric bonus challenge, the player fights a tiger for the chance to improve punching or kicking power. The game predates the fighting-game boom unleashed by Street Fighter II and was followed by Taito's related Solitary Fighter in 1991.

games.title: Violent Storm
games.description:
Konami's Violent Storm (1993) is a colorful, three-player, side-scrolling beat-'em-up set after a devastating world war. The vigilantes Wade, Boris, and Kyle pursue the Geld gang after its lieutenant kidnaps their friend Sheena. Their journey spans seven stages, from crumbling streets and a runaway train to an industrial furnace, a botanical garden, and the villain's museum. Each hero has a distinct balance of speed, strength, and techniques.

Combat is full of interactive touches: enemies can be struck while grounded, pipes and other dropped weapons can be picked up, and crates reveal food and bonuses. Powerful crowd-clearing special attacks cost health, giving players a reason to mix ordinary combos with more desperate moves. The game is also unusually playful for a post-apocalyptic brawler, with improvised projectiles and hidden Konami references, including arcade cabinets for Scramble and Penta in a later stage. Its enormous sprites, expressive animation, and energetic soundtrack have made it a cult favorite among fans of Final Fight-style cooperative action.

games.title: Viper
games.description: Leland's Viper (1988) is a military-themed shooting game and the follow-up to Danger Zone. The player uses a trackball and two buttons to aim at incoming aircraft as helicopters, fighters, and bombers swoop through the combat area in looping attack patterns. Its emphasis on tracking fast targets across a horizontally oriented screen gives it a different physical feel from joystick-driven scrolling shooters. The game uses Leland's distinctive multi-processor arcade hardware and remains a relatively obscure entry in the company's late-1980s catalog.

games.title: Viper Phase 1
games.description:
Viper Phase 1 is Seibu Kaihatsu's 1995 space-based spin-off of the Raiden shooter series, built for the Seibu SPI arcade system. Set against a rebellion among humanity's distant colonies, it puts players in heavily armed starfighters for eight vertically scrolling stages. Battles range from swarms of small craft to giant warships, installations, and elaborate bosses, with the methodical movement and powerful weaponry associated with Raiden.

A distinctive part of the game is its end-of-stage scoring, which rewards medals, enemies destroyed, ammunition or bombs conserved, and overall destruction percentage. Regional revisions change weapon balance: the American release grants continuous access to secondary weapons but makes them less damaging than their limited-ammunition counterparts. The original and revised editions are both worthwhile because the adjustments meaningfully affect strategy and difficulty.

games.title: Mahjong Vitamin C
games.description: Mahjong Vitamin C: Anata ga Sensei yo! is a 1989 Japanese arcade mahjong game from Home Data with a hospital-themed presentation. Players compete in Japanese mahjong against computer opponents, with adult-oriented live-action reward sequences following victories. Its unusual mixture of traditional tile play and photographic presentation reflects a particular niche of late-1980s Japanese amusement software.

games.title: Vivid Dolls
games.description: Vivid Dolls is a 1998 territory-capture puzzle game developed by Visco for Seta's Aleck64 arcade system, a platform closely related to the Nintendo 64. It follows the Qix tradition: players venture out from safe territory, draw boundaries, and try to claim sections of the playfield while exposed to hazards. The game belongs to the adult-themed branch of the genre popularized by Gals Panic. Its use of the relatively rare Aleck64 hardware makes it a notable curiosity among late-1990s Japanese arcade puzzles.

games.title: V-Liner
games.description:
V-Liner is a 2001 electronic video-slot game developed by Dyna and BreezaSoft for SNK's Neo Geo MVS arcade hardware. Instead of the fighting games and shooters normally associated with the Neo Geo, it uses the system's colorful 2D graphics to present a coin-operated reel-gambling interface. Its six-button panel and joystick-related controls make this a distinctive commercial use of the MVS platform.

Several revisions survive, including v0.53, v0.54, v0.6e, v0.7a and v0.7e. Unlike most well-known Neo Geo games, V-Liner never received a standard AES home-console release. Its niche gambling purpose demonstrates the flexibility, and occasional unexpected uses, of SNK's cartridge-based arcade system.

games.title: Virtual Mahjong
games.description: Virtual Mahjong is a Japanese mahjong title developed by Micronet for Sega's ST-V arcade hardware, which shares much of its architecture with the Sega Saturn. The game uses a dedicated mahjong-button panel rather than ordinary joystick controls, a distinction that matters when configuring it in an emulator. It also appeared on the Saturn and was followed by My Fair Lady: Virtual Mahjong II. Its appeal lies chiefly in its place among the specialist board-game releases that broadened the ST-V catalog beyond action and racing games.

games.title: Varia Metal
games.description:
Varia Metal is a 1995 vertically scrolling shooter by Excellent Systems set against the invading Ocayea Empire. The two-player game assigns the pilot Grey to the first player and Atuja to the second, sending their ships against mechanical formations and large bosses. Green power-up spheres strengthen ordinary fire, while holding the firing button charges a more powerful laser attack, creating a rhythm of rapid shooting and deliberately timed heavy blasts.

Licensed boards also appeared under the New Ways Trading name. The game's unusual audio hardware and reported scarcity in Japan make it an obscure mid-1990s shoot-'em-up rather than a major genre hit, but its charged-shot system gives it a recognizable tactical twist.

games.title: Volfied
games.description:
Taito's Volfied (1989) is a science-fiction successor to the classic territory-capture game Qix. Instead of drawing abstract lines across an empty field, players pilot the small ship Monotros around alien-controlled planets. Leaving the safety of an established boundary exposes the ship to attacks while it cuts off sections of the playfield. A stage is cleared by claiming at least 80 percent of the available area, with the location of the main enemy determining which side of a new line becomes safe territory.

Each stage introduces a different large alien and smaller roaming enemies, adding colorful character to the geometric contest. Capturing smaller enemies inside completed territory can earn bonuses, while certain captured objects reveal useful power-ups. The need to balance ambitious land grabs against the risk of having an unfinished line struck gives Volfied its addictive tension. It became one of the best-known descendants of Qix and later reached numerous home computers and consoles.

games.title: Virtual On 2: Oratorio Tangram
games.description:
Cyber Troopers Virtual-On: Oratorio Tangram is Sega's 1998 sequel to the original Virtual-On, featuring high-speed one-on-one combat between giant humanoid robots known as Virtuaroids. Players maneuver through 3D arenas, managing distance, jumps, dashes, and weapon attacks while attempting to outmaneuver another pilot or a computer-controlled rival. The series is especially associated with its distinctive paired flight-stick controls.

The AdvanceMAME entry represents the early Model 3 arcade release of Oratorio Tangram, also known as M.S.B.S. version 5.2. Later revisions, including 5.4 and 5.6, altered and extended the game on subsequent arcade hardware. Its combination of arena fighting and mech piloting helped give Sega's 3D arcade catalog a style quite different from its conventional fighting games.

games.title: 906III Video Poker
games.description:
906III Video Poker is an early MAME designation for a single-player electronic draw-poker game associated with Cal Omega and Casino Electronics Inc., dating to 1985. The preserved game was subsequently identified as Gaming Draw Poker and catalogued as Cal Omega - Game 23.9, making the older AdvanceMAME name potentially confusing alongside later CEI 906-III poker machines.

Rather than an action game, it presents a conventional video-poker challenge: the player works with a hand of cards, discarding and drawing replacements in pursuit of a winning poker combination. The original hardware uses a 6502-family processor, programmable sound generation, and a horizontal raster display. Its changing identifiers in MAME reflect the process of identifying and documenting early coin-operated gambling hardware.

games.title: Virtua Racing
games.description:
Sega AM2's Virtua Racing (1992) was a watershed moment in arcade racing, demonstrating that real-time, filled-polygon 3D graphics could create a convincing and immediately playable motorsport spectacle. Originally developed to test Sega's new Model 1 hardware, the prototype was impressive enough to become a full commercial game. Players drive a Formula One-style car against a packed field on three tracks of increasing difficulty: Big Forest, Bay Bridge, and Acropolis. The races are governed by timed checkpoints, sharp corners, rival cars, and the ever-present risk of a costly spin.

Its celebrated V.R. View System lets drivers cycle among four camera positions, from a close driving perspective to elevated broadcast-style views. Flat-shaded polygons might look stark beside later textured racers, but the smooth 3D course design, large screen, and substantial dedicated cabinets were spectacular for the time. The game could also be played in linked multiplayer installations.

Virtua Racing became a major commercial success and laid the groundwork for Sega's Daytona USA and other 3D arcade racers. Its home ports are historically interesting too: the Mega Drive cartridge contained a special Sega Virtua Processor chip to make polygon rendering possible on the console.

games.title: Vegas Roulette
games.description: Vegas Roulette is a 1989 electronic roulette machine by World Game. Rather than requiring a physical wheel, it presents roulette-style wagering on a vertical video display with a nine-button control panel. The Z80-based electronics and AY-3-8910 audio hardware are typical of compact late-1980s gambling cabinets, but the roulette format distinguishes it from the contemporary wave of poker and fruit machines. The preserved arcade program also circulates under related regional labels, including El Circulo and Kasino '89.

games.title: Virtua Striker 2
games.description:
Virtua Striker 2 is Sega's 1997 Model 3 sequel to its pioneering 3D arcade football game. International sides compete in brisk, stadium-based matches viewed from a fixed television-like camera. Rather than simulating every tactical detail, it concentrates on instant pick-up-and-play action: an eight-way stick and a small group of buttons handle passing, shooting, and defending, with automatic player selection keeping the pace brisk.

The polygonal players, animated crowds, and dramatic camera work helped make it a showcase for Sega's arcade hardware. It also began an unusually long cycle of progressively updated Virtua Striker 2 editions, culminating in late-1990s revisions that led toward the Dreamcast version. Its accessible controls made it particularly well suited to head-to-head competition in an amusement arcade.

games.title: Virtua Striker 2 '98
games.description: Virtua Striker 2 '98 is Sega's 1998 arcade revision of Virtua Striker 2 for Model 3 hardware. It retains the series' instantly accessible 3D international football matches, using joystick movement and dedicated buttons for passes, shots, and tackles, while bringing the original 1997 release forward as a new annual edition. Its chief historical significance is as part of Sega's continuing cycle of arcade updates rather than a separate football design. The later '99 and '99.1 editions followed the same revision-based approach.

games.title: Virtua Striker 2 '99.1
games.description: Virtua Striker 2 '99.1 is a late Model 3 revision of Sega's fast-paced 3D arcade football sequel. The fundamental game remains recognizably Virtua Striker 2: players select an international team, switch automatically to the player nearest the action, and combine quick passes, tackles, and charged shots in short stadium matches. The '99.1 designation marks a particular stage in Sega's succession of updated arcade versions, following the '98 and '99 revisions and preceding the later 2000-era releases. It is best approached as a historically distinct tournament-era update, not an entirely new installment.

games.title: Vampire Savior: The Lord of Vampire

variants.title: Vampire Savior: The Lord of Vampire (Europe 970519)
Vampire Savior: The Lord of Vampire (Asia 970519)
Vampire Savior: The Lord of Vampire (Brazil 970519)
Vampire Savior: The Lord of Vampire (Hispanic 970519)
Vampire Savior: The Lord of Vampire (Japan 970519)
Vampire Savior: The Lord of Vampire (USA 970519)

games.description:
Capcom's Vampire Savior: The Lord of Vampire (1997), the third principal Darkstalkers game, is one of the studio's most inventive two-dimensional fighters. Its story follows Jedah Dohma, a resurrected demon nobleman who summons supernatural combatants into a bizarre realm to collect their souls. The cast blends horror-film archetypes with outrageous visual comedy, including Morrigan, Demitri, Felicia, and new arrivals Jedah, Lilith, Q-Bee, and the gun-toting B. B. Hood.

On Capcom's CPS-II hardware, the game delivers exceptionally fluid animation and a fast, aggressive rule set. Instead of resetting health between traditional rounds, its damage-gauge system allows combat to flow almost continuously; recoverable life and the ability to keep pressure on a downed opponent change the usual rhythm of a match. Chain combos, air movement, and character-specific super moves reward experimentation.

Vampire Savior is widely regarded as a high point of Capcom's sprite-based fighting artistry. Its expressive characters and unusually ambitious mechanics have sustained an enthusiastic competitive following, while regional naming changes and later roster revisions add to its complicated arcade history.

games.title: Vampire Savior 2: The Lord of Vampire

variants.title: Vampire Savior 2: The Lord of Vampire (Japan 970913)

games.description:
Vampire Savior 2: The Lord of Vampire is a Japanese-only 1997 revision of Capcom's Darkstalkers fighter, released alongside the related Vampire Hunter 2. It preserves Vampire Savior's fast CPS-II combat and flowing damage-gauge system but changes the roster: Donovan, Huitzil, and Pyron return, while Jon Talbain, Rikuo, and Sasquatch are removed. These changes make it a distinct variation for players interested in the series' different character matchups.

Its blend of chain combos, supernatural special moves, and elaborate animation remains recognizably Vampire Savior, but this is not simply a Western retitling of the same game. The Japanese arcade revisions are an important part of Darkstalkers history, showing how Capcom reshuffled a successful fighting game's roster without creating a full new sequel.

games.title: Vs. BaseBall
games.description: Vs. BaseBall is Nintendo's 1984 arcade adaptation of its early Famicom baseball game, released for the Nintendo Vs. System. Players pitch, bat, and field in an overhead-style representation of the sport, trying to outscore either a computer opponent or another player. Six teams are available, with uniform colors standing in for real-world professional clubs rather than officially licensed names. Its significance lies in bringing one of Nintendo's formative home sports games into a coin-operated, competitive setting.

games.title: Vs. Freedom Force
games.description:
Vs. Freedom Force is Sunsoft's 1988 light-gun game for Nintendo's Vs. System, based on the company's NES Zapper shooter. As an anti-terrorist operative, the player moves through an airplane, airport, city streets, and an enemy hideout, shooting armed attackers who appear from doors, windows, and behind obstacles. Innocent civilians and hostages may appear in the same scenes, making rapid target recognition just as important as accuracy.

Power-up icons can be activated by shooting them, and occasional bonus rounds turn the gun into a tool for answering a word puzzle. Its mixture of scrolling shooting-gallery action and hostage-rescue decisions makes it a distinctive late release for Nintendo's coin-operated Vs. hardware.

games.title: VS Gong Fight
games.description: VS Gong Fight is a 1984 boxing game developed by Kaneko and also distributed under the name Ring Fighter. Seen from the side, two boxers trade blows in a ring as players use a directional joystick and separate punch and block buttons. In solo play, a computer-controlled, dark-silhouetted opponent supplies the opposition; a second person can instead take the other corner. The visible energy gauges and straightforward exchange of offense and defense place it among the early arcade attempts to turn boxing into a head-to-head action game.

games.title: Vs. Gradius
games.description:
Vs. Gradius is Konami's 1986 Nintendo Vs. System adaptation of the Famicom version of Gradius, rather than a direct conversion of the original arcade circuit board. The player pilots the Vic Viper through horizontally scrolling waves of enemies and giant mechanical bosses, collecting power capsules to move a selection cursor along the famous upgrade bar. Choosing when to activate Speed Up, Missile, Double, Laser, Option, or Shield can be as important as dodging enemy fire.

This coin-operated edition introduces arcade-specific changes, including a continue feature, a different ending message, and a new credit sound. Unlike the finite seven-stage structure of the original, Vs. Gradius can continue cycling through progressively more demanding play. It is an interesting example of an arcade version derived from a console adaptation of an arcade classic.

games.title: Vs. Gumshoe
games.description: Vs. Gumshoe is Nintendo's 1986 light-gun platform game for the Vs. arcade system, adapted from the unusual NES Zapper title. Detective Stevenson advances across obstacle-filled scenes while the player shoots on-screen hazards with the gun. Crucially, shooting Stevenson himself makes him jump, so the same weapon is used both to protect the detective and to steer him over gaps and other dangers. This hybrid of shooting gallery and automatic-scrolling platform game is among Nintendo's most experimental light-gun designs.

games.title: J-League Soccer V-Shoot
games.description: J-League Soccer V-Shoot is a 1994 Namco arcade football game built around Japan's newly prominent professional J.League. Unlike international-team soccer cabinets, it lets players choose from twelve contemporary Japanese league clubs, with team and player details reflecting the period. The fast-moving action is viewed on a scrolling pitch and controlled through ordinary joystick-and-button soccer commands. An officially licensed title running on Namco's NB-1 hardware, it captures the early-1990s surge of interest in domestic professional football in Japan.

games.title: Vs. Mahjang
games.description: Vs. Mahjang is Nintendo's 1984 Vs. System adaptation of the Famicom Mahjong game, offering competitive Japanese tile play in a coin-operated format. Players form hands using the familiar draw-and-discard rhythm of riichi-style mahjong, with the arcade version designed around the Vs. System's dual-screen capabilities. It stands apart from the action-heavy reputation of Nintendo's arcade catalog and illustrates how early Famicom board games also found their way into amusement centers.

games.title: Versus Net Soccer
games.description: Konami's Versus Net Soccer (1996) is an international football game with 28 selectable national teams and an unusually flexible choice of viewpoint. Players can switch between a side-on camera and a higher, semi-overhead view of the three-dimensional action. In dual-monitor installations, opposing players can even use different camera angles simultaneously. This focus on customizable presentation distinguishes it from many contemporary arcade soccer games, which generally fixed both competitors to the same broadcast view.

games.title: Vs. Pinball
games.description: Vs. Pinball is Nintendo's 1984 coin-operated adaptation of its Famicom pinball game, released on the Vs. System. The table is split into upper and lower playfields that appear as the ball passes between them. Players operate the flippers to keep the ball alive, strike targets, and earn bonuses, with a separate Breakout-like bonus sequence providing a change of pace. The arcade edition adds refinements and difficulty variations compared with the original home version and can be played in Vs. System cabinets designed for competitive coin-op sessions.

games.title: Vs. Super SkyKid
