games.description: Vs. Super SkyKid is a Nintendo Vs. System arcade release of Namco's colorful side-scrolling flying game. Players guide a small cartoon biplane through enemy territory, firing at aerial opponents, avoiding obstacles, and carrying out bombing attacks on ground targets. The aircraft can perform a loop to escape danger, while the game's playful presentation contrasts with the more militaristic shooters of its era. Its appearance on Nintendo hardware represents a less common coin-operated version of Namco's Sky Kid series.

games.title: Vs. Slalom
games.description:
Vs. Slalom is the original 1986 arcade release of Rare's downhill skiing game, published by Nintendo on the Vs. System before its NES conversion. The player races against the clock down 24 courses spread across three mountains of increasing difficulty. Flags, trees, snowmen, sledders, and rival skiers make every run a test of timing and route choice, while jumps allow particularly well-timed escapes from hazards.

The game is historically significant as an early Rare production by Tim and Chris Stamper, with music by David Wise. Its large skier sprites, changing scenery, and progressively tougher courses helped establish the British studio's reputation for technically accomplished games on Nintendo hardware.

games.title: Vs. Soccer
games.description: Vs. Soccer is Nintendo's 1985 Vs. System version of the Famicom sports game Soccer. A scrolling overhead pitch follows the action as one or two players compete in quick football matches, selecting teams, match length, and a difficulty setting. Passing, shooting, and tackling are complemented by familiar rules such as throw-ins, goal kicks, corners, and penalties. The uncomplicated controls and clearly drawn field make it a representative early Nintendo approach to arcade-friendly team sports.

games.title: Vs. Tennis
games.description:
Vs. Tennis is Nintendo's 1984 arcade adaptation of its foundational Famicom tennis game and one of the titles that helped launch the Nintendo Vs. System. Players time ground strokes, volleys, and lobs across singles or doubles matches, balancing court position against shot placement. Dedicated dual-monitor cabinets could show the action to opposing competitors, and arcade configurations support multiplayer competition and cooperative doubles.

Its simple visual presentation belies a sharp focus on timing and anticipation. Vs. Tennis was a successful early Vs. System attraction and helped demonstrate that familiar home-console sports games could thrive when presented as quick, social arcade contests.

games.title: Vs. Tetris
games.description:
Vs. Tetris is Tengen's arcade interpretation of Alexey Pajitnov's falling-block puzzle, developed for Nintendo's Vs. System before Tengen's better-known NES Tetris release. Players rotate and position descending tetrominoes to form complete horizontal lines, which disappear to make room for new pieces. As the pace increases, a single misplaced block can create an increasingly difficult stack to recover.

The Vs. edition has comparatively simple block graphics and an operator-dependent cooperative two-player mode. Its place in Tetris history is intriguing because it belongs to the overlapping wave of Japanese and Western arcade adaptations that appeared before the game's rights and licensing situation was fully resolved.

games.title: Vs 10-Yard Fight
games.description: Vs. 10-Yard Fight is the Nintendo Vs. System edition of Irem's early American football game, released in arcades under regional licensing arrangements. The action is viewed from above, with the field scrolling vertically as the ball advances. Rather than choosing from a detailed playbook, players decide in real time whether to run with the quarterback, hand off to a back, or throw to a receiver; on defense, they control a selected player while teammates move automatically. Matches escalate through high-school, college, professional, playoff, and championship opposition. This edition preserves the unusually direct, action-focused approach of the original 10-Yard Fight.

games.title: Vulcan Venture

variants.title: Gradius II - GOFER no Yabou (Japan New Ver.)
Gradius II - GOFER no Yabou (Japan Old Ver.)
Gradius II - GOFER no Yabou (Japan Older Ver.)

games.description:
Vulcan Venture is the export title of Konami's Gradius II (1988), a celebrated successor to the original side-scrolling space shooter. Once again, the Vic Viper battles the Bacterion Empire, now led by Gofer, through a succession of hostile planets, mechanical installations, and enormous bosses. Defeated enemies release power capsules, and players use the series' signature selection bar to purchase speed, missiles, lasers, defensive shields, and orbiting weapon duplicates.

Gradius II adds selectable weapon configurations, letting players tailor their arsenal before launching. Its stages push the series toward more spectacular scenery and increasingly elaborate patterns of enemy fire, culminating in a memorable succession of bosses drawn from the game's own history. The export version introduces changes to terminology and presentation, such as calling Options 'Multiples' and Ripple Laser 'Pulse Laser', and allows continues.

The result is one of Konami's defining late-1980s shooters, admired for its music, dramatic encounters, and high difficulty. It set an influential template for later Gradius entries while remaining distinctly recognizable as the game distributed overseas under the Vulcan Venture name.

games.title: Vulgus
games.description:
Vulgus (1984) holds a special place in arcade history as Capcom's first released video game. This vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter places a small spacecraft against relentless formations of alien craft over alternating planetary and space backgrounds. The ship has unlimited ordinary shots but a restricted supply of more powerful bombs, with POW items replenishing ammunition and supplying bonuses.

Rather than moving through a conventional finite campaign, the player survives an increasingly difficult sequence of enemy waves and repeating scenery. Vulgus does not yet display the elaborate level design of Capcom's later 1942 or 1943, but it already shows the company's interest in clear projectile combat, varied enemy patterns, and a demanding high-score chase. Its greatest significance is as the starting point of Capcom's long arcade development history.

games.title: Wacko
games.description:
Bally Midway's Wacko is a wonderfully eccentric early-1980s arcade shooter starring Kapt'n Krooz'r, a green alien in a domed spacecraft. The player moves with a trackball and aims shots using a joystick, but merely hitting every monster is not enough: enemies must be shot in matching pairs to disappear. On later stages, shooting mismatched creatures can create hybrid mutants, making careful target selection increasingly important.

The game is also famous for its deliberately tilted cabinet, an uncommon piece of arcade furniture that matches the off-kilter humor on screen. Its designer originally conceived a gentler theme before the cast was revised into stranger cartoon monsters. Wacko remains a memorable example of how developers experimented with both physical controls and unusual rules during the early arcade boom.

games.title: Waku Waku 7
games.description:
Sunsoft's Waku Waku 7 (1996) is a Neo Geo fighting game that affectionately parodies Japanese anime, manga, and other video games. Seven eccentric protagonists compete to collect seven magical Waku Waku Balls, which can supposedly grant a wish. Its roster ranges from an exaggerated heroic adventurer and a magical girl to a cat-eared fighter and a creature that resembles a cheerful mascot, with each character fighting in a noticeably different style.

Under the cartoon comedy is a capable four-button fighter, complete with special techniques, dramatic super attacks, and zooming battle screens. A bonus encounter with Bonus Kun, a martial-arts punching bag, openly lampoons the genre's familiar karate heroes. The colorful artwork and irreverent character animations have made Waku Waku 7 a small cult favorite among Neo Geo collectors.

games.title: Wall Crash
games.description: Wall Crash is a mid-1980s Italian Breakout-style game from Midcoin. Players use a rotary dial to position a paddle at the bottom of the screen and bounce a ball against a wall of bricks, trying to clear the playfield without letting the ball escape. Certain blocks reveal bonuses or change the rules temporarily, including explosive effects and additional paddle support. It is a compact example of the wave of European arcade bat-and-ball games that expanded Atari's familiar Breakout formula with power-ups.

games.title: Wall Street
games.description: Wall Street is an unusual 1982 arcade action game on Century's CVS hardware that mixes two completely different challenges under a stock-market theme. First, the player controls rescuers who must bounce falling brokers safely toward a waiting ambulance. The second sequence puts the player in the role of a broker gathering money around a town, returning it to a designated base while avoiding or shooting hostile tanks. Its deliberately absurd premise and abrupt shifts of genre make it an oddity among early-1980s arcade releases, rather than a conventional financial simulation.

games.title: Wanted
games.description: Wanted is a 1984 Western-themed shooting game by Sigma Enterprises, distinct from Sega's unrelated game of the same name. Seen from behind the gunfighter, it presents fixed-screen frontier confrontations with outlaws and other attackers approaching from different directions. Players move and aim using an eight-way joystick and fire with a single button, clearing successive encounters without being overwhelmed. Its compact, vertically oriented arcade presentation makes it a lesser-known example of the mid-1980s revival of Western shooting-gallery games.

games.title: Wardner
games.description:
Wardner, developed by Toaplan and released in 1987, is an atmospheric fantasy platform game also known as Wardner no Mori in Japan and Pyros in the United States. A young hero enters an enchanted forest to rescue his companion from the sorcerer Wardner, battling monsters and avoiding traps as he progresses through five scrolling stages. The hero's magical projectiles can be strengthened, and coins collected along the way can be spent in shops at the end of stages.

The shop system gives the action an appealing light role-playing flavor: a player can invest in better equipment, extra protection, or supplies before confronting the next area. The large monsters, sinister forest settings, and precise jumps recall Ghosts 'n Goblins, but the magical combat and between-stage economy give Wardner its own personality. It remains one of Toaplan's distinctive departures from the shooters for which the company became famous.

games.title: War: Final Assault

variants.title: War: Final Assault (GUTS 1.3 Apr 20 1999, GAME Apr 20 1999)

games.description:
War: Final Assault is Atari Games' 1999 arena-based, three-dimensional action shooter, built around a commando mission against the forces of General Yuri Nienov. Players choose from four characters with different attributes and fight through a series of enemy-filled environments, collecting weapons, health, and additional time while following objective markers. The campaign culminates in boss encounters and rewards thorough exploration with keys needed to reach the true finale.

Unlike many contemporary coin-op shooters, it can be played from first- or third-person viewpoints and supports both cooperative campaign play and competitive head-to-head combat. Its unusual mixture of arcade time pressure, console-like roaming, and multiplayer deathmatches illustrates the industry's experiments with 3D combat at the end of the 1990s.

games.title: War Gods
games.description:
Midway's War Gods is a mid-1990s three-dimensional one-on-one fighting game created in the wake of Mortal Kombat's enormous success. Its fighters are humans transformed into supernatural beings after coming into contact with alien ore, and their battles combine martial-arts strikes, powerful special moves, and spectacular finishing attacks. The roster includes ten principal combatants competing for dominance over the ore's mysterious power.

War Gods keeps a familiar punch-and-kick control scheme but adds a dedicated 3D movement button, allowing fighters to step around attacks and change their relative depth in the arena. Midway advertised its textured polygon characters using the term 'digital skin', seeking a more organic appearance than the angular models of earlier 3D games. Its dedicated board's hard disk and experimental combat system mark a transitional point between the studio's digitized-sprite fighters and its later polygon-based action games.

games.title: Warlords
games.description:
Atari's Warlords, copyrighted 1980 and commercially released in 1981, is a brilliant multiplayer reinterpretation of Breakout. Four castles occupy the corners of a square arena, each guarded by a movable shield. Ricocheting fireballs gradually knock bricks out of the castle walls until an exposed monarch is struck. Players can catch a fireball with their shields and release it as a more powerful shot, turning defense into a calculated opportunity for attack.

Its distinctive appeal is social: as many as four people can attack and defend simultaneously, forming temporary alliances and breaking them as the surviving castles become vulnerable. The cocktail-table version is especially associated with this chaotic four-way contest, while computer-controlled Black Knights take empty seats. With simple controls and instantly readable rules, Warlords became one of Atari's most enduring experiments in competitive arcade design.

games.title: War of the Bugs or Monsterous Manouvers in a Mushroom Maze
games.description: War of the Bugs, also known by its long subtitle Monsterous Manouvers in a Mushroom Maze, is an early-1980s shooter closely modeled on Centipede. The player controls a winged insect near the bottom of a mushroom-filled playfield, firing upward at descending creatures. Shots can clear obstructing mushrooms, but they also reshape the paths taken by the segmented centipede-like enemies. Survival depends on controlling the congestion near the lower edge while reacting to bugs approaching from several directions. Its resemblance to Atari's hit is part of its historical identity as a Galaxian-hardware-era imitation.

games.title: Warp & Warp
games.description:
Namco's Warp & Warp (1981), released in North America as Warp Warp through Rock-Ola, is an inventive single-screen action game built around two contrasting worlds. In Space World, the player shoots wandering Berobero aliens in an open arena. In Maze World, the same enemies must be defeated by planting delayed bombs among walls and corridors, requiring careful timing to avoid the explosion yourself.

A central warp zone lets the player switch between the two modes, and bonus opportunities reward well-planned attacks and patterns of kills. The ability to choose when to enter each world distinguishes Warp & Warp from games that simply alternate stages automatically. Its blend of shooting and bomb placement anticipated several later maze-action ideas while retaining the brisk, score-focused character of Namco's early arcade catalog.

games.title: Warrior
games.description:
Warrior, released by Vectorbeam in 1979, is a landmark two-player fighting game and one of the earliest arcade titles devoted entirely to direct one-on-one combat. Two armored knights duel on a top-down vector display, each moving around a battlefield punctuated by dangerous pits. A single joystick controls a knight's movement and sword position, and victory comes from striking the opponent or maneuvering them into a deadly fall.

The simple sword-fighting contest predates the fighting-game conventions established in the 1980s and 1990s by many years. Its minimalist vector graphics and requirement for two human participants make it feel more like a tense physical duel than a later computer-controlled tournament fighter. Warrior is consequently a key historical reference point when tracing the origins of versus fighting games.

games.title: Warrior Blade - Rastan Saga Episode III

variants.title: Warrior Blade - Rastan Saga Episode III (Japan)

games.description:
Warrior Blade: Rastan Saga Episode III is Taito's 1991-copyrighted fantasy beat-'em-up, released in Japanese arcades in 1992. Instead of the lone swordsman of the earlier Rastan games, it offers three playable adventurers: Rastan, the warrior; Dewey, a mercenary; and Sophia, a thief. One or two players fight their way through castles, forests, swamps, and other hostile locations, sometimes taking part in mounted sequences on horses or dragons.

A remarkable feature is its exceptionally wide double-screen presentation, adapted from Taito's panoramic Darius-style hardware. The broad battlefield lets the game stage large confrontations and sweeping scenery while retaining close-range swordplay. Treasure, character-specific attacks, and fantasy monsters make it feel closer to Golden Axe than to the straightforward platform action of the original Rastan, giving the final major arcade episode of the series a very different identity.

games.title: Warzard / Red Earth
games.description:
Warzard, released outside Japan as Red Earth, was Capcom's first CPS-III arcade game in 1996. It is an experimental fantasy fighter that combines one-on-one combat with an almost role-playing-style boss campaign. Instead of a large tournament roster, players choose among four heroes: Leo, a lion-headed king; Tao, a martial artist; Tessa, a sorceress; and Kenji, a ninja. They battle an assortment of enormous monsters and villains on the path to the evil conqueror Valdoll.

The single-player Quest Mode rewards victories with experience and character growth, and the elaborate boss encounters require players to learn attacks more like those of action-game enemies than conventional fighting opponents. A separate versus mode allows the four heroes to fight one another. With lavish animation and distinctive watercolor-like fantasy artwork, Red Earth showed off Capcom's new hardware and anticipated some of the genre-blending experiments that would later become common in fighting and action RPGs.

games.title: Wanpaku Safari
games.description:
Wanpaku Safari is a 1998 Sega children's ride attraction rather than a conventional arcade racing game. A child sits in a lion-shaped ranger vehicle and goes on a safari-park patrol, with the on-screen adventure centered on helping animals in trouble. The machine combines a physical ride with animated video-game elements, using a straightforward button interface appropriate for young players. Its premise is a friendly animal-rescue outing, not a speed-based competition.

Released in Japan in November 1998, Wanpaku Safari ran on Sega's ST-V arcade hardware, a system closely related to the Sega Saturn. It is part of Sega's lesser-known mechatronic amusement history, in which arcade electronics were incorporated into dedicated rides and attractions rather than standard upright video cabinets.

games.title: Water Ski
games.description: Taito's Water Ski (1983) turns a towboat ride into a frantic obstacle course. The player controls a water-skier being pulled along a scrolling body of water, steering around rocks, boats, sharks, and other hazards while trying to reach the next checkpoint before time expires. Buttons allow the skier to adjust speed and jump, creating opportunities to clear small obstacles or launch from ramps for bonus points. A crash sends the skier back to a checkpoint and wastes precious time, so reading the towboat's route is as important as reacting to hazards. Its unusual theme makes it stand out from the many car and motorcycle racing games of its time.

games.title: Water Balls
games.description: Water Balls is a 1996 color-matching puzzle game from ABM Electronics, built around a comical mouse operating a miniature water-powered launcher. The player catches colored balls with a stream of water, adjusts or changes their color, and fires them back toward matching groups to clear the screen. It resembles the arcade puzzle tradition of Puzzle Bobble but gives the familiar matching task a distinctive water-pump mechanism. Its playful audiovisual presentation includes an arrangement associated with the Liberty Bell March and sampled movie dialogue.

games.title: Wonder Boy III - Monster Lair

variants.title: Wonder Boy III - Monster Lair (set 5, World, System 16B, 8751 317-0098)
Wonder Boy III - Monster Lair (set 1, System 16A, FD1094 317-0084)
Wonder Boy III - Monster Lair (set 2, Japan, System 16B, FD1094 317-0085)
differences: Hardware configuration: set 2, Japan, System 16B, FD1094 317-0085.

variants.title: Wonder Boy III - Monster Lair (set 3, World, System 16B, FD1094 317-0089)
differences: Hardware configuration: set 3, World, System 16B, FD1094 317-0089.

variants.title: Wonder Boy III - Monster Lair (set 4, Japan, System 16B, FD1094 317-0087)
differences: Hardware configuration: set 4, Japan, System 16B, FD1094 317-0087.

games.description:
Wonder Boy III: Monster Lair is Westone's 1988 arcade hybrid of platform adventure and horizontal shoot-'em-up, published by Sega. Leo and Priscilla, known in some versions as Papillo, cross brightly colored fantasy landscapes while firing magical projectiles and collecting fruit. A continuously draining health meter pushes the characters onward, and food dropped from enemies or scenery keeps the journey alive.

The game divides its stages into two contrasting halves. The first is a running-and-jumping platform section; the second puts the hero on a flying creature for a shooting sequence culminating in a large boss. Two-player cooperative action and the constant need to gather food make it considerably more hectic than Wonder Boy in Monster Land. Its curious genre combination gives the third arcade Wonder Boy a character of its own.

games.title: Beach Festival World Championship 1997
games.description: Beach Festival World Championship 1997 is a beach-volleyball arcade game released by the Korean company Comad in 1997. Men and women representing different countries compete in fast, accessible matches, with an emphasis on the timing and positioning needed to return, set, and spike the ball. Its international tournament presentation places it among the many late-1990s arcade sports games that adapted traditional team games to quick, button-driven play.

games.title: World Beach Volley

variants.title: World Beach Volley (set 1, PIC16C57 audio CPU)

games.description: World Beach Volley is a 1995 arcade beach-volleyball game developed by Playmark. The game focuses on quick two-on-two matches, with players controlling their side of the net through a joystick and attack buttons. Team selection and the sandy seaside courts give it a lighter atmosphere than indoor-volleyball games, while successful rallies depend on positioning and accurately timed returns. It is a comparatively obscure European contribution to the arcade sports genre of the mid-1990s.

games.title: Wonder Boy in Monster Land

variants.title: Wonder Boy in Monster Land (Japan New Ver.)
Wonder Boy in Monster Land (Japan not encrypted)
Wonder Boy in Monster Land (Japan Old Ver.)
Wonder Boy in Monster Land (English, Virtual Console)

games.description:
Wonder Boy in Monster Land, developed by Westone and published by Sega in 1987, transformed the original Wonder Boy's straightforward running and jumping into an influential action adventure with role-playing elements. The hero sets out to reclaim his homeland from the evil Meka Dragon, fighting monsters through towns, caves, castles, and other interconnected fantasy environments. Hearts represent health, and the player's equipment changes noticeably as the quest progresses.

Enemies drop gold that can be spent in shops on armor, shields, boots, healing items, and stronger weapons. Hidden doors, secret treasures, and the need to manage money and time encourage exploration rather than pure speed. The familiar arcade timer still adds pressure, ensuring that shopping and searching never completely interrupt the action.

Its combination of side-scrolling combat, character progression, and discoverable secrets became a defining formula for later Wonder Boy and Monster World games. It is particularly notable as an arcade title that managed to evoke a longer role-playing quest without abandoning the pace of a coin-operated platformer.

games.title: Wonder Boy
games.description:
Wonder Boy is a 1986 Sega arcade platformer developed by Escape, the studio later known as Westone. Players guide a young caveman, Tom-Tom, through forests, coastlines, caves, and volcanic landscapes to rescue his kidnapped girlfriend. Each area is divided into short stages filled with enemies, pits, and obstacles, while a continuously diminishing vitality meter forces the player to collect fruit to stay alive.

A stone hatchet provides a ranged attack, eggs can contain useful items or surprises, and a skateboard dramatically changes the pace by sending the hero hurtling through stages. The simple two-button movement and jumping are easy to learn, but higher stages require precise timing and a good memory for hazards. Finding hidden dolls and bonus items adds replay value beyond merely reaching the exit.

The game became a major hit and the foundation of a long-running series that later evolved in very different directions. Its underlying design was also licensed to Hudson Soft, leading to the famous Adventure Island series, an unusual case of one arcade platformer's mechanics flourishing under two distinct identities.

games.title: Tecmo World Cup '90
games.description:
Tecmo World Cup '90 is Tecmo's 1989 arcade football game, a successor to the earlier Tehkan World Cup. Players select from eight national teams, including Brazil, Italy, Japan, and West Germany, then compete on a scrolling overhead pitch. Joystick movement and two action buttons support an immediate, fast-moving blend of passing, shooting, and defense, with little of the tactical menu management found in contemporary console simulations.

Its World Cup theme coincided with the buildup to the 1990 tournament, although the selectable national sides are not a strictly accurate list of qualifiers. The game's popularity also inspired unauthorized conversions, notably Euro League, which replaced the national-team selection with European club sides.

games.title: Euro League
games.description: Euro League is an unauthorized arcade conversion of Tecmo World Cup '90, retaining the underlying scrolling football action but replacing its eight national teams with eight European clubs. Players still use the original game's joystick-based passing, shooting, and tackling to compete in fast, overhead-view matches. The change of teams rather than the invention of new mechanics is what defines this bootleg, which reflects the common practice of rebranding successful arcade sports games for different audiences.

games.title: Mahjong Wakuwaku Catcher
games.description: Mahjong Wakuwaku Catcher is a 1993 Japanese mahjong arcade game developed by Nichibutsu. It uses a dedicated, multi-button mahjong control panel to select tiles and perform game actions rather than relying on a conventional joystick. The game's unusually wide horizontal display and specialist tile-game hardware place it firmly within Nichibutsu's early-1990s mahjong catalog. Detailed, independently verified accounts of its special modes are scarce, so its core mahjong format and physical controls are the clearest documented features.

games.title: World Class Bowling
games.description:
World Class Bowling is Incredible Technologies' mid-1990s arcade take on ten-pin bowling, using a trackball rather than a simulated throwing animation driven by button presses. Players roll the ball by pushing the trackball forward, adjusting aim and using dedicated hook controls to curve it toward the pins. Up to four people can compete in the familiar ten-frame format, making it a natural social arcade attraction.

The same immediately understandable physical interface that helped make Incredible Technologies' Golden Tee series successful translates neatly to bowling: a smooth roll improves precision, and subtle changes in spin separate strikes from difficult spares. It was later expanded by World Class Bowling Deluxe.

games.title: World Class Bowling Deluxe
games.description:
World Class Bowling Deluxe is Incredible Technologies' 1999 revision of its popular trackball bowling game. The essential control scheme remains: push the trackball to release the ball and use the hook controls to curve the delivery toward the pins. Deluxe extends the familiar regulation ten-frame game with Flash Bowling, a bonus-oriented variation in which changing point values add a timing element to each shot.

Designed for quick competitive sessions, it preserves the approachable feel of real bowling while adding the score-chasing incentives of a coin-operated game. The combination of conventional rules and an arcade-specific scoring mode distinguishes Deluxe from the earlier World Class Bowling release.

games.title: World Cup Volley '95
games.description:
World Cup Volley '95, also catalogued as World Cup Volleyball '95, is a 1995 sports arcade game by Data East. Players select a national team from a roster of twelve countries and compete in volleyball matches shown from an elevated side-on view. The emphasis is on positioning, receiving the ball and timing attacks, with joystick movement and action buttons translating the sport's quick exchanges into an arcade-friendly format. Its tournament theme and international team selection distinguish it from more abstract ball games.

Released in February 1995, it uses Data East's later ARM-based hardware and YMZ280B sample playback. Japan and Asia revisions survive, along with an Extra Version, giving the game a small but interesting regional history. Despite arriving amid the fighting-game and 3D boom, it is a comparatively traditional two-dimensional sports title.

games.title: WEC Le Mans 24
games.description:
Konami's WEC Le Mans 24 (1986) is a spectacular sprite-scaling racing game inspired by the endurance race at Le Mans. The player drives a high-performance car along a winding circuit, trying to reach successive checkpoints before the clock runs out. Opposing traffic, roadside scenery, and sharp corners punish careless steering, with crashes dramatically tossing or spinning the car off line. The game compresses the atmosphere of an endurance event into a much shorter arcade contest.

Its sense of speed was heightened by a deluxe moving cabinet and controls that demanded careful braking and counter-steering. The race also progresses from daylight into darkness, requiring the player to contend with night driving. The result was among the more convincing and visually impressive arcade driving experiences before the polygonal revolution, and a notable achievement in Konami's late-1980s racing catalog.

games.title: Wedding Rhapsody
games.description:
Wedding Rhapsody is a 1997 Konami quiz game that turns preparing for a wedding into a humorous test of knowledge and decision-making. An engaged couple must earn money, navigate everyday complications, and eventually stage their marriage ceremony. Answering questions quickly brings in more wedding funds, while wrong answers deplete a limited stock of lives. Between quiz stages, story events offer choices that change the couple's relationship, their health, their finances, and how friends and relatives feel about the marriage. These developing circumstances shape the kind of wedding, and the ending, that the player receives.

Built for Konami's PlayStation-derived GV arcade system, it features a notably large bank of roughly 6,000 questions assembled with help from Sophia University's quiz research club. The game is remembered for unusually demanding questions and absurdly mischievous story options: even an apparently happy engagement can be steered toward a lonely ceremony if the couple behaves selfishly. This blend of knowledge quizzes and lighthearted relationship simulation sets it apart from ordinary score-driven trivia machines, and gives the otherwise familiar multiple-choice format an entertaining narrative payoff.

games.title: Welltris
games.description:
Welltris is an inventive follow-up to Tetris designed by Alexey Pajitnov with Andrei Snegov. Instead of blocks falling straight down a flat playing field, pieces descend along the four walls of a square well and slide onto its floor. Players rotate and steer each piece before it arrives, attempting to complete straight rows or columns on the floor. A blocked wall becomes temporarily unavailable, making poor stacking decisions affect where future pieces can enter.

The concept transforms a familiar line-clearing puzzle into a spatial-planning challenge without requiring true three-dimensional blocks. After originating on home computers, Welltris appeared in arcades in 1991. It remains one of the most distinctive early attempts to develop the Tetris formula into something genuinely different.

games.title: Western Express
games.description: Western Express is a bootleg version of Data East's 1986 action game Express Raider, known as Western Express in some original markets. The player stages a train robbery in the American West, alternating between two very different sequences. On the roof of a moving train, the hero punches and kicks guards while ducking obstacles and making his way toward the locomotive. In the other sequence, he rides alongside on horseback and shoots outlaws appearing in carriage windows, taking care not to hit innocent passengers. This unauthorized set preserves the parent game's distinctive mixture of platform brawling and shooting; its chief historical interest is as a surviving bootleg ROM variant.

games.title: Wheel Of Fortune
games.description: Wheel of Fortune is a 1989 arcade adaptation of the American television word-puzzle show, developed by Incredible Technologies for GameTek. Players spin a prize wheel, select letters, and attempt to solve concealed phrases before their rivals, with bankrupt results threatening accumulated winnings. Its appeal is the instantly recognizable cycle of spinning, guessing, and deciding when enough letters have been revealed to risk a solution. Unlike a conventional general-knowledge quiz, it translates a specific televised format into a compact coin-operated word game.

games.title: Wayne Gretzky's 3D Hockey
games.description:
Wayne Gretzky's 3D Hockey is Atari Games' exuberant 1996 ice-hockey arcade game, trading strict sports simulation for oversized hits, spectacular shots, and high-scoring matches. Its polygonal teams skate across a full rink while players pass, shoot, body-check, and contend for the puck. Special effects can turn a goaltender into a brick wall, set the net ablaze after a powerful shot, or produce a cartoonish ambulance after an especially brutal check.

Licensed by the NHL and its players' association, the game could accommodate up to four players and offered competition alongside statistics and tournament-style play. Its exaggerated action made it an accessible alternative to home hockey simulators and a clear descendant of the arcade sports philosophy represented by games such as NBA Jam.

games.title: World Grand Prix
games.description:
WGP: Real Race Feeling, also known as World Grand Prix, is Taito's late-1980s motorcycle road-racing game. Riders compete on courses inspired by real racing circuits, negotiating corners, braking points, and rival traffic while trying to maintain speed. Its arcade controls were designed to convey the distinctive challenge of steering a powerful racing motorcycle rather than treating the machine like a car with two fewer wheels.

The game stands out for its attention to handling and its ambition to reproduce competitive motorcycle racing in a cabinet. It followed the broader trend toward more physically involving late-1980s racing hardware while remaining a relatively uncommon alternative to car-focused games.

games.title: World Heroes
games.description:
World Heroes is a 1992 Neo Geo fighting game by Alpha Denshi, later known as ADK, built around a tournament of combatants gathered from different historical periods. A time-traveling scientist, Dr. Brown, brings together ninjas, wrestlers, martial artists, and exaggerated versions of famous figures to discover the strongest fighter in history. Their plans are interrupted by the shape-shifting alien Geegus.

The most distinctive mode is Death Match, where the environment itself can become a hazard through traps and special arena conditions. Ordinary fights use joystick commands and a compact attack system that distinguishes light and heavy strikes by button timing. World Heroes helped establish the Neo Geo as a home for competing Street Fighter II-era franchises, and its cheerful historical absurdity became the basis for several increasingly elaborate sequels.

games.title: World Heroes 2
games.description:
World Heroes 2 is ADK's 1993 Neo Geo sequel to its time-traveling tournament fighter. It brings back the original eight combatants and adds six new challengers, expanding the eccentric lineup of historical caricatures and fantasy warriors to fourteen regular fighters. Rivalries still play out in standard one-on-one bouts, but the series' signature Death Match mode introduces more elaborate hazards and arena rules.

The sequel refines character techniques, adds defensive and offensive options, and gives the roster more room for varied matchups. Its blend of familiar fighting-game conventions with environmental gimmicks makes it one of the more distinctive Neo Geo alternatives to Capcom's Street Fighter franchise.

games.title: World Heroes 2 Jet
games.description:
World Heroes 2 Jet is ADK's 1994 refinement of the World Heroes series for the Neo Geo. It retains the time-traveling cast and basic fighting controls of World Heroes 2 but modifies moves, rebalances fighters, and adds newcomers including Ryofu and Jack. The competition is recast as the World Heroes Battle Fest, giving the familiar tournament a new narrative setting.

The most significant changes are in its modes of play, particularly the Tournament and Forging of Warriors challenges, which offer alternatives to straightforward one-on-one progression. Jet bridges the more experimental early installments and the mechanical overhaul that would arrive with World Heroes Perfect the following year.

games.title: Wheels & Fire
games.description: Wheels & Fire is a rare arcade driving game developed by the Spanish manufacturer TCH during the 1990s. It presents racing from a simulated three-dimensional driving perspective and uses steering and acceleration controls to negotiate the course. Its coin-operated hardware and obscure regional distribution distinguish it from the better-known Japanese arcade racers of the decade. Documentation of its game modes and course structure is limited, so its most securely established features are its road-racing premise and specialized driving controls.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Wheels Runner
games.description: Wheels Runner is an obscure racing game from International Games, with an overhead view of cars negotiating a selection of changing tracks. The courses include different surfaces, such as paved roads and dirt, shifting the visual rhythm from one race to the next. It uses steering-wheel controls rather than the ordinary joystick typical of many contemporary action games. Surviving documentation offers little reliable information about its precise release year, but its top-down, circuit-based format is identifiable.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Who Dunit
games.description:
Who Dunit is Exidy's 1988 light-gun adventure, combining a shooting gallery with a comic murder mystery. The player protects Max as he explores his grandfather's mysterious house in search of the key to a chest in the attic. Shooting hostile creatures and environmental dangers keeps Max alive, but the gun also serves as an indirect control device: firing at certain objects opens a route, and shooting Max can make him jump or perform an action.

The design is related to Exidy's earlier Crossbow, but the detective-story setting and interactive hazards give it a more whimsical personality. Rather than simply clearing every target, players must guide a vulnerable character through rooms while uncovering the secret behind the crime.

games.title: World Heroes Perfect
games.description:
World Heroes Perfect is ADK's 1995 conclusion to its main Neo Geo fighting-game series. Sixteen regular fighters, plus hidden and boss characters, meet in a final contest that retains the series' fantastical mixture of real-world historical inspirations and over-the-top special attacks. Its most important innovation is a move to a conventional four-button layout, separating light and heavy punches and kicks instead of relying on the timing-sensitive system of earlier games.

Additional attack variations and refined special-move inputs make the combat more responsive and technically demanding. Perfect is generally remembered as the most polished version of ADK's idiosyncratic fighting formula, preserving its flamboyant personalities while bringing the mechanics closer to the standards established by other leading mid-1990s arcade fighters.

games.title: Wiggie Waggie
games.description: Wiggie Waggie is a 1994 adult-themed brick-breaking game published by Promat. It follows the Breakout and Thunder & Lightning tradition: a paddle keeps a ball in play while the player breaks away blocks to uncover images of women. Its attraction is principally the pairing of conventional ball-and-paddle action with progressively revealed artwork, a common formula in certain early-1990s arcade markets.

games.title: Wild Fang / Tecmo Knight
games.description:
Wild Fang, released internationally as Tecmo Knight, is Tecmo's brutally stylized 1989 fantasy beat-'em-up. Players control armored heroes riding into battle on strange creatures to stop an army of monstrous invaders. Two riders can cooperate, smashing ogres, demons, and other enemies in side-scrolling stages while collecting rewards from fallen foes.

The game's defining mechanic is its unusual choice of mounts. The powerful humanoid Smokeman fights at close range with punches and kicks, while a tiger uses a longer-reaching spiked weapon; the player can switch between them during combat. Temporary transformations introduce an even more destructive dragon form. The exaggerated violence, large grotesque enemies, and creature-riding mechanics give Tecmo Knight an identity far removed from the urban street brawlers of the era.

games.title: Wild Pilot
games.description: Wild Pilot is a 1992 rail shooter in which the player acts as an airborne bounty hunter. A companion pilots a biplane along a predetermined route while the player concentrates on aiming and firing at enemy aircraft and other threats. The game builds toward encounters with heavily armored bosses whose health must be worn down with repeated accurate shots. Its division between automatically controlled flight and manually directed fire gives it the character of a flying shooting gallery rather than a conventional free-movement airplane shooter.

games.title: Willow
games.description:
Capcom's Willow (1989) is a side-scrolling action game loosely based on the 1988 fantasy film. The player alternates between Willow Ufgood, a young magician, and Madmartigan, a skilled swordsman, as they battle the forces of Queen Bavmorda to protect the infant Elora Danan. The six-stage journey moves through fantasy landscapes filled with enemies, hidden rewards, and imposing bosses.

The two heroes have different styles of attack, and defeated enemies leave behind gold that can be spent in shops on stronger weapons and defensive improvements. This equipment system gives the game a touch of action-RPG progression without slowing down the platforming and combat. Its detailed animation and vibrant scenery make Willow one of Capcom's more memorable licensed arcade productions of the late 1980s, distinct from the role-playing adaptation released for the NES.

games.title: Wily Tower
games.description: Wily Tower, also known as Atomic Boy, is a 1984 vertical platform game that sends the player climbing a lattice of pipes and machinery. The objective is to deactivate power switches connected to a central computer while avoiding roaming robots. Instead of relying on an ordinary projectile weapon, the hero jumps onto generators to release limited-use electrical disrupters that can destroy nearby enemies. Certain robots become tougher after passing through machinery, requiring additional care and attacks. Its mixture of climbing, switch hunting, and indirect combat makes it an unusual industrial-themed platformer.

games.title: Winding Heat
games.description:
Konami's Winding Heat (1996) is a three-dimensional arcade road racer built around speed, drifting, and the race against a ticking clock. Players select from a sizable lineup of cars with different acceleration, grip, handling, and top-speed characteristics, then drive through scenic courses while avoiding traffic and trying to reach each goal in time. Tight corners reward controlled slides, making the steering feel more demanding than a straightforward hold-the-accelerator driving game.

A time-trial option removes rival traffic for players who want to concentrate on lap performance. Its emphasis on road-car handling and linked arcade competition places Winding Heat in Konami's 1990s driving lineage alongside titles such as GTI Club.

games.title: Wing Force
games.description:
Wing Force is an unreleased 1993 vertically scrolling arcade shooter developed by A.I. for the planned publisher Atlus. It features two-player action and a choice of four wing or weapon types, sending the pilots through enemy formations and bosses in a style reminiscent of Raiden. Contemporary advertising showed the game, but it never reached normal commercial distribution.

For many years it was known mainly from promotional material. A surviving prototype board was rediscovered and dumped in the mid-2010s, allowing its gameplay to be preserved in emulation. Wing Force is therefore particularly interesting as a rescued arcade project rather than a forgotten commercial hit.

games.title: Wing War
games.description:
Sega's Wing War (1994) is a polygonal aircraft-combat game for Model 1 hardware, released in both conventional and specialized simulator cabinet configurations. Instead of following a scrolling shooting path, the player takes control of a plane in three-dimensional aerial duels, aiming guns and missiles at rival pilots. Its roster spans different eras of aviation, giving encounters a playful contrast between classic and more modern aircraft.

Like Virtua Racing, it provides several viewing angles, while the flight controls include a yoke and, in advanced play, throttle management. Its dogfight-focused action differs from the realistic mission structures of later flight simulators, stressing rapid targeting and spectacle. Wing War was the last Sega game built for the original Model 1 system and one of the few major Model 1 releases not converted to a home platform at the time.

games.title: Wink
games.description: Wink is a 1985 Italian brick-breaker by Midcoin, developed as an elaboration of the company's earlier Wall Crash. Players move a paddle with a rotary control and bounce a ball into brick patterns that gradually uncover a picture. A particularly unusual feature is musical: each brick destroyed can sound a note from a recognizable tune associated with the image, such as the Neapolitan song Santa Lucia. This combination of paddle action, picture revelation, and a melody assembled through play gives Wink a distinctive identity among Breakout derivatives.

games.title: Winning Run
games.description:
Namco's Winning Run (1988) was among the first major arcade racing games to present Formula One action using fully filled, real-time shaded polygons. Developed for the pioneering Namco System 21 hardware, it puts the driver behind the wheel of a racing car in a 3D world, beginning with a qualifying session before moving into a timed Grand Prix. Players choose between easier and more technically demanding driving options, then negotiate the course while contending with rival vehicles and the pressure of the clock.

Its futuristic 3D graphics were a remarkable achievement for the late 1980s, well before polygon racing became familiar through Virtua Racing and Daytona USA. Rather than relying on sprite scaling, Winning Run used dedicated hardware to draw solid 3D geometry and create a more convincing sense of approaching corners. It occupies an important transitional place between the sprite-based racing classics and the polygon-heavy arcade driving boom of the 1990s.

games.title: Winning Run '91

variants.title: Winning Run '91 (Japan) (1991/03/05, Main Ver 1.0, Sub Ver 1.0)

games.description:
Winning Run '91 is Namco's 1991 continuation of its early polygonal Formula One racing series, running on System 21 hardware. Players drive from a cockpit-style view, using steering, acceleration, and braking to negotiate a three-dimensional circuit against the clock. The game retains the emphasis on a technically demanding driving feel and shaded polygon scenery that made the original Winning Run historically notable.

Unlike a completely new racing franchise, this edition refines the existing formula and preserves the recognizable solo Grand Prix format. It is an interesting snapshot of how Namco continued developing dedicated 3D arcade driving technology before more powerful systems transformed the genre.

games.title: Winning Spike
games.description: Winning Spike is Konami's 1997 arcade volleyball game, depicting fast rallies from a side-on view of the court. Players use an eight-way joystick and action buttons to position their athletes, return the ball, and attempt well-timed attacks over the net. Energetic commentary accompanies play, lending the matches the presentation of a televised sporting contest. Its straightforward controls and short rallies make it a natural fit for quick competitive arcade sessions.

games.title: Winter Heat
games.description:
Winter Heat is Sega's 1997 winter-sports companion to DecAthlete, created for the Saturn-derived ST-V arcade hardware. Players choose from a cast of fictional international athletes and compete across eight events, including downhill skiing, ski jumping, slalom, cross-country skiing, bobsleigh, and several forms of speed skating. Every discipline uses its own combination of rapid button pressing and precisely timed inputs.

Like DecAthlete, the game's appeal comes from transforming athletic technique into an energetic contest of timing and dexterity, particularly when players compete side by side. The arcade version's compact selection of events also distinguishes it from the expanded Saturn home release. Winter Heat remains a characteristic example of Sega's accessible, multi-event sports design.

games.title: Wiping
games.description:
Wiping is a 1982 maze-action game from Nichibutsu in which the hero is a small vacuum cleaner tasked with clearing a dirty floor. Moving through compact rooms, the player removes patches of dust while avoiding germs that roam the maze. Soap hidden beneath the dirt can be collected and used to deal with enemies, while other concealed prizes reward thorough cleaning.

Its humorous domestic setting and combination of territory clearing, enemy avoidance, and item discovery give it an appealing resemblance to other early-1980s maze games without simply copying Pac-Man. An updated version later appeared as Rug Rats, making Wiping an interesting example of a small arcade concept revised for a different market.

games.title: Witch
games.description: Witch is a 1992 Japanese video pinball and medal game developed by Vic Tokai and published under Sega's name. Rather than controlling a walking character, players interact with a pinball-inspired playfield and a set of cabinet buttons, in a format aimed at the Japanese medal-amusement market. Its video-based approach and compact Z80 hardware distinguish it from conventional electromechanical pinball tables. Several board and software variations survive, including a Sega-licensed version and the related Witch Star, making it an intriguing example of pinball imagery crossing into video-medal gaming.

games.title: Wit's
games.description: Wit's is a 1989 arcade maze contest from Athena that turns the light-cycle idea from Tron into a dedicated game. Players navigate a rectangular arena while leaving a solid trail behind them, attempting to force rivals to crash into a wall or another trail. Speed bursts and a limited jump ability allow sudden escapes or aggressive maneuvers that would not be possible with ordinary turning alone. Human opponents can join a match, making it a tense multiplayer test of anticipating another player's route and avoiding the maze both sides continually create.

games.title: Wiz
games.description:
Wiz is a 1985 fantasy platform game from Seibu Kaihatsu starring a wizard who must travel from the depths of the earth through the surface world toward a final confrontation with a dragon in the sky. The hero jumps between platforms, avoids bizarre creatures, and fights using a staff and a selection of magical attacks. Different spells include stronger projectiles, fire, bombs, protective effects, and abilities that manipulate enemies or the passage of time.

Switching magical abilities rather than relying on a single fixed weapon is the game's main strategic attraction. The varied magical tools make Wiz a more elaborate action platformer than its modest appearance initially suggests.

games.title: Wizard Fire
games.description:
Wizard Fire, known in Japan as Dark Seal II, is Data East's 1992 follow-up to the isometric fantasy beat-'em-up Gate of Doom. One or two players choose from five adventurers, including a knight, wizard, bard, dwarf, and elf-like hero, then battle through monster-filled medieval environments. The heroes have different strengths and resistances, while spells, equipment, and useful items add tactical decisions to the usual brawling.

Its diagonally viewed stages, elaborate monsters, magical effects, and cooperative battles make it resemble a tabletop fantasy adventure transformed into a fast arcade action game. The sequel expands the playable cast and carries forward the original's blend of close combat, spellcasting, and dungeon exploration.

games.title: Wiz Warz
games.description:
Wiz Warz is an unreleased 1984 arcade action game in which the player guides a wizard around the walls of an arena, firing magical bolts at approaching creatures. A rotary movement control and separate firing stick are used to maneuver and attack; electrifying sections of wall can destroy enemies, while shooting treasure earns points before devils collect it. Storm clouds introduce additional hazards.

The game reportedly reached a playable, near-finished state but was canceled, with only a single machine once known to exist. Its surviving instructions and distinctive combination of movement, magic, and environmental attacks make Wiz Warz an intriguing arcade prototype rather than a commercially established release.

games.title: Wizz Quiz
games.description:
Wizz Quiz is a mid-1980s quiz arcade game released by Konami and also distributed in versions associated with Zilec-Zenitone. It challenges players to answer timed trivia questions from categories including television and film, sports, music, history, and general knowledge. Two people can compete simultaneously on the same question, giving it a more immediate head-to-head format than a conventional turn-taking trivia machine.

Contemporary trade coverage describes animated wizard characters and comic punishments for incorrect answers. The game was also sold as a conversion kit using Track & Field hardware, an economical approach that let operators turn an established action cabinet into a question-and-answer attraction.

games.title: Windjammers / Flying Power Disc
games.description:
Windjammers, released by Data East in 1994 as Flying Power Disc in Japan, is a fiercely competitive disc-throwing sports game for the Neo Geo MVS. Its simple premise combines air hockey with the reflexes and positioning of a fighting game: two athletes patrol opposite sides of a court, catching a flying disc and hurling it into their opponent's goal. Six selectable characters differ in movement speed, throwing strength, and spectacular special shots, while courts feature different scoring-zone layouts and obstacles.

The battle for position is more involved than it first appears. Players can dash to intercept a shot, lob the disc over an opponent, curve throws, or bank them off the side walls. Goal sections award three or five points, while a missed airborne catch costs two. Rallies accelerate as opponents return shots, making anticipation crucial. The original also includes whimsical intermissions such as disc bowling and a dog-catching challenge.

Long prized by competitive Neo Geo players, Windjammers enjoyed a second life through modern re-releases and tournament play. Its unusual blend of approachable rules and high-level mind games eventually led to Windjammers 2 in 2022.

games.title: Wild Arrow
games.description:
Wild Arrow is a 1982 American electronic gambling game by Meyco Games, one of the company's early experiments in replacing traditional casino equipment with a video screen. The surviving color release uses an Intel 8088 processor and a horizontal display. Unlike a joystick action game, it was intended for a dedicated casino-style cabinet; its precise wagering and scoring rules are not reliably described in the available records.

Its hardware history is unusually well documented. Early versions were programmed directly in 8080 machine code for a black-and-white board shared with Meyco's blackjack product. Later color revisions preceded a redesigned 8088 system with modular software written in C and assembly language. This progression makes Wild Arrow a small but revealing example of the rapid technical change in early video gambling.

games.title: World Court
games.description:
Namco's World Court (1988), also known as Pro Tennis: World Court, takes the approachable tennis action of the Famicom's Family Tennis into Japanese arcades on Namco System 1 hardware. Players choose singles or doubles, select from twenty competitors, including two robot players, and compete on hard, grass, or clay courts themed after New York, London, and Paris.

Movement uses an eight-way joystick, while different stroke buttons emphasize placement or power. Serves, faults, net shots, and deuce rules give the lighthearted presentation recognizable tennis structure. The arcade game supports two human players, while the related PC Engine and TurboGrafx-16 versions introduced additional features, including a distinctive tennis-themed role-playing quest. Namco returned to the sport in 1992 with Super World Court.

games.title: Wild Guns
games.description:
Wild Guns (SNES bootleg) is an unauthorized coin-operated adaptation of Natsume's 1994 Super Nintendo shooting-gallery game, appearing in arcade form around 1996. Rather than an original arcade design, this set runs the console game's software on converted hardware, bringing its unusual Western-and-science-fiction setting to a coin-op cabinet. The player chooses Annie or Clint and faces gunmen, machines, and imposing mechanical bosses across scrolling shooting-gallery scenes.

The action mixes foreground dodging with a separate aiming reticle: holding fire directs the sights instead of moving the character, so shooting and evasive movement demand careful timing. Players can jump, roll, catch and throw back dynamite, use a lasso to stun foes, and collect stronger weapons or screen-clearing bombs. This bootleg is historically interesting as a commercial arcade conversion of a game originally created for home consoles, not as a separate Natsume arcade sequel.

games.title: Wonder League Star - Sok-Magicball Fighting
games.description:
Wonder League Star: Sok-Magicball Fighting is a colorful 1995 Korean baseball game credited to Mijin and associated with SemiCom. Its cartoon-style presentation favors exaggerated characters and spectacular pitches and hits over a realistic baseball broadcast. Two players can compete using joystick-and-button controls.

The release is also notable for its hardware history. It uses a Motorola 68000-based board related to SemiCom's other mid-1990s games and employs a protected microcontroller; preservation work required recovering the protection data before the game could be emulated correctly. The Mijin credit reflects a name SemiCom used on Korean arcade releases.

games.title: Water Match
games.description:
Sega's Water Match (1984) is an unusual multi-event aquatic sports game that asks players to imitate swimming and paddling motions with two eight-way joysticks. Events include freestyle, backstroke, butterfly, and breaststroke swimming, as well as canoeing and rowing. Rather than simply hammering a button for speed, players must coordinate two controls in patterns appropriate to each discipline.

Freestyle and backstroke call for alternating up-and-down movements, while butterfly and breaststroke require rotating the sticks in opposite directions. Rowing demands synchronized movements; canoeing involves steering and compensating for the boat's drift. With its distinctive twin-stick physical routine, Water Match is a striking example of the inventive control schemes inspired by the early-1980s multi-sport arcade boom.

games.title: Wonder Momo
games.description:
Wonder Momo is Namco's eccentric 1987 Japanese side-scrolling action game, staged as a live superhero performance at the fictional Namco Theater. Players control Momo, an actress starring in a parody of television's costumed-hero shows. She kicks enemy performers across the stage, dodges attacks, and builds a Wonder meter that lets her transform into the masked heroine Wonder Momo.

In superhero form she can hurl a returning Wonder Hoop, unleash energy attacks, and perform the screen-sweeping Wonder Typhoon. The transformation is temporary, so timing it around approaching bosses matters. The theatrical framing is part of the gameplay: curtains divide acts, Japanese voice clips accompany the action, and intrusive audience photographers can temporarily stun Momo. The game also stands out for its female lead and playful spoofing of Japanese tokusatsu conventions.

Originally an arcade exclusive in Japan, Wonder Momo later reached the PC Engine, compilation releases, and modern digital platforms. Its distinctive heroine subsequently inspired a webcomic, an animated series, and a later game.

games.title: Wonder Planet
games.description:
Data East's Wonder Planet (1987) is a colorful, vertically scrolling space shooter that combines airborne combat with ground-target bombing and a shop-based upgrade system. Players steer a starship over successive planets, using forward shots against flying enemies and bombs against installations beneath the craft. Destroyed targets yield money that can be spent at shops on engine speed, missiles, stronger bombs, protective barriers, and other equipment.

Collectible letters can be assembled into bonus words such as EXTRA, MONEY, and BLAST, adding another incentive to explore the stages. Planet-ending bosses demand effective use of both weapon types. The combination of mid-stage shopping, distinct air-to-ground targeting, and bright science-fiction scenery gives Wonder Planet an identity beyond its conventional scrolling-shooter framework.

games.title: Warriors of Fate

variants.title: Tenchi wo Kurau II - Sekiheki no Tatakai (Japan 921031)

games.description:
Warriors of Fate (1992), released in Japan as Tenchi wo Kurau II: Sekiheki no Tatakai, is one of Capcom's most accomplished three-player arcade beat-'em-ups. A follow-up to Dynasty Wars, it draws on the Romance of the Three Kingdoms setting as interpreted through the Tenchi wo Kurau manga. The five playable warriors are Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, Zhao Yun, Huang Zhong, and Wei Yan, renamed for the Western release, where the historical conflict was recast as a fantasy war.

Across nine stages, players fight through dense ranks of soldiers, archers, and powerful enemy generals. The two-button controls conceal a substantial move set of throws, dashing strikes, aerial attacks, and character-specific techniques. Swords, axes, and other dropped weapons add variety, while special attacks can break up crowds at a cost to health. A particularly memorable mechanic lets fighters summon and mount warhorses, gaining mounted attacks and, for most characters, distinctive long-reaching weapons.

Warriors of Fate demonstrates Capcom's knack for giving a cooperative brawler both visual spectacle and tactical depth. Its large, sharply animated characters, elaborate bosses, and QSound audio distinguish it from earlier CPS-1 games, while the Japanese and export versions preserve notably different names, dialogue, and story sequences.

games.title: Wolf Pack
games.description:
Wolf Pack is an unreleased Atari submarine-combat prototype from 1978, designed around a periscope-style viewing and aiming arrangement. The player operates a submarine weapon, lining up shots at enemy surface vessels. A rotary control and firing button support its naval targeting concept.

The prototype is especially remembered for experimenting with digitized speech at a very early point in arcade history. Despite this ambitious presentation, Atari never put Wolf Pack into general production. Surviving game code and documentation make it an intriguing glimpse of an alternative direction for late-1970s arcade shooters rather than a commercially released classic.

games.title: Wonder League '96
games.description: Wonder League '96 is a 1996 Korean baseball arcade game developed by SemiCom and a follow-up to the company's earlier Wonder League Star. It belongs to SemiCom's small collection of colorful sports titles on 68000-based arcade hardware. Its arcade presentation is built around baseball competition rather than a simulation-style management game, and it supports two players. Documentation of this particular revision's rules and special moves is limited, so it is best distinguished by its place in SemiCom's short-lived Wonder League series rather than by unverified gameplay features.

games.title: Wonder Stick
games.description: Wonder Stick is a Korean adult-themed territory-capturing puzzle game released by Yun Sung in the late 1990s. Players guide a penguin-like character across a grid, laying out lines to surround sections while avoiding roaming enemies. Captured areas disappear to reveal portions of an underlying illustration; clearing enough territory completes the picture and the stage. Unlike a straight Qix imitation, the game uses a tag or marker connected to the drawn line, and enclosed spaces are cleared through the marker's movement around their boundary. Its cartoonish playfield contrasts with the adult images revealed as a reward. A censored variant is also documented.
research_notes: Exact release year is not established.

games.title: Woodpecker
games.description: Woodpecker (1981) is an obscure single-screen platform game closely related to Naughty Mouse and built on Pac-Man-derived arcade hardware. The player climbs between levels of a vertically arranged playfield, attempting to reach a destination at the top while avoiding or negotiating the woodpeckers that emerge from large eggs along the sides. Its compact layout, simple four-way movement, and hazards arranged on multiple platforms place it among the experimental early-1980s platform games that preceded standardized scrolling designs. The game is also remembered by emulator historians for the unusual protected hardware needed to preserve its operation.

games.title: War of the Worlds
games.description: Cinematronics' War of the Worlds (1981) is a rare vector-graphics shooter inspired by H. G. Wells's invasion novel. A small ground-based tank moves laterally beneath advancing Martian fighting machines, firing repeatedly to knock out their legs. An emergency shield protects the player from incoming fire, but its limited supply makes judicious use essential. The game was effectively a vector-era take on Space Invaders, with looming walkers in place of descending alien formations. It never entered regular mass production after disappointing location and trade-show tests, leaving only a handful of machines. Its rarity and distinctive Martian imagery have made it an unusual footnote in Cinematronics' vector-game history.

games.title: Wizard of Wor
games.description:
Wizard of Wor, developed by Dave Nutting Associates and released by Midway in 1981, is a celebrated maze shooter built around tense, single-screen dungeon battles. One or two players control armed Worriors, hunting Burwors, Garwors, and Thorwors through winding corridors. Some enemies become invisible, demanding attention to the radar display, and clearing the maze can bring more dangerous opponents such as the Worluk and the Wizard himself.

Its two-player mode is particularly memorable. Partners can coordinate their fire to survive the increasingly hostile dungeons, but friendly fire is enabled, and deliberately shooting the other Worrior scores points at the expense of their life. That uneasy balance between cooperation and betrayal adds personality to a game already rich in ambushes and sudden reversals.

Wizard of Wor also helped establish synthesized speech as an arcade attraction. The Wizard's taunting voice, unusual stereo sound presentation, and relentless maze escalation gave it a distinctive character that survived numerous home-computer and console conversions.

games.title: WOW New Fantasia
games.description: WOW New Fantasia is a 2002 adult-themed territory-capture puzzle game by Korean developer Comad. Following the Qix and Gals Panic formula, the player traces lines to claim sections of a playfield while avoiding roaming threats. Capturing enough territory reveals a hidden picture and permits progress to the next stage. This installment distinguishes itself with an international character-selection theme, presenting models associated with different parts of the world. Its underlying play is closely related to earlier Fantasia games, with the challenge coming from safely cutting large areas of the screen before enemies can intercept the drawing cursor.

games.title: World PK Soccer
games.description: World PK Soccer is an unusual early-1990s Jaleco soccer attraction built around the physical act of taking a penalty kick. Rather than using a conventional joystick to control a full match, the player kicks a ball-shaped fixture on the cabinet, whose mechanism measures the force of the strike. The game translates that input into an attempt to score past the goalkeeper. Its appeal lies in this combination of an electronic soccer contest and a mechanical strength-and-timing challenge. World PK Soccer belongs to the class of arcade attractions in which the cabinet itself is an essential part of the game, and emulating the video display alone cannot reproduce the whole experience.

games.title: World PK Soccer V2
games.description: World PK Soccer V2 is Jaleco's 1996 follow-up to its penalty-kick-themed World PK Soccer. This edition uses Jaleco's Mega System 32 arcade platform and retains the penalty-kick attraction format, with a pedal input associated with its specialized kicking apparatus rather than a full eleven-a-side match. The game belongs to Jaleco's unconventional sports-arcade catalog, where compact competitive challenges are made for quick coin-operated sessions. The surviving V2 program is catalogued as version 1.1, documenting a later technical revision of Jaleco's unusual physical soccer cabinet.

games.title: World Rally
games.description:
World Rally, developed by Zigurat Software and released by Gaelco in 1993, is an overhead-view rally racer that translates the excitement of sliding through narrow roads into an unusually immediate arcade format. Players tackle timed stages set in different countries, negotiating hairpins, mud, snow, and changing road surfaces while avoiding crashes that cost precious seconds. Each rally consists of several stages, and the clock is the constant opponent.

Despite its bird's-eye viewpoint, the driving has a satisfying sense of momentum. Skilled players learn to position the car before each corner and carry speed through slides rather than simply steering after the road bends. The cabinet's wheel, accelerator, and gear controls reinforce the racing theme. A successful European arcade release, World Rally led directly to World Rally 2: Twin Racing.

games.title: World Rally 2: Twin Racing
games.description:
World Rally 2: Twin Racing (1995) expands Gaelco's overhead rally formula with new locations, new hazards, and a cabinet designed for direct head-to-head competition. The 'Twin Racing' name refers to paired driving stations, each with its own screen, steering wheel, and pedals, connected to one game board. Players can now race against a nearby opponent rather than simply compare times.

The action remains built around short, unforgiving special stages, with tight corners, obstacles, and surface changes testing car control. Four difficulty levels and varied international courses give the sequel more breadth, while its dual-screen setup makes it a distinctive example of Gaelco's interest in competitive arcade hardware.

games.title: Vs. Wrecking Crew
games.description:
Vs. Wrecking Crew is Nintendo's arcade adaptation of the 1985 demolition-themed action-puzzle game starring Mario and Luigi. Armed with oversized hammers, players navigate scaffold-like single-screen stages and smash designated walls, ladders, and other objects while dodging enemies. Because Mario cannot jump, completing a stage is often a matter of planning the order in which obstacles are destroyed.

Doors, barrels, and rival demolition worker Foreman Spike complicate the layouts, and careless hammering can make an objective unreachable. The Vs. System version brings Nintendo's construction-site puzzle platforming into the competitive coin-operated environment, where efficient routes and careful timing matter more than ordinary jumping skills.

games.title: Wrestle War
games.description:
Sega's Wrestle War (1989) is a professional-wrestling arcade game in which players take a wrestler through a succession of increasingly difficult ring opponents. Matches combine movement, strikes, grappling, and pin attempts, asking players to weaken rivals before trying to finish a bout. Its large wrestlers and ringside presentation emphasize the spectacle of late-1980s wrestling.

Built for Sega's System 16 hardware, Wrestle War was later adapted for the Mega Drive/Genesis in markets outside North America. Despite its title, it is unrelated to the similarly named American wrestling pay-per-view event.

games.title: War of Aero - Project MEIOU
games.description: War of Aero: Project MEIOU is a 1993 vertically scrolling science-fiction shooter by Yang Cheng. Piloting a small futuristic craft, the player battles successive waves of enemy ships, defensive installations, and large bosses over urban and mechanical landscapes. Movement, continuous fire, and collectible weapon upgrades supply the essential arcade-shooter rhythm. Its most distinctive feature is the ability to deploy smaller satellite weapons, adding coverage around the main craft. The dense formations and increasingly elaborate enemies place War of Aero in the tradition of early-1990s Japanese-style scrolling shooters. Its promotional art is a curiosity in its own right: the flyer reused imagery from Irem's Image Fight with a Japanese disclaimer explaining that it did not depict the game.

games.title: World Stadium
games.description:
Namco's World Stadium (1988) brings the popular Family Stadium style of Japanese baseball from the Famicom to the arcade. Cartoon-like players and an overhead view of the diamond keep the sport immediately readable, with pitching, batting, fielding, and base running compressed into quick coin-operated contests. Its cheerful presentation is closer to an accessible sports game than a statistical baseball simulation.

The arcade series also received World Stadium '89 and World Stadium '90 updates, reflecting Namco's practice of revising team rosters and presentation across seasons. These versions helped sustain the familiar Family Stadium aesthetic in Japanese game centers.

games.title: Wing Shooting Championship V2.00
games.description:
Wing Shooting Championship, represented here by the V2.00 revision, is a two-player light-gun target-shooting game centered on hunting birds. Players choose among simulated firearms such as pump-action, semiautomatic, over-and-under, side-by-side, and single-shot shotguns before tackling a succession of timed shooting events.

Its six hunting scenarios include quail, pheasant, goose, and duck targets, with accuracy and reaction time determining results. The game's sporting-clays atmosphere and varied firearm handling distinguish it from the more common arcade light-gun battles against criminals, monsters, or military targets.

games.title: World Series: The Season
games.description:
World Series: The Season (1985) is Cinematronics' ambitious arcade baseball game for one player against the computer or two players head to head. It represents pitching and batting with distinctive spring-loaded joysticks, while dedicated base-running controls support advancing and retreating runners. These unusually physical inputs give its baseball action a feel far removed from the standard joystick-and-one-button sports cabinet.

The game's presentation emphasizes full games and baseball statistics, including high-score tables for batting average and earned-run average. Its attention to authentic baseball situations and specialized controls made it a notable mid-1980s attempt to capture the sport in an arcade setting.

games.title: World Soccer Finals
games.description: World Soccer Finals is a 1990 arcade football game from Leland supporting up to four players. Its central attraction is team play: two human players can cooperate on one side against two opponents, turning the usual joystick-based soccer match into a lively multiplayer contest. The four-person arrangement is the defining attraction: friends can play alongside one another instead of having to alternate turns. It makes World Soccer Finals an interesting entry in Leland's varied American arcade catalog.

games.title: World Tennis
games.description: World Tennis is an obscure 1982 unlicensed arcade tennis game. It features a female player character and simple joystick-and-button controls, with alternating play rather than simultaneous head-to-head matches when two people participate. The game is catalogued as a bootleg running on hardware associated with early Data East arcade titles.
