Its basic tennis format and sparse surviving documentation distinguish it from better-known licensed or officially branded tennis games of the period.

games.title: Wally wo Sagase!

variants.title: Wally wo Sagase! (rev B, Japan, FD1094 317-0197B)
differences: Hardware configuration: rev B, Japan, FD1094 317-0197B.

variants.title: Wally wo Sagase! (rev A, Japan, FD1094 317-0197A)
differences: Hardware configuration: rev A, Japan, FD1094 317-0197A.

games.description:
Wally wo Sagase! is Sega's 1992 Japanese arcade adaptation of Where's Waldo?, known in Japan as Where's Wally?. Up to three people simultaneously use trackballs to move their cursors across crowded, illustrated scenes, searching for Wally and other specified targets before time expires. The compact timed challenges translate the familiar picture-book hunt into a fast multiplayer arcade contest.

The game consists of themed levels subdivided into several searches, with pressure mounting as the clock runs down. Its unusual three-trackball configuration, licensed picture-book subject, and Sega System 18 hardware make it a particularly distinctive early-1990s coin-op curiosity.

games.title: Wild Western
games.description:
Wild Western is a 1982 Taito action shooter in which a mounted sheriff protects a moving train from bands of robbers. The view looks down on the landscape as horsemen race along the track, and the player must aim at attackers while avoiding rocks, cacti, trains, and incoming shots. Allowing too many bandits to board the train also means disaster.

The game's most recognizable control feature is the ability to shoot in different directions while guiding the horse, creating a juggling act between pursuit and marksmanship. Its Old West theme, scrolling terrain, and intermittent bonus rounds make it a memorable variation on the early overhead shooter.

games.title: WWF: Wrestlemania
games.description:
WWF WrestleMania: The Arcade Game (1995), developed by Midway, transforms professional wrestling into a larger-than-life fighting game. Digitized images of eight WWF stars, including Bret Hart, Shawn Michaels, The Undertaker, Razor Ramon, and Doink the Clown, clash with the speed and outrageous special effects of an arcade fighter rather than a traditional sports simulation.

Matches use strikes, grapples, signature moves, and absurd visual gags: wrestlers unleash supernatural attacks, cartoonish projectiles, and exaggerated knockdowns. The Intercontinental and WWF Championship routes escalate from individual bouts to matches against multiple opponents. Its theatrical blend of wrestling personalities with the spectacle of Mortal Kombat-era arcade combat makes it one of the most distinctive wrestling games of the decade.

games.title: WWF Superstars
games.description:
WWF Superstars (1989) is Technos Japan's lively arcade wrestling game based on the late-1980s World Wrestling Federation. Players form a two-man tag team from six popular wrestlers: Hulk Hogan, Randy Savage, the Ultimate Warrior, Big Boss Man, Jim Duggan, and the Honky Tonk Man. The team faces progressively tougher opponents on a tour that culminates in a championship confrontation.

Matches emphasize grapples, strikes, Irish whips, and well-timed tags rather than the fantastical effects of later wrestling fighters. Its colorful, oversized wrestlers and crowd-pleasing finishing moves helped establish a formula Technos expanded dramatically in WWF WrestleFest two years later.

games.title: WWF WrestleFest
games.description:
WWF WrestleFest, released by Technos Japan in 1991, is one of the most fondly remembered arcade wrestling games. It expands the tag-team action of WWF Superstars with ten selectable WWF personalities, including Hulk Hogan, the Ultimate Warrior, Jake Roberts, Ted DiBiase, Mr. Perfect, and the Legion of Doom. Large, expressive sprites, booming sound effects, and an exuberant crowd presentation recreate the spectacle of early-1990s televised wrestling.

The Saturday Night's Main Event mode sends teams through a series of tag matches, while Royal Rumble throws multiple wrestlers into the ring and rewards survival and eliminations. Up to four players can participate, and the grappling system encourages well-timed attacks, reversals, and partner coordination. Its blend of accessible action and faithful wrestling theatrics made WrestleFest a lasting favorite of arcade sports fans.

games.title: Wai Wai Jockey Gate-In!
games.description: Wai Wai Jockey Gate-In! is a 1984 Japanese horse-racing arcade game developed by Casio and released by Jaleco. Players guide a horse and jockey through track races using a four-way joystick and two buttons, with the emphasis on timing and successfully negotiating obstacles while competing with other racers. The game supports two players and appeared well before the more elaborate horse-racing attractions of the 1990s. Its title incorporates 'wai wai', an expression evoking a noisy cheering crowd, an appropriate name for a compact, competitive arcade interpretation of horse racing.

games.title: Waku Waku Pajero
games.description:
Waku Waku Pajero is a 1990 Sega kiddie ride themed around the Mitsubishi Pajero, rather than a conventional arcade driving game. The on-screen program is titled 'Jungle Exploration' and accompanies a short vehicle-themed trip featuring animals. Its physical steering wheel provides simple left-and-right input, while a button can sound the vehicle's horn; the experience is primarily an animated, educational ride rather than a race with laps and opponents.

Released in Japan in April 1990, the machine used Sega's System C-2 electronics, derived from the Mega Drive hardware family. That combination of a specialized vehicle cabinet, simple interaction, and familiar arcade components makes it an instructive example of Sega's early-1990s children's amusement business. AdvanceMAME preserves the video program, although emulation does not reproduce the physical ride itself.

games.title: X-Day 2
games.description:
X-Day 2 is Namco's 1995 Japanese sequel to its eccentric arcade fortune-telling attraction X-Day. Presented as a futuristic life-expectancy diagnostic service, it asks players a succession of personal yes-or-no questions and produces tongue-in-cheek predictions rather than testing encyclopedic knowledge. This sequel broadens the original theme by examining both physical lifespan and romantic lifespan, giving its mock-scientific personality assessment a distinctly dark sense of humor.

Released in Japan in July 1995, the game uses Namco's NA-series arcade hardware and an unconventional attraction-style presentation. Although sometimes catalogued as a quiz, its appeal lies more in interactive fortune telling and the unsettling idea of an arcade machine estimating a person's remaining time than in conventional trivia scoring.

games.title: Xeno Crisis
games.description: Xeno Crisis is a one- or two-player top-down arena run-and-gun shooter developed and published by Bitmap Bureau for the Neo Geo MVS in 2019. Players control battle-hardened marines clearing procedurally arranged alien-infested outpost rooms using twin-stick style eight-way firing, dodge rolls, grenades, and temporary heavy weapons.

games.title: Xenophobe
games.description:
Xenophobe (1987) is Bally Midway's strange and inventive science-fiction run-and-gun game, famous for dividing its arcade monitor into three independent horizontal views. Each section follows a different player, allowing up to three people to explore and fight at the same time without forcing everyone to share a camera. Players take the roles of eccentric technicians and adventurers sent to clear alien infestations from space installations.

The action involves navigating rooms, using lifts, gathering supplies, and blasting grotesque creatures before an installation's self-destruct timer expires. Different weapons and equipment can be found during the mission, while the aliens' varied behavior creates a tense mixture of exploration and frantic combat. The simultaneous three-view presentation was an unusually bold solution to multiplayer screen sharing.

Designed by Brian Colin, Xenophobe blends comic-book caricature with horror-film imagery. Its title and creatures openly evoke the science-fiction cinema of the period, but its unusual cabinet and independent multiplayer exploration give it a gameplay identity of its own.

games.title: Xevious 3D/G
games.description:
Xevious 3D/G is Namco's mid-1990s polygonal revival of its influential 1982 scrolling shooter. Players once again pilot the Solvalou, attacking airborne enemies with a forward-firing weapon and ground installations with a separate bombing system. The familiar tactical split between air and land targets remains, but textured 3D scenery, changing camera angles, and new enemy formations bring a very different visual perspective.

Unlike the original, this installment supports simultaneous two-player action, and later sections move the camera to a more dramatic behind-the-craft viewpoint. New weapons and boss encounters broaden the campaign while retaining recognizable Xevious imagery. It is an interesting example of Namco reinterpreting a foundational 2D arcade series during the transition to polygonal graphics.

games.title: Xevious
games.description:
Xevious, released by Namco in 1982 and designed by Masanobu Endo, was a landmark in the development of scrolling shooters. Players pilot the Solvalou fighter over forests, roads, rivers, and mysterious geometric ruins while fighting an invading mechanical army. Its central innovation is the separation of aerial and ground combat: the zapper destroys flying enemies, while the blaster drops bombs onto ground targets marked by a forward reticle.

The game's continuous landscape, detailed enemy designs, and sixteen linked areas gave it a stronger sense of journey than the largely static shooting games that preceded it. Hidden Sol towers and secret flags rewarded experimentation with the bombing system, and enemy patterns made the battlefield feel responsive rather than entirely scripted. The huge Andor Genesis mothership became one of the defining arcade spectacles of the era.

A major Japanese arcade success, Xevious helped popularize the vertically scrolling shooter and influenced countless successors. Its recognizable music, intricate background art, and secrets made it an enduring Namco icon, spawning revisions, sequels, and many home conversions.

games.title: Xexex
games.description:
Konami's Xexex (1991) is a visually spectacular horizontal shooter that combines ideas from R-Type and Irem's X Multiply. Players pilot the Flintlock spacecraft to rescue Princess Irene from the villain Klaus, navigating biomechanical landscapes filled with enormous enemies and intricately animated hazards. The ship's defining weapon is the Flint, a detachable organic-looking pod with extendable tentacles that can attack enemies and absorb incoming threats.

Managing the Flint's position is as important as firing the main weapon: it can be launched ahead, recalled, and used to cover dangerous spaces. The Japanese edition provides a selection of weapon upgrades and traditional lives, while international versions substantially revise the weapons and replace lives with a health meter, making regional choice unusually significant.

Xexex is remembered for Konami's elaborate pixel art, scaling effects, and distinctive sound design. Although not as commercially ubiquitous as Gradius, its intricate stage construction and unconventional weapon system have earned it a strong reputation among shooter enthusiasts.

games.title: X-Files
games.description: X-Files is a 1999 Korean tile-matching arcade game from dgPIX Entertainment, loosely invoking the title of the American science-fiction television series. Despite its name, it is not a narrative adaptation or investigative adventure. Its play is based on matching pairs of mahjong-style tiles in the manner of solitaire tile-removal games such as Match It. The unusual combination of a familiar television-inspired name and conventional tile-puzzle mechanics makes it a minor curiosity among late-1990s Korean arcade releases.

games.title: X-Men: Children of the Atom

variants.title: X-Men: Children of the Atom (Japan 941208 rent version)

games.description:
X-Men: Children of the Atom (1994) is Capcom's first Marvel-licensed arcade fighting game and an important step toward the Marvel vs. Capcom series. Using the CPS-2 hardware, it translates the exaggerated action of Marvel's X-Men comics into fast, vividly animated one-on-one battles. Ten playable heroes and villains include Wolverine, Cyclops, Storm, Psylocke, Iceman, Colossus, Sentinel, and Spiral, while Juggernaut and Magneto await as major opponents.

The combat builds upon Street Fighter II and Darkstalkers but pushes character mobility and spectacle much further. Super jumps, air combat, dramatic screen-filling attacks, and the X-Power gauge support explosive battles that feel distinctly comic-book-like. Characters retain recognizable powers rather than simply sharing conventional martial-arts moves.

The game was both an impressive licensed adaptation and a technical showcase for Capcom's animation artists. Its success established the visual vocabulary and high-flying combat style later developed in X-Men vs. Street Fighter and the broader crossover fighting series.

games.title: X-Men
games.description:
Konami's X-Men (1992) is one of the defining licensed arcade beat-'em-ups of the early 1990s. Visually inspired by the 1989 television pilot X-Men: Pryde of the X-Men, it lets players choose Wolverine, Cyclops, Storm, Colossus, Nightcrawler, or Dazzler and battle through the forces of Magneto. Sentinels fill the streets, while familiar villains such as Pyro, Blob, Juggernaut, and Mystique guard the route to Magneto's asteroid base.

Each mutant has ordinary attacks, jumps, and a distinctive special power that can devastate nearby enemies at the cost of health. The game was distributed in two-, four-, and spectacular six-player configurations. The six-player deluxe cabinet uses two monitors to create a very wide playfield, allowing the entire mutant team to fight together.

Its combination of recognizable comic characters, cooperative action, large animated sprites, and memorable voice samples made X-Men a fixture of 1990s arcades. The enormous multiplayer cabinet remains especially iconic, emphasizing the communal appeal of the beat-'em-up genre.

games.title: X Multiply
games.description:
X Multiply is Irem's 1989 horizontal-scrolling shooter, a disturbing biological science-fiction counterpart to R-Type. Set during a microscopic alien invasion, it puts players in control of the X-002 fighter as it battles grotesque organisms and mechanical defenses within a living host. The stages use organic textures and unsettling enemy designs to create a claustrophobic atmosphere.

Instead of R-Type's detachable Force pod, the ship acquires a pair of long, flexible mechanical tentacles. Their positioning changes as the player maneuvers, and because the appendages are invulnerable they can block enemy fire while damaging targets above, below, or behind the craft. Learning to bend these weapons around obstacles is central to the game's challenge.

The unusual defensive-offensive weapon system and elaborate body-horror imagery helped make X Multiply a cult favorite. Its tentacle concept also influenced Konami's later Xexex.

games.title: X-Men Vs. Street Fighter
games.description:
X-Men vs. Street Fighter (1996) was a major turning point for Capcom's arcade fighting games, bringing Marvel mutants and Street Fighter veterans together in the first title of the Marvel vs. Capcom crossover line. Rather than choosing a single character, players select two-person teams, switching fighters during a match and calling on their partner for spectacular combined attacks.

The system emphasizes super jumps, air combos, rapid special moves, and the dramatic Variable Combination team supers. A resting character can recover a portion of damaged health, making tag timing a strategic choice as well as a spectacle. Characters such as Wolverine, Cyclops, Ryu, Chun-Li, and Cammy confront each other in animated battles that stretch Capcom's CPS-2 hardware.

Its tag-team system became foundational to the later Marvel crossover games. At the time, the sheer speed of the combat and the idea of superheroes and martial-arts stars sharing the same fighting roster made it a standout arcade event.

games.title: Xor World

variants.title: Xor World (different hardware, ver 1.1, checksum 3333BA, prototype)

games.description: Xor World (different-hardware prototype) is an alternate board version of the unreleased 1990 puzzle game Xor World. Like the main prototype, it is a falling-block puzzle in which pieces must be arranged efficiently before they accumulate to the top of the playfield. This particular set is distinguished in emulator catalogs by its different hardware and version 1.1 program rather than by any reliably documented new rules. Its surviving form provides an uncommon example of a puzzle game that underwent hardware changes without achieving a regular commercial arcade release.

games.title: Xor World
games.description: Xor World is a 1990 arcade puzzle prototype built around falling-block play in the broad tradition of Tetris. The challenge is to arrange descending pieces while preventing the growing stack from overwhelming the available space. Although it was preserved as a playable arcade set, Xor World is chiefly notable for its prototype status. A separate version was also found on different hardware, illustrating how the design was tested or adapted before its intended release was abandoned.

games.title: Xain'd Sleena
games.description:
Xain'd Sleena, also distributed as Solar-Warrior, is a distinctive 1986 action game by Technos Japan that combines side-scrolling platform combat with space-shooter interludes. Players control Xain, a heavily armed space warrior tasked with liberating five conquered planets. In the original version, the planets can be selected in different orders, while the American Solar-Warrior edition imposes a fixed sequence.

On each planet Xain runs, jumps, and fires through hostile terrain, battling enemy soldiers and machines before confronting a boss. Between planets, the action shifts to a horizontally scrolling spaceship sequence, providing a striking change of pace. This alternation between on-foot combat and space flight, together with the variable stage order, made Xain'd Sleena unusually ambitious for its period.

games.title: X the Ball
games.description:
X the Ball (1991) is an unusual arcade redemption game from Rare based on the traditional 'spot the ball' competition. The machine displays a football scene with the ball removed; players study the positions and gazes of the footballers, then place an X where they believe the missing ball belongs.

A limited number of attempts are available, and accurate guesses can earn prize tickets. This makes the experience more a test of visual judgment than a conventional football video game. It is an unusual early example of Rare working in the coin-operated redemption market.

games.title: XX Mission
games.description:
XX Mission is a 1986 vertically scrolling military shooter from UPL, built around the need to attack targets at different heights. Players pilot a fighter aircraft over forests, seas, and defended installations, using one firing system against planes and helicopters and another against tanks and ground emplacements.

The air-to-ground attack has an unusually generous supply compared with bomb-limited shooters, encouraging players to keep both weapon types in use. Pickups enhance the craft's attacks, while the steady advance of enemy formations and fortified targets recalls Xevious. Its restrained graphical style and dual-layer combat distinguish it from UPL's more eccentric action games.

games.title: Xybots
games.description:
Xybots (1987), designed by Ed Logg for Atari Games, is a striking hybrid of maze exploration and third-person shooting. One or two players guide Rock Hardy and Ace Gunn through a sprawling underground robot complex, firing on mechanical enemies while searching for exits, collecting useful items, and conserving energy. Each player receives a separate perspective in two-player mode.

The cabinet uses an unusual twistable joystick: tilting it moves the character while rotating its top changes the viewing direction. This permits navigation through pseudo-3D corridors without a second stick, a control scheme far ahead of the standard first-person shooter era. Between levels, players can use collected resources to improve their characters' capabilities.

Its mixture of strategic exploration, cooperative play, and direct firefights gave Xybots a character all its own. It remains particularly interesting for the way its physical controls anticipated later approaches to navigating three-dimensional game spaces.

games.title: Xing Yen Man Guan
games.description:
Xing Yen Man Guan, more commonly romanized Xingyun Manguan, is a 1996 Chinese mahjong medal game from International Game System (IGS). Players use a dedicated mahjong-style control panel to manage their tiles and pursue winning hands, while the game's betting and credit system adds a gambling-oriented layer to the traditional tabletop rules. Operator settings include wager levels and an optional double-up feature, distinguishing it from a straightforward recreational mahjong simulation.

The game uses a Motorola 68000, an OKI sample-based sound chip, and a horizontal display. AdvanceMAME also preserves Wan Li Chang Cheng, or 'Great Wall', as a closely related alternate version. Its emulation history is particularly notable: the IGS graphics and protection hardware originally caused corrupted displays and lockups, and reverse-engineering work gradually made this obscure game playable. The two variants document a specialized Chinese arcade market where mahjong, medal play, and gambling-style features often overlapped.

games.title: Xyonix
games.description: Xyonix is an obscure late-1980s Korean falling-block puzzle game by Philko. It closely follows the Tetris style of play, with shaped blocks descending into a well and the player attempting to organize them before the pile reaches the top. The game includes several modes and decorates its presentation with imagery recalling Korea's historical dynastic era. Rather than building its identity on a novel character or story, Xyonix belongs to the wave of regionally produced puzzle titles that followed Tetris's explosive arcade popularity.

games.title: Go Go Mr. Yamaguchi / Yuke Yuke Yamaguchi-kun
games.description: Go Go Mr. Yamaguchi, also called Yuke Yuke Yamaguchi-kun, is an obscure 1985 action shooter featuring a small jungle explorer. Players guide Mr. Yamaguchi through hostile surroundings, firing at approaching human and other enemies while avoiding their attacks. The game is a minor example of the character-driven action shooters found in Japanese arcades during the mid-1980s. Surviving descriptions establish its explorer protagonist and combat premise, but little detailed information about its stage structure has been documented.

games.title: Yamato
games.description:
Yamato (1983) is a naval-combat arcade shooter presented from the perspective of a battleship's gun positions. Enemy aircraft and ships approach from the distance while the player directs weapons using separate sights for different attacks. Unlike a conventional scrolling shooter, the action is framed as defending the ship from an oncoming fleet.

The challenge lies in switching attention between aerial and surface threats and placing shots accurately as targets move across the horizon. Its distinctive first-person naval viewpoint and dual-targeting system make Yamato a memorable early attempt to portray large-scale warship combat in the arcade.

games.title: Yam! Yam!?
games.description: Yam! Yam!?, also known as Wise Guy, is a 1990 single-screen maze puzzle game in which a small bear-like character must push gems into designated openings before time runs out. Its grid of walls, movable objects, and restricted corridors rewards planning more than speed: a badly positioned gem can block a route or prevent a stage from being completed. Other movable objects, including peppers and skulls, add complications to the puzzles, and some situations allow several objects to be pushed together. The game belongs to the tradition of box-pushing action puzzlers but uses a bright, comic arcade presentation.

games.title: 10-Yard Fight
games.description:
Irem's 10-Yard Fight (1983) is an early arcade American-football game notable for presenting the field from a vertically scrolling overhead perspective. Players control the team directly rather than selecting elaborate tactical formations, advancing upfield through running plays, lateral passes, and throws to receivers. On defense, the player chooses a defender and attempts to stop the opposing drive.

The action strips the sport down to quick decisions, timing, and field position, making it understandable to players unfamiliar with full playbook management. An influential early treatment of American football in arcades, 10-Yard Fight also became widely known through its later Nintendo Entertainment System conversion.

games.title: Mahjong Yarunara
games.description:
Mahjong Yarunara is a 1991 Japanese adult-themed mahjong game by Dynax. It belongs to the strip-mahjong arcade tradition, pairing the familiar challenge of Japanese mahjong hands with anime-style character scenes unlocked by defeating opponents.

Its interest is principally as an example of the specialized mahjong cabinets common in Japanese amusement venues of the period. The title focuses on one-player competition against computer opponents rather than the action-oriented mechanics of more conventional video arcade games.

games.title: Yes/No Sinri Tokimeki Chart
games.description: Yes/No Sinri Tokimeki Chart is a Japanese personality-test attraction released by Taito in March 1992 for the F2 arcade system. Instead of asking players to identify factual trivia, it poses a sequence of psychological or romantic questions answered with two dedicated buttons marked Yes and No. The results are presented as an entertaining personal assessment, making it closer to an electronic magazine quiz than an action game. This Japan-only release is a distinctive example of arcade hardware being used for a lightweight social and fortune-telling experience.

games.title: Yie Ar Kung-Fu
games.description:
Konami's Yie Ar Kung-Fu (1985) is one of the most important precursors of the modern one-on-one fighting game. Players control Oolong, an unarmed martial artist who must defeat a succession of eleven opponents to earn the title of Grand Master. Each rival has a distinctive combat style and weapon, from throwing stars and staffs to unusual physical attacks, forcing the player to adjust their distance and timing.

A joystick and attack buttons allow an unusually broad range of kicks and punches, including standing, crouching, and jumping techniques. Health bars and individualized opponents create a recognizable fighting-game structure, but without the mirror-match tournament format later associated with Street Fighter II.

A major success in its day, Yie Ar Kung-Fu helped establish the vocabulary of varied martial-arts opponents and move-based duels that defined the fighting genre. Its influence persisted through arcade sequels, home versions, and Konami compilations.

games.title: Yosaku to Donbei
games.description: Yosaku to Donbei is a 1979 Japanese fixed-screen shooter that adapts the Space Invaders formula to a humorous rural setting. Instead of firing at alien craft, the player controls a small farmer trying to shoot down rows of crows occupying a tree. A large bird replaces the familiar bonus UFO that flies across the top of the screen. As the birds work their way across the playfield, a lumberjack chops away sections of the tree, bringing the targets progressively closer. The simple comic premise and unmistakable Invaders-style rhythm make it an interesting example of the rapid experimentation that followed the original game's success.

games.title: Mahjong Yoshimoto Gekijou
games.description: Mahjong Yoshimoto Gekijou (1994) is a Japanese mahjong arcade game by Nichibutsu made in cooperation with the Yoshimoto Kogyo entertainment company. Its distinguishing feature is the use of digitized performers associated with Japanese comedy rather than a roster of conventional illustrated mahjong opponents. Players compete in mahjong games to advance through its entertainment-themed presentation. The involvement of a major Japanese talent agency makes the title an unusual intersection of licensed celebrity culture and the specialized arcade mahjong market of the 1990s.

games.title: Youjyuden
games.description: Youjyuden is a 1986 top-down fantasy shooter in which a small, bearded warrior wearing a horned helmet advances through hostile territory. Viewed from above, the character fires short-range projectiles at approaching creatures and other enemies while maneuvering to avoid contact and counterattacks. Its compact combat range creates a different rhythm from the distant shooting of typical military run-and-gun games: the player must approach enemies closely enough to attack while leaving room to evade. The fantasy imagery and overhead action place it alongside the more obscure Japanese arcade shooters of the mid-1980s.

games.title: Yu-Jan
games.description:
Yu-Jan is a 1999 Japanese mahjong arcade game released by Yubis and developed in association with T.System. Its title means roughly 'Play Mahjong'. It uses the Seta Multi Amenity Cassette System (MACS), a comparatively obscure cartridge-based arcade platform, with a dedicated mahjong button layout for selecting tiles and carrying out the usual draw, discard, and hand-completion actions. The game is designed for solo play rather than simultaneous competitive action.

Yu-Jan forms a closely related pair with Yu-Ka, released on the same system but devoted to hanafuda flower cards. Both use Seta's ST0016-based hardware, which helps explain why their presentation and control arrangements differ from mainstream joystick-driven arcade games. The survival and emulation of these cartridges preserves a small corner of Japan's late-1990s tabletop arcade scene.

games.title: Yu-Ka
games.description:
Yu-Ka is a 1999 Japanese hanafuda game published by Yubis and developed by T.System. Its name means roughly 'Play Hanafuda', and its preserved program is associated with hana-awase, a form of play using traditional illustrated flower cards. Players select cards from their hand and capture corresponding cards on the table, building scoring combinations through the familiar matching-by-month structure of hanafuda rather than the numbered tiles of mahjong.

The game runs on Seta's Multi Amenity Cassette System (MACS), using dedicated hanafuda controls rather than a standard arcade joystick. It is the card-game counterpart to Yu-Jan, the mahjong release from the same year and developer partnership. Their shared hardware and different traditional games make the pair an unusual example of specialized Japanese tabletop software surviving on a cartridge-based arcade platform.

games.title: (Medal) Yumefuda
games.description:
Yumefuda, meaning 'Dream Cards', is a Japanese hanafuda medal game released by Alba in May 1991. It presents play with the traditional flower-card deck in a coin-operated betting format, making it distinct from action-oriented arcade games and from Western poker machines. The attraction is the formation of scoring card combinations through hanafuda play, with a dedicated card-selection control layout and a medal-oriented credit system.

The game is preserved in AdvanceMAME as '(Medal) Yumefuda [BET]' and runs on Alba's Z80-based hardware with AY-3-8910 sound. Its small-scale electronics and specialized controls reflect the long Japanese tradition of arcade machines devoted to mahjong, hanafuda, and other tabletop pastimes, many of which remained little known outside their domestic market.

games.title: Yuuyu no Quiz de GO!GO!
games.description:
Yuuyu no Quiz de GO!GO! is a Japanese arcade trivia game developed by Taito and released around 1990-1991. It is built around the television-variety-show appeal of Yuuyu, the nickname of singer and former Onyanko Club member Yukiko Iwai. Players answer a succession of questions through dedicated cabinet buttons, progressing through a bright, show-like presentation in which pop-idol culture is as important to the atmosphere as general knowledge.

The game was later adapted for the Super Famicom in 1992, giving it a life beyond Japanese amusement centers. It also received renewed attention when it was featured in the television series GameCenter CX. Its crossover between celebrity entertainment, quiz competition and arcade presentation makes it a recognizable period piece from the height of Japan's early-1990s variety-game boom.

games.title: Zarya Vostoka
games.description: Zarya Vostoka (1984), whose Russian title means 'Dawn of the East', is Nova Games' follow-up to Intrepid. It retains the earlier game's secret-agent premise and multiroom maze structure. Players guide a spy with a four-way joystick through an embassy, using elevators to reach different floors, searching rooms for essential items, and avoiding pursuing guards. The game runs on hardware related to Intrepid, but its surviving software has historically presented preservation and emulation difficulties. As a result, its broad infiltration objective is better documented than its full sequence of missions and hazards. It remains an intriguing, little-seen sequel to an unusual arcade espionage game.

games.title: Zaviga
games.description:
Zaviga is a 1984 Data East scrolling shooter with a transforming vehicle that can switch between aircraft and ground-combat forms. The action follows a winding canyon from a high, nearly overhead viewpoint, with the playfield scrolling upward as enemy aircraft, machines, and defensive positions appear ahead. The player's weapons include forward-firing guns and ground attacks.

Changing altitude and form is crucial to surviving the mixed threats. The route can shift sideways, requiring the pilot to follow the terrain while targeting enemies at different elevations. This aircraft-and-tank combination gives Zaviga a more distinctive tactical hook than the average early vertical shooter.

games.title: Zaxxon
games.description:
Sega's Zaxxon (1982) was a visual and technical milestone for arcade shooters, using a convincing isometric projection to give its scrolling battlefield an unprecedented sense of height and depth. Players pilot a spacecraft through heavily defended fortresses, weaving between walls, radar towers, fuel tanks, and enemy fighters. Flying high or low matters as much as steering left and right: an on-screen altimeter and the ship's shadow help judge the height needed to clear obstacles.

The mission alternates between fortress assaults and a space battle before culminating in a confrontation with the imposing Zaxxon robot. Fuel must be replenished by shooting storage tanks, making accurate attacks essential to survival as well as scoring. The dramatic diagonal scrolling and large illustrated environments made the game immediately recognizable.

A major arcade success, Zaxxon became synonymous with the early-1980s fascination with pseudo-3D graphics. Its viewpoint influenced numerous isometric action games and prompted a long series of home conversions, spin-offs, and sequels.

games.title: Zed Blade / Operation Ragnarok
games.description:
Zed Blade, known in Japan as Operation Ragnarok, is NMK's 1994 horizontal shooter for the Neo Geo MVS. Players choose between three pilots and their spacecraft, each with different mobility characteristics, before battling through eight enemy-filled stages across a futuristic Solar System. A second player can join, turning the dense shooting into cooperative action.

A distinctive feature is the ability to configure three weapon categories, including forward fire, rear fire, and missile-type ordnance. Collectible upgrades strengthen these systems, so the starting loadout and subsequent pickups have a real effect on how the craft handles attacking waves and large bosses. Its colorful visuals and energetic music made it one of the more approachable, though still challenging, Neo Geo shooters.

games.title: Zektor
games.description:
Zektor (1982) is Sega's elaborate color-vector space shooter, built for the G80 vector system. The player's ship must liberate eight cities captured by alien robots, each of which challenges the pilot before a series of defensive encounters. The ship rotates, thrusts, and fires freely in a play style descended from Asteroids and Sega's earlier vector shooters.

City liberation involves fighting agile Roboprobes and other threats through successive attack waves. Some enemies are protected by shields that must be worn down before the craft itself can be destroyed. The game's synthesized speech and vivid vector displays give personality to an otherwise abstract space-combat premise. Zektor is especially prized for its unusual combination of named adversaries, evolving objectives, and classic vector shooting.

games.title: Zero Hour
games.description: Zero Hour is a 1980 arcade space shooter by Universal, unrelated to the much later tactical computer game of the same name. Players guide a small spaceship across a top-down playfield, firing at enemy craft while avoiding falling meteorites, hostile bombs, and collisions. Special red meteorites offer an increased score when destroyed. After clearing the enemy formation, the game changes to a delicate landing sequence in which the player's craft must descend safely onto a landing pad for bonus points. This alternation between shooting and precision landing gives the title a simple but memorable progression beyond a straightforward alien-wave game.

games.title: Zero Point
games.description:
Zero Point is Unico's 1998 light-gun shooting-gallery game, a close contemporary of Namco's Point Blank series. One or two players tackle a succession of very short target-shooting challenges, each introduced with its own rules. Some tasks demand rapid fire at colored targets, while others punish mistakes such as hitting bombs, civilians, or the other player's targets.

Players choose sets of minigames from a grid, then attempt the individual challenges in any order. A limited supply of hearts makes missed objectives consequential. Its constantly changing tasks and friendly competitive presentation emphasize accuracy and reactions rather than a continuous shooting-game storyline.

games.title: Zero Point 2
games.description:
Zero Point 2 (1999) is Unico's sequel to its light-gun shooting-gallery game, retaining the quick-fire minigame structure while adding richer prerendered visuals and a world-travel theme. Players select a difficulty and one of several whimsical characters, then choose destinations from a world map, each offering a cluster of shooting challenges.

Before each minigame, illustrated instructions indicate the required targets and the objects that must be avoided. Some rounds require frequent reloading, while others introduce unusual shooting conditions. As in Point Blank and the first Zero Point, success depends on reading the objective instantly and hitting the right targets under a tight time limit.

games.title: Zero Team 2000
games.description:
Zero Team 2000 is Seibu Kaihatsu's 2000 reissue of its 1993 cooperative arcade brawler Zero Team, not an entirely new game. Up to four players take members of the Zero Team through side-scrolling city stages, punching, kicking, throwing enemies, and picking up weapons while fighting gangs and larger bosses. Its straightforward three-button controls and simultaneous multiplayer play reflect the early-1990s beat-'em-up tradition.

This edition runs on Seibu's revised V33-based hardware rather than the original board. Unlike New Zero Team, which rearranged some stages, Zero Team 2000 restores the original level order and adds nonvolatile high-score storage. Its interest to arcade historians lies in this late commercial revision of a game first released seven years earlier.

games.title: Zero Target
games.description: Zero Target, released in Japan as Gekitsui Oh, is a 1985 Data East aerial-combat shooter that alternates between distinct attack situations. Players maneuver a fighter aircraft and fire at formations of enemy planes, then enter a sequence involving ground targets such as tanks and helicopters. Surviving requires careful aiming and quick reactions as enemy fire intensifies. The game also includes a landing challenge, rewarding a successful approach with bonus points and punishing a crash. This mixture of air combat, low-level attacks, and precision landing gives Zero Target a structure different from a continuous scrolling shooter.

games.title: Zero Wing
games.description:
Zero Wing is a 1989 horizontal shooter developed by Toaplan. Players pilot the ZIG starfighter through eight stages of alien formations, winding mechanical terrain, and imposing bosses in a struggle against the cyborg CATS. Power-ups enhance three color-coded weapons, including spread fire, lasers, and homing attacks.

Its signature mechanic is the Seizer Beam, which captures certain enemies and holds them in front of the craft as protection or launches them into other targets. This gives the player an extra layer of offense and defense beyond ordinary shooting. The arcade version also supported a simultaneous two-player variation.

Although respected for its carefully paced shooter design, Zero Wing gained extraordinary notoriety through the English introduction in the later European Mega Drive version, source of the internet phrase 'All your base are belong to us.' That mistranslation is part of the console port's history, not a feature of the original arcade release.

games.title: Zero Zone
games.description: Zero Zone is a 1993 adult-themed falling-block puzzle game by Korean developer Comad, closely modeled on Columns. Groups of colored pieces descend into a narrow playfield, and the player rotates their order to create lines of three or more matching colors. Successful matches clear space, while a stack that reaches the top ends the game. The puzzle action is interspersed with revealing images, tying a familiar color-matching mechanic to the adult arcade market. Its fast, easy-to-understand rules place it alongside the many Columns-inspired regional puzzle games of the early 1990s.

games.title: Zig Zag

variants.title: Zig Zag (Galaxian hardware, set 1)
variants.version: (bootleg Dig Dug conversion on Galaxian hardware, set 1)

variants.title: Zig Zag (Galaxian hardware, set 2)
variants.version: (bootleg Dig Dug conversion on Galaxian hardware, set 2)

games.description:
Zig Zag is an early-1980s unlicensed take on Namco's Dig Dug, surviving in versions for different arcade hardware. The player tunnels through underground soil, trying to eliminate roaming enemies while avoiding contact with them. Falling rocks can be used as weapons, but the mechanics vary between the preserved versions.

The Galaxian-related hardware conversion is especially distinctive because it changes how enemies are defeated: the familiar air pump is absent, requiring close-range contact, while a temporary pickaxe upgrade can increase digging speed. Unlike Dig Dug, the game omits the vegetable bonus items. These alterations make the conversion more than a simple graphics swap and a useful example of early arcade bootleg adaptation.

games.title: Zing Zing Zip
games.description:
Zing Zing Zip is a 1992 vertically scrolling military shooter developed by Allumer and published by Tecmo. Players select between two aircraft with different handling strengths, then battle streams of enemy planes, tanks, and trains using forward fire and powerful bombs. Weapon pickups improve firepower and add missile support, while large bosses punctuate the campaign.

The game's most unusual feature is a barrel-roll maneuver that briefly makes the aircraft invulnerable, offering a skill-based way out of crowded bullet patterns. Its bright, exuberant presentation and punishing formations make it a recognizable entry in the crowded early-1990s shooter field.

games.title: Zintrick / Oshidashi Zentrix
games.description:
Zintrick / Oshidashi Zentrix is a bootleg Neo Geo MVS cartridge adaptation of ADK's Oshidashi Zintrick, originally released for the Neo Geo CD in 1996. Unlike a conventional arcade game ported home, this set reverses the process by bringing a CD-exclusive title onto cartridge hardware without an official MVS release.

The game is a competitive sideways falling-block puzzler. Players send pairs of colored blobs horizontally into their playfields, matching groups of three or more to clear them. Chains and combinations send obstructing gray pieces to an opponent, so the aim is not merely to keep one's own field tidy but to overwhelm the rival. The unofficial cartridge conversion is a noteworthy preservation curiosity within the Neo Geo library.

games.title: Zip & Zap
games.description: Zip & Zap is a 1995 adult-themed brick-breaking game by Barko Corp, adapted from the arcade design of Thunder & Lightning. Players control a paddle to keep a ball in play and remove blocks from a series of arrangements, using the ricochets to reach difficult parts of the screen. Its main distinguishing feature is the replacement of the original game's presentation with adult-oriented imagery. As a derivative of a familiar Breakout-style design, it is best understood as a themed hack rather than a fundamentally new ball-and-paddle game.

games.title: Zen Nippon Pro-Wrestling Featuring Virtua

variants.title: Zen Nippon Pro-Wrestling Featuring Virtua (J 971123 V1.000)

games.description:
Zen Nippon Pro-Wrestling Featuring Virtua is a 1997 Sega ST-V arcade wrestling game based on Japan's All Japan Pro Wrestling promotion. Its roster combines real wrestlers from the promotion with two unusual guest competitors, Wolf Hawkfield and Jeffry McWild from Sega's Virtua Fighter series. The matches are presented with polygonal 3D wrestlers and shifting camera angles.

Players use strikes, grapples, holds, counters, and taunts, with different moves depending on positioning and button combinations. An injury system adds another layer of ring strategy. The crossover guests and fully three-dimensional presentation make this one of Sega's more distinctive licensed wrestling projects.

games.title: Zoar
games.description: Zoar is a 1982 Data East vertically scrolling shooter in which the player attacks airborne enemies and ground installations across an advancing landscape. The craft can fire at targets in the sky and bomb objects beneath it, requiring attention to threats on two different levels. Passing aircraft, guns, and other hazards demand steady movement and accurate timing. Between combat sequences, the player can attempt to land on an airstrip for bonus points. This mixture of conventional shooting, bombing, and landing sequences gives Zoar a distinctive structure among early scrolling shooters.

games.title: Zodiack
games.description: Zodiack is a 1983 vertically scrolling space shooter developed by Orca. Players pilot the Zogram craft through alien formations and obstacles, blasting enemy ships while navigating a continually advancing starfield. The game changes its objective as the mission progresses, eventually requiring attacks on enemy bases and their defenses. Its recognizable set-piece involves destroying installations around a hostile launch complex, then returning toward a friendly base. These changing attack and return phases make Zodiack more varied than a simple endless wave shooter, even though its controls and presentation remain rooted in the early-1980s arcade tradition.

games.title: Zombie Raid
games.description:
Zombie Raid is a 1995 horror-themed light-gun shooter from American Sammy, set in a village troubled by disappearances and grave robberies. Players follow detective Edward Windsor through graveyards, castles, and laboratories, firing on zombies, monsters, and other grotesque enemies. The gun-based cabinet uses a pump-action reloading mechanism that adds a physical rhythm to the frantic action.

Scenery can be shot apart to reveal supplies and bonuses, and the arsenal expands beyond the starting handgun to stronger weapons. Innocent bystanders must be spared, since shooting them reduces health. Its Gothic horror setting, destructible details, and unusual shotgun controls give Zombie Raid a particular flavor among the many arcade rail shooters of the 1990s.

games.title: Zoo Keeper
games.description:
Zoo Keeper, developed by Taito America and released in 1982, is one of the most inventive single-screen platform games of the golden arcade era. Players control Zeke, a beleaguered zookeeper whose animals keep escaping and whose girlfriend Zelda has been captured. In the main stage type, Zeke runs around the border of an animal enclosure, continually rebuilding its brick wall while leaping over escaped creatures.

Other stages change the action completely. Zeke must leap across moving platforms to reach Zelda and tackle bonus rounds built around jumping animals for escalating scores. The risk-reward system is especially ingenious: jumping over multiple animals in a single bound awards huge points, encouraging dangerous feats instead of merely surviving.

Its brightly colored characters, bouncy animation, and alternating stage types made Zoo Keeper an enduring cult favorite. The game's unusual blend of enclosure management, platforming, and spectacular score opportunities remains recognizable decades later.

games.title: Zunzunkyou No Yabou
games.description: Zunzunkyou no Yabou is a bizarre 1994 Japanese arcade shooter published by Sega and developed by Minato Giken. Players control a small statue-like figure in enclosed, single-screen arenas, dodging enemies while firing upward. Each confrontation features strange opponents and eccentric scenery drawn from a playful mixture of world cultures and cartoon imagery. The game resembles an arena-based parody of the vertically oriented shooter: instead of piloting a spacecraft through a scrolling landscape, players reposition around a compact battlefield and line up shots against enemies overhead. Its offbeat presentation, Sega System C-2 hardware, and unusual player character make it one of the stranger Japanese arcade shooters of the period.

games.title: Zupapa!
games.description:
Zupapa! is a bright, whimsical Neo Geo platform game developed by Face and finally released by SNK in 2001. One or two players control the long-eared heroes Zupapa and Zupipi through single-screen stages packed with monsters, toy-like environments, and cheerful animation. Its central mechanic revolves around tiny helper creatures called Zooks, which can be thrown at enemies to trap them.

Once a target is covered in Zooks, it becomes a star-like bomb whose explosion can defeat other enemies. Using more helpers increases the blast's reach, rewarding clever positioning and chain reactions. Themed worlds, power-ups, and boss battles give the familiar Bubble Bobble-style framework a personality of its own.

Zupapa! has an unusual release history. Face demonstrated the game as early as 1994, but the finished MVS cartridge did not reach arcades until 2001, making it a rare example of a long-delayed Neo Geo project eventually receiving an official release.

games.title: Zwackery
games.description:
Zwackery is Bally Midway's 1984 fantasy action game starring Zachary 'Zak' Thwacker, a cartoon wizard seeking to restore a princess who has been transformed into a frog. Players explore interconnected platform-style screens, defeat monsters, search for keys and treasure, and use spells to overcome obstacles and confront the evil Ghoulum. The game's colorful storybook setting and elaborate character animation distinguish it from the arcade's more common science-fiction themes.

The controls are unusually complex for the period. Alongside movement and buttons, a rotary control helps direct Zak's sword and shield, making combat a matter of orientation as well as timing. Players can stab or spin weapons, block attacks, and collect magical powers while moving through doors and passages that connect the screens.

Zwackery was an early showcase for Midway's MCR-68 hardware and marked an important arcade design credit for artist Brian Colin, later associated with Rampage and Xenophobe. Its ambitious mechanics and eccentric fantasy world have made it a cult curiosity.

games.title: Zzyzzyxx
games.description:
Zzyzzyxx is a charmingly strange 1982 arcade maze-platform game developed by Advanced Microcomputer Systems and published by Cinematronics. Its hero moves through a shifting structure of horizontally sliding brick rows, gathering presents to impress his sweetheart Lola. The obstacles are not fixed: openings continuously change position, and the villainous Rattifers roam the passages looking for an opportunity to intercept him.

Players must time their movement between rows, collect enough gifts, and use special equipment to create or break bricks and trap pursuers. The combination of moving architecture and enemy avoidance makes the game more a test of anticipation than a conventional static maze chase. It was also distributed in a conversion-kit form under the simpler title Brix.

Although obscure, Zzyzzyxx is remembered for its inventive moving-brick playfield and its almost unbeatable claim to the last alphabetical position in arcade game lists.
